ashtavakra.1.11.context: After telling Janaka that he is the ever-free witness, Ashtavakra quotes a popular saying. The next verse (1.12) says the Self only seems to be caught in samsara, through error.
ashtavakra.1.11.core_teaching: The Self is always free, so bondage lasts only through the conviction of being bound. Holding the conviction of freedom dissolves it.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The Self never really enters bondage. Our thought that we are bound keeps the bondage going. Thinking constantly of oneself as the free Self removes the binding thought, and one finds one was always free.

ashtavakra.1.11.practical_reading: It helps you notice self-limiting stories ('I'm stuck', 'I'm broken') and practise identifying with what is free in you, while still dealing with real problems.
misreadings: Not 'positive thinking' or manifesting outcomes
Does not mean that external constraints such as illness, poverty or oppression are imaginary or self-caused
cautions: Can be misheard as blaming people for their suffering ('you're bound because you think so'). Use care with depression or oppression.
Jalim Singh's gloss ties it to one's thought at the moment of death; avoid that framing near bereavement.
not_for: Someone with clinical depression who may hear blame
People facing structural injustice, if framed as a matter of mindset only
speaks_to: Someone trapped in a story of being stuck or unworthy
Someone after a setback who has absorbed 'I'm a failure'

ashtavakra.1.16.context: Toward the end of chapter 1, Ashtavakra piles up images of the Self as the ground of the world (1.10, the snake seen in a rope). This verse says the universe is pervaded by consciousness and strung on it; 1.17 then lists the Self's qualities.
ashtavakra.1.16.core_teaching: The Self is the consciousness that pervades and holds the world, so one should not shrink into a petty, limited self-image.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The Self is the substance of the universe, which cannot exist without it as its ground. 'Small-minded' means thinking of oneself in a way unlike this true nature.

ashtavakra.1.16.practical_reading: It is an invitation to step out of petty reactions such as grudges, comparison and small anxieties by remembering a larger identity.
misreadings: Not grandiosity or ego inflation ('I am everything, so I matter most')
'Pettiness' here means identifying with the limited self, not a moral insult
cautions: Jalim Singh's claim that the world is unreal can feel dismissive to someone in acute loss
not_for: Someone in mania or grandiosity
speaks_to: Someone stuck in resentment or comparison
Someone who feels small or insignificant

ashtavakra.1.17.context: This is the last of the descriptions of the Self in chapter 1, before 1.18–20 contrast form (unreal) with the formless (permanent) and use the images of a mirror and space in a pot.
ashtavakra.1.17.core_teaching: The verse describes the Self, and anyone resting in it, as needing nothing, unchanging, deep and unshaken, and urges holding to consciousness alone.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Cool, because the heat of passion cannot reach the Self. Unfathomable, because consciousness is beyond relative knowledge. Unperturbed by inner or outer events. He reads the verse as telling you what you are, then urging: desire consciousness alone.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Nirapekṣa means free of the six 'waves' (hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, birth, death) and the body's six changes. The Self is their witness, hence changeless and cool, meaning blissful. Be established in consciousness, free of action.

ashtavakra.1.17.practical_reading: In a heated moment, the verse is a portrait to recall gently: the cool, deep, unshaken witness behind the reaction.
misreadings: Not a demand to suppress emotion or manufacture calm
Not a relational ideal of needing no one
cautions: 'Needing nothing' could be heard as 'don't need anyone' by someone lonely or avoidant
not_for: Someone grieving who would hear 'be cool and unshaken'
speaks_to: People wanting an image of steadiness

data_flags.translation_note: 'Self-reliant' for nirbhara is not supported. Nityaswarupananda has 'devoid of bulk and form', Richards 'formless', Baijnath (1904) 'ever full'. Suggest 'full' or 'weightless'. Commentators read the first half as a description ('you are...') and only the last word as a command; our all-imperative 'Be...' is...

ashtavakra.1.2.context: This is the opening of the dialogue. King Janaka has just asked three questions in 1.1: how knowledge, liberation and dispassion are gained. This is Ashtavakra's first reply, and from 1.3 he turns straight to the teaching that Janaka is the witnessing consciousness, not the elements.
ashtavakra.1.2.core_teaching: Freedom starts with two practices together: loosening the grip of sense-objects, and actively cultivating forbearance, honesty, kindness, contentment and truthfulness, which purify the mind for self-knowledge.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Shunning objects means dropping the 'this is mine' attachment born of identifying with body and mind, plus sense-control. The virtues purify the mind: non-attachment is the negative half of practice, virtue the positive. Cites Ramakrishna on sincerity and truth.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Objects can't literally be abandoned while the body lives; obsessive attachment is what goes. Be content with what prarabdha brings, don't lie or grovel to get things, see their faults. He mocks nakedness and begging as false renunciation.

ashtavakra.1.2.practical_reading: In daily life it works as a two-step practice: notice what hooks you and hold it at arm's length, and deliberately practise patience, honesty, kindness, contentment and truthfulness.
misreadings: Not a call to reject all pleasures or possessions; Jalim Singh says objects are still used, and it is the attachment that goes
Forgiveness (kṣamā) is forbearance grown inside, not a duty to put up with ongoing harm
Not a moral checklist that earns freedom; in the text it prepares the mind for self-knowledge
cautions: 'Poison' language about desire can feed shame in someone struggling with appetite, addiction or body image. Frame it as loosening a grip, not as self-disgust.
not_for: A person being pressured to 'forgive' an abuser
Someone with an eating disorder or compulsive guilt about desire, if read as 'desire is poison'
speaks_to: Someone feeling pulled around by cravings, shopping, scrolling or habits
A person wanting a concrete first step in inner work
Someone rebuilding trust after dishonesty who wants to practise truthfulness

ashtavakra.1.4.context: This is part of Ashtavakra's opening reply. In 1.3 he tells Janaka that he is none of the five elements but the consciousness that witnesses them. This verse states the result of resting as that witness: happiness, peace and freedom, right now.
ashtavakra.1.4.core_teaching: Freedom is not a distant goal. It follows at once from no longer identifying with the body and abiding as consciousness.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The essence of Advaita practice. Identifying with the body loads its birth, ageing, disease and death onto the Self. Drop that and you know yourself as consciousness at once; body and mind only hide it, as clouds hide the sun.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Bondage lasts only while the 'knot' of mutual superimposition between consciousness and the inert mind remains; as heated iron seems to burn, the Self seems to act. Cut the knot and freedom is immediate; moksha is not elsewhere.

ashtavakra.1.4.practical_reading: It can be used as a pause practice: step back, notice the body and its sensations as things you are aware of, and rest in that awareness for a few breaths.
misreadings: Not a dissociation technique or a denial of bodily needs or pain
'Right now' is a claim about the Self, not a promise that problems vanish instantly
cautions: For someone with dissociation, depersonalisation or trauma, 'set the body apart' can be destabilising; grounding in the body may be what they need
not_for: People experiencing dissociation or depersonalisation
Someone with a new serious diagnosis who needs their body taken seriously
speaks_to: Someone over-identified with appearance, ageing or illness
Anxious people who need a felt moment of calm
Seekers who think freedom is far away

ashtavakra.1.5.context: Continuing the opening instruction, after saying Janaka is not the elements (1.3), Ashtavakra strips away social and perceptual identities: caste, stage of life, anything the eye can see. Next (1.6) he says merit and demerit, pleasure and pain belong to the mind.
ashtavakra.1.5.core_teaching: The Self has none of the labels that society or perception give it. It is the unattached, formless witness, and knowing this is the basis of happiness.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Āśrama means the four stages of life. The Self is never an object of sense-knowledge, so neither caste nor āśrama can be said of it, and the Self as such has no obligation to perform the duties tied to them.

ashtavakra.1.5.practical_reading: It can loosen an identity built on status, caste, job title or stage of life: what you are underneath is the one who sees all these roles.
misreadings: Not a social programme against caste, though it is often quoted against caste pride; its claim is about the Self
Not licence to drop duties while one still identifies with the body; Jalim Singh's answer concerns the knower
cautions: Caste is a live and painful subject. Avoid implying that discrimination does not matter because 'you are not your caste'.
Jalim Singh's tika says varna duties are for the ignorant; don't present that as the verse's plain meaning.
not_for: Someone facing caste discrimination, if it sounds like 'just transcend it'
speaks_to: Someone feeling reduced to a label such as caste, job, age or marital status
A person in a life transition (retirement, empty nest) whose role has changed

ashtavakra.1.8.context: Ashtavakra has just said (1.6–1.7) that merit and demerit, pleasure and pain belong to the mind, and that Janaka is the one seer, neither doer nor enjoyer. Here the doer-sense is pictured as a snakebite. In 1.9 the next step is to burn the forest of ignorance with the conviction 'I am pure awareness'.
ashtavakra.1.8.core_teaching: The conviction 'I am the doer' is a poison that binds. The antidote is a firm conviction that the Self does not act; body and mind do.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: It is a black serpent because egoism brings spiritual death. The nectar revives and removes pain: in the same way, destroying egoism revives spiritual awareness and frees one from worldly misery.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The conceit 'I do this and will enjoy its fruit' is the black snake whose bite keeps the whole world in birth and death. Only the firm conviction 'I am not the doer' cures it; nothing else brings happiness.

ashtavakra.1.8.practical_reading: It applies to over-responsibility and control. Notice the inner claim 'everything depends on me', do your part, and let outcomes rest with the larger web of causes.
misreadings: Not an excuse to avoid accountability for one's actions
The verse denies doership to the Self altogether; it is not a teamwork message about sharing the load
cautions: Our line softens the doctrine. Fine as application, but say so if quoting the verse itself.
not_for: Someone avoiding responsibility for harm they caused
Someone who already feels powerless, since it could deepen helplessness
speaks_to: Managers or parents carrying everything on themselves

data_flags.translation_note: The translation is accurate. The line and misuse note change 'I am not the doer' into 'not the ONLY doer'. Both commentators deny doership to the Self entirely (the body-mind acts). It works as pastoral advice, but readings should not attribute 'only' to the verse.

ashtavakra.10.3.context: This verse is from chapter 10, 'Quietude' (upaśama). Verses 10.1–2 urge giving up desire and seeing wealth, friends and property as a dream lasting a few days. Verse 10.4 says bondage consists of craving alone.
ashtavakra.10.3.core_teaching: Samsara is present wherever craving is. Firm dispassion frees one from craving and brings happiness.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Our entanglement in the world has desire as its root; free of desire, the world loses its hold. 'Firm' dispassion means non-attachment even to objects one already possesses, and dropping desire for things not yet obtained.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Whatever object craving arises for is a cause of samsara. Quoting the Yoga Vasishtha: the world rides the chariot of wishes, drawn by the senses, driven by craving, which grows with the mind as horns grow with a cow.

ashtavakra.10.3.practical_reading: Use it as a diagnostic: where you feel the treadmill, look for the craving underneath.
misreadings: Not that all wanting is evil; it concerns compulsive thirst
Not 'escape the world'; samsara here is a state, not a place
cautions: In addiction contexts, pair it with practical support; craving is not only a mindset
not_for: Someone in active addiction without support, if presented as a matter of willpower

ashtavakra.10.7.context: Chapter 10 continues. Verses 10.5–6 said everything is impermanent and that enjoyments have been had over countless lives. Here the aims of wealth, pleasure and even dharma are dismissed as resting places; 10.8 then says: stop.
ashtavakra.10.7.core_teaching: Wealth, pleasure and even good deeds have never given the mind rest in the wilderness of worldly life. Enough of looking to them for peace.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Giving up the wish for dharma, artha and kama is the cause of liberation. Even someone given the whole wealth-filled earth still craves heaven, and the lustful and greedy cannot see faults. Wandering in samsara, one never finds rest.

ashtavakra.10.7.practical_reading: It speaks to burnout from achievement, and even from doing good: rest is not a reward waiting at the end of enough effort or virtue.
misreadings: Not against good deeds or ethics
Not 'nothing matters'
cautions: Nityaswarupananda calls dharma worthless as an ideal; that can unsettle a reader whose ethics are their anchor. Our misuse note is a guardrail, softer than the commentary.
not_for: Someone using it to justify dropping ethical commitments
speaks_to: Volunteers or caregivers who hoped service would bring peace

ashtavakra.10.8.context: This closes chapter 10. After saying nothing has ever given the mind rest (10.7), Ashtavakra urges stopping, at least now. Chapter 11 then lists the certainties that make the wise calm.
ashtavakra.10.8.core_teaching: After countless lives of painful, exhausting action, stop desire-driven activity now.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Our present body and misery result from past actions, and the process continues as long as we keep acting. To escape misery we must stop worldly activity at once, since all that labour brought no lasting happiness.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Having taught the calming of craving, Ashtavakra now teaches the calming of action (uparāma). Over many births you have done exhausting deeds and wandered in birth and death; without this withdrawal no one gains the joy of liberation in life.

ashtavakra.10.8.practical_reading: It can be permission to rest from frantic striving and the compulsion to keep doing. For householders, it calls for stopping the inner treadmill rather than abandoning duties.
misreadings: Our misuse note ('rest, not quitting your obligations') is a guardrail; both commentators read 'stop' as withdrawing from worldly action
Not a judgement that your work has been worthless
cautions: 'Now, at last, stop' could be misheard by someone with suicidal thoughts
The 'how many births' framing assumes rebirth, which not every reader shares
not_for: Someone with suicidal thoughts
Someone considering walking away from dependants
speaks_to: Someone who can't stop working even on holiday

ashtavakra.11.1.context: This opens chapter 11, 'Wisdom', a series of verses about 'one who knows for certain that...' (niścayī). Next, 11.2 assigns everything to Ishvara, 11.3 assigns fortune to destiny, and 11.4 assigns pleasure, pain, birth and death to destiny.
ashtavakra.11.1.core_teaching: Knowing for certain that arising, passing and changing belong to the nature of things, one stays unperturbed and easily finds peace.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Everything exists, changes and is destroyed; nothing is permanent. Seeing this clearly, one stops clinging to things and finds peace, since mental pain comes from attachment to what passes.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: All changes, gross and subtle, come from maya and its impressions, not from the changeless Self, as iron moves near a still magnet. One certain that the Self is unattached and the body perishable finds peace without effort.

ashtavakra.11.1.practical_reading: When things change or break, remember that change is the nature of things, not a personal attack.
misreadings: Not that loss doesn't hurt
Not fatalism about what can be changed
cautions: After fresh loss, 'it's just nature' can feel minimising
not_for: The first days of grief
speaks_to: Change at work, moving house, ageing
Someone who takes every change personally

ashtavakra.11.3.context: This is the third of the 'certainties' in chapter 11. Verse 11.2 said Ishvara is the maker of all; 11.4 says pleasure and pain, birth and death come from destiny, and 11.5 that suffering comes from anxious thought.
ashtavakra.11.3.core_teaching: One who is certain that hard and good times come in their own time, by destiny, is content and settled, neither longing nor grieving.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Fate is the mysterious power of karma. Whoever sees this life's ups and downs as the result of past karma is not shaken by changes of fortune, neither longing for what he lacks nor grieving for what is lost.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Objection: if God made everything, inequality would make God partial. Answer, citing Gita 5.14: the Lord creates neither agency nor karma; fortune follows beginningless karma, which ripens like seeds when conditions gather.

ashtavakra.11.3.practical_reading: It loosens anxiety over what you cannot control, while you keep acting on what you can.
misreadings: Not a reason to stop trying
Not 'you deserved your misfortune'
cautions: Karma-and-destiny framing can feel like blame to someone facing illness, poverty or abuse; never imply they caused it
not_for: Victims of injustice or abuse
Someone with a seriously ill child or a serious illness
speaks_to: Someone on a lucky streak who fears it will end

ashtavakra.11.5.context: This verse is from chapter 11. After 11.3–4 assign fortune and pain to destiny, it says the mind's dwelling is what turns them into suffering. Verse 11.6 then describes one who knows 'I am not the body'.
ashtavakra.11.5.core_teaching: Here, suffering is born of anxious dwelling and nothing else. One certain of this drops it and becomes happy, calm and free of craving everywhere.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The preceding verses say suffering comes through karma and is unavoidable. But if we detach the mind when it comes, it will not affect us; dwelling on it intensifies it.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: He uses it to explain how one acts without being bound: here, suffering comes from worry alone. One sure of this drops worry, becomes calm and steady, and though acting does not experience the fruits.

ashtavakra.11.5.practical_reading: It separates pain from the extra suffering of rumination: deal with the problem, and drop the loop.
misreadings: Not that all suffering is imaginary
Real problems still need attention
cautions: Telling someone with an anxiety disorder 'suffering is only worry' can sound dismissive; pair it with care
not_for: Someone in physical pain or acute crisis
Clinical anxiety, if framed as 'just stop worrying'

ashtavakra.13.1.context: Chapter 13, 'Happiness', is Janaka's seven-verse song, each verse ending 'I live happily' (yathāsukham). In 13.2 he adds that he has set aside the strains of body, speech and mind.
ashtavakra.13.1.core_teaching: The ease of inwardly having nothing is rare even for the outward renunciate. So Janaka drops both renouncing and acquiring, and lives at ease.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Svāsthya literally means being established in the Self; this tranquillity is uncaused and inherent. Even a loincloth implies relative consciousness, and renunciation also presupposes ego and attachment, so true happiness lies beyond both.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The steadiness that comes from dropping attachment to all objects does not arise if one is attached even to a loincloth. So the disciple gives up attachment to both renouncing and taking, and rests in the Self's bliss.

ashtavakra.13.1.practical_reading: It addresses spiritual or minimalist striving: inner ease comes not from owning less or more, but from being driven by neither grabbing nor giving up.
misreadings: Not against simplicity or monastic life
Not 'anything goes' in consumption
not_for: Someone whose poverty is not chosen, if 'having nothing' is romanticised
speaks_to: Someone caught between consumerism and guilt-driven minimalism
People who renounced outwardly but feel no peace

ashtavakra.13.3.context: This is from Janaka's song of happiness (chapter 13). After setting aside the strains of body, speech and mind (13.2), here he does what comes without the sense of 'I did it'. Verse 13.4 continues the theme of action and non-action; 18.20 repeats the thought.
ashtavakra.13.3.core_teaching: Knowing that in truth the Self does nothing, Janaka simply does whatever comes to be done and stays at ease.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Everything done is done by body, mind and senses with the ego; the Self is beyond them. While one lives in a body, some activity such as eating and sleeping continues, and he does it unattached. Cites Gita 3.8.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Objection: if all action stops, the body will die. Reply: what body and senses do is not done by the Self. Seeing this, the wise eat, drink and act free of ego, and stay in their blissful nature.

ashtavakra.13.3.practical_reading: A way of working: do what is in front of you, fully, without the extra weight of 'I must be the one who achieves this'.
misreadings: Not drifting without plans or commitments
Not denying responsibility for what one does
not_for: Someone avoiding accountability
speaks_to: New parents doing endless small tasks

ashtavakra.15.1.context: This opens chapter 15, 'Knowledge of the Self', where Ashtavakra repeats the core teaching to steady Janaka. Verse 15.2 then compresses the whole teaching into one line.
ashtavakra.15.1.core_teaching: A clear intellect is fulfilled by even a casual teaching, while an unprepared one stays confused despite a lifetime of inquiry.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Self-knowledge dawns at once on an intellect purified by discipline and the four qualifications (discernment, dispassion, the six virtues, longing for freedom). A ready disciple needs little instruction; the unready misconceive the Self however long they inquire.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Three grades of aspirant: the best awakens on hearing the great saying once, the middling through repeated hearing and reflection, the lowest after long study and worship. He cites Virochana, taught repeatedly without understanding.

ashtavakra.15.1.practical_reading: It suggests shifting from collecting teachings to preparing the mind through honesty, calm and sincerity, so that simple truths can land.
misreadings: Not that some people are hopeless
Not anti-study; it is about readiness
cautions: Can make a long-time seeker feel inferior ('a muddled mind'); frame it as readiness that grows
not_for: Someone who already feels stupid or inadequate
speaks_to: Seekers who have read everything and feel stuck
Someone overloaded with courses and books

ashtavakra.15.10.context: This continues 15.9 in chapter 15. Verse 15.11 widens the view from the body to the whole universe, pictured as waves on the ocean.
ashtavakra.15.10.core_teaching: Whether the body lasts till the end of the age or ends today, pure consciousness gains or loses nothing.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The body's conditions make not the slightest difference to the Self, so do not fear death. He cites Vivekachudamani 560–564 and Gita 2.17.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The seer is distinct from the seen: the body is seen and you are the seer. Whether it lasts an aeon or falls now, you neither persist nor perish with it, since you are what lends it existence.

ashtavakra.15.10.practical_reading: With fears about health and mortality, it reminds you that your worth and being are not measured by lifespan.
misreadings: Not indifference to health or life
Not 'it doesn't matter if I die'
cautions: 'Let it go even today' must never reach someone with suicidal thoughts
not_for: Suicidal ideation or self-harm
Fresh bereavement
The first days after a terminal diagnosis
speaks_to: Reflective people facing old age or illness with some steadiness

ashtavakra.15.11.context: In chapter 15, after the body (15.10), the whole universe rises and falls like waves in the ocean that you are. Verse 15.12 adds that nothing is separate from you, so what is there to accept or reject?
ashtavakra.15.11.core_teaching: In you, the boundless ocean, the world's waves rise and fall by their own nature; they neither add to you nor take away from you.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: 15.10 taught letting go of the body; this verse, of the universe. Creation and dissolution happen in time; the Self is beyond time. As waves neither add to nor subtract from the ocean, the universe adds nothing to the Self.

ashtavakra.15.11.practical_reading: In turbulent times, events are waves; you can let them move without being diminished.
misreadings: Not indifference to world events or to others' suffering
cautions: The 'imagined world' framing (Jalim Singh) can feel dismissive during a collective tragedy
not_for: Fresh personal tragedy

ashtavakra.15.19.context: This comes near the end of chapter 15. Verse 15.18 said that in the ocean of the world, One alone was, is and will be. Verse 15.20 adds: give up even contemplation and hold nothing in the mind.
ashtavakra.15.19.core_teaching: Don't churn the mind with plans and counter-plans. Become still and rest in your own blissful Self.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Be free of affirmations and negations, ideas such as 'I shall do this' and 'I shall not do this'.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: O conscious one, don't disturb your mind with willing and doubting. Free of them, abide in your own blissful nature.

ashtavakra.15.19.practical_reading: For decision paralysis and second-guessing: make the decision, then stop re-arguing it in your head.
misreadings: Not avoiding decisions
Not forcibly suppressing thought
not_for: Someone who urgently needs to make a safety decision, if read as 'stop thinking'

ashtavakra.15.2.context: In chapter 15, right after saying a pure mind needs little teaching (15.1), Ashtavakra gives the teaching in one line. Verse 15.3 says this knowledge makes the talkative silent and the busy idle, which is why pleasure-seekers avoid it.
ashtavakra.15.2.core_teaching: Liberation is losing the relish for sense-objects; bondage is relishing them. That is all there is to know, and the rest is up to you.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Ashtavakra describes the essence of bondage and liberation in a few words and points to the aspirant's one duty. He cross-refers 10.4 (bondage is craving alone).

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: He quotes the saying that the mind alone causes bondage and liberation: attached to objects it binds, free of them it liberates. Having understood this much, do as you wish.

ashtavakra.15.2.practical_reading: A simple self-test: where am I still savouring what hooks me? 'Do as you wish' hands the responsibility back to the student.
misreadings: 'Do as you wish' is not licence; it assumes the relish is already gone
Not hatred of the senses
not_for: Someone who might take 'do as you wish' as permission for harmful behaviour
speaks_to: Someone wanting a clear, compact teaching

ashtavakra.15.4.context: In chapter 15, after noting that pleasure-seekers avoid this knowledge (15.3), Ashtavakra restates the witness teaching. Verse 15.5 extends it to likes and dislikes.
ashtavakra.15.4.core_teaching: You are not the body or its owner, neither doer nor enjoyer, but consciousness: the ever-present witness that needs nothing. Live freely.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: A brief note: 'free' (nirapekṣa) means not depending on or conditioned by anything.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Doership and enjoyership belong to the mind, which you witness. Image: a lamp in a dance hall lights host, audience and dancer alike; the body is the hall, ego the host, intellect the dancer, consciousness the lamp.

ashtavakra.15.4.practical_reading: For identity shaped by body image or performance, notice that you are the awareness in which body, deeds and results appear.
misreadings: Not neglect of the body or health
Not that your actions don't matter
cautions: 'Not your body' can sound like rejecting the body to someone with body-image distress or dissociation
not_for: Dissociation
Eating disorders, if it encourages ignoring the body

ashtavakra.15.5.context: This chapter 15 verse follows 15.4 (not the body, not the doer). Next, 15.6 says to see the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self.
ashtavakra.15.5.core_teaching: Attraction and aversion belong to the mind, and the mind is never you. You are changeless awareness, so live freely.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The aspirant should neither love nor hate in the narrow, selfish sense, since that means identifying with the mind. He adds that universal love, which grows from true self-knowledge, is not what is to be dropped.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Friend, enemy and stranger are all distinctions of the mind. Attraction and aversion cannot be the Self's nature, since scripture calls the Self attributeless; if they were natural to it, liberation would be impossible.

ashtavakra.15.5.practical_reading: It creates space around reactive likes and dislikes: notice 'I don't like this' as a passing mental event, not who you are.
misreadings: Not suppression of feelings
Nityaswarupananda explicitly says universal love is not what is meant to be dropped
not_for: Someone told their legitimate anger at injustice is 'just the mind'
speaks_to: Reactivity, irritability, strong dislikes of people
Someone who confuses their moods with their identity

ashtavakra.15.8.context: In chapter 15, after the ocean image (15.7), Ashtavakra presses Janaka with repeated encouragement. Verses 15.9–10 then apply this to the body's coming and going.
ashtavakra.15.8.core_teaching: An insistent call to trust that you are knowledge itself, the Lord, beyond nature, and not to slip back into confusion.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Ashtavakra is impressing the Self's nature on the disciple. Until it is realised, one finds it hard to believe that the Self is what the sages say; 'beyond nature' means unaffected by it and controlling it.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Don't fall into the twin errors of doubting and misconceiving your conscious nature. He defines consciousness as self-luminous, lighting other things without needing anything else, and contrasts it with inert objects that know neither themselves nor others.

ashtavakra.15.8.practical_reading: A reassurance when doubt creeps in: you are more than what is happening to you.
misreadings: Not 'you are God' in an egoistic sense
Not blind belief; śraddhā here is trust in the teaching while understanding matures
not_for: Someone in grandiosity
speaks_to: Someone who has lost faith in themselves

ashtavakra.15.9.context: In chapter 15, after urging faith (15.8), Ashtavakra applies the teaching to the body. Verse 15.10 continues: let the body last an aeon or end today.
ashtavakra.15.9.core_teaching: The body with its senses comes, stays and goes; the Self neither comes nor goes. So why mourn?

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The Self does not share the body's nature: the body changes and the Self does not. 'It' refers to the body's changes, such as death. He cites Gita 2.13 and 2.18.

ashtavakra.15.9.practical_reading: Later in grief, or with fear of death, it can offer perspective: something in you, and in the one you love, is not subject to coming and going.
misreadings: Not a rule against mourning
Not 'the person who died doesn't matter'
cautions: It directly questions grieving; never use on Day 1 of a grief plan
Jalim Singh's reading relies on rebirth (the subtle body travelling to other worlds), which can feel dismissive in fresh grief
not_for: Fresh bereavement
Child loss
Suicidal ideation
speaks_to: Later stages of grief seeking meaning

ashtavakra.16.1.context: This opens chapter 16, 'Special instruction'. Verse 16.2 says that whether you enjoy, work or meditate, your mind will still long for the state beyond all desire. Verse 16.11 repeats the refrain: even with Shiva, Vishnu or Brahma as teacher, there is no ease without forgetting all.
ashtavakra.16.1.core_teaching: However much scripture one recites or hears, one does not rest in the Self until everything, every mental construction, is forgotten.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Self-knowledge is experience, not intellect; scripture says the Self isn't gained by speech, intellect or Veda study. 'Forget all' means being conscious of the Self alone and seeing everything as the Self, not a deep-sleep blankness.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Quoting the Panchadashi: study and reflect, then drop the texts as a grain-seeker drops straw. Objection: in deep sleep all is forgotten, yet no one is freed. Reply: ignorance remains in sleep; the liberated forget ignorance too.

ashtavakra.16.1.practical_reading: After study, let the concepts go and live from what you have understood.
misreadings: Not anti-learning or anti-scripture
Not mental blankness, and not forgetting responsibilities
cautions: In a scripture app, 'forget the scriptures' needs framing: study first, then go beyond concepts
not_for: Someone with memory loss or dementia, if read literally as 'forget everything'
speaks_to: People who intellectualise their inner life

data_flags.translation_note: Narrowed. The Sanskrit says no abiding in oneself 'without forgetting everything' (sarvavismaraṇāt ṛte). Our translation ('until you forget them all') and line ('set them all down') limit 'all' to the scriptures. Nityaswarupananda and Richards both have 'forget all / everything'. Suggest: 'you will not be...

ashtavakra.16.10.context: In chapter 16, after 16.9 on fleeing the world, Ashtavakra targets spiritual pride. Verse 16.11 says that even a divine teacher cannot help without the forgetting of all.
ashtavakra.16.10.core_teaching: Whoever is proud even of liberation, and still possessive about the body, is neither knower nor yogi, only a sufferer.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Abhimāna can mean egoism or conceit. Thinking 'I shall be free' or 'I am free' keeps the ego; pride in spiritual attainment is the opposite of knowledge. Claimed knowledge full of ego is a sad delusion that breeds misery.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Whoever boasts 'I am a knower, I see past and future, I am liberated' is no knower. Whoever says 'I'm a yogi, I do dhauti, neti and basti daily' is no yogi. Such a person only suffers.

ashtavakra.16.10.practical_reading: It addresses spiritual ego: a wellness identity, pride in practice streaks, or feeling superior for being 'more spiritual'.
misreadings: Not against practice or yogic techniques
Not a licence to label others as spiritual egotists
not_for: A beginner who might feel their sincere effort is being mocked
speaks_to: Someone noticing pride in their practice

ashtavakra.16.2.context: 16.1: you can recite and hear scriptures endlessly, but you won't rest in yourself without 'forgetting everything'. 16.2 is this verse. 16.3: everyone suffers from straining, and the lucky one who grasps this teaching finds peace. 16.4 praises the 'master idler' for whom even blinking is effort.
ashtavakra.16.2.core_teaching: No activity, whether pleasure, work or even meditation, satisfies on its own; what the mind really wants is the state where wanting itself stops.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), notes
commentaries.gist: Enjoyment, work and concentration all show the Self is not yet realised; none gives lasting satisfaction. The mind yearns for the Self, which lies beyond all quests and can't be realised until desire is gone.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903)
commentaries.gist: Reads the verse positively: whatever you do, enjoy, act or meditate, your mind, emptied of hope by self-knowledge, will be at peace; actions done without hope do not bind, since hope is bondage.

ashtavakra.16.2.practical_reading: If you've tried pleasure, productivity and even spiritual practice and still feel restless, the restlessness isn't a sign you picked the wrong activity; it points to wanting something none of them can give.
misreadings: Not 'nothing is worth doing'
Not anti-meditation; it says meditation as a goal-driven activity won't finish the job either
cautions: For someone flat or depressed, 'nothing satisfies' can confirm hopelessness; frame it as a pointer, not a verdict
Next verses (16.4 'master idler') need explanation if quoted
not_for: someone with clinical depression, unless paired with grounding and support
speaks_to: trying everything and still feeling empty

ashtavakra.16.3.context: 16.1: you can recite and hear many scriptures, but you will not be at ease without forgetting everything. 16.2: enjoy, work or meditate, and your mind will still long for what lies beyond all desire. 16.3 is this verse. 16.4: only the 'master idler', to whom even blinking is a strain, is happy. 16.5: freed from 'this is done, that is not', the mind no longer cares about the four aims of life.
ashtavakra.16.3.core_teaching: Suffering comes from the strain of desire-driven striving. Seeing this clearly is itself the teaching that frees.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Ashtavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama) notes
commentaries.gist: All exertion presupposes a desire for something not yet had; satisfied desire breeds more desire, unsatisfied desire hurts. Uprooting desire makes one inwardly inactive, though outwardly one may still act.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baijnath, The Ashtavakra Gita (translation with brief notes)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: every exertion brings pain though no one recognises it, and whoever takes this single lesson to heart finds peace. His note on 16.1 says the last word of this teaching is silence.

ashtavakra.16.3.practical_reading: Notice the extra layer of strain (gripping, urgency, needing a particular outcome) on top of what you are doing, and release that even while you keep doing the work.
misreadings: Not against effort or responsibility; Nityaswarupananda says outward activity may continue
Not 'parenting should feel effortless'
The next verse's 'master idler' means inner non-grasping, not laziness
cautions: If 16.4 is quoted, explain it; for a tired parent 'master idler' can sound like a dig
not_for: someone already unable to get started, who may hear it as permission to give up

ashtavakra.16.9.context: In chapter 16, verse 16.8 contrasted attachment to objects with aversion to them and said both bind. Here the attached person wants to flee the world; 16.10 then targets spiritual pride.
ashtavakra.16.9.core_teaching: The attached person wants to escape the world in order to escape pain. One free of attachment has no pain and is not distressed even while living in it.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The attached person thinks sorrow's cause lies in the world. But attachment to the world, not the world itself, is the root of misery; free of attachment one can live as happily in the world as anywhere.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The attached want to leave the world to escape the pain objects bring; the dispassionate are untroubled though the world continues. Quoting the Panchadashi: a tree with fire in its hollow can't turn green, nor an ignorant mind find peace.

ashtavakra.16.9.practical_reading: It addresses 'geographical cures': changing job, city or partner won't fix an inner restlessness that travels with you.
misreadings: Not advice to stay somewhere harmful
Not against changing circumstances when that is needed
cautions: Must not be used to keep someone in an abusive relationship or an unsafe job
not_for: Someone in danger who needs to leave
speaks_to: Someone who has changed jobs or cities repeatedly and still feels the same

ashtavakra.17.1.context: This opens chapter 17, 'The true knower', a long portrait. Verse 17.2 says the knower is never distressed, since the whole universe is filled by him; 17.3 says sense-objects don't please one who delights in the Self.
ashtavakra.17.1.core_teaching: The one who is content, with clear senses, always delighting alone in the Self, has gained the fruit of both knowledge and yoga.
ashtavakra.17.1.practical_reading: It points to being at ease in your own company and finding contentment without constant stimulation.
misreadings: Not a recommendation of isolation for everyone
Not a judgement on people who need others
cautions: There are two traditional readings: metaphysical aloneness (Nityaswarupananda) and literal solitude for renunciates (Jalim Singh). Our note's 'not counsel to the lonely' is a guardrail, not what Jalim Singh says.
Can wound someone who is lonely or isolated
not_for: Isolated or lonely elderly people
Someone withdrawing because of depression

ashtavakra.17.4.context: This is part of chapter 17's portrait. In 17.3 sense-objects don't please one who delights in the Self, as neem leaves don't please an elephant fond of sallaki leaves. Verse 17.5 adds: rare is one who desires neither enjoyment nor liberation.
ashtavakra.17.4.core_teaching: Rare is the person who neither keeps dwelling on pleasures already had nor longs for those not yet had.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Every enjoyment leaves an impression in the mind that makes us want the thing again and again. Only self-knowledge removes this pull.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: One who is not attached to past enjoyments, does not long for new ones, and is content in the Self is one in crores, or perhaps not even one.

ashtavakra.17.4.practical_reading: For nostalgia and anticipation: notice yourself replaying past pleasures or fantasising about future ones, and come back to the present.
misreadings: Not against happy memories or healthy planning
not_for: Someone grieving who treasures memories of a loved one
speaks_to: Compulsive anticipation (the next trip, the next purchase)

ashtavakra.17.7.context: This verse is from chapter 17's portrait. In 17.5–6 the great-souled person desires neither enjoyment nor liberation, and is drawn to nothing and averse to nothing among the four aims, or life and death. Here he neither wants the world dissolved nor resents its going on.
ashtavakra.17.7.core_teaching: The knower neither longs for the world to end nor resents its going on, and so lives happily on whatever livelihood comes.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The knower has no wish for the world to dissolve and no aversion to its staying. Whether it remains or perishes, he stands as its witness and ground, and is accomplished, blessed and worthy of honour.

ashtavakra.17.7.practical_reading: For world-weariness: neither wishing everything would stop nor resenting that life goes on, but living simply on what comes.
misreadings: Not passivity about earning or providing for others
Not indifference to the world's suffering
cautions: 'Longing for the world to end' sits close to a suicidal wish; the verse counters it, but handle with care
Nityaswarupananda says the knower makes no effort for his living; that is not a model for householders
not_for: Suicidal ideation, unless handled by a person who can support them
speaks_to: Someone resentful that life goes on after a loss (later stage)

ashtavakra.18.100.context: This closes the hundred-verse eighteenth chapter, in which Ashtavakra describes how the freed person lives: not excited by praise, not hurt by blame, not afraid of death (18.99). Chapter 19 then turns to Janaka, who answers with his own account of resting in the Self.
ashtavakra.18.100.core_teaching: Peace is not a matter of location. The settled person does not chase society or flee to solitude, because neither attraction nor aversion is driving the choice; they remain the same wherever life puts them.

commentaries.who: Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (1903, Hindi)
commentaries.gist: The calm, freed person does not rush toward crowded places, because he has no attachment to them, nor toward the forest, because he has no aversion to people. In town or forest he stays steady and the same.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Reads the verse plainly: the tranquil one runs after neither the crowd nor the wilderness and remains the same in any condition and place. He adds no separate note to this verse.

ashtavakra.18.100.practical_reading: A reader who keeps thinking peace lies in a different place (a quieter city, a retreat, a busier social life) can use this to notice that the restlessness travels with them; the work is on the chasing, not on the address.
misreadings: Not a rule against solitude or retreats, nor against social life; it rejects running to either out of craving or aversion.
Not a description of indifference to people; Jalim Singh frames it as freedom from attachment and aversion.
cautions: Describes the state of a jivanmukta; a reader who cannot yet feel 'the same everywhere' should not read it as a judgement on themselves.
not_for: someone who needs to leave an unsafe home or workplace: the verse is about inner chasing, not about staying put in harm
acute loneliness, where telling the reader the crowd does not matter could feel dismissive
speaks_to: restlessness that keeps looking for the right place
someone torn between moving to the city and moving away from it
people who feel calm only on holiday

ashtavakra.18.11.context: In chapter 18, verses 18.9–10 describe the yogi who has gone silent, beyond distraction and focus, pleasure and pain. Verse 18.12 says that for him there is no dharma, wealth, pleasure or discrimination.
ashtavakra.18.11.core_teaching: For the yogi whose nature is free of mental distinctions, it makes no difference whether he rules or begs, gains or loses, lives in society or in the forest.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Feeling different in these conditions is possible only for a mind bound by relative consciousness. Someone who has gone beyond it may still notice extremes of fortune, but they seem shadowy and unsubstantial.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The one liberated in life feels no elation even on gaining heaven's kingdom and no disturbance living by begging. Gain and loss are equal to him, and in forest or at home he remains the same.

ashtavakra.18.11.practical_reading: For status swings such as promotion or redundancy, crowd or solitude: the steady person stays themselves.
misreadings: Not that circumstances don't matter for wellbeing or justice
not_for: Someone in acute financial crisis who needs practical help

ashtavakra.18.2.context: Chapter 18, 'Peace', opens with praise of the Self (18.1). This verse says happiness requires letting go of everything; 18.3 adds the burning pain of obligation.
ashtavakra.18.2.core_teaching: One may acquire everything and enjoy plenty, but no one is happy without letting go of everything.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: He quotes Bhartrihari's Vairagya Shataka: every possession (pleasure, rank, wealth, honour, beauty, learning, the body itself) carries its own fear, and renunciation alone is fearless. Sense-enjoyment and true happiness contradict each other.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The rich suffer disease, rivalry, fear of kings and thieves, and sleepless guarding of wealth; given the earth they'd want heaven. Renouncing means knowing the world as unreal, as one 'gives up' a barren woman's nonexistent son.

ashtavakra.18.2.practical_reading: 'Letting go of everything' can be read as releasing ownership and clinging, so that you can hold what you have without fear.
misreadings: Not that one must give away all possessions
Not contempt for wealth itself
not_for: Someone in poverty, as it could romanticise lack
speaks_to: Fear of losing what one has

ashtavakra.18.20.context: In chapter 18, verse 18.19 says nothing is done by the content, desireless sage even if he seems to act. Verse 18.21 compares him to a dry leaf blown by the wind of past impressions. The thought repeats Janaka's 13.3.
ashtavakra.18.20.core_teaching: The steady person has no stubborn attachment to doing or to not doing; he does what comes to be done and stays at ease.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: What comes, comes as a matter of course through prarabdha. He no longer acts or refrains by personal will, and willed actions breed unhappiness when frustrated; free of ego, he is the same in action and inaction.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The wise person insists on neither activity nor withdrawal, being free of the pride of doership. If prarabdha brings either, he does it happily and stays unattached.

ashtavakra.18.20.practical_reading: For guilt about doing versus resting: do what is actually in front of you, and rest when that is what comes, without rigid rules.
misreadings: Not aimlessness
Not avoiding planning
not_for: Someone procrastinating on something urgent

ashtavakra.18.3.context: In chapter 18, right after 'no happiness without letting go of everything' (18.2), Ashtavakra names the burning pain of obligation. Verse 18.4 says this existence is mere imagination.
ashtavakra.18.3.core_teaching: For one whose inner being is scorched by the sun of obligations, there is no happiness without the cooling downpour of calm.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: A strong note: duty as usually understood is slavery dressed as virtue, arising from taking the world as real, and it scorches the soul. When the mind's waves settle and desires go, calm pours like ambrosia on the parched heart.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The pain born of actions done as duties is like the sun's heat. One whose mind is burnt by it can never find happiness without the nectar-rain of peace.

ashtavakra.18.3.practical_reading: For burnout and the tyranny of 'shoulds': cultivate inner calm so that obligations stop burning you, even when they remain.
misreadings: Not permission to abandon dependants or commitments
Nityaswarupananda's 'duty is slavery' is one commentator's strong view, not a modern ethic to pass on
cautions: Caregivers with real, unavoidable duties may hear them dismissed; stress calm within duty
not_for: Someone looking for justification to walk out on dependants
speaks_to: People who feel scorched by endless obligations

ashtavakra.18.39.context: This verse is part of a run in chapter 18 (roughly 18.33–44) contrasting the confused (mūḍha) with the wise (dhīra). Verse 18.41 adds that mind-control comes naturally to the wise but escapes the one who strains for it.
ashtavakra.18.39.core_teaching: The confused do not find peace precisely because they chase it; the wise, clear about the truth, are always at peace.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: We lack peace because we don't know the Self, which is calm by nature. The very desire for peace comes from ignorance, so while that desire lasts, peace is not attained.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The deluded person seeks peace by forcibly restraining the mind and so does not get it. The wise person, having ascertained the Self, does not desire peace, and therefore has it.

ashtavakra.18.39.practical_reading: For anxious meditation: stop forcing calm, and let understanding and allowing bring it.
misreadings: Not that seeking help for anxiety is wrong
Not a licence to call people fools
cautions: The 'fool' framing can shame anxious readers; use 'a restless mind'
not_for: Someone with an anxiety disorder who needs treatment, if framed as 'just stop trying'
speaks_to: Anxiety about not being calm enough

ashtavakra.18.55.context: In chapter 18, verse 18.54 says the wise feel no attachment whether they meet a learned brahmin, a god, a holy place, a woman, a king or a friend. Verse 18.56 adds that pleased, he is not pleased, and pained, he is not pained.
ashtavakra.18.55.core_teaching: Even when ridiculed and scorned by servants, children, spouse, grandchildren and relatives, the yogi is not disturbed in the least.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Because he is completely free of the aversion that disturbs the mind.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The jivanmukta's mind is neither agitated when servants, sons, wives, daughters and relatives insult him nor elated when they honour him, since the delusion behind attraction and aversion is gone.

ashtavakra.18.55.practical_reading: For family friction: stay steady inside when family teases or criticises, without retaliating.
misreadings: Inner calm is not tolerating abuse; boundaries are still right
Not a model of the uncaring elder
cautions: Must never be used to tell someone to endure domestic abuse, elder abuse or contempt from family
not_for: Anyone experiencing domestic or elder abuse

ashtavakra.18.58.context: In chapter 18, verse 18.57 says the sense of obligation is itself samsara. Verse 18.59 then describes the wise person's ease in everyday acts.
ashtavakra.18.58.core_teaching: The confused mind is restless even when doing nothing; the skilful one stays calm even while doing everything that needs doing.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The skilful person's mind is calm because there is no egoistic feeling even amid activity. He cross-refers 18.29, 18.47 and 18.49.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The ignorant person, even sitting idle in an empty temple or on a mountain, is agitated by his own thoughts. The wise, though body and senses are busy in the world's eyes, stays unagitated, being free of willing.

ashtavakra.18.58.practical_reading: You can be frazzled on holiday and calm on a busy day: peace is a state of mind, not a schedule.
misreadings: Not a glorification of overwork
Not shaming people who cannot rest
not_for: Someone in burnout who would hear 'keep working, calmly'

ashtavakra.18.59.context: This verse follows 18.58's contrast between the restless and the skilful. Verse 18.60 compares the wise person to a vast, undisturbed lake.
ashtavakra.18.59.core_teaching: The calm-minded person sits, sleeps, comes and goes, speaks and eats at ease, even in everyday affairs.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: No note; he translates it as the equanimous sage living happily in practical life.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The one liberated in life stays in the Self's bliss in all dealings. Sitting, rising, sleeping, eating, drinking, doing every action, the knower stays calm-minded.

ashtavakra.18.59.practical_reading: A mindful-living practice: bring ease into the most ordinary acts, such as eating, walking, talking and sleeping.
misreadings: Not that a wise person never struggles
Not that you have failed if daily life is hard
cautions: For someone with insomnia or chronic pain, 'sleeps happily' may sting
not_for: Someone in acute distress for whom daily life is unmanageable

ashtavakra.18.61.context: In chapter 18, after the wise person as a calm lake (18.60), this verse contrasts inner and outer action. Verse 18.62 says the fool often shows aversion to his possessions.
ashtavakra.18.61.core_teaching: Even the confused person's withdrawal turns into activity, while even the wise person's activity bears the fruit of stillness.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The deluded person, though outwardly inactive, is inwardly very active. The wise person, though outwardly active, is inwardly still, because he does not identify with body and senses. He cites Gita 4.18.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The fool's senses may look withdrawn to the world, but that withdrawal is really activity because the ego remains. The knower's activity is really withdrawal and yields liberation, because pride is absent.

ashtavakra.18.61.practical_reading: For time off and retreats: a restless mind turns rest into busyness, while a still mind finds rest even at work.
misreadings: Not against retreats or rest
Not a glorification of constant activity
not_for: Someone who badly needs real rest
speaks_to: People who cannot relax on time off

ashtavakra.18.81.context: In chapter 18, verse 18.80 says that for the seer there is no heaven, hell or even liberation-in-life. Verse 18.82 adds that the desireless one neither praises the good nor blames the wicked.
ashtavakra.18.81.core_teaching: The steady person neither longs for gain nor grieves at its absence; his cool mind is filled as if with nectar.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: His only note glosses the nectar as the nectar of immortal bliss.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The one liberated in life neither asks for gain nor grieves at loss; his mind is satisfied and glad with the nectar of supreme bliss.

ashtavakra.18.81.practical_reading: For swings of gain and loss (markets, sales targets, exam results): do your work and let the mind stay cool whatever the result.
misreadings: Not against prayer or ambition as such
Not indifference to other people's real losses
not_for: Someone who has recently suffered a devastating loss

ashtavakra.18.91.context: In chapter 18, verse 18.90 says only the desireless one knows without knowing and sees without seeing. Verse 18.92 adds that for the sage who embodies guileless sincerity there is neither licence nor restraint, nor even the settling of truth.
ashtavakra.18.91.core_teaching: Beggar or king, whoever is desireless shines: the one for whom judging things as good or bad has melted away.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Because he finds the same Self in all things, good and evil.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: One with no craving for 'fine' things and no aversion to 'poor' ones shines, whether king or mendicant. His examples are Janaka and Rama among kings, and Jadabharata, Dattatreya and Yajnavalkya among renunciates.

ashtavakra.18.91.practical_reading: On status: what makes a person admirable is freedom from craving, not wealth or position.
misreadings: 'No good or bad' concerns preferences about things, not abandoning ethics
cautions: Dropping 'good and bad' can be misread as moral relativism, especially next to 18.92 (beyond licence and restraint); frame carefully
not_for: Someone who could use it to dismiss moral responsibility

ashtavakra.18.98.context: Chapter 18 nears its end. Verse 18.97 says the blessed one is not distracted in distraction and not even wise in his wisdom. Verses 18.99–100 close with evenness toward praise, blame, life, death and place.
ashtavakra.18.98.core_teaching: The liberated one is at ease in every condition and the same everywhere; free of craving, he does not brood over what he has or hasn't done.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Ego and its offspring, desire, come before every sense of action and duty. Free of them, the liberated soul is unconcerned with all his apparent actions, past, present and future.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The one liberated in life stays at ease in whatever situation prarabdha brings and is never anxious. He is content about deeds done and tasks ahead, insists on nothing, and so does not recall what was done or left undone.

ashtavakra.18.98.practical_reading: For rumination and regret: once you have done what you can, including making amends, stop replaying the tape.
misreadings: Not a way to dodge accountability
Not forgetting the lessons learned
cautions: For someone who has harmed others, 'don't dwell on what you did' must be paired with making amends
not_for: Someone avoiding facing harm they caused

data_flags.translation_note: 'Even everywhere' is garbled; samaḥ sarvatra means 'the same everywhere'. Kṛtakartavya-nirvṛta has two readings: 'done with what needed doing' (ours) or 'free of the idea of done and to-be-done' (Nityaswarupananda, Richards; Jalim Singh: content about past and future tasks). Suggest: 'at ease in any state,...

ashtavakra.18.99.context: This is the penultimate verse of chapter 18. Verse 18.100 closes it: the calm one runs neither to crowds nor to the forest and stays the same anywhere. Chapters 19–20 then give Janaka's final responses.
ashtavakra.18.99.core_teaching: The free one is not elated by praise or angered by blame; he neither dreads death nor clings to life.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Being identified with the one absolute Self, there is for him no praiser or praise, no blamer or blame, and no life or death.

ashtavakra.18.99.practical_reading: The praise-and-blame half applies to work and social media. The life-and-death half suits people reflecting on mortality from a stable place.
misreadings: Not that life isn't worth living
Not indifference to others' opinions or feedback
cautions: 'Neither clings to life', and Jalim Singh's 'no wish to live longer', must not reach someone with suicidal thoughts
Mentions death
not_for: Suicidal ideation
Fresh bereavement
speaks_to: Reflecting on mortality in later life

ashtavakra.2.14.context: Chapter 2 is Janaka's ecstatic response to Ashtavakra's teaching. A run of verses (2.11–2.14) begins 'aho aham', 'how wonderful I am'. In the next verse (2.15) he says knower, knowing and known are not ultimately real.
ashtavakra.2.14.core_teaching: Seeing himself as consciousness, Janaka marvels that as an individual he owns nothing, yet as the Self everything that can be spoken of or thought is his.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: 'Nothing' because only the Self exists, or because the unattached Self owns nothing. 'Everything' because the Self projects and supports the universe. 'Speech and mind' marks the phenomenal world, since only phenomena can be named or thought.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Nothing related to me is real; only Brahman is. Whatever mind and speech can reach is unreal and has no real link to the conscious Self, so Janaka bows to his own wondrous Self.

ashtavakra.2.14.practical_reading: The paradox can be applied to possessiveness: hold nothing as 'mine', and you can meet everything with ease and wonder.
misreadings: 'I bow to myself' is not ego-worship; it is reverence for the Self as consciousness
Not a claim to own the world materially
cautions: Out of context, 'I bow to myself' can sound narcissistic; explain that the speaker is marvelling at consciousness
not_for: Someone in grandiosity
Someone who has just lost everything materially and needs practical help, if it sounds glib
speaks_to: Someone after a loss of possessions or status who finds unexpected freedom
Moments of awe or joy after an insight

ashtavakra.3.1.context: This opens chapter 3, 'Test of the disciple's realisation'. After Janaka's exultant chapter 2, Ashtavakra probes whether the realisation is real, pointing out contradictions such as attachment to wealth and sex (3.1–3.8). From 3.9 he describes the true knower.
ashtavakra.3.1.core_teaching: If you truly know yourself as one and imperishable, the urge to keep piling up wealth should fall away. Continued craving shows the gap between claimed and real understanding.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Janaka is not yet fully established, so Ashtavakra tests him, pointing out anomalies in his behaviour to improve him. A realised person knows himself as perfect and immortal and wants nothing; how could he long for wealth?

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Having examined Janaka's experience, the teacher tests him again. Knowing the Self as free of all limits of time, place and object, why do you still seem to delight in collecting worldly wealth? What is the cause?

ashtavakra.3.1.practical_reading: It works as a self-check: when your spiritual talk and your spending or acquiring habits don't match, notice it without self-condemnation.
misreadings: Not against earning a living, or against a king managing a treasury; the target is delight (rati) in accumulating
A test aimed at someone claiming realisation, not a blanket condemnation of the wealthy
cautions: Can shame someone anxious about money for legitimate needs
not_for: Someone in financial hardship working to meet basic needs
speaks_to: Someone noticing compulsive accumulation or a never-enough feeling
Someone whose stated values and spending don't match

ashtavakra.3.10.context: After the test verses, from 3.9 Ashtavakra describes the genuine knower. This verse deals with praise and blame; the next deals with fear of death.
ashtavakra.3.10.core_teaching: One who sees his own body's activity as if it belonged to someone else cannot be shaken by praise or blame aimed at that activity.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Praise and blame always refer to behaviour carried out through body and mind. One who sees bodily and mental activity as unconnected with the Self is unaffected by them. He cites Gita 3.27–28.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Another person's body is a place of activity separate from my Self, and so is my own. The knower who sees this never feels elation at praise or agitation at blame; if he does, he is not yet a knower.

ashtavakra.3.10.practical_reading: With feedback and criticism, watch your own conduct as a fair observer would, take what is useful, and let the sting pass.
misreadings: Not indifference to feedback or to how one's actions affect others
Not dissociation from one's body
cautions: For someone with depersonalisation, 'see your body as someone else's' can be distressing
not_for: People with dissociation
Someone who needs to take responsibility for harm
speaks_to: Someone hurt by criticism, reviews or social media

ashtavakra.3.11.context: This is still the portrait of the true knower (3.9–3.14). After praise and blame (3.10), Ashtavakra asks how one who sees the world as illusion could fear death.
ashtavakra.3.11.core_teaching: One who sees the world as mere appearance and has lost fascination with it cannot be terrified, even as death approaches.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: One cannot be interested in what does not truly exist. The Self is birthless and deathless; birth and death are illusory, so the knower has no reason to fear the body's dissolution. He cites Gita 2.13–18.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The visible world is maya's product and so unreal. The knower who sees this doesn't brood over where bodies come from or go, and isn't afraid as death approaches; if bewildered by it, he is no knower.

ashtavakra.3.11.practical_reading: It can soften fear of mortality by loosening fascination with worldly drama, best for people facing ageing or illness who are already reflective and steady.
misreadings: Not that life or people don't matter
Not a test in which fearing death means spiritual failure
cautions: Mentions death directly. 'The world is illusion' can feel dismissive in fresh grief or after a terminal diagnosis.
Not for anyone with suicidal thoughts, since 'the world is a mere show' can feed detachment from life
not_for: Fresh bereavement
Suicidal ideation
The first days after a terminal diagnosis
speaks_to: Reflective people facing ageing or mortality with some steadiness already
Anxiety about death in someone not in crisis

ashtavakra.3.12.context: This continues the portrait of the knower (3.9–3.14). After fearlessness at death (3.11), the knower is shown unmoved even by disappointment.
ashtavakra.3.12.core_teaching: The one whose mind stays free of craving even when hopes fail, content in self-knowledge, is beyond comparison.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Ordinary people cling harder to their desires when disappointed. The realised person has no desire and so no real disappointment; even when he fails at some action, he does not hold on to the desire and suffer.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The knower's mind is free even of the wish for liberation; gaining or losing anything brings neither joy nor grief. His wishes have ended and he is content in the Self's bliss, so no one compares with him.

ashtavakra.3.12.practical_reading: When a hope collapses, notice the extra suffering that comes from clinging harder, and rest in what does not depend on outcomes.
misreadings: Not advice to stop hoping or planning
cautions: 'Even in despair' can be misused to tell someone with depression that their despair is a spiritual failing
not_for: Clinical depression or hopelessness with any risk
speaks_to: After a rejection, failed exam, lost job or broken plan
Someone who clings harder after disappointment

ashtavakra.3.14.context: This is the last verse of chapter 3 and closes the portrait of the knower. In chapter 4 Janaka replies that the knower, even while enjoying, cannot be compared with the deluded.
ashtavakra.3.14.core_teaching: For one free of inner passion, of opposites and of wishes, whatever comes unsought brings neither pain nor satisfaction.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Pleasure and pain arise when the senses meet objects we are drawn to or repelled by. With neither attraction nor repulsion, experiences allowed to come as a matter of course produce neither.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: The knower whose mind is cleansed, who is free of dualities like heat and cold and of all cravings for objects, experiences through prarabdha whatever destiny brings and feels neither joy nor sorrow.

ashtavakra.3.14.practical_reading: Take life's small pleasures and inconveniences as they come, without chasing or resisting them.
misreadings: Not numbness or an inability to enjoy
Not passivity toward problems that need action
cautions: Could make depressive numbness sound like an ideal
not_for: Someone experiencing depressive numbness or anhedonia
speaks_to: People wanting steadiness through ordinary ups and downs

ashtavakra.3.3.context: This is part of Ashtavakra's test of Janaka (3.1–3.8). Verse 3.2 compared craving to greed for 'silver' that is really mother-of-pearl. Here the image is the ocean and its waves; 3.4 turns to sexual attachment.
ashtavakra.3.3.core_teaching: One who knows himself as the ocean-like ground in which the world arises has no reason to behave like someone in need.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: All fear, misery, helplessness and want come from seeing the universe as other than one's self. As waves are nothing but the sea, the universe is nothing but the Self; such knowledge should make one serene, fearless and self-contained.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Waves appear in the sea without separate reality of their own, and so does the world. One who has realised 'I am the ground of all' does not run toward objects like a poor man driven by thirst.

ashtavakra.3.3.practical_reading: When you feel a frantic sense of lack, recall the fullness the waves rise from before chasing the next thing.
misreadings: Not contempt for the poor; dīna describes an inner state of neediness
The barb is aimed at someone who claims knowledge, not at someone struggling
cautions: The 'beggar' image can wound someone in real poverty; prefer 'like someone in need'
not_for: Someone in actual material deprivation
speaks_to: Frantic striving, fear of missing out, never-enough feelings
Someone who knows spiritual ideas but still feels desperate

ashtavakra.5.4.context: Chapter 5 gives four short ways to laya, the dissolution of the separate sense of self.
