Verses 1–3 dissolve the external world (it is not separate from you; it appears like silver seen in a shell). This fourth verse dissolves the inner world of feelings through evenness, up to life and death.
ashtavakra.5.4.core_teaching: Complete in yourself, even toward pain and pleasure, hope and despair, life and death, let the separate sense of self dissolve.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Verses 1–3 dissolve the outer world; this one dissolves the inner world of thoughts and feelings. Joy and sorrow, hope and despair, life and death toss us only while we take ourselves as imperfect and other than the Self.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: You are full with the Self's bliss. Pleasures and pains arising in the body by destiny belong to the not-Self and are unreal, like dream objects or a rope-snake. Contemplating 'all this is Brahman' is what laya means.

ashtavakra.5.4.practical_reading: It can be a short contemplation on evenness: notice the swing between pain and pleasure, hope and despair, and rest in what does not swing.
misreadings: Not indifference to living or dying
'Dissolve' (laya) means dissolving the separate-self sense, not death or self-erasure
cautions: 'Equal in life and death' and 'dissolve now' must never reach someone with suicidal thoughts
No prasang is attached to this verse in our data
not_for: Suicidal ideation or self-harm
Fresh grief
Despair
speaks_to: Meditators wanting a short contemplation on equanimity

ashtavakra.8.1.context: Chapter 8 is a four-verse definition of bondage and liberation. Our entry joins 8.1 (bondage) and 8.2 (freedom). In 8.3 Ashtavakra restates them as attachment or non-attachment to any sense-experience, and 8.4 traces both to the 'I'.
ashtavakra.8.1.core_teaching: Bondage is the mind wanting, grieving, grasping, rejecting, delighting or raging over anything. Freedom is the mind no longer moved in those ways.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: He gives separate translations for 8.1 and 8.2 and adds no note on either. His note on the next verse explains 'sense-experience' as any sense-organ and cites Gita 2.67 (senses carrying the mind away).

ashtavakra.8.1.practical_reading: It can become a check-in: which of the six movements (wanting, grieving, grabbing, pushing away, elation, anger) is running me right now?
misreadings: Not a rule against feeling; it describes being driven by feelings
Not 'grief is bondage, so stop grieving'
cautions: Grieving is listed as bondage, and Jalim Singh's gloss names not grieving when loved ones die. Never use on Day 1 of a grief plan.
Our data joins two verses under the reference 8.1
not_for: Fresh bereavement
Someone who has been told their feelings are wrong
speaks_to: Someone wanting a simple map of what agitates the mind

ashtavakra.8.4.context: This closes chapter 8. After defining bondage as the mind's attachment (8.1–8.3), Ashtavakra locates its root in the 'I'. Chapter 9 then turns to dispassion.
ashtavakra.8.4.core_teaching: Ego-identification is bondage and its absence is liberation. Knowing this, one can lightly stop grasping and rejecting.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: Egoism is bondage because it identifies the Self with body and mind; without ego the Self is known as one without a second. With this knowledge one becomes perfectly tranquil, free of desire and aversion.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: As long as the ego sits there ('I am a brahmin, I am learned, I am a renunciate'), liberation cannot happen. When the ego's superimposition on the body ends, one becomes free without effort, neither doer nor enjoyer.

ashtavakra.8.4.practical_reading: 'Lightly' is the key: instead of straining to drop things, notice the 'I' that grasps and loosen the grip with some playfulness.
misreadings: Not self-annihilation or low self-worth
Not passivity; it is about neither clinging nor recoiling
cautions: 'No I' language can confuse someone with a fragile sense of self or depersonalisation
not_for: Someone with low self-worth who would hear 'have no self'
Dissociation
speaks_to: Someone stuck in ego battles at work or home

ashtavakra.9.1.context: This opens chapter 9, 'Detachment' (nirveda). Jalim Singh says its eight verses set out what dispassion looks like, to steady Janaka's experience. Verses 9.2–9.3 add that it is rare for anyone to lose the urge to live, enjoy and know, and that everything is transient.
ashtavakra.9.1.core_teaching: Neither duties nor the pairs of opposites ever come to an end, for anyone. Seeing this, become intent on letting go through disenchantment, free of compulsive vows and observances.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: 'Done and undone' is the insistence that this must be done and that must not; the pairs are pleasure and pain. Since these never cease for anyone embodied, don't insist on them: be avratī, holding stubbornly to nothing.

ashtavakra.9.1.practical_reading: Applied to the endless to-do list: the list never ends, so stop waiting to finish everything before you are at peace, and hold obligations more lightly.
misreadings: Not permission to drop responsibilities
Avratī does not mean breaking promises; both commentators read it as freedom from desire-driven vows and insistence
cautions: Nityaswarupananda's note leans toward renouncing the world; for householders, frame it as letting go inwardly
not_for: Someone looking for a reason to abandon dependants
speaks_to: Perfectionists waiting to finish everything before resting

ashtavakra.9.4.context: This verse belongs to chapter 9, 'Detachment'. Verse 9.3 called everything transient. Here, no time or age of life is free of life's swings; in 9.5 Ashtavakra turns to the disagreements among sages.
ashtavakra.9.4.core_teaching: No time or stage of life is free of opposites. One who stops fighting them and lives on what comes reaches fulfilment.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: No age can be imagined of unmixed good and joy, so we cannot expect lasting peace from life's process. The way is to step out of it, staying unattached to and unmoved by its experiences. He cites Gita 2.14.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903), bhavartha
commentaries.gist: Quoting the Adhyatma Ramayana: pleasure and pain follow each other like day and night, mixed like water and mud, and no embodied being escapes them. So the wise drop the wish about them and leave the body to prarabdha.

ashtavakra.9.4.practical_reading: It addresses 'I'll be happy when...' thinking: every stage has its swings, so make peace now and respond to what actually comes.
misreadings: Accepting life's swings is not accepting mistreatment
Not fatalism about situations that can be changed
not_for: Someone in an abusive or unsafe situation
speaks_to: Someone waiting for a future stage (marriage, retirement, children grown) to be happy

ashtavakra.9.5.context: In chapter 9, after saying no age is free of opposites (9.4), Ashtavakra points out how sages disagree. In 9.6 he says the true guru is someone who has realised the truth and frees others, not someone with opinions.
ashtavakra.9.5.core_teaching: Seeing how the views of sages, saints and yogis differ, a person stops relying on mere opinion and becomes calm.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), verse notes
commentaries.gist: The verse refers to the schools of philosophy, each with a different highest good (he cites Gita 2.42–43 and Vivekachudamani 58–61). Those indifferent to worldly objects and intent only on self-realisation gain this quietude, which comes with renunciation.

ashtavakra.9.5.practical_reading: With information overload, when every expert disagrees, step back from the debate and turn to direct inner understanding.
misreadings: Not anti-intellectualism or contempt for other traditions
cautions: Jalim Singh's reading is sectarian (anti-Nyaya); don't present that tone as the verse's
not_for: Someone who needs to make an informed decision and might take it as 'all views are equally useless'
speaks_to: Someone exhausted by conflicting advice on parenting, health or spirituality

avadhuta.1.18.context: Chapter 1 is Dattatreya's song of the one Self. In 1.14 he already asks why one runs here and there like a ghost when the Self is inside and outside; 1.15-17 say union and separation, and the five sense objects, do not belong to the Self. Here he turns to his own mind directly.
avadhuta.1.18.core_teaching: The mind's frantic searching comes from treating the Self as something somewhere else; seeing it as one's own undivided being, and letting go of clinging to objects, is what brings ease.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: The mind roams like a ghost looking for the Self as if it were separate; that is the basic mistake. See it as non-different, drop attachment to objects, because sorrow lasts only as long as clinging does.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as a call to the mind to stop wandering bewildered, to realise the Atma as indivisible, give up desire and be happy.

avadhuta.1.18.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a self-talk practice: when the mind is spinning, name it and speak to it, then ask what it is chasing and whether letting go of that one thing would bring rest.
misreadings: Not contempt for the mind or for the reader; it is the sage scolding his own mind gently.
'Drop attachment' is not 'stop caring about people'; Paramananda means clinging to sense objects as sources of happiness.
cautions: The ghost image is mild here, but for someone with intrusive thoughts or anxiety disorders, 'just drop it and be happy' can sound like blame; pair with practical steps.
not_for: clinical anxiety or panic, where 'be happy' would be glib
grief in its first days
speaks_to: restless searching for meaning in the next thing
someone who keeps changing plans and is tired

avadhuta.1.68.context: Near the end of chapter 1, after many verses negating every attribute of the Self, Dattatreya stops arguing and sums up. The next verses speak of the knower dissolving into the whole like pot-space into space, wherever he dies.
avadhuta.1.68.core_teaching: After all the reasoning, the point is simple: what you are is not the chatter but the sky-like awareness in which it moves.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Dattatreya tells his own mind there is no use in more talk; the world is what is open to debate, but the settled conclusion already given is that you are pure awareness, unstained and unattached like space.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: what is gained by so much talk and intellectual wrangling? The real essence has been told: thou art the highest Self, unlimited like space.

avadhuta.1.68.practical_reading: Useful when overthinking: notice when analysis has stopped helping, return to one simple truth, and let the commentary in the head be weather in a large sky.
misreadings: Not anti-intellectual; it ends discussion only after the teaching has been given.
Not telling the reader their thoughts or worries are meaningless.
cautions: Advaita identity language ('you are reality itself') can feel abstract or alienating to someone who needs comfort; it works better as a pause than as an argument.
not_for: someone whose 'chatter' is a real problem needing practical decisions
people in crisis who need concrete help
speaks_to: someone tired of their own inner debate

avadhuta.2.1.context: Chapter 2 opens with two verses on the teacher. Kannoo Mal's introduction links them to Dattatreya's well-known twenty-four gurus (earth, water, a pigeon, a prostitute, a child and others): wisdom is taken wherever it is found. The chapter then returns to the Self.
avadhuta.2.1.core_teaching: Judge teaching by its truth, not by the teacher's age, status, learning or lifestyle; you would not throw away a jewel because of where it was lying.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Reads 2.1 with 2.2: do not weigh whether the guru knows poetry or lexicons; take the essence a teacher has and leave the rest. A boat carries you across whether or not it is painted.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (introduction)
commentaries.gist: Sums up a key piece of advice of the text: a seeker should pick up wisdom wherever he finds it, like a bee gathering honey from many flowers, never despising its source. Cites 2.1-2 and the twenty-four gurus.

avadhuta.2.1.practical_reading: Learn from unlikely people: a junior colleague, a child, someone whose life you would not choose. Ask 'is this true?' before 'who said it?'
misreadings: Not an endorsement of abusive or exploitative teachers; it is about not dismissing truth for superficial reasons, not about excusing harm.
Not a claim that the teacher's conduct never matters.
cautions: In a reader's life this could be misused to justify staying under a harmful guru or boss; editors should frame it as 'take the good', not 'tolerate everything'.
not_for: someone currently in an exploitative spiritual or workplace relationship
speaks_to: someone dismissing advice because of who gave it

avadhuta.2.2.context: Second of the two opening verses on teachers in chapter 2. It follows 2.1's jewel-in-the-mud image with a second image: an unpainted boat.
avadhuta.2.2.core_teaching: Substance matters more than polish. A plain boat still gets you to the other shore; a plain teacher or plain words still carry truth.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Do not judge the guru by literary accomplishment; take the essence. He adds: do not just pierce your ears and join someone's sect; become one who takes in virtues, since without knowledge and dispassion no one is freed.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (introduction and translation)
commentaries.gist: Reads the verse about the guru: whether or not he has poetic learning, the wise take the good in him; a boat without vermilion painting still carries passengers across.

avadhuta.2.2.practical_reading: When choosing what to read, whom to listen to or how to judge your own work, ask whether it carries you across, not whether it is impressive.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of beauty or craft.
Not specifically about this app's own texts; the classical readers read it about teachers.

avadhuta.2.24.context: Late in chapter 2, after verses on the knower's identity with the Self, Dattatreya names the qualities of the one who reaches the highest. The next verse compares the knower's death to a pot breaking and its space merging with space.
avadhuta.2.24.core_teaching: Freedom is marked by three things together: no grudges or cravings, active goodwill toward every being, and a steady, settled understanding.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Only the knower who is free of attachment and aversion, wishes the good of all and the harm of none, has firm knowledge of the Self and is steady reaches the highest state; no one else does.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as one free from passions and animosity, disposed to do good to all beings, of firm convictions and strong mind, who attains the supreme goal.

avadhuta.2.24.practical_reading: A short self-check for a day: what am I clinging to, whom am I resenting, and what one thing can I do for someone else's good?
misreadings: 'Free of attachment' does not mean cold; the same line asks for active care for all beings.
Not a demand to have no feelings.
cautions: Holding up 'no aversion' to someone who has been wronged can feel like being told to stop protecting themselves; the verse is about inner grudges, not about losing boundaries.
not_for: a person in an abusive situation, where 'no aversion' could be heard as 'make peace with it'
speaks_to: service-minded people who want a spiritual frame

avadhuta.2.7.context: After 2.3-6 describe the Self as effortless, all-pervading and bodiless, 2.7 deals with thoughts: they are not the Self's doing. 2.8-9 follow with the image of qualities that are inseparable from their substance, as coolness is from water.
avadhuta.2.7.core_teaching: Thoughts come and go on their own like bubbles in water; the Self only witnesses them and does not need to chase, fight or own them.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: The movements of the inner mind are not produced by me; like bubbles in water they rise and merge back by themselves, and I am simply their witness.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Renders the first half as a warning not to think that it is I who drive the mind's deceptive impulses; they arise and dissolve like bubbles in a river.

avadhuta.2.7.practical_reading: A plain mindfulness instruction: when a thought bubbles up, notice it, do not grab it, and watch it pop.
misreadings: Not 'nothing you think or do matters' or a denial of responsibility for actions.
Not saying thoughts are bad; only that they are not who you are.
cautions: For obsessive or intrusive thoughts this can help, but 'they dissolve by themselves' is not a promise that distressing thoughts will stop quickly.
not_for: someone using detachment to avoid a decision that does require action
speaks_to: meditation beginners frustrated by a busy mind

avadhuta.3.34.context: Chapter 3 is a long hymn whose verses end with the refrain 'I am the nectar of knowledge, of one taste, like the sky.' From 3.34 on, a run of verses asks 'Why do you weep, friend?' and lists things the Self does not have: age, death, birth, form, change.
avadhuta.3.34.core_teaching: Weeping over ageing, death and birth belongs to identifying with the body; the Self one truly is does not age, die, get born or change.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Dattatreya speaks to his own mind: weeping out of fear of age and death is mistaken, since your nature is free of them; you were never born, so birth's pain is not yours; resolve that you are knowledge, one, all-pervading.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'friend' as the heart; it has no birth pangs, old age, death or change, and the speaker is deathless knowledge, unchanging and all-pervading like space.

avadhuta.3.34.practical_reading: Some teachers use the refrain as a meditation when afraid of ageing or illness: notice what in you watches the body change and has not itself changed.
misreadings: Not a rebuke to anyone who is grieving a death.
Not a claim that the body's pain is unreal or unimportant.
cautions: Strong caution for grief: 'why do you weep?' said to a mourner can feel dismissive and shaming. Our setting ('a grieving friend') makes this worse; it should not be used on Day 1 of any grief plan.
Speaks of death and birth directly.
not_for: fresh bereavement
someone who has just had a frightening diagnosis and needs to be heard first
children's grief
speaks_to: fear of one's own death, in a calm reflective moment
illness that is changing the body

data_flags.translation_note: The translation omits the refrain's last line, which the verse ends on: 'I am the nectar of knowledge, of one taste, vast as the sky' (jñānāmṛtaṃ samarasaṃ gaganopamo 'ham). Our setting also says Dattatreya speaks 'to a grieving friend'; Paramananda reads it as addressed to...

avadhuta.3.46.context: This closes chapter 3's long refrain-hymn. Having negated every attribute of the Self, Dattatreya ends by negating even the act of renouncing; chapter 4 opens by asking how there can be invocation or farewell, flowers or meditation, for the formless.
avadhuta.3.46.core_teaching: Letting go is the path, but holding on to the identity of 'one who has let go' is a new bondage; one's nature is already free and needs neither.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Give up the world, then give up renunciation too; know both renouncing and its absence as poison. The pride 'I am a renouncer' is itself very painful; only by dropping pride in both do you find full happiness.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Give up the world, give up renunciation, give up both renouncing and not renouncing; the Atma is by nature spotless and immortal.

avadhuta.3.46.practical_reading: Watch for spiritual pride: the diet, the detox, the minimalism or the quitting can become a new identity to defend. Let that go too.
misreadings: Not permission to drop all discipline because 'renunciation is poison'; the verse comes after renunciation, not instead of it.
Not saying the world or family is poison.
cautions: 'Let go of the world' could be read by a depressed reader as withdrawal from life; the classical reading is about dropping self-image, not dropping out.
not_for: someone already withdrawing from people and duties in depression
speaks_to: someone defining themselves by what they gave up

avadhuta.7.9.context: Chapter 7 describes the wandering avadhuta in rhymed couplets: rags from the road, beyond merit and sin, beyond union and separation. The next verse asks how one still tied to ideas of duality or non-duality can be free.
avadhuta.7.9.core_teaching: The free person is not driven either to grab experiences or to refuse them; he moves through life unhurried, in a joy that does not depend on either.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: The yogi absorbed in the Self is free of union and separation, of permitted and forbidden enjoyment; such a one moves slowly, slowly in natural bliss, that is, he reaches the joy of the Self.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Renders the ascetic as one free of union and disunion, an enjoyer free of enjoyment and non-enjoyment, who gradually attains the spontaneous felicity projected by the mind.

avadhuta.7.9.practical_reading: Slow down: walk, eat and work at a pace that is not chasing a reward or proving a discipline.
misreadings: Not laziness or passivity.
Not a rejection of pleasure; it is freedom from both craving and refusing it.
not_for: someone struggling with addiction who needs firm abstinence, not 'neither enjoying nor refusing'
speaks_to: all-or-nothing habits around food or pleasure
someone who wants to enjoy life without guilt or compulsion

avadhuta.8.2.context: Chapter 8 opens with Dattatreya asking forgiveness for three 'faults' of worship (pilgrimage to the all-pervading, meditating on what is beyond thought, praising what is beyond words). Verses 2-4 then list a sage's qualities, borrowed from the Bhagavata's list of a saint's marks.
avadhuta.8.2.core_teaching: A portrait of quiet strength: steadiness of mind, gentleness, purity, few needs and moderation, rooted in a single refuge.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: One whose intellect is not spoiled by desire, who has mastered the outer senses, is gentle, pure, holds nothing, wants nothing, eats little, is calm, steady and speaks little: that one is a knower of the Self.

commentaries.who: Bhaktivedanta Book Trust purport to Bhagavata 11.11.29-32 (Gaudiya Vaishnava)
commentaries.gist: Treats these lines as part of a list of twenty-eight saintly qualities; following Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati it calls taking full shelter of Krishna the key one, from which the others grow.

avadhuta.8.2.practical_reading: Pick one quality as a day's practice: eat a little less, speak a little more gently, or let one wish go unpursued.
misreadings: Not a call to own nothing or to starve; mita-bhuk means moderate.
Not a checklist to judge oneself harshly against.
cautions: For readers with eating disorders, 'eats moderately' should not be the line a reading builds on.
not_for: readers with disordered eating
someone already feeling they fall short of every ideal

avadhuta.8.3.context: Second of the three borrowed Bhagavata verses listing a sage's marks at the start of chapter 8, before Dattatreya explains each syllable of the word 'avadhuta'.
avadhuta.8.3.core_teaching: Inner depth shows outwardly as alertness, steadiness, humility that still honours others, friendliness and compassion.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Ever watchful, of deep nature, patient, having conquered the six vices (desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy), without pride, skilled in all work, friendly to all and kind: such a one is called a sadhu.

commentaries.who: Bhaktivedanta Book Trust purport to Bhagavata 11.11.29-32 (Gaudiya Vaishnava)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the six as hunger, thirst, lamentation, illusion, old age and death; amānī as not puffed up even if famous; māna-da as respecting everyone as part of Krishna.

avadhuta.8.3.practical_reading: Give credit and respect freely today without asking for any back.
misreadings: 'Seeking no honour' is not low self-worth or accepting disrespect.
not_for: someone whose self-esteem is already crushed and who hears 'seek no honour' as 'you deserve none'
speaks_to: being kind without being a pushover

avadhuta.8.4.context: Third of the borrowed Bhagavata verses at the start of chapter 8. Paramananda ends his gloss with 'such am I', reading the list as the sage's self-description.
avadhuta.8.4.core_teaching: Compassion, harmlessness, patience with everyone, truthfulness to the core, evenness and helpfulness belong together as marks of a free person.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: One who is compassionate, forbearing, bears malice to no embodied being, sees one Self everywhere, speaks only truth, is free of birth and death and helps everyone: such am I.

commentaries.who: Bhaktivedanta Book Trust purport to Bhagavata 11.11.29-32 (Gaudiya Vaishnava)
commentaries.gist: Akṛta-droha: never offensive in return even when offended; titikṣu: forgives and forgets offences against oneself; sarvopakāraka: works for others' welfare. Frames all of it as devotion to Krishna.

avadhuta.8.4.practical_reading: Practise one act of patience today with someone who tests you, and one act of help no one asked for.
misreadings: Titikṣā is a quality of the saint, not a demand on someone being harmed to keep putting up with it (our_note says this well).
cautions: For readers being mistreated, 'patient with all beings' must not be read as 'tolerate abuse'.
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship
speaks_to: wanting to be a kinder person

avadhuta.8.6.context: After 8.5 says these marks should be known by all seekers, 8.6-9 explain the word a-va-dhū-ta syllable by syllable. This verse gives 'a'.
avadhuta.8.6.core_teaching: The first mark of the free person is release from the noose of expectation, which leaves a steady, clean joy.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Free of the noose of hope for pleasures of the world; pure in waking, dream and sleep, or in past, present and future, or in childhood, youth and age; always immersed in Brahman's bliss. This is the meaning of 'a'.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: The letter 'a' shows that he is free from the net of hope, free from beginning, middle and end, and always abiding in happiness.

avadhuta.8.6.practical_reading: Notice one expectation you are holding over a person or outcome today and loosen it; see what is left when you are not waiting for it.
misreadings: Not 'abandon hope' in the sense of despair; āśā here is craving for outcomes.
cautions: 'Free of hope' can land badly with someone depressed or hopeless; frame as freedom from clinging expectation, never as giving up.
not_for: someone who feels hopeless or suicidal

avadhuta.8.7.context: Second of the four syllable-verses explaining a-va-dhū-ta: this gives 'va'. The next verse gives 'dhū' (body covered in dust, mind cleansed, beyond concentration and meditation).
avadhuta.8.7.core_teaching: The free person has let go of old cravings, speaks in ways that do no harm, and lives in the present rather than in the future's worries.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: He has dropped both good and bad latent desires, since he no longer needs even purification; his words cause no one pain; he lives on what the present brings, absorbed in joy, without worrying about the future.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: The letter 'va' shows he is bereft of desires, his speech is free of evil, and he abides in all existing things.

avadhuta.8.7.practical_reading: Three practices in one: drop one old craving, say nothing today that wounds, and do the task in front of you without rehearsing tomorrow.
misreadings: 'Lives in the present' is not 'make no plans'; Paramananda means not being consumed by future anxiety.
speaks_to: habits that come from old cravings

bg.1.28.context: Arjuna has asked Krishna to drive the chariot between the two armies so he can see whom he must fight; Krishna stops before Bhishma and Drona and tells him to look. Arjuna sees fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, friends and in-laws on both sides. Here Sanjaya reports that pity overwhelms him and he begins to speak; in the following verses his body gives way, his bow slips, he argues against the war and finally sits down in the chariot, refusing to fight.
bg.1.28.core_teaching: Not yet a teaching but the crisis that prompts the Gita: love and pity for people on the other side overwhelm even the greatest warrior. Commentators read the pity differently, Ramanuja as noble compassion and fear of wrongdoing, the Advaita line as grief born of seeing bodies as 'mine'.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898 (summary closing ch. 1)
commentaries.gist: Calls Arjuna most noble and compassionate: though the Kauravas had plotted to kill the Pandavas (the lac house), he saw them as kin, was overcome by pity and fear of wrongdoing, and sat down refusing to fight.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Introduces Arjuna's speech, which runs to the end of the chapter: seeing his kinsmen drawn up to fight, his limbs, hands and feet give way and his mouth goes completely dry.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901, introduction at 2.10, not a comment on this verse
commentaries.gist: Gives no comment on chapter 1. His introduction at 2.10 reads the whole passage up to 2.9 as grief and delusion born of 'I am theirs and they are mine', which cause samsara and are removed only by self-knowledge.

bg.1.28.practical_reading: Teachers use this moment to normalise breakdown: the Gita opens with its hero shaking, not with a lecture. Freezing when a conflict involves people you love is human, and the first step is to say honestly what is happening, as Arjuna does to Krishna.
misreadings: Not a portrait of cowardice: Ramanuja stresses Arjuna's compassion and righteousness here.
Not Arjuna's own claim of pity; that half is Sanjaya's narration.
Not a teaching about whether to fight one's family; it is a narrative moment that the rest of the Gita answers.
cautions: Setting is a war against one's own family; may stir pain for readers in family conflict or estrangement.
The Advaita reading calls this pity delusion; avoid telling a distressed reader that their compassion is a fault.
not_for: Someone in an abusive family situation who might read it as a nudge to confront or 'fight' family
A reader looking for a clear answer or instruction; the verse offers none yet
speaks_to: Freezing when a conflict involves family or people you love
Physical overwhelm before a hard confrontation (shaking, dry mouth, weak limbs)
Feeling ashamed of breaking down when others expect you to be strong
Disputes with relatives, old mentors or close colleagues

data_flags.attribution_note: Mixed speakers. The first half (kṛpayā parayāviṣṭo viṣīdann idam abravīt) is Sanjaya narrating to Dhritarashtra; only the second half, after 'arjuna uvāca', is Arjuna speaking to Krishna. Govindacharya's translation of Ramanuja's text makes this explicit (Arjuna, overcome by compassion, became sad and spoke). Our Sanskrit...
data_flags.translation_note: Our translation turns Sanjaya's description ('filled with deep pity, despairing, he said this') into Arjuna's first-person 'I am overcome with pity and sorrow'. Arjuna's own sentence only begins in this verse ('Krishna, seeing these my own people standing here, eager to fight...') and is completed...

bg.1.29.context: Krishna has driven the chariot between the two armies at Arjuna's request. Arjuna sees teachers, uncles, sons, grandsons and friends on both sides and is overcome by pity. Here he describes what that sight is doing to his body. Next he says he sees bad omens and wants no victory, kingdom or pleasure bought by killing his own people.
bg.1.29.core_teaching: This verse isn't a teaching. It is Arjuna's honest report of grief and fear taking over his body. The classical commentators treat the whole stretch from 1.2 to 2.9 as the diagnosis: grief and confusion that come from the sense of 'mine'. The rest of the Gita answers it.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Shankara does not comment on chapter 1 verse by verse. At 2.10 he says 1.2–2.9 shows where grief and delusion come from: the feeling 'I am theirs and they are mine', which overpowers clear judgement.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Closing chapter 1, Ramanuja calls Arjuna noble and compassionate, affectionate even towards kin who had tried to kill him. Overcome by pity and fear of doing wrong, he shrank back, grieving at losing them.

bg.1.29.practical_reading: It works as a way to name the body's signs of overwhelm (shaking, dry mouth, a spinning mind) before trying to fix anything. The Gita takes the breakdown seriously enough to give it a full chapter before any advice begins.
misreadings: Not simply cowardice. Ramanuja reads pity, love for kin and fear of doing wrong; Shankara reads grief and confusion born of attachment.
Not a clinical description. Calling it a 'panic attack' is a modern analogy, so present it as one.
Not a verse that tells the reader to push through bodily distress. It only describes the distress.
cautions: The setting is a battle against one's own family; killing kin is what Arjuna dreads.
Prabhupada's reading (fear from a bodily view of life) can sound dismissive to someone with real anxiety symptoms. Use it lightly.
Used on Day 1 of 'work feels unsafe'. Later Gita verses push Arjuna to stand up and fight; the writer should not carry that over as 'stay and endure an unsafe workplace'.
not_for: someone having physical symptoms that may need medical help; the verse names distress but cannot treat it
a reader being harmed at work, if the plan goes on to frame staying as duty
speaks_to: body-level dread before a confrontation or hard conversation
freezing when people you care about are on the other side
feeling that you are falling apart before something you have to do

data_flags.translation_note: Our Sanskrit and ref cover 1.29 and 1.30, but the English renders only 1.29 (limbs, mouth, trembling, hair). It leaves out 1.30: the Gandiva bow slipping from his hand, his skin burning, being unable to stand, and his mind seeming to spin. Add the second...

bg.1.47.context: This verse closes chapter 1. Arjuna has argued that killing kin would destroy families and their ways of life, and has said he would rather be killed unarmed. Sanjaya, narrating to the blind king, reports that Arjuna drops his bow and arrows and sits down in the chariot. Chapter 2 opens with Krishna rebuking this weakness.
bg.1.47.core_teaching: The narrative low point: grief has taken away Arjuna's will to act. The commentators read it as the state the teaching is about to address, not as a final verdict on him.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Arjuna was compassionate towards kin who had plotted to burn him alive. Overcome by pity and fear of unrighteousness, he refused to fight. Grieving at the thought of separation from them, he let the bow go and sat down.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Sridhara treats it as Sanjaya answering 'what happened next?'. Arjuna, his mind agitated by grief, sat down on the chariot in the midst of battle.

bg.1.47.practical_reading: It names the moment of putting everything down when you can't go on. The story doesn't end there: the next verses are about getting help and finding a way forward.
misreadings: Not the Gita's verdict that giving up is right or wrong. It is the starting point the teaching answers.
Not a call to shame someone for stopping. Ramanuja stresses Arjuna's compassion.
cautions: Used on Day 1 of 'losing hope': it mirrors the low point. The writer should point forward (2.7, where he asks for help) and not leave the reader at the collapse.
Shankara's frame calls this grief 'delusion'. Do not tell a hopeless reader that their despair is a delusion.
The battle context (killing kin) sits right behind the verse.
not_for: a reader who needs to be told they are not failing, if the reading frames stopping as weakness
speaks_to: the moment you put everything down and sit with it
feeling too overwhelmed by grief to go on
being stuck between duty and love

bg.10.1.context: Chapters 7 to 9 have described the Lord to be worshipped and briefly named his glories. Chapter 10 opens with Krishna offering, unasked, to speak again, because Arjuna delights in hearing and for his good. What follows is the teaching that no one knows his origin (10.2-3), the 'seed' verses of devotion (10.8-11), and then the long list of his glories.
bg.10.1.core_teaching: The teacher speaks again, without being asked, because the student is delighted to listen and because the teacher wants the student's good.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Hear once more my supreme word, which reveals the highest reality; I speak it to you who delight in my words as if drinking nectar, out of a wish for your good.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Because you rejoice at hearing of my greatness, and wishing your good, namely the birth and growth of devotion to me, I will speak further about my glory; listen with attention.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Chapters 7 to 9 described the Lord to be worshipped and touched on his glories; chapter 10 lays them out in detail so that one can see the Lord everywhere.

bg.10.1.practical_reading: Teachers draw from it that eagerness to learn draws out the teacher, and that the Gita's teaching is offered as care for the listener's good.
misreadings: Not a claim that only the 'dear' or chosen deserve the teaching.
not_for: someone who needs a concrete teaching, since this verse is a preface
speaks_to: someone who loves learning about the sacred
a reader who wants to feel the teaching is offered for their good

data_flags.translation_note: Minor. 'Prīyamāṇāya' means 'to you who are delighted (by hearing)'; Shankara (Sastri) says Arjuna delights in the words as if drinking nectar. Govindacharya's Ramanuja renders it '(My) beloved', explaining 'because you delight in hearing my greatness', so 'dear to me' has some support in Ramanuja,...

bg.10.11.context: Krishna has described devotees who keep their minds on him, enlighten one another and delight in speaking of him (10.9), and said he gives them the understanding by which they reach him (10.10). This verse completes that promise. Arjuna then praises Krishna and asks to hear his glories in full (10.12-18).
bg.10.11.core_teaching: Out of compassion, the divine dwells within those who love it and lights the lamp of understanding from inside, dispelling the darkness of confusion.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Out of compassion the Lord dwells in the devotee's mind and dispels ignorance with the lamp of discernment. The lamp is fed by devotion, fanned by meditation, trimmed by virtue, and sheltered from the winds of sense and attachment.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Out of pure grace the Lord becomes the very content of the devotee's thought and reveals his qualities there. This dispels the darkness of ignorance, which is past karma that breeds desire for things other than him.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The Lord dwells within their intellect to bless them. With the shining light of knowledge he destroys the darkness of worldly existence, which comes from ignorance.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Develops the lamp image as Shankara does. Like any light, knowledge needs no further act to remove darkness: once self-knowledge dawns, ignorance is simply gone.

bg.10.11.practical_reading: Teachers read it as reassurance that clarity is not only earned but given: keep turning toward the divine in love, and understanding will dawn from within, often when you stop forcing it.
misreadings: Not a promise of sudden answers to every problem; the darkness meant is spiritual confusion about what is real.
Not passivity; the commentators assume steady devotion and meditation.
cautions: A reader in a dark period may feel unchosen if no light comes; stress that the compassion is offered to all who turn.
not_for: depression framed as 'ignorance' to be dispelled by devotion alone

bg.10.20.context: Arjuna has asked Krishna to describe his glories in full, so that he can meditate on him in them (10.16-18). Krishna begins the list with this verse: first and foremost he is the self in the heart of every being, and the beginning, middle and end of all beings. The particular glories follow from 10.21 (among the Adityas, Vishnu; among lights, the sun...).
bg.10.20.core_teaching: The divine is first of all the innermost self present in every heart, and the source, sustenance and end of every being's life.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The Lord is the inner Self in the heart of all beings, always to be meditated on; one unable to do so should meditate on him in the glories that follow. He is beings' origin, continuance and dissolution.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: All beings are the Lord's body and he dwells in their hearts as their self, which means their support, controller and owner; he cites 15.15 and 18.61.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: First he states his own sovereign form: as inner controller with omniscience he dwells in all minds; he is the cause of every being's birth, life and end.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Meditate on the Lord as the innermost Self. Those who can meditate on the Self as non-different are the best-prepared aspirants; others should think of him in the things listed next.

bg.10.20.practical_reading: Teachers use it to turn the search inward: before looking for God in great things, notice the presence in your own heart and in others', through every stage of life.
misreadings: Not a claim that our impulses are God's voice; commentators speak of the self as witness and controller, not of every thought.
cautions: 'The end of beings' touches on death; mild, but notice it in grief contexts.
not_for: fresh grief, if 'I am the end of beings' would sound like God caused the death
speaks_to: someone who feels God is far away
a person at a life transition (birth, midlife, ageing)
someone wanting to see the sacred in others

bg.10.41.context: Krishna has listed his chief manifestations (10.20-39), from the sun among lights to the Ganga among rivers, and said they have no end (10.40). This verse gives the rule behind the list; the chapter closes (10.42) with Krishna saying he upholds the whole universe with a single fraction of himself.
bg.10.41.core_teaching: Every instance of excellence, beauty, prosperity or strength in the world is a small spark of the divine's own splendour, and can be recognised as such.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Gives only a short gloss: 'my splendour' means the Lord's (Ishvara's). The next verse adds that one part of the Lord sustains the whole world, so knowing the countless details matters less.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Whatever shows lordly power, wealth or splendour, or energy and drive in any undertaking, comes from a mere fraction of the Lord's power, his irresistible energy.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: A summary after the long list: anything marked by greatness, strength, grace or excellence is born of a portion of the Lord's splendour.

bg.10.41.practical_reading: Teachers turn it into a gratitude practice: when something moves you by its excellence or beauty, a person's skill, a landscape, a piece of music, see it as a glimpse of the divine and give thanks.
misreadings: Not a reason to worship powerful or wealthy people.
Not 'only the excellent carry the divine'; elsewhere the Gita sees the divine in all beings.
Not an endorsement of power used badly; the commentators mean the excellence itself as a sign.
cautions: A reader feeling small or unaccomplished might hear that the divine shows only in the outstanding; pair with verses on the divine in every heart (e.g. 18.61).
not_for: someone comparing themselves unfavourably to high achievers
contexts that would sacralise wealth or status

bg.10.9.context: Krishna has said that the wise, knowing him as the source of all, worship him with love (10.8). Here he describes how such devotees live: minds on him, lives given to him, enlightening one another and always speaking of him, content and joyful. 10.10-11 add that he gives them the yoga of understanding and, out of compassion, lights the lamp of knowledge in their hearts.
bg.10.9.core_teaching: Devotion flourishes in company: people who share a love of God and speak of it together find contentment and joy in that sharing.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Minds on the Lord, their senses drawn into him or their lives given to him, they teach one another and speak of him as endowed with knowledge, strength and power, and find contentment and delight as in a beloved.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Unable to sustain themselves without the Lord, they tell each other the qualities each has experienced and narrate his lovely deeds; the speakers are content in speaking for its own sake, the listeners delight beyond measure in hearing.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: This is worship born of love: with minds and senses given to the Lord, the wise explain him to one another with reasoning and scripture and sing of him, and are always content and delighted.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The devotee's life is consecrated to the Lord; he delights in talking of the Lord's wisdom and power and feels the satisfaction of being in the company of the Beloved.

bg.10.9.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to satsang and spiritual friendship: speaking about what you love with others who love it deepens both understanding and joy.
misreadings: Not a call to talk only about God or to withdraw from other relationships.
not_for: someone hurt by a religious group, for whom community talk may sting
someone isolated with no such company, unless offered as an invitation
speaks_to: friends or couples who share a faith
a person whose devotion feels lonely

bg.11.24.context: Krishna has granted Arjuna divine sight to see his cosmic form (11.8). Arjuna praises the vision (11.15-22), then admits that the worlds are terrified, and so is he (11.23). In this verse he says his inner self trembles and he finds neither courage nor peace; next he sees the warriors of both armies rushing into its blazing mouths (11.25-30).
bg.11.24.core_teaching: Faced with the full, overwhelming reality of the divine, Arjuna's courage and calm give way; the Gita lets even its hero be honestly terrified.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Glosses the vision: reaching the heavens, blazing, many frightening colours and shapes, mouths gaping, eyes huge and flaming; seeing it, Arjuna's inner self is terrified and he finds neither firmness nor peace.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: 'Touching the sky' means reaching the supreme heaven beyond material nature, as the Vedic texts use the word; the form is the support of matter and souls in every state.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Not only am I afraid: seeing you filling the sky, radiant, many-coloured, mouths open and great eyes blazing, my mind is shaken and I find neither steadiness nor calm.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Dhṛti can also mean patience and strength, and śama self-control; the cosmic vision has frightened Arjuna considerably.

bg.11.24.practical_reading: Teachers use it to validate overwhelm: meeting something too vast to process (a diagnosis, a disaster, the scale of loss) can shake even a strong person, and saying so honestly is where steadiness begins.
misreadings: Not a sign that Arjuna's faith failed; terror before the infinite is a recognised religious response.
Not a picture of God as a monster; the chapter ends in the gentle form (11.49-51).
cautions: The surrounding verses (11.26-30) describe warriors crushed between teeth; avoid quoting that imagery to a frightened or grieving reader.
Pair with 11.49-51, where Krishna calms Arjuna.
not_for: someone in acute panic or trauma, unless paired with the reassurance of 11.49
children, given the violent imagery nearby
speaks_to: overwhelm in the face of something vast
someone who feels they should be braver

bg.11.33.context: Arjuna, seeing the cosmic form devour the warriors of both armies, asks who Krishna really is (11.31). Krishna says he is Time, the destroyer, and that these warriors will not survive even without Arjuna (11.32). This verse urges him to rise and be the instrument; 11.34 names Drona, Bhishma, Jayadratha and Karna as already slain and tells him to fight without distress.
bg.11.33.core_teaching: The larger course of events is already in motion beyond any one person's control; Arjuna is asked to rise and play his part as an instrument rather than imagine he is the sole cause.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: The fame is for defeating Bhishma and other great warriors whom even the gods could not beat, fame that comes only from good karma. The enemies are Duryodhana's side; Savyasachin means one who shoots with the left hand too.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Arise and fight, win glory and your rightful kingdom. The Lord has already marked these unrighteous men for destruction; Arjuna has only to serve as the instrument, like a weapon in that work.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The Lord, as all-destroying Time, has all but killed these enemies before the battle begins. Arjuna should simply be the instrument and win the fame of defeating Bhishma and Drona.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Arjuna is to be only the apparent or nominal cause; the Lord has slain them long before. He repeats the classical glosses on fame, the enemies and Savyasachin.

bg.11.33.practical_reading: Teachers read 'be the instrument' as freedom from the burden of being the only cause: you do your part fully, and let go of the illusion that everything depends on you.
misreadings: 'Be the instrument' is not 'I am not responsible for what I do' (as our misuse note says).
Not fatalism ('everything is fixed, so effort is pointless'); Krishna is urging action.
Must never be used to justify harming others as 'God's will'.
cautions: The literal context is killing kin and teachers in war, by the cosmic form that devours lives; this is the most violent image in the group. For a new-beginnings plan, keep to 'rise and do your part' and avoid quoting 'already slain'.
'Already set in motion' could distress a reader who fears things are out of their hands.
not_for: grief or bereavement (death imagery)
readers with violent intrusive thoughts or in conflict situations
someone seeking to justify harm
speaks_to: feeling that everything depends on you

bg.11.41.context: After the overwhelming vision and his hymn of praise (11.36-40), Arjuna turns personal: he remembers calling Krishna 'Krishna, Yadava, friend' without knowing his greatness, out of carelessness or affection. In 11.42 he lists slights made in jest, at play, resting, sitting and eating, and asks forgiveness; in 11.44 he asks Krishna to bear with him as a father, friend or lover would.
bg.11.41.core_teaching: Seeing who his friend truly is, Arjuna regrets the casual way he treated him, and admits it came both from carelessness and from love.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Thinking of Krishna as a friend of his own age, with a mistaken understanding, Arjuna spoke to him presumptuously as 'Krishna, Yadava, friend', not knowing this greatness of the cosmic form, through a distracted mind or through affection.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Ignorant of Krishna's majesty, through confusion or through love, Arjuna treated him as a mere friend and rashly called him 'Krishna, Yadava, friend'; he joins this with the jests and shared meals of the next verse.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Here Arjuna begins asking forgiveness over two verses: thinking you an ordinary friend, I addressed you with disrespect, out of carelessness or affection; 'I ask your forgiveness' comes in the next verse.

bg.11.41.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to taking those closest to us for granted: familiarity can hide someone's worth, and it is never too late to acknowledge it.
misreadings: Not a teaching that friendship or affection toward God (or anyone) is wrong; Arjuna names affection, not only carelessness, and Krishna keeps the friendship.
Not an argument for formality in relationships.
cautions: For a grieving reader, regret for 'taking someone for granted' can deepen guilt over things left unsaid to someone now gone.
not_for: someone consumed by guilt after a death
someone in a relationship where the other person's 'greatness' is used to demand submission
speaks_to: regret for taking a spouse, parent or friend for granted
a long friendship one has stopped seeing clearly

data_flags.corrected_ref: Bhagavad Gita 11.41 (same in all editions checked). DATA ERROR: our record's id is bg.11.41 but its ref is '11.41–42' and its sanskrit and translation contain both 11.41 and 11.42, while a separate record bg.11.42 repeats 11.42.

bg.11.42.context: Continuing from 11.41, Arjuna lists the slights: jokes at Krishna's expense while walking, resting, sitting or eating, alone or in front of others; for all of it he asks the immeasurable one's forgiveness. He goes on to praise Krishna as father of the world (11.43) and asks him to bear with him as a father, friend or lover would (11.44).
bg.11.42.core_teaching: Arjuna owns even the small, everyday slights of a long friendship and asks for forgiveness for all of them.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Whatever slight was done for fun, while walking, lying down, sitting or eating, when Krishna was absent or in front of him, Arjuna asks the immeasurable one to forgive it all.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Whatever slight came in play, in private without the friends or in front of the friends who joked along, for that whole set of offences Arjuna asks the one of unfathomable power to forgive.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Seeing the cosmic form, Arjuna asks pardon for his familiar conduct: he treated the origin of the universe as a friend, joked with him and took liberties, not knowing his greatness.

bg.11.42.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to the everyday texture of close relationships: small jokes and casual neglect accumulate, and naming them honestly is part of repair.
misreadings: Not a call to stop joking with or enjoying people we love.
Not a model of grovelling; it is a sincere apology within an ongoing friendship.
cautions: Can intensify guilt for a bereaved reader thinking of casual moments with someone now gone.
not_for: someone already overwhelmed by guilt
fresh grief
speaks_to: wanting to apologise for small, repeated slights
realising one has been careless with a close friend
making amends in a long marriage or friendship

bg.11.44.context: Having asked forgiveness for treating Krishna casually (11.41-42) and praised him as the father of the world, beyond compare (11.43), Arjuna prostrates and asks Krishna to bear with him as a father with a son, a friend with a friend, a lover with the beloved. In the next verse he asks to see Krishna's familiar form again.
bg.11.44.core_teaching: Arjuna appeals to the closest human bonds as the model for divine forgiveness: the patience a parent, friend or lover shows the one they love.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Bowing and laying his body low, Arjuna seeks the Lord's grace: just as a father forgives a son's fault, a friend a friend's, and a lover the beloved's, so the Lord should bear with and forgive him.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: As a father or friend, approached with a bow, is gracious even to a son or friend who has erred, so you, supremely compassionate and dear, should bear everything from me, who am dear to you.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Falling flat like a staff in prostration, Arjuna asks the Lord of the world to forgive his offences, as a father bears a son's fault out of compassion, an unconditional friend a friend's, and a lover a beloved's.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Arjuna asks to be taken to the Lord's bosom as a mother takes her child, to have his past faults overlooked, since they were done in ignorance and he now comes in submission.

bg.11.44.practical_reading: Teachers use it to show what asking forgiveness looks like: humility, honesty, and trust in the other's love, without demanding the outcome.
misreadings: Asking for forgiveness is not demanding it; the other person still decides (our existing misuse note is right).
Not a model for forgiving an abuser because they are 'family'.
cautions: Parent and lover images can hurt readers with an absent or harmful parent or a broken relationship.
not_for: someone being pressured to forgive or to seek forgiveness from someone who harmed them
speaks_to: someone wanting to apologise to a parent, partner or close friend
a person who fears they are beyond forgiveness
someone longing for a gentler image of God

bg.11.45.context: After his apology (11.41-44), Arjuna admits he is thrilled to have seen what no one has seen, yet his mind is shaken by fear; he asks Krishna to be gracious and show him that earlier form. 11.46 names it: crowned, four-armed, with mace and discus. Krishna answers that no one else has seen this vision (11.47-48) and then reassures him (11.49).
bg.11.45.core_teaching: Awe and fear can come together; after seeing something overwhelming, it is natural and right to ask to return to what is familiar and gentle.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Seeing the cosmic form, never before seen by him or anyone, Arjuna is delighted yet his mind is confounded with fear; so he asks to be shown only the form he wore as Arjuna's friend.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Beholding the most marvellous and awesome form, Arjuna is satisfied yet filled with fear; he asks the Lord, God even of Brahma, to take again his other, benign form and to be gracious.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Having asked pardon, Arjuna now prays over two verses: he is thrilled yet his mind trembles with fear, so to end his distress he asks to be shown that same form.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: To an ordinary person the cosmic form is overwhelming and terrifying, though to a yogi it uplifts; Arjuna asks to see only the form Krishna wears as his friend.

bg.11.45.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to big experiences (a birth, a revelation, a crisis): you may feel wonder and fear at once, and asking for the familiar and gentle is not weakness.
misreadings: Not a rejection of the vision; Arjuna is grateful and afraid at once.
Not a sign that seeking comfort means a lack of faith.
not_for: someone who needs encouragement to face something rather than step back from it
speaks_to: mixed feelings of wonder and fear
someone longing for the familiar after upheaval

bg.11.49.context: Arjuna has begged, frightened, to see Krishna's gentle form again (11.45-46). Krishna, having told him that no one else has seen this vision (11.47-48), now comforts him: do not be afraid or bewildered; free of fear and glad at heart, see my familiar form again. Sanjaya then narrates the change (11.50).
bg.11.49.core_teaching: The divine does not leave the frightened one in terror: Krishna meets fear with tenderness and returns to the form his friend can bear.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Let there be no fear and no confusion from seeing this terrible form; freed of fear and glad in mind, behold again the four-armed form with conch, discus and mace, the form you love.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Let the distress and bewilderment caused by the fierce form cease; I will show you the gentle form you are used to; see that form of mine.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: If seeing this terrible form still distresses you, then I will show you that same form: let there be no distress or confusion, and look on it, free of fear and with a glad mind.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Seeing Arjuna in terror, the Lord withdrew the cosmic form, took his usual gentle form, and consoled him with sweet, loving words.

bg.11.49.practical_reading: Teachers read it as a picture of how comfort works: first 'don't be afraid', then something familiar to hold on to.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of Arjuna's fear; Krishna responds to it and changes what he shows.
not_for: someone whose fear is a warning they should act on (danger, abuse), if 'don't be afraid' would sound like 'ignore it'
speaks_to: fear and confusion after a shock
someone who needs gentleness rather than more challenge
a reader who imagines God as only fearsome

bg.11.50.context: Krishna has just told Arjuna not to fear and to look again on his familiar form (11.49). Sanjaya, narrating to the blind king, reports that Krishna did so: he showed his own form again and, becoming gentle in appearance, comforted the terrified Arjuna. Arjuna then says he is himself again (11.51).
bg.11.50.core_teaching: Having shown the overwhelming truth, the divine returns to a gentle, approachable form in order to comfort the one who is afraid.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Having spoken so, Vasudeva again showed his own form, the one born in Vasudeva's house, and, becoming gentle in body, the great-souled one consoled the frightened Arjuna.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The Lord showed his own four-armed form again and, taking the familiar gentle body, reassured Arjuna, who had been frightened by seeing an unfamiliar form; 'great-souled' means one whose will is always true.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: He showed again his own crowned, four-armed form as before, and, gentle in appearance, reassured the frightened Arjuna; 'mahātmā' means the one with the cosmic form, or the compassionate one.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: 'His own form' means his form as the son of Vasudeva.

bg.11.50.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that the infinite also chooses to be near and gentle; comfort is part of how the divine meets us.
misreadings: Not a sign that the cosmic vision was false; both forms are his.
speaks_to: someone who has been frightened and needs reassurance
a reader who wants to know God also comforts

bg.11.51.context: Krishna has returned to his gentle form and comforted Arjuna (11.50). Arjuna says that, seeing this gentle human form again, he is now composed and back to his natural state. Krishna then tells him how rare the vision was and that only undivided devotion makes it possible (11.52-54).
bg.11.51.core_teaching: Seeing the familiar, gentle face of the one he trusts, Arjuna recovers his composure and himself.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Seeing this gentle, serene human form, his friend's form, Arjuna says he has now become calm in mind and returned to his natural state.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Seeing Krishna's own most gentle form in human shape, of unsurpassed beauty, tenderness and grace, Arjuna has become composed and is restored to his nature.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Freed of fear, Arjuna says his mind is now calm and he has returned to his normal, healthy state.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: His thoughts are collected, his fear gone, his senses work again; he compares himself to an erring child embraced by its mother, or a calf that sees its mother again, and says he feels alive.

bg.11.51.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to recovering after a shock: a familiar face, a trusted presence, helps us come back to ourselves.
misreadings: Not a claim that the overwhelming vision was bad; Arjuna needed both.
not_for: someone still in the middle of a crisis, for whom 'I feel like myself again' may not yet be true
speaks_to: coming back to oneself after panic or shock
the comfort of a trusted, familiar person
someone who prefers a personal, human image of the divine

bg.11.54.context: Krishna has told Arjuna that the form he saw is very hard to see; even the gods long for it (11.52), and it cannot be seen through Vedas, austerity, gifts or sacrifice (11.53). Here he names the one way: by undivided devotion he can be known, truly seen and entered. 11.55 then sums up the whole path.
bg.11.54.core_teaching: What no ritual, learning, gift or austerity can achieve, love that looks to nothing but God achieves: knowing God, seeing God and entering into God.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Undivided devotion never turns to anything but the Lord, so that no senses perceive anything but Vasudeva. By it he can be known from scripture, directly seen, and entered, which is liberation.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Vedic study, sacrifice, gifts and austerity without devotion cannot show him as he is; by single-minded devotion he can be known, seen and entered. He cites the Katha Upanishad: not by learning, but whom he chooses.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: By devotion fixed on the Lord alone, this cosmic form can be truly known through scripture, seen directly and entered into by identity, and by no other means.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Single-minded, unbroken devotion that seeks nothing but the Lord is the sole means; egoism and duality vanish, and the devotee, illumined, merges in him.

bg.11.54.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that the heart, not credentials, is the way in: sincere, undivided love matters more than learning or ritual performance.
misreadings: Not anti-learning or anti-ritual in every case; it says these do not suffice without devotion.
Not exclusivist hostility to others.
not_for: a reader alienated by personal-God devotion
speaks_to: someone who feels unqualified (not learned, not ritually observant)
a person drawn to devotion over philosophy
someone wanting a direct relationship with God

bg.11.55.context: Krishna has just said that only undivided devotion lets him be known, seen and entered (11.54). He closes the chapter of the cosmic vision with a summary of the whole path: work for him, hold him as highest, love him, drop clinging, and hate no being. Chapter 12 then takes up Arjuna's question about the best kind of devotee.
bg.11.55.core_teaching: The whole Gita in one line: work for God, make God your goal, love God, let go of clinging, and bear no hatred toward any being.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: One who does all acts, even Vedic study, as worship; for whom the Lord is the aim of every effort; whose sole object of love he is; free of attachment to anything else and hating no one.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The supreme secret, essence of all scripture: one who works for the Lord, takes him as supreme goal, is his devotee, unattached to sons and the like, and hostile to no creature, reaches him, and no one else does.

bg.11.55.practical_reading: Teachers offer it as a five-point rule for daily life: do your work as an offering, keep your highest aim in view, love, hold things lightly, and refuse hatred.
misreadings: No hatred doesn't mean no boundaries; you can wish someone no harm and still keep away (our existing misuse note is right).
Not a call to stop loving family; 'free of attachment' means free of clinging.
cautions: Shankara's and Sivananda's 'no enmity even toward one who has done great injury' can feel like pressure on survivors of abuse or violence to forgive or reconcile; frame it as release from hatred, not as excusing harm.
Lists of attachments to drop (wife, children, kin) can sound cold to a reader grieving or caring for family.
not_for: a survivor of abuse who is being pushed to forgive
fresh grief, where 'drop attachment' may feel like being told to stop loving
speaks_to: someone wanting a single, practical summary of the Gita
a person carrying resentment that is eating at them
someone wanting to bring faith into their work

bg.12.10.context: Krishna's ladder in 12.8-11 runs from the most demanding to the most accessible: fix mind and intellect on him (12.8); if not, practise (12.9); if not, work for him (12.10); if not, give up the fruits of action (12.11). 12.12 then praises the last step. This is the third rung: if even practice is too hard, make works done for him your aim; even that leads to perfection.
bg.12.10.core_teaching: When focused inner practice is too hard, action done for God's sake is itself a full path, leading step by step to perfection.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: If you cannot manage practice, be devoted to works done for the Lord; even without practice, doing actions for him brings perfection, by way of a purified mind, then concentration, then knowledge.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Do the Lord's works with great love: building temples, tending gardens, lighting lamps, sweeping and cleaning, gathering flowers, worship, chanting his names, circling and bowing. Doing these soon leads to steady remembrance and to him.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: If unable to practise, make central the acts done to please the Lord, such as fasting on Ekadashi, vows and singing his names; even such acts, done for him, bring liberation.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Mere actions for the Lord bring purity of mind, then meditation, knowledge and liberation. Serving humanity while feeling you serve the Lord in all is also action for his sake, together with worship and meditation.

bg.12.10.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to people who find meditation hard: serve, cook, clean, volunteer, care for others, and do it as an offering; that counts fully.
misreadings: Not 'any work is spiritual'; the point is work done for God's sake.
Not a lesser path to be ashamed of; Krishna says it reaches perfection.
not_for: someone already overworking, who may hear 'do more' (pair with 12.11's letting go)
speaks_to: someone who can't sit still for meditation
volunteers, carers and people whose devotion is practical
someone who feels unspiritual because they are always busy

bg.12.11.context: Last rung of the ladder in 12.8-11: fix the mind on Krishna; if not, practise; if not, work for his sake (12.10); and if even that is too hard, give up the fruit of all actions. The next verse (12.12) then praises this last, most accessible step, and 12.13-20 describe the person who lives it.
bg.12.11.core_teaching: Even someone who cannot meditate, practise, or work specifically for God can still act and hand over the results; that release, done with self-control, is a real path in its own right.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: For one too unready for works that ripen into love of God: take up contemplation of the self (the path of chapters 1-6), doing works without craving reward. This purifies, leads to self-vision, and finally to supreme love of God.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: An alternative for one who cannot steadily perform rites for the Lord: surrender to him and give up the fruit of all acts, thinking 'I act as he directs within my ability; results are his.' Living so, grace brings blessedness.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Calls this the easiest path, the last after meditation (12.8), practice (12.9) and work for the Lord (12.10). Even acts done from personal motives can be offered to God as duty, fruits renounced, senses controlled.

bg.12.11.practical_reading: Teachers offer it to people who feel they 'can't do spirituality properly': keep doing your ordinary work, but do it well and let go of how it lands; that release is itself the practice.
misreadings: Not 'stop caring about results' or giving up planning; it is giving up the anxious claim on outcomes.
Not a lesser or second-class path in Sridhara and Sivananda; it is presented as fully valid (Shankara does rank it lower, as a means for one who cannot follow the higher paths).
cautions: Shankara frames this as the course for someone not able to take up the higher paths; avoid presenting the reader as 'failing' the earlier rungs.
Theistic framing (taking refuge in God) may not suit every reader.
not_for: someone whose results genuinely matter for survival (job loss, medical outcome) and may hear 'let go of results' as 'don't try'
a reader who needs a call to agency rather than release
speaks_to: someone who feels too busy, scattered or tired for meditation or prayer
a person stuck on whether their work will succeed
someone who feels spiritually inadequate and needs an entry point

bg.12.12.context: Having offered the ladder in 12.8-11, Krishna praises its last step. Knowledge, meditation and renouncing the fruit of action are compared, ending with peace that follows at once from renunciation. Then 12.13-20 begin the portrait of the devotee who is dear to him.
bg.12.12.core_teaching: Releasing one's claim on the results of action brings peace without delay; the commentators read the ranking as encouragement to take up this step, not as a literal claim that it outranks meditation for everyone.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: If devotion is too hard, try self-knowledge; failing that, contemplation of the self; failing that, works with their fruit given up. That removes sin and brings peace, which leads back up to contemplation, self-vision and supreme love of God.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Knowledge grounded in teaching and reasoning surpasses practice without understanding; meditation surpasses that; renouncing the fruit surpasses meditation, because non-attachment plus the Lord's grace quickly brings release from worldly existence.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
