commentaries.gist: Follows Shankara: the ranking praises renouncing fruits to spur aspirants into selfless action. Adds that desire is the enemy of peace; renouncing fruits purifies the heart and weakens desire, and the sage does it naturally.

bg.12.12.practical_reading: Used to say that peace is not earned only by long meditation: the moment you stop gripping the outcome of a task, the agitation around it eases.
misreadings: Not a claim that meditation and study are worthless.
Not 'stop caring how things turn out'; peace comes from releasing the grip, not from indifference.
Not a promise that circumstances improve at once; it is the mind that settles.
cautions: Shankara explicitly calls the ranking 'mere praise'; a reading should not overstate it as a literal hierarchy.
not_for: someone in acute grief, where 'peace at once' may sound glib
a person facing an outcome they cannot afford to let go of without support
speaks_to: someone exhausted by over-investing in outcomes (exams, promotions, launches)
a person who finds sitting meditation hard and feels behind

bg.12.13.context: After offering a graded set of practices (12.8-12), Krishna begins describing the devotee who is dear to him (12.13-20, a passage Sivananda notes is called the 'Amritashtakam'). This verse opens the list and runs on into 12.14: content, self-controlled, firm in resolve, mind and intellect given to him.
bg.12.13.core_teaching: The person dear to the divine bears ill-will to no one, is friendly and compassionate, holds loosely to 'I' and 'mine', stays even through pain and pleasure, and forgives.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Reads 'friendly and compassionate' by rank: no malice toward superiors, friendship toward equals, compassion toward those below. Out of compassion he feels others' pain and pleasure as his own.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Opens the eight verses he calls 'Amritashtakam'. The devotee bears no ill will even to one who hurts him, feels the sufferer's pain and tries to relieve it, and is forgiving like the earth.

bg.12.13.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a practical checklist for relationships: drop grudges, be friendly, act on compassion, hold possessions and status loosely, and forgive, which also frees oneself.
misreadings: Forgiving is not excusing harm or staying in danger (as our misuse note says).
Not emotional suppression; 'even in pain and pleasure' is about not being driven by them, not about not feeling them.
cautions: Ramanuja's reading (those who harm you do so under God's direction, matching your own past faults) could be deeply harmful to someone being abused; never use it in that context.
Shankara's 'unchanged when insulted or struck' describes a renunciant's inner state; it is not advice to tolerate violence.
not_for: someone currently being abused or bullied, if read as 'just forgive'
fresh betrayal, where 'hate no one' may feel invalidating
speaks_to: loneliness eased by reaching out in friendship

bg.12.14.context: Second verse of the eight-verse portrait (12.13-20) of the devotee Krishna loves, continuing the sentence begun in 12.13 (no hatred, friendliness, compassion, no 'mine' or 'I', even in pain and pleasure, forgiving). Each verse ends with the refrain 'such a one is dear to me'.
bg.12.14.core_teaching: The person God loves is inwardly settled: content whatever they receive, disciplined, clear about what is true, and with thinking and feeling directed to God.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Applies it to the karma-yogi: content with whatever chance brings for bodily needs, always meditating on the self as distinct from matter, firm in the scriptural knowledge of spirit, convinced that works done without seeking reward are worship of Vasudeva.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Treats 13-14 as the traits that quickly win grace: contented whether or not things are gained, cheerful, vigilant, self-restrained, firm in conviction about the Lord, mind and intellect dedicated to him.

bg.12.14.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a portrait to grow toward: contentment that does not depend on getting things, steady habits, and a settled sense of what you live for.
misreadings: Contentment here is not complacency or giving up on improving one's circumstances.
Not a test the reader must already pass to be loved; it describes a direction of growth.
cautions: Sivananda grounds contentment in past karma ('what comes is the fruit of your past actions'), which can feel blaming to someone suffering.
Shankara applies the list to monastic renunciates; a lay reader should not be made to feel excluded.
not_for: someone in material hardship, who may hear 'be content' as 'accept deprivation'
a reader feeling unlovable, if framed as conditions for being dear to God
speaks_to: a person seeking an inner anchor amid changing circumstances

bg.12.15.context: Part of the eight-verse portrait (12.13-20) of the devotee dear to Krishna. After content and self-control (12.14), this verse turns to relationships: the person is no source of fear to others and is not shaken by them, and is free of four disturbing emotions.
bg.12.15.core_teaching: The person God loves threatens no one and is not threatened by anyone; free of elation, resentment, fear and agitation, they are safe to be around and hard to unsettle.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Applies it to the renunciate. Joy is the mind's exhilaration on getting what it desired, showing in bristling hair and tears; one free of joy, envy, fear and sorrow is dear to the Lord.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: This person never acts so as to trouble the world, and nothing the world does can trouble him, since he has no antagonism toward anyone; so he gives rise to neither delight nor anger in others' regard.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: No one feels threatened by him, nor he by anyone. Elation is joy at getting what one wants, jealousy is envy at another's gain, fear is terror, anxiety a mind ruffled by fear; he is free of all four.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The devotee harms no creature in thought, word or deed, so none fears him; seeing the world as his own Self, he fears nothing. Joy, anger, fear and anxiety leave him on their own, like animals fleeing a forest fire.

bg.12.15.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to everyday relationships: be someone people feel safe around, and do not let others' moods or opinions set your own.
misreadings: Not 'never disagree or cause any discomfort'; it means not causing needless harm or fear.
Not suppressing emotion; it describes freedom from being driven by it.
cautions: For someone being harmed by others, 'not agitated by the world' must not imply they should simply absorb mistreatment.
not_for: someone in an abusive situation, who may hear it as 'don't be upset by it'
acute anxiety disorder, if presented as a standard to meet rather than a direction
speaks_to: someone who is easily rattled by others' reactions
a person aware that their temper unsettles family or colleagues

bg.12.16.context: Continues the portrait of the beloved devotee (12.13-20). After the social marks of 12.15, this verse lists practical and inner traits: wanting nothing extra, clean, competent, impartial, untroubled, and no longer launching desire-driven projects.
bg.12.16.core_teaching: The beloved devotee is not dependent on things, is clean and competent, stays impartial and untroubled, and has stopped launching projects out of craving.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Indifferent to body, senses and objects; pure inside and out; able to decide rightly on the spot; not taking a friend's side; habitually giving up actions aimed at desired objects of this world or the next.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Wants nothing but the self; keeps the body on scripturally allowed food; skilled in enjoined duties; unconcerned with other matters; unmoved by the heat, cold and hardship those duties bring; drops every undertaking that scripture does not require.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Indifferent even to things that come unasked; clean within and without; dexterous, meaning not lazy; not taking sides; free of anguish; habitually giving up undertakings aimed at visible or unseen results.

bg.12.16.practical_reading: Teachers draw from it a picture of calm competence: do what is yours to do well and promptly, keep inner and outer life clean, and stop piling on new pursuits driven by wanting.
misreadings: 'Giving up all undertakings' is not quitting work or ambition; the commentators limit it to desire-driven ventures (Ramanuja keeps all enjoined duty).
'Unconcerned' is impartiality, not apathy.
'Pure' is not a matter of ritual status.
cautions: Sivananda's 'not troubled even if beaten by a wicked man' should not be presented as advice to endure abuse.
not_for: someone who has lost motivation or is depressed, who might hear 'give up undertakings' as permission to withdraw
a young person just starting out who needs encouragement to begin things
speaks_to: someone overextended by too many projects
a person who wants to be dependable and calm at work

bg.12.17.context: Part of the portrait of the beloved devotee (12.13-20). It restates and deepens 12.13's evenness: four reactions (exulting, hating, grieving, craving) are named and set aside, along with attachment to good and bad deeds.
bg.12.17.core_teaching: The devotee is not thrown about by gain and loss: no exulting, hating, grieving or craving, and no clinging even to merit, since both good and bad works bind.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: He does not rejoice on gaining the desirable, does not fret at the undesirable, does not grieve at parting with something loved, and does not long for what he lacks.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Neither pleased by the pleasant nor upset by the unpleasant, not grieving at losing what was wanted nor longing for the unattained; habitually renouncing merit and demerit, and devoted.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Expands 12.13: he does not rejoice in getting desirable things, hate the undesirable, grieve at parting from loved ones, or crave the unattained; he has renounced the good and evil actions that bring pleasure and pain.

bg.12.17.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to emotional swings: notice the cycle of thrill, resentment, grief and craving, and practise not being carried away by it, without pretending not to feel.
misreadings: Not 'feeling grief is wrong'; the ideal is not being swept away, and this is a description of a mature devotee, not a rule for the bereaved.
'Giving up good and evil' is not moral indifference; it means not clinging even to merit.
cautions: Explicitly names not grieving; Ramanuja's example is the loss of wife, son or wealth. Do not use on day 1 of a grief plan or for someone recently bereaved.
'Renouncing good and evil' can be misheard as relativism.
not_for: fresh grief or bereavement
someone who has been told not to show emotion and needs permission to feel
speaks_to: someone caught in emotional highs and lows over outcomes
a person whose mood depends on wins and losses

bg.12.18.context: Penultimate pair in the portrait of the beloved devotee (12.13-20). It lists pairs of opposites (friend and foe, honour and insult, cold and heat, pleasure and pain) toward which the devotee stays even, and adds freedom from attachment; 12.19 completes the sentence.
bg.12.18.core_teaching: Evenness across the pairs of opposites, including how one is treated by others, marks the devotee; it rests on having no attachment.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Read with 12.19 for the renunciate who knows the Supreme: he has no attachment to any object, is content with the bare means of bodily sustenance, and his thought rests steadily on the highest reality.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: 12.13 already ruled out hating foe or friend; here the equanimity is stronger: staying even when actually face to face with them, and bearing honour and disgrace alike.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Same to foe and friend; even in honour and dishonour, meaning free of joy and sorrow at them; alike in heat and cold, happiness and misery; not attached to anything.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The ordinary person is ruled by honour and dishonour, cold and heat, pleasure and pain; the devotee keeps a balanced mind, unmoved by attraction and repulsion, and is attached to nothing.

bg.12.18.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to criticism and praise at work and in families: your worth is not set by who flatters or insults you, and you can treat a rival with the same fairness as a friend.
misreadings: Being the same in insult does not mean tolerating abuse; it means one's worth is not decided by it.
'Same to enemy and friend' is not naivety about who is safe; it is freedom from hatred and favouritism.
cautions: Incomplete sentence: pair with 12.19 or note that it continues.
For someone being harassed or abused, 'stay even in dishonour' must not be framed as 'accept it'.
not_for: someone currently in an abusive relationship or facing discrimination
acute humiliation or public shaming, if offered without compassion first
speaks_to: someone whose self-worth swings with others' opinions

bg.12.19.context: Closes the sentence begun in 12.18 and the list of marks of the beloved devotee; 12.20 then sums up that those who follow this 'immortal dharma' with faith are exceedingly dear to Krishna, ending chapter 12.
bg.12.19.core_teaching: The devotee is unmoved by praise or blame, sparing with words, content with whatever comes, not bound to a home or comfort, and steady in mind; such a person is dear to God.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: 'Without a home' means free of love for house and the like, the mind being set on the self; such a person bears honour and disgrace equally and is dear to the Lord. This closes the account of bhakti-yoga.

bg.12.19.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to approval-seeking: let praise and criticism pass through, speak less, be content with enough, and hold possessions and places lightly.
misreadings: Not 'never ask for credit' or never advocate for yourself.
'Homeless' is not a recommendation to abandon family or housing for a lay reader; even Ramanuja reads it as non-attachment to home.
'Silent' is not shutting people out.
cautions: Literal 'homeless' (Shankara, Sridhara, Sivananda) describes a wandering renunciate; it may land badly with someone facing housing insecurity.
Our line paraphrases aniketa as 'not status', which is not supported by the commentaries.
not_for: someone who is actually homeless or displaced
a person being silenced or whose voice needs to be heard
speaks_to: someone hooked on praise or wounded by criticism
a person seeking simplicity and contentment

bg.12.2.context: Arjuna has asked (12.1) which worshippers know yoga better: those devoted to Krishna as described at the end of chapter 11, or those who meditate on the imperishable, unmanifest reality. Krishna answers here: those who fix their minds on him and worship him, always united, with supreme faith, are the most perfect in yoga. 12.3-4 add that the others also reach him, and 12.5 that their path is harder for embodied beings.
bg.12.2.core_teaching: Devotion to God in a personal form, held constantly and with deep faith, is the most complete form of yoga.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Those who fix their mind on the Lord in his cosmic form, omniscient, ruler of all masters of yoga, free of passion, and worship him with steadiness and supreme faith are the best yogis; the others also reach him (12.3-4).

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Those who, out of intense love, fix their minds on the Lord and worship him with supreme faith, longing for constant union, are the best yogis, meaning they reach him easily and soon.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Answering Arjuna: the first kind are best. Those who make the mind one-pointed on the Lord endowed with omniscience and other qualities, devoted through works done for him, and worship him with highest faith are the most united.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Devotees who fix their minds on the Lord in the cosmic form and worship him day and night, living for him alone, are rightly called the best yogis; what of those who contemplate the formless? That comes next.

bg.12.2.practical_reading: Teachers draw from it that a heartfelt relationship with God, kept up daily with trust, is not a lesser path than philosophy; for most people it is the more natural one.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of those who seek the formless; 12.3-4 says they reach him too.
Not a call to blind belief; 'supreme faith' goes with steady practice.
not_for: a reader who meditates on the formless and might hear this as a ranking against them (show with 12.3-4)
speaks_to: someone unsure whether heartfelt devotion is 'enough'
a person drawn to a personal God rather than abstract philosophy
someone wanting to deepen daily trust

bg.12.4.context: Answering which devotee is best (12.1-2), Krishna turns to those who worship the imperishable, unmanifest reality (12.3). This verse completes the sentence: with senses restrained, even-minded everywhere and delighting in the welfare of all beings, they too reach him. 12.5 adds that the path of the unmanifest is harder for embodied beings.
bg.12.4.core_teaching: Those who seek the formless also reach the goal, provided their search comes with self-restraint, an even mind and active goodwill toward every being.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Restraining the senses, even-minded in gaining what is wanted or unwanted, and devoted to all beings' welfare, they reach the Lord; nothing needs to be said about that, since the knower is the Lord's own self (7.18).

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Reads 'the imperishable' as the individual self's nature. Seeing all selves as alike, these meditators wish all beings well, since ill will comes from identifying with unequal bodies; they too reach a self like the Lord's.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Evenness comes to those free of likes and dislikes; love and hatred make a person think of harming others, so when they are destroyed through meditation on the Self, the yogi becomes intent on others' welfare.

bg.12.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that whatever your path, the signs of real progress are the same: self-control, steadiness and care for others.
misreadings: Not a claim that the formless path is wrong; it is called harder (12.5), not invalid.
speaks_to: contemplatives and meditators drawn to the formless
someone whose spirituality expresses itself as service
a person bridging different spiritual approaches

bg.12.6.context: Having said that the path of the unmanifest is harder for embodied beings (12.5), Krishna describes the devotees he rescues: those who lay all their actions in him, hold him as supreme and meditate on him with undivided devotion (12.6). For them, minds set on him, he soon becomes the one who lifts them out of the ocean of death and rebirth (12.7). He then gives his ladder of practices (12.8-11).
bg.12.6.core_teaching: Those who offer all their work to God and turn to God single-mindedly do not have to save themselves: God soon lifts them out of the cycle of death and rebirth.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Read with 12.7: those who renounce all actions in the Lord and meditate with exclusive devotion on his cosmic form alone, minds fixed on him, he soon lifts out of the ocean of mortal samsara, so hard to cross.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Those who lay in him all their acts, worldly and Vedic, take him as sole goal, and find meditation, worship and praise so dear they are like the goal itself: these he soon lifts from the sea of mortal existence.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: For his devotees, perfection comes without strain by his grace: offering all actions to him and worshipping with one-pointed devotion, they are soon lifted by him from the death-filled ocean of samsara.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Even on the path of devotion one should not abandon action; dedicate its fruits to the Lord. To one who surrenders completely, the Lord comes quickly and lifts him from the mortal plane.

bg.12.6.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to the exhaustion of trying to save oneself: offer the work, keep turning toward God, and trust that you will be lifted, not left to swim alone.
misreadings: Not a promise of rescue from every worldly difficulty; the ocean is samsara, the round of death and rebirth.
Not a reason to stop acting; the verse says offer actions, not drop them.
cautions: 'Ocean of death' imagery; take care with readers who are grieving or in suicidal crisis.
Rests on rebirth doctrine.
not_for: someone in a mental-health crisis, where 'death' and 'ocean' imagery could land badly
a reader who needs practical help and may hear 'God will lift you' as 'wait'
speaks_to: feeling overwhelmed and unable to save oneself
someone ready to surrender effort to God
a person seeking assurance that grace meets effort

data_flags.corrected_ref: Bhagavad Gita 12.6-7. DATA ERROR: the record's id and ref say 12.6, but its sanskrit and translation contain both 12.6 and 12.7 (12.6 alone is an incomplete relative clause; 12.7 carries the promise). Set ref to 'Bhagavad Gita 12.6–7' or split the record.

bg.12.7.context: Arjuna has asked who is better: those devoted to Krishna's personal form or those who meditate on the imperishable unmanifest (12.1). Krishna says both reach him but the unmanifest path is harder for embodied beings (12.2-5); those who offer all actions to him and meditate on him with single devotion (12.6) are lifted by him swiftly (12.7). Hence: fix your mind on me (12.8).
bg.12.7.core_teaching: For those whose minds rest wholly in the divine, the divine itself becomes the rescuer who lifts them, soon, out of the cycle of mortality and struggle.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Comments on 12.6-7 together: those who give all actions to the Lord and contemplate him alone are lifted soon from the 'ocean' of mortal samsara. It is called an ocean because it is so hard to cross.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Covers both worldly work and religious rites. Those who hand all their acts to the Lord and worship him single-mindedly, finding joy in the worship itself, are soon delivered from samsara, which keeps souls from reaching him.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Reads 12.6-7 together: devotees reach realisation easily by grace. Those who offer all actions to the Lord and worship him wholeheartedly are quickly rescued from the ocean of birth and death.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The devotee who surrenders completely, offers the fruits of action to the Lord and fixes the mind on him alone is soon lifted from the round of birth and death.

bg.12.7.practical_reading: Teachers use it to comfort those who feel they are drowning: you do not have to swim out alone; resting the heart in the divine lets you be carried.
misreadings: Not a promise that troubles will end immediately in this life; the 'ocean' is the whole cycle of worldly existence.
Not passivity; the preceding verse (12.6) describes offering one's actions, not abandoning them.
cautions: Names death directly ('ocean of death'); fine for a devotion plan, but handle gently for bereaved readers.
'Drowning' imagery in the line could be triggering for someone who has lost a loved one to drowning.
not_for: fresh bereavement, if death imagery is foregrounded
someone in danger who needs practical help now
speaks_to: wanting rescue rather than more effort

bg.12.8.context: Krishna's ladder in 12.8-11 runs from the most demanding to the most accessible: fix mind and intellect on him (12.8); if not, practise (12.9); if not, work for him (12.10); if not, give up the fruits of action (12.11). 12.12 then praises the last step. This verse is the first and highest step: rest the whole mind and understanding in him, and from then on you will live in him.
bg.12.8.core_teaching: The most direct path: let both your thinking and your deciding rest in God, and you will come to live in God.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Fix the mind, which deliberates, on the Lord in his cosmic form, and settle the intellect, which decides, in him; then after the body falls you will surely dwell in him as his very self.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Since he is the highest goal, easy and quick to reach, fix your mind on him and resolve that he alone is the supreme goal; right after that resolve you will dwell in him.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Steady the mind on the Lord and settle the deciding intellect in him; gaining knowledge by his grace, after the body ends you will dwell in him as his self, and he cites scripture for this.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Fix your purposes and thoughts on the Lord and give up thoughts of sense objects; fix your resolving intellect there too, and you will live in him as himself. This is the yoga of meditation.

bg.12.8.practical_reading: Teachers present it as the ideal to aim at, while stressing that the Gita immediately offers easier steps (12.9-11) for those not ready.
misreadings: Not a demand that everyone must manage this before anything else counts; Krishna immediately offers alternatives.
Not 'stop thinking'; it is about where mind and judgement rest.
not_for: a beginner who might feel this is out of reach (start with 12.9-11)
speaks_to: someone ready for deeper devotion or meditation
a person whose thinking and choices feel scattered

bg.12.9.context: Krishna's ladder in 12.8-11 runs from the most demanding to the most accessible: fix mind and intellect on him (12.8); if not, practise (12.9); if not, work for him (12.10); if not, give up the fruits of action (12.11). 12.12 then praises the last step. This is the second rung: if you cannot hold the mind steady on him yet, seek him through repeated practice.
bg.12.9.core_teaching: If the mind won't stay on God, don't give up: bring it back again and again, and that repetition itself is a path to God.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: If you cannot fix the mind steadily as described, then by practice, gathering the mind from everything and placing it again and again on one support, and the concentration that follows, seek to reach the Lord.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: If you cannot fix it at once, seek him by practice: dwelling again and again on him as an ocean of countless good qualities, his beauty, gentleness, friendliness, motherly love, compassion and sweetness.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: For one unable, an easier means: draw back the scattered mind again and again by remembering the Lord, and strive to reach him through that practice.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Practice means repeatedly withdrawing the mind from sense objects and fixing it on the Lord. If you cannot do it all the time, do it for some time; worship of images, feeling God's presence in them, also helps.

bg.12.9.practical_reading: Teachers present it as permission to be a beginner: wandering is expected; the practice is the returning.
misreadings: Not mechanical repetition; Ramanuja ties the practice to loving reflection on God's qualities.
speaks_to: someone whose mind wanders in prayer or meditation
a beginner who feels they are failing
someone who needs a realistic next step

bg.13.25.context: Krishna has explained that the self is a witness distinct from nature (prakriti) and that whoever understands this is not reborn. Here he names the different routes by which people come to see that self. The next verse adds a further group who simply hear the teaching from others and practise it with faith.
bg.13.25.core_teaching: There is more than one route to the same inner realisation: meditation, discriminating knowledge, and selfless action. Commentators read these as suited to different temperaments and stages, not as rival truths.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Meditation withdraws the senses into the mind and the mind into inner awareness, an unbroken flow 'like oil'. Sankhya is reflecting 'the gunas act; I am their witness'. Action done for the Lord counts as yoga by purifying the mind.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: The perfected see the self through meditation; less advanced ones ready the mind through the path of knowledge; those unfit for it, those preferring an easier road, and public figures setting an example follow karma-yoga, which carries knowledge within it.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: These are alternative routes to the same discriminating knowledge (he adds Patanjali's eight-limbed yoga as a fourth). They can be practised in sequence, but are listed separately because people differ in which they take up.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Many paths suit different temperaments: meditation, analytical inquiry that identifies with the silent witness, and karma-yoga that offers action and its fruit to the Lord.

bg.13.25.practical_reading: Modern teachers use it to reassure people who 'can't meditate': some find depth in stillness, some in study and reflection, some in honest work done for others. Pick the route that fits your nature and do it wholeheartedly.
misreadings: Not 'any path is fine, so no discipline is needed'; each route is a demanding practice.
Not a ranking that dismisses action; Ramanuja treats karma-yoga as a complete means.
cautions: Doctrinal and comparatively abstract; better for a 'why/steady' day than for acute distress.
not_for: Acute crisis where the reader needs comfort rather than a map of paths
speaks_to: Feeling like a failure at meditation
Wondering whether one's spiritual practice is 'the right one'
Active, practical people who think spirituality isn't for them
Couples or families with different styles of practice

bg.13.26.context: Right after naming meditation, discriminating knowledge and selfless action as routes to seeing the self, Krishna adds a fourth group: people who cannot follow any of those but hear the truth from teachers and worship or reflect with faith. Then he goes on to explain that everything that is born arises from the union of field and knower.
bg.13.26.core_teaching: Even someone with no capacity for subtle philosophy or demanding practice is not shut out: hearing the truth from trustworthy teachers and living by it with faith also carries a person across. The door is open to the ordinary seeker.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Some cannot know the self by these means; they learn from teachers and contemplate the teaching with full faith, relying wholly on others' instruction. Even they cross beyond death; how much more those who can weigh evidence themselves.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Those not yet able for the paths hear sages who have seen the truth; even those who can only believe what they hear are purged of sin and gradually take up karma-yoga. 'Also' marks these degrees of capacity.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: A means of release for the least equipped: not knowing how to realise the self by knowledge or yoga, they meditate on what they hear from teachers and, devoted with faith to that hearing, slowly pass beyond transmigratory existence.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Calls this the yoga of worship: some listen with unshakable faith to their teachers, others study books by realised sages and live by them; they too overcome death, since there are paths to suit every temperament.

bg.13.26.practical_reading: Teachers use it to honour the listener: you don't have to be a scholar or an adept; attending to good teaching, trusting it and returning to it daily is itself a path. It is a warm verse for beginners and for those who learn by ear.
misreadings: Not 'blind belief is enough'; Ramanuja and Sridhara describe listening as the start of gradual purification and practice.
'Crossing death' is not a promise that oneself or a loved one will be spared physical death.
cautions: Mentions death; in grief, 'they cross beyond death' may be heard as a promise about a loved one's fate, which the verse does not make.
not_for: Someone harmed by a manipulative teacher or group, for whom 'rely on what others tell you' could reopen that wound
speaks_to: Feeling not clever, educated or disciplined enough for spiritual life
Beginners and people who learn by listening (satsang, katha, podcasts)
Older readers who come to scripture late

bg.13.28.context: Krishna has just said that everything that comes into being arises from the joining of the field (body, nature) and its knower. He now says that the one who sees the same imperishable reality in all perishing beings is the one who truly sees. The next verse says such a person no longer harms the self by the self.
bg.13.28.core_teaching: True seeing is recognising one unchanging reality present equally in every living being, which does not perish when bodies perish. Everything else is a partial or distorted view.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: The Supreme Lord dwells without difference in all beings, from Brahma to the unmoving, imperishable while they perish. All see, but wrongly, like a diseased eye seeing several moons; only one who sees the one undivided self truly sees.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: 'Supreme lord' here is the self, ruler of the body, senses and mind it dwells in. Seeing it as the same knower in every body, apart from divine, human or other forms, and undecaying while bodies decay, is true seeing.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Having described the bondage that comes from lack of discrimination, Krishna gives its cure: seeing the Supreme Lord present equally, as pure existence, in all moving and unmoving beings, and not perishing when they perish. Only that person sees rightly.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Heat is the same in different fires, gold in different ornaments, light from many lamps; so the one Lord in all beings, who is not destroyed when they are.

bg.13.28.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to how we treat people: the same worth lives in a beggar and a king, a rival and a friend. It is also used, gently and later in mourning, to say that what was most real in a person is not destroyed with the body.
misreadings: Not a denial that loss is real or that bodies and lives matter.
Not a reason to be indifferent to suffering because 'the self is untouched'.
cautions: Mentions perishing; in fresh grief 'the undying within the dying' can sound like 'nothing was really lost'. Use only once the reader is ready for consolation of this kind.
not_for: The first days of a bereavement
Someone angry at platitudes about the soul
speaks_to: Prejudice, contempt or feeling superior to others
Loneliness and a sense of separateness
Caregivers and hospice workers looking for meaning
Grief some time after a loss, when the reader seeks what endures

bg.13.29.context: Following the statement that true seeing finds the same undying reality in all beings, Krishna gives its result: the one who sees this does not harm the self by the self and reaches the highest goal. He goes on to say that it is nature that acts, while the self is not the doer.
bg.13.29.core_teaching: Seeing the same reality in all beings ends the way we wound ourselves: mistaking ourselves for the body and its fortunes. That clear sight is what leads to freedom.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: No one literally destroys himself; but the ignorant ignore the self, take the body for it and lose body after body, so they are 'slayers of the self'. One who sees the Lord everywhere is not, and is liberated.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: 'Lord' is the soul, ruler and support of every body; seeing it as the same conscious knower in all bodies, one does not harm it by wrong thinking, saves it from samsara, and reaches the highest goal, seeing the self.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The ignorant 'destroy the Self' by identifying with the body and the mind's changes and failing to see the one Self in all; the liberated sage sees it everywhere.

bg.13.29.practical_reading: Teachers read it as: much of our suffering is self-inflicted through a narrow, body-bound view of who we are, and widening that view to see the same life in others also eases how we treat ourselves.
misreadings: Not about self-harm in the clinical sense; 'killing the self' is a metaphor for ignorance of one's nature.
Not saying the body or physical health doesn't matter.
cautions: The traditional language of 'self-slayers' (and Sridhara's citation of the Isha Upanishad line about such people going to sunless worlds) must never be used with a reader who mentions self-harm or suicidal thoughts; route those to real help instead.
Avoid phrasing that implies a struggling reader is 'hurting themselves' by not seeing correctly.
not_for: Any reader expressing self-harm or suicidal thoughts
Someone already blaming themselves for their pain
speaks_to: Wanting a wider, kinder sense of self

bg.13.33.context: Krishna has said that the supreme self, though dwelling in the body, neither acts nor is tainted. This verse gives the first of two images: space pervades everything yet nothing clings to it. The next verse adds the image of the one sun lighting the whole world.
bg.13.33.core_teaching: The self present in every body is not stained by what the body does or undergoes, just as space contains everything and is soiled by none of it.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: As all-pervading space, being subtle, is never soiled, so the self present everywhere in the body is not soiled. (A footnote from Anandagiri adds that space pervades mire and the like without being affected.)

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Space is in contact with everything yet, being subtle, takes on none of their properties; the self, very subtle, dwells in the bodies of gods, humans and others without being sullied by their peculiar qualities.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: As space is present even in mud but, being subtle and untouched, is not muddied, so the self in a superior, middling or lowly body is not joined to that body's merits or defects.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Being subtler than the body, the self, like ether, pervades all yet is tainted by nothing; it is unattached and actionless, so virtue and vice cannot touch it.

bg.13.33.practical_reading: Teachers use it to separate who you are from what has happened to you or around you: illness, ageing, social status or past events do not soil your deepest identity. It is also used against judging people by their bodies, caste or circumstances.
misreadings: Not a licence to act carelessly because 'my self is untouched'; the Gita elsewhere holds people responsible for their actions.
Not a denial that harm done to a person is real.
cautions: For survivors of abuse or assault, 'you are unstained' can be healing, but should never imply the harm did not matter or that they should simply rise above it.
not_for: Someone using it to excuse their own harmful actions
A reader who needs their hurt acknowledged first
speaks_to: Shame or feeling 'dirty' because of the past
Body image struggles, illness or disability affecting self-worth
Being judged by status, caste or background
Wanting an image of inner spaciousness for meditation

bg.13.8.context: Krishna has described the 'field' (the body-mind and its changes) and is now listing the qualities that make up true knowledge, about twenty in all, over five verses ending with 'the opposite of this is ignorance'. This verse opens that list; the next verses add dispassion, absence of ego, seeing the pain of birth, death, age and illness, and non-clinging to family and home.
bg.13.8.core_teaching: Knowledge, for the Gita, is shown in character: humility, no pretence, non-harm, patience, honesty, respect for one's teacher, purity, steadiness and self-restraint are themselves what knowing means.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Glosses each quality. Humility is lack of self-esteem; patience is staying unmoved when wronged. Purity is outer (water and earth) and inner (clearing attachment). Steadiness means putting all effort into the path of liberation alone.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Reads humility as not slighting good people and simplicity as piety without show. Harmlessness covers word, thought and deed, and steadiness is unshakable confidence in scripture's spiritual teaching. Self-control turns the mind from other pursuits.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Opens 13.7-11, which list the means to know the self as distinct from the field. Humility means not boasting of one's virtues; harmlessness means not causing pain; purity is both outer and inner.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: These qualities make up wisdom or lead to it; where all are present, self-knowledge has dawned. He gives long practical glosses, for instance on humility as shunning praise and on hypocrisy as wanting to seem what one is not.

bg.13.8.practical_reading: Teachers use the list as a self-check, especially in success: true learning shows up as humility, honesty and patience rather than as status or display.
misreadings: Patience and humility aren't silence in the face of mistreatment (as our misuse note says).
Not a call to blind obedience; 'serving the teacher' assumes a genuine teacher of truth.
cautions: 'Service of the teacher' can be exploited in abusive guru settings; keep it to respect and learning.
not_for: someone being mistreated by an authority figure, if read as 'be patient and serve'

bg.13.9.context: Krishna has just called the body the 'field' and the self its 'knower', and now lists about twenty traits that together he calls knowledge: humility, patience, purity, steadiness and so on. This verse adds dispassion toward sense pleasures, freedom from ego, and repeated reflection on what birth, death, old age and illness involve. The list ends by calling everything opposite to it ignorance, and Krishna then turns to what is to be known.
bg.13.9.core_teaching: Knowledge shows itself as a changed relationship to pleasure and to the self-image: a person who honestly reflects on what embodied life involves loses the compulsive pull of sense pleasures and turns inward. The reflection is a means to dispassion, not an end in itself.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Dispassion toward pleasures seen and unseen. Reflect on the evil in birth, death, old age (decline, contempt), sickness and pain; or: these are miseries because they cause pain. This breeds indifference to bodily pleasure and turns the senses inward.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Dispassion is distaste for what is not the self, seeing its defects; non-egoism is not taking the body for the self or claiming what is not 'mine'. Reflection: while embodied, birth, death, ageing and disease are unavoidable.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Takes 7-11 as one list of means to knowing the pure self; 'seeing' means repeatedly pondering the misery and evil bound up with birth, death, old age and sickness.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The wise person's senses no longer run after objects and he does not even like to talk about them; egoism is the thought 'I am superior to all'; he never forgets the troubles of birth, ageing and sickness.

bg.13.9.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a reality check: remembering that bodies age and fall ill loosens the grip of status and constant gratification and makes room for what lasts. Sivananda defines the ego to be dropped very concretely, as the feeling 'I am better than everyone'.
misreadings: Not a call to despise the body or to dwell morbidly on death and disease.
Not saying pleasure is evil; the point is freedom from its compulsive pull.
Not a claim that life is only suffering; Shankara says birth and the rest are painful because they cause pain, not in their own nature.
cautions: Names death, old age and disease directly; for someone newly diagnosed, caring for a dying parent, or freshly bereaved, 'reflect on the defect of illness' can feel cold.
For readers prone to health anxiety or depressive rumination, contemplating disease and death may amplify distress; frame as perspective, not as an exercise to dwell on.
not_for: Fresh grief or a new serious diagnosis
Health anxiety or obsessive fears about illness
Someone already anhedonic or depressed for whom 'turn away from pleasure' reads as confirmation
speaks_to: Restlessness from chasing pleasure, novelty or status and still feeling empty
Ego bruises and the need to look important
Midlife or ageing reflections: what actually matters when the body changes
Wanting to simplify and live with fewer cravings

bg.14.12.context: Krishna gives the signs by which a person can tell which guna is dominant: when clarity and knowledge shine through the senses, sattva has grown (14.11); this verse gives the signs of rajas; the next gives those of tamas. He goes on to say what each leads to at death and as fruit.
bg.14.12.core_teaching: Greed, compulsive busyness, endless new ventures, inner restlessness and craving are the signs that rajas has taken over. They are diagnostic signs to notice, not a verdict on action itself.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Greed is wanting to take others' property; activity is action in general; unrest is giving vent to joy, attachment and the like; desire is thirst for all things in general. These are the marks of rajas predominating.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Greed is close-fistedness with one's own money; activity is busyness without definite purpose; undertaking is fruit-seeking work; disquiet is restlessness of the senses; craving is for sense-objects. Seeing these, infer that rajas is ascendant.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Greed is desire for wealth that keeps growing however much is gained; undertakings are efforts like building houses; restlessness is the constant 'after this I'll do that'; desire is wanting whatever one sees, good or bad.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Greed includes wanting more wealth though one has enough; restlessness is 'I'll do this, then that, then a third': desire, will and action never end.

bg.14.12.practical_reading: A close fit for modern burnout: the to-do list that never ends, starting new projects before finishing old ones, and wanting more as soon as one gets something. Teachers suggest noticing these signs early and pausing before acting on them.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of work or ambition; the Gita elsewhere commands action.
Not saying all new projects are bad; the issue is compulsion and restlessness.
cautions: Generally safe. Avoid making a reader feel judged for having to work long hours out of necessity.
not_for: Someone in poverty or financial distress for whom 'greed' framing about earning would be unfair
speaks_to: A mind that won't switch off at night

bg.14.13.context: Third in a set of three verses giving recognisable signs of each guna: sattva (14.11), rajas (14.12) and here tamas. Krishna then describes where a person goes at death depending on which guna prevails.
bg.14.13.core_teaching: When tamas grows, the mind loses clarity, effort dries up, attention slips and judgement becomes confused. Recognising these signs lets a person see what state they are in.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Darkness is absence of discrimination; inertness, its result, is extreme inactivity; heedlessness and error are also effects of that darkness. These mark tamas predominating.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Obscurity is absence of understanding; inertness is disinclination to work; heedlessness is attention turned toward wrongdoing; error is the intellect's tendency to see things distorted. Where these are rife, infer tamas is ascendant.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Darkness is lack of discrimination, inactivity is absence of effort, inadvertence is not remembering one's duty, and delusion is a mistaken resolve. By these signs know tamas has increased.

bg.14.13.practical_reading: Used as a mirror for foggy, stuck periods: noticing 'I can't see clearly, I'm not starting anything, I keep missing things' is itself the first bit of clarity. Teachers pair it with small, concrete steps.
misreadings: Not a diagnosis of anyone's character.
Not identical to depression; overlapping symptoms need care, not moral judgement.
cautions: The signs (fog, inertia, confusion) closely resemble clinical depression, grief and burnout; never imply the reader is 'tamasic' or to blame.
Sivananda's commentary says tamas must be destroyed at all costs; avoid that tone with distressed readers.
not_for: Someone in depression, grief or burnout
A reader who already feels like a failure
speaks_to: Wanting language to observe one's own low states

bg.14.22.context: Arjuna has asked how to recognise someone who has gone beyond the three gunas, how such a person behaves, and how they get there. Krishna's answer runs through 14.26; this first verse gives an inner sign. Sridhara notes Arjuna had asked a similar question about the person of steady wisdom in chapter 2.
bg.14.22.core_teaching: One who has gone beyond the gunas neither resents clarity, restlessness or dullness when they arise, nor craves them when they pass. The mark is an inner freedom from aversion and longing toward one's own changing states.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: The unknowing resent these states: 'tamas deludes me', 'rajas pulls me from my true nature', 'even sattva binds me to happiness'. The one beyond the gunas neither resents nor longs for them; only he can perceive this mark.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Lucidity, activity and folly are the effects of the three gunas; the sign of one beyond them is not hating them when they arise toward unwanted things and not longing for them when they are absent toward wanted things.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Though the steady sage was described in chapter 2, Arjuna wants detail, so six verses follow. This one gives a sign known only to oneself: not hating the gunas' effects as they arise, nor wanting them when they cease.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Answers Arjuna's first question; when sattva shines the sage is not proud of his learning, and when called to act for the world he acts without aversion.

bg.14.22.practical_reading: Modern teachers read it as a way to relate to moods: low days and high days both come and go, and fighting the low or clinging to the high adds a second layer of suffering. Notice the state without hating it or chasing it.
misreadings: Not 'feel nothing' or suppress emotion.
Not a reason to ignore persistent low mood that needs care.
cautions: Gentle and broadly safe; still, a reader in clinical depression should not hear 'just don't mind it'.
not_for: Someone in acute crisis needing practical help rather than acceptance language
speaks_to: Mood swings and frustration with one's own states
Chasing peak experiences and feeling flat afterwards

bg.14.23.context: Part of Krishna's answer (14.22-26) to Arjuna's question about the person beyond the gunas. After the inner sign in 14.22, this verse begins describing how such a person conducts himself. It continues with equanimity in pleasure and pain, praise and blame.
bg.14.23.core_teaching: The one beyond the gunas stays like a neutral witness, not pushed around by the play of moods and circumstances, knowing that these are nature's movements and not the self.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Like a neutral who takes no side, the self-knowing renunciate does not swerve from discrimination; thinking 'the gunas, turned into body, senses and objects, act on one another', he stays unshaken in his own nature.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Delighting in seeing the self, he is indifferent to all else; unagitated by the desires and aversions the gunas produce, he reflects that it is their nature to display themselves, keeps quiet, and does not act at their prompting.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Begins the signs others can see, answering 'how does he behave?': he rests like a witness, not shaken from his nature by pleasure and pain, knowing 'I have no connection with these', steady and unwavering.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: He is like a spectator at a match or a play, or the sky unmoved when the wind blows, free of likes and dislikes as the gunas come and go.

bg.14.23.practical_reading: Teachers connect it to witness practice in meditation and daily life: stepping back half a pace from a surge of anger or anxiety and saying 'this is a state passing through' before reacting.
misreadings: Not emotional numbness or not caring about people.
Not passivity in the face of wrong; Arjuna is still asked to act.
cautions: For readers who dissociate or feel detached after trauma, 'be unconcerned' could reinforce disconnection; frame as steadiness, not distance.
not_for: Someone already emotionally numb or dissociated
A reader who needs to feel and express grief
speaks_to: Being swept along by moods and reactions

bg.14.24.context: Arjuna has asked (14.21) how one who has gone beyond the three qualities (gunas) lives and how he gets there. Krishna describes such a person (14.22-25): not resenting the qualities' moods nor craving them, sitting like a witness, and, in this verse, the same in pain and pleasure, praise and blame. In 14.26 he names the way: unwavering devotion.
bg.14.24.core_teaching: One who has gone beyond the play of moods rests in the self, so pain and pleasure, wealth and worthlessness, praise and blame no longer throw them off balance.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Describes the self-knower who stands like a neutral bystander while the qualities act on one another as body, senses and objects. He stays in his own nature and does not take himself to be the doer.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Pleasure and pain are alike to him because he abides in his real nature. Hence earth, stone and gold have equal worth to him, and he is calm before praise or blame.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Like a post in the ground, to which night and day mean nothing, the sage resting in the Self is above the pairs of opposites. Praise and blame cannot move him.

bg.14.24.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to success and failure: let praise and criticism pass through without defining you, and stay rooted in who you are rather than in how you are rated.
misreadings: Not indifference to people or to doing good work.
Not 'money doesn't matter' as a practical rule; it describes inner freedom from being ruled by gain and loss.
cautions: Ramanuja's example (staying undistracted by a son's birth or death) would be painful for a grieving reader; do not use in grief contexts.
not_for: fresh grief or loss
someone told to 'not care' about real injustice

bg.14.25.context: Close of Krishna's description of the person beyond the gunas (14.22-25): even in honour and insult, equal to friend and foe, having let go of self-serving projects. Krishna then answers the last question, how one goes beyond the gunas, with unswerving devotion (14.26).
bg.14.25.core_teaching: Someone free of the gunas is not lifted by honour or crushed by insult, treats friend and foe alike, and no longer launches projects for personal gain. What a seeker practises with effort becomes natural in the realised.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Some neutrals seem to others to favour one side; he appears the same to both. He gives up all works for seen or unseen results except bodily upkeep. These traits are discipline while effortful, marks of realisation when natural.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The same in honour and dishonour and toward friend and foe, habituated to renouncing undertakings aimed at visible or invisible results; one who lives so is said to have transcended the gunas.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Balanced in honour and dishonour and the same to friend and foe, he rests in his own nature as existence, knowledge and bliss, untouched by the play of the gunas.

bg.14.25.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to approval-seeking: steadiness that doesn't depend on praise or criticism, and fairness that doesn't change with who is on 'our side'. It is a description of maturity to grow toward, not a rule to fake.
misreadings: Not 'tolerate disrespect or abuse'; it is about not being shaken inside.
Not 'stop all work or ambition'; Shankara is describing a renunciate's ideal, and householder readings stress letting go of self-seeking.
Not 'treat an abuser the same as a friend' in practical decisions.
cautions: Ramanuja's gloss on 14.24-25 cites even-mindedness at the birth or death of one's children; do not use that framing with bereaved parents.
A reader being bullied or abused should not hear this as 'just stay equal'.
not_for: Someone currently being abused or harassed
Bereaved parents
speaks_to: Sensitivity to criticism or praise at work or online

bg.14.8.context: Krishna is describing how each of the three gunas binds the embodied self: sattva through attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas through attachment to action, and here tamas through heedlessness, laziness and sleep. The next verses summarise and then give the signs by which each guna can be recognised.
bg.14.8.core_teaching: Dullness clouds judgement and holds a person down through inattention, inertia and sinking into sleep. Naming it is the first step to rising out of it.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Very brief: tamas, the third guna, is born of unwisdom and causes delusion, that is, non-discrimination, in all embodied beings, binding them through heedlessness, indolence and sloth.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Ignorance is the reverse of right perception, seeing a thing as other than it is. Heedlessness is attention drifting from the task at hand; sloth is inability to engage in work; sleep is the senses, then the mind, shutting down.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Tamas comes from nature's concealing power and so confounds every embodied being. Inadvertence is negligence, laziness is lack of effort, and sleep is the mind shutting down through fatigue.

bg.14.8.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a self-check on drift: scrolling, putting things off, sleeping to escape. The remedy suggested is small, steady attention and action rather than self-blame.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of rest or sleep; nidra here is sleep used as escape or dullness.
Not a moral label for people who are ill, exhausted or depressed.
cautions: Symptoms of depression, burnout, chronic illness, medication side effects and new-parent exhaustion overlap with 'laziness and sleep'; never frame these as tamas or a character flaw.
Sivananda's commentary is harsh in tone; do not echo that harshness to a struggling reader.
not_for: Someone in depression or burnout
Chronic fatigue or illness
Sleep-deprived new parents
speaks_to: Using sleep, screens or substances to avoid life
Wanting to understand one's own sluggish patterns without shame

bg.15.15.context: Krishna is describing how his power sustains the world: as the light of sun, moon and fire, as the force holding up the earth, as the digestive fire in bodies. Here he moves inward: he sits in every heart and is the source of memory and knowledge. He then distinguishes the perishable, the imperishable and the Supreme Person beyond both.
bg.15.15.core_teaching: The divine is present within every being, and the very capacities to remember, know and forget arise from that inner presence. The whole Veda points to this one reality.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: As inner ruler in the heart, centre of all consciousness and impulse, the Lord is the source of memory, of knowledge by perception, inference, scripture and yoga, and of its loss (or, reading apohana otherwise, of reasoning).

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: As inner ruler in every heart, the Lord causes memory of past experience, sense-knowledge and their loss; he is known in the Vedas as the various gods, started the Vedanta teaching lineage, and knows the Vedas' meaning.

bg.15.15.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that the divine is not far away but as close as one's own thinking and remembering; insight and even forgetting are held within a larger presence. It suits practices of turning inward to the heart.
misreadings: Not a claim that God causes someone's dementia or memory loss as punishment.
Not about reading the Vedas as a requirement for knowing God.
cautions: Shankara (echoed by Sivananda) ties loss of memory and knowledge to bad deeds. Never use this verse or that reading with someone facing dementia, brain injury or memory loss in themselves or a parent; it can read as karmic blame.
not_for: Dementia, Alzheimer's or memory-loss situations
Someone ashamed of forgetting or cognitive decline
speaks_to: Wanting an inward focus for prayer or meditation
Students and seekers wondering where insight comes from

bg.15.5.context: Krishna has pictured worldly existence as an upside-down ashvattha tree, told Arjuna to cut it with the axe of non-attachment and to seek refuge in the primal Person. This verse describes the people who actually reach that goal. The next verse describes the goal itself, a light beyond sun and moon from which no one returns.
bg.15.5.core_teaching: Those who reach the lasting goal are marked by freedom from pride and confusion, victory over clinging, steady inner focus, the fading of cravings, and release from being tossed between pleasure and pain.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: 'Ever dwelling in the self' means constantly contemplating the Supreme Self's nature; with desires gone without taint they become renunciates; the eternal goal they reach is the Lord's own being.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Those who take the Lord as refuge shed love of the non-self, conquer attachment to guna-born pleasures, are absorbed in self-knowledge and freed from joy and grief; for them every stage is accomplished by his agency and easily traversed.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Pride is stiff egoism; moha is failing to tell the real from the unreal; those who stay free of likes and dislikes amid pleasant and unpleasant things have conquered attachment.

bg.15.5.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a portrait of inner freedom to grow toward: less pride, less clinging, fewer compulsive wants, less being thrown about by good and bad days. Ramanuja softens it: for those who take refuge, these stages are carried through by grace and become easy.
misreadings: Not a checklist one must complete before being worthy of grace; Ramanuja reads it as made possible by refuge.
Not a call to stop loving family; 'attachment' is the possessive, clinging kind.
cautions: Sridhara names attachment to children as the fault overcome; avoid that example with new or grieving parents.
not_for: Someone in fresh loss for whom 'free from attachment' sounds like 'stop loving'
speaks_to: Wanting a picture of spiritual maturity
Tired of being ruled by pride or approval
Someone on a long practice who needs a sense of direction

bg.15.7.context: Having described the supreme abode from which there is no return, Krishna explains who it is that keeps returning: the individual soul, an eternal part of him, which gathers the mind and senses. The following verses describe it carrying them from body to body as the wind carries scent, and say the deluded cannot see this while yogis can.
bg.15.7.core_teaching: Each living soul is an eternal part of the divine that, while embodied, gathers mind and senses around itself. The schools differ on how literally 'part' is meant, but all read it as a statement of the soul's divine origin and dignity.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: The jiva is a portion of the Supreme like the sun reflected in water or space in a jar: when water or jar goes, it rejoins the whole for good. The partless Lord has 'parts' only through imagined adjuncts.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: The soul is an eternal portion of the Lord; enmeshed in beginningless karma it becomes god, human and so on, limited in knowledge and power, dragging the senses about; treading the path of 15.4-5 it regains its nature.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: If those who reach God never return, yet all merge in him in dissolution and deep sleep, who transmigrates? A part of the Lord that through ignorance has become the embodied soul, drawing the senses back to the world.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Explains how the individual soul arises: a ray of the Lord enters nature, draws the five senses and mind to itself and takes a body; uses the image of the sun reflected in water.

bg.15.7.practical_reading: Teachers use it to affirm the worth of every person: whoever you are, you are not an accident or a stranger to the divine but a part of it. It is also used to explain why spiritual life feels like returning home.
misreadings: Not 'I am God' in an ego-inflating sense; even Shankara's reading dissolves the ego rather than enlarging it.
Not a settled single doctrine: Advaita and Vishishtadvaita read 'part' very differently.
cautions: Introduces the soul moving from body to body (15.8); in grief this may be heard as a claim about a loved one's rebirth, which can comfort some and unsettle others.
not_for: Fresh grief if the reading pivots to rebirth
speaks_to: Feeling far from God or spiritually homeless
Questions about what a soul is

bg.16.1.context: Chapter 16 opens with no question from Arjuna: having just said that whoever understands his teaching becomes wise, Krishna sorts people into those fit and unfit for it. Verses 16.1-3 list the 'divine endowment', 16.4 lists the opposite, and 16.5 tells Arjuna which side he is on.
bg.16.1.core_teaching: The qualities that lead to freedom start with fearlessness and an honest, clean mind, and include generosity, self-restraint, study, discipline and integrity. They are a portrait of the person ready for wisdom.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Purity of heart is dealing without deception or falsehood, doing business honestly. Knowledge is learning from scripture and teacher; yoga is making it direct experience. Fearlessness, purity and this steadfastness are the divine nature par excellence.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Fear is pain at foreseeing loss of what is dear or arrival of what is hated; fearlessness is its absence. Charity is giving honestly earned wealth to deserving recipients. Uprightness is consistency of thought, speech and deed toward others.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The chapter distinguishes the fit from the unfit seeker of knowledge. Fearlessness is absence of fear; purity of heart is perfect serenity of mind; charity is properly sharing one's food; study may also mean repeating holy names; uprightness is straightforwardness.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The divine and demonic natures mentioned in chapter 9 are now described in detail; the first verses draw the line between the god-like person and the asura.

bg.16.1.practical_reading: Used as a character inventory: courage, honesty in dealings, generosity, discipline, study and straightforwardness. Teachers often start with fearlessness because the others are hard to practise while afraid.
misreadings: Not a list one must fully possess before beginning spiritual life; Shankara's own commentary on 14.25 notes such qualities are practised before they become natural.
Not a test to sort other people into good and bad.
cautions: Generally safe and encouraging. Avoid using it to shame an anxious reader for not being 'fearless'.
not_for: Someone already in harsh self-judgement who will read it as a list of failures
speaks_to: Wanting to build character or integrity
Starting a new chapter and choosing values
Parents thinking about the virtues they hope to model

bg.16.11.context: Part of Krishna's long portrait of the 'demonic' mindset (16.6-20): people who deny any moral order and live only for gratification. This verse describes their endless anxieties and their conviction that pleasure is all there is. It leads into their schemes for wealth (16.12) and their boasting thoughts (16.13-15).
bg.16.11.core_teaching: A life that treats gratification as the only goal is not carefree; it is consumed by endless worry that lasts until death, because there is always more to secure and nothing beyond it.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: They give themselves up to cares without measure that end only with death, and are convinced that enjoying sense-objects such as sound is the highest human end, with nothing beyond it.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Death waits for them today or tomorrow, yet they cling to schemes so vast they would need until the world's dissolution to complete, revel in desire as life's summit, and are sure nothing lies beyond.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Always worried with innumerable cares until death, holding sense-gratification as life's highest aim; he links this to the materialist aphorisms of Brihaspati that pleasure is the only human end and the conscious body is the self.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Their minds are engrossed in acquiring and preserving countless sense objects, beset by worries and anxieties, firmly believing that enjoyment is everything.

bg.16.11.practical_reading: Teachers use it to name the anxiety that comes with consumerism and status-chasing: the more one lives for acquisition, the more there is to worry about. Ramanuja's image of planning for centuries while life is short is a sharp mirror for workaholism.
misreadings: Not a description of people with anxiety disorders; the worry here comes from a worldview that pleasure is everything.
Not a condemnation of enjoyment as such.
cautions: Part of the 'demonic nature' passage; a reader with anxiety must never be told their worry makes them demonic.
Mentions death.
not_for: Someone with clinical anxiety
A reader already ashamed of worrying
speaks_to: Consumerism and the treadmill of wanting more
A sense that success has brought more worry, not less
Questioning whether material life is 'all there is'

bg.16.12.context: Continues the description of the demonic mindset (16.6-20): after endless worry and the belief that pleasure is everything (16.11), such people are dragged by countless expectations and pile up wealth by any means. Their inner monologue follows in 16.13-15.
bg.16.12.core_teaching: When desire and anger become one's refuge, a person is pulled in every direction by countless expectations and starts gathering wealth by whatever means, just for gratification.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Bound by a hundred bands of false hope they are pulled here and there; they gather wealth for sensual enjoyment, not for dharma, and by unjust means such as taking other people's wealth.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Fettered by the bonds of hopes, wholly devoted to cultivating and gratifying passion as life's highest call, they long to amass riches by illegitimate methods to feed it.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Expectation itself is the tie, a hundred of them dragging them hither and thither; with lust and anger as their supreme resort they strive to heap up wealth by theft and other foul means.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Bound by expectations and craving every kind of object, they amass wealth only for pleasure, never for righteous ends, and can become merciless.

bg.16.12.practical_reading: Used to examine how expectations tie us down and how the drive for more can quietly bend ethics at work or in business.
misreadings: Not 'give up all hope'; 'asha' here is craving-driven expectation, not hope in the sense that sustains a struggling person.
Not a condemnation of earning money honestly.
cautions: For a reader in despair, 'hope is a noose' could be devastating if quoted alone; avoid with anyone hopeless or in crisis.
not_for: Anyone in despair or hopelessness
Someone in financial hardship who may hear it as judgement on wanting money
speaks_to: Ethical pressure at work to cut corners
Greed and anger feeding each other

bg.16.13.context: Krishna gives voice to the demonic mind (16.13-15): what I gained today, what I'll get tomorrow, enemies I've beaten, my wealth and birth. 16.16 says such people, deluded, fall into a foul hell.
bg.16.13.core_teaching: The acquisitive mind lives in a running tally of 'got this, will get that, mine, and more to come', a loop that never arrives at enough.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Their thought runs: this I have gained today, this desire I will attain, this is mine, and next year this wealth too will be mine, and I will be known as a wealthy man.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: The stress is on 'by me': land, sons and money were all gained by my own exertion, with no unseen cause; whatever I desire I will fulfil myself, and I will earn more by my own effort.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: This begins four verses describing their 'fanciful kingdom', which, construed with verses 15-16, ends in their falling into hell; 'desire' means whatever pleases the mind.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Imagines their inner voice: next year this wealth too shall be mine and people will call me lord; such people become conceited through their wealth.

bg.16.13.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a mirror for the 'more' loop of modern life: next promotion, next purchase, next milestone. Ramanuja adds a second mirror: the belief that everything we have is self-made.
