misreadings: Not saying planning or saving is wrong; the problem is a mind that defines itself by accumulation.
Krishna is quoting, not endorsing, these words.
cautions: Belongs to the 'demonic' passage that ends in hell imagery (16.16); keep the reading on self-reflection, not condemnation.
not_for: Someone in poverty or job loss for whom any gain is survival
speaks_to: Self-made pride that leaves no room for gratitude

bg.16.15.context: End of the quoted inner monologue (16.13-15) of the arrogant mind: wealth gained, enemies slain, and here pride in riches and birth, even religious acts used for display. Krishna then says such people, caught in delusion, fall into a foul hell (16.16).
bg.16.15.core_teaching: Pride in wealth and pedigree can swallow even good acts: worship and charity become tools for outdoing others and enjoying acclaim. Krishna calls this a delusion born of ignorance.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: 'By myself I am rich and well-born; who else won every happiness by his own effort? I will sacrifice, give and be merry, with no need of the Lord's grace': so think those blinded by ignorance.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Rich and aristocratic, they mean to win a greater name than other sacrificers through their rituals, to give gifts to flatterers and to enjoy themselves; ignorance has filled them with false notions.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Imagines the boast in full: richer than the god of wealth, of nobler family than any; who in the world could equal me?

bg.16.15.practical_reading: Used to examine the motive behind generosity and religiosity: giving for applause, philanthropy for image, piety for status. Also a warning about pride of family, caste or class.
misreadings: Not saying wealth or good birth are bad in themselves.
Not discouraging giving; it questions giving for self-display.
cautions: Part of the 'demonic nature' section with hell imagery around it; frame as self-examination.
not_for: Someone already struggling with low self-worth
speaks_to: Philanthropy or social-media giving for image

bg.16.17.context: After the arrogant inner monologue (16.13-15) and its fall (16.16), Krishna describes how such people practise religion: rituals in name only, done for display and without regard to the proper way. He goes on to say they hate the divine present in themselves and others (16.18).
bg.16.17.core_teaching: Religion done from pride becomes performance: rituals for the name and image, without humility, sincerity or care for how it should be done.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Self-honoured: they credit themselves with every good quality, but the righteous do not; their sacrifices ignore the parts and obligations scripture enjoins.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: They flatter themselves, think themselves perfect and so do nothing, puffed up by pride of wealth, learning and birth; they perform sacrifices merely to be known as 'a sacrificer', for show and without rule.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Their resolve 'I will sacrifice' (16.15) is driven by ostentation and conceit, not pure motives: glorified only by themselves, not humble, they sacrifice in name only, or to gain titles, showily rather than with devotion.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: They rate themselves very highly but are not honoured by the pious; they have no humility or meekness.

bg.16.17.practical_reading: A check on religious or charitable display: grand functions for status, donations for the plaque, piety performed for social standing. Teachers contrast it with quiet, humble practice.
misreadings: Not condemning ritual or public worship as such; the target is pride and hypocrisy.
Not a licence to judge others' piety as fake.
cautions: Easy to use for judging others; keep the reading turned inward.
not_for: A reader who already feels their faltering practice is 'fake'

bg.16.2.context: Second of three verses (16.1-3) listing the divine qualities. After this list, Krishna describes the opposite, 'demonic', traits and then reassures Arjuna that he was born with the divine ones.
bg.16.2.core_teaching: A good nature shows in how we treat others: not harming, speaking truly, calming anger, not gossiping, feeling for those who suffer, not grasping, being gentle, having a sense of shame about wrongdoing, and being steady.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Truth is speaking of things as they are, avoiding the unpleasant and the false. Absence of anger is suppressing anger that arises when struck or reviled. Compassion is for the suffering; steadiness is not moving tongue or limbs in vain.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Truth is speech that is true and beneficial to all; wrathlessness is no resentment toward those who cause pain; sympathy is feeling others' grief; gentleness is the opposite of hard-heartedness; modesty is shame at doing what is unworthy.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Truthfulness is speaking as one perceived; absence of anger is the mind unstirred even when beaten; renunciation here is generosity; no slander means no backbiting; kindness is toward the distressed; steadiness is avoiding useless activity.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Ahimsa is non-injury in thought, word and deed; truth means speaking things as they are without harsh words or lies.

bg.16.2.practical_reading: A practical ethic for speech and relationships: tell the truth kindly, don't gossip, let anger settle before acting, notice who is suffering. Teachers often pick one quality a week to practise.
misreadings: 'Freedom from anger' does not mean never feeling anger or never standing up to injustice; it is about not being driven by it.
'Modesty' (hri) is shame at wrongdoing, not shame about oneself.
cautions: Someone suffering abuse should not hear 'no anger, be gentle' as an instruction to accept it.
not_for: A reader in an abusive relationship who needs permission to protect themselves first
speaks_to: Wanting to be kinder in speech

bg.16.21.context: After describing the demonic nature and its downward path, Krishna distils it: desire, anger and greed are the three gates to ruin, and should be given up. The next verse promises that one freed from them does what is truly good and reaches the highest; he then makes scripture the guide for what to do and avoid.
bg.16.21.core_teaching: Desire, anger and greed are the root of all the destructive traits just described; they ruin a person's capacity for any real good, so they are to be abandoned.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: By merely entering this gate the self is ruined, that is, made fit for no human end whatever; since lust, wrath and greed are so ruinous, everyone should abandon them. The next verse praises that abandonment.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: The demonic nature is itself the hell; lust, wrath and greed are the door, the cause leading to it and the ruin of souls. Fling these three far away, since they lead to the most dreadful hell.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Of all the demonic vices described, these three are the basis of the rest; they lead to lower births, so they should be shunned by all means.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Calls them highway robbers and the three fountain-heads of misery, enemies of peace, devotion and knowledge: when they arise one loses balance and discrimination.

bg.16.21.practical_reading: One of the most quoted self-help verses in Indian homes: watch three triggers, craving, anger and greed, because almost every regrettable action comes through one of them.
misreadings: Not saying that feeling desire or anger makes you damned; it is about being ruled by them.
'Kama' is craving or lust, not every healthy wish.
cautions: Hell imagery can frighten readers with religious anxiety or scrupulosity; use the softer 'self-ruin' framing.
Anger at genuine injustice or abuse should not be shamed.
not_for: Someone with scrupulosity or fear of damnation
An abuse survivor whose anger is part of healing
speaks_to: Wanting a simple rule for self-control

bg.16.22.context: The positive side of 16.21: freed from desire, anger and greed, a person does what is good for the self and reaches the highest goal. Krishna then says that one who sets scripture aside and follows impulse reaches neither happiness nor the goal (16.23-24).
bg.16.22.core_teaching: Once free of desire, anger and greed, a person finally does what is genuinely good for themselves, which those three had been blocking, and this leads to the highest goal.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Freed from lust, wrath and greed, the gates to a hell of pain and delusion, a person does good to himself, since what blocked him is gone, and so even attains liberation. Scripture is the authority for renouncing and practising.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: These three doors of darkness breed wrong notions about the Lord; one who shakes them off can work for the soul's good, gains true knowledge of the Lord, acts in harmony with him and reaches him.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: States the special result of renouncing the three: rid of these gates to darkness, a person practises austerity, yoga and other disciplines that are good for him, and thereby attains liberation.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Once these gates are abandoned the way opens: the aspirant finds the company of sages, receives and practises instruction, hears, reflects, meditates and realises the Self.

bg.16.22.practical_reading: A hopeful companion to 16.21: when a craving or anger loosens its grip, the good thing you've been meaning to do suddenly becomes possible. Freedom from the three is presented as a release, not a loss.
misreadings: Not a promise that once you've slipped you are excluded; the verse is about the effect of release whenever it happens.
cautions: Generally safe; mild religious framing ('highest goal').
not_for: No strong contraindications
speaks_to: Recovery from addiction or anger patterns
Wanting to do good but feeling blocked

bg.16.3.context: Last of the three verses (16.1-3) listing the divine endowment, closing with 'these belong to one born for the divine nature'. Krishna next lists the demonic traits (hypocrisy, arrogance, anger, harshness) and then reassures Arjuna.
bg.16.3.core_teaching: Strength and gentleness belong together in a good character: boldness and endurance alongside forgiveness, freedom from malice and freedom from arrogance.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Tejas means energy, not bright skin. Forgiveness is being unaffected when beaten or reviled, unlike absence of anger, which suppresses it once arisen. Fortitude lifts a drooping body and senses. Pride is thinking oneself worthy of high honour.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Lustre is a presence proof against the attacks of evil men; forgiveness is no vengeful feeling toward those who make one suffer; fortitude is continuing to do right under the heaviest misfortune; non-interference is not obstructing others' purposes.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Boldness is courage; forgiveness is not getting angry when humiliated; fortitude steadies a mind drooping under pain. These twenty-six traits from fearlessness on belong to one born for divine wealth, one for whom well-being is in store.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Tejas is the aspirant's bold, unbroken march toward the Self, which nothing can tempt or slow and which overcomes the downward pull of tamas.

bg.16.3.practical_reading: Teachers pair forgiveness with strength: you can refuse to be dominated and still not carry hatred. Fortitude is presented as a learnable inner muscle that gets you through exhausting stretches.
misreadings: Forgiveness is not an obligation to stay in harm's way or to excuse wrongdoing; Ramanuja's 'not being overpowered by the wicked' sits right beside it.
Not saying the forgiving person never feels hurt.
cautions: For abuse survivors, lead with tejas and dhriti (strength, endurance) rather than with forgiveness.
not_for: Someone currently being harmed who may hear 'forgive' as 'stay'
speaks_to: Struggling to forgive without becoming a doormat
Exhaustion and needing endurance (caregivers, exams, long projects)

bg.16.4.context: Chapter 16 opens with a long list of divine qualities (16.1-3: fearlessness, purity, compassion, forgiveness, freedom from excessive pride). This verse gives the contrasting demonic set. Krishna then says the divine qualities lead to freedom and the demonic to bondage, and reassures Arjuna not to worry: he is born with the divine ones (16.5).
bg.16.4.core_teaching: Hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and lack of discernment are the traits that lead a person into bondage; naming them helps one recognise and drop them.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Ostentation is pretending to be righteous; arrogance is pride of learning, wealth or connections. Insolence is false or flattering speech, and ignorance is misjudging one's duties.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Defines each trait: piety displayed to win flattery; exultation in pleasures that blinds right and wrong; self-importance without merit; wanting others to suffer; contempt for the good. The 'non-divine' are those who defy the Lord's laws.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Gives brief glosses: ostentation as sanctimony, arrogance as pride in wealth or learning, rudeness as harshness, ignorance as lack of discrimination. These mark one born to the demonic endowment.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Calls religious hypocrisy the worst kind of pretence. The arrogant cannot bear to see others prosper, and the ignorant cannot tell right from wrong. Calling Arjuna 'Partha' signals that he has none of these traits.

bg.16.4.practical_reading: Teachers use the list as a mirror, especially when things go well: success can quietly breed show, arrogance and harshness, and noticing them early keeps one free.
misreadings: A mirror for yourself, not a label to throw at others (as our misuse note says).

Not a fixed, inborn type of person; for a modern reader treat the list as tendencies to notice in oneself (an application: the classical commentators describe a type, Ramanuja as those who defy the Lord's laws).
cautions: 'Demonic' and 'born with' are loaded words; avoid implying a reader is inherently bad.
16.5 immediately reassures Arjuna; consider echoing that reassurance.
not_for: someone with harsh self-criticism or shame, who may take it as a verdict
judging others
speaks_to: noticing arrogance or harsh speech in oneself

bg.16.5.context: Having listed the divine qualities (16.1-3) and the demonic ones (16.4), Krishna says the first lead to freedom and the second to bondage. Seeing Arjuna anxiously wondering which kind he is, he reassures him. He then describes the demonic mindset at length (16.6-20).
bg.16.5.core_teaching: Good qualities lead toward freedom and their opposites toward bondage; and Krishna gently tells an anxious Arjuna not to worry about which he is, because he is born for the good.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: The divine nature leads to liberation; the demonic and fiendish natures to sure bondage. Seeing Arjuna wonder 'am I demonic or divine?', the Lord says: do not grieve, you are born for the divine lot; happiness lies ahead.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: The divine character is obedience to the Lord's will, leading in time to release; the demonic is violating his commands, leading downward. Seeing Arjuna fear for his own nature, he reassures him: you are Pandu's son, of the divine kind.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: One with divine wealth is fit for the knowledge taught; one with demonic wealth stays bound. Arjuna is perturbed, doubting whether he is fit, and the Lord cheers him: do not sorrow, you are born for divine wealth.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Since Arjuna was already grief-stricken and dejected, Krishna reassures him not to be alarmed by the description of the demonic qualities.

bg.16.5.practical_reading: Teachers use it for the person who worries they are fundamentally bad: the very worry is a sign of conscience. The Lord's first response to self-doubt is reassurance, not a test.
misreadings: Not a licence to label other people 'demonic'.
Not a fixed caste of souls; the chapter is meant to steer conduct.
Not a promise that one need not strive.
cautions: The divine/demonic binary can feed scrupulosity or religious OCD if the reading dwells on the demonic side; keep the focus on reassurance.
not_for: Contexts where the reader wants to judge someone else as 'demonic'
speaks_to: Guilt and fear of being unworthy
Spiritual anxiety after reading harsh teachings
Needing reassurance from a trusted guide

bg.17.15.context: Krishna is describing three kinds of austerity: of body (17.14), speech (this verse) and mind (17.16), before sorting each by the three qualities (17.17-19). It sits in a chapter on how faith shapes food, worship, discipline and giving.
bg.17.15.core_teaching: Disciplined speech is speech that is at once truthful, kind and helpful, and does not wound; together with regular study of sacred texts, this is the 'austerity' of speech.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: All four marks must be present together: speech that is harmless but untrue, or true but harsh, does not count. His example of such speech: 'Be calm, my son; study and practise yoga, it will do you good.'

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Speech austerity means words that hurt no one, spoken truthfully, sweetly and gently, along with regular recitation of scripture.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Glosses the first mark as speech that causes no worry or fear. It must also be true, pleasant to hear and lead to good; Vedic study is included.

bg.17.15.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a filter before speaking, especially in anger: is it true, is it kind, is it helpful, will it wound needlessly? If not, wait or rephrase.
misreadings: Kind speech doesn't mean avoiding hard truths (as our misuse note says); it means saying them without cruelty.
Not mere politeness; truthfulness is required alongside kindness.
cautions: The Manu rule Sivananda quotes ('do not speak an unpleasant truth') can be read as 'stay silent'; for a reader being mistreated, emphasise that truthful, non-cruel speech still includes speaking up.
not_for: someone told to silence legitimate complaints in the name of 'pleasant speech'

bg.17.16.context: Following the austerities of body (17.14) and speech (17.15), Krishna names the austerity of mind. Next (17.17-19) he says these disciplines are sattvic when done with faith and without wanting reward, rajasic when done for show, and tamasic when done with self-torment or to harm others.
bg.17.16.core_teaching: The discipline of the mind is a calm, gentle, quiet, self-restrained and sincere heart; inner austerity is about the quality of one's attention and intentions.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Good-heartedness shows in a bright face. Silence is really control of thought, of which quiet speech is the effect. Purity of nature means honesty of purpose in dealing with others.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Glosses each term: a mind free of anger, a mind that delights in others' happiness, restraint of speech, the mind held on holy objects, and no straying thoughts away from the self.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Serenity is composure; kindliness is freedom from harshness; silence is a sage's practice of meditation. Purity of heart means no deceit in conduct.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: A serene mind is like a lake without a ripple. Silence includes staying calm amid outside disturbance, and purity of nature means freedom from cunning, lust, anger and greed.

bg.17.16.practical_reading: Teachers suggest small practices: a few minutes of quiet, noticing harsh thoughts before they become words, and acting without hidden motives; joy rests on a clear, kind mind.
misreadings: Not emotional suppression; serenity here is clarity, not numbness.
'Silence' does not mean withdrawing from people.
not_for: someone told to stay quiet about harm

bg.17.18.context: Krishna has described austerity of body, speech and mind (17.14-16) and said that when done with faith and no desire for reward it is sattvic (17.17). This verse gives the rajasic kind, done for honour and display; the next gives the tamasic kind. He then turns to the three kinds of giving.
bg.17.18.core_teaching: Discipline undertaken to be praised and honoured, or for show, is driven by rajas; its rewards are unstable and fleeting.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Good reception means people saying 'here is a great ascetic'; honour is rising to greet and bowing; worship is washing feet, adoring and feeding. Done for these and with hypocrisy, it is rajasic and unstable, its effect transient.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Regard in others' minds, praise in their words and worship by their bodies are what it seeks; done for such fruit and to parade, it is rajasic, unstable because ever fearful of falling, and not lasting.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Respect is verbal praise ('he is a man of great austerity'), honour is physical worship such as rising and saluting, adoration includes gaining wealth; such ostentatious austerity is fleeting and unstable.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Penance done without sincere belief, for show and to increase self-importance, so that the world will honour and praise the performer, bears fruit only in this world.

bg.17.18.practical_reading: Used to examine motives behind visible discipline: fasting, fitness, spiritual routines or hard work done mainly for likes, admiration or reputation tend to collapse when the audience disappears.
misreadings: Not saying recognition is evil or that one must hide all practice.
Not condemning discipline; it distinguishes motives.
cautions: Generally safe; avoid implying a reader's struggling practice is fake.
not_for: Someone whose self-worth is fragile and who needs encouragement to keep going
speaks_to: Performing spirituality or fitness on social media
Burnout from effort driven by approval

bg.17.19.context: Third of the three kinds of austerity (17.17-19): after the sattvic (faithful, desireless) and the rajasic (for honour and show), this is the tamasic kind, done from deluded stubbornness, by tormenting oneself or to harm someone. Earlier (17.5-6) Krishna had condemned people who torture the body in fierce austerities not sanctioned by scripture.
bg.17.19.core_teaching: Discipline that comes from deluded stubbornness, that punishes one's own body, or that aims to harm someone else is the darkest kind and does not lead to good.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Mahadeva Sastri gives only the verse here: austerity from a foolish notion, with self-torture, or to ruin another, is tamasic; he moves straight on to the three kinds of gift.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Austerity undertaken by the resolve of the foolish, without regard to one's own capacity, to torture oneself, or to hurt others, is called tamasic.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Austerity practised from foolhardiness born of non-discrimination, with self-torture, or to destroy another, as in black magic, is tamasic.

bg.17.19.practical_reading: Teachers use it against self-punishing discipline: crash fasting, overtraining, sleep deprivation to 'prove' devotion, or efforts driven by spite or rivalry. Ramanuja's 'without regard to one's own capacity' is a good everyday test.
misreadings: Not saying all hard effort is bad; it is about self-torment and harmful intent.
Not a ban on fasting or discipline that fits one's capacity.
cautions: Touches on self-inflicted pain. It can gently support a reader who punishes themselves, but avoid graphic examples (Sivananda lists extreme self-mortifications) and route any mention of self-harm to proper help.
not_for: A reader disclosing self-harm (needs care, not scripture)
Someone with an eating disorder if the reading focuses on fasting
speaks_to: Efforts driven by spite or wanting to beat someone

bg.17.20.context: After the three kinds of austerity, Krishna sorts giving by the three qualities. This verse describes the best (sattvic) gift; the next two describe giving reluctantly or for return (rajasic, 17.21) and giving at the wrong place or time, to the unworthy, or with contempt (tamasic, 17.22).
bg.17.20.core_teaching: The best giving is done simply because giving is right, to someone who cannot repay, with attention to where, when and to whom it will truly help.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Give because giving is a duty, not for reward, to someone who can give nothing back, at the right place and time, to a fit recipient.

bg.17.20.practical_reading: Teachers apply it as giving without strings: give where there is real need, at a time it helps, without wanting thanks or a return, as a natural expression of gratitude.
misreadings: Not 'give only to the deserving' in a judgemental sense.
Not giving to be seen or to earn something; that is the rajasic kind (17.21).
cautions: Classical commentators define the 'worthy recipient' as a learned brahmin and the right place/time as pilgrimage sites and eclipses; use a modern need-based reading (giving to whoever truly needs it) rather than the caste-specific one, and say it is an application. Sridhara names a Brahmin explicitly; Shankara and Sivananda describe a learned, pious recipient.
not_for: someone financially stretched, if read as an obligation to give money
contexts where it would imply some people are unworthy of help

bg.17.21.context: Krishna has just described sattvic giving: given because it ought to be given, to a worthy person who cannot repay, at the right place and time (17.20). This verse gives the rajasic kind; the next gives the tamasic kind (to the unworthy, at the wrong time, with contempt). He then closes the chapter with 'Om tat sat'.
bg.17.21.core_teaching: A gift given to get something back, to earn merit or reward, or given grudgingly is the restless, self-interested kind of giving; it falls short of giving freely because it should be given.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Given hoping the recipient will in time return the service, or that the gift will win some unseen reward, or given reluctantly: such a gift is rajasic.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Gifts given expecting a return, aiming at a reward, or unwillingly; the last includes giving inferior or damaged things while keeping the good for oneself, which betrays the unwillingness.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Given expecting the person to return the service in time, or seeking a fruit such as heaven, or grudgingly: that gift is rajasic.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Includes giving in the hope of public praise, or so that one's sins will be washed away, and feeling grieved at heart after giving.

bg.17.21.practical_reading: Teachers use it to look at the strings attached to our generosity: favours tracked in a ledger, donations for tax or reputation, help given resentfully. The invitation is to give lighter, not to stop giving.
misreadings: Not 'don't give unless your motives are pure'; imperfect giving is still better than none.
Not condemning reciprocity in ordinary relationships.
cautions: Avoid shaming someone who gives out of obligation in a hard family situation.
not_for: Someone being financially exploited who needs to set limits, not give more freely

bg.17.3.context: Arjuna has asked (17.1) about people who worship with faith but ignore scriptural rules: is their state sattvic, rajasic or tamasic? Krishna answers that faith is of three kinds, born of each person's nature (17.2), and here that faith takes the shape of one's inner nature and defines the person. He then shows how worship, food, sacrifice, austerity and giving reveal the three kinds.
bg.17.3.core_teaching: Everyone has faith of some kind, shaped by their inner nature, and that faith in turn shapes who they are. To know a person, look at what they truly trust and give themselves to.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: 'Nature' (sattva) is the mind with its specific past tendencies; each person's faith follows it, and a person is what his faith is. Which faith someone has must be inferred from its effects, chiefly whom they worship (17.4).

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Faith arises toward whatever matches the quality of one's mind (which here implies body and senses too); a person is faith embodied and becomes what he has faith in, so faith in a meritorious act leads to its corresponding fruit.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Faith is sattvic, yet mixed with rajas and tamas it becomes threefold, and by habit past faith reproduces itself. This holds for those living by mere custom; those with scriptural discernment conquer their nature, and their faith is sattvic alone.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: A person's faith shows his character; a man is what his faith has made him, and his conduct is shaped by it.

bg.17.3.practical_reading: Teachers read it as 'you become what you deeply trust': what you give your attention and loyalty to shapes your character. Sridhara's note adds hope: faith can be refined by understanding.
misreadings: Not 'positive thinking makes anything true'.
Not saying a person's nature is fixed forever; Sridhara says discernment can transform it.
Not a judgement on people who are going through doubt.
cautions: Someone in a crisis of faith or doubt could hear 'you are your faith' as 'without faith you are nothing'; frame gently.
not_for: Someone in a painful loss of faith who needs acceptance, not definition
speaks_to: Reflecting on what one really believes and lives for
Wanting to change one's habits by changing what one trusts
Understanding why people differ in their spiritual inclinations

bg.17.8.context: Krishna has said that food, sacrifice, austerity and giving are each of three kinds (17.7). This verse describes the food liked by sattvic people; the next two describe rajasic food (too bitter, sour, salty, hot, causing pain and illness) and tamasic food (stale, putrid, leftover, impure).
bg.17.8.core_teaching: Food that supports long life, clarity, strength, health and cheer, and that is tasty, wholesome and appealing, is what a person of clear, balanced nature is drawn to. What we like to eat reflects and reinforces our state.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Brief gloss: sattvic foods increase life, energy, strength, health, joy and cheerfulness; 'oleaginous' means oily or fatty, and 'substantial' means lasting long in the body.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Sattvic food promotes life and the mind's intelligence (since knowledge arises from sattva, 14.17), strength, health, comfort felt during digestion, and zest for congenial work; it is tasty and sweet, mixed with ghee and the like, substantial and pleasing.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Sattva is vivacity, sukha serenity of mind, priti relish; savoury means juicy, substantial means its essence stays long in the body, agreeable means pleasing at first sight. Such foods are liked by the sattvic.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Pure food builds vitality and also mental energy; sattva includes the inner strength that keeps the mind steady in distress; hridya means food pleasing to see and not smoky or burnt.

bg.17.8.practical_reading: Teachers use it to connect eating with clarity: fresh, wholesome, satisfying food supports a steady mind. It is about qualities of food and its effect, not a fixed list of allowed items.
misreadings: Not a strict diet code or a basis for food shaming.
Not anti-fat: the verse actually praises food with healthy fat.
cautions: Food-purity framing can harm readers with eating disorders or orthorexia; avoid moralising food.
Not medical or nutritional advice; 'sweet and oily' should not be pushed on someone with diabetes or heart disease.
not_for: Eating disorders or disordered eating
Food insecurity, where choosing ideal food is not possible
speaks_to: Wanting to eat in a way that supports calm and energy
Mindful eating and gratitude for food
Cooking and feeding a family with care

bg.18.10.context: Having defined sattvic relinquishment (18.9), Krishna describes the person established in it: he neither resents unpleasant work nor clings to pleasant work. He then adds that no embodied person can give up action altogether (18.11).
bg.18.10.core_teaching: The person of genuine relinquishment, clear and free of doubt, takes up whatever needs doing without resenting the unpleasant parts or getting attached to the pleasant ones.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: 'Evil' action is desire-driven work that perpetuates samsara; he does not hate it. 'Good' is obligatory work; he is not attached to it as a means to liberation. Permeated by discriminating sattva, he gains wisdom and his doubts are cut.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Having renounced attachment, fruit and agency, full of sattva and doubt-free, he is neither troubled by acts with unwanted results nor attached to those yielding heaven, children or cattle, since 'mine' is gone and every end but Brahman given up.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: He does not hate painful work, like a dawn bath in winter, nor relish pleasant work, like a noon bath in summer; one who endures humiliation and forgoes heaven's joys reasons that such passing pleasures and pains hardly matter.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: All actions are equally welcome to him; he is neither elated by pleasant work nor put off by disagreeable work.

bg.18.10.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to the parts of a job or role we love and hate: do the tedious paperwork without sulking, and the glamorous work without getting possessive. Sridhara's cold-bath example makes it concrete.
misreadings: Not that one should have no preferences at all, or must accept harmful work.
Not indifference to quality; it is about not being ruled by liking and disliking.
cautions: Broadly safe.
not_for: Someone in genuinely harmful or degrading work who needs to change it
speaks_to: Resenting boring or unpleasant parts of work or caregiving

bg.18.11.context: Having described sattvic relinquishment and the person established in it, Krishna explains why giving up the fruit, rather than action itself, is the real renunciation: no one with a body can stop acting altogether. He then describes what happens to the results of action for renouncers and non-renouncers (18.12).
bg.18.11.core_teaching: As long as we live in a body we cannot stop acting, so the real renunciation is giving up our claim on the results, not giving up action.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: 'Body-wearer' means one who identifies with the body; such a person cannot give up action completely, so doing obligatory work while giving up only the fruit, he is called an abandoner by courtesy. Only the knower can abandon all action.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: One in a body cannot give up work entirely, since getting food and drink is unavoidable; so the daily rites remain, and one who gives up their fruit, which implies giving up agency and attachment too, is the true renouncer.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Wouldn't renouncing all action be better for undistracted knowledge? No: one who identifies with the body cannot give it up entirely (3.5), so one who keeps acting while relinquishing the fruit is the real relinquisher.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: A human who grumbles at having to act is a fool; can fire give up its heat? While living in a body you cannot give up action entirely.

bg.18.11.practical_reading: A liberating verse for busy people: spirituality is not about escaping work but changing your relationship to its payoff. You can be fully engaged and inwardly free.
misreadings: Not that the renunciate life is worthless; Shankara keeps full renunciation for the realised.
Not 'don't care about results' as an excuse for sloppy work.
cautions: Broadly safe.
not_for: No strong contraindications
speaks_to: Householders who feel spiritual life requires leaving the world
Wanting to work without being consumed by results

bg.18.14.context: Krishna has said (18.13) he will explain the five causes of every action as taught in Sankhya. He names them here and adds (18.15) that every action of body, speech or mind, right or wrong, has these five causes; so one who sees the self as the sole doer does not see truly (18.16).
bg.18.14.core_teaching: No action has a single cause: body, agent, instruments, efforts and an unseen divine factor all contribute, so it is a mistake to see oneself as the only doer.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: The seat is the body, where desire, aversion, pleasure, pain and knowledge show themselves; the doer is the experiencing self shaped by its adjuncts. The divine factor is the gods, such as the sun, who let the organs work.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: The seat is the body, where the soul resides; the doer is the soul, able to know and act; then the organs and vital breaths. The fifth, 'daiva', is the Supreme Self, the inner guide who completes every act.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The seat is the body; the doer is ego, the knot of spirit and matter; then the senses and the breaths. The fifth is the deities over the senses, such as the sun, or the inner ruler who directs all.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Follows Shankara: the body is the seat; the doer is ego, which wrongly takes credit for what nature does. He glosses 'daivam' as the presiding deities and also as destiny. Without any one of the five, action cannot happen.

bg.18.14.practical_reading: Teachers use it to loosen the grip of fear and over-responsibility: you are one real contributor among several causes, so do your part fully but do not carry the whole outcome alone.
misreadings: Not 'it wasn't my fault' (as our misuse note says); you own your part.
Not fatalism; effort is itself one of the five causes.
'Adhiṣṭhāna' is the body, not 'the setting/environment' as our line implies.
cautions: The passage continues (18.17) with the claim that one free of ego 'does not kill even if he kills'; do not extend the reading there.
not_for: someone avoiding accountability for harm they caused

data_flags.translation_note: Flagged false for the LINE (the translation itself is acceptable). Translation acceptable ('the seat' for adhiṣṭhāna is right). Two issues in our data: (1) the line and prasang call adhiṣṭhāna 'the setting', but every commentator read here (Shankara, Ramanuja, Sridhara, Sivananda) glosses it as the...

bg.18.16.context: Krishna has listed five factors behind every action of body, speech or mind: the body as base, the doer, the instruments, the various efforts, and providence (daiva) (18.13-15). Here he says anyone who sees the self alone as the doer, ignoring these, does not truly see. The next verse, much debated, says one free of the sense of 'I did it' is not bound even by what he does.
bg.18.16.core_teaching: Every action arises from several factors together. Seeing oneself as the sole author of what happens, for good or ill, is a failure of understanding.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Every act is done by the five causes; the ignorant, untrained by Vedanta, teacher or reasoning, identify with them and see the pure Self as agent. Seeing, they do not see, like a passenger who thinks he is running.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: The individual self is an agent, but only with the Supreme Self's sanction; whoever thinks his own self acts with full independence has a warped understanding and does not see the other factors that make up his agency.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Since these five cause all action, whoever, with an understanding unrefined by scripture and teacher, regards the Self, free of adjuncts and unattached, as the agent is foolish and does not see truly.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The Self is always actionless, the silent witness of activity; the egoistic person thinks himself the real agent and so is bound by actions.

bg.18.16.practical_reading: Teachers use it two ways: against pride ('I did this all myself') and against crushing guilt ('it was all my fault'). Many factors, including circumstance and grace, shape every outcome.
misreadings: Not a way to dodge responsibility; you are still one of the five causes.
Not 'nothing is my doing'; Ramanuja insists the self is a real agent.
Do not chain it to 18.17 ('even if he kills') without careful framing.
cautions: Can ease survivor's guilt or self-blame after a loss, but must not be used to dismiss the feeling or to excuse real wrongdoing.
The next verse (18.17) about killing is easily misread; keep readings on this verse.
not_for: Someone avoiding accountability for harm they caused
A reader who needs their guilt heard before it is reframed
speaks_to: Self-blame after a failure or loss
Pride in sole credit for success
Team settings where blame is being assigned
Perfectionists who feel everything rests on them

bg.18.20.context: Krishna has said that knowledge, action and the doer each come in three kinds according to the gunas (18.19). This verse gives sattvic knowledge: seeing one undivided reality in all beings. Rajasic knowledge sees only separate entities (18.21), and tamasic knowledge clings to one small thing as if it were everything (18.22).
bg.18.20.core_teaching: The clearest kind of knowledge sees a single, unchanging reality running through all beings, undivided even though they appear separate.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Knowledge that sees one immutable Self in all beings, from unmanifest matter to unmoving things, undivided across bodies as space is, is direct right perception of the non-dual Self and is sattvic. Dualistic systems are rajasic or tamasic.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Beings are divided as brahmana, kshatriya, student, householder and so on, or as fair or tall; seeing in them one self, alike as consciousness, unchanging amid changing bodies, with no stake in the act's fruit, is sattvic knowledge.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The knowledge that sees, in all beings from Brahma to the unmoving, distinct from one another, the one undivided, imperishable, changeless substance, the Supreme Self, is sattvic.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Pure knowledge sees no difference in what is perceived: one imperishable essence behind seeming diversity, unity in diversity, all things rooted in the One.

bg.18.20.practical_reading: Teachers use it against tribalism and contempt: the same life looks out of every face, whatever the label of caste, class, religion or nation. It is also a meditation on unity.
misreadings: Not a denial that people differ or that differences matter in practical life.
Not a license to ignore injustice because 'all is one'.
cautions: Broadly safe.
not_for: No strong contraindications

bg.18.23.context: After the three kinds of knowledge, Krishna turns to the three kinds of action. This is sattvic action; rajasic action (18.24) is driven by desire and ego and done with great strain, tamasic action (18.25) is begun blindly. The three kinds of doer follow.
bg.18.23.core_teaching: Good action is one's proper work done without clinging, without being pushed by likes and dislikes, and without craving its reward.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Brief gloss: 'ordained' means obligatory (nitya) action; sattvic action is not done under the impulse of love or hatred, and is done by one not desiring its fruit.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Duty is what is prescribed for one's varna and stage of life; done free of attachment such as the sense of agency, of love of fame and hatred of infamy (that is, without vanity), and of desire for fruit.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: An action prescribed as a regular rite, done without hankering, not out of love for one's son or hatred toward an enemy, by a disinterested agent, is sattvic.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Such pure action is done wholeheartedly, offered to the Lord without caring for reward, and the doer experiences great joy.

bg.18.23.practical_reading: A test for one's own work: am I doing this because it's right, or because I like it, hate someone, want praise or fear blame? Ramanuja's 'not for fame, not from fear of disgrace' is especially sharp.
misreadings: Not 'feel nothing while working'; it is about motive, not emotion.
Not a defence of duties that cause harm.
cautions: Broadly safe.
not_for: No strong contraindications

bg.18.24.context: Second of three kinds of action (18.23-25): after sattvic action done without attachment or craving, this is rajasic action, done for desired ends, with ego, and with great strain. Tamasic action follows.
bg.18.24.core_teaching: Action driven by desire for results and by ego, carried out with exhausting strain, is the restless rajasic kind.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Done for pleasures as fruit, by the egotistic, at great cost of effort. 'Egotistic' contrasts with an ordinary humble Vedic devotee, not the self-realised, who could never seek fruit or toil so; even a sattvic doer has some ego.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Done aiming at fruit, with the self-love of being its performer, and with great strain; that is, done with the conceit 'what an enormous work this is, and I have done it'.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Done by one craving fruit, or with deep-rooted egotism such as 'who else is a Vedic scholar like me?', and with great strain: such action is rajasic.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The passionate person boasts of his actions in public and can never work without expecting reward; only a liberated sage is wholly free of egoism.

bg.18.24.practical_reading: Teachers link it to hustle and martyrdom: work done to prove oneself, with the inner narrative 'I'm the only one carrying all this', tends to be exhausting and brittle.
misreadings: Not saying hard work is bad; strain driven by ego and craving is the issue.
Not judging people who must work very hard to survive.
cautions: Avoid implying that someone overworking out of financial necessity is egoistic.
not_for: Someone working multiple jobs out of necessity
speaks_to: The 'only I can do this' feeling

bg.18.25.context: Third of three kinds of action (18.23-25): tamasic action is begun in confusion, without weighing its consequences, cost, harm or one's own ability. Krishna then describes the three kinds of doer (18.26-28).
bg.18.25.core_teaching: Action begun blindly, without considering consequences, cost, harm to others or one's own capacity, is the darkest kind.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Undertaken from delusion without regard to consequence, to the loss of power and wealth it will cause, to injury to living beings, or to one's own ability to complete it: such action is tamasic.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Done heedless of the pain that follows, the money it costs and the hurt it causes creatures, boasting that one can finish it, and from ignorance that the Supreme Person is the real doer: such action is tamasic.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Begun from sheer delusion, without considering the good or evil that will follow, the expense, injury to others, or one's own strength: such action is tamasic.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The tamasic person acts blindly, never asking whether he has the capacity, what it will cost or what will result, and so harms others.

bg.18.25.practical_reading: Works as a four-point checklist before a big decision: What follows from this? What will it cost? Who could be hurt? Can I actually carry it through?
misreadings: Not a call to over-deliberate or never take risks; it targets acting blindly.
cautions: Avoid shaming someone who made an impulsive decision during a crisis.
not_for: Someone already paralysed by over-thinking
speaks_to: Impulsive decisions: debts, risky ventures, angry messages

bg.18.26.context: In chapter 18 Krishna sorts knowledge, action and the doer by the three qualities. Having described sattvic, rajasic and tamasic action (18.23-25), he turns to the doer: this verse is the sattvic doer, followed by the rajasic doer, driven by craving, greed and swings of joy and grief (18.27), and the tamasic doer, careless, stubborn, lazy and procrastinating (18.28).
bg.18.26.core_teaching: The best kind of worker acts wholeheartedly and with staying power, but without clinging to results or making the work about themselves, and stays steady whether it succeeds or fails.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Success means gaining the fruit of the act. The sattvic agent is unaffected by success or failure because he acts on the authority of scripture, not from desire for results.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: The sattvic agent seeks no fruit and takes no pride in being the doer. He has the fortitude to bear the hardships a task brings and the zeal to keep at it, and stays unmoved whether it succeeds or fails.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Glosses each mark: no longing for results, no boasting, steadiness and zeal, and neither elation nor dejection at the outcome of work undertaken.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The pure agent works wholeheartedly without pride, weighs whether an action is worth doing, builds courage and will, and keeps a balanced mind through success and failure.

bg.18.26.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a portrait of healthy ambition: bring energy and grit to the work, let the work speak instead of your ego, and keep your balance through wins and losses.
misreadings: Not lack of ambition or care; enthusiasm (utsāha) is part of the ideal.
Not suppressing feelings about outcomes; it is about not being thrown off course by them.
not_for: someone burnt out, if 'steadiness and enthusiasm' is pressed as a demand

bg.18.27.context: Second of three kinds of doer (18.26-28): the sattvic doer is free of attachment and ego, steady and enthusiastic, unmoved by success or failure (18.26). This verse describes the rajasic doer; the tamasic doer follows.
bg.18.27.core_teaching: The restless kind of doer is attached, hungry for results, greedy, willing to harm, impure in motive, and thrown between elation at success and dejection at failure.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Greedy means thirsting for others' property and not giving one's own to the worthy; cruel means harming others; impure lacks outer and inner purity; he rejoices at what he wants and grieves at the unwanted or at losing the wanted.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: He hungers for fame, power and honour, expects the benefit, will not spend what the work requires, gets it done through cruelty to others, lacks the purity work needs, and is enslaved by joy and grief at outcomes.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Attached to children and the like, longing for results, covetous of others' property, inclined to violence, not observing prescribed cleanliness, and elated or dejected at gain or loss: such an agent is rajasic.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: He strives wholeheartedly wherever he imagines worldly gain, keeps whatever he gains for himself and his family, rejoices at success and is overcome by grief at failure.

bg.18.27.practical_reading: A mirror for result-driven work: if every win sends you soaring and every setback crushes you, and you cut corners or step on people to get results, rajas is running the show.
misreadings: Not saying that feeling happy or sad about outcomes is a sin; it describes being swung by them.
Not a label to pin on colleagues.
cautions: 'Swayed by sorrow' should not be applied to someone grieving a real loss.
not_for: Someone grieving
Someone already crushed by a failure who needs comfort
speaks_to: Emotional roller-coaster of targets and reviews
Leaders who push people too hard

bg.18.28.context: Last of three kinds of doer (18.26-28). After the sattvic doer (detached, steady, enthusiastic) and the rajasic one (attached, greedy, swung by outcomes), this is the tamasic doer. Krishna then turns to the three kinds of intellect and resolve (18.29).
bg.18.28.core_teaching: The dull, inert kind of doer is unfocused, crude, rigid, deceitful, spiteful, lazy, gloomy and endlessly procrastinating.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Vulgar is uncultured, like a child; unbending bows to nobody; deceptive hides his real power; wicked sets people at variance; indolent fails even in duty; desponding is always depressed; procrastinating takes a month over what should be done today.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Unqualified for scripture-prescribed work, unlettered, disinclined even to begin, fond of sorcery, bent on imposing on others, slack in work begun, always gloomy, and harbouring deep, long vengeance against others: such is the tamasic agent.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Careless, lacking discrimination, not humble, hiding his strength, insulting others, wanting in effort, sorrowing, and not accomplishing in a month what should be done that day or the next: such an agent is tamasic.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Through his vulgar nature he cannot tell proper from improper action; full of vanity and stiff, he bows to no deity or sage and is ready for evil deeds.

bg.18.28.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a mirror for one's own patterns, especially procrastination and rigidity, with Shankara's line about putting off for a month what should be done today. The remedy is small, steady effort.
misreadings: Not a label for anyone with depression, ADHD or burnout.
Not a character verdict on others.
cautions: 'Despondent' and 'lazy' overlap heavily with depression; never imply a struggling reader is tamasic. Arjuna himself is despondent at the start of the Gita, which teachers can point to with compassion (editor's note, not from the commentaries).
not_for: Depression, grief or burnout
Neurodivergent readers who struggle with task initiation
speaks_to: Stubbornness and inability to take advice

bg.18.30.context: After sorting knowledge, action and doer by the three qualities, Krishna turns to understanding (buddhi): this verse describes the clear, sattvic kind; the next two describe understanding that confuses right and wrong (rajasic, 18.31) and that sees everything upside down (tamasic, 18.32). Resolve (dhṛti) and happiness follow.
bg.18.30.core_teaching: Clear understanding knows when to engage and when to step back, what is right to do and not do, what is truly dangerous and what is safe, and what binds versus what frees.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Since they stand beside bondage and liberation, pravṛtti and nivṛtti mean the paths of action and of renunciation. The sattvic intellect also knows what scripture requires or forbids in each place and time, and what leads to fear or safety.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Pravṛtti is the discipline for worldly good, nivṛtti the discipline for release. The sattvic intellect knows what to do in each time, place and circumstance; fear comes from breaking scripture, fearlessness from keeping it.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Reads the pair ethically: being drawn to right action and refraining from wrong. The sattvic understanding also knows what to do in each place and time, and the ways to bondage and to freedom.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Follows Shankara: pravṛtti is the path of work and nivṛtti the path of renunciation. The pure intellect guides daily conduct by knowing what to do and avoid, and the causes of fear, bondage and freedom.

bg.18.30.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a decision checklist: Should I engage or step back? Is this right to do? Is my fear pointing to real danger? Will this choice bind me or free me?
misreadings: Not 'wait until you are certain'; nivṛtti is not procrastination.
Classically the 'should and should not' is defined by scripture; modern readers apply it to conscience and context.
not_for: someone in acute crisis needing immediate support rather than reflection

bg.18.31.context: Krishna sorts the intellect (buddhi) by the gunas. The sattvic intellect knows when to act and when to withdraw, what to do and avoid, what to fear and not, what binds and what frees (18.30). This verse is the rajasic intellect; the tamasic one, which inverts right and wrong, follows (18.32).
bg.18.31.core_teaching: An intellect clouded by restlessness does not discern right and wrong, or what to do and avoid, clearly; it is not inverted, just unreliable and mixed.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Dharma is what scripture ordains and adharma what it forbids; the rajasic intellect understands these, and what should and should not be done, wrongly, that is, contrary to what all authorities have settled.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: It does not rightly discern the two kinds of dharma (of active life and of withdrawal) and their opposites, nor what a person ought and ought not to do according to time, place and circumstance.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: 'Incorrectly' means in a way that leaves one in doubt; the rest he calls self-evident.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: No English word fits dharma: it is what raises you toward the Self, adharma what hurls you into ignorance; the rajasic intellect confuses them.

bg.18.31.practical_reading: Useful for moments when you are too agitated to judge well: rushed, angry or desperate minds blur moral lines. Teachers advise slowing down before deciding.
misreadings: Not saying every moral uncertainty is a character flaw; Ramanuja notes right action depends on time, place and circumstance.
cautions: Broadly safe.
not_for: No strong contraindications
speaks_to: Decisions made in a rush or while angry

bg.18.32.context: Third of three kinds of intellect (18.30-32): after the clear sattvic intellect and the unreliable rajasic one, this is the tamasic intellect, covered by darkness, which takes wrong for right and sees everything in reverse. The three kinds of resolve (dhriti) follow.
bg.18.32.core_teaching: When the intellect is covered by darkness it does not merely blur right and wrong but inverts them, seeing everything upside down.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Very brief: enveloped in darkness, it sees adharma as dharma and takes a wholly perverted view of all things to be known.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Wrapped in tamas, it perceives everything contrariwise: wrong as right, right as wrong, fact as figment, fancy as fact, the higher ideal as base and the base as higher.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: An understanding that grasps things in an inverted way is tamasic. Of the mind's many functions, understanding, tenacity and happiness are singled out because they chiefly lead to right and wrong, fear and fearlessness.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: It treats virtues as vices and regards what scripture calls good as wholly wrong, viewing everything in a perverted light.

bg.18.32.practical_reading: A warning about rationalisation: the mind can build convincing cases for what is clearly harmful. Teachers suggest checking big moral conclusions against trusted people and principles.
misreadings: Not a tool for labelling those who disagree with you as 'tamasic'.
cautions: Easily weaponised in arguments; keep it as self-examination.
not_for: Someone being gaslit who may already doubt their own perceptions
speaks_to: Situations where harmful behaviour has been normalised

bg.18.33.context: Having sorted the intellect by the gunas, Krishna does the same for dhriti, the resolve or firmness that sustains a course. This is the sattvic kind; rajasic resolve clings to duty, pleasure and wealth for their rewards (18.34), and tamasic resolve clings to sleep, fear and grief (18.35).
bg.18.33.core_teaching: The best kind of resolve, sustained by steady concentration, holds mind, breath and senses on course without wavering.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Yoga here is samadhi, concentration; the firmness always joined to it holds the activities of thought, breath and senses back from rushing into ways opposed to scripture. (Anandagiri's footnote: firmness without such concentration cannot reliably restrain them.)

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Yoga is meditation on the Lord, the means to release, pursued single-mindedly; the purpose that keeps mind, vitality and senses engaged in achieving it, discarding every fruit opposed to liberation, is sattvic.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The tenacity that is unswerving, thinking of nothing else, through concentration of mind, and by which one regulates the functions of mind, breaths and senses, is sattvic.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Firmness alone cannot restrain mind, life-force and senses; it must be joined with concentration, by which the senses are withdrawn into the mind.

bg.18.33.practical_reading: Teachers connect it to the steadiness built by daily practice: breath, attention and habits held on course by a clear purpose, rather than by willpower spikes.
misreadings: Not suppression or rigid self-control for its own sake; Ramanuja frames it as staying engaged toward a meaningful goal.
cautions: Broadly safe.
not_for: No strong contraindications
speaks_to: Building a meditation or study habit

bg.18.34.context: Second of three kinds of resolve (18.33-35). After the sattvic resolve that holds mind and senses steady in yoga, this is rajasic resolve: holding fast to duty, pleasure and wealth (the worldly aims) for what they will bring. The tamasic kind follows.
bg.18.34.core_teaching: Determination that pursues duty, pleasure and wealth for their payoffs is the restless kind of resolve: strong, but transactional.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: When a person is firmly convinced that dharma, pleasure and wealth must always be secured, and desires the fruit of whichever one occupies his attention at the moment, his firmness is rajasic.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Dharma, pleasure and wealth here stand for the powers of mind, life and senses directed toward them; the will that, from longing for fruit and attachment, keeps those energies aimed at these ends rather than liberation is rajasic.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The tenacity that holds primarily to duty, pleasure and wealth, never letting them go, and through attachment becomes desirous of their fruit, is rajasic.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The person of rajasic firmness clings passionately to the threefold aim of life, dharma, wealth and pleasure, and wants the rewards of his actions.

bg.18.34.practical_reading: A mirror for ambitious people: drive can be admirable and still be transactional, including 'being good' for the rewards it brings. Teachers invite keeping the drive and loosening the bargain.
misreadings: Not saying duty, pleasure or wealth are wrong; they are legitimate aims, and the issue is grasping for fruit.
cautions: Broadly safe.
not_for: No strong contraindications
speaks_to: Doing good for recognition or reward

bg.18.35.context: Last of three kinds of resolve (18.33-35): the tamasic kind is the stubbornness with which a person of poor understanding keeps holding on to sleep, fear, grief, despondency and intoxication. Krishna then begins the three kinds of happiness (18.36).
bg.18.35.core_teaching: The darkest kind of resolve is the persistence with which we hold on to sleepiness, fear, grief, despondency and intoxication, as if they were duties.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: The dull person prizes sensual gratification and never gives up indulgence; he regards sleep, fear, grief, depression and lust as things always to be resorted to. That firmness is tamasic.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Madam is the stupor that comes from enjoying objects; the unwise person does not check, and even abets, the mind and life-forces dragging him into sleep and fancies; fear, grief and despair stand for the things that cause them.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: A person whose intellect lacks discrimination does not give up sleep and the rest but indulges in them again and again; that tenacity is tamasic.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Paints the tamasic person harshly as indolent, sinful and addicted to sleep, fearful through attachment to the body, discontented, lustful and conceited.

bg.18.35.practical_reading: Teachers use it to notice how we can cling to familiar misery, rehearsing fears and grievances, numbing out, because letting go feels unsafe. The first step is seeing the habit.
misreadings: Not a judgement on grief, depression or anxiety as illnesses or natural responses to loss.
Not 'stop grieving'; it names a habit of clinging, not the feeling itself.
cautions: Lists grief (shoka) and despondency (vishada) among things tamas clings to; never use on Day 1 of a grief plan or for a reader in depression. It can sound like blame.
Mentions intoxication; handle carefully with readers in addiction recovery (supportive framing only).
not_for: Fresh grief
Clinical depression or anxiety
Anyone in crisis
speaks_to: Recognising patterns in recovery, once stable

bg.18.36.context: Having sorted knowledge, action, doer, intellect and resolve, Krishna turns to happiness. He introduces three kinds and begins with the best: the joy one grows into through practice, which ends sorrow. The next verse says it is like poison at first and nectar at the end; rajasic happiness (18.38) is the reverse.
bg.18.36.core_teaching: There is a happiness that does not arrive in a rush but grows through steady practice and familiarity, and it brings sorrow to an end.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Brief gloss: 'hear' means pay steady attention; 'practice' means familiarity and repetition; 'the end' of pain means its cessation or alleviation. The description of sattvic pleasure follows.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Knowledge, act and actor all serve the aim of happiness, which is threefold; in the best kind one gradually draws exquisite delight through long habituation and finally reaches the end of the pain of samsara.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Sattvic happiness is relished through familiarity, not suddenly like sense pleasure, and in it one reaches the cessation of all pain; it is like poison at first and nectar at the end (37).

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Even a little of the pleasure experienced in the Self brings pain to an end; he cross-refers to 6.20-30 on the joy of meditation.

bg.18.36.practical_reading: Teachers use it to encourage persistence: meditation, study, music, exercise or service may feel effortful at first, but the joy they give deepens with practice and outlasts quick pleasures.
misreadings: Not a promise that practice will remove all pain quickly.
Not dismissing ordinary pleasures; it contrasts depth and durability.
cautions: Gentle; 'end of sorrow' should not be framed as a deadline for someone grieving.
not_for: Fresh grief if framed as 'practice will end your sorrow'
speaks_to: Starting a new practice and finding it hard
Seeking lasting rather than quick satisfaction

bg.18.37.context: Krishna is describing three kinds of happiness (18.36-39). This is the sattvic kind, hard at first and sweet later, born of a clear mind. It is contrasted with sense-pleasure, sweet at first and bitter later (18.38), and with the dull pleasure of sleep, sloth and heedlessness that deludes from start to finish (18.39).
bg.18.37.core_teaching: The deepest happiness often feels hard at the beginning, because it asks for effort and restraint, but it ripens into something sweet, rising from a clear and settled mind.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: It feels like poison at first because gaining knowledge, detachment and meditation takes great effort. It becomes nectar as knowledge and detachment mature, arising from a clear mind or clear knowledge of the Self.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: This happiness has to be won by hard effort early in yoga, so before it is tasted it seems bitter. Through practice it is finally felt as nectar, born of the calm of a mind turned wholly to the self.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Reads 18.36-37 together: this happiness grows through practice and familiarity, not suddenly like sense pleasure, and ends all pain. It is bitter while the mind is being controlled, then sweet once agitation and dullness clear.

bg.18.37.practical_reading: Teachers use it for starting hard, good habits: the first days of exercise, study or meditation feel bitter, but the joy they lead to is lasting. Expect the hard start rather than read it as a sign you are on the wrong path.
misreadings: Not 'suffering is good in itself' or 'if it hurts, it must be right'.
Not a reason to stay in a harmful situation waiting for it to turn sweet.
cautions: Sivananda's gloss stresses severe austerities and sense-subjugation; keep the modern reading to ordinary healthy effort.
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship or harmful job, if read as 'endure, it will get better'
depression framed as necessary 'poison'

bg.18.38.context: Having described sattvic happiness, bitter at first and sweet later (18.37), Krishna describes its mirror image: pleasure from the senses meeting their objects, sweet at first and bitter later. The tamasic kind, delusion from start to finish, follows (18.39).
bg.18.38.core_teaching: Pleasure that comes only from the senses meeting their objects tastes sweet at first but turns bitter, because it fades and leaves loss behind.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: A grain of sense pleasure comes with a mountain of pain, fear and attachment. Chasing the means to it breeds lies and wrongdoing, and indulgence dulls the senses and the mind.

bg.18.38.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to choices like scrolling, binge eating or impulse buying: notice the after-taste, and choose the joys that leave you better off.
misreadings: Not 'all pleasure is bad'; it contrasts kinds of happiness by where they lead.
Not shame about the body or normal enjoyment.
cautions: Classical commentaries are strongly ascetic here (Sridhara: pain here and hereafter; Shankara and Ramanuja mention hell); avoid shaming tones for modern readers, especially those with addiction or body-image struggles.
not_for: someone already ashamed of their habits, if framed moralistically
speaks_to: understanding why some pleasures leave one empty

bg.18.39.context: Last of three kinds of happiness (18.36-39). Sattvic happiness is bitter at first and nectar later; rajasic is sweet at first and poison later; this tamasic kind deludes from start to finish and comes from sleep, sloth and heedlessness. Krishna then says nothing in creation is free of the three gunas (18.40).
bg.18.39.core_teaching: The lowest kind of happiness, born of dullness, laziness and inattention, clouds the mind both while it is enjoyed and afterwards.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Very brief: the pleasure that deludes the self both at first and 'in the sequel', meaning after it ends, and that arises from sleep, indolence and heedlessness, is tamasic.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: It enthrals the self while enjoyed and when its results appear. Delusion hides things' true nature: sleep plainly does, sloth dulls the senses and so the intellect, heedlessness is inattention to the work at hand. So suppress rajas and tamas.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Self-deluding from the first moment and afterwards, it arises from sleep, lassitude and inadvertence, which he explains as fantasising while neglecting the duty at hand.

bg.18.39.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to numbing pleasures: binge-watching, oversleeping, intoxication, idle fantasy. They feel like relief but leave you foggier.
misreadings: Not condemning rest, sleep or leisure in healthy measure.
Not a judgement on people with fatigue or illness.
cautions: Overlaps with exhaustion and depression; avoid shaming rest. Sivananda's mention of liquor needs care with readers in recovery.
not_for: Depression, chronic fatigue or illness
New parents and carers short of sleep

bg.18.45.context: Krishna has just listed the duties that arise from the nature (svabhāva) of each of the four varṇas (18.41-44). Here he states the principle behind the list and announces that he will explain how one's own work leads to perfection; the next verse gives the answer: by worshipping, through that work, the one from whom all beings come.
