bg.18.45.core_teaching: Doing one's own work wholeheartedly is itself a path to the highest good; the commentators add that this works because such work, done without craving for results and as worship, purifies the mind for knowledge or devotion.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Each devoted to the duty ordained by his nature gains a perfection that is the body and senses made fit for the path of knowledge once their impurities are washed out; he notes duty alone does not directly give liberation.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Every person devoted to his own duty reaches the final state of perfection, the supreme abode; the following verses explain the manner.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Perfection here means fitness for knowledge; the verse and a half that follows explains how sincere performance of one's own duty leads to knowledge of the truth.

bg.18.45.practical_reading: Teachers use it to dignify ordinary work: putting full attention and integrity into the job in front of you, as an offering rather than a scramble for reward, is itself spiritual practice.
misreadings: Not a promise that any job brings success or status; 'perfection' is inner readiness, not worldly achievement.
Not a licence for workaholism; the stress is on the spirit of the work, not its quantity.
Not to be read as divine endorsement of caste-assigned occupations (see cautions).
cautions: The verse sits inside the varṇa list (18.41-48) and every classical commentator, and Sivananda, ties 'one's own work' to caste duty. Our misuse note ('the work that fits your nature', not birth) is a modern reading; present it as such rather than as what the commentaries say.
For someone unemployed or stuck in work they hate, 'perfection through your own work' can sound like blame.
not_for: Someone who has just lost their job
A person trapped in exploitative or abusive work
Readers sensitive to caste, if the context is not explained
speaks_to: Feeling your ordinary job is spiritually meaningless
Comparing your path with others' and feeling behind
Wanting to bring care and integrity to daily work
Early career: finding work that fits your temperament

bg.18.46.context: Krishna has just listed the work natural to each of the four varnas (18.41-44) and said that each person reaches perfection by being devoted to their own work (18.45). This verse says how: by worshipping, through that work, the source of all beings. The next verses (18.47-48) say one's own path, even imperfect, is better than another's, and that every undertaking has flaws.
bg.18.46.core_teaching: Ordinary work, done as worship of the source that moves and pervades all life, is itself a path to fulfilment; one need not leave one's work to find the sacred.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'his own duty' as each person's caste duty, as described just before. Worshipping the Lord, the inner ruler, through that duty brings perfection only in that it makes one fit for the path of knowledge.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Perfection means reaching the Lord by his grace, through worshipping him by one's acts as the inner self of all, since everything comes from him and is pervaded by him.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The Lord is the inner ruler from whom all beings' activity proceeds and who pervades the universe as its cause. Worshipping him through one's own duty, a person attains perfection.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Doing one's own duty carries out the will of the Supreme. Worshipped with the 'flowers' of action, the Lord grants dispassion and discernment. He too glosses 'own duty' by caste, and perfection as fitness for self-knowledge.

bg.18.46.practical_reading: Teachers apply it as 'work as worship': do your own job carefully and sincerely, as an offering, instead of measuring it against others' work.
misreadings: Work as worship doesn't mean overwork or tolerating exploitation (as our misuse note says).
'Own work' is classically one's varna duty (Shankara, Sivananda say so explicitly); the modern application to one's chosen vocation is a reinterpretation, not the classical sense.
cautions: The immediate context is the varna list (18.41-45); avoid quoting the surrounding verses in a way that implies caste-based work.
not_for: someone stuck in exploitative work, if read as 'accept it as worship'
someone pressured into a family or caste occupation

bg.18.47.context: Having said one reaches perfection by worshipping the divine through one's own work (18.46), Krishna repeats a line from 3.35: one's own dharma, even imperfect, is better than another's done well. He adds that action fitting one's nature brings no fault, and next (18.48) that one should not abandon such work for its flaws, since all work has some. For Arjuna, this means not abandoning his warrior duty.
bg.18.47.core_teaching: It is better to walk one's own path, imperfectly, than to imitate someone else's path, however well; acting in line with one's own nature does not bring fault.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Like a worm born in a poison that does not harm it, one who does the duty set by one's nature incurs no sin. So one should not abandon one's own duty.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'one's own dharma' as karma yoga, which comes naturally to an embodied person with active senses, and 'another's' as jnana yoga. That needs prior mastery of the senses and carries risks, so action is the safer path.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Applies it directly to Arjuna: a Brahmin's life of alms is not better for him than his own duty of fighting, even though it means killing kinsmen. Doing the duty set by one's nature brings no sin.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Repeats the worm-in-poison image and adds that sweet cane juice kills the same worm. One's own appointed duty, however hard, frees from bondage, while another's brings danger.

bg.18.47.practical_reading: Teachers use it against comparison: your path will look messier than others' highlight reels, but living honestly from your own nature beats a polished copy of someone else's life.
misreadings: Not 'stick to the role you were born into' (as our misuse note says), though editors should know the classical commentators do read it in terms of varna.
Not a reason never to grow or change direction.
Not a defence of doing harm because it is 'my nature'.
cautions: Caste: the classical reading is explicitly varna-based; the modern 'personal fit' reading is a reinterpretation. Be transparent rather than claiming the tradition says otherwise.
In context the verse urges Arjuna to fight; keep the war context out of comparison-plan readings.
not_for: someone pressured to stay in a family or caste occupation
someone using 'my nature' to excuse harm

bg.18.48.context: Krishna has said one's own path, though imperfect, is better than another's (18.47). Here he adds that one should not give up one's natural work because it has faults, since every undertaking is wrapped in some fault, as fire in smoke. In the story, this answers Arjuna's wish to abandon fighting because of the violence it involves; Krishna then moves to the state beyond action (18.49 onward).
bg.18.48.core_teaching: Do not abandon the work that is yours just because it has flaws: every undertaking carries some imperfection, as every fire carries smoke.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Every duty is faulty, since all is made of the three gunas, so taking up another's duty escapes no fault and brings fear. One without self-knowledge cannot give up action entirely, so should not abandon his own.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Karma yoga comes naturally and is free of danger, so do it even when it is painful. Even one fit for jnana yoga should follow it, since both paths have faults and hardships and only action is safe.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Answers Arjuna's worry about the violence in his own duty: another's duty has its faults too. Use fire's heat and ignore its smoke; take the good part of work for purifying the mind.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: All duties, one's own and others', are mixed with the three qualities. Taking up another's duty brings no gain and brings fear, and one without self-knowledge cannot stop acting, so should not abandon action.

bg.18.48.practical_reading: Teachers use it against perfectionism: no job, relationship or project is free of drawbacks; rather than quitting at the first sign of smoke, use the warmth and light and work around the smoke.
misreadings: Not 'never change jobs' (as our misuse note says); it answers perfectionism, not a reason to stay where you are harmed.
Not acceptance of wrongdoing as 'just smoke'.
cautions: Used in a new-beginnings plan, a 'do not abandon' verse may feel contradictory to someone who has just made a change; frame it as 'your new path will also have smoke; that is normal'.
Classical 'sahaja karma' is birth-based duty; same caste caveat as 18.47.
not_for: someone in an abusive job or relationship
someone pressured into inherited occupations
speaks_to: doubting a path because it has drawbacks
new beginnings that turn out imperfect

bg.18.49.context: After saying that one reaches perfection through one's own work offered to the Lord (18.45-48), Krishna turns to the higher perfection beyond that: the state of freedom from action. This verse names who reaches it, and the following verses (18.50-55) describe how such a person settles into Brahman.
bg.18.49.core_teaching: When attachment, self-will and craving fall away, a person reaches a freedom in which action no longer binds; the schools differ on whether this means formal renunciation (Shankara) or a contemplative stillness reached while still doing one's duty (Ramanuja, Sridhara).

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Unattached to fruits, mind conquered, desire gone because all sense of being the doer is handed over to the Lord; through relinquishing fruits while still doing one's duty he reaches the highest stage of meditation, where the senses fall still.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Unattachment means no egotism and no desire for results; by renouncing attachment to work and its fruit he reaches a purity in which activity ceases, the state of the highest renunciate.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Free of attachment to family, body and property, the mind turns inward; knowing the Self, one may still act for the world's good yet is not bound, since the sense of being the doer has gone.

bg.18.49.practical_reading: Modern teachers read it as inner freedom: you can keep working and caring while loosening the grip of needing outcomes, possessions and approval.
misreadings: Not a call to abandon family or responsibilities; Ramanuja and Sridhara keep the person working.
'Unattached' does not mean cold or indifferent to people.
Not a quick technique; the commentators place it at the end of a long discipline.
cautions: Shankara explicitly names detachment from children and spouse; in a reading for someone grieving or estranged from family this could sound like approval of withdrawal.
not_for: Someone isolated or estranged who may hear it as 'detach from people'
Fresh grief over a family member
speaks_to: Exhaustion from needing every outcome to go your way
Midlife questions about what you actually need

bg.18.53.context: Krishna is describing the person who has reached the perfection of knowledge: pure in mind, steady, living simply in solitude (18.51-52). This verse lists what that person has dropped, and the next verse says that, having become Brahman, they neither grieve nor crave.
bg.18.53.core_teaching: Peace and fitness for the highest come from dropping a specific set of inner habits: ego, aggressive will, arrogance, craving, anger, accumulation, and the sense of ownership.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Ego is identifying with the body; strength means force fused with passion, not physical strength; arrogance follows elation and breaks dharma. He gives up even possessions needed for the body, becoming a wandering renunciate, fit for Brahman.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Ego is taking the not-self for the self; 'strength' is the force of old impressions feeding it; pride follows. Free of 'mine' and serene in the self's bliss, the meditator becomes fit to realise the self's true nature.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Even the ego of 'I am detached' is dropped, along with rashness, spiritual pride, desire and anger; free of 'mine' even toward what comes unasked, and tranquil, he can rest in 'I am Brahman'.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Notes that people grow arrogant through wealth or learning and then transgress; the aspirant regards even the body as not his own and so becomes peaceful and fit for Brahman.

bg.18.53.practical_reading: Teachers turn the list into a self-audit: notice where you push, show off, accumulate, or say 'mine', and loosen one of these today; peace follows the loosening.
misreadings: Not a rule that owning things is sinful for householders; Shankara's 'even bodily necessities' applies to the formal renunciate.
Not telling anyone to suppress anger by force; the commentators speak of a mind that has outgrown it.
'Ego' here is not healthy self-respect or boundaries.
cautions: A long list of faults can feel like an indictment to someone already self-critical; offer one item, not all six.
not_for: Someone with low self-worth who needs encouragement, not a list of faults
A person being exploited who needs to assert themselves
speaks_to: Ambition that has turned into constant pushing
Arguments driven by needing to win
Clutter and the urge to acquire

bg.18.54.context: Continuing the portrait of the one fit to become Brahman (18.53), Krishna describes the result: serenity, no grief, no craving, equal regard for all beings, and supreme devotion. The next verse says that through this devotion one knows him truly and enters him.
bg.18.54.core_teaching: Inner clarity shows itself as freedom from both grief and craving and as equal regard for all, and this state opens into the highest devotion; Advaita reads that devotion as knowledge, Vishishtadvaita as loving bliss in God.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Having reached Brahman, serene, he does not grieve over failures or wants and longs for nothing; this describes his nature, not a command. He feels others' joys and pains as his own and attains the highest devotion, that of knowledge.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Resting in Brahman, he does not grieve for what is lost or crave what he lacks, since he no longer identifies with the body; free of likes and dislikes, he attains devotion that sees all beings as the Lord.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Adds that 'the same to all beings' can mean feeling others' pain as one's own: such a heart is tender, rejoices and suffers with others, and has dropped jealousy and prejudice.

bg.18.54.practical_reading: Teachers present it as a picture of where practice leads, not a demand: a steadier heart that feels for everyone and is less tossed between loss and wanting.
misreadings: Not a command not to grieve; Shankara says it describes the nature of one established in Brahman.
'Same to all' is not emotional flatness; Shankara and Sivananda read it as feeling everyone's joy and pain as your own.
cautions: 'Neither grieves' will land badly on someone newly bereaved unless framed as a distant horizon rather than a standard to meet.
Ramanuja's 'indifference toward every creature except the Lord' is a strong phrasing that can sound cold; don't quote it to a lonely reader.
not_for: Fresh grief
Someone being told by others to 'just get over it'
speaks_to: Longing for inner steadiness after a turbulent period
Swinging between disappointment and wanting more
Wanting to love people more evenly, beyond one's own circle

bg.18.56.context: Having described the path of knowledge and renunciation (18.49-55), Krishna returns to the person who keeps working. This verse says that even one constantly busy with every kind of work reaches the eternal state by his grace if they rely on him; the next verse urges Arjuna to offer all action inwardly.
bg.18.56.core_teaching: A full, busy working life is no barrier to the highest goal, provided one relies on the divine rather than on one's own sense of being the doer; the result is a gift of grace, not a wage.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Whoever does all actions, even forbidden ones, yet takes refuge in the Lord with the whole self centred in him reaches by the Lord's grace the eternal abode of Vishnu.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: All works, including those done with a desire, performed while ascribing all authorship to the Lord and trusting him, lead to him, the goal that is eternal and infinite.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Concludes how worship through one's duties brings liberation: doing regular, occasional and even desire-prompted acts in the way described, with the Lord as sole refuge instead of heaven as the aim, one reaches his eternal state by grace.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Worship the Lord with the flowers of good actions; work done as worship purifies the heart. Like drains flowing into the Ganga, the devotee merged in the Lord is not tainted by occasional lapses.

bg.18.56.practical_reading: Teachers use it for busy people: you don't have to leave your job or family to grow spiritually; keep the work, change what you lean on.
misreadings: Not 'anything goes if you are devoted'; Shankara's and Sivananda's mention of forbidden acts concerns grace toward lapses, not permission.
Not a promise of worldly success; the 'home' is the spiritual goal.
Not saying effort is pointless because grace does it all; the person keeps working.
cautions: The classical gloss that even prohibited actions do not bar the devotee can be misused to excuse harm; leave it out of readings.
not_for: Someone rationalising harmful behaviour
A person told their suffering is 'grace' and should not be challenged
speaks_to: Busy professionals or parents who feel too occupied for spiritual life
Guilt about not having time to practise

bg.18.57.context: Following the promise that one who keeps working while relying on the Lord reaches him (18.56), Krishna turns it into direct instruction to Arjuna: offer all action inwardly, keep him as the goal and the mind on him. The next verse states the result and the danger of ego.
bg.18.57.core_teaching: Surrender here is inner, not outer: keep acting, but hand over the sense of ownership and authorship, hold the divine as the goal, and keep the mind steady on it.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: With the discerning faith that knowledge, not works, finally liberates, dedicate all actions with visible and invisible results to the Lord as in 9.27, regard him as the goal and rest on steady-mindedness as your refuge.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Dedicate in thought, knowing your self belongs to and is guided by the Lord, both the doership and the object of your works to him; doing everything with him as goal and fruit is buddhi-yoga.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Offer all actions to the Lord mentally, treat him as life's highest end, and, even while working, keep the mind fixed on him through a resolute intellect, as in 4.24's 'the offering is Brahman'.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Surrender all actions to the Lord while holding to discrimination; through it you see yourself as distinct from body and activity and resting in his being.

bg.18.57.practical_reading: Teachers make it a daily practice: before a task, offer it inwardly; during it, keep returning attention to what you serve; after it, let go of the result.
misreadings: Not quitting one's work; the giving-up is mental (cetasā).
Not abandoning judgement; buddhi-yoga means more discernment, not less.
not_for: Someone who reads 'surrender' as passivity in a situation that needs action
speaks_to: Feeling scattered and needing one anchor
Wanting to turn routine work into practice

bg.18.58.context: Right after telling Arjuna to keep his mind on him (18.57), Krishna states the two outcomes: with mind on him, grace carries him through every difficulty; refusing out of ego leads to ruin. The next verses warn that Arjuna's own nature will make him fight anyway.
bg.18.58.core_teaching: Turned toward the divine, a person is carried through difficulties by grace; the real danger is the ego that thinks it already knows better and will not listen.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: With your heart on the Lord, by his grace you cross the hard obstacles rooted in ignorance; if you refuse out of the conceit of being learned, or think 'I am independent, why obey another', you will be ruined.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Ego is the notion 'I know well what should and should not be done'; ignoring the Lord on that basis brings ruin, since no creature but he truly knows what is right or governs as he does.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Fixing your mind on him, you overcome all worldly troubles by grace; if from the notion that you are wise you will not listen, you fail to reach life's goal.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Through one-pointed devotion you cross pitfalls, temptations, illness and the other troubles of saṃsāra; but if through pride you disregard the teaching, thinking 'I know everything', you will be ruined.

bg.18.58.practical_reading: Teachers read it as a warning about the know-it-all mind: when stuck, the block is often the refusal to listen; humility opens a way through.
misreadings: Not a threat of divine punishment for doubt; the commentators locate the ruin in acting from conceit.
Not a demand to obey any human authority who claims to speak for God.
cautions: 'You will perish' is harsh language; for an anxious or scrupulous reader, frame it as a natural consequence of ego, not a threat.
Can be weaponised by controlling teachers or relatives demanding obedience.
not_for: Anxious or scrupulous readers prone to fear of punishment
Someone in a coercive religious or family setting
speaks_to: Facing a hard stretch and needing reassurance
Pride that blocks you from asking for help

bg.18.6.context: Arjuna has asked the difference between sannyasa (renunciation) and tyaga (relinquishment). Krishna notes the competing views, then gives his own: sacrifice, giving and austerity must not be abandoned because they purify even the wise (18.5), but they too must be done without attachment or desire for results. He then sorts relinquishment into three kinds (18.7-9).
bg.18.6.core_teaching: Krishna's final position on renunciation: do not give up good action; give up clinging to it and to what it gets you. This is his firm conclusion.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: The purifying acts of worship, gift and austerity must still be done by the seeker of liberation, without attachment or fruits. He rejects reading 'even these' as desire-driven rites, which the Gita calls an inferior, binding path.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Because sacrifice, gift and austerity purify and are themselves worship of the Lord, the seeker must practise them daily until death, like meditation itself, giving up the sense of 'mine' in them and their fruits.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: This is how they become purifying: do them giving up attachment, the idea of being the doer, treating them purely as worship of the Lord, and giving up desire for fruit; this is my decided, therefore best, view.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: A summary of karma-yoga: the fault lies not in action itself but in attachment and expecting reward.

bg.18.6.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to all meaningful work and service: keep doing the good thing, but loosen the grip of 'my project, my credit, my outcome'. Ramanuja's 'every day until the end' frames it as a lifelong practice, not a one-off decision.
misreadings: Not 'stop caring about outcomes' to the point of carelessness; the action itself is to be done fully.
Not an endorsement of quitting good work in the name of detachment.
cautions: Broadly safe. For someone grieving a failed project, 'let go of results' should come with acknowledgement of the loss.
not_for: Someone exhausted who needs permission to rest, not a reminder to keep acting
speaks_to: Volunteers and caregivers who feel unappreciated
Professionals attached to credit or outcomes
People tempted to drop spiritual or service practices because they feel 'detached'

bg.18.61.context: Krishna has just told Arjuna that if, out of ego, he refuses to fight, his own nature will drive him to it anyway (18.59-60). Here he names who stands behind that nature: the Lord in every heart. The next verse (18.62) says: take refuge in him with your whole being, and by his grace you will find supreme peace.
bg.18.61.core_teaching: The divine is not far off: it dwells in the heart of every being and is the hidden power behind all their movement.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: The Lord dwells in all hearts and, through maya, makes beings whirl like wooden dolls on a machine. 'As if' is to be understood. He reads 'Arjuna' here as 'pure-hearted'.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: The Lord dwells in the heart, seat of awareness and activity. He makes the body a machine, sets the soul on it and turns it by his maya of the gunas, in keeping with the qualities each was born with.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The previous two verses gave the Sankhya view, that beings are driven by nature and duty; here Krishna gives his own. The inner ruler moves all beings by his power like a puppeteer, citing the Upanishads on the indwelling ruler.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The Lord gave each of us this marvellous machine, the body, and by his power it moves. He is the real actor within, turning beings like dolls on a machine.

bg.18.61.practical_reading: Teachers use the first half for loneliness and self-worth: the divine lives in your heart and in everyone else's, so you are never empty of it and never wholly alone.
misreadings: Not fatalism or 'I am a puppet, so nothing is my responsibility'; the very next verse calls for a free act of refuge.
Not an excuse for harm done ('God made me do it').
cautions: The puppet/machine image can feel disempowering or frightening to an anxious or depressed reader; use the first half only, as our data suggests.
not_for: readers struggling with a sense of no control, if the second half is included
someone excusing harmful actions

bg.18.62.context: Krishna has just said that the Lord dwells in the heart of every being and turns them as if mounted on a machine by his power (18.61). Here he tells Arjuna to take refuge in that Lord with his whole being. Next he says he has now taught the most secret wisdom and leaves Arjuna to reflect and choose (18.63).
bg.18.62.core_teaching: Complete, wholehearted refuge in the Lord within brings peace and the lasting goal as his gift; Ramanuja adds that refuge means following his guidance in what one actually does.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Seek the Lord as sole refuge with your whole being for relief from the distress of saṃsāra; by his grace you will gain supreme peace and the supreme eternal abode.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Since every soul depends on the Lord, give up self-conceit and take refuge in him with all your heart; by his grace you gain supreme peace and his eternal abode.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Surrender totally and keep no secret desires; desire and ego are the two main obstacles to surrender; run to the Lord for shelter from the sorrows of saṃsāra.

bg.18.62.practical_reading: Teachers read refuge as trust lived out: bring your whole self, worries included, to the divine, and act from that trust rather than from fear.
misreadings: Not giving up effort or judgement; the very next verse asks Arjuna to reflect fully and then choose.
Not refuge in a human guru or institution.
cautions: Ramanuja's reading that refuge means carrying out God's directions, including the war, should not become 'do what you are told'.
not_for: Someone being told to 'just surrender' instead of getting medical or practical help
A reader without theistic belief, unless reframed
speaks_to: Feeling overwhelmed and needing to lean on something larger
Anxiety that comes from trying to control everything
A crisis where one has done what one can

bg.18.63.context: Krishna has urged Arjuna to take refuge in the Lord in his heart (18.61-62). Here he rounds off the teaching and leaves the decision to Arjuna after full reflection. Then, out of love, he adds one final 'most secret' word (18.64-66): fix your mind on me, take refuge in me, do not grieve.
bg.18.63.core_teaching: After giving his teaching, Krishna does not command; he asks Arjuna to reflect on all of it and then choose freely.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: 'It' means the whole teaching just given by the omniscient Lord. Reflect on all of it, then act as you see fit. He then introduces a further word: devotion to the Lord is the secret of success in karma yoga.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: The secret wisdom covers karma yoga, jnana yoga and bhakti yoga. Arjuna should examine them all and freely choose the one that suits him.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The gracious, all-knowing Lord closes the teaching of the whole Gita here. If Arjuna reflects on it fully, his delusion will lift; then he may act as he likes.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The teaching is the essence of the Vedas, revealed to Arjuna because he is dear to the Lord. Whoever lives by it reaches peace and the highest knowledge.

bg.18.63.practical_reading: Teachers highlight that even God leaves the choice to the person: gather wisdom, think it through completely, and then own your decision.
misreadings: Not 'anything goes'; the freedom comes after full reflection on the whole teaching.
Not 'I've told you everything' (see translation note).
not_for: someone in crisis who needs direct guidance or help now rather than open choice
speaks_to: after gathering advice, choosing for oneself

data_flags.translation_note: Flagged false for the LINE (the translation itself is acceptable). Translation fine. Line error: 'I've told you all I know' is not in the verse, which says 'thus this knowledge, more secret than all secrets, has been declared to you by me'. Krishna also goes...

bg.18.64.context: Krishna has just left Arjuna free to reflect and choose (18.63). Now, unprompted, he says he will repeat the most secret teaching once more because Arjuna is dear to him. The next two verses (18.65-66) give that teaching: fix your mind on me and take refuge in me alone.
bg.18.64.core_teaching: The final teaching is given out of love rather than duty or gain: the teacher repeats what matters most because the student is dear.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Though already said more than once, the Lord repeats it not from fear or hope of reward but because Arjuna is his firm, beloved friend; what he will tell is the highest good, the means to knowledge.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Of the three paths, bhakti-yoga is pre-eminent and so most secret (as in 9.1); because Arjuna is dear and devoted, the Lord again states what is for his good.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: For those unable to absorb the whole profound teaching, the Lord kindly gives its essence in three verses; he repeats it because Arjuna is very dear to him.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The repetition is to make a deep impression; Krishna seeks nothing from Arjuna, who is his beloved friend and disciple, and so tells him the supreme good.

bg.18.64.practical_reading: Teachers stress the tenderness: before the hardest truth, Krishna reassures Arjuna that he is loved; good counsel lands best when the listener knows they are cared for.
misreadings: Not favouritism toward a chosen few; the commentators tie it to Arjuna's devotion and readiness.
not_for: Little risk; may feel hollow to someone grieving the loss of the person who loved them most
speaks_to: Needing to hear something important from someone who cares
Mentors and parents wanting to give counsel with warmth

bg.18.65.context: After leaving the choice to Arjuna (18.63), Krishna says he will tell him his supreme word, the most secret of all, because Arjuna is dearly loved (18.64). This verse gives it: fix your mind on me and you will come to me. The next verse (18.66) completes it with the call to take refuge in him alone.
bg.18.65.core_teaching: Keep your mind, love, worship and reverence turned toward the divine, and you will reach it; this is given as a personal promise, out of love.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: 'You will reach me' means: by taking Vasudeva alone as aim, means and end. Knowing the Lord's word is true and that liberation follows from devotion, one should take him as the highest and only refuge.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: 'Mind on me' means meditation so vivid it approaches direct experience, steeped in love; worship and bowing must express inner love, not mere ritual. The promise is a real pledge: the Lord cannot bear separation from one who loves him.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Remember the Lord, be devoted to him alone, worship him and bow to him. Through knowledge gained by his grace you will come to him; do not doubt it, since you are dear to him.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Bring the wandering mind back to the Lord again and again; let tongue, hands and feet all serve him, and give up hatred of any creature. Taking him as sole refuge is the secret of devotion.

bg.18.65.practical_reading: Teachers turn it into a simple daily practice: remember the divine during the day, offer what you do, bow inwardly, and rest in the assurance that you are loved.
misreadings: Not a demand for exclusive ritual at the expense of duties; Sivananda reads it as including work done for God.
Not conditional love in a transactional sense; the reason given is 'you are dear to me'.
not_for: non-theistic readers, if framed as obligation
speaks_to: longing to feel loved by God

bg.18.66.context: This is the culmination of Krishna's final 'most secret' word (18.64-66): after asking Arjuna to fix his mind on him (18.65), he asks him to take refuge in him alone and promises release from all sin. Krishna then says who should hear this teaching (18.67-71) and asks if Arjuna's confusion is gone (18.72); Arjuna says it is (18.73).
bg.18.66.core_teaching: Stop relying on your own observances to save you; take refuge wholly in the divine, which promises to free you from every fault, so there is no need for anguish.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: 'All dharmas' includes adharma too: the verse teaches giving up all works. Seeking the Lord alone means knowing 'I am that Lord', the one Self in all. He then argues at length that self-knowledge alone leads to the highest good.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: First reading: keep practising karma, jnana and bhakti yoga as worship, but give up fruit, ownership and doership, seeing the Lord as doer, goal and means. Alternative: give up endless expiatory rites and take the merciful Lord as refuge.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The Lord reveals something more secret still. Trusting that everything comes through devotion, leave behind servitude to scriptural injunctions and take refuge in him alone. Do not fear sin for setting duties aside; he will free you.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Calls this the answer to Arjuna's plea in 2.7. Following Shankara, he reads it as knowing the one Self; for devotees, it means working ceaselessly for the Lord while surrendering every fruit and taking him as sole refuge.

bg.18.66.practical_reading: Teachers use it to lift the weight of guilt and spiritual scorekeeping: you are not saved by flawless performance; lean wholly on grace, put down the anxiety, and then act.
misreadings: Not 'do nothing' or 'ignore your duties' (as our misuse note says); Ramanuja's main reading keeps the disciplines and gives up their fruit, ownership and doership, and Arjuna goes on to fight.
Not a license to keep doing wrong.

Among the most debated verses in the Gita: Shankara reads it as renouncing all works for self-knowledge, Sridhara as leaving servitude to injunctions, Ramanuja in two ways, and Govindacharya notes it is the 'charama-śloka', one of the three mysteries of Ramanuja's school. Avoid presenting one reading as the only one.
cautions: For a guilt plan, pair the promise of release with responsibility for repair, so it does not read as cheap absolution.
not_for: someone using faith to avoid accountability
readers hurt by religious authority, if 'abandon all dharmas' is read as demanding total submission
speaks_to: spiritual exhaustion from trying to be perfect

bg.18.7.context: First of three kinds of relinquishment (18.7-9). Having said that purifying actions must be done without attachment (18.6), Krishna says that dropping one's obligatory duties out of confusion is tamasic. The next verse covers dropping them out of fear of hardship, and the one after describes the sattvic way.
bg.18.7.core_teaching: Abandoning one's real duties is not genuine renunciation; doing so out of confusion is the darkest kind of giving up.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Abandoning an obligatory duty is not proper, since it purifies one who does not yet know; to call a duty obligatory and then drop it is self-contradictory. Such abandonment comes from ignorance, and ignorance is tamas.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Without action even the body cannot be sustained (3.8); food consecrated through sacrifice nourishes a mind fit for holy knowledge (citing the Chandogya), unconsecrated food breeds error. So ceasing prescribed duties is wrong, and abstention from misconception is tamasic.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Giving up desire-prompted work is proper, as it binds; but giving up obligatory rites, which liberate by purifying the mind, comes from the deluded idea that what is prescribed should be dropped; that delusion is tamasic.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Prescribed duties purify the ignorant person; one who renounces what he should do as duty is deluded by ignorance, and such renunciation is of the nature of darkness.

bg.18.7.practical_reading: Teachers use it for the temptation to walk away from responsibilities in the name of spirituality, burnout or confusion. Before dropping something, ask whether it comes from clarity or from fog.
misreadings: Not 'you can never leave a role, job or relationship'; it targets abandonment out of confusion.
Not a defence of harmful duties; 'niyata' meant scriptural duties, and modern readers should not stretch it to obligations that harm.
cautions: Someone in an abusive marriage, exploitative job or unsafe family situation must not hear this as 'staying is your duty'.
For a reader in depression, 'abandoning duty from delusion' can sound like blame; pair with compassion.
not_for: Anyone in an abusive or unsafe situation
Someone who has thoughtfully decided to leave a harmful role
speaks_to: Spiritual bypassing: dropping duties because they seem 'worldly'
Neglecting family or health obligations out of overwhelm

bg.18.73.context: Krishna has asked whether Arjuna listened with a focused mind and whether his confusion born of ignorance is gone (18.72). Arjuna answers here, the last words he speaks in the Gita. Sanjaya then closes the account (18.74-78), rejoicing in the dialogue and declaring that where Krishna and Arjuna are, there is fortune, victory and sound conduct.
bg.18.73.core_teaching: Through the teaching and grace, Arjuna's confusion lifts and he recovers his true self-understanding; he stands steady, free of doubt, ready to act.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Delusion is the ignorance behind all worldly evil, as hard to cross as an ocean; 'memory' is recognising the Self. The exchange shows the purpose of the whole teaching: to end delusion and bring self-recognition, as the Upanishads say.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Delusion was mistaking the self for matter and thinking duty binds rather than serves as worship. Arjuna regains knowledge of the self as distinct from matter and the Lord's servant; freed from grief born of misplaced pity, he will fight.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Arjuna's delusion about the Self is gone and he recalls his true nature, through grace. Now free of doubt about his duty, he rises to fight as told.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Calls delusion maya's strongest weapon. All spiritual practice aims at ending it and gaining self-knowledge, after which doubts and karma fall away (Isha Upanishad 7).

bg.18.73.practical_reading: Teachers use it as the shape of a good decision: confusion lifts when you remember who you are and what you value; then you can stand firm and act.
misreadings: Not blind obedience (as our misuse note says); it follows Krishna's 'reflect on it fully, then do as you wish' (18.63), and Ramanuja and Shankara present it as the fruit of regained knowledge.
Not a promise that every doubt vanishes forever.
cautions: In the story the action Arjuna commits to is fighting a war; keep the decision-plan reading on clarity and commitment.
not_for: someone being pressured to obey an authority figure

bg.18.78.context: Krishna has asked whether Arjuna's delusion is gone; Arjuna says it is and that he will do as told (18.72-73). Sanjaya, who has narrated the whole dialogue to the blind king Dhritarashtra, describes his thrill at hearing it and closes with this conviction about which side will prevail.
bg.18.78.core_teaching: Where the divine guide and the committed doer stand together, success and right order follow; for Sanjaya this is also a pointed hint to the king about the war's outcome.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Glosses briefly: 'wherever' means on whichever side; Krishna is lord of yoga since all yoga springs from him; the archer bears the Gandiva; 'there' is the Pandavas' side, where fortune, victory, growing prosperity and policy stand.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Krishna is lord of every arrangement of beings, governing all; where he and Partha, whose only refuge is the Lord's feet, are together, fortune, victory, power and righteousness dwell permanently.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Sanjaya is hinting to Dhritarashtra to give up hope for his sons' rule, seek Krishna's refuge and make peace with the Pandavas; he then sums up the Gita as devotion, aided by self-knowledge given by grace, leading to liberation.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Calls this the 'one-verse Gita', whose recitation carries the merit of the whole; follows Shankara's gloss on 'wherever' and 'lord of yoga'.

bg.18.78.practical_reading: Teachers apply it as a partnership: inner guidance and wholehearted effort together; neither prayer without action nor action without guidance.
misreadings: Not a guarantee of worldly success to anyone who claims God is on their side.
The 'wisdom plus effort' reading is a modern allegory; the commentators read it literally about Krishna, Arjuna and the war.
cautions: Victory language can sound triumphal to someone who has just failed or lost; avoid pairing with defeat.
not_for: Someone who has just failed and may hear it as 'you lacked God'
Partisan or 'God is on our side' contexts
speaks_to: Starting a venture and wanting to align effort with guidance
Teams: the value of a guide and a doer working together
Closing a period of study or reflection

bg.18.8.context: Second of the three kinds of relinquishment (18.7-9): after dropping duty out of delusion (tamasic), this is dropping it because it is painful or physically taxing (rajasic). The next verse gives the sattvic alternative.
bg.18.8.core_teaching: Giving up a duty simply because it is hard or physically demanding is self-protective, not renunciation, and it does not bring the inner freedom real renunciation brings.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Whoever abandons an act as painful, from fear of bodily trouble, makes a rajasic abandonment and does not obtain its fruit, liberation, which belongs to renouncing all action together with wisdom.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Earning the means for work and its fatigue pain the mind; dropping one's duties out of that dread to practise meditation alone is rajasic and against scripture. Work purifies the mind not by visible means but through the Lord's grace.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Without the knowledge 'I am not the doer', giving up regular rites simply because they are irksome, from fear of bodily trouble, is rajasic, since pain belongs to rajas; such a person does not gain the fruit, steadiness in knowledge.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Religious duties need determination and persistence; one may begin an action but drop it before completion because of difficulty or physical suffering.

bg.18.8.practical_reading: A check on avoidance: are you stepping back from something because it is wrong for you, or because it is uncomfortable? Ramanuja's note fits anyone tempted to quit work to 'focus on spirituality'.
misreadings: Not 'never quit' or 'ignore your body's limits'; it warns against fleeing from mere discomfort.
Not a glorification of exhaustion.
cautions: Chronic illness, disability, pregnancy, injury and burnout are real limits; do not use this verse to shame someone who has stepped back for health reasons.
not_for: Someone with chronic illness, injury or burnout
Caregivers at breaking point
speaks_to: Procrastination and avoidance of hard tasks
Wanting to quit when work gets physically or emotionally demanding
People romanticising leaving work for a 'spiritual' life

bg.18.9.context: Third of the three kinds of relinquishment (18.7-9): after the tamasic (from confusion) and rajasic (from fear of strain), the sattvic kind is to keep doing one's duty because it ought to be done, while giving up attachment and the fruit. Krishna next describes the person established in this relinquishment (18.10).
bg.18.9.core_teaching: True relinquishment keeps the action and drops the clinging: do what needs doing because it should be done, without attachment and without demanding a payoff.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Even the supposed fruits of obligatory work, such as self-purification or avoiding the sin of omission, are to be given up. Done without attachment or longing, such work makes the mind pure and tranquil, fit for contemplation of the Self.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: All duties of one's varna and stage of life are modes of worship of the Lord and ends in themselves; done without 'my-ness' and without seeking fruit, this is sattvic renunciation, sattva being the source of right knowledge.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: When compulsory work is performed with the understanding that it ought to be done, giving up attachment to it and to its fruit, that relinquishment is sattvic.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The pure person does the actions that fall to his lot, according to capacity and nature, without pride in being the doer or hope of gain.

bg.18.9.practical_reading: Teachers use it for daily duties that bring no applause: caring for parents, routine work, chores. Doing them because they are right, without bargaining for reward, is itself freedom.
misreadings: Not 'never question your duties'; choose wisely, then act without clinging.
Not that duties must be joyless; Ramanuja treats them as worship worthwhile in themselves.
cautions: Avoid using it to keep someone locked in harmful or exploitative obligations.
not_for: Someone in an exploitative arrangement being told it is their 'duty'
speaks_to: Caregivers and parents doing unglamorous daily work
Wanting a healthier relationship to obligation

bg.2.11.context: Arjuna has said 'I will not fight' and fallen silent (2.9); Krishna, as if smiling (2.10), now begins the teaching proper. This verse opens the section on the deathless self that runs to 2.30, followed by arguments from duty (2.31-38).
bg.2.11.core_teaching: Krishna points to the contradiction between Arjuna's grief and his learned arguments: those who know what the self truly is do not grieve as he does, for the dead or the living. It sets up the teaching that the self is eternal and the body changes by nature.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Bhishma and Drona need no grief: they are good men and eternal in their real nature. Arjuna mourns yet talks like the wise, showing folly and wisdom together; knowers of the self mourn neither living nor dead.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Arjuna's talk of ancestors losing offerings (1.42) assumes a soul distinct from the body, yet he grieves. For those who know the true natures of body and soul, neither the lifeless body nor the living soul is cause for grief.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Arjuna's grief comes from not discriminating self from body. He mourns kin who are not truly objects of sorrow and, though rebuked at 2.2, keeps uttering learned-sounding words without being wise; the wise grieve for neither dead nor living.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Says the Gita's philosophy begins here. Bhishma and Drona are eternal in their real nature; knowers of the self do not mourn living or dead because they know the self is unborn and death is only the body's disintegration.

bg.2.11.practical_reading: Teachers read it as an invitation to look at what grief is attached to: the changing body and circumstances, or the person's deeper being, which the Gita says does not end. Many stress it answers grief that has frozen Arjuna in the middle of his duty, not the ordinary tears of loss.
misreadings: Not 'don't cry' or 'your grief is wrong'.
Not contempt for mourners; the point concerns knowing the self, not suppressing feeling.
Not 'the dead don't matter'.
cautions: Literally tells the listener not to grieve; on Day 1 of a grief plan it would land as dismissive.
The eternal-self frame can feel like a brush-off to fresh loss.
The line ('talking like you know better') can feel scolding.
not_for: Fresh bereavement (first days or weeks)
Loss of a child, or loss to suicide
Anyone already being told by others to 'move on'
speaks_to: Grief that has become paralysis and stops someone doing what must be done
Anticipatory grief, fear of losing someone
Readers ready to ask what in a person does not die
Overthinking that dresses fear in clever arguments

bg.2.12.context: Krishna's first argument after 2.11 for why the wise do not grieve. It is followed by the image of the self passing through childhood, youth and old age into another body (2.13) and the advice to endure passing heat and cold (2.14).
bg.2.12.core_teaching: None of them, Krishna, Arjuna or the kings, ever began to exist or will cease to exist: the self persists through past, present and future, so death of the body is not the end of the person.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: I, you and these kings existed through past births and deaths and will continue after these bodies die: as the self we are eternal in all three times. The plural refers to different bodies, not many selves.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: As the Lord has always existed, so have Arjuna and all these souls, and all will exist forever. Spoken by a teacher removing ignorance, the 'I, you, all of us' shows that souls are many and distinct from God.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The Lord, though his body of divine play appears and disappears, is beginningless; Arjuna and the kings, being parts of him, always existed and always will. Having no birth or death, they need no grief.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Speaks of the immortality of the soul: it exists in past, present and future, and a person continues to exist after the physical body dies; there is life beyond.

bg.2.12.practical_reading: Teachers apply it as perspective on identity: the 'you' that persists through childhood, youth and age is more than passing circumstances, so loss and change do not erase who someone is.
misreadings: Not a claim that bodies or personalities are permanent.
Not a reason to treat life or death lightly because 'no one really dies'.
cautions: About death and continuity of the self; comforting to some, abstract or dismissive to others in fresh grief.
Schools differ (one self appearing as many, or many real selves); avoid presenting one view as the only meaning.
not_for: A reader of another faith or none, in acute grief, who may experience it as doctrine imposed
Someone who needs practical, not metaphysical, help right now
speaks_to: Wondering whether a loved one who has died still exists
Existential anxiety, a sense of being more than one's roles

bg.2.13.context: Krishna has just smiled at Arjuna's grief and told him the wise mourn neither those who have died nor those still alive (2.11), since none of them ever did not exist (2.12). This verse is his first illustration. Next he turns to pleasure and pain as passing sense-contacts that must be endured (2.14–15).
bg.2.13.core_teaching: The self stays the same through childhood, youth and old age, and it passes into another body in the same way. Death is therefore one more transition of the body, and the wise are not bewildered by it.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The Self passes unchanged through the stages of life. It does not die when childhood ends or get born when youth begins. It enters another body just as unchanged, so the wise are not troubled.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Nobody grieves moving from infancy to youth, so the wise do not grieve moving between bodies. Selves are eternal, bound by past deeds, and win freedom by doing their duties without craving the fruit.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Answering the objection that individual souls are born and die: across life's stages we know 'I am the same person', and the self takes a new body through the subtle body. A newborn's instinct to suckle shows past impressions.

bg.2.13.practical_reading: Teachers use the familiar sense of being the same 'me' who was once a child to make a continuing self feel intuitive. The steadiness it offers is not being thrown when the body changes.
misreadings: Not a claim that ageing or death doesn't matter. It is about not being thrown into confusion by them.
Not just about ageing. The second half is about death and rebirth.
cautions: This passage teaches rebirth. To a newly bereaved reader, a doctrine that the dead simply move on can feel like it skips over their loss.
In context the verse supports Krishna's argument that the wise do not grieve (2.11). Writers should not pass that on as 'you should not grieve'.
not_for: someone in the first raw days of a bereavement who needs their grief acknowledged, not explained
readers who do not hold a belief in rebirth, unless it is framed as the Gita's view
speaks_to: noticing how much you have changed and are still you
wanting a sense of continuity beyond a loss

bg.2.14.context: Just after the image of the self passing through childhood, youth and old age (2.13), Krishna anticipates a further worry: even if the self is eternal, we still suffer heat and cold, pleasure and pain. He says these come and go and must be borne. The next verse (2.15) says the steady person who is not shaken by them is fit for immortality.
bg.2.14.core_teaching: Pleasure and pain arise when the senses meet things, and by nature they begin and end. So bear them without being carried away by either joy or grief.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Cold or heat that pleases at one moment hurts at another. Because sense-contacts begin and end, they are impermanent, so endure them bravely and do not hand yourself over to joy or grief because of them.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Cold and heat stand for every kind of experience. Bear them with courage until your appointed duty is complete. They come and go, and they cannot disturb one whose karma has run out.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The same object pleases at one moment and hurts at another, so sensations are impermanent. It is the mind that feels pleasure and pain. Bear them patiently and cultivate a balanced mind.

bg.2.14.practical_reading: In stress, the verse invites you to notice that this discomfort, like weather, has a beginning and an end. Patience means bearing it without adding panic or despair.
misreadings: Not a call to tolerate harm, abuse or unsafe conditions. Those are not passing sensations to wait out (as our misuse note says).
Not 'feel nothing'. Shankara and Sridhara mean not being swept away by joy or grief, not numbness.
cautions: Sridhara applies the verse directly to the pain of losing loved ones. If it is reused in a grief context, that reading can sound like it reduces bereavement to a passing sensation.
not_for: someone in an abusive or unsafe situation
chronic pain or illness that will not 'pass', where 'it comes and goes' can feel invalidating
speaks_to: a stressful stretch that will pass
physical or emotional discomfort you can't change right now

bg.2.15.context: Krishna has said the self passes through childhood, youth and age (2.13) and that the contacts of the senses bring heat and cold, pleasure and pain, which come and go and must be endured (2.14). This verse gives the reason to endure them; 2.16 then distinguishes the unreal from the real.
bg.2.15.core_teaching: The person who is not knocked over by the passing contacts of pleasure and pain, and holds steady through both, becomes fit for freedom. Endurance grounded in understanding, not mere toughness, is the point.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The wise person who neither exults in pleasure nor sinks in pain, unaffected by heat and cold because he sees the eternal self, and who bears the opposites calmly, becomes fit for immortality, meaning liberation.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: A courageous person who regards unavoidable pain as equal to pleasure is untroubled by blows; for such a one, doing the duties of his station without seeking reward leads to immortality, not for one who cannot bear pain.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Rather than trying to remedy the sense-contacts, one should simply endure them, since that yields a great result; the person not overpowered by them, unperturbed in pleasure and pain, becomes fit for liberation through knowledge.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Pleasure and pain come from identifying the self with the body. Endurance (titiksha) builds will-power and is a qualification on the path of knowledge; alone it does not liberate, but joined with discrimination and dispassion it leads to immortality.

bg.2.15.practical_reading: Teachers apply it as training in equanimity: let good and bad days come and go without letting either decide who you are, and build the steadiness to keep doing what matters through both.
misreadings: Not numbness or hiding what you feel.
Not a demand to tolerate harm that can and should be stopped; the examples are unavoidable passing experiences (heat, cold, pleasure, pain).
cautions: A reader in acute pain may hear 'stay the same in pain' as being told their suffering is a failure of composure.
not_for: Someone enduring abuse who needs permission to leave, not to endure
Acute grief or crisis, where 'be the same in pain and pleasure' sounds dismissive
speaks_to: Mood swings tied to success and failure
Long stretches of discomfort that must be borne (recovery, caregiving, exam preparation)

bg.2.16.context: After telling Arjuna to endure passing pleasure and pain (2.14-15), Krishna gives the principle behind it: what is unreal has no being and what is real never stops being. The next verses (2.17-18) say that what pervades all is imperishable while bodies come to an end, so 'fight'.
bg.2.16.core_teaching: What changes and passes, such as heat, cold, pleasure, pain and the body, does not have real being; what is truly real, the self, never ceases. Seeing this difference makes endurance possible.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Heat, cold and their causes are not truly real, being changing effects, as a pot is never perceived apart from clay. What awareness never loses is real, what it loses is unreal; the self is the real.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Asat is the non-sentient body, whose nature is to change; sat is the conscious soul, whose nature is constancy. Seers of truth have settled the essential nature of each, so the body's passing is no ground for grief.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Answers how hard things like heat and cold can be endured: by discrimination. Being non-self, they have no reality in the self; the self, whose nature is being, never ceases; knowers of truth have settled both.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The changeless self alone always exists; the ever-changing world of names and forms is unreal, like a mirage or the snake seen in a rope. The sage sees through name and form to existence-knowledge-bliss.

bg.2.16.practical_reading: Teachers use it to separate what passes (moods, circumstances, praise and blame) from what lasts in you, so that you stop staking your whole self on what is changing.
misreadings: Not 'the world is fake, nothing matters'; even the Advaita reading uses it to ground endurance and right action.
Schools disagree sharply on what the 'unreal' is; avoid presenting one reading as the only one.
cautions: Abstract and philosophical; calling a reader's pain 'unreal' would land badly in distress.
not_for: Someone in pain who could hear it as 'your suffering isn't real'
Fresh grief
speaks_to: Anxiety about losing status, possessions or approval
Wanting a fixed point when everything is changing

bg.2.2.context: Sanjaya has just described Arjuna in tears, overcome by pity (2.1). These are Krishna's first words in the Gita: a sharp question about where this collapse came from. The rebuke continues in 2.3; Arjuna then lays out his dilemma (2.4-2.8) and at 2.7 asks to be taught.
bg.2.2.core_teaching: Krishna questions the timing and source of Arjuna's collapse: at the decisive moment he has slid into a confusion that noble people do not indulge and that serves neither this life nor the next.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Asks from what cause this confusion has come over Arjuna in a crisis; it is not something honourable people take up, it does not lead to heaven, meaning it is unrighteous, and it brings disrepute.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Reads 2.2-2.3 together: Krishna rebukes a sadness felt out of place, not approved by the wise, harmful to higher aims, inglorious and born of a faint heart, and urges him to shake it off and stand up to fight.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901, introduction at 2.10
commentaries.gist: Does not comment on 2.2; his introduction at 2.10 treats everything up to 2.9 as the display of grief and delusion that the teaching from 2.11 removes.

bg.2.2.practical_reading: Teachers read it as a wake-up question rather than contempt: when you notice yourself shutting down exactly when action matters, ask where the paralysis came from instead of simply obeying it.
misreadings: Not a model for shaming someone's tears or fear.
Not Krishna's whole answer: he starts by appealing to honour and duty, and the deeper teaching begins at 2.11 (Shankara's 2.10 introduction).
cautions: The tone is a rebuke; for a reader in grief, depression or burnout it can feel like being scolded for struggling.
Words like 'disgrace' and 'ignoble' can feed shame.
not_for: Fresh grief or bereavement
Depression or burnout, where a reprimand lands as blame
Someone already flooded with shame
speaks_to: Freezing or backing out at a decisive moment (an exam, interview, hard conversation) and wanting a firm nudge
Someone who has asked a friend to be blunt with them
Noticing that a sudden doubt is really fear

bg.2.20.context: Krishna has just said that whoever thinks the self kills, or is killed, does not understand (2.19). This verse gives the reason. The next verse asks how one who knows this could kill or cause killing (2.21). The passage is part of Krishna's answer to Arjuna's horror at killing his kin in battle.
bg.2.20.core_teaching: The self is free of every change that bodies go through, including birth, growth, decay and death. Whatever happens to the body, the self is not destroyed.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The verse denies all six changes every being undergoes, from birth to death. The Self has no parts and no qualities to lose, and 'not slain' means it is not altered when the body is.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Birth and death belong to bodies, not to the self. 'Ancient' here means old yet always new, something that can be experienced ever freshly. Bodies perish; the self cannot.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The Self is free of the six transformations from birth to death. Being indivisible, it neither grows nor declines. Birth and death touch only the physical body, never the all-pervading Self.

bg.2.20.practical_reading: The verse offers the thought that what a person most deeply is was not ended by the death of their body. Many readers find that a comfort to hold, not an argument to accept.
misreadings: Not a reason to skip mourning or to treat a death as unimportant (as our misuse note says).

Not, in context, a general statement about loss. It is part of Krishna's argument that Arjuna can fight without the self being harmed. The writer should not carry that 'so killing doesn't matter' logic into a grief reading.
cautions: Used on Day 1 of the grief plan ('see'). The surrounding verses (2.11, 2.25, 2.27) draw the conclusion 'therefore you should not grieve'. On a day meant to name the feeling, that conclusion can land as a dismissal. The writer should validate the grief first.
Mentions death and slaying directly.
This passage teaches rebirth. To a newly bereaved reader, a doctrine that the dead simply move on can feel like it skips over their loss.
not_for: someone in the first days of a loss who needs space to mourn, unless the reading leads with acknowledgement
grief after violent death, where the battle context can be jarring
speaks_to: wanting to believe something of a loved one continues
a sense that a person was more than their body

bg.2.22.context: This continues Krishna's argument (2.19–25) that the self is never killed and so Arjuna's grief is misplaced. Just before, he asks how one who knows the self as indestructible could kill or be killed (2.21). Just after, he says weapons, fire, water and wind cannot touch it (2.23).
bg.2.22.core_teaching: Death is like changing clothes. The self lets go of a worn-out body and takes on a new one, and the self itself is not changed by this.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Like a person changing old clothes for new, the embodied Self leaves old bodies and enters new ones without itself undergoing any change.

bg.2.22.practical_reading: For those who hold the Gita's view, the image can soften the finality of death: the person has set down a body, not ceased to be. It works as a picture to rest in, not a reason to stop missing someone.
misreadings: Not a line for brushing off someone else's grief (our misuse note is right).
Not a claim that the dead are better off, or that the death was good, even though one classical reading (Ramanuja, about warriors) goes that way.
cautions: This is a strong caution. Used on Day 2 of the grief plan, but both Ramanuja and Sridhara read the verse as removing grounds for grief. Ramanuja even says a warrior's death is matter for rejoicing. The writer must not carry over 'no need to grieve'.
'Worn-out' fits old age. For the death of a child, a young person or a sudden death, the image can feel wrong or hurtful.
This passage teaches rebirth. To a newly bereaved reader, a doctrine that the dead simply move on can feel like it skips over their loss.
not_for: loss of a child or a young person
sudden or violent death
early, raw grief
speaks_to: wanting a gentle picture of death as transition
a reader whose own tradition holds rebirth
anticipatory grief for an elderly loved one

bg.2.23.context: This is part of Krishna's run of reasons (2.19–25) why the self is never destroyed. It follows the clothes image (2.22). The next two verses call the self uncuttable, eternal and beyond thought, and conclude that knowing this, Arjuna should not grieve (2.25).
bg.2.23.core_teaching: Nothing in the physical world, whether weapon, fire, water or wind, can damage the self, because it is not a physical thing made of parts.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The Self has no parts. Weapons cannot divide it, fire cannot reduce it to ash, water cannot loosen it by wetting, and wind cannot dry what has no moisture.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The verse spells out the earlier question, 'how can it be slain?', by showing that no means of destruction exists. Water cannot even soften it.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The Self is indivisible, without parts, extremely subtle and infinite, so sword, fire, water and wind have no hold on it.

bg.2.23.practical_reading: For a grieving reader it offers one image of steadiness: whatever happened to the body, the self was beyond its reach. It can be held quietly, without arguing anyone out of their sorrow.
misreadings: Not a statement that the body's suffering didn't matter.
Not 'nothing can hurt you' in an everyday sense. It is about the self, not the person's feelings or circumstances.
cautions: Used on Day 4 of the grief plan. The argument it belongs to ends at 2.25 with 'knowing this, you should not grieve', and Ramanuja repeats it. Writers should keep that conclusion out of the reading.
The list of weapons and fire may be painful after a violent death, an accident or a cremation.
not_for: grief after violent death or fire, where the images may be too literal
speaks_to: needing an image of something in a loved one that was untouched by what happened
finding steadiness on a hard day of grief

bg.2.25.context: Part of Krishna's description of the self that cannot be cut, burnt, wetted or dried (2.23-24). This verse closes the description with three more marks and draws the conclusion: do not grieve. From 2.26 he argues that even on the opposite view grief is not fitting.
bg.2.25.core_teaching: The self is not something the senses grasp, the mind can picture, or anything can alter; knowing it so, there is no ground for grieving over it, or for thinking 'I kill, they are killed'.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The self is beyond the senses, so unmanifest; what is not perceived cannot be thought, so unthinkable; having no parts, it cannot change as milk does. Knowing this, do not grieve or see yourself as slayer.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The soul cannot be shown like divisible physical things, nor conceived as having this or that familiar quality; it is a unique kind of entity and so cannot be modified. Knowing this, Arjuna has no cause for grief.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Unmanifest: not an object of the eye and senses; unthinkable: not an object of the mind; unchangeable: not touched by the organs of action. 'Is said to be' brings in scriptural authority for the self's eternity.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Follows Shankara closely: the self cannot be seen, so cannot be thought of, and does not change form like milk turned by buttermilk; so do not mourn, nor think of yourself as slayer.

bg.2.25.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a reminder that the deepest part of a person is not what illness, ageing or loss can reach, which can steady both the grieving and the dying.
misreadings: Not a prohibition on mourning; it concerns grief over the self being destroyed.
Not a claim that the body or personality is unchanging.
cautions: Ends in 'you should not grieve'; would feel dismissive early in a grief plan.
Assumes an eternal self; can feel like doctrine to a reader who does not share it.
not_for: The first days of bereavement
A reader who wants practical help, not metaphysics
speaks_to: Facing serious illness or ageing in oneself or a loved one
Reflective grief some time after a loss
Fear that a person is 'gone completely'

bg.2.26.context: Having described the deathless self (2.17-25), Krishna now argues from the other side: suppose Arjuna holds the common view that the self is born and dies. Even so (2.27), birth leads certainly to death and death to birth, so grief over the inevitable is unfitting.
bg.2.26.core_teaching: Even on the view that the self is born and dies with the body, being crushed by grief is not warranted, because birth and death are bound to follow each other.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Grants the popular view that the self is born with each body and dies with it; even so Arjuna should not grieve, since death is inevitable for what is born and birth for what has died.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: If Arjuna still takes the self to be nothing but the body, constantly born and dying, there is still no ground for grief: for changing bodies, birth and death are an unavoidable law of nature.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
