commentaries.gist: Having shown that the self has neither birth nor destruction, Krishna now argues that even if the self were born and died with the body, grief would still be out of place.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Krishna takes up the popular supposition for argument's sake; even then one should not grieve, because birth and death follow each other by an unrelenting law of nature.

bg.2.26.practical_reading: Teachers point out that the Gita meets you where you are: whatever you believe about what happens after death, being destroyed by grief does not follow from it. It invites steadiness, not a particular metaphysics.
misreadings: Not a request to stop feeling grief; 'like this' (evam) targets grief that overwhelms.
Not Krishna's own view of the self; it is a concession for argument.
cautions: Still ends in 'you should not grieve'; time it well after a loss.
Can sound like logic used against feelings.
not_for: Early grief
A reader whose grief is being policed by others
speaks_to: Readers unsure about an afterlife who still want steadiness
Grief that has gone on to the point of stopping a person's life
People who find metaphysical comfort unconvincing

bg.2.27.context: The second half of Krishna's concessive argument begun in 2.26: even if the self is born and dies, death is certain for the born and birth for the dead. In 2.28 he adds that beings come from the unmanifest and return to it.
bg.2.27.core_teaching: Birth and death are bound together and cannot be avoided; grieving as if the inevitable could have been otherwise adds suffering without changing anything.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Death comes without fail to what is born and birth to what has died; since both are unavoidable, one ought not to grieve over them.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Death is certain for the born and rebirth for the dead; nothing that never was can come to be, so birth and death are only changes of state of something ever-existent, as yarn becomes cloth. Do not lament the unavoidable.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Death comes to the born when the karma that produced the body is exhausted; rebirth follows the dead because of the deeds done in that body. A wise man is not meant to grieve over what is inevitable.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Birth and death are certainly unavoidable, each following the other, so one should not grieve over an inevitable matter.

bg.2.27.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to acceptance: preparing for and accepting the death of the old or sick, and spending energy on care and presence rather than on fighting what cannot be changed.
misreadings: Not a reason to stop caring for the sick or to hurry someone's mourning.
Not fatalism about preventable harm; it concerns what is truly unavoidable.
cautions: Explicit rebirth doctrine; can feel dismissive to fresh grief or to readers who do not hold it.
Not for a sudden or untimely death, where 'inevitable' would sound cruel.
not_for: Loss of a child, accidental or violent death, suicide loss
The first weeks of bereavement
speaks_to: Anticipatory grief for an ageing parent

bg.2.28.context: Continuing the argument that grief is not fitting even for bodies, Krishna says beings are unseen before birth and after death, visible only in between. Next (2.29) he says the self is seen, spoken of and heard of as a wonder, and few truly know it.
bg.2.28.core_teaching: Beings come out of the unseen and return to it; only the middle span is visible. Seeing the whole arc softens the despair of thinking the visible part is all there is.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Sons and friends, as bodies, are unseen before birth, seen in the middle, unseen after death. He quotes a consolation verse (came from the unseen and went back; not yours, nor you his) and asks why lament mere appearances.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Beings, though ever-existent, pass from an unmanifest state before birth to a manifest middle and back to the unmanifest; such change is a law of nature and gives no cause for sorrow.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Bodies exist in causal form in the unmanifest (pradhana) before birth, are manifest between birth and death, and dissolve back; grieving them is like someone who has woken up still mourning friends lost in a dream.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The body, made of five elements, is visible only in its middle state. Family ties form through the body by attachment; like planks meeting and parting in a river or pilgrims at an inn, relatives unite and separate.

bg.2.28.practical_reading: Teachers use it to widen the frame in grief: a life is a visible stretch between two mysteries, and remembering the whole arc can ease the feeling that everything has simply ended.
misreadings: Grief is natural; the verse widens the frame, it doesn't forbid tears.
Not 'the person was never real'; the dream and illusion comparisons are about the body's passing appearance.
cautions: The commentaries compare bodies to a dream or illusion and quote 'he is not yours, nor you his'; avoid passing these images to a grieving reader.
Ends in a rhetorical 'why lament?', which can feel dismissive early in grief.
not_for: Fresh bereavement
Pregnancy loss or child loss
A reader who feels their grief is being minimised
speaks_to: Reflective grief some time after a loss
Birth and death in the family prompting big questions
Readers drawn to the mystery of where we come from

bg.2.3.context: Krishna continues the opening rebuke of 2.2. He addresses Arjuna as Partha, son of Pritha, and as 'scorcher of foes', recalling who he is. Arjuna replies in 2.4 by asking how he could shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, men he should revere.
bg.2.3.core_teaching: This faint-heartedness is not who Arjuna is; it is small and can be thrown off. Krishna calls him to stand up, before giving any reasons, which come later.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Glosses klaibyam as cowardice: do not be overcome by it, it does not befit you; shake off this mean, contemptible faint-heartedness and rise for battle, chastiser of foes.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Treats 2.2-2.3 together: a sadness out of season, unworthy and springing from weakness of heart; Krishna tells him to shake it off and stand up. Arjuna, still gripped by affection, pity and fear of wrongdoing, does not accept this.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Translates klaibyam as 'impotence' and the rest as a call to cast off mean weakness of heart and stand up; offers no separate comment on this verse.

bg.2.3.practical_reading: Teachers use it as the line a true friend says once: this smallness is not you. Name the shrinking, stand up, and take the next step; the reasons can follow.
misreadings: Not 'feelings are weakness' or 'man up'.
Not a statement about gender; Sridhara glosses klaibya as cowardice, i.e. loss of nerve.
Not the whole answer: the reasoned teaching begins at 2.11.
cautions: 'Unmanliness' can read as gendered shaming; consider 'faint-heartedness'.
A rebuke; not for acute grief or a reader who is already blaming themselves.
not_for: Clinical depression, trauma or panic responses
Grief
Someone being pressured into a fight they would be wise to walk away from
speaks_to: Talking yourself out of something you are capable of
Cold feet before a commitment or a performance
Needing a push after a long period of hesitation

bg.2.30.context: This verse concludes the teaching on the deathless self that began at 2.11. From 2.31 Krishna turns to a second line of argument: Arjuna's own duty as a warrior, and the dishonour of withdrawing.
bg.2.30.core_teaching: The self in every body can never be killed; therefore no being, Bhishma or anyone else, is to be grieved over as destroyed.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Though anyone's body is killed, the self cannot be; so grieve for no creature, Bhishma or anyone. This closes the argument from absolute truth; the next verses add the argument from duty.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Whatever body it inhabits, god's or mineral's, the dweller remains eternal and invulnerable though the body is slain; all selves are equal in essence while bodily variety is passing, so there is no reason to grieve for any being.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Concludes the brief teaching on the self's incomprehensibility with the point that one should not grieve for it; he says the meaning is quite clear.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The body of any creature may be destroyed but the self cannot be killed, so one should not grieve for any creature, Bhishma or anyone else.

bg.2.30.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that the essential being of a loved one, and of every creature, is not destroyed by death, and that all beings share that same deathless nature.
misreadings: Not a reason to hurry anyone through mourning a person or a pet.
Not a licence to harm, on the grounds that 'the self cannot be killed'.
cautions: Direct instruction not to grieve; unsuitable for early grief.
In context it supports going to war; avoid any reading that minimises violence.
not_for: Fresh loss
Violent or traumatic death
Readers who might hear it as 'your loss doesn't count'
speaks_to: Grief that has settled and is looking for meaning
Loss of an animal companion, read gently (Ramanuja: the same self in all beings)

bg.2.38.context: Krishna has just argued from worldly honour: a warrior who flees a righteous war loses duty and fame and earns disgrace (2.31–37). This verse closes that argument. With 2.39 he moves from the knowledge of the self to the yoga of action.
bg.2.38.core_teaching: Act from duty with an even mind towards pleasure and pain, gain and loss, win and defeat. Action done in that spirit does not bind or stain the one who acts.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: 'Treating alike' means not liking one outcome and disliking the other. Shankara adds that the command to fight is only incidental. The worldly arguments of 2.31–38 just remove grief; the real subject is knowledge of the Self.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Knowing the self as distinct from the body, keep the mind unshaken by pain, gain, loss, victory or defeat. Seek no reward such as heaven and fight as a duty. The 'sin' avoided is the bondage of worldly existence.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: This is the yoga of equanimity, poise in action. Work done with a balanced mind purifies the heart instead of binding. Such balance is built through continuous struggle and vigilance.

bg.2.38.practical_reading: Before a feared task, settle that you will meet a win or a loss with the same steadiness, then commit fully. The fear of the outcome loses some of its grip once the outcome is no longer what defines you.
misreadings: Not 'outcomes don't matter'. It means not being ruled by liking one and dreading the other.
Not a licence to harm others because you feel detached. 'No sin' is tied to doing a rightful duty, not to the attitude alone.
cautions: The verse is literally an order to go into battle against kin. Keep the generalisation to 'act' explicit.
Sridhara links it to Arjuna's fear of sin. Readers with scrupulosity or guilt may need the 'no sin' promise framed carefully.
not_for: someone being pushed into a fight or conflict that is actually wrong
speaks_to: fear of failing at something important
dreading a result you can't control
needing to commit to a hard task

bg.2.40.context: Krishna has just announced that he will now teach the yoga of action, by which Arjuna can break the bondage of karma (2.39). This verse is his first promise about it. The next verse contrasts the single resolute mind of this path with the scattered minds of the desire-driven.
bg.2.40.core_teaching: Unlike ordinary ventures, an effort on the path of desireless action is never wasted and cannot backfire. Even a small beginning protects you from the great fear of endless rebirth.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Unlike farming, nothing attempted on this path is wholly lost. Unlike medicine, it cannot cause harm. However little you do, it saves you from the great fear of saṃsāra, of birth and death.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Even if a duty begun this way is interrupted and left unfinished, no fruit is lost and no harm follows. Ordinary worldly and ritual efforts fail when interrupted and can backfire.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Worldly work and desire-driven rites can fail or backfire through defects. In action done for the Lord, defects do not count, so nothing begun is wasted, and even a start frees one from transmigration.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Each act of karma-yoga purifies the heart at once, so there is no uncertainty, as there is in farming, and no risk, as with a wrong medicine. Krishna praises it to build Arjuna's interest.

bg.2.40.practical_reading: Small, sincere steps on an inner practice count, even if you are interrupted or fall short. Starting is itself protective, so you don't have to do it perfectly or completely for it to matter.
misreadings: Not 'no effort is ever wasted' in worldly terms. Shankara and Sivananda explicitly contrast it with farming and medicine, where effort can fail. It does not promise that an exam, launch or project will succeed.
The 'great fear' is the fear of rebirth and bondage, not everyday anxiety, though teachers extend it.
cautions: Used on Day 3 of 'fear of failure'. The writer must not turn it into a promise that worldly effort always pays off. The commentators say the opposite about worldly effort.
not_for: someone who needs to hear that a real-world failure was not their fault, if framed as 'effort is never lost'
speaks_to: fear that starting something will be wasted
feeling that half-done efforts don't count

bg.2.41.context: Following the promise that nothing on this path is wasted (2.40), Krishna contrasts its single resolve with minds driven by many desires. The next verses (2.42–44) criticise people who love the flowery Vedic promises of heaven and power and so never reach a settled mind.
bg.2.41.core_teaching: On this path the understanding has one settled aim. People driven by many desires have thoughts that branch without end, and that scatter keeps them bound.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: On the path to liberation there is one resolute thought, born of right knowledge, which overturns all opposing ones. Following many-branched thoughts makes worldly life endless; when they cease, it ceases too.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The seeker of liberation has a single settled conviction about the self, so all their work points to one aim. Those after rewards like heaven have minds that branch endlessly.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: In work done as worship there is one settled conviction: that devotion to the Lord will surely save him. The desire-driven have endless thoughts because their desires are endless.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The yogi gathers the mind's scattered rays through discrimination, dispassion and concentration and stops wavering. The worldly mind breeds countless thoughts; control the thoughts and the mind is controlled.

bg.2.41.practical_reading: When a choice feels impossible, ask what your one real aim is. Many options branch out of many wants, and naming the aim prunes them.
misreadings: Not 'be decisive and pick fast'. The resolve comes from clarity about one's highest aim, not from speed.
Not a criticism of considering options carefully. Its target is minds pulled by countless desires.
cautions: In context (2.42–44) the 'irresolute' are those attached to ritual rewards and pleasures. The writer should not imply that an anxious decision-maker is shallow or worldly.
not_for: someone whose indecision comes from real constraints or danger, not scattered wants
speaks_to: going round in circles on a decision
needing to find the one thing that matters

bg.2.44.context: Krishna has just contrasted the single, resolute understanding of the yoga of action (2.41) with the scattered minds of those who delight in the Vedas' promises of heaven and pleasure (2.42-43). This verse concludes that thought; 2.45 tells Arjuna to rise above the three gunas.
bg.2.44.core_teaching: When the mind is hooked on comfort and power and keeps being lured by promises of more, a clear and single-minded understanding cannot settle in it.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Reading 2.42-44 together: the undiscriminating love Vedic passages promising heaven, cattle and progeny, say nothing else exists, and talk in pleasant 'flowery' words; minds identified with pleasure and power, blinded by this, never form a resolute conviction.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: 'Flowery' speech is pleasant like a flower but bears no further fruit; it is uttered by those devoted to the reward-promising parts of the Veda who deny any goal beyond heaven, and it keeps them in rebirth.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Those who hold heaven as the highest goal speak attractive words about rites that bring enjoyment and power; people carried away by them do not reach the one-pointed resolve that turns the mind wholly toward the Lord.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: People clinging to pleasure and power cannot steady the mind or meditate; always planning to acquire wealth and power, they stay restless and lack poised understanding.

bg.2.44.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to modern distraction: when attention is constantly captured by the promise of more comfort, status or reward, it cannot settle on one clear purpose. Fewer lures make room for focus.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of enjoyment or wealth as such; the problem is being carried away by them.
Not an attack on the Vedas as a whole; commentators read it as a critique of reading them only for rewards.
cautions: Can sound moralising to someone already struggling with addiction or compulsive behaviour; frame it as about attention, not character.
not_for: Someone in financial hardship, for whom 'chasing comfort' would feel insulting
A reader seeking comfort in grief
speaks_to: Scattered focus, constantly chasing the next thing
Career choices driven only by perks and status
Feeling unable to commit to one path

bg.2.45.context: Following the critique of reward-seeking ritualism (2.42-44), Krishna tells Arjuna to rise above the three gunas. In 2.46 he adds that for one who knows, the Vedas are like a small pond when the land is flooded; 2.47 gives the famous teaching on action without claim to its fruits.
bg.2.45.core_teaching: Scripture addresses people according to their desires; Arjuna is told to rise above that whole realm of wanting, bear the opposites, rest in clarity, and stop being consumed by getting and keeping.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The Vedas' ritual portion concerns samsara, the triad of gunas; be desireless, free of the opposites that cause pleasure and pain, abide in sattva, and do not worry over gaining or keeping, which makes virtue impossible. Be vigilant.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Translates the verse as a call to rise above the three qualities and the pairs, keep to sattva, be unconcerned about gaining and guarding things, and stay concerned with the self; gives little separate comment.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: If heaven is not the goal, why do the Vedas teach rites for it? They speak to the desire-filled under the gunas. Rise above them: endure heat and cold, joy and sorrow, keep to fortitude, and do not chase acquisition.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Explains the three gunas and the pairs of opposites (heat and cold, gain and loss, praise and blame); one anxious to gain new things or keep old ones is restless and cannot meditate or practise virtue.

bg.2.45.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to anxiety about getting and holding on: plan and provide, but do not let acquiring and protecting become the centre of life; keep a clear, steady core beneath the ups and downs.
misreadings: Not 'don't save or plan'; it's about not being consumed by getting and holding.
Not a rejection of scripture as such; Shankara and Sridhara say only the ritual portion addressed to desire-driven people is meant.
cautions: 'Free from the urge to acquire and keep' may grate on someone struggling to make ends meet.
not_for: Someone in genuine financial crisis who needs practical help
A reader who could take it as advice to neglect responsibilities to family
speaks_to: Constant worry about money, possessions or security
Feeling pulled between opposites (praise and blame, gain and loss)
Wanting a calmer centre amid ambition

bg.2.47.context: Krishna has criticised people who perform rituals to gain heaven and power (2.42–46). Now he tells Arjuna how to act instead. The next verse defines yoga as evenness in success and failure (2.48), and 2.49–50 call those who work for the fruit 'pitiable'.
bg.2.47.core_teaching: Do the work that is yours and drop the craving for its results. But don't use that as a reason to stop acting: inaction is not the answer either.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: You are fit for works, not yet for the path of pure knowledge. While working, never thirst for results, since that thirst binds you to rebirth. Nor cling to inaction, asking what use painful works are without their fruits.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Answering 'why work if worship brings every result?': you have a right only to action. Do not hanker after results, which bind; undesired results do not arise. But fear of binding work should not push you into inaction.

bg.2.47.practical_reading: Put your full attention on the part you control, which is the effort, the craft and showing up, and let the result be what it will be. Fear of the outcome is not a reason to stop.
misreadings: Not 'don't care about results' or 'don't plan' (our misuse note is right). Shankara and Sridhara target craving and motive, not planning.
Not a call to quit because results aren't guaranteed. The verse's last clause rules out inaction.
cautions: Ramanuja ties the teaching to duties prescribed for one's station, and Sivananda mentions caste. If quoted, frame these as the commentators' setting, not a prescription.
not_for: someone being told their pay, credit or fair outcome doesn't matter, e.g. by an employer
speaks_to: burnout from tying self-worth to outcomes

bg.2.48.context: Right after saying that one's claim is to the action, not the fruit (2.47), Krishna explains how to act: steady in yoga, without attachment, even in success and failure. He then calls this evenness 'yoga' and says action done for the fruit is far inferior to action guided by this understanding (2.49).
bg.2.48.core_teaching: Work while anchored, letting go of clinging, and stay the same whether it succeeds or fails. That evenness is what yoga means.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Work for God's sake, dropping even the attachment of wanting God pleased. Here 'success' is the knowledge that dawns when a mind purified by desireless work becomes clear. Evenness in success and failure is itself the yoga.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Yoga here is single-minded devotion to the Lord. Set in it, act without the sense of being the doer, relying on the Lord and indifferent to success or failure, offering the work to him.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Act for God's sake with a balanced mind; balance is yoga. Success is reaching self-knowledge through a heart purified by desireless work; failure is falling short of it by working for rewards.

bg.2.48.practical_reading: Once you have decided, carry the work out steadily and judge yourself by how you acted, not by how it turned out. Let success and failure both teach without either one knocking you over.
misreadings: Not indifference. Our misuse note is right that you can learn from success and failure without being thrown.
In the commentaries 'success' often means inner purification or knowledge, not worldly success. Don't overstate the verse as a productivity tip.
cautions: Ramanuja's gloss names the work as 'war and the like'. The original setting is battle.
not_for: someone grieving a failure that cost them deeply, if 'stay the same' is pressed too hard
speaks_to: acting on a decision without obsessing over the result
staying steady through ups and downs at work

bg.2.49.context: Comes just after the teaching on action without claim to fruits (2.47) and the definition of yoga as evenness of mind (2.48). Krishna now ranks fruit-driven action far below action done with that even understanding; 2.50 adds that 'yoga is skill in action'.
bg.2.49.core_teaching: Work done only for the payoff is far lower than work done with a steady, even mind; make that understanding your shelter, because living for results keeps a person small and anxious.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Action for reward is far below action with even mind, since it causes birth and death; seek refuge in wisdom, knowledge of the supreme. Those driven by thirst for fruit are wretched, as the Gargi passage says.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Work done for gain is far below work done with steady mind whatever happens: the latter removes the suffering of samsara and leads to liberation, the former breeds samsara. Reward-seekers are pitiable because they miss liberation, the lasting wealth.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Work prompted by desire is far inferior to karma yoga done with one-pointed resolve; so take refuge in that wisdom, or in the Lord who dwells in the intellect. Those impelled by results are wretched, citing the Brihadaranyaka.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Action with evenness of mind is the yoga of wisdom; such a yogi is untouched by success or failure. Action done expecting fruit is far inferior because it binds and causes birth and death.

bg.2.49.practical_reading: Teachers use it to reframe work: aim for doing it well with a steady mind, not for the reward alone. When results become the only reason, success and failure both make you anxious and small.
misreadings: Not 'ambition is wrong'. It's about not letting rewards be the only reason you work.
Not contempt for people who need their pay; kṛpaṇa describes an inner poverty, not an income level.
cautions: 'Pitiable' or 'wretched' can sting a reader who feels trapped in a job they do only for money.
not_for: Someone in financial distress for whom pay is survival
A reader already feeling judged for their choices

bg.2.50.context: Krishna has just said that action done for its fruit is far inferior to action guided by even-minded understanding, and that those who work for fruit are pitiable (2.49). This verse gives the payoff: such understanding frees one from the binding force of both good and bad deeds. The next verse says the wise who give up the fruit are freed from rebirth (2.51).
bg.2.50.core_teaching: Acting with an even mind frees you even in this life from the binding force of both good and bad deeds. That is the 'skill in action' yoga means: action that no longer binds.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The even-minded person casts off both merit and sin through purity and knowledge. Yoga is a skill because works that would bind lose that nature when done with equanimity, the mind resting on the Lord.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Whoever acts under the shelter of this understanding is freed from countless accumulated good and evil deeds that bind. Keeping the mind calm while acting is great cleverness, and it takes enormous effort to cultivate.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: By the Lord's grace such a person is freed here and now from deeds leading to heaven or hell. Skill in action is the knack of turning binding acts into means of liberation by doing them for the Lord.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Only work done for its fruit binds. Done with an even mind resting in the Lord, it brings no binding fruit and is 'no work at all'. The poised yogi credits all action to the Divine within.

bg.2.50.practical_reading: The skill worth building is doing your work fully without letting it hook you, so that praise, blame, success and failure don't keep score inside you. Effort without that hook is lighter and often clearer.
misreadings: Not 'yoga = being efficient or excellent at your job'. In all four commentaries the skill is acting without being bound.
Not 'good and bad don't matter'. It is about freedom from the binding results of one's deeds, not moral indifference.
cautions: Our translation's 'results' wording can feed the misreading that the verse says outcomes don't matter. Correct it to 'deeds'.
not_for: someone looking for a productivity slogan; the verse is about inner freedom
speaks_to: wanting to work well without anxiety

data_flags.translation_note: 'Casts off both good and bad results' misstates sukṛta-duṣkṛte, which means good and bad deeds: merit and sin (Shankara), accumulated good and evil deeds (Ramanuja), work leading to heaven and hell (Sridhara). Suggest 'casts off both good and bad deeds (merit and demerit) here in...

bg.2.52.context: Krishna has praised action done with evenness of mind, which frees one from birth's bonds (2.50-51). Here he says when this happens: when understanding crosses the mire of delusion. 2.53 continues: when the mind stands unshaken, you will reach yoga; Arjuna then asks about the person of steady wisdom (2.54).
bg.2.52.core_teaching: Once understanding clears the fog of confusing body and self, the endless chase after more promises, opinions and rewards loses its pull; what one has heard of and might yet hear no longer drives one.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: When your understanding crosses the mire of delusion, which confounds self and not-self and turns the mind toward sense objects, and becomes pure, you will grow weary of all that has been heard and is still to be heard.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The mire of delusion is mistaking the not-self, the body, for the self. With a purified mind, things heard and yet to be heard will seem of no use and you will not care for them.

bg.2.52.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to information overload and advice-seeking: when you are clear inside, you stop needing every new opinion, course or promise, and can act from what you know.
misreadings: Not 'stop learning' or 'scripture is useless'; it is about the pull of promised rewards and endless opinions.
Not cynicism or boredom.
cautions: The line 'you'll tire of all you've heard' could read as anti-learning; the commentators mean indifference to promised rewards and things not worth pursuing (Ramanuja, Sridhara), not to learning itself.
not_for: A student who needs encouragement to keep studying
Someone whose disillusionment is closer to depression than clarity
speaks_to: Overwhelm from too much advice or information
Seeking one more course, book or opinion instead of acting
A season of disillusionment that is turning into clarity

bg.2.53.context: Completes the thought of 2.52: when understanding, unsettled by conflicting things heard, stands firm, you reach yoga. This prompts Arjuna's question in 2.54: what are the marks of a person of steady wisdom? The rest of the chapter answers.
bg.2.53.core_teaching: A mind pulled in many directions by conflicting teachings and promises reaches yoga when it settles and stays unmoved in the self.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Your understanding, perplexed by hearing of many ends and means for the active and the retired life, will stand without distraction or doubt in the self; then you gain yoga, the insight born of discrimination.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Hearing Krishna's teaching cultures the reason to reflect on the subtle self; when it is firmly planted in a mind purified by unselfish work, Arjuna will reach yoga, vision of the self. Arjuna then asks about steady wisdom.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The understanding, now distracted by hearing of many scriptural and worldly enjoyments, will rest unwavering in the Lord, where the mind settles; then you gain the fruit of yoga, knowledge of the truth.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: When the intellect, tossed by conflicting opinions about the path of action and the path of renunciation, rests immovable and free of doubt in the self, you attain self-knowledge.

bg.2.53.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to confusion from too many voices: stop collecting opinions, settle into a steady practice, and clarity comes from stillness rather than from one more piece of advice.
misreadings: Not a call to ignore all teachers; it is about a mind that never settles.
not_for: Someone who needs to seek expert advice (medical, legal) and might take this as permission not to
speaks_to: Paralysis from conflicting advice (career, health, parenting)
Spiritual seekers who keep switching paths
Wanting to build a steady meditation or prayer practice

bg.2.55.context: Arjuna has asked four questions about the person of steady wisdom: how to describe them, how they speak, sit and move (2.54). This is the first answer, and the description continues to the end of the chapter (2.55-72).
bg.2.55.core_teaching: Steady wisdom shows when a person lets go of the desires crowding the mind and is content from within, not depending on anything outside to feel whole.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: One who drops every desire in the heart and is content in the innermost self, wanting nothing outside, as one who has gained immortal nectar, has steady knowledge. Without that contentment, dropping desires would look like madness.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: When the mind is wholly occupied with the self and finds satisfaction there, other desires in the heart are banished; this is the highest stage of steady wisdom. The next verses describe lower stages.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: A seeker's means of knowledge, once natural, are the marks of the realised. Delighting in the self, whose nature is supreme bliss, one drops desire for paltry things of oneself; that marks steady wisdom.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Someone who has sugar candy does not crave coarse jaggery: one who tastes the bliss of the self does not thirst for sense pleasures, and all the world's pleasures together seem worthless to him.

bg.2.55.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to contentment: notice how much of the mind's restlessness is wanting, and practise finding enough within (in prayer, meditation, or simply being present) so that outer things become extras rather than needs.
misreadings: Not 'never want anything'; the point is inner contentment that does not depend on desires being met.
Not self-absorption; 'the self' here is the deepest self, not the ego.
cautions: A reader with depression-related loss of desire (anhedonia) is not describing steady wisdom; avoid praising 'not wanting anything' in that context.
not_for: Someone in depression or apathy
Someone who needs encouragement to pursue a healthy goal
speaks_to: Seeking contentment that does not depend on circumstances

bg.2.56.context: Arjuna has asked how a person of steady wisdom (sthita-prajña) speaks, sits and walks (2.54). Krishna answers in 2.55–72. He has just said that such a person is content in the self after giving up all desires (2.55). This verse describes their inner state, and the next says they are neither elated by good nor resentful of bad (2.57).
bg.2.56.core_teaching: The steady person isn't knocked over by sorrow and doesn't hunger for more pleasure. They are free of the attachment, fear and anger that drive most reactions.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The sage is not distressed by calamities from body, other beings or nature. His desire does not grow as pleasures come, unlike a fire fed with fuel. Free of attachment, fear and wrath, he has steady knowledge.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Even when misery arrives he is not shaken, and amid pleasures he wants nothing more. Attachment, affection, fear and anger have left him, and that marks his wisdom as steady.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The sage is not shaken by the three kinds of affliction: illness of one's own body, natural disasters, and harm from other creatures. Even in comfort, he does not long for sensual pleasures.

bg.2.56.practical_reading: Ramanuja's breakdown is useful for anger. Anger usually points to something we wanted or feared losing, and to someone we blame for blocking it. Seeing that chain is the first step to not being run by it.
misreadings: Not 'feel nothing'. A steady mind still feels, it just isn't ruled by sorrow, fear or anger (our misuse note is right).
Not a standard to measure yourself against harshly. It describes a sage, and the commentators treat it as the fruit of long practice.
cautions: Ramanuja explicitly lists the impending loss of a loved one among the things the sage does not grieve over. Avoid using that gloss with a bereaved reader.
not_for: someone whose anger is a healthy response to real mistreatment, if the reading implies they should just let it go
speaks_to: fear of losing what you have
wanting steadiness that doesn't depend on circumstances

bg.2.57.context: Part of Krishna's description of the person of steady wisdom (2.55-72). Sridhara takes this verse as the answer to Arjuna's question 'how does such a person speak?'. The next verse gives the image of the tortoise drawing in its limbs.
bg.2.57.core_teaching: Steady wisdom shows in how a person meets whatever comes: without clinging, neither inflated by good fortune nor embittered by bad.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The sage is unattached even to the life of the body; he does not exult in pleasure or recoil from pain when they come, and free of delight and distress, his discriminating knowledge becomes steady.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: A lower stage of steady wisdom: one who forms attachments nowhere, staying unconcerned, neither over-joyed when something liked happens nor hostile when something disliked happens.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The sage has even mind, rooted in the self; he does not praise someone who helps him or censure someone who harms him. This answers Arjuna's question about how such a sage speaks.

bg.2.57.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to reacting less: let good news and bad news land without being swept up or embittered, so that your words and choices come from a steady place.
misreadings: Not coldness or not loving anyone; Ramanuja reads it as an unconcerned attitude to events, not lack of love.
Not suppressing joy or sorrow; it is about not being ruled by them.
cautions: 'Without attachment anywhere' (Sridhara: even to sons) can sound cold to parents, caregivers or the newly bereaved.
not_for: A grieving parent or partner
Someone who already feels emotionally numb or disconnected
speaks_to: Emotional swings with good and bad news (results, reviews, markets)
Wanting to respond rather than react
Leaders who need to stay steady for others

bg.2.58.context: Arjuna has asked how a person of steady wisdom (sthita-prajña) speaks, sits and walks (2.54). Krishna answers in 2.55–72. After describing the sage's even response to good and bad (2.57), Krishna gives the tortoise image. The very next verse warns that objects fall away from someone who abstains, but the taste for them lingers until the Supreme is seen (2.59).
bg.2.58.core_teaching: Being able to pull the senses back from what pulls at them, at will and as easily as a tortoise pulls in its limbs, is a mark of settled wisdom.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The seeker on the path of knowledge withdraws the senses from all objects, as a tortoise draws in its limbs in fear. Shankara then raises a problem: a sick man's senses withdraw too, yet his taste for objects remains.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Drawing the senses back from their pleasures like a tortoise, and fixing the mind on the self, is one of four ascending stages in training the will towards steady wisdom.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The tortoise is chosen because it withdraws its limbs effortlessly. The yogi's control of the senses becomes just as easy and natural.

bg.2.58.practical_reading: When wanting spikes, practise a small tortoise move: close the tab, put the phone face-down, step back from the shop window. Then notice the pull fade. Repeated, the withdrawal gets easier.
misreadings: Not mere abstinence. The next verse (2.59), and Shankara's question here, say the taste can remain even when objects are avoided.
Not a call to shut out people or the world. It is about not being dragged by the senses.
cautions: Sivananda says the one who practises this is 'dead to the world'. Don't use that framing with a reader who is withdrawn, isolated or depressed.
not_for: someone already isolating or emotionally shut down
eating-disorder contexts, where 'withdraw from objects' could reinforce restriction

bg.2.59.context: Within Krishna's portrait of the person of steady wisdom. He has just compared such a person to a tortoise drawing in its limbs (2.58). Here he notes that holding back from objects is not enough, since the craving remains; 2.60-61 warn how strong the senses are and give the remedy.
bg.2.59.core_teaching: Abstaining from something removes the thing but not the longing for it; the longing itself falls away only when something higher is seen and tasted.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Even an ignorant ascetic who abstains from all objects finds the senses withdraw, but the inclination for them stays; only on seeing Brahman as 'I am That' does that subtle attachment go. So steadiness of right knowledge must be gained.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Objects are the food of the senses; starving the senses removes the objects but leaves the craving. When the self is seen as far more blissful than any sense object, even that residue of craving vanishes.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Lazy, sick or fasting people also turn from objects, so that alone marks no wisdom. For the body-identified abstainer experience stops but craving stays; in the wise it ends on realising the Supreme.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: By austerity and abandoning objects, the objects may turn away from the ascetic, but the longing remains; only knowledge of the self destroys the subtle tendencies (vasanas) and attachments entirely.

bg.2.59.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to habits and cravings: white-knuckle abstinence alone rarely lasts; lasting change comes when something more meaningful fills the place the craving held.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of fasting or harsh self-denial as the path; the verse says denial alone does not work.
Not 'give in to cravings because you can't beat them'.
cautions: 'Abstaining' and the food imagery (nirāhāra) could be misread by a reader with disordered eating; avoid framing around food restriction.
not_for: Readers with eating disorders, if framed around food or fasting
Someone in early addiction recovery who could hear 'abstinence isn't enough' as permission to stop abstaining
speaks_to: Breaking a habit or addiction and finding the craving still there

bg.2.6.context: Arjuna has refused to fight, asking how he could attack Bhishma and Drona and saying it would be better to live on alms than enjoy blood-stained wealth (2.4-2.5). Here he admits he cannot even tell which course is better. In 2.7 he confesses his confusion and asks Krishna to teach him as a disciple.
bg.2.6.core_teaching: Arjuna voices a double uncertainty: he cannot judge which path is right or what the outcome will be, and even victory would be hollow because it would cost the lives of the people he loves.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Even if they chose the unrighteous course, they could not say whether victory or defeat would be better; in fact victory would be defeat, since the very people without whom they would not wish to live stand before them.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Summarising 2.4-2.8: Arjuna thinks it more honourable to be killed by the Kauravas than to win unjustly; he humbly asks Krishna, as disciple and refuge-seeker, what is truly best, and Krishna sees his pity is misplaced.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901, text and translator's gloss
commentaries.gist: No commentary on this verse; the translator's gloss frames the choice as begging without killing versus fighting as duty. Shankara's 2.10 introduction treats this whole section as grief and delusion.

bg.2.6.practical_reading: Teachers point out that honest not-knowing is where real guidance starts: Arjuna's admission that he cannot see the right choice leads straight to his asking for help in the next verse.
misreadings: Not the Gita's conclusion that victory is worthless; it is Arjuna's confusion, which Krishna goes on to answer.
Should not be quoted as Krishna's teaching.
cautions: Contains 'we would not wish to live' after killing loved ones; avoid foregrounding this phrase for a reader who may be having thoughts of not wanting to live.
not_for: Someone expressing they do not want to live
Someone who needs reassurance that their choice is right
speaks_to: Being stuck between two bad options
Decisions where 'winning' would hurt people you love (family business, inheritance, divorce, a dispute with relatives)
Not knowing what success would even look like
The moment just before asking for help

bg.2.60.context: After saying craving survives mere abstinence (2.59), Krishna warns that the senses can forcibly drag off even a wise person who is trying. 2.61 gives the remedy: restrain them and sit with the mind on him.
bg.2.60.core_teaching: The pull of the senses is strong enough to overpower even the wise and the diligent; knowing this, one should guard the mind rather than trust intelligence alone.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The senses are dangerous: they agitate the mind of one inclined toward objects and carry it off by force, even while the person is alert and has discriminating knowledge. Hence the next verse's call to devotion.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Without seeing the self, cravings never fully cease, and the powerful senses drag off even a persevering sage's mind; sense-conquest depends on seeing the self and seeing the self on sense-conquest, which makes the path of knowledge hard.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Without control of the senses steady wisdom is impossible, so during practice one must struggle hard; the distracting senses violently lead astray even a discerning person striving for liberation.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The senses are like horses: kept under control they carry you safely to the goal; turbulent ones throw you into sense objects and you never reach the abode of peace.

bg.2.60.practical_reading: Teachers use it to remove shame from relapse and distraction: even the wise get dragged off, so don't be surprised; plan for it, set up your environment, and return.
misreadings: Not 'you're helpless, so don't try'; the next verse gives the way.
Not a judgment that the senses or the body are evil.
not_for: Someone using it to excuse harmful behaviour toward others
speaks_to: Relapse after a period of discipline
Being pulled into a phone, food or anger despite knowing better
Smart people surprised by their own impulses

bg.2.61.context: The remedy for the overpowering senses of 2.60. Sridhara reads it as the answer to Arjuna's question 'how does such a person sit?'. Next (2.62-63) Krishna traces how dwelling on objects leads through attachment, desire and anger to ruin.
bg.2.61.core_teaching: Gather in all the senses and sit collected with the mind on the Lord; for the one whose senses are mastered, wisdom becomes firm.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Controlling the senses, one should sit calm and intent on Vasudeva, the innermost self of all, thinking 'I am no other than He'; the knowledge of one who has mastered the senses by such practice is steady.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The way out of the circle (sense-control needs self-vision and vice versa) is to rein in the senses and make Krishna the mind's object; this burns away impurity and longing, and the mastered senses then allow seeing the self.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Controlling all the senses, the yogi should sit devoted to the Lord; this answers Arjuna's question 'how does he sit?': with senses controlled, free of activity.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Control the senses and sit focused on the Lord as the Supreme with a calm mind; such a yogi's wisdom is steady. Notes Shankara's reading of mat-paraḥ as contemplating 'I am no other than He'.

bg.2.61.practical_reading: Teachers apply it as a daily practice: sit, gather the attention in from all directions, and rest it on God or on what you hold highest; self-control grows more easily from that anchor than from struggle alone.
misreadings: Not repression by force alone; commentators stress that fixing the mind on the Lord is what makes restraint possible.
not_for: A reader who rejects devotional framing, unless 'me' is explained
speaks_to: Starting a meditation or prayer practice
Trying to change a habit and failing by willpower alone

bg.2.62.context: Arjuna has asked how a person of steady wisdom (sthita-prajña) speaks, sits and walks (2.54). Krishna answers in 2.55–72. He has just said the senses can carry off even a wise man's mind, so one should fix the mind on him (2.60–61). Here he traces how merely thinking about objects starts a chain that ends in ruin. The chain continues in 2.63.
bg.2.62.core_teaching: Dwelling on something breeds attachment, attachment hardens into desire, and desire that gets blocked turns into anger.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Dwelling on objects in detail, on their beauty and so on, breeds attachment. When something blocks the desire that follows, it turns into wrath.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Without centring the mind on the Lord, efforts to master the senses fail, because old tendencies keep it brooding. Brooding tightens attachment into craving that can't rest unsatisfied, then anger at whoever seems to obstruct it.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: After the outer senses, Sridhara turns to the uncontrolled mind. Daydreaming about objects as pleasant breeds attachment, then stronger desire, then anger at anyone who stands in its way.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Dwelling on an object's attractions makes us want to possess it and strive for it. When the desire is thwarted, anger arises, and we turn hostile towards whoever blocks us.

bg.2.62.practical_reading: Anger often starts upstream, in something we kept turning over in our minds and came to need. Catching the dwelling stage early is easier than stopping anger once it flares.
misreadings: Not 'all thinking is dangerous'. The problem is brooding on objects as desirable.
Not a claim that the person who angers you is innocent. It explains how anger arises in you, without judging the situation.
cautions: Anger at real injustice or abuse is not the 'blocked desire' this verse describes. The writer should not frame such anger as the reader's own fault.
not_for: someone whose anger is a response to abuse or discrimination, if framed as 'your desire is the problem'
speaks_to: anger that seems to come from nowhere
resentment when something wanted is withheld

bg.2.63.context: This continues the chain begun in 2.62 (dwelling, then attachment, then desire, then anger). Here anger leads on to ruin. Krishna then gives the alternative: one who moves among objects with the senses controlled, free of attraction and aversion, attains clarity (2.64–65).
bg.2.63.core_teaching: Anger clouds judgement, clouded judgement makes you forget what you know, and once discernment is gone you are lost.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Wrath blurs right and wrong, so an angry man may insult even his teacher. What scripture and teacher taught no longer comes to mind. Discernment fails, and since a person is human by discerning right from wrong, he is ruined.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: From anger comes infatuation, where one can no longer tell right action from wrong 'and so does anything'. Then he forgets the effort he had begun to master the senses, the will is wrecked, and he perishes.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Delusion is losing sight of what must not be done. Memory of the teachings lapses, intelligence is dulled until he is as if dead.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: An angry man loses discrimination between right and wrong, says and does whatever he likes, and is swept along by impulse into irrational action.

bg.2.63.practical_reading: When angry, you forget what you know and value. Pausing before speaking or acting protects your judgement until the surge passes.
misreadings: Not 'never feel anger' (our misuse note is right). It warns about anger that overrides judgement.
'Perishes' is about losing one's moral bearings and life's aims, not literal death.
cautions: The language is stark ('ruin', 'perishes'). For a reader already ashamed of an angry episode, emphasise the way back (2.64–65) so the reading doesn't feel like condemnation.
not_for: a reader in a situation of ongoing harm, if the reading implies their anger is the main danger
speaks_to: saying things in anger you later regret

bg.2.64.context: Just after the famous chain of ruin (2.62-63: dwelling on objects breeds attachment, desire, anger, delusion, loss of memory and of judgment). This verse is the positive alternative; 2.65 adds that in that serenity all sorrows end and understanding steadies.
bg.2.64.core_teaching: You do not have to flee the world: moving among things with the senses under control and free of grabbing and pushing away, a self-governed person reaches serenity.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: After 2.62-63 trace ruin to brooding on objects, this gives the way out: senses naturally move by liking and disliking; the seeker meets only unavoidable objects, senses freed of both, mind obedient, and gains peace.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Whoever fixes the mind on the Lord as in 2.61 has his taints wiped away; his senses lose craving and loathing and come under control, and he gains prasāda, a clear and cheerful purity of the inner organ.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Answers the doubt that senses drawn to objects can never be held: one whose senses, governed by a controlled mind, are free of attachment and aversion finds serenity even while experiencing objects. Answers 'how does he move?'

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Mind and senses carry currents of attraction and repulsion; the disciplined person moves among objects free of both, taking only what the body needs, and reaches peace.

bg.2.64.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to living in the world rather than escaping it: eat, work, use your phone and enjoy things, but practise noticing the grab and the push-away, and let calm come from not being ruled by them.
misreadings: Not a call to withdraw from life; it explicitly describes moving among objects.
Not suppression of all preference; it is about not being driven by craving and aversion.
not_for: A reader in acute distress who needs comfort more than discipline
speaks_to: Wanting peace without leaving work or family
Mindful consumption, eating, spending, screen use
Irritability over small likes and dislikes

bg.2.65.context: After the downward chain of 2.62–63, Krishna shows the upward path. Someone who moves among objects with senses free of attraction and aversion attains serenity (prasāda) (2.64). This verse says what serenity brings, and the next says the undisciplined have no peace and so no happiness (2.66).
bg.2.65.core_teaching: When the mind becomes clear and serene, sorrow falls away and understanding quickly settles into steadiness.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: With serenity, all miseries of body and mind end, and the understanding steadies, settled in the Self. So the devout person uses only necessary, permitted objects, with senses free of love and hate.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: When the mind is cleared of the blemish that hides the self, sorrows born of entanglement with matter cease, and a clear understanding that lights up the self follows.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Sridhara reads the verse plainly: once serenity is gained, all misery is destroyed, and the serene person's wisdom quickly becomes steady.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: With peace of mind, hankering for sense-objects goes, the intellect rests steadily in the Self, and the miseries of body and mind come to an end.

bg.2.65.practical_reading: Joy that lasts follows clarity, not the other way round. Small practices that settle the mind make room for a gladness that doesn't depend on circumstances.
misreadings: Not 'if you still feel sorrow, you are not serene enough'. The verse describes a fruit of practice, not a test.
cautions: 'All sorrows end' is strong language. For a reader in grief or depression, frame it as a direction to move in, not a promise or a standard.
not_for: someone in acute grief or clinical depression, if presented as 'just get serene and the sorrow ends'
speaks_to: wanting joy that is steadier than mood
noticing how a calm mind changes everything else

bg.2.66.context: This is part of Krishna's portrait of the person of steady wisdom (2.55–72), given in answer to Arjuna's question in 2.54. Having said that serenity ends sorrow (2.65), Krishna states the converse here: without a collected mind there is no understanding, no contemplation, no peace and so no happiness. The next verse explains why: the roving senses carry the mind away (2.67).
bg.2.66.core_teaching: Happiness depends on peace, peace on contemplation, and contemplation on a collected mind. Without inner steadiness the whole chain fails.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: One who cannot fix the mind has neither self-knowledge nor devotion to it, so no peace. Happiness is the senses' freedom from thirst. While thirst lasts, we cannot catch even a whiff of happiness.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Trying to master the senses by one's own effort, without fixing the mind on the Lord, gives no clear insight, hence no contemplation of the self, no stilling of cravings, and no lasting bliss.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Without sense-control even scriptural knowledge of the Self can't take hold, let alone stay steady. Meditation settles the intellect in the Self. Without it there is no peace, and so no bliss of liberation.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Thirst for sense-objects is the enemy of peace. While it lasts, the mind stays restless and happiness can't arise. Only when the thirst dies can one meditate and rest in the Self.

bg.2.66.practical_reading: Under stress we chase relief in more input, more doing, more checking. The verse turns that around: some daily practice of collecting the mind comes first, and peace and happiness grow out of it.
misreadings: Not 'stressed people are undisciplined'. The verse names a mechanism, not a moral failing.
Not 'happiness is impossible for you'. It names the conditions for happiness.
cautions: Used on Day 2 of the stress plan ('why'). The 'no happiness for the undisciplined' phrasing can read as blame. The writer should frame it as cause and effect, not judgement.
not_for: someone with clinical anxiety or ADHD, if framed as a lack of discipline
speaks_to: feeling unable to settle or focus

bg.2.67.context: This is part of Krishna's portrait of the person of steady wisdom (2.55–72), given in answer to Arjuna's question in 2.54. It explains why the uncollected have no understanding (2.66): the mind trails after the roaming senses and loses its course. The next verse concludes that wisdom is settled in one whose senses are fully withdrawn from their objects (2.68).
bg.2.67.core_teaching: When the mind keeps following wherever the senses wander, it loses its own course, the way wind drives an unsteered boat off course.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: A mind engrossed in sense-objects destroys the power to tell Self from not-Self. Like wind driving a ship off the sailors' intended course, it pulls awareness away from the Self towards objects.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: If the mind is allowed to ramble after the senses, it steals away the understanding that was focused on the self and fills the will with sensuous thoughts, like a ship tossed by violent winds.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Even one sense that the mind slavishly follows is enough to sweep wisdom away, so many certainly will. It is like a ship on the sea whose helmsman has lost his wits.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: A mind that keeps company with the senses and dwells on their objects destroys discrimination. It pulls the seeker off the spiritual path, as wind pushes a boat off course.

bg.2.67.practical_reading: Overthinking often starts with one hook (a notification, a remark, a craving) that the mind follows, then follows the next. Noticing 'my mind just followed that' is how you take back the rudder.
misreadings: Not 'the senses are evil'. The problem is a mind with no hand on the rudder.
Strictly, the verse is about senses pulling the mind outward, not about anxious rumination. Present the application to overthinking as an extension.
not_for: someone whose racing thoughts come from trauma or a clinical condition, if presented as a matter of willpower
speaks_to: feeling 'swept away' by moods or impulses

bg.2.69.context: Near the end of Krishna's portrait of the person of steady wisdom. He has said that peace and happiness belong to the one whose senses are withdrawn (2.66-68). This paradox follows; 2.70 gives the image of the ocean that stays still as rivers pour in.
bg.2.69.core_teaching: What ordinary minds are blind to, the deepest reality, is where the sage is awake; and the world of objects in which everyone is busily awake is, for the sage, like night.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The supreme reality is night to the ignorant, as day is night to night-wanderers; the self-controlled yogi, woken from ignorance, is awake to it. The world of perceiver and perceived, where others seem awake, is a dream-night to the sage.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Knowledge of the self is dark as night to all creatures, but the conqueror of the senses is wide awake in it, seeing the self; the sense-bound understanding where others are alive does not shine for that sage.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Answers the objection that no one is so withdrawn: abiding in the self is night to those darkened by ignorance, yet there the self-controlled is awake; the sense world where others wake is night to the sage.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: What is real for worldly people is illusion for the sage and vice versa: he lives in the self as his day, while sense enjoyment, the ordinary person's day, is night to him.

bg.2.69.practical_reading: Teachers use it to validate living by different values: what others overlook (inner life, stillness) can be what you are most awake to, and what they chase can matter little to you.
misreadings: Not contempt for ordinary people or worldly life.
Not literally about sleeping at night (though it is sometimes quoted that way).
cautions: Could feed a sense of superiority if framed as 'you versus the crowd'.
not_for: Someone feeling isolated or alienated, who might hear it as confirmation that they don't belong
Insomnia or literal sleep problems
speaks_to: Feeling out of step with peers' priorities
Spiritual awakening that changes what matters

bg.2.7.context: Krishna has just told Arjuna to shake off his faint-heartedness and stand up (2.2–3). Arjuna replies that he cannot fight his revered elders Bhishma and Drona, and does not know which outcome would be worse (2.4–6). Here he gives up arguing and asks to be taught. Two verses later he says 'I will not fight' and falls silent, and Krishna begins teaching at 2.11.
bg.2.7.core_teaching: Arjuna admits that his own judgement has failed him and asks, as a student, for a clear answer. Commentators see this surrender of pride as what makes the teaching possible.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Two things overcame his natural courage: helplessness at the thought of living on after killing them, and fear of the sin of destroying family. Unsure whether a warrior may quit battle to beg, he asks as a disciple taking refuge.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Arjuna humbly approaches Krishna as disciple and refuge-seeker. Krishna sees him undone by misplaced affection and pity, mistaking a lawful war for wrong, and resolves to teach self-knowledge joined to action done without interest in results.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Shankara reads 1.2–2.9 as showing how grief and delusion, born of 'mine'-ness, overpower judgement and make people abandon their duty. Because only self-knowledge removes them, Krishna begins teaching at 2.11.

bg.2.7.practical_reading: Clarity often starts with admitting 'I don't know what's right here' and asking someone wiser, humbly and with a real question, rather than arguing for the choice you have already half made.
misreadings: Not a model of handing your judgement over completely. The rest of the Gita reasons with Arjuna at length.
Not proof that compassion is a defect. The commentators fault the confusion that pity caused here, not kindness itself.
cautions: Some renderings call Arjuna's pity a 'taint' (Sivananda). A reader whose distress comes from caring about people should not come away feeling their care is a flaw.
not_for: someone being pressured to defer to an authority figure against their own conscience
speaks_to: being torn between two choices that both seem wrong
admitting you are confused and need guidance
the first honest step of asking for help

data_flags.attribution_note: The speaker and listener fields (Arjuna to Krishna) are right, but the setting sentence reads 'Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed…'. This verse is Arjuna's plea to Krishna. Fix the setting to something like 'Arjuna, in tears and refusing to fight, asks Krishna to teach...

bg.2.70.context: This is part of Krishna's portrait of the person of steady wisdom (2.55–72), given in answer to Arjuna's question in 2.54. After saying the sage is awake to what others sleep through (2.69), Krishna uses the ocean image. The chapter closes with the verse on giving up 'mine' and ego (2.71) and a final word on the state of Brahman (2.72).
bg.2.70.core_teaching: Desires and sense-impressions will keep flowing in. Peace belongs to the one who takes them in without being moved, like the ocean, not to the one who keeps craving.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The ocean, filled from every side, stays within its bounds, unchanged. So the sage meets desires amid objects that absorb into the Self without enslaving him. He attains peace (liberation); the one who longs for objects does not.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The sea is full in itself and the same whether rivers enter or not. When sense-objects reach the self-mastered person, he stays calm, because his satisfaction comes from knowing the self.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Objects still reach such a sage through past karma already in motion (prārabdha), as rivers keep pouring into a sea that never overflows. They leave him unaffected, and he attains liberation.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Like the full ocean, the sage resting in his own nature is not disturbed by desires of every kind entering from all sides. He attains peace; the one full of cravings does not.

bg.2.70.practical_reading: You can't stop the inflow of demands, wants and noise, but you can become roomier. When fulfilment comes from within, inputs pass through without capsizing you.
misreadings: Not 'suppress every desire'. The image is about the inflow not disturbing you, not about blocking it.
Not 'take on everything'. It is about inner steadiness, not accepting unlimited demands.
cautions: In the stress plan, 'let everything flow in' could be heard as 'absorb all the pressure'. The writer should make clear it means inner steadiness, not unlimited capacity.
not_for: someone overloaded who needs to set limits, if framed as 'be an ocean, take it all in'
speaks_to: wanting calm that doesn't depend on circumstances

bg.2.71.context: This is part of Krishna's portrait of the person of steady wisdom (2.55–72), given in answer to Arjuna's question in 2.54. It comes just after the ocean image (2.70) and just before the closing verse on the Brahman-state (2.72). It sums up the portrait: giving up desire, longing, 'mine' and ego brings peace.
bg.2.71.core_teaching: The person who lets go of desires, longing, possessiveness and ego moves through life at peace.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Desires here are the objects one wants to enjoy. Whoever gives them up without craving, free of 'my-ness' and of 'I-ness' (mistaking the body for the self), sees the self and attains peace.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: He ignores what he has and does not yearn for what he lacks. Free of ego, hence of ownership over the means of enjoyment, he moves about as past karma carries him, and attains peace.

bg.2.71.practical_reading: Comparison feeds on 'mine' and on an 'I' that measures itself against others. Holding what you have lightly, and loosening the need to rank yourself, leaves room for peace.
misreadings: Not 'love your people less'. Dropping 'mine' is about possessiveness (our misuse note is right).
Not a demand to become a monk, although Shankara frames it around the renouncer. The commentators read it as an inner stance.
cautions: 'Bare necessities' language (Shankara, Sivananda) could be heard as glorifying deprivation by a reader struggling financially.
not_for: someone in financial hardship, if framed as 'want less'

bg.2.72.context: The last verse of chapter 2, sealing Krishna's portrait of the person of steady wisdom (2.55-72), just after the person who gives up all desires and 'I' and 'mine' attains peace (2.71). Arjuna's next question (3.1) is why, if understanding is higher, he is urged to this terrible action.
bg.2.72.core_teaching: This steady state is abiding in the Absolute; whoever reaches it is not confused again, and even reaching it at the end of life brings final peace.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The 'Brahmic state' is unselfish work grounded in knowing the eternal self, leading to steady wisdom; one who adopts it, even in old age, is not drawn back into samsara and reaches the bliss of the self.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Concludes by praising the path of knowledge: one purified by worshipping the Lord who reaches this is not again deluded by transmigration; resting in it even a moment at death brings nirvana in Brahman, how much more if from boyhood.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Renouncing everything and living in Brahman is the Brahmic state; held even at death it brings liberation. Cites Vidyaranya's Panchadasi reading 'end-time' as the moment ignorance ends.

bg.2.72.practical_reading: Teachers say it is never too late: steadiness found even late in life, or at its end, is real and freeing; and it encourages starting now rather than waiting.
misreadings: Not 'you can postpone spiritual life until old age'; the commentators praise starting early.
Not a judgment on how a particular person died.
cautions: Mentions the hour of death (antakāle); can comfort the dying or the elderly but may raise worry for the bereaved about a loved one's state of mind at death. Shankara reads it as 'the last period of life', which is gentler.
not_for: A grieving family member anxious about how their loved one died
Fresh bereavement
speaks_to: Older readers wondering if it is too late to change
Facing the end of life with calm
Wanting a lasting, not temporary, peace

bg.2.8.context: Having asked to be taught as Krishna's disciple (2.7), Arjuna explains why he needs help: nothing he can imagine gaining would remove this grief. In 2.9 he declares he will not fight and falls silent; Krishna, smiling as it were, begins the teaching at 2.11.
bg.2.8.core_teaching: Arjuna recognises that his grief is not the kind any outward gain can fix, not even the greatest kingdom on earth or in heaven. Commentators see this honest admission as the starting point of the inner teaching.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Told to decide for himself, Arjuna replies he sees no action that would remove a grief drying up his senses, even with everything coveted: an unrivalled kingdom on earth or lordship over the gods.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898 (comment on 2.4-2.9)
commentaries.gist: Krishna sees Arjuna made helpless by misplaced affection and pity, mistaking a lawful war for wrong; he resolves that only knowledge of the self, joined with action done without interest in results, will lift this confusion.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901, introduction at 2.10, not a comment on this verse
commentaries.gist: Reads 1.2 to 2.9 as showing grief and delusion, the cause of samsara; since nothing but self-knowledge ends them, Krishna begins his teaching at 2.11.

bg.2.8.practical_reading: Teachers use it to name grief that no achievement, purchase or distraction can touch, and to say that admitting this is the first step toward a different kind of help.
