misreadings: Not a statement that grief is hopeless: in the Gita this admission opens the teaching.
Not a rejection of worldly success as such.
cautions: Vivid grief imagery; good for naming grief, but best paired with what follows (2.11 onward) so it does not end in despair.
not_for: Someone looking for quick motivation
A reader at risk of hopelessness, if used alone without the verses that answer it
speaks_to: Grief or heartbreak that success does not touch
Realising you need a different kind of help, not more of the same

bg.3.11.context: Krishna has said that action done as sacrifice does not bind (3.9). He then recounts how Prajapati created beings along with sacrifice and told them to prosper by it (3.10); this verse continues that speech, and 3.12 adds that one who enjoys the gods' gifts without offering back is a thief. 3.14 describes the cycle: food from rain, rain from sacrifice, sacrifice from action.
bg.3.11.core_teaching: Life is a cycle of mutual giving: humans offer to the powers that sustain the world, and those powers sustain humans; by nourishing one another, all reach the highest good.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: By sacrifice nourish the gods such as Indra, and they will nourish you with rain and the like. The 'highest good' is knowledge of Brahman reached in due course, or else it may mean heaven.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Prajapati is Narayana, who out of mercy created beings with sacrifice so they could worship him. Worship the gods, who form his body; they will give food and rain; serving each other this way, you reach liberation.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Explains how sacrifice yields enjoyments: please the gods with oblations and they will please you by producing food through rain; pleasing each other, you and the gods both gain what you desire.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Deva means 'shining one'. Sacrifice nourishes gods like Indra, who give rain; the highest good may be self-knowledge freeing from rebirth or heaven, depending on the aspirant's motive.

bg.3.11.practical_reading: Teachers widen it to interdependence: family, community, nature and society sustain us, and we sustain them; giving back is not charity but taking part in the cycle that keeps everyone alive.
misreadings: Not a transaction ('pay the gods, get rewards'); Ramanuja reads the highest good as liberation, Shankara as knowledge of Brahman in due course (or heaven).
Not Krishna's own direct command; it is Prajapati's founding instruction, quoted.
not_for: Someone in a one-sided or exploitative relationship who might read it as 'keep giving'
speaks_to: Team, family or community life where everyone carries part of the load

data_flags.attribution_note: Krishna is quoting. In 3.10-12 Krishna reports what Prajapati, the creator, said to the first beings when he created them along with sacrifice; Govindacharya's Ramanuja and Vireswarananda's Sridhara print these verses as Prajapati's quoted words. So the words are Prajapati's, addressed to humankind, relayed by...

bg.3.13.context: Follows the account of Prajapati's command and the warning that one who enjoys the gods' gifts without offering is a thief (3.10-12). Next comes the cycle of food, rain, sacrifice and action (3.14-15) and the judgment that one who does not keep this wheel turning lives in vain (3.16).
bg.3.13.core_teaching: Food and goods received should first be offered and shared; living on what remains after giving frees one from fault, while living only for oneself turns even eating into a wrong.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Those who eat what remains after offering to the gods and others are freed from sins incurred at the household's five places of harm to small creatures; selfish people who cook only for themselves eat sin itself.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Those who cook with honestly earned means to worship the Supreme, who indwells the gods, and eat the remainder are freed from sins blocking self-knowledge; those who treat his gifts as their own eat sin.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Those who eat the remnants of the daily offerings are freed from sins committed through the five household agencies of harm; so those who sacrifice are pre-eminent, and those cooking only for themselves partake of sin.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Names the five places where small life is harmed daily (pestle and mortar, grinding stone, hearth, water-pot place, broom) and the five great daily offerings, to gods, sages, ancestors, beings and guests, that wash those sins away.

bg.3.13.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to offering food before eating, feeding guests and animals, and sharing first; more broadly, to receiving life's goods with gratitude and giving some away before consuming.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of people who live alone or cannot afford to share; the target is selfishness.
Not a ritual technicality only; the spirit is gratitude and sharing.
cautions: Harsh words ('wicked', 'eat sin') around food may shame a reader with an eating disorder, food insecurity, or who eats alone.
not_for: Someone facing food insecurity or poverty
Readers with eating disorders
Someone lonely and eating alone
speaks_to: Generosity and sharing in a household
Feeling that consumption has become empty

bg.3.17.context: After condemning one who does not keep the wheel of offering turning (3.16), Krishna names the exception: the one who rests wholly in the self has nothing left to do (3.17-18). Yet he immediately adds 'therefore act, unattached' (3.19), citing Janaka (3.20) and his own example (3.22).
bg.3.17.core_teaching: The one whose joy, satisfaction and contentment come wholly from the self has no further duty to fulfil; such a person acts, if at all, not from need.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The renunciate devoted to self-knowledge, whose joy is in the self rather than sense objects, who is satisfied by the self rather than food and drink, and content without outer possessions, has nothing left to do.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Reading 3.17-19 together: one whose satisfaction lies in the self rather than food, gardens, music or fragrance, to whom the self is already evident, needs no means to reach it; yet Arjuna is told to work unattached, as duty.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Having prescribed action to purify the ignorant, Krishna now says it is useless for the wise: one gratified in the self, happy in its bliss and free of desire for enjoyment, has no duties to perform.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The sage does not depend on outside objects for happiness; finding joy and contentment within, he has nothing to do, having in effect done all actions and satisfied all desires.

bg.3.17.practical_reading: Teachers use it to point to a contentment that does not depend on achievement, and then, with the following verses, to say that such a person still works, out of care for others rather than need.
misreadings: Not permission to drop responsibilities because 'I'm content'; 3.19-22 say to act anyway.
Not self-centredness; 'self' means the deepest self, not the ego.
cautions: Read alone, it could support withdrawal; pair with 3.19 or 3.22.
not_for: Someone using spirituality to avoid responsibilities to family or work
Depression-related withdrawal
speaks_to: Wanting contentment that doesn't depend on success
Retirement or a life transition where external roles fall away
Freedom from the need for approval

bg.3.19.context: Krishna has just said that one who delights only in the self has no remaining duty and nothing to gain from acting or not acting (3.17–18). 'Therefore', he tells Arjuna, who is not yet in that state, to keep acting without attachment. The next verses cite Janaka and the need to set an example for the world (3.20–21).
bg.3.19.core_teaching: Keep doing what needs doing, without clinging to the outcome. Unattached action itself leads to the highest goal.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Doing action without attachment, for the Lord's sake, purifies the mind, and through that purity a person attains liberation.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Until the self is realised, work disinterestedly, as duty, without thinking 'I am the doer'. Even for the knower, action is safe and sets a good example. Practised so, karma-yoga leads to the self.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Action is useless only to one who already has knowledge. Everyone else should do prescribed duties well, without attachment to their fruit, and reach liberation through a purified mind and knowledge.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Actions done without attachment, for the Lord's sake, purify the heart and so lead to self-realisation.

bg.3.19.practical_reading: In a new beginning, don't wait for certainty or a perfect plan. Keep steadily doing the work in front of you without gripping the result, and the steadiness itself carries you forward.
misreadings: Not 'work non-stop'. 'Constantly' refers to a steady unattached attitude, not overwork.
Not 'whatever you do is fine if you're detached'. It is about action that ought to be done.
not_for: someone who needs permission to stop or rest
speaks_to: starting over and needing a steady rhythm
anxiety about whether a new path will pay off

bg.3.2.context: Chapter 3 opens with Arjuna's objection (3.1): if understanding is better than action, why urge him to this terrible deed? Here he asks for one decisive teaching. Krishna replies (3.3) that there are two paths, knowledge for the contemplative and action for the active, and then shows why action cannot be abandoned.
bg.3.2.core_teaching: Arjuna honestly says the teaching so far sounds contradictory to him, praising both knowledge and action, and asks for one clear path to the highest good.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The Lord speaks clearly, but to Arjuna's dull understanding it seems mixed; hence 'as it were': Krishna, who set out to remove confusion, cannot really confuse him. If knowledge and action are for different seekers, teach me one.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: If knowledge is the means to seeing the self and requires withdrawing the senses, why command me to violent action that engages every faculty? Your speech seems double; tell me one consistent course to the highest good.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Praise of action in some places (righteous war, 2.31) and of knowledge in others sets his mind swinging; the compassionate Lord cannot really perplex anyone, so 'seem' reflects Arjuna's ignorance. He asks for the one better way.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Arjuna asks Krishna to teach him one of the two, knowledge or action, by which he may attain the highest good, liberation.

bg.3.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it to honour honest confusion: asking a teacher or mentor 'just tell me the one thing to do' is a valid, even necessary, step, and the Gita answers it at length.
misreadings: Not evidence that the Gita is incoherent; Arjuna himself says 'as if'.
Not Krishna's teaching; it is the student's question.
not_for: A reader who needs grounding or comfort rather than a question
speaks_to: Students and seekers who feel they are being told opposite things

bg.3.20.context: After saying that the self-content person has no duty, but Arjuna should still act without attachment (3.17–19), Krishna gives precedent: King Janaka and others reached perfection through action. Then he adds a second reason, the good of the world, and explains that people copy the great (3.21). He then offers himself as the example (3.22–24).
bg.3.20.core_teaching: Wise people like Janaka reached fulfilment while still acting in the world. Even if you needed nothing for yourself, the world's welfare would be reason enough to act.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: If Janaka and Asvapati had knowledge, they kept acting to set an example. If not, action purified their minds. Either way, Arjuna, born a warrior, should act to protect and guide people.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Royal sages like Janaka, though leaders of the wise, reached self-realisation by works alone. So karma-yoga is commended even to those qualified for the path of knowledge.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Sridhara cites approved precedent: Janaka and others were purified in mind by action and so reached perfection. Even just to give people an incentive, you should act.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Perfection here means liberation. Janaka and others had full self-knowledge, yet kept acting to set an example and guide people.

bg.3.20.practical_reading: When nothing feels meaningful for yourself, acting for others can still make sense: a small task done for someone else, or keeping a commitment others rely on.
misreadings: Not 'your worth is your usefulness'. The verse offers a reason to act, not a measure of a person.
Not 'ignore your own emptiness and keep busy'.
cautions: Used on Day 6 of 'nothing matters'. If the reader may be depressed, 'keep working for the world' should be offered gently, with a small, concrete act, not as an obligation.
not_for: someone in a depressive crisis who needs care, not duty

bg.3.21.context: Krishna has just told Arjuna to act for the world's welfare (3.20). This verse explains why: people imitate their leaders. He goes on to say that he himself, who needs nothing, keeps acting, because if he stopped, people would follow and the world would fall into ruin (3.22–24).
bg.3.21.core_teaching: People take their cue from those they look up to. So anyone with standing is responsible for the standard their conduct sets.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Whatever authority a leading person follows, in spiritual or worldly matters, his followers take as their authority too.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The masses copy a great person, and whichever scripture he treats as authoritative, whether it teaches action or renunciation, people follow.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Humans are social and imitative. They take their sense of right and wrong from those they regard as morally superior and try to walk in their footsteps.

bg.3.21.practical_reading: With success comes influence. People around you, especially juniors, family or followers, will copy how you work, treat others and handle pressure, so set the standard you want them to follow.
misreadings: Not 'successful people are better people'. The verse is about responsibility, not superiority.
Not 'image management'. The point is real conduct, not appearances.
cautions: Ramanuja frames the leader's duty in terms of the duties of his caste (varṇa) and stage of life. Don't import that framing.
not_for: someone already crushed by others' expectations, if framed as 'everyone is watching you'
speaks_to: being a parent or role model

bg.3.22.context: Krishna has cited Janaka, who reached perfection through action, and said that whatever the best person does, others follow (3.20-21). Now he offers himself as the example; 3.23-24 explain that if he stopped working, people would follow suit and the worlds would fall into ruin.
bg.3.22.core_teaching: Krishna, lacking nothing and owing nothing, still keeps working, because others take their cue from him and the world depends on that example.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Krishna has nothing to achieve in the three worlds, since there is nothing he lacks; yet he engages in action. The next verses give the reason: people follow his path.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: As Lord of all he has no binding work and nothing to gain; he works ceaselessly only for the world, since if he grew idle all would copy him and the worlds would fall into ruin.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Krishna offers himself as the example in 3.22-24: he has no duty and nothing unattained in the three worlds, yet keeps working; if he stopped, people would follow his footsteps to ruin.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: As Lord of the universe Krishna has no personal reason to act, yet he acts; Arjuna, a leader with noble qualities, should likewise set an example so that others do not take the wrong path.

bg.3.22.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to leadership and parenting: even when you personally need nothing more, keep showing up and doing the work well, because people around you learn from what you do.
misreadings: Not a celebration of endless busyness; the motive is care for others, not need.
not_for: Someone in burnout who might hear 'keep working no matter what'
speaks_to: Leaders, parents, teachers and elders whose example matters
People who have 'made it' and are wondering why to keep working
Retirement and the question of purpose

bg.3.25.context: After giving himself as the example of one who acts though he needs nothing (3.22-24), Krishna draws the lesson for the wise. 3.26 adds that the wise should not unsettle those attached to action, and 3.27 explains the difference between the wise and the unwise doer.
bg.3.25.core_teaching: The wise should work with the same energy the unwise bring to their ambitions, but without attachment, so as to sustain and guide the world.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The ignorant act expecting 'this result will be mine'; the knower of the self should act with the same diligence but unattached, for the world's welfare, which is the only reason left for him to act at all.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Treats 3.25-26 together: though the wise person has full self-knowledge and no interest in results, he should work just like the work-attached, because the world takes him as its pattern and learns right conduct from his example.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Concludes that even knowers of the self should act for the world's welfare out of compassion: as the ignorant work engrossed in results, the wise should work unattached, wishing the world good.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The ignorant work expecting fruit; the wise person serves not for his own ends but so that the world, following his example, gains peace, purity of heart and knowledge.

bg.3.25.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to working wholeheartedly for shared good: bring full effort to your work, but measure it by what it does for others rather than by your personal gain.
misreadings: Not contempt for ambitious people; they are the model for energy, not the target.
Not 'appear busy for show'; the motive is the welfare of others.
not_for: Someone exhausted by caregiving or service who needs rest, not more effort
speaks_to: Finding meaning in work beyond personal rewards

bg.3.26.context: Continues from 3.25: the wise act unattached for the world's sake. Here Krishna adds a caution about teaching: do not unsettle those whose faith lies in action. 3.27-29 explain the difference between the wise and the unwise doer.
bg.3.26.core_teaching: Those who know more should not shake the conviction of people who are growing through their work; instead, by doing the work well themselves, they should encourage others in it.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The ignorant believe 'I should do this and enjoy its result'; the wise should not unsettle that conviction, but should do the same work diligently and well himself and so get them to do theirs.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The unwise are seekers who cannot yet take up the path of knowledge, for whom works are the sole means. The wise should not unsettle them but enter wholeheartedly into works to encourage them by example.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Objection: shouldn't the wise, out of pity, teach them the self is a non-agent? No: that would turn them from work before knowledge arises, leaving them with neither. Make them work, by working carefully yourself.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Do not unsettle the belief of those who work for fruit; set an example by doing your duties diligently without attachment, encourage them in their duties, and once their hearts are purified, sow the seeds of selfless service.

bg.3.26.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to mentoring, parenting and teaching: meet people at their stage, don't knock down a beginner's motivation with advanced ideas, and lead by example rather than lecture.
misreadings: Not a licence to withhold honest information or keep people in the dark for one's own benefit.
Not elitism; the motive given is kindness to the learner.
cautions: 'The ignorant' can sound condescending; soften in readings.
not_for: Situations of abuse or deception, where 'don't unsettle them' could be misused to justify silence
speaks_to: Someone eager to share a new insight that might discourage others

bg.3.27.context: Explains the inner difference between the wise and the unwise, who may do the same work (3.25-26). Next, 3.28 says the knower of the gunas and their functions sees that 'gunas act upon gunas' and is not attached.
bg.3.27.core_teaching: All activity is carried out by nature's forces working through body, senses and mind; it is the ego's confusion that claims, 'I alone am doing this.'

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: All actions are done by the gunas, nature's modifications appearing as body and senses. One whose mind is deluded by ego identifies with body and senses, takes on their attributes, and through ignorance thinks 'I am the doer'.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Activities arise from matter's three qualities; one blinded by ahamkara, the mistaken notion that the non-self body is the self, takes the body's doings for the self's and thinks 'I am the doer'.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Answers 'if the wise must act too, how do they differ from the ignorant?': actions are done by the senses, products of nature, but the ignorant, superimposing the self on the senses through ego, thinks 'I am doing this'.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Nature is the balance of sattva, rajas and tamas; when it is disturbed, body, senses and mind form. Deluded by ego, a person identifies with these, ascribes their attributes to the self, and thinks 'I am the doer'.

bg.3.27.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to pride and anxiety alike: much of what we do rides on forces and help beyond us, so hold both credit and blame more lightly and act without the burden of being the sole doer.
misreadings: Not a denial of moral responsibility ('nature did it, not me').
Not 'nothing I do matters'.
cautions: Could be misused to excuse harmful behaviour; frame it as freedom from ego, not from accountability.
not_for: Someone trying to avoid accountability for harm done
A reader who already feels powerless
speaks_to: Pride in success, or crushing self-blame for failure
Wanting to work with less ego

bg.3.30.context: Krishna has explained that actions are really done by the forces of nature, though the ego thinks 'I am the doer' (3.27–29). Here he tells Arjuna how to act: offer every action to him, keep the mind on the self, and fight without hope, possessiveness or fever. The next verses promise freedom to those who follow this teaching with faith (3.31–32).
bg.3.30.core_teaching: Offer all your actions to the Lord, keep your mind on the inner self, drop expectation and possessiveness, and do your work free of anguish.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Surrender all actions to Vasudeva, the Self of all, with the thought: 'I, the agent, do this for the Lord's sake, as his servant.' 'Fever' means anguish or grief.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Place all acts in Krishna, the inner Self of all beings, contemplating the self as his body, ruled from within. Desireless and free of 'mine' and cankering care, 'fight' here means discharge all prescribed duties.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: You have not yet realised the truth, so act. Offer each action to the Lord, knowing the Inner Ruler guides you. Drop expectation and any sense that the action is for your own ends, and banish grief.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Surrender all actions with the thought 'I do everything for the Lord's sake'. Fever here means grief or sorrow.

bg.3.30.practical_reading: Before a stressful task, consciously hand it over, as an offering or simply as 'not mine to control'. Then do it without the anxious grip. The fever (the heat of worry and grief) can drop while the work still gets done.
misreadings: Not handing over your judgement or responsibility (our misuse note is right). The commentators still expect full, careful action.
Not literally a call to fight, except in Arjuna's setting. Ramanuja reads 'fight' as 'do your prescribed duties'.
cautions: The 'me' is Krishna. For a general audience, 'something higher' is acceptable, but don't misrepresent the verse as non-theistic.
not_for: someone whose stress comes from being pressured to do something wrong
speaks_to: needing to let go of control

bg.3.33.context: Krishna has urged Arjuna to act, surrendering all action to him (3.30-32), and warned that those who reject this teaching are lost. This verse explains why many do not follow it: beings follow their nature. 3.34 immediately says not to fall under the sway of like and dislike, and 3.35 that one's own duty, even imperfect, is better than another's.
bg.3.33.core_teaching: Everyone, even the wise, acts out of their ingrained nature, so sheer suppression achieves little; the work is to understand that nature and not be ruled by its likes and dislikes (3.34).

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Nature is the store of past impressions showing at birth; even the knower acts by it, the ignorant all the more, so prohibition seems powerless. He raises the objection that effort and teaching are then pointless, answered in 3.34.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Even a wise person who knows from scripture that the self differs from matter is carried along by habits formed in past association with matter; against such ingrained tendencies, what can scripture's restraint do?

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Answers why everyone doesn't simply do their duty unattached: disposition, shaped by past impressions, is powerful; even a wise man aware of good and bad acts according to it, so what can mere restraint of the senses do?

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Warns that this verse does not mean there is no room for effort: read it with 3.34, which shows one can master nature by rising above liking and disliking; the steady meditator controls it.

bg.3.33.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to self-change: forcing yourself against your grain rarely lasts; know your temperament, work with it, and watch your likes and dislikes rather than fighting yourself head-on.
misreadings: Not 'I can't change, it's my nature'. The next verse says not to come under the sway of likes and dislikes.
Not a dismissal of discipline; it questions brute suppression.
cautions: Read alone, it can sound fatalistic; always pair with 3.34.
not_for: Someone excusing harmful behaviour as 'just my nature'
speaks_to: Accepting one's temperament in career and relationships
Frustration that knowing better doesn't change behaviour

bg.3.34.context: Answers the fatalism that 3.33 might suggest. 3.35 follows with the teaching that one's own duty, even done imperfectly, is better than another's done well; then Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will (3.36).
bg.3.34.core_teaching: Every sense meets its objects with built-in liking and disliking; you cannot stop these arising, but you can refuse to be ruled by them, and that is where effort counts.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Here lies the scope for effort: nature drags a person only through liking and aversion, toward neglecting one's own duty. Whoever checks these with their opposite follows the teaching, not his nature; they are enemies, like robbers on the road.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Every sense object attracts love from old habit and aversion when enjoyment is blocked; these grip whoever attempts the path of knowledge and drive him back to his inherited nature, so they are his strongest enemies.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: If inclination follows nature, are injunctions useless? No: liking for pleasant objects and aversion to unpleasant ones are fixed in every sense, yet scripture says not to come under their sway, for they block the way.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Here lies the scope for personal effort: nature pulls through the two currents of attraction and aversion; control them by discrimination and inquiry and you can conquer nature and attain lasting peace.

bg.3.34.practical_reading: Teachers apply it as a pause practice: notice the pull or the push before acting, name it, and choose instead of reacting; you don't have to obey every craving or irritation.
misreadings: Not 'never like or dislike anything'; it is about not being ruled.
Not self-hatred toward one's desires.
not_for: Someone already rigidly over-controlled or scrupulous

bg.3.35.context: Krishna has warned that everyone acts according to their nature and that attraction and aversion lie in wait in every sense-object (3.33–34). This verse concludes the section. It also prompts Arjuna's next question: what makes a person do wrong even against their will (3.36)?
bg.3.35.core_teaching: Doing your own proper duty imperfectly is better than doing someone else's well. Even death in your own duty is better, because another's path brings danger.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Here 'own dharma' means karma-yoga, which comes naturally and safely to someone bound to matter. The path of knowledge is excellent but hard and risky for them. Even if death comes first, progress carries over to the next birth.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: A warrior's duty is to fight a righteous battle. Arjuna should fight, even at the cost of his life, and not abandon his duty for the path of renunciation, which belongs to others.

bg.3.35.practical_reading: Modern teachers apply it against comparison: a life lived honestly on your own terms, even clumsily, beats a polished imitation of someone else's. (This is an application. The classical commentators tie svadharma to one's station or one's suited path.)
misreadings: Do not present 'your own calling' as what the verse plainly means. That is a modern reading.
Not an endorsement of caste or birth-assigned roles. The app should not carry the classical station-based reading forward uncritically either.
Not 'never try something new'. It warns against abandoning your own path out of imitation or fear.
cautions: Mentions death ('better is death in one's own duty'). Handle carefully with a distressed reader.
Caste: three of the four commentaries read it in terms of varṇa or station, and Shankara and Sridhara mention hell. The editor should decide how the app frames this.
not_for: someone being told to stay in a role imposed by family, caste or gender
a reader with suicidal thoughts (the 'death' line)
speaks_to: feeling pressure to live someone else's life

bg.3.36.context: Krishna has just said that attraction and aversion lie in wait in the senses and should not be allowed to rule, and that one's own duty is better than another's (3.34–35). Arjuna asks what drives people into wrongdoing even against their will. Krishna's answer names desire, which becomes anger, as the enemy (3.37–43).
bg.3.36.core_teaching: Arjuna asks the question everyone asks: why do I do the wrong thing when part of me doesn't want to, as if something forces me?

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Shankara pictures a person dragged and constrained the way a king's servant is pushed into tasks. Krishna answers that he will name the enemy who is the source of all evil.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Arjuna asks what impels a person who wants to pursue the path of knowledge, dragging him as if by force into evil ways.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Arjuna doubts anyone can avoid coming under desire's sway. Even people who restrain desire and anger through discernment are seen slipping back, so he suspects a deeper prompter at the root of both.

bg.3.36.practical_reading: Naming the pattern ('I keep doing this even though I don't want to') is the first honest step. The Gita treats it as a real question deserving a real answer, not as proof that you are bad.
misreadings: Not an excuse ('something forced me'). The answer that follows locates the force in one's own desire, which can be mastered.
Not a verdict that the asker is wicked. It is a sincere question from the Gita's hero.
cautions: Used on Day 1 of the guilt plan. Krishna's answer calls desire the 'enemy' and 'greatly sinful' (3.37). For a reader with heavy guilt or shame, keep the focus on understanding, not condemnation.
If the reader's 'wrong thing' is an addiction, the verse speaks to it, but the plan should not imply that willpower alone is the fix.
not_for: a reader who has been harmed and is blaming themselves for another person's wrongdoing

bg.3.37.context: Krishna answers Arjuna's question (3.36): the force that drives people to wrongdoing is desire, which becomes anger when blocked. He goes on to say it covers wisdom like smoke covers fire or dust a mirror (3.38–39), and that one must master the senses to slay it (3.41–43).
bg.3.37.core_teaching: Desire, and anger as its blocked form, both born of restless passion, can never be satisfied. That is the real enemy behind wrongdoing.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Desire is the whole world's enemy and the source of all evil. When obstructed, it becomes wrath, so wrath is desire itself. Rousing rajas, it drives people to act; we hear them say 'desire made me do it'.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Craving for sense-objects, sharpened by past habit, is a devouring foe. Blocked, it turns into hatred towards whoever stands in the way, even leading to violence. It obstructs the path of knowledge.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Anger is desire frustrated, so conquering desire conquers anger. It arises from rajas and fades as sattva (clarity) grows. It cannot be appeased by feeding it; it must be overcome.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Desire is the root of wrong action. Anger is desire unfulfilled, turned against whatever obstructs it. Born of rajas, desire stirs a person into restless striving to possess.

bg.3.37.practical_reading: Behind a flash of anger there is usually a want or expectation that got blocked. Tracing anger back to the desire underneath gives you something you can actually work with.
misreadings: Not 'all desire is evil'. The commentators target craving, the insatiable kind driven by rajas.
Not 'you are your anger'. It is called an enemy precisely because it is not the self.
cautions: Strong words ('greatly sinful', 'enemy'). For a reader ashamed of anger, frame desire as something that can be understood and mastered, not a mark of badness.
not_for: anger at injustice or abuse, if framed as 'your desire is the problem'
speaks_to: frustration when things don't go your way

bg.3.38.context: Arjuna has asked what drives a person to do wrong even against his will (3.36). Krishna answers that it is desire, which turns into anger, the all-consuming enemy (3.37). This verse illustrates how desire covers; 3.39 names what is covered, knowledge, and 3.40 says where desire lives: senses, mind and intellect.
bg.3.38.core_teaching: Desire veils clear seeing as smoke veils fire, dust a mirror and the membrane an unborn child: the light is still there, but hidden, to different degrees.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: As a bright fire is wrapped in the dark smoke born with it, so 'this' is covered by desire; he then asks what 'this' is and answers with the next verse: knowledge.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: 'This' is the whole world of creatures, immersed in desire as fire is wrapped in smoke, a mirror's brightness dimmed by a stain, or an embryo sheathed in its membrane.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Shows desire's hostile nature: as fire is covered by its own smoke, a mirror by outside dust, and a foetus fully sealed by its membrane, so knowledge is covered by desire in all three ways.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: 'This' means the universe and also knowledge; 'that' which covers it is desire.

bg.3.38.practical_reading: Teachers use the images to encourage: clarity is not lost, only covered; sometimes a little effort clears it (dust), sometimes it takes patience and time (the womb).
misreadings: Not 'all desire is evil'; the subject is the desire that drives one to wrongdoing (3.36-37).
Not a statement about pregnancy or embryos as impure; it is an image of covering.
cautions: The womb image could feel odd or sensitive for readers dealing with pregnancy or pregnancy loss.
not_for: Readers in pregnancy loss, if the embryo image is foregrounded
speaks_to: Feeling that craving or obsession has clouded judgment
Wanting hope that clarity can return
Understanding why we act against our better judgment

bg.3.39.context: Explains 3.38: what desire covers is knowledge. 3.40 names desire's seats (senses, mind, intellect), and 3.41 begins the remedy: first control the senses.
bg.3.39.core_teaching: Desire is like a fire that can never be filled; it covers even a wise person's understanding, and the wise feel it as an enemy all along, not only after the damage is done.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The wise know even beforehand that desire leads them astray, so it is their constant enemy; the ignorant treat it as a friend while craving and learn otherwise only when suffering comes. It never has enough.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The wise person's understanding of the self is clouded by an eternal foe disguised as lust, which breeds fascination with enjoyment; it is insatiable and inexhaustible, wanting another thing as soon as it gets one.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: To the ignorant, desire brings pleasure during enjoyment and harm after; to the wise, who remember its harm, it is pain even then, hence their constant enemy. Never satisfied however fed, and leading to grief, it is like fire.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Quotes Manu: desire grows with enjoyment as fire with ghee; all the wealth of the earth would not satisfy one man of desire. The ignorant welcome desire as a friend; the wise know beforehand it brings misery.

bg.3.39.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to the treadmill of wanting: getting what you crave rarely ends the craving, it feeds it; noticing this early is the first freedom.
misreadings: Not condemnation of all wishes and aspirations; it concerns compulsive craving.
Not shaming people for desires; it names a universal pattern.
not_for: Someone in early recovery who may hear 'enemy' as self-condemnation, unless framed gently
speaks_to: Consumerism, endless scrolling, chasing the next upgrade

bg.3.4.context: Krishna has answered Arjuna's request for one path by saying there are two, knowledge for contemplatives and action for the active (3.3). Now he explains why action cannot simply be dropped: not starting it, or merely renouncing it, does not bring freedom. 3.5 adds that no one can stay without acting even for a moment.
bg.3.4.core_teaching: Freedom from the bondage of action is not reached by avoiding action, and perfection is not reached by renouncing alone; rightly done action purifies the mind and is itself the way.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Action (worship) done in this or past lives destroys sin, purifies the mind and so yields knowledge. The knower's freedom from action is not reached by not acting; action is its means, and bare renunciation does not perfect.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Neither by not doing prescribed work nor by abandoning it midway does one reach the actionless state of knowledge; work done as worship of the Supreme without seeking reward is what makes one fit for knowledge.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Until the mind is fully purified and knowledge arises, the duties of one's station must be done. Answers the objection that scripture calls renunciation the way to liberation: mere renunciation, without knowledge, does not bring perfection.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Actionlessness and perfection mean resting in one's own nature, existence-knowledge-bliss, through self-knowledge. Someone who just sits idle has not reached it: the mind keeps planning and scheming, and thought is real action.

bg.3.4.practical_reading: Teachers apply it against avoidance dressed as wisdom: quitting, withdrawing or refusing to start does not by itself bring peace; growth comes through engaged, well-intentioned work.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of monastic renunciation; it rejects renunciation without inner readiness.
Not 'never rest'.
not_for: Someone in burnout who genuinely needs rest or to leave a harmful situation
speaks_to: Wanting to quit a job or role in the hope that peace will follow
Procrastination framed as 'waiting until I'm ready'
Spiritual seekers tempted to withdraw from responsibilities

bg.3.41.context: Krishna has named desire as the enemy that covers knowledge (3.37-39) and said it lodges in the senses, mind and intellect (3.40). This verse begins the remedy: start with the senses. 3.42-43 then point to what is higher than the senses, mind and intellect, and close the chapter with the call to slay desire.
bg.3.41.core_teaching: Because desire works through the senses, begin there: get the senses in hand first, then cast off the desire that wrecks both learning and lived understanding.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: First master the senses, then cast off desire, the sinful destroyer of jñāna, knowledge of the self learned from scripture and teacher, and vijñāna, the personal experience of what was taught. Next he asks where one stands to do this.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Desire breeds dislike for the self and love for sense pleasures; so steer the senses from their natural pursuits into the duties of karma yoga, and vanquish this great sinner that destroys knowledge and deeper knowledge of the self.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Control senses, mind and intellect at the very outset, before delusion sets in, and kill or give up sinful desire, which destroys both self-knowledge and scriptural knowledge (or knowledge from teaching and knowledge from meditation).

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Jñāna is indirect knowledge from scripture; vijñāna is direct experience through self-realisation. Control the senses first, then kill desire.

bg.3.41.practical_reading: Teachers apply it as 'start with the doorway': manage what you see, hear and consume (screens, environments, company) before trying to wrestle with the craving itself.
misreadings: Not hatred of the body or the senses; it is about where to begin.
Not that every desire is sinful; the 'sinful one' is the compulsive desire of 3.37.
cautions: Violent language ('slay') and 'sinful' may feed self-hatred in a struggling reader; frame as steady practice.
not_for: Someone with harsh self-criticism or scrupulosity
speaks_to: Breaking a habit by changing environment and inputs
Anyone whose cravings keep undoing what they know

bg.3.42.context: After telling Arjuna to begin by controlling the senses (3.41), Krishna lays out a ladder of inner faculties, senses, mind, intellect and what lies beyond. 3.43 concludes: knowing what is beyond the intellect, steady yourself and slay desire. Chapter 4 then turns to the ancient lineage of this teaching.
bg.3.42.core_teaching: There is an order within: senses, then mind, then intellect, and beyond the intellect the self, the witness of all; knowing this ladder shows where to stand when fighting desire.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Compared with the gross body the senses are subtler and wider; mind, made of wishes and doubts, is above them; intellect, which decides, is above mind; above intellect is the self, its witness, whom desire bewilders by veiling knowledge.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Reads the series as obstacles to self-knowledge: senses, then the mind, then the misdirected intellect; and 'that' beyond the intellect is desire, rooted in the heart, which asserts mastery even when everything else is quiet.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Shows the self, on which the mind can be fixed to control the senses: senses are subtler than objects, mind directs senses, intellect decides before mind wills, and beyond the intellect, its innermost witness, is the self.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Senses are subtler than the body; the mind directs the senses; the intellect, able to discriminate, rescues the doubting mind; the self, the witness, is above the intellect, which borrows its light from the self.

bg.3.42.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a map of inner authority: the senses pull, the mind deliberates, the intellect decides, and your deepest self watches all of them; act from the top of the ladder, not the bottom.
misreadings: Not a ranking of people by intelligence.
Not a denial of the body's worth.
not_for: A reader in acute emotional distress who needs comfort rather than a model
speaks_to: Wanting a simple model of the inner life

bg.3.43.context: The closing verse of chapter 3, completing the answer to Arjuna's question about what drives people to wrongdoing (3.36). Chapter 4 opens with Krishna revealing the ancient lineage of this teaching (4.1).
bg.3.43.core_teaching: Knowing the self that stands beyond even the intellect, and steadying the mind from that place, one can overcome desire, the enemy that is so hard to pin down.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Knowing the self as higher than the intellect, and composing the mind by the purified mind, slay desire, which is hard to conquer because its nature is complex and hard to grasp.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Know that desire, which can overpower even the intellect, is the enemy of the path of knowledge; firmly resolve to keep the mind established in the self, and destroy this inveterate foe in the shape of lust.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Desire and the like are changes in the intellect, while the self is their changeless witness; knowing this, pacify the mind by the intellect so convinced, and kill this hard-to-subdue enemy.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Restrain the lower self by the higher. Desire is hard to conquer but not impossible: discrimination, dispassion and steady practice overcome it, raising sattva overpowers rajas, and the direct way is prayer and repeating God's name.

bg.3.43.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to standing in your deepest self when cravings arise: from that place, watch the mind and steady it rather than being swept along; the struggle is real but winnable.
misreadings: Not violence toward oneself; 'slay' is aimed at compulsive desire.
Not 'desire is easy to beat'; the verse calls it hard to overcome.
cautions: Martial language ('slay the enemy') can feed self-hatred; frame as steadying, not attacking oneself.
not_for: Someone in a crisis of self-blame
speaks_to: Long struggles with a habit or craving
Wanting to act from one's best self

bg.3.5.context: Supports 3.4: since no one can remain without acting, simply giving up action is impossible. 3.6-7 then contrast the person who holds back outwardly while dwelling on objects with the one who works unattached.
bg.3.5.core_teaching: No embodied person can stop acting even for a moment; nature's qualities keep moving everyone, so the real question is not whether to act but how.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: 'Everyone' means every being ignorant of the self; the wise, unshaken by the gunas, are a separate case. So karma yoga is for the unknowing, and one who does not yet know the self should not neglect his duty.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: No one stays still even a moment; resolve to do nothing and the qualities of matter, stirred by past deeds, force action. So karma yoga must first wear away past sin and master the gunas before knowledge is possible.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Renouncing action can only mean being unattached to it, since giving it up is impossible: no one, wise or ignorant, stays inactive even a moment, being driven by attachment and aversion arising from their own nature.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Sattva, rajas and tamas drive the ignorant helplessly to act; sattvic action helps toward liberation while rajasic and tamasic action binds. One who knows the self has crossed beyond the gunas.

bg.3.5.practical_reading: Teachers use it to drop the fantasy of a life without demands: you will be doing something every moment anyway, so choose to act well and with the right spirit rather than wishing to escape action.
misreadings: Not 'you have no free will'; later verses (3.34) say not to fall under the sway of like and dislike.
Not an excuse: 'my nature made me do it'.
cautions: 'Helplessly' could feed fatalism in a discouraged reader; pair with 3.7 or 3.34.
not_for: Someone with depression who feels unable to act and could read 'helplessly' as confirmation
speaks_to: Restlessness and the impossibility of 'doing nothing'

bg.3.6.context: Follows 3.5 (no one can stay without acting). Krishna names the false renunciate who holds the body still while the mind feasts on objects. 3.7 praises the opposite: controlling the senses with the mind and working unattached.
bg.3.6.core_teaching: Outward restraint while the mind keeps dwelling on what it craves is self-deception, not renunciation.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: One who holds back hands and other organs of action while his mind dwells on sense objects is deluded within and is called a hypocrite, a person of sinful conduct.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Someone still burdened with past sin, who has not mastered his senses, tries for self-knowledge while his thoughts dwell lovingly on objects; he pretends to one thing while doing another, misses the mark and fails.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Censures the ignorant renouncer: holding back speech and hands under the pretext of meditating on the Lord while the impure mind keeps returning to objects makes one a hypocrite, a cheat, an egotist.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Lists the five organs of action; whoever restrains them but sits revolving thoughts of sense objects is self-deluded, a hypocrite. Both organs and thoughts must be controlled, the mind fixed on the Lord.

bg.3.6.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to honesty with oneself: giving something up only outwardly, while fantasising about it all day, changes little; work on the mind's attention, not only the hands.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of everyone who gets distracting thoughts in meditation; it targets deliberate pretence and dwelling.
Not 'so you might as well indulge'; 3.7 gives the better way.
cautions: A reader with intrusive thoughts (for example OCD) could take 'hypocrite' as an accusation; avoid using it for unwanted thoughts.
not_for: Readers with intrusive thoughts or scrupulosity
Someone already harsh on themselves
speaks_to: Outward discipline that hides inner craving (diets, detoxes, vows)
Wanting integrity between thought and action

bg.3.7.context: The positive contrast to 3.6. Krishna then tells Arjuna to do his obligatory work, since action is better than inaction and even keeping the body alive needs action (3.8), and that work done as sacrifice does not bind (3.9).
bg.3.7.core_teaching: Better than sham withdrawal is to guide the senses with the mind and get to work, without craving for results; that person excels.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: If the unknowing person, fit only for action, restrains the organs of knowledge by the mind and acts with hands and speech, unmindful of results, he is worthier than the hypocrite of 3.6.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: One who reins in the senses by the mind and does the scripturally enjoined duties natural to his situation, seeking self-vision, excels even the follower of knowledge, since the path of works is free of that path's dangers.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: One who turns the senses toward God through the mind and practises the way of action without desire for fruit excels, because his mind is purified and he gains knowledge.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Whoever acts with the organs of action while controlling the senses of knowledge by the mind, without expecting fruit and without egoism, is far worthier than the hypocrite.

bg.3.7.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to doing the day's work wholeheartedly but without being hooked on the payoff, with the mind steering the senses rather than the other way round.
misreadings: Not workaholism; the key word is 'unattached'.
not_for: Someone in burnout who might hear it as 'just keep working'
speaks_to: Wanting a practical spirituality in a busy working life

bg.3.8.context: Arjuna has asked why, if understanding is higher than action, Krishna urges him into terrible action (3.1–2). Krishna answers that no one can stay actionless even for a moment (3.5), and that holding back the body while the mind dwells on objects is hypocrisy (3.6). This verse draws the practical conclusion. The next says action done as sacrifice does not bind (3.9).
bg.3.8.core_teaching: Do the work that is yours to do. Acting is better than withdrawing, and even keeping the body alive requires action.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Bounden duty is the regular obligatory act, not done for a specific reward. Action beats inaction in its results, as experience shows: by inaction you cannot even get through life's journey.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Action is 'inherent' because the embodied self is joined to matter, so working comes naturally and safely. Here 'inaction' means the path of pure knowledge, which is harder for one unused to it.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Perform the prescribed duties, such as the daily rites and meditation. Action is higher than abstaining from work; give up all work and you could not even maintain your body.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Living itself involves natural, unavoidable actions. It is ignorance to think one can live doing nothing, and neglecting one's obligatory duties is itself a fault.

bg.3.8.practical_reading: When you're stuck, do the next small thing that is yours to do. Action, even modest, gets life moving again; waiting until you feel ready usually doesn't.
misreadings: Not 'any activity beats rest'. The verse is about one's proper duties, not busyness.
Not a condemnation of rest, illness or recovery. Even 'keeping the body going' is counted as action.
cautions: For someone burnt out or depressed, 'action is better than inaction' can feel like pressure. The writer should keep the action small and humane.
not_for: someone who needs rest or medical care and is being urged to push on

bg.4.10.context: Follows 4.9: whoever truly knows Krishna's divine birth and deeds is not reborn but comes to him. Here he says many have reached that state. 4.11 adds that he meets each person in the way they approach him.
bg.4.10.core_teaching: Many before you have let go of craving, fear and anger, given themselves wholly to the Lord, been purified by understanding and reached his own state: the path is well travelled.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: 'Absorbed in me' means knowing Brahman, seeing their identity with the Lord; 'refuge in me' means firm devotion to knowledge alone. Knowledge is itself the austerity, needing no other; purified by its fire, many have reached liberation.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Countless souls, free of desire, fear and anger, wholly given to and relying on him, have been purified by meditating on the truth of his incarnations and acts, and have come to his state.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Knowing his compassion in protecting dharma through his incarnations, people grow free of attachment, fear and anger, fix their minds on him, and purified by self-knowledge and duty done as austerity, both by his grace, attain his being.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Self-knowledge ends attachment; knowing oneself as the deathless self ends fear; seeing the self everywhere leaves no room for anger. The fire of wisdom burns latent tendencies, cravings and sins as fire burns cotton.

bg.4.10.practical_reading: Teachers use it as encouragement: craving, fear and anger can be outgrown, and many ordinary people have done it through devotion and understanding; you are not the first.
misreadings: Not 'never feel fear or anger'; it describes where the path leads.
not_for: Someone whose anger is a healthy response to injustice they need to address
A reader in acute anxiety who may feel judged for still being afraid
speaks_to: Anxiety or anger one wants to outgrow
Feeling alone on a spiritual path
Fear and attachment that keep one from trusting

bg.4.11.context: After saying that many have reached his state (4.10), Krishna answers an implied charge of favouritism. In 4.12 he notes that people who want quick results from action worship the gods, since success from action comes quickly in the human world.
bg.4.11.core_teaching: The Lord responds to each person according to how they approach him, without favouritism; in all their ways of seeking, people are in some sense following his path.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: He rewards each as they seek him: desired ends to seekers of fruit, knowledge to the dutiful, liberation to renouncers, relief to the distressed; never from favour or aversion. All follow the path of the Lord in all forms.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Not only through incarnations: in whatever form or way his devotees choose to conceive and seek him, he adapts himself and appears to them, so that they can enjoy him with every faculty, though he transcends thought and speech.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Is he partial, uniting only his devotees to himself? No: whether people worship with desires or without, he blesses them with what they seek; even those worshipping Indra and other gods walk his path.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: He grants each the objects sought according to their motives: what selfish worshippers ask for, liberation to those who seek self-knowledge unselfishly. He is partial to no one.

bg.4.11.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say God meets people where they are: in a crisis, in curiosity, in longing for results, or in pure love, the response comes in the form the seeker can receive.
misreadings: Not 'all paths are identical' or 'whatever you do leads to the same goal'; the classical readings are more nuanced.
Not 'God gives whatever you ask for'.
cautions: Interfaith readings should not claim the classical commentators taught that all religions lead to the same end.
not_for: Someone who reads it as transactional ('I worshipped, why didn't I get what I asked?')
speaks_to: Feeling one's way of praying or seeking is 'not right enough'
Returning to faith after a gap

bg.4.17.context: Krishna has said that even sages are bewildered about what action and inaction are, and promised to explain the action that frees (4.16). This verse says all three need understanding. The next verse gives the famous paradox: the wise see inaction in action and action in inaction (4.18).
bg.4.17.core_teaching: What counts as right action, wrong action and non-action is not obvious. It has to be understood carefully, because the way of action is deep.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: There is much to learn about action enjoined by scripture, about unlawful action, and about inaction. The true nature of all three is hard to grasp, and Krishna goes on to explain it.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Three things must be known: action that leads to liberation; the many actions (daily, occasional, desire-driven) and the earning they require; and akarma, which here means knowledge. So the path of action is abstruse.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: People assume action is bodily movement and inaction its absence. But the true nature of enjoined action, of forbidden action and of non-action must each be learned. Their way is mysterious.

bg.4.17.practical_reading: Before a hard decision, slow down and look at what you are actually doing, what would be wrong, and what not acting would really mean. Rarely is any of the three as obvious as it first seems.
misreadings: Not 'everything is relative'. The verse says right and wrong action must be understood, not that they don't exist.
Not 'doing nothing is always an option'. The next verse shows that inaction can itself be a form of action.
not_for: someone who needs a clear, immediate safety decision rather than reflection
speaks_to: not knowing whether to act or wait

data_flags.attribution_note: Speaker and listener are right, but the setting is wrong for this verse. 'Krishna reveals the ancient lineage of this teaching and why he comes into the world' describes 4.1–8. Verse 4.17 sits in 4.16–18, where Krishna says even the wise are confused about what...

bg.4.18.context: Krishna has just said (4.16-17) that even sages are confused about what action is, and that action, wrong action and inaction must each be understood, for the way of action is deep. This verse states the paradox; 4.19-23 then describe the person whose actions are burnt up by knowledge, who acts without attachment and so is not bound.
bg.4.18.core_teaching: Whether we are bound depends less on whether the body moves than on the doer behind it: work done without the sense 'I am the doer' or without craving for its fruit does not bind, while sitting idle with the ego intact is still action.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: To the ignorant, true inaction looks like action and vice versa; both assume an agent, which belongs to ignorance. The self is actionless; one who sees this amid activity, and sees idleness as action, is wise.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: A-karma here is knowledge of the self. The wise see that knowledge in the work they do, contemplating the self while working, and see contemplation itself as a kind of act; such a person is fit for liberation.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Work done as worship of the Lord is really inaction, since it leads to knowledge and does not bind; not doing prescribed duty is really action, leading to sin and bondage. One who sees this is wise.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Bondage comes from the idea 'I am the doer'. If one stands as witness of nature's activity, much work is no action; if one sits idle but keeps the idea of agency, that idleness is action.

bg.4.18.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to burnout and to procrastination alike: you can be extremely busy and inwardly quiet if you drop the anxious 'it all depends on me', and you can be lying on the sofa while your mind churns, which is still exhausting activity.
misreadings: Not permission to do nothing because 'everything is really inaction'.
Not a claim that what you do doesn't matter morally; Sridhara reads neglect of duty as binding action.
Not a productivity slogan about 'staying calm while busy' only; it is about the sense of doership.
cautions: Abstract and paradoxical; a reader in acute distress may find it confusing rather than steadying unless the reading explains it simply.
not_for: Someone in depression being told their inactivity is 'really action' in a blaming way
A reader looking for concrete, practical instruction for a crisis today
speaks_to: Burnout from feeling everything depends on oneself
Guilt about resting, or restlessness while resting
People caught between 'doing more' and 'stepping back'
Overthinkers whose minds stay busy when the body stops

bg.4.20.context: Part of Krishna's portrait (4.19-23) of the one whose actions are 'burnt in the fire of knowledge'. 4.19 described one whose undertakings are free of desire-driven plans; this verse says such a person, though fully busy, does nothing; 4.21-22 add that he works with mind controlled, content with what comes, and is not bound.
bg.4.20.core_teaching: When attachment to results is gone and contentment comes from within, even full engagement in work does not create bondage; the action is, in effect, no action.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Having dropped concern for action and fruit through knowledge, content and seeking nothing for himself, he might give up action, but where that is impracticable works on as an example; knowing the actionless self, he does nothing.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Free of any link with results, content in the eternal self and not dependent on matter, such a person may seem intent on work, yet does nothing binding, since inwardly he is cultivating knowledge.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Giving up attachment to action and its fruit, content with his own bliss and so needing nothing for gaining or keeping, he does nothing even while fully engaged in natural or prescribed action; his actions become non-actions.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Repeats the idea of inaction in action for emphasis: one who works without egoism or attachment, for the world's good, does nothing though always active; like someone favoured by the king, he needs no lesser support.

bg.4.20.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to working hard without needing the outcome or others' validation to feel whole: give full effort, then let the result go, and the job stops eating you.
misreadings: Not 'do whatever you like, it doesn't count'.
Not indifference to the people affected by your work.
Not a call to stop caring about doing the work well.
cautions: 'Ever content' can sound like a standard a struggling reader fails; present it as a direction, not a test.
not_for: Someone being exploited at work, who might read it as 'don't care about pay or recognition'
A reader in grief or crisis who cannot yet feel 'content'
speaks_to: Overwork driven by the need to prove oneself
People whose mood rises and falls with each result at work
Caregivers and volunteers who give a lot and want to stop keeping score
Anyone dependent on praise or approval to feel settled

bg.4.21.context: Continues Krishna's portrait (4.19-23) of one who acts without binding. After 4.20 (content, dependent on nothing), this verse adds giving up expectation and possessiveness; 4.22 adds contentment with what comes unbidden and evenness in success and failure; 4.23 says the whole action of such a person melts away.
bg.4.21.core_teaching: Action does not taint one who has dropped craving for outcomes and possessiveness and keeps mind and body in hand; Shankara applies it to the renunciate's bare upkeep, Ramanuja to any selfless worker.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: One free of desire, mind and body controlled, owning nothing, doing only what bare bodily existence needs, incurs no sin; for a seeker of liberation even merit binds. 'Bodily action' cannot mean any act done with the body.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Without longing for fruit, with the mind's anxieties restrained, and giving up selfish love of material things, one who works for life as a mere bodily function incurs no evil, meaning samsara; such karma yoga alone leads to self-vision.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Free of desire, body and mind subdued, possessions relinquished, acting with the body but without sense of agency, he is not bound; for one with knowledge, natural acts like begging alms to sustain the body bring no sin.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The liberated sage keeps only actions needed for the body's maintenance and has given up possessions; for a seeker of liberation even righteousness is a golden fetter, and the sage is free of both good and evil.

bg.4.21.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that much of what wears us out is not the work but the grasping around it: expectations about outcomes and the urge to own and control. Doing simple, needed tasks without that grasping keeps the heart clean.
misreadings: Not 'live without hope' or 'expect nothing good from life'.
Not a demand to give away everything one owns (that is Shankara's reading for monks, not a rule for householders).
Not a license for any bodily act: Shankara explicitly rejects reading it as 'whatever is done with the body is sinless'.
cautions: Our current English 'without hope' could be read by a depressed user as endorsing hopelessness; fix before use.
Ideal of owning nothing can feel shaming to people anxious about money.
not_for: Readers in despair or depression (unless the translation is fixed)
People facing financial hardship, for whom 'give up all possessions' lands badly
speaks_to: People exhausted by possessiveness and control
Those learning to do ordinary chores and work without resentment
Minimalists or people simplifying their lives
Anyone anxious about outcomes of daily work

data_flags.translation_note: 'Without hope' for nirāśīḥ is misleading and risky in a wellbeing app: commentators read it as free of desire or longing for fruit (Shankara: one from whom desires have gone; Ramanuja: without longing for results), not hopelessness. Suggest 'Free of craving, mind and body controlled,...

bg.4.22.context: Krishna is describing the wise who act without being bound (4.18–23). Before this, he says that one who has given up attachment to results, ever content and dependent on nothing, does nothing even while acting (4.20–21). After it, he says that for one whose work is done as sacrifice, all action dissolves (4.23).
bg.4.22.core_teaching: The person who is content with what comes, steady through life's opposites, free of envy and even in success and failure, can act without being bound by the action.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: He is content with what comes unasked, unshaken by opposites and free of envy. Whether he gets his bodily needs or not, he stays calm, knowing the Self is not the doer, so in truth he does nothing.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Content with whatever arrives unsought, enduring opposites, without jealousy, and unmoved whether luck brings something or nothing, he stays unbound even while performing actions.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The sage is satisfied with whatever comes by chance and stays balanced. Others see him acting, but he knows the qualities of Nature do everything. His actions are burnt in knowledge like roasted seeds.

bg.4.22.practical_reading: Comparison lives on envy and on keeping score of others' gains. Practising contentment with what has come to you, and evenness about wins and losses, loosens its grip while you keep working.
misreadings: Not 'never want anything better'. It is about contentment and freedom from envy, not giving up effort.
Not 'blame yourself for everything'. Ramanuja's gloss (tracing harm to one's own past karma) is a doctrinal point, not advice to take on blame for others' wrongs.
cautions: Ramanuja's reading of 'free of malice' (attribute harm to your own past deeds, not to others) could be heard by a mistreated reader as 'it's your fault'. Avoid it in that context.
not_for: someone who has been wronged and needs to name it

bg.4.24.context: Krishna has just said (4.23) that the entire action of one who works as a sacrifice melts away. This verse gives the vision behind that: every element of the offering is Brahman. It opens a list (4.25-33) of the many kinds of sacrifice people perform, ending with the claim that the sacrifice of knowledge is highest.
bg.4.24.core_teaching: For one who sees the one reality in every part of an act (the doer, the means, the offering, the receiver, the result), the act stops binding and becomes a path to that reality itself.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: For one who knows Brahman, the ladle, oblation, fire, offerer, act and result are nothing but Brahman, as mistaken silver is only mother-of-pearl; so his action is no action. The verse praises knowledge by describing it as a sacrifice.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The ladle, oblation, fire and offerer are all effects of Brahman and so are Brahman; whoever contemplates every act as ensouled by Brahman reaches the self's Brahman-like nature, and work itself becomes knowledge and the means to self-vision.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: This is the sacrifice of wisdom: the ideas of instrument, action and result are replaced by Brahman, so action melts away, as 4.23 says; for the self-realised, all life becomes such a sacrifice.

bg.4.24.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to ordinary tasks, especially eating and cooking: treat the food, the hands, the fire and the meal as sacred, and a routine act becomes worship. Many families say it as a grace before meals.
misreadings: Not literal ritual instruction about fire sacrifices.
Not pantheism in a casual 'everything is God, so nothing matters' sense; the commentators link it to knowledge or contemplation that changes how one acts.
