cautions: Abstract metaphysics; pair with a concrete practice (e.g. a mindful meal) for readers who are struggling.
not_for: Someone with an eating disorder, if the reading centres on food
A reader wanting practical, problem-solving help today
speaks_to: Bringing a sense of the sacred into routine chores and meals
People who feel their daily work is meaningless
Those wanting a short daily recitation

bg.4.34.context: This is part of Krishna's praise of knowledge (4.33–42), which ends chapter 4. Krishna has just said that the sacrifice of knowledge is higher than any material offering, and that all action culminates in knowledge (4.33). This verse says how to get it: from those who have seen the truth. The following verses describe what that knowledge does: it ends delusion and carries even the worst wrongdoer across (4.35–36).
bg.4.34.core_teaching: Learn the deepest knowledge from people who have actually realised it. Approach them with humility, ask real questions and serve.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Go to teachers, prostrate humbly, and ask: what is bondage, what is liberation, what is knowledge, what is ignorance? Serve them. Only knowledge passed on by those who have realised the truth, not merely learned it, is effective.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Learn the self-knowledge taught in 2.17–39 from the wise, step by step as you carry on your work, through reverence, timely questions and service. Pleased, they will discern what you truly want to know and teach it.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Prostrate fully before realised people, ask them where your worldly existence comes from and how it can end, and attend on them. Those learned in scripture and with direct experience will instruct you.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Seek a teacher both learned in scripture and established in Brahman; book learning alone is not enough. Prostration alone can be hypocrisy. What counts is faith, sincere questions and wholehearted service.

bg.4.34.practical_reading: In your first week with the Gita: find a trustworthy teacher, study circle or commentary, come with humility, ask your real questions, and give something back. Learning deepens in relationship, not just reading.
misreadings: Not 'obey a guru unquestioningly'. paripraśna means probing questions, and the commentators insist the teacher must have truly realised what they teach.
Not 'service' in the sense of unpaid labour or submission to anyone claiming authority.
cautions: Guru-devotion language (prostration, service, perfect faith) has been exploited by abusive teachers. The writer should stress discernment in choosing a teacher.
not_for: someone leaving or recovering from a high-control religious group
speaks_to: having questions you're afraid to ask

bg.4.36.context: This is part of Krishna's praise of knowledge (4.33–42), which ends chapter 4. Krishna has said that with this knowledge Arjuna will never again fall into such delusion and will see all beings in himself and in Krishna (4.35). This verse makes the strongest claim, and the next gives the fire image (4.37).
bg.4.36.core_teaching: No one is beyond redemption. Even the worst wrongdoer can cross the whole ocean of their wrongdoing on the boat of true knowledge.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Knowledge is a boat for crossing the whole sea of wrongdoing. To a seeker of liberation, Shankara adds, even merit is something to be left behind.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Even if you were a greater sinner than the greatest, the bark of self-knowledge would carry you across the sea of long-hoarded sins.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Even someone foremost among wrongdoers will cross the entire sea of wrongdoing easily, with knowledge as the only vessel needed.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The boat of self-knowledge carries one across the ocean of sin. Sivananda points to 9.30 for the same assurance.

bg.4.36.practical_reading: Guilt can make a person feel permanently defined by what they did. The verse insists that real understanding can carry anyone across: the past does not get the final word.
misreadings: Not 'understanding cancels the harm done to others' (our misuse note is right). It is about inner liberation, not erasing consequences or skipping amends.
Not a licence ('I can do wrong now and get knowledge later').
cautions: Used on Day 2 of the guilt plan. 'Most sinful of all sinners' can sting a reader already full of shame. Emphasise the promise, not the label.
not_for: someone avoiding responsibility for ongoing harm to others
speaks_to: wanting to start again after wrongdoing

bg.4.37.context: This is part of Krishna's praise of knowledge (4.33–42), which ends chapter 4. After promising that knowledge carries even the worst wrongdoer across (4.36), Krishna gives a stronger image: knowledge does not just cross over past actions, it burns them up. The next verse says there is no purifier equal to knowledge (4.38).
bg.4.37.core_teaching: Real knowledge of the self works like fire on fuel. It takes away the power of past actions to keep binding a person.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Knowledge cannot literally burn actions. It makes them impotent. Actions whose effects have already begun, which produced this body, run their course; knowledge destroys only those not yet bearing fruit.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: As a kindled fire burns a bundle of sticks, knowledge of the self's true nature reduces to ashes the whole long-accumulated mass of sin clinging to the individual soul.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: This verse prevents a misreading of the last one: sin is not just crossed while it remains, like an ocean, but destroyed. All actions burn, except prārabdha.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Like roasted seeds, actions burnt by knowledge cannot sprout or bind a person to rebirth. Without the sense 'I do this' and without desire for fruit, action loses its potency. Prārabdha is the usual exception.

bg.4.37.practical_reading: Understanding can change your relationship to the past: old actions stop dictating who you are. Making amends and living with consequences still belong to the same honest process.
misreadings: Not 'no consequences'. Shankara, Sridhara and Sivananda all say knowledge does not burn up prārabdha karma, the past action whose effects have already begun (it produced this body). Those effects still play out.
Not a way to skip accountability (our misuse note is right).
cautions: Used on Day 3 of the guilt plan. The prārabdha point supports the plan's message that amends still matter, and the writer can use it.
not_for: someone looking for absolution while still harming others
speaks_to: feeling defined by what you did

bg.4.38.context: Krishna has been extolling knowledge: it is the highest sacrifice (4.33), learned by approaching the wise with humility and service (4.34), and it carries even the worst wrongdoer across sin, burning actions as fire burns wood (4.36-37). This verse calls it the supreme purifier; 4.39-40 then name the qualities that win it and the doubt that loses it.
bg.4.38.core_teaching: Understanding the self cleanses more deeply than any rite or penance, and it is not handed over from outside: it ripens within a person who has been made ready by steady practice, in its own time.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: No purifier equals wisdom. The seeker of liberation who has made himself fit through karma yoga and the yoga of concentration will, after long practice, find that wisdom himself, within himself.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Nothing in the universe is as purifying as knowledge of the self; it destroys all sin. Perfected by practising karma yoga as taught, which is easy, one realises the self's nature within oneself in due course.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Among penances and yogas nothing purifies like knowledge. Why doesn't everyone pursue knowledge alone? Because it comes of itself, in time, only to one made fit by intense karma yoga, not without it.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: There is no purifier like self-knowledge; one who has reached perfection through steady practice of karma yoga and meditation finds it in himself after a time.

bg.4.38.practical_reading: Teachers use it to encourage patience with inner growth: keep doing the practice and the work honestly, and clarity arrives on its own schedule, from within, rather than by forcing it.
misreadings: Not 'knowledge' as information or intellectual learning; it means insight into the self.
Not a promise of quick results ('in time' means after long practice, per Shankara).
cautions: 'Purifier' language can imply the reader is impure or guilty; frame it as clearing confusion rather than washing away sin for a reader carrying shame.
not_for: Someone in acute crisis needing immediate relief, for whom 'in due time' may feel dismissive
speaks_to: People feeling stuck in spiritual or personal practice
Those carrying guilt who want a path forward

bg.4.39.context: Following 4.38 (knowledge as the supreme purifier, found within in time), Krishna names the three conditions for gaining it: faith, devotion to it, and mastery of the senses. 4.40 then describes the opposite case, the person of doubt, and 4.41-42 close the chapter by urging Arjuna to cut doubt with the sword of knowledge and rise.
bg.4.39.core_teaching: Trust, steady devotion to the means and self-restraint together bring real understanding, and understanding quickly brings deep peace.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Faith alone may be slow, so devotion to the means, like attending the teacher, is added; then sense-mastery. Together they surely bring wisdom, being impossible to fake, unlike outward show, and wisdom swiftly brings liberation.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Having received knowledge by instruction (4.34), growing ever more devoted as it ripens and drawing away from outward pulls of the senses, one soon reaches the height of wisdom and then supreme peace, spiritual bliss.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Only one who trusts the teacher's teaching, is wholly devoted to it and controls the senses gains knowledge; until then one follows the way of action to purify; after knowledge nothing remains to do and peace follows at once.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: One who has faith, serves his teacher and hears his teaching, and has subdued the senses, surely gains knowledge and quickly reaches peace; all three qualifications are needed, one alone will not suffice.

bg.4.39.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to any real learning or healing: trust the process, keep showing up, and rein in distractions, and understanding comes, bringing a calm that outlasts moods.
misreadings: Not 'just believe and everything will be fine'; faith is one of three conditions.
Not blind obedience to any guru; the context is sincere study with a genuine teacher.
cautions: Faith framed as a condition can make a doubting reader feel excluded; pair with the reassurance that sincere effort counts.
not_for: Someone harmed by a manipulative teacher or religious authority
A reader in a faith crisis who may hear it as a reproach
speaks_to: People starting a practice or course of study
Those who have lost peace and want a path back

bg.4.40.context: After naming faith, devotion and self-control as the way to knowledge (4.39), Krishna describes the unfit seeker: ignorant, faithless or doubting. Next (4.41-42) he says actions do not bind one whose doubts are cut by knowledge, and urges Arjuna to cut the doubt in his heart with the sword of knowledge and stand up.
bg.4.40.core_teaching: Of the obstacles to understanding, chronic doubt is the worst: it blocks not only spiritual progress but ordinary happiness, because nothing can be wholeheartedly begun or enjoyed.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The ignorant and the faithless are ruined, but not as much as the doubter, the most sinful of all: even this common world, the next, and happiness escape him, since he doubts them too. So do not doubt.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The ignorant lacks instruction, the non-earnest lacks fervour after instruction, the sceptic doubts what he received; one who doubts the self taught to him forfeits worldly goals and the next world, let alone liberation, since all depend on that conviction.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Describes the unfit seeker: one who hasn't grasped the teacher's teaching, or grasped it without faith, or has faith but doubts it will bear fruit in him. The doubter loses everything: wealth and marriage here, merit hereafter, and happiness.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The faithless lacks faith in himself, scripture and his teacher. The doubter's condition is deplorable: unsure of the next world, he cannot rejoice in this one either, being so suspicious; he has no happiness.

bg.4.40.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to paralysing second-guessing: constant doubt about every choice drains joy and stops all progress, so at some point you commit to a path and test it by living it.
misreadings: Not a ban on questions or critical thinking; Arjuna questions Krishna throughout.
Not a threat that doubters will be destroyed; 'perishes' means failing to reach the goal.
Not condemnation of someone wrestling honestly with faith.
cautions: Strong condemnatory language ('most sinful', 'perishes'); can wound readers with anxiety, OCD-type doubt, or faith struggles.
Should not be used with someone grieving who doubts God's goodness.
not_for: Readers with anxiety or obsessive doubt, who may hear it as a verdict
Someone in a faith crisis after loss
Survivors of spiritual abuse who were punished for questioning
speaks_to: People who never commit to a path and feel stuck
Cynicism that has drained joy from life

bg.4.41.context: After warning that the doubter is lost (4.40), Krishna turns to the one whose doubts are cut by knowledge: actions no longer bind such a person. The chapter closes in 4.42 with a direct command: cut the doubt in your heart, born of ignorance, with the sword of knowledge, resort to yoga and stand up.
bg.4.41.core_teaching: When action is offered or let go through yoga, doubt is cut by understanding, and the mind is steady and watchful, one's actions no longer chain one.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: One who sees the Supreme renounces both merit and demerit through that knowledge, his doubt cut by realising the self's oneness with the Lord; seeing all action as the play of the gunas and ever watchful, he is not bound.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Works done by karma yoga from the standpoint of wisdom lose their binding power; doubts about the self are dispelled by self-knowledge; the mind reaches unshakable certainty; then no string of deeds can bind such a person.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Concludes chapters 3-4 on action then knowledge: one who offers actions to the Lord in worship, whose ego-sense about the body is destroyed by knowing he is not the agent, and who is alert, is not bound by actions.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Cites Madhusudana for 'ever watchful'. One established in the identity of individual and supreme soul has his doubts cut; his actions, burnt in the fire of wisdom, do not bind.

bg.4.41.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to acting with a clear head after a period of confusion: once you have thought it through and settled your doubt, act fully and steadily, offering the result, and stop being dragged back by every action's aftermath.
misreadings: Not 'nothing you do has consequences'.
Not suppressing doubts; the doubt is cut by understanding, not ignored.
cautions: Paired with 4.40's harsh view of doubt; keep the tone encouraging.
not_for: Someone avoiding responsibility for harm they've done, who might read it as 'my actions don't bind me'
speaks_to: Moving from long indecision into committed action
People haunted by guilt over past actions
Those seeking inner steadiness at work

bg.4.42.context: This ends chapter 4. Krishna has just said that the doubter perishes and finds no happiness in this world or the next, while one who has given up action through yoga and cut doubt by knowledge is not bound (4.40–41). Here he tells Arjuna to cut his doubt, take up yoga and stand up. Chapter 5 opens with Arjuna, still uncertain, asking which is better: renunciation or action.
bg.4.42.core_teaching: Cut through the doubt that ignorance has planted in your heart with clear understanding. Then commit to the path of action and stand up.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: With the knowledge of the self that Krishna has taught, sever your long-standing doubts about the self. Practise karma-yoga as instructed, and arise to carry out his teaching.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Cut the doubt arising from grief, born of not knowing the Self, with the sword of discrimination between Self and body. Take up karma-yoga and first of all rise for the battle at hand, which is righteous for a warrior.

bg.4.42.practical_reading: At a new start, some doubt is natural. But when it becomes a loop that keeps you from moving, use what you know to cut it, choose your path and take the first step today.
misreadings: Not 'never question anything'. The doubt meant here is confusion about the self that paralyses action, not honest inquiry (4.34 praises questioning).
Not literally 'go to war', except in Arjuna's case.
cautions: Shankara and Sivananda call doubt 'most sinful'. For an anxious or OCD-prone reader, that can feed self-blame. Frame it as 'doubt that stops you', not 'doubting is a sin'.
not_for: someone whose doubt is a healthy warning about a harmful choice

bg.4.7.context: Krishna has told Arjuna that he first taught this yoga to Vivasvan (4.1); Arjuna asks how, since Vivasvan lived long before (4.4). Krishna answers that both have had many births, which he remembers (4.5), and that, though unborn, he takes birth through his own power (4.6). This verse and 4.8 say when and why he comes.
bg.4.7.core_teaching: Whenever the order that sustains life weakens and its opposite rises, the divine comes into the world: there is no fixed schedule, only the need.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Dharma here is the religion embodied in the order of castes and stages of life, the means to prosperity and liberation; whenever it decays and its opposite rises, the Lord manifests himself through his own maya.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: No fixed periods are set for the Lord's incarnations: whenever and wherever the dharma of the varnas and ashramas declines and adharma grows, he manifests himself of his own free will.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Answers the question 'when do you come into being?': whenever righteousness decreases and unrighteousness predominates.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Dharma is what sustains and holds together, with no exact English equivalent: what elevates a person toward knowledge and liberation; adharma is what drags one down into worldliness and ignorance.

bg.4.7.practical_reading: Teachers use it as hope in dark times: decline is not the end of the story. Many also read it as a call to take part in restoring what is right, rather than waiting passively.
misreadings: Not 'wait for rescue'. Many read it as a call to be the force that restores what is right.
Not a basis for declaring a particular leader or person an avatar.
cautions: Classical commentaries define dharma in caste terms (varṇa-āśrama); avoid carrying that into modern readings.
Political or communal misuse is common; keep it personal and ethical.
not_for: Someone waiting passively for a rescuer in an unsafe situation
Communal or political contexts where it could be used against others
speaks_to: Despair at injustice or decline in society, workplace or family

bg.4.8.context: Completes 4.7: why the Lord comes. 4.9 adds that whoever truly knows his divine birth and deeds is not born again but comes to him; 4.10 says many have reached his state this way.
bg.4.8.core_teaching: The divine comes into the world, again and again, to protect the good, end the harm done by wrongdoers and set dharma back on its feet.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The good are those on the right path. Comments briefly; with 4.9 he adds that the Lord's birth is through maya, divine and not ordinary, and one who knows it truly is liberated.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The good are devotees who cannot live without seeing him, for whom a moment apart is an age; he comes so they may see him, to destroy evildoers, and to restore Vedic dharma, the mode of his worship.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: He comes to protect those doing their duties, slay those who do vile deeds, and so make dharma secure. Chastising the wicked is not cruelty, any more than a mother disciplining her child.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society) (commentary printed under 4.7-8)
commentaries.gist: The good are those who live righteously, serve others with their bodies, and are free of selfishness, lust and greed; the Lord comes in every age to protect them and restore righteousness.

bg.4.8.practical_reading: Teachers apply it as reassurance that goodness is protected, and as an invitation to align with that protecting work through one's own fairness and courage.
misreadings: Not a licence to punish people you judge wicked; the work of setting right belongs to the divine and to justice.
Not 'my side is the good side'.
cautions: 'Destroy the wicked' can be weaponised in conflict; avoid in contexts of anger at a specific person.
May raise the question 'why wasn't I protected?' for someone who has suffered harm.
not_for: Someone wanting revenge
A victim of harm who may hear it as a broken promise
speaks_to: Feeling unprotected or overwhelmed by wrongdoing around you
Ramanuja's reading: longing for God's presence

bg.5.10.context: In chapter 5 Krishna is reconciling renunciation and action. He has just said that the one who knows the truth thinks 'I do nothing at all' even while seeing, hearing and eating, since only the senses move among their objects (5.8–9). This verse gives the lotus-leaf image. The next says yogis act with body, mind and intellect only to purify themselves (5.11).
bg.5.10.core_teaching: Whoever acts while offering the action up and letting go of attachment stays unstained by it, as a lotus leaf sits in water without getting wet.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: He offers all actions to the Lord, like a servant acting for his master, without attachment even to liberation. The only result of acting this way is a purified mind.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Here 'brahman' means matter. Whoever sees that seeing and hearing belong to matter and the senses, ascribes actions to it, and thinks 'I do nothing' is untouched by the error of taking matter for the self.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Objection: one who feels 'I am the doer' must be tainted, so how can he renounce? Answer: offering actions to the Lord and dropping attachment to fruit, he is untouched by good or evil deeds, like a lotus leaf.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Several verses in chapters 4–5 make one point: the yogi who acts without ego or attachment to results, offering everything to the Lord, is not tainted, gains purity of heart and, through it, self-knowledge.

bg.5.10.practical_reading: In a stressful environment you can do your work fully without letting the drama and politics soak in. The 'leaf' is the inner distance that comes from doing the work as an offering, not as a bid for approval.
misreadings: Not 'stay silent about wrongdoing' (our misuse note is right). Being unstained is about inner freedom, not complicity.
Not 'nothing you do can be wrong if you're detached'. The verse is about how a rightful action is done.
not_for: someone in an abusive situation who needs to leave, not stay 'unstained'
speaks_to: feeling contaminated by a toxic environment
wanting to stay clean inside while staying engaged

bg.5.11.context: Krishna has said (5.8-10) that the knower thinks 'I do nothing' while the senses move among objects, and that one who acts offering everything to Brahman is untouched by sin like a lotus leaf by water. This verse describes how karma yogis work; 5.12 contrasts the peace of the one who drops the fruit with the bondage of the one driven by desire.
bg.5.11.core_teaching: Those on the path of action use every faculty, body, mind, intellect and senses, to work without attachment, aiming not at rewards but at an inner cleansing.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: 'Mere' means free of egotism, resolved 'I act only for the Lord, not myself', and applies to each faculty. Yogins act unattached to results only for purity of mind; so Arjuna's duty is simply to act.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Free of clinging to fruits such as heaven, karma yogis let body, mind, intellect and senses do the work as instruments of self-purification, which means breaking the bonds of past deeds on the self.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Selfless actions lead to liberation: giving up attachment to fruit, such people bathe with the body, meditate with the mind, ascertain truth with the intellect, and hear and speak of the Lord with the senses, to purify the mind.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Yogis here are karma yogis, free of egoism and selfishness, working to purify the heart without attachment to results and dedicating every action to the Lord; 'only' means free from egoism and applies to all four faculties.

bg.5.11.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to doing ordinary work, exercise, study and conversation as practice: when the point is to become clearer and kinder rather than to gain, the same tasks change their effect on you.
misreadings: Not 'work for free' or 'don't seek a livelihood'.
Not mechanical, mindless activity; the faculties are used deliberately but without ego.
cautions: 'Purification' can imply the reader is dirty or guilty; frame as clarity.
not_for: Someone with scrupulosity or obsessive guilt about impurity
A reader exhausted by unpaid labour, who may hear it as 'keep giving'
speaks_to: People who want their daily work to have inner meaning
Those beginning a spiritual practice through service

bg.5.12.context: After 5.11 (yogis act with body, mind, intellect and senses for inner purification), Krishna sums up the contrast: the integrated person who lets go of results finds lasting peace, while the one driven by desire clings to results and is bound. 5.13 then describes the self-controlled person who, having renounced all actions in mind, dwells at ease in the body, the 'city of nine gates'.
bg.5.12.core_teaching: The same work can free or bind: done with the result handed over, it brings lasting peace; done in the grip of desire for the result, it chains the doer.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The steady one, resolved 'I act for the Lord, not for my benefit', gives up the fruit and reaches liberation by stages: purity of mind, knowledge, renunciation of action, steadiness in knowledge. The unsteady, led by desire, is firmly bound.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The right performer wants nothing but the self, gives up the fruit and works only to purify himself, reaching the lasting joy of the self; the one who craves other fruits, driven by lust, stays bound in samsara.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Answers how the same actions bind some and free others: the one devoted solely to the Lord, acting without seeking fruit, gains liberation; the outward-turned one, impelled by desire and attached to fruit, is completely bound.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The harmonious person says 'I act for my Lord, not for gain' and reaches peace through four stages; the unbalanced person thinking 'I did this and will get that' is firmly bound.

bg.5.12.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to work and relationships: do your part fully and let go of controlling the payoff; the more you need a particular outcome, the more every setback owns you.
misreadings: Not refusing fair pay, recognition or planning; it is about not being chained to them (as our misuse note says).
Not passivity about outcomes that affect others.
cautions: 'Bound' language can feel judgmental to someone anxious about money or results; keep the tone compassionate.
not_for: Someone in financial crisis who might hear 'don't care about the money'
A reader in fresh grief over an outcome that cannot be undone
speaks_to: Anxiety about results at work or in exams
People whose self-worth hangs on outcomes
Those recovering from disappointment after a big effort

bg.5.18.context: This is part of Krishna's description of the sage who has realised Brahman (5.18–26), late in chapter 5. Krishna has just said that knowledge dispels ignorance like the sun (5.16), and that those whose minds are absorbed in it are freed from rebirth (5.17). This verse defines their vision. The next says those whose minds rest in this sameness have conquered worldly existence here and now (5.19).
bg.5.18.core_teaching: The wise see the same Self in every being, however different their species, learning or social status.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The wise see one principle, Brahman, in unlike things. The brahmin and the 'dog-cooker' illustrate differences of conduct; the cow, elephant and dog, differences of species.

bg.5.18.practical_reading: Success tempts us to rank people by status. The verse asks for the opposite practice: treat the person who serves you, the stranger and the colleague with the same regard you give the powerful.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of the caste hierarchy its examples come from. Its point is that those distinctions don't touch the Self.
Not 'treat everyone identically in practice'. Shankara notes it is about seeing the same Self, not about erasing all practical distinctions.
cautions: This is a strong caution about caste. Shankara and Sivananda explicitly rank the beings by guṇa and group the outcaste with animals as tamasic. Shankara's comment goes on to discuss a law about not eating such persons' food. Do not reproduce those rankings. Ramanuja's reading (all selves equal in essence) is the safest to lead with.
Our line's 'an outcast' should be reworded.
not_for: readers who may be hurt by casual use of caste terms
speaks_to: treating people fairly regardless of status

bg.5.19.context: Krishna has just said (5.18) that the wise look with the same eye on a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste. This verse says such people have already overcome birth and becoming while still alive, because their minds rest in Brahman, which is the same in all. It leads into 5.20's portrait of the person who is neither elated nor crushed.
bg.5.19.core_teaching: A mind that rests in the sameness of the one reality in every being is already free in this life; that sameness is Brahman itself, so such people already stand in Brahman.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: 'Here' means even during practice: whoever sees all selves as equal has overcome samsara. Freed of matter's taint, the self is the same in all, so resting in that sameness is resting in Brahman; such people are as liberated.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Answers the objection that Gautama's law forbids treating unequal people alike: these sages have overcome samsara while alive and reached Brahman; the fault Gautama names applies to someone still acting as an honour-giver, before that attainment.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: When the mind stays balanced, birth and death are conquered and freedom is gained. Brahman is pure and attributeless, so dwelling in an outcaste or a dog does not affect it; it is one and equal in all.

bg.5.19.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that peace is not postponed to an afterlife: a mind that stops ranking people and outcomes as higher and lower is already free of much of its torment, today.
misreadings: Not a claim that social inequality or mistreatment doesn't matter; the 'sameness' is about the one Self in all, not about ignoring injustice.
Not indifference or emotional flatness; it is steadiness of the mind.
cautions: The surrounding verse (5.18) and Shankara's discussion use caste examples ('dog-eater', rules for honouring brahmins); keep that out of a modern reading or handle it explicitly.
'Conquering birth' presupposes rebirth doctrine.
not_for: someone currently facing discrimination, who may hear 'see everyone as the same' as dismissing their experience
acute grief, where an abstract statement about Brahman can feel distant
speaks_to: someone worn out by comparison, ranking and status games
a person who judges others (or themselves) by background or rank
someone who wants calm now rather than 'someday'

bg.5.2.context: Chapter 5 opens with Arjuna, still confused after chapter 4 praised both knowledge and action, asking which one is better: renouncing action or the yoga of action (5.1). Krishna answers that both lead to the highest good but action done as yoga is better; the following verses say the true renouncer is one without hate or craving and that the two paths reach the same goal (5.3-6).
bg.5.2.core_teaching: Both stepping back from action and acting selflessly can lead to freedom, but for most people engaged, unattached action is the better path.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Renunciation and karma yoga both lead to liberation by giving rise to knowledge; but karma yoga is better than mere renunciation not accompanied by knowledge. Renunciation with knowledge, he notes, is a far higher path.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Renunciation here means ceasing from work, that is, the path of knowledge. Each path can independently lead to bliss, but karma yoga is better than the renunciation of works; the following verses explain why.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Krishna does not prescribe action for one who knows the self; he tells Arjuna, who still takes the body for the self, to take up selfless action as the means to knowledge, cutting through doubt born of grief and delusion.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Both lead to liberation, but karma yoga is better than renunciation without self-knowledge, while renunciation with knowledge is superior; karma yoga is easy and so suits most people.

bg.5.2.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to the urge to quit everything when overwhelmed: for most people the way through is not walking away but continuing to act while letting go of the grasping and resentment around the work.
misreadings: Not 'never rest, retire or take a break'.
Not a dismissal of monks or contemplative life; Shankara holds renunciation with knowledge to be higher.
Not 'activity for its own sake is good'.
cautions: Can sound like pressure to keep going for a burnt-out reader; pair with the point that the action meant is unattached, not driven.
not_for: Someone in burnout who genuinely needs to stop and rest
A person leaving an abusive situation, who should not read it as 'stay and keep acting'
speaks_to: People tempted to quit a job, family role or commitment out of frustration
Those torn between withdrawal and engagement
Retirees wondering how to stay meaningfully engaged

bg.5.20.context: Continuing from 5.19's picture of those whose minds rest in sameness, Krishna describes the knower of Brahman: not thrilled by the pleasant, not shaken by the unpleasant. The next verse (5.21) says such a person, unattached to outer contacts, finds happiness within.
bg.5.20.core_teaching: Swings of elation and dismay belong to someone who takes the body-and-mind to be the whole self; the person settled in the deeper self keeps a steady, undeluded understanding through both.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Elation and dejection at getting the liked and disliked happen to those who see only the body as self, not to one who sees the Self alone. Steadiness is a doubt-free conviction that one faultless Self is in all beings.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Whatever pleasant or unpleasant things come by past karma, do not react with joy or agitation. Steady intellect means fixed on the stable self; undeluded means not merging the unstable body with it. This is practice, after learning from teachers.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: A mark of one who has reached Brahman: not exultant over the pleasant, not dejected by the unpleasant, because the intellect is unwavering and delusion has gone.

bg.5.20.practical_reading: Modern teachers apply it to the daily swing of good and bad news (results, messages, markets): let events register, but do not let each one decide your inner weather.
misreadings: Not 'suppress your feelings' or 'never be happy'; it is about not being thrown around by gain and loss.
Not a test the reader is failing if they feel hurt; commentators describe the realised state (Shankara) or a long practice (Ramanuja).
cautions: 'Do not be troubled by the unpleasant' can sound dismissive to someone in fresh grief or shock; frame it as a direction to grow toward, not an instruction for today.
not_for: fresh bereavement or trauma
someone who already numbs or suppresses feelings and needs permission to feel
speaks_to: someone on an emotional roller-coaster driven by outcomes
a person whose mood depends on praise, likes or approval

bg.5.21.context: This is part of Krishna's description of the sage who has realised Brahman (5.18–26), late in chapter 5. Krishna has just described the knower of Brahman as neither elated by the pleasant nor shaken by the unpleasant (5.20). This verse describes their inner joy. The next adds that pleasures born of contact are wombs of sorrow, with a beginning and an end (5.22).
bg.5.21.core_teaching: When the mind is no longer hooked by outer pleasures, it finds a joy within. Joined to Brahman, that joy does not run out.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: When the mind is not tied to external sense-objects, the sage finds the joy in the Self. Absorbed in deep contemplation of Brahman, he gains imperishable bliss, so one should turn the senses from momentary pleasures.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Whoever stops clinging to pleasures from things other than the self, and begins to delight in the self within, unites his mind to repeated contemplation of the self and gains imperishable bliss.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Unattached to outer objects, he first finds the serene joy of inner withdrawal. Then, with his mind absorbed in Brahman through yoga, he enjoys a bliss that never decays.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: To enjoy the imperishable happiness within, withdraw the senses from their objects and go deep into meditation on the Self.

bg.5.21.practical_reading: Notice the difference between pleasure that needs something outside you and the quieter gladness that comes in stillness. Giving the second a few minutes a day helps it grow.
misreadings: Not 'outer joys are bad'. It contrasts dependent pleasure with independent joy.
Not a call to withdraw from relationships.
cautions: The very next verse (5.22) calls sense-pleasures 'wombs of sorrow'. In a joy plan, the writer should not slide into treating all ordinary happiness as suspect.
not_for: someone with anhedonia or depression, if framed as 'joy is simply within, just find it'

bg.5.22.context: Krishna has said (5.21) that one unattached to outer contacts finds happiness in the self. Here he explains why: pleasures born of contact breed sorrow and do not last. The next verse (5.23) praises the person who can withstand the surge of desire and anger before the body falls.
bg.5.22.core_teaching: Pleasures that depend on contact with objects start, end and leave pain behind, so a discerning person does not rest their happiness on them.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Pleasures from sense contact end in sorrow and are seen to last only a short time; one who knows their real nature does not delight in them.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Answering how giving up pleasant things can be a human good: even while they last, such pleasures are mixed with rivalry and envy, so they cause sorrow; and they begin and end, so the discerning do not delight in them.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: People seek joy in perishable objects and end up carrying sorrow; between the start and end is only a brief, hollow pleasure. Withdraw the senses and fix the mind on the blissful Self within.

bg.5.22.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to the comedown after a purchase, a binge or a scroll: enjoy what comes, but don't stake your lasting happiness on things that, by their nature, end.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of joy, food, friendship or beauty; the point is where lasting happiness can be found.
Not a reason for guilt about ordinary pleasures.
cautions: Shankara's language is severe (he says the deeply deluded, 'like animals', delight in objects); avoid carrying that tone to a reader.
For someone with depression or anhedonia, 'pleasures breed sorrow' may reinforce hopelessness.
not_for: someone depressed whose small pleasures are a lifeline right now
someone already prone to guilt or self-denial
speaks_to: the emptiness after chasing a high (shopping, scrolling, partying)
someone noticing a habit that no longer satisfies
a person rethinking what they've built their happiness on

bg.5.23.context: This is part of Krishna's description of the sage who has realised Brahman (5.18–26), late in chapter 5. Krishna has just called sense-pleasures wombs of sorrow with a beginning and an end (5.22). Here he says the truly disciplined and happy person can withstand the surge of desire and anger right here, in this life. The next verse describes the one whose joy and light are within (5.24).
bg.5.23.core_teaching: Whoever can withstand the surge of desire and anger here and now, for as long as they live, is the disciplined one, and truly happy.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Even while still practising, in the body, one who draws on the satisfying experience of the self to resist the rush of desire and passion is fit for yoga, and finds bliss in the self.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Desire and anger are powerful enemies of peace and need strong effort to overcome. The happiest person is the one who has mastered them, not the one with great wealth or a picture-perfect family.

bg.5.23.practical_reading: Anger arrives as a surge in the body: heat, trembling, a clenched jaw. You don't have to act on it. Riding out the wave without obeying it is a skill you can practise today.
misreadings: Not 'never feel desire or anger'. It is about withstanding the surge, not having no surge.
'Before leaving the body' is about the whole span of life, not a hint about death.
cautions: Mentions death ('before release from the body'; Shankara: 'up to the point of death'). One of Sridhara's alternative readings compares the steady person to a corpse unmoved by mourners or the funeral pyre. Don't use that gloss with a distressed reader.
not_for: a reader with suicidal thoughts, if the 'before death' phrasing is emphasised

bg.5.24.context: This is part of Krishna's description of the sage who has realised Brahman (5.18–26), late in chapter 5. After the person who withstands desire and anger (5.23), Krishna describes the one whose happiness, delight and light are all within. The following verses say such sages, free of sin and doubt and devoted to all beings' welfare, attain Brahman's peace (5.25–26).
bg.5.24.core_teaching: The yogi whose happiness, delight and light all come from within attains the peace of Brahman, even while living.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: 'Within' means in the Self. Such a yogi attains liberation, the bliss in Brahman, while still living on earth, himself becoming Brahman.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Having let go of external pleasures, he longs for the joy of self-experience. The self is his pleasure-garden and knowledge of the self his only light. Such a Brahman-like yogi gains the bliss of self-enjoyment.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Subduing desire and anger is not enough. Happiness must rest in the Self, not in objects; one's play must be within, and one's attention inward rather than on entertainments. Only then is one absorbed in Brahman.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Within means in the Self. Such a yogi attains liberation while still living, becoming a jīvanmukta.

bg.5.24.practical_reading: Joy that comes from within (from meaning, presence, a quiet mind) is less fragile than joy that depends on events. Notice where your gladness comes from, and tend the inner source.
misreadings: Not 'needing nothing and no one'. It describes where the deepest joy comes from, not a rejection of people.
cautions: Used on Day 1 of the joy plan ('see'). Keep it invitational. A reader without much inner joy right now should not come away feeling deficient.
not_for: someone isolated, if framed as 'you don't need others'
speaks_to: wanting joy that doesn't depend on circumstances

bg.5.25.context: Krishna is describing those who reach the peace of Brahman (brahma-nirvāṇa): 5.24 speaks of one whose joy and light are within, and 5.26 adds that this peace is near for those free of desire and anger. This verse adds a social mark: delight in the welfare of all beings.
bg.5.25.core_teaching: Inner purification, clarity and self-mastery go together with active goodwill to all beings, and this combination is what reaches the peace of Brahman.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Renunciates of right vision, whose sins are gone, doubts cut and senses restrained, and who are devoted to the welfare of all beings, which he glosses as non-harming, attain liberation.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Freed from pairs like heat and cold, minds held on the self, devoted to all beings' good as to their own, intent on seeing the self: such people lose every obstacle to the self and reach the bliss of Brahman.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Seers of right vision with impurities gone, doubts cut, minds controlled, and compassionate, devoted to the good of all, attain liberation.

bg.5.25.practical_reading: Teachers stress that the Gita's inner peace is not private escape: clearing your own confusion and caring for others' welfare are one path.
misreadings: Not a claim that only 'sinless' people deserve peace; kṣīṇa-kalmaṣa describes a wearing-away that happens on the path.
Not a call to self-sacrifice to the point of burnout.
cautions: 'Faults/sins destroyed' can trigger shame in a reader already burdened by guilt.
not_for: exhausted caregivers who may hear 'delight in the welfare of all' as one more demand
someone in heavy guilt or shame
speaks_to: someone who finds steadiness through service or volunteering
a person stuck in indecision who wants clarity
someone looking for a spirituality that includes others

bg.5.28.context: In the closing verses of chapter 5, Krishna sketches meditation for the first time: shut out outer contacts, steady the gaze, even out the breath (5.27). This verse names the result: a sage with senses, mind and intellect in hand, free of desire, fear and anger, is free already. 5.29 adds that knowing the Lord as friend of all beings brings peace, and chapter 6 develops meditation in detail.
bg.5.28.core_teaching: When desire, fear and anger have fallen away and the faculties are steady, freedom is not a later reward; the person is already free.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Read with 5.27: the renunciate who withdraws from sense objects, steadies gaze and breath, controls senses, mind and intellect, aims only at liberation and is free of desire, fear and anger, is liberated; nothing further remains for him to do.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Describes the posture: sit upright, gaze at the nose-tip, even breath. One whose faculties no longer stray from contemplating the self, free of desire, fear and anger, is free even while still practising, as at the goal.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: By this method, the sage whose senses, mind and intellect are controlled and whose goal is liberation, free of desire, fear and anger, is liberated even while alive.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Desire, fear and anger make the mind restless; without them there is perfect peace. With the faculties subdued, the sage contemplates constantly and attains freedom. A muni is one who reflects.

bg.5.28.practical_reading: Teachers use the trio of desire, fear and anger as a check-in: notice which of the three is driving you right now, and return to the breath before acting.
misreadings: Not a claim that feeling fear makes you unspiritual; fear can be protective, and the verse describes the goal.
Not a breathing trick that instantly liberates; Ramanuja and Shankara frame it within sustained practice.
cautions: For someone in real danger, 'be free of fear' should not be read as 'ignore the threat'.
not_for: someone in an unsafe situation where fear is a needed signal
someone with trauma who may experience breath and gaze techniques as triggering without guidance
speaks_to: someone reactive or quick to anger
someone who wants to see what inner freedom looks like in practice

bg.5.29.context: Krishna has just sketched meditation: shut out external contacts, fix the gaze between the brows, even out the breath, and be free of desire, fear and anger (5.27–28). This verse closes chapter 5 with what the meditator should know. Chapter 6 then teaches meditation in detail.
bg.5.29.core_teaching: Knowing the Lord as the one who receives every offering, rules all the worlds and is the selfless friend of every being, a person comes to peace.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: I am Narayana, author and goal of all sacrifices and austerities, everyone's friend, doing good without expecting return. Dwelling in all hearts, I dispense the fruits of action and witness all thought. Knowing me brings peace, saṃsāra's end.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Knowing Krishna as receiver of sacrifices, Lord of lords and intimate friend of every creature, one finds peace. Work done as worship is easiest, and who would not gladly serve a universal friend?

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Liberation needs knowledge, not just sense-control. Know the Lord as the one who protects his devotees' offerings, the great Lord, and the disinterested well-wisher or inner ruler of all; by his grace one attains peace.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The Lord is the friend of all beings, doing them good without expecting anything back, dwelling in their hearts as silent witness. Knowing him, they attain peace and liberation.

bg.5.29.practical_reading: In loneliness, the verse offers a companion that is always present: the divine as a well-wisher who wants your good and expects nothing in return. Many readers find that thought steadying, alongside human connection.
misreadings: Not 'you don't need human friends'. It offers a deeper companionship, not a replacement.
Not a transactional God. The commentators stress that the Lord does good without expecting return.
cautions: Theistic verse: 'me' is Krishna. Our line's 'the divine' is a reasonable softening, but don't strip the theism entirely.
not_for: a non-theistic reader, unless framed as the Gita's view
someone in crisis who needs human support urgently

bg.5.3.context: Having said that karma yoga is better than renunciation (5.2), Krishna explains why: the person who neither hates nor craves is already a true renouncer, even while acting. In 5.4-5 he says only the immature see knowledge and action as different paths; both reach the same goal.
bg.5.3.core_teaching: Renunciation is an inner state, not a robe or a place: whoever has stopped hating and craving is a renouncer while fully engaged in life, and is freed easily.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The karma yogi who neither hates pain and its causes nor desires pleasure and its sources is a perpetual renouncer, even while acting; free of the pairs, he is easily released. Sankhya and Yoga share one goal.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The karma yogi who has tasted the bliss of the self desires nothing but the self, so has nothing to hate and can endure the pairs; such a person is a constant renouncer, practising knowledge, and easily escapes bondage.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Praising the karma yogi as a renouncer shows why action is better: one free of attachment and aversion, working for the Lord, is a renouncer even while working, and being pure-minded is easily freed through knowledge.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Giving up work from laziness, family quarrels, calamity or unemployment does not make a renouncer; the karma yogi above liking and disliking, success and failure, praise and blame, is one, even without formal vows.

bg.5.3.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to people who think peace requires leaving: you don't need to move to a monastery or quit your life; dropping resentment and craving where you are is the real letting go.
misreadings: Not a call to suppress all feeling; it concerns hatred and craving.
Not 'you are a renunciate, so you have no obligations'.
cautions: A reader full of anger or longing may feel judged; present it as a direction, not a test they are failing.
not_for: Someone whose anger is a healthy response to injustice or abuse
speaks_to: People who fantasise about escaping their lives to find peace
Those working on resentment or envy

bg.6.1.context: Chapter 6 opens by settling a question that ran through chapter 5: is it better to renounce action or to act? Krishna answers that the real renouncer and yogi is the one who does what needs doing without depending on its results, not the one who simply drops ritual and work. 6.2 adds that no one becomes a yogi without giving up self-centred intention (saṅkalpa), and the chapter then moves to meditation.
bg.6.1.core_teaching: Renunciation is an inner letting-go of the claim on results, not an outward quitting of work; someone who does their duty that way already has what the renouncer seeks.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Free of thirst for results, one who does obligatory work as duty excels other workers and may be called renouncer and yogi, through renouncing desire for fruit; the one without sacred fire and rites is not the only renouncer.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: One who acts as worship of the Supreme Person, the friend of all, treating the action itself as the whole purpose, has both knowledge-discipline and action-discipline; the one who merely abstains from prescribed work has only the first.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Chapter 6 unfolds meditation. Because chapter 5 praised knowledge and action can feel painful, people might renounce rashly; so Krishna praises action-yoga as even better than such renunciation.

bg.6.1.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to the urge to quit when work feels pointless: the freedom you want comes from loosening your grip on outcomes while still doing what's needed, not from walking away.
misreadings: Not 'never leave a job or role'; it concerns the inner motive, not a rule against change.
Not a dismissal of monastic life; Shankara keeps formal renunciation and calls this praise of the worker.
not_for: someone in an exploitative or harmful job who needs permission to leave
someone already over-functioning, who may hear 'keep doing your duty' as 'never rest'
speaks_to: burnout that tempts someone to drop everything
someone who equates being spiritual with withdrawing from responsibilities
a person anxious about whether their work will 'pay off'

bg.6.16.context: After describing how to sit and focus in meditation (6.10-15), Krishna turns to daily habits. This verse rules out extremes of eating and sleeping; 6.17 gives the positive form: yoga removes sorrow for one who is moderate in food, recreation, effort, sleep and waking.
bg.6.16.core_teaching: Inner discipline does not grow from extremes: overindulgence and harsh deprivation in food and sleep both block it; the body needs to be kept in measured health.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: No yoga for one who eats beyond his measure or not at all; he cites scripture that the right amount sustains, excess harms, too little fails. Or the yoga-texts' measure: half the stomach food, a quarter water, a quarter air.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Overeating and fasting, too much and too little recreation, too much sleep and too much waking, overexertion and no exertion: all of these obstruct yoga.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: States the rules of diet for the practitioner over two verses: samadhi does not arise for one who eats far too much or nothing at all, nor for one given to oversleeping or excessive waking.

bg.6.16.practical_reading: Modern teachers read it as the Gita's case for balance: sleep, food and rest are part of spiritual practice, and crash diets, all-nighters or bingeing undermine a steady mind.
misreadings: Not a diet plan or a call to restrict food; it rejects both excess and deprivation.
Not a judgement on people whose sleep is disrupted by things outside their control (new parents, shift workers, illness).
cautions: Food and fasting language can be sensitive for readers with eating disorders; keep the emphasis on moderation and self-care, not on control.
Sivananda's gloss (fill half the stomach) is traditional advice, not medical guidance.
not_for: someone with an active eating disorder, unless framed carefully around nourishment
an exhausted new parent or carer who cannot choose their sleep
speaks_to: burnout from overwork and too little sleep
swinging between indulgence and strict regimes
someone who thinks spiritual seriousness means severe austerity

bg.6.17.context: Krishna has just described the seat, posture and gaze for meditation (6.10-15) and warned that yoga is not for one who eats or sleeps too much or too little (6.16). This verse states the positive rule; the next verse (6.18) says when a meditator is called settled: when the mind rests in the self, free of craving.
bg.6.17.core_teaching: The meditation that ends sorrow rests on an ordinary, measured life: eating, moving, working and sleeping in the right amount and at the right time, with neither indulgence nor self-punishing austerity.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Moderation means food and recreation, such as walking, kept within set limits, and sleep and waking at fixed hours. For such a person yoga ends the misery of worldly existence.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Lists both extremes as harmful to meditation: overeating and fasting, overwork and idleness, too much sleep and too little. For the measured person meditation removes every affliction, which he reads as loosening all bondage.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Reads it as the answer to who attains yoga: one who is restrained in food, movement, work, sleep and waking reaches the yoga that destroys misery.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Urges the middle way for the yoga student. Austerity is a means, not the goal, and becomes harmful when it turns into self-torture; he cites the Buddha's early extreme fasting as what fails.

bg.6.17.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a rhythm check: steady habits of sleep, food, work and rest are part of inner practice, and both burnout and harsh self-denial undermine a calm mind.
misreadings: Not a diet rule or a call to strict food control.
Not an endorsement of extreme discipline; the point is balance, and the classical readers explicitly reject self-torture.
'Yoga' here is meditative discipline, not an exercise routine.
cautions: Food and 'moderation' framing can be triggering for readers with disordered eating; keep the emphasis on rest and rhythm, not restriction.
For an exhausted reader, avoid implying their sorrow comes from their own lack of moderation.
not_for: readers struggling with eating disorders
caregivers or shift workers whose exhaustion is imposed by circumstance, if framed as personal failing
fresh grief, where 'balance ends sorrow' would feel glib
speaks_to: stress with irregular sleep and meals
wanting a calmer mind through daily habits

bg.6.19.context: Krishna has just said a meditator is 'settled' when the restrained mind rests in the self alone and craves nothing (6.18). He now gives the image of a lamp in a windless place. The following verses (6.20-23) describe the joy beyond the senses found in that stillness, which even heavy sorrow cannot shake.
bg.6.19.core_teaching: A mind gathered in meditation is like a flame sheltered from wind: steady and still, yet still shining. Stillness here is clarity, not blankness.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Those who know the ways of the mind gave this simile: through practice the yogi's mind becomes one-pointed, like a lamp sheltered from the wind.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: The steady flame illustrates the self itself: when every outward distraction is shut out, the self shines steady and bright in its own light of awareness for the meditator.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Gives this as the picture of a mind absorbed in the self: the controlled yogi's mind stays steady and bright like a flame out of the wind.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Calls it a favourite simile among yogis for concentration; a steady mind works like a searchlight for finding the hidden treasures of the self.

bg.6.19.practical_reading: Teachers use the image for attention that is quiet but awake: you do not fight the flame, you shelter it from the winds of craving and distraction, and its light steadies by itself.
misreadings: Not 'a good mind has no thoughts'; it describes the fruit of practice, not a test you must pass today.
Not emotional numbness; the commentators stress that the flame keeps shining.
The 'windless place' implies creating shelter and conditions, not forcing the mind still.
cautions: An overthinking reader may feel like a failure because their mind flickers; pair it with 6.26 and 6.35, where wandering and returning are expected.
not_for: someone in acute panic, if presented as a standard they must reach now
someone whose restlessness is from trauma, if 'just be still' is implied
speaks_to: wanting an image of calm to hold onto
starting or deepening a meditation habit

bg.6.20.context: Krishna has just given the image of a lamp in a windless place (6.19). Verses 20 to 23 form one sentence defining yoga by its experience: the stilled mind, seeing the self and content in it (6.20), a joy beyond the senses (6.21), a gain beyond all gains that sorrow cannot shake (6.22), and so the disconnection from sorrow (6.23).
bg.6.20.core_teaching: Through steady practice the restless mind comes to rest, and in that stillness a person sees their own self and finds a contentment that needs nothing from outside.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: When the mind, held back from all wandering by practice, comes to rest, and when one perceives the Self, supreme consciousness and light, through an inner instrument purified by concentration, one is content in that Self alone.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The mind restrained by practice delights in yoga, recognising it as unsurpassed happiness; seeing the self with the mind, one is content in the self without needing anything else.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Here 'yoga' means samadhi, and these verses define it by its nature and its fruit: the mind's activity stilled (he cites Patanjali's definition of yoga) and contentment in the self rather than in objects. The clauses complete in 6.23.

bg.6.20.practical_reading: Teachers use it to describe what meditation is for: not a blank mind, but the quiet in which you stop needing the world to entertain or reassure you.
misreadings: Not a promise that a short session will bring this state; the commentators tie it to sustained practice.
Not a rejection of relationships or the world; contentment within is the point.
not_for: someone in acute distress who may feel judged for not being able to quiet their mind
speaks_to: someone curious about meditation and what it leads to
restlessness and constant need for stimulation
someone who has glimpsed calm and wants to understand it

bg.6.22.context: Within the definition of yoga in 6.20-23, this verse names two marks of the state: once gained, no other gain seems greater, and established in it one is not moved even by heavy sorrow. 6.23 concludes: know this disconnection from sorrow as yoga, and practise it with an undejected mind.
bg.6.22.core_teaching: The settled state of yoga is a gain that outranks every other, and a person grounded in it is not thrown off balance even by great suffering.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Having gained the Self, one does not think any other gain greater; established in the truth of the Self, one is not moved even by great pain, such as being struck by a weapon.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Explains the steadiness: the joy of the self is unsurpassed, so no other gain is thought higher; settled in it, one is not overwhelmed even by heavy hardship like heat and cold.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Self-realisation fulfils all desires, so no gain is higher. Pain and sorrow are felt while identified with body and mind; one rooted in the sorrowless Self is not shaken even by heavy sorrow.

bg.6.22.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to finding an inner anchor that holds when life is hard: it does not stop sorrow from coming, but it can stop sorrow from overturning you.
misreadings: Not a claim that a spiritual person feels no grief or pain.
Not a measure to judge whether someone's practice is 'real' by how much they suffer.
cautions: Ramanuja's own example is the loss of a virtuous son: do not use this verse to tell a bereaved parent they should not be shaken.
For fresh grief, 'not shaken even by heavy sorrow' can read as a rebuke; frame it as a ground to return to later, not a test today.
not_for: fresh bereavement, especially of a child
someone in acute crisis or trauma
speaks_to: someone looking for an inner anchor before or during hard times
a person who has found that achievements didn't satisfy
someone who wants a steadiness that does not depend on circumstances

bg.6.23.context: Verses 6.20-22 describe the stilled mind seeing the self, a joy beyond the senses, and a state where even heavy sorrow does not shake one. Here Krishna names that state 'yoga' and urges practice with resolve; the method follows in 6.24-26 (drop desires, withdraw gradually, bring the wandering mind back).
bg.6.23.core_teaching: Yoga is redefined as unhooking from sorrow, and it is to be practised with conviction and without losing heart, even when progress is slow.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Calls severing contact with pain 'yoga' (union) with a touch of irony. The verse then stresses again that the practice needs firm resolve and a heart that does not sink.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Gathers 6.20-23: meditation is the state in which the mind rests content in the self and is not shaken even by grave losses such as a son's death. One should enter it with conviction and a contented, unworried mind.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: After the benefits in 6.20-22, the Lord asks for firm conviction and a heart that does not lose courage. A wavering seeker gives up at the first obstacle; one should be bold, cheerful and self-reliant.

bg.6.23.practical_reading: Teachers read it as permission to keep going when practice feels slow: the goal is loosening sorrow's grip, and the only requirement named is not giving up heart.
misreadings: Not a promise that sorrow will never touch you; it describes loosening its hold through practice.
Not 'if you still suffer, you lack resolve'.
cautions: For a reader losing hope, 'with determination' could sound like a demand; lean on the gradualness the commentators stress at 6.25 (Sridhara: by degrees, 'not all on a sudden').
Do not present meditation as a substitute for help when despair is severe.
not_for: clinical depression framed as a willpower problem
very fresh loss, where 'unhook from sorrow' may feel dismissive
speaks_to: losing heart in a practice or recovery

bg.6.25.context: Krishna has said to drop desires born of imagination and restrain the senses with the mind (6.24). This verse says the withdrawal should be gradual; the next (6.26) adds what to do when the restless mind wanders off.
bg.6.25.core_teaching: Calm comes gradually: with patient, steady understanding one lets the mind settle in the self and stops feeding other thoughts.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: The mind is to rest in the self, held there by a firm intellect, with the conviction that the self is all. He calls this the highest form of yoga.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Distinguishes mind-born desires, which can be dropped by ceasing to dwell on them, from bodily sensations like heat and cold, which can only be borne with indifference. The mind is drawn back slowly, by steady will.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Withdrawal should come through gradual practice, not all at once. When the latent impressions of the past unsettle the mind, steady it by concentration; in the end even the act of meditating falls away.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Calm comes by degrees through long, steady practice. When the mind keeps turning toward the self, it naturally stops chasing sense pleasures.

bg.6.25.practical_reading: Teachers stress the 'little by little': settling the mind is trained gradually, and patience with yourself is part of the method rather than a lack of it.
misreadings: Not 'suppress all thoughts by force'; the classical readers insist on gradual, unforced withdrawal.
Not instant emptiness; 'thinking of nothing' is the end of a process.
cautions: Readers with anxiety may hear 'think of nothing' as an impossible demand; foreground the gradualness.
not_for: someone who needs to process a pressing problem rather than set it aside
intrusive thoughts from trauma or OCD presented as something to simply stop

bg.6.26.context: After saying to withdraw gradually and settle the mind in the self (6.25), Krishna gives the practical rule for when it strays. The next verses (6.27-28) describe the deep peace and joy that come to the yogi whose mind is calmed this way.
bg.6.26.core_teaching: Wandering is the mind's nature; the practice is simply to notice where it has gone and bring it back, every time.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Sense objects pull the mind away by its natural weakness. Seeing their fleeting nature and cultivating detachment lets one bring the mind back to rest in the self.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Wherever the fickle mind runs after what it likes, effort should pull it back and settle it in the self, persuading it that true happiness lies there.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Even after the mind is controlled, restlessness can make it stray again. Then draw it back from that very object and steady it in the self.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Likens the mind to a bull that keeps running off and must be led home again and again. Give it a taste of the self's joy, and over time it stops wandering.

bg.6.26.practical_reading: Teachers make this the core of everyday meditation: the return, not the wandering, is the practice. Each time you notice and come back counts as success.
misreadings: Not 'a wandering mind means you are bad at this'; the verse assumes it will wander.
Not harsh self-policing; the commentators pair restraint with making the self more attractive than the distraction.
cautions: In the someone-left plan the 'wandering' is likely to the person who left; avoid implying that thinking of them is a failure.
not_for: presenting grief-thoughts as distractions to be suppressed
someone needing to deal with an urgent real problem their mind keeps returning to

bg.6.27.context: Krishna has just told the meditator to bring the wandering mind back to the self wherever it strays (6.26). This verse names what follows: the highest happiness comes to the yogi whose mind is calm and whose restlessness (rajas) has settled. 6.28 repeats that such a yogi easily touches the boundless joy of contact with Brahman.
bg.6.27.core_teaching: When repeated practice settles the mind's restless energy, a happiness higher than any other comes on its own.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Unsurpassed bliss comes to the yogi of deeply calm mind, whose afflictions such as delusion have waned, who has become Brahman (liberated while living, sure that all is Brahman) and is beyond merit and demerit.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The mind fixed unwaveringly on the self burns away every impurity, so rajas is destroyed and the yogi abides in his own true nature; the highest happiness he reaches is the experience of the self.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: By repeatedly mastering the mind through withdrawal and the like, when rajas wanes the yogi, calm and untainted, reaches the joy of samadhi of its own accord.

bg.6.27.practical_reading: Teachers draw from it that happiness is less something you chase than something that arrives when agitation settles.
misreadings: Not 'calm people are better people'; it describes the fruit of practice.
Not a promise of constant bliss.
