not_for: someone in depression who may feel blamed for not being calm or happy
speaks_to: a meditator wondering if practice leads anywhere

bg.6.29.context: Toward the end of the meditation teaching, Krishna describes the vision it opens: the yogi sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self. 6.30 adds the devotional side (whoever sees me everywhere is never lost to me), and 6.32 turns it into ethics: feeling others' joy and pain as one's own.
bg.6.29.core_teaching: Deep meditation removes the sense of separation: one sees the same essential reality in every being, though traditions explain that sameness differently.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The yogi sees all beings, from the creator Brahma to a clump of grass, as one with the Self, and sees the same in all of them: that is, he knows the Self and Brahman to be one.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Freed from matter, every self has the same form, pure knowledge; inequality belongs to matter. So the yogi sees his self as like all beings and all as like himself: seeing one self, all are seen through their similarity.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: This is direct realisation of Brahman: with a concentrated mind one sees the self, free of body-limits, present in all beings, and all beings in the self without difference.

bg.6.29.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to empathy and belonging: seeing yourself in others softens judgement and loneliness, and grounds compassion (as 6.32 makes explicit).
misreadings: Not 'everyone is the same so differences and boundaries don't matter'.
Not a single doctrine: Shankara and Sridhara read identity with Brahman, Ramanuja the likeness of all selves.
not_for: someone who needs to separate from a harmful person and may hear 'see yourself in them' as a call to merge or stay
speaks_to: loneliness and feeling separate from others
someone wanting to grow in empathy
a person drawn to the unity at the heart of many spiritual traditions

bg.6.30.context: Krishna has described the yogi who sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self (6.29). Here he restates it in the first person: whoever sees 'me' everywhere is never out of my sight. Next (6.31-32) he praises one who worships him as present in all beings and who feels others' joy and pain as his own.
bg.6.30.core_teaching: One who sees the divine in everything and everything resting in the divine is never separated from it, and the divine never loses sight of that person.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: One who sees the Lord, the Self of all, in every being, and all beings in him, has realised the unity of the Self. Lord and sage never leave each other, since their self is one.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'Me' through the likeness of the pure self to the Lord. One who sees that likeness in all selves is one the Lord never hides from; the Lord holds him as his own and always shows himself to him.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Seeing the Lord in every being is the chief means to self-realisation. The Lord never loses sight of such a person and shows himself to him with grace.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Describes the vision of oneness: the Lord dwells in the sage and the sage in the Lord, and neither ever lets go of the other.

bg.6.30.practical_reading: Teachers use it to widen attention: noticing the sacred in people, nature and ordinary moments becomes a way of never being wholly alone.
misreadings: Not 'if you feel alone, you have failed to see God'.

Readings differ on who 'me' is: Shankara and Sivananda read it as the one Self of all; Ramanuja reads it through the likeness of every pure self to the Lord; Sridhara as the Lord seen in every being. All are traditional.
cautions: Used on loneliness Day 1 ('see'): it offers presence, but avoid suggesting spiritual vision replaces human connection.
not_for: a reader who is not religious, if pressed as a doctrinal claim
someone isolated who needs practical human contact first
speaks_to: longing for a sense of being held
spiritual connection in nature or people

bg.6.32.context: Krishna has spoken of the yogi who sees the divine in all beings (6.29-31). Here he names the highest yogi as one who measures others' joy and pain by his own. Immediately after (6.33-34) Arjuna objects that such evenness seems impossible because the mind is so restless.
bg.6.32.core_teaching: The highest yogi treats every being's joy and pain as he would his own, and so harms no one and wishes all well.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Seeing that what pleases or pains oneself pleases or pains every creature, such a person harms no one. Harmless and devoted to right knowledge, he is the highest yogi.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The best yogi feels that others find pleasure and pain just as he does, so he wishes only good for every being and harm to none.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Such a person harms no one and wishes all well, out of a large and gentle heart. This rests on knowing the one Self in all.

bg.6.32.practical_reading: Teachers apply it as everyday empathy and non-harm: before acting or speaking, ask how this would feel if it were done to you, and let that shape what you do.
misreadings: Not 'take on everyone's pain until you are depleted'.
Ramanuja's reading is about equanimity, not emotional fusion; the empathy reading (Shankara, Sridhara) is the basis for our line.
cautions: Ramanuja's example (a son's death seen with the same detachment as another's) would be jarring for a grieving reader; do not use that reading in grief contexts.
not_for: people-pleasers or caregivers already over-absorbing others' pain, if read as a call to carry more
someone being harmed, if read as 'feel for your abuser'

bg.6.33.context: Krishna has just completed his teaching on meditation and equal vision (6.29-32). Arjuna answers frankly that he cannot see this evenness lasting, because the mind is restless; in 6.34 he compares the mind to the wind. Krishna agrees (6.35) and says it can be held through practice and dispassion.
bg.6.33.core_teaching: Arjuna voices the honest objection every practitioner feels: the ideal of an even mind seems impossible to sustain when the mind keeps moving.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Arjuna says that for the yoga of evenness Krishna has taught, he cannot perceive any steady, unwavering continuance, because the mind is fickle.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The yoga taught is seeing all selves as equal, alike in consciousness and, when freed, alike to the Lord, against our constant experience of difference (gods, humans, soul and God). Arjuna cannot grasp how it could stay steady.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Thinking it impossible, Arjuna says: evenness, the mind free of dullness and distraction and resting as the self alone, cannot be held for long, because the mind is restless.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Arjuna finds this yoga hard to practise: his mind is restless and unsteady and wanders in the blink of an eye, so he cannot keep steady concentration.

bg.6.33.practical_reading: Teachers use it to reassure beginners: even Arjuna said 'my mind won't stay still', and the Gita answers with patience and practice, not scolding.
misreadings: Not proof that meditation is impossible; Krishna's answer comes in 6.35.
Not a confession of weakness to be ashamed of.
cautions: Shown alone, it ends on doubt; pair with 6.35 (practice and dispassion) when used in a plan.
not_for: a reader who needs reassurance today and would get only the question without the answer (show with 6.35)
speaks_to: a meditation beginner who feels like a failure
someone who finds spiritual ideals unrealistic

bg.6.34.context: Krishna has just described the highest yogi as one who sees all beings' joy and pain as his own (6.32). Arjuna objects (6.33-34) that such steady evenness cannot last, because the mind is too restless. Krishna's answer follows at once (6.35): practice and dispassion.
bg.6.34.core_teaching: Arjuna honestly names how hard the mind is to steady: it is restless, agitating, strong and obstinate, as hard to hold as the wind. The Gita takes this complaint seriously and answers it.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: The mind is not only fickle but stormy: it shakes the body and senses and hands them over to outside influences. It cannot be cut through, and restraining it is harder even than holding back the wind.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Arjuna cannot grasp seeing all selves as equal, since experience shows difference everywhere. If the mind will not stay put on everyday things, holding it on the self is harder still; he asks for a method.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Glosses each word: fickle by nature, able to agitate body and senses, too strong even for discrimination, and bound by attachment. Holding it is as impossible as shutting the wind in a pot.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The mind keeps changing its objects and is pulled outward by the five senses, which makes it restless. He adds a traditional link: the mind arises from the subtle element of air, hence its wind-like nature.

bg.6.34.practical_reading: Teachers find comfort in the fact that the Gita's hero says this out loud: struggling with a restless mind is normal and worth naming honestly, and it is the starting point for practice rather than proof you cannot do it.
misreadings: Not the Gita's verdict that the mind cannot be trained; it is Arjuna's objection, which Krishna answers in 6.35.
Should not be used alone as a closing thought; pair with 6.35.
cautions: As Day 1 'see' it validates the struggle well, but the reading should signal that an answer comes, so it does not end in helplessness.
not_for: as a final word without the answer that follows
someone who already feels hopeless, if not paired with 6.35
speaks_to: feeling at the mercy of one's thoughts

bg.6.35.context: Arjuna has said the mind is as hard to hold as the wind (6.34). Krishna agrees without argument, then gives the two means: practice and dispassion. He adds (6.36) that yoga is hard for the uncontrolled but reachable for one who strives by the right means.
bg.6.35.core_teaching: Krishna grants that the mind is restless and hard to control, but says it can be trained by steady practice and by loosening its cravings.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Accepts that the roving mind is hard to subdue, but says it is governable through steady effort and dispassion; his note links the pair to Patanjali's Yoga Sutra 1.12.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Krishna grants Arjuna's point, then names the means. Practice means repeatedly turning the mind toward the self and away from sense objects; dispassion means loosening attachment to them. Together they bring the mind to rest in the supreme Self.

bg.6.35.practical_reading: Teachers read it as a two-handed method: build a small daily habit of returning attention (practice), and gently loosen what keeps pulling you away (letting go). Progress is by repetition, not a single breakthrough.
misreadings: Not 'just try harder'; it names a method, not willpower.
Vairāgya is not coldness toward people; the commentators mean losing the craving for sense pleasures.
cautions: Sivananda's and Shankara's 'seeing the defects' in pleasures can sound world-denying; for modern readers, frame dispassion as loosening grip, not disgust.
not_for: clinical anxiety or OCD presented as solvable by practice alone
someone who needs to feel and process emotion rather than detach from it
speaks_to: building a meditation or focus habit

bg.6.36.context: Krishna has just said the mind is caught by practice and dispassion (6.35). Here he adds his own judgement: yoga is hard for the undisciplined, but within reach for one who strives by the right means. This prompts Arjuna's next question (6.37): what happens to someone who starts with faith but falls short?
bg.6.36.core_teaching: Yoga is hard without discipline, but anyone who keeps trying with the right method can reach it.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: An uncontrolled self is a mind not trained by practice and detachment. One who has mastered the mind and keeps striving can reach yoga by the proper means.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: The mind is tamed by growing love for the self, through dwelling on its excellence, and distaste for other things by seeing their flaws. Such control comes through karma yoga done as worship of the Lord.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Without the practice and dispassion just described, yoga is out of reach. With the mind brought under control by them, and continued effort through the same means, it can be attained.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Self-control here means the mind trained through constant dispassion and meditation. With the right means and steady effort, self-realisation becomes possible.

bg.6.36.practical_reading: Teachers use it as realistic encouragement: the goal is not reserved for the naturally calm, but for anyone who keeps practising with a sound method.
misreadings: Not 'only the already-disciplined can succeed'; the second half is the point: striving by the right means makes it possible.
Not a moral judgement on people who struggle.
cautions: The first half ('hard for the uncontrolled') could sting someone starting over after a setback; lead with the second half.
not_for: someone already self-critical about lack of discipline, if the first half is stressed

bg.6.37.context: Krishna has said yoga is reachable by one who strives (6.36). Arjuna asks about the person who began with faith but whose effort was weak and whose mind fell away before the goal; he goes on (6.38-39) to fear such a person is lost like a torn cloud, with neither world. Krishna's reassurance begins at 6.40.
bg.6.37.core_teaching: Arjuna voices the fear of every sincere beginner: if I start with faith but my effort fails before the end, is it all wasted?

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Arjuna asks about someone who believes in yoga but does not strive, and whose mind slips away from it at the moment of death. Having left worldly works and not yet won knowledge, does he come to nothing?

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Arjuna asks the fate of one who is earnest yet, for lack of steady application, lets his mind slide from yoga and so never reaches its perfection.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Describes the person as sincere at the start, with real faith and no pretence, who then grows slack in practice and lukewarm in dispassion. His mind drifts to sense objects and he falls short of knowledge.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Pictures someone with faith in yoga who cannot yet master the senses. Their mind wanders at the last breath, and they die without reaching self-knowledge; Arjuna asks what becomes of such a person.

bg.6.37.practical_reading: Teachers use Arjuna's question to normalise the fear of failing at something you care about: the question is legitimate, and the Gita answers it with reassurance (6.40).
misreadings: Not a statement that slipping means ruin; it is a question, and the answer is 'no'.
Should not be used without the answer in 6.40.
cautions: The classical frame is death and what follows it; keep the reading on everyday effort unless the plan intends afterlife themes.
not_for: readers near end of life or grieving, where 'what end does he come to' may evoke death
as a standalone without the reassurance
speaks_to: procrastination from fear of wasted effort
having slipped in a practice or resolution

bg.6.38.context: Having heard that the restless mind can be trained (6.35-36), Arjuna asks what happens to someone who has faith but lacks discipline and falls away before reaching the goal (6.37). This verse is his fear in an image: a torn cloud, cut off from both worlds, dissolving. He asks Krishna to resolve the doubt (6.39), and Krishna replies that no one who does good comes to ruin (6.40).
bg.6.38.core_teaching: Arjuna gives voice to the fear that half-hearted or failed spiritual effort leaves a person worse off than never trying: cut off from ordinary rewards and short of the goal.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Arjuna asks whether one who has slipped from both the path of works and the path of yoga, supportless and confused on the way to Brahman, is destroyed like a torn cloud, or not.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Like a cloud fragment that breaks from a large cloud and vanishes before reaching another: his works, done without desire for fruit, will not win heaven, and he has strayed from the path to Brahman, so does he perish?

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Having offered his actions to God he gets no heavenly reward, and with yoga unfinished he gets no liberation: fallen from both, he may dissolve midway like a cloud that has left one and not reached another.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: This yoga demands one-pointed devotion; the aspirant turns from the world and even from heaven, so some held that if he failed he would lose everything. Hence Arjuna's question.

bg.6.38.practical_reading: Teachers use it for the fear of 'falling between two stools': having given up the old life for a new path (or a career change, or recovery) and fearing that slipping means losing everything.
misreadings: Not the Gita's verdict; it is Arjuna's fear, which Krishna rejects in 6.40.
Not a warning against trying something new.
cautions: Shown alone it leaves the reader with fear; pair with 6.40 ('no one who does good comes to ruin').
The 'path to Brahman' assumes a spiritual frame and, in the answer, rebirth.
not_for: someone already despairing, unless shown with Krishna's answer
a reader who needs a quick reassurance and will see only the question
speaks_to: fear of having wasted years on a path that didn't 'work'
someone who relapsed or fell short after real effort
a person between two lives, no longer at home in either

bg.6.39.context: Arjuna has just asked whether someone who falls away from yoga perishes like a torn cloud (6.37-38). Here he asks Krishna to cut that doubt completely, saying no one else can. Krishna's answer begins in 6.40: neither in this world nor the next is such a person lost.
bg.6.39.core_teaching: Arjuna turns his deepest worry over to the one teacher he trusts can answer it fully, rather than leaving it half-resolved.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Arjuna asks Krishna to remove this doubt entirely, since no other, whether sage or god, can destroy it; so Krishna alone should cut it.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: No one other than Krishna, who by his own nature sees everything directly, all at once and always, can cut this doubt.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: The doubt must be removed by Krishna, the all-knowing; there is no other who can dispel it.

bg.6.39.practical_reading: Teachers use it to model bringing a real fear to the right person (teacher, mentor, God) instead of carrying it alone or settling for a half-answer.
misreadings: Not a claim that no human help is worth seeking.
Not an endorsement of total dependence on a single guru.
cautions: Shown alone it is a plea without an answer; pair with 6.40.
not_for: someone isolated who may read 'no one but you' as 'no human can help me'
speaks_to: someone with a doubt that keeps returning
a person who needs to ask for help directly
someone whose faith is shaken after falling short

bg.6.40.context: Arjuna has asked whether one who falls short in yoga is lost in both worlds like a torn cloud (6.37-39). Krishna answers that such a person is never destroyed; the following verses (6.41-45) say he is reborn in a pure or wise family, regains his earlier understanding and strives again, so no effort is lost.
bg.6.40.core_teaching: Sincere effort toward the good is never wasted: one who falls short is not ruined in this life or after, and the effort carries forward.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Explains 'tāta' as son: a father lives on in his son, and a disciple counts as a son. One who fails in yoga will not fall to a lower birth, here or hereafter.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Whoever sincerely takes up this yoga and falls away loses nothing, either the enjoyments of heaven or the spiritual goal. Even a little of such practice is never wasted.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: No loss of standing here and no hell hereafter: he has taken up yoga with faith, so he is a doer of good. 'My child' is an affectionate address in ordinary speech.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The one who falls short in this life is not destroyed and will not take a lower birth; verses 41-44 describe what follows. 'Tāta' means son, since a disciple is regarded as one.

bg.6.40.practical_reading: Teachers use it as one of the Gita's most hopeful lines: no honest effort toward good is wasted, even if you fall short, and you can pick up where you left off.
misreadings: Not a promise of worldly success or protection from hardship.
Not 'effort does not matter'; the reassurance is for one who sincerely began.
cautions: The surrounding passage relies on rebirth; for a reader in grief or fearing death, keep to 'nothing good is lost' rather than afterlife detail.
not_for: someone grieving a death, if pressed as a claim about the departed's fate
someone avoiding responsibility for harm, if read as blanket absolution
speaks_to: fear that past effort was wasted

bg.6.43.context: Answering Arjuna's fear, Krishna says that one who falls from yoga is never lost (6.40): after a stay in good worlds they are born into a pure and prosperous home, or into a family of wise yogis (6.41-42). This verse says that there they regain the understanding of their former life and strive harder for perfection; 6.44 adds that the old practice carries them on.
bg.6.43.core_teaching: Spiritual progress is not wiped out by failure or death: the understanding gained is recovered and becomes the starting point for even greater effort.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Born in a family of yogis, he regains contact with the understanding he had in the previous body, and from the impressions formed earlier strives even harder for perfection.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: In that birth he regains the same yoga-directed understanding from his former body, and like someone waking from sleep strives again for perfection, so that obstacles do not stop him.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: In either kind of birth (a prosperous home or a family of yogis) he regains the understanding directed to Brahman from his former body and makes still greater effort toward liberation.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Past efforts in yoga are not wasted; impressions (samskaras) of thought and practice are stored and revived in the next birth, driving the aspirant to strive with more vigour.

bg.6.43.practical_reading: Teachers apply it, by extension, to any return after a lapse: what you learned and practised before resurfaces quickly when you begin again.
misreadings: Not a promise that nothing needs to be done again; it says one strives more.
The verse itself is about a later birth, not only about relapse within one life.
cautions: Rests on rebirth; a writer should not slip this into a grief context as 'you'll meet again' or 'it continues in the next life' without care.
not_for: fresh grief, where talk of the next birth may feel dismissive
someone who rejects rebirth and would find the frame alienating unless it is named as an application
speaks_to: someone returning to a practice (prayer, music, study, sobriety) after a long gap
fear that a setback erased all progress
late starters who feel they are beginning from zero

bg.6.44.context: Continuing his reassurance about the one who falls from yoga (6.40-45), Krishna explains why they strive again (6.43): the momentum of former practice pulls them on even against their will. Even someone who merely wants to know yoga goes beyond the rewards of ritual. 6.45 completes the arc: persistent striving, over many births, reaches the goal.
bg.6.44.core_teaching: Practice builds a momentum that outlasts lapses and even rebirth; sincere interest alone already lifts a person beyond merely ritual religion.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Past practice carries him along even unwillingly. Stronger wrongdoing may overpower it for a while, but once that is spent it resumes; it is never destroyed. Even one who only wishes to know yoga transcends Vedic ritual's fruits.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Even a mere inquirer into yoga resumes the inquiry from a past life, comes back to karma-yoga, and finally transcends 'word-Brahman', the nameable material world, reaching the self whose nature is knowledge and bliss.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Even if some obstacle makes him unwilling, past practice turns him from sense objects and sets him in Brahman. If even a mere inquirer who slipped goes beyond the Veda's ritual fruits, how much more the one who practises.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The force of past yogic impressions carries him toward the goal even unconsciously or unwillingly; a strong evil karma may suppress them for a time, but they resume.

bg.6.44.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to habits and practice: days when you show up without wanting to still count, because built-up practice carries you when motivation fails.
misreadings: Not 'you'll get there whether you try or not'; 6.45 stresses diligent striving.
Not a dismissal of ritual worship in general; it ranks a seeker's inner inquiry above ritual done for rewards.
cautions: The 'former practice' is from a previous life in the verse's own frame; modern applications to this life are extensions.
not_for: someone who feels trapped by compulsive habits, for whom 'carried along against your will' may sound fatalistic
speaks_to: someone whose motivation has dropped but who keeps showing up
a returning practitioner after a break
a curious beginner who wonders if mere interest counts

bg.6.45.context: This verse closes Krishna's answer to the fear of falling from yoga (6.37-45): the yogi who strives with diligence, cleansed over many births, finally reaches the highest goal. Krishna then concludes the chapter by ranking the yogi above ascetics, scholars and ritualists (6.46-47).
bg.6.45.core_teaching: Final attainment comes through sustained, earnest effort that accumulates over a very long time (many lives); no sincere effort is wasted.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Striving ever harder, the purified yogi gathers a little impression in each of many births; perfected by that accumulation, he gains right vision and then reaches the highest goal.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Cleansed by merit gathered over many births, the earnestly striving yogi, even one who once wavered, certainly reaches the highest goal.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: If even a slack yogi reaches the highest goal, then surely one who strives more and more, purified by yoga and perfected over many births into right knowledge, does.

bg.6.45.practical_reading: Teachers use it to counter impatience: real change is slow and cumulative, and steady effort, not a single breakthrough, gets you there.
misreadings: Not 'it will take lifetimes, so why bother now'; every effort counts toward it.
Not a claim that suffering is deserved for past 'sins'.
cautions: Rests on rebirth and the language of 'sin' cleansed; handle carefully for readers who reject rebirth or carry guilt.
not_for: someone wanting quick relief, who may hear 'many births' as hopeless
a reader carrying heavy guilt, for whom 'cleansed of sin' may sting
speaks_to: someone discouraged by how far they still have to go
long-haul efforts: recovery, healing, mastering a craft

bg.6.5.context: Krishna opens chapter 6 by saying the true renouncer is one who does their duty without depending on its fruit (6.1). For one climbing to yoga, action is the means; for one who has arrived, calm is (6.3–4). This verse says the climb is one's own to make. The next explains: the self is a friend to one who has mastered it, and acts like an enemy to one who hasn't (6.6).
bg.6.5.core_teaching: Lift yourself up by your own effort and don't drag yourself down. Depending on how you treat yourself, you are your own best friend or your own worst enemy.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Here 'by the self' means by the mind. A mind detached from sense-pleasures lifts the self to higher things; turned towards objects, it harasses the self. So the mind is the self's friend or foe, depending on its use.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Since attachment binds and non-attachment frees, use your discriminating self to lift yourself out of worldly bondage and never degrade yourself. The self freed from attachment is your benefactor; otherwise it is your enemy.

bg.6.5.practical_reading: Notice how you talk to yourself. Treat yourself as you'd treat a friend who's struggling: encourage the next step instead of piling on, because you can be the one who pulls you up.
misreadings: Not 'you're alone, so don't ask for help' (our misuse note is right). Arjuna himself asks for help.
Not 'it's all your fault'. The verse is about agency, not blame.
cautions: This is a strong caution. Shankara and Sivananda say outward friends are obstacles or 'enemies in reality' for a seeker. The verse is used in the losing-hope and comparison plans, and possibly by lonely readers, so the writer must not pass on that view.
For a reader losing hope, 'raise yourself by yourself' can sound like 'you're on your own'. Pair it with permission to seek support.
not_for: someone in crisis who needs to hear that others can and should help them
a lonely reader, if Shankara's or Sivananda's view of friends is carried over

bg.6.6.context: Krishna has just said (6.5) 'lift yourself by yourself; do not let yourself sink', because the self alone is one's friend and one's enemy. This verse explains when each is true. 6.7 then describes the calm of the self-mastered person in heat and cold, honour and insult.
bg.6.6.core_teaching: The same inner self that can rescue you can also harm you; which it becomes depends on whether you have brought it under your own direction.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The self is friend to the one who has mastered the body-and-senses complex, that is, controlled the senses. For one who has not, his own self harms him just as an outside enemy would.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The mind is friend to whoever has won it back from sense-objects; an unwon mind works against one's own highest good. He cites the Vishnu Purana: the mind alone causes bondage and freedom.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: For one who has subdued the body-and-senses by himself, that self is his own friend; for the unsubdued, the same self harms him like an enemy.

bg.6.6.practical_reading: Teachers use it for self-talk and habits: you can be your own best ally or your own worst critic, and training the mind is how you choose which.
misreadings: Not self-hatred or 'beat yourself into shape'; the aim is to befriend oneself.
Not a claim that people struggling with mental illness simply lack willpower.
cautions: For someone with depression or an anxiety disorder, 'your mind is your enemy if you haven't conquered it' can sound like blame; pair it with 6.5's call to lift yourself and with help from others.
not_for: someone in a mental-health crisis who needs outside help, not a self-mastery message
someone already blaming themselves for everything
speaks_to: someone starting a discipline (exercise, study, sobriety)
a person who wants to rely on themselves

bg.6.7.context: Following 'the self is the friend of the self' (6.6), Krishna describes the self-mastered, calm person: steady in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour. 6.8-9 continue the portrait (a clod and gold alike; even-minded toward friend and foe).
bg.6.7.core_teaching: Once a person has mastered themselves and grown calm, their deepest self stays composed through the opposites of physical comfort, emotional pleasure and pain, and social respect or insult.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: For the self-controlled renunciate whose inner instrument is serene, the supreme Self becomes directly his own self; he should also be the same in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and humiliation.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: For one whose mind is unshaken by heat, cold, pleasure, pain, honour and dishonour, the self is well established in its own nature; 'supreme self' here means the individual self, higher than its earlier states.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Only for the self-mastered, free of attachment and the like, does the self stay settled in itself even when cold and heat come; alternatively, the supreme Self abides in his heart.

bg.6.7.practical_reading: Modern teachers apply it to criticism and praise at work or online: let your worth rest somewhere deeper than the day's reception.
misreadings: Steadiness under insult is not accepting mistreatment; you can stay composed and still object or leave (our existing misuse note is right).
Not endurance of physical harm (cold, heat) as a virtue in itself.
cautions: Someone being humiliated or abused should not hear this as 'just stay calm and take it'.
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship or workplace
someone whose dignity has just been violated and needs validation first
speaks_to: someone whose mood follows how others treat them

bg.6.8.context: Part of Krishna's portrait of the one who has climbed to yoga (yogārūḍha), after 6.7's calm in honour and insult. This verse adds inner contentment through knowledge and direct experience, and an even regard for a clod, a stone and gold. 6.9 extends the evenness to people.
bg.6.8.core_teaching: Someone who has both understood and directly experienced the truth is inwardly satisfied, unshaken and master of the senses, so objects that others value differently no longer pull them.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Jñāna is understanding what scripture teaches; vijñāna is making it one's own experience. Satisfied by both, the person is unshakable and sense-controlled, and is called 'joined in yoga'; earth, stone and gold are alike to him.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Content in knowing the self and its distinctness from matter; firm in the self unchanged through every body; since material things no longer please him, clod, stone and gold are equal. Such a karma-yogi is fit for meditation.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Jñāna is knowledge from teaching, vijñāna direct experience; content with these and wanting nothing, changeless and sense-controlled, he sees nothing among earth, stone and gold as to be grasped or rejected. He has climbed to yoga.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Jñāna is theoretical knowledge from study, vijñāna direct realisation. Kūṭastha means changeless like an anvil: iron is hammered on it, but it stays the same, as the yogi stays unaffected by contact with objects.

bg.6.8.practical_reading: Teachers use it to distinguish book knowledge from lived understanding, and to describe freedom from the pull of possessions and money.
misreadings: Not a reason to neglect money, savings or family finances (our existing misuse note is right); it is about not being ruled by them.
Not anti-intellectual: knowledge is half of what satisfies the yogi.
not_for: someone in financial hardship who may hear 'gold and earth are the same' as indifference to their need
speaks_to: someone caught in comparing possessions or salary
a learner frustrated that knowing something isn't the same as living it

bg.6.9.context: Having described the yogi as even toward clod and gold (6.8), Krishna now extends that evenness to people: well-wishers, friends, enemies, neutrals, relatives, the virtuous and wrongdoers. Such a person excels. 6.10 then begins the practical instructions for meditation.
bg.6.9.core_teaching: The highest yogi meets every kind of person, friend or foe, good or wicked, with the same unclouded judgement, free of attachment and aversion.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Glosses each term, then says equal-minded means not preoccupied with 'who is this, what has he done' toward any of them, the good or the sinful. Such a person is the best of those established in yoga.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Because the self is his only aim, he needs nothing from friends and has no quarrel with foes; this equal regard makes him most fit for the practice of yoga.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: One whose judgement toward all these, from natural well-wisher to wrongdoer, is free of attachment and aversion is superior even to the one just described.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Equal vision means impartiality: making no distinction of caste, creed or colour and loving all as one's own self.

bg.6.9.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to family feuds and office politics: treat people fairly without letting old grudges or favouritism decide your response.
misreadings: Even-minded is not naive: you can be fair to someone and still keep a boundary (our existing misuse note is right).
Not a demand to trust everyone equally or to stop distinguishing right from wrong.
cautions: A reader hurt by a relative or partner may hear 'be the same toward the hateful' as pressure to reconcile or forgive before they're ready.
not_for: someone recently harmed by a specific person
someone being pressured to 'treat everyone the same' as a way of excusing abuse
speaks_to: someone carrying grudges that weigh on them

bg.7.1.context: Chapter 6 ended by saying the best yogi is the one who worships Krishna with faith, his inner self absorbed in him (6.47). Chapter 7 opens by promising to explain how, with mind attached to him and taking refuge in him, Arjuna will know him fully and without doubt. The next verse (7.2) promises knowledge together with realisation, after which nothing remains to be known.
bg.7.1.core_teaching: Full, doubt-free knowledge of the divine comes to someone whose mind is lovingly fixed on God, who leans on God alone and keeps up practice.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Others rely on rites, austerity or gifts for their goals; this yogi, mind intent on the Lord, relies on him alone. So he will know the Lord fully, with all his greatness, strength and power, beyond doubt.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: 'Mind attached to me' means loving so intensely that a moment's lapse in thinking of my qualities and deeds would imperil one's existence; 'relying on me' means having me as sole prop. Hear how such a one knows me fully.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Having taught the self and yoga, the Gita now describes the Lord's form to be worshipped, since 6.47 named his worshipper best: hear how, with no other refuge, you will know me with all my powers, free of doubt.

bg.7.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it as an invitation: knowing God is less an intellectual project than the fruit of a mind that keeps turning toward God and leans on God.
misreadings: Not a demand for blind attachment; commentators pair attachment with practice (yoga) and knowledge.
not_for: a reader alienated by devotional, personal-God language (who might prefer chapter 6's meditative verses)
speaks_to: someone who wants a more personal relationship with God
someone ready to lean on faith after trying to do everything alone

bg.7.11.context: Part of the list in 7.8-11 where Krishna names himself as the essence in things: taste in water, light in sun and moon, sound in space, the life in all beings. This verse names him as strength without craving and as desire that does not go against dharma. 7.12 adds that all states of goodness, passion and dullness come from him, but he is not in them; they are in him.
bg.7.11.core_teaching: Strength and desire are not unspiritual in themselves; when strength is free of greed and desire stays within what is right, the divine is present in them.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Kāma is thirst for things not present, rāga attachment to things present. The Lord is the strength free of both, enough to sustain the body; and the desire scripture allows, such as for food and drink needed to live.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: All these distinctive things arise from the Lord, exist for him and abide in him as his body; so he is present as their inner form.

bg.7.11.practical_reading: Teachers use it to make peace with ambition and desire: wanting things, or being strong, is not a spiritual failing; the question is whether greed drives it and whether it stays within what is right.
misreadings: Not a licence for any desire someone labels 'righteous'.
Not a call to suppress all desire; it explicitly sanctifies right desire.
cautions: Sridhara's example of permitted desire (within marriage, for children) is narrow and traditional; do not present it as the verse's only meaning.
not_for: someone using spiritual language to justify a harmful desire
speaks_to: someone ashamed of ambition, desire or physical strength
athletes and people who rely on their strength
someone trying to tell healthy wanting from compulsive wanting

bg.7.14.context: Krishna has said that the whole world, deluded by states made of the three qualities, does not recognise him, who is beyond them (7.13). Here he admits this divine māyā is hard to cross, but those who take refuge in him alone cross it. 7.15 says the wrongdoers and deluded do not turn to him, and 7.16 begins the four kinds of people who do.
bg.7.14.core_teaching: The confusing pull of the world, woven from nature's qualities, is too strong to escape by one's own effort alone; turning to God as one's sole refuge carries one across it.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Daivī means supernatural, wondrous: the Lord's power of the three qualities, hard to cross; yet those who worship him with unswerving devotion cross even this, and then know him.

bg.7.14.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to patterns we cannot break by willpower alone (compulsions, recurring confusion): admitting it is hard is honest, and surrender or seeking refuge is part of the way through.
misreadings: Not fatalism ('it's all illusion, nothing matters').
Not a claim that only one sect's worship works; the point is single-hearted refuge.
cautions: Shankara's 'all is illusion' reading and Ramanuja's 'māyā is real' reading conflict; don't present one as the Gita's only meaning.
not_for: someone who needs practical, professional help and might hear 'just surrender'
a reader with no theistic frame, unless the refuge idea is opened up
speaks_to: feeling stuck in confusion or a cycle you can't break alone
a person learning to surrender or to ask for help

bg.7.16.context: Krishna has just said that the deluded and wrongdoers do not turn to him (7.15). Here he names four kinds of people with good merit who do. He goes on (7.17-18) to say the wise one, ever steady in single devotion, is dearest, though all four are noble.
bg.7.16.core_teaching: People come to the divine by different doors: trouble, curiosity, need, or wisdom. All are counted among the good; the Gita does not shut out those who come because they are hurting or need something.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the distressed as someone in danger from a robber, a tiger or illness; the seeker of knowledge wants to know the Lord's nature; the wise one knows the true nature of Vishnu.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Ranks the four, each above the one before: the distressed want lost fortune back, the wealth-seeker wants new fortune, the seeker wants the self freed from matter. The wise one knows the self belongs to the Lord.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Gives examples of each kind: Draupadi and the elephant Gajendra in distress, Janaka and Uddhava as seekers, Dhruva and others seeking gain, Shuka as the wise. Whatever the motive, devotion purifies it in time.

bg.7.16.practical_reading: Teachers use it to welcome beginners: it is fine to come to spiritual life because you are in pain, curious, or in need. Motives can deepen over time.
misreadings: Not a ranking that shames the distressed or needy; 7.18 calls all four noble.
Not a claim that God rewards only people of merit in a transactional way.
cautions: Sridhara's remark that only those with past merit turn to God could feel exclusionary; avoid it with a newcomer.
not_for: contexts that would rank people's worth by motive
speaks_to: coming to the Gita in a crisis
wondering if one's motives are 'pure enough'

bg.7.18.context: Krishna has named four kinds of people who turn to him: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of gain, and the wise (7.16), and said the wise one, ever devoted, is especially dear (7.17). Here he says all four are noble, but the wise one he holds as his very self. 7.19 adds that such a person, who sees 'Vasudeva is all', is rare and comes after many births.
bg.7.18.core_teaching: Whatever brings people to God, need, curiosity or longing, is honoured as noble; but the one who knows God and wants nothing but God is closest of all, as God's own self.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: All are noble; no devotee is not dear. But the wise one is the Lord's very Self, not different, firm in the conviction that he himself is Vasudeva, and seeks the Lord alone as the highest goal.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: All are 'generous' because whoever accepts anything from the Lord gives him everything. The wise one cannot sustain himself without the Lord; so the Lord says he cannot sustain himself without that devotee, who is therefore his own self.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Do the other three stay bound? No: all are noble and will be liberated. But the wise one is the Lord's very self, since, mind fixed on him alone, he takes him as highest goal and wants no other result.

bg.7.18.practical_reading: Teachers draw comfort from the first half (turning to God in trouble is noble, not selfish) and challenge from the second (grow toward loving God for God's own sake).
misreadings: Not a put-down of people who pray when in need; Krishna calls them noble.
Not a claim that the wise become God in a way that erases the relationship (Ramanuja reads mutual dependence).
cautions: Our current misuse note about grace and responsibility doesn't match this verse; replace it.
not_for: a reader who may hear the ranking as 'my faith is second-class'
speaks_to: someone who turned to faith only in a crisis and feels it doesn't 'count'
a seeker wondering how God regards different motives
someone longing for intimacy with God

data_flags.translation_note: Translation is fine; the line is not. The verse calls the jñānī, the one who knows/the wise devotee, 'my very self'. The line says 'The one who loves me is my very self', which swaps knowledge for love; Ramanuja's jñānī is a devotee, but even...

bg.7.21.context: Krishna has said that people whose understanding is carried away by desires turn to other deities (7.20). Here he says that whatever form a devotee worships with faith, he himself makes that faith firm; 7.22 says the devotee gains his wishes, though they are granted by Krishna, and 7.23 says such results are finite, while his own devotees reach him.
bg.7.21.core_teaching: God honours and steadies sincere faith in whatever form a person worships, because every such form is ultimately God's; but the context also says worship for limited ends brings limited results.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Whatever deity-form a person moved by desires wishes to worship with faith, the Lord makes that very faith steady.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Those deities are the Lord's own bodies, as the Upanishad's inner-controller passage teaches. Even when the worshipper of Indra and others does not know this, the Lord recognises the faith as aimed at his body and makes it unobstructed.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Whichever deity-form, which is really the Lord's own form, a devotee wants to worship with faith, the Lord as inner controller makes that faith firm.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Tanu means a deity here. The Lord, the indweller of all, steadies the faith of one who worships lesser divinities, a faith born of impressions from a past birth.

bg.7.21.practical_reading: Teachers use it to encourage respect for other people's ways of worship: sincere faith is honoured, and growth comes by deepening it, not by being mocked out of it.
misreadings: Not a simple statement that all worship is equal; 7.20 and 7.23 rank desire-driven worship below devotion to the Supreme.
Not permission to belittle someone's chosen deity or practice.
cautions: Reading it as pure pluralism skips the hierarchy in 7.20-23; reading it as sectarian skips 'I make that faith steady'. Present both.
not_for: a reader looking for a proof-text that their tradition alone is right
speaks_to: someone unsure whether their way of worship 'counts'
a person whose faith feels unsteady

bg.7.27.context: Krishna has said he knows all beings past, present and future, but no one knows him (7.26). This verse gives the reason: from birth, the delusion of the opposites, born of desire and aversion, confuses every being. 7.28 adds that people whose wrongdoing has ended, freed from that delusion, worship him with firm resolve.
bg.7.27.core_teaching: Every being is confused from birth by the pull of wanting and the push of aversion, which split experience into pleasant and unpleasant and hide the deeper reality.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Desire and aversion, opposed like heat and cold and tied to pleasure, pain and their causes, give rise to the delusion of opposites, which overwhelms all beings at birth.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Likes and dislikes practised toward pleasure and pain in earlier births leave impressions; so at birth itself the same pairs appear as things to want or hate and delude beings.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: At birth, desire for the pleasing and aversion to the unpleasant breed loss of discernment amid heat and cold, pleasure and pain; beings identify with the body ('I am happy, I am miserable'), and so do not know the Lord.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Pleasure brings attachment and pain brings aversion, rooted in the instinct to preserve the body. Overwhelmed by these, a person cannot see even the outer world as it is, let alone the inner Self.

bg.7.27.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to reactivity: much of our confusion comes from automatic liking and disliking, so noticing the pull and push is the first step toward clear sight.
misreadings: Not a claim that having preferences is sinful.
Not fatalism about human nature; 7.28 describes people freed from this delusion.
not_for: someone in crisis who needs comfort rather than a diagnosis of human confusion
speaks_to: someone caught in reactive likes and dislikes
a person trying to understand why they keep misjudging situations
meditators working with craving and aversion

bg.7.7.context: Krishna has said that his two natures, the lower material one and the higher one that is life itself, are the womb of all beings, and that he is the origin and dissolution of the whole world (7.4-6). Here he concludes that nothing is higher than him and that all things are strung on him like gems on a thread. The verses that follow (7.8-11) name him as the taste in water, the light in sun and moon, and so on.
bg.7.7.core_teaching: The divine is the single, unseen thread that runs through and holds together everything that exists; nothing stands above or apart from it.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: There is no other cause beyond the supreme Lord; he alone is the world's cause. So all beings and the whole universe are threaded through him, like cloth on long threads or gems on a string.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: All sentient and insentient things form the Lord's body and depend on him as their soul, held together like gems on a thread; he cites the Upanishadic inner-controller passages, where earth and the rest are his body.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Nothing is a superior, independent cause of the world's creation and dissolution; he is also the cause of its continuance, since the whole world is strung on and supported by him.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The image of gems and thread only shows that all beings are threaded on the Lord; the thread is not the cause of the gems. Since Brahman is all in all, nothing is higher.

bg.7.7.practical_reading: Teachers use the image for coherence and belonging: the scattered pieces of a life, and all the different people in it, are held on one thread.
misreadings: Not pantheism in the simple sense; commentators keep the Lord as cause, self or support of the world, not just its sum.
not_for: someone in acute pain who needs concrete comfort rather than metaphysics
speaks_to: feeling that life is fragmented or meaningless
someone looking for what connects all things
a reader drawn to contemplative images of unity

bg.8.14.context: Krishna has just described the yogi who leaves the body uttering Om and remembering him (8.12-13). Here he offers an easier assurance: for the one who remembers him constantly, every day, with mind on nothing else, he is easy to reach. 8.15-16 add that great souls who reach him do not return to rebirth, the home of sorrow.
bg.8.14.core_teaching: God is not remote or hard to reach for someone who keeps God in mind steadily over a lifetime; constancy, more than intensity, makes the difference.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: 'Constantly' means without break; 'always' means over a long time, not six months or a year but for life. To the yogi whose mind goes to nothing else and who remembers the Lord thus, he is easily reached.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: One who loves the Lord so much that he cannot sustain himself without remembering him: for such a one the Lord himself, unable to bear separation, chooses him, ripens his worship and removes what stands in the way.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Reaching the Lord by concentration at death comes only through daily practice. To one who remembers him every day with mind on nothing else, he is easily attained, and not to others.

bg.8.14.practical_reading: Teachers use it as encouragement: a small, unbroken daily remembrance (a name, a prayer, a pause) brings the divine near more surely than occasional intense effort.
misreadings: Not a claim that God is unreachable for those who forget or lapse; the stress is on how near God is to the constant.
Not a call to give up all other thoughts and responsibilities.
cautions: Sivananda's line that on-and-off remembrance does not reach God could discourage someone restarting a practice; foreground 'easy to reach'.
not_for: someone in guilt over lapses in practice who may hear 'only the constant'
speaks_to: someone who feels God is distant
a person building a simple daily practice
someone who prefers steadiness over dramatic spiritual experiences

bg.8.6.context: Arjuna has asked, among seven questions, how the Lord is to be known at the time of death (8.2). Krishna answers that whoever leaves the body remembering him attains him (8.5), and generalises here: whatever one remembers at the end, one goes to, because one has always dwelt on it. 8.7 draws the conclusion: so remember me at all times, and fight.
bg.8.6.core_teaching: What fills the mind at death determines where one goes next, and what fills the mind then is whatever one has dwelt on throughout life.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Whatever being, such as a particular deity, one thinks of when life departs, one reaches that alone, because one has practised dwelling on it; the final thought is what leads to the next body.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: One reaches after death whatever one remembers at the end; and the final thought arises only about what was dwelt on earlier.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: The last thought decides the next birth, and the predominant thought of a life is what occupies the mind at death; impressions from practice produce that memory. He cites the wasp and caterpillar image.

bg.8.6.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that the habits of attention we build every day are what will be left in us at the end; what we keep returning to, we become.
misreadings: Not a test that one last moment can pass or fail; every commentator ties the last thought to lifelong habit.
Not a claim that someone who died afraid, confused or unconscious is condemned.
cautions: About death and rebirth; for a bereaved reader it can trigger worry about a loved one's final moments (sudden death, dementia, sedation). Sridhara (on 8.7) notes the dying cannot make effort, which is why lifelong remembrance matters; never imply a loved one 'failed' at the end.
Not for anyone in suicidal crisis or facing imminent death without careful framing.
not_for: fresh grief, especially after a sudden or difficult death
someone with health anxiety or fear of death
speaks_to: someone reflecting on what they let fill their mind
someone preparing calmly for mortality, or caring for a dying person with faith

bg.8.7.context: Having said that the mind's final content decides one's destination (8.6), Krishna draws the conclusion for Arjuna: remember me at all times, and fight. With mind and understanding offered to him, Arjuna will surely reach him. The following verses (8.8-10) describe meditation on the supreme Person through practice.
bg.8.7.core_teaching: Remembering God is not a retreat from life: keep God in mind all the time and keep doing your work, and with mind and judgement offered to God you will reach God.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Therefore remember the Lord at all times as scripture teaches, and fight, that is, do your own duty. With mind and intellect offered to Vasudeva you will reach him as remembered; there is no doubt.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Since only prior impressions produce memory at death, when a helpless person cannot make an effort to remember, remember me always. Constant remembrance needs a pure mind, so do your duty of fighting to purify it.

bg.8.7.practical_reading: Teachers present it as integration: carry a quiet remembrance of the divine through the workday instead of separating spiritual life from ordinary duties.
misreadings: 'Fight' means do your rightful work; it is not a call to pick battles or endorse violence (our existing misuse note is right).
Not a claim that remembering God guarantees worldly success.
cautions: Ramanuja and Sivananda frame duty in caste-and-stage-of-life terms; a modern reading should speak of one's responsibilities, not caste duty.
not_for: someone in a conflict where 'fight' could be heard literally
a reader facing death who needs comfort rather than an instruction
speaks_to: someone who feels their busy life leaves no room for spirituality
a person wanting to work with a calmer, offered mind
someone torn between duty and devotion

bg.8.8.context: After 'remember me at all times and fight' (8.7), Krishna explains how remembrance becomes steady: a mind trained by repeated practice, not straying elsewhere, reaches the supreme divine Person. 8.9-10 then describe that Person and the yogi's meditation at the hour of death.
bg.8.8.core_teaching: Steady remembrance is built by practice: repeatedly bringing the mind back to one object until it stops wandering is the means of reaching the Supreme.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Practice is repeating one thought of the Lord, uninterrupted by any other; that is yoga. With the mind so occupied, meditating as scripture and teacher instruct, one reaches the supreme Person, the one in the sun's orb.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Practice means training the mind on the object of meditation even at times outside set worship and duties. Thinking of the Lord at death with a mind so trained, one reaches him, gaining glory comparable to his.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Practice, a stream of like thoughts, is the inner means of continuous remembrance; with that one-pointed, non-wandering mind, meditating on the luminous supreme Lord, one reaches him.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Abhyasa is constant repetition of one idea of God, shutting out other thoughts and keeping a continuous flow of the divine thought; like rivers losing their names in the ocean, the sage becomes one with the Supreme.

bg.8.8.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to any devotional or meditative habit: the mind is trained not by one great effort but by returning, again and again, to the same point.
misreadings: Not a technique to get whatever you visualise; the object is the Supreme.
Not a demand that the mind never wander; practice is the returning.
not_for: someone who feels guilty for a wandering mind and may hear 'not straying' as a standard they fail
speaks_to: someone building a daily prayer or meditation habit
a distracted mind that keeps drifting
someone wondering how 'remembering God always' is possible

bg.9.17.context: In a run of verses (9.16-19) Krishna names himself as every part of worship and of the world: the ritual, the offering, the fire (9.16); here, father, mother, sustainer and grandfather of the world, the one to be known, the purifier, Om and the three Vedas. 9.18 continues: the goal, supporter, witness, refuge and friend.
bg.9.17.core_teaching: The divine relates to the world as every kind of parent and source: begetting, nurturing, sustaining, preceding it, and also as what is worth knowing and what makes pure.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: The Lord is the world's father, mother, dispenser of the fruits of action and grandsire; also what is to be known, the purifier, Om, and the Rig, Sama and Yajur Vedas.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: The Lord himself stands to this universe of moving and unmoving things as father, mother, patriarch and grandsire; he is also the one to be known, the holy, Om, and the three Vedas.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Dhātā is the dispenser of the fruits of action; the purifier is what cleanses, such as expiation; Om and the Vedas too are the Lord.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Dhātā can mean supporter or dispenser of fruits. He maps father to the Lord with attributes, mother to primordial Nature, grandfather to the absolute Brahman; the purifier is like a bath in the Ganga or Gayatri japa.

bg.9.17.practical_reading: Teachers use it to widen the image of God beyond one role: the same presence that begets also mothers, sustains and purifies, which can comfort people who feel unparented.
misreadings: Not a replacement for a parent who is gone (our existing misuse note is right).
Not a gendered claim that God is only male; the verse names God as mother as well.
cautions: Parent imagery can hurt readers with absent, abusive or recently deceased parents; use gently.
not_for: someone whose parent was abusive, unless framed carefully
fresh grief for a parent, where it may feel like a substitution
speaks_to: someone who feels alone or unparented
new parents reflecting on what parenting means
someone who wants a warmer, more familial image of God

bg.9.18.context: In 9.16-19 Krishna describes himself as everything in worship and in the world: the ritual and the offering, father, mother and grandsire of the world, heat and rain, immortality and death. This verse is the most personal of the list, naming what he is to each being. Next (9.20-21) he contrasts worship done for heavenly rewards.
bg.9.18.core_teaching: The divine is not distant: it is at once the goal, the support, the one who sees, the home, the refuge and the friend of every being, as well as the source and end of all.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Glosses each title. The Lord shelters and frees those who come to him in distress, and is a friend who does good expecting no return. As the imperishable seed, he keeps all growth going while the world lasts.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Glosses each name: the refuge to whom souls turn to gain their hopes and escape harm, the friend who wishes all well, the inexhaustible cause. He links the list to a Subala Upanishad passage.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Defines each term in turn: goal as the fruit of action, refuge as protector, friend as one who does good. The seed is eternal, unlike a rice seed that perishes.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Repeats the classical glosses (shelter for the distressed, friend who expects no return) and draws the practical conclusion: take refuge at the Lord's feet.

bg.9.18.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a litany for times of isolation: repeating these names reminds the reader they are supported, seen and befriended even when no one else is near.
misreadings: Not a promise that one will never feel alone or that people are unnecessary.
'Witness' is not surveillance or judgement here; the commentators place it beside refuge and friend.
cautions: The full verse also names him as dissolution (pralaya); if quoted whole, the ending may need gentle handling for someone grieving.
For a reader with religious trauma, 'witness' may feel like being watched; emphasise friend and refuge.
not_for: readers who are not theistic, if pressed doctrinally
someone who needs practical help, if offered as a substitute
speaks_to: needing a sense of home or belonging

bg.9.22.context: Krishna has just said that those who perform rites for heavenly rewards enjoy heaven but return when their merit runs out (9.20-21). In contrast, those who think of him alone are carried by him. Next (9.23-24) he says even worship of other gods reaches him, though not in the proper way.
bg.9.22.core_teaching: Those who turn to the divine wholeheartedly are looked after: what they lack is brought and what they have is protected, by the divine itself.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Applies the verse to renunciates who see the Lord as their own Self. Other devotees still work for their own gain and safety; these do not even wish for life or death, so the Lord himself provides for them.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Reads yoga-kṣema spiritually: for those whose only hope is the Lord and who long for lasting union with him, he grants that union, from which there is no return, and keeps it secure for ever.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: For those who desire nothing but the Lord, he himself secures what they need, including wealth and its protection and finally liberation, without their asking.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Since such devotees have no selfish aims, the Lord looks after their bodily needs like food and clothing and guards what they have, as parents care for children.

bg.9.22.practical_reading: Teachers read it as relief from carrying everything alone: wholehearted trust loosens anxiety about the future, while one still does one's part.
misreadings: Not 'God will pay the bills, so don't plan' (as our misuse note says).
Classical readers differ on what is 'carried': Ramanuja means spiritual attainment and freedom; Sridhara includes material welfare. Avoid promising material outcomes.
cautions: For someone losing hope after financial or health loss, a promise of provision can backfire if things do not improve; frame it as being held, not as a guarantee.
not_for: someone in financial crisis, if read as 'don't take practical steps'
someone whose prayers seem unanswered, if read as a transactional promise
speaks_to: feeling one must hold everything together alone

bg.9.26.context: Krishna has said that worshippers go to whatever they worship (9.25). He now shows how easy devotion to him is: any simple thing offered with love is enough. The next verse (9.27) widens this to offering everything one does, and 9.28 says this frees one from karma's bonds.
bg.9.26.core_teaching: The divine is pleased by love, not by the value of the gift: the simplest thing offered with a sincere heart is received.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Comments only briefly, with a plain rendering: whatever simple thing the pure-minded offer with devotion (leaf, flower, fruit, water), the Lord partakes of it. He uses it to lead into the next verse, 'therefore offer everything'.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Devotion here means a love so strong that the devotee cannot bear to live without offering something. The Lord, who lacks nothing, receives such an offering as if it were a rare treat beyond all hope.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Shows how easy devotion is. The supreme Lord is not won by costly rites, as petty gods are, but by love alone, so he gladly accepts even a leaf from a selfless devotee.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Recalls Sudama's handful of parched rice and Shabari's berries. Leaf and flower are symbols; what the Lord wants is a devoted heart, a golden temple built within.

bg.9.26.practical_reading: Teachers turn it into a small daily act: a flower, a glass of water, a moment of attention offered with love counts. What matters is the heart, not the size of the gesture.
misreadings: Not a statement that ritual objects themselves earn favour; the love is the point.
Not dismissive of elaborate worship, but it removes cost as a barrier.
cautions: In the grief plan, a simple offering can be a gentle ritual; note it is an offering to God, distinct from tarpan or śrāddha offerings for the departed, though readers may connect them.
not_for: non-theistic readers, if presented as required worship
speaks_to: wanting a simple way to express love or devotion
feeling one has little to give
grief that needs a small ritual act

bg.9.27.context: Having said that even a leaf offered with love is accepted (9.26), Krishna widens the offering to the whole of life: work, food, worship, giving and discipline. The next verse (9.28) says that living this way frees one from the bonds of karma's good and bad fruits.
bg.9.27.core_teaching: Every ordinary act, from eating to working to giving, can be done as an offering to the divine; nothing needs to be set apart as special.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Covers acts done by one's own choice as well as the sacrifices and gifts that scripture requires. All of them should be done as an offering to the Lord, and the next verse says what follows from that.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Covers ordinary work done to live, eating, and prescribed rites and gifts. Offer all of it to the Lord, including oneself as doer and enjoyer and even the gods one worships, since all depend on him.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Nothing special needs to be gathered for the Lord, unlike the materials of a sacrifice. Do every act, natural or prescribed, in such a way that it becomes an offering to him.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: Calls this the simplest yoga, to begin today. Dedicating every act frees one from karma's bondage and slowly dissolves greed and ego, as a river gives up its name in the sea.

bg.9.27.practical_reading: Teachers suggest a simple practice: before a meal, a task or a gift, dedicate it silently. Everyday life itself becomes devotion, without adding extra rituals.
misreadings: Not 'anything is fine if I call it an offering'; the offering presupposes acts that are fit to offer.
Not a call to overwork in God's name.
cautions: 'Whatever you eat' may touch readers with eating difficulties; keep the focus on dedication, not food control.
not_for: readers seeking to justify harmful acts as 'offerings'
non-theistic readers, if framed as obligation
speaks_to: wanting devotion in a busy life

bg.9.29.context: Krishna has just said that offering all action to him frees one from karma (9.27-28). Here he answers an implied objection: if he favours devotees, is he partial? He says he is equal to all, yet devotees dwell in him and he in them. The next verses (9.30-32) extend this to wrongdoers who turn and to those of low social standing.
bg.9.29.core_teaching: The divine is impartial and rejects no one, but those who turn to it in love come to dwell in it, and it in them; the closeness comes from the turning, not from favouritism.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Uses the image of fire: it warms only those who come near, without favouring anyone. Likewise, grace reaches devotees because their devotion has made them fit for it, not because the Lord is partial.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Caste, looks, character and learning count for nothing: no one is rejected as unworthy and no one has a special claim. Only taking the Lord as refuge counts, and he dwells in such devotees as if they were his superiors.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Answers the charge of partiality: like fire or the wish-granting tree, the Lord helps those who come near. This is the power of devotion, not favouritism.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The Lord condemns and favours no one; the ego alone opens the gap. Sunlight is reflected only in a clean mirror, and devotion is what cleans the mind.
