bg.9.29.practical_reading: Teachers use it to answer 'why does God seem far from me?': the divine is equally near to all, and turning toward it is what lets one feel that nearness.
misreadings: Not 'God is indifferent to you'; 'same to all' means no one is shut out.
Not a reason to judge others as less loved.
cautions: A reader who feels God has abandoned them might hear 'I warm only those who come near' as blame; emphasise that no one is rejected.
not_for: someone in a crisis of faith who may hear it as 'it's your fault God feels absent'
speaks_to: feeling excluded by status or background

bg.9.30.context: Krishna has said he is equal to all, yet devotees dwell in him (9.29). He now extends this to the worst-behaved: wholehearted turning makes one count as good. He continues (9.31) that such a person soon becomes righteous and finds lasting peace, and (9.32) that people of any birth or station can reach the highest.
bg.9.30.core_teaching: A person's past wrongdoing does not shut the door: one who turns wholeheartedly to the divine is to be seen as good, because the decisive thing, their resolve, is now right.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1901)
commentaries.gist: Such a person is 'rightly resolved': his resolve is good. Shankara's note runs into the next verse: by giving up evil ways outwardly and by the force of that inner resolve, he becomes righteous.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya (1898)
commentaries.gist: Even one who breaks his caste's rules deserves honour as a true devotee if he worships the Lord alone. His mind rests on the Lord as cause of all, his master, teacher and friend; his lapses should not be belittled.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: If a very wicked person worships the Lord alone and no other god, regard him as among the best. His resolve, that worship of the Lord alone will bless him, is a worthy one.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (Divine Life Society, modern)
commentaries.gist: The holy resolve means resolving to give up one's evil ways. He cites Ratnakar who became Valmiki, and others transformed by turning to God. Outward change and inner resolve together make one righteous.

bg.9.30.practical_reading: Teachers use it against crushing guilt: your past does not define your worth; a sincere turn toward the good changes your direction now, and change follows.
misreadings: Not 'devotion erases harm done to others' (as our misuse note says); turning includes making amends.
Not instant sainthood; 9.31 says the person 'soon becomes' righteous, i.e. through change.
Not a license to keep doing wrong while claiming devotion; Shankara and Sivananda tie the 'right resolve' to giving up evil ways outwardly.
cautions: A reader harmed by someone else may hear this as excusing their abuser; keep the reading self-directed.
For a reader with heavy guilt, pair with practical repair, not only reassurance.
not_for: someone using faith to avoid accountability
a reader processing harm done to them by another
speaks_to: guilt and shame over past actions

data_flags.translation_note: Flagged false for the LINE (the translation itself is acceptable). Translation fine. Line shifts the verse: 'count yourself among the good' and 'the moment you turn' make it self-assessment and instant. The verse says such a person 'should be regarded' (mantavyaḥ) as good because his...

bg.9.31.context: Krishna has said that even a wrongdoer who turns wholeheartedly is to be regarded as good (9.30). Here he explains why: such a person soon becomes righteous and reaches lasting peace, and he asks Arjuna to proclaim that his devotee is never lost. Next (9.32-33) he says people of every background can reach the highest.
bg.9.31.core_teaching: Wholehearted turning changes a person quickly toward goodness and lasting peace; one who belongs to the divine in love is never lost.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Through worship even a wicked person soon becomes righteous-minded and gains lasting peace. Krishna tells Arjuna to proclaim this boldly before clever doubters, with drums and raised hands.

bg.9.31.practical_reading: Teachers read it as hope after wrongdoing: change can come sooner than you fear, and peace is possible for someone who sincerely turns around.
misreadings: Not a guarantee against consequences of past actions in this life.
Not a reason to judge others' sincerity; nor a promise of instant transformation.
cautions: Some readers will take this as 'anything goes' and others as 'you are a fraud if you still slip'. Avoid both; Ramanuja says the devotee is protected even while his conduct is still flawed, and Shankara and Sivananda pair the promise with giving up evil ways.
not_for: someone not yet willing to change harmful behaviour, if read as blanket assurance
speaks_to: guilt and fear of being beyond help
needing reassurance that change is possible

bg.9.34.context: This is the closing verse of chapter 9. Krishna has said that a leaf, flower, fruit or water offered with love is accepted (9.26), that everything one does should be offered to him (9.27), and that even a wrongdoer who turns to him wholeheartedly is to be counted good (9.30). He sums up the whole path of devotion here: mind, love, worship and reverence turned to him.
bg.9.34.core_teaching: Devotion engages the whole person, thought, love, action and humility, and a life gathered toward God in this way arrives at God.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: Fix your mind on Vasudeva, be devoted, worship and bow to him; having concentrated the mind with him as the highest goal, you will reach him, who is the Self of all beings and their supreme goal.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: Let the heart rest on the Lord unbroken, like a stream of poured oil: Lord of all, free of flaw, home of every excellence, lotus-eyed, cloud-hued, radiant; so devotion becomes loving contemplation.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Concluding the mode of worship: mind on me, be my devotee and servant, worship me, bow to me; with me as the highest aim and mind fixed, you will reach me, who am supreme bliss.

commentaries.who: Swami Sivananda (modern, Divine Life Society)
commentaries.gist: Fill your mind with the Lord and put head, heart and hands to him; surrender without reserve and life is transformed, sorrow falls away, and one crosses beyond death.

bg.9.34.practical_reading: Teachers present it as a four-part daily practice anyone can begin with: a thought, a feeling of love, a small offering, and a bow.
misreadings: Not a demand to abandon family or work; the chapter's offering includes everything one does (9.27).
Not exclusivist hostility to others; it describes wholehearted devotion.
cautions: The verses just before (9.32-33) contain caste and gender hierarchy language; do not pull that context into a reading without addressing it.
not_for: a reader alienated by devotional, personal-God language
speaks_to: someone wanting a simple, whole-hearted devotional practice
a person whose spiritual life feels scattered
someone longing for closeness to God

bg.9.6.context: Krishna has just stated a paradox: all beings rest in him, yet he is not contained in them, and in another sense they do not rest in him; behold his divine power (9.4-5). This verse gives the image: as the vast wind, moving everywhere, always stays in space, so all beings are in him. 9.7-8 go on to the cycles in which beings dissolve into and re-emerge from his nature.
bg.9.6.core_teaching: All beings, however restless, exist within the divine the way moving wind exists within space: held and contained, yet without the divine being touched or limited by them.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri 1901
commentaries.gist: As the great, all-moving wind always stays in space, so all beings stay in the Lord, all-pervading like space, without any contact.

commentaries.who: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), tr. A. Govindacharya 1898
commentaries.gist: As the mighty wind is held and moves in supportless space by the Lord's power, so all beings rest in him, unseen. He cites a verse naming clouds, tides, moon's phases and winds as Vishnu's marvels.

commentaries.who: Sridhara Swami (Subodhini), tr. Swami Vireswarananda
commentaries.gist: Shows by example a support-and-supported relation without contact: wind, though vast and everywhere, needs space yet is not attached to it, since space has no parts; so all beings rest in the Lord.

bg.9.6.practical_reading: Teachers use the image for anxiety and restlessness: however much your life is blowing about, it is still held in a stillness that is not disturbed by it.
misreadings: Not a claim that the world is unimportant to God.
not_for: someone who needs practical support rather than a metaphysical image
speaks_to: anxiety and a sense of constant motion
someone who wants an image of being held

bh.niti.100.context: In the run praising action: after verses on merit from former lives protecting a person anywhere (97) and on good conduct turning poison to nectar (98), this verse turns practical. The next verse compares wasting a human birth to cooking sesame husks in a jewelled pot over sandalwood.
bh.niti.100.core_teaching: Before any undertaking, good or bad, weigh where it will lead; the results of rash acts lodge like a barb and keep burning for the rest of one's life.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses rabhasa as rashness, āvipatteḥ as up to the time of death, śalya as a foreign body causing great pain, and vipāka as ripening, hence result.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Same reading: the result must be considered beforehand; the issue of acts done in hot haste is, till death, like a dart in the vitals; the figure is simile.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, tr. (London, 1886)
commentaries.gist: Takes the point of looking to the end as freedom from births in another state, a more otherworldly reading than the Bombay editors give.

bh.niti.100.practical_reading: Quoted as a pause-before-you-act rule: a hasty word or decision can leave a regret that outlasts the moment by decades.
misreadings: Not advice to avoid all risk or decision
Not a claim that every regret is permanent or unforgivable
cautions: For someone already tormented by a past rash act, 'burns until death' can deepen shame
not_for: someone stuck in regret over a past mistake
anxious over-planners who need encouragement to act
speaks_to: about to send an angry message or make an impulsive decision
big financial, career or relationship choices

bh.niti.102.context: In the praise-of-action run, right after the image of wasting a human birth (100) and before the verse that, for a person with great past merit, a wild forest becomes a city (102). Despite the heading, these verses keep conceding what earlier deeds have already fixed.
bh.niti.102.core_teaching: However heroic or skilled the effort, what is not destined will not happen and what is destined will not be undone; the reason given is the force of past deeds.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Draws the moral that one may attempt the hardest and most dangerous things to bring about what is fated not to happen, or to avoid what is fated, and will fail.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Disputes half of Telang's moral: the verse says nothing about avoiding the fated; it says wealth sought by pearl-diving, Meru's gold, war or trade will not come if it is not destined.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Explains 'all sciences and arts' as the traditional fourteen sciences and sixty-four arts, and construes 'by the force of karma' with 'never happens'.

bh.niti.102.practical_reading: Teachers pair it with the verses on effort: do everything you can, then loosen your grip on the result, because outcomes depend on more than you.
misreadings: Not a reason not to try; nearby verses praise industry (Niti 86)
Not a claim that every detail of life is pre-written
cautions: Read alone it is fatalistic; it can crush someone who tried everything and failed, or sound dismissive after a loss
Pair it with an effort verse, as our misuse note says
not_for: someone deciding whether to try at all
fresh bereavement, where 'it was meant to be' can feel cruel
speaks_to: after giving one's best and still not getting the result (exam, job, fertility treatment, business)
letting go of obsessive control over outcomes

bh.niti.104.context: A question-and-answer verse (praśnottara) among the closing stanzas of the Niti collection, after the runs on fate and action. Riddle catechisms like this were a common teaching form.
bh.niti.104.core_teaching: A catechism of values: real gain is good company, real loss is a missed moment, real courage is self-mastery, real wealth is learning.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Gives both senses of samaya-cyuti (missing the right moment; breaking an engagement) and glosses kingship as the capacity to command and enforce obedience.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Translates nipuṇatā as being devoted to one's religious principles, anuvratā as a wife devoted to her husband, and happiness as not going on a journey.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains samaya-cyuti as letting slip an opportunity and kingship as the power whose fruit is command; quotes the Sanskrit commentary on the rest.

bh.niti.104.practical_reading: Teachers lift single lines: self-mastery as courage, learning as wealth, and the real cost of missed timing.
misreadings: 'Happiness is not living abroad' is a period sentiment about exile and homesickness, not a judgment on migrants
The 'beloved = faithful wife' line reflects its time; do not present it as teaching on marriage roles
cautions: Contains gendered and dated definitions; quote selectively and say so
Can sting for emigrants or people working far from home
not_for: readers living abroad or homesick (the apravāsa line)
conversations about marriage or gender roles
speaks_to: someone who keeps letting opportunities pass

bh.niti.105.context: A short āryā verse among the closing Niti stanzas, describing the rare good person; the neighbouring verses praise steadiness that does not bend in misfortune.
bh.niti.105.core_teaching: Only here and there is the world adorned by people who never speak harshly, always speak kindly, are faithful in marriage and do not speak ill of others.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Explains the paradox: 'poor' in disagreeable language means not given to harsh words, 'rich' in agreeable language means habitually kind; the world is only sparsely adorned by such people.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Gives the same reading and glosses parivāda as censure of others.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, tr. (London, 1886)
commentaries.gist: Renders the first compound as poor men whose words are of no account, inverting the sense; a warning that old translations can mislead on this verse.

bh.niti.105.practical_reading: A reminder that kind speech and refusing to gossip are rare and beautiful; useful for reflecting on how we talk about people who are not in the room.
misreadings: Not praise of material poverty; 'poor' and 'rich' refer to speech
cautions: The fidelity clause names 'their own wives' in the original; our translation modernises it
not_for: someone hurting from a partner's infidelity, where the fidelity clause may sting

bh.niti.106.context: Near the end of the Nitishatakam. In Wortham's arrangement the section 'The Praise of Action' runs from 94 to the end (110), and its closing verses praise the dhīra, the steadfast person. The next verse in Wortham/Kale says such a person is not pierced by love's arrows, burned by anger or snared by greed.
bh.niti.106.core_teaching: Steadiness that is part of one's nature survives rough treatment, just as a flame keeps rising however the torch is held.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation and notes (1902 ed., Niti 106)
commentaries.gist: Glosses kadarthita as despised, afflicted, worried; the courage of the heroic cannot be subdued, as a downturned flame does not point to the ground. Discusses Telang's alternative reading.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation and notes (1886, Niti 106)
commentaries.gist: The constant man keeps his virtue in misfortune; notes the Hitopadesha version, where it is the steady person's understanding that is not lost when troubled.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 226)
commentaries.gist: Doubtful-block verse.

bh.niti.106.practical_reading: After a knock to your confidence, remind yourself of a quality in you that did not change because someone treated you badly; act from it today.
misreadings: Not 'strong people never feel humiliated'.
Not a test the reader is failing if they feel shaken.
cautions: For a reader who feels not good enough, 'the steadfast are unshakeable' can read as proof they are not steadfast; frame the flame as something they already have.
not_for: someone currently being abused, if it implies they should simply endure

bh.niti.107.context: Among the closing Niti verses on the steady person (dhīra). Just before, a constant person's courage is like a flame that points upward even when the torch is held down (106); just after, one hero lights up the whole earth like the sun.
bh.niti.107.core_teaching: The truly steady person is not wounded by desire, not burned by anger and not dragged by greed; such a person has conquered more than any king.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Translates: the firm man whose mind is not pierced by glances, consumed by anger, or ensnared by greed for many objects prevails in the three worlds; discusses the variant verbs for the arrows.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Prefers the idea of piercing for the glance-arrows and reads the three clauses as parallel negations describing the courageous man.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Defends his chosen verb because piercing suits arrows and 'burning' already goes with the fire of anger.

bh.niti.107.practical_reading: Used to redefine strength as inner mastery: anger and greed are named as enemies, and not being ruled by them is the real victory.
misreadings: Not a claim that women are dangers; the glance-as-arrow is a stock image for desire
Not a demand to feel nothing; it is about not being cut, burned or dragged
cautions: The first image casts women's glances as weapons; our line rightly omits it
not_for: someone ashamed of their feelings or desires, who may hear condemnation

bh.niti.14.context: Closes the section on fools in the Chaukhamba and Kale ordering, after verses on people without learning being beasts in human form. It sums up the section's advice: avoid company with the closed and foolish, whatever the comfort on offer.
bh.niti.14.core_teaching: The company you keep matters more than the comfort of your surroundings; hardship among the simple is better than luxury among fools.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Living with forest folk in rough terrain is somehow bearable, but living with great fools is to be shunned even if it came with a royal palace or heaven.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang (1874/1893 edition: notes citing two Sanskrit commentaries, one by Ramarshi)
commentaries.gist: Notes that a similar idea occurs in the Dhammapada.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Compares Proverbs 17:12, that meeting a bear robbed of her cubs is better than meeting a fool in his folly.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi (1948 critical edition: textual status)
commentaries.gist: Ranked Group II (no. 320): in more than one manuscript version but not the secure core; absent from the southern recension.

bh.niti.14.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to choosing environments: a modest job, flat or town with decent people can be better than a prestigious one among people who drag you down.
misreadings: Not contempt for tribal or rural people; the contrast is between hardship and bad company.
Not a licence to call anyone you dislike a fool and cut them off.
cautions: Can sound misanthropic; keep it about one's own choices of company.
not_for: someone lonely or isolated who needs connection, not more distance
a reader in a family situation they cannot leave
speaks_to: weighing a prestigious but toxic workplace
choosing friends or a peer group
someone who left comfort for integrity

bh.niti.16.context: In the section praising the learned, which opens with verses on poets living poor in a king's land. This verse tells rulers to drop their pride before people whose wealth is learning, because that wealth is beyond the reach of thieves, time and loss.
bh.niti.16.core_teaching: Learning is a wealth that cannot be stolen, keeps giving joy, grows when shared and survives every loss; those who hold it deserve respect from the powerful.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Learning cannot be stolen; unlike money, whose earning brings pain, it yields indescribable happiness and grows by being taught. Kings should drop their anger toward the learned, since no one can rival them.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Addresses kings: before those who own this hidden, imperishable wealth that grows by giving, stop your arrogance; who can equal them?

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Kale's translation stresses that the 'secret wealth of knowledge' survives even the end of the world and increases when given to those who ask.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Explains kalpānta as the destruction at the end of a kalpa, a day of Brahma: learning outlasts even the world's dissolution.

bh.niti.16.practical_reading: A reminder that skills and understanding are the one asset no layoff, theft or market crash takes; and that teaching what you know enlarges it rather than spending it.
misreadings: Not a claim that learned people are above criticism; it is aimed at the arrogance of power.
Not a dismissal of material security.
cautions: Mentions the end of an age (kalpānta), a cosmic not personal image; harmless for most readers.
not_for: someone struggling to learn or excluded from education, who may feel shut out
a reader in financial crisis who needs practical help, not consolation
speaks_to: someone who lost money or a job but kept their skills
students doubting the worth of study
people facing condescension from the powerful

bh.niti.18.context: In the praise of the learned, directly after verses telling kings not to slight scholars. The swan, famed for separating milk from water, stands for the scholar's discernment; the angry Creator stands for a king who can banish a scholar but not take his skill.
bh.niti.18.core_teaching: Circumstances, comforts and position can be taken away; a cultivated skill of discernment cannot.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as indirect speech (aprastuta-praśaṃsā): an angry king can only stop a scholar living in his realm, not take the skill his learning produced, so a king should not be angry with scholars.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Adds the explicit parallel: a king may seize a poet's wealth or bar him from court, but cannot snatch his poetic gift or learning; wherever such people go, they shine.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Quotes the scholiast: no one can take away the virtue of one whose good quality is part of his nature.

bh.niti.18.practical_reading: When you lose a role, a city or a comfortable setting, what you have cultivated in yourself travels with you; build skills that do not depend on one employer.
misreadings: Not a claim that losses do not hurt; the verse admits the swan really loses its lake.
Not a statement that fate is hostile; the 'angry creator' is a figure for an angry patron.
cautions: For someone who just lost a home or job, lead with the acknowledgment of loss before the consolation.
not_for: fresh bereavement (the 'what remains' framing can feel dismissive)
someone whose skill itself was damaged by illness or injury
speaks_to: job loss or being pushed out of a position
relocation or exile from a familiar place

bh.niti.19.context: In the praise of learning, following verses on learning as unstealable wealth and the swan's discernment. It narrows the point to speech: cultivated speech is the ornament that lasts when jewellery and grooming fade.
bh.niti.19.core_teaching: External adornments fade; speech refined by learning and care is the one ornament that stays and truly makes a person attractive.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Goes through each adornment (armlets, pearl necklaces, bath, sandal and musk, jasmine, oiled hair) and says none adorns; refined speech alone does, as an ornament that never perishes.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: All ornaments are perishable; the beauty pure speech creates is lasting, so effort should go to the ornament of speech.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates 'saṃskṛtā' as speech 'possessed in a refined state' and the last clause as the one ornament that fades not.

bh.niti.19.practical_reading: Invest in how you speak: clarity, kindness and accuracy outlast looks and clothes, at interviews, in families and as we age.
misreadings: Not a sneer at grooming or dress; the comparison is about what lasts.
'Refined' does not mean elite Sanskrit or English; it means speech cultivated with care.
not_for: someone with a speech or language disability, unless framed as care rather than polish
speaks_to: preparing for interviews or public speaking
parents teaching children how to speak to others

bh.niti.20.context: Part of the praise of learning, right after the verse on speech as the lasting ornament. It piles up titles for learning: beauty, hidden treasure, source of comfort and fame, teacher of teachers, kin abroad, highest deity, honoured by kings.
bh.niti.20.core_teaching: Learning gives a person everything that beauty, money, family and status promise, and it goes with you everywhere, including far from home.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Learning is the beauty that shows without ornaments; teacher of teachers because it teaches the highest truth; kin abroad because it earns hospitality; highest deity because it can grant liberation; honoured in royal assemblies where wealth is not.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Learning is the best form, a secret treasure, giver of comfort and fame, revered even by elders, a companion abroad; one is honoured among kings for learning, not money; without it a person counts as a beast.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Renders 'gurūṇāṃ guruḥ' as 'the greatest benefactor' and keeps the closing line that one destitute of learning is a beast.

bh.niti.20.practical_reading: Speaks strongly to people building a life abroad: what you know becomes your network and your standing where you have no family.
misreadings: The closing 'a person without learning is a beast' is rhetorical; it must not be used to demean the unschooled.
Not a claim that degrees equal worth.
cautions: The final quarter is harsh; quote the verse selectively as our line does.
not_for: someone who could not study or left school early
readers with learning disabilities if the last quarter is quoted
speaks_to: students and migrants starting out in a new country

bh.niti.21.context: In the praise of learning, a chain of 'if you have X, what need of Y?' questions. Some items are virtues that make outward aids unnecessary (patience, a friend, learning, modesty, poetry); others are evils that are bad enough on their own (anger, rival kin, wicked people).
bh.niti.21.core_teaching: Inner qualities do the work of outer aids: patience protects better than armour and a true friend heals better than medicine; and inner faults like anger harm more than any outside enemy.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Forbearance blocks anger when insults come, so nothing can harm; anger is an inner enemy; rival heirs alone can burn up your wealth; a friend gives health; flawless learning secures every enjoyment; shame at wrongdoing is the ornament.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Summarises: forbearance is the greatest armour, anger the greatest enemy, co-heirs destroy like fire, a friend is the best medicine, the wicked are more venomous than snakes, faultless knowledge the best wealth.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Notes a variant 'vacanena' for 'kavacena' and reads 'anger, what need of enemies' as the inner passions being the worst foes.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates vrīḍā as 'a scrupulous conscience' and the kinsmen clause as kin doing the destructive work of fire.

bh.niti.21.practical_reading: Teachers take the first half as a checklist: cultivate patience instead of defences, notice that your own anger costs more than any rival, and value one true friend above remedies.
misreadings: The 'kinsmen are fire' clause is about inheritance rivalry, not a statement that family is bad.
Not a rejection of medicine or of wealth; it is a comparison of worth.
cautions: Contains a bitter line on kinsmen; avoid quoting it whole to someone in a family dispute or grieving a relative.
not_for: someone in an inheritance or family feud (the kinsmen clause will inflame)
a reader needing medical care who might hear 'no need of medicine'
speaks_to: people who react with anger and want to change
someone grateful for a friend in illness
reflection on what really protects us

bh.niti.23.context: In the praise of learning. Ramachandra Budhendra notes that, having praised the learned, the poet now states the benefit of good company (satsaṅgati). The verse lists what good company does and ends with a rhetorical question.
bh.niti.23.core_teaching: Spending time with good people improves almost everything about us: our thinking, our honesty, our standing and our peace of mind.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Good company removes dullness, makes one truthful, brings honour, removes sin through teaching dharma and clears the mind through teaching knowledge; so keep company with the good, not the wicked.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Company of the good takes away slowness of mind, brings truth into speech, raises respect, ends wrongdoing and spreads one's name; there is nothing it does not accomplish.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang (1874/1893 edition: notes citing two Sanskrit commentaries, one by Ramarshi)
commentaries.gist: Reads the phrase about truth in speech as making a person habitually truthful.

bh.niti.23.practical_reading: Choose friends, colleagues and mentors deliberately; the people around you shape your habits of mind and speech more than any resolution.
misreadings: Not a reason to look down on or shun people who are struggling; 'good company' means people of good character, not of high status.
not_for: someone isolated who cannot easily find such company (it may feel like blame)
speaks_to: someone starting at a new college or job
parents thinking about a child's peer group
feeling stuck and needing new influences

bh.niti.25.context: In the North Indian ordering it sits among the verses praising learning, just after a verse praising great poets. It is a list of the good things of a householder's life, ending with the claim that they come when Hari (Vishnu), who removes the world's troubles, is pleased.
bh.niti.25.core_teaching: The blessings of an ordinary good life (family, work, friends, peace of mind, learning) are to be recognised as grace, not taken for granted.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Heads it 'the fruit of divine grace': only when Vishnu, protector of the worlds, is pleased does one gain a virtuous son, faithful wife, kind master, loving friend, trustworthy servant, untroubled mind, lasting wealth and learning.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the attendants as 'honest servants' and the closing clause as these being obtained when Hari, who gratifies desires and pleases the world, is propitiated.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi (1948 critical edition: textual status)
commentaries.gist: Group III (no. 807): attested only in single versions or anthologies, with a different reading of the last line; the least secure class of verses ascribed to Bhartrihari.

bh.niti.25.practical_reading: Read as a gratitude list: name what is already good in your household, work and friendships, and treat it as gift rather than entitlement.
misreadings: Not a test of divine favour: lacking a child, spouse, kind boss or wealth does not mean God is displeased with you.
Not a prescription of gender roles; the Sanskrit names son and wife, but the point is gratitude for good relationships.
cautions: Implies that these blessings follow divine pleasure; for readers who are childless, widowed, single, unemployed or ill, it can read as a judgment.
not_for: infertility or child loss
divorce or widowhood
job loss or a harsh boss
chronic illness or depression (the 'mind at ease' line can sting)

bh.niti.26.context: A compact list of ethical restraints and virtues, called the path to the good that is common to all scriptures. In the North Indian order it closes the run of verses on learning and good company before the verse on three kinds of people (Niti 27).
bh.niti.26.core_teaching: Underneath differences of doctrine, every tradition agrees on a basic path: non-harm, honesty, not taking what is not yours, timely generosity, restraint of craving, humility and compassion.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Grounds each item in scripture: non-harm ('do not injure any being'), regarding others' goods as clods of earth, giving within one's means. This path is unbroken in all traditions and leads to every good.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Lists the virtues it names (non-violence, non-stealing, truthfulness, generosity, keeping out of talk about others' wives, freedom from greed, humility, kindness to all) as qualities that lead a person onto the path of welfare.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Renders the close as 'the way of happiness common in all the scriptures, that never fails in its operation'.

bh.niti.26.practical_reading: A short, interfaith ethical checklist for a day: harm no one, take nothing that is not yours, tell the truth, give what you can when it is needed, notice and interrupt craving, be kind.
misreadings: Not a claim that all religions are identical in doctrine; it says they agree on this ethical floor.
'Silence about others' wives' is about not gossiping or leering, not about women's speech.
cautions: The original includes a clause about not discussing other men's wives; if quoted whole, render it neutrally as not gossiping about others' partners.
not_for: someone in scrupulosity or moral OCD who may turn the list into self-punishment
speaks_to: someone wanting a simple moral compass
starting a fresh habit or vow

bh.niti.27.context: In the North Indian order it follows the list of universal virtues; in Ramachandra Budhendra's southern order it comes right after the verse on the gods churning the ocean, who did not stop for jewels or poison until they got nectar. He reads the two together: obstacles are expected, and the best keep going.
bh.niti.27.core_teaching: People differ less in talent than in how they meet obstacles: some never start, some stop when it gets hard, the best keep going through repeated setbacks.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: The low do not begin from fear of obstacles; the middling begin and are shaken off; the best, endowed with steadiness, finish despite repeated blows. Like the gods who churned on through poison until nectar appeared.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Calls it the difference between low, middling and high natures: the high-minded person completes what he starts without counting obstacles.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Notes the verse is quoted in the Mudrarakshasa, Act 2, and gives Wilson's verse translation of it there.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi (1948 critical edition: textual status)
commentaries.gist: Group II (no. 277): attested in several versions but among the verses Kosambi marks as open to suspicion.

bh.niti.27.practical_reading: Used to encourage finishing: expect obstacles as part of any real project, and judge yourself by whether you keep returning after setbacks, not by whether setbacks come.
misreadings: Not a judgment that people who hesitate are worthless; teachers use it to invite movement up the scale.
Not an argument never to quit anything; stopping a harmful or mistaken course is not what it describes.
cautions: Labels the hesitant 'low' (nīca); for someone ashamed of not starting, lead with the 'middling' and 'best' as steps.
not_for: someone in burnout or depression who needs rest, not more push
a reader ashamed of not having started
someone staying in an abusive situation out of 'perseverance'
speaks_to: someone halfway through a hard project
students facing exams or a long course
founders and job seekers after repeated rejections
anyone tempted to give up after a setback

bh.niti.28.context: Closes the run of verses on the learned and the good in the North Indian order. It lists the hard code of good people and asks who taught them this 'sword's-edge vow'. A near-twin (Niti 64) ends with the same question.
bh.niti.28.core_teaching: Good people keep a demanding code even under pressure: they do not beg from the wicked or burden struggling friends, earn honestly, refuse what is base even at great cost, and keep their dignity in trouble.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: An honest livelihood is dear to them; nothing base, even at risk of life, rejecting the excuse that emergencies have no rules. Who taught them this vow? No one: it comes naturally to them.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Asks who set the good on this path, sharp as a sword's edge, where one cannot ask the wicked, cannot ask a poor friend for money, must keep an honest living and stay steady in trouble.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Following Telang, reads 'uccaiḥ stheyam' as retaining one's dignity in misfortune.

bh.niti.28.practical_reading: A guide for hard times: borrow from the right people or not at all, do not lean on a friend who is also struggling, keep earning honestly, and hold your head up while you get through it.
misreadings: Not a ban on asking for help; it rules out begging from the wicked and burdening the struggling.
'Even at the cost of life' is rhetorical intensity, not advice to risk one's life.
cautions: The 'even at the cost of life' phrase should not be quoted to someone in crisis; it is about integrity, not sacrifice.
not_for: a person in danger who needs to ask anyone for help
someone already too proud to seek support
suicidal ideation
speaks_to: financial hardship and the temptation of shortcuts
someone deciding whom to ask for help

bh.niti.3.context: The opening verse of the section on fools (murkha-paddhati), right after the poet's complaint that the learned are jealous, the powerful proud and the rest ignorant. Ramachandra Budhendra introduces it as the answer to 'what kind of person is the fool?': not the ignorant, but the half-learned. The next verses list impossible feats that are still easier than pleasing such a mind.
bh.niti.3.core_teaching: The ignorant can be taught and the expert can be reasoned with, but a person proud of a little learning is closed to everyone. The real 'fool' of this section is the half-learned, conceited mind.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: The ignorant are set right by mere instruction; the true expert grasps distinctions at once; but one who thinks himself a pandit on a scrap of learning cannot be settled by any words. He is the real fool.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Heads the verse 'half knowledge causes trouble': the simple and the truly learned are easy to bring round, but one who struts on a little knowledge cannot be pleased even by Brahma, let alone by people.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang (1874/1893 edition: notes citing two Sanskrit commentaries, one by Ramarshi)
commentaries.gist: The commentator explains durvidagdha as 'arrogant'; Ramarshi as 'imperfectly educated'. Telang compares the English saying that a little learning is a dangerous thing.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Compares St Paul (1 Corinthians 8:2: whoever thinks he knows something does not yet know as he ought) and Pope's 'a little learning is a dangerous thing'.

bh.niti.3.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a mirror before a verdict: the hardest person to teach is the one who has learned just enough to stop listening, and that can be any of us after a first success, a course or a few articles.
misreadings: Not a licence to label people who disagree with you as half-learned; commentators place the danger in the conceit, which the reader should check in themself first.
Not contempt for beginners or the unschooled: the verse says the ignorant are easy to teach.
cautions: Satire. Read flat it can sound arrogant; frame it as self-examination.
not_for: someone already feeling stupid or 'not enough'
a reader in a painful family conflict who might use it to write off a relative
speaks_to: frustration at arguing with someone who will not listen
students and new professionals after early success
managers dealing with confident but shallow expertise

bh.niti.31.context: In the section on honour and spirit (mana-shaurya), after verses on the lion who will not eat what is beneath him. The dog and the elephant are two ways of depending on a patron: fawning, or steady self-respect.
bh.niti.31.core_teaching: Even when you depend on someone, you can keep your dignity; grovelling for favour is the mark of a small spirit.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: The dog shows its own lowness before the giver; the elephant looks on gravely and eats only after many coaxing words. These are the examples of the low and the high person.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Calls it the illustration of high and low: the small person, like a dog, shows grovelling humility to get fed; the great one stays dignified like the king of elephants and lives with self-respect.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the dog showing its mouth and belly and points to a parallel in the Hitopadesha.

bh.niti.31.practical_reading: At work or with patrons and donors, do your job well and be courteous without flattery; self-respect is compatible with depending on others.
misreadings: Not contempt for dogs or for anyone who must work for a living; it is about the posture of flattery.
Not a licence for arrogance or making others coax you; the elephant's quality is composure.
not_for: someone who has had to plead to survive (it can shame them)
a reader in a coercive relationship
speaks_to: someone tempted to flatter a boss or client
people in service jobs keeping their dignity
job seekers and freelancers dealing with gatekeepers

bh.niti.4.context: Second verse of the section on fools. Ramachandra Budhendra says that in two verses (this and the next, on oil from sand and water from a mirage) the poet shows how hard it is to win the obstinate fool's mind. It follows the verse on the half-learned (Niti 3).
bh.niti.4.core_teaching: Feats that look impossible can be managed with some method, but there is no method for winning over a mind that has dug in against you. Effort spent there is wasted.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Each danger named can be overcome by some means: a trick, a boat, a charm against snakes. For the fool possessed by stubbornness (durāgraha) there is no means at all, so his mind cannot be won.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Reads the closing optative as advice: one may brave crocodile, sea and snake, but should not even try to please the obstinate fool's mind.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang (1874/1893 edition: notes citing two Sanskrit commentaries, one by Ramarshi)
commentaries.gist: Glosses pratiniviṣṭa as perverse, headstrong in holding a contrary opinion.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Explains the image by the old fable that crocodiles carry pearls between their teeth.

bh.niti.4.practical_reading: Used as permission to stop: when someone has made up their mind against you, more argument rarely helps; save your energy for what can move.
misreadings: Not a claim that people never change; the target is the dug-in posture (pratiniveśa), not the person's whole future.
Not advice to write off family or colleagues after one disagreement.
cautions: Can harden contempt for a specific person; pair with Niti 3 and 8, which turn the same lens on oneself.
not_for: someone grieving an estrangement who may hear it as 'they will never change'
a reader looking for reasons to cut off help-seeking
speaks_to: deciding when to stop trying to convince someone

bh.niti.40.context: Early in the section on wealth (artha-paddhati), which opens with a verse saying that caste, virtue and character may all go to ruin so long as money remains. This verse notes with wry wonder how the same person seems to become someone else once the money is gone.
bh.niti.40.core_teaching: Nothing about a person changes when they lose money, yet how they are seen and treated changes completely; the poet marvels at this.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Though senses, mind and speech stay as before, without wealth a person enters a strange state; the wonder is that when the warmth of money ends he seems in a moment a different man.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates: the same limbs, deeds, intellect and speech, yet without the warmth of wealth the man instantly becomes another being, and calls this strange.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi (1948 critical edition: textual status)
commentaries.gist: Group III (no. 512): found only in isolated versions or anthologies; reads 'the same deeds' rather than 'the same name'.

bh.niti.40.practical_reading: For someone who has lost income: the change you feel in others' eyes is about them and the world's habits, not about your worth or abilities.
misreadings: Not saying that money makes the person; the wonder is aimed at the world's judgement.
Not advice to chase wealth to be respected.
cautions: Can deepen shame if read as 'without money you are nobody'; frame the wonder as criticism of the world.
not_for: someone in acute financial crisis without support, unless paired with practical help
a reader already ashamed of poverty, if read flatly
speaks_to: feeling treated differently after losing status
retirement and loss of a title

bh.niti.41.context: In the section on wealth. Ramachandra Budhendra introduces it as the answer to an objection that money without virtues achieves nothing: the verse claims money brings every virtue with it. It sits between verses on how people treat the poor and how wealth is lost.
bh.niti.41.core_teaching: Society credits the rich with every virtue: birth, learning, eloquence, looks. The verse states it as a law of the world.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as hyperbole (atiśayokti): wealth is said to produce qualities it has no real connection with. Within his section it states the worldly power of money.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: These days birth, learning, eloquence and looks are credited to whoever has money; a poor man with every virtue gets no respect. All virtues seem to live in gold.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates plainly: whoever has wealth is noble, learned, a sound critic, an orator and handsome; all virtues resort to wealth.

bh.niti.41.practical_reading: A clear-eyed observation to steady someone who feels overlooked: if people defer to the wealthy, that reflects social habit, not the real distribution of worth.
misreadings: Not advice that money is what makes a person good; our_note is right that read flat it inverts the point.
The tradition reads it less as satire than as realistic, exaggerated observation; either way it is description, not a value to adopt.
cautions: Easily misused as cynicism; pair with Niti 40 and 43.
not_for: someone in financial distress who might hear 'without money you have no worth'
speaks_to: feeling invisible next to wealthier relatives or colleagues
noticing status bias at work or in marriage talks
young people under pressure to show off money

bh.niti.42.context: Ramachandra Budhendra says that with this and the next verse the poet shows how wealth and other goods are destroyed. It is a list of twelve causes of ruin, from a king's bad counsel to a person's careless spending.
bh.niti.42.core_teaching: Good things are rarely lost in one blow; they wear away through specific neglects: bad advice, attachment, spoiling, not studying, bad company, drink, inattention, distance, coldness, misconduct and carelessness.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Draws the lessons: a king should take good counsel, an ascetic avoid attachment, a son not be over-pampered, the wise avoid bad company and drink, farming be watched, friendship tended, wealth guarded from unworthy recipients.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'saṅga' as attachment to objects of sense, since detachment is the ascetic's whole aim.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the last clause as wealth dissipated by misdirected charity or careless expenditure.

bh.niti.42.practical_reading: A maintenance checklist for a life: friendships need warmth, relationships need presence, money needs attention, children need limits, and judgement needs good advisers.
misreadings: 'Affection is lost by living away' is an observation about neglect, not a verdict that migrants' families stop loving them.
Not an endorsement of harsh parenting; the tradition's maxim about beating children should not be carried over.
cautions: Ramachandra Budhendra supports 'spoiling ruins a son' with a maxim recommending beating over pampering; do not reproduce that in a modern reading.
The distance clause may sting readers living abroad or in long-distance relationships.
not_for: someone abroad who already feels guilty about distance from family
a parent grieving a child who went astray (the 'bad son ruins a family' clause)
speaks_to: parents thinking about indulgence and limits
people managing money or a small business

bh.niti.43.context: In the section on wealth, following the list of ways good things are lost. It names the only three ways wealth can go and warns the hoarder.
bh.niti.43.core_teaching: Wealth will leave you one way or another: by giving, by using, or by loss. Whoever neither gives nor uses it chooses loss by default.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Giving to the worthy is the best exit, one's own enjoyment the middle, loss to thieves the worst. He quotes a verse: dharma, fire, king and thief are wealth's four heirs; slight the eldest, dharma, and the others take it.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Wealth should be given and enjoyed, otherwise it is destroyed through theft and the like.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the three as charity, enjoyment and destruction, the conditions to which wealth is subject.

bh.niti.43.practical_reading: Teachers use it against hoarding and anxious saving with no purpose: plan to give and to use what you have, or circumstances will decide for you.
misreadings: Not a case against saving for needs, emergencies or dependants; the target is the miser who neither gives nor uses.
Not a licence for extravagance.
not_for: someone who has just lost savings to fraud or disaster (it can sound like blame)
a reader in poverty
speaks_to: people who never let themselves enjoy what they earn

bh.niti.45.context: In the section on wealth. Ramachandra Budhendra reads the subject as a rich man fallen into poverty who longs for a handful of grain and, rich again, looks on the earth as straw. The conclusion: the size of things depends on our state.
bh.niti.45.core_teaching: Need makes small things great and plenty makes great things small; values are not fixed in things but in our condition.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: A wealthy man ruined by fate longs for a handful of barley; enriched again, intoxicated by money, he thinks the whole earth straw. Nothing is great or small by itself; one's state enlarges or shrinks things.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Nothing has a fixed weight or lightness; things grow or shrink in importance with people's circumstances, as the poor man craves half a handful of grain and the rich man thinks the world dry grass.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Reports Telang's explanation: since the same things are thought great or small in different states of life, it is the state that makes them appear so.

bh.niti.45.practical_reading: Remember when little things felt like everything; that memory guards against contempt when life is full, and against despair when it is lean.
misreadings: Not saying poverty and wealth are equal; it is about perception.
not_for: someone currently hungry or destitute, for whom it may sound like philosophising

bh.niti.46.context: In the section on wealth, a piece of statecraft addressed to a king. The earth is compared to a cow and the people to its calf; Ramachandra Budhendra stresses that the comparison is a simile, and that without caring for the people the king will get no wealth.
bh.niti.46.core_teaching: A ruler who wants prosperity must first nourish the people; cared-for people make the land fruitful.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Addresses the king: if you want to milk the earth for wealth, nourish the people like the calf; well cared for, the land yields grain and riches. Caring for them is necessary for every gain.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Heads it 'all aims are achieved only by caring for the people': just as nourished cattle give generously, the jewel-bearing earth gives when the people are well protected.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Notes that the earth-cow image is common (go means both cow and earth) and compares the Raghuvamsha on King Dilipa milking the earth for sacrifices.

bh.niti.46.practical_reading: Managers, parents and community leaders apply it directly: invest in people's wellbeing before asking for output.
misreadings: Not a licence to treat people as resources to be milked; the verse's frank revenue logic should be softened into care.
cautions: The image is instrumental (feed the calf so you can milk the cow); keep the emphasis on nourishing.
not_for: an employee feeling exploited (it may read as their boss's playbook)

bh.niti.49.context: In the section on wealth. Ramachandra Budhendra introduces it: do not be abject in wanting to get, since gain and loss rest on what is destined. The pot-and-water image closes the argument.
bh.niti.49.core_teaching: Grovelling before the rich does not increase what you get; keep your composure and dignity. The verse grounds this in the idea that one's portion is fixed.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Brahma's writing gives the same in the desert as on golden Meru. So be steady; abjectness before the wealthy earns only blame, never more money. A pot takes the same water from well or ocean.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Whatever is written in one's fortune is obtained anyway and more is unreachable even with great effort, so be steady and do not show neediness to the rich.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as predestination of one's share, with enjoyment proportioned to one's capacity, like the pot.

bh.niti.49.practical_reading: Keep your self-respect with wealthy clients, relatives or bosses; flattery and desperation rarely change the outcome, and they cost you.
misreadings: Not an argument against effort or ambition, nor a justification of poverty or inequality as 'written'.
Our line wisely keeps the dignity and drops the fatalism; the fate premise should not be pressed on a reader.
cautions: Built on fatalism ('it is written on your forehead'); can feel dismissive to someone struggling economically or facing injustice.
not_for: someone in poverty or debt
victims of wage theft or discrimination (fate framing excuses injustice)
speaks_to: someone tempted to flatter a rich relative or client

bh.niti.51.context: Closes the section on wealth in the North Indian order. It follows a verse addressed to the cloud as the chataka's only support; now the poet turns to the chataka, the bird said to drink only rain, and advises it not to plead before every cloud.
bh.niti.51.core_teaching: Not everyone who looks powerful will actually help; choose carefully whom you ask, and do not humble yourself before everyone.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: As the chataka should not beg every cloud, since some only thunder, a person in need should not ask whoever seems a giver; test first, then make your request known.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates: the clouds are not all such that a supplication should be addressed to them; some wet the earth, others roar for nothing.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Treats verses 50 and 51 as a dialogue between the chataka and the cloud, with the moral in the last line: do not plead before everyone.

bh.niti.51.practical_reading: When asking for jobs, loans, mentorship or help, put your energy into the people who actually come through; do not spend your dignity on those who only make noise.
misreadings: Not advice never to ask for help.
Not a reason to judge all who decline as 'empty clouds'.
not_for: someone who has run out of people to ask (it may feel like 'stop asking')
speaks_to: someone repeatedly let down by promises
deciding whom to ask for help

bh.niti.53.context: Opens the Nitishatakam's portrait of wicked people right after the list of their marks (cruelty, causeless quarrels, envy of the good and of relatives). It is followed by the verse on how the wicked brand every virtue as a vice.
bh.niti.53.core_teaching: Talent or learning does not make a harmful person safe; judge people by how they treat others and keep your distance from those who harm.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, notes (1902 ed., Niti 53)
commentaries.gist: Explains the old belief that a certain kind of serpent carries a jewel in its crest that shines at night; records Telang's note that the verse is attributed to Chanakya and appears in older anthologies.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation and notes (1886, Niti 53)
commentaries.gist: Renders it plainly (avoid an evil man though learned; a jewelled snake is no less feared) and cross-references the Hitopadesha.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 27)
commentaries.gist: Core verse.

bh.niti.53.practical_reading: If someone who keeps hurting you is admired for their brilliance or charm, give yourself permission to step back anyway; distance is a reasonable response to harm.
misreadings: It means keeping distance from people who harm you, not labelling everyone who annoys you.
Not contempt for learning or talent.
cautions: If the reader is in an abusive situation, the verse supports distance, but safety planning and support matter more than a verse; include a pointer to help.
not_for: ordinary disagreements with decent people
speaks_to: a charming or brilliant person who harms you

bh.niti.54.context: In the Nitishatakam's section on the wicked: right after the advice to avoid a learned but wicked man (53), the poet catalogues how spiteful people re-label each virtue as its nearest vice, and ends asking which virtue they have not stained.
bh.niti.54.core_teaching: Malicious critics can turn any virtue into a fault by renaming it; their verdict says more about them than about the person judged.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation and notes (1902 ed., Niti 54)
commentaries.gist: Explains that 'is counted as' must be supplied in each clause, and that muni here means a reserved, silent person; the verse asks what virtue the wicked have not stigmatised.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation and notes (1886, Niti 54)
commentaries.gist: Focuses on 'aṅkitaḥ', branded: the good's virtues are branded as vices by the evil-minded; compares a Greek proverb on the same idea.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 24)
commentaries.gist: Core verse; reads 'ṛjau vimatitā' (the honest are called stupid).

bh.niti.54.practical_reading: When someone's criticism of you is just your strength described unkindly (your calm called coldness, your care called weakness), name the trick and stop absorbing it.
misreadings: Not every criticism is spite; it is a tool for recognising malice, not for dismissing fair feedback.
cautions: Avoid encouraging the reader to label everyone who criticises them as wicked.
not_for: someone who needs to hear honest correction

bh.niti.55.context: Placed at the turn between the section on the wicked and the section on the good, it works as a hinge: a balance sheet of what makes all other faults or merits redundant. It follows the verse on honour and precedes the 'seven thorns in my mind' verse.
bh.niti.55.core_teaching: One inner quality outweighs a pile of outward ones: greed and slander are enough to spoil a person, while truthfulness and a clean mind already do the work that penance and pilgrimage are meant to do.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Greed alone is enough blame; backbiting leads to ruin like the gravest sins; truth purifies more than fasts; a mind free of malice is the root of liberation, so pilgrimage adds nothing. Conclusion: work to acquire good qualities.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: A ranking: no flaw beyond greed, no sin above slander, no penance above truth; learning is the chief wealth and ill fame hurts worse than death. So drop greed and take up truth.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Links the last clause to the Roman ideal of preferring death to dishonour (Horace on Regulus), i.e. a classical honour-code sentiment.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Calls greed the greatest evil because most others spring from it; on goodness of heart, says courteous conduct wins over strangers, so such a person never lacks kin.

bh.niti.55.practical_reading: Use it as an audit: before adding rituals, good causes or possessions, check the one inner thing that would make them pointless (greed, gossip) or unnecessary (honesty, a clean mind).
misreadings: Not a dismissal of pilgrimage or practice as such; the verse ranks inner purity above them.
The last clause ('if disgrace, what need of death') is rhetoric about honour, never a suggestion that a disgraced person is better dead.
cautions: Last clause equates disgrace with death; avoid for anyone facing public shame, scandal, exam failure or job loss, and never quote it alone. Our misuse line already flags this; keep it.
not_for: anyone living through public humiliation or with suicidal thoughts
someone being shamed by their community
speaks_to: someone tempted to buy their way to virtue with rituals or donations
a person trying to stop gossiping
someone wanting a simple inner checklist

bh.niti.57.context: In the section on the wicked, among verses about the dangers of court life. It is followed directly by the famous verse on how hard service to a master is (silent servants are called dumb, talkative ones forward).
bh.niti.57.core_teaching: A person ruled by fierce anger has no one truly close: like fire, they hurt even those who serve and feed them.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: No one counts as their own for violently angry kings; even someone who serves them well will be burned, as fire burns the sacrificer who touches it. Therefore such a king should not be served.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Everyone fears a hot-tempered ruler, so none is his own; heads it 'the harm of anger' and draws the lesson that a ruler should not be fierce in temper.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as no one being a favourite of fiercely angry kings, with fire burning the sacrificer who touches it; takes the sacrificer in a general sense.

bh.niti.57.practical_reading: Two directions: if you have a temper, notice that it pushes away the very people who look after you; if you work or live near someone like that, it names why loyalty does not make you safe.
misreadings: Not a reason to stay close to a volatile person in the hope that devotion will protect you.
Not a claim that the people who get burned deserved it.
cautions: Can describe an abusive household or boss; for a reader in that situation, pair it with practical safety and support, not acceptance.
not_for: someone being told to tolerate an abusive partner or parent
speaks_to: someone whose temper is costing them relationships
a leader reflecting on how their anger lands

bh.niti.58.context: From the Nitishatakam's group of verses on wicked or difficult people (Wortham's section 52-61). Just before, the poet lists 'seven thorns' in his heart, including a wicked man at court, and warns that an angry king has no friends. This verse describes the courtier's or servant's trap: every way of behaving is twisted into a fault.
bh.niti.58.core_teaching: When you serve someone powerful, any behaviour can be read as a fault; the problem lies in the position, not necessarily in you.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation and notes (1902 ed., Niti 58)
commentaries.gist: Calls service the hardest thing even for sages; notes that yogis are credited with superhuman insight through contemplation, yet even they cannot fathom it; 'apragalbha' means timid.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation and notes (1886, Niti 58)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as rules of behaviour impossible to learn even for an ascetic, and records that the verse also appears in the Hitopadesha.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 35)
commentaries.gist: Core verse; same text in substance ('dhṛṣṭaḥ pārśve...').

bh.niti.58.practical_reading: If every choice you make at work gets criticised, recognise the double bind for what it is; stop trying to find the one 'right' behaviour and anchor in your own standard.
misreadings: Not a claim that all feedback from a manager is unfair.
Not advice to stop trying; it describes a structural bind.
cautions: Can feed cynicism about authority if used alone; pair with a constructive step.
not_for: someone receiving fair, specific feedback they need to hear
speaks_to: feeling nothing you do is right at work
being judged whichever way you act

bh.niti.60.context: Near the end of the section on the wicked: having described the wicked, the poet contrasts their friendship with the friendship of the good, just before the next verse on deer, fish and the good being harassed by hunters, fishermen and slanderers for no reason.
bh.niti.60.core_teaching: Judge a friendship by its direction, not its start: the false kind opens big and shrinks, the true kind starts small and keeps growing.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Forenoon shadow is long and shrinks; afternoon shadow is short and grows. So the friendship of the wicked begins large and wanes, that of the good begins slight and increases; a sensible person should act on this.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Explains the two shadows the same way and draws the plain rule: make friends with the good, not with the wicked.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Calls it a clever picture of friendship as found in the world: insincere friendship is most demonstrative at the start, good friendship hardly visible at first but steadily increasing.

bh.niti.60.practical_reading: Be slow to trust intense early warmth, and patient with quiet friendships that seem modest now; watch which way each one is moving over months.
misreadings: Not a claim that every friendship that starts warmly is false.
Not a reason to write off a friend after one cold patch.
not_for: someone isolated and lonely who might hear it as 'distrust anyone friendly'
speaks_to: someone hurt by a friendship that burned bright and faded
a new arrival in a city or job making friends
someone doubting a slow, steady friendship

bh.niti.62.context: Opens the section on the good (sujana-paddhati) in both the northern and the southern ordering, right after the verses on the wicked. It is a salutation to people who carry a list of qualities.
bh.niti.62.core_teaching: Goodness is a cluster of everyday habits (seeking good company, enjoying others' merits, humility before teachers, love of learning, faithfulness, devotion, self-mastery) and the people who carry them deserve honour.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Each quality is set against its opposite: longing for the company of the wise (a door to liberation, citing Yoga Vasishtha), joy in others' merits rather than fault-finding, humility to the teacher, faithfulness, devotion to Shiva as the supreme deity.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'strength in ātma-damana' as prowess when oneself is slighted, not indifference, quoting a saying that forbearance is the usual ornament but valour suits the moment of insult.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the self-mastery clause as power to restrain the mind; those who hold these qualities are truly great, to be saluted and imitated.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates it as a bow to people in whom the listed sterling qualities reside, including devotion to the trident-holder (Shiva) and strength to restrain the self.

bh.niti.62.practical_reading: Pick one item from the list (enjoying someone else's success, seeking better company, studying) and practise it this week; notice the people around you who already live it and honour them.
misreadings: Not a sectarian test; the devotion clause names Shiva, but the list is broadly ethical.
Self-mastery here is not self-suppression or swallowing mistreatment.
cautions: Includes 'love for one's own wife' and devotion to Shiva; render inclusively (faithfulness to one's partner) if used for a general reader.
not_for: someone using lists of virtues to judge themselves harshly
speaks_to: someone choosing role models or mentors
a student wanting a character checklist
someone trying to stop envying others

bh.niti.63.context: Second verse of the section on the good: after saluting good people, the poet lists the qualities that come to the great-souled by nature, each matched to its proper occasion.
bh.niti.63.core_teaching: Greatness shows as the right quality at the right time: steadiness when things go wrong, patience when they go right, clear speech among people, courage in a real fight, love of learning.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Pairs each quality with what it excludes: steadiness without dejection in trouble, patience without arrogance in prosperity, eloquence rather than silence in a learned court, valour rather than flight; all native to the great.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Gives word meanings and stresses that these are inborn characteristics of the great-souled, not traits put on for show.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the qualities and notes that the frequent mention of Vedic study in these poems suggests Bhartrihari was not a Buddhist.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Notes it also appears in the Hitopadesha and that the variant words for 'love of fame' carry the same sense.

bh.niti.63.practical_reading: Ask which situation you are in today, setback or success, and practise the matching virtue: steadiness for the first, restraint and patience for the second.
misreadings: 'Natural to the great' is not a claim that ordinary people cannot learn these qualities.
Courage 'in battle' is about rising to a real contest, not a licence for aggression.
not_for: someone in acute crisis who may hear 'the great are naturally steady' as a judgement on their distress
speaks_to: someone in a setback looking for steadiness
students and young professionals building character

bh.niti.64.context: In the section on the good. Its refrain 'who taught the good this sword's-edge vow?' echoes an earlier verse (Niti 28, the first asidhara-vrata), making this the second list of hard, quiet disciplines of good people.
bh.niti.64.core_teaching: Real goodness is a set of quiet asymmetries: hide your own kindnesses, announce others' kindness to you, welcome people warmly, stay humble when rich, and speak of others without contempt.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Secret giving bears greater fruit; rise to greet a visitor; after a favour stay silent (citing Manu, do not proclaim a gift); speak publicly of favours received, or you become ungrateful; talk of others without censure.
