commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Calls it a very hard rule of the good: giving without publicising, honouring guests, never mentioning one's own help but telling everyone of others', no pride in prosperity, never speaking scornfully of anyone.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Notes the sword-edge vow was proverbial for an extremely hard discipline (also explained as continence beside a young wife) and that the verse is quoted in the Kuvalayananda.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Explains 'upakṛti' as favours received from others, set against the kindness one has done oneself, and the sword-edge vow as a proverb for a near-impossible task.

bh.niti.64.practical_reading: Do one kind thing today and tell no one; publicly thank someone who helped you; notice whether your talk about absent people carries a hint of contempt.
misreadings: Not a ban on ever acknowledging one's own work (for instance, at a job review).
Secret giving is not secrecy about money from a spouse or family.
not_for: someone whose unpaid work is already invisible and unthanked (carers, homemakers); it may sound like 'stay invisible'
speaks_to: someone who wants recognition for their help
someone who wants to stop gossiping

bh.niti.66.context: A short couplet in the section on the good, on how the minds of the great respond to fortune and misfortune; it follows the verse on the natural ornaments of the great.
bh.niti.66.core_teaching: The great are gentle and generous when things go well, and unbreakably firm when things go badly; the usual human pattern (hard in success, soft in trouble) is reversed.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: In prosperity their heart turns tender, never hard; in disaster it becomes hard as a rock pile, meaning their steadiness does not loosen. He quotes a verse describing the good as unshaken in danger and not puffed up in wealth.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: In good times the great are compassionate; in adversity they bear it with a heart hard like mountain rock.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Compares Proverbs on the righteous as an everlasting foundation and Horace's just man whom nothing shakes.

bh.niti.66.practical_reading: When things are good, let it make you kinder and more giving; when things are hard, let it make you firmer, not harder on others.
misreadings: Hardness in adversity is firmness of resolve, not coldness towards people or suppressing grief.
cautions: 'Be hard as rock in adversity' can be heard as 'don't feel'; for grief or distress, frame it as steadiness, not emotional shutdown.
not_for: someone in fresh grief who needs permission to be soft
speaks_to: someone in a tough stretch who needs to hold steady
someone newly comfortable who wants to stay kind

bh.niti.67.context: In the section on the good, on how surroundings shape character. Three fates of one drop of water illustrate the low, middling and high results of association.
bh.niti.67.core_teaching: The same drop vanishes, sparkles or becomes a pearl depending on where it lands; as a rule, people too become low, middling or excellent according to their company.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: On hot iron not even the water's name survives; on a lotus leaf it looks like a pearl without being one; in the oyster it becomes one. His text applies this to low, middling and best people.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: As a rule, low company makes one low and ruins one, middling company middling, best company best: this is the power of association.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Reads the three as an ascending scale of dispositions: one that leaves no result, one pleasing to look at, and one both beautiful and valuable.

bh.niti.67.practical_reading: Look at where you spend your hours and with whom; move a little of that time toward people and places that bring out your best.
misreadings: Not a licence to look down on people as 'hot iron'.
'Prāyeṇa' (as a rule) is a hedge: company shapes but does not wholly determine a person.
cautions: Can read as blaming people stuck in harsh environments; frame as encouragement to seek good company, not judgement of anyone's origins.
not_for: someone who cannot leave their environment (it may feel like a verdict)
speaks_to: a student or young adult choosing friends
someone leaving a toxic workplace or group
parents thinking about a child's company

bh.niti.68.context: In the section on the good: defines three relationships by their conduct rather than their title, and calls finding all three a reward of past merit. The following verse in the southern text and the friend-marks verse (Niti 73) take up the friend again.
bh.niti.68.core_teaching: A son, a wife or a friend is defined by how they act, not by the label; the real thing in each is rare and counted as a blessing earned by goodness.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: A son is one who pleases his father by obedience and good conduct, not merely one born; a wife one devoted to her husband's welfare; a friend one alike in trouble and prosperity. Only the meritorious gain all three.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: A virtuous son, a wife who seeks her husband's good and a friend with equal sympathy in joy and sorrow are obtained only through great merit.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the three definitions plainly and the close as only the meritorious securing this triad.

bh.niti.68.practical_reading: Our card uses only the friend line: be the friend who shows up the same way in someone's bad week as in their good one.
misreadings: Not a judgement that people without a good child, spouse or friend lack merit.
The wife clause is one-sided; do not use it to prescribe roles.
cautions: Ties having good family and friends to past merit; for someone estranged, widowed, childless or friendless it can sound like blame. Our record already restricts the card to the friend line; keep that.
not_for: someone estranged from family or in a difficult marriage
someone grieving a child or spouse
speaks_to: someone reflecting on what a real friend is

bh.niti.70.context: Closes the section on the good with a summary portrait built on paradoxes: rising by bowing, praising oneself by praising others, serving oneself by serving others, defeating slanderers by patience.
bh.niti.70.core_teaching: The good win by apparent reversals: humility lifts them, praising others reveals their own worth, working for others gets their own work done, and patience leaves slanderers exposed.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Humility itself is the cause of their rise; they reveal their virtues by praising others, never by self-praise; they achieve their ends by putting others' work first; they pain harsh speakers by forbearance alone, not by fierceness.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the third line as making the harsh-mouthed wicked ashamed by forgiveness alone; the good, of wondrous conduct, are honoured by all.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the third clause as censuring calumniators, whose mouths are noisy with harsh words of accusation, with their patience alone.

bh.niti.70.practical_reading: Next time you are criticised unfairly, try answering with calm and good work rather than a counter-attack; next time you want credit, give some away first.
misreadings: Patience with slander is not silence about abuse or harassment (our misuse line says this; keep it).
Not a strategy of fake humility to get ahead.
cautions: For someone being bullied or harassed, 'answer with patience' must not become 'put up with it'.
not_for: a victim of harassment or abuse
speaks_to: someone facing gossip or unfair criticism at work

bh.niti.71.context: Opens the section on helping others (paropakara-paddhati). Three natural images of fullness that bows down rather than puffing up.
bh.niti.71.core_teaching: Real abundance bends toward others: as fruit-laden trees and rain-heavy clouds hang low, the good become humbler as they prosper, because what they have is for giving.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Trees bow under fruit; clouds hang low to rain everywhere; the good, though prosperous, are not fierce. This is natural to benefactors, who do not count effort for others as hardship; quotes 'trees bear fruit for others'.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Trees, clouds and good men bend because their fruit, water and wealth exist for others, not themselves; humility is the innate dharma of those who help.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Notes the stanza also occurs in Kalidasa's Shakuntala with a minor variant ('āgamaiḥ' for 'udgamaiḥ').

bh.niti.71.practical_reading: Measure success by how much lower it lets you bend toward others: more patience, more listening, more sharing.
misreadings: Not an argument that the poor or struggling are less humble or less good.
speaks_to: someone who admires quiet, generous people

bh.niti.72.context: In the section on helping others, right after the verse on the humility of benefactors; it lists the true ornaments of a compassionate person. It echoes an earlier verse (Niti 65) on the ornaments of the great.
bh.niti.72.core_teaching: Each part of the body is truly adorned by its right use (the ear by learning, the hand by giving, the whole body by serving others), not by jewellery or perfume.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: The ear shines by hearing dharma teaching, not gold earrings; the hand by giving to the worthy, not a golden bracelet; the body by doing good, not musk-sandal paste. These natural ornaments last; jewellery perishes.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Learning, giving and service produce a lasting beauty in ear, hand and body that perishable earrings, bracelets and sandal paste cannot; so these are what the good collect.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Cross-refers to the earlier ornament verse and to the New Testament on inner rather than outward adornment.

bh.niti.72.practical_reading: Before dressing up for an occasion, ask what your hands, ears and time will actually do there: learn something, give something, help someone.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of jewellery or self-care; it ranks them below use.
speaks_to: someone caught up in appearance or status
a wedding or festival season reflection

bh.niti.73.context: In the section on helping others, a definition of the true friend (san-mitra-lakṣaṇa), placed among verses on benefactors. It answers the friend-line of Niti 68.
bh.niti.73.core_teaching: A true friend is known by six acts: checking your wrongs, steering you to good, keeping your secrets, speaking up for your strengths, staying in your trouble, and giving in time of need.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Turns you from sin by advice on dharma, urges you to good deeds, hides your secrets, proclaims your virtues, stays even in deep trouble, gives what is needed in calamity; cross-refers to Niti 68.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: A good friend stops harmful acts, sets you to beneficial ones, hides what should be hidden, publicises your merits, stays in adversity and supplies help when needed.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as the wise describing the marks of a true friend, including helping you in time of need.

bh.niti.73.practical_reading: Use it both ways: test one friendship against the six marks, and pick one mark to practise for a friend this week, such as telling someone else what you admire about them.
misreadings: Keeping secrets does not mean covering up harm or abuse; the first mark is stopping wrongdoing.
not_for: someone recently betrayed by a friend may find it painful; pair with gentleness
speaks_to: someone wondering if a friendship is real
someone who wants to be a better friend

bh.niti.75.context: In the section on helping others, a four-way classification of people by how they treat others' interests. The punchline is the last class, who destroy others' good for no gain at all.
bh.niti.75.core_teaching: People range from those who give up their own interest for others, to those who help when it costs them nothing, to those who harm others for gain, to those who harm others for no reason at all, the last being worse than any name.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Ranks them as best, middling, demon-like and a fourth group so far outside the three that they cannot be classed, the very lowest; advice: join the best class you can.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Gives the four grades in order (some good people, ordinary people, human-demons, and those we cannot even name) with word-by-word meanings.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the first class as the noblest, the second as men of the middle order, the third as demons in human form; we know not what to call the fourth.

bh.niti.75.practical_reading: An honest mirror: most of us live in the 'ordinary' band; the verse invites one step up, and a hard look at any harm we do out of spite or habit with nothing to gain.
misreadings: Not a licence to label people demons.
Being 'ordinary' (helping without self-harm) is not condemned.
cautions: Harsh language ('demons in human form'); for someone recently hurt by another person it can feed rage or rumination.
not_for: someone consumed by anger at a specific person
speaks_to: someone reflecting on their motives for helping
someone puzzled by pointless cruelty or trolling

bh.niti.76.context: In the section on helping others: a small kitchen parable explaining the friendship of the good, right after the four kinds of people and the marks of a true friend.
bh.niti.76.core_teaching: Good friends give each other what they have, cannot bear to see each other suffer, and are calmed only by being together again.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Milk gave water its sweetness and whiteness; water, unable to bear the milk's heating, sacrificed itself; milk rose to follow it into the fire and settled only when water was added. True friends cannot bear each other's pain.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Water, remembering the milk's gift of its qualities, burns itself away; milk then tries to leap into the fire and calms only when water is added. Good friends share qualities, bear hardship, and are healed by reunion.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Calls it a fine moral drawn from a kitchen fact: well-heated milk boils over, and adding water settles it.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as friends acting together against a common enemy, at the cost of their own lives, and cites a Hitopadesha line on water quenching fire.

bh.niti.76.practical_reading: Notice who has given you something of themselves; when they are under strain, show up, and when you are boiling over, let a friend's presence settle you.
misreadings: Not a call to self-destruction for a friend; the image is mutual care, not martyrdom.
cautions: The image of 'offering itself into fire' can be heard as self-sacrifice; avoid for someone in a codependent or self-erasing relationship.
not_for: someone in a codependent relationship
someone grieving a friend's death (the reunion image may sting)
speaks_to: someone grateful for a close friend
someone missing a friend who has moved away

bh.niti.78.context: Near the end of the section on helping others: a run of twelve imperatives summing up the conduct of the good, before the verse asking how many such people there really are.
bh.niti.78.core_teaching: Goodness is a daily practice of small decisions: let go of craving and pride, forgive, tell the truth, learn from the wise, respect those who deserve it, reach out even to opponents, guard your name, and be kind to anyone in pain.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Gives each command a reason: cut craving with dispassion or hope's ropes bind you; forgive insults or temper wrecks your work; win over enemies, citing the Gita's evenness to foe and friend, or they exploit your weak spots.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'praśraya' as humility toward teachers and elders, to be made visible, and 'guard your good name' as making one's birth worthwhile.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Lists these as the very form of good conduct and human duty; renders the enemy clause as keeping even enemies content.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates with the variant 'do not parade your good qualities' and discusses the grammar of the imperatives.

bh.niti.78.practical_reading: Choose one of the twelve for today (for example, one kind act for someone suffering, or one conciliatory message to someone you are at odds with).
misreadings: Winning over an enemy is not tolerating harm (our misuse line; keep it).
'Guard your good name' is not image management at the cost of honesty.
cautions: Forbearance and conciliation should not be pressed on someone in an abusive situation.
not_for: a victim of abuse being urged to 'win over' the abuser
speaks_to: someone wanting a daily practice list
someone struggling with craving or ambition

bh.niti.79.context: Closes the section on helping others in the southern text. A portrait of the rare good person, ending in the question 'how many are there?'.
bh.niti.79.core_teaching: The rarest goodness is consistent in thought, word and deed, and magnifies the smallest good in others while rejoicing inwardly at it; such people are few.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Devoted to good acts with all three instruments (mind, speech, body); they enlarge even others' tiny virtues and are glad at heart; 'how many' means few, since such qualities are uncommon.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Such people, full of the nectar of good deeds and delighted by others' small merits, can be counted on one's fingers.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Reads the question as expecting the answer 'but few', comparing the Gita's 'among thousands, scarcely one strives for perfection'.

bh.niti.79.practical_reading: Turn the usual habit around: today, make a mountain out of someone's small good deed (say it aloud, thank them) and a molehill of their small fault.
misreadings: Not a claim that good people do not exist; it says they are rare and precious.
speaks_to: someone wanting to appreciate others more

bh.niti.8.context: In the section on fools, after verses on the impossibility of pleasing the conceited, the speaker turns the charge on himself: he too was blind with pride when he knew a little. The cure was learning, bit by bit, in the presence of the wise.
bh.niti.8.core_teaching: Pride grows from knowing a little; real contact with deeper knowledge shows how much one does not know, and that recognition dissolves pride as a fever breaks.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Cites the maxim 'little learning, great pride' and the Upanishadic idea that one who has a teacher truly knows. Whoever knowing little thinks himself all-knowing is the fool; whoever knowing much counts himself a fool is wise.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Plain sense: with a little knowledge I strutted like a rutting elephant; once I began learning from scholars I saw I was a fool, and the pride left like a fever.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Notes the double meaning of mada (rut and vanity) and disagrees with Telang's reading: people are puffed up by little knowledge, not great.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Reports Telang's view that 'knowing a little' is the speaker's later judgment: when I knew what I now see was only a little.

bh.niti.8.practical_reading: A model of honest self-correction: the sign that you are learning is that you feel less certain; seek out people who know more than you and let them deflate you.
misreadings: Not a call to self-contempt; 'I am a fool' is the healthy recognition that ends arrogance, not a verdict on one's worth.
cautions: Readers with low self-esteem may hear 'I am a fool' literally; emphasise the relief of the fever breaking.
not_for: someone in acute shame or self-criticism
a reader who already feels stupid
speaks_to: students moving from beginner confidence to real study
anyone humbled by a mentor or a new field

bh.niti.81.context: Opens the Nitishatakam's section in praise of constancy (Wortham: 'With this sloka begins the section on the praise of firmness'). It recalls the churning of the ocean: the gods kept churning past the precious jewels that surfaced and past the deadly poison until the nectar came up. The next verses describe the steadfast person indifferent to hard ground or soft couch, and unmoved by praise or blame.
bh.niti.81.core_teaching: The steadfast are neither distracted by early rewards nor scared off by early dangers; they keep going until the real goal is reached.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation and notes (1902 ed., Niti 80)
commentaries.gist: Explains that thirteen precious things came up before nectar, the fourteenth; points to the churning story in the Ramayana (Bala-kanda) and Bhagavata (book 8).

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation and notes (1886, Niti 80)
commentaries.gist: Notes this verse opens the section on firmness; renders the gods as not turned aside by pearls of great price or fear of poison.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 52)
commentaries.gist: Core verse; same text in substance.

bh.niti.81.practical_reading: When a resolve produces an early win or an early scare, treat both as stages of the churning; ask what the 'nectar' was and keep going toward that.
misreadings: Steadiness is not refusing to reassess a goal.
Not glorifying pushing through genuine danger to health.
cautions: The 'poison' stage can be read as 'ignore warning signs'; keep the reassessment caveat.
not_for: someone whose goal is harming them and who needs permission to stop
speaks_to: not settling for an early partial reward
persisting through a scary middle stage

bh.niti.82.context: In the section on steadfastness (dhairya-paddhati), right after the verse on the gods who kept churning the ocean despite jewels and poison until they got the nectar. It portrays the person of spirit who is indifferent to comfort while pursuing a goal.
bh.niti.82.core_teaching: Someone fully committed to a purpose stops keeping score of comfort and discomfort; floor or bed, plain or fine food, rags or silk, all are equal next to the work.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Whether on hard ground or a soft couch, plain greens or rich food, rags or golden robes, the high-minded seeker of a goal counts neither pain nor pleasure but stays even while pursuing the work.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: A person bent on accomplishing a task with a firm mind sleeps on thorny ground or a soft bed as place and time require and takes whatever food or clothing comes; only the goal matters.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Compares Gita 2.15: the steady person unmoved by these contacts, the same in pain and pleasure, is fit for immortality.

bh.niti.82.practical_reading: In a demanding season (exams, a start-up, caring for someone), let go of comparing your comforts with what you had or what others have; keep your eye on the purpose.
misreadings: Not a glorification of neglecting sleep, food or health.
Not a reason to impose hardship on others who did not choose the goal.
cautions: Can feed hustle culture; for someone near burnout, pair with rest (see Niti 86 misuse line).
not_for: someone burnt out or neglecting health
someone in poverty not by choice (it may romanticise hardship)
speaks_to: founders and people in demanding projects
someone adjusting to a drop in lifestyle

bh.niti.83.context: Closes the section on steadfastness in the southern text; in the northern order it sits among the steadfastness verses. It pairs eight strengths with the quality that makes each beautiful, then crowns character as the ornament of all.
bh.niti.83.core_teaching: Every strength has a matching restraint that makes it admirable (power with courtesy, courage with few words, learning with humility, wealth with wise giving, authority with forgiveness), and character underlies them all.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Contrasts each ornament with its spoiling opposite: courtesy not wickedness in lordship, measured speech not rambling in a hero, humility not arrogance in learning, giving to the worthy not to flatterers in wealth; character outranks them all.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: Glosses each pair word by word: courtesy adorns prosperity, measured use of speech adorns valour, calm adorns knowledge, humility adorns learning, using wealth for a worthy recipient adorns money.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates restraint over the senses as the ornament of learning and good character as 'the root of all' and the ornament of all things.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Renders the last line as natural disposition, parent of the virtues in each, being the highest ornament.

bh.niti.83.practical_reading: Name your main strength (skill, money, authority, knowledge) and practise its matching restraint today: the expert listens, the boss forgives, the strong one speaks less.
misreadings: 'Forgiveness adorns the powerful' does not ask the powerless to forgive abuse.
speaks_to: new managers and people with authority

bh.niti.84.context: In the section on steadfastness, after the verses on the person of spirit indifferent to comfort. It names the four great pressures (opinion, fortune, life, time) and says none moves the steadfast off the just path.
bh.niti.84.core_teaching: The steadfast do not let praise or blame, gain or loss, or even the timing of death decide their conduct; they hold to what is right.

commentaries.who: Ramachandra Budhendra (Sanskrit tika, southern recension; Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1914)
commentaries.gist: Whether the shrewd blame or praise, wealth comes or freely goes, death comes now or in another age, the steadfast do not move a single footstep from the just path; that path, not opinion, is their highest aim.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: The firm-minded do not care for blame or praise, whether wealth is gained or not, or even death; they never stray from the just path and do only what is just.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates the steadfast ('persons of mental calibre') as not swerving from the path of justice whatever politicians say or wealth does.

bh.niti.84.practical_reading: Before a hard decision, set aside what people will say and what it will cost you, and ask only what is right; then take one step on that path.
misreadings: Not stubbornness: 'the right path' is justice, not one's own opinion.
Not contempt for feedback.
cautions: Mentions death ('let death come today'); fine as resolve, but avoid for a reader with suicidal thoughts or fresh bereavement.
not_for: someone in fresh grief or with thoughts of death
someone being rigid who needs to hear others
speaks_to: whistle-blowers and people under pressure to cut corners
someone facing criticism for a principled choice
someone tempted by money to compromise

bh.niti.85.context: In the Kale/Wortham ordering it is in the section on steadfastness, just after a verse about fate (the rat and the snake). It offers a counterweight: for good people, setbacks tend not to last.
bh.niti.85.core_teaching: Like a ball that bounces back when struck down, people of good conduct usually recover; their misfortunes tend not to last.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Notes the double meaning: applied to the ball the word means well-rounded, applied to people it means those whose conduct is well regulated; translates the close as the misfortunes of the virtuous being generally evanescent.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham (1886 translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Credits Telang with pointing out the pun on 'sādhu-vṛtta' and compares a related verse about the good falling like a ball.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi (1948 critical edition: textual status)
commentaries.gist: Group II, no. 270: a stanza whose authenticity there is reason to doubt; a close variant (no. 276) contrasts the noble, who rebounds like a ball, with the ignoble, who falls like clay.

bh.niti.85.practical_reading: After a setback, ask what helps you bounce: your habits, values and relationships ('being well-rounded') are what let you rise again.
misreadings: Not a promise that suffering is always short (our misuse line; keep it).
Not a claim that people whose hardship lasts must lack virtue.
cautions: Implies good people recover quickly; for chronic illness, long grief or long unemployment it can sound like blame. 'Prāyeṇa' (as a rule) must be kept in any reading.
not_for: chronic illness or disability
long or complicated grief
someone in a prolonged crisis
speaks_to: someone after a recent setback (exam, job, breakup)

bh.niti.86.context: In the northern order it comes in the steadfastness/fate stretch, right after the ball verse, as a counter to fatalism: whatever fate does, effort is the friend that keeps you from sinking.
bh.niti.86.core_teaching: The worst enemy is the inertia inside us, and the best friend is steady effort; one who keeps working does not go under.

commentaries.who: Janardana Shastri Pandey (Sanskrit vyakhya and Hindi bhasharth, Motilal Banarsidass 1974)
commentaries.gist: External enemies spoil one's work, but sloth is an enemy inside the body, so how could success come? Effort helps like a kinsman, since one who works can hope for results; so abandon sloth and stay industrious.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale (1902 edition: English translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Translates sloth as a dreadful enemy in the body and industriousness as the friend by which one is never ruined; notes a rhetorical flaw in the second line's construction.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi (1948 critical edition: textual status)
commentaries.gist: Group II, no. 216 (doubtful authenticity), reading 'having made which one does not sink'.

bh.niti.86.practical_reading: When stuck, do the smallest next action rather than waiting to feel ready; effort, even small, is the friend that gets you moving.
misreadings: Rest is not laziness; burnout needs rest, not more effort (our misuse line; keep it).
Not a judgement on people with depression, illness or disability whose low energy is not sloth.
cautions: For a reader with depression or chronic fatigue, 'laziness is your enemy' can deepen shame; frame as gentle small steps.
not_for: someone depressed or burnt out
someone with chronic illness or fatigue
speaks_to: someone restarting after a long pause

bh.niti.87.context: In Wortham's arrangement this verse belongs to the section on the Power of Fate (84-93), not the section on constancy (80-83): it follows the fable of the rat and the starving snake, the ball that bounces back, and the line that idleness is the great enemy, and is followed by Indra's defeat despite all his advantages. It is the hopeful counterweight inside that fate section.
bh.niti.87.core_teaching: Loss and decline in nature are followed by regrowth; remembering this cycle keeps the good from being consumed by their misfortunes, even when they feel them.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation and notes (1902 ed., Niti 87)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the verb for the moon as 'waxes, grows in bulk'; good men are not grieved when overpowered by difficulties.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 246)
commentaries.gist: Doubtful-block verse; critical text ends 'na vidhureṣu' (not in adversities).

bh.niti.87.practical_reading: On a bad day, look for one thing in your life that has already grown back after being cut down; let it remind you that this low phase is a phase.
misreadings: Not a promise that a particular person or relationship will return.
Not 'the wise feel nothing'; they feel it but are not consumed.
cautions: Used in 'someone-left': the renewal image is about fortunes, not people. Wortham's own note points out that Job and Horace apply the same image to say the dead do not return. Do not imply that someone who left or died will come back.
'Good people are not tormented' can sound like a judgement on a reader who is tormented; stress 'not consumed', not 'not affected'.
not_for: fresh bereavement read as 'they will come back'
someone who needs permission to grieve before hearing about regrowth
speaks_to: hope after loss of status or work

data_flags.translation_note: Our Sanskrit does not match the GRETIL text it cites. GRETIL reads 'kṣīṇo 'py upacīyate punaś candraḥ | ... santapyante na duḥkheṣu' (not consumed in their sorrows); Kosambi reads '... na vidhureṣu' (in misfortunes); Kale's translation ('not troubled in this world when plunged in misery')...

bh.niti.90.context: Sits in the run of verses on fate (daiva). Just before it, Indra loses a battle despite Brihaspati, the thunderbolt and Vishnu on his side (88); just after, a bald man who seeks shade under a palm is killed by a falling fruit (90). Between these fables of helplessness, this short verse concedes karma's hold and then insists on careful conduct. The verses praising action begin a few stanzas later.
bh.niti.90.core_teaching: What happens to us, and even the way our minds lean, is shaped by earlier deeds; that is no excuse. The wise still act only after careful deliberation.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Warns that the first half could suggest a person is wholly at the mercy of past deeds, but says thinkers hold one can shape one's future by present deeds; compares Gita 6.5 (raise yourself by yourself).

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the fruit as the pleasure or pain that deeds bring and sees an allusion to the traditional divisions of karma; renders the close as acting only after mature consideration.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Takes karma as acts done in a past life and links the verse to the following stanzas on merit stored from former births; otherwise grammatical notes.

bh.niti.90.practical_reading: Teachers use it to hold two truths together: you did not choose your starting conditions or even all your habits of mind, but you still owe the next decision your full attention.
misreadings: Not fatalism: 'tathāpi' (even so) turns the verse toward responsibility
Not a claim that people deserve what happens to them
cautions: The first line can sound like blaming a person's misfortune on their past deeds; do not apply it to someone's illness, loss or abuse
not_for: someone grieving or harmed, for whom 'karma' can sound like blame
a reader already paralysed by overthinking
speaks_to: feeling boxed in by circumstances or old patterns
after a setback, when tempted to stop thinking things through

bh.niti.93.context: Among the verses on the power of fate. Just before, the poet sees sun and moon seized by eclipse, elephants and snakes in bonds and wise men in poverty, and concludes fate is mighty (91). Just after, no one can wipe away what fate has written on the forehead (93). This verse turns the theme into a cry against a Creator who wastes his finest work.
bh.niti.93.core_teaching: A lament, not a lesson: fate creates a person of rare goodness, an ornament to the world, and then breaks them at once; the poet calls this folly.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Explains puruṣa-ratna as a jewel of a man endowed with every virtue; records a commentator who places the folly in creating such a person at all if he must soon be destroyed; notes the verse recurs in the Vairagyashataka.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Translates it as fate first producing an ornament of the earth and then making him short-lived, and exclaims at fate's folly; takes tāvat as emphatic, 'indeed creates'.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Prefers 'the jewel man' over 'a jewel-like man' and reads the opening as 'does indeed create, but then...'.

bh.niti.93.practical_reading: Used in grief writing to give permission to protest an early death instead of explaining it away; the poet does not console, he names the unfairness.
misreadings: Not a theological claim that God is foolish; it is a poet's lament inside a section on fate
Not a consolation; it gives no reason for the loss
cautions: Directly about the sudden death of an outstanding person; raw for fresh grief, especially an untimely death
Blaming the Creator may jar for devout readers
not_for: a reader who needs reassurance that loss has meaning
someone facing their own serious diagnosis, who may read it as a verdict
speaks_to: grief over someone taken too soon
anger at the unfairness of a loss
feeling the world wasted someone good

bh.niti.95.context: Opens the praise of action in Wortham's arrangement and answers the run of verses on fate just before it. The next verse bows to the karma that made Brahma toil like a potter, sent Vishnu through ten incarnations, made Shiva beg with a skull and keeps the sun circling. The argument climbs from gods to fate to deeds.
bh.niti.95.core_teaching: Gods answer to fate, and fate only delivers what deeds have earned, so the real power lies in deeds; the poet bows to karma, over which even fate has no say.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, tr. and notes (Bombay, 1902)
commentaries.gist: Notes the gods are finite, their rule ending with the aeon; fate has no arbitrary power and dispenses fruit strictly by men's actions; the poet distinguishes vidhi from karman; the figure is a climax.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Says Bhartrihari makes karma the thing on which even fate's course depends; translates the fruit as that of settled deeds done in a former state.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, tr. (London, 1886)
commentaries.gist: Places it at the head of 'The Praise of Action' and ends with adoration paid to works over which fate has no power.

bh.niti.95.practical_reading: Teachers use it to move attention from luck and divine favour to conduct: what you do is the one lever every other power must respect.
misreadings: Not irreverence toward the gods; it is a rhetorical ladder
Not a promise that present effort always wins; in the commentators' reading karma includes past deeds whose fruit is already fixed
cautions: Can feed self-blame if read as 'whatever happened to you, you caused'
not_for: someone suffering a loss they did not cause
a reader wrestling with guilt
speaks_to: feeling dependent on luck or other people's favour
wanting to take ownership of one's life

bh.vairagya.10.context: Our data places it at the close of the opening censure of craving. After the portraits of the ageing body (8-9), the poet gives an extended allegory: expectant craving is a river full of hazards that only pure-minded yogis cross.
bh.vairagya.10.core_teaching: Expectant craving is a dangerous river: fed by wishes, churned by longing, full of passions, doubts and delusion, it uproots fortitude; only yogis of pure mind reach the far shore and rejoice.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Reads vitarka as scheming thoughts of greed, the birds on the river, and dhairya-druma as the trees of patience and fortitude that it destroys.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Renders āśā as Desire: passions are the crocodiles, doubts the birds, infatuation the eddies, anxiety the steep banks; happy the pure-hearted ascetics who have crossed.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: His free version makes the yogis blissful because, with pure minds, they never crossed this river at all.

bh.vairagya.10.practical_reading: Used to map anxiety: each feature of the river (wishes, worry, doubt, attachment) names a mental habit to notice; helpful for people caught in rumination about outcomes.
misreadings: Not against hope in the sense of courage or faith; āśā here is grasping expectation
cautions: Our gloss 'a river called Hope' can mislead a reader in despair; make clear it means anxious expectation
not_for: someone in depression or despair who needs hope in the ordinary sense
readers in crisis
speaks_to: chasing a goal that keeps moving

bh.vairagya.100.context: The last verse of the Vairagyashataka in Madhavananda's (Nirnaya Sagar) order: after the yogi's longing for Himalayan samādhi with antelopes rubbing against him (98) and the plea to Shiva (99), the knower says goodbye to the five elements that made up his body.
bh.vairagya.100.core_teaching: At the end, the knower thanks earth, wind, fire, water and sky as family: through their company he gained merit and the clear knowledge that dispelled delusion, and now he merges into Brahman.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Says the endearing terms suit the blissful parting of a yogin who has passed through the subtle essences of the five elements in the stages of yogic practice.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Reads the sage as saying the elements nursed and helped him, since knowledge of Brahman is impossible without a body made of them; he takes leave with grateful recollection.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: take my last salutation; today I melt into Brahman, my heart purified and delusion gone through your good company.

bh.vairagya.100.practical_reading: Used as a model of a grateful farewell: thanking the body and the natural world for what they made possible.
misreadings: Not a wish to die; it is the culmination of a realised life
cautions: A farewell at death; moving at end of life or a funeral, but avoid for anyone expressing a wish to die
Rebirth/merging doctrine may not console every mourner
not_for: anyone with suicidal thoughts
fresh, raw grief where 'merging into Brahman' may sound dismissive
speaks_to: gratitude for the body and nature

bh.vairagya.12.context: In the section on the futility of trying to give up sense objects (viṣaya-parityāga-viḍambana). Just before, the poet finds even merit earned for heavenly pleasures frightening (11); just after, he marvels that the wise can drop wealth they actually enjoy while he cannot drop pleasures he only imagines (13).
bh.vairagya.12.core_teaching: Every pleasure and possession will leave us anyway; the only choice is whether we let go freely, which brings lasting peace, or have it torn away, which brings anguish.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Distinguishes two kinds of separation from pleasures, being left and renouncing; the peace that comes from having given them up is the difference; compares Gita 2.71.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Takes the stress on voluntary separation in the last line as the key, and compares the Gita's passage from 2.70 onward on the one who is not moved by desires.

commentaries.who: Madhavananda-style translation reproduced by Arunachala Ashrama
commentaries.gist: Adds that renouncing them oneself leads to the bliss of self-possession, while their tearing away greatly afflicts the mind.

bh.vairagya.12.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to possessions, status, youth and habits: practise letting go before life takes them, so that loss when it comes is less of a wound.
misreadings: About things and pleasures, not advice to leave people before they leave you
Not a reason to refuse enjoyment; the point is the grip
cautions: Read near a bereavement, 'let go before it is taken' can sound like blaming the mourner for grieving
not_for: fresh grief over a person
someone who has just lost a job or home involuntarily
speaks_to: downsizing, retirement, ageing out of a role
fear of losing what one has

bh.vairagya.18.context: In the Vairagyashatakam's section mocking our failure to give up pleasures. The verse before contrasts Shiva, master of himself even in union with Gauri, with sensualists who can neither enjoy pleasures nor let them go; the verse after says what we call happiness is only the relief of thirst, hunger and lust.
bh.vairagya.18.core_teaching: Unlike the moth and the fish, we see the danger in our cravings and still cling to them; this shows how deep delusion runs, not merely ignorance.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, translation with notes (1916, no. 18)
commentaries.gist: Renders the insect as not knowing the fire's burning power and the fish as ignorant of the hook, while we, with full discernment, keep desires full of dangers; calls the power of delusion inscrutable. Situates it between verses on Shiva's mastery and on pleasure as mere relief.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation (1902 ed., Vairagya 21)
commentaries.gist: Moth and fish act through ignorance; we who know better do not give up sense-objects complicated by a net of difficulties; infatuation is mysterious.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation (1886, Vairagya 21)
commentaries.gist: We know the entanglements fortune lays and still keep our desires, wandering in a thicket of error.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 160)
commentaries.gist: Core verse; reads 'māhātmyam'.

bh.vairagya.18.practical_reading: Pick one craving you already know is bad for you and name it honestly; knowing is not enough, so add one small practical barrier between you and it.
misreadings: Not a claim that all desire is bad.
Not a reason for self-contempt; the poet includes himself in 'we'.
cautions: Can feed shame for someone struggling with addiction or compulsive behaviour; frame it as a shared human pattern and point to real help where needed.
not_for: someone in active addiction crisis as a stand-alone message
speaks_to: knowing something is bad for you and doing it anyway

bh.vairagya.19.context: In the section on the futility of giving up sense objects: after the moth and the fish who do not know their danger (18), and before the man with mansions, sons, wealth and a loving wife who thinks the world permanent (20).
bh.vairagya.19.core_teaching: What we call pleasure is mostly relief: drinking when thirsty, eating when hungry, embracing when desire burns. People mistake the cure of a disease for happiness itself.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Says the point is that worldly happiness is a temporary remedy for the diseases of worldly life; once that is seen, one stops chasing it and seeks lasting peace in renunciation.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders the last line as mistaking the mere cure of pain for pleasure itself, and notes Tawney compares a passage in Plato's Republic.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses viparyasyati as thinking wrongly, misunderstanding; translates the meal as rice with vegetables and condiments.

bh.vairagya.19.practical_reading: A tool for noticing that much 'pleasure' is just the ending of discomfort; useful for examining cravings like snacking, scrolling or shopping that relieve an itch rather than satisfy.
misreadings: Not saying eating, drinking or marital love are sinful
Not a call to deny the body its needs
cautions: Mentions meat and sexual desire; our line rightly keeps only the thirst image for general readers
not_for: someone with an eating disorder (food as 'disease' framing)
a reader in physical hardship or hunger

bh.vairagya.21.context: In the section censuring begging and servility (yācñā-dainya-dūṣaṇa). The next verses call the belly the root of all humiliation (22) and say a proud man would sooner wander a forest or beg in a holy city than plead among his equals (23).
bh.vairagya.21.core_teaching: Self-respect would never let a man beg for his own sake; only the sight of his hungry family drives him to ask, with a choking voice, for help.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as no self-respecting man saying 'give me' for his own petty stomach, in a voice faltering for fear of refusal, if he did not see his wife and children suffering.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: States the sense plainly: a strong-minded man would not go about begging but for the state of his family; it is they who compel him.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Explains the broken, choked syllables and notes a commentator's analysis of the compound; translates 'his accursed stomach'.

bh.vairagya.21.practical_reading: Speaks to the humiliation of asking for money, loans or favours for one's family, and honours the love that swallows pride.
misreadings: Not contempt for people who ask for help
Not a teaching that providing is only a man's role
cautions: Vivid picture of hungry crying children and a wife in rags; painful for readers in poverty or debt
Gendered household roles
not_for: someone in acute financial crisis looking for hope (the verse offers none)
readers sensitive to gender roles
speaks_to: a parent swallowing pride to ask for help
job loss, debt, borrowing from relatives

bh.vairagya.29.context: In our data's section on begging and servility (the Nirnaya Sagar order). Madhavananda's nearby verses praise forest food and the begging bowl over flattering the rich (26-30).
bh.vairagya.29.core_teaching: Contented people already have unbroken joy and greedy people are never satisfied, so a mountain of gold helps no one; the poet does not want it.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Explains that Meru, the fabled gold mountain, serves no one: the contented are happy without it and the greedy are never satisfied; its gold glorifies only itself, so the poet will not covet it.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reports that the Sharngadhara Paddhati ascribes the stanza to Vidyapati; discusses how the closing question should be construed.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Translates: for whose sake was Meru, so full of wealth, created, since its golden splendour is confined to itself; finds part of the last sentence superfluous.

bh.vairagya.29.practical_reading: Used to question hoarding: wealth that sits unused helps neither the content (who do not need it) nor the greedy (who are never filled).
misreadings: Not a condemnation of earning; the target is greed and hoarded wealth
cautions: Low risk; mild reproach of the greedy
not_for: someone in real poverty, for whom 'wealth helps no one' may ring false

data_flags.translation_note: First half is fine. The second half is garbled: the Sanskrit asks for whose sake the Creator made Meru, that great store of riches whose golden glory stays within itself, and ends 'Meru does not please me' (Madhavananda, Wortham, Joglekar). Ours ('for whom did fate...

bh.vairagya.3.context: One of the opening verses that censure craving (tṛṣṇā-dūṣaṇa). Verse 2 lists hard travel, servility and eating at others' doors; this verse lists treasure-hunting, alchemy, sea voyages, courting kings and graveyard rites; verse 4 adds smiling through tears before the rich. Each ends by speaking directly to Desire.
bh.vairagya.3.core_teaching: A catalogue of everything done for gain, even occult shortcuts, ends with nothing gained; the poet tells his own craving to be content now and let him go.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Footnotes the cremation-ground nights as part of secret rites by which people invoked supernatural agencies to obtain riches.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Notes that fortunes are still wrecked by alchemy, that power through incantation was a common chase, and that the cremation ground on full-moon or eclipse nights was the usual place for it.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Takes the opening as digging because one suspects treasure is there, and weighs Ramarshi's glosses on the smelting phrase, finding one strained.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: In his free rendering the worthless cowrie becomes a cowrie 'of blessedness', giving the futility a spiritual edge.

bh.vairagya.3.practical_reading: Speaks to the exhaustion of chasing money through scheme after scheme (speculation, quick-rich plans, endless side ventures) and to the moment of finally saying 'enough' to the wanting itself.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of honest work or ambition as such
Not a claim that effort never pays
cautions: Mentions cremation-ground rites; harmless but may need a gloss
not_for: someone struggling to meet basic needs, for whom 'enough craving' can sound contemptuous
a young person who needs encouragement to work
speaks_to: burnout after years of chasing money
losses from risky schemes or speculation

bh.vairagya.31.context: Opens the section on the instability of enjoyments (bhoga-asthairya). Just before, the begging bowl is praised as free of every anxiety (30); just after, the poet lists how each good thing is preyed on by something else, birth by death and youth by age (32).
bh.vairagya.31.core_teaching: Every good thing we hold (pleasure, family, wealth, honour, strength, beauty, learning, virtue, the body) carries its own fear of loss; only dispassion is without fear.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates each pair plainly and ends that all things of this world pertaining to man are attended with fear; renunciation alone stands for fearlessness.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Discusses the 'silence' versus 'honour' readings, finding reticence a virtue that does not belong in this list; renders the close as asceticism alone free from danger.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Notes the 'silence' reading breaks the stanza's symmetry, so 'honour' is better: where there is a high sense of one's greatness there is danger of misery.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely as a litany ending: all in this life is fraught with fear; renunciation alone is fearless.

bh.vairagya.31.practical_reading: Teachers use it to show that anxiety is the shadow of attachment: every role and asset we cling to brings a matching fear, so loosening the grip loosens the fear.
misreadings: Dispassion is not giving up on life or people; it is holding things without clutching
Not a claim that anyone's fear is baseless
cautions: Mentions disease, old age and death in one breath; may feed health anxiety if read alone
not_for: someone in acute grief or fear, who may hear 'you should not have been attached'
a reader with health anxiety, without framing
speaks_to: anxiety about losing status, money, looks or health
high achievers who feel constantly threatened

bh.vairagya.33.context: In the section on the instability of enjoyments: after the list of how each good is preyed on by another (32) and before the call to wise teachers to put forth energy since the world is unsubstantial (34).
bh.vairagya.33.core_teaching: Health is uprooted by countless ills, fortune lets disasters in after it, and death swallows everything born; nothing fate has made is stable.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates health as rooted out by ailments of body and mind, perils finding open access wherever fortune alights, death annexing all that is born again and again.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Explains the grammar of 'makes its own' (complete subjection) and quotes Telang: what indeed has unbridled destiny created well-constituted?

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: around the root of health are a thousand worms of danger and disease; where is the Providence that made anything that did not die?

bh.vairagya.33.practical_reading: Used to puncture the illusion of permanence in health and prosperity, as a prompt to hold them gratefully and lightly.
misreadings: Not a reason to neglect health or prudence
Not cynicism about good fortune as such
cautions: Bleak and death-focused; can deepen despair or health anxiety
not_for: a reader newly diagnosed or bereaved
someone depressed or anxious about health
speaks_to: sudden illness or reversal after a good period
reflecting on the fragility of success

bh.vairagya.35.context: In the section on the instability of enjoyments, between the call to wise teachers to strive since the world is unsubstantial (34) and the verse that life is a wave and even embraces end (36).
bh.vairagya.35.core_teaching: Pleasures flash like lightning, life is as fragile as a drop on a wind-tossed lotus leaf, youth's longings do not last; knowing this, the wise should turn quickly to yoga.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Renders life as insecure as a drop on the edge of a lotus leaf dispersed by wind, and asks the wise to fix their minds firmly in yoga, easily reached through patience and equanimity.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Reads life as water in a small bank of clouds scattered by wind; explains that reaching samādhi needs strong courage against obstacles listed by Patanjali; discusses the compound.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, tr. (London, 1886)
commentaries.gist: Renders pleasure as lightning in a canopy of cloud and life as fleeting clouds, the cloud reading Joglekar also follows.

bh.vairagya.35.practical_reading: Used as an urgent nudge to start a meditation or spiritual practice now rather than 'later, when life settles'.
misreadings: Not saying pleasure is evil; it is fleeting
Not a demand to abandon family or work
cautions: Moderate; reminder of mortality
not_for: someone grieving a sudden death, where 'life is fragile' can feel like a lecture
speaks_to: young adults noticing how fast years go
after a near miss or health scare

bh.vairagya.36.context: Follows the call to turn to yoga (35) in the section on the instability of enjoyments; the next verse surveys the womb, youth and old age and asks if there is any happiness at all (37).
bh.vairagya.36.core_teaching: Life, youth, wealth, pleasures and even the embrace of loved ones are brief; fix the mind on Brahman to cross the ocean of worldly fear.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Explains the 'fear' of the world as the dread of finding oneself bound by an afflicted world with no way out; attachment to Brahman is the crossing.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses arthāḥ as riches momentary like a thought; records Krishna Shastri's explanation of the embrace phrase; asks the reader to fix attention on Brahman.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely, saying our most beloved one is only for a moment, and urging the reader to give the heart to Brahman to cross this ocean.

bh.vairagya.36.practical_reading: Used to invite reflection on what lasts when every relationship and possession is temporary; in a devotional reading, to anchor the heart in the divine.
misreadings: Not telling anyone to stop loving family
Not saying human love is worthless; it is saying it is not permanent
cautions: 'Even the embrace of loved ones does not last' is very painful for the newly bereaved or separated
Our_note: it pushes the mind away from family ties
not_for: fresh grief or divorce
new parents or lovers in a joyful season, where it can feel like a cold shower
speaks_to: after the end of a relationship, once the rawness has passed

bh.vairagya.38.context: In the section on the instability of enjoyments, after the survey of womb, youth and old age (37) and before the call to stop chasing enjoyments and fix the mind on its true abode (39).
bh.vairagya.38.core_teaching: With old age crouching, illness attacking and life leaking away, it is a wonder that people still spend their time doing what harms them.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates the close as how wonderful that man still goes on doing wicked deeds.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses ahitam ācaranti as doing injury to themselves or leading an evil life; parisravati as dribbling, passing away; the jar is cracked.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: old age watches, roaring like a tigress; life flows out like water from a broken jar; curious that men still do evil.

bh.vairagya.38.practical_reading: Used as a wake-up call to stop spending limited time on grudges, self-destructive habits and petty harm.
misreadings: Not fear-mongering about ageing; the point is the use of time
cautions: Predatory image of old age; can frighten older or ill readers
not_for: elderly or ill readers already afraid
health anxiety
speaks_to: someone stuck in a feud or grudge
a reminder to use time well

bh.vairagya.4.context: Early in the Vairagyashatakam's censure of craving: in the preceding verses the poet confesses digging for treasure, smelting ore, crossing seas and humbling himself before kings, all fruitless. Here he lists the humiliations he swallowed to win favour and asks hope or desire how much longer it will make him dance. The next verse in popular editions continues the confession: for the sake of a life as unstable as water on a lotus leaf, he shamelessly recited his own merits before the rich.
bh.vairagya.4.core_teaching: Unexamined hope for gain or approval can make us swallow insults and fake our feelings; naming that pattern is the first step out of it.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, translation (1916, no. 4)
commentaries.gist: Places it in servile attendance on wealthy wicked people: shabby treatment borne, tears suppressed, forced smiles, bows to men dulled by wealth; addresses Desire, whose yearning is never satisfied.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation (1902 ed., Vairagya 6)
commentaries.gist: Renders the addressee as 'disappointed Greed' and stresses enduring taunts while intent on propitiating the powerful.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation (1886, Vairagya 6)
commentaries.gist: Frames the abuse as suffered in hope of gain, the laughter as forced from a void heart, and asks foolish desire how much further it will lead him.

bh.vairagya.4.practical_reading: Notice what you put up with because you hope it will pay off (the promotion, the approval); ask whether that hope is still worth the price you are paying in self-respect.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of all hope; it targets the hope that keeps one in humiliation.
Not a judgement on people who must endure a bad job to survive.
cautions: Describes suppressed tears and forced laughter; can land heavily on someone in an abusive workplace. Avoid implying their hope is the problem.
not_for: someone with no option to leave a degrading situation, unless paired with practical support

bh.vairagya.41.context: Opens the section on the working of Time (kāla-mahimā). Just after, Time plays dice on the board of the world (42). The roll-call of a vanished court recalls the king-poet of tradition.
bh.vairagya.41.core_teaching: A whole brilliant world (city, king, court, poets, beauties, princes, bards) now survives only as memory; the poet bows to Time, by whose power it all passed.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Glosses Kāla as time or the principle of change, and has the whole scene fleeting away along the way of memory.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Compares Niti 34; likens 'gone into memory' to the English phrase 'a matter of history'; notes the Sharngadhara Paddhati quotes a related stanza right after it.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Reads the pronoun 'that' throughout as 'that well-known, familiar', giving continuity of remembered grandeur; translates 'homage to father Time'.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely as a roll-call of beautiful cities, mighty monarchs and moon-faced women all swept from memory, with salutation to Time.

bh.vairagya.41.practical_reading: Used for reflection when an era of life ends (a workplace, a home, a generation): honouring what was, without bitterness, and bowing to change.
misreadings: Not nihilism; it is an elegy that ends in a bow
cautions: Gentle; suitable for loss of a place or era
not_for: very fresh loss of a person, where 'only memory' may feel too stark
speaks_to: the end of an era: a closed business, a sold family home, a changed hometown

bh.vairagya.42.context: Follows the salutation to Time (41) in the section on Time; next comes the sun's daily coming and going that shortens life (43).
bh.vairagya.42.core_teaching: Households fill and empty, from many to one, from one to many, and finally to none: Time plays a game on the world's board, throwing night and day as dice, with living beings as its pieces.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Explains 'home' as also a square of a checkerboard; expert Kāla moves the pieces, casting the two dice of day and night, until none remain at the end of the game.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Takes the two players as the male and female personifications of destruction, Shiva and Parvati, whose dice game is famous in the Puranas; notes the house/square pun.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Follows Telang: Kāla and Kālī play dice on the earth as a dice-board, living beings as pieces tossed night and day.

bh.vairagya.42.practical_reading: A way to see family change across generations (weddings, births, deaths, children moving away) as one long game no one controls.
misreadings: Not saying life is random or meaningless
cautions: Depicts households emptying and death as a game; can feel callous to the bereaved
not_for: fresh bereavement
anyone feeling powerless or used by fate
speaks_to: a family home after elders have died

bh.vairagya.43.context: In the section on Time, after Time's dice game (42) and before the verse on people running the same daily course without shame at being fooled by repetition (44).
bh.vairagya.43.core_teaching: Each day shortens life, yet busy with work we never notice; seeing birth, age, trouble and death all around, we feel no alarm, as if drunk on heedlessness.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates the end as the world gone mad from drinking the stupefying wine of delusion.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Allows that 'time is not felt' can be construed with the busy affairs; glosses the wine as made of delusion.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Notes Tawney compares a stanza of the Palatine Anthology, and that the verse also occurs in the Śāntiśataka.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: crushed by many works we do not feel time fly; seeing birth, age, danger and death, we are not afraid.

bh.vairagya.43.practical_reading: Used to challenge busyness: a full calendar can hide the fact that days, and with them life, are passing.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of work; it is about heedless work
cautions: Mild; mentions death
not_for: someone who cannot slow down because of financial necessity (may feel like blame)
speaks_to: feeling years have vanished in routine

bh.vairagya.44.context: Part of the run of verses on Time in the Vairagyashatakam: just before, the poet says life shrinks with each sunrise and sunset while business hides the passing of time, and that the world has gone mad on the wine of delusion. Here he observes people treating each day as a repeat of the last and pursuing the same routines without ever feeling ashamed of the treadmill.
bh.vairagya.44.core_teaching: Treating life as an endless loop of identical days lets it slip away unnoticed; the verse asks us to wake up to the repetition and to time passing.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, translation with notes (1916, no. 44)
commentaries.gist: Explains that desire, which never ages, makes stale pursuits look fresh; in truth worldly pursuits are as repetitive as day following night.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation (1902 ed., Vairagya 75)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as ignorant people busily running their diverse vocations, and asks why we are not ashamed of being disgraced by such repetitive worldly life.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation (1886, Vairagya 78)
commentaries.gist: Stresses that we assume days and nights go on indefinitely, resume each task where we left it, and endure the world's pains while enjoying the same sense-objects over and over.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 316)
commentaries.gist: Doubtful-block verse; critical text reads the 'enjoyed again' variant.

bh.vairagya.44.practical_reading: When the week feels like a loop, stop and ask what this particular day is for; change one small thing so it is not simply a rerun of yesterday.
misreadings: Not contempt for ordinary work or routine as such; the target is mindless repetition driven by craving.
Not a call to quit one's responsibilities.
cautions: The 'we feel no shame' language can shame someone already depleted; many people repeat exhausting routines out of necessity, not delusion.
Includes the poet himself ('we'); keep that inclusive tone.
not_for: someone trapped in a routine by caregiving or poverty who would hear it as an accusation
someone with depression for whom 'same day again' is a symptom, not a choice
speaks_to: feeling like a hamster on a wheel

bh.vairagya.47.context: Third of three stanzas (45-47) in the section on Time where the poet speaks as a man whose life has achieved nothing: no merit, no learning, no glory, no love, no service to parents. The next verse turns to parents and childhood friends long gone (48).
bh.vairagya.47.core_teaching: Looking back, the speaker finds he has gained neither learning nor wealth, not truly cared for his parents, not known love; his time has gone like a crow's, scrounging for scraps from others.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Says stanzas 45-47 strike an anomalous note: the poet plays a man whose life was a failure, to show the vanity of a householder's aims; the poet cares more for drama than psychological precision.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses śuśrūṣā as attendance or service and the crow image as yearning for food meant for others; compares the third line of stanza 11.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, tr. (London, 1886)
commentaries.gist: Renders it with 'reverence towards our elders' not paid, generalising beyond parents.

bh.vairagya.47.practical_reading: Used for an honest life-audit: naming what was neglected (learning, family, love) as a spur to change while there is time.
misreadings: Not saying the reader's life is wasted
Per Madhavananda, a dramatic persona, not a model of how a seeker should think
cautions: Regret about not caring for parents can trigger guilt, especially after a parent's death
Mentions missed romantic love
not_for: someone whose parents recently died
readers prone to depression or harsh self-judgement
speaks_to: someone resolving to reconnect with parents while they live

bh.vairagya.48.context: In the section on Time, after the failed-life stanzas (45-47) and before the arithmetic of a hundred-year life (49).
bh.vairagya.48.core_teaching: Our parents are long gone and those we grew up with are now memories; we ourselves, closer to falling each day, are like trees on a crumbling sandy riverbank.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the first line as parents now on intimate footing with Eternity, long dead; in old age we approach our fall day by day like trees on a sandy bank.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Translates: those from whom we were born have long since left us, those we grew up with are mere recollection, our fall comes nearer daily.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
