commentaries.gist: Discusses Ramarshi's gloss of the first word as 'familiar with Time' and finds it unsupported by anything in the verse except the section heading.

bh.vairagya.48.practical_reading: Speaks to the moment one becomes the oldest generation: honouring those gone and accepting one's own place on the bank.
misreadings: Not morbid: it is about seeing one's place in time
cautions: About the death of parents and peers and one's own nearing death; strong grief trigger
not_for: fresh bereavement on Day 1 of a grief plan
young readers or anyone with death anxiety
speaks_to: becoming the elder of the family

bh.vairagya.49.context: In the section on Time, after the trees on the crumbling riverbank (48) and before the actor who exits behind Death's curtain (50).
bh.vairagya.49.core_teaching: Do the arithmetic of a hundred-year life: half goes in sleep, much in childhood and old age, and the rest in illness, separation and serving others; where is happiness in so restless a life?

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Works through the arithmetic: the remaining middle portion is about twenty-five years, full of troubles, illness and separation, spent in servitude; cites Telang in support of the simpler reading.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Ends with life more uncertain than ripples on the surface of water.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely as 'where is happiness in this life?', with the hundred years parcelled out among sleep, decrepitude, childhood and serving others.

bh.vairagya.49.practical_reading: Our_note calls it deliberately bleak. Teachers use it to make time feel finite, a prompt to protect the hours that are truly one's own.
misreadings: Not a claim that life has no joy; it is rhetorical arithmetic meant to shock
cautions: Deliberately bleak; can deepen depression
Mentions illness and separation
not_for: anyone depressed or hopeless
caregivers or people with chronic illness, for whom 'the rest goes in sickness and service' may feel like a sentence
speaks_to: feeling time is eaten by work and obligations

bh.vairagya.50.context: Our data places it at the close of the section on Time; it gathers the section's images into one: life as a play of quick costume changes ending in exit.
bh.vairagya.50.core_teaching: A person plays child, lover, pauper and rich man, each for a moment, and then, made up with wrinkles like an actor, exits behind the curtain of Death.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Calls the actor comparison very impressive: as an actor retires behind the curtain after many parts, so a man, after many roles on the world's stage, retires behind the seat of Death.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates the exit as going behind the scene that veils the abode of Yama, after the role ends with diseased limbs and a wrinkled body.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely, addressing 'O actor man', who vanishes from the stage when death beckons from the wings.

bh.vairagya.50.practical_reading: Used to loosen identification with any one role (rich, poor, young, successful): they are costumes in a short play.
misreadings: Not saying life is fake; it is saying roles are temporary
cautions: Ends with death; moderate for the bereaved
not_for: fresh grief
someone in a health crisis
speaks_to: identity crisis after losing a role or status
sudden change of fortune, up or down

bh.vairagya.51.context: Opens the section comparing the monk and the king (yati-nṛpati-saṃvāda). An ascetic speaks to a king as an equal or better; the next verse sets kingly power over riches against the ascetic's command over words and ideas (52).
bh.vairagya.51.core_teaching: A learned ascetic tells a king: you have wealth and fame, I have wisdom and a poet's renown; if you turn away from me, I want nothing from you either.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Says the sloka is addressed by a monk to a king to show the vanity of his possessions: the king is rich only in wealth, the monk in wisdom, which commands even a king's respect.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'mānada' as a vocative (one who humbles enemies) and translates: the difference between both of us is not at all great; if you are cold to us, we are wholly indifferent to you.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: there is infinite difference between us, so we are not the persons to wait upon kings.

bh.vairagya.51.practical_reading: Used to support self-respect before the powerful: learning and integrity are their own wealth, and one need not court approval.
misreadings: Self-respect, not contempt for others or for wealth
Not licence for arrogance toward employers or elders
cautions: Low risk
not_for: someone whose pride is already isolating them
speaks_to: feeling small before rich or powerful people
scholars, teachers, artists undervalued by the market

data_flags.translation_note: Our Sanskrit reads 'mānadhanātidūram' (very far apart in honour and wealth), and Madhavananda and Vivekananda translate a great or infinite difference between ascetic and king. Our English says the gap 'is not wide', which follows Telang/Joglekar's variant reading (vocative 'mānada', 'not very far'). Either change...

bh.vairagya.53.context: In the monk-and-king dialogue: after the monk's claim of mastery over words (52) and before the verse listing fruits, water, bare ground and bark as enough (54).
bh.vairagya.53.core_teaching: Bark or silk, the contentment is the same; the poor one is whoever craves endlessly, and when the mind is content there is no rich or poor.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Adds that one satisfied with even the little he has is as good as rich.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Prefers the silk reading because it contrasts better with bark, and compares Shakespeare's line that the poor but content man is rich enough.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Also prefers the silk reading and finds the 'distinctionless distinction' phrase puzzling, suggesting a sense of greatness for viśeṣa.

bh.vairagya.53.practical_reading: A favourite on contentment: redefine poverty as unending craving, so that comparison with richer people loses its sting.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of real material poverty or of fighting it
cautions: Can sound glib to someone in real deprivation
not_for: someone facing real hardship (unpaid rent, hunger)
speaks_to: comparison and envy (social media, relatives, colleagues)
financial anxiety that is really about status

bh.vairagya.57.context: In the monk-and-king dialogue, after 'who are we to go to see a king?' (56) and before the verse mocking kings who rejoice over a fragment of an earth that hundreds of rulers have already enjoyed (58).
bh.vairagya.57.core_teaching: Great beings have created, ruled, conquered and given away whole worlds like straw; what is this fever of pride in people who rule a few towns?

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the fourteen divisions as the entire created universe, set against pride in ruling a few towns.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Paraphrases the close as asking why people become so infatuated by sovereignty over a few cities; notes the verse is also in the Kāvyasaṅgraha.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Explains the locative absolute 'when there is lordship over a few towns' and translates the end as a fever of pride or passion.

bh.vairagya.57.practical_reading: Used to puncture status pride: any title or position is tiny on the scale of history.
misreadings: Not contempt for leadership or responsibility
cautions: Low risk
not_for: someone who has just lost a position and feels worthless (may sound like 'it never mattered')
speaks_to: a promotion going to one's head

bh.vairagya.6.context: In the opening censure of craving. It follows verses on servile flattery and on risking one's fragile life for gain (4-5) and comes just before the famous 'we did not enjoy pleasures, they enjoyed us' (7). The poet sees that his worldly life copied the outward acts of ascetics with none of their inner reasons.
bh.vairagya.6.core_teaching: The worldly person ends up doing what sages do (enduring, giving up comfort, bearing hardship, fixing the mind) but for the wrong reasons, and so misses every fruit those acts bring the sages.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Adds the hidden motives in brackets: forgiving from inability to right one's wrongs, giving up home comforts as an exile in quest of riches.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Sums up: neither the pardoning nor the leaving of home involved self-denial; the pain endured chasing earthly things equalled an ascetic's, yet produced no merit.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Gives the same sense of the first line, prefers a reading of the second for syntactic uniformity, and finds the Sanskrit commentary on this verse involved and unclear.

bh.vairagya.6.practical_reading: Teachers use it to ask why we do what we do: the same act (patience, sacrifice, long hours, discipline) can build us or empty us depending on its motive.
misreadings: Not saying forgiveness or sacrifice are worthless; it is about motive
cautions: Can feel accusatory to someone who sacrificed out of necessity, e.g. migrant workers or carers
not_for: someone who endured abuse, who may hear 'you didn't really forgive'
exhausted caregivers

bh.vairagya.61.context: The poet turns from describing kings and ascetics to addressing his own heart. He asks why it wears itself out courting other people's favour every day, and answers that a mind serene within already holds a wish-granting jewel. Nearby verses rebuke the mind for roaming everywhere except inward.
bh.vairagya.61.core_teaching: Approval chased from others is exhausting and unreliable; a mind settled within is itself the source of what one is looking for.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, translation with notes (1916, no. 61)
commentaries.gist: Notes the alternative reading kleśa-kalitam ('a chaotic mass of troubles'); explains the self-arisen wish-gem as almost a yogic power, and takes vivikta as being free of the need for others' company.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation (1902 ed., Vairagya 33)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as the heart suffering much distress to please others daily, whereas when wish-gem powers rise in it spontaneously and it is inwardly satisfied, nothing desired is out of reach.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation (1886, Vairagya 34)
commentaries.gist: Reads the point as: a purified heart would have its desires met and would stop seeking others' favours because it would be at rest inside.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 167)
commentaries.gist: Core verse; critical text points the resolve toward liberation (vimukti) rather than toward seclusion.

bh.vairagya.61.practical_reading: Notice how much daily energy goes into managing other people's opinion of you, and try one stretch of the day where you act from your own settled sense of what is right rather than from the wish to be liked.
misreadings: Not permission to ignore other people's needs or feedback.
Not 'manifesting': the wish-gem is inner contentment, not a guarantee of external outcomes.
cautions: For a carer or employee who cannot stop pleasing others without real cost, the verse can sound like blame; frame it as relief, not fault.
not_for: someone whose safety depends on placating another person (abuse, coercive work); they need practical help, not an inner-calm verse

bh.vairagya.62.context: In the section on stimulating wisdom in the mind (mano-sambodhana), after the verse asking why the heart labours to win other people's favour (61) and before the call to leave the labyrinth of sense objects (63).
bh.vairagya.62.core_teaching: The mind is told to stop its restless wandering: things unfold as they will, so without brooding on the past or scripting the future, the poet accepts what comes unbidden.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates: rest somewhere; whatever happens in whatever way happens so by itself; not thinking over the past nor resolving about the future, I enjoy what comes without engaging my thoughts.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Says bluntly that the second line is fatalism.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Quotes Kale's alternative: things turn out best when left to their natural course rather than forced by exertion.

bh.vairagya.62.practical_reading: Used for the worry loop: once you have done your part, stop rehearsing the past and pre-living the future, and let the next thing arrive.
misreadings: Not an argument against planning or responsibility
Telang calls the second line fatalism; do not present it as a general life philosophy
cautions: Fatalistic ground ('what will be will be') can feel dismissive to someone facing a fixable problem
not_for: someone who needs to act (medical decisions, unsafe situations)
a person in crisis

bh.vairagya.67.context: In the section on the mind. The preceding verse says enjoy if real pleasure can be found, otherwise plunge into meditation (66); Madhavananda notes that this verse then shows the uselessness of fulfilled desires, and the next (68) names what is worth having: devotion to Shiva, fear of birth and death, solitude, dispassion.
bh.vairagya.67.core_teaching: Wealth that grants every wish, victory over enemies, friends won with money, a body lasting an aeon: so what? None of it is the real goal.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Frames the 'so what' as the poet preaching the uselessness of fulfilled worldly desires, since all worldly pleasures are transient and limited.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses kalpa as a day of Brahma, 432 million years, and points to the next stanza for what the poet prefers to all this.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely and joins it to the next verse: the only thing to be desired is renunciation that gives all love to Shiva.

bh.vairagya.67.practical_reading: Used to test goals: after each achievement ask 'and then what?' until you reach something that does not need another 'so what'.
misreadings: Read alone it can deepen 'nothing matters'; the tradition reads it with the next verse, which names devotion and dispassion as the answer
cautions: Can feed nihilism or depression if given without verse 68
not_for: someone depressed or without purpose
a young person just starting to build a life
speaks_to: chasing the next promotion or purchase

bh.vairagya.7.context: The climax of the opening censure of craving: right after the verse on doing ascetics' deeds for the wrong reasons (6) and before 'wrinkles on the face, only craving stays young' (8). Vivekananda joined verses 5 to 8 into one passage in his free translation.
bh.vairagya.7.core_teaching: We think we consume pleasures, practise discipline and spend time; in truth pleasures consumed us, worry scorched us, we passed while time stayed, and we aged while craving stayed young.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Explains each pair as an ironic pun: time is not gone because it is ever-present and infinite, but we are gone because death draws near; the effect cannot be kept in translation.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'we were enjoyed' as becoming the objects of enjoyment (by death) and 'we were heated' as by worldly anxieties instead of austerities.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely within a combined passage: we did not enjoy, enjoyments enjoyed us; we did no penance, penances burnt us.

bh.vairagya.7.practical_reading: Widely quoted on consumerism and ageing: the habit of wanting outlives the body and the years spent feeding it.
misreadings: Not a rejection of all joy; the target is craving (tṛṣṇā)
Not despair about growing old
cautions: Blunt about ageing and lost time; may sting for readers carrying heavy regrets
not_for: someone in depression who already feels life is wasted
terminally ill readers, without careful framing
speaks_to: feeling used up by work or consumption

bh.vairagya.70.context: Our data calls it the closing verse of the section on the mind: after the call to meditate on the infinite Brahman beside which world-sovereignty looks pitiable (69); the next section opens with 'what use are the Vedas...' (71).
bh.vairagya.70.core_teaching: The restless mind roams underworld, sky and every direction, yet never, even by accident, turns to the pure Brahman that is its own self and its peace.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Explains ātmanīna as belonging to the self, since the self's real state is Brahman; the other reading would mean submerged in the self.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Notes Ramarshi takes mānasa as vocative; 'even by mistake' means you not only fail to think of Brahman on purpose, you never stumble on it.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: all this searching is the mind's fickleness; you never remember the Lord within, so how can you be happy?

bh.vairagya.70.practical_reading: Used in meditation teaching to name mind-wandering and invite the attention home.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of curiosity or travel
cautions: Low risk
not_for: someone with ADHD or anxiety who may hear blame for a restless mind
speaks_to: constant searching for the next thing

bh.vairagya.71.context: Opens the section discriminating the lasting from the passing (nitya-anitya-vastu-vicāra), after the mind's fruitless roaming (70). The next verse pictures Meru toppling and the seas drying at the end of an age (72).
bh.vairagya.71.core_teaching: Scripture, ritual and learning that only earn a place in heaven are trading; the one thing worth having is entry into the bliss of the self, which burns up worldly sorrow.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Says the vast śāstras here mean logic, grammar and the six philosophical systems, vast because of their commentary and argument; heaven is likened to a village of huts.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Calls the rest mere mercenary affairs, except the one way into the place where there is joy in one's self, which destroys worldly misery like the final fire.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Records Ramarshi's gloss of svātmānanda-pada as the seat where there is joy in oneself.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: freedom alone lifts the weight of the world and reveals the Self's blessedness; the rest is shop-keeping.

bh.vairagya.71.practical_reading: Used to warn against transactional religion (rituals done to get something) and to point to inner peace as the aim of practice.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of scripture or ritual; a warning against treating them as a transaction
Not anti-learning
cautions: Can offend readers devoted to ritual if not framed
not_for: someone whose ritual practice is their main comfort in grief

bh.vairagya.73.context: In the section on the lasting and the passing: after the image of Meru falling at the world's end (72) and before the verse on young women fleeing an old man's grey hair (74). Both are portraits of old age.
bh.vairagya.73.core_teaching: A lament on old age: the body fails, and the family stops listening; the wife no longer cares for him and even his son turns hostile.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates it as a list of bodily decline ending with relatives not valuing one's words, the wife not nursing, and even the son of an aged man turning hostile.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses ādriyate as heeding, śuśrūṣate as serving, and cites a parallel for the line about the hostile son.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, tr. (London, 1886)
commentaries.gist: Renders the family lines as servants ceasing to obey, the wife not submissive and the son an enemy.

bh.vairagya.73.practical_reading: Our misuse note reads it as a call to keep listening to the old; teachers use it to awaken compassion for ageing parents and to prepare for one's own old age.
misreadings: A lament, not a prediction of every family's future
Not permission to neglect elders
cautions: Graphic bodily decline (drooling, deafness, blindness); painful for those caring for ageing parents or ageing themselves
Family-conflict theme
not_for: elderly readers feeling neglected (may confirm their fear)
someone estranged from a parent or child
speaks_to: adult children caring for ageing parents

bh.vairagya.75.context: In the section on the lasting and the passing, after two portraits of old age (73-74) and before the poet's indecision about how to spend a life of a few blinks (76).
bh.vairagya.75.core_teaching: While the body is healthy, old age far off and the senses strong, make a great effort for your highest good; once the house is burning, it is too late to dig a well.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates it as a call for mighty exertion for one's supreme good while health, senses and life last, for digging a well once the house is on fire avails nothing.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the words and quotes Telang that the closing question is an idiom like the English 'what shall we say to such a thing'.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely with urgency: now, now, struggle on, rendering great help to yourself; no use digging a well in a burning house.

bh.vairagya.75.practical_reading: One of the most usable verses for younger readers: do the inner work (practice, character, relationships) now, while you have energy, not after a crisis.
misreadings: Not saying it is ever too late to begin; it is about not postponing
cautions: For someone already ill or old, 'too late' can sting
not_for: someone newly diagnosed or elderly who may hear 'you missed your chance'
speaks_to: young and middle-aged readers postponing what matters
starting a spiritual or health practice

bh.vairagya.76.context: In the section on the lasting and the passing, right after 'dig the well before the house burns' (75). Having urged effort, the poet admits he does not know which path to choose.
bh.vairagya.76.core_teaching: Ascetic retreat, devoted family life, deep study or poetry? With a life that lasts a few blinks, the poet confesses he does not know which to choose.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates: since man's life lasts a few twinklings of the eye, we do not know which of these to undertake.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Notes some take the scripture and poetry phrases as one item but finds it happier to take them separately; renders the close 'we do not know what to do'.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Says resorting to the Ganges stands for leaving the world, and discusses Ramarshi's long gloss, preferring to take the options separately.

bh.vairagya.76.practical_reading: A rare honest verse about indecision; teachers use it to name the paralysis of too many good paths, before choosing one.
misreadings: Not a claim that all paths are equal or pointless; the indecision is left unresolved
cautions: Low risk; may mirror anxiety for an indecisive reader
not_for: someone already paralysed by indecision who needs a clear step
speaks_to: choosing between spiritual life and family duties

bh.vairagya.8.context: A short verse right after 'craving did not age, we did' (7), making the same point through the ageing body. Verse 9 then pictures an old man on a stick still startled by death.
bh.vairagya.8.core_teaching: The body visibly ages in every part, but craving alone keeps getting younger.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates it plainly: the face attacked by wrinkles, the head painted white, the limbs enfeebled, desire alone rejuvenating.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses each word and compares a Panchatantra stanza (V.38) making the same point that desire does not age.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Cross-refers to the 'bhogā na bhuktāḥ' verse and to stanza 15 of the Mohamudgara (Bhaja Govindam) as a parallel.

bh.vairagya.8.practical_reading: A mirror for later life: the body slows, but the mind's wanting (status, possessions, control) may not; noticing that gap is a place to begin.
misreadings: Not mockery of old people
Not saying older people should stop enjoying life
cautions: Describes bodily ageing plainly; can feel unkind to someone distressed about ageing or illness
not_for: someone with body-image distress or a recent diagnosis
older readers who already feel discarded
speaks_to: noticing that wants do not fade with age
habits that persist despite changed circumstances

bh.vairagya.82.context: Late in the Vairagyashatakam the poet has just said that moonlight, poetry and good company all lose their charm once the mind sees how fleeting they are, and that the wise leave palaces for the forest. Here he lists the goods of the renunciant's life and marvels at them as the ripened fruit of some great austerity. The verses that follow turn to devotion to Shiva, including the one declaring Shiva and Vishnu not different in essence.
bh.vairagya.82.core_teaching: A plain, self-respecting life (free movement, honest food, good company, study aimed at calm, a quiet mind) is treated as a rare blessing, the ripened fruit of great effort, to be wondered at rather than taken for granted.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, translation with notes (Advaita Ashrama 1916, no. 82)
commentaries.gist: Glosses upaśama as the ending of the world's illusions and worries; says this is the only fruit of such study, whereas other vows promise worldly prosperity. Renders the close as the poet unable, even after lifelong reflection, to name the austerity behind it.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation (1902 ed., Vairagya 49)
commentaries.gist: Takes the long reflection as the poet's own, and describes the mind as moving only slowly toward external objects; the learning's fruit is the vow of sense-control.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation (1886, Vairagya 51)
commentaries.gist: Lists rest at will, food without degradation, friendship with the noble-minded and an undisturbed mind as fruits of the highest vow of tranquillity, then admits he cannot tell what penance wins this state.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 308)
commentaries.gist: Places the verse in the doubtful block; his text reads 'bahir aticirasyāpi', confirming the long-reflection reading.

bh.vairagya.82.practical_reading: Read as a gratitude exercise: name the ordinary freedoms and dignities you already have (choosing your own hours, food you did not have to beg for, good friends, a mind that is not racing) and notice them as gifts rather than entitlements.
misreadings: Not a boast that one has earned one's comforts; the tone is wonder, not desert.
Not praise of luxury; the goods listed are those of a simple, even ascetic, life.
Not a claim that people lacking these goods failed to earn them.
cautions: The 'fruit of past austerity' frame can imply that hardship is deserved; avoid for a reader in poverty, dependency or humiliating work.
Original context is the renunciant's life, not a householder's comforts.
not_for: someone who has just lost their freedom, job or home
someone forced to depend on others for food or money
speaks_to: appreciating good company and a calm mind

data_flags.translation_note: Minor: 'for long' belongs to the poet's reflection, not to the mind looking outward. Kale, Wortham and Madhavananda all read it as 'though I have pondered it for a long time, I do not know what noble austerity has ripened into this', with the mind...

bh.vairagya.84.context: In the section on the worship of Shiva. Madhavananda explains that the previous verse names Shiva as the only refuge, so this verse removes a doubt: the poet does not set Shiva above Vishnu in essence; his love is simply turned to Shiva.
bh.vairagya.84.core_teaching: Shiva and Vishnu are not different in essence; still, the poet's heart is given to Shiva: one truth, one chosen form of love.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Calls this ishta-nishtha, devotion to one's own ideal: no real difference between Shiva and Vishnu, but the poet is by nature attached to Shiva; lists four senses of 'inner self of the universe'.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Glosses vastu-bheda-pratipatti as a belief in difference and compares a Gita construction for the grammar.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: in Shiva or Vishnu I see no difference, but my love is for Him with the young moon on His forehead.

bh.vairagya.84.practical_reading: Used to model devotion without sectarianism: love your chosen form of the divine wholeheartedly without denying others.
misreadings: Not a ranking of Shiva over Vishnu
Not religious relativism that makes devotion pointless
cautions: Low risk; sectarian readers may bristle
not_for: readers outside Hindu devotion without context
speaks_to: devotees who feel torn between deities

bh.vairagya.9.context: Follows 'only craving stays young' (8) and precedes the river of hope (10). An old man's view: the wish for pleasure gone, respect gone, peers dead, eyesight failing, and still the body flinches at death.
bh.vairagya.9.core_teaching: Even when every reason to cling to life has fallen away, the body still recoils from death; the poet calls this clinging foolish.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Adds that the friends went to heaven before being overtaken by old age, allows that the blindness may be cataract, and calls the body's alarm a silliness.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses mūḍha as impudent or shameless and timira as an eye disease; offers two senses for the lost respect: pride of manhood or esteem among men.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, notes with extracts from two Sanskrit commentaries incl. Ramarshi (Bombay Sanskrit Series, 1893 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Prefers 'respect among men' and cites Tawney's comparison with verses of Maecenas on clinging to life even when crippled.

bh.vairagya.9.practical_reading: Teachers use it to name the instinctive fear of death that survives every argument, as a starting point for inner work rather than for shame.
misreadings: Not contempt for the elderly or for fear of death
Not encouragement to neglect one's health
cautions: Mentions the death of friends, frailty, failing sight and fear of dying; heavy for the elderly, the bereaved or the ill
not_for: recent bereavement
someone with a terminal diagnosis or a dying parent
health anxiety
speaks_to: noticing that fear of death persists despite age

bh.vairagya.92.context: In the section on the way of life of a free ascetic (avadhūta-caryā), after the verse that a worn loincloth, begged food and a calm mind outweigh rule over three worlds (91), and before the poet's farewell to Lakshmi, goddess of wealth (93).
bh.vairagya.92.core_teaching: To a great mind the whole universe is a small thing and cannot stir greed, just as a small fish's flick cannot churn the ocean.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Explains: as a fish cannot set the ocean swaying, the universe, a mere image in pure consciousness, cannot move the wise, who are one with that consciousness, to covetousness.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Translates: what is a mere collection of worlds to tempt one whose mind is under control? Is the ocean ever agitated by a small fish's gambols?

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely: this universe is only a little circle; what is there to desire in it?

bh.vairagya.92.practical_reading: Our line widens it from greed to not being shaken by small things, which the ocean image supports: a deep mind is not stirred by petty provocations.
misreadings: Not contempt for the world or for small people
cautions: Low risk
not_for: someone whose distress is serious (it can minimise real pain as a 'small fish')
speaks_to: being thrown by small annoyances or criticism

bh.vairagya.94.context: In the section on the free ascetic, after the farewell to Lakshmi (93) and before the portrait of the real ascetic living on alms, unattached, clothed in rags (95).
bh.vairagya.94.core_teaching: The sage sleeps like a king: earth for a bed, his arm for a pillow, the sky a canopy, the breeze a fan, the autumn moon a lamp, and Renunciation as his bride.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Translates the sage as lying down happily and peacefully, rejoicing in abnegation as his wife, like a monarch of undiminished glory.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Renders: though he has renounced all desires, the sage stretches out like a monarch, delighting in renunciation as his woman.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, free oral tr. recorded by Sister Nivedita, 1898 (Complete Works vol. 9)
commentaries.gist: Renders it freely, ending: what king is there who can sleep like me in pleasure?

bh.vairagya.94.practical_reading: Used to celebrate simplicity: contentment turns the simplest surroundings into a palace.
misreadings: Not romanticising homelessness or poverty
cautions: Could feel glib to someone without a home
not_for: someone facing homelessness or insecure housing

bh.vairagya.96.context: In the section on the free ascetic, after the portrait of the real ascetic in rags (95) and before the verse that the Creator provides air for snakes and grass for beasts, so a livelihood exists for the self-devoted too (97).
bh.vairagya.96.core_teaching: People speculate loudly about who the wandering yogi is, outcaste, brahmin, labourer, ascetic or great sage; the yogis walk on, neither angry nor flattered.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, tr. and notes (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati, 1916)
commentaries.gist: Explains the social labels for the reader: the caṇḍāla is beyond the four castes, the śūdra is the fourth, the twice-born are the first three; the yogis go their way neither pleased nor displeased.

commentaries.who: K. M. Joglekar, notes and tr. (Bombay, 1911; Telang's text; cites Ramarshi, Krishna Shastri, Kale)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the yogi as one whose intellect is keen at separating reality from appearance, and the crowd as garrulous with doubts; translates that ascetics are neither irritated nor pleased.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, tr. (London, 1886)
commentaries.gist: Renders the guesses as questions put directly to the wanderer ('Are you a Chandala?'), sharpening the scene.

bh.vairagya.96.practical_reading: Used to steady people who are constantly labelled or judged: let others argue about who you are and keep walking.
misreadings: The verse sets caste labels aside as other people's chatter; it does not endorse them
cautions: Names caste categories, including an outcaste term; explain rather than repeat them
not_for: readers hurt by caste discrimination, unless the labels are carefully framed
speaks_to: being judged, gossiped about or misjudged

dheesh_gita.1.4.context: The text opens with Suta thanking his guru Vyasa for the Puranas and Gitas already taught, recalling Vyasa's teaching that the Lord is called Dhisha because he presides over the intellect, and asking to hear the Gita in which Ganesha taught the seers. Vyasa then narrates.
dheesh_gita.1.4.core_teaching: The divine both stands beyond the mind and, out of compassion, works through it; that is why Ganesha is called lord of the intellect and gives freedom to those who turn to him.
dheesh_gita.1.4.practical_reading: A prayer-frame for clear thinking: ask for help not only with the outcome but with the mind that will choose.
misreadings: Not a claim of Vedic origin for this text; 'the Vedas call him Dhisha' is the text's own statement.
cautions: The Dheesh (Dhisha) Gita is one of five sectarian 'Gitas' (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi. The 1989 second edition's preface calls them previously unpublished. I found no older manuscript tradition or classical commentary; date and authorship are unverified.
not_for: readers expecting a canonical Purana passage

data_flags.corrected_ref: Dheesh (Dhisha) Gita 1.5-6 in both Bharat Dharma Mahamandal editions read (the printed numbering counts the speaker line 'suta uvaca' as 1). Our '1.4-5' is off by one.
data_flags.attribution_note: Speaker Suta is correct, but he is addressing his teacher Vyasa, not 'Shaunaka and the sages'. He reports what he once heard from Vyasa and asks Vyasa to recite the Dhisha Gita.

dheesh_gita.1.42.context: The seers tell Ganesha that by his grace they long ago received the Vedas and succeeded in studying their meaning, but because they did not know his real form their minds found no peace. Having come to his world for refuge, they ask (1.46-47) for the essential knowledge that gives lasting peace.
dheesh_gita.1.42.core_teaching: Learning and accomplishment did not bring peace; peace came only from turning toward the source with humility and asking to know it.
dheesh_gita.1.42.practical_reading: For the high achiever who is still restless: name it honestly, then stop adding achievements and ask what kind of knowing would actually settle you.
misreadings: Not anti-learning; the seers' study is praised. It says study without inner knowing did not bring peace.
cautions: The Dheesh (Dhisha) Gita is one of five sectarian 'Gitas' (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi. The 1989 second edition's preface calls them previously unpublished. I found no older manuscript tradition or classical commentary; date and authorship are unverified.
not_for: someone who needs practical help rather than surrender language
speaks_to: students and professionals who feel empty

data_flags.corrected_ref: Dheesh Gita 1.45 in both Mahamandal editions (1.42 there is the speaker line 'rishaya ucuh'). Our ref is off by three.

dheesh_gita.1.46.context: Ganesha answers: he abides as being-consciousness-bliss above the seven stages of knowledge. Though all-pervading and formless, devotees see him in many forms, gross or as light, and are fulfilled. He then describes a ladder beyond sense objects, senses, subtle elements, mental states and mahat, where his wise devotees see him; knowing this, the seers will find lasting peace (1.55).
dheesh_gita.1.46.core_teaching: The formless divine meets each loving devotee in the form they long for, and that meeting is real and fulfilling, even though the final truth lies beyond all forms.
dheesh_gita.1.46.practical_reading: Permission to relate to the divine in whatever form helps you, an image, a name, a light, without worrying whether it is the 'right' one.
misreadings: Not saying forms are mere imagination to be outgrown; the text affirms the devotees' fulfilment.
cautions: The Dheesh (Dhisha) Gita is one of five sectarian 'Gitas' (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi. The 1989 second edition's preface calls them previously unpublished. I found no older manuscript tradition or classical commentary; date and authorship are unverified.

data_flags.corrected_ref: Dheesh Gita 1.50-51 in both Mahamandal editions. Our '1.46-47' is off by four.

dheesh_gita.4.19.context: In a chapter on dharma, Ganesha says his sustaining power keeps the stars in orbit (4.19-20). Then: beings are nourished by his Prakriti's dharma-filled motherly nature and rise through the classes of birth (sprouting, sweat-born, egg-born, womb-born) to human birth, where alone knowledge of right and wrong makes them travellers on the road to freedom (4.22-26).
dheesh_gita.4.19.core_teaching: All life is held and fed by a sustaining order that works like a mother's care, carrying beings step by step toward freedom.
dheesh_gita.4.19.practical_reading: A grounding thought on a hard day: you have been carried this far by more care than you can see.
misreadings: Not a promise that nothing bad will happen; the verse is cosmological.
cautions: The Dheesh (Dhisha) Gita is one of five sectarian 'Gitas' (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi. The 1989 second edition's preface calls them previously unpublished. I found no older manuscript tradition or classical commentary; date and authorship are unverified.
The surrounding verses describe rebirth through animal species to human birth; avoid building readings on that for someone grieving a pet or a child.
not_for: someone who feels abandoned by caregivers, where 'motherly care at the heart of things' could ring false without acknowledgement

data_flags.corrected_ref: Dheesh Gita 4.21 in both Mahamandal editions (chapter 4, 'Dharma-vijnana-nirupana'). Our '4.19' is off by two.

dheesh_gita.7.27.context: Ending their hymn on Ganesha's cosmic form, the seers say that those who, drunk on their own independence, ignore his hints wander in the painful wheel of birth and death (7.27). They then pray, in a stanza echoing the Gayatri, that his radiance guard their minds and urge them to good action. Vyasa says the seers fell silent, thrilled and in tears, and Ganesha smiled and answered.
dheesh_gita.7.27.core_teaching: A prayer for the mind itself: may the divine light protect it from wrong action and turn it toward the good, day and night.
dheesh_gita.7.27.practical_reading: A short morning prayer before a day of choices; can be said before work or study.
misreadings: Not a replacement for the Vedic Gayatri; it is modelled on it.
cautions: The Dheesh (Dhisha) Gita is one of five sectarian 'Gitas' (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi. The 1989 second edition's preface calls them previously unpublished. I found no older manuscript tradition or classical commentary; date and authorship are unverified.
The verse just before speaks of those who ignore the divine suffering in samsara; do not quote 7.27 alongside this as a warning to a struggling reader.

data_flags.corrected_ref: Dheesh Gita 7.28 (chapter 7, 'Virat-svarupa-varnana') in both Mahamandal editions. Our '7.27' is off by one.

hans_gita.10.context: Just before, the swan warns that word-arrows fly from the mouth and wound the hearer's vitals day and night, so the wise should never shoot them (12.288.8-9). This verse turns to the other side: what to do when you are the target.
hans_gita.10.core_teaching: When someone attacks you with words, answer with calm; the one who stays unprovoked keeps their goodness and, in the epic's moral accounting, gains the attacker's merit.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: If someone pierces a wise man with word-arrows, he should keep peace; one who, provoked, rejoices without yielding to anger takes away all the provoker's merit.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition text (12.288) as a textual check
commentaries.gist: Critical text 12.288.10 reads 'pratimṛṣyate' (endures) where ours reads 'pratihṛṣyate' (rejoices): the core instruction, calm under verbal attack, is the same.

hans_gita.10.practical_reading: When a message or comment stings, wait before replying; reply only from calm, or not at all.
misreadings: Not 'accept abuse silently forever'; it governs your reaction, not whether to set boundaries.
The 'merit transfer' is the epic's moral language, not a promise of revenge.
cautions: For someone being bullied or abused, 'stay cheerful' can sound like 'it's your job to absorb this'; pair with permission to step away.
not_for: victims of ongoing abuse or harassment

data_flags.corrected_ref: Mahabharata 12.288.10 (BORI critical edition, Mokshadharma, Hamsa Gita). Ganguli/Roy translation: Santi Parva section CCC (300). Our data's '12.305.10' matches neither; the verse number within the chapter (10) is correct.

hans_gita.11.context: Continues the swan's teaching on insult (12.288.10-12). Right after, the swan says of himself: when abused I say nothing, when struck I forgive; the noble rank forgiveness, truth, straightness and kindness highest.
hans_gita.11.core_teaching: Restraining the flare of anger that insult provokes, without letting the heart turn bitter, is a real achievement and preserves one's goodness.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: The righteous person who, joyful and free of malice, subdues the blazing wrath that, if indulged, would make him speak ill and become an enemy, takes away the merit of others.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition text (12.288) as a textual check
commentaries.gist: Same wording in the critical text (12.288.11); 12.288.12 follows with the swan's own example of forgiving abuse and blows.

hans_gita.11.practical_reading: When anger flares after a slight, notice the heat, breathe, and decide not to let it poison how you see the person.
misreadings: Not 'never feel anger'; it is about holding back the blaze and keeping the heart clean.
cautions: Same caution as 12.288.10 for people facing repeated mistreatment.
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship

data_flags.corrected_ref: Mahabharata 12.288.11 (BORI critical edition, Mokshadharma, Hamsa Gita). Ganguli/Roy translation: Santi Parva section CCC (300). Our data's '12.305.11' matches neither; the verse number within the chapter (11) is correct.

hans_gita.17.context: Just before, 12.288.16 says that one who, though reviled, does not revile back burns the reviler and takes his merit. Just after, 12.288.18 says one should forgive the worse, the better and the equal alike, and that one who is dishonoured, struck and abused reaches success this way.
hans_gita.17.core_teaching: The highest steadiness is not just restraining retaliation but not even wishing harm on the one who hurt you.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: One who answers harsh words with no harsh word, does not flatter back when praised, and has the fortitude neither to strike back nor wish the striker evil, finds his company always sought by the gods.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition text (12.288) as a textual check
commentaries.gist: Critical text 12.288.17 has the same wording; the swan frames it as a description of a character the gods desire, not as a command.

hans_gita.17.practical_reading: Notice the urge to get even, even in thought; let it pass without feeding it.
misreadings: Not 'do nothing when harmed'; it is about non-retaliation and not wishing harm, not about refusing protection or justice.
cautions: For someone who has been assaulted, 'when struck does not strike back' must never be framed as a duty; this is an ideal of character, not instruction to a victim.
not_for: victims of violence or assault
anyone being told to forgive too soon

data_flags.corrected_ref: Mahabharata 12.288.17 (BORI critical edition, Mokshadharma, Hamsa Gita). Ganguli/Roy translation: Santi Parva section CCC (300). Our data's '12.305.17' matches neither; the verse number within the chapter (17) is correct.

hans_gita.21.context: Immediately before, the swan says: when cursed I do not curse back; I know self-control is the door to immortality; and he reveals a secret, that nothing is higher than the human state (12.288.20). This verse follows with the image of the moon emerging from clouds.
hans_gita.21.core_teaching: Freed from wrongdoing, the steady person waits patiently for the right time, and through that patience reaches fulfilment.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: Freed from sin like the moon from murky clouds, the wise man, shining, attains success by patiently waiting for his time. Ganguli places it right after the line that no status is higher than humanity.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition text (12.288) as a textual check
commentaries.gist: Critical text 12.288.21 (GRETIL e-text) matches our wording, including 'dhanebhya'; the moon image and Ganguli's 'murky clouds' imply 'ghanebhya' (from clouds). Placed right after 'nothing is higher than the human state'.

hans_gita.21.practical_reading: When results are slow, keep your conduct clean and wait; clarity often comes the way the moon clears clouds, not by force.
misreadings: Not 'wait passively for luck'; the patience follows self-purification and restraint.
not_for: situations needing urgent action

data_flags.corrected_ref: Mahabharata 12.288.21 (BORI critical edition, Mokshadharma, Hamsa Gita). Ganguli/Roy translation: Santi Parva section CCC (300). Our data's '12.305.21' matches neither; the verse number within the chapter (21) is correct.

hans_gita.25.context: Part of the swan's teaching on speech: revilers are keener to talk of a person's faults than of his virtues (12.288.23); the one whose speech and mind are guarded gains everything (12.288.24). This verse then tells the wise not to answer abuse with abuse.
hans_gita.25.core_teaching: Answering insult with insult feeds the other's anger and damages you; the wise reply is restraint.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: The wise should never revile the undeserving in return with dispraise and insult; he should not extol others (merely because they extol him), and should never injure himself.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition text (12.288) as a textual check
commentaries.gist: Critical text 12.288.25 reads differently in its first line: a wise person grows (in merit) through the abuse he receives from a fool; therefore he should not make the other grow (in anger) nor harm himself.

hans_gita.25.practical_reading: Before replying to a rude person, ask whether the reply will cool things or heat them, and whether it will cost you your own peace.
misreadings: It governs your reply, not whether to accept mistreatment (our_note says this well).
cautions: 'The ignorant' can sound contemptuous; better framed as 'someone acting without understanding'.

data_flags.corrected_ref: Mahabharata 12.288.25 (BORI critical edition, Mokshadharma, Hamsa Gita). Ganguli/Roy translation: Santi Parva section CCC (300). Our data's '12.305.25' matches neither; the verse number within the chapter (25) is correct.

hans_gita.26.context: Follows the advice not to answer abuse with abuse (12.288.25). The next verse says the sacrifices, gifts and austerities of an angry man are taken away by Yama and his toil is wasted.
hans_gita.26.core_teaching: Insult need not disturb the one who receives it; the real damage falls on the one who gives it.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: The wise and learned man regards revilement as nectar; reviled, he sleeps without anxiety, while the reviler meets with destruction.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition text (12.288) as a textual check
commentaries.gist: Same wording in the critical text (12.288.26).

hans_gita.26.practical_reading: If an insult replays at night, remind yourself the injury is theirs to carry; you can let it go and sleep.
misreadings: Not 'seek out humiliation' or 'enjoy being insulted' (Medhatithi explicitly rejects this reading).
'The insulter is ruined' states a consequence; it is not a curse to wish on someone.
cautions: For a reader being humiliated at home or work, 'be satisfied by insult as by nectar' can sound like endorsement of mistreatment; use Medhatithi's framing (equanimity, not appetite for disrespect).
not_for: victims of ongoing emotional abuse
children being bullied

data_flags.corrected_ref: Mahabharata 12.288.26 (BORI critical edition, Mokshadharma, Hamsa Gita). Ganguli/Roy translation: Santi Parva section CCC (300). Our data's '12.305.26' matches neither; the verse number within the chapter (26) is correct. Near-parallel in Manusmriti 2.162-163 (verified on wisdomlib, Ganganath Jha's edition): 2.162b has 'amṛtasyeva cākāṅkṣed avamānasya' and 2.163 ends 'avamantā vinaśyati'. It is a close parallel, not the identical verse.

hans_gita.31.context: Just before, the swan lists truth, self-control, straightness, kindness, steadiness and forbearance, and says he has found nothing more purifying than truth (12.288.29-30). After this verse he says a person becomes like those he lives with and serves, as cloth takes the colour of the dye (12.288.32-33).
hans_gita.31.core_teaching: Having seen both humans and gods, the swan's testimony is that truth is the way up and the way across.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: I do not know anything more sacred than truth; having roved among humans and deities, I declare that truth is the only means of reaching heaven, as a ship is the only means of crossing the ocean.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition text (12.288) as a textual check
commentaries.gist: Same wording in the critical text (12.288.31); preceded by 'I found nothing more purifying than truth' (288.30).

hans_gita.31.practical_reading: Make one choice today where the truthful option is harder, and take it.
misreadings: Not license for hurtful 'honesty'; the same chapter ranks true and kind speech above true speech alone (12.288.38).

data_flags.corrected_ref: Mahabharata 12.288.31 (BORI critical edition, Mokshadharma, Hamsa Gita). Ganguli/Roy translation: Santi Parva section CCC (300). Our data's '12.305.31' matches neither; the verse number within the chapter (31) is correct.

hans_gita.40.context: After the swan's long answer, the Sadhyas ask four short questions (12.288.39): by what is the world covered, why does it not shine, why do people abandon friends, why do they not reach heaven? This is the answer. Two more question-and-answer pairs follow.
hans_gita.40.core_teaching: Four diagnoses in one line: ignorance hides the world, envy dims us, greed costs friendships, attachment keeps us from the higher goal.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: The world is enveloped by ignorance; men fail to shine because of malice; people cast off friends because of covetousness; men fail to reach heaven because of attachment.

commentaries.who: BORI critical text, Yaksha Prashna parallel (3.297 *1383)
commentaries.gist: The same question and answer is put to Yudhishthira by the Yaksha in a passage the critical edition relegates to the apparatus; there the world does not shine because of tamas (darkness).

hans_gita.40.practical_reading: Look at one friendship that has cooled and ask honestly whether wanting something (money, status, attention) played a part.
misreadings: Not a judgement that anyone who lost a friend was greedy.
cautions: Could sting a reader who was abandoned by a friend; better used for self-reflection than for explaining someone else's loss.
not_for: someone freshly hurt by a friend's betrayal (could read as blaming them)

data_flags.corrected_ref: Mahabharata 12.288.40 (BORI critical edition, Mokshadharma, Hamsa Gita). Ganguli/Roy translation: Santi Parva section CCC (300). Our data's '12.305.40' matches neither; the verse number within the chapter (40) is correct. A near-identical pair appears in the Yaksha Prashna, but only as a star passage (3.297.57 *1383) excluded from the BORI critical text; it reads 'tamasā' where we have 'mātsaryāt'. Our_note's recalled parallel is confirmed.

hans_gita.42.context: The Sadhyas ask (12.288.41): who alone among brahmanas is happy, who alone stays silent among many, who alone is strong though weak, who alone avoids quarrels? The swan answers each with 'the wise one' (prājña).
hans_gita.42.core_teaching: Wisdom shows as quiet contentment, the ability to stay silent in a crowd, inner strength without outer power, and staying out of quarrels.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: Only the brahmana possessed of wisdom is always happy, can keep silence while living among many, is regarded as strong though actually weak, and avoids quarrels. Footnote (Nilakantha): the verse shows the merits of one whose ignorance has gone.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition text (12.288) as a textual check
commentaries.gist: Same wording in the critical text (12.288.42); the question at 288.41 names 'among brahmanas'.

hans_gita.42.practical_reading: In a heated group chat or meeting, practise being the one who does not need to join the fight.
misreadings: Not that silence is always right; it is about not being dragged into quarrels.
not_for: someone who needs to speak up against wrongdoing and might hear 'stay quiet'

data_flags.corrected_ref: Mahabharata 12.288.42 (BORI critical edition, Mokshadharma, Hamsa Gita). Ganguli/Roy translation: Santi Parva section CCC (300). Our data's '12.305.42' matches neither; the verse number within the chapter (42) is correct.

hans_gita.7.context: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma what he thinks of truth, self-control, forgiveness and wisdom, which the learned praise. Bhishma tells of the Sadhya gods meeting Prajapati in the form of a golden swan and asking for the one best practice that frees a person from all bonds. This verse is the swan's first answer.
hans_gita.7.core_teaching: The core work is discipline, self-restraint, truth and inner guarding, ending in untying the heart's knots so that likes and dislikes no longer rule you.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: Renders the answer as penance, self-restraint, truth and subjugation of mind, untying the heart's knots and mastering the agreeable and disagreeable. Footnote (from the commentator Nilakantha): tapas is doing one's own duties; knots mean attachments and desires.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition text (12.288) as a textual check
commentaries.gist: The critical text has this verse as 12.288.7 with the same wording as ours; the swan goes on to warn at once against wounding speech (288.8-9).

hans_gita.7.practical_reading: Choose one 'knot' today, a grudge, a craving, a fear, and loosen it a little, so that a like or dislike does not decide your next action for you.
misreadings: Not about suppressing feelings; it is about not being ruled by them.

data_flags.corrected_ref: Mahabharata 12.288.7 (BORI critical edition, Mokshadharma, Hamsa Gita). Ganguli/Roy translation: Santi Parva section CCC (300). Our data's '12.305.7' matches neither; the verse number within the chapter (7) is correct.

kabir.kk.66.context: In Kabir's sakhis grouped under love and affection, this opens the section. The next sakhi says the guru lives in Banaras and the disciple across the sea, yet one with real virtue never forgets; the third says whoever is truly dear will come to you sooner or later, and one you gave body and mind to never leaves. Hazari Prasad Dwivedi quotes the pair to describe Kabir and his guru Ramananda: love does not recognise distance or caste.
kabir.kk.66.core_teaching: Real love is not measured in distance: the lily in the water and the moon in the sky are far apart yet joined, and whoever is dear to someone stays close to them. In context it is said of guru and disciple, and of God and devotee.

commentaries.who: Pushpapal Singh, Kabir Granthavali Satik (Hindi gloss, 1962)
commentaries.gist: The lily is in water and the moon far away, yet their love stays whole; whoever is someone's beloved is very close even while far. Names the figure as drishtant (illustrative example).

commentaries.who: Hazari Prasad Dwivedi, Kabir (1960 ed.), chapter on outer practice
commentaries.gist: Uses the sakhi of Ramananda and Kabir: love ignores distance, difference and caste; even if the guru were in Banaras and Kabir overseas, the guru's affection would reach him.

commentaries.who: Surrounding sakhis (Kabir Granthavali, ed. Shyamsundar Das, section 44)
commentaries.gist: The section continues: the guru in Banaras, the disciple on the sea-shore, never forgotten; the beloved comes sooner or later; one given body and mind never leaves. Sets the verse in devotional love.

kabir.kk.66.practical_reading: Used today to comfort people separated by distance: closeness is held in the heart, not in kilometres. A reader far from family can treat the bond as already present, and keep it alive by remembering.
misreadings: Not a claim that distance never hurts or that missing someone is a mistake.
In Kabir it is mainly about guru/God; do not present it as a family poem without saying it widens his image.
cautions: For someone separated by death, 'those we love are never far' can feel like a platitude; use gently.
For a reader whose loved one has cut contact, it may sound like denial.
not_for: fresh bereavement as a first response
estrangement or rejection by the loved one
speaks_to: living far from parents or family

kabir.kk.71.context: In Tripathi's anthology this couplet sits in a short run of petitions. Just before it the poet asks with what face he can plead when he does wrong in the Lord's very sight (70); just after, he says the Lord alone is merciful and all his running ends there, like a crow on a ship at sea that has no other perch (72). The ordering is the anthologist's, not necessarily Kabir's.
kabir.kk.71.core_teaching: The devotee owns his faults and asks pardon, appealing not to his merit but to the bond: a father's honour is tied to his child, even a bad one, so keeping the child is the father's own concern.

commentaries.who: Surrounding couplets in Kavita-Kaumudi (Tripathi, 1918), nos. 69-72
commentaries.gist: The neighbouring sakhis ask for the company of saints and the gift of compassion and humility, confess shame at sinning in God's sight, and call the Lord the only refuge, like a crow at sea with nowhere else to land.

commentaries.who: Ram Naresh Tripathi, introduction to the Kabir section (Kavita-Kaumudi, 1918)
commentaries.gist: Tripathi says Kabir wrote no books: he spoke sakhis and songs, disciples memorised them and they were compiled later; his couplets work almost like proverbs in everyday speech.

commentaries.who: Sung variant inside the bhajan 'नैया पड़ी मंझधार गुरु बिन कैसे लागे पार' (Kavitakosh)
commentaries.gist: The couplet survives in bhajan singing, reworded with Kabir's signature: the faults are servant Kabir's, the Lord cherishes the poor, and a father's name covers an unworthy son. There it frames the guru as ferryman.

commentaries.who: David Lorenzen, 'Kabir and the Avatars' (Kervan 25/1, 2021)
commentaries.gist: Scholars work from three older collections (Dadu Panth Granthavali, Sikh Adi Granth, Kabir Panth Bijak); the oldest manuscripts are western, and Callewaert grades songs by their presence in early manuscripts and gives little weight to later bhajan collections.

kabir.kk.71.practical_reading: For someone weighed down by guilt, the couplet shows a way to ask forgiveness from belonging rather than performance: you remain someone's child even when you have fallen short, and you can return on that basis.
misreadings: Not a licence to keep doing wrong because pardon is assured: the couplet before it is a confession of shame.
Not about a human father's duty to tolerate or cover up a child's wrongdoing.
'Father' is a relational image for God, not a sectarian doctrine; Kabir's God is also called Ram, Sain, Allah.
cautions: Father imagery can hurt readers whose father was absent, abusive or has recently died.
'Kaput' (bad son) is a harsh self-label; don't let the reading reinforce self-loathing in someone already full of shame.
Gendered (son/father) wording; the writer may need to widen it to 'child'.
not_for: readers estranged from or harmed by their father, unless reframed
situations needing accountability and repair toward someone the reader has hurt (the couplet is about being forgiven, not making amends)
speaks_to: feeling too unworthy to pray or ask for help
coming back after a long lapse
being the 'black sheep' of the family

kabir.sdg.samrathai.1.context: The chapter is about God's all-sufficiency (samarthai). It opens with Kabir saying he did nothing and could do nothing; whatever was done, Hari did. This couplet follows: the one with nobody has God. Next comes the famous image that even with the seven seas as ink, every forest as pens and the earth as paper, God's qualities could not be written down; later, the Lord as a merchant who weighs the whole world without scales.
kabir.sdg.samrathai.1.core_teaching: God is the refuge exactly of the friendless; whoever belongs to God finds everyone drawn to him; and no petitioner at the Lord's court is sent away with nothing.

commentaries.who: Kavitakosh bhavarth (volunteer gloss on the selection page)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as: when someone has no support anywhere, You alone are that support; once You are someone's, all others seek ties with him; nobody who reached Your court was ever turned away, all found shelter.

commentaries.who: Surrounding sakhis of 'Samrathai kau ang' (Das Granthavali text on Kavitakosh)
commentaries.gist: The chapter's theme is God's sole agency: Kabir did nothing, Hari did all; effort fails without Ram's help, every branch one steps on bends; the Lord turns a mustard seed into a mountain and back.

commentaries.who: David Lorenzen, 'Kabir and the Avatars' (Kervan 25/1, 2021)
commentaries.gist: Places the Granthavali among the three older Kabir collections; its manuscripts are western and early, and Agrawal argues it is the most reliable source of Kabir's compositions.

kabir.sdg.samrathai.1.practical_reading: For someone who feels utterly alone, the couplet says that having no one is the very condition in which God is nearest, and that no one is excluded from that court. Teachers often add its second claim: leaning on God tends to open human doors too.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that friends and family will reappear: 'whoever has You has everyone' is a spiritual claim, not a social promise.
Not a reason to refuse human help or community.
'Dargah' is a metaphor for God's court, not an endorsement of a particular shrine.
cautions: For a lonely reader who also feels God-forsaken, the line can sting; acknowledge the loneliness before offering the comfort.
Mixed Persian and Hindi devotional words (dargah, sain, mahrum): don't frame Kabir's God as narrowly Hindu or Muslim.
not_for: readers angry at God or in spiritual abandonment, where it may feel glib
someone in danger who first needs practical help
speaks_to: loneliness and having no one to turn to
migration or living far from family
after bereavement or a breakup leaves one without support

mbh.12.103.34.context: Yudhishthira asks how a king should deal with a mild enemy, a fierce one, and one with many allies. Bhishma retells Brihaspati's advice to Indra: hide hostility behind sweet words, wait for the right moment, use spies and division, attack enemies one at a time. This verse sits in that hard-edged statecraft.
mbh.12.103.34.core_teaching: People disregard a leader who is only soft and recoil from one who is only harsh; authority needs both, each at its proper time.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: a mild king is disregarded, a fierce one inspires dread, so be neither only fierce nor only mild but both; it sits amid advice on concealment, timing and dividing enemies.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.104.33 and 12.138.64 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The same maxim reappears in Bharadvaja's counsel (12.138.64), which spells out the timing: harsh when it is time for harshness, gentle when it is time for gentleness.

mbh.12.103.34.practical_reading: For parents, managers and teachers: kindness without boundaries gets ignored, boundaries without kindness breed fear. Read the moment.
misreadings: Firmness means clarity and consequences, not cruelty (our misuse note is right).
Not license to be unpredictable or manipulative.
cautions: From advice on handling enemies by deceit and force; take only the balance principle.
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship being told to be gentler
readers seeking justification for harshness
speaks_to: someone who is a pushover or too harsh

mbh.12.104.16.context: Yudhishthira asks how a righteous king who has lost his officers, army and treasury should find happiness. Bhishma tells of Prince Kshemadarshi of Kosala, who, after failing to win back his kingdom, asks the sage Kalakavrikshiya what he can do short of suicide, theft or begging refuge. The sage says all possessions are unstable, grief cannot restore them, wise people want only what is attainable and bear others' prosperity, and he could live contentedly alone in the forest. In the next section the sage offers a strategy for recovering the kingdom if the prince still has the strength, and later reconciles him with King Janaka. This verse comes early in the sage's first reply, after he tells the prince that what earlier generations acquired has all perished.
mbh.12.104.16.core_teaching: Things arise and pass by their nature; grief has no power to reverse that, so endless grieving over what is gone is futile.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: everything acquired by forebears has perished; things that were are no more and grief cannot restore them; where are your father and grandfather? Everyone now twenty or thirty will be dead within a century.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.105 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text matches. The prince's question openly lists suicide among the options he wants to avoid, which frames the whole consolation.

mbh.12.104.16.practical_reading: After losing a job, status or money: grieve, but notice that rumination cannot change the fact; redirect energy to what can still be done.
misreadings: Feeling grief is human; the point is not to feed it endlessly (our misuse note is right).
Counsel about lost wealth and position, not a death (our note is right).
cautions: The prince has mentioned suicide as an option he is trying to avoid; never quote the setting for a distressed reader.
The sage's reasoning also invokes dead parents and everyone's death; it can feel cold.
not_for: fresh bereavement
suicidal thoughts
speaks_to: job loss, business failure, lost status
someone stuck replaying a financial loss

mbh.12.104.28.context: Yudhishthira asks how a righteous king who has lost his officers, army and treasury should find happiness. Bhishma tells of Prince Kshemadarshi of Kosala, who, after failing to win back his kingdom, asks the sage Kalakavrikshiya what he can do short of suicide, theft or begging refuge. The sage says all possessions are unstable, grief cannot restore them, wise people want only what is attainable and bear others' prosperity, and he could live contentedly alone in the forest. In the next section the sage offers a strategy for recovering the kingdom if the prince still has the strength, and later reconciles him with King Janaka. Here, after the prince says Time swept his kingdom away and he lives on alms, the sage tells him not to grieve over past or future.
mbh.12.104.28.core_teaching: Set your desire on what can actually be had, enjoy what is in front of you, and do not grieve over a future that has not arrived.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: never grieve for past or future; desiring only the obtainable, enjoy present possessions and do not mourn what is absent; be glad of what you win with ease, and keep a pure disposition.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.105.27-29 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text uses a direct imperative ("desire attainable things"); the next verses warn that the foolish blame the Ordainer and envy others when stripped of former prosperity.

mbh.12.104.28.practical_reading: A grounding practice for anxious or deprived seasons: list what is within reach and enjoyable today, and catch yourself pre-grieving imagined futures.
misreadings: Not "stop hoping or planning"; it is about longing for the impossible and anticipatory grief.
cautions: Same frame as the previous verse (a ruined prince); may sound dismissive to someone facing real scarcity.
not_for: people in poverty told to want less
fresh grief
speaks_to: someone fixated on a lost or unattainable goal

mbh.12.104.33.context: Yudhishthira asks how a righteous king who has lost his officers, army and treasury should find happiness. Bhishma tells of Prince Kshemadarshi of Kosala, who, after failing to win back his kingdom, asks the sage Kalakavrikshiya what he can do short of suicide, theft or begging refuge. The sage says all possessions are unstable, grief cannot restore them, wise people want only what is attainable and bear others' prosperity, and he could live contentedly alone in the forest. In the next section the sage offers a strategy for recovering the kingdom if the prince still has the strength, and later reconciles him with King Janaka. Here the sage says a foolish man stripped of fortune blames the Ordainer and resents others' undeserved prosperity; the prince is free of that vice, so he should bear others' good fortune.
mbh.12.104.33.core_teaching: Make peace with other people's good fortune even when you lack it; the wise can take joy in fortune that is not theirs, while resentment drives fortune away.

commentaries.who: Ganguli translation (Santi sec. CIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: endure others' prosperity though you have none; the dexterous enjoy prosperity vested in others; prosperity leaves one who hates others.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha, as reported in Ganguli's note 5
commentaries.gist: Nilakantha glosses kuśala as "free from envy" and "elsewhere" as "in an enemy": the non-envious can enjoy fortune even when it sits with a rival. Ganguli says he does not follow this.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.105.33 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Only the first two lines are in the constituted text (reading janāḥ for narāḥ); the line about fortune draining from the resentful is absent there.

mbh.12.104.33.practical_reading: A practice against envy: when someone else succeeds, try sharing in it (mudita) rather than measuring yourself; resentment only adds a second loss.
misreadings: Not "accept injustice"; it addresses envy, not unfairness.
Not a promise that being gracious brings money back.
cautions: Line 3 is textually weak; avoid building a reading on it.
not_for: someone whose "rival" harmed them
infertility or loss where others' joy is acutely painful
