speaks_to: envy of peers' success (promotions, weddings, babies)
someone recovering from a setback while others thrive

mbh.12.104.57.context: Yudhishthira asks how a righteous king who has lost his officers, army and treasury should find happiness. Bhishma tells of Prince Kshemadarshi of Kosala, who, after failing to win back his kingdom, asks the sage Kalakavrikshiya what he can do short of suicide, theft or begging refuge. The sage says all possessions are unstable, grief cannot restore them, wise people want only what is attainable and bear others' prosperity, and he could live contentedly alone in the forest. In the next section the sage offers a strategy for recovering the kingdom if the prince still has the strength, and later reconciles him with King Janaka. This image comes in the sage's closing advice to live alone and content in the forest; he says a person in the prince's plight can live happily so. The next section offers a political route back instead.
mbh.12.104.57.core_teaching: A deep lake stirred up clears by itself; likewise one whose understanding is formed regains clarity from within, without forcing.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: a large turbid lake resumes tranquillity of itself; a wise man disturbed by such matters becomes tranquil of himself. The sage pairs this with life alone in the forest, compassionate and content.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.105.52 and star passage 246 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Only the lake half-line is in the constituted text; the explicit comparison to the wise person is a manuscript addition, as our backticks show.

mbh.12.104.57.practical_reading: When upset, stop stirring: give the mind stillness and let understanding do its work, the way silt settles when the water is left alone.
misreadings: Not "just wait, time heals": it is wisdom that settles the mind (our note is right; the line is not).
Not "suppress feelings".
cautions: In context tied to withdrawing alone to the forest; do not suggest isolation to a struggling reader.
not_for: clinical depression where waiting it out is unsafe advice
someone who needs to act urgently
speaks_to: anger or agitation after a blow-up

mbh.12.108.3.context: Yudhishthira asks which of the many branches of duty matters most. Bhishma names honouring mother, father and teacher. He goes straight on to say their commands should be followed whether or not they accord with dharma, likens the three to the three sacred fires, ranks the mother above ten fathers and the teacher above both, and says parents should never be slain or punished even if they offend.
mbh.12.108.3.core_teaching: Of the many duties, Bhishma rates honouring one's mother, father and teachers as foremost; living by it brings both good standing and spiritual reward.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: worship of mother, father and preceptor is most important; their commands should be done whether consistent with righteousness or not; they are the three fires; the mother outweighs ten fathers, yet the teacher outranks both.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.109 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text keeps the obedience verses immediately after this one, so the library's choice to stop at 109.3 is a real editorial cut.

mbh.12.108.3.practical_reading: A call to gratitude and respect toward those who raised and taught us: visiting, caring for aging parents, thanking teachers.
misreadings: Not obedience into harm (our misuse note is right; the very next verses ask for it, which is why they are cut).
Not a ranking of people's worth.
cautions: Surrounding verses demand obedience even against dharma and say parents should go unpunished whatever they do; never pair with readers from abusive or controlling homes.
Can feel like guilt for adult children setting boundaries.
not_for: survivors of parental abuse
estranged children
someone pressured by family to give up a choice

mbh.12.113.9.context: Yudhishthira asks how a king without allies should behave toward a far stronger enemy. Bhishma tells how the Ocean asked the rivers why they carry away great trees but never the reeds on their banks. Ganga answers that rigid trees resist and are uprooted, while the reed bends to the flood, knows time and place, and rises after. Bhishma concludes that one who will not yield to an overwhelming foe is destroyed, and the wise adopt the reed's conduct.
mbh.12.113.9.core_teaching: Flexibility under overwhelming force is survival, not defeat: bend while the flood passes, then stand again where you were.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CXIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the cane bows to the current and resumes its posture after; it knows time and opportunity. Bhishma: whoever will not yield to a mightier foe soon perishes. Ganguli's note: true policy is waiting till the foe weakens.

commentaries.who: Kautilya, Arthashastra 12.1 (Shamasastry translation)
commentaries.gist: The weak king attacked by a powerful one should live like a reed in a current, an opinion credited to Bharadvaja; Kautilya qualifies it: bowing to everyone breeds despair, so seek a strong protector or a fortress.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.114 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Same parable in the constituted text; it is framed as statecraft for a weak ruler facing a stronger enemy.

mbh.12.113.9.practical_reading: In a crisis you cannot win head-on (a layoff wave, an illness, a market crash), adapt, conserve and wait, without abandoning who you are.
misreadings: Bending under pressure is not giving up your values (our misuse note is right).
Not a rule to submit to mistreatment (our note is right); it is strategy for surviving overwhelming force.
cautions: Do not give to someone in an abusive relationship as advice to "bend".
not_for: abuse, harassment or coercion
someone being pressured to compromise their integrity

mbh.12.114.15.context: Yudhishthira asks how a wise person should respond when a harsh, foolish man abuses him in public. Bhishma says such talk is like a crow cawing in the woods; the backbiter is like a dog, and whoever tries to answer him in kind is like a donkey sinking in ashes. The person who bears abuse in assemblies, he ends, is never hurt by words.
mbh.12.114.15.core_teaching: Public slander reveals the slanderer: it displays his own faults as plainly as a snake shows its raised hood.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation (Santi CXIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli reads it as the evil person who broadcasts a great-souled man's faults merely advertising his own nature, like a snake spreading its hood; trying to hit back, he adds, leaves you like a donkey stuck in ash.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Kumbakonam 12.114.14-16)
commentaries.gist: The verse is flanked by advice to avoid such a person entirely and not to answer back; retaliation only drags you down.

mbh.12.114.15.practical_reading: When someone runs you down in front of others, you do not need to win the exchange; what they say mostly shows who they are.
misreadings: Not a licence to dismiss all criticism as 'their faults'; it is about malicious public slander.
Not advice to stay silent about abuse or harassment that needs reporting.
cautions: The surrounding text uses insulting animal comparisons (dog, ass) for the slanderer; keep the reading free of contempt.
not_for: situations of ongoing bullying or harassment where action, not endurance, is needed
speaks_to: being belittled or passed over in public

mbh.12.114.8.context: Yudhishthira asks how a modest, learned man should respond when a conceited fool abuses him in an assembly. Bhishma: one who bears abuse without anger takes the abuser's merit; abusive talk is like a bird's harsh cry; such a man boasts of his insults; then this verse. The slanderer only exposes his own nature; avoid him, and do not trade words, since a quarrel between the high and the low is disapproved by the calm.
mbh.12.114.8.core_teaching: The praise or blame of a thoughtless person has no real power over you; it is noise, like a crow cawing in the forest.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CXIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: what can a vulgar fellow do by praise or blame? He is a crow cawing uselessly in the woods; if mere words could prove accusations they would matter; the slanderer only displays his own nature; avoid him.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.115 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The constituted text reads prākṛto ("a common person"), confirming that the verse is about an unthinking critic, not about everyone's opinion.

mbh.12.114.8.practical_reading: For online abuse or public insults: you do not owe a response to noise. Save your energy for criticism that comes from thought and goodwill.
misreadings: Fair criticism is worth hearing (our misuse note is right).
Not contempt for ordinary people; prākṛta here means the thoughtless abuser.
cautions: The surrounding passage uses harsh labels for the abuser (bastardy, dog); keep the reading calm.
If the "abuse" is harassment or threats, ignoring it may not be safe; real help comes first.
not_for: harassment or threats needing action
someone dismissing legitimate feedback
speaks_to: people-pleasers hooked on approval (praise too is noise)

mbh.12.138.46.context: Yudhishthira asks how a king surrounded by enemies keeps his wits. Bhishma tells of the mouse Palita, who finds a cat caught in a hunter's net, a mongoose below and an owl above. Reasoning that a cornered enemy may make peace, he says this verse to himself, then offers to gnaw the cat free in exchange for protection. Both keep the deal, but afterwards the mouse refuses the cat's friendship, arguing that alliances rest on interest.
mbh.12.138.46.core_teaching: In a crisis, an intelligent adversary who understands shared interest is a better partner than a well-meaning fool; the mouse bets his life on that.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CXXXVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one afflicted by a stronger foe should make peace even with an enemy; better a learned enemy than a fool for a friend; my life is in the cat's hands, so let me address him about his own liberation.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.136.42-46 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: In the constituted text the mouse calls the cat a fool just before and hopes alliance may make him a wise enemy; the maxim is tactical self-talk in apaddharma, not a general rule.

mbh.12.138.46.practical_reading: In negotiations or emergencies, judge partners by competence and aligned interest, not by sentiment; and choose wise counsel even when it comes from someone you dislike.
misreadings: Not "ditch kind but simple friends".
Not a call to trust enemies; the mouse stays wary throughout.
cautions: The story's closing moral is cynical: friendships are interest-based. Use for strategy, not for questions about real friendship.
not_for: someone hurt by a friend's foolish mistake
loneliness

data_flags.translation_note: Only the first half is translated. The second half says: my life now rests on my enemy, the cat. Without it the maxim loses its point (an emergency alliance with a natural enemy). BORI reads śreyān ("better") and apaṇḍitam.

mbh.12.140.66.context: Yudhishthira asks how a king should act in a decaying age beset by robbers. Bhishma says he will describe policy for hard times, "setting compassion aside", via Kaninka's counsel to the Sauvira king: keep the rod ready, be humble in speech but razor-sharp at heart, make peace without trusting, cut enemies at the root. Just before this verse: people despise the soft and fear the harsh, so be harsh at the time for harshness and soft at the time for softness. Kaninka ends by saying this conduct is only for times of distress.
mbh.12.140.66.core_teaching: Gentleness, used well, prevails over both gentle and fierce opponents; nothing is beyond it, which makes it sharper than harshness.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CXL)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: be stern when sternness is needed, mild when mildness is; by mildness the mild are cut and the fierce destroyed; nothing mildness cannot effect, so it is sharper than fierceness. All this is for seasons of distress.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.138.2-9 and 63-66 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The constituted text frames the counsel as policy for calamity with compassion set aside, opens with the ever-raised rod, and places this verse after the be-harsh-or-soft-in-season maxim.

mbh.12.140.66.practical_reading: In conflict, calm and courteous persistence often achieves more than force: it disarms the hostile and does not provoke resistance.
misreadings: Not a teaching on meekness (our note is right): gentleness here is a means of prevailing.
Not "soft is always enough"; the preceding verse says be harsh when it is time.
cautions: Comes from a ruthless, explicitly compassion-suspending speech; do not present Kaninka as a gentle sage.
not_for: someone in an abusive situation being told to be gentler
readers seeking manipulation tactics
speaks_to: dealing with difficult colleagues or customers

mbh.12.144.12.context: Yudhishthira asks about the merit of protecting one who seeks refuge. Bhishma tells a story that Parashurama (Bhargava) once told King Muchukunda: in a storm a fowler, who has caged a female pigeon, shelters under a tree where her mate lives. The male pigeon laments his missing wife; she, in the cage, urges him to honour the fowler as a guest. He welcomes the fowler, lights a fire for him and, having no food, throws himself into it as a meal. The shaken fowler frees the female, who then also enters the fire; the fowler renounces his trade and later dies in a forest fire, and all three reach heaven. This verse is in the male pigeon's lament that night, before he knows his wife is caged below.
mbh.12.144.12.core_teaching: Home is where the beloved is; without them even a palace is a wilderness.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CXLIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: a house is not a home, the wife is the home; even the foot of a tree is home with one's spouse, and without her a palace is a desolate wilderness. The praise includes her never eating or sitting before him.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.142.4-10 and star passages 364-368 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The constituted lament keeps the core (empty home, no medicine or ally like a wife); the tree-and-palace couplet and much of the praise are manuscript additions.

mbh.12.144.12.practical_reading: Used for couples and families who have moved, downsized or live simply: belonging is in the relationship, not the building.
misreadings: Not the wife's duty to be the husband's "home" at her own expense.
cautions: The surrounding praise idealises a wife who never eats before her husband, and the story ends with the widowed pigeon throwing herself into the fire because she cannot live without him. Never use this story for widowhood or partner loss.
The pigeon fears his wife is lost; for someone whose partner has died or left, it can deepen pain.
not_for: widowhood or recent partner loss
divorce
readers in controlling relationships
speaks_to: couples who have moved, migrated or downsized

mbh.12.144.13.context: Yudhishthira asks about the merit of protecting one who seeks refuge. Bhishma tells a story that Parashurama (Bhargava) once told King Muchukunda: in a storm a fowler, who has caged a female pigeon, shelters under a tree where her mate lives. The male pigeon laments his missing wife; she, in the cage, urges him to honour the fowler as a guest. He welcomes the fowler, lights a fire for him and, having no food, throws himself into it as a meal. The shaken fowler frees the female, who then also enters the fire; the fowler renounces his trade and later dies in a forest fire, and all three reach heaven. This follows the tree-and-palace couplet; the constituted text nearby says there is no ally like a wife in pursuing dharma.
mbh.12.144.13.core_teaching: A spouse is a partner across every sphere of life and the one you can rely on when far from home.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CXLIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the spouse is one's associate in virtue, profit and pleasure, the trusted companion abroad, the best medicine in sickness; there is no friend or refuge like a wife.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.142.8-10 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: This couplet is a manuscript addition, but the constituted text says the same in its own words: a wife is the companion on life's road, the best medicine, the best ally in dharma.

mbh.12.144.13.practical_reading: For marriage reflection: a partner is a companion in values, work and joy alike; trust is built for the times you are far from home.
misreadings: Not a statement that a woman's worth is in serving her husband.
cautions: Same story cautions as the previous verse (self-immolation of both pigeons; widow cannot live without husband).
not_for: widowhood or partner loss
readers in unhappy or controlling marriages
singles who feel judged
speaks_to: partners supporting each other through moves or work abroad

mbh.12.145.5.context: Yudhishthira asks about the merit of protecting one who seeks refuge. Bhishma tells a story that Parashurama (Bhargava) once told King Muchukunda: in a storm a fowler, who has caged a female pigeon, shelters under a tree where her mate lives. The male pigeon laments his missing wife; she, in the cage, urges him to honour the fowler as a guest. He welcomes the fowler, lights a fire for him and, having no food, throws himself into it as a meal. The shaken fowler frees the female, who then also enters the fire; the fowler renounces his trade and later dies in a forest fire, and all three reach heaven. Here the pigeon, urged by his caged wife, greets the cold fowler as a guest who has sought refuge, then lights a fire and offers himself as food.
mbh.12.145.5.core_teaching: Duty to a guest who seeks shelter does not depend on who he is: as a tree shades even the woodcutter, hospitality is owed even to an enemy at your door.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CXLVI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: you are welcome, this is your home; hospitality should be shown even to a foe; the tree does not withdraw its shade from one who comes to cut it; a householder of the five sacrifices is especially bound.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.142.22-26 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The constituted text grounds the welcome in duty to one who has sought refuge and the householder's five daily offerings; the tree-and-shade couplet itself is a manuscript addition.

mbh.12.145.5.practical_reading: Basic dignity and care are owed even to people we dislike when they come to us in need: the stranger, the rival, the difficult relative at the door.
misreadings: Kindness is not letting someone keep harming you (our misuse note is right).
Not a general rule to be kind to whoever harms you (our note is right; the line drifts toward it).
cautions: In the story this hospitality ends in the pigeon's self-sacrifice in the fire, followed by his widow's; never let the reading glorify self-destruction.
Do not offer to someone being harmed by the "guest".
not_for: abuse survivors
someone being told to keep sheltering a person who hurts them
suicidal readers (story context)
speaks_to: humanitarian work with people seen as enemies
professionals (doctors, lawyers) serving people they dislike

data_flags.corrected_ref: Not in the BORI constituted text: BORI star passage 374, after 12.142.24. Ganguli, Santi Parva section CXLVI (wisdomlib) includes it. Our chapter number 145 matches neither.

mbh.12.17.3.context: Bhima has urged Yudhishthira to stop grieving and enjoy the kingdom they won. Yudhishthira answers that discontent, attachment and pride drive Bhima's love of rule: even the sole ruler of the earth has one stomach, desire can never be filled, so conquer the stomach first. In the same speech he quotes Janaka's saying that nothing of his burns if Mithila burns.
mbh.12.17.3.core_teaching: Owning more than one can use adds nothing to what one person actually needs; so praising accumulation and power for their own sake is misplaced.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XVII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the peerless monarch of the whole earth will have but one stomach, so why applaud this life? Desire is like fire fed with fuel; subdue the stomach with little food and conquer it first.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.17 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Same chapter and numbering. The speech goes on (12.17.17-18) to quote Janaka's verse about Mithila burning, linking this verse to the renunciation sayings elsewhere in the Shanti Parva.

mbh.12.17.3.practical_reading: A check on status-chasing: ask what you will actually use or enjoy, and notice how much striving serves appetite rather than need.
misreadings: Not a rule against earning, providing or leading; Yudhishthira is answered by his family and does take up the rule.
Not advice to under-eat.
cautions: The next lines in Ganguli praise subduing hunger with little food; avoid for readers with disordered eating.
Spoken by a grieving man arguing against his duties; the epic does not endorse his conclusion.
not_for: people in poverty or food insecurity
eating disorders
someone deciding to abandon responsibilities
speaks_to: someone burnt out from chasing more

mbh.12.17.4.context: Continues the previous verse: after "one stomach", Yudhishthira says desire cannot be filled in a day, in months, or in a lifetime, and compares it to fire that grows when fed and dies down when not.
mbh.12.17.4.core_teaching: Desire is structurally unfillable: feeding it does not satisfy it, so a whole life spent filling it never arrives at enough.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XVII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: desires cannot be filled in a day or many months, not in a whole lifetime; fire fed with fuel blazes, unfed it goes out.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.17.4 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text has the same thought with minor wording differences; the "unfillable desire" idea recurs in Yayati's sayings and in Manki's song later in the Shanti Parva.

mbh.12.17.4.practical_reading: Notice the pattern of "one more" (purchase, promotion, follower count) and test whether feeding it ever produced lasting satisfaction; practise contentment as a skill.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of all wanting; it is about craving as a bottomless hunger.
cautions: Same context as 12.17.3: grief-driven argument against duty; the fire-and-food image continues into fasting advice.
not_for: someone whose basic needs are unmet
eating disorders
speaks_to: compulsive buying, scrolling or achievement treadmills
someone who "has everything" and is still restless

mbh.12.172.18.context: Bhishma ends the tale of Gautama, a destitute brahmin who was fed and sheltered by the crane Rajadharman and enriched by the crane's friend, the Rakshasa king Virupaksha, then killed his sleeping host for food on the way home. Virupaksha has Gautama killed; the crane is revived by the divine cow Surabhi and asks Indra to revive Gautama too; Gautama goes home and is later cursed to hell. Bhishma, who heard it from Narada, draws the lesson about ingratitude and friendship. After this verse he adds that one must never betray a friend, should always be grateful, and that everything, including help in danger, comes through friends.
mbh.12.172.18.core_teaching: Ingratitude destroys a person's name, standing and peace, because no one can trust him; the text treats it as a wrong with no ritual expiation.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CLXXIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: whence can an ungrateful person have fame, place or happiness? He is not to be trusted and can never escape; no one should injure a friend; be grateful, since everything comes through friends.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.167.16-21 and star passage 449 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: In the constituted text; a longer manuscript version adds that expiations exist for killing a brahmin or drinking liquor but none for ingratitude.

mbh.12.172.18.practical_reading: Remember who helped you and honour it; trust, once broken by using people and discarding them, is hard to rebuild.
misreadings: Not a tool to demand gratitude from people we have helped.
Not "you owe your abuser"; gratitude is for real kindness.
cautions: "Ungrateful" is often used to silence children or partners leaving controlling situations; never pair with them.
The story has a killing, caste-laden language and a curse to hell; keep the reading on the principle.
not_for: abuse survivors told they are ungrateful
depressed readers who cannot feel gratitude and blame themselves
speaks_to: reflecting on how we treat benefactors and mentors
repairing a relationship after taking someone for granted

data_flags.translation_note: The translation drops the final clause "kṛtaghne nāsti niṣkṛtiḥ" (for the ungrateful there is no expiation), which is the point Bhishma stresses (expiations exist for grave sins, none for ingratitude). The line reorders the logic, making trust the cause of the other losses.

mbh.12.172.20.context: Bhishma ends the story of the ungrateful brahmin Gautama, who killed the crane Rajadharma that had fed and enriched him. In Ganguli's text the story does not end at the murder: the crane is revived by the cow Surabhi's milk-froth and nectar, and even asks Indra to bring Gautama back to life; Gautama goes home and is later cursed for his ingratitude. Bhishma then draws the moral: the ungrateful have no fame, no refuge and no expiation; be grateful and good to friends.
mbh.12.172.20.core_teaching: A grateful, friendly disposition is the soil of a good life; much of what we gain, materially and otherwise, comes to us from or through friends.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation and footnote (Santi CLXXIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's Bhishma closes: be grateful and work for your friends' good, since much can be gained from friends. His footnote explains that 'mitrāt' means both 'from' and 'through' a friend: friends give, or help one win, wealth and honour.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Kumbakonam 12.172.18-21)
commentaries.gist: The verse sits between the sharp warning that ingratitude has no expiation (v.18-19) and the claim that gaining a friend is better than gaining wealth (v.21).

mbh.12.172.20.practical_reading: Read as a daily practice: notice who has helped you, say so, and treat friendship as something you invest in rather than use.
misreadings: Not a transactional 'make friends because they are useful'; the story's point is the moral horror of exploiting a benefactor.
Not a claim that people without friends are to blame for their hardship.
cautions: The source story is violent (a friend killed for food) and the surrounding verses speak of hell for the ungrateful; keep the reading on gratitude, not damnation.
not_for: someone who was exploited or betrayed by a 'friend' and may hear it as pressure to stay grateful to them
someone isolated and friendless, unless framed as hope
speaks_to: noticing who has quietly supported you

mbh.12.172.21.context: Bhishma ends the tale of Gautama, a destitute brahmin who was fed and sheltered by the crane Rajadharman and enriched by the crane's friend, the Rakshasa king Virupaksha, then killed his sleeping host for food on the way home. Virupaksha has Gautama killed; the crane is revived by the divine cow Surabhi and asks Indra to revive Gautama too; Gautama goes home and is later cursed to hell. Bhishma, who heard it from Narada, draws the lesson about ingratitude and friendship. This couplet belongs to a longer manuscript version of Bhishma's closing lesson on friendship; the constituted text and Ganguli say more briefly that strength and every good come through friends.
mbh.12.172.21.core_teaching: A friend is worth more than money: wealth comes easily through friends, and a friend makes effort possible.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. CLXXIII, n. 3)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: everything may be obtained from or through a friend, honours, enjoyments, escape from danger; the wise honour friends. His note explains the ablative as both "from" and "through" friends.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.167.21 and star passage 449 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text: be grateful and friend-seeking; truth and strength arise from a friend. This exact couplet appears only in the manuscript expansion, which also says a friend is called true wealth.

mbh.12.172.21.practical_reading: Invest in friendships as you would in savings: relationships open doors and give courage that money alone cannot.
misreadings: Not "make friends for what they can get you"; it praises friendship over wealth.
cautions: Comes at the end of a story of betrayal and murder; keep the reading on friendship.
not_for: someone just betrayed by a friend
isolated readers who may feel shamed for having few friends
speaks_to: someone choosing between a career move and staying near friends

mbh.12.173.21.context: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how to push away grief when wealth is lost or a wife, son or father dies. Bhishma tells how a brahmin came to King Senajit, who was stunned by his son's death, and talked him out of his grief; he first tells the king that he too will soon be mourned, that people meet and part like two logs drifting on the ocean, and that joy and sorrow follow each other. This verse closes that point; the vulgate line just before says joy and sorrow turn like a wheel. The talk then moves to the body as the seat of pleasure and pain and to letting go of craving.
mbh.12.173.21.core_teaching: Happiness and sorrow take turns in every life, so the present sorrow is not permanent; neither state is held for ever.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli, Santi sec. CLXXIV)
commentaries.gist: The brahmin's ground is that nothing, not even his own self, is truly 'his', and that unions are like driftwood that meets and parts; Ganguli's note adds that joy and grief end with the body.

commentaries.who: Sanskrit Wikisource text (vulgate) and BORI 12.168.18-19
commentaries.gist: Both set this verse right after the claim that sorrow follows happiness and happiness follows sorrow; the vulgate adds the wheel image, which BORI keeps only as a manuscript addition (star passage 460).

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 12.168
commentaries.gist: Same wording in the constituted text; the episode is the opening of the Mokshadharma, answering how to dispel grief at loss.

mbh.12.173.21.practical_reading: When a hard season feels endless, remember that states change; this is a reason to hold on, not a promise about timing.
misreadings: Not a promise that a specific loss will be undone or 'made up for'.
Not an instruction to stop feeling grief now.
cautions: Spoken to a father whose son has just died; the surrounding speech calls him deluded and says one should not feel affection for children because separation is certain. Use this verse alone, not its frame, for grieving parents.
'You will be happy again' can feel dismissive in the first days of a bereavement.
not_for: a parent in the first weeks after a child's death
chronic illness or depression where 'it will pass' sounds like minimising
speaks_to: a long low patch after a job loss, breakup or failure
someone who feels stuck in a bad season
people who need perspective that moods and fortunes change

mbh.12.173.40.context: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how to push away grief when wealth is lost or a wife, son or father dies. Bhishma tells how a brahmin came to King Senajit, who was stunned by his son's death, and talked him out of his grief; after describing how only the wise who have gone beyond pairs of opposites stay untroubled, he turns to effort: idleness is pleasant and ends in pain, capable effort is painful and ends in joy. The next verses tell the king to meet whatever comes with an undefeated heart.
mbh.12.173.40.core_teaching: Ease that avoids effort ends in sorrow, while capable effort, though hard, leads to happiness; good fortune stays with the diligent.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource)
commentaries.gist: Reads it spiritually: idleness means not taking up the means to knowledge; prosperity means yogic powers and fortune means knowledge. Records a variant first line.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXIV)
commentaries.gist: Parses the first half as two statements, that happiness ends in misery and that idleness is misery, with cleverness in action the cause of happiness; prosperity lives with the capable.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 12.168.29 and 12.27.30
commentaries.gist: The same maxim appears twice in the Shanti Parva consolations, once in Vyasa's speech to Yudhishthira and once here, which shows it was a stock saying.

mbh.12.173.40.practical_reading: Notice which comforts are really avoidance; do the slightly hard thing today that your future self will thank you for.
misreadings: Not a glorification of overwork or hustle.
Not a judgement on rest, illness or depression; Nilakantha's reading is about neglecting the spiritual path.
cautions: Comes in a consolation to a bereaved father; do not use it to tell a grieving person to 'get busy'.
Can shame people with low energy from illness or depression.
not_for: burnout or exhaustion
depression, chronic fatigue or illness
fresh grief
speaks_to: someone choosing between comfort and a demanding goal
students and early-career people building habits

mbh.12.173.41.context: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how to push away grief when wealth is lost or a wife, son or father dies. Bhishma tells how a brahmin came to King Senajit, who was stunned by his son's death, and talked him out of his grief; right after saying that effort, not idleness, brings fortune, he gives this rule for meeting events: take each as it comes without being conquered by it. The next verse says thousands of occasions for grief and fear daily overwhelm the undiscerning, but not the wise.
mbh.12.173.41.core_teaching: Meet each pleasant or painful thing as it actually arrives, without letting joy or sorrow take control of the heart.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource)
commentaries.gist: Pleasant and unpleasant are what produce joy and pain; 'undefeated' means not brought under the sway of a heart made of elation and grief.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXIV)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as enjoying or enduring what comes with an unconquered heart, placed between the praise of capable effort and the warning about daily causes of grief.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 12.168.30 and 12.26.26
commentaries.gist: The same couplet occurs in Vyasa's consolation of Yudhishthira as well as here, so it is a recurring teaching of the Shanti Parva consolations.

mbh.12.173.41.practical_reading: Deal with today's actual event, good or bad, one at a time, without letting it decide who you are.
misreadings: Not 'feel nothing'; the heart is undefeated, not absent.
Not passive acceptance of harm that can be changed.
cautions: Part of a speech to a bereaved father; gentle as a verse, but avoid implying the reader is 'defeated' if they are grieving.
not_for: someone enduring abuse or injustice they could act against
the rawest days of loss
speaks_to: people swept up by highs and lows
anyone facing a run of unexpected events

mbh.12.173.42.context: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how to push away grief when wealth is lost or a wife, son or father dies. Bhishma tells how a brahmin came to King Senajit, who was stunned by his son's death, and talked him out of his grief; having told him to meet each event with an undefeated heart, he says that every day countless occasions of grief and fear seize the person without discernment but not the wise. The next verse lists who is untouched: the learned, attentive to good teaching, free of envy and self-controlled.
mbh.12.173.42.core_teaching: Grief and fear arise from countless daily triggers, but they take hold only where discernment is missing.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource)
commentaries.gist: Grief is rooted in being parted from what one wants, fear in meeting what one does not want; 'enter' means they spread through a person by producing their effects.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXIV)
commentaries.gist: Follows the vulgate 'fear' reading and continues that sorrow cannot touch the wise, the self-restrained and the non-envious.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 12.168.31; 12.317.2; 3.2.15
commentaries.gist: Here the constituted text pairs grief with joy, not fear; the grief-and-fear form is the one used at 12.317.2 and in the Vana Parva.

mbh.12.173.42.practical_reading: You cannot stop triggers arriving, but you can learn to recognise them and decline to let each one take over.
misreadings: Not 'anxious people are fools'; it is about cultivated discernment.
Not a claim that wise people never feel anything.
cautions: The verse labels the overwhelmed person 'mūḍha' (deluded); it can shame readers with anxiety disorders or depression.
Original audience is a grieving father.
not_for: clinical anxiety or panic
someone in acute grief who would hear it as 'you are a fool to suffer'
speaks_to: people learning not to react to every provocation

mbh.12.173.47.context: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how to push away grief when wealth is lost or a wife, son or father dies. Bhishma tells how a brahmin came to King Senajit, who was stunned by his son's death, and talked him out of his grief; after saying that whatever desire one gives up fills one with happiness, and that the person who runs after desires is destroyed with them, he states this famous comparison. It is followed by a reflection on past karma and on drawing the senses in like a tortoise.
mbh.12.173.47.core_teaching: The quiet that comes when craving ends outweighs every pleasure of earth or heaven.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'world' as the human world, 'divine' as heavenly, and the end of craving as vairāgya, dispassion.

commentaries.who: Vyasa's bhashya on Yoga Sutra 2.42 (Rama Prasada tr.)
commentaries.gist: Quotes this saying to support the sutra that contentment brings unsurpassed happiness; Vachaspati Mishra links it to Yayati's giving up of desire.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXIV) and BORI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it as the felicity of the destruction of all desires; BORI shows the line repeated in Manki's song, so it is a refrain of these chapters.

mbh.12.173.47.practical_reading: Notice the relief when you stop chasing one more thing; contentment is a positive happiness, not a consolation prize.
misreadings: Not a call to stop meeting basic needs.
Not contempt for ordinary enjoyment; it is a comparison of degree.
cautions: To a grieving reader, calling grief a 'craving' to end would be harsh; keep it to desire and acquisition.
not_for: someone in poverty or deprivation
fresh grief, where longing for a person is not craving to be cured
speaks_to: people who achieved goals and still feel empty

mbh.12.173.53.context: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how to push away grief when wealth is lost or a wife, son or father dies. Bhishma tells how a brahmin came to King Senajit, who was stunned by his son's death, and talked him out of his grief; having urged him to give up even a limb of the body if it is the root of grief, fear or toil, and to draw in the senses like a tortoise, he names the mechanism: whatever is imagined as 'mine' becomes the cause of anguish. He goes on to say that one who neither fears nor is feared, and neither desires nor hates, reaches Brahman.
mbh.12.173.53.core_teaching: Pain at loss is in proportion to how much we have made a thing 'mine'; possessiveness is the seed of anguish.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXIV)
commentaries.gist: Renders the idea of 'meum' as a source of grief and heartburn; his note says the verse appears twice in his text, and the Bombay edition does not repeat it.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource) on the preceding verse
commentaries.gist: On the instruction just before: the root of toil should be dropped even if it is part of one's own body, how much more wealth or wife.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 12.168.41, 12.268.8
commentaries.gist: Constituted text says the thing taken as 'mine' wholly becomes a cause of anguish; the same couplet returns in a later Janaka passage.

mbh.12.173.53.practical_reading: Hold roles, possessions and even plans a little more loosely; care for them without making your peace depend on keeping them.
misreadings: Not 'don't love people'.
Not a claim that grief is wrong or a sign of selfishness.
cautions: In the story it is said to a father whose son has died; read as 'your grief comes from possessiveness' it would wound a bereaved parent.
not_for: bereaved parents or partners
someone who has just lost a home or livelihood
speaks_to: fear of losing a job title or status

mbh.12.173.64.context: Closing his consolation of the grieving King Senajit, the brahmin cites the verses of Pingala, a courtesan who was deprived of her lover at the place of meeting and, in that hard moment, turned her mind to peace. She says she lived long beside the true beloved within without knowing him, that she is now awake, and ends with this verse. Bhishma then says Senajit was persuaded and became glad.
mbh.12.173.64.core_teaching: Clinging expectation keeps one awake and suffering; dropping it brings the deepest ease.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource)
commentaries.gist: Treats Pingala's song as allegory: the lover always near is the bliss-giving Self in the heart, and the one-pillared, nine-doored house is the body.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXIV)
commentaries.gist: Follows the same reading: she lived beside the Supreme Self without knowing him, is now awake to it, and sleeps happily once free of desire and hope.

commentaries.who: Bhagavata Purana 11.8.44 (parallel)
commentaries.gist: The Bhagavata's Pingala ends with the same thought: desire is the greatest misery, its absence the greatest happiness, and having cut off hope for lovers she slept happily.

mbh.12.173.64.practical_reading: When your peace hangs on someone else's message, arrival or approval, practise setting the expectation down so you can rest.
misreadings: Not 'hopelessness is happiness'; Hindi readers may hear nirāśā as despair.
Not a judgement on Pingala for her profession; the tradition presents her as a teacher.
cautions: High risk of being heard as endorsing despair by a depressed reader.
Mentions a courtesan and a lover; handle without moralising.
not_for: depression or hopelessness
someone waiting on a medical result or a missing person
speaks_to: waiting for a call, text or reply

mbh.12.174.15.context: Yudhishthira asks what good a person should seek while time destroys all beings. Bhishma tells of a Veda-reciting brahmin whose son, called Medhavin, asked him how to live given that life slips away. The father gave the conventional sequence: Vedic study, sons, household fires and sacrifices, then the forest. Having said that death snatches people while their minds are elsewhere, the son tells his father to do his good today, because death drags people off with their tasks undone. This verse follows; the next asks who knows whose death will come today, and urges a life of dharma while young.
mbh.12.174.15.core_teaching: Because death does not wait for our work to be finished, the work of one's highest good should not be postponed.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (BORI 12.169.13)
commentaries.gist: The verse just before tells the father to do 'what is good' (śreyas) today; the urgency is about the highest good, not about chores.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource) on 174.13
commentaries.gist: Explains the 'flowers' a person is busy picking when death comes as the fruits of desire-driven rites, so the rush the son condemns is the rush after desires.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXV)
commentaries.gist: Renders the line plainly and continues that one should practise virtue in the prime of life since life is transitory.

mbh.12.174.15.practical_reading: Do the important thing you keep deferring, the apology, the call, the practice, before the less important urgent things.
misreadings: Not a productivity hack or a case for overwork.
Not 'never rest'.
cautions: Its force rests on death; an anxious reader may hear it as pressure.
not_for: burnout
health anxiety
someone grieving a person who died with things left unsaid (can induce guilt)
speaks_to: people who keep waiting for the 'right time'

mbh.12.174.16.context: Yudhishthira asks what good a person should seek while time destroys all beings. Bhishma tells of a Veda-reciting brahmin whose son, called Medhavin, asked him how to live given that life slips away. The father gave the conventional sequence: Vedic study, sons, household fires and sacrifices, then the forest. After urging him to do tomorrow's work today, the son asks who knows whose death will come today and says one should be devoted to dharma while still young. He then describes how death carries off people absorbed in sons, cattle, fields and shops.
mbh.12.174.16.core_teaching: Since no one knows the day of death, a good life cannot be left for old age; dharma begun young bears fruit here and hereafter.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXV)
commentaries.gist: No one knows whether death comes today, so virtue should be practised in the prime of age; it brings fame here and felicity hereafter.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 12.169.14-15
commentaries.gist: Puts the image more vividly as death's army entering someone's camp today, and gives the life-is-uncertain line as having no fixed cause.

commentaries.who: Sanskrit Wikisource (vulgate) text
commentaries.gist: Gives our three-line form with 'anityaṃ khalu jīvitam'; the father's final acceptance of the son's view closes the chapter.

mbh.12.174.16.practical_reading: Do not save kindness, honesty or practice for retirement; begin living the life you admire now.
misreadings: Not a claim that young people will die soon.
Not 'fame is the goal'; fame is a by-product.
cautions: Death theme; afterlife promise may feel glib to the bereaved.
not_for: parents who have lost a child
people with severe health anxiety
speaks_to: young adults deferring values until 'after settling down'

data_flags.translation_note: Omits the third line of our own Sanskrit: if dharma is done, there is fame here and happiness after death. Otherwise accurate.

mbh.12.174.20.context: Yudhishthira asks what good a person should seek while time destroys all beings. Bhishma tells of a Veda-reciting brahmin whose son, called Medhavin, asked him how to live given that life slips away. The father gave the conventional sequence: Vedic study, sons, household fires and sacrifices, then the forest. The son describes how death seizes people absorbed in family and acquisition, like a tiger carrying off a sleeping deer. This verse gives the inner voice of such a person, ticking off done, to-do and half-done; the next says death carries off the man attached to field, shop and home before he reaps the fruit of his work.
mbh.12.174.20.core_teaching: A life spent in endless to-do lists, enjoying the striving itself, is overtaken by death before it turns to what matters.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource)
commentaries.gist: Defines 'to be done' as what one wishes to do, 'done-not-done' as half-finished, and 'īhā' as craving.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXV)
commentaries.gist: The surrounding lines picture death bearing away the man attached to field, shop and home before he has obtained the fruit of his acts.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 12.169.19-20
commentaries.gist: Same verse; manuscripts add lines about people thinking 'let this be mine, let that be mine' until death takes them.

mbh.12.174.20.practical_reading: Look up from the task list now and then and ask whether the busyness serves anything you care about.
misreadings: Not 'work is pointless'.
Not a judgement on people who must work long hours to survive.
cautions: Death theme; can feed guilt in people already overwhelmed.
not_for: someone in burnout or overwhelmed by obligations
someone grieving a sudden death
speaks_to: people who feel life is passing while they manage tasks

data_flags.translation_note: 'Attached to his little comforts' misreads 'īhā-sukha-āsakta'. Nilakantha glosses īhā as craving; the phrase means caught up in the pleasure of wanting and striving. Suggest: 'while a person is caught up in the pleasure of planning and striving, death takes him'. The line is fine.

mbh.12.174.35.context: Yudhishthira asks what good a person should seek while time destroys all beings. Bhishma tells of a Veda-reciting brahmin whose son, called Medhavin, asked him how to live given that life slips away. The father gave the conventional sequence: Vedic study, sons, household fires and sacrifices, then the forest. Near the end, the son resolves to live by truth and non-harm and to offer only inner sacrifices of restraint, study, prayer and meditation, not animal sacrifice. He sums up in this verse, then says he needs no son to save him and asks his father what wealth or wife will help when he dies. Bhishma says the father followed his son's advice.
mbh.12.174.35.core_teaching: Knowledge is the truest sight, truthfulness the truest discipline, attachment the deepest sorrow, and letting go the deepest happiness.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXV)
commentaries.gist: Gives the fourfold maxim in the vulgate form with truth as the supreme penance, as part of the son's closing resolve.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource) on 174.32
commentaries.gist: The inner sacrifices the son takes up are sense-restraint, reflection on the Upanishads, japa, meditation and service; this is the 'tyāga' he means.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 12.169.33 and 12.316.6
commentaries.gist: The maxim circulated in several forms; the critical text here praises knowledge as both the best eye and the best strength.

mbh.12.174.35.practical_reading: When choosing between holding on and letting go, remember that clinging tends to cost more than it gives.
misreadings: 'Rāga' is attachment, not love or affection for people.
Not a call to abandon family duties; the speaker is a renunciant.
cautions: Comes from a son rejecting the householder path; avoid using it to belittle family life.
not_for: fresh grief, where 'no sorrow like attachment' can sound like blame
speaks_to: people weighing what to let go of
students and seekers wanting a compact rule
someone caught in a draining attachment

mbh.12.174.9.context: Yudhishthira asks what good a person should seek while time destroys all beings. Bhishma tells of a Veda-reciting brahmin whose son, called Medhavin, asked him how to live given that life slips away. The father gave the conventional sequence: Vedic study, sons, household fires and sacrifices, then the forest. The son asks how he can speak so calmly while the world is under attack, surrounded, and struck by unfailing things. The father asks what he means, and the son answers with this verse: death strikes, old age surrounds, and the passing days and nights are what fall. He goes on to say that each night shortens life and that death takes people before their desires are fulfilled.
mbh.12.174.9.core_teaching: Every passing day and night shortens life, so one should wake up to mortality instead of postponing what matters.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource)
commentaries.gist: On the son's earlier phrase: the nights are 'unfailing' because each one succeeds in carrying away some of one's life.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXV)
commentaries.gist: Death assails the world, decrepitude surrounds it, and the irresistible things that come and go are the nights that keep lessening human life.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 12.169.5-9
commentaries.gist: The constituted text frames the whole dialogue with the son's opening worry that a person's life drains away quickly.

mbh.12.174.9.practical_reading: Treat today as a real portion of a limited life: pick one thing that truly matters and stop deferring it.
misreadings: Not a reason for panic or morbid dread.
Not a rejection of family life as such; it criticises postponing the highest good.
cautions: Death-centred; can trigger health anxiety or fresh grief.
not_for: the recently bereaved
people facing terminal illness or with strong death anxiety
speaks_to: birthdays and milestones that prompt reflection

mbh.12.175.11.context: Yudhishthira asks how happiness and misery come to the rich and the poor. Bhishma recalls verses of Shamyaka, a man who had found peace and freedom, as told to him long ago at Hastinapura by a destitute renunciant brahmin. The verses praise owning nothing: the poor man sleeps and wakes happily, and when poverty and kingship were weighed on a balance, poverty proved heavier. This verse gives the difference; the next says neither fire, death nor robbers can touch the one who has let go of wealth, and then describes the arrogance that wealth breeds.
mbh.12.175.11.core_teaching: Wealth brings constant anxiety about loss, which the person who owns nothing is free of.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource)
commentaries.gist: Someone else told Bhishma what Shamyaka sang; the speaker was destitute, lacking food and clothing; the poor man's path is free of enemies and hard to reach for those full of desire.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXVI)
commentaries.gist: Translates the weighing of poverty against sovereignty and the rich man's agitation; his note says the commentator's view of the speaker strains the grammar of the last verse.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 12.170
commentaries.gist: Same text; the chapter ends with Bhishma saying that for this reason he holds renunciation to be the highest.

mbh.12.175.11.practical_reading: Notice how much worry each new possession or commitment brings, and weigh that cost before acquiring more.
misreadings: Not a case against earning a living or supporting a family.
Not a romantic view of real poverty.
cautions: Can sound glib to readers in financial hardship.
not_for: someone struggling to pay for basics
someone who has just lost their savings or job
speaks_to: anxiety about protecting wealth or status

data_flags.attribution_note: Disputed. The text says a brahmin told Bhishma what Shamyaka had sung; Nilakantha (followed by Ganguli) takes the reciter to be someone other than Shamyaka. Safer: 'Verses of Shamyaka, as recited to Bhishma'. Name: Śamyāka in BORI and Wikisource; Śampāka is a variant reading; Ganguli...

mbh.12.175.22.context: Yudhishthira asks how happiness and misery come to the rich and the poor. Bhishma recalls verses of Shamyaka, a man who had found peace and freedom, as told to him long ago at Hastinapura by a destitute renunciant brahmin. After showing how wealth breeds pride, waste and finally theft and punishment, the verses advise treating these sorrows with understanding as a medicine, knowing the way of the world. This is the closing verse; Bhishma then says this is why he regards renunciation as foremost.
mbh.12.175.22.core_teaching: Happiness, the highest good and fearless rest all come only through letting go.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource) on 175.21
commentaries.gist: The 'medicine' the verses prescribe for great sorrows is a remedy applied through understanding.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXVI)
commentaries.gist: Renders the threefold 'without renunciation' and Bhishma's conclusion that renunciation is foremost.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 12.170.21-23
commentaries.gist: Places the verse after the advice to understand the world's mixture of the stable and unstable, and ends with Bhishma's verdict for renunciation.

mbh.12.175.22.practical_reading: Find one thing you are gripping, a grudge, a plan, a possession, and loosen your hold on it so you can rest.
misreadings: Not 'abandon your family or responsibilities'.
Not 'give up on life'.
cautions: 'Let go of everything' must never be read as giving up on life; avoid for any reader who may be at risk of self-harm.
Literal total renunciation is the original sense.
not_for: anyone expressing hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm
someone in acute grief
speaks_to: people unable to sleep from worry over possessions or plans

data_flags.attribution_note: As for 12.175.11: verses of Shamyaka, recited to Bhishma by a brahmin whom Nilakantha takes to be someone else.

mbh.12.176.25.context: Yudhishthira asks what a man should do when thirst for wealth overwhelms him and he cannot get it. Bhishma tells of Manki, who after repeated failures spent his last money on two young bulls; a startled camel ran off with both dangling from its neck. Watching them carried to their death, Manki sees through desire and sings to it: you have made me your toy; I know your root, you are born of my own resolving, and I will stop resolving you. He ends by choosing tranquillity.
mbh.12.176.25.core_teaching: Desire grows from our own mental fixing on things; stop feeding that fixation and desire withers at the root.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation and footnote (Santi CLXXVII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli takes saṃkalpa as 'Will': desire springs from it, so giving it up destroys desire at the root. His footnote muses that if kama means a formed desire for specific objects, resolve can indeed be called its base.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli, Santi CLXXVII)
commentaries.gist: Manki adds that wealth gives anxiety when gained and grief like death when lost; he resolves to bear insults and seek happiness within, and Bhishma presents him as a model of one freed from attachment.

mbh.12.176.25.practical_reading: Catch the moment a want is being built up in your mind, the planning and picturing, and stop feeding it; that is where desire gets its strength.
misreadings: Not a demand to give up all goals; Manki's insight is about compulsive craving that keeps hurting him.
Not self-blame for loss.
cautions: Manki's song comes out of loss and despair; for a reader who has just lost money or a job, keep the tone gentle, not 'you brought it on yourself'.
not_for: someone in fresh financial crisis who needs practical help first
speaks_to: letting go after a financial loss

mbh.12.176.43.context: Yudhishthira asks how a man who keeps striving and fails to gain wealth can be happy. Bhishma tells of Manki, who after repeated failures spent his last money on a pair of young bullocks; while being trained they ran at a resting camel, which rose and bolted with both dangling from its neck to their death. Manki first blames fate, then turns on Desire itself: he knows its root is mental intention and will no longer feed it. Casting Desire off, he vows forbearance and gentle speech, then says he will live content on whatever comes and has entered Brahman like a man plunging into a cool lake in summer.
mbh.12.176.43.core_teaching: One freed from desire answers insult with patience, harm with non-harm, and hostility with kind words.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource)
commentaries.gist: 'Kṣipamāṇa' means those who scorn or revile; in the next verse 'content' means living on what comes without feeding Desire.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXVII)
commentaries.gist: Renders the vow of forgiveness, non-retaliation and agreeable speech as the fruit of Manki's renunciation, followed by his list of new virtues: tranquillity, truth, self-restraint, forgiveness and compassion.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 12.171.42-45
commentaries.gist: Constituted text puts the vow right after Manki casts off Desire, and frames the whole song as born of nirveda, disenchantment.

mbh.12.176.43.practical_reading: When someone is harsh, choose not to retaliate and reply in a calm, kind tone, while still protecting yourself.
misreadings: Not 'stay in an abusive situation'.
Not 'never set boundaries or seek justice'.
cautions: A renunciant's vow; applied to a victim of abuse it could be harmful.
not_for: victims of abuse, harassment or bullying
someone seeking justice for a serious wrong
speaks_to: someone wanting to stop escalating conflicts

mbh.12.176.56.context: Bhishma ends the story of Manki and adds, on the same theme, the verse sung by Janaka, king of Videha, who had reached peace. He then moves to the sage Bodhya and his six teachers. The saying is very widely shared: Buddhist literature gives the same words to King Janaka in the Mahajanaka Jataka, where his queen sets fires around Mithila to call him back from renunciation.
mbh.12.176.56.core_teaching: One who owns nothing inwardly has a wealth that cannot be lost; even if his city burns, nothing of his is burned.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXVIII)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as a paradox, unlimited wealth and yet nothing owned, so the burning of Mithila is no loss to him.

commentaries.who: Naomi Appleton, 'Janaka' (Univ. of Edinburgh, 2016)
commentaries.gist: In the Buddhist Mahajanaka Jataka the renouncing king answers his queen's fires with this verse; Appleton notes it recurs across Hindu, Buddhist and Jain literature, exploring duty versus renunciation.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 12.171.56, 12.17.18, 12.268.4
commentaries.gist: Constituted text has the exclamatory 'ah, endless'; the Shanti Parva quotes the verse in three places.

mbh.12.176.56.practical_reading: Hold your role and belongings as a steward, not an owner, so a loss does not destroy your sense of self.
misreadings: Not 'don't care for anything'; care without clutching.
Not a model for a leader ignoring a real disaster.
cautions: The burning-city image would hurt someone who has lost a home to fire or disaster.
not_for: survivors of fire, flood or displacement
someone who has just been robbed or evicted
speaks_to: fear of losing a position or possessions
leaders who feel their identity depends on their role

mbh.12.176.63.context: Bhishma says the old saying of the sage Bodhya also concerns disenchantment. A king (in the vulgate the son of Nahusha, Yayati; in BORI Nahusha himself) asks the calm Bodhya what understanding gives him peace. Bodhya says he teaches no one, but names his six teachers: Pingala, the osprey, the snake, the bee, the arrow-maker and the maiden. The verses explaining each teacher follow under the heading 'Bhishma said' in both the vulgate and the manuscripts BORI records. After Pingala, the osprey: carrying meat it is set upon by birds that have none, and by dropping the meat it is left in peace. Next come the snake that lives in another's hole, the bee, the absorbed arrow-maker and the maiden's single bangle.
mbh.12.176.63.core_teaching: What we grab makes us a target; letting go of the prize ends the conflict and brings peace.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXVIII)
commentaries.gist: Gives the six teachers and, under 'Bhishma continued', the osprey set on by birds without meat and finding happiness once it gives the meat up.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha (Bharatabhavadipa notes on Sanskrit Wikisource)
commentaries.gist: Explains the 'sāraṅga' in the list as a bee and its 'following' as imitation; the passage containing this verse is bracketed in the Wikisource text as an addition.

commentaries.who: Bhagavata Purana 11.9.2 (parallel)
commentaries.gist: The Bhagavata's brahmin teacher uses the same image: stronger hawks without prey attack the one holding meat, and it finds happiness by dropping it.

mbh.12.176.63.practical_reading: If holding on to something is drawing constant conflict, a promotion fight, a family property, an argument, consider whether dropping it buys you peace.
misreadings: Not 'always give in to bullies'.
Not 'never own anything'.
cautions: Could be read as advice to surrender rights to aggressors; keep it to voluntary letting go.
not_for: someone being coerced or robbed
someone fighting for something they need to live
speaks_to: rivalry over a prize or position

data_flags.attribution_note: Speaker error. Bodhya only lists his six teachers; this gloss on the osprey is introduced with 'Bhishma said' in Wikisource, in BORI's star passage and in Ganguli ('Bhishma continued'). Correct to Bhishma, to Yudhishthira. Listener: Yayati in the vulgate, Nahusha in BORI.

mbh.12.176.67.context: Bhishma says the old saying of the sage Bodhya also concerns disenchantment. A king (in the vulgate the son of Nahusha, Yayati; in BORI Nahusha himself) asks the calm Bodhya what understanding gives him peace. Bodhya says he teaches no one, but names his six teachers: Pingala, the osprey, the snake, the bee, the arrow-maker and the maiden. The verses explaining each teacher follow under the heading 'Bhishma said' in both the vulgate and the manuscripts BORI records. After Pingala, the osprey, the snake and the bee, the arrow-maker: a man so intent on his arrow that he did not notice the king passing beside him. Last is the maiden whose single shell bangle makes no noise, a lesson in solitude.
mbh.12.176.67.core_teaching: Total absorption of the mind in one task makes it oblivious to every distraction, even a passing king; this is the model of concentration.

commentaries.who: Ganguli (Santi sec. CLXXVIII)
commentaries.gist: The maker of shafts was so attentive to his work that the king passing by went unnoticed; it stands among Bodhya's lessons in detachment.

commentaries.who: Bhagavata Purana 11.9.13 (parallel)
commentaries.gist: Uses the same arrow-maker as an image of a mind fixed so completely on the Absolute that it no longer registers inside or outside.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 12.171.61 and star 475
commentaries.gist: The constituted text only names the six teachers; the explanations, including this one, survive as a manuscript addition headed 'Bhishma said'.

mbh.12.176.67.practical_reading: Give one task your undivided attention for a stretch, phone away, and let lesser things pass by unnoticed.
misreadings: Not 'ignore people or authority'.
Not a celebration of workaholism; the point is the gathered mind.
cautions: Low risk. Avoid framing it as a judgement on readers who struggle with attention.
not_for: someone neglecting people around them through over-absorption in work

data_flags.attribution_note: Same speaker error as 12.176.63: the gloss is spoken by Bhishma, not Bodhya. Listener Yayati (vulgate) or Nahusha (BORI).

mbh.12.177.24.context: Yudhishthira asks how a person can move through the world free of grief. Bhishma tells how Prahlada asked a serene, childlike wandering brahmana the secret of his contentment. The sage says beings arise and perish by their own nature, every union ends in parting, so he neither rejoices nor grieves; he feasts or fasts, sleeps in palaces or on bare ground, as things come. This verse states his rule, and Bhishma ends by saying whoever keeps this vow lives happily.
mbh.12.177.24.core_teaching: Contentment comes from neither rejecting what rightfully arrives nor straining after what is hard to get. The sage's peace rests on seeing that gain and loss come and go by their own course.

commentaries.who: Bhagavata Purana 7.13 (parallel retelling)
commentaries.gist: The Bhagavata retells Prahlada meeting a dust-covered sage near the Sahya hills who lives the python's way: no effort for gain, rich or poor food and bedding accepted as they come, python and bee as teachers.

mbh.12.177.24.practical_reading: Teachers use the ajagara ideal for non-grasping contentment: enjoy what comes honestly and stop the anxious chase after what is out of reach. For a householder it is usually applied to cravings and comparison, not to giving up work or responsibilities.
misreadings: Not a counsel of laziness or of abandoning needed effort; it is an ascetic's vow, and even he accepts only what is lawful (dharmya).
Not a claim that whatever happens is fine; the surrounding speech is about inner equanimity, not about tolerating harm.
cautions: The surrounding speech is close to fatalism: the sage says everything comes by its own nature or destiny, and Ganguli's note glosses him as not grieving even at a son's death. Avoid pairing it with fresh grief.
For a reader in poverty or job loss, 'don't chase what is hard to get' can sound dismissive.
not_for: someone who needs to pursue medical care, a job or justice and is being told to stop trying
low mood with loss of motivation, where 'don't chase' could deepen withdrawal
fresh bereavement
speaks_to: fatigue from chasing promotions, money or status
wanting to enjoy what one already has
simplifying life after a period of striving

mbh.12.178.12.context: A prosperous merchant carelessly runs down the young ascetic Kashyapa with his chariot; humiliated and in pain, Kashyapa decides a poor man has no use for life and resolves to die. Indra appears as a jackal and points out what he already has: a human body, hands, learning. The jackal cannot pull out a thorn or brush off biting insects. He goes on to say craving grows like fire fed with fuel, and that he refuses suicide himself. Kashyapa then recognises Indra and returns home.
mbh.12.178.12.core_teaching: What one already has, a human body with working hands, is a greater gain than the money one is grieving for; despair over wealth forgets this. The jackal's wider point is that craving is never satisfied, so contentment, not more gain, ends sorrow.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation and notes)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders the jackal as listing what hands make possible: removing thorns and insects, building shelter, clothing, food. His note on the thirst image says even copious drinking only slakes thirst for a while before it returns.

commentaries.who: BORI critical text (enjoylearningsanskrit translation)
commentaries.gist: The critical text (12.173.11-12) has the jackal exclaim how fully those with hands achieve their aims: creatures like him long for hands as Kashyapa longs for wealth, and no gain beats having hands.

mbh.12.178.12.practical_reading: Used as a reminder to count basic capacities (a working body, hands, the chance to act) when a setback or humiliation makes life feel worthless.
misreadings: Not an argument that a person in despair should simply feel grateful and get over it; in the story the jackal also stays to talk Kashyapa through it.
The ranking of births (jackal below human, brahmin above others) is the jackal's worldview, not a teaching to pass on.
cautions: The story is about a man resolving to end his life. Do not serve this verse as a response to suicidal thoughts; such a reader needs crisis support, not a parable.
The jackal's speech includes caste and rebirth hierarchy (he says he was reborn a jackal for being a sceptic) which can alienate modern readers.
Gratitude-for-hands framing can hurt readers with limb loss or disability.
not_for: anyone expressing suicidal thoughts or self-harm
readers with disability or limb loss
acute grief
speaks_to: feeling worthless after a humiliation or financial setback
forgetting ordinary blessings in a bad week

mbh.12.178.26.context: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that wisdom is the best refuge, through the story of Kashyapa: knocked down by a proud rich merchant's chariot, the young brahmin resolves to die, saying a poor man has no use for life. A jackal (Indra in disguise) tells him how fortunate he is to have hands and a human birth, says taking one's life is sinful, and explains that no condition brings contentment: the rich want kingship, kings want godhood, gods want Indra's throne. Then comes this verse on craving that grows with each gain.
mbh.12.178.26.core_teaching: Getting what you want does not satisfy craving; like fire fed with fuel, it only blazes higher.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation and footnote (Santi CLXXX)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's jackal says getting what we want never brings contentment; thirst returns however much water there is, and the urge to acquire flares with each gain like fire with fresh fuel. His note: quenched thirst always returns.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Kumbakonam 12.178.24-27)
commentaries.gist: The jackal lists the endless ladder of wanting (wealth, kingship, godhood, Indra's seat) and then reminds Kashyapa that both joy and sorrow are already in him, so why lament.

mbh.12.178.26.practical_reading: If each thing you get only sharpens the wanting, the answer is not one more thing; notice the fire before feeding it.
misreadings: Not a rule against ever wanting or earning anything.
Not contempt for the poor.
cautions: The frame story is a young man resolved to die after humiliation; do not foreground it.
The jackal's argument includes caste-ranking of births (brahmin as highest); leave it out.
not_for: someone in real poverty, who may hear it as 'stop wanting basics'
speaks_to: chasing the next purchase or promotion

mbh.12.210.16.context: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma what a person seeking liberation should repeat and remember as death approaches. Bhishma relates that Narada once put this question to Narayana, who told him to begin with Om, bow, and recite a prayer; Narada then offers a long litany of refuge (verses 14 onward), of which this is the third verse. The chapter closes saying that one who studies this secret 'anusmriti' gains steady understanding and freedom from distress.
mbh.12.210.16.core_teaching: A prayer of surrender: the devotee takes refuge in the Lord who governs all time. In context it is meant to be kept in mind daily and especially at the moment of death.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text, Kumbakonam 12.210 (no classical commentary found)
commentaries.gist: Vishnu says whoever learns this remembrance and recalls it when departing reaches his state; the chapter ends that for one devoted to Janardana the single mantra of homage to Narayana is enough.

mbh.12.210.16.practical_reading: Can be used as a short prayer of refuge for anxiety about the future, since it names the Lord as master of past, present and future.
misreadings: Not a promise that taking refuge will change outward events.
cautions: In context this is a deathbed recitation; keep that framing away from readers who are suicidal or fear dying.
Southern-recension only: avoid citing it as part of the critical-edition Mahabharata.
not_for: readers who do not want devotional content
contexts presenting it as 'core' Mahabharata
speaks_to: wanting a simple prayer of surrender

mbh.12.230.31.context: Indra, having defeated the asuras, asks Brahma where his old rival Bali is; Brahma says he lives as an ass (or camel, bull or horse) in an empty house, and forbids Indra to kill him, telling him to ask Bali for instruction instead. Indra rides up on Airavata and taunts Bali with his lost splendour. Bali first says his treasures lie hidden and will reappear when his time returns, then delivers this rebuke; he adds that the wise neither grieve in misery nor exult in prosperity.
mbh.12.230.31.core_teaching: Mocking a fallen rival does not fit the dignity of the one on top. Bali answers contempt without self-pity, pointing to the boaster's lack of wisdom.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: In Ganguli's rendering Bali says such taunting is unworthy of Indra's name and lineage, that the wise feel neither grief in misery nor glee in good times, and that Indra will talk differently once he falls too.

commentaries.who: BORI critical text (enjoylearningsanskrit translation)
commentaries.gist: The critical text (12.216.26) gives the same rebuke: boasting at one who has lost everything, while oneself prospering, befits neither Indra's fame nor his lineage.

mbh.12.230.31.practical_reading: Applied to winners who gloat and to people being mocked after a fall: dignity lies in not answering contempt with self-pity, and success does not entitle anyone to look down on others.
misreadings: Not a claim that the fallen person must stay silent about mistreatment.
cautions: Bali is in a degraded animal birth; the story uses rebirth imagery that some readers may find strange.
not_for: situations of ongoing bullying or abuse, where the reader needs protection rather than composure
speaks_to: being mocked or pitied after a fall

mbh.12.231.41.context: In the second chapter of the dialogue Indra taunts Bali again. Bali answers at length that Time, not anyone's own deeds, gives and takes away; he says that if Time had not turned against him he could strike Indra down with his fist even now, but this is not the time for valour. He goes on to say thousands of Indras have passed and Indra too will pass.
mbh.12.231.41.core_teaching: Bali reads his situation as a season set by Time: strength is not lost but held back, because this is a time for forbearance. Time establishes things and also brings them to their end, so the present turn will also change.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation and note)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it as: this is not the time for prowess but for peace and tranquillity; Time establishes all things and leads them to their final consummation. His footnote says the literal phrase is 'Time cooks everything'.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha, as reported in Ganguli's note on the same speech
commentaries.gist: On Bali's claim that the slayer is not the doer, Nilakantha (via Ganguli) glosses 'slain' as the lifeless body: whoever thinks himself the agent is the deluded one. Ganguli links this to Bhagavad Gita 2.19.

mbh.12.231.41.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to strategic patience: in some seasons the wise choice is to hold back, conserve strength and wait, knowing circumstances will turn.
misreadings: Not resignation to injustice: Bali says he could fight and chooses not to because the time is wrong.
Not proof that nothing one does matters; the next chapter (Shri's speech) adds that Bali's own lapses in conduct are why fortune left him.
cautions: Bali's doctrine that Time, not people, is the doer can feel dismissive to someone harmed by a specific person.
Mentions being 'swept away by Time'; mild mortality theme.
not_for: someone in an abusive or unsafe situation who needs to act now
someone told to 'wait' when urgent help is needed
speaks_to: a setback where pushing harder would backfire
waiting out a hard season at work

mbh.12.231.62.context: Near the end of his long reply on Time, Bali tells Indra that many thousands of Indras, greater than he, have passed away and Indra will too.
