Royal Fortune, which Indra thinks is his to keep, lived in them and in Bali before moving on; Bali tells Indra to stop boasting and be calm, since she will leave him quickly too. In the next chapter Shri herself steps out of Bali's body and explains to Indra why she left him.
mbh.12.231.62.core_teaching: Success and power are not possessions: fortune has moved through countless holders and will move on, so pride in it is a mistake. Bali says it calmly, which is itself the lesson.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders Fortune as unsubstantial and unreal, never dwelling long in one place, having lived in thousands of Indras superior to Indra, and warns that, seeing his vanity, she will soon desert him too.

commentaries.who: Sequel in the text: Shri's own explanation (Ganguli section CCXXV)
commentaries.gist: Shri says Time moves her, yet adds she dwells in truth, gifts, vows, austerity, prowess and virtue; Bali lost these and grew boastful, so she left. She then divides herself among earth, waters, fire and the good.

mbh.12.231.62.practical_reading: Used to keep success in perspective: a title, a market position or a winning streak has been held by many before and will pass to others, so hold it lightly and do not look down on those who lost it.
misreadings: Not a claim that effort and conduct are irrelevant; the sequel ties fortune to virtues like truthfulness and generosity.
cautions: The sequel says fortune left Bali because of his faults; a reader who has lost a job or business could hear blame. Keep the focus on impermanence, not fault.
For someone at the bottom, 'it will move on' may sound like empty comfort.
not_for: fresh job loss or bankruptcy where the reader needs practical support
readers prone to self-blame
speaks_to: staying humble after a win or promotion
envy of someone who now has what you lost
founders or leaders anxious to hold on to success

mbh.12.25.31.context: Yudhishthira tells Vyasa no pleasure reaches him while widows lament. Vyasa replies that everything comes in its time, quotes the grieving King Senajit on how dwelling on loss feeds it, then adds this verse in his own voice and turns to telling Yudhishthira that battle, just rule and generous gifts are a king's sacrifice and yoga.
mbh.12.25.31.core_teaching: The pairs of opposites, pleasure and pain, gain and loss, life and death, visit everyone in rotation; seeing that, one keeps steady, neither crushed nor elated.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XXV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: after reporting Senajit, Vyasa says happiness and misery, prosperity and adversity, gain and loss, death and life wait on all creatures in turn, so the wise man of tranquil soul is neither elated nor depressed.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.26.13-31 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Senajit's song runs 12.26.14-28 and is closed at 26.29; this verse (26.31) belongs to Vyasa. Its BORI ending asks the steady person to neither exult nor be angry.

mbh.12.25.31.practical_reading: Used for equanimity in volatile seasons: when things go very well or very badly, remember the wheel turns for everyone and keep your footing.
misreadings: Not "feel nothing"; it targets being thrown off balance.
Not fatalism about injustice.
cautions: Lists death and life among the alternations; to someone freshly bereaved the call to stay unmoved can feel like being told not to mourn.
Vyasa's next move is to send Yudhishthira back to kingship and war-as-sacrifice.
not_for: fresh grief
someone suffering ongoing injustice
speaks_to: someone riding a high or a low (markets, career, health swings)
a person comparing their bad season to others' good ones

data_flags.attribution_note: Speaker is Vyasa, not Senajit. In BORI 12.26.29 Vyasa closes the quotation ("thus spoke the wise Senajit"); verses 30-31 are Vyasa's own summary. Ganguli agrees: the line "This is what Senajit said" comes before this verse. Listener Yudhishthira is correct.

mbh.12.26.29.context: Yudhishthira blames himself for Bhishma's fall and the deaths of the young and says he will sit and starve. Vyasa restrains him, tells him not to grieve beyond measure, and lists the certainties: unions end in separation, heaps in depletion, rises in falls, life in death. He ends by saying Yudhishthira was made for action and must not avoid it.
mbh.12.26.29.core_teaching: Coming together and coming apart are built into every born life, as bubbles form and vanish on water; seeing this is meant to limit excessive grief, not to forbid it.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XXVII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: Vyasa first says "this cannot be" to the fast, then that everything born meets dissolution like bubbles; everything risen falls, union ends in separation, life in death; and Yudhishthira was created for work.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.27.22-32 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The constituted text frames it as Vyasa forbidding a resolved fast unto death; his first line is "you should not grieve beyond measure". The next verse is the stock maxim that unions end in separation, life in death.

mbh.12.26.29.practical_reading: A way to hold impermanence gently: every relationship has a beginning and an end, which is a reason to cherish it now and to grieve without being destroyed.
misreadings: Not "relationships don't matter because they end".
Not "stop grieving"; Vyasa objects to grief beyond measure that turns into self-destruction.
cautions: The setting is a resolve to starve oneself to death. Any reading must not echo that setting for a reader who mentions not wanting to live; point to real help instead.
Impermanence talk can feel cold to fresh grief.
not_for: acute grief
suicidal thoughts
someone afraid of abandonment who may hear "everyone leaves"
speaks_to: endings: moves, breakups, children leaving home, retirement
someone learning to hold relationships lightly and dearly

mbh.12.268.9.context: Jajali performed such severe austerities that birds nested and raised their young in his matted hair, and he grew proud of his merit. A voice from the sky said he was not the equal of Tuladhara, a merchant of Varanasi. Jajali went to him; Tuladhara already knew his story. Asked where a trader got such wisdom, Tuladhara says dharma is the ancient way of friendliness and doing good to all; he buys and sells without cheating, harms no one, keeps his scales even toward all beings, and then states this definition.
mbh.12.268.9.core_teaching: The one who truly knows dharma is not the great ascetic but the person who is a constant friend to all and works for everyone's good in action, thought and speech. Ordinary honest life, lived without harm, can carry the highest goodness.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's Tuladhara buys and sells without cheating, harms no creature or as little as necessity allows, and says his scales are even toward all: he weighs every being as equal, neither praising nor blaming others.

commentaries.who: Nilakantha, as reported in Ganguli's notes
commentaries.gist: The commentator notes that the second line spells out what this 'eternal dharma with its mysteries' consists of: universal friendliness and doing good. Ganguli's note on the scales says Tuladhara counts a Brahmana no heavier than a Chandala.

mbh.12.268.9.practical_reading: Teachers use Tuladhara to say goodness is available in ordinary work: deal fairly, wish everyone well, and let thought, word and action match. Spiritual pride in one's practice is the trap Jajali fell into.
misreadings: Not a claim that austerity or practice is worthless; the point is that pride in it is.
'Friend to all' does not mean having no boundaries with people who harm you.
cautions: The chapter goes on into criticism of animal sacrifice and farming as cruel; some readers may find it preachy if they read on.
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship who might hear 'be a friend to all' as 'keep accommodating'
speaks_to: people who feel their ordinary job is spiritually second-rate
wanting a simple test of a good life

mbh.12.27.12.context: After the war Yudhishthira, burning with grief for slaughtered kin, has resolved to end his life; Vyasa consoles him with Ashma's discourse to Janaka on how to bear the coming and going of kin and wealth. Ashma says a ruler should understand the sorrows of his people in order to remedy them, and gives this two-cause analysis. He goes on at length about time and destiny bringing gain and loss, old age and death to everyone, and urges bearing both joy and sorrow without elation or collapse.
mbh.12.27.12.core_teaching: Mental pain has two sources, a confused mind or something unwanted happening; seeing which one you are facing is the start of healing.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation and footnote (Santi XXVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli names the two causes as a deluded mind and the arrival of misfortune, with no third; his note adds that the many other woes listed spring from these same two.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli, Santi XXVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ashma frames the analysis as knowledge a king needs to relieve his subjects' sorrows, then stresses that old age, death, gain and loss come to all in time's course.

mbh.12.27.12.practical_reading: Ask of a painful feeling: is this about what actually happened, or about how my mind is spinning around it? Each needs a different response.
misreadings: Not 'it's all in your head'; one of the two causes is a real, unwanted event.
Not dismissing grief as delusion.
cautions: The frame story is Yudhishthira resolved to end his life; do not foreground this.
The chapter leans heavily on destiny and time as the cause of all fortune, which can feel fatalistic or dismissive to fresh grief.
not_for: acute suicidal distress (refer to support, not analysis)
the first days of bereavement
speaks_to: understanding why loss hurts so much
rumination after a breakup or departure
sorting what can be changed from what can't

mbh.12.27.40.context: Vyasa, trying to lift Yudhishthira's grief, tells how the sage Ashma answered King Janaka, who asked how one should meet the arrival and loss of kin and wealth. Ashma describes how pleasure and pain take turns, how time carries everyone, and how family ties are like travellers meeting on a road; he ends by telling Janaka to live by scripture, honour ancestors and do his duties, and Janaka goes home free of grief. This verse follows the image of countless mothers, fathers, sons and wives met over many lives, and of family as a meeting on a road.
mbh.12.27.40.core_teaching: In loss, step back and ask where you came from, where you are going and who you are; seeing life as a brief shared stretch of road steadies the mind.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XXVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: our union with wives, kin and friends is like travellers at a roadside inn; asking where am I, where shall I go, who am I, for whom do I grieve, one gains calm. Life turns like a wheel.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.28.36-41 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Verse 40ef adds that dwelling with dear ones is impermanent and samsara turns like a wheel; a manuscript line repeats that brother, mother, father and friend are a meeting on the road.

mbh.12.27.40.practical_reading: A contemplative prompt for later grief or life transitions: widen the frame beyond the immediate loss and ask what you are and what your journey is.
misreadings: Not "they were never really yours, so don't mourn".
Not a way to argue someone out of grief; the data's own misuse note is right.
cautions: Context assumes rebirth (countless parents and children over many lives); can feel dismissive to fresh grief.
The inn/road image for family can wound a newly bereaved spouse or parent.
not_for: fresh bereavement, especially of a child or partner
someone feeling abandoned
speaks_to: someone overwhelmed who needs to step back

mbh.12.27.49.context: Vyasa, trying to lift Yudhishthira's grief, tells how the sage Ashma answered King Janaka, who asked how one should meet the arrival and loss of kin and wealth. Ashma describes how pleasure and pain take turns, how time carries everyone, and how family ties are like travellers meeting on a road; he ends by telling Janaka to live by scripture, honour ancestors and do his duties, and Janaka goes home free of grief. Here Ashma has just said that physicians fall ill, elixir-makers age, and ascetics and generous givers still meet old age and death.
mbh.12.27.49.core_teaching: Time spent does not come back for anyone born: days, months, years, nights are gone once gone. The point is to see time's one-way flow clearly and live accordingly.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XXVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: for all creatures born, years, months, fortnights, days and nights once passed never return; man is carried by Time, willing or not, onto the broad road all must walk.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.28.44-51 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The constituted text lists fortnights and nights in the second half-line, not "no reunion". The surrounding verses stress that medicine, elixirs, austerity and generosity do not stop aging and death.

mbh.12.27.49.practical_reading: Teachers use the line to sharpen priorities: time is the one resource that never refunds, so spend today on what and whom you value.
misreadings: Not a statement that the dead are lost forever (that comes only from the weak variant).
Not a reason for panic about time; Ashma uses it to steady the mind.
cautions: With our variant ("beings do not meet again") the verse is stark for anyone grieving; prefer the BORI reading.
Context dwells on illness and aging that medicine cannot stop.
not_for: fresh grief
health anxiety
someone with a terminal diagnosis unless they ask for this frame
speaks_to: someone deciding what matters this year

data_flags.translation_note: Our second half-line ("na punar vai samāgamaḥ", no reunion) is a variant not found in BORI or Ganguli. BORI: for all born beings neither fortnights nor nights come back; Ganguli likewise lists years, months, fortnights, days and nights. Our "do not meet again in the...

mbh.12.27.52.context: Vyasa, trying to lift Yudhishthira's grief, tells how the sage Ashma answered King Janaka, who asked how one should meet the arrival and loss of kin and wealth. Ashma describes how pleasure and pain take turns, how time carries everyone, and how family ties are like travellers meeting on a road; he ends by telling Janaka to live by scripture, honour ancestors and do his duties, and Janaka goes home free of grief. The verse follows the line that union with wife and kin is a meeting on the road, and precedes the question: where today are your father and grandfather? You do not see them, nor they you.
mbh.12.27.52.core_teaching: Permanent companionship is not available to anyone, not even with one's own body; seeing this loosens the shock of separation.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XXVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: no one gains lasting companionship with anyone, not even with one's own body, so how with another? Then: where are your sire and grandsire now? Follow the scriptures and your duties.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.28.50-53 and 12.307.9 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Same wording in the constituted text; a near-identical line returns at 12.307.9 in a later consolation, showing it is a stock teaching of the Shanti Parva.

mbh.12.27.52.practical_reading: Used to hold people and health with open hands: every bond, including with our own body, is on loan, which is a reason for tenderness now.
misreadings: Not "don't get attached to anyone".
Not contempt for the body.
cautions: Next lines turn to dead fathers and grandfathers; mind readers recently bereaved of a parent.
Mentions parting from one's own body; handle with care for serious illness.
not_for: fresh bereavement
terminal illness unless the reader seeks this frame
health anxiety

mbh.12.272.23.context: Yudhishthira asks whether a hard, painful duty should be done quickly or after long thought. Bhishma tells of Chirakari ('the one who acts slowly'), son of the sage Gautama, mocked as lazy for weighing everything. Suspecting his wife (Ahalya) of infidelity, Gautama orders Chirakari to kill his mother and leaves for the forest. Chirakari agrees, then deliberates at length on what is owed to a father and to a mother. This verse closes his reflection on the father: the father is dharma, heaven and the highest austerity, and unlike a flower or fruit that drops away, he never releases his child. He then turns to think about his mother.
mbh.12.272.23.core_teaching: Flowers and fruit detach naturally, but a father's bond with his child does not, even when that love costs him pain. Chirakari uses this to weigh the father's claim before weighing the mother's.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it as the flower falling from its stalk and the fruit from its tree, while the father, whatever his distress, never abandons the son; Chirakari then sets out to think about the mother.

commentaries.who: Sanskrit glosses printed with the Kumbakonam text (several match Nilakantha as Ganguli reports him)
commentaries.gist: The notes name the mother as Ahalya and, on Gautama's later speech, say the wrong arose from Indra's lust and Ahalya committed no transgression.

mbh.12.272.23.practical_reading: Read as a tribute to a parent's steady love, the kind that holds on through a child's mistakes and the parent's own pain.
misreadings: Not a statement that adult children never become independent.
In the story this praise of the father is weighed and finally outweighed by the mother's claim; it does not license obeying a harmful order.
cautions: The surrounding story is a father ordering his son to kill his mother over suspected infidelity; Indra had seduced her in disguise. Domestic violence and sexual deception themes.
Idealised fathers can hurt readers with absent or abusive fathers.
not_for: readers estranged from or harmed by their father
father-loss grief in its first days
speaks_to: a father who has struggled to love a difficult child

data_flags.translation_note: Our Sanskrit reads 'puruṣaṃ' and the translation follows it ('a grown person is freed from his bonds'). That word is a corruption: the digital Kumbakonam text has the garbled 'puraṣpaṃ', the BORI text reads 'puṣpaṃ' (flower), and Ganguli translates 'flower'. Correct sense: 'A flower is...

mbh.12.272.28.context: Yudhishthira asks whether a hard, painful duty should be done quickly or after long thought. Bhishma tells of Chirakari ('the one who acts slowly'), son of the sage Gautama, mocked as lazy for weighing everything. Suspecting his wife (Ahalya) of infidelity, Gautama orders Chirakari to kill his mother and leaves for the forest. Chirakari agrees, then deliberates at length on what is owed to a father and to a mother. Having weighed the father, he now thinks about the mother: she is the fire-stick from which his body was kindled, the comfort in every trouble, and anyone who comes home and calls 'Mother!' does not grieve or feel old.
mbh.12.272.28.core_teaching: As long as a person has a mother to turn to, they remain a child at heart, sheltered, however old and however many descendants they have.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: a person whose mother lives, even with sons and grandsons and at a hundred years, seems a child of two; the son who enters his house calling 'Mother' does not grieve and is not touched by decrepitude.

commentaries.who: Sanskrit glosses printed with the Kumbakonam text
commentaries.gist: The note glosses dvihāyanavat as 'like one two years old' and records a manuscript variant in which the person at a hundred years simply 'counts as a one-year-old'.

mbh.12.272.28.practical_reading: Used to honour the comfort of a living mother and to encourage adult children to keep turning to and caring for her.
misreadings: Not a claim that adults should stay dependent.
cautions: Painful for readers whose mother has died, who never had one, or whose mother was harmful.
Part of the deliberation over an order to kill the mother.
not_for: recent mother-loss
estrangement or maternal abuse
readers who are themselves struggling mothers and may feel judged
speaks_to: Mother's Day or a mother's birthday
adult children caring for an ageing mother

mbh.12.272.29.context: Yudhishthira asks whether a hard, painful duty should be done quickly or after long thought. Bhishma tells of Chirakari ('the one who acts slowly'), son of the sage Gautama, mocked as lazy for weighing everything. Suspecting his wife (Ahalya) of infidelity, Gautama orders Chirakari to kill his mother and leaves for the forest. Chirakari agrees, then deliberates at length on what is owed to a father and to a mother. Thinking about his mother, he says she protects her son whether he is able or helpless, thin or strong.
mbh.12.272.29.core_teaching: A mother's protection does not depend on how able or deserving the child is; no other carer is bound to the child in the same way.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: able or disabled, lean or robust, the son is always protected by the mother, and by the ordinance no one else is his protector.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's explanatory note on the same reflection
commentaries.gist: Ganguli explains that the father stands for all the gods together, while the mother gathers in herself all beings, mortal and divine; the Kumbakonam gloss on that verse likewise calls her the protector in this world.

mbh.12.272.29.practical_reading: Applied to unconditional care: love that does not wait for the child to succeed. Also read as a call to give such care back to an ageing mother.
misreadings: Not a rule that only mothers can nurture, or that a mother who struggles has failed.
cautions: Idealised motherhood can wound readers with absent or harmful mothers, and mothers who feel they fall short.
Story context: an ordered matricide.
not_for: maternal estrangement or abuse
mothers struggling with guilt or postpartum depression
speaks_to: a parent caring for a child with disability or illness

mbh.12.272.30.context: Yudhishthira asks whether a hard, painful duty should be done quickly or after long thought. Bhishma tells of Chirakari ('the one who acts slowly'), son of the sage Gautama, mocked as lazy for weighing everything. Suspecting his wife (Ahalya) of infidelity, Gautama orders Chirakari to kill his mother and leaves for the forest. Chirakari agrees, then deliberates at length on what is owed to a father and to a mother. Among his reflections on the mother, he says it is only on losing her that a person truly becomes old and sorrowful and finds the world empty.
mbh.12.272.30.core_teaching: Losing one's mother is the moment one truly ages and the world feels empty. Chirakari says it to show what killing her would destroy.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: only when deprived of his mother does the son become old and grief-stricken, and the world look empty to him.

commentaries.who: Bibek Debroy (translator of the critical edition), column on Chirakari
commentaries.gist: Debroy summarises the deliberation as a weighing of the father's supremacy against the mother as the one who nurtures and protects, which leads Chirakari to delay.

mbh.12.272.30.practical_reading: Often quoted at a mother's death to name the particular emptiness of that loss. It validates grief rather than correcting it.
misreadings: Not a claim that life cannot be full again after a mother's death.
cautions: Directly about losing a mother: strong for naming grief, but it intensifies rather than consoles. Best on a 'see' day, not 'steady'.
Story context: an ordered matricide.
not_for: readers whose mother is gravely ill (may feel like a premonition)
estrangement or maternal abuse
speaks_to: feeling suddenly 'grown up' or old after a parent's death

mbh.12.272.31.context: Yudhishthira asks whether a hard, painful duty should be done quickly or after long thought. Bhishma tells of Chirakari ('the one who acts slowly'), son of the sage Gautama, mocked as lazy for weighing everything. Suspecting his wife (Ahalya) of infidelity, Gautama orders Chirakari to kill his mother and leaves for the forest. Chirakari agrees, then deliberates at length on what is owed to a father and to a mother. This line is the climax of his praise of the mother; he next derives her names (dhātrī, jananī, ambā) from what she does, and asks what thinking person could kill her.
mbh.12.272.31.core_teaching: Nothing shelters, guides, protects and is as dear as a mother. In the story this recognition is what stays Chirakari's hand.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: no shelter like the mother, no refuge, no defence, and no one so dear; he then explains her names as she who bore, gave birth to, and nourished the child.

commentaries.who: Sanskrit glosses printed with the Kumbakonam text
commentaries.gist: On the verse that follows, the note glosses vīrasū as 'mother of heroic sons', part of the name-derivations that extend this praise.

mbh.12.272.31.practical_reading: A widely quoted line in Hindu homes for honouring mothers and for gratitude cards and tributes.
misreadings: Not a ranking that makes other caregivers lesser.
cautions: Hard for readers with maternal loss, estrangement or abuse.
Story context: an ordered matricide.
not_for: maternal estrangement or abuse
recent mother-loss (unless the plan's purpose is honouring her)
speaks_to: adult children returning to care for a mother

mbh.12.272.51.context: After long reflection Gautama returns in tears. He realises Indra came to his hermitage disguised as a brahmin guest, and that his wife was not at fault; the lapse was his own carelessness. He confesses that jealousy plunged him into a sea of wrongdoing, believes he has had his wife killed, and prays that his slow son has lived up to his name.
mbh.12.272.51.core_teaching: Jealousy brings ruin even to the disciplined; Gautama owns that his own jealousy, not his wife's fault, drove him to order a killing.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation and note)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's Gautama says neither his wife nor Indra but his own heedlessness is to blame; the note says the commentator attributes this exculpation of Indra to Gautama's purity, though Ganguli thinks Indra plainly was at fault.

commentaries.who: Sanskrit glosses printed with the Kumbakonam text (several match Nilakantha as Ganguli reports him)
commentaries.gist: The notes name the mother as Ahalya and, on Gautama's later speech, say the wrong arose from Indra's lust and Ahalya committed no transgression.

mbh.12.272.51.practical_reading: Used to show the value of owning one's jealousy: naming it as one's own, rather than blaming the other person, is where repair begins.
misreadings: Not a statement that jealousy is unforgivable; Gautama's confession leads to reconciliation.
cautions: Involves suspected infidelity, sexual deception by Indra, and an order to kill a wife. Avoid for readers in or leaving abusive relationships.
Victim-blaming risk: the text clears the wife, but the setting could still trigger.
not_for: victims of partner jealousy or control
readers dealing with infidelity trauma
speaks_to: regret after acting in anger toward a partner

mbh.12.272.69.context: Gautama finds his son holding the weapon, the mother alive; Chirakari throws the weapon down and bows. Gautama embraces him for a long time and blesses him, saying his delay has made them happy for ever. He then recites verses praising slowness: in friendship, anger, pride and painful duties, the slow one is praised.
mbh.12.272.69.core_teaching: Friendships should be formed and ended slowly; what is built with care lasts.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's version of the verse speaks of carrying out a friend's death or abandoning a begun project only after long delay, then says friendship formed after long examination lasts long.

commentaries.who: Bibek Debroy (translator of the critical edition), column on Chirakari
commentaries.gist: Debroy presents the story as a case for slowness as wisdom; among Gautama's maxims he gives taking a long time before severing a friendship.

mbh.12.272.69.practical_reading: Applied to friendship and trust: don't rush into intimacy, and don't cut people off in a moment of anger.
misreadings: Not advice to stay in a friendship that is harming you.
cautions: Story context: an ordered killing of a mother/wife.
not_for: readers who need to leave a controlling or abusive friendship quickly
speaks_to: a friendship strained by a quarrel
moving to a new city and making friends

mbh.12.272.70.context: Gautama's second and third verses in praise of slowness, spoken right after he finds his wife alive: delay is praised in passion, pride, hostility, wrongdoing and unpleasant duties, and above all when a relative, friend, servant or wife is suspected of a fault that has not been proved.
mbh.12.272.70.core_teaching: When emotions run hot, or when someone close seems to have wronged you but the facts are unclear, slowness is a virtue: delay prevents harm that cannot be undone.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: in giving way to wrath, haughtiness, pride, disputes or sin, and in unpleasant tasks, delay deserves applause; when a fault of a relative, friend, servant or wife is not proved, the one slow to punish is praised.

commentaries.who: Bibek Debroy (translator of the critical edition), column on Chirakari
commentaries.gist: Debroy notes that while procrastination usually has a bad name, Gautama approved of Chirakara's delay and so did Bhishma, citing the praise of slowness in anger, pride and other unpleasant situations.

mbh.12.272.70.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a rule for conflict at home and work: pause before reacting to an unverified accusation, especially against people close to you.
misreadings: Slowing down is not ignoring a wrong once it is clear.
Not a licence to delay duties out of avoidance.
cautions: The story's suspicion is of a wife's infidelity and the ordered 'punishment' is murder; keep the domestic-violence frame away from readers in unsafe homes.
not_for: someone being harmed now who needs to act, not wait
speaks_to: suspecting a partner, colleague or family member before the facts are in

mbh.12.272.73.context: After telling how Gautama blessed his son and praised slowness, Bhishma draws the moral for Yudhishthira and continues: one should restrain anger long, honour elders long, and think long before answering questions on dharma. Gautama and his son later ascend to heaven.
mbh.12.272.73.core_teaching: Deliberate carefully and decide without haste; then you will not spend a long time in regret.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: in every act a person should reflect long before settling what to do, and so avoid grief for a long time; one who does not nurse anger and thinks before acting does nothing to repent.

commentaries.who: Bibek Debroy (translator of the critical edition), column on Chirakari
commentaries.gist: Debroy reads the episode as an argument for reconsidering slowness as a virtue rather than a vice, noting Bhishma endorses it.

mbh.12.272.73.practical_reading: Used for big decisions: sleep on it, gather facts, consult, then act; the time spent thinking is less than the time you would spend regretting.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of chronic procrastination or of avoiding urgent decisions.
cautions: Story context: an ordered matricide.
not_for: emergencies where delay causes harm
anxious over-thinkers already paralysed by indecision
speaks_to: impulsive people trying to slow down

mbh.12.28.14.context: Arjuna asks Krishna to comfort Yudhishthira. Krishna retells how Narada consoled King Srinjaya after his son died: this verse opens Narada's speech, followed by the lives of sixteen great kings, each said to surpass the boy and yet to have died, with the refrain that Srinjaya should not grieve. Srinjaya says his grief is gone and asks for his son; Narada restores him.
mbh.12.28.14.core_teaching: Narada places one death inside the shared human condition: speaker, listener and all beings will die still tangled in joy and sorrow, so lament cannot set one apart.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XXIX)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: Narada says all of us, subject to happiness and misery, must die, so why sorrow, then recites ancient kings to dispel grief. Srinjaya, comforted, asks; Narada gives back his son Suvarnashthivin.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.29 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The Sixteen Kings episode is in the constituted text; its refrain tells Srinjaya not to grieve for a son lesser than those kings. The BORI reading of this verse speaks of living on, not dying, unfreed from joy and sorrow.

mbh.12.28.14.practical_reading: At its gentlest it says grief is shared, not a personal punishment: everyone, including those who comfort you, is in the same condition.
misreadings: Not "your loss is small because everyone dies".
Our misuse note says the story "is not telling a grieving parent to stop crying"; in fact its refrain does say "do not grieve". The verse should not be presented as validating tears either.
cautions: The son is miraculously restored at the end; a bereaved parent may find that painful.
The refrain compares the dead child unfavourably with legendary kings.
Speaks plainly of death to someone grieving a child.
not_for: bereaved parents in early grief
children

mbh.12.305.14.context: Yudhishthira asks what Bhishma thinks of truth, self-control, forgiveness and wisdom. Bhishma recounts how the unborn Lord of creatures (Prajapati/Brahma), wandering as a golden swan, was questioned by the Sadhya gods about the highest good. The swan answers with a string of maxims on restraint of speech and anger, forbearance under insult, truth, and the company one keeps. Just before, the swan says truth is the secret of the Veda, self-restraint the secret of truth, and freedom the secret of self-restraint; he never answers abuse with abuse.
mbh.12.305.14.core_teaching: The truly wise person is the one who can withstand the rush of speech, anger, craving, appetite and lust when they rise, not by never feeling them but by not being carried off.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the one who subjugates the rising impulse of speech, of wrath in the mind, of thirst, and of the stomach and the organ of pleasure is the one I regard as Brahmana and Muni.

commentaries.who: Sanskrit glosses printed with the Kumbakonam text
commentaries.gist: The note explains vidhitsā as a particular thirst, the force of craving; 'brāhmaṇa' as one devoted to Brahman; 'muni' as one given to meditation.

mbh.12.305.14.practical_reading: Teachers use it for urge-surfing: notice the surge to speak, snap, crave or binge, and let it pass before acting. The verse names the urge as normal and the mastery as the achievement.
misreadings: Not a call to suppress emotions; it is about not acting on them in the moment.
Not a rule that bodily needs are shameful.
cautions: Mentions sexual urge; fine for adults but keep plain. Can sound shaming to someone with an eating disorder or addiction; frame as gradual skill, not willpower verdict.
not_for: readers in active eating disorders or addiction relapse, unless framed with care

data_flags.translation_note: Minor: 'the itch to scheme' is not supported. The Kumbakonam gloss reads vidhitsā as a special thirst, the surge of craving (from dhe, to drink), and Ganguli renders it 'thirst'. Suggest 'the surge of craving'. The verse also says 'him I call a brāhmaṇa and...

mbh.12.305.15.context: Yudhishthira asks what Bhishma thinks of truth, self-control, forgiveness and wisdom. Bhishma recounts how the unborn Lord of creatures (Prajapati/Brahma), wandering as a golden swan, was questioned by the Sadhya gods about the highest good. The swan answers with a string of maxims on restraint of speech and anger, forbearance under insult, truth, and the company one keeps. This follows the verse on withstanding the surges of speech, anger and craving.
mbh.12.305.15.core_teaching: A simple ladder of worth: freedom from anger over anger, forbearance over impatience, humanity over inhumanity, knowledge over ignorance.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one who does not yield to wrath is superior to one who does; so too the renouncer, the one with manly virtues, and the knowing; assailed with harsh speech, one should not assail in return.

commentaries.who: Sanskrit glosses printed with the Kumbakonam text
commentaries.gist: The note glosses 'ajñāna' here as the person lacking knowledge, the deluded one.

mbh.12.305.15.practical_reading: Used as a quick self-check in conflict: the calmer, more patient response is the stronger one.
misreadings: Not a ranking of people to look down on; it ranks qualities to grow toward.
cautions: Can sound judgemental to someone who struggles with anger; frame as direction, not verdict.
not_for: someone whose anger is a response to ongoing injustice and who needs validation first

mbh.12.305.23.context: Yudhishthira asks what Bhishma thinks of truth, self-control, forgiveness and wisdom. Bhishma recounts how the unborn Lord of creatures (Prajapati/Brahma), wandering as a golden swan, was questioned by the Sadhya gods about the highest good. The swan answers with a string of maxims on restraint of speech and anger, forbearance under insult, truth, and the company one keeps. It sits among verses on bearing insult calmly: the man of restrained soul who becomes a pillar to others is spoken of kindly by all, and revilers dwell on faults more than merits.
mbh.12.305.23.core_teaching: Critics and rivals speak far more readily of a person's faults than of their virtues; knowing this helps one not to be shaken by criticism.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: revilers never come forward to speak of a person's merits as they speak of his demerits.

commentaries.who: Sanskrit glosses printed with the Kumbakonam text
commentaries.gist: The note glosses nairguṇya as fault and anuyuñjakāḥ as those who compete or vie with one, so the verse is about rivals' talk.

mbh.12.305.23.practical_reading: Applied to criticism at work or online: negative feedback travels faster than praise, so weigh it rather than take it as the whole truth.
misreadings: Not a reason to dismiss all criticism as envy.
cautions: Could feed defensiveness in a reader who needs to hear honest feedback.
not_for: someone avoiding legitimate accountability
speaks_to: being judged by rivals or in-laws

mbh.12.305.27.context: Yudhishthira asks what Bhishma thinks of truth, self-control, forgiveness and wisdom. Bhishma recounts how the unborn Lord of creatures (Prajapati/Brahma), wandering as a golden swan, was questioned by the Sadhya gods about the highest good. The swan answers with a string of maxims on restraint of speech and anger, forbearance under insult, truth, and the company one keeps. It comes right after verses saying the wise man treats insult like nectar and sleeps in peace, while the reviler perishes.
mbh.12.305.27.core_teaching: Good acts done in anger lose their merit: worship, gifts, austerity and offerings made by an angry person are carried off, and his effort is wasted.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the sacrifices, gifts, penances and fire-offerings made in anger have their merits robbed by Yama; the toil of an angry man is entirely fruitless.

commentaries.who: Vidura's parallel counsel (Udyoga Parva, Ganguli XXXVI)
commentaries.gist: Vidura's version of the Sadhyas' dialogue likewise warns against angry, harsh words and teaches bearing reproach silently, saying the patient bearer takes on the slanderer's virtues.

mbh.12.305.27.practical_reading: Used to show that anger spoils even good work: help given resentfully, or service done angrily, loses its value for giver and receiver.
misreadings: Not a teaching that angry people are doomed; it urges letting anger settle before acting.
cautions: Mentions Yama (death); mild.
Can feel condemning to someone who has been angry for good reason.
not_for: readers whose anger is a response to abuse or injustice and needs to be heard first
speaks_to: caregivers or volunteers who feel resentful

mbh.12.305.32.context: Yudhishthira asks what Bhishma thinks of truth, self-control, forgiveness and wisdom. Bhishma recounts how the unborn Lord of creatures (Prajapati/Brahma), wandering as a golden swan, was questioned by the Sadhya gods about the highest good. The swan answers with a string of maxims on restraint of speech and anger, forbearance under insult, truth, and the company one keeps. The swan has just said truth is the ladder to heaven like a ship across the sea; he then turns to the power of company, and adds that the gods keep company with the good.
mbh.12.305.32.core_teaching: A person comes to resemble the people they live among and look up to, and what they aspire to be; like cloth taking a dye, character takes the colour of its company.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: a person becomes like those he dwells with, those he reverences, and what he wishes to be; serving the good or the wicked, the ascetic or the thief, he takes their hue like cloth in dye.

commentaries.who: Vidura's parallel counsel (Udyoga Parva, Ganguli XXXVI)
commentaries.gist: Vidura gives the same simile: whoever waits upon the good or the wicked, the ascetic or the thief, soon takes the companion's colour like cloth soaked in dye.

mbh.12.305.32.practical_reading: Teachers use it for choosing friends, workplaces and media with care, and for aspiration: decide who you want to become and spend time near such people.
misreadings: Not a reason to shun people who are struggling or to cut off family for being imperfect.
cautions: A reader stuck in a bad environment (home, job) may feel blamed for absorbing it.
not_for: readers who cannot leave their environment and may feel doomed by it
speaks_to: choosing friends or a peer group
starting a new job or city

data_flags.translation_note: 'The people one argues with' follows the Kumbakonam word saṃvivadate but misleads: BORI reads 'lives with' and Ganguli translates 'dwells with'; even saṃvivadate can mean 'converses with'. Suggest 'the people one lives among'. The rest, and the line, are accurate.

mbh.12.305.38.context: Yudhishthira asks what Bhishma thinks of truth, self-control, forgiveness and wisdom. Bhishma recounts how the unborn Lord of creatures (Prajapati/Brahma), wandering as a golden swan, was questioned by the Sadhya gods about the highest good. The swan answers with a string of maxims on restraint of speech and anger, forbearance under insult, truth, and the company one keeps. This verse closes the swan's main speech; the Sadhyas then ask what covers the world and why friends are abandoned.
mbh.12.305.38.core_teaching: Speech can be graded: silence is better than idle speech; true speech is better; true speech that is also right is better still; and true, right speech that is also kind is best.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: silence is better than speech, truth better than silence, truth joined with righteousness better still, and best what is true, righteous and agreeable.

commentaries.who: Vidura's parallel (Udyoga Parva, Ganguli XXXVI)
commentaries.gist: Vidura gives the same ladder with the last two swapped: after truth, say what is agreeable, and if agreeable, then what accords with morality.

commentaries.who: Medhatithi on Manu 4.138 (related rule)
commentaries.gist: On 'speak the true, speak the pleasant', Medhatithi says an unpleasant truth should not be spoken where avoidable and one should rather stay silent, but a pleasant falsehood is never allowed.

mbh.12.305.38.practical_reading: A widely used four-step filter for speech: is it better than silence, is it true, is it right, is it kind.
misreadings: Not an excuse to avoid saying a needed hard truth; the steps add to truth, they do not replace it.
Not 'silence is always best'; silence is only the first rung.
cautions: Readers who were silenced in abusive settings may hear 'silence is better' as a rebuke; emphasise the ladder upward.
not_for: someone deciding whether to report abuse or wrongdoing (silence is not the virtue there)

mbh.12.305.8.context: Yudhishthira asks what Bhishma thinks of truth, self-control, forgiveness and wisdom. Bhishma recounts how the unborn Lord of creatures (Prajapati/Brahma), wandering as a golden swan, was questioned by the Sadhya gods about the highest good. The swan answers with a string of maxims on restraint of speech and anger, forbearance under insult, truth, and the company one keeps. This is near the start of the swan's reply: after naming austerity, self-restraint, truth and mastery of mind, he turns to speech.
mbh.12.305.8.core_teaching: Do not speak to wound: words that cut another to the quick, cruel speech, and anything that makes another person flinch are to be avoided, because such speech harms the hearer and degrades the speaker.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: do not wound others' vitals, do not utter cruel speeches, never take scriptural lectures from a mean person, and never say words that pain or burn others and lead to hell.

commentaries.who: Medhatithi on Manu 2.161 (same opening phrase)
commentaries.gist: Medhatithi explains aruntuda as speech that strikes the vitals; even when one has been hurt one should not answer so, and even words said in jest that pain others are to be avoided.

commentaries.who: Vidura's parallel counsel (Udyoga Parva, Ganguli XXXVI)
commentaries.gist: In Vidura's version harsh, angry words scorch the vitals and heart; the man who pierces others with word-thorns is called the worst of men, carrying hell on his tongue.

mbh.12.305.8.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to everyday speech: before speaking in anger, ask whether the words are meant to wound. Avoid taunts aimed at someone's tender spots.
misreadings: Not a ban on honest criticism; it targets speech meant to wound.
Not a demand that a hurt person stay silent about being hurt.
cautions: A reader who has been verbally abused may feel the verse is aimed at them; frame it as validating that such words do real harm.
not_for: readers being told to tolerate abuse silently
speaks_to: sarcasm and cutting remarks at work

mbh.12.305.9.context: Yudhishthira asks what Bhishma thinks of truth, self-control, forgiveness and wisdom. Bhishma recounts how the unborn Lord of creatures (Prajapati/Brahma), wandering as a golden swan, was questioned by the Sadhya gods about the highest good. The swan answers with a string of maxims on restraint of speech and anger, forbearance under insult, truth, and the company one keeps. This verse follows directly on the warning against wounding speech.
mbh.12.305.9.core_teaching: Harsh words are arrows that land only on the vulnerable places and leave the hearer hurting day and night, so the wise never shoot them.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: word-shafts fall from the lips and the one pierced burns incessantly; they strike only the vitals, so the learned should never aim them at others.

commentaries.who: Vidura's parallel counsel (Udyoga Parva, Ganguli XXXIV)
commentaries.gist: Vidura adds that a forest felled by axes grows back, but a heart wounded by ill-spoken words never recovers; arrows can be drawn out of the body, the word-dagger cannot.

mbh.12.305.9.practical_reading: Used both as a brake on one's own tongue and as recognition for someone still hurting from words said to them long ago.
misreadings: Not a claim that the hurt person is weak for being affected.
cautions: For a reader wounded by words, the first half validates the hurt; the second half, addressed to the speaker, should not read as blame.
not_for: readers currently in a verbally abusive situation who need safety steps, not reflection
speaks_to: regret over something said in anger
being hurt by a parent's, partner's or boss's words

mbh.12.337.11.context: Narada, visiting the young Shuka (Vyasa's son, who is set on liberation), offers to teach him what is for his highest good, and passes on what the sage Sanatkumara once told a gathering of rishis about knowledge, renunciation, restraint and truth. This verse sits in a run of maxims on restraining desire and anger, just before the famous line on truth and benefit.
mbh.12.337.11.core_teaching: Each good thing has its own thief: anger drains disciplined practice, envy spoils prosperity, praise and insult corrupt learning, and carelessness endangers the self.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation and footnote)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's note: an ascetic's power is spent the moment he curses in anger, which is why forgiveness is a Brahmana's strength; learning is guarded by neither performing for honour nor acting so as to dishonour it.

commentaries.who: BORI critical text (enjoylearningsanskrit translation)
commentaries.gist: Same four pairings in the critical text: austerity guarded from anger, prosperity from envy, knowledge from both honour and dishonour, the self from negligence.

mbh.12.337.11.practical_reading: Used as a checklist for protecting what one has built: don't let a temper undo years of discipline, don't let comparison sour success, don't study for applause, and don't drift.
misreadings: Not a call to hoard success out of fear; 'guarding prosperity from envy' includes one's own envy of others.
not_for: someone in acute grief or crisis; it is a maintenance teaching, not a consolation
speaks_to: people who lose ground through flashes of anger
comparison and envy at work or on social media

mbh.12.337.13.context: Narada, visiting the young Shuka (Vyasa's son, who is set on liberation), offers to teach him what is for his highest good, and passes on what the sage Sanatkumara once told a gathering of rishis about knowledge, renunciation, restraint and truth. Just before, Sanatkumara says there is nothing higher than truth; this verse then refines what counts as truth.
mbh.12.337.13.core_teaching: Truthful speech is good, but the measure of truth is finally the welfare of beings: what is truly for the good of all is what deserves the name of truth.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation and footnote)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli warns the line is often misread: it does not license sacrificing truth for convenience, only covers rare cases where a fact would cause real harm, such as betraying hiding travellers to robbers.

commentaries.who: Medhatithi on Manu 4.138 (related rule)
commentaries.gist: Manu: speak what is true and pleasant; never a pleasant falsehood. Medhatithi adds that where a truth would only wound, one may stay silent, but must not speak a comforting lie.

commentaries.who: Parallel in the hunter's teaching (Vana Parva, BORI 3.203.42)
commentaries.gist: The same idea recurs in the Vana Parva: telling the truth is the better course, and what most fully benefits creatures is regarded as the highest truth.

mbh.12.337.13.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to hard conversations: tell the truth, but choose which true words to say, when and how, so that they help rather than merely discharge.
misreadings: Not a licence for white lies or convenient untruth (Ganguli explicitly rejects this).
Not a reason to withhold truths someone needs, such as a diagnosis or a safety risk.
cautions: Readers recovering from being lied to 'for their own good' may find the verse uncomfortable; frame it as choosing helpful truths, not replacing truth.
not_for: someone deciding whether to conceal wrongdoing; it should not read as permission to deceive
speaks_to: people who use 'just being honest' as cover for cruelty
parents deciding what to tell children

mbh.12.338.12.context: Narada comes to the young Shuka and offers teachings to dispel grief. He says the man of little understanding suffers from meeting the unwanted and losing the loved; grieving for what is past only adds a second sorrow to the first; those who see the course of life clearly do not weep. Then come these lines: when pain arrives that no effort can ward off, do not keep dwelling on it. He adds that mental pain is cured by wisdom as bodily pain by medicine, and that where grief can be averted one should act on the remedy as soon as the chance appears.
mbh.12.338.12.core_teaching: For pain that nothing can fix, the medicine is to stop brooding on it; dwelling feeds it, it does not dissolve it.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation and footnote (Santi CCCXXXI)
commentaries.gist: In Ganguli's rendering, when an unavoidable grief arrives one should stop dwelling on it, since refusing to brood is its cure and brooding feeds it. His note on the nearby 'one sorrow becomes two' line: indulging sorrow makes it grow.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli, Santi CCCXXXI)
commentaries.gist: Narada pairs this with the advice that where grief can be averted, one should apply a remedy as soon as an opportunity arises, so the counsel is limited to what truly cannot be changed.

commentaries.who: Parallel in BORI apparatus (12.198, *540)
commentaries.gist: The same verses appear attributed to Manu, followed by the line that wisdom heals mental pain as medicine heals the body, showing this was a stock teaching.

mbh.12.338.12.practical_reading: When you have done all you can and the pain remains, gently steering attention away from rumination is a remedy, not avoidance.
misreadings: Not 'suppress your feelings'; it targets brooding, and only where nothing can be done.
Not an instruction to forget the person who left.
cautions: The same passage says the wise do not shed tears; for grief, keep the anti-rumination point and leave out the no-tears line.
not_for: early grief that needs expression
situations where something can and should still be done
speaks_to: pain one can no longer act on

mbh.12.338.13.context: In the next chapter Narada continues to Shuka with a teaching on sorrow: brooding over loss multiplies it, mental pain yields to understanding as bodily pain to medicine, everything joined must separate, and contentment is the only wealth that satisfies. It prepares Shuka's turn from worldly life toward liberation. Just before, Narada says that pain one cannot ward off should not be dwelt on, since thinking about sorrow only enlarges it.
mbh.12.338.13.core_teaching: Pain has two kinds of remedy: medicine for the body and clear understanding for the mind. Using each where it belongs is what knowledge makes possible.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: mental griefs should be killed by wisdom, physical ones dispelled by medicine; this is the power of knowledge, and one should not act like people of little understanding.

commentaries.who: Shaunaka's parallel counsel (Vana Parva, Ganguli section II)
commentaries.gist: In the Vana Parva the same pairing appears: disease is allayed by medicine, while mental affliction is eased by withdrawing the mind and by yoga, and wise physicians treat the mind first.

mbh.12.338.13.practical_reading: Often quoted to legitimise caring for the mind as seriously as the body: understanding, reflection and good counsel are remedies too.
misreadings: Not advice to rely on 'wisdom' instead of treatment for depression, anxiety or other mental illness; in modern terms mental health care can be medicine too (our misuse note is right).
cautions: Anyone with a mental health condition could hear 'solve it with wisdom'. Pair it with explicit permission to seek professional help.
not_for: users in crisis or with suicidal thoughts (route to support, not reflection)
speaks_to: people who dismiss their own emotional pain
caregivers balancing physical and emotional needs

mbh.12.338.15.context: In the next chapter Narada continues to Shuka with a teaching on sorrow: brooding over loss multiplies it, mental pain yields to understanding as bodily pain to medicine, everything joined must separate, and contentment is the only wealth that satisfies. It prepares Shuka's turn from worldly life toward liberation. Here Narada turns from private loss to calamities that strike a whole people.
mbh.12.338.15.core_teaching: When a calamity is shared by everyone, private lament is not the fitting response; if there is any means to act against it, one should act instead of mourning.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one should not lament individually over a misfortune that concerns a whole community, but seek to avert it and apply a remedy as soon as an opening appears.

commentaries.who: BORI critical text (enjoylearningsanskrit translation)
commentaries.gist: The critical text has the same verse; it is followed by the observation that in life misery outweighs happiness, which frames action, not despair, as the sane response.

mbh.12.338.15.practical_reading: Applied to shared crises (a pandemic, layoffs, a flood): don't sink into solitary despair over what is happening to everyone; look for the one practical thing you can do.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of collective grief or of mourning after a disaster.
Not a claim that individual action can fix systemic problems.
cautions: For someone who has personally lost a loved one in a shared disaster, 'don't grieve' lands badly.
not_for: personal bereavement in a mass tragedy

mbh.12.338.19.context: In the next chapter Narada continues to Shuka with a teaching on sorrow: brooding over loss multiplies it, mental pain yields to understanding as bodily pain to medicine, everything joined must separate, and contentment is the only wealth that satisfies. It prepares Shuka's turn from worldly life toward liberation. Just before, Narada notes that wealth brings pain in earning, keeping and losing it, so its loss should not be mourned.
mbh.12.338.19.core_teaching: Climbing from one level of wealth to the next does not satisfy; the unsatisfied are ruined by the chase, while the wise arrive at contentment.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: people of little understanding, reaching one grade of wealth after another, never find contentment and perish in misery; the wise are always content.

commentaries.who: Shaunaka on thirst (Vana Parva, Ganguli section II)
commentaries.gist: Shaunaka calls the thirst for possessions the root of anxiety, a disease without beginning or end that the unwise cannot give up; those who renounce it find happiness.

mbh.12.338.19.practical_reading: Used against lifestyle creep and status chasing: notice that each raise or upgrade resets the target, and decide what 'enough' looks like.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of earning or of ambition as such.
Not advice to someone struggling financially to be content with deprivation.
cautions: Can feel tone-deaf to a reader in financial hardship.
not_for: people facing poverty, debt or job loss

mbh.12.338.21.context: In the next chapter Narada continues to Shuka with a teaching on sorrow: brooding over loss multiplies it, mental pain yields to understanding as bodily pain to medicine, everything joined must separate, and contentment is the only wealth that satisfies. It prepares Shuka's turn from worldly life toward liberation. This verse follows the reflection that everything joined will separate and everything high will fall.
mbh.12.338.21.core_teaching: Craving has no end point, so happiness cannot come from satisfying it; contentment is the highest happiness and the only wealth the wise count.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: thirst is unquenchable, contentment the highest happiness, so the wise regard contentment as their most precious wealth.

commentaries.who: Shaunaka on thirst (Vana Parva, Ganguli section II)
commentaries.gist: The Vana Parva describes the same thirst as endless, dwelling in the heart and consuming a person like a self-fed fire; giving it up is named the way to happiness.

mbh.12.338.21.practical_reading: Teachers use it to reframe wealth: contentment is something one practises, a kind of income that does not depend on the next purchase.
misreadings: Not a glorification of poverty or a reason to stop providing for a family.
cautions: Avoid for readers in real material need.
not_for: financial hardship or loss of livelihood

mbh.12.338.22.context: In the next chapter Narada continues to Shuka with a teaching on sorrow: brooding over loss multiplies it, mental pain yields to understanding as bodily pain to medicine, everything joined must separate, and contentment is the only wealth that satisfies. It prepares Shuka's turn from worldly life toward liberation. It follows directly on 'contentment is the real wealth' and leads into Narada's point that one should seek the self rather than objects.
mbh.12.338.22.core_teaching: Life is running out continuously, not even pausing for a blink; since the body itself does not last, it makes no sense to fix one's mind on anything as if it were permanent.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one's allotted life runs on without stopping even for a moment; when the body itself is not durable, what else could be thought of as lasting?

commentaries.who: BORI critical text (enjoylearningsanskrit translation)
commentaries.gist: Same verse in the critical text: life does not stand still even a moment, so in impermanent bodies there is no lasting thing to contemplate.

mbh.12.338.22.practical_reading: Used as a memento mori for priorities: time is the scarcest resource, so spend attention on what matters rather than on what will pass anyway.
misreadings: Not a counsel of despair or of 'nothing matters'.
cautions: Mortality theme; may unsettle someone who is ill, elderly and anxious, or recently bereaved.
not_for: terminal illness or health anxiety
fresh bereavement

mbh.12.338.9.context: In the next chapter Narada continues to Shuka with a teaching on sorrow: brooding over loss multiplies it, mental pain yields to understanding as bodily pain to medicine, everything joined must separate, and contentment is the only wealth that satisfies. It prepares Shuka's turn from worldly life toward liberation. This verse comes early: having said that what is gone does not return however much one regrets it, Narada names the cost of brooding.
mbh.12.338.9.core_teaching: Grief that keeps replaying a loss adds a second injury to the first: the loss itself, and the suffering one renews by dwelling on it.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation and footnote)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it as getting sorrow for sorrow, two griefs instead of one; his note adds simply that sorrow grows when indulged.

commentaries.who: BORI critical text (enjoylearningsanskrit translation)
commentaries.gist: Identical wording in the critical text; the surrounding verses stress that what has passed cannot be regained and that wise people, seeing life and death clearly, do not keep weeping.

mbh.12.338.9.practical_reading: Teachers use it to distinguish mourning from rumination: feel the loss, but notice when replaying it has become a second wound one keeps reopening.
misreadings: Not a command to stop grieving or to grieve quickly.
Not a judgement on people who are still sad long after a loss.
cautions: Mentions death directly. For fresh bereavement it can sound like 'stop grieving'; use only after the first weeks, and frame as noticing rumination, not forbidding tears.
Narada's wider teaching tells Shuka not to shed tears at all; do not import that stance into a reading for a grieving user.
not_for: recent bereavement (days or weeks)
pregnancy or child loss
anyone who might hear it as blame for still hurting
speaks_to: rumination over a past loss, breakup or failure

mbh.12.46.122.context: Near the end of the hymn, after praising Krishna as the cosmic person and in his many forms, Bhishma says that those who bow to Govinda have no fear; manuscripts add that one bow to Krishna equals ten horse-sacrifices. The hymn closes with Bhishma's petition and a final salutation.
mbh.12.46.122.core_teaching: Bowing to Krishna, pictured in his familiar dark form and yellow garment, is offered as refuge from fear.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XLVIII, n. 18)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: those who worship Govinda of unfading prowess are freed from all fears; the next lines say one bow to Krishna equals ten horse-sacrifices and frees from rebirth. His note identifies atasi as flax.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.47.60 and 12.51.8 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The verse is in the constituted text, but the ten-horse-sacrifice lines between its halves are manuscript additions. Bhishma repeats the first line to Krishna's face at 12.51.8.

mbh.12.46.122.practical_reading: Used as a short prayer for anxious moments: picture the beloved form, bow inwardly, and let that be a place to stand.
misreadings: Not a promise that nothing bad will happen (our misuse note is right).
Not "fear means weak faith".
cautions: Spoken by a dying man; the hymn also contains rebirth and hell imagery nearby.
not_for: anxiety disorders where the reader may feel blamed for still being afraid
readers who reject devotional framing
speaks_to: devotional readers seeking a short prayer

mbh.12.46.125.context: Part of a block of salutations that some manuscripts insert in the closing section of Bhishma's hymn, between "those who bow to Govinda have no fear" and his final petition.
mbh.12.46.125.core_teaching: Vishnu is praised as protection against dread and as the one thing to hold onto when life's current spins you.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XLVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: salutations to the one who dispels fear of hell, a boat for those plunged in the eddies of worldly life; then to the friend of brahmins, cows and the world, Krishna and Govinda.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, star passage 93 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The editors relegated this salutation block to the apparatus as a manuscript addition; our brackets reflect that. It is devotional expansion, not the oldest layer.

mbh.12.46.125.practical_reading: An image for overwhelming periods: when life swirls, you do not need to swim out, only to hold on to something steady.
misreadings: Not fear-based religion; the stress is on rescue, not on hell.
cautions: Mentions hell; soften or drop that half for anxious readers.
Late devotional addition; present as part of the received hymn, not as Bhishma's oldest words.
not_for: readers with religious fear or scrupulosity

mbh.12.46.127.context: Same inserted block as the preceding salutation, near the end of Bhishma's hymn; it is the classic statement of the power of the name Hari within the Mahabharata.
mbh.12.46.127.core_teaching: The name Hari is presented as food for the journey, medicine and rescue from grief: a portable refuge.

commentaries.who: Ganguli translation with note 19 (Santi sec. XLVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli calls the two syllables the travelling stock for life's wilderness and the cure for worldly attachments; his note gives two readings of saṃsāra: attachments, or the round of rebirths ended by contemplation.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, star passage 93 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Relegated to the apparatus as a manuscript addition, as our brackets show; it reflects later name-devotion (nāma-māhātmya) layered onto the hymn.

mbh.12.46.127.practical_reading: A simple practice for hard days: repeat the name as provisions on a long road, a small, carryable source of steadiness.
misreadings: Not a cure that replaces medical, legal or emotional help (our misuse note is right).
Not magic words; in context it is the fruit of a lifetime's devotion.
cautions: Late devotional addition; present it as part of the recited hymn tradition.
not_for: readers who might use prayer instead of treatment
non-devotional users
speaks_to: devotional readers in grief or illness
someone wanting a simple daily practice

mbh.12.46.131.context: Bhishma's last petition in the hymn, after "may my sins perish as everything is full of Vishnu". He then bows saying "namah", and Krishna, perceiving his devotion, grants him divine knowledge. Bhishma repeats the same plea when Krishna stands before him (12.51.9).
mbh.12.46.131.core_teaching: Having done his part and taken refuge, Bhishma hands the choice of what is truly good for him to Krishna.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XLVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: I seek your protection and am devoted, desiring a happy end; lotus-eyed best of gods, think of what will be for my good. Bhishma then bows and Krishna grants him knowledge of past, present and future.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.47.62 and 12.51.9 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: In the constituted text in both places: once in the hymn, once said face to face when Krishna arrives, right after Bhishma repeats the flax-flower verse.

mbh.12.46.131.practical_reading: A prayer of trust after effort: I have done what I could; let what is truly good, not just what I want, unfold.
misreadings: Not a reason to stop making choices (our misuse note is right).
Shreyas is the truly good, not guaranteed comfort.
cautions: A deathbed prayer for a good end; for ill or elderly readers it may land as "prepare to die".
not_for: someone avoiding a decision
readers frightened by mortality
speaks_to: letting go of control after doing one's part

mbh.12.46.14.context: Janamejaya asks how Bhishma on the arrow-bed gave up his body and what yoga he held. Vaishampayana describes him, surrounded by sages, concentrating within, then turning in deed, mind and word to Krishna and singing the long hymn (Bhishma-stava-raja). Krishna, far away, perceives it, grants him knowledge, and sets out with the Pandavas to visit him.
mbh.12.46.14.core_teaching: Facing death in great pain, Bhishma gathers his whole being, act, thought and word, into one movement of attention toward Krishna.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. XLVIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: surrounded by sages like the moon among stars, Bhishma with pure heart and joined palms thought of Krishna in mind, word and act and praised him in a strong, cheerful voice.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.47.1-7 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The chapter is framed by Janamejaya's question about Bhishma's death; long lists of attending sages are manuscript additions. The hymn is placed here although Bhishma's teaching and death come later in the book.

mbh.12.46.14.practical_reading: A model for prayer or meditation in hard moments: bring body, mind and words to one point instead of letting pain scatter them.
misreadings: Not a claim that devotion removes pain; Bhishma is still on the arrows.
cautions: A deathbed scene with physical suffering; consider the reader's situation (illness, caregiving).
not_for: someone frightened of dying who did not ask for this
readers who reject devotional framing

mbh.12.51.11.context: Krishna has asked Bhishma to teach Yudhishthira. Bhishma protests that in Krishna's presence he cannot speak: his arrow-wounds burn, his mind is clouded, his breath is failing, he cannot tell the directions or sky from earth, and he lives only by Krishna's power, so Krishna should teach. Krishna then grants him freedom from pain, hunger and confusion and clear vision.
mbh.12.51.11.core_teaching: In extreme pain and disorientation, Bhishma admits he has no footing of his own and is sustained only by the divine.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: Bhishma says his mind is agitated by arrow pain, vitals burning, utterance failing; he cannot distinguish the compass points or sky from earth and is barely alive through Krishna's energy, so Krishna should speak.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.52 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Same wording in the constituted text; the verse belongs to Bhishma's refusal to teach, which Krishna answers with the boon that removes his pain.

mbh.12.51.11.practical_reading: Gives words to utter depletion: it is honest to say "I can't tell up from down; I am held up by something beyond me".
misreadings: Not passivity; the next scene has Bhishma teaching for days. (Our misuse note cites Gita 18.63, which is not from this context.)
cautions: Describes severe pain and dying; can be strongly validating or frightening for the seriously ill.
not_for: readers in crisis who need practical help first
non-devotional users
speaks_to: exhaustion, illness, burnout at its worst
devotional readers who feel they are holding on by grace

mbh.12.53.17.context: Next morning the Pandavas and Krishna return. Krishna asks whether Bhishma slept well and whether his mind is clear and free of pain. Bhishma answers with this verse and adds that past, present and future, all the Vedic and regional duties, and kingcraft are now clear to him, so he feels young and able to teach.
mbh.12.53.17.core_teaching: Bhishma testifies that by Krishna's grace his burning, fog, exhaustion and pain lifted at once, clearing him for his last work.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: burning, stupefaction, fatigue, exhaustion, illness and pain have left me in a single day; past, present and future are clear as a fruit in my hand.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.54 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text addresses Govinda; the relief is the fulfilment of the boon Krishna gave at 12.52. Bhishma still dies weeks later at the solstice.

mbh.12.53.17.practical_reading: For relief after a hard stretch: name what has eased and give thanks, without assuming the struggle is over.
misreadings: Not a promise of healing; keep up medical care (our misuse note is right).
Relief here is to enable service, not an escape from death.
cautions: Readers with chronic pain may feel their own lack of relief as lack of grace.
not_for: chronic or terminal illness without relief
readers who might stop treatment
speaks_to: a fog lifting after depression (with care)

mbh.12.53.23.context: Same morning conversation. Having reported his relief and clarity, Bhishma says meditation on Krishna has made him feel young and able to speak the good; he then asks why Krishna does not teach Yudhishthira himself, and Krishna replies that he wants Bhishma's fame to grow.
mbh.12.53.23.core_teaching: Remembrance of the divine renews even the old and wounded, making them able to give what is truly good to others.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: strengthened by meditation on Krishna, Bhishma feels young again and competent to discourse on what is beneficial, then asks why Krishna does not teach himself.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.54 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Same verse in the constituted text; Krishna's answer is that he steps back so Bhishma's words will be honoured as long as the world lasts.

mbh.12.53.23.practical_reading: For elders and mentors: inner renewal can come late in life, and its natural use is passing on what one knows.
misreadings: Not a promise of physical youth.
cautions: Bhishma is still dying; avoid suggesting the body will recover.
not_for: readers in active decline who may feel failure for not feeling renewed
speaks_to: older readers taking on mentoring or teaching
renewal after a long illness or depression
someone asked to step up and teach

mbh.12.55.16.context: Bhishma opens his instruction: a king should honour gods and brahmins, and always strive in exertion (utthāna), since fate does nothing without it; fate and effort go together, but effort is primary. Then this verse: do not burn with distress over a failed undertaking; apply yourself again. He moves on to truth as the king's chief means of success.
mbh.12.55.16.core_teaching: A failed undertaking is not a reason for self-torment; a leader returns to the task with renewed effort, because exertion, not fate alone, brings results.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LVI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: exertion and destiny operate together but exertion is superior, since destiny is inferred from results of effort; do not grieve if what you began ends badly, exert yourself in it with redoubled attention.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.56.14-16 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The constituted text sets the verse after a call to constant exertion (utthāna); its second line instead commends discipline (vinaya) as the king's highest policy, so "try again" rests on the vulgate reading.

mbh.12.55.16.practical_reading: For anyone leading a project: when it fails, skip the self-punishment, review, and re-engage with more care; that is what responsibility looks like.
misreadings: Not "never feel disappointed"; it targets the self-torment that stops the next attempt.
Not "repeat the same thing blindly"; Ganguli stresses redoubled attention.
cautions: Addressed to a king about statecraft; frame for leaders, parents, managers rather than as universal pressure to keep trying.
not_for: someone whose "undertaking" was a relationship that ended for good reason
burnout
speaks_to: a failed launch, campaign, exam or project
managers and team leads after a setback

mbh.12.7.13.context: Right after the war Yudhishthira mourns Karna and all the slain. He describes how parents strive and pray for sons, carry them anxiously, and wonder whether they will live and grow strong; then he says those young men now lie dead and their parents' hopes are void. From this grief he argues for leaving the kingdom.
mbh.12.7.13.core_teaching: Children are the object of long, costly hope: parents take on disciplines to have them and carry them with anxious expectation. In context the point is how much is lost when such children die.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. VII)
commentaries.gist: In Ganguli the verse opens a lament: parents ask whether their sons will survive and bring them joy, and now those youths are slain and the parents' expectations are fruitless.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition (textual note: 12.7.13-14 and 12.146.13)
commentaries.gist: The same first line returns at 12.146.13, where the sage Indrota rebukes King Janamejaya: parents strive for sons, yet his family's hopes in him came to nothing. Both uses stress hopes that can be dashed.

mbh.12.7.13.practical_reading: Can prompt gratitude for what parents invested before we were even born, and compassion for their worries; it also helps new parents name the weight of hope they carry.
