misreadings: Not a claim that parents' love is purely selfless; the passage openly includes their hope of support.
Not a guilt lever ("look what your parents gave up").
cautions: In context this leads straight into the deaths of young sons and their parents' ruined hopes. Avoid for bereaved parents or anyone who has lost a child or a pregnancy.
Talks of conceiving and carrying children; can hurt readers facing infertility.
not_for: bereaved parents
infertility or pregnancy loss
estranged or abused children who would hear guilt
speaks_to: new or expecting parents reflecting on what they hope for
adult children making peace with what their parents gave

mbh.12.7.34.context: Yudhishthira has called the war a sin. He says a sin can be cancelled by good acts and lists the means of expiation, then argues that renunciation is best, since the renouncer commits no new sins; so he will go to the forest. Arjuna immediately disputes this, praising wealth and kingship.
mbh.12.7.34.core_teaching: A wrong already done is not the end of the story: it can be outweighed by deliberate good action, beginning with owning it and feeling its weight.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. VII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli lists the means and adds that the renouncer is held incapable of new sin, which is why Yudhishthira decides to go to the woods and hand Arjuna the kingdom.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition (textual note, 12.7.34 and star passage 8)
commentaries.gist: Only the first line is in the constituted text; the itemised list of expiations is a manuscript addition, matching the brackets in our Sanskrit.

mbh.12.7.34.practical_reading: For someone stuck in guilt: name the wrong honestly, let the regret be real, then do concrete good, ideally repairing harm where possible, rather than either denying it or drowning in it.
misreadings: Not "good deeds cancel the need to apologise or repair harm to the person hurt".
Not Yudhishthira's conclusion that one should abandon one's duties; the epic rejects that.
cautions: Uses the language of sin (pāpa); a scrupulous or depressed reader may hear accusation. Lead with the hope, not the sin.
Spoken by a man in acute guilt-driven grief who is about to be argued out of his plan.
not_for: someone who was harmed and is told to absorb it
obsessive guilt spirals
readers wanting to buy off a wrong with charity
speaks_to: guilt over a past wrong and wanting a way forward

mbh.12.80.17.context: Yudhishthira asks what a king's counsellor should be like and whom to trust. Bhishma lists kinds of friends, warns that anyone can turn and that total trust ruins while total distrust is like death, gives the marks of an enemy and of the best friend, then turns to kinsmen: fear them like death, since a kinsman cannot bear a kinsman's rise, yet the kinless are easily overrun; honour them in word and act while privately staying wary. This verse comes right after the marks of an enemy (one who thinks your loss will bring him gain).
mbh.12.80.17.core_teaching: The surest mark of a true friend is that your success does not sting them and your losses grieve them.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LXXX)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one whose fall would follow yours should be trusted like a father; a friend is like your own self who fears when calamity strikes you and rejoices at your prosperity; those who wish you harm are foes.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.81.3-19 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: In the constituted text the best-friend verse sits among warnings that friends change, that one should trust and suspect selectively, and that an enemy is one who expects to gain by your loss.

mbh.12.80.17.practical_reading: Use it as a mirror more than a test: can I be glad, not threatened, when a friend does well, and truly sorry when they struggle?
misreadings: Not a tool for suspicion ("prove you're not jealous").
Not "friends must never feel envy"; the mark is how they act on it.
cautions: Context is a king's guide to trust and suspicion, not a warm essay on friendship.
not_for: someone already paranoid about friends
a reader grieving a lost friendship
speaks_to: someone hurt that a friend wasn't happy for them

mbh.12.80.36.context: Yudhishthira asks what a king's counsellor should be like and whom to trust. Bhishma lists kinds of friends, warns that anyone can turn and that total trust ruins while total distrust is like death, gives the marks of an enemy and of the best friend, then turns to kinsmen: fear them like death, since a kinsman cannot bear a kinsman's rise, yet the kinless are easily overrun; honour them in word and act while privately staying wary. The very next verse adds that one also knows oneself wronged by one's own kin; there are virtues and faults in them.
mbh.12.80.36.core_teaching: For all their friction, kin are the refuge when outsiders wrong you, because they feel the insult as their own.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LXXX)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: fear kinsmen as death, for they cannot bear your prosperity; yet the kinless are despised and overrun; kinsmen are the refuge of one afflicted by others; honour them while privately wary.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.81.33-38 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text: the verse is balanced by the next, which admits one is also wronged by kin and that both good and bad are seen among them; hence honour them in word and deed.

mbh.12.80.36.practical_reading: A reminder that family conflicts can coexist with deep loyalty; when the world turns on you, the people who share your name often show up.
misreadings: Not "family is always safe" (our own note is right).
Not a reason to tolerate mistreatment at home.
cautions: Must not be shown to someone wronged by their own family.
Bhishma's surrounding advice includes outward trust with inner mistrust of kin; not a model of healthy family life.
not_for: domestic abuse or family estrangement
LGBTQ readers rejected by family
someone without family
speaks_to: someone humiliated at work or in public whose family rallied
reconciling with relatives after a feud

mbh.12.81.11.context: Krishna tells Narada his clan is split between the Ahuka and Akrura factions; each urges him to drop the other, and both having and not having them is painful. He compares himself to the mother of two gamblers playing each other and asks what would be good for himself and his kin. Narada prescribes the 'weapon not of iron': sharing, forbearance, sincerity, gentleness and respect.
mbh.12.81.11.core_teaching: When two people you love are pitted against each other, you cannot root for either one's defeat; that is the torn position of the peacemaker.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation and footnote (Santi LXXXI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's Krishna is like the mother of two brothers gambling against each other who prays that both may win; the footnote on the Ahuka-Akrura rivalry explains why he needs both sides.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text: Narada's counsel (Ganguli, Santi LXXXI)
commentaries.gist: Advises winning kin with food shared, forgiveness, sincerity, mildness and honour, and soft words that turn away anger.

mbh.12.81.11.practical_reading: For a parent between two quarrelling children (or a friend between two friends), it names the ache of loving both and wanting neither to lose; Narada's answer points to patience and gentle speech.
misreadings: Not advice to stay neutral at all costs where one party is harming the other.
cautions: Fix the translation before use: as written it suggests taking sides is unavoidable, which is the opposite of the image.
not_for: situations of abuse between family members, where neutrality is harmful

data_flags.translation_note: Our translation reverses the sense. The Kumbakonam line 'naikasya jayam āśaṃse dvitīyasya parājayam' means 'I wish neither for the victory of one nor for the defeat of the other'; the BORI text reads 'I wish for victory to one and no defeat to the other',...

mbh.12.81.21.context: Bhishma tells how Krishna confided in Narada about his own clan: he gives them half of what he has and bears their cruel words, which grind his heart like fire-sticks, and he is caught between rival factions like the mother of two gamblers. Narada says the trouble is internal and partly of Krishna's own making, and that force would bring slaughter, so he should use a soft weapon to correct his kinsmen's tongues and carry the burden of leadership like a strong ox on a rough road. Krishna asks what this weapon is; this verse is Narada's answer.
mbh.12.81.21.core_teaching: To hold a quarrelsome family together, the effective weapon is not force but steady generosity, forbearance, sincerity, gentleness and due respect to each person.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LXXXI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: giving food as one can, forgiveness, sincerity, mildness and honour where due are a weapon not of steel; Narada adds that the calamity is internal, born of Krishna's own acts, and only the strong carry such loads.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.82 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text lists titikṣā and dama (restraint) beside sincerity; the episode frames this as advice to the head of a clan on preventing internal destruction, not to a victim.

mbh.12.81.21.practical_reading: For whoever holds a family or team together: feed people, absorb some provocation, be straight and gentle, and give each their due; these win more than confrontation.
misreadings: Patience with family is not tolerating abuse (our misuse note is right).
Not passivity: Narada calls it a weapon to be sharpened and used.
cautions: Counsel to the person with power and responsibility in the family, not to one being harmed by it (our note is right).
not_for: someone being abused or controlled by family
a child or dependent told to keep the peace
speaks_to: eldest siblings, parents and heads of households managing feuds
someone tired of being the peacemaker

mbh.12.81.22.context: Bhishma tells how Krishna confided in Narada about his own clan: he gives them half of what he has and bears their cruel words, which grind his heart like fire-sticks, and he is caught between rival factions like the mother of two gamblers. Narada says the trouble is internal and partly of Krishna's own making, and that force would bring slaughter, so he should use a soft weapon to correct his kinsmen's tongues and carry the burden of leadership like a strong ox on a rough road. This verse continues the description of the soft weapon.
mbh.12.81.22.core_teaching: When relatives are on the verge of saying bitter or petty things, use your own words to settle their hearts, speech and minds before the quarrel starts.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LXXXI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: with soft words alone turn away the anger of kinsmen about to utter cruel speeches, and mollify their hearts, minds and slanderous tongues; take up the weight of leading the clan.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.82.22 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text reads kaṭūni ca laghūni ca and śamayasva, confirming the meaning; it continues Narada's soft-weapon list for a leader keeping a clan from splitting.

mbh.12.81.22.practical_reading: De-escalate early: when you sense a family gathering heading for a fight, a warm, timely word can defuse it before anyone says what they will regret.
misreadings: Not "always swallow your truth"; it is about timing and tone.
Not the responsibility of a child or a victim to manage adults' anger.
cautions: Same as the previous verse: advice to the one with standing in the family.
not_for: someone facing verbal abuse at home
people-pleasers who already over-manage others' moods

mbh.12.81.6.context: Yudhishthira asks how to win over kinsmen who turn hostile; Bhishma recounts Krishna confiding in Narada. Krishna says he gives his kin half of what he has and bears their harsh words, yet those words grind his heart like a fire-stick; his clan is split between the Ahuka and Akrura factions and he cannot side with either. Narada answers that this trouble is internal and partly of Krishna's own making, and that the only weapon that works on kin is one not made of iron: sharing food, forbearance, sincerity, gentleness and due respect.
mbh.12.81.6.core_teaching: Cruel words from one's own family keep burning long after they are spoken; even Krishna felt this.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation and footnote (Santi LXXXI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli has Krishna's heart ground by his kinsmen's cruel words as a fire-stick is ground; his footnote explains that Ahuka and Akrura each urged Krishna to drop the other, so keeping both and losing both hurt equally.

mbh.12.81.6.practical_reading: It names the particular sting of harsh words from family, and then (in Narada's answer) points to patience, generosity and soft speech as the way to work on such relationships.
misreadings: Not a reason to keep absorbing abuse indefinitely; Krishna asks for a remedy, and Narada also says he has partly brought the trouble on himself.
Not 'family is always toxic'.
cautions: Narada's reply partly blames Krishna; a writer should not imply the reader caused the cruelty done to them.
not_for: someone in an abusive family situation who needs safety, not patience
speaks_to: being the peacemaker in a divided family
feeling unappreciated by kin you support

mbh.12.84.5.context: Bhishma recounts how Indra asked Brihaspati for the one thing that makes a person loved by all and famous. Brihaspati answers: conciliatory, pleasant speech (sāntva). He adds that a gift without kind words pleases no one, that even people deprived of their goods can be reconciled by sweet speech, and that a king who must punish should still speak gently. Bhishma tells Yudhishthira to practise it.
mbh.12.84.5.core_teaching: Warm, welcoming speech is the single practice that wins general goodwill: the silent frowner is disliked, while one who greets first with a smile is loved.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LXXXIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: agreeableness of speech is the one thing that wins regard from all; the silent, frowning man is hated, while one who addresses others first with smiles gratifies everyone.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.85 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text matches; the short chapter also says even those whose goods are taken can be reconciled by gentle words, showing sāntva as a political skill as well as a courtesy.

mbh.12.84.5.practical_reading: Be the one who greets first: a smile and an opening word at work, home or a new place changes how people receive you.
misreadings: Not flattery or manipulation, even though the passage notes sweet speech can soften people who have been wronged.
Not a judgment on quiet or shy people.
cautions: Can sting for socially anxious or depressed readers who find smiling hard; frame as a small practice, not a verdict.
not_for: social anxiety or depression framed as a fault
someone told to smile at an abuser
speaks_to: starting at a new job, school or neighbourhood
someone noticing they come across as cold

mbh.12.84.7.context: Bhishma recounts how Indra asked Brihaspati for the one thing that makes a person loved by all and famous. Brihaspati answers: conciliatory, pleasant speech (sāntva). He adds that a gift without kind words pleases no one, that even people deprived of their goods can be reconciled by sweet speech, and that a king who must punish should still speak gently. Bhishma tells Yudhishthira to practise it. This verse follows the smile-and-speak-first verse.
mbh.12.84.7.core_teaching: How you give matters as much as what you give: a gift without warmth pleases no one, like a meal with no seasoning.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Santi sec. LXXXIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: even gifts made without agreeable speech do not delight, like rice without curry; sweetness of speech never fails and never pains any heart.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 12.85.7 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: Same wording in the constituted text; vyañjana is the condiment or relish served with rice.

mbh.12.84.7.practical_reading: When you help or give, add the words: a note, a kind sentence, attention. Help delivered coldly can feel like a transaction or a humiliation.
misreadings: Not "words matter more than real help"; the gift is still the food.
not_for: someone in need being told to be grateful for cold help
speaks_to: caregivers and parents who give a lot but feel unappreciated

mbh.13.10.25.context: Yudhishthira asks about the fruits of good and evil acts. Bhishma answers that deeds follow their doer like a calf finding its mother among a thousand cows, and ripen in their season like fruit. In that run of images he observes that everything in an ageing body wears out except craving.
mbh.13.10.25.core_teaching: Age wears down every faculty, yet craving does not age with it; desire outlives the very senses that serve it.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: with age the hair greys, teeth loosen, eyes and ears dim, but the one thing that never abates is the desire for enjoyment.

commentaries.who: Shaunaka on thirst (Vana Parva, Ganguli section II)
commentaries.gist: Shaunaka describes the same thirst as something that does not decay with the decay of the body, a fatal disease the unwise cannot renounce.

commentaries.who: Bhartrihari, Vairagya Shataka (Wortham 1886)
commentaries.gist: Bhartrihari's renunciation verse makes the same contrast in the first person: face wrinkled, hair grey, limbs weak, yet desire alone stays strong.

mbh.13.10.25.practical_reading: Used to notice that wanting does not retire on its own; letting go has to be practised, at any age.
misreadings: Not mockery of old age or of older people's wishes.
Not a claim that all desire is shameful.
cautions: Could feel harsh to an older reader already struggling with failing health; avoid an ageist tone.
not_for: someone newly diagnosed with an age-related illness

mbh.13.11.26.context: A hunter's poisoned arrow misses a deer and strikes a great tree, which withers. A parrot that has lived in its hollow all its life will not leave, and wastes away with it. Indra, disguised as a brahmin, asks why it clings to a dead tree when the forest is full of others. The parrot answers with this verse; Indra, pleased by its compassion, offers a boon, and the parrot asks that the tree live again.
mbh.13.11.26.core_teaching: Loyalty is proved in hard times: one who lived on another's support when things were good should not abandon them when they fall into trouble.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli frames the tale as an illustration of compassion: the grateful parrot, out of affection for the lord of the forest, stays motionless and fasting, withering along with the tree, which amazes Indra.

commentaries.who: BORI critical text (enjoylearningsanskrit translation)
commentaries.gist: In the critical text the parrot says it relied on the tree while it was strong and asks how it could forsake it now; Indra is then pleased by its kindness and knowledge of dharma.

mbh.13.11.26.practical_reading: Applied to staying by people and institutions that supported you when they hit hard times: an ageing parent, a mentor in decline, a struggling family business.
misreadings: Not a call to stay in an abusive or harmful relationship (our misuse note is right).
Not a rule that one may never leave a failing workplace.
cautions: A reader in an abusive relationship could hear 'don't leave'; keep the benefactor framing explicit.
not_for: domestic abuse or coercive relationships
someone deciding to leave a toxic job
speaks_to: gratitude to those who helped us

mbh.13.161.111.context: Yudhishthira asks why people die young when scripture promises a hundred years. Bhishma answers that conduct (ācāra) is what lengthens life and brings prosperity, and gives a long list of rules, moral and ritual side by side: on anger and truthfulness, speech, hygiene, food, sleep, hospitality and whom to honour. It comes late in the list, among rules on purification and on avoiding the company of those who have fallen from their duties.
mbh.13.161.111.core_teaching: Don't slander others or say hurtful things, and don't needlessly stir up anyone's anger if you want a good life.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: never indulge in calumny or say what is disagreeable; one who wants his own good should never provoke the wrath of others against himself.

commentaries.who: Medhatithi on Manu 4.138 (related rule)
commentaries.gist: Manu pairs truth with pleasant speech; Medhatithi explains that a true but needlessly hurtful remark is better left unsaid, and a pleasant lie is never allowed.

mbh.13.161.111.practical_reading: Applied to gossip and needless provocation: skip the remark that only stirs resentment, especially behind someone's back.
misreadings: Not a rule to avoid every conflict or never disagree.
Not advice to appease an abuser to avoid their anger.
cautions: A reader living with someone volatile could hear 'don't provoke them', which shifts blame; avoid that framing.
not_for: anyone living with an abusive or volatile partner

mbh.13.161.119.context: Yudhishthira asks why people die young when scripture promises a hundred years. Bhishma answers that conduct (ācāra) is what lengthens life and brings prosperity, and gives a long list of rules, moral and ritual side by side: on anger and truthfulness, speech, hygiene, food, sleep, hospitality and whom to honour. This verse sits among household rules, just before the advice to keep pigeons and parrots at home for good fortune.
mbh.13.161.119.core_teaching: Give a place in your home, as far as you are able, to the vulnerable people connected to you: aged relatives, friends in need, and those who have fallen poor; doing so brings blessing and long life.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: an old kinsman or a friend who has become poor should be settled in one's house and cared for like family; doing so brings fame and long life.

commentaries.who: BORI critical text (enjoylearningsanskrit translation)
commentaries.gist: The critical text lists aged relatives, friends and anyone who has become poor, to be housed at home as a source of blessing and longevity; the sister and teacher do not appear.

mbh.13.161.119.practical_reading: Applied to multigenerational households and taking in relatives or friends who have fallen on hard times.
misreadings: Not an obligation beyond one's means ('svaśaktitaḥ', as one is able).
cautions: Could weigh on readers already stretched by caregiving or unable to house family; stress 'as you are able'.
not_for: caregivers already at breaking point
readers estranged from family for safety reasons
speaks_to: caring for ageing parents or relatives
helping a friend through job loss

mbh.13.161.14.context: Yudhishthira asks why people die young when scripture promises a hundred years. Bhishma answers that conduct (ācāra) is what lengthens life and brings prosperity, and gives a long list of rules, moral and ritual side by side: on anger and truthfulness, speech, hygiene, food, sleep, hospitality and whom to honour. This verse comes near the start, right after Bhishma says that even people without accomplishments live long if they keep to good conduct and are free of malice.
mbh.13.161.14.core_teaching: A long and good life rests on plain virtues: freedom from anger, truthfulness, harmlessness, freedom from envy and straight dealing.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one free from wrath, truthful, injuring no creature, without malice, crookedness or insincerity lives a hundred years; even the unaccomplished live long through right conduct and faith.

commentaries.who: BORI critical text (enjoylearningsanskrit translation)
commentaries.gist: The critical text has the same verse unchanged as 13.107.14, opening Bhishma's catalogue of what lengthens or shortens life.

mbh.13.161.14.practical_reading: Teachers read the 'hundred years' as the fruit of a calm, honest life: less anger and envy means less stress and fewer broken relationships.
misreadings: Not a medical promise; a short life or illness is not proof of bad character.
cautions: Someone grieving a person who died young, or who is seriously ill, could hear blame in the longevity promise.
not_for: grief over an early death
serious illness
speaks_to: people wanting a simple ethical checklist

mbh.13.161.35.context: Yudhishthira asks why people die young when scripture promises a hundred years. Bhishma answers that conduct (ācāra) is what lengthens life and brings prosperity, and gives a long list of rules, moral and ritual side by side: on anger and truthfulness, speech, hygiene, food, sleep, hospitality and whom to honour. Here Bhishma turns to speech: wounding words shot from the mouth leave the hearer grieving day and night, a forest cut down grows back but a heart hurt by words does not, and arrows can be drawn out of flesh but not words out of the heart.
mbh.13.161.35.core_teaching: Physical wounds can be treated, but cruel words lodge in the heart where they cannot be pulled out, so one should not speak them.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation and footnote)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: barbed and broad-headed arrows can be extracted, word-shafts cannot, being embedded in the heart; his note on the preceding verse says such wounds fester and can even lead to death.

commentaries.who: Vidura's counsel (Udyoga Parva, Ganguli XXXIV)
commentaries.gist: Vidura gives the same image: weapons can be drawn from the body, but a dagger of words plunged into the heart cannot; a forest cut down regrows, a heart wounded by ill speech never recovers.

mbh.13.161.35.practical_reading: Used both as a brake on one's own tongue and as recognition that words said to someone long ago can still hurt.
misreadings: Not a claim that the hurt can never heal with time and care.
Not blame for someone who is still affected by words.
cautions: For readers hurt by words the verse validates the pain; avoid implying they are permanently damaged.
not_for: someone in an ongoing verbally abusive situation who needs safety steps
speaks_to: being hurt by a parent's or partner's words
parents and managers who criticise sharply

mbh.13.161.36.context: Yudhishthira asks why people die young when scripture promises a hundred years. Bhishma answers that conduct (ācāra) is what lengthens life and brings prosperity, and gives a long list of rules, moral and ritual side by side: on anger and truthfulness, speech, hygiene, food, sleep, hospitality and whom to honour. This verse follows the passage on wounding speech, then moves to avoiding atheism, scorn of the Vedas, malice, pride and harshness.
mbh.13.161.36.core_teaching: Never ridicule people for what they lack or cannot help: a disability, lack of schooling, old age, plain looks, poverty or weakness.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one should not taunt a person who lacks a limb or has an extra one, the unlearned, the miserable, the ugly or poor, or one destitute of strength.

mbh.13.161.36.practical_reading: Applied to teasing, body-shaming and class snobbery: humour that targets what someone cannot help is cruelty.
misreadings: Not merely etiquette; it is about dignity of people with disabilities, the poor and the old.
cautions: Our translation's 'lack of standing' could be read as caste or status; avoid reintroducing Manu's 'low birth' category.
speaks_to: people who were mocked for their body or background

data_flags.translation_note: Two problems. (1) 'Vayo'dhikān' means those advanced in years, the old, not 'age' generally; better 'for being old'. (2) The last item: our 'lack of standing' matches no reading. Kumbakonam has satyahīnān ('lacking truth', probably a corruption), BORI and Ganguli have sattvahīnān ('lacking strength or...

mbh.13.161.45.context: Yudhishthira asks why some people die young and how one gains long life, fame and prosperity. Bhishma answers that conduct (achara) is the cause, and gives a long list of daily rules: rise before the sun, greet parents and teachers first on rising, clean the teeth, honour elders by standing and offering a seat, avoid malice. The list mixes timeless courtesies with rules of ritual purity, caste and marriage of its time.
mbh.13.161.45.core_teaching: Good conduct in small daily things, like rising early and greeting one's parents and teachers first, is what builds a long and good life.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation (Anusasana CIV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's Bhishma says not to lie in bed after sunrise, and to make amends if one does; the first act on rising should be to greet parents, teachers or other honoured elders, and this is what wins long life.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli, Anusasana CIV)
commentaries.gist: Bhishma's thesis is that conduct, more than learning or wealth, gives long life; he adds that old people should be greeted by standing and offering a seat, and that malice shortens life.

mbh.13.161.45.practical_reading: A daily act of respect, such as greeting your parents first thing (or calling them, if far away), is a small habit that shapes a good life.
misreadings: Not a literal promise that early risers live longer.
Not a demand to obey parents unconditionally, though the same chapter says so elsewhere.
cautions: The same chapter tells readers to obey parents' and teachers' commands without judging them, and includes caste and gender rules; do not import these.
For someone estranged from or grieving parents, 'greet your parents' can hurt.
not_for: someone whose parents have died recently
someone estranged from abusive parents
speaks_to: living far from parents and wanting a daily connection

mbh.13.162.12.context: Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should treat his younger brothers and how they should treat him. Bhishma says the eldest should act toward them as a teacher toward pupils, then gives rules on correcting faults, keeping the family united, dividing property, and the reverence due to father, mother and eldest brother. It is part of a run of rules on property: an eldest who wrongs his brothers forfeits his share, self-earned property abroad may be kept, and partition in the father's lifetime must be equal.
mbh.13.162.12.core_teaching: When a father divides family property among his sons in his lifetime, he must never give unequal shares.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: if unseparated brothers wish to portion the family property while their father lives, the father should give equal shares to all his sons.

commentaries.who: Ganguli's note on this chapter
commentaries.gist: Ganguli notes that many verses of this lesson come from Manu, while flagging where the epic's ranking of teachers departs from Manu.

mbh.13.162.12.practical_reading: Applied to wills, gifts and inheritance today: treat children even-handedly and transparently, because perceived favouritism outlives the parent.
misreadings: The text speaks of sons only; a modern reading should include daughters rather than reinforce exclusion.
cautions: Gendered source rule; don't present it as endorsing sons-only inheritance.
not_for: someone currently fighting a bitter inheritance case, where it may feel like taking sides

mbh.13.162.15.context: Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should treat his younger brothers and how they should treat him. Bhishma says the eldest should act toward them as a teacher toward pupils, then gives rules on correcting faults, keeping the family united, dividing property, and the reverence due to father, mother and eldest brother. Having said that dharma is the highest good, Bhishma ranks those owed reverence and ends with the mother, then adds that after the father's death the eldest brother stands in his place.
mbh.13.162.15.core_teaching: In the reverence owed, the mother surpasses father and every teacher, even the whole earth; no teacher is equal to a mother.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation and footnotes)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the Vedic instructor outweighs ten ordinary teachers, the father ten such instructors, the mother ten fathers or the whole earth. His note flags that this teacher ranking is inconsistent with Manu.

commentaries.who: Medhatithi on Manu 2.145 (parallel)
commentaries.gist: Manu: the ācārya excels ten sub-teachers, the father a hundred ācāryas, the mother a thousand fathers. Medhatithi says the numbers are only praise; the point is the ascending order, with the mother highest.

mbh.13.162.15.practical_reading: Widely quoted to honour mothers as a child's first and greatest teacher.
misreadings: Not a ranking that makes fathers or teachers unimportant.
cautions: Painful for readers whose mother has died, who were harmed or abandoned by their mother, or who are estranged.
Mother's Day style use can exclude those who cannot have children.
not_for: recent loss of a mother
maternal abuse or estrangement
pregnancy loss or infertility

mbh.13.162.4.context: Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should treat his younger brothers and how they should treat him. Bhishma says the eldest should act toward them as a teacher toward pupils, then gives rules on correcting faults, keeping the family united, dividing property, and the reverence due to father, mother and eldest brother. This verse opens the practical advice, right after Bhishma says a teacher of good conduct produces disciples of the same kind.
mbh.13.162.4.core_teaching: A wise elder sometimes chooses not to see small lapses, and when correction is needed does it indirectly rather than by open rebuke.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the eldest should at times be blind to his younger brothers' acts and, though wise, seem not to understand them; their transgressions should be corrected by indirect means.

commentaries.who: Ganguli on the next verse (reason given in the text)
commentaries.gist: Bhishma's reason follows at once: if the eldest corrects openly, enemies pained by the brothers' harmony seize on it to sow discord between them.

mbh.13.162.4.practical_reading: Used by parents, older siblings and managers: let minor mistakes pass, and correct privately and gently rather than in public.
misreadings: Not a licence to ignore real harm, danger or abuse (our misuse note is right).
not_for: situations involving abuse, addiction or safety, where 'looking away' is harmful
speaks_to: older siblings and parents of teens

mbh.13.162.5.context: Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should treat his younger brothers and how they should treat him. Bhishma says the eldest should act toward them as a teacher toward pupils, then gives rules on correcting faults, keeping the family united, dividing property, and the reverence due to father, mother and eldest brother. This verse explains the previous one: why the eldest should correct his brothers indirectly.
mbh.13.162.5.core_teaching: Families are split from outside by people envious of their good fortune, and open rebukes within the family give those people their opening.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: if, where brothers live in harmony, the eldest corrects them openly, enemies grieved by that harmony set themselves to divide them and sow dissension.

commentaries.who: BORI critical text (enjoylearningsanskrit translation)
commentaries.gist: The critical text has only the two lines: people openly divided at heart, or enemies burning at prosperity and wanting discord, would undo what was built. The bracketed southern line is absent.

mbh.13.162.5.practical_reading: Applied to family and team unity: keep disagreements in-house and be wary of outsiders who feed on rifts.
misreadings: Not a reason to distrust every in-law or outsider.
Not a case for hiding abuse to protect family image.
cautions: The 'enemies outside' framing can feed suspicion of in-laws; keep it about not giving rifts an audience.
not_for: families where the harm is internal and needs to be named

data_flags.translation_note: Our translation's last sentence ('Those who stay close are not divided') comes only from the bracketed southern insertion, and the first part drops the condition that Ganguli makes clear: it is open, direct correction by the eldest that gives envious outsiders their opening. Ganguli: if...

mbh.13.162.6.context: Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should treat his younger brothers and how they should treat him. Bhishma says the eldest should act toward them as a teacher toward pupils, then gives rules on correcting faults, keeping the family united, dividing property, and the reverence due to father, mother and eldest brother. It follows the warning about outsiders, and leads into rules that an eldest who wrongs his brothers loses his rank and his share.
mbh.13.162.6.core_teaching: The eldest sibling carries the family's fortunes: his conduct can build it up, and his misconduct is usually what brings it down.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: it is the eldest who either enhances the family's prosperity or destroys it entirely; if he lacks sense and behaves wickedly, the whole family is ruined.

commentaries.who: BORI critical text (enjoylearningsanskrit translation)
commentaries.gist: The critical reading of the second half: where the eldest degenerates, he destroys the whole family into which he was born.

mbh.13.162.6.practical_reading: A reminder to anyone in a lead role in a family (eldest child, head of household) that their behaviour sets the tone for everyone.
misreadings: Not a claim that the eldest is to blame for every family breakdown.
Not a reason to load an eldest daughter or son with responsibility for everyone.
cautions: Eldest children who already over-function for their families may feel more burdened; frame as influence, not total responsibility.
not_for: eldest children already carrying guilt for a family crisis they did not cause
speaks_to: eldest siblings and heads of joint families

mbh.13.175.8.context: Yudhishthira asks which of non-violence, Vedic rites, meditation, sense-control, austerity and service to teachers is best. Brihaspati answers that one who sees all beings as oneself leaves no harm behind, and then compresses dharma into this rule. He goes on: in giving and refusing, pleasure and pain, judge by reference to yourself, since harm returns to the harmer and care to the one who cares.
mbh.13.175.8.core_teaching: Don't do to another what you would find hurtful yourself; this is dharma in brief, and conduct that departs from it is driven by desire.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one should never do to another what one regards as injurious to oneself; this is the rule of righteousness in brief, and acting otherwise out of desire is unrighteousness.

commentaries.who: Brihaspati's next verses (same chapter)
commentaries.gist: The teaching continues: in refusing and giving, joy and sorrow, the pleasant and unpleasant, judge by your own case; whoever injures is injured in turn, and whoever cherishes is cherished.

commentaries.who: Wikipedia, Golden Rule (comparative context)
commentaries.gist: The Golden Rule article cites this Anushasana verse (critical edition 13.113/114) as the Mahabharata's statement of the rule, alongside other religious traditions.

mbh.13.175.8.practical_reading: Used as a quick test before acting or speaking: would I accept this if it were done to me?
misreadings: Not a claim that the rest of dharma is unnecessary; it is a summary, not a replacement.
speaks_to: conflict with a neighbour or colleague

mbh.13.254.145.context: After Bhishma teaches Yudhishthira the thousand names of Vishnu and their benefits, the southern text adds a short dialogue: Arjuna asks the lotus-eyed Lord to protect his devoted followers, and the Lord replies that one who wishes to praise him with a thousand names is praised by him even with one verse. Further verses addressed to Vasudeva and the Infinite follow.
mbh.13.254.145.core_teaching: A short prayer asking the Lord to be the protector of those who love him; in the recited hymn it prompts the assurance that sincere praise, even in a single verse, reaches him.

commentaries.who: Kumbakonam text (surrounding verses)
commentaries.gist: The Lord's reply that immediately follows: whoever wishes to praise him with the thousand names, he is praised by that person even with a single verse, without doubt.

commentaries.who: Shankara-bhashya edition of the hymn (Ananthakrishna Sastry tr.)
commentaries.gist: The text printed with Shankara's commentary closes with the colophon after the verse promising that those who worship the lotus-eyed Lord never meet defeat; the Arjuna dialogue is not part of it, so no classical commentary covers this verse.

mbh.13.254.145.practical_reading: Used as a closing prayer of refuge: asking for protection without bargaining, and trusting that heartfelt devotion counts more than length of recitation.
misreadings: Not a promise that devotees will be spared all hardship.
cautions: Devotional and Vaishnava; best in devotional plans.
not_for: secular readers
someone angry at God after a loss, for whom 'protect your devotees' may sting
speaks_to: people who recite the Vishnu Sahasranama
anxious readers seeking a simple prayer of refuge
those who feel their prayers are too short or imperfect

mbh.13.273.39.context: When the sun turns north, Yudhishthira brings the family, Krishna and the materials for the funeral rites to Bhishma. Bhishma bids farewell, tells Dhritarashtra not to grieve and to treat the Pandavas as his own sons, then praises Krishna and asks his leave to die. Krishna grants it, saying Bhishma has committed no wrong in this world, and Bhishma gives up his life.
mbh.13.273.39.core_teaching: At the end of his life Bhishma asks Krishna to protect him as one wholly devoted, and to give him leave to go.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's Bhishma praises Krishna, asks the lotus-eyed one to rescue him, begs leave to depart, and commends the Pandavas to his care; Krishna grants leave, saying Bhishma has not committed a single transgression.

commentaries.who: Bhagavata Purana 1.9 (later retelling, vedabase)
commentaries.gist: The Bhagavata retells Bhishma's death: as the sun turns north he stops teaching, fixes his eyes and mind on Krishna standing before him, and passes away absorbed in him.

mbh.13.273.39.practical_reading: Used as a model of a peaceful, prepared death: settling affairs, blessing family, and letting go into trust.
misreadings: Not a teaching that one may choose the time of death; Bhishma's boon is unique in the story.
cautions: About dying. Suitable for end-of-life, hospice or anticipatory grief only with care; can be very painful soon after a death.
Any echo of choosing one's death must not reach a reader at risk of self-harm.
not_for: users expressing suicidal thoughts
fresh bereavement
young readers facing a sudden loss
speaks_to: devotional reflection on a good death

mbh.13.43.45.context: In a southern-only Anushasana chapter, Narayana tells Garuda that neither gods nor demons know him in truth, that he takes form whenever dharma is oppressed, and that fasts, vows and penance alone cannot reach him. This verse then names Hari as the refuge of those sunk in delusion, and the meditative renouncer as one who comes to him directly.
mbh.13.43.45.core_teaching: Those stuck deep in confusion and worldly pursuit still have a refuge in Hari; those who are single-minded and meditative reach him through renunciation.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Kumbakonam 13.43, no classical commentary found)
commentaries.gist: The preceding verses say that minds clouded by passion and inertia cannot see him even through great penance, and that fasts and vows alone do not reach the highest goal; the following verses praise non-violence and steadiness.

mbh.13.43.45.practical_reading: Read as reassurance that being deep in confusion does not disqualify anyone from grace; the way out is turning toward the divine, not first becoming perfect.
misreadings: The second half should not be read as saying only renunciates are saved.
cautions: Explicitly sectarian Vaishnava framing; fits devotional plans better than general ones.
not_for: secular or non-Vaishnava readers looking for practical counsel
speaks_to: feeling too lost or worldly to deserve spiritual help

mbh.13.9.9.context: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma whether destiny or human effort is stronger. Bhishma recites how Vasishtha once put the same question to Brahma. Brahma answers with the image of seed and field, then argues at length, with examples of gods and kings, that the doer reaps his own acts and that exertion is what makes destiny bear fruit.
mbh.13.9.9.core_teaching: Destiny and effort are not rivals: destiny is the seed, effort the field, and nothing grows without both; but since effort is the part in one's hands, it is the decisive one.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: as tilled soil left unsown yields nothing, so destiny avails nothing without exertion; one's acts are the soil and destiny, the accumulated acts of past births, is the seed.

commentaries.who: Kumbakonam edition chapter summary
commentaries.gist: The southern text's chapter heading frames Bhishma's whole answer as proving, with illustrations, that human effort prevails even over fate.

commentaries.who: BORI critical text (enjoylearningsanskrit translation)
commentaries.gist: The critical text has both verses (13.6.7-8) unchanged: a field sown without seed is fruitless, so fate fails without effort; effort is the field, fate the seed.

mbh.13.9.9.practical_reading: Used against both fatalism and hustle-culture pride: circumstances and inheritance are the seed you were given, and the work you put in is the ground where it grows or fails.
misreadings: Not 'everything is up to you'; the verse keeps a real role for what one is given.
Not a claim that failure proves lack of effort.
cautions: A reader blaming themselves for an outcome outside their control (illness, layoffs) could hear 'you didn't try enough'.
not_for: grief over a loss nobody could have prevented
infertility or illness, where 'effort' framing can wound
speaks_to: after a setback, choosing to try again

data_flags.translation_note: First half reversed: the Sanskrit (uptaṃ kṣetram bījaṃ vinā) says a field sown/tilled without seed bears nothing, i.e. effort without destiny; Ganguli and the BORI translation both read it so. Ours says 'seed sown without a field'. The second half (effort = field, destiny =...

mbh.14.12.15.context: After the war Yudhishthira is crushed by grief and guilt and wants to renounce the throne. In chapters 11 to 13 Krishna answers him: the enemies were outside, but now the war is inside, with his own mind; what binds is the sense of 'mine', not owning things; and desire itself (in the Kama Gita) boasts that it survives every weapon used against it. Krishna urges him to rule and perform the horse sacrifice rather than retreat to the forest. In this chapter Krishna explains that there are two kinds of illness, bodily and mental, and that the great battle with Bhishma and Drona is over; a new one has come.
mbh.14.12.15.core_teaching: After the outer war comes a harder one, fought alone with one's own mind, where no weapon or ally can help; losing it leaves one in misery.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: Krishna says Yudhishthira must now fight his own mind; in this war there is no need of missiles, friends or attendants, the battle to be fought alone has come, and defeat in it leaves one wretched.

commentaries.who: Pradip Bhattacharya, essay on the Ashvamedha Parva
commentaries.gist: Bhattacharya reads Krishna's counsel as telling Yudhishthira that the war with Drona and Bhishma is finished and his real fight is inward: to master himself and take up his own duty.

mbh.14.12.15.practical_reading: Used for the moment after an outer crisis ends and the inner one begins: guilt, grief or anxiety that no one else can fight for you, though others can support you.
misreadings: Not a statement that one should face mental struggles without help; it says outer tools cannot do the work for you.
cautions: A person with depression could hear 'you must do this alone'; pair with encouragement to seek support.
not_for: someone in a mental health crisis who needs to reach out, not go it alone
speaks_to: aftermath of a crisis, divorce or job loss

mbh.14.13.13.context: After the war Yudhishthira is crushed by grief and guilt and wants to renounce the throne. In chapters 11 to 13 Krishna answers him: the enemies were outside, but now the war is inside, with his own mind; what binds is the sense of 'mine', not owning things; and desire itself (in the Kama Gita) boasts that it survives every weapon used against it. Krishna urges him to rule and perform the horse sacrifice rather than retreat to the forest. Krishna introduces the verses sung by Desire itself, which old sages recite. Desire says it cannot be killed by any being without the right method, and lists one method after another in which it simply reappears.
mbh.14.13.13.core_teaching: Desire cannot be killed by force: whatever weapon or method one uses against it, it reappears as attachment to that very method.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's text has prayer-muttering instead of a weapon: Kama deludes such a striver by posing as his own ego, and reappears likewise in sacrifice, Vedic study, patience, austerity, even the quest for liberation.

commentaries.who: Bibek Debroy, 'A Dirge for Desire' (Open magazine)
commentaries.gist: Debroy calls the Kama Gita short but profound: desire reappears in weapons, sacrifices, rites, austerities and even the pursuit of moksha, and is overcome only through non-attachment.

mbh.14.13.13.practical_reading: Applied to habits and cravings: white-knuckled suppression often turns into a new obsession (with the diet, the discipline, the spiritual practice); what works is loosening the grip, not fighting harder.
misreadings: Not an argument that self-discipline is useless.
Not permission to indulge every desire because it 'can't be beaten'.
cautions: For someone in recovery from addiction it could sound defeatist; pair with Krishna's answer (dropping possessiveness) and with support.
not_for: someone in early addiction recovery without support

mbh.14.13.3.context: After the war Yudhishthira is crushed by grief and guilt and wants to renounce the throne. In chapters 11 to 13 Krishna answers him: the enemies were outside, but now the war is inside, with his own mind; what binds is the sense of 'mine', not owning things; and desire itself (in the Kama Gita) boasts that it survives every weapon used against it. Krishna urges him to rule and perform the horse sacrifice rather than retreat to the forest. This verse opens chapter 13: renunciation of outer things alone does not bring success, and the next verses say death and Brahman both live within a person and fight unseen.
mbh.14.13.3.core_teaching: The sense of 'mine' is itself death, and 'not mine' is the eternal: bondage and freedom are a matter of possessiveness, not of possessions.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's Krishna: the two-syllabled 'mama' is death and the three-syllabled 'na mama' is eternal Brahman; both dwell within and wage an unseen war.

commentaries.who: Bibek Debroy, 'A Dirge for Desire' (Open magazine)
commentaries.gist: Debroy notes that 'mrityu' and 'mama' are both two syllables, treating the sense of ownership as a form of death and its absence as the eternal.

commentaries.who: Pradip Bhattacharya, essay on the Ashvamedha Parva
commentaries.gist: Bhattacharya paraphrases the teaching as 'mine' leading to death and 'not mine' to eternity, part of Krishna's push for Yudhishthira to rule rather than withdraw.

mbh.14.13.3.practical_reading: Applied to attachment in relationships, careers and possessions: notice the grip of 'mine' (my child, my title, my house) and hold things as care, not ownership.
misreadings: Not advice to give everything away or abandon responsibilities; Krishna is urging Yudhishthira to rule.
Not coldness toward loved ones.
cautions: For a bereaved parent or spouse, 'not mine' can feel like being told not to have loved; avoid in fresh grief.
not_for: recent bereavement
pregnancy or child loss
speaks_to: identity tied to job or status

mbh.14.13.6.context: After the war Yudhishthira is crushed by grief and guilt and wants to renounce the throne. In chapters 11 to 13 Krishna answers him: the enemies were outside, but now the war is inside, with his own mind; what binds is the sense of 'mine', not owning things; and desire itself (in the Kama Gita) boasts that it survives every weapon used against it. Krishna urges him to rule and perform the horse sacrifice rather than retreat to the forest. These verses follow directly on 'mama is death': Krishna contrasts a king without possessiveness and a forest hermit who still clings.
mbh.14.13.6.core_teaching: Freedom is measured by possessiveness, not possessions: a ruler of the whole world who does not cling is free, while a forest hermit who clings to his few things is in death's jaws.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: what matters the world to one who rules the whole earth yet is not attached to it; but a forest recluse living on roots who craves worldly things may be said to bear death in his mouth.

commentaries.who: Bibek Debroy, 'A Dirge for Desire' (Open magazine)
commentaries.gist: Debroy draws the same contrast: one who has conquered the world but has no sense of ownership is unbound, while a forest-dweller who clings to objects is in the jaws of death; inner attitude, not withdrawal, decides.

mbh.14.13.6.practical_reading: Used against the idea that spirituality requires quitting one's life: you can hold a job, home and wealth lightly, or cling to very little very tightly.
misreadings: Not a justification for accumulating wealth as long as one 'feels detached'.
Not a dismissal of renunciation.
not_for: people in poverty, for whom talk of 'ruling the earth' is remote
speaks_to: professionals wondering if success and spirituality conflict

mbh.14.32.12.context: In the Anugita, Krishna recounts a Brahmana's teaching to his wife. The Brahmana names three sets of inner foes (from goodness, passion and darkness) and cites old verses of King Ambarisha. Ambarisha says he has conquered many faults and all enemies, but one great fault, greed, remains; from it come desire, anxiety and rebirth. This verse is his conclusion.
mbh.14.32.12.core_teaching: Having seen greed clearly, restrain it with steadiness and seek rule over oneself; that is the only true kingdom, and the self rightly understood is its king.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation and Nilakantha note)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: subduing cupidity by intelligence, one should desire sovereignty in one's own soul; there is no other. Citing Nilakantha, he notes that the 'faults' Ambarisha subdued are attachment, greed and the like.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, Anugita (SBE 8, ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: Telang's version: restraining avarice by courage, one should wish for sovereignty in the self; this is sovereignty and there is no other, for the self properly understood is the sovereign.

mbh.14.32.12.practical_reading: Used as a reframe of ambition: the hardest and most worthwhile conquest is over one's own greed and cravings.
misreadings: Not a rejection of worldly responsibility; Ambarisha remained a king.
not_for: someone in financial distress, where 'greed' framing misfires
speaks_to: impulse spending and greed at work

mbh.14.52.7.context: After the Anugita, Krishna has Daruka yoke the chariot and they set out for Hastinapura. On the way Arjuna thanks him: through Krishna's grace the king has won, enemies are slain, and the Pandavas, with him as protector, crossed the Kuru ocean using him as their raft. He then praises Krishna as the soul of the universe.
mbh.14.52.7.core_teaching: Arjuna gratefully acknowledges that the Pandavas survived the war only because Krishna was their protector, the raft on which they crossed.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: through Krishna the Pandavas have a powerful protector; having obtained him for their raft, they have crossed the Kuru ocean. Arjuna then salutes him as soul and maker of the universe.

commentaries.who: BORI critical text (enjoylearningsanskrit translation)
commentaries.gist: The critical text has the two-line verse only; the extra line asking protection 'here and hereafter' is not there.

mbh.14.52.7.practical_reading: Used for gratitude after coming through a hard period: naming who or what carried you across.
misreadings: Not a claim that the war or its suffering was good.
cautions: The 'ocean' is a war in which countless people died; keep the gratitude framing, not triumph.
not_for: someone who did not come through (bereaved by the same crisis)
speaks_to: gratitude after recovering from illness or crisis

mbh.14.53.15.context: Returning to Dvaraka after the war, Krishna meets the ascetic Uttanka in the desert. Uttanka asks whether Krishna has established lasting brotherhood between the Kurus and Pandavas. Krishna says he tried hard but they would not be reconciled, so they destroyed one another, ignoring his counsel and Bhishma's and Vidura's. Uttanka, furious that Krishna did not force them to stop, threatens a curse; Krishna asks him to first hear his teaching on the self, and goes on to explain his nature and his repeated pleading with the Kauravas.
mbh.14.53.15.core_teaching: One can make every honest effort for peace, but cannot force others to accept it.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation (Asvamedha LIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's Krishna says he tried his utmost to bring the Kauravas to accord, failed, and so they all died; he adds that neither intellect nor strength can override what is ordained.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (BORI 14.53.19)
commentaries.gist: Later in the same reply Krishna repeats the point: in human form he pleaded with them piteously, but in their delusion they would not accept his beneficial words.

mbh.14.53.15.practical_reading: When a rift in the family or with a friend will not heal despite real effort, you can recognise that you did what you could; reconciliation needs both sides.
misreadings: Not 'give up after one attempt'; Krishna stresses sustained effort.
Not fatalism excusing inaction; the destiny line comes after effort.
cautions: The answer goes on to the total slaughter of both families, and Uttanka's anger at Krishna mirrors a reader's anger; acknowledge that anger rather than dismissing it.
not_for: someone who has not yet tried to repair a relationship and may use it as an excuse
speaks_to: guilt over a rift you could not repair

data_flags.attribution_note: Krishna to the sage Uttanka is correct, but the setting is out of order: when Krishna says this, Uttanka has only asked, hopefully, whether Krishna made peace between the cousins. Uttanka's rage and threat to curse come immediately after, in response to this answer.

mbh.14.66.15.context: Krishna returns to Hastinapura for the horse sacrifice. Uttara's son is born dead, struck in the womb by Ashvatthama's weapon. Kunti rushes to Krishna, praises him, and reminds him of his vow to revive the child. Krishna, by the power of his truthfulness, brings the infant back to life, and he is named Parikshit.
mbh.14.66.15.core_teaching: In the family's darkest moment Kunti declares Krishna their only refuge and foundation; the whole line now depends on him.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: choked with tears, Kunti tells Krishna that Devaki is honoured for bearing him, that he is their refuge and glory, and that the race depends on him; she asks him to revive the child as he vowed.

commentaries.who: Bhagavata Purana 1.8 (parallel episode, vedabase)
commentaries.gist: The Bhagavata places Kunti's famous prayers right after Krishna shields Uttara's unborn child: she recalls every danger he saved them from and says the Pandavas have no other protector.

mbh.14.66.15.practical_reading: Used as a prayer of total dependence in crisis, when all human resources have run out.
misreadings: Not a promise that prayer will reverse a death (our misuse note is right).
cautions: The scene is a stillbirth. Keep this card away from pregnancy loss, stillbirth, infant loss and infertility, as our note says.
Even outside those contexts, the story's miracle can make readers whose loved ones were not saved feel abandoned.
not_for: pregnancy loss, stillbirth, infant or child loss
bereavement after a loved one was not saved
speaks_to: family emergencies where one turns to prayer
devotional readers seeking words of refuge

mbh.14.92.69.context: At the close of Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice a mongoose, half its body golden, declares the great rite worth less than a poor gleaner's gift. During a famine in Kurukshetra a brahmin living by gleaning, with his wife, son and daughter-in-law, had at last gathered a little barley flour when a hungry guest arrived; each gave his own share. The guest revealed himself as Dharma and praised the gift; the mongoose, rolling in the spilt flour, turned half gold. Dharma speaks this as he praises the gift: because hunger destroys judgement and steadiness, the one who conquers hunger to give conquers heaven.
mbh.14.92.69.core_teaching: Hunger drives out judgement, a sense of right and steadiness; that is why giving while starving is so great a feat.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: hunger destroys wisdom and drives off righteous understanding, and one overwhelmed by it casts off fortitude; therefore one who conquers hunger conquers heaven.

commentaries.who: Devdutt Pattanaik on the half-golden mongoose
commentaries.gist: Pattanaik reads the tale as measuring generosity by what it costs the giver: the poor man gave his last meal, feeling another's hunger while rising above his own.

mbh.14.92.69.practical_reading: Read today as both admiration for those who give in hardship and realism about what deprivation does to anyone's choices.
misreadings: Not a claim that poor people are less moral.
Not a demand that people in need give away what they have.
cautions: Readers facing food insecurity may feel judged; use the compassionate reading.
not_for: eating disorders or fasting contexts
readers in acute food insecurity, if framed as moral test

mbh.14.92.75.context: At the close of Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice a mongoose, half its body golden, declares the great rite worth less than a poor gleaner's gift. During a famine in Kurukshetra a brahmin living by gleaning, with his wife, son and daughter-in-law, had at last gathered a little barley flour when a hungry guest arrived; each gave his own share. The guest revealed himself as Dharma and praised the gift; the mongoose, rolling in the spilt flour, turned half gold. Dharma says heaven's door is seen by those who give according to their ability, then states this rule of proportion.
mbh.14.92.75.core_teaching: Giving is measured by proportion to one's means: a hundred from a thousand, ten from a hundred, and a little water from one who has nothing, all bear equal merit.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one who gives a hundred having a thousand, ten having a hundred, or a handful of water having nothing, all earn equal merit; Rantideva, stripped of wealth, reached heaven by a little water given with a pure heart.

commentaries.who: Devdutt Pattanaik on the half-golden mongoose
commentaries.gist: Pattanaik: the king's ritual charity was vast in wealth but small in proportion to what he had, while the beggar's last meal was everything; generosity is measured by its cost to the giver.

mbh.14.92.75.practical_reading: Encourages people with little to give without embarrassment, and people with much to measure their giving honestly against their means.
misreadings: Not a claim that large donations are worthless.
not_for: someone pressured to give beyond their means
speaks_to: people who feel their small contribution doesn't count
students and young earners starting to give

mbh.14.92.77.context: At the close of Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice a mongoose, half its body golden, declares the great rite worth less than a poor gleaner's gift. During a famine in Kurukshetra a brahmin living by gleaning, with his wife, son and daughter-in-law, had at last gathered a little barley flour when a hungry guest arrived; each gave his own share. The guest revealed himself as Dharma and praised the gift; the mongoose, rolling in the spilt flour, turned half gold. After the Rantideva example, Dharma states this principle and adds the case of King Nriga, who gave thousands of cows but fell into hell for giving one that was not his.
mbh.14.92.77.core_teaching: Dharma is pleased not by grand gifts but by small ones that were honestly earned and sincerely given.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli (translation)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the deity of righteousness is never gratified so much by costly gifts as by things of little value, lawfully acquired and given with devotion and faith; Nriga fell for giving one cow not his own.

commentaries.who: Pradip Bhattacharya, essay on the Ashvamedha Parva
commentaries.gist: Bhattacharya reads the mongoose episode as the epic's verdict on the great sacrifice: lavish gifts do not equal one poor man's offering to a guest who was Dharma himself, and no number of rituals makes one virtuous.

mbh.14.92.77.practical_reading: Used to stress the ethics of giving: clean money and a sincere heart matter more than the size or publicity of a donation.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of large-scale philanthropy.

mbh.3.12.134.context: Draupadi has just recounted the dice hall, being dragged by the hair while menstruating, and every earlier plot against the Pandavas, and has wept that she has no husbands, sons, kin, or even Krishna. Krishna replies that the wives of those she is angry with will weep as she does, that he will do all he can for the Pandavas, and that she will be queen again; this cosmic oath seals it. Arjuna confirms it, and Dhrishtadyumna names who will kill whom.
mbh.3.12.134.core_teaching: Krishna gives his unbreakable word that the wrong done to Draupadi will be answered. The impossibilities listed stress that the cosmos would break before his promise does.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XII
commentaries.gist: In Ganguli the oath directly follows the promise that her tormentors' wives will weep over their slain husbands and that she will be a queen again, so the vow is about justice through war.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.13.117 matches our Sanskrit. The same second line reappears in a starred passage of Udyoga 5.80, where Krishna renews his word to Draupadi before his peace mission.

mbh.3.12.134.practical_reading: Teachers often take it as an image of a promise that holds when everything else gives way; for a reader it can say that someone sees the wrong done to them and will not forget it.
misreadings: Not a call to personal revenge.
Not a promise that a particular outcome will arrive on our timetable.
cautions: In the text the vow foretells killing; keep a reading on 'being seen and stood by', as our misuse note says.
Context includes sexual humiliation and assault on Draupadi; avoid graphic retelling for a distressed reader.
not_for: someone nursing a wish for vengeance
a reader who wants a guarantee of a specific result
speaks_to: feeling abandoned after being publicly wronged
needing to hear that a promise to you will be kept

mbh.3.12.46.context: Soon after the dice game, Krishna and allied kings visit the exiled Pandavas in the Kamyaka forest. Krishna erupts in anger and promises the deaths of Duryodhana, Karna and Shakuni; Arjuna soothes him by reciting Krishna's divine deeds. Krishna answers with this declaration of mutual belonging and adds that the two of them are the ancient sages Nara and Narayana. Draupadi then comes forward and pours out her grief to him.
mbh.3.12.46.core_teaching: Krishna declares a complete, two-way bond with Arjuna: whatever belongs to one belongs to the other, and their friends and enemies are shared. The epic grounds this in their identity as Nara and Narayana rather than in mere friendship.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it as a pledge of mutual possession and shared friends and foes, then moves straight into the Nara-Narayana identity, so the bond reads as metaphysical kinship, not only affection.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: The verse stands unchanged in the constituted text at 3.13.38, followed by the Nara-Narayana verse. A near-identical line recurs in Udyoga 5.89.28, where Krishna says whoever hates the Pandavas hates him.

mbh.3.12.46.practical_reading: Read devotionally, it says the one who turns to God is held as God's own, not as a stranger. In a human key it describes the kind of friendship where your people become my people.
misreadings: Not a license to treat one's personal opponents as God's enemies; it was spoken while Krishna's anger at the Kauravas was being calmed.
Not a general promise about any human friendship; it rests on the special Nara-Narayana identity.
cautions: 'Whoever hates you hates me' can feed us-versus-them thinking for a reader in an active conflict.
not_for: someone in a feud seeking divine endorsement against another person
speaks_to: a deep friendship or partnership that feels like kinship

mbh.3.133.13.context: Indra as a hawk and Agni as a dove test King Ushinara at his sacrifice. The dove takes refuge on the king's thigh; the hawk claims it as his ordained food and argues that saving one bird will starve him and his family, so the king must weigh the duties and choose the weightier. The king replies that abandoning a refugee is the gravest wrong, offers anything else, and finally puts his own flesh on the scale until he climbs on himself; the gods reveal themselves and bless him.
mbh.3.133.13.core_teaching: When duties conflict, weigh them and follow the one that carries more weight. The story shows the principle is sound but can be used to tempt; the king honours it by paying the cost himself rather than giving up the one who trusted him.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CXXXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli gives the hawk's case: a virtue that blocks another virtue is not virtue; compare opposing duties and adopt the preponderant. The king suspects the hawk is Garuda and still refuses to abandon a refugee.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.131.10-12 (hawk) and 3.130.17-19 name the king Ushinara; Shibi's own telling is at 3.197.

commentaries.who: Adam Bowles, 'The failure of dharma', Seminar 608 (2010)
commentaries.gist: Argues the epic's leitmotif is the subtlety of dharma, shown through dilemmas in which each option conforms to some dharmic norm; this hawk-and-dove dilemma fits that pattern.

mbh.3.133.13.practical_reading: Faced with two real obligations, slow down and weigh them honestly rather than grabbing the convenient one; be wary when the 'greater good' happens to cost someone else everything.
misreadings: Not a license to sacrifice a vulnerable person for the many; the king refuses exactly that.
The speaker uses the principle to tempt; do not present it as the story's moral without the king's answer.
cautions: The story ends with the king cutting his own flesh; avoid literal self-sacrifice imagery for a reader at risk of self-harm.
not_for: someone being pressured to give up a dependent or a promise 'for the greater good'
speaks_to: a hard choice between two obligations (family vs work, two people who need you)
a promise to someone who trusted you

data_flags.attribution_note: Speaker correct (the hawk, Indra in disguise), but the listener in this passage is King Ushinara, not Shibi (BORI 3.130.17-19, 3.131.22, 26; Ganguli CXXX-CXXXI). The tale is told by the sage Lomasha to Yudhishthira at the Jala and Upajala rivers. The version with Shibi Aushinara...

mbh.3.135.10.context: Ashtavakra, born bent in eight places by his father Kahoda's curse, learns in his twelfth year that Kahoda was defeated in debate by Bandin at King Janaka's court and made to enter the water. With his uncle Shvetaketu he goes to Janaka's sacrifice; the gatekeeper bars boys and asks him to recite a hard verse. Ashtavakra answers that growth is not measured by bodily size, then that grey hair does not make an elder, and is admitted.
mbh.3.135.10.core_teaching: Maturity is shown by what a person produces in wisdom and conduct, not by age or size.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CXXXIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it: true growth cannot be inferred from bodily development, as knots on the Salmali do not show its age; a slender, short tree bearing fruit is full-grown, a fruitless one is not.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.133.9, a trishtubh verse in the same wording; the gatekeeper's challenge and Ashtavakra's replies run through 3.133.

mbh.3.135.10.practical_reading: Judge people, including yourself, by the fruit of their lives rather than by age, size or title.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of elders; Ashtavakra himself honours learning.
cautions: Mild. The frame story involves a father's curse and apparent drowning.
not_for: a reader using it to wave away experienced advice
speaks_to: someone who feels small next to bigger peers

mbh.3.135.12.context: The gatekeeper has said boys learn from the old and only grow wise with time. Ashtavakra replies that grey hair does not make an elder; the gods count the young who understand as elders; sages measure greatness by learning, not years, wealth or kin. He then asks to be announced to Janaka and goes on to defeat Bandin, which frees his father.
mbh.3.135.12.core_teaching: Seniority belongs to understanding, not to age; a young person who knows is an elder in the eyes of the gods.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CXXXIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one is not old because his head is grey; the gods count as old the child who has knowledge; sages do not measure merit by years, grey hair, wealth or friends.

commentaries.who: Medhatithi on the parallel Manusmriti 2.156 (tr. Ganganath Jha)
commentaries.gist: Explains that grey hair alone does not make one venerable; the young person who keeps studying is called an elder by the gods, and since the gods know all, the verse is praise of the learner.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.133.11 matches our Sanskrit.

mbh.3.135.12.practical_reading: Listen to wisdom wherever it comes from, including from people much younger than you; age earns respect, but understanding earns authority.
misreadings: Not contempt for the old; it denies that age alone confers wisdom.
cautions: None significant.
not_for: a reader using it to justify disrespect toward elders
speaks_to: a young person whose ideas are dismissed
an older person learning from the young

mbh.3.152.27.context: Searching for the Saugandhika flower for Draupadi, Bhima finds an old monkey blocking his path and cannot lift its tail; it is his brother Hanuman, who shows his giant form and teaches about the yugas and the duties of the orders. Sending him on, Hanuman warns him not to take the flowers by force from Kubera's garden, to keep to his own dharma, and adds this verse; next he says that wrong sometimes passes under the name of right and right under the name of wrong.
mbh.3.152.27.core_teaching: Knowing what is right needs study and the company of experienced elders; brilliance alone is not enough.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CXLIX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: without knowing duties and serving the old, even someone like Brihaspati cannot understand profit and religion; one must discriminate cases where vice passes as virtue and virtue as vice.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.149.26. The apparatus shows a near-identical line in a Southern insertion in Vidura's counsel (Udyoga 5.39), about learning that is not understood without serving elders.

mbh.3.152.27.practical_reading: Before acting on a strong conviction, test it with people who have lived through similar choices.
misreadings: Not blind deference to anyone older.
cautions: None significant; context is a gentle teaching after humbling Bhima's pride.
not_for: situations where 'elders' are the source of harm
speaks_to: a capable person tempted to go it alone
after being humbled by a mistake

mbh.3.183.30.context: Yudhishthira, impressed by the serpent's learning, asks how delusion could overtake one so wise who once lived in heaven. Nahusha answers with this verse and confesses that the intoxication of power made him fall; now awakened, he is teaching Yudhishthira. He then tells how he made sages carry his palanquin and touched Agastya with his foot.
mbh.3.183.30.core_teaching: Success can cloud the judgement even of the wise and brave, and the one living in comfort does not notice it happening.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CLXXX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: prosperity intoxicates even the wise and valiant, and those in luxury lose their reason; Nahusha says he too fell this way and, restored to awareness, now instructs Yudhishthira.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.178.30. A Southern insertion (BORI Appendix I.20) expands it: pride sits in power as surely as heat in fire, and an eye darkened by power regains clarity only after the salve of a fall.

mbh.3.183.30.practical_reading: Good times are exactly when to check yourself: ask trusted people whether success has changed how you treat others.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of success itself.
cautions: None significant.
not_for: someone in poverty or failure, for whom it may sound like 'better that you didn't succeed'
speaks_to: after a fall from a high position

mbh.3.183.33.context: Nahusha's confession: ruling heaven in Indra's place, he travelled in a celestial car, took tribute from sages, gods and every being, and drained the power of anyone he looked at.
