A thousand brahmarshis carried his palanquin; he touched Agastya with his foot and was cursed to fall as a serpent. Agastya told him Yudhishthira would release him.
mbh.3.183.33.core_teaching: Pride at the height of power made Nahusha blind to others, and that blindness caused his fall.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CLXXX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: revelling in pride in his celestial car he thought of nothing else, exacted tribute from all three worlds, had Brahmarshis draw his car, and was cursed when his foot touched Agastya.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.178.33-38 gives the confession in the same order; Udyoga 5.11-17 tells the fuller story of Nahusha's rise and fall.

mbh.3.183.33.practical_reading: Notice when you stop thinking about the people who carry you; that loss of attention is an early sign of pride.
misreadings: Not a story about divine punishment for success; the fault is contempt for others.
cautions: None significant.
not_for: a reader already crushed by shame who needs mercy more than a mirror
speaks_to: someone reflecting honestly on past arrogance

mbh.3.183.43.context: Nahusha has just described how Agastya's curse and his promise of release showed him the power of tapas and of true brahmanhood. He concludes that truth, self-control, austerity, yoga, harmlessness and constant giving (or knowledge) are what bring people to their goal, not birth or family. He then releases Bhima and rises to heaven.
mbh.3.183.43.core_teaching: What brings a person to the highest good is cultivated character and practice, not birth or family.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CLXXX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: truth, charity, self-restraint, penance, harmlessness and constancy in virtue, not race or family connections, are the means by which a man must always secure salvation.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.178.43 reads dānanityatā and sadā puṃsām. Earlier in the same dialogue (3.177) Yudhishthira argues a Brahmin is known by conduct, not birth.

mbh.3.183.43.practical_reading: What you practise every day, honesty, restraint, kindness, generosity, shapes you more than where you come from.
misreadings: Do not present the epic as uniformly anti-caste; the same dialogue also says mixing has made birth hard to determine.
cautions: Caste is a sensitive topic; keep the focus on conduct over birth without making broad historical claims.
not_for: none in particular
speaks_to: someone judged by background or family

mbh.3.183.5.context: The python holding Bhima is King Nahusha, cursed by Agastya. He agrees to free Bhima if Yudhishthira answers his questions; after an exchange on who is a Brahmin, Yudhishthira in turn asks him what leads to the highest state. Nahusha names giving to the worthy, kind speech, truth and harmlessness; asked which weighs more, he answers that it depends on the weight of the task at hand.
mbh.3.183.5.core_teaching: No single virtue always outranks another; their relative weight depends on what the situation demands.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CLXXX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli gives the answer to the snake: the relative merit of truth, charity, kind speech and harmlessness is measured by their gravity in effect; sometimes truth, sometimes giving, is the more praiseworthy.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.178.3-7: Yudhishthira asks, the serpent (sarpa uvāca) answers that weight depends on the task (kāryagarīyastva, kāryāpekṣam).

mbh.3.183.5.practical_reading: When two good values pull apart, such as honesty and kindness, ask which one the situation actually needs most rather than applying a fixed rule.
misreadings: Not moral relativism; all four virtues remain binding, only their ranking shifts.
cautions: None significant.
not_for: someone looking for permission to lie
speaks_to: ethical dilemmas at work or home
choosing between telling a hard truth and being generous

data_flags.attribution_note: Wrong speaker. Yudhishthira asks the question (3.178.3: which is weightier, giving or truth, harmlessness or kind speech?) and the serpent Nahusha answers with this verse. Fix: speaker 'Nahusha (as the serpent)', listener 'Yudhishthira'. Our_note ('Yudhishthira on the relative weight of virtues') should also be corrected.

mbh.3.192.43.context: Markandeya tells the Pandavas of the end of an age: the world became one ocean and he wandered alone, exhausted, finding no rest, until he saw a radiant child on a banyan bough. The child drew him in through his mouth, and inside he saw all the worlds intact; then he was released. The child, revealing himself as Narayana, explains that he showed the universe because he knew Markandeya's distress at seeing everything destroyed.
mbh.3.192.43.core_teaching: God notices the distress of the one who feels alone in a destroyed world and answers it by showing that nothing is truly lost; all is held within him.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CLXXXVIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: seeing one expanse of water and all creatures destroyed, Markandeya was afflicted with melancholy; knowing this, the Lord showed him the universe within his body, then brought him out.

commentaries.who: Bhagavata Purana 12.9 (Bhaktivedanta VedaBase), parallel telling
commentaries.gist: The Bhagavata version has Markandeya ask to see the Lord's illusory power; he is drawn in by the infant's breath, sees the universe intact, and feels lamentation and bewilderment before the vision ends.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.187.42; Markandeya's vision runs through 3.186-187.

mbh.3.192.43.practical_reading: When everything familiar seems swept away, the story offers the image of being seen in one's fear and shown that what matters is still held somewhere.
misreadings: Not a promise that what was lost will be restored in the same form.
cautions: Imagery of total destruction; can resonate with catastrophic loss (disaster, death of many). Keep the comfort in 'you were seen', not in 'it will all come back'.
not_for: fresh bereavement where 'all is preserved' may sound dismissive
speaks_to: feeling utterly alone in a crisis

mbh.3.192.56.context: Ending his account, Markandeya tells the Pandavas that the child he saw is Krishna of the Vrishnis, sitting among them; seeing him, the sage's memory of the vision returns. He calls Krishna the father and mother of all beings and urges them to seek his refuge. The Pandavas, the twins and Draupadi bow to Krishna, who comforts them with sweet words.
mbh.3.192.56.core_teaching: Krishna is parent to every being and the proper refuge; the sage invites the Pandavas to take shelter in him.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CLXXXVIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: Markandeya says this Madhava is father and mother of all creatures and bids the Kuru bulls seek his refuge; they and Draupadi bow down and Krishna consoles them.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.187.52-55 identifies the child with Krishna and ends with this call to refuge.

mbh.3.192.56.practical_reading: For a devotional reader, it invites trust: the divine is as near and caring as a parent.
misreadings: Not a substitute for practical help or care.
cautions: Parent imagery can be painful for a reader with an absent or harmful parent; offer it as what a parent should be.
not_for: a non-devotional reader who wants practical guidance

mbh.3.210.44.context: The Brahmin ascetic Kaushika burns a crane with an angry look, is rebuked by a devoted housewife who reads his mind, and is sent to learn dharma from a meat-seller in Mithila. The Dharmavyadha receives him, explains that he follows his inherited trade honestly and serves his parents, and teaches the conduct of the good (śiṣṭācāra). In this stretch he lists rules of conduct: avoid falsehood, do good unasked, never abandon dharma from desire, anger or hatred, do not over-rejoice or over-grieve, and do not give up right conduct even in poverty.
mbh.3.210.44.core_teaching: Hold to what is right whatever passion pulls at you, and keep an even mind through pleasant and unpleasant events.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCVI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one should never cast off virtue from lust, wrath or malice, never joy immoderately at good fortune or grieve immoderately at bad, and never leave virtue when poverty comes.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, Karma Yoga, 'What is Duty?' (Complete Works vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: Retells the Vyadha story to argue that doing the duty of one's station wholeheartedly and without attachment to results leads to the highest realisation; no duty is impure.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.198.40-41; the whole chapter is the Vyadha's account of śiṣṭācāra.

mbh.3.210.44.practical_reading: Name the feeling that is pushing you to cut a corner (wanting, anger, resentment) and decide not to let it make the choice; likewise, ride highs and lows without being carried off.
misreadings: Not a call to suppress all emotion; it warns against over-reacting and against letting feelings override principle.
cautions: For someone in fresh grief, 'do not burn with distress' can sound like 'do not grieve'; avoid that framing.
not_for: fresh bereavement
speaks_to: holding steady through good and bad news

mbh.3.210.46.context: The Brahmin ascetic Kaushika burns a crane with an angry look, is rebuked by a devoted housewife who reads his mind, and is sent to learn dharma from a meat-seller in Mithila. The Dharmavyadha receives him, explains that he follows his inherited trade honestly and serves his parents, and teaches the conduct of the good (śiṣṭācāra). Here he says: whatever one judges beneficial, commit to it; do not return wrong for wrong; the one who wants to do evil destroys himself and only imitates the wicked.
mbh.3.210.46.core_teaching: Commit yourself to what is good and do not let another's wrong turn you into a wrongdoer.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCVI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: urge the soul toward what it judges beneficial; never return wrong for wrong but deal honestly even with those who wronged you; whoever wishes to sin slays himself.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, Karma Yoga, 'What is Duty?'
commentaries.gist: Presents the Vyadha as an ordinary householder whose honest, unattached work and care for his parents made him a teacher of a proud ascetic; goodness is shown in everyday conduct.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.198.42-43, same wording.

mbh.3.210.46.practical_reading: When someone treats you badly, protect yourself if needed but refuse to copy their behaviour; your conduct stays yours.
misreadings: Not a demand to stay silent or unprotected, as our misuse note says.
cautions: Do not use it to tell a victim to 'take the high road' instead of seeking safety or justice.
not_for: a reader being told not to report abuse

mbh.3.210.51.context: The Brahmin ascetic Kaushika burns a crane with an angry look, is rebuked by a devoted housewife who reads his mind, and is sent to learn dharma from a meat-seller in Mithila. The Dharmavyadha receives him, explains that he follows his inherited trade honestly and serves his parents, and teaches the conduct of the good (śiṣṭācāra). He has just said the sinful swell like bellows full of wind and that the inner self exposes the fool as sunlight reveals forms; then this contrast between the self-praising fool and the accomplished person who shines without adornment.
mbh.3.210.51.core_teaching: Real accomplishment shows itself; self-praise cannot make an empty person shine.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCVI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the fool cannot always shine by self-praise; the learned man, even without beauty, shows his lustre by not speaking ill of others or well of himself.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.198.46 matches our Sanskrit.

mbh.3.210.51.practical_reading: Spend energy on the work rather than on promoting yourself; good work becomes visible.
misreadings: Not a rule against ever presenting one's work; it targets empty self-praise.
cautions: Readers whose real work goes unnoticed may find 'it will shine anyway' untrue to their experience.
not_for: someone whose work is being actively overlooked through bias
speaks_to: impostor feelings next to loud peers

mbh.3.210.53.context: The Brahmin ascetic Kaushika burns a crane with an angry look, is rebuked by a devoted housewife who reads his mind, and is sent to learn dharma from a meat-seller in Mithila. The Dharmavyadha receives him, explains that he follows his inherited trade honestly and serves his parents, and teaches the conduct of the good (śiṣṭācāra). After warning that self-praise does not make anyone shine, he turns to how wrongdoing is undone: by remorse for the misdeed and the resolve not to repeat it, as with the expiations the scriptures prescribe.
mbh.3.210.53.core_teaching: Genuine remorse frees one from a past wrong, and a firm resolve not to repeat it frees one from the next.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCVI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: repentance washes off the sin, and the resolve never to repeat it saves one from future sin, much as scriptural expiations do; virtue drives off sins done in ignorance.

commentaries.who: Medhatithi on the parallel Manusmriti 11.230 (tr. Ganganath Jha)
commentaries.gist: Insists remorse and renunciation are two distinct acts: first the mental pain of repentance, then the resolve not to act so again; together with confession and expiation they purify.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.198.48; starred line *1012 adds a third release through resolving to practise dharma.

mbh.3.210.53.practical_reading: Owning a mistake has two parts: feeling its weight honestly, then deciding concretely what you will do differently.
misreadings: Not a teaching that guilt must be endless; remorse is meant to release, not to trap.
Not a substitute for making amends to the person harmed.
cautions: For a reader stuck in shame, stress release; avoid language that deepens guilt.
not_for: someone using regret to avoid repairing harm to others

mbh.3.210.59.context: The Brahmin ascetic Kaushika burns a crane with an angry look, is rebuked by a devoted housewife who reads his mind, and is sent to learn dharma from a meat-seller in Mithila. The Dharmavyadha receives him, explains that he follows his inherited trade honestly and serves his parents, and teaches the conduct of the good (śiṣṭācāra). Continuing on release from wrongdoing, he says the gods and the inner witness see every deed, that one who covers the faults of the good seeks salvation, and that a person who turns to doing good after sinning is cleansed like the moon coming out of clouds, or as sunrise dispels darkness.
mbh.3.210.59.core_teaching: Turning to good after wrongdoing frees a person from past wrongs; their goodness reappears like the moon from behind clouds.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCVI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one who seeks redemption after sin is purged and looks pure and bright like the moon emerged from clouds, washed as the rising sun dispels darkness.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.198.52; a similar image (the moon freed from darkness) recurs at 3.34.76.

mbh.3.210.59.practical_reading: A past mistake does not define you; steady good action now lets who you are show through again.
misreadings: Not a claim that consequences vanish or that harmed people must forget.
cautions: Hopeful and broadly safe; avoid implying instant absolution for serious harm to others.
not_for: a victim being told their abuser is now 'cleansed'

mbh.3.211.34.context: The Brahmin ascetic Kaushika burns a crane with an angry look, is rebuked by a devoted housewife who reads his mind, and is sent to learn dharma from a meat-seller in Mithila. The Dharmavyadha receives him, explains that he follows his inherited trade honestly and serves his parents, and teaches the conduct of the good (śiṣṭācāra). Near the end of his account of śiṣṭācāra, after listing many virtues of the good, he sums up their way in three steps, then adds freedom from malice, forbearance, peace, contentment and pleasant speech.
mbh.3.211.34.core_teaching: The way of the good comes down to three things: never betray or harm, give, and always speak the truth.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCVI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: these three constitute the perfect way of the virtuous: do no wrong to anybody, give alms, and always be truthful.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.198.89 reads anuttamam; the summary closes the Vyadha's long list of śiṣṭa virtues.

mbh.3.211.34.practical_reading: A simple daily check: did I harm or betray anyone, did I give something, did I tell the truth?
misreadings: Not a full ethics; the surrounding text lists many more virtues.
cautions: None significant.
not_for: none in particular

mbh.3.211.8.context: The Brahmin ascetic Kaushika burns a crane with an angry look, is rebuked by a devoted housewife who reads his mind, and is sent to learn dharma from a meat-seller in Mithila. The Dharmavyadha receives him, explains that he follows his inherited trade honestly and serves his parents, and teaches the conduct of the good (śiṣṭācāra). Kaushika asks how to recognise good conduct; the Vyadha lists sacrifice, giving, austerity, Veda and truth as present in it, then serving elders, truth, freedom from anger and giving, and then this chain of essences.
mbh.3.211.8.core_teaching: Truth is the core of sacred knowledge; self-restraint is the core of truth; renunciation is the core of self-restraint. All three show in the conduct of the good.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCVI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the essence of the Vedas is truth, of truth self-control, and of self-control abstention from worldly pleasures; these are seen in virtuous behaviour.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.198.62; a starred variant elsewhere has 'mokṣa' for tyāga; the verse belongs to the Vyadha's definition of śiṣṭācāra.

mbh.3.211.8.practical_reading: Honesty depends on self-control, and self-control on being willing to let go of what you want in the moment.
misreadings: Not a call to renounce the world; the speaker is a working householder.
cautions: None significant.
not_for: none in particular

mbh.3.213.43.context: The Brahmin ascetic Kaushika burns a crane with an angry look, is rebuked by a devoted housewife who reads his mind, and is sent to learn dharma from a meat-seller in Mithila. The Dharmavyadha receives him, explains that he follows his inherited trade honestly and serves his parents, and teaches the conduct of the good (śiṣṭācāra). In a later chapter Kaushika asks about the fruits of action and rebirth. The Vyadha explains that deeds follow the doer, that the sinful never reach the end of their wrongs, and that one should strive for virtue; the grateful, envy-free person who keeps to good reaps the four goods.
mbh.3.213.43.core_teaching: Freedom from envy and gratitude keep a person on the path of good action, which brings happiness, right living and prosperity.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCVIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: whoever, grateful and free from malice, strives to do good attains wealth, virtue, happiness and heaven; one must follow the standard of the good.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.200.40; part of the Vyadha's teaching on karma and rebirth in 3.200.

mbh.3.213.43.practical_reading: Gratitude and freedom from envy are practices: noticing what others have given you and not measuring yourself against them.
misreadings: Not a guarantee of material reward (prosperity-gospel reading).
cautions: Our 'line' can sound like 'be grateful and good things will come'; a reader in hardship may hear blame.
not_for: someone in poverty or loss who may hear 'you lack gratitude'
speaks_to: comparison and envy on social media

mbh.3.216.50.context: The Brahmin ascetic Kaushika burns a crane with an angry look, is rebuked by a devoted housewife who reads his mind, and is sent to learn dharma from a meat-seller in Mithila. The Dharmavyadha receives him, explains that he follows his inherited trade honestly and serves his parents, and teaches the conduct of the good (śiṣṭācāra). By this chapter the teaching has moved to the self, the senses and yoga: the Vyadha describes renunciation, self-restraint and equanimity as the way to knowledge, and in that setting urges harmlessness, friendliness toward all, and making no enemies in this life.
mbh.3.216.50.core_teaching: Harm no being and live in friendliness; this precious life is not to be spent in enmity.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCXII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: we must not harm any creature, must live in amity with all, and in this present existence must not avenge ourselves on anyone; self-abnegation, peace and equanimity lead to enlightenment.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.203.45; context is the Vyadha's teaching on yoga and renunciation in 3.203.

mbh.3.216.50.practical_reading: Life is short; let go of grudges that eat your time and energy, and lead with friendliness.
misreadings: Not a demand to befriend people who harm you; it forbids nursing enmity.
cautions: None significant.
not_for: a reader who needs to keep distance from an abuser
speaks_to: family estrangement one wants to soften

mbh.3.234.14.context: Krishna and Satyabhama visit the Pandavas in the forest. Satyabhama asks Draupadi privately what vow, charm, drug or spell keeps her five husbands devoted. Draupadi answers that she is asking about the practices of wicked women: a husband who learns his wife uses spells fears her like a snake in his bedroom, and the frightened have no peace. She then describes her own devoted service in detail.
mbh.3.234.14.core_teaching: Control by manipulation destroys peace, and without peace there is no happiness; love cannot be secured by tricks.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCXXXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: a husband who learns his wife uses incantations and drugs dreads her like a serpent in his chamber; how can the fearful have peace, or the peaceless happiness? A husband is never won by spells.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.222.12; the chapter (3.222) then lays out Draupadi's own conduct of service as the real 'charm'.

mbh.3.234.14.practical_reading: Relationships built on control or manipulation breed fear; trust grows where each person feels safe.
misreadings: Do not carry over the chapter's model of wifely service as the lesson; only this point travels, as our note says.
cautions: The surrounding chapter describes extreme self-effacing wifely service; a reader in a controlling marriage could hear it as an endorsement of submission.
not_for: a reader in a coercive relationship if the rest of the chapter is invoked
speaks_to: jealousy or control in a relationship
anxiety about keeping a partner's love

mbh.3.262.51.context: In the eleventh year of exile Yudhishthira broods over his brothers' suffering, which he blames on himself. Vyasa visits, praises giving and austerity, and tells of Mudgala, who refused heaven when told that merit runs out and the fall from heaven is bitter, and sought instead the state beyond grief. Vyasa then tells Yudhishthira not to grieve: joy and sorrow come in turn like a wheel, and after the thirteenth year he will regain his ancestral kingdom.
mbh.3.262.51.core_teaching: Joy and sorrow alternate in every life like spokes coming round on a wheel; neither state is permanent.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCLIX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: misery after happiness and happiness after misery revolve round a man like a wheel; Vyasa promises the kingdom after the thirteenth year and bids him let the fever of his heart go.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.247.44-47: Vyasa's consolation follows the Mudgala story, in which heaven itself is rejected because it too ends.

mbh.3.262.51.practical_reading: In a hard season, remember it is a season; in a good one, hold it lightly.
misreadings: Not a promise of a specific happy ending; the same wheel turns joy into sorrow too.
cautions: Can feel glib to someone in acute grief; it works better for prolonged hardship than for a fresh death.
not_for: fresh bereavement
someone currently happy who would hear only 'it won't last'
speaks_to: long hardship (job loss, illness, exile, a bad year)
fear that bad times will never end

mbh.3.264.10.context: Duryodhana, having pleased the irascible sage Durvasa, asks him to visit the Pandavas after Draupadi has eaten, when the sun-given vessel can no longer produce food. Durvasa arrives with ten thousand disciples and goes to bathe before the meal; Draupadi, with nothing to serve, prays to Krishna in her mind. Midway through the prayer she addresses him as the giver of boons, endless, the refuge of the refuge-less, the primordial Person beyond mind and breath.
mbh.3.264.10.core_teaching: God is the way for those who have no way, though beyond the grasp of mind and senses.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCLXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: she calls him supreme, infinite and giver of all good, asks him to be the refuge of the helpless, and calls him the primordial being beyond the reach of the mind.

mbh.3.264.10.practical_reading: Even when every path seems closed, prayer can open the mind to a way you had not seen; keep taking the practical steps you can.
misreadings: As our misuse note says: a way, not necessarily the one we wanted.
cautions: Textually late episode.
not_for: someone whose 'no way out' involves danger to life; point to real-world help first

mbh.3.264.11.context: Duryodhana, having pleased the irascible sage Durvasa, asks him to visit the Pandavas after Draupadi has eaten, when the sun-given vessel can no longer produce food. Durvasa arrives with ten thousand disciples and goes to bathe before the meal; Draupadi, with nothing to serve, prays to Krishna in her mind. This is the heart of the prayer, the act of taking refuge; it continues with a description of Krishna's form and a plea to rescue her as he did from Duhshasana. Krishna appears at once, leaving Rukmini's side.
mbh.3.264.11.core_teaching: Draupadi surrenders herself to Krishna's protection, trusting his tenderness toward those who seek refuge.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCLXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: she calls him ruler of all and lord of Brahma, seeks his protection, and asks him, ever kind to those who take refuge, to cherish her with his kindness.

mbh.3.264.11.practical_reading: Asking for help is itself an act of trust; it can be the first step out of panic.
misreadings: Not a promise of instant rescue.
cautions: Textually late episode.
not_for: a reader angry that their own prayers were not answered

mbh.3.264.40.context: Krishna has asked Draupadi for food, eaten a single particle of rice and greens from the vessel's rim, and wished that the Lord of the universe be satisfied; at the river the sages suddenly feel full, and Durvasa, fearing the Pandavas' power and their devotion to Hari, flees with them. When the Pandavas still worry the sages will return at night, Krishna appears and tells them this, adding that they need not fear and that the virtuous do not come to grief.
mbh.3.264.40.core_teaching: Krishna says he came quickly because Draupadi thought of him in their danger.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCLXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: knowing their danger from the wrathful Rishi and implored by Draupadi, Krishna came speedily; the sage has fled, and the virtuous never suffer; then he takes leave.

mbh.3.264.40.practical_reading: Being remembered and remembering others in their need matters; reaching out quickly to a friend in trouble is its human echo.
misreadings: As our misuse note says, not a promise that every prayer is answered the same day.
cautions: Textually late; also the claim that the virtuous never suffer sits badly with readers who are suffering.
not_for: someone in grief whose call for help was not answered

mbh.3.264.44.context: Relieved by Krishna's assurance, the Pandavas and Draupadi thank him with this image of drowning people reaching a boat, and bid him go in peace. He returns to Dvaraka and they continue their forest life; the narrator closes by saying this is how Duryodhana's plots were foiled.
mbh.3.264.44.core_teaching: With Krishna as protector, an impassable danger has been crossed, like the drowning who reach a boat.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCLXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: freed of their anxiety, they say they escaped the difficulty by his aid as the drowning reach shore by a boat, and bid him depart in peace.

mbh.3.264.44.practical_reading: After getting through a crisis, name who or what carried you through and say thank you.
misreadings: Not a promise that every crisis is crossed.
cautions: Textually late episode.
not_for: someone still in the middle of a crisis
speaks_to: gratitude for support in a crisis

mbh.3.264.8.context: Duryodhana, having pleased the irascible sage Durvasa, asks him to visit the Pandavas after Draupadi has eaten, when the sun-given vessel can no longer produce food. Durvasa arrives with ten thousand disciples and goes to bathe before the meal; Draupadi, with nothing to serve, prays to Krishna in her mind. This verse opens her prayer with a string of names; she goes on to ask him to protect her now as he once did from Duhshasana.
mbh.3.264.8.core_teaching: In a moment of helplessness Draupadi calls on Krishna by his names, appealing to him as the one who removes the distress of those who turn to him.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCLXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: Draupadi inwardly prays, invoking Krishna as son of Devaki and lord of the universe who dispels the difficulties of those who bow to him, and asks rescue as he once saved her from Dussasana.

mbh.3.264.8.practical_reading: When there is nothing left to do, naming what you trust and calling on it can steady the mind.
misreadings: As our misuse note says, not a promise that help comes in a set form or time.
cautions: Textually late; present it as a beloved traditional story rather than core epic text.
not_for: a reader whose prayers went unanswered in a loss, if framed as 'call and he comes'

mbh.3.28.27.context: In the forest Draupadi presses Yudhishthira to answer the Kauravas with force. She cites Prahlada: neither constant forgiveness nor constant force is right; the always-forgiving are trampled and the never-forgiving are feared like a snake in the house. He then lists the occasions for forgiveness, beginning with this one, and says force belongs to all others. Draupadi concludes that the Kauravas, who wrong them continually, are not a case for forgiveness.
mbh.3.28.27.core_teaching: Forgiveness has proper occasions; a past benefactor's earlier kindness should weigh in his favour when he offends. In the critical text this applies to offences that are not grave.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXVIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli follows the vulgate: a former benefactor is to be forgiven even a serious wrong, out of remembrance of his service. He frames the list as Prahlada's answer that might and forgiveness each have their time.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: The constituted text has 'garīyasi, 'not too grave', so the critical edition restricts this forgiveness to lesser offences. The next verses: deliberate offenders who plead ignorance are punished even for small faults; a first offence is forgiven, a second is not.

commentaries.who: Abhinav Agarwal, Swarajya column using Debroy's critical-edition translation
commentaries.gist: Summarises Prahlada's middle path: forgive a former benefactor if the crime is not too great, forgive stupidity and first offences, examine unintended ones, punish knowing offences; Draupadi says now is not the time for forgiveness.

mbh.3.28.27.practical_reading: When someone with a long record of kindness hurts you, their history can rightly count toward giving them another chance, as long as the hurt is not grave or repeated.
misreadings: Not a rule that benefactors, parents or mentors may do anything and must be forgiven.
Draupadi cites it to show forgiveness's limits, not to urge more forgiveness.
cautions: A reader hurt by a parent, partner or patron 'who did so much for you' may hear pressure to excuse serious harm; use the critical reading and the misuse note.
not_for: abuse or repeated serious harm by a caregiver or benefactor
coercive relationships where past help is used as leverage
speaks_to: a falling-out with an old friend, mentor or relative after a hurtful act
deciding whether to give a second chance

data_flags.translation_note: Our translation ('even badly') follows the vulgate reading aparādhe garīyasi, which Ganguli also renders as a grave wrong. The BORI critical text reads aparādhe 'garīyasi, i.e. 'when the offence is NOT grave'. Debroy's critical-edition rendering (as quoted in Swarajya) likewise limits it to crimes 'not...

mbh.3.28.28.context: Second item in Prahlada's list of times for forgiveness, quoted by Draupadi. Immediately after it he says that those who offend knowingly and then claim it was unintended should be punished even for a small offence; a first offence is forgiven, a second punished. Draupadi uses the list to argue that the Kauravas fall outside it.
mbh.3.28.28.core_teaching: Wrongs born of ignorance or poor judgement deserve forgiveness, because good sense is not easy for anyone to have at all times. Deliberate wrongs dressed up as mistakes do not qualify.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXVIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it as forgiving offenders who acted from ignorance and folly, since wisdom is hard to come by, and immediately contrasts those who offend knowingly and then plead ignorance, who are not to be pardoned.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Same sense in the constituted text 3.29.26; the following verses 27-29 set the limit (knowing offenders punished, a second offence punished, unintended acts forgiven only after careful inquiry).

commentaries.who: Abhinav Agarwal, Swarajya column using Debroy's critical-edition translation
commentaries.gist: Notes Prahlada's reason: learning is not easily available to people, so offences from stupidity are forgiven, while offences done with full knowledge are punished as crookedness.

mbh.3.28.28.practical_reading: Before judging a hurt, ask whether it came from carelessness or ignorance; such mistakes can be met with patience, especially from the young or inexperienced.
misreadings: Not a reason to excuse someone who keeps 'not knowing' after being told.
cautions: Pair with the misuse note: one mistake is different from a pattern of harm.
not_for: repeated, knowing harm presented as 'I didn't mean it'
speaks_to: irritation at someone's clumsy or thoughtless hurt
parents, teachers or managers dealing with others' mistakes

mbh.3.28.6.context: In the forest, Draupadi argues that Yudhishthira's endless patience with the Kauravas is wrong, and quotes Prahlada's answer to Bali. Prahlada lists the harms of always forgiving (servants and strangers disregard you, and wrongdoers grow bold) and of never forgiving (you are hated and lose friends), then gives the times for forgiveness: a past benefactor, an offence from ignorance, a first offence; a deliberate or repeated wrong should be met with firmness. Draupadi concludes it is time to act; in the next section Yudhishthira replies at length that anger destroys and forgiveness is eternal virtue.
mbh.3.28.6.core_teaching: Neither force nor forgiveness is right in every case; wisdom is knowing which the situation calls for.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation (Vana XXVIII)
commentaries.gist: Prahlada says neither might nor forgiveness is always good, then lists when to pardon (a past benefactor, an error of ignorance, a first offence) and when to be firm (deliberate or repeated wrongs), weighing time, place and strength.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli, Vana XXIX)
commentaries.gist: Yudhishthira answers Draupadi that anger is the root of ruin, that whoever does not answer anger with anger heals both parties, and that forgiveness and gentleness are eternal virtue.

mbh.3.28.6.practical_reading: Used to say that letting things go is not always kindness: decide each time whether this moment needs forgiveness or a firm line.
misreadings: Not a licence for revenge; Prahlada lists the harms of the never-forgiving person too.
Not a rule that you must forgive everything to be good.
cautions: Draupadi uses the verse to argue for war; the reading should stay with everyday boundaries.
Prahlada's examples include harsh punishment of servants; do not import them.
not_for: someone wanting justification for retaliation
speaks_to: deciding whether to let something go
being taken for granted because you always forgive
setting boundaries after being passed over

mbh.3.29.12.context: Part of Yudhishthira's case against anger. Right after this verse he adds that a weak man who flares up against a stronger persecutor destroys himself, and that the wise man who does not let persecution rouse his anger rejoices hereafter, having passed over his persecutor with indifference.
mbh.3.29.12.core_teaching: Not answering anger with anger protects both people; the one who stays calm acts like a doctor to both.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXIX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one who does not react against an enraged man saves himself and others from great fear and is the physician of both; the passage then advises the weak to suppress anger toward the strong.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.30.9 matches (paraṃ, 'the other'). The following verses about the weak man and the persecutor are also in the critical text.

mbh.3.29.12.practical_reading: In a heated exchange, the person who refuses to escalate often ends the fight for both; calm can be a form of care.
misreadings: Not an instruction to stay with an abusive person and absorb their rage.
cautions: The surrounding verses tell a weak person persecuted by a stronger one to swallow their anger; this can harm a reader in an abusive or unsafe situation. Keep the misuse note.
not_for: a reader in an abusive relationship
workplace harassment
speaks_to: arguments with a partner, parent or colleague that keep escalating
someone who wants to be the calmer person

mbh.3.29.20.context: Draupadi has argued that a king without tejas (fiery energy) is despised. Yudhishthira redefines tejas: the wise do not count outward wrath as strength; the truly tejasvin is the one who restrains anger as it arises. He adds that the ignorant mistake anger for energy.
mbh.3.29.20.core_teaching: Real strength is mastering anger with insight the moment it arises, not displaying it.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXIX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders tejas as force of character: the learned credit it to one who suppresses risen wrath by wisdom, and he adds that the ignorant mistake anger for energy.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.30.17 has the same sense; the chapter is Yudhishthira's sustained answer to Draupadi's praise of tejas in 3.29.

mbh.3.29.20.practical_reading: The moment anger flares is the moment that tests strength; noticing it and steadying it is the strong act.
misreadings: Not a claim that feeling anger is weakness; the point is what one does with it.
cautions: One side of a debate; Draupadi and Bhima reply, and the epic does not simply endorse Yudhishthira.
not_for: a reader being told their justified anger is a character flaw
speaks_to: a leader or parent who wants to model calm strength

mbh.3.29.28.context: Yudhishthira argues that if the injured always returned injury and the punished always punished back, people would destroy one another and even birth would fail; the world continues only because some are as forgiving as the earth. He goes on to say one should forgive every injury, then quotes Kashyapa's verses on kshama.
mbh.3.29.28.core_teaching: Peace among people depends on some who absorb injury without retaliating; quarrels grow from anger and end through forbearance.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXIX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it within a chain: if injury were always returned, fathers, sons and spouses would slay each other and creatures could not be born; the earth-like forgiving keep life going.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.30.25 matches; 3.30.31 restates that creatures live because forgiving people like the earth exist.

mbh.3.29.28.practical_reading: Someone has to be the first to stop returning the hurt; in families and friendships that choice is often what keeps the relationship alive.
misreadings: Not a demand that one person in a relationship absorb all the harm.
cautions: The same speech says one should forgive under every injury, which Prahlada's limits in 3.28 contradict; do not present it as the epic's final word.
not_for: a reader in an abusive or exploitative relationship

mbh.3.29.40.context: Having argued that forgiveness keeps the world alive, Yudhishthira quotes Kashyapa's gatha: forgiveness is dharma, sacrifice, the Vedas, Brahman, truth, austerity, purity, and what upholds the world; the forgiving reach the highest worlds. He ends by urging Draupadi to let go of her anger, expecting Bhishma, Krishna, Vidura and others to press Dhritarashtra for peace.
mbh.3.29.40.core_teaching: Praise poetry that identifies forbearance with every high value: truth, discipline, purity, the sacred itself. It is what holds the world together.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXIX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli presents it as Kashyapa's hymn: forgiveness is virtue, sacrifice, Veda, Brahma, truth, stored merit, asceticism and holiness, and the world is held together by it; the forgiving attain Brahma's world.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.30.36-39; c-pada reads kṣamayā coddhṛtaṃ jagat. 3.30.39 adds that kshama is the energy of the energetic.

commentaries.who: Abhinav Agarwal, Swarajya column using Debroy's critical-edition translation
commentaries.gist: Quotes these verses, then argues Yudhishthira's forgiveness here was partly calculation about Kaurava strength, and that Draupadi and Bhima saw it as confusion; Vyasa then sends Arjuna for weapons.

mbh.3.29.40.practical_reading: Forbearance is presented not as weakness but as a discipline as demanding as any austerity; choosing it can be an act of strength.
misreadings: Not an obligation to forgive someone who is still harming you.
Not the epic's conclusion: Draupadi and Bhima answer it, and Prahlada's limits stand.
cautions: High praise of forgiveness can feel like pressure to a reader who is not ready; keep the misuse note.
not_for: fresh betrayal or ongoing abuse
a reader being pressured by others to 'just forgive'
speaks_to: someone who has chosen to forgive and wants to understand that choice as strength

mbh.3.29.8.context: Yudhishthira's reply to Draupadi's call for force. He opens by saying anger is both what destroys people and, when mastered, what makes them prosper; then he lists what the angry do: they sin, kill even their teachers, insult their elders, and cannot tell what should be said. He concludes that one like him cannot indulge such a force.
mbh.3.29.8.core_teaching: Anger blinds judgement: under its grip a person loses the sense of limits in speech and action.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXIX
commentaries.gist: In Ganguli the line sits in a list of anger's effects: the angry man may kill the innocent, honour the guilty, insult superiors, even destroy himself. Yudhishthira uses it to explain why he keeps his own anger down.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.30.5 is the same. The chapter opens (3.30.1) with the claim that anger is both man's slayer and, if mastered, his prosperer.

commentaries.who: Abhinav Agarwal, Swarajya column using Debroy's critical-edition translation
commentaries.gist: Summarises Yudhishthira's counsel: an angry person cannot see the right course or his own limits; the author adds that this forbearance looks like calculation, and that Draupadi and Bhima reject it.

mbh.3.29.8.practical_reading: When anger rises, delay speaking and acting; words said in that state are the ones most often regretted.
misreadings: Not a rebuke of the wronged person's feelings; it is about what anger does to judgement.
cautions: Spoken to Draupadi, whose anger was just. Do not turn it on a reader who has been wronged and is angry about it.
not_for: a reader whose anger at real injustice is being dismissed by others
speaks_to: someone who regrets things said in a fight
a hot temper at work or home

mbh.3.297.7.context: Savitri knows, from Narada's prophecy, that her husband Satyavan will die on a set day. Four days before it she begins a severe three-night vow, standing without food. Her blind father-in-law, the exiled king Dyumatsena, is distressed at its harshness; she reassures him with this verse, and he replies that he cannot ask her to break it. On the fated day she goes into the forest with Satyavan, and later wins his life back from Yama.
mbh.3.297.7.core_teaching: A resolve begun with determination is carried through by that same determination.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation (Vana CCXCIV)
commentaries.gist: In Ganguli, Savitri asks her father-in-law not to grieve: she began the vow with steady resolve, and such resolve is what brings a vow to completion; he says he cannot ask her to give it up.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 3.280.5-7
commentaries.gist: Dyumatsena calls the three-night observance extremely severe; Savitri answers with this verse; he replies he is unable to say 'break your vow'.

mbh.3.297.7.practical_reading: When others worry you have taken on too much, your own steady resolve is both the reason you started and the thing that will carry you through.
misreadings: Not a case for ignoring health in extreme fasting or vows.
Not 'willpower conquers death'; Savitri's victory comes through wisdom and Yama's boons.
cautions: Background is foreknowledge of a husband's death; avoid for a reader facing a partner's terminal illness unless intended.
not_for: someone in an unhealthy restriction pattern (fasting, overwork)

mbh.3.298.24.context: Markandeya tells the exiled Yudhishthira the story of Savitri. On the day Satyavan is fated to die, he falls asleep in her lap in the forest; Yama himself comes, draws out his life and heads south, and Savitri follows. Each time Yama tells her to turn back, she speaks a few lines on dharma and on the good; pleased, he grants a boon each time, anything except Satyavan's life. This is her first speech: Yama has told her she has done all she owes her husband and must go back; she says she will go wherever he is taken, then claims the friendship of fellow-travellers before offering her teaching.
mbh.3.298.24.core_teaching: A short shared walk already creates a bond; on that basis Savitri earns the right to be heard even by Death.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCXCV
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the wise hold that walking only seven paces with someone makes a friendship; keeping in view the friendship she has thus formed with Yama, she asks him to listen.

commentaries.who: Abhinav Agarwal, 'On Conditions and Exceptions' (Swarajya column)
commentaries.gist: Reads her conduct as strategy: she never badgers Yama, keeps him pleased with wise words, and accepts each condition he sets, then turns his own promise into the means of winning Satyavan back.

commentaries.who: Scholarly readings summarised on Wikipedia ('Savitri and Satyavan')
commentaries.gist: Scholars broadly agree Savitri wins by speech rather than devotion alone; Brad Weiss argues that by speaking dharma to the god of dharma she leaves him no choice but to grant boons.

mbh.3.298.24.practical_reading: Before asking something hard of someone, find the real bond you share, however small, and speak from it rather than from demand.
misreadings: Not a manipulation trick; in the story it opens a sincere teaching on dharma.
cautions: The setting is a husband's death; the happy ending (he is restored) can sting for a reader who is widowed or recently bereaved.
not_for: recent loss of a spouse, if the restoration story is foregrounded

mbh.3.298.31.context: Markandeya tells the exiled Yudhishthira the story of Savitri. On the day Satyavan is fated to die, he falls asleep in her lap in the forest; Yama himself comes, draws out his life and heads south, and Savitri follows. Each time Yama tells her to turn back, she speaks a few lines on dharma and on the good; pleased, he grants a boon each time, anything except Satyavan's life. After her first boon (sight and strength for her blind, exiled father-in-law), Yama says she looks tired and should go back; she replies that there is no weariness beside her husband and offers this verse. Yama praises it and grants a second boon (the return of her father-in-law's kingdom).
mbh.3.298.31.core_teaching: Contact with good people always bears fruit, so seek it and stay in it; this is the classical root of satsaṅga.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCXCV
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: even one interview with the pious is highly desirable, friendship with them more so; intercourse with the virtuous is never fruitless, so one should live among the righteous.

commentaries.who: Yama's response in the text (BORI 3.281.30)
commentaries.gist: Yama calls her words agreeable to the mind and increasing the wisdom even of the wise, and grants a second boon: the narrative itself endorses the teaching.

commentaries.who: Abhinav Agarwal, Swarajya column
commentaries.gist: Notes that her line that communion with the virtuous is never fruitless earns the second boon, part of her pattern of pleasing Yama with wisdom rather than pleading.

mbh.3.298.31.practical_reading: Choose your company deliberately: one honest conversation with a person of good character can change your week, so seek such people out and spend time near them.
misreadings: Not snobbery about 'good' and 'bad' people; it is about the effect of character on those around it.
cautions: Death setting (see the story).
not_for: someone who has just been hurt by a person they trusted as 'good'

mbh.3.298.36.context: Markandeya tells the exiled Yudhishthira the story of Savitri. On the day Satyavan is fated to die, he falls asleep in her lap in the forest; Yama himself comes, draws out his life and heads south, and Savitri follows. Each time Yama tells her to turn back, she speaks a few lines on dharma and on the good; pleased, he grants a boon each time, anything except Satyavan's life. After the second boon she praises Yama: he restrains creatures by law, not by whim, which is why he is called Yama. She then states the eternal dharma of the good, adding in the next verse that the good show mercy even to enemies who come to them. Yama likens her words to water for the thirsty and grants a third boon (a hundred sons for her father).
mbh.3.298.36.core_teaching: Goodness has three parts: wish no being harm in act, mind or speech; help; and give.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCXCV
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the eternal duty of the good toward all creatures is never to injure them in thought, word or deed, but to love them and give them their due; the good show mercy even to foes seeking protection.

commentaries.who: Yama's response in the text (BORI 3.281.36)
commentaries.gist: Yama says her words are like water to someone thirsty and grants a third boon; the god of dharma accepts this as a true statement of dharma.

commentaries.who: Scholarly readings summarised on Wikipedia ('Savitri and Satyavan')
commentaries.gist: Scholars broadly agree Savitri wins by speech rather than devotion alone; Brad Weiss argues that by speaking dharma to the god of dharma she leaves him no choice but to grant boons.

mbh.3.298.36.practical_reading: Check all three channels today: an action, a thought and a sentence. Is any of them carrying ill will? Then add one act of help and one of giving.
misreadings: 'No ill will' is not the same as having no boundaries or never saying no.
cautions: Death setting (see the story).
not_for: someone currently being harmed, if read as 'you must not resent your abuser'
speaks_to: resentment you want to let go of

mbh.3.298.44.context: Markandeya tells the exiled Yudhishthira the story of Savitri. On the day Satyavan is fated to die, he falls asleep in her lap in the forest; Yama himself comes, draws out his life and heads south, and Savitri follows. Each time Yama tells her to turn back, she speaks a few lines on dharma and on the good; pleased, he grants a boon each time, anything except Satyavan's life. Told she has come far enough, she answers that her mind runs farther still, praises Yama as Vaivasvata and Dharmaraja, and says that people trust the good more than they trust even themselves; this verse explains why. Yama says he has never heard such words and grants a fourth boon (a hundred sons for her and Satyavan), which will force Satyavan's return.
mbh.3.298.44.core_teaching: Trust is not demanded; it grows from goodwill toward everyone, which is why people instinctively rely on the good.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCXCV
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one does not place even in oneself the confidence one places in the righteous; goodness of heart alone inspires the confidence of all creatures, which is why people rely on the righteous.

commentaries.who: Yama's response in the text (BORI 3.281.43)
commentaries.gist: Yama says he has heard nothing like it from anyone and offers a fourth boon, the one Savitri will use to win back her husband.

commentaries.who: Scholarly readings summarised on Wikipedia ('Savitri and Satyavan')
commentaries.gist: Scholars broadly agree Savitri wins by speech rather than devotion alone; Brad Weiss argues that by speaking dharma to the god of dharma she leaves him no choice but to grant boons.

mbh.3.298.44.practical_reading: If you want to be trusted at work or at home, look less at proving yourself and more at whether people can feel you want their good.
misreadings: Not a claim that good people are never betrayed or that trusting the good is always safe.
cautions: Death setting (see the story).
not_for: someone whose trust has just been betrayed by a 'good' person

mbh.3.298.50.context: Markandeya tells the exiled Yudhishthira the story of Savitri. On the day Satyavan is fated to die, he falls asleep in her lap in the forest; Yama himself comes, draws out his life and heads south, and Savitri follows. Each time Yama tells her to turn back, she speaks a few lines on dharma and on the good; pleased, he grants a boon each time, anything except Satyavan's life. Her last teaching, given after the fourth boon: the good are never cast down, their company is never fruitless, by truth they keep the sun moving and by austerity hold up the earth; knowing this, they act for others without looking for return, and kindness to them is never wasted. Yama then offers a boon beyond compare, and she asks for Satyavan's life.
mbh.3.298.50.core_teaching: The good help others as a settled way of life, not as a trade, and do not watch for repayment.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCXCV
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: knowing this to be the eternal practice of the good, the righteous keep doing good to others without expecting any benefit in return; a good office done to the virtuous is never wasted.

commentaries.who: Yama's response in the text (BORI 3.281.50)
commentaries.gist: Yama says the more she speaks such meaningful words on dharma, the greater his regard for her, and offers an incomparable boon; she asks for Satyavan's life.

commentaries.who: Abhinav Agarwal, Swarajya column
commentaries.gist: Observes that her early boons are all for others (her father-in-law, her father) before any for herself, and that her victory comes from judgement and timing as much as devotion.

mbh.3.298.50.practical_reading: Do one helpful thing today and notice whether you are quietly keeping score; let it go unrecorded.
misreadings: Not a demand to let others exploit you (our misuse note is right); it describes a disposition, not a duty to accept mistreatment.
cautions: Can feed self-neglect in people-pleasers or caregivers already giving too much.
not_for: someone in an exploitative relationship
burnt-out caregivers if read as 'give more'
speaks_to: parents and caregivers who feel unthanked

mbh.3.31.2.context: Draupadi has protested that the Ordainer treats people like puppets, rewarding the wicked and crushing the good. Yudhishthira calls her speech fine but faithless (nāstikya) and answers that he does not practise dharma for its fruit: he gives because giving is due and sacrifices because sacrifice is due. He goes on to warn against doubting dharma and insists that dharma does bear fruit, even if its workings are hidden.
mbh.3.31.2.core_teaching: Right action is done because it is right, not as a trade for reward. Yudhishthira still holds that dharma bears fruit; it is just not his motive.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: he acts from duty, not for fruits, following scripture and the conduct of the good; whoever wants dharma's fruits is a 'trader in virtue', and he then urges Draupadi not to doubt that virtue bears fruit.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical text the explicit 'trader in dharma' line is only a starred insertion (*0111); the constituted text makes the same point at 3.32.5: one who tries to milk dharma does not obtain its fruit.

mbh.3.31.2.practical_reading: Do the decent thing because it is decent, not because it will be noticed or repaid; this guards against bitterness when good acts go unrewarded.
misreadings: Not a claim that goodness has no results; Yudhishthira says it does.
Not a dismissal of Draupadi's suffering; it answers her theology, not her pain.
cautions: Said in reply to a woman in exile protesting injustice; avoid using it to tell a suffering reader that complaining is faithless.
not_for: a reader angry at real injustice who needs their protest heard first
speaks_to: someone whose good deeds go unthanked
burnout from doing right and seeing others prosper by doing wrong

mbh.3.314.112.context: At the end of the twelve years of exile, the Pandavas chase a deer that has carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks. Thirsty, the four younger brothers in turn drink from a lake despite a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's questions before drinking. The Yaksha asks whether Brahminhood comes from birth, conduct, study or learning. Yudhishthira answers that conduct alone decides it, that conduct must be guarded, and that scholars of bad conduct are fools; the next line says even a four-Veda scholar of bad conduct is lower than a Shudra. TEXTUAL CAUTION: this verse is NOT in the BORI critical text; it belongs to a long passage relegated to Appendix I, No. 32 (inserted after 3.297.61). It is in the vulgate and in Ganguli, and is famous, but an editor should not cite it as critical-edition text.
mbh.3.314.112.core_teaching: Learning is proved in conduct; study without practice does not make anyone wise.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCCXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: neither birth, study nor learning makes a Brahmin, only behaviour; those who study scripture, if addicted to wicked habits, are illiterate wretches; he only is learned who performs his duties.

mbh.3.314.112.practical_reading: Take one idea you have read or heard about recently and do it today; that is what makes it yours.
misreadings: Not anti-learning (our misuse note is right).
Not a general claim that all readers are fools.
cautions: Surrounding lines are framed in caste terms (Brahmin vs Shudra); keep any reading on conduct over credentials and avoid reproducing the caste comparison.
Textually late (appendix).
speaks_to: students and readers who feel stuck in theory

data_flags.translation_note: Overstated. The question is 'what makes one a Brahmin: birth, conduct, study or learning?' Yudhishthira says conduct (vṛtta). Ganguli reads the verse conditionally: readers and teachers of scripture, if given to vices (vyasanin), are fools; the learned one is the one who acts rightly. Ours...

mbh.3.314.114.context: At the end of the twelve years of exile, the Pandavas chase a deer that has carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks. Thirsty, the four younger brothers in turn drink from a lake despite a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's questions before drinking. Asked right after the Brahminhood question and just before the four famous questions (who is happy, what is the wonder, what is the path, what is the news). TEXTUAL CAUTION: this verse is NOT in the BORI critical text; it belongs to a long passage relegated to Appendix I, No. 32 (inserted after 3.297.61). It is in the vulgate and in Ganguli, and is famous, but an editor should not cite it as critical-edition text.
mbh.3.314.114.core_teaching: Small practical habits bring their own rewards: kind speech brings affection, reflection brings success, friendship brings ease.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCCXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: agreeable speech makes one agreeable to all, acting with judgment obtains what one seeks, many friends make life happy, and devotion to virtue wins a happy state hereafter.

mbh.3.314.114.practical_reading: Before one decision today, pause and think it through; and say one kind thing you would normally leave unsaid.
misreadings: Kind speech is not flattery; reflection is not endless hesitation.
cautions: Textually late (appendix).
not_for: someone who is isolated and cannot easily 'make many friends'

mbh.3.314.116.context: At the end of the twelve years of exile, the Pandavas chase a deer that has carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks. Thirsty, the four younger brothers in turn drink from a lake despite a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's questions before drinking. Near the end the Yaksha asks four questions at once and promises that if they are answered the dead brothers will live. This is the answer to the second, the 'wonder'. TEXTUAL CAUTION: this verse is NOT in the BORI critical text; it belongs to a long passage relegated to Appendix I, No. 32 (inserted after 3.297.61). It is in the vulgate and in Ganguli, and is famous, but an editor should not cite it as critical-edition text.
mbh.3.314.116.core_teaching: The strangest thing is our denial: we watch others die every day and still live as if we will not.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCCXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: countless creatures go to Yama's abode daily, yet those remaining believe themselves immortal; nothing could be more wonderful.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda, Jnana Yoga, 'Maya and Illusion' (Complete Works vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: Cites Yudhishthira's answer as an example of Maya: death stalks everywhere, yet we think we will live forever; such contradictions run through all of life.

commentaries.who: Swami Harshananda, Concise Encyclopedia of Hinduism, 'Yakṣapraśna' (Hindupedia)
commentaries.gist: Harshananda's summary gives the same answer as the greatest wonder, within his account of the dialogue.

mbh.3.314.116.practical_reading: Let mortality sharpen priorities: what would you stop postponing if you took seriously that your time is limited?
misreadings: Not morbid; it is a wake-up call, not a counsel of despair.
cautions: Directly about death; can land very hard on someone in fresh grief or facing a diagnosis. Textually late (appendix).
not_for: fresh bereavement
someone with a terminal diagnosis or suicidal thoughts

mbh.3.314.119.context: At the end of the twelve years of exile, the Pandavas chase a deer that has carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks. Thirsty, the four younger brothers in turn drink from a lake despite a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's questions before drinking. Answer to the third of the four last questions, 'what is the path?'. TEXTUAL CAUTION: this verse is NOT in the BORI critical text; it belongs to a long passage relegated to Appendix I, No. 32 (inserted after 3.297.61). It is in the vulgate and in Ganguli, and is famous, but an editor should not cite it as critical-edition text.
mbh.3.314.119.core_teaching: When argument and texts don't settle the question, follow the path walked by people of great character.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCCXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: argument reaches no certain conclusion, the Srutis differ, no single Rishi's view is accepted by all, the truth of duty is hidden in caves; so the path is that along which the great have gone.

commentaries.who: Krishnadasa Kaviraja, Caitanya-caritamrta Madhya 17.186, with A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami's notes (Vedabase)
commentaries.gist: Quoted by Caitanya; the word glosses take guhā as the heart of a realised person and mahājana as self-realised predecessors whose path one should accept.

commentaries.who: Swami Harshananda, Concise Encyclopedia of Hinduism, 'Yakṣapraśna' (Hindupedia)
commentaries.gist: Harshananda: disputation goes nowhere, scriptures contradict, no single sage is the final authority, dharma's principles are deeply hidden; hence the way is what great people tread.

mbh.3.314.119.practical_reading: When advice conflicts and you can't reason your way out, look at someone whose life you admire and ask what they actually did in your situation.
misreadings: 'Mahājana' does not mean the majority or the crowd (our misuse note and our_note are right).
cautions: Textually late (appendix).
not_for: someone being pressured to conform by family or community, if mahājana is read as 'what everyone does'

mbh.3.314.120.context: At the end of the twelve years of exile, the Pandavas chase a deer that has carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks. Thirsty, the four younger brothers in turn drink from a lake despite a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's questions before drinking. Answer to the last of the four questions, 'what is the news?'. The Yaksha then asks who is truly a person. TEXTUAL CAUTION: this verse is NOT in the BORI critical text; it belongs to a long passage relegated to Appendix I, No. 32 (inserted after 3.297.61). It is in the vulgate and in Ganguli, and is famous, but an editor should not cite it as critical-edition text.
mbh.3.314.120.core_teaching: The one constant headline is Time quietly cooking every being, day and night, season by season.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCCXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: this ignorant world is a pan, the sun its fire, days and nights the fuel, months and seasons the ladle, and Time the cook of all creatures: this is the news.

mbh.3.314.120.practical_reading: Next time the news feeds feel urgent, remember the one story that is always running, and spend today on what matters if time is short.
misreadings: Not fatalism; it puts daily anxieties in proportion.
cautions: About mortality; heavy for the grieving. Textually late (appendix).
not_for: fresh grief
someone facing serious illness

mbh.3.314.121.context: At the end of the twelve years of exile, the Pandavas chase a deer that has carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks. Thirsty, the four younger brothers in turn drink from a lake despite a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's questions before drinking. Having heard all four last answers, the Yaksha says the questions were answered truly and asks one more. After this answer he offers to revive one brother of Yudhishthira's choice.
mbh.3.314.121.core_teaching: The richest person is the one whose peace no longer depends on pleasant or unpleasant, past or future.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCCXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the report of good deeds reaches heaven and earth, and as long as it lasts one is a man; the one to whom agreeable and disagreeable, weal and woe, past and future are the same possesses every kind of wealth.

commentaries.who: Bibek Debroy, 'The Ideal King' (Open magazine column)
commentaries.gist: Debroy reports the answer as: a person who treats pleasure and pain, and past and future, as equal is a man who possesses all riches.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: 3.297.62-64 in the constituted text, with sarvadhanī; our 'puruṣa ucyate' ending matches the star passage *1384.

mbh.3.314.121.practical_reading: Notice how much of today's mood depends on what happened yesterday or might happen tomorrow; each time you come back to the present evenly, you are richer.
misreadings: Not indifference to others' pain; it is about not being thrown by one's own ups and downs.
cautions: Equanimity can sound like 'don't feel' to someone in acute distress.
not_for: fresh grief

data_flags.translation_note: Incomplete. The Yaksha asks two things: who is a person (puruṣa), and who possesses all wealth (sarvadhanī). In BORI and Ganguli, Yudhishthira first says a person is one whose good deeds' fame touches heaven and earth, and then that the one for whom pleasant/unpleasant, joy/sorrow,...

mbh.3.314.132.context: At the end of the twelve years of exile, the Pandavas chase a deer that has carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks. Thirsty, the four younger brothers in turn drink from a lake despite a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's questions before drinking. Satisfied, the Yaksha lets him choose one brother to revive. He chooses Nakula. The Yaksha asks why not Bhima, whom he loves, or Arjuna, on whom they all depend; he answers with this verse and adds that Madri should have a son as Kunti does. Pleased that he puts non-cruelty above gain and pleasure, the Yaksha revives all four and reveals himself as Dharma.
mbh.3.314.132.core_teaching: Fairness and non-cruelty come before advantage: Yudhishthira gives up his strongest brothers so that his stepmother is not left without a son.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCCXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: abstention from injury is the highest virtue, higher even than the highest object; he practises it, so let Nakula live; as Kunti is to him so is Madri, and he wants to act equally toward both mothers.

commentaries.who: Bibek Debroy, 'The Ideal King' (Open magazine column)
commentaries.gist: Debroy frames the choice of Nakula as a test of impartiality: Yudhishthira will not leave his own dharma and sees no difference between his mothers; the Yaksha, Dharma himself, revives all.

commentaries.who: Swami Harshananda, Concise Encyclopedia of Hinduism, 'Yakṣapraśna' (Hindupedia)
commentaries.gist: Harshananda's epilogue: the Yaksha was Yama-Dharma, was greatly pleased by the answers, revived all the brothers and granted further boons.

mbh.3.314.132.practical_reading: When you have to choose who benefits, ask who would be left out or hurt, not only what helps you most.
misreadings: Not a rule that one should always choose against one's own interest.
cautions: The story begins with four brothers lying dead; gentle reading needed for the bereaved.
speaks_to: a choice between advantage and decency

mbh.3.314.61.context: Same riddle sequence at the lake: with his four brothers lying dead, Yudhishthira answers a quick run of paired riddles. This pair contrasts the weight of a mother and the height of a father with the speed of the mind and the multitude of worries. The episode ends with all the brothers restored.
mbh.3.314.61.core_teaching: Parents carry a weight and height beyond measure, while the mind outruns the wind and worries outnumber the grass.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation (Vana CCCXI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli gives the answer as: the mother outweighs the earth, the father stands higher than heaven, the mind outruns the wind, and our thoughts outnumber the grass.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 3.297.40-41
commentaries.gist: The critical text asks what is most abundant among men and answers 'worry', rather than comparing it with grass.

mbh.3.314.61.practical_reading: Honour what your parents mean to you, and notice how fast and many the worries are, so you need not believe every one.
misreadings: Not a ranking of mothers over fathers.
cautions: For readers estranged from or grieving a parent, the praise of parents can hurt.
not_for: someone with an abusive parent

mbh.3.314.65.context: At the end of the twelve years of exile, the Pandavas chase a deer that has carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks. Thirsty, the four younger brothers in turn drink from a lake despite a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's questions before drinking. This pair comes early in the series of riddles, just after questions about what does not close its eyes in sleep and what has no heart. It is followed by questions on the guest of all beings and on what walks alone.
mbh.3.314.65.core_teaching: Each stage of life has its true support, and at the end only what one has given goes with one.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCCXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the exile's friend is his companion, the householder's is the wife, the sick man's the physician, and the friend of one about to die is charity.

commentaries.who: Bibek Debroy, 'The Ideal King' (Open magazine column)
commentaries.gist: Debroy's retelling gives the same set of answers, including that charity is the friend of one about to die.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: 3.297.44-45 is in the constituted text; the critical reading for the traveller's friend is sārtha (companion), not vidyā.

mbh.3.314.65.practical_reading: Ask who or what is your real support in your current season (travel, home, illness), and remember that generosity is the one thing that stays with you to the end.
misreadings: Not a claim that the spouse is one's only friend, or that the sick should rely on nothing but doctors.
cautions: Mentions dying; gentle but direct. 'Spouse is the friend at home' may sting for the widowed, separated or single.
not_for: recent widowhood or divorce
a reader facing their own death, if 'charity' is read as a transaction

data_flags.corrected_ref: BORI critical edition 3.297.44-45; Ganguli Vana Parva sec. CCCXI. Our numbering (3.314.65) matches neither.

mbh.3.314.71.context: At the end of the twelve years of exile, the Pandavas chase a deer that has carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks. Thirsty, the four younger brothers in turn drink from a lake despite a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's questions before drinking. Here the Yaksha asks, in his compressed riddle-style, what single thing leads to each of four goods. The next questions ask what is a man's self, his god-given friend, his livelihood and his refuge.
mbh.3.314.71.core_teaching: Four goals, four foundations: diligence for dharma, giving for good name, truth for heaven, character for happiness.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCCXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it as 'refuges': liberality the highest refuge of virtue, gift of fame, truth of heaven, good behaviour of happiness.

commentaries.who: Swami Harshananda, Concise Encyclopedia of Hinduism, 'Yakṣapraśna' (Hindupedia)
commentaries.gist: Harshananda glosses dākṣya as integrity, the source of dharma; charity the source of fame; truth the source of heaven; character (śīla) the source of happiness. He notes Nilakantha's commentary leaves many answers enigmatic.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: 3.297.48-49 is in the constituted critical text.

mbh.3.314.71.practical_reading: Pick one of the four for today: do a task well, give something, tell the truth where it costs, or act in character when no one is watching.
misreadings: Not a promise that happiness follows automatically from good character in the short term.
not_for: acute grief or crisis, where a list of virtues can feel cold

mbh.3.314.75.context: Four Pandava brothers have drunk from a guarded lake against a voice's warning and lie dead on its bank. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's riddles first; this pair is one of a rapid series of short questions and answers. At the end he is offered one brother's life, picks Nakula over his own full brother, and the Yaksha, revealed as Dharma, revives all four.
