mbh.3.314.75.core_teaching: Of the good things a person can have, the ones Yudhishthira ranks highest are inner or bodily rather than bought: skill, learning, health, and above all contentment.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation (Vana Parva CCCXI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli ranks skill as the most praiseworthy thing, knowledge as the finest possession, health as the greatest gain and contentment as the highest happiness; he adds no footnote here.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli, Vana CCCXI)
commentaries.gist: The section frames every answer as tested wisdom under pressure: the brothers lie dead, and the episode closes when Yudhishthira chooses Nakula on grounds of non-injury and fairness, and all are revived.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 3.297.52-53
commentaries.gist: The critical text has the same question and answer, with 'lābhānāṃ śreṣṭham ārogyam' (health the best of gains) and 'sukhānāṃ tuṣṭir uttamā'.

mbh.3.314.75.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a gratitude check: count skill, learning, health and contentment as real wealth before measuring life by money or status.
misreadings: Not a claim that ill or less-skilled people are worse off as persons; it ranks goods, not people.
Contentment here is not giving up effort; Yudhishthira also prizes skill and learning.
cautions: Health named as 'the best gain' can sting for a reader who is chronically ill or disabled; frame it as appreciation, not a test they fail.
The scene's backdrop is four brothers lying dead; keep the riddle tone, not the deaths, in the foreground.
not_for: someone newly diagnosed or in chronic pain, unless framed gently
someone in acute financial hardship who may hear 'be content' as dismissal
speaks_to: wanting to notice what is already enough

mbh.3.314.79.context: At the end of the twelve years of exile, the Pandavas chase a deer that has carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks. Thirsty, the four younger brothers in turn drink from a lake despite a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's questions before drinking. Just before, he has said that non-cruelty is the highest dharma and that the controlled mind does not grieve; next the Yaksha asks why one gives to different kinds of people.
mbh.3.314.79.core_teaching: Four things to drop and what each frees: pride for being loved, anger for freedom from sorrow, craving for true wealth, greed for happiness.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCCXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: pride renounced makes one agreeable, wrath renounced leads to no regret, desire renounced makes one wealthy, avarice renounced makes one happy.

commentaries.who: Swami Harshananda, Concise Encyclopedia of Hinduism, 'Yakṣapraśna' (Hindupedia)
commentaries.gist: Harshananda's summary: renouncing pride makes one lovable, anger frees one from grief, desire makes one wealthy, greed makes one happy.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: 3.297.56-57 is in the constituted critical text.

mbh.3.314.79.practical_reading: Notice which of the four is loudest in you today and set it down once: skip the point-scoring, hold back one angry reply, or decline one want.
misreadings: 'Give up anger and you will not grieve' does not mean grief is a sign of anger or that a grieving person has failed.
cautions: 'Na śocati' (does not grieve) could be misread by a grieving reader as blame; keep the reading on anger's regrets.
not_for: fresh bereavement, if 'na śocati' is foregrounded

mbh.3.314.89.context: At the end of the twelve years of exile, the Pandavas chase a deer that has carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks. Thirsty, the four younger brothers in turn drink from a lake despite a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's questions before drinking. This begins a run of definitions (austerity, restraint, forbearance, shame; then knowledge, calm, compassion, straightness; enemies and disease; steadiness and fortitude) that the critical edition sets aside as a later addition but most popular versions include. TEXTUAL CAUTION: this verse is NOT in the BORI critical text; it belongs to a long passage relegated to Appendix I, No. 32 (inserted after 3.297.61). It is in the vulgate and in Ganguli, and is famous, but an editor should not cite it as critical-edition text.
mbh.3.314.89.core_teaching: Virtues are defined by what they do inside us: real austerity is doing one's own work, real patience is bearing life's swings.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCCXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: staying in one's own religion is asceticism, restraint of mind the true restraint, forgiveness is enduring enmity, and shame is withdrawing from unworthy acts.

mbh.3.314.89.practical_reading: When things swing between good and bad today, treat the steadiness itself as the practice, and let 'shame' mean simply stopping before the thing you know is wrong.
misreadings: Kṣamā here is not 'put up with mistreatment'; it is bearing heat and cold, gain and loss.
cautions: Textually late (appendix).
not_for: someone being told to tolerate abuse

mbh.3.314.91.context: At the end of the twelve years of exile, the Pandavas chase a deer that has carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks. Thirsty, the four younger brothers in turn drink from a lake despite a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's questions before drinking. Part of the definitions passage that follows the questions on the way, water, food and poison. TEXTUAL CAUTION: this verse is NOT in the BORI critical text; it belongs to a long passage relegated to Appendix I, No. 32 (inserted after 3.297.61). It is in the vulgate and in Ganguli, and is famous, but an editor should not cite it as critical-edition text.
mbh.3.314.91.core_teaching: Calm, compassion and honesty are states of mind: a quiet mind, a wish for everyone's happiness, an even and undivided heart.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCCXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: true knowledge is that of Divinity, true tranquillity that of the heart, mercy is wishing happiness to all, simplicity is equanimity of heart.

mbh.3.314.91.practical_reading: Use the definitions as a check: is my mind quiet, do I wish this person well, am I the same inside as I appear?
misreadings: Calm is not suppression; it is a mind that has settled.
cautions: Textually late (appendix).

mbh.3.314.93.context: At the end of the twelve years of exile, the Pandavas chase a deer that has carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks. Thirsty, the four younger brothers in turn drink from a lake despite a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's questions before drinking. Part of the definitions passage; next he defines delusion, pride, idleness and grief. TEXTUAL CAUTION: this verse is NOT in the BORI critical text; it belongs to a long passage relegated to Appendix I, No. 32 (inserted after 3.297.61). It is in the vulgate and in Ganguli, and is famous, but an editor should not cite it as critical-edition text.
mbh.3.314.93.core_teaching: The hardest enemy is inside (anger), the incurable illness is greed, and goodness is measured by care for all beings.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCCXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: anger is an invincible enemy, covetousness an incurable disease; the honest man desires the weal of all creatures and the dishonest is unmerciful.

mbh.3.314.93.practical_reading: When angry, remember it is the opponent that is hardest to beat, so do not fight it head-on: pause. Treat greed as a symptom that recurs rather than something one more purchase will cure.
misreadings: Not a statement that angry people are bad; it says anger is hard to conquer.
cautions: Textually late (appendix). 'Disease' metaphor: avoid applying to a reader's actual illness.
not_for: someone whose anger is a justified response to injustice, if read as 'your anger is the problem'

mbh.3.314.97.context: At the end of the twelve years of exile, the Pandavas chase a deer that has carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks. Thirsty, the four younger brothers in turn drink from a lake despite a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira agrees to answer the Yaksha's questions before drinking. Part of the definitions passage, after the lines on delusion and grief and before those on who is learned. TEXTUAL CAUTION: this verse is NOT in the BORI critical text; it belongs to a long passage relegated to Appendix I, No. 32 (inserted after 3.297.61). It is in the vulgate and in Ganguli, and is famous, but an editor should not cite it as critical-edition text.
mbh.3.314.97.core_teaching: Ritual words are turned inward: the true bath cleans the mind, the true gift is protection of others.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. CCCXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: steadiness is staying in one's own religion, patience is subjugation of the senses, a true bath washes the mind clean of impurities, and charity is protecting all creatures.

mbh.3.314.97.practical_reading: Pair a daily ritual (a shower, a donation) with its inner version: let go of one resentment, and protect someone who needs it.
misreadings: Not dismissive of outer ritual; it says what the ritual points to.
cautions: Textually late (appendix).
speaks_to: wanting inner meaning in daily habits
guilt and wanting a fresh start

mbh.3.32.14.context: Draupadi apologises for seeming to slander dharma but presses her point: every living thing must act; only the immobile live without acting. Those who trust only fate and those who trust only chance are the worst of people; the one who believes in effort is praised. She credits this teaching to a learned Brahmin, reciting Brihaspati's doctrine, whom she heard in her father's house.
mbh.3.32.14.core_teaching: Waiting on fate without effort leads to ruin; human effort is required alongside whatever destiny brings.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXXII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: believers in destiny and in chance are both the worst of men; one who lies idle trusting destiny perishes like an unburnt pot in water; only those who trust in action deserve praise.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.33.12; the surrounding chapter weighs daiva (fate), haṭha (chance) and puruṣakāra (effort) and concludes one must act.

commentaries.who: Abhinav Agarwal, Swarajya column using Debroy's critical-edition translation
commentaries.gist: Reads Draupadi's speech as a call to act now: only the immobile can live without acting, and believers in destiny or chance are both wrong.

mbh.3.32.14.practical_reading: Hoping things will change is not a plan; take the next concrete step yourself.
misreadings: Not a claim that outcomes are fully in our control; the same speech says success depends on many factors.
cautions: The 'fool' language can shame a reader who is stuck because of depression or illness rather than idleness.
not_for: a reader paralysed by depression or grief who needs gentleness, not a push
speaks_to: someone ready to stop waiting and start

mbh.3.32.48.context: Draupadi illustrates effort and what lies beyond it: the farmer breaks the soil, sows, and then waits, because rain is the cause he cannot supply (3.33.44). If rain fails, he is blameless; he tells himself he did all a person could, and the wise do not reproach themselves. She then says not to despair when effort does not succeed.
mbh.3.32.48.core_teaching: Do your full share of the work; when an outcome depends on forces beyond you and fails, you are not at fault and should not condemn yourself.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXXII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: the tiller ploughs and sows and then sits silent, the clouds being the cause; if they fail him he is absolved, tells himself he did what others do, and does not indulge in self-reproach.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.33.44-46 has the full image (ploughing, sowing, waiting on Parjanya); the next verses list success as depending on many factors combined.

mbh.3.32.48.practical_reading: After giving something your honest best, separate what was yours to do from what was not; failure in the second part is not a verdict on you.
misreadings: Not an excuse for half-effort; the farmer did everything others do.
cautions: Gentle and widely usable; careful only when the 'outcome' is a death or illness, where 'not your fault' must not sound dismissive.
not_for: a reader who has not yet tried and is looking for permission not to
speaks_to: self-blame after a failed exam, interview, venture or pregnancy attempt
caregivers who did everything and still lost

mbh.3.32.50.context: Right after the farmer image, Draupadi says no one should fall into despair saying 'I work and do not succeed'. Success comes from many factors together; if one is missing the result is reduced or absent, but without beginning there is no fruit at all. The wise bring together place, time, means and auspicious circumstance as best they can.
mbh.3.32.50.core_teaching: Lack of success so far is no reason to despair; action can go either way, but not acting guarantees no result.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. XXXII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: one should not despair at acting without success, because there are two other causes besides exertion; success depends on a union of circumstances, but without exertion there can be none.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.33.47-48: effort ends in success or non-success, non-action in neither; results come from many factors combined, and with no undertaking there is no fruit.

mbh.3.32.50.practical_reading: Keep going after setbacks: each try carries a real chance, while giving up removes it.
misreadings: Not a promise that persistence always pays off.
cautions: For someone exhausted by repeated failure (e.g. long job search, infertility), pair with rest and with 3.32.48's 'do not blame yourself'.
not_for: situations where stopping is the wise and healthy choice

mbh.3.32.58.context: Draupadi, still pressing Yudhishthira to act, argues that every creature must act, that those who trust only fate or chance are the worst of men, and that success depends on effort combined with circumstances, so one should not despair at failure. Immediately before this line she says a person should seek out the weak points of enemies; immediately after, that success depends on acting according to time and circumstance. She closes by naming her source: Brihaspati's teachings as recited by a learned brahmin at her father's house.
mbh.3.32.58.core_teaching: Never look down on yourself; one who despises himself cannot flourish.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation (Vana XXXII)
commentaries.gist: Renders: no man should ever disparage himself, for the man who disparages himself never earns high prosperity; success depends on acting according to time and circumstances.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli, Vana XXXII)
commentaries.gist: Draupadi also says no one should despair at failure, since success needs several conditions besides exertion, but without exertion there is none; confident, active people succeed.

mbh.3.32.58.practical_reading: Self-contempt is not humility; it drains the energy you need to act. Treat yourself as someone worth effort.
misreadings: Not arrogance or self-promotion.
Not 'confidence guarantees success'; Draupadi says success depends on many factors.
cautions: The line sits in a speech that also advises searching out enemies' weaknesses and wishing them ill; keep it on self-respect.
not_for: someone in a depressive episode who may hear 'don't despise yourself' as one more thing they are failing at, unless framed gently
speaks_to: low confidence before a new effort

mbh.3.57.15.context: Kali has entered Nala and Pushkara keeps winning with Kali's help; for months Nala gambles away gold, chariots and robes and will not see his ministers or citizens. Damayanti summons the charioteer Varshneya and tells him the more Nala loses, the stronger his passion for the dice, that he no longer heeds friends or even her. She asks Varshneya to take their two children to her father in Vidarbha.
mbh.3.57.15.core_teaching: Losses can feed a compulsion rather than stop it; Damayanti sees the pattern clearly and acts to protect her children.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. LX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli gives the line to Damayanti, speaking to Varshneya: the more the king loses to Pushkara, the greater his ardour for play, and he heeds neither friends nor her; she sends the children to safety.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text 3.57.11-16 frames it as bhaimī uvāca to Vārṣṇeya; the verse continues that the dice obey Pushkara and turn against Nala, and that he no longer listens to friends.

mbh.3.57.15.practical_reading: Chasing losses is a known trap: the more one loses, the harder stopping feels. Damayanti's response models seeing it clearly and protecting those who depend on you.
misreadings: Not a moral verdict on Nala's character; the text attributes the compulsion to Kali's possession, and he later recovers.
cautions: Gambling and addiction; avoid shaming language toward someone with a compulsion.
The story continues with Nala abandoning Damayanti in the forest.
not_for: using it to label a person with addiction as weak or bad
speaks_to: someone watching a loved one spiral into gambling or another compulsion
someone noticing their own 'chasing losses' pattern

data_flags.attribution_note: Wrong speaker. This is Damayanti speaking to Nala's charioteer Varshneya (BORI 3.57.11-13; Ganguli LX), inside the sage Brihadashva's narration to Yudhishthira. Fix: speaker 'Damayanti', listener 'Varshneya, Nala's charioteer'; nested in Brihadashva's tale to Yudhishthira.

mbh.3.58.30.context: Having lost his kingdom, Nala wanders the forest with Damayanti, half-starved, and keeps pointing out the road to Vidarbha. She fears he means to send her away and says she will soothe his weariness, since nothing heals sorrow like a wife. Nala agrees and swears he would sooner give up himself than her, yet that same night, still under Kali's influence, he cuts her half-garment and abandons her as she sleeps.
mbh.3.58.30.core_teaching: In hardship, a loving companion is the best medicine. Damayanti offers herself as that companion when Nala has lost everything.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Vana sec. LXI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: Damayanti says physicians hold that in every sorrow nothing equals a wife; Nala agrees there is no friend or medicine like a wife for a man in distress, and swears not to forsake her.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Constituted text: Damayanti 3.58.27 (no remedy like a wife, physicians say); Nala 3.58.28 (no friend or medicine like a wife for the distressed). Our verse merges the two.

mbh.3.58.30.practical_reading: When someone you love has lost everything, staying close can matter more than advice; a steady companion is itself a kind of medicine.
misreadings: Not a claim that a wife exists to heal her husband; our line rightly widens it to any partner.
cautions: Right after this, Nala abandons her; a reader who was left by a partner may find it painful.
Gendered frame (wife as medicine for a man); keep our gender-neutral line.
not_for: someone recently abandoned or widowed
someone pressured to stay with a partner who harms them
speaks_to: standing by a partner through job loss, debt or illness
feeling grateful for a partner who stayed

mbh.5.129.11.context: Duryodhana has stormed out of the assembly after rejecting Krishna's terms. Dhritarashtra sends Vidura to fetch Gandhari. She says to bring their kingdom-mad son back, then turns on her husband: he is most to blame, knowing the boy's wickedness and still following him; now Duryodhana is ruled by lust and anger and cannot be turned by force, and Dhritarashtra is reaping the fruit of giving the kingdom to a fool with bad friends.
mbh.5.129.11.core_teaching: A parent who knows a child's wrongdoing and still goes along with it carries the greater share of blame.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section CXXIX
commentaries.gist: Gandhari says Dhritarashtra, so fond of his son, is greatly to blame, for he knows the son's sinfulness yet follows his counsel; the son is now a slave of lust, wrath and delusion.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (129.11-14) adds her charge that he gave the kingdom to an ignorant, wicked son with bad ministers and now reaps the result.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 127.9-14: she says a kingdom cannot be held by one without discipline, and ends asking how a wise man can ignore a split within his own family.

mbh.5.129.11.practical_reading: Used for parents and leaders: affection that excuses known wrongdoing is not love; enabling has consequences, for the child too.
misreadings: Not a statement that parents are to blame for everything an adult child does.
Not a reason to cut off a struggling child; it targets going along with known wrong.
cautions: Can land as guilt for parents of children with addiction or mental illness; distinguish enabling from support.
not_for: Parents grieving a child's wrongdoing who already blame themselves
Parents whose adult child acts beyond their influence
speaks_to: A parent who keeps covering for a child
A manager protecting a favourite who behaves badly

mbh.5.129.27.context: Gandhari, to Duryodhana: a kingdom cannot be won, kept or enjoyed by willfulness; whoever cannot govern his senses cannot rule long; desire and anger drag a man from his goals. The senses, restrained, make understanding grow like fire with fuel; unrestrained, they kill, as in this verse. Next: whoever tries to master his ministers without mastering himself is lost.
mbh.5.129.27.core_teaching: Unruly senses can destroy their owner, just as unbroken horses can kill a poor charioteer on the road.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section CXXIX
commentaries.gist: If not controlled, the senses can slay their possessor like unbroken, furious horses killing an unskilful driver; restrained, they make intelligence grow like fire fed with fuel.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (129.26-27) has the same pair: senses guided to virtue and profit increase intelligence; untrained, they kill like horses with a bad driver.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text: Vidura uses the identical image at 34.57-58, right after calling the body a chariot, the self its driver and the senses its horses, the Katha Upanishad figure.

mbh.5.129.27.practical_reading: Used for impulse control and habits: skill at the reins, built daily, decides whether energy carries you or wrecks you.
misreadings: Not a call to suppress or hate the senses; a good charioteer uses strong horses.
cautions: Avoid for readers in eating-disorder recovery, where 'control' language can harm.
not_for: Someone with compulsive self-control issues (e.g. disordered eating)
speaks_to: Someone whose temper or appetite keeps causing damage
A leader who knows their impulses are a risk

mbh.5.129.29.context: Gandhari has just said that whoever tries to master his ministers before himself, or his enemies before his ministers, is helpless and lost. This verse gives the right order; the next says fortune stays with one whose senses and ministers are mastered, who punishes wrongdoers and acts after reflection.
mbh.5.129.29.core_teaching: Conquer yourself first, as you would an enemy or a country; only then will efforts to lead advisers or overcome rivals bear fruit.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section CXXIX
commentaries.gist: One who conquers his own self first, taking it for a foe, will not seek in vain to conquer counsellors and enemies.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (129.28-29) gives the order self, then ministers, then enemies, with the self 'thought to be an enemy'.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 127.27-28 and Vidura's identical lines at 34.54-55 read 'as a territory'; the teaching is a stock maxim of kingship shared by Vidura and Gandhari.

mbh.5.129.29.practical_reading: Used for leadership and relationships: fix your own reactivity before trying to manage others.
misreadings: Not self-hatred; 'as an enemy' means with the seriousness of a campaign, not with contempt.
cautions: 'Treat yourself as an enemy' should not be given to someone with harsh self-criticism; prefer the 'territory' reading.
not_for: Someone with severe self-criticism or self-harm thoughts
speaks_to: Someone who keeps trying to change others first
A person preparing for a hard negotiation

mbh.5.129.44.context: Gandhari reminds Duryodhana that Bhishma, his father and Bahlika once gave the Pandavas their share to avoid a split, and he now enjoys the whole earth cleared by their heroism. Give them their due: half the earth is enough for you and your ministers. Fighting such disciplined, capable cousins will cost you great happiness; calm your friends' anger and rule justly.
mbh.5.129.44.core_teaching: Half of what you hold is more than enough; share what is due to others, listen to those who wish you well, and you will gain honour instead of ruin.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section CXXIX
commentaries.gist: Half the earth is enough to support Duryodhana and his counsellors; acting on well-wishers' words brings fame, while a quarrel with the self-controlled Pandavas would strip him of prosperity.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (129.43-45) has her urge him to give the Pandavas their due share if he wants to enjoy the earth with his ministers.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 127.40-46: she grounds it in the earlier peaceful division and says thirteen years of wrong are enough. Dhritarashtra says the same 'half is enough' at 57.3.

mbh.5.129.44.practical_reading: Used for inheritance and business disputes: enough is enough; giving others their fair share protects what you have and your name.
misreadings: Not advice to accept half of what is rightfully yours from someone who wronged you; it is said to the one holding more than his share.
cautions: Inheritance and property quarrels are raw; keep it advisory, not accusing.
not_for: Someone being cheated who might hear 'settle for half'
speaks_to: A business partner tempted to keep everything
Someone who can't stop wanting more

mbh.5.129.54.context: Last words of Gandhari's speech. She has warned that Bhishma, Drona and Kripa, equally fond of the Pandavas, will not truly fight against Yudhishthira, and that the whole earth would die for Duryodhana's sake. She ends: greed never brings wealth; give it up and make peace. Her plea fails; Duryodhana does not relent.
mbh.5.129.54.core_teaching: No one is seen to prosper through greed; so stop grasping, my son, and make peace.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section CXXIX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli closes the section with her saying men never acquire wealth by avarice; give it up and desist.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (129.54) renders it as a mother's request to quench his avarice.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 127.47-53 sets it after her warning that the elders' loyalty is to dharma and the war would destroy the earth.

mbh.5.129.54.practical_reading: Used as a check on chasing more: greed tends to cost more than it gains; the mature move is to stop and settle.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of earning or ambition as such.
cautions: In the story her advice fails; don't promise readers that the other side will listen.
not_for: Someone struggling to afford basics, for whom 'greed' framing is irrelevant and hurtful
speaks_to: Someone in a money dispute who can't let go
A parent pleading with an adult child
Someone noticing they always want more

mbh.5.133.14.context: Vidula, having told her son to rise, says a coward is content with little like a small stream or a mouse's handful; better to die tearing out an enemy's fang, or to watch like a hawk for an opening. Then this image, and the next line: a moment's blaze beats smouldering for long. She goes on that a man who does his human work in battle owes nothing to dharma and need not reproach himself.
mbh.5.133.14.core_teaching: Better to blaze brightly, even briefly, than to smoulder without flame just to stay alive; give full effort rather than a cautious half-life.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section CXXXIII
commentaries.gist: Blaze up like a brand of tinduka wood even for a moment, never smoulder like a flameless chaff fire; blazing briefly is better than smoking forever.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (133.14-15) has the same: blaze up for a moment rather than smoke away fireless out of a desire to live.

commentaries.who: Sri Aurobindo, 'Vidula' (free verse paraphrase, CWSA vol. 5)
commentaries.gist: Aurobindo's free verse paraphrase makes it a call to rise and fight, contrasting the swift flame with smoke 'afraid to die'; he warns his poem sacrifices the letter to the spirit.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 131.9-16: the surrounding verses urge fighting even at risk of life and close with 'why do you live?'

mbh.5.133.14.practical_reading: Used for wholehearted effort: in a project, a relationship or a career move, a committed attempt beats years of half-hearted hedging.
misreadings: Not a glorification of burning out or reckless risk (our misuse note is right).
Not a judgement that a quiet, modest life is worthless.
cautions: Explicitly devalues clinging to life, and the context urges risking death; must never be served to a reader expressing despair, hopelessness or suicidal thoughts.
Martial and gendered shaming in the wider speech.
not_for: Anyone in despair or with suicidal ideation
Someone already exhausted or burned out
A grieving reader
speaks_to: Someone hesitating over a bold, worthwhile step
A person coasting who wants to commit fully
Someone after a setback ready to try again

mbh.5.133.17.context: Before the war Kunti sends Yudhishthira the story of the Kshatriya queen Vidula, who found her son lying dejected after the king of Sindhu defeated him. This verse sits inside her opening tirade: she tells him to blaze up for a moment rather than smoulder, says the sensible do not keep lamenting, and then demands that he either show his valour or meet death, asking what he is living for.
mbh.5.133.17.core_teaching: Once a result is in, success or failure, the wise do not sit in lament; they move straight to the next necessary act and do not let fear for themselves hold them back.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Udyoga sec. CXXXIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli renders it as the sensible person not grieving over gain or loss but doing what must be done next, careless even of his life. It falls in a scathing speech urging prowess or a warrior's death.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 5.131.14-17 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The constituted text has the plural "the wise do not grieve". The verses after it tell the son to show valour or go to the certain end, and twice ask him what he lives for.

mbh.5.133.17.practical_reading: Used against rumination after a setback: let the result register, then find the very next concrete step and take it, instead of waiting for the sting to fade before acting again.
misreadings: Not a call to be careless with one's life or health: the phrase about not hoarding life is a warrior's readiness to risk battle.
Not "never feel grief": the target is prolonged lament that blocks action.
cautions: The surrounding speech is shaming and martial: Vidula calls her son a eunuch and asks what he is alive for. Never pair with a reader who sounds hopeless or mentions not wanting to live.
Keep "does not hoard his life" out of any reading for someone in distress; it can read as indifference to living.
not_for: bereavement
depression or suicidal thoughts
someone being pushed by family into dangerous risks
speaks_to: someone replaying a failure (exam, rejection, lost deal) who needs to restart
a person who has just got a result, good or bad, and is drifting
athletes, founders, job-seekers after a loss

data_flags.corrected_ref: Mahabharata 5.131.15 in the BORI critical edition; Ganguli, Udyoga Parva section CXXXIII (wisdomlib). Our id 5.133.17 matches neither BORI chapter nor verse; it follows another edition's numbering.

mbh.5.133.21.context: Still in Vidula's first speech. Just before, she says a sinking man should drag the enemy down with him and that even someone cut off at the roots must not despair. Just after, she tells him to raise up the family line that sank because of him. Her son has not yet answered.
mbh.5.133.21.core_teaching: Even when everything seems cut away, take up your burden again as a good horse leans into a heavy load; rouse your strength and self-respect and recognise the capacity for effort that is yours.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Udyoga sec. CXXXIII)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: horses of mettle put out all their strength for heavy loads; remembering them, gather strength and honour and know what your manhood consists in. Raise the family that sank through you.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 5.131.18-19 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The verse straddles 18ef-19ab; the preceding half-verse says that even one whose roots are cut must never despair. The reading is ājāneyakṛtaṃ, "the deed of a thoroughbred".

mbh.5.133.21.practical_reading: A call to pick up an abandoned responsibility after a defeat: remember what steady, well-trained effort looks like and act from self-respect rather than from shame.
misreadings: Pauruṣa here means effort and agency, not machismo; the gendered insults around it are not the teaching.
Not "push through no matter what": a thoroughbred pulls well because it is trained and cared for.
cautions: The surrounding speech shames the son in gendered terms ("neither man nor woman"); a reading should borrow the courage, not the tone.
not_for: burnout or exhaustion where rest is the need
someone whose self-worth is already under attack at home
speaks_to: someone who has dropped a duty after a setback
rebuilding a business or career after failure
a student going back to study after failing
someone who needs to remember their own capacity

mbh.5.133.7.context: Kunti, asked by Krishna for a message to her sons, tells the old tale of Vidula, a proud and learned queen who found her son lying in despair after defeat by the king of Sindhu. She opens by disowning him as no son of hers; this verse is her first positive instruction, followed by 'Rise, coward, don't lie there defeated'. Over four chapters she shames, argues and encourages until he rises.
mbh.5.133.7.core_teaching: Do not hold yourself cheap or settle for scraps; set your mind on what is truly good, drop fear, and gather your strength.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section CXXXIII
commentaries.gist: Vidula tells her prostrate son not to disgrace his soul or let it be satisfied with little, to set his heart on his welfare and abandon fear, and then to rise.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (133.7) gives it as: do not think lightly of your own self or let it be content with a little; set your mind on great good things and lose your misgivings.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 131.1-7 sets the frame (Kunti's tale) and puts this line right after Vidula's contemptuous opening and before 'Rise, coward'.

mbh.5.133.7.practical_reading: Used to rebuild self-respect after failure: don't shrink your ambitions to match your low mood; aim at something good and take the first step.
misreadings: Not 'think big at any cost'; 'sukalyāṇa' is the good, not mere success.
The verse is the kind core of a harsh speech; don't import the shaming that surrounds it.
cautions: Surrounding verses call the son a coward and a eunuch and urge him to fight even to death; quote only this verse to a low reader.
not_for: Someone with clinical depression who needs care rather than a call to 'stop fearing'
speaks_to: Someone who has given up after a defeat
A person settling for far less than they can do
Someone rebuilding confidence after job loss or a failed venture

mbh.5.135.25.context: The son finally pushes back: her heart is steel, and with no treasury or allies how can he win? Then he asks her for a way and promises to follow it. Her tone changes from scorn to counsel. This is her first piece of advice; she goes on to say results are uncertain but effort is the only route, and then gives a plan to win over the enemy's disaffected.
mbh.5.135.25.core_teaching: Past failures are no reason to think less of yourself, because fortunes come and go; but a fresh start should be made with judgment, not from wounded resentment.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Udyoga sec. CXXXV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's mother tells her son not to disgrace himself by expecting failure: what was not gained has been gained, what was gained has been lost, and goals should never be pursued in anger and folly.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 5.133.18-23 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The constituted text heads this "the mother said". It answers the son's question about how to win without treasury or allies, so it is counsel given on request, no longer rebuke.

mbh.5.135.25.practical_reading: Separate the failure from the self: a bad run is a fact about circumstances, not a verdict on worth. Then check the motive for the comeback; restarting out of anger or to prove someone wrong tends to go badly.
misreadings: Not a promise that fortune will return; it says fortunes change, both ways.
Not permission for a revenge project; the second half warns against exactly that.
cautions: Vidula's follow-up plan is wartime statecraft (recruiting the enemy's angry and humiliated). Keep the reading at the level of self-respect and wise beginnings.
not_for: acute bereavement (the verse is about fortunes, not people)
someone whose loss came from another's abuse, who may hear it as "move on"
speaks_to: someone who has turned a failure into an identity ("I am a failure")
restarting after bankruptcy, divorce, a failed exam or a layoff
someone tempted to act out of resentment

mbh.5.135.26.context: Directly continues the previous verse. After saying fortunes come and go, Vidula argues that uncertainty is no excuse: effort gives two possible outcomes, idleness only one. The next verses warn that whoever decides in advance that everything is uncertain shuts himself off from success, and urge him to act in the conviction that it will succeed.
mbh.5.135.26.core_teaching: Every outcome is uncertain, so uncertainty cannot justify not trying: action gives two possibilities, success or not; inaction gives only one, nothing.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Ganguli translation, Udyoga sec. CXXXV)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: success is always uncertain, yet people act and sometimes succeed; those who abstain never do. Whoever settles beforehand that results are uncertain makes success unreachable; cast off sloth and act believing it will happen.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, 5.133.23-26 (textual note)
commentaries.gist: The constituted text spells out both halves: inaction has one outcome, effort has two (fruit or no fruit), and knowing impermanence in advance should not be used to push away growth.

mbh.5.135.26.practical_reading: A reply to fear of failure and procrastination: you cannot remove uncertainty, but you can choose between a chance and a certainty of nothing. Apply, launch, ask, start.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that effort pays off; it explicitly allows that some who try do not succeed.
Not a judgment on people who tried and failed.
cautions: Spoken to rouse a reluctant prince to war; for someone who tried hard and lost, it can sound like blame.
not_for: grief
someone exhausted after repeated effort who needs rest or comfort
someone whose failure was outside their control
speaks_to: someone hesitating to apply, launch, or ask

mbh.5.136.1.context: Kunti, through Krishna, urges Yudhishthira to fight for his kingdom by retelling how Queen Vidula roused her son Sanjaya, who lay dejected after defeat by the king of Sindhu. In this closing speech Vidula explains why a leader must not show fear: when the king looks frightened, kingdom, army and counsellors lose heart, some defect to the enemy, and loyal friends stand by helplessly. She tells him he still has friends and hidden treasure, and he rises to win his kingdom back.
mbh.5.136.1.core_teaching: In a crisis a leader may be shaken inside, but should not act as a shaken person, because others take their courage or their panic from him.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation (Udyoga CXXXVI)
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's Vidula says a king must not let any calamity show on him, because when the people see their king afraid, the realm, the army and the counsellors all lose heart and drift apart.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Kumbakonam 5.136; Ganguli CXXXVI)
commentaries.gist: Vidula pairs the warning with encouragement: he still has friends who share his joys and sorrows, and resources he does not know of; Kunti says the story should be told to a ruler overcome by despair.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition 5.134.1-2
commentaries.gist: Same verse in the critical text, followed by the line that on seeing a shaken king the realm, army and ministers all fall apart.

mbh.5.136.1.practical_reading: For someone carrying responsibility at work or at home: you can feel fear and still choose steady actions, because the people around you take their cue from what you do.
misreadings: Not 'hide your feelings from everyone'; Vidula's own point is about the leader's conduct before those who depend on him.
Not an argument for bravado or denial.
cautions: Vidula's speeches as a whole are harsh and shaming before they turn encouraging; do not borrow their tone for a reader who already feels like a failure.
not_for: someone who needs permission to admit fear and ask for help
burnout from always having to look strong
speaks_to: a parent holding steady for children

mbh.5.27.26.context: Thirteen years after the dice game, the Pandavas ask for their kingdom back. Dhritarashtra sends Sanjaya, who praises Yudhishthira's righteousness and urges him to live on alms rather than fight: life is short, war would kill Bhishma, Drona and kin, and victory cannot save anyone from age and death. Yudhishthira replies (sec. XXVIII) that dharma must be discerned, not assumed, and defers to Krishna, who (sec. XXIX) defends the Pandavas' claim and blames the Kauravas' greed.
mbh.5.27.26.core_teaching: No conquest saves anyone from age, death and the swings of joy and sorrow; Sanjaya uses this to argue against war.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Udyoga sec. XXVII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: even after winning the sea-girt earth one is not freed from decrepitude and death, pleasure and pain; knowing this, do not engage in war, or else hand everything to your counsellors and flee.

commentaries.who: Yudhishthira's and Krishna's replies, Ganguli Udyoga secs. XXVIII-XXIX
commentaries.gist: Yudhishthira answers that virtue and vice can wear each other's look and must be discerned; Krishna says Sanjaya cannot claim to know dharma better and that the Kauravas' covetousness makes conflict inevitable.

commentaries.who: Wikipedia, 'Udyoga Parva' (summary)
commentaries.gist: Summarises Sanjaya's mission: he argues that war means losses on both sides and that the Pandavas would be miserable even in victory; Yudhishthira says they want peace but the kingdom must be returned.

mbh.5.27.26.practical_reading: Use it to check ambition: will this prize really change what I most fear? But notice when someone uses 'nothing lasts' to talk you out of a fair claim.
misreadings: The epic does not endorse Sanjaya's conclusion; the verse is part of a pressure argument that the Pandavas and Krishna reject. Do not present it as 'give up what is yours'.
cautions: Speaker is pleading for the side that did wrong; a reader dealing with injustice (stolen inheritance, workplace wrong) should not be told to drop it on this verse's authority.
Mentions old age and death.
not_for: someone seeking justice for a real wrong
victims being pressured to 'let it go'

data_flags.translation_note: Incomplete: drops the last quarter, 'knowing this, do not wage war' (BORI: evaṃ vidvān naiva yuddhaṃ kuruṣva). That clause is the point of the verse: the truth about mortality is being used as an argument for giving up a just claim. Add: 'Knowing this, do...

mbh.5.33.106.context: One of Vidura's numbered lists for Dhritarashtra. In the vulgate it comes after the eight 'creams of happiness' (meeting friends, embracing a son...) and before the riddle of the nine-doored house. In the critical text it sits in ch. 35, after the Keshini story, and the next verse adds wryly that when a king honours someone, that one 'quality' outshines all eight.
mbh.5.33.106.core_teaching: Eight qualities make a person shine: wisdom, good family, self-control, learning, courage, few words, giving as much as one can, and gratitude.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Lists the eight as wisdom, high birth, self-restraint, learning, prowess, moderation in speech, gifts according to one's power, and gratitude.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Gives the same list in ch. 33 and again, almost word for word, in ch. 35, where the next verse says royal favour alone makes all the qualities seem to shine.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 5.35.45 only. The following verse (35.46) undercuts it: a single 'quality', being honoured by a king, eclipses the eight, a sly comment on court life.

mbh.5.33.106.practical_reading: Used as a character checklist, especially the less obvious items: speaking little, giving within one's means, and gratitude.
misreadings: 'Kaulya' is not a claim that only the high-born can shine; read with Vidura's own line that conduct matters more than birth (5.34.39).
cautions: The lineage item can exclude readers from marginalised or broken families; consider rendering it as 'good upbringing' only with a note.
not_for: A reader estranged from or ashamed of their family background
speaks_to: Someone wanting a short list of qualities to grow
Parents thinking about the character they hope to pass on

mbh.5.33.108.context: Vidura, after the riddle of the nine-doored house, tells Dhritarashtra the ten who do not know dharma; immediately after, he introduces the story of Prahlada, Virochana and Sudhanvan (told in the next chapter), about judging truthfully against one's own son.
mbh.5.33.108.core_teaching: Some states blind a person to right and wrong: intoxication, carelessness, frenzy, exhaustion, anger, hunger, haste, greed, fear and lust. The wise do not decide or act from inside them.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Lists the ten who do not know virtue (the intoxicated, inattentive, raving, fatigued, angry, starving, hasty, covetous, frightened and lustful) and says the wise should avoid their company.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same ten, with the same conclusion: a wise man should shun the company of all these.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.82-83. The next lines introduce Prahlada's judgement against his own son, aimed at Dhritarashtra, whose love for Duryodhana is itself one of these blinding states.

mbh.5.33.108.practical_reading: Modern teachers turn it into the HALT-style rule: do not make big decisions when hungry, angry, rushed, exhausted, frightened or craving; wait until the state passes.
misreadings: Not a judgement on people with mental illness ('unmatta'); read it as temporary states anyone can be in.
cautions: Avoid implying that people who are hungry or poor are morally blind.
not_for: A reader with a psychiatric condition who may hear 'deranged' as a label for themselves
speaks_to: Someone about to send an angry message or make a rushed decision
A person learning to pause before reacting
Someone in a craving or panic moment

mbh.5.33.119.context: Part of a run of verses on the conduct of the noble (arya-shila) near the end of chapter 33; just before: the one who never boasts and never speaks harshly is loved by all; just after: the verse on not gloating over one's own joy.
mbh.5.33.119.core_teaching: Noble conduct: leave settled quarrels settled, neither puff up nor collapse, and do not use your own hardship as an excuse for wrongdoing.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Has it as one who does not rake up old hostilities, behaves neither arrogantly nor with too much humility, and even in distress never does an improper act.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same: does not revive settled disputes, is neither too arrogant nor too humble, and does not do wrong because he is in distress.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.93 reads that the noble do not sink in spirit and do not turn resentful when they are down, a slightly different emphasis from 'do no wrong'.

mbh.5.33.119.practical_reading: Applied to family feuds and office grudges: once something is settled, do not reopen it to win again; and hard times do not license cutting corners.
misreadings: Not a demand to stay silent about an unresolved wrong; it concerns quarrels that have actually died down.
cautions: Someone in genuine hardship may feel judged; keep the focus on not harming others, not on shame for struggling.
not_for: A survivor whose 'settled' quarrel was never actually resolved or acknowledged
speaks_to: Someone tempted to reopen an old family argument
A person under financial pressure tempted to cut ethical corners
Someone swinging between pride and self-abasement

mbh.5.33.120.context: Follows directly on the verse about not rekindling quarrels, in Vidura's account of noble conduct; next comes the man who learns the customs and languages of many countries.
mbh.5.33.120.core_teaching: A good person does not gloat over his own good fortune, takes no pleasure in another's pain, and does not regret a gift once given.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Reads it as one who neither exults in his own happiness nor delights in another's misery, and does not repent after giving: a man of good nature and conduct.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same three marks: no exulting in one's happiness, no gladness at another's distress, no repenting after a gift.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.94 ends with the giver not boasting about it, which pairs 'no regret' with 'no bragging' about generosity.

mbh.5.33.120.practical_reading: Teachers use the last clause for generosity: once you give, let it go, neither keeping score nor regretting it.
misreadings: Not a ban on enjoying good fortune; the point is gloating.
Not a rule that one must keep giving where gifts are being exploited.
cautions: Someone who gave money or care and was taken advantage of may feel blamed for regretting it.
not_for: A person financially exploited by someone they helped
speaks_to: Someone who gave and now second-guesses it
A person tempted by schadenfreude toward a rival
Someone wanting a simple test of good character

mbh.5.33.14.context: Sanjaya has returned from the Pandavas, rebuked Dhritarashtra, and will deliver Yudhishthira's message at court the next day. Unable to sleep, the king sends for Vidura and asks what is good for one who is sleepless and burning. Vidura's first answer is this list, followed by a pointed hope that none of these has befallen the king and that he is not grieving because he covets others' wealth. He then goes on to the marks of the wise and the fool.
mbh.5.33.14.core_teaching: Sleeplessness is a symptom: it comes to the threatened, the powerless, the robbed, the craving and the guilty, so ask which one you are.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, English translation (1883-96), Udyoga sec. XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli: sleeplessness overtakes the thief, the lustful, one who has lost his wealth, one who has failed, and the weak attacked by the strong; Vidura hopes none of these has overtaken the king, nor coveting others' wealth.

commentaries.who: Wikipedia, 'Udyoga Parva' (Prajagara sub-parva summary)
commentaries.gist: Places this at the opening of chapters 33-40: Dhritarashtra admits Sanjaya's message has disordered his senses and kept him awake, and Vidura's counsel follows.

commentaries.who: Textual note: BORI critical edition (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: 5.33.13 in the constituted text, wording identical to ours.

mbh.5.33.14.practical_reading: On a sleepless night, ask honestly which of these is keeping you up: a threat, a loss, a want, or something you know you did wrong. Each needs a different response.
misreadings: Not a claim that every insomniac is guilty or greedy; the list mixes victims (the attacked, the robbed) with wrongdoers.
cautions: Insomnia can be medical or linked to depression or anxiety; do not imply it is always moral. Avoid suggesting a sleepless reader is a 'thief'.
not_for: clinical insomnia or depression, if read as moral diagnosis

mbh.5.33.29.context: Dhritarashtra cannot sleep the night Sanjaya returns from the Pandavas, and sends for Vidura. Vidura first tells him plainly that he has handed power to Duryodhana, Shakuni, Karna and Duhshasana, then begins a long list of the marks of the wise (pandita) and the fool; this is the line he calls the first mark.
mbh.5.33.29.core_teaching: Wisdom is shown less by cleverness than by a sequence: quick understanding, slow and full listening, acting on the understood purpose rather than on desire, and restraint about other people's business.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Renders the four marks as quick understanding, patient listening, pursuing aims with judgement rather than desire, and not spending one's breath on others' affairs unasked; calls this the foremost sign of wisdom.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Similar reading, but spells out the third mark as weighing the effects of an action and not following it merely for pleasure; the last as not attaching oneself to other people's affairs unsolicited.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical text the verse (33.22) sits in a run of 'he is called wise' verses: before it, the wise act to the full of their ability and slight nothing; after it, they do not crave the unattainable.

mbh.5.33.29.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a checklist for meetings and family talks: understand fast, but let the other person finish; decide from the facts rather than from what you want to be true; offer advice when it is asked for.
misreadings: Not a ban on helping someone in danger or speaking up about wrongdoing; it targets officious meddling, not care.
'Quick understanding' is not a demand to answer quickly; the same line asks for long listening.
cautions: A reader who processes slowly (learning difference, grief fog, depression) could hear 'understands quickly' as a verdict on them.
not_for: A person being told to 'stay out of it' when they are trying to protect someone being harmed
A reader already harsh on themselves for being slow or indecisive
speaks_to: Someone stepping into a role where they must listen and decide (new manager, new parent, caregiver)
People who react fast and regret it
Someone tempted to fix other people's lives uninvited

mbh.5.33.30.context: Part of Vidura's list of the marks of the wise, spoken to the sleepless Dhritarashtra. It follows the 'first mark' verse (quick understanding, long listening) and precedes the verse on finishing what one starts.
mbh.5.33.30.core_teaching: A trained mind does three things: it lets go of what is out of reach, it does not dwell on mourning what is gone, and it stays clear-headed when trouble comes.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Reads it as a description of people whose intellects are wise: they do not strive after the unattainable, do not grieve over what is lost, and do not let calamity cloud their minds.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same three marks; Dutt's wording for the last is that the wise do not lose their senses in calamities.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.23: one of a series of 'marks of the wise'; the next verse praises deciding first and then acting without stopping midway, so the context is steadiness in action, not consolation.

mbh.5.33.30.practical_reading: Often used to separate healthy acceptance from rumination: notice which hopes are no longer possible, allow sorrow without building a life around it, and keep the mind available for practical next steps when things go wrong.
misreadings: Not a command to stop grieving or a timetable for grief.
Not contempt for ambition; it is about what truly cannot be had.
cautions: Describes a mature state; read to someone newly bereaved it can sound like 'wise people don't mourn'. Pair it with permission to grieve.
Our note already says it 'describes more than it comforts'; agreed.
not_for: Fresh bereavement (first weeks after a death)
Miscarriage or loss of a child
Anyone told by others to 'move on' too quickly
speaks_to: Someone stuck replaying a lost opportunity, job or relationship long after the fact
A person facing a setback who needs to keep their head
Someone chasing something that is clearly closed to them

mbh.5.33.31.context: Vidura, continuing his marks of the wise for Dhritarashtra on the night before Sanjaya delivers Yudhishthira's message in court. It follows the verse on not chasing the unattainable and precedes 'they delight in noble deeds'.
mbh.5.33.31.core_teaching: Decide first, then begin; once begun, carry the work through without stalling, use time well, and keep yourself in hand.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Gives the sense as someone who, having commenced a thing, strives until it is completed, never wastes time and keeps his soul under control.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Stresses the order: he exerts after deciding on a course, does not stop in the middle, does not waste time, and has himself under control.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.24, same reading. It belongs to the same cluster as the 'six faults' list later in the chapter (sleep, sloth, procrastination), which names the opposite habits.

mbh.5.33.31.practical_reading: Used as a simple work rule: do the deciding up front, then protect the doing; most unfinished projects stall in the middle, not at the start.
misreadings: Not a rule never to stop a plan that has turned out wrong; the decision step is supposed to be real deliberation.
cautions: Can feel accusing to someone with burnout, chronic illness or ADHD who cannot always finish what they start.
not_for: A person in burnout who needs rest, not more push
Someone whose work stopped because of illness or caregiving
speaks_to: A student or professional who procrastinates after starting
Someone who wants a calm, practical maxim for discipline

mbh.5.33.33.context: Another of Vidura's marks of the wise in his night counsel to Dhritarashtra; it comes after 'they delight in noble deeds' and before the wise man who knows the nature of all beings.
mbh.5.33.33.core_teaching: The wise are not inflated by honour or burnt by insult; like a deep river pool, the surface may be touched but the depth does not churn.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Reads it as one who does not exult at honours or grieve at slights and stays cool and unagitated like a lake in the Ganga's course.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same sense; Dutt places the lake near the Ganga and calls the wise man unagitated by honour or insult.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.26. The next verse defines the wise by knowledge of beings, of how acts connect, and of human means, so the equanimity here rests on understanding, not indifference.

mbh.5.33.33.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to praise and criticism at work and online: take both as information, not as a verdict on your worth, so neither swells nor sinks you.
misreadings: Not emotional numbness or 'never feel hurt'; it is about not being thrown off balance.
Not a reason to ignore legitimate feedback.
cautions: Someone being repeatedly humiliated or bullied should not be told to simply stay unruffled; the harm still needs addressing.
not_for: Victims of ongoing workplace bullying or abuse who need action, not composure
speaks_to: Someone stung by a public slight or a bad review
Someone riding high on praise and wanting to stay grounded
People pleasers who feel every comment deeply

mbh.5.33.42.context: Having listed the marks of the wise, Vidura turns to the marks of the fool (mudha) for Dhritarashtra. This verse sits among them, after the man who befriends enemies and hates friends.
mbh.5.33.42.core_teaching: Three habits mark a fool in practical affairs: talking his plans around, doubting everything, and dawdling where speed is needed.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Gives the fool as one who divulges his projects, doubts in all things and spends long over what needs little time.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same three items: the fool gives out his intended acts, has doubts in every case and delays what should be done quickly.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.34. Later Vidura makes the matching positive rule: do not speak of what you intend, show what you have done (38.16), which supports the 'divulging' reading.

mbh.5.33.42.practical_reading: A plain warning for decision-makers: guard plans until they are ready, separate useful doubt from chronic second-guessing, and move fast on time-sensitive things.
misreadings: Not an attack on careful thinking; 'doubts everything' means habitual indecision, not honest questioning.
cautions: A verdict ('fool'); our note is right that it lands only where the reader asked to be challenged. Anxiety disorders and OCD involve compulsive doubt that is not foolishness.
not_for: Someone with anxiety or depression whose indecision is a symptom
A reader already ashamed of being slow
speaks_to: Someone who asked for a blunt push on procrastination
Founders or managers who leak plans and stall decisions

data_flags.translation_note: First clause disputed. 'saṃsārayati kṛtyāni' (literally 'makes his affairs go around') is rendered by both Ganguli ('divulges his projects') and Dutt ('gives out his intended acts') as broadcasting one's plans, not as dragging tasks out. Slowness is already the third clause. Suggested: 'He lets his...

mbh.5.33.45.context: From Vidura's marks of the fool, spoken to Dhritarashtra. Just before: the worst of men who enters uninvited and talks unasked; just after: the one who wants something hard to get without knowing his strength or using proper means.
mbh.5.33.45.core_teaching: Two kinds of folly are singled out: blaming others for a fault one shares, and raging where one has no power to change anything.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Renders it as the man who, himself guilty, casts blame on others, and who, though impotent, gives vent to anger: the most foolish of men.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same: the worst fool blames others when he himself is to blame, and is angry though unable to do anything.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.36, same reading. It closes a sub-list of foolish conduct that began with befriending enemies and hating friends (33.33-35).

mbh.5.33.45.practical_reading: Used as a mirror for projection (the fault I point at is often my own) and as a nudge to turn helpless anger into either action or acceptance.
misreadings: Not saying anger at injustice is foolish; the target is futile rage that changes nothing and harms the one raging.
cautions: Our note is right: the second half would wound someone powerless against a real wrong (an abuse survivor, a person facing discrimination). Their anger is not folly.
not_for: Survivors of abuse or injustice who are angry and have little power
Someone grieving with anger at a death
speaks_to: Someone noticing they criticise others for their own habit
Someone stewing about things they cannot affect (news, distant people)

mbh.5.33.55.context: Vidura has just told Dhritarashtra that Truth is the one boat to heaven. He then praises kshama: its only fault is that people mistake it for weakness. In the vulgate the passage goes on: forgiveness subdues everything, a fire falling on grassless ground goes out by itself.
mbh.5.33.55.core_teaching: Forbearance is often misread as weakness, but that misreading is not its fault: it is a strength, a virtue in those who have no power and an adornment in those who do.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Says the only defect of the forgiving is that people think them weak; that defect should be disregarded, since forgiveness is a great power, a virtue of the weak and an ornament of the strong.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same argument, but Dutt has forgiveness as an ornament for weak and strong alike, followed by the image of the 'sword of pacification' a wicked man cannot defeat.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical text only the first verse (33.47) survives; the 'greatest strength / ornament' lines are in the apparatus. The constituted text goes straight on: dharma is the one highest good, forbearance the one supreme peace (33.48).

commentaries.who: Counter-teaching in the epic: Prahlada to Bali, Vana Parva 3.29 (BORI e-text)
commentaries.gist: Draupadi cites Prahlada's ruling that neither force nor forgiveness is always best; the right one depends on time and person. This balances Vidura's praise.

mbh.5.33.55.practical_reading: Teachers use it to separate forgiveness from weakness: choosing not to retaliate can be strength, and other people's misreading of it is their problem, not proof you were wrong.
misreadings: Forgiving is not staying in harm's way or excusing abuse (our misuse note is right).
Not a duty to reconcile or to restore trust.
The epic itself (Prahlada, Vana 3.29) says forbearance is not always the right response.
cautions: Anyone in an abusive situation can hear it as pressure to keep forgiving. Keep the misuse note attached.
Do not cite the second half as 'critical edition' text.
not_for: Someone currently being abused or coerced
A survivor pressured by family to 'forgive and forget'
speaks_to: Someone who let a slight go and is now called a pushover
A person in power deciding whether to retaliate
Someone working toward forgiving an old hurt on their own timeline

mbh.5.33.85.context: In the middle of Vidura's numbered lists (ones, twos, threes... sixes). Just before: if one of the five senses leaks, wisdom drains out like water from a leaky skin bag. Just after: six people to abandon like a leaking boat (a teacher who cannot teach, a king who does not protect...).
mbh.5.33.85.core_teaching: Whoever wants to flourish must drop six habits: sleep, lethargy, fear, anger, idleness and procrastination.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Lists the six faults to be avoided by one seeking prosperity as sleep, drowsiness, fear, anger, indolence and procrastination.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same six, described as defects to be shunned by anyone desiring prosperity in this world.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.66. A few verses later (33.69) Vidura names the six good qualities never to be given up: truth, giving, diligence, freedom from envy, forbearance and steadiness.

mbh.5.33.85.practical_reading: Commonly taught as a habit audit for students and professionals; the pair at the end (idleness, procrastination) is the one most people recognise.
misreadings: Not a case against healthy sleep or rest; read 'sleep' as indulgence and dullness.
Fear and anger are named as habits to master, not feelings never to have.
cautions: Insomnia, depression, chronic fatigue and anxiety can look like these 'faults'; do not present them as moral failings.
not_for: Someone depressed, chronically ill or exhausted
New parents short on sleep
speaks_to: A student or professional wanting a crisp self-discipline checklist
Someone who sees procrastination eating their goals

mbh.5.33.96.context: Vidura's six-item lists to Dhritarashtra: six faults to drop, six people to abandon, six who forget their benefactors, then these six joys of the living world, then six who are always unhappy.
mbh.5.33.96.core_teaching: Ordinary happiness is concrete: health, no debt, home, good company, a dependable living and a life without fear.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Lists health, being free of debt, living at home, companionship with the good, certainty about one's livelihood and fearless living as the six things that make people happy.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same six, with Dutt calling the third the reverse of exile and the fifth confidence in one's own livelihood; he then gives the second list of six joys.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical edition this verse is relegated to the apparatus (*183), along with the 'six always unhappy' verse that follows; the constituted text moves from six virtues (33.69) to the six enemies of the heart.

mbh.5.33.96.practical_reading: Used as a gratitude list and a planning frame: look after health, avoid debt, invest in good friends and a reliable income, and build a life where you are not afraid.
misreadings: Not saying people abroad, in debt or ill cannot be happy; it names common supports of ease.
cautions: Our note is right that 'living at home' can sting migrants, students abroad and those displaced.
Readers in debt, unemployed, ill or living in fear may read it as a list of what they lack.
not_for: A refugee, migrant worker or someone forced to live away from family
Someone drowning in debt or newly unemployed
A person living with abuse (no 'fearless living')
speaks_to: Someone taking stock of what already supports them
A young adult planning finances and career
Someone rethinking success in simpler terms

mbh.5.33.97.context: Right after the six joys of life, Vidura gives Dhritarashtra its mirror: six kinds of people who are always unhappy.
mbh.5.33.97.core_teaching: Some misery is a disposition: envy, contempt, discontent, a short fuse, constant suspicion and dependence on other people's luck keep a person unhappy whatever happens.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Names the six always-miserable as the envious, the malicious, the discontented, the irascible, the ever-suspicious and those depending on others' fortunes.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same list; Dutt likewise calls them always miserable and places them directly after the six joys.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: This verse is part of the same interpolated block (*183) as the six joys and is absent from the critical text.

mbh.5.33.97.practical_reading: Teachers use it to show that some unhappiness is self-generated and changeable: envy and suspicion can be noticed and worked on.
misreadings: Not a description of people who depend on others through illness, age or disability.
Suspicion after real betrayal is not the same as a suspicious temperament.
cautions: 'Living off another's fortune' can shame dependants (students, homemakers, disabled or elderly readers).
Calling someone 'always unhappy' because of their traits can deepen depression.
not_for: A person dependent on family or care for reasons outside their control
Someone who has been betrayed and is learning to trust again
A depressed reader
speaks_to: Someone noticing envy or suspicion souring their days
A reader who wants a sharp self-check on discontent

mbh.5.34.19.context: Within Vidura's practical maxims for a ruler: take wealth like a garland-maker who plucks flowers without cutting roots (34.18), then weigh what follows from acting and from not acting (34.19); some undertakings should not be begun at all because effort would be wasted (34.20).
mbh.5.34.19.core_teaching: Before acting, think through both futures, the one where you act and the one where you do not, and then decide.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt, 34.19: having considered what will befall him after doing an act or not doing it, a man should do it or not.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical text the verse follows the garland-maker image and precedes the advice not to begin what cannot succeed, so it is about prudent statecraft and effort, not about avoiding all risk.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIV
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's section XXXIV abridges this stretch: he gives the same idea in general form (consider the agent, the act and its purpose; act or desist after weighing consequences) but not this verse word for word.

mbh.5.34.19.practical_reading: A simple two-question decision tool for career moves, conversations and purchases: picture acting, picture not acting, and compare honestly.
misreadings: Not a recipe for endless deliberation; the verse ends in a decision either way.
cautions: Someone with anxiety may turn it into rumination; keep it as a short exercise.
not_for: A reader caught in obsessive what-if thinking
speaks_to: Someone facing a big decision (job, move, confrontation)
An impulsive decider who wants a pause rule
Someone stuck because they only considered the risks of acting

mbh.5.34.43.context: Vidura has just told Dhritarashtra that birth is no measure without good conduct, and that conduct ranks above lineage even among the low-born (34.39). Then this verse on envy; then advice to avoid what intoxicates and to curb the pride of learning, wealth and family (34.41-42).
mbh.5.34.43.core_teaching: Envy of others' wealth, looks, strength, family, happiness, luck or honours is a sickness that never runs out, because there is always someone with more.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt, 34.42: one who envies other people's wealth, beauty, prowess, birth, happiness, luck and reward suffers a disease that has no cure.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical text (34.40) the verse follows Vidura's claim that conduct outweighs lineage, so envy of others' birth and status is the very thing he has just declared beside the point.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIV
commentaries.gist: Ganguli does not translate this verse; his section XXXIV skips from statecraft maxims to the 'self as friend and foe' passage. Listed only so the editor knows it was checked.

mbh.5.34.43.practical_reading: Teachers use it on social-media comparison: the list of envied things is endless, so the disease is too, unless you stop measuring.
misreadings: Not a claim that wanting a better life is envy; the target is resentment at others having more.
cautions: Calling envy a disease is fine as metaphor; do not imply someone struggling with real deprivation is merely envious.
not_for: A person facing genuine injustice or discrimination who is told their grievance is 'envy'
speaks_to: Someone eaten up by comparison with peers or siblings
A person scrolling and feeling worse
Someone resentful of a colleague's recognition

mbh.5.34.7.context: Dhritarashtra, admitting he looks back on his own guilt, asks Vidura what Yudhishthira intends.
