Vidura says he will speak the truth unasked, then warns: do not set your heart on gains got by unfair means (34.6); and if work done with proper means still fails, do not let your mind sink (34.7). He goes on to weigh consequences before acting.
mbh.5.34.7.core_teaching: If you used fair and proper means and the work still failed, there is no reason for the mind to sink; the duty was the right method, not the guaranteed result.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIV
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: a man of intelligence must not grieve when a purpose of his fails despite fair and proper means; it is paired with the warning not to set the heart on unjust means.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt, 34.7: if an aim cannot be achieved even with proper means, the intelligent man does not distress his mind about it.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 34.6-7 makes the pair explicit: do not hanker after deeds that succeed by false, improper means; and do not wilt when deeds done by proper means fail.

mbh.5.34.7.practical_reading: Used for honest failure: an exam, interview, pitch or treatment plan done well that still did not work. Review the method, then release the outcome instead of punishing yourself.
misreadings: Not an excuse to skip learning from failure; it presupposes the means really were sound.
Not 'results don't matter'.
cautions: About undertakings, not deaths; told to a caregiver whose loved one died despite good care it may sound cold unless framed gently.
not_for: Fresh bereavement after medical efforts failed
Someone whose failure came from cutting corners and who needs to own it
speaks_to: Someone who did everything right and still failed an exam or lost a job
Founders after an honest venture fails
Someone who keeps relitigating a sound decision that turned out badly

mbh.5.34.75.context: Vidura has listed qualities never found in the base (self-knowledge, patience, steadiness in dharma). He then says fools wound the wise with abuse and slander, and that the abuser takes on the wrong; next he says forgiveness is the strength of the virtuous (34.72) and that guarding speech is hardest of all.
mbh.5.34.75.core_teaching: Abuse and slander rebound: the one who utters them takes the moral stain on himself, and the one who bears them with forbearance is freed.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIV
commentaries.gist: Reads it as fools trying to injure the wise by reproach and evil speech, thereby taking the sins of the wise upon themselves, while the wise, freed of those sins, are forgiven.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt: the speaker of malice takes on the load of the wise man's sins, which the wise man casts off by forgiving the ignorant.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 34.71; the next verse (34.72) names forbearance as the strength of the good, and the passage then moves to the forest-and-axe image of wounding words.

mbh.5.34.75.practical_reading: Used to help someone not internalise insults: the ugliness belongs to the one who spoke, and not retaliating keeps you free of it.
misreadings: Bearing an insult calmly does not mean accepting ongoing abuse (our misuse note is right).
Not a promise that the abuser will be punished.
cautions: For people in abusive relationships it can be heard as 'just endure it'. Keep the misuse note attached.
not_for: Someone living with domestic or ongoing abuse
A child or employee being bullied by someone with power over them
speaks_to: Someone insulted or slandered at work or online
A person tempted to answer abuse with abuse

mbh.5.34.79.context: In Vidura's teaching on speech: guarding the tongue is hardest (34.73), well-spoken words bring good, ill-spoken ones harm (34.74), then this verse; then arrows can be pulled from the body but not a word-arrow lodged in the heart (34.76-77).
mbh.5.34.79.core_teaching: Physical damage, even a forest cut down, regrows; a wound made by cruel words does not close over.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIV
commentaries.gist: A forest pierced by arrows or cut by hatchets may grow again, but a heart wounded by ill-spoken words never recovers; Ganguli continues that word-arrows cannot be extracted.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (34.78) has the forest cut down by scythes growing back while the heart pierced with harsh words never recovers.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 34.75-77: the next verses say word-arrows fly from the mouth, make the struck one grieve night and day, and the wise should never loose them at others, so the verse is a warning to speakers.

mbh.5.34.79.practical_reading: A warning before speaking in anger to a partner, child or colleague; and, for the hurt person, a recognition that the wound is real.
misreadings: Not a claim that people can never recover from verbal hurt; it stresses how deep such wounds go so that speakers hold back.
cautions: Read to someone carrying old verbal abuse, 'does not heal' can sound hopeless; frame it as validation and as a warning to the speaker.
not_for: A survivor of long verbal abuse who needs hope of healing, unless reframed
speaks_to: Someone about to say something cruel in anger
Parents and partners in heated arguments
Someone told their hurt over words is an overreaction

mbh.5.35.51.context: Vidura ends the story of Keshini's suitors: Prahlada, asked to judge between his own son Virochana and the brahmin Sudhanvan, ruled truthfully against his son and so saved him. Vidura draws the moral for Dhritarashtra: do not lie for the sake of land out of love for your son. Then this verse; then a person's aims succeed as he turns his mind to the good.
mbh.5.35.51.core_teaching: Providence does not guard people like a herdsman with a stick; it protects by giving them clear judgement.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXV
commentaries.gist: After Prahlada's honest verdict against his son, Vidura tells the king not to lie for land; the gods do not protect men with clubs like herdsmen but grant intelligence to those they would protect.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt, 35.39-40: so do not speak untruth for land and ruin yourself with your sons; the gods give intelligence, not a club, to those they protect.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: The matching verse in the critical text is 34.78: when the gods intend someone's defeat, they first take away his judgement. Read together: protection and ruin both work through the mind.

mbh.5.35.51.practical_reading: Teachers use it against magical thinking: do not wait for rescue; good judgement, sought and used, is the form help usually takes.
misreadings: Not saying the gods abandon people; it says how protection works.
cautions: The paired idea (those headed for ruin lose their judgement) can sound like blaming victims of misfortune.
not_for: Someone who suffered a disaster and fears it means God withdrew favour
speaks_to: Someone waiting for a sign before making a needed decision
A believer wanting to connect faith with practical wisdom

mbh.5.35.60.context: After a list of those as guilty as brahmin-slayers, Vidura gives Dhritarashtra a set of tests of character; the next verse lists what steals what (age steals beauty, pride steals everything).
mbh.5.35.60.core_teaching: Every quality has its test: gold by fire, good character by conduct, honesty by dealings, courage by danger, steadiness by money trouble, and friends and enemies by hard times.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXV
commentaries.gist: Lists gold tested by fire, the well-born by deportment, the honest by conduct, the brave in panic, the self-controlled in poverty, and friends and foes in calamity.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt, 35.49, gives the same series, ending with friends and enemies known in seasons of difficulty and danger.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 35.42; immediately followed by 35.43, the list of thieves of beauty, patience, life and character, the next verse in our corpus.

mbh.5.35.60.practical_reading: Used to reassure someone that hard times are revealing who their real friends are, and to judge people by how they deal, not by how they present.
misreadings: Not saying suffering is good for people; it is about what difficulty reveals.
cautions: Someone who discovered friends left them in crisis may find it confirming but painful.
not_for: A person mid-crisis who feels abandoned and needs comfort first
speaks_to: Someone learning who stood by them in a crisis
A person deciding whom to trust in business

mbh.5.35.61.context: Follows the 'tests of character' verse in Vidura's counsel; next he says prosperity is born of good deeds, grows by activity, roots by skill and lasts by self-control. In the vulgate Vidura repeats the verse in ch. 37, just before Dhritarashtra asks why people do not live their full hundred years.
mbh.5.35.61.core_teaching: Each good thing has a thief: age takes beauty, craving patience, death life, envy goodness, anger prosperity, bad company character, lust shame, and pride takes everything.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXV
commentaries.gist: Gives decrepitude destroying beauty, ambitious hopes destroying patience, death life, envy righteousness, anger prosperity, low company good behaviour, lust modesty, and pride everything.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (35.50) has the same list; the vulgate repeats it in ch. 37 (Dutt 37.8) with some items reordered.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 35.43; the critical edition keeps it once and puts the ch. 37 repetition in the apparatus.

mbh.5.35.61.practical_reading: Teachers focus on the controllable thieves (craving, envy, anger, company, pride) and leave age and death as the frame that makes the rest urgent.
misreadings: 'Āśā' here is craving or grasping expectation, not hope in the healthy sense.
cautions: Opens with ageing and death; for a dying or elderly reader, or someone bereaved, the first half may hurt (our line wisely omits it).
not_for: A bereaved reader
An elderly or seriously ill reader if the full verse is used
speaks_to: Someone noticing anger or pride costing them
A person in bad company recognising its effect

mbh.5.35.79.context: Vidura has just said the one who draws wisdom from the wise is truly wise; then this ladder of foresight (day for night, dry season for rains, youth for age, life for the hereafter); then what the wise praise once it is safely past (food digested, a hero home from battle).
mbh.5.35.79.core_teaching: Live with foresight at every scale: do by day what lets you rest at night, in good seasons what carries you through hard ones, in youth what eases old age, and all your life what brings peace after death.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXV
commentaries.gist: Renders the four steps as day for night, eight months for the rains, youth for a happy old age, and the whole of life for happiness hereafter.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt, 35.67-68: the same ladder, ending with doing in this life what lets one live happily after death.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 35.57-58. Spoken to a king who cannot sleep because of what he has allowed; the first rung, sleeping at peace, is pointed (our note agrees).

mbh.5.35.79.practical_reading: Used for sleep and conscience (finish today's honest work so you can rest), for saving and health, and for long-term ethical living.
misreadings: Not a gospel of anxiety about the future; it is about preparing, then resting.
cautions: Mentions old age and life after death; an older reader with regrets about youth may feel it is 'too late'.
not_for: An elderly reader full of regret
Someone terminally ill
speaks_to: Someone losing sleep over unfinished or unclean business
A young adult thinking about saving and health
Someone wanting a simple frame for long-term living

mbh.5.36.37.context: Vidura is counselling the sleepless king. After retelling the sage Atreya's teaching to the Sadhyas on not returning insult, he answers Dhritarashtra's question about what makes a family great: good conduct rather than wealth. Then he turns to friendship: one whose anger you fear, or whom you must serve warily, is no friend; a true friend is one you can trust like a father. He adds that a well-wisher, even unrelated, is a real kinsman and refuge.
mbh.5.36.37.core_teaching: A true friend is someone you can trust like a parent; if you fear their anger or must tiptoe around them, it is only an acquaintance.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation (Udyoga XXXVI)
commentaries.gist: In Ganguli's version, someone whose temper you dread, or whom you must serve nervously, is not a friend; the real friend is one you can rely on as on a father, and other ties are friendships in name only.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Kumbakonam 5.36.38; Ganguli XXXVI)
commentaries.gist: The next verse adds that even someone unrelated who behaves as a friend is a true kinsman, refuge and protector; the passage goes on to warn against fickle, ungrateful friends.

mbh.5.36.37.practical_reading: If you are always bracing for someone's temper, that is a sign the relationship is not the friendship it claims to be.
misreadings: Not 'cut off anyone who is ever angry'.
cautions: For a reader being hurt by someone close, this may prompt hard conclusions; pair with support.
not_for: someone without safe alternatives who may feel more trapped by the realisation

mbh.5.36.44.context: Vidura has been speaking about friends (a friend's worth is known only when asked for help). Then this verse against brooding; then: people die and are born again and again, rise and fall, ask and are asked, lament and are lamented; joy and sorrow, gain and loss come by turns, so the steady neither exult nor grieve.
mbh.5.36.44.core_teaching: Brooding costs looks, strength, judgement and health, gets back nothing and pleases one's enemies; so do not hand your mind over to grief.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVI
commentaries.gist: Has sorrow killing beauty, strength and understanding and bringing disease; grief dries up the body, wins nothing and gladdens foes; so do not yield to grief.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt, 36.43-44, gives the same four losses and the same advice not to give way to grief.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 36.42-43. The verses right after (36.44-45) set it within the turning of births, deaths, gains and losses, so the reason given is impermanence, not toughness.

mbh.5.36.44.practical_reading: Teachers use it on rumination and chronic worry: notice what brooding costs your body and mind, and that it changes nothing, then turn to what can be done.
misreadings: Not 'stop grieving' to a bereaved person; it addresses an anxious, brooding king.
cautions: A grief plan must not put this on Day 1: it tells the reader not to grieve and then moves to rebirth (people die and are born again), which can feel dismissive of fresh loss.
Says brooding brings disease; avoid implying that a reader's illness is their fault.
not_for: Fresh bereavement
Someone with clinical depression who cannot 'choose' to stop brooding
Someone whose grief is being policed by others
speaks_to: Someone ruminating over a setback for weeks
An anxious person whose worry is affecting sleep and health

mbh.5.36.5.context: Vidura retells the dialogue of Atreya and the Sadhyas. Atreya's first teaching is to untie the knots of the heart and treat the pleasant and unpleasant alike; then this verse; then do not revile or humiliate others, avoid harsh words that burn the vitals, and be coloured by good company like cloth in dye.
mbh.5.36.5.core_teaching: Do not answer abuse with abuse. The hurt held in by the one who forbears burns the abuser, and the forbearer gains the abuser's merit.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli has Atreya say one should not return slanders: the pain felt by the one who bears silently consumes the slanderer, and the bearer takes over the slanderer's virtues.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt's ch. 36 continues the thought: a wise man pierced by word-arrows should bear them, remembering that the slanderer's good deeds become his.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical text the sage is introduced as wandering in the form of a swan (36.2); the verses after this one forbid reviling, humiliating others, betraying friends and harsh speech.

mbh.5.36.5.practical_reading: Used to break the cycle of retaliation: you do not have to answer an insult, and the restraint itself works in your favour.
misreadings: Not a wish for harm to come to the other person (our misuse note is right).
Not a demand to suppress all feelings; it acknowledges the forbearer's anger (manyu) exists.
cautions: The 'merit transfer' idea is traditional; avoid making it sound like a revenge mechanism.
not_for: Someone in an abusive relationship who needs to leave or report, not endure
speaks_to: Someone insulted and itching to hit back
A person in an online flame war
Someone who wants dignity in a conflict

mbh.5.36.50.context: Dhritarashtra confesses that Yudhishthira, like a flame, has been wronged by him and will destroy his foolish sons in battle; so everything and his own mind are always agitated, and he asks for the unagitated state. Vidura answers with four things and adds: by understanding one drives off fear, by austerity one wins the great, by serving teachers one gains knowledge, by renunciation peace.
mbh.5.36.50.core_teaching: Asked for a mind that is not always anxious, Vidura names learning, austerity, mastery of the senses and the giving up of greed as the only roads to peace.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVI
commentaries.gist: Has Dhritarashtra confess he deceived Yudhishthira and that everything seems fraught with danger; Vidura sees no good for him except in knowledge, asceticism, restraint of the senses and abandoning avarice.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 36.47-50: the confession (36.47) frames the question; Vidura's follow-up (36.50) adds that understanding drives out fear and renunciation brings peace, so greed (keeping the kingdom) is the live issue.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt's ch. 36 continues with Vidura's warning that those at odds with their own kin cannot sleep even on soft beds, which ties the remedy back to making peace with the Pandavas.

mbh.5.36.50.practical_reading: Often used for chronic anxiety in a moral key: some unrest comes from what we are holding onto; learning, discipline and letting go of 'more' are the steady remedies.
misreadings: Not a claim that all anxiety is guilt or greed.
Not a replacement for treatment of an anxiety disorder.
cautions: In context the anxious man is anxious because he did wrong; do not imply that to an anxious reader.
not_for: Someone in acute panic or a mental-health crisis
A reader with anxiety who might hear it as moral blame
speaks_to: Someone whose mind is always restless and who wants a path, not a quick fix
Someone whose anxiety is tied to something they know they must give up or set right

mbh.5.36.62.context: Vidura argues for kinship unity to Dhritarashtra: threads together bear the shuttle, firebrands blaze only when brought together; then the lone tree and the grove; then a single man, however gifted, is thought beatable by enemies; kinsmen grow together like lotus stalks in a lake. The point is that Kauravas and Pandavas need each other.
mbh.5.36.62.core_teaching: A lone tree, however strong, can be torn down by the wind; trees that grow together withstand storms by leaning on each other. So do kin.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVI
commentaries.gist: Has the single tree, though gigantic and deep-rooted, smashed by a mighty wind while trees in close order resist stronger winds by mutual dependence; so too with relatives.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 36.60-62: the next verse applies it directly: enemies think a single man, even a virtuous one, can be uprooted like a lone tree.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt's ch. 36 frames the same image with the threads and firebrands, all arguing that relatives estranged from each other lose sleep and prosperity.

mbh.5.36.62.practical_reading: Used for families, teams and communities: strength is in mutual support, and isolation makes even capable people vulnerable.
misreadings: Not an argument for staying in a harmful family to preserve unity.
cautions: Can sting someone isolated, estranged or without family support.
not_for: Someone who left an abusive family
A lonely or isolated reader who may feel doomed
speaks_to: Siblings or partners in a quarrel
A team leader trying to rebuild cohesion
Someone trying to go it alone and burning out

mbh.5.36.68.context: Vidura has said the sick enjoy nothing, so health matters. Then this verse asking the king to swallow his manyu. Then he reminds Dhritarashtra that he warned him at the dice game to stop Duryodhana, and urges peace with the Pandavas. Earlier (5.27) Dhritarashtra's envoy Sanjaya had pressed the same verse on Yudhishthira, the wronged party, urging him to drop war.
mbh.5.36.68.core_teaching: Resentment is a harsh, sickening drink that leads to wrongdoing; the good swallow it and the bad cannot. Swallow it and be at peace.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVI
commentaries.gist: Calls anger a bitter, pungent, acrid, hot drink and a headache not born of illness that the unwise cannot digest; Vidura asks the king to swallow it and find peace.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation, Udyoga section XXVII (Sanjaya to Yudhishthira)
commentaries.gist: The same image is used earlier by Sanjaya to urge Yudhishthira, the injured party, to swallow his wrath and give up war: the epic shows the advice used by both sides.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 36.66 and 27.23. In ch. 36 it is followed by Vidura recalling his warning at the dice game, so it is aimed at the powerful king's resentment of the Pandavas.

mbh.5.36.68.practical_reading: Teachers use it for anger management: feel the anger, but do not act it out; it hurts the holder first.
misreadings: Swallowing anger means not acting it out, not denying a real hurt (our misuse note).
Not counsel that victims should silently absorb wrongs; Vidura says it to the one holding power.
cautions: The epic itself shows the line being used to pressure a wronged party (Sanjaya to Yudhishthira); be careful offering it to someone who was wronged.
not_for: Someone who has been abused and is just finding their anger
A person being told by others to 'swallow it' about injustice
speaks_to: Someone in a position of power nursing a grudge
A person who acts out anger and regrets it
Someone with a long-running resentment toward a relative

mbh.5.37.10.context: Dhritarashtra asks why, if the Vedas promise a span of a hundred years, people do not reach it. Vidura answers with these six 'sharp swords'; he then lists grave sinners (one who violates a trusting friend's wife, etc.) whom the messengers of death drag away.
mbh.5.37.10.core_teaching: Arrogance, overtalking, meanness, anger, self-seeking and betraying friends are the real swords that cut life short; it is these, Vidura says, and not death, that kill.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVII
commentaries.gist: Has Dhritarashtra ask why men fall short of the Vedic hundred years; Vidura names six sharp swords (in Ganguli's text excess of pride, of speech, of eating, anger, desire of enjoyment, internal dissension) that kill, not death.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (37.10-11) gives too much pride, too much talk, lack of restraint, anger, quarrels with relations and enmity with friends; the different lists show the verse varied across manuscripts.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 37.8-10: Dhritarashtra's question (37.8) and Vidura's answer; the BORI list matches ours except 'ativivitsā' for 'ātmavidhitsā'.

mbh.5.37.10.practical_reading: Teachers read it as 'how we shorten our own lives': not literally, but by the corrosion of pride, anger and broken trust on health and relationships.
misreadings: Not a claim that anyone who died young had these faults.
cautions: Must not reach a bereaved reader: 'these, not death, kill people' can imply the person who died was at fault.
Literal health claims should not be drawn from it.
not_for: Anyone recently bereaved, especially of a young person
Someone seriously ill
speaks_to: Someone noticing anger or arrogance damaging their health and relationships
A person tempted to betray a friend's trust

mbh.5.37.46.context: Vidura warns Dhritarashtra that the wrath of Bhishma, Drona and Yudhishthira could burn the world, while together his hundred sons, Karna and the Pandavas could rule the earth. He says the Dhartarashtras are a forest and the Pandavas its tigers: do not cut down the forest with its tigers. Then this verse.
mbh.5.37.46.core_teaching: Forest and tiger protect each other: without the forest the tigers are exposed, without the tigers the forest is cut down. The two branches of the family need each other.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVII
commentaries.gist: Vidura names the Dhartarashtras the forest and the Pandavas its tigers, begs the king not to cut the forest down or drive the tigers out, and states the mutual protection.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (37.45-46) has the same image: do not cut down the forest with the tigers, or drive the tigers away to be killed; each protects the other.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 37.41-42. A related image occurs earlier in BORI 5.29.48 (a tiger without forest is killed, a forest without tiger is felled), showing it was a stock political proverb.

mbh.5.37.46.practical_reading: Used for family businesses, partners and rival departments: the side you want to cut away may be the one protecting you.
misreadings: Not an argument that every family conflict must be kept together at any cost.
cautions: If one 'side' in a family is abusive, the mutual-protection frame can pressure the harmed side to stay.
not_for: Someone who left an abusive family member
speaks_to: Siblings or co-founders in a feud
A family where one branch wants to cut off another
Rival teams who depend on each other

mbh.5.37.51.context: Vidura says one who follows dharma, artha and kama each in season gains all three; then this verse on reining in anger and elation; then he lists the five kinds of strength, of which strength of arm is the least.
mbh.5.37.51.core_teaching: Whoever can check the first rush of anger and of excitement, and keeps his head in misfortune, becomes a fit vessel for good fortune.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVII
commentaries.gist: Gives it as: one who restrains the force of both anger and joy and never loses his senses in calamities wins prosperity.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (37.51) says whoever restrains the force that rises from anger and from joy wins prosperity, as does one who keeps his wits in distress.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 37.47, same reading. It is followed by the five strengths (37.48-52): arms, good advisers, wealth, birth, and above all wisdom, so the restraint is presented as the base of real power.

mbh.5.37.51.practical_reading: Teachers stress the pairing: elation can mislead as much as anger, so pause on both before deciding or spending.
misreadings: Not a call to suppress joy; it is about not acting on the first surge.
cautions: Mild verse; few risks.
not_for: A depressed reader for whom any joy is rare and should not be dampened
speaks_to: Someone who makes rash decisions when excited or angry
A person newly successful who wants to stay steady
Someone facing a crisis who needs calm

mbh.5.38.16.context: Vidura on mantra (state counsel): the king whose counsels are unknown to outsiders and insiders enjoys power long (38.15); then this verse; then counsel should be taken on a hilltop, palace terrace or treeless wilderness, and not shared with an unwise friend or a wise but undisciplined one.
mbh.5.38.16.core_teaching: Do not announce what you are about to do; let only finished acts be seen. That way plans concerning duty, pleasure or gain are not leaked.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVIII
commentaries.gist: Renders it as never speaking of what one intends to do, letting whatever one does in virtue, profit and desire be unknown until done, so that counsels are not divulged.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (38.16-17) gives the king's secrecy rule: do not speak of what you intend, and do not let others know plans made for virtue, gain or pleasure; consult in a lonely place.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 38.15-18 shows the setting is statecraft secrecy: where to hold counsel, and whom not to trust with it, rather than personal modesty.

mbh.5.38.16.practical_reading: Modern teachers apply it to goals and projects: work quietly, let results speak, and avoid the false satisfaction (and exposure) of announcing plans too early.
misreadings: Not a rule for secrecy in relationships where openness builds trust.
Not a ban on asking for advice; Vidura elsewhere says to consult the wise.
cautions: For someone whose isolation is part of the problem, 'keep plans to yourself' may reinforce it.
not_for: Someone hiding plans from a partner or family in a way that erodes trust
A person in recovery who needs accountability partners
speaks_to: Someone who announces goals and then stalls
People who seek validation before doing the work

mbh.5.39.2.context: Dhritarashtra has just said man is like a wooden puppet on strings, subject to destiny, and asks Vidura to go on. Vidura replies that even Brihaspati, speaking out of season, earns contempt; then one becomes dear by gifts or sweet words; and then he reminds the king that he told him at Duryodhana's birth to give that son up.
mbh.5.39.2.core_teaching: Even the wisest words are despised if spoken before their time; timing is part of wisdom.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIX
commentaries.gist: Has Vidura reply to the king's 'puppet of destiny' complaint: speaking out of season, even Brihaspati incurs reproach and the charge of ignorance.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (39.2) gives the same: even Vrihaspati speaking before the right time is charged with ignorance and insulted.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 39.1-4: Dhritarashtra's fatalism (39.1) is the trigger, and the verses after note that people attribute good to those they love and evil to those they hate, which is why Vidura's advice has gone unheard.

mbh.5.39.2.practical_reading: Used for feedback and hard conversations: the right message at the wrong moment is often wasted; choose the time as carefully as the words.
misreadings: Not a reason never to speak an unwelcome truth; Vidura himself keeps speaking it.
cautions: A person whose valid warning was ignored may feel blamed for 'bad timing'.
not_for: A whistleblower or survivor told their disclosure was 'badly timed'
speaks_to: A professional whose good ideas keep being dismissed

mbh.5.39.51.context: Vidura on choosing friends: the wise do not befriend the proud, ignorant, fierce, rash or unrighteous (39.36); then this list of who is wanted as a friend; then the senses, neither starved nor indulged.
mbh.5.39.51.core_teaching: Everyone wants a friend who is grateful, principled, truthful, generous, loyal, self-controlled and steady.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIX
commentaries.gist: Gives the desirable friend as grateful, virtuous, truthful, large-hearted, devoted, master of his senses, keeping his dignity and never forsaking a friend.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (39.50-51) sets the list after a warning against friendship with the proud, ignorant, fierce and rash: the grateful, virtuous, truthful, generous, devoted and self-controlled are the friends to seek.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 39.36-37: the verse is the positive pair of the warning against befriending the proud, foolish, fierce and rash.

mbh.5.39.51.practical_reading: Used as a mirror for friendship: the qualities we want in friends are the ones to cultivate in ourselves.
misreadings: Not a test to drop friends who fall short; it is an ideal.
cautions: Lonely readers may feel this is a standard they or their friends fail.
not_for: A very lonely reader without friends right now
speaks_to: Someone who wants to be a better friend

mbh.5.39.56.context: Vidura on success: the person who knows remedies for the future, is resolute in the present and learns from the past does not fail (39.41); then this verse; then auspiciousness, effort, learning, initiative and the frequent company of good people bring prosperity, and perseverance is its root.
mbh.5.39.56.core_teaching: What a person does repeatedly in deed, thought and word takes possession of him; so make the good your habit.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIX
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: whatever a man pursues in word, deed and thought wins him for its own, so he should always pursue his good.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (39.55-56): whatever a man pursues in deed, thought or speech draws him to itself, so one should follow a virtuous course.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 39.42; the following verses name the habits that bring flourishing (39.43) and say perseverance is the root of prosperity (39.44), so this is a teaching on habit formation.

mbh.5.39.56.practical_reading: A favourite verse on habit: you become what you practise, so small repeated good acts, thoughts and words shape character.
misreadings: Not a claim that intrusive thoughts make you bad; it is about what one chooses to dwell on and do.
cautions: People with OCD or intrusive thoughts may fear their thoughts 'take them over'; frame as chosen habits.
not_for: A reader with OCD-type intrusive thoughts if framed as thought-policing
speaks_to: A person trying to change what they dwell on

mbh.5.39.6.context: Immediately before, Vidura reminds Dhritarashtra: when Duryodhana was born, I told you to give up this one son; by giving him up your hundred sons would prosper, by keeping him they would perish. Then this verse; then 'that is no loss which brings gain; the real loss is what, once gained, destroys much'.
mbh.5.39.6.core_teaching: Judge a gain or a loss by what it leads to: a gain that brings ruin is not worth prizing, and a loss that brings growth is.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIX
commentaries.gist: Places the maxim right after Vidura's reminder that he urged the king to abandon Duryodhana at birth to save his hundred sons; a gain leading to loss should not be prized, a loss bringing gain should.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (39.5-7) gives the same sequence: abandon this one son for the hundred; then the maxim, and that true loss is what, once obtained, causes much loss.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical edition the Duryodhana recollection and this maxim are both in the apparatus (*231); the constituted text keeps only 39.5 ('that is no loss which brings gain'), still in the same argument.

mbh.5.39.6.practical_reading: Used in planning and ethics: a short-term gain that damages health, relationships or integrity is a loss; a sacrifice that clears the way to growth is a gain.
misreadings: Not a general warrant to cut people off; in its context it argues for abandoning a child, which modern readers should not draw from it.
cautions: Context is a father being told to abandon his newborn son. Do not use with parents of difficult children, estranged children, or anyone considering cutting off a family member.
Not for grief: the 'loss that brings gain' frame is wrong for a death.
not_for: Parents struggling with a difficult child
Anyone grieving a death or pregnancy loss
Someone pressured to cut off a family member
speaks_to: Someone weighing a lucrative job that costs their health or values
A person deciding to give up a habit, deal or role that looks like a gain

mbh.5.39.63.context: Vidura is counselling the anxious, sleepless king. This verse sits in a list of people with whom Prosperity (Shri) does not stay: the grief-stricken, the idle, the uncontrolled, and the straightforward and modest person whom dull minds mistake for weak and bully. Nearby Vidura also says perseverance is the root of prosperity and that forgiveness is fitting for the strong and the weak alike.
mbh.5.39.63.core_teaching: Small-minded people misread straightforwardness and modesty as weakness, and try to exploit it.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli, translation (Udyoga XXXIX)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as the humble and modest man being regarded as weak and persecuted by people of misdirected intelligence, in a passage about whom Prosperity avoids.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Kumbakonam 5.39; Ganguli XXXIX)
commentaries.gist: The same discourse praises perseverance as the root of prosperity and says forgiveness suits both the powerful and the weak; it describes how the world behaves rather than telling the honest to change.

mbh.5.39.63.practical_reading: If your honesty or modesty is being taken advantage of, the problem is the misreading, not the virtue; keep it, and add firmness.
misreadings: Not advice to stop being straightforward; it names a risk.
Not a reason to become suspicious of everyone.
cautions: As a descriptive line it can confirm a reader's bitterness; pair it with an action (a boundary) rather than leaving it as 'people are cruel'.
not_for: someone already prone to seeing others as enemies
speaks_to: being passed over because you don't self-promote

mbh.5.40.12.context: After lists of auspicious things to keep at home, Vidura says he will give the king his highest teaching: never abandon dharma for desire, fear, greed, or even to save one's life. He follows it with: dharma is eternal, pleasure and pain are passing; and with the deaths of great kings who left everything behind.
mbh.5.40.12.core_teaching: The highest counsel: never give up what is right, whether out of desire, fear or greed, not even to save your life.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XL
commentaries.gist: Calls it the highest of all teachings: virtue should never be forsaken from desire, fear or temptation, nor for life itself; virtue is everlasting, pleasure and pain transitory.

commentaries.who: Bharata Savitri, Svargarohana Parva 18.5.50 (BORI e-text)
commentaries.gist: The same words reappear in the four closing verses Vyasa is said to have taught Shuka, which the epic says one should recite at dawn: the epic's own summary of its message.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In ch. 40 the critical text follows it (40.12) with dharma as eternal, pleasure and pain as passing, and an exhortation to stand in the eternal and be content.

mbh.5.40.12.practical_reading: Used as a personal anchor: under pressure from desire, fear or money, ask what is right and hold to it.
misreadings: Not a demand that someone in danger refuse to compromise to survive.
cautions: 'Not even for your life' is absolute; a reader who lied or complied to stay safe (abuse, coercion) should not hear it as condemnation.
Can feed scrupulosity in anxious readers.
not_for: A survivor who had to comply or lie to stay safe
A reader with scrupulosity/religious OCD
speaks_to: Someone under pressure to do something wrong at work
A person tempted to compromise integrity for money or approval
Someone who wants one guiding principle

mbh.5.40.18.context: Vidura describes death plainly: kings who ruled great lands are gone; a son raised with care is carried to the pyre by weeping relatives and burnt like wood; others enjoy his wealth, birds and fire his body; only merit and sin go with him; kin turn back like birds from a tree without fruit. Then this verse.
mbh.5.40.18.core_teaching: At death everyone else turns back; only one's own deeds go along. So gather goodness carefully, a little at a time.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XL
commentaries.gist: After the image of the dead son carried to the pyre and relatives turning back like birds from a fruitless tree, says only one's own acts follow, so merit should be earned carefully and gradually.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (40.15-18) gives the same funeral scene: the body thrown on the pyre like wood, wealth enjoyed by others, only virtue and sin accompanying the dead.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical text only the first line is constituted (40.16cd); the exhortation to gather dharma slowly is in the apparatus. The tree-and-birds simile beside it is also an addition (*241), echoing Yudhishthira at 5.70.20.

mbh.5.40.18.practical_reading: Used to turn attention from possessions to conduct: small daily goodness is the only thing that is truly ours.
misreadings: Not saying relatives' love does not matter; it is about what accompanies the self.
cautions: The surrounding passage describes a son's body being burnt on the pyre; extremely painful for bereaved parents.
Rebirth and karma framing can feel cold to fresh grief.
not_for: Anyone recently bereaved, especially parents who lost a child
Someone with health anxiety or fear of death
speaks_to: Someone re-evaluating priorities after a wake-up call
A person chasing possessions who wants perspective

mbh.5.40.2.context: Opening of Vidura's last chapter of counsel. He has just said the good, when pleased, give happiness; then this verse; then lists sins equal to killing a brahmin (victory by lies, deceit toward the king, insincerity before a teacher).
mbh.5.40.2.core_teaching: Whoever gives up even a great gain that is tainted with wrong, of his own accord, sleeps at ease, rid of sorrows as a snake sheds its old skin.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XL
commentaries.gist: Has the one who forsakes of his own accord a great object because it is unrighteous live happily, casting off foes like a snake its slough.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (40.2) reads it as giving up, without any outside pressure, a great object tainted by unrighteousness, and resting happily like a snake casting off its worn-out skin.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 40.2. Addressed to a king who has just said he cannot sleep and who is holding a kingdom that is not his; 'sleeps at ease' answers his insomnia directly.

mbh.5.40.2.practical_reading: Used for ethical decisions at work and in money: walking away from a tainted deal brings a relief that keeping it never does.
misreadings: Not a promise that giving up the gain costs nothing.
cautions: Someone who already took a tainted gain may feel condemned; the verse still points to release.
not_for: A person in poverty for whom 'walk away from money' sounds glib
speaks_to: Someone tempted by a lucrative but dishonest opportunity
A person losing sleep over money or property they know isn't rightly theirs

mbh.5.40.22.context: Just before, Vidura calls the self a river whose holy ford is merit, water truth, banks steadiness and waves self-restraint; bathing there purifies. Then this second river image. After it: consult elders when unsure, and guard the body with steadiness.
mbh.5.40.22.core_teaching: Life is a river of the senses with desire and anger lurking like crocodiles; build a boat of steadiness and cross its dangerous passages.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XL
commentaries.gist: Calls life a river whose waters are the five senses and whose crocodiles and sharks are desire and anger; make self-control your raft and cross the eddies of repeated births.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (40.21-22) also pairs the two rivers: the soul as a holy river of truth and self-control, then self-control as the boat across the river of the senses and its monsters of desire and anger, beyond repeated births.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 40.19-20 pairs two rivers: the self as a holy river to bathe in (truth, steadiness, restraint) and the senses as a dangerous river to cross.

mbh.5.40.22.practical_reading: Used for impulse control: the senses keep moving like water; desire and anger are the real dangers; steadiness is the vessel, built in calm times.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of the senses themselves; they are the water one has to cross, not an enemy.
cautions: The crossing is of repeated births; keep the rebirth frame light for readers who do not share it.
not_for: Someone grieving who may hear 'cross the river' as about death
speaks_to: Someone struggling with cravings or temper
A person in a turbulent period needing a steadying image

mbh.5.40.23.context: Right after the river images, Vidura tells Dhritarashtra to honour and consult a kinsman ripe in wisdom, dharma, learning and years. The irony is plain: Vidura is that kinsman, and at the end of the chapter Dhritarashtra admits he agrees with him but turns the other way whenever he is with Duryodhana.
mbh.5.40.23.core_teaching: Whoever honours a kinsman mature in wisdom, goodness, learning and years, wins his goodwill and asks him what should and should not be done, is never confused.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XL
commentaries.gist: Has the one who worships and gratifies friends eminent in wisdom, virtue, learning and years, and asks their advice, never misled; the chapter ends with Dhritarashtra admitting he turns away from such advice when near Duryodhana.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (40.23) has friends 'old' in wisdom, virtue, knowledge and age, honoured and then asked what to do and not do; such a person is seldom deceived.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 40.21; the next verses on guarding the body by steadiness, the eyes, the mind and action show it as part of a discipline, not only deference.

mbh.5.40.23.practical_reading: Used to encourage seeking mentors: approach them with respect, ask clearly about what to do and not do, and then actually listen.
misreadings: Not 'always obey elders'; it is about seeking counsel from those mature in wisdom and goodness, not just age.
cautions: Someone harmed by an elder relative may find 'honour the elder kinsman' painful.
not_for: A person whose elder relatives are controlling or abusive
speaks_to: A young professional looking for a mentor
Someone who asks for advice but never follows it

mbh.5.42.13.context: Sanatsujata has just shown death unfolding as brooding on objects, then desire, then anger, and said that the wise cross death by steadiness. This verse states the rule; the next calls desire darkness and a hell in which people run headlong like drunk men toward a pit.
mbh.5.42.13.core_teaching: Whoever follows desires goes down with them; whoever puts them aside shakes off whatever stain clings to him.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, Sanatsujatiya (SBE 8, 1882), notes drawing on Shankara and Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: Telang notes Nilakantha's gloss on being destroyed by desire with the old image of five creatures each ruined by one sense; for the 'taint' shaken off, Shankara says merit and sin, Nilakantha says misery.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XLII
commentaries.gist: Gives it as: the follower of desires is destroyed with them, while the one who renounces desire drives away every kind of woe; desire is darkness and hell for creatures.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (42.13) reads 'destroyed soon after the desires', i.e. the person outlives his pleasures only to fall with them.

mbh.5.42.13.practical_reading: Used for compulsive wanting: chasing every urge drains the person, while consciously dropping one desire leaves a felt lightness, like dust shaken off.
misreadings: Not a rejection of all wanting or of ordinary enjoyment; the target is being led by desire.
Not a promise that renouncing desire fixes every outer problem.
cautions: Can feel shaming to someone struggling with addiction; pair with compassion and practical help.
not_for: Someone in recovery who already feels guilt-ridden and needs encouragement, not a warning
speaks_to: Someone caught in a cycle of craving, shopping, scrolling or comfort habits
A person who keeps getting what they want and still feels empty

mbh.5.42.35.context: Sanatsujata is describing the true brahmana, who lives unknown among kin and does not mistake the inner self, which is without marks, unmoving and pure, for something else. The verse calls such a mistake theft of the self. The same couplet in the Adi Parva is Shakuntala's rebuke to King Dushyanta, who pretends not to know her.
mbh.5.42.35.core_teaching: To take oneself for something other than one really is, is a theft of the self, the root from which every other wrong can follow.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, Sanatsujatiya (SBE 8, 1882), notes drawing on Shankara and Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: Telang's notes, from Shankara, read it of the inner self wrongly identified with the body and senses; he compares the Isha Upanishad's 'slayers of the self'.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XLII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli makes it doctrinal: one who regards the soul as the acting and enjoying self robs the soul of its true nature.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt's Udyoga (42.36) also reads it doctrinally, of one who thinks heaven is won by ritual action alone; in his Adi Parva, Shakuntala uses it of a man who thinks one thing and shows another.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical edition places the couplet in the main text only in Shakuntala's speech (1.68.26), after she tells the king his heart is witness to truth and falsehood; in Udyoga it survives as a manuscript insertion.

mbh.5.42.35.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to authenticity: living a false front, or denying what one knows to be true, costs the person their own self first.
misreadings: Not a licence to judge people who mask for safety (e.g. at an unsafe workplace or home).
In its Udyoga setting it is about self-knowledge, not social honesty; do not present the social sense as Sanatsujata's meaning.
cautions: 'Thief' and 'sin' are harsh words for someone who hides parts of themselves out of fear (identity, illness, trauma).
not_for: Someone who conceals an identity or history for their safety
Someone with impostor feelings who would hear it as an accusation
speaks_to: Someone tired of performing a role that isn't them
A person who knows the truth of a situation but is denying it

mbh.5.42.4.context: Vidura, a shudra by birth, declines to teach about death and the self and calls the ancient sage Sanatsujata to answer the sleepless king. Dhritarashtra has heard that Sanatsujata teaches there is no death, yet gods and demons practised austerity to escape it; which is true? This verse is the opening answer, followed by: the demons fell by heedlessness, the gods became Brahman by heedfulness, and death does not eat creatures like a tiger.
mbh.5.42.4.core_teaching: Death in the sense that matters is not the end of the body but heedlessness, falling away from awareness of one's real self; staying awake to it is the deathless state.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, Sanatsujatiya (SBE 8, 1882), notes drawing on Shankara and Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: Telang reports Shankara: Sanatsujata sets his own view beside 'the wise'; delusion means taking the not-self for the self, and heedlessness means falling from one's natural condition as Brahman, the root of that delusion.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XLII
commentaries.gist: Renders the key terms as ignorance and its absence: the learned call ignorance death, and freedom from ignorance is immortality; demons fell through it, gods reached Brahman by its absence.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (42.4-6) likewise makes ignorance the great death, adds that Yama is one kind of death, and that pursuing self-knowledge is immortality.

mbh.5.42.4.practical_reading: Teachers read it as a call to wakefulness: much of what we fear as 'death' is already happening when we live on autopilot, and attention to what we really are is the remedy.
misreadings: Not a denial that the body dies or a reason to dismiss someone's fear of dying.
'Heedlessness' here is spiritual forgetfulness, not ordinary carelessness or a productivity lapse.
cautions: About death throughout; for a reader facing a terminal diagnosis or fresh bereavement, 'death is only heedlessness' can sound like it waves away real loss.
not_for: Someone newly bereaved
Someone facing a serious illness who needs comfort, not a redefinition of death
speaks_to: Someone feeling they are sleepwalking through life
A reader drawn to contemplative practice and mindfulness
Someone anxious about mortality in a general, philosophical way

mbh.5.43.61.context: Dhritarashtra asks what mauna (silence, the sage's discipline) is, and whether one reaches the highest by it. Sanatsujata answers that the Self is itself called mauna because neither Veda nor mind reaches it, then says one should seek it within, sit quiet without even wishing, and only then gives this verse. Next he plays on 'vaiyākaraṇa': one who analyses all things from their root.
mbh.5.43.61.core_teaching: Outer silence or retreat does not make one a sage; knowledge of one's real nature, the Imperishable, does. In the critical reading, true mauna is itself that knowledge.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, Sanatsujatiya (SBE 8, 1882), notes drawing on Shankara and Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: Telang's text says one becomes a sage by mauna, not by forest life; he notes Shankara elsewhere glosses mauna as the end of all sense of anything other than the self, and that 'forest' is not unimportant either.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XLIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli, on the vulgate, says one is not a muni by yoga-meditation alone or by living in the woods; whoever knows his own nature is the best of munis.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text (43.33-35): search for it within, sit silent without stirring even the mind, and Brahman turns toward you; then the verse, with 'by mauna one becomes a muni'.

mbh.5.43.61.practical_reading: Used against spiritual window-dressing: retreats, silence and quitting the world are means, not proof; the test is self-knowledge carried into ordinary life.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of silence, retreat or meditation practice, which the same passage recommends.
Not 'you can be wise without any discipline'.
cautions: Reading variant reverses the first half; avoid putting a strong anti-silence claim in Sanatsujata's mouth.
not_for: Someone who needs silence and rest for their mental health and could hear it as 'that's useless'
speaks_to: Someone who thinks they must quit their life or go on retreat to grow
A meditator wondering whether practice is becoming performance

data_flags.translation_note: Reading conflict. Our text (Wikisource vulgate) reads 'maunān na sa munir bhavati ... svalakṣaṇaṃ tu yo veda', 'not by silence ... who knows his own nature'. The BORI critical text and Telang (following Shankara's text) read 'maunād dhi sa munir bhavati ... akṣaraṃ tat tu...

mbh.5.71.26.context: Sanjaya has left; Yudhishthira opens his heart to Krishna. He has asked for only five villages and Duryodhana refuses even those. He then diagnoses Duryodhana's greed as a chain of losses, and moves straight on to what poverty does to a person, which is his own situation.
mbh.5.71.26.core_teaching: Coveting what belongs to others sets off a chain: greed destroys judgement, then the sense of shame, then right conduct, then fortune, and finally the person.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXII
commentaries.gist: Follows the same steps: avarice destroys intelligence, shame is then lost, virtue declines, prosperity goes, and poverty is a person's death.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (72.19-20) makes the subject a man of noble family who still wants others' wealth, and ends the chain with poverty as death.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 70.16-19: Yudhishthira's request for five villages, Duryodhana's refusal while claiming all as his own, then this chain.

mbh.5.71.26.practical_reading: Used as a warning about small compromises: the first loss is clear thinking, and the rest follows quietly.
misreadings: Not a statement that the poor are morally fallen; the chain begins with greed, and in context the speaker is the one dispossessed.
cautions: Ends in 'poverty is death', which can wound a reader in financial hardship; omit or frame it.
not_for: A reader in financial distress who might hear 'loss of wealth destroys the person'
speaks_to: Someone tempted to cut a corner for money
Someone watching a colleague or relative slide through greed

mbh.5.71.28.context: Directly after the greed chain, Yudhishthira turns to his own case: the dispossessed are shunned. He goes on to say this shunning feels like death, that some in poverty choose death, exile, madness or servitude, and that wealth supports both dharma and pleasure.
mbh.5.71.28.core_teaching: When someone loses their means, relatives, friends and even priests drift away from them, as birds leave a tree that no longer flowers or fruits.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXII
commentaries.gist: Kinsmen, friends and Brahmanas shun a poor man as birds avoid a tree with no flower or fruit; Yudhishthira adds that being shunned so feels to him like death.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (72.21) keeps the image of cousins, friends and Brahmanas turning away from one stricken with poverty.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 70.20-26 continues with being shunned as like death, and the desperate paths the poor are driven to.

mbh.5.71.28.practical_reading: Read as an honest naming of a painful social fact: support can thin out when you are no longer useful, and that says more about the birds than the tree.
misreadings: Not advice to value people by what they can give.
Not a claim that all friends are fair-weather.
cautions: The surrounding verses (not ours) speak of people choosing death in poverty; do not quote them to someone in crisis.
not_for: Someone in acute financial crisis with suicidal thoughts (the context dwells on death)
speaks_to: Someone who lost a job or business and noticed people falling away
A person learning who their real friends are

mbh.5.71.37.context: Yudhishthira has said that natural death is the common road no one escapes, but loss of fortune is worse than death. Then this comparison, and after it a portrait of the man who falls from comfort: blaming the gods, raging at servants, envying friends, sinking into delusion and cruelty.
mbh.5.71.37.core_teaching: Someone born poor is not hurt as much as someone who had good fortune, grew up in ease, and then lost it.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXII
commentaries.gist: One poor from birth is less distressed than one raised in luxury who is then stripped of prosperity.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (72.30) has the same contrast between lifelong want and loss after great prosperity and happiness.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 70.27-32 frames it: loss of fortune is worse than death, and it is followed by the fallen man's slide into anger and cruelty.

mbh.5.71.37.practical_reading: Used to validate the particular pain of downward change (job loss, divorce, displacement): it is real, and comparing yourself with those who never had it does not cancel it.
misreadings: Not a ranking that dismisses the suffering of those born poor.
The verse observes pain; it does not by itself prescribe self-compassion (that is our line's addition).
cautions: The next verses describe how such a person turns bitter; avoid pairing it with 5.71.38 for a reader in fresh loss.
not_for: A reader who grew up poor, who may feel their hardship minimised
speaks_to: Someone whose family or business has fallen on hard times
An expat or migrant who lost status
Someone after divorce or a layoff adjusting to less

mbh.5.71.38.context: Part of Yudhishthira's portrait of the man who fell from comfort through his own fault: he blames the gods, no scripture eases him, he lashes out at servants and friends, then anger and confusion lead him to cruelty. Yudhishthira is speaking of the general case, with his own family's fall in the background.
mbh.5.71.38.core_teaching: One who falls into ruin through his own fault blames the gods and fate, and never himself; that refusal starts a further slide into anger and harm.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXII
commentaries.gist: Such a person blames the gods with Indra (and, in Ganguli's wording, himself); scripture does not soothe him, and he turns angry with servants and spiteful to well-wishers.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (72.31) says he blames the gods with Indra and rarely himself.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 70.30-32 continues: anger comes, then confusion, then cruel acts.

mbh.5.71.38.practical_reading: Used as a mirror for honest self-review after a setback: ask what was in my control before blaming luck, God or others.
misreadings: Not a claim that all misfortune is self-caused; the verse is about trouble that came 'through his own fault'.
Not for telling someone else their suffering is their fault.
cautions: Sharp if aimed at a reader in pain; can sound like victim-blaming.
not_for: Someone grieving or suffering through no fault of their own
Survivors of abuse or disaster
speaks_to: Someone ready to take responsibility after a mistake
A reader stuck in blaming others for a setback

mbh.5.71.67.context: Yudhishthira is weighing war. He says defeat is no better than death, the victor also loses, the brave and decent are the ones killed, and the survivor regathers strength and seeks to wipe out the winner. Then this verse; after it, the man with enemies sleeps as if with a snake in the house.
mbh.5.71.67.core_teaching: Victory breeds enmity and defeat breeds misery; only the one who has let go of winning and losing sleeps in peace.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXII
commentaries.gist: The survivor seeks to destroy the victor; victory creates animosity, the defeated lives in sorrow, the peaceful sleeps happily, while the one who provoked hostility sleeps as if sharing a room with a snake.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (72.60-61) has the same sequence and the same sleep contrast.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 70.54-61 shows the reasoning: both sides lose, the decent die, and the exterminator earns lasting infamy.

commentaries.who: Parallel: Dhammapada 201 (Sukhavagga, Thanissaro tr.)
commentaries.gist: A near-identical Buddhist verse: winning breeds hostility, the loser lies in pain, and the calmed one sleeps easily, having left victory and defeat.

mbh.5.71.67.practical_reading: Used for rivalry, office politics and family disputes: keeping score keeps you awake; stepping out of the win-lose frame is what lets you rest.
misreadings: Not an argument that nothing is worth standing up for; the Pandavas' peace offer is refused and the epic then judges the war just.
Not advice to let an abuser 'win'.
cautions: The surrounding speech is about war and killing; keep the reading on everyday conflict.
not_for: Someone being harmed who needs to protect themselves, who might hear 'just stop fighting'
speaks_to: Someone stuck in a long-running quarrel
A competitive person who can't switch off
Someone losing sleep over a workplace rivalry

mbh.5.71.71.context: Yudhishthira says long feuds never die because someone always survives in the family and someone is always there to retell the wrong. Then this verse. He goes on that, short of exterminating the enemy, which would be crueller, peace comes only by giving something up, and he chooses to seek peace through Krishna's embassy.
mbh.5.71.71.core_teaching: Hostility is never ended by more hostility; like fire fed with ghee, it only grows.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXII
commentaries.gist: As long as one of the enemy's family lives, there are narrators to remind him of the past; enmity is not ended by enmity but fed by it, like fire by clarified butter.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (72.64-65) has the same image and, like Ganguli, reads the following line as saying peace otherwise comes only by total annihilation.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 70.62-66 adds that the alternative, cutting the enemy off at the root, is crueller, so Yudhishthira prefers renouncing his claim to that.

commentaries.who: Parallel: Dhammapada 5 (Yamakavagga, Thanissaro tr.)
commentaries.gist: The Buddhist parallel: hostilities are never stilled by hostility, only by non-hostility, an unending truth; brooding on wrongs keeps them alive.

mbh.5.71.71.practical_reading: Used for retaliation spirals in families, workplaces and online: each response feeds the fire; someone has to stop adding fuel.
misreadings: Not a demand to pretend the wrong never happened (our misuse note is right).
In the epic, peace is offered and refused and a righteous war follows; the verse is not pacifism at any price.
cautions: Someone in an abusive situation should not be told that resisting is 'adding fuel'.
not_for: A victim of ongoing abuse who needs to set firm boundaries or seek justice
speaks_to: A person in a long family feud
Someone hurt by a public argument that keeps escalating

mbh.5.71.92.context: Krishna has offered to go as envoy to Hastinapura. Yudhishthira objects that Duryodhana will not heed even good advice and the assembled kings are his men, so he does not want Krishna walking into their midst. Krishna replies that he knows Duryodhana's wickedness, that by going they escape the world's blame, and that no assembly of kings can stand before him if they try to harm him.
mbh.5.71.92.core_teaching: Nothing, not wealth, not godhood, not sovereignty over the gods, is worth a friend's safety; Yudhishthira would rather lose the gain than risk Krishna.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXII
commentaries.gist: Yudhishthira does not want Krishna among the Kshatriyas obedient to Duryodhana: if any mischief were done to him, neither happiness nor godhood nor sovereignty over the gods would delight them.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (72.83-85) has the same objection and the same condition, 'if any ill happens to you'.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 70.82-86 reads 'rodhena' (by your detention) and gives Krishna's reply that the kings could not stand before him.

mbh.5.71.92.practical_reading: Used for loyalty in friendship: a person who loves you will not trade your safety for their goal.
misreadings: It is not about betrayal; it is about fear for a friend's safety.
Not a reason to block a friend's own brave choice; Yudhishthira voices his fear, then lets Krishna go.
cautions: Current translation and line state something the verse does not say; correct before use.
not_for: Someone using concern to control a partner's choices
speaks_to: Someone worried about a loved one taking a risk for them
A reader reflecting on what they would not trade for success

data_flags.translation_note: MISREAD. 'tava droheṇa' (BORI 'tava rodhena') here means 'with harm (or confinement) coming to you', not 'by betraying you'. Yudhishthira is begging Krishna not to go to the hostile Kaurava court, because no gain, not even godhood or lordship of the gods, would please the...

mbh.5.81.26.context: After Yudhishthira's peaceable words and Bhima's turn toward peace, Draupadi, in tears, reminds Krishna who she is: Drupada's daughter, his dear friend, wife of five heroes, yet dragged into the hall by the hair and treated as a slave while her husbands lived. This verse recalls her silent cry. She then recalls Dhritarashtra's boon freeing the Pandavas, curses the strength of Bhima and Arjuna while Duryodhana lives, and asks Krishna to turn his anger on the Kauravas.
mbh.5.81.26.core_teaching: Abandoned by those who should have defended her, Draupadi turned inwardly to Krishna for protection; she recalls it now so that peace does not erase that wrong.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXXII
commentaries.gist: When the Pandavas sat silent without wrath, she called on Govinda in her heart, 'save me'; the speech opens with her grief at the talk of peace.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (82.26) gives the same scene: the sons of Pandu gazed at her without wrath or effort to free her, and she thought of Govinda.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 80.20-32: her lineage, the hair-dragging, this verse, the boon, her curse on her husbands' strength, and her plea that Krishna's anger fall on the Kauravas.

mbh.5.81.26.practical_reading: Teachers use it for the moment of abandonment: when people who should act only watch, one can still reach for an inner refuge, and later name what happened.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of silent endurance; her speech is a demand that the wrong be answered (our misuse note is right).
Not a story about the sari miracle; this text does not mention it.
cautions: Recalls sexual humiliation and public assault; can trigger survivors. Avoid for readers disclosing abuse unless the reading centres their voice and safety.
not_for: A reader in a current abusive situation (needs practical safety guidance, not a devotional reframe)
speaks_to: Someone let down by family who stood by while they were mistreated
A person who prayed in a moment of helplessness
Someone whose pain is being smoothed over in the name of peace

mbh.5.95.46.context: In the Kuru assembly Krishna, addressing Dhritarashtra, delivers the Pandavas' message: they kept the exile pact trusting him as a father, now he must keep it too. This verse asks for reciprocal conduct; the next asks him to set them on the right path and keep to his own. Then Krishna turns to the assembly with the Pandavas' charge that onlookers to injustice are themselves struck down.
mbh.5.95.46.core_teaching: Respect runs both ways: the young owe the elder obedience, and the elder owes them guidance; if they stray, it is the father's duty to bring them back, and to keep to the right path himself.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XCV
commentaries.gist: The Pandavas ask him to behave like a father or brother and a preceptor; they will act as disciples; if they go wrong, a father should set them right, and he should also walk the path of righteousness.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (95.45-47) gives the same reciprocal duty of elder and younger, ending with 'set us in the proper path and follow it yourself'.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 93.40-46 shows the context (thirteen years of exile kept on trust) and that the reciprocal-conduct line is a manuscript insertion.

mbh.5.95.46.practical_reading: Used for parents and mentors: authority comes with the duty to correct with care, and to model the path one asks of others.
misreadings: Not 'children must obey whatever the parent says'; the elder's own duty is the point.
In context the elder (Dhritarashtra) is failing; it is a plea from the wronged, not a defence of parental control.
cautions: A reader estranged from a harmful parent may find 'father sets you right' painful.
not_for: Someone whose parent is abusive or controlling
speaks_to: Parents of teenagers or young adults
Adult children asking a parent to step up

mbh.5.95.48.context: Krishna has asked Dhritarashtra to restrain his sons. Now he gives the Pandavas' words to the kings: in an assembly that knows dharma, injustice should not happen. If right is killed by wrong while members watch, they are killed with it; dharma, wounded, comes to the hall, and those who don't remove the arrow are wounded too, as a river tears out the trees on its banks. The dice hall, where elders sat silent, is behind every word.
mbh.5.95.48.core_teaching: Where wrong overcomes right while the assembly watches, the watchers share the guilt; silence in the face of injustice is itself a wound.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XCV
commentaries.gist: Where righteousness is overpowered by unrighteousness in the presence of virtuous members, they are the ones slain; those who do not draw out the arrow are pierced by it, as a river uproots the trees on its bank.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (95.48-50) has the same sequence, including the river eating away its bank trees.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 93.47-50: the river image, then the claim that the Pandavas, who kept silent with their eyes on dharma, are now speaking what is true and just.

mbh.5.95.48.practical_reading: Used for bystander responsibility: at work, in families, online, staying silent while someone is wronged makes us part of it; speak, or at least do not lend cover.
misreadings: Not a call to attack individuals publicly or to shame people who were afraid to speak.
Not about every disagreement; it is about clear injustice.
cautions: A reader who froze during someone else's abuse (or their own) may hear blame; pair with compassion.
not_for: A survivor who could not act during their own assault
speaks_to: Someone deciding whether to speak up about harassment or fraud at work
A family member who has seen mistreatment
Someone serving on a board, jury or committee

meera.kk.10.context: Mira asks Hari to glance her way just a little: she keeps looking at him and he does not look back, so hard is his heart. Her hope rests on his glance alone; she has no other place. For her he is the only one, while he has millions like her. She has stood pleading so long that dawn has broken, and she ends by offering her life to the imperishable Lord.
meera.kk.10.core_teaching: Loving complaint to a Lord who seems not to answer: the devotee may say God seems hard and still keep all her hope there.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text of the pada (Kavitakosh)
commentaries.gist: The complaint grows: for her he is everything, for him she is one of millions; she has pleaded all night till dawn; yet the song ends in self-offering, not anger.
