commentaries.who: Rita Dubey and Rambaksh Jat, e-PG Pathshala (UGC/INFLIBNET) Hindi MA module 27 (on the related pada 'घड़ी अंक नहीं आवङै')
commentaries.gist: Describes Mira's direct address to Krishna as a blend of earnest prayer, statement of pain, reproach (upalambha), petition and longing; this pada is a pure case of that reproachful-loving mode.

commentaries.who: Nora Melnikova (Cracow Indological Studies, 2018)
commentaries.gist: Notes that Mira padas show her in many moods, from a desolate lover reaching out to an angry, scolding beloved; complaint against Krishna is a recognised strand of the corpus.

meera.kk.10.practical_reading: It gives permission to tell God that silence hurts. Teachers present it as honest prayer that keeps the relationship alive rather than quitting it.
misreadings: Not a claim that God is actually cruel.
Not a call to keep begging a person who ignores you.
cautions: The closing line 'देस्यूँ प्राण अकोर' (I will give my life as an offering) is devotional self-surrender, but could be misheard by someone with suicidal thoughts; do not quote it in distress plans.
Calling God hard-hearted can free some readers and unsettle others.
not_for: a reader with suicidal thoughts if the closing line is included
someone pining after a person who has clearly ended contact

meera.kk.11.context: Hari is the support of her life and breath; in all three worlds she has no shelter but him. She has looked over the whole world and nothing pleases her without him. She ends: Mira is your servant, do not forget her.
meera.kk.11.core_teaching: Hari is the one support that holds when nothing else does; the devotee asks only not to be forgotten.

commentaries.who: Kavitakosh word glosses (raga Hamir version)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'आसरो' as support, 'मंझार' as in, 'रावरी' as yours: no support in the three worlds without you; I am your servant.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text of the pada (Kavitakosh)
commentaries.gist: The refrain returns after each line, and the song closes with a plea not to be forgotten, so the statement of dependence ends as a request for remembrance.

commentaries.who: Rita Dubey and Rambaksh Jat, e-PG Pathshala (UGC/INFLIBNET) Hindi MA module 27 (parallel phrase in 'घड़ी अंक नहीं आवङै')
commentaries.gist: Glossing Mira's 'you are my life-breath', the module explains that Krishna is the support of her life and her very living rests on it; without him food and sleep leave her.

meera.kk.11.practical_reading: For someone whose usual supports have fallen away, it names a support that does not depend on circumstances; teachers pair it with the closing plea to be remembered.
misreadings: Not a rejection of human help or relationships.
Not a claim that nothing in the world has value.
cautions: 'No shelter but you' for a reader with no human supports: add encouragement to reach people too.
not_for: someone isolating themselves who needs to hear about human connection
speaks_to: when every other support has failed

meera.kk.12.context: Mira tells her own mind to touch Hari's feet, lovely, cool and lotus-soft, which take away the threefold fire. The pada then lists what those feet did: Prahlad touched them and gained Indra's rank (Shukla's text), Dhruva was made immovable by them, they spanned the universe, freed Gautama's wife (Ahalya), and lifted Govardhan to humble Indra's pride. It ends calling Girdhar the one who carries others across.
meera.kk.12.core_teaching: Turning the restless mind toward the Lord's feet cools every kind of burning suffering, as it did for Prahlad, Dhruva and Ahalya.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text of the pada (Kavitakosh)
commentaries.gist: The comfort is grounded in stories: the same feet raised Prahlad, steadied Dhruva, freed Ahalya and humbled Indra, so the mind is urged to seek them.

commentaries.who: Acharya Ramchandra Shukla, Hindi Sahitya ka Itihas (1929), Krishna-bhakti section, via Hindwi
commentaries.gist: Shukla prints this as one of two representative Mira padas. He describes her worship as madhurya bhava, Krishna as beloved or husband, and notes her padas are partly Rajasthani-mixed, partly literary Braj, all absorbed in love.

commentaries.who: Tulsidas, Ram Rajya passage (Ramcharitmanas), with gloss from Pushp-Parag (ed. Tekchand Shastri), via Hindwi
commentaries.gist: Names the three kinds of suffering (daihik, daivik, bhautik) and glosses them as bodily illness like fever, calamity like famine, and harm from creatures; this is the 'threefold fire' Mira says the feet remove.

meera.kk.12.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a self-talk practice: when the mind is burning with anxiety, anger or worry, deliberately direct it to a cooling, steady image of the divine.
misreadings: Not a promise that physical or circumstantial suffering will vanish.
Not a substitute for treatment of anxiety disorders.
cautions: Prahlad and Dhruva stories involve child abuse and rejection by a parent; if the reading expands on them, keep that in mind.
not_for: readers who need practical steps rather than contemplation in an emergency

meera.kk.13.context: Mira rejoices: she has found the jewel of Ram's name, a priceless thing given by her true guru, who in kindness made her his own. It is the capital of many lives; she lost all that the world counts. It does not run out when spent, thieves cannot take it, it grows each day. With truth as the boat and the guru as boatman she has crossed the ocean of becoming, and sings his praise with joy.
meera.kk.13.core_teaching: The Name received through the guru's grace is a wealth that grows by being spent and that nothing can take away; worldly losses are small beside it.

commentaries.who: Hindwi (Rekhta Foundation) prose gloss; text sourced to Mira Vani (Rajkamal Prakashan, 2004)
commentaries.gist: She has found Ram's wealth; the satguru kindly adopted her and gave a priceless thing; losing the world she gained the wealth of births; it cannot be spent or stolen; the guru rows truth's boat across.

commentaries.who: Nora Melnikova (Cracow Indological Studies, 2018), on the guru tradition
commentaries.gist: The Raidas-as-guru link grows from Anantadas's story of a Chittaur queen initiated by Raidas, later identified with Mira; modern devotional writers make it central. Treat the guru's identity as tradition.

meera.kk.13.practical_reading: Teachers use it to contrast inner wealth with outer: what is found in practice and grace cannot be stolen or used up. It suits readers after financial or material loss.
misreadings: Not a money or prosperity promise (our misuse note is right).
Not contempt for honest work or wealth; 'lost all the world's' is about attachment.
cautions: 'Lost everything in the world' can feel flip to someone in real financial hardship; acknowledge the loss first.
not_for: readers in acute poverty if framed as 'money doesn't matter'
speaks_to: after financial loss or job loss

meera.kk.14.context: Mira asks someone, anyone, to bring word that the Lord is coming. He neither comes nor writes; he has a habit of keeping her hoping. Her eyes won't obey her and stream like monsoon rivers. She is helpless and has no wings to fly to him. She ends: when will you meet me? I have become your servant, caught in your snare.
meera.kk.14.core_teaching: Tears in waiting are not a failure of will; the longing for the beloved overflows on its own.

commentaries.who: Hindwi (Rekhta Foundation) prose gloss; text sourced to Mira Vani (Rajkamal Prakashan, 2004)
commentaries.gist: Someone tell me the Lord is coming; he neither comes nor sends a letter, and keeps tempting me; my eyes won't listen; I am helpless and have no wings; when will you meet me, I am caught in your toils.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text of the pada (Kavitakosh)
commentaries.gist: The monsoon image sits between 'he does not even write' and 'I have no wings to fly to him': the tears are the body's answer to helplessness, not drama.

commentaries.who: Rita Dubey and Rambaksh Jat, e-PG Pathshala (UGC/INFLIBNET) Hindi MA module 27 (general observation on Mira's padas)
commentaries.gist: Mira never describes the experience of meeting God; her songs voice the wish and the faith that meeting will surely come, but in the padas it never actually happens.

meera.kk.14.practical_reading: It gives permission to cry. For someone who cannot stop tearing up, the line says the eyes have their own will and that is human, not weakness.
misreadings: Not a call to keep waiting for someone who has stopped writing back.
cautions: 'He neither comes nor writes' can sharply touch readers ghosted by a partner or estranged from a child; may comfort or reopen a wound.
not_for: readers who need to move on from a relationship, if framed as 'keep waiting'

meera.kk.2.context: In its fuller form the song begins with Mira crazed with love and no one knowing her pain; only the wounded know a wound, only a jeweller knows a jewel; her bed is on a stake and her beloved's in the sky; she roams from forest to forest and finds no physician. This last line resolves it: the only healer is Krishna.
meera.kk.2.core_teaching: The ache of love in separation (viraha) is not something any ordinary remedy can treat; only the beloved Lord's presence heals it.

commentaries.who: Hindwi (Rekhta Foundation) prose gloss; text sourced to Mira Vani (Rajkamal Prakashan, 2004)
commentaries.gist: On the fuller Hindi form: she is lovesick and roams forest to forest finding no doctor; her pain will end only when the dark, lovely Krishna treats it himself.

commentaries.who: Rita Dubey and Rambaksh Jat, e-PG Pathshala (UGC/INFLIBNET) Hindi MA module 27, vyakhya of 'हेरी मैं तो दरध-दिवाणी'
commentaries.gist: The pain of not meeting the beloved is known only to Mira, and no physician can be found; it will go only when her Giridhar himself comes as the physician, because only he shares the experience.

commentaries.who: Nora Melnikova, 'Mirabai: a Saint or a Rebel?' (Cracow Indological Studies 20.2, 2018), summarising Hawley
commentaries.gist: The earliest-attested Mira padas speak only of love for Girdhar and the suffering of separation (viraha), with almost no biographical detail; this line belongs to that register.

meera.kk.2.practical_reading: Teachers use the image to say some heart-pain is not a problem to fix but a longing to be met. It can validate that an ache is real and turn the reader toward the source of love rather than numbing the pain.
misreadings: Not medical advice and not a reason to avoid doctors, therapy or medicine (our misuse note is right).
Not a claim that suffering proves holiness.
Not romantic advice to wait for a human partner to heal you.
cautions: Can be twisted into 'pray instead of getting treatment'; keep the misuse note visible.
Same song as meera.kk.3; do not use both in one plan without saying so.
not_for: someone in acute medical or psychiatric crisis
a reader being pressured to 'just pray' instead of seeking care
speaks_to: a long ache nobody around understands
when advice and fixes have not helped

meera.kk.3.context: Mira speaks to a companion: she is mad with love and no one knows her pain. Only someone wounded knows a wound, only a jeweller a jewel. Her bed is on a stake, her beloved's in the sky, so how can they meet? She wanders forest to forest seeking a physician, and ends saying the pain will go only when Krishna is the physician.
meera.kk.3.core_teaching: Love-longing is a wound only the wounded understand; Mira names her isolation and points to Krishna as the only cure.

commentaries.who: Hindwi (Rekhta Foundation) prose gloss; text sourced to Mira Vani (Rajkamal Prakashan, 2004)
commentaries.gist: Addressed to a sakhi: she is love-crazed and unknown in her pain; her bed is a stake while the beloved's is in the sky; only the wounded or a true jeweller understands; she roams finding no doctor until Krishna heals.

commentaries.who: Rita Dubey and Rambaksh Jat, e-PG Pathshala (UGC/INFLIBNET) Hindi MA module 27
commentaries.gist: Social bonds kept Mira from Krishna and the world missed her feeling. Real communication needs shared experience, so she forgives friend and foe alike: well-wishers advise from inexperience. Only Krishna knows this pain.

commentaries.who: Nabhadas, Bhaktamal (early 17th c.), via Hindwi
commentaries.gist: The earliest hagiography: Mira cast off public shame and the chains of family to worship Girdhar; the wicked tried to kill her with poison, which she drank like nectar. The family-hostility setting comes from this tradition, not from this pada.

commentaries.who: Nora Melnikova (Cracow Indological Studies, 2018)
commentaries.gist: Early sources give almost no biography beyond her leaving family ties and surviving poison; fuller details of her family life arrive only later, especially with Priyadas. Read biographical settings as tradition.

meera.kk.3.practical_reading: For someone whose pain feels invisible, the line affirms that only those who have been through it truly understand. That also explains, and lets one forgive, well-meant advice that misses the mark; it can nudge the reader toward people with lived experience, and devotionally toward bringing the pain to God.
misreadings: Not 'no one can ever help me': the song points to the one who can.
Not a romanticising of suffering.
Not evidence about Mira's family life.
cautions: Impaling-stake and wound imagery in the fuller pada is intense.
'Only the wounded know' can feed isolation in a depressed reader; pair it with an invitation to connect.
Duplicate song with meera.kk.2.
not_for: a reader in crisis who is withdrawing from everyone
anyone the line might convince that no one can understand them

meera.kk.4.context: The pada goes on to list those the Lord has already saved: the sinner Ajamil, the elephant king drowning in the lake, the courtesan Ganika who rose to heaven, Kubja and the Bhil woman (Shabari); there are too many to count and the Vedas and Puranas tire of telling. It closes with Mira the servant taking refuge and asking the Lord to listen with both ears.
meera.kk.4.core_teaching: Mira surrenders and asks to be kept, resting her plea on the Lord's record of rescuing sinners and outcasts rather than on her own worth.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text of the pada (Kavitakosh)
commentaries.gist: The plea is backed by precedent: Ajamil, Gajendra the elephant, Ganika, Kubja and Shabari were all saved though counted low or sinful; the list is endless, so Mira too may be kept.

commentaries.who: Nora Melnikova (Cracow Indological Studies, 2018), on the Mira corpus
commentaries.gist: Padas under Mira's name range widely in style and persona; the few early-attested ones are about love and separation, and this refuge-and-rescue song is not among them.

meera.kk.4.practical_reading: Teachers read it as permission to ask for help without credentials: everyone on the list was 'unworthy', so no one is too far gone to be held.
misreadings: Not passivity: taking refuge is an active choice.
The labels in the fuller pada ('नीच', 'अधम', 'गणिका') reflect period caste and gender attitudes, not an endorsement.
cautions: If quoting the fuller pada, the caste-laden word 'नीच' (low) is applied to Kubja and the Bhil woman; paraphrase with care.
not_for: a reader who needs to act against immediate danger; on its own it can read as passive waiting

meera.kk.5.context: The pada: without your sight I get no peace for a moment; food and sleep desert me; I wander like a wounded woman and no one knows my pain; my days and nights are wasted, my life spent pining, my eyes worn out with weeping; had I known love brings such pain I would have beaten a drum through the town telling everyone not to love. Then this line: I watch the road and sweep the path. It ends asking when he will come, for meeting him is joy.
meera.kk.5.core_teaching: Longing turned into readiness: she keeps the path swept and watches for the beloved, so the waiting becomes its own devotion.

commentaries.who: Rita Dubey and Rambaksh Jat, e-PG Pathshala (UGC/INFLIBNET) Hindi MA module 27, vyakhya of this pada
commentaries.gist: Mira addresses Krishna directly, mixing prayer, pain, reproach (upalambha), petition and longing. After saying she would have warned the town against love, she turns back to prayer: watching his road, sweeping it so his coming is easy.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text of the pada (Kavitakosh)
commentaries.gist: The line comes after the song's lowest point (sleeplessness, wasted days, 'let no one love') and turns despair into active watching before the final hope that meeting him will be joy.

commentaries.who: Hindwi prose gloss on the parallel pada 'दरस बिन दूखन लागे नैन' (text sourced to Mira Vani, Rajkamal 2004)
commentaries.gist: The same 'watching the road' formula: with a fixed gaze she waits for him, the night of separation feels endless, and she has no one to tell her ache to.

commentaries.who: Nora Melnikova (Cracow Indological Studies, 2018)
commentaries.gist: Viraha, the lonely woman's longing for an absent beloved, is the core theme of the earliest Mira songs.

meera.kk.5.practical_reading: Teachers use the image for prayerful waiting that stays active: you cannot make the beloved come, but you can keep the path clean and keep looking. It suits anyone waiting on something they cannot hurry.
misreadings: Not a recommendation to put life on hold for someone.
Not a promise of when the waiting will end.
cautions: The same pada says she lost her life pining and wanted to warn everyone never to love; don't quote neighbouring lines to a heartbroken reader.
Not eating and not sleeping are named in the pada; the reading should not romanticise these.
not_for: fresh bereavement, where 'waiting for his return' can feed denial
someone waiting for an abusive partner to change
speaks_to: waiting for someone to come home or call

meera.kk.6.context: Mira begs the beloved to come to her house: she will offer body, mind and wealth and sing his praises. She sets his virtues against her faults, admits she has no merit, and ends asking when he will meet her, since her eyes ache without him.
meera.kk.6.core_teaching: Humility (dainya) before the Lord: she claims no merit and rests her hope on the beloved's generous nature.

commentaries.who: Hindwi (Rekhta Foundation) prose gloss; text sourced to Mira Vani (Rajkamal Prakashan, 2004)
commentaries.gist: Without the beloved the whole world tastes bitter; she will offer him everything; he is an ocean of virtues and she is full of faults with not one merit; she is miserable without his sight.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text of the pada (Kavitakosh)
commentaries.gist: The refrain 'come to my house, beloved' frames each confession, so the admission of faults is an invitation, not a withdrawal; it closes on aching eyes and 'when will you meet me'.

meera.kk.6.practical_reading: Teachers use it for coming to God without a record of achievements: admit the gap honestly and invite the divine in anyway.
misreadings: Not self-hatred: the confession serves an invitation.
Not a statement that the reader is worthless.
cautions: 'All the faults are mine, all the virtue yours' can mirror the language of controlling relationships; frame it as humility before grace only.
Self-deprecation can reinforce low self-worth in a depressed reader.
not_for: readers with severe shame unless carefully framed
anyone in an abusive relationship where the self-blame pattern is already present

meera.kk.8.context: Mira pleads to be heard: she is being swept away in the ocean of worldly life, and asks to be pulled out if the Lord wills. No one in this world is truly hers; the true kinsman is Raghubar. Mother, father and clan all look after their own interest. She ends: hear Mira's plea and set her at your feet, as you will.
meera.kk.8.core_teaching: A cry for rescue that leaves the outcome to the Lord's will, made after human ties have proved unreliable.

commentaries.who: Kavitakosh word glosses (variant page, raga Darbari)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'काढ़ो' as pull out, 'इण' as this, and 'गरजी' as selfish, supporting the reading that relatives act from self-interest while the Lord is asked to rescue.

commentaries.who: Nabhadas, Bhaktamal (early 17th c.), via Hindwi
commentaries.gist: Tradition remembers Mira breaking with family honour to worship Girdhar and surviving a poisoning attempt; this pada's complaint about kin is read against that story.

commentaries.who: Acharya Ramchandra Shukla, Hindi Sahitya ka Itihas (1929), via Hindwi
commentaries.gist: Shukla reports the legend that, harassed by relatives for keeping saints' company, Mira wrote to Tulsidas for advice, then rejects it as imagination since she died in samvat 1603. Family-conflict readings are tradition, not record.

meera.kk.8.practical_reading: For someone overwhelmed, it models a two-part prayer: say plainly that you are going under, then hand over the outcome. Teachers stress the second half: 'if you will' is trust, not resignation.
misreadings: Not a general verdict that families are selfish.
Not a reason to cut off family.
cautions: Calls parents and clan self-interested: may validate estrangement or wound a reader whose family is their support; quote only the plea in most plans.
Drowning imagery ('being swept away') for a reader with suicidal thoughts: pair with real-world help lines.
not_for: family-reconciliation plans
readers using 'drowning' language about their own life without added support
speaks_to: being overwhelmed or swept away by events

rahim.193.context: Alphabetical placement in the 1926 edition. The editor notes that some of Rahim's dohas have unclear sense because of copying errors; this one's second line is a likely example.
rahim.193.core_teaching: Repeated remembrance is the best thing there is: through it, those who have been parted come together again.

commentaries.who: Rahim-Kavitavali (1926), editor's introduction
commentaries.gist: Tiwari warns that no old manuscript of the dohas was found, that copying has loosened language and sense, and that several dohas' meaning is not clear; read line two of this doha with that caution.

commentaries.who: Kavitakosh 'Rahim Dohavali - 5' (variant witness)
commentaries.gist: Same doha with 'यहै जान अवतार' and 'मिलें', confirming the wording; it offers no gloss.

rahim.193.practical_reading: For someone missing a person, it honours remembering as a real form of closeness, something that can bring the absent near.
misreadings: Not a promise that the dead will physically return or that a lost relationship will be restored.
Not a doctrine about why avatars happen.
cautions: 'The separated meet again' can be read as reincarnation or afterlife reunion; with fresh grief this may comfort or feel like a promise the text does not make.
not_for: fresh bereavement if framed as a promise of reunion
readers trying to let go of a harmful relationship
speaks_to: hope of reunion after a rift

rahim.61.context: In the 1926 edition the dohas are arranged alphabetically, so there is no thematic context. The editor counts about 17 devotional and 11 love (shringar) dohas among some 250; our note reads this one as devotional, though it fits human love equally.
rahim.61.core_teaching: When the beloved already lives in the heart, nothing needs reporting: one's joys and sorrows are already known.

commentaries.who: Rahim-Kavitavali (1926), editor's introduction (Surendranath Tiwari)
commentaries.gist: Tiwari describes Rahim as generous, patient and deeply trusting in God, and sorts his dohas: mostly ethical maxims, with a smaller group of devotional and love dohas. This one sits at that devotion-love border.

commentaries.who: Kavitakosh 'Rahim Dohavali' text (variant witness)
commentaries.gist: The variant 'took body and mind' makes the beloved the active one who has claimed the poet and settled in his heart, which sharpens the point that nothing remains to be told.

rahim.61.practical_reading: For someone who cannot find words to pray, it says you do not need them: the one who lives in your heart already knows. It also fits a close human bond where explanations are unnecessary.
misreadings: Not advice to stop talking to a partner because 'they should just know'.
Not a reason to hide one's troubles from people who can help.
cautions: For a reader whose loved one has died, 'the one in your heart already knows' can comfort or ache; use gently.
not_for: relationship conflict where communication is the actual need

rahim.89.context: Alphabetical placement in the 1926 edition; the very next doha (90) continues the thought: the lowly man watches everyone but no one watches him, and whoever does look after the lowly becomes like Dinabandhu, the Friend of the lowly.
rahim.89.core_teaching: Lowliness has a hidden sweetness the world cannot see: it makes God, the Friend of the lowly, one's own kin.

commentaries.who: Surrounding doha no. 90, Rahim-Kavitavali (1926)
commentaries.gist: The paired doha shifts from receiving to giving: the poor notice everyone but are noticed by none; whoever does notice them becomes like Dinabandhu himself.

commentaries.who: Rahim-Kavitavali (1926), editor's introduction
commentaries.gist: Tiwari recounts that after Akbar's death Rahim's property was seized and he wandered in poverty, still besieged by petitioners, and reads several dohas as voicing that experience and his trust in God.

commentaries.who: Hariram Vyas parallel (Hindwi, from Bholanath Tiwari, Hindi Niti-Kavya-Dhara, 1984)
commentaries.gist: Vyas's version: the blind world does not know that humility is a philosopher's stone; by becoming lowly one gains a kinsman like Dinabandhu. Same idea, different signature.

rahim.89.practical_reading: For someone brought low by failure, illness or loss of status, it suggests that the lowered place is where God draws near and where one learns to see others who are low.
misreadings: Not a call to accept humiliation or abuse (our misuse note is right).
Not praise of poverty as such.
cautions: Telling someone freshly humiliated that lowliness is 'sweet' can sound dismissive; lead with their pain.
not_for: readers being bullied or abused, where 'humility' could be misheard as 'accept it'
speaks_to: after a public failure or demotion

rahim.91.context: Alphabetical placement in the 1926 edition. The thought echoes Rahim's better-known counsel elsewhere to keep one's sorrow to oneself because people will only mock it; here the alternative is given: tell it to Raghuvir, who listens and helps.
rahim.91.core_teaching: People may mock your sorrow; Rama hears it and, having heard, helps.

commentaries.who: Rahim-Kavitavali (1926), editor's introduction
commentaries.gist: Tiwari stresses Rahim's full trust in God, quoting dohas where he leaves every matter to the Lord and does not fear in war, forest, sickness or calamity because the one who kept him in the womb still keeps him.

commentaries.who: Parallel doha no. 168, Rahim-Kavitavali (1926)
commentaries.gist: Rahim's companion counsel: keep the ache of your heart hidden, because people who hear it will only make fun and none will share the load. Doha 91 supplies the other half: there is one listener who does not mock.

commentaries.who: Kavitakosh 'Rahim Dohavali' text (variant witness)
commentaries.gist: Gives the same doha with 'धरत' for 'धरैं', confirming the wording apart from that verb form.

rahim.91.practical_reading: For someone who has been laughed at or dismissed after sharing pain, it says there is one listener who does not mock and who acts. Writers can add: also find the people who listen like that.
misreadings: Not advice never to share sorrow with people.
Not a claim that everyone mocks suffering.
cautions: Could reinforce 'no one cares' for a reader already isolated; pair with encouragement to find safe listeners.
not_for: readers who need to be urged toward therapy or friends, if framed as 'tell only God'
speaks_to: being mocked or dismissed after opening up

ram_gita.24.context: Rama has argued (5.7-23) that ritual action cannot remove ignorance and that knowledge alone frees; that the duties of one's station purify the mind first. Here he names the means: faith, the teacher's grace and the great saying 'tat tvam asi'. Verses 25-27 then explain how the words That and Thou are understood.
ram_gita.24.core_teaching: Faith, a pure mind and a teacher's grace, applied to the teaching that you are one with the Self, make a person happy and as unshakable as a mountain.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: Stresses that the unity taught by 'That art thou' is realised through a guru's grace and personal contact, not mere verbal teaching; notes that such teachers are rare, which is why many read Vedanta and few realise it.

commentaries.who: Anonymous Sanskrit tika in a Nepali printed Rama Gita (commentator not named in the scan)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'unshakable' as having an inner organ no longer agitated by craving for sense objects.

ram_gita.24.practical_reading: Steadiness grows from three things together: trust, good guidance and a clear understanding of who you are; check which of the three is missing.
misreadings: Not a promise of instant calm by repeating a phrase; the commentators insist on preparation and a teacher.
cautions: Advaita identity claims can feel abstract; best paired with the image of the mountain rather than the doctrine.

ram_gita.34.context: Rama has explained the gross, subtle and causal bodies and the three states, all of which belong to the intellect, not the Self (5.28-33). Here he gives the method: negate everything with 'not this, not this', taste the Self, then let the world go. Verse 35 states what the Self is.
ram_gita.34.core_teaching: Once one has tasted the Self by negating what one is not, the world can be let go the way one sets down a fruit after drinking its juice.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: Notes that for one who has reached realisation through neti neti, the world ceases to assert itself and he becomes indifferent to its joys and sorrows; but this is the state of the jivanmukta, not of everyone.

commentaries.who: Anonymous Sanskrit tika in a Nepali printed Rama Gita (commentator not named in the scan)
commentaries.gist: Answers the objection that the world is enjoyed: as with a coconut or orange, one drinks the sweet juice and leaves the rest; once the essence is taken, the remainder is dropped, since it brings fear.

ram_gita.34.practical_reading: In a smaller key: take what is nourishing from an experience, a job, even a relationship that has ended, and let the husk go without bitterness.
misreadings: Not 'the world is worthless, discard people'; Baij Nath limits it to the jivanmukta's inner detachment.
Not a call to quit responsibilities.
cautions: For someone who feels used and discarded by others, the 'shell' image could sting; avoid in breakup or abandonment contexts.
not_for: someone who has just been left or let go
depression with withdrawal from life
speaks_to: letting go after a chapter ends

ram_gita.35.context: Follows the neti neti method (5.34). The next verse asks: if the Self is such, how does a sorrowful world appear in it? Answer: through ignorance and superimposition, which knowledge removes in a moment (5.36); 5.37 defines superimposition.
ram_gita.35.core_teaching: What you truly are is untouched by the changes of birth, growth, decline and death: whole, self-luminous and one.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: The embodied self, taken to be subject to birth and death, is not subject to any of them; free of them it is the limitless Brahman itself, as the Upanishadic saying 'this Self is Brahman' declares.

ram_gita.35.practical_reading: In times of change (ageing, illness, a move), some teachers suggest resting attention on the awareness that has watched every change and is still here.
misreadings: Not a denial that bodies age and die, or that loss hurts.
cautions: Restates Gita 2.20's theme of the deathless Self; can feel dismissive to fresh grief if offered as consolation for a death.
not_for: fresh bereavement
terminal diagnosis without pastoral care
speaks_to: fear of ageing or death in reflective moments

ram_gita.37.context: After saying the world appears in the blissful Self only through ignorance (5.36), Rama defines superimposition with the rope-snake example. Verse 38 adds that the first superimposition is the notion 'I' on the Self, and 39 turns to deep sleep as evidence.
ram_gita.37.core_teaching: Suffering comes from mistaking one thing for another, like a rope for a snake; the world and the 'I' are laid over the one reality by confusion.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913) (translation and surrounding notes)
commentaries.gist: Superimposition is what is imposed on another thing through illusion, as a rope is taken for a snake; so the world is laid on the Lord, and the Self is taken to be happy, miserable, born and dying.

commentaries.who: Anonymous Sanskrit tika in a Nepali printed Rama Gita (commentator not named in the scan)
commentaries.gist: Introduces the next verse as saying the first superimposition is ego (ahaṅkāra) on the Self, the cause of all saṃsāra; and earlier compares the disappearance of the world on knowledge to the snake vanishing when the rope is seen.

ram_gita.37.practical_reading: When fear or anger spikes, pause and look again; much of what frightens us is a rope taken for a snake.
misreadings: Not 'your problems are imaginary'; it is about seeing clearly, which may still call for action.
cautions: Telling someone in real danger that it is 'just a rope' would be harmful; keep it to misperception and anxiety.
not_for: real threats or trauma

ram_gita.39.context: After defining superimposition (5.37-38), Rama gives the evidence of deep sleep: the mind's states cease there and the Self is experienced as happiness. 5.40-41 then explain how consciousness and intellect seem to borrow each other's qualities, like fire and iron.
ram_gita.39.core_teaching: Wanting, clinging and even pleasure and pain belong to the mind; in dreamless sleep they stop and we are simply at ease, which hints that ease is our nature.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: Explains the pairs: desire and aversion, attachment and non-attachment, happiness and misery are states of the intellect, which vanish in deep sleep when the Self is known as bliss; cites the Brihadaranyaka's description of deep sleep.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Adhyatma Ramayana, Hindi translation (numbering check)
commentaries.gist: Same verse number; the Hindi rendering stresses that these are properties of the intellect and the cause of saṃsāra, absent in deep sleep.

ram_gita.39.practical_reading: Notice how a good night's sleep resets you even though nothing outside changed; ease does not always need new things.
misreadings: Not an argument that unconsciousness is the goal.
cautions: For readers with insomnia, avoid making sleep sound like the measure of spiritual health.
not_for: chronic insomnia sufferers as the main hook

ram_gita.46.context: After the 'I am' contemplations of 5.43-44 and the image of a sick man cured by an elixir (5.45), Rama gives the posture of meditation. 5.47-51 then describe merging the universe into the Self and meditating on Om (A, U, M).
ram_gita.46.core_teaching: Sit apart, quiet the senses, steady the mind and contemplate the one Self with undivided attention.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: Uses the verse to set out the seven stages of yoga (right desire, right thought, non-attachment, purity, non-cognition of objects, turiya, beyond turiya), adding that in his day few pass the third stage.

commentaries.who: Anonymous Sanskrit tika in a Nepali printed Rama Gita (commentator not named in the scan)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as nirvikalpa samadhi; 'no other means' means free of the error that anything besides knowledge of truth liberates; 'kevala' is unattached; the mind never strays to another object.

ram_gita.46.practical_reading: A plain meditation instruction: a quiet corner, phone away, a few minutes of resting attention on awareness itself.
misreadings: Not a demand to leave family for a cave; a 'secluded place' can be a quiet room.
not_for: people with trauma for whom unguided silent sitting can be destabilising

ram_gita.5.context: After the coronation, Rama tells Lakshmana old stories of dharma (sarga 5.2). Lakshmana, his mind purified by devotion, finds Rama in seclusion, bows, praises him as pure knowledge (5.4) and makes this request. Rama, pleased, begins the teaching at 5.6-7 with the steps that lead to a teacher.
ram_gita.5.core_teaching: The teaching begins with a humble request: refuge first, then the ask to be taught a simple way across confusion.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913) (translation reading)
commentaries.gist: Lakshmana takes refuge in Rama's feet, which free one from worldly life and which yogis cherish, and asks for the knowledge to cross the impassable ocean of nescience quickly and easily.

ram_gita.5.practical_reading: Asking for help is itself the first step; name the confusion and ask someone wiser to show you a way through.
misreadings: Not passivity; the request leads straight into a demanding discipline.
cautions: Within the Adhyatma Ramayana the whole Rama Gita is narrated by Mahadeva (Shiva) to Parvati.

ram_gita.52.context: After the Om meditation that merges gross, subtle and causal into pure awareness (5.48-51), Rama describes the result. 5.53 says such a yogi sees him; 5.54 says he lives on until his past karma is spent and then merges in Rama.
ram_gita.52.core_teaching: The freed person rests content in the Self's own joy, free and still like a waveless ocean.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: This is the state where the mind has merged in the Self; not a void or nothingness but something very real, beside which what now seems real looks unreal; the goal of all religion.

commentaries.who: Anonymous Sanskrit tika in a Nepali printed Rama Gita (commentator not named in the scan)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'still ocean' as one whose waters have no waves of contact with sense objects; such a one is liberated while living.

ram_gita.52.practical_reading: An image to rest in: beneath surface waves the ocean is still; on busy days return to that stillness for a few breaths.
misreadings: 'Forgetting all else' is not neglecting people or duties; it describes absorption.
cautions: Describes an advanced state; avoid making a struggling reader feel they are failing.

ram_gita.58.context: After the austere path of knowledge and samadhi (5.46-57), Rama adds that until one sees everything as himself, one should be devoted to worshipping him. He then says this teaching is the essence of the Vedas (5.59) and that he purifies those who serve him (5.61).
ram_gita.58.core_teaching: Knowledge and devotion are joined: keep worshipping until you see the divine everywhere, and to the faithful the divine is present in the heart day and night.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: Rama here reveals that the secret of knowledge lies in uninterrupted devotion; those who seek the goal by knowledge alone find it hard, while for the devotee the Lord removes obstacles unnoticed, as for Prahlada, Bhishma, Vyasa and Narada.

commentaries.who: Anonymous Sanskrit tika in a Nepali printed Rama Gita (commentator not named in the scan)
commentaries.gist: Links it to Gita 4.11, 'as people approach me, so I receive them': the faithful worshipper sees the Lord in the heart day and night.

ram_gita.58.practical_reading: Keep a daily practice of love and attention, even a small one, while understanding grows.
misreadings: Not that worship is only for beginners to discard later; Baij Nath presents devotion as the secret of knowledge.

ram_gita.61.context: After telling Lakshmana that the visible world is maya and he should purify his mind by meditating on Rama (5.60), Rama makes this promise. The chapter ends with 5.62 on the merit of reading the Rama Gita.
ram_gita.61.core_teaching: Whether one worships the divine as formless or with form, even sometimes, sincere inner worship makes one one with Rama and a source of blessing to the world.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: Contemplation with attributes and without attributes leads to the same goal, one leading into the other; the devotee merges into the knower, as Bhishma and Prahlada did through the Lord with attributes.

ram_gita.61.practical_reading: Reassurance for the irregular practitioner: sincere remembrance, even occasional, counts.
misreadings: Not that occasional practice makes discipline unnecessary; 'pure heart' is the condition.
cautions: Within the Adhyatma Ramayana the whole Rama Gita is narrated by Mahadeva (Shiva) to Parvati.
speaks_to: people who pray irregularly and feel guilty
debates about form vs formless worship

rcm.1.1.sortha.4.context: The Manas opens with seven Sanskrit shlokas and then five Awadhi sorathas. The first four invoke deities (Ganesha, then Vishnu in two forms by most readings, then Shiva), and the fifth bows to the guru. This is the fourth, to Shiva, who in the poem is both the first teller of Ram's story and Tulsidas's guide. Right after it the poet turns to the guru and the dust of his feet.
rcm.1.1.sortha.4.core_teaching: Tulsidas comes to Shiva as the compassionate one who loves the helpless and who mastered desire, and asks for grace before he begins. He bases his claim on his own lowliness, not his merit.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, as compiled in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: A prayer to Shiva alone. Each epithet points ahead to an episode the poem will tell: burning Kama, pitying the widowed Rati, marrying Uma, and then narrating Ram's story to her.

commentaries.who: Karunasindhu, Shivlal Pathak and Baba Janakidas, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Read 'Umaraman' as invoking Uma and Shiva together, as the half-woman Lord. Janakidas adds that Parvati too 'crushed Kama', through her own renunciation.

commentaries.who: Baijnath's tika, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The jasmine and moon qualities (softness, coolness, nectar, light) all serve others without any motive. So the poet trusts that Shiva will show him the same unmotivated grace.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji and another note, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The two similes voice the poet's wish that his own heart become soft as jasmine and clear as the moon. By naming Shiva's love for the 'dīn', he claims kinship through his own helplessness.

rcm.1.1.sortha.4.practical_reading: Teachers read the line as a way to ask for help from honest need rather than from merit. Admitting that you feel small is treated as the opening, not the obstacle.
misreadings: Not a rejection of love or marriage: commentators square 'Uma's lord' with 'Kama's crusher' as love without craving, or as a prayer that the poet's own heart be freed of desire.
Not a sectarian statement: the opening sorathas honour several deities in turn.
cautions: A devotional prayer. A secular reader may need the context that this is the poet asking for grace before a large task.
not_for: someone who wants practical steps rather than prayer
a reader put off by devotional address
speaks_to: feeling small or unqualified before a big piece of work
people drawn to Shiva as the compassionate one

rcm.1.102.chaupai.2.context: After their marriage, Shiva sits under the great banyan on Kailash. Parvati, remembering her previous birth as Sati and the doubt that cost her so much, sits at his left and asks: if you are truly pleased with me and know me as your own, take away my ignorance and tell me the story of Ram. This is the start of the Shiva-Parvati dialogue that frames the Manas.
rcm.1.102.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Parvati reasons that someone sheltering under a wish-tree need not suffer want, so she, living in Shiva's grace, asks him to clear her confusion. Asking honestly for understanding is itself an act of trust.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: She recalls that in her last birth Shiva neither was pleased with her nor treated her as his own, so her ignorance remained. Now that he has, she argues, ignorance has no reason to stay.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note
commentaries.gist: She calls him the wish-tree and 'heap of joy' because he has just honoured her. The ending confirms it: 'by your grace my sorrow is gone' (120.3). The ignorance is not knowing Ram's true nature.

commentaries.who: Baijnath and Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Baijnath: 'your own servant' means serving in mind, deed and word. Panjabi: seating her on his left shows he has forgotten all her past offences.

commentaries.who: P. P. Pr., in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Traces the stages: servant and master become student and teacher ('you are guru of the three worlds'), and the purpose is named: confusion removed, sorrow ended, joy gained.

rcm.1.102.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it to encourage people to bring their doubts openly to someone they trust, especially after an old mistake. Being accepted again is the time to ask.
misreadings: Not a claim that devotees never face hardship: the 'poverty' here is confusion of mind.
not_for: someone in material poverty, who may hear the wish-tree image as mocking
speaks_to: lingering doubt or confusion about faith
returning to a teacher or partner after a past rupture
wanting to understand, not just believe

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 108, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 108, half-lines 3-4'). NOT 1.102.

rcm.1.109.chaupai.5.context: Parvati has asked how the formless Brahman could be the prince she saw grieving in the forest. Shiva first rebukes those who confuse the two without discernment (115). He then states the principle in this line, and goes on: just as there is no difference between water and ice, the formless Lord takes form out of love.
rcm.1.109.chaupai.5.core_teaching: God with form and God without form are not two. The formless, unborn One takes on form, compelled by the love of devotees.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: 'No difference' means that just as the formless has no delusion or defect, neither does the embodied form, though it may seem to show grief or confusion.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, 'Samanvaya' reading
commentaries.gist: Brahman always has divine qualities such as mercy and love. 'Nirguna' means those qualities are unmanifest, 'saguna' that they are manifest. One reality, two states.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, Advaita reading
commentaries.gist: Brahman is truly without any qualities, pure being, consciousness and bliss. The embodied form is how it appears. Manas Piyush sets out both readings without forcing one.

commentaries.who: Karunasindhu, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Parvati's question is shaped by her old doubt: if Shiva says the formless becomes embodied, she will see that as Sati she failed to grasp that Ram himself is that Brahman.

rcm.1.109.chaupai.5.practical_reading: Teachers use it to reconcile people who feel torn between an abstract spirituality and a personal, devotional God: the same reality is approached both ways, and love is what makes it near.
misreadings: Not a ranking of form-worship below formless meditation, or the reverse.
not_for: a reader in acute distress who needs comfort rather than theology
people put off by doctrinal debate
speaks_to: tension between philosophical and devotional faith
interfaith or inter-sect conversations within Hinduism

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 116, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush cites '116. 1' and numbers the half-lines 1-2). NOT 1.109 and NOT chaupai 5.

rcm.1.112.chaupai.2.context: Shiva is answering Parvati's doubt about Ram's nature. He says that Ram, the Lord whose name he himself repeats in Kashi to free the dying, is the supreme Self. Then he contrasts the name said helplessly with the Lord remembered lovingly. He closes by telling Parvati that doubting such a Lord destroys knowledge and dispassion.
rcm.1.112.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Even saying Ram's name helplessly burns away old wrongs. Remembering him with love makes the ocean of worldly life as easy to cross as a hoofprint.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: 'Helplessly' covers saying it when falling, yawning, in pain or fear, or because one is among saints, like Ajamila calling his son Narayana. Its contrast with 'reverently' gives two grades of fruit.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The name is fire and past sins are a mountain of cotton: one spark burns it all. It cites a Padma Purana verse. Saying the name and hearing it have the same fruit.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar and V. Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ramkumar: devotion yields the fruit of both action (sins destroyed) and knowledge (liberation). Tripathi: helpless utterance burns sin, but loving remembrance carries one across.

rcm.1.112.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers encourage people that no practice is wasted, and that loving, regular remembrance makes life's difficulties feel smaller.
misreadings: Praise of remembrance, not a promise that life's problems will vanish; practical help still matters.
Not 'past actions have no consequences in this life'.
cautions: Speaks of sins across many births, a rebirth doctrine that some readers may find heavy.
not_for: someone in acute crisis who would hear 'just remember God' as dismissive
speaks_to: people who can only manage a little practice

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 119, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 119, half-lines 3-4'). NOT 1.112.

rcm.1.113.chaupai.1.context: Shiva has finished explaining Ram's nature (Bal Kand 116-119). Parvati, joyful, tells him his words have cleared her delusion. Then she asks the next questions: why the formless took a human body, and the story of the avatar, which Shiva goes on to tell.
rcm.1.113.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Words of real understanding cool a mind burned by confusion as moonlight relieves the autumn heat. Doubt resolved brings peace as well as knowledge.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Shiva called his words sun-rays that end the night of error. Parvati calls them moon-rays that end the day's burning. The same speech dispels darkness and soothes heat.

commentaries.who: Prof. Lala Bhagwandin, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Shiva sees his words as removing darkness. Parvati finds they also bring peace, so she chooses the moon, which does both. She then says her sorrow has gone too.

commentaries.who: P. P. Pr., in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: A dissenting note: her claim is partly polite deference. Shiva later says the 'shadow' of her old delusion still lingers, so full clarity comes only with the whole story.

rcm.1.113.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to describe the relief of a good explanation from a trusted teacher, friend or counsellor: understanding is also emotional rest.
misreadings: Not a claim that one conversation ends all doubt: the commentary notes she still needs the rest of the story.
not_for: someone still in the middle of doubt, for whom the resolved ending may feel out of reach
a reader whose questions were dismissed by a teacher
speaks_to: relief after a long doubt is answered

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 120, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush cites '1. 120. 1'). NOT 1.113.

rcm.1.127.chaupai.1.context: Narada, proud of having resisted Kama, falls in love with a princess at a bride-choice (svayamvara) staged by Vishnu's illusion. He asks Vishnu for Vishnu's own handsome form. Vishnu answers with this image of the doctor and vanishes. Narada, still deluded, does not grasp the hint and is mocked at the ceremony for his monkey face.
rcm.1.127.chaupai.1.core_teaching: As a good doctor refuses a sick person the food that would harm him, the Lord withholds what we crave when it would hurt us. Refusal can be care.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The patient cannot tell harmful food, the doctor can. Narada is sick with desire and asks for a woman, his 'harmful food'. Vishnu says 'listen' so Narada can never say he was not told.

commentaries.who: Lamagoda ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Calling him 'sage, yogi' is quiet irony. The yogi who boasted of conquering desire has become a 'deluded sage'.

commentaries.who: P. P. Pr., in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Narada has a fever of lust with greed, and soon anger. A patient denied bad food curses the doctor, as Narada will. The good doctor bears it calmly for the patient's sake.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Shiva Purana
commentaries.gist: The same image appears there: as a fine physician helps the afflicted, because you are dear to me.

rcm.1.127.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to reframe disappointment, a job or relationship that did not work out, as a possible protection, and as a model for parents and mentors who must sometimes refuse.
misreadings: Not every refusal is for your good; this is a way to reframe, not a reason to accept harm.
Not a justification for controlling others 'for their own good'.
cautions: In the story the 'treatment' is public humiliation. Avoid implying that humiliation is good for people.
not_for: someone being denied basic rights or care by another person who claims it is 'for their good'
fresh grief after a loss that was not a choice
speaks_to: craving something one suspects is bad for one
parents saying no to a child

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 133, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 133, half-lines 1-2'). NOT 1.127.

rcm.1.135.sortha.1.context: Shiva tells Parvati about another cause of Ram's avatar: Svayambhuva Manu and Shatarupa. Manu ruled for ages by divine command, and his children included Dhruva's father and Devahuti, mother of Kapila. In old age he grieved that his life had passed without devotion to Hari. He handed over the kingdom and went with Shatarupa to the Naimisha forest for austerity, where Ram promised to be born as their son.
rcm.1.135.sortha.1.core_teaching: Even a righteous life of duty can leave the heart unfulfilled. Seeing that late is painful, but it becomes a turning point toward what matters.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Two griefs: ages spent in enjoyment, and old age reached at home with life passing without devotion. He felt aversion to both and resolved to leave them. Dharma leads to detachment, detachment to devotion.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Manu cannot be called a sensualist. 'No detachment' means household life left no room for it. His remorse is shown to teach the world.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note
commentaries.gist: Manu kept dharma all his life, so why regret? Tulsidas's teaching: dharma brings happiness, not devotion, and without devotion there is no liberation. It cites Kavitavali: wealth and power mean nothing without love for Ram.

rcm.1.135.sortha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use Manu as a model for midlife and retirement reflection: a dutiful life can still lack what matters most, and it is not too late to turn.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of family or working life: Manu's rule was by divine command and righteous.
Not 'your life was wasted': his grief leads straight to fulfilment.
cautions: Can sting for an older reader who feels their life has been wasted. Pair it with Manu's turn and its fruit.
not_for: an elderly reader who is ill or dying and cannot 'begin again'
someone already sunk in regret without hope

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand soratha 142 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'soratha 142'). NOT 1.135.

rcm.1.141.chaupai.3.context: King Manu and Queen Shatarupa, after long austerity, see the Lord appear and are told to ask any boon. Manu says that seeing the Lord's feet fulfils every wish, yet one great longing remains, which feels too much to ask because of his own smallness: like a pauper before the wishing tree who hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power. The Lord tells him to drop the hesitation, since nothing is withheld from him; Manu then asks for a son like the Lord himself.
rcm.1.141.chaupai.3.core_teaching: We hesitate to ask for what we truly want because we feel too small for it, not knowing how generous the giver is.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Pandit Ramkumar
commentaries.gist: Manu casts himself as the pauper and the Lord as the wishing tree whose power he does not grasp, so he shrinks from asking. The 'great wealth' he wants is the Lord's lifelong presence as a son.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Karunasindhuji
commentaries.gist: Sees here the attitude of 'karpanya' surrender: however much one has practised, one should never think 'I have done something'; humility and love, not years of austerity, win the Lord.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Vijayanand Tripathi
commentaries.gist: The poverty here is ignorance: the deluded person assumes the highest joy is not for him, so he does not even ask for it.

rcm.1.141.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Feeling 'not good enough' can stop us asking for what we really want; the verse invites naming the wish anyway, trusting the giver's generosity.
misreadings: Not 'ask God for wealth'; the 'much' Manu wants is the Lord's lasting presence.
cautions: Devotional framing; for a non-devotional reader, keep the point about hesitating to ask.
not_for: someone whose request has already been refused painfully
speaks_to: feeling unworthy of what you want
hesitating to ask for help or a raise

data_flags.attribution_note: Listener is wrong. In the Manas, Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva had come to Manu many times and he did not ask them for anything; the one who now stands before Manu and Shatarupa and offers the boon is the Supreme Lord in his own form...

rcm.1.15.chaupai.2.context: In the opening salutations Tulsidas bows in turn to Brahma and then to Shiva and Parvati, before Vishnu's forms and Ram's family. This pair of lines comes in that series. Right after it he praises Shiva and Parvati for the Shabar mantras made for the good of the world in the Kali age.
rcm.1.15.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Tulsidas names Shiva and Parvati as his own teacher and parents, the friends of the helpless who give every day. They wish him well without any motive, and they stand to Ram as servant, master and friend.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Guru because Shiva teaches what is good for us. Mother and father because they do us good. Kin to the helpless, and providers who sustain. The poet says they wish him well in every way, the world in one way.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note
commentaries.gist: Ties the line to the tradition (Mool Gosain Charit) that Tulsidas's parents abandoned him at birth (Vinaya 275) and Bhavani fed the infant. Hence 'father and mother' carries personal weight.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note on 'servant, master, friend'
commentaries.gist: The Manas shows Shiva as Ram's servant (bowing to him), as master (Ram worships him at Rameshwaram) and as friend. The name Rameshwar is read all three ways.

rcm.1.15.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Readers use it to name where they found care when human parents or teachers were absent, and to see a divine source of steady, unmotivated goodwill.
misreadings: Not a slight on human parents: it describes Tulsidas's own life and devotion.
cautions: The traditional backstory of Tulsidas being abandoned by his parents comes from a later hagiography (Mool Gosain Charit), which scholars treat as tradition rather than verified biography.
not_for: a reader in fresh grief for a parent who may not want a substitute offered
speaks_to: people without parents, or estranged from them
gratitude toward a teacher who was like a parent

rcm.1.153.sortha.1.context: Shiva tells the story of King Pratapbhanu (who will be reborn as Ravana). Lost while hunting, the king meets an old enemy disguised as a hermit. The false ascetic wins his trust by seeming to shun fame, saying public honour is a fire that burns the forest of austerity. Tulsidas interjects with this warning. The king's trust leads to a Brahmin's curse and his ruin.
rcm.1.153.sortha.1.core_teaching: A fine appearance and sweet words can deceive the clever as easily as the foolish. Judge by conduct, not by looks or speech, as the beautiful, sweet-voiced peacock eats snakes.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The king was first fooled by the holy dress, now by the sweet words, hence 'nectar speech'. 'Mudh na chatur' is a Gahora idiom: fools and clever alike are fooled.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note
commentaries.gist: Dress and speech are fair but conduct foul, as with the wicked who speak sweetly like peacocks and devour great snakes. It cites a Dohavali couplet naming Shurpanakha, Maricha, Putana and Ravana.

commentaries.who: V. Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: A swindler first secures trust, then spreads his net, as Manthara did with Kaikeyi.

commentaries.who: Alternative reading, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Some read 'fools are deceived, not the clever', meaning true devotees. The king, lacking devotion and craving immortality, was a fool in that sense.

rcm.1.153.sortha.1.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to scams, charismatic fraudsters and 'godmen': polish and piety are not proof of honesty, and intelligence is no protection.
misreadings: Not a reason to distrust all religious people or all kind speech.
The peacock is an image only; no moral judgement of the bird.
not_for: someone already paranoid or isolated, who may hear 'trust no one'
speaks_to: evaluating a charismatic leader or guru
shame at being fooled ('even the clever are')

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand soratha 161 (ख), the second closing verse of doha-group 161 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush prints it under 161). NOT 1.153.

rcm.1.180.chhand.4.context: At Ram's birth the Lord appears to Kausalya in his four-armed divine form. She praises him, then knowledge dawns and he smiles and reminds her of her past births' austerity (as Manu and Shatarupa). Her mind turns from awe to a mother's longing, and she asks him to become a baby. He cries like a newborn, and the queens come running.
rcm.1.180.chhand.4.core_teaching: Love asks God to be near rather than grand. Kausalya prefers her child's cry to the divine form, and the Lord gladly becomes small for love.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: His smile and the story he told were meant to take away her knowledge of his godhood. Once she felt like a mother, she called him 'child' instead of 'Lord' and asked for his infant play.

commentaries.who: Pandeyji and Manas Piyush note
commentaries.gist: The joy of his infancy is called beyond compare: even Brahma, Shiva and the sages long for it. Devotees love the Lord's play more than the Lord's majesty.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The smile is compassion: by his Vidya-maya he replaced dry knowledge with the sweetness of parental love (vatsalya).

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Adhyatma Ramayana 1.3.29
commentaries.gist: There Kausalya likewise asks the Lord of the universe to withdraw his unearthly form and show his tender childhood.

rcm.1.180.chhand.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it for the preciousness of ordinary moments with a baby: no greatness compares with being simply loved, and the sacred is met in the small.
misreadings: Not a rejection of God's greatness, only a preference for intimacy.
cautions: Centres a mother and newborn. Could be painful for a reader facing infertility or infant loss.
not_for: someone grieving a miscarriage, stillbirth or infant death
a reader struggling with infertility
speaks_to: devotion that prefers intimacy to awe

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 192, chhand stanza 4 (the 'bhae pragat kripala' birth hymn; Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 192, half-lines 7-8'). NOT 1.180.

rcm.1.186.doha.1.context: After the naming ceremony the mothers cuddle the boys, sometimes in their laps and sometimes in a fine cradle, calling them pet names. Tulsidas pauses to marvel at who is lying there. The next lines describe the child's beauty limb by limb, then say Ram, father and mother of the world, gave joy to the people of Kosala.
rcm.1.186.doha.1.core_teaching: The infinite, unborn, all-pervading Absolute lies in a mother's lap, because love has won it over.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Love made the Lord give up his limits: the all-pervading came to one place, the vast became a child, the stainless played on earth, the unborn was born. All this is 'prem-bhakti-bas'.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note
commentaries.gist: Tulsidas's habit: whenever he describes the Lord's sweetness he adds a touch of majesty, so readers do not mistake him for an ordinary child.

commentaries.who: Khara, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: One of three matching dohas in the childhood section (198, 201, 205). Each states the Lord's transcendence, then the love that binds him: first Kausalya's, then both parents', then the townspeople's.

commentaries.who: Baijnath and P. P. Pr., in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: They see hidden childhood rites in these lines: Baijnath the infant's first showing to the sun, P. P. Pr. the first feeding of cow's milk.

rcm.1.186.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that love brings the vast near: in caring for a child, a parent, or anyone, we hold something infinite.
misreadings: Not a reduction of God to a human infant: the verse insists on both.
cautions: Mother-and-infant imagery may be painful for readers facing infertility or infant loss.
not_for: someone grieving a baby or unable to have children
speaks_to: the wonder of caring for a baby
feeling God is too vast to reach

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 198 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush prints '198'). NOT 1.186.

rcm.1.19.chaupai.3.context: Tulsidas is in the long praise of Ram's name (Bal Kand 19-28). Here he argues that name and form are two adjuncts of the inexpressible Lord, and that the form depends on the name. He goes on to say the name is a witness and interpreter between the formless and the embodied God.
rcm.1.19.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Even something in your hand cannot be recognised without its name. But remembering the name, even without seeing the form, brings that form into the heart with love. That is why Tulsidas puts the name above the form.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Proof within the Manas: Hanuman did not recognise Ram until Ram told him his name (Kishkindha Kand), and then he fell at his feet.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Call a name among sleepers and only that person answers. The form, with all its qualities, lives subtly within the name, and praising the name pleases the one named.

commentaries.who: Lala Bhagwandin, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Shows Tulsidas's philosophical skill. Without names nothing can be known or told apart: someone who knows the shapes but not the names will mix up a mango and an amla.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation (1883)
commentaries.gist: Same sense: without the name the form is not recognised even in your hand, but meditating on the name without seeing the form fills the soul with devotion.

rcm.1.19.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers use it to explain why calling a loved one's name, or God's, brings their presence near even when they are absent or unseen.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of the form or of images. Tulsidas says both are the Lord's, and he will go on to praise the form.
not_for: a reader who wants a practical rather than devotional reflection
speaks_to: missing someone far away or gone
a devotee who cannot visit a temple or see the deity

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 21, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 21, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 1.19: our id and label are off by two.

rcm.1.19.doha.1.context: This doha closes the stretch on name and form in the praise of Ram's name (Bal Kand 19-28). Next Tulsidas turns to the four kinds of devotees (yogis, seekers, the distressed and the wise) who all reach their goal through the name.
rcm.1.19.doha.1.core_teaching: Keep Ram's name on the tongue like a jewel-lamp on a threshold. Like a lamp in a doorway, it lights both the inner life and the outer world.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Why a jewel-lamp? An oil lamp can run dry or blow out, like other practices that need money and are upset by desire and anger. The name, like a gem's light, cannot be extinguished. It should never leave the tongue.

commentaries.who: Vedanti Bhushan Pt. Ramkumar Das, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Dehari' means threshold, by the Amarakosha: body as house, mouth as door, tongue as the sill where the lamp sits. Manas Piyush agrees and cites the 'threshold-lamp' maxim of light on both sides.

commentaries.who: Nange Paramhans, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Reads 'dehari' as a lamp-stand. The tongue holds the name as a stand holds a lamp, and should be used for nothing else. Manas Piyush rejects this sense as unattested in lexicons.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation (1883)
commentaries.gist: Translates it as placing Ram's name like a jewelled lamp at the door of the tongue, for light within and without.

rcm.1.19.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to encourage japa through the day, at work, on the road, at home, so that one practice brightens both inner peace and outer conduct.
misreadings: Not a magic formula that removes outer problems by itself.
not_for: someone in acute crisis who needs practical help first
speaks_to: keeping steady speech and thought at work

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 21 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 21'). NOT 1.19: our id and label are off by two.

rcm.1.196.chaupai.3.context: Vishwamitra comes to Ayodhya to ask for Ram (and Lakshman) to protect his sacrifice from demons. Dasharath offers land, cows, wealth, even his own body and life, but says he cannot give Ram. The sage is unmoved. Vasishtha explains things to the king, his doubts clear, and he hands both boys over with blessings.
rcm.1.196.chaupai.3.core_teaching: A parent's love makes some partings almost impossible, especially when the child faces danger. Yet growing up means the child must sometimes go.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: He first calls all sons dear as life, so the sage cannot simply ask for another, then singles out Ram as dearer than life. Separation from Ram is worse than death to him, as the Ayodhya Kand will show.

commentaries.who: Baba Haridas, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He offered his body and life and the sage stayed silent. Realising breath cannot really be given, he tries again: the others he might give, but Ram is his very senses' master.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji and Ramcharan Mishra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Panjabi: the eldest is most dear, and his life depends on seeing Ram. Mishra: the sons are like the breath, but Ram is the consciousness that gives breath life.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Valmiki 1.20
commentaries.gist: In Valmiki Dasharath admits he could not himself fight Ravana's forces, so how could he send boys? Tulsidas renders this as 'nothing is dearer than body and life'.

rcm.1.196.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Readers apply it to parents letting children leave for school, hostel, a job or the army: the fear is real and honoured, and letting go becomes possible with wise counsel.
misreadings: Love that never lets go can hold a child back; in the story he does let Ram go.
not_for: a parent whose child has died, who may find the 'letting go' frame painful

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 208, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 208, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 1.196.

rcm.1.247.chaupai.1.context: At the bride-choice, every king has failed to move Shiva's bow, and Janaka has despaired aloud. Ram rises at his guru's word and comes to the bow. He looks at the frozen crowd and then at Sita, who is in agony, each instant like an age. He reflects that help after the moment is useless, bows to his guru in his mind, lifts the bow in an instant and breaks it.
rcm.1.247.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Help, love or action that comes after the moment is no help at all. Seeing someone suffering, act while it still matters.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Even a little relief on time (one inch of the bow moved) would have been water to the thirsty. Lifting and breaking it would be nectar, worthless if Sita has already died of grief. It cites a Dohavali couplet.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram looked on her as 'abode of grace', because she had staked love, not merit. The Lord is moved more by pure love than by austerities.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush textual note
commentaries.gist: Commentators debate 'sudha': nectar revives the dead, so is it really useless? Some take 'sudha' as plain water, others (Unmani tika) as 'up to' or the Ganga. The point stands: timeliness.

rcm.1.247.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Widely quoted as a maxim on timely action: a call, an apology, care for an ageing parent, treatment, a decision. Do it while it can still help.
misreadings: Not a reason for panic or recklessness: Ram acts calmly, after bowing to his guru.
Not a judgement on those who missed a moment through no fault of their own.
cautions: The images of dying of thirst and 'regret is useless' can wound someone who arrived too late for a loved one's death. Avoid for fresh grief or guilt.
not_for: someone grieving a death they could not prevent or reach in time
a reader with anxiety who may hear only 'too late'
speaks_to: someone waiting for you to act

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 261, chaupais 1-2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 261, half-lines 1-4'). NOT 1.247, and our text covers two chaupais, not one.

rcm.1.25.chaupai.3.context: Tulsidas compares the ages: in the first age the Lord was pleased by meditation, in the second by sacrifice, in the third by worship. The fourth, Kali, is rooted in impurity, with minds swimming like fish in a sea of sin. In such a terrible time, he says, the name is the wish-fulfilling tree. The next line adds that in Kali the name is the only support.
rcm.1.25.chaupai.3.core_teaching: In a hard age the name of Ram grants what one truly needs and frees one from the world's tangle. It cares for a person here and hereafter as parents care for a child.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Here the name's greatness is shown through time: in every age and every world, those who repeat it became free of sorrow.

commentaries.who: Shri Sudarshan Singh, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The name grants wishes the way parents do: it guards your ultimate good and refuses what would harm you, as parents deny a sick child bad food. Compare Narada's story (Bal Kand 133).

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note
commentaries.gist: A wishing tree gives wealth, duty and pleasure but not liberation, and grants even harmful wishes. The name differs on both counts. 'Remembering' means no effort: the net of opposites dissolves.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation (1883)
commentaries.gist: In these fearful times the name is the only tree of life, and meditating on it stills all commotion.

rcm.1.25.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers use it to reassure people who feel the times are against them: the simplest practice, remembering God, is enough to begin, and it looks after what is truly good for you, not just what you want.
misreadings: Not a promise that every wish will be granted: the commentators stress it gives like a parent, withholding what harms.
Not a reason to skip medical, legal or emotional help.
cautions: The surrounding verses describe the Kali age bleakly. Keep the focus on the comfort, not on 'the age is sinful'.
not_for: someone awaiting a specific outcome (a diagnosis, a job, a court ruling) who may hear a promise
speaks_to: needing to feel parented or protected

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 27, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 27, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 1.25: our id and label are off by two.

rcm.1.25.chaupai.4.context: This continues the praise of the name in the Kali age, after the line calling the name a wish-tree and a parent. Tulsidas says the paths of earlier ages (rites, devotion, knowledge) are out of reach, and the name alone supports. The doha that follows compares the name to Narasimha protecting Prahlad.
rcm.1.25.chaupai.4.core_teaching: When the usual spiritual paths feel out of reach, the name of Ram is still a support. And when the age deceives, the name sees through it, as Hanuman saw through Kalanemi.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Rites need wealth and correct procedure, devotion needs a pure mind, and knowledge needs dispassion and restraint. All are hard when minds are restless. The name has none of these preconditions.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'No karma': people have fallen from their duties. Good deeds are done for praise, worship is outward show, and knowledge is mere words. So the name is the only real recourse.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Kali is deceitful. It knows the name's power, so it attacks by trickery, as Kalanemi did in a sage's disguise. The name, like Hanuman, sees through and destroys the deceit.

commentaries.who: Janakisharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The three paths denied here (discernment, action, devotion) are the meditation, sacrifice and worship of the earlier ages named just before.

rcm.1.25.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers offer it to people who feel they 'can't do' spirituality (no time, no discipline, no learning): one simple remembrance is still open to them.
misreadings: Not a rejection of ethical action, devotion or study: it is a claim about the easiest refuge.
cautions: Depicts the present age as degraded. Avoid framing the reader's own life as corrupt.
not_for: a reader who would hear 'no devotion, no discernment' as a judgement on themselves
speaks_to: feeling unable to keep up any practice
burnout, exhaustion, depression that make discipline impossible
