data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 27, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 27, half-lines 7-8'). NOT 1.25: our id and label are off by two.

rcm.1.258.doha.1.context: Ram has broken Shiva's bow at Sita's bride-choice (svayamvara). Parashurama, Shiva's devotee and the destroyer of kings, storms in demanding to know who broke it. Lakshman goads him with mocking replies while Ram stays courteous. In the end Parashurama tests Ram with Vishnu's bow, recognises him, and leaves praising him. Parashurama has been reciting his feats: twenty-one times he rid the earth of kings, his axe killed Sahasrabahu. Lakshman tells him to go on if he is not satisfied, since a hero who reviles does not look well. Then he says this.
rcm.1.258.doha.1.core_teaching: The truly capable prove themselves in action, not words. Boasting in front of an opponent is the mark of insecurity.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Lakshman's earlier jibes imply Parashurama is shameless, angry, a babbler. His pride in killing Sahasrabahu and ridding the earth of kshatriyas fuels his rage at a boy who does not fear him.

commentaries.who: Lamagoda ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Notes the humour: Lakshman needles Parashurama's self-praise, then his abuse.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing a Subhashita
commentaries.gist: A verse on self-praise: virtues one claims for oneself bring no grace. Virtues others recognise do, so the wise never proclaim their own.

rcm.1.258.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use the maxim at work and in sport: let results speak, and be wary of those who keep announcing what they can do.
misreadings: Not a ban on ever speaking about one's abilities (interviews, applications).
In context it is a taunt that inflames the sage, so the scene is not a model of how to say it.
cautions: Calls the boaster a coward, which is harsh if aimed at a reader. Use as a self-check, not a label.
not_for: someone who needs encouragement to speak up for themselves
speaks_to: impostor feelings next to loud colleagues

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 274 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush '274'). NOT 1.258.

rcm.1.26.chaupai.1.context: This is the last line of the long praise of Ram's name. Having said the name works in every age, Tulsidas says it works whatever the mood in which it is said. He then bows to Raghunath and begins, confessing his faults and trusting Ram to set them right.
rcm.1.26.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Whatever the mood in which the name is said, with love, with ill will, in irritation or in laziness, it brings good everywhere. Its power does not depend on the speaker's state.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Four modes: 'bhav' is loving relationship (servant to master, child to parent), 'kubhav' hostile feeling like envy or enmity, 'anakh' anger from a love that has turned sulky, 'alas' the name slipping out in grief or fatigue.

commentaries.who: Vijay Dohavali, as cited in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Gives examples: Shiva repeated the name with love, Valmiki with 'wrong' feeling (the reversed name), Kumbhakarna in sloth, and Ravana in anger.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note
commentaries.gist: 'Kubhav' also covers self-seeking motives, repeating it for show, joking, or mere semblance of the name. Even these are not wasted.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation (1883)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as repeating the name 'whether in joy or in sadness, in action or in repose', bliss spreads all around.

rcm.1.26.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to tell people not to wait until they feel devout: begin the practice tired, irritable or doubtful, and keep going.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of careless or mocking use of sacred names: it praises the name's generosity.
Not a claim that inner feeling does not matter at all: the Manas elsewhere prizes loving remembrance most.
not_for: someone who needs to hear that their feelings matter, not just the ritual
readers who feel pressured into religious practice
speaks_to: feeling too low, angry or tired to pray
restarting a practice after a lapse

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 28, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush cites it as '28. 1'). NOT 1.26: our id and label are off by two.

rcm.1.26.chaupai.2.context: Having bowed to Raghunath and begun, Tulsidas lists his own shortcomings. His mind and wit are poor, his poetry lacks every grace, his fortune is small. He trusts that Ram, whose kindness never tires, will set everything right. The next lines describe how a good master accepts his servant's honest effort, and Ram most of all.
rcm.1.26.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Grace does not wait for the servant to deserve it. Ram cares for Tulsidas by looking at his own compassionate nature, not at the servant's poor record, and his kindness never tires.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: 'He will set right' assumes something is spoilt, and earlier lines say what: mind and wit, the poetry's craft, and luck. 'In every way' means all of these will be mended.

commentaries.who: Manas Prakash, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Once grace is given it keeps growing. If a devotee errs, the Lord thinks he gave too little grace and takes the fault on himself.

commentaries.who: Karunasindhu, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Reads 'अघाती' also as 'अघ-हाती', the destroyer of sin: without his grace no other god's favour removes wrongdoing.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note on 'good master'
commentaries.gist: Other masters pay by service rendered. Ram shows kindness without service. It cites Kavitavali: at Ram's door alone the poor, the weak and the wayward are called in and honoured.

rcm.1.26.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it with people weighed down by their own failings: grace is not a wage for good behaviour, so one can start from where one is.
misreadings: Not a licence to stop trying: Tulsidas goes on to work hard at the poem.
Grace does not erase consequences or responsibility toward people one has hurt.
not_for: a reader who would use it to excuse harm to others without making amends
speaks_to: a lapse in practice or conduct
being cared for despite one's failings

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 28, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 28, half-lines 3-4'). NOT 1.26: our id and label are off by two.

rcm.1.26.doha.1.context: Tulsidas has said that Ram, a good master, accepts honest effort and looks at the heart. Now he cites the proof: the stones of the bridge to Lanka floated, and monkeys and bears became his trusted counsellors. In the next doha (28 ख) he jokes that everyone laughs at Ram for having such a servant as Tulsidas.
rcm.1.26.doha.1.core_teaching: The one who made stones float and made monkeys and bears into wise counsellors will honour the love and hope of even a dull servant. Grace makes the unfit fit.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The examples are deliberate. Telling Ram's story needs a sound mind, and his is poor. Ram gave monkeys wisdom, so he will give it too. The floating stones carried an army across, and the endless story will carry him.

commentaries.who: Sant Gursahay Lal, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Love' is his remembering the name and bowing to Raghunath before beginning. 'Liking' is his wish to be set right.

commentaries.who: Unmani tika, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Stones that sink and drag others down were made into boats that carry others. Animals fit only to be made to dance became counsellors. If Ram did that, he will fulfil a human servant's wish.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing the Bhagavata (5.19.7)
commentaries.gist: Birth, beauty, eloquence and intellect do not win Ram's favour. He made friends of forest creatures to show it.

rcm.1.26.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers offer it to anyone who feels unqualified, whether a first-time parent, a new student or a beginner: earnest love counts, and help comes for what one cannot do alone.
misreadings: Not a slur on animals or on 'foolish' people: the point is that grace raises up whoever it touches.
not_for: a reader who would take 'foolish servant' or 'monkeys and bears' as an insult to themselves
non-devotional readers looking for practical self-worth advice
speaks_to: starting a creative or service project without credentials

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 28 (क), the first of two dohas numbered 28 (Gita Press). NOT 1.26: our id and label are off by two.

rcm.1.260.doha.1.context: Ram has broken Shiva's bow at Sita's bride-choice (svayamvara). Parashurama, Shiva's devotee and the destroyer of kings, storms in demanding to know who broke it. Lakshman goads him with mocking replies while Ram stays courteous. In the end Parashurama tests Ram with Vishnu's bow, recognises him, and leaves praising him. Lakshman has just told Parashurama that he spares him only because he is a Brahmin, and that he has grown big at home without facing a real warrior. The assembly cries out 'wrong!', Ram silences Lakshman with a glance, and seeing the sage's anger blazing up, speaks soothing words.
rcm.1.260.doha.1.core_teaching: Sharp replies feed an angry person's fire like ghee. Cooling, humble words are what put it out.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: All of Lakshman's replies are bitter, the last especially. Parashurama raises his axe and the hall cries out. Ram stops Lakshman by a sign, then speaks water-like words.

commentaries.who: Swami Prajnananand, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Lakshman, Vishvamitra and Ram had all asked forgiveness, yet Parashurama kept accusing. His capacity to forgive had gone: anger had destroyed forbearance.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note on 'Bhriguvar'
commentaries.gist: Lakshman addresses him by his ancestor Bhrigu's name. Bhrigu kicked Vishnu, and his descendant raises an axe, so the name fits.

rcm.1.260.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it for conflict at home and work: when someone is angry, do not add fuel. Speak in a way that lowers the heat.
misreadings: Not a demand that people being abused must always placate their abuser.
Not a dismissal of Lakshman's loyalty: the issue is the effect of his words.
not_for: someone facing an abusive or violent person, where safety, not soothing words, is the priority
speaks_to: managing an angry boss or customer
a sibling or friend who escalates conflicts

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 276 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush '276'). NOT 1.260.

rcm.1.261.doha.1.context: Ram has broken Shiva's bow at Sita's bride-choice (svayamvara). Parashurama, Shiva's devotee and the destroyer of kings, storms in demanding to know who broke it. Lakshman goads him with mocking replies while Ram stays courteous. In the end Parashurama tests Ram with Vishnu's bow, recognises him, and leaves praising him. Parashurama has just told Ram that his brother is a great sinner, and that Ram is not like him. Lakshman laughs and replies with this. He goes on with mock humility about the broken bow (next verse).
rcm.1.261.doha.1.core_teaching: Anger is the root of wrongdoing: in its grip people do what they should not and turn against everyone.

commentaries.who: Ramcharan Mishra, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Lakshman's laughter signals irony: a calm reply that is really a counter-thrust.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note
commentaries.gist: It answers 'your brother is a great sinner': if anger is sin's root and anger rides on you, who is the sinner? It links Hanuman's reflection on anger in Valmiki 5.55.5-6: the angry may kill even their guru.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note
commentaries.gist: Implies that anger is why Parashurama cannot recognise Ram, and why he speaks harshly to the one his own guru worships.

rcm.1.261.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers quote the maxim on its own: notice anger rising, because most regrettable words and acts begin there.
misreadings: Not a teaching that all anger is sinful, including anger at injustice.
In the scene Lakshman uses it as a taunt, which inflames rather than cools. Do not present it as a model of how to calm someone.
not_for: someone whose justified anger at abuse or injustice is being dismissed

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 277 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush '277'). NOT 1.261.

rcm.1.262.chaupai.1.context: Ram has broken Shiva's bow at Sita's bride-choice (svayamvara). Parashurama, Shiva's devotee and the destroyer of kings, storms in demanding to know who broke it. Lakshman goads him with mocking replies while Ram stays courteous. In the end Parashurama tests Ram with Vishnu's bow, recognises him, and leaves praising him. Right after saying anger is the root of sin, Lakshman puts on a show of humility: I am your servant, be kind, a broken bow won't mend through anger, your feet must ache, sit down. The jibes continue until Ram steps in again.
rcm.1.262.chaupai.1.core_teaching: As a saying: anger cannot undo what is done. In the scene it is mockery that inflames rather than calms.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush gloss (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Paraphrases the lines and the one after: if the bow is so dear, let us call a skilled craftsman to join it, which is plainly sarcastic.

commentaries.who: Ramcharan Mishra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The whole exchange is a play of retort and counter-retort. Lakshman's laughter marks irony beneath polite words.

rcm.1.262.chaupai.1.practical_reading: The half-line 'a broken thing won't mend through anger' is used on its own as gentle advice to stop raging over what cannot be undone, but say it kindly, not as Lakshman does.
misreadings: Not a model of how to talk to an angry person: in context it is sarcasm that stokes the fire.
Not 'just get over it' for a real loss.
cautions: Sarcastic tone. If quoted to someone grieving a loss ('it won't mend'), it can sound dismissive.
not_for: someone grieving a death or a broken relationship
an angry reader who would hear mockery
speaks_to: rumination over a past mistake or loss
family arguments about something broken or lost

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 278, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 278, half-lines 1-2'). NOT 1.262.

rcm.1.27.chaupai.2.context: Tulsidas has just confessed that his audacity is so great that even hell would turn up its nose, and that he is afraid of his own fear, yet Ram never took notice of it even in a dream. Here he says the Lord, having heard and looked and considered, praised his devotion. The next lines say the Lord keeps no mistake in mind, and give the examples of Sugriva and Vibhishana.
rcm.1.27.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Even when what we say or do comes out badly, Ram looks at the intention in the heart and is pleased by it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Hearing, seeing and weighing describe how the Lord takes in a devotee's devotion. 'Su-chit chakh' means considering with the mind.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Objects to the plain reading: Ram knows all and needs no hearing or seeing, and self-praise spoils merit. Reads instead: I have heard from guru and scripture that the Lord looks for the heart's clear eye.

commentaries.who: Sudhakar Prasad Mishra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Replies: Tulsidas is reassuring himself, not boasting to others. And love explains it all: Ram ate Sudama's rice, Shabari's tasted berries and Vidura's greens.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation (1883)
commentaries.gist: Though the story is spoilt by the telling, Ram accounts it good, since the will is good.

rcm.1.27.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to clumsy prayers, awkward apologies and imperfect work: sincerity is what is received.
misreadings: Not an excuse for careless words toward people: it describes God's reading of intent, not a rule that others must ignore how we speak.
not_for: someone hurt by another's 'well-meant' words, who may hear their pain dismissed
speaks_to: fear of saying the wrong thing
perfectionism in creative or devotional work
people with speech or language difficulties

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 29, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 29, half-lines 3-4'). NOT 1.27: our id and label are off by two.

rcm.1.27.chaupai.3.context: This continues from the line that Ram is pleased by the good in a servant's heart even when the telling is spoilt. Tulsidas says the Lord does not keep a mistake in mind and remembers the heart a hundred times. His example is pointed: the misdeed for which Ram killed Bali, Sugriva and Vibhishana later committed too, yet Ram honoured them.
rcm.1.27.chaupai.3.core_teaching: The Lord does not hold on to a devotee's lapse but keeps recalling the good in their heart. The proof is that he overlooked in his friends the very wrong he punished in an enemy.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: A slip is an act. If word and deed go wrong but the heart is good, Ram is pleased. He cites Dohavali: what is made by the mind, Ram treats as well made.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Valmiki 2.1.11 and Gita 9.30
commentaries.gist: Ram is satisfied by a single kindness and does not recall a hundred wrongs. Whoever worships single-mindedly, even with bad conduct, is to be counted good.

commentaries.who: Nange Paramhans, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Bali's sin was taking his younger brother's wife. Sugriva then took Tara, and Vibhishana Mandodari. Ram overlooked these because of their devotion. Bali, an enemy of a devotee, was punished, then forgiven when he took refuge.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation (1883)
commentaries.gist: The Lord is not mindful of a chance fault but always considers the heart. Sugriva and Vibhishana did what Bali was killed for, yet Ram honoured them.

rcm.1.27.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers use the first half for people stuck in guilt: God remembers your good heart more than your slip. The Bali example is usually only mentioned, not dwelt on.
misreadings: Not a model for overlooking repeated harm in human relationships, especially sexual or domestic wrongs.
Not 'mistakes have no consequences': Bali's story shows they do; the point is about the heart of one who turns to God.
cautions: The illustration involves Bali's killing and the taking of a brother's wife or widow. Handle carefully, or use only the first half for a distressed reader.
not_for: someone dealing with infidelity or abuse, who might hear 'forget the wrong'
a reader being pressured to forgive a repeat offender
speaks_to: fear that one's failings define one

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 29, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 29, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 1.27: our id and label are off by two.

rcm.1.3.chaupai.4.context: In the opening salutations Tulsidas compares the gathering of saints to the sacred confluence at Prayag and says its effect is immediate: crows become cuckoos and herons become swans. Valmiki, Narada and Agastya told how it changed them, and whatever wisdom, fame or good end anyone has reached came through it. This line follows. The next line says even rogues are reformed by such company.
rcm.1.3.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Clear judgement grows from keeping holy company, and that company is itself a gift of grace. Practices are flowers, but satsang is the root and also the fruit.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Reads a chain: Ram's grace brings satsang, satsang brings discernment, and discernment brings release. Grace is why everyone does not simply seek satsang. He cites parallels from Vinaya Patrika and Sundar Kand.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Without God's grace a person develops no taste for, or trust in, the words of the good. Other practices bring other fruits, but satsang depends on grace alone.

commentaries.who: Baijnath and Baba Janakidas, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Baijnath: satsang is the root of two trees, discernment and joy. Janakidas: even knowing satsang's power is itself learned in satsang.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation (1883)
commentaries.gist: Renders satsang as 'intercourse with the good', attainable only by Ram's blessing. Good works are its flowers and perfection its fruit.

rcm.1.3.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to the people and conversations we choose. Judgement is shaped by whom we spend time with, and finding people who make us better is a grace worth recognising and seeking.
misreadings: Not a claim that people without mentors cannot think: the verse is about where discernment grows.
Not a call to cut off ordinary friends. Manas Piyush also notes that a brief meeting is not enough: the Manas elsewhere stresses long association (Garuda's doubt clears only after long satsang).
cautions: For someone isolated by illness, grief or circumstance, 'without satsang there is no discernment' could feel like a judgement. Frame it as an invitation to seek company, not a verdict.
not_for: someone who has no access to company right now and would feel blamed
a reader being pressured to leave friends or family
speaks_to: gratitude for a mentor or circle that changed you

rcm.1.3.chaupai.5.context: This continues Tulsidas's praise of the saints: satsang is the root of joy, and the gift of grace. Here he gives its proof: it reforms the worst. He then turns to the opposite worry, whether the good are spoiled by bad company, before saying even the gods cannot fully tell the glory of saints. Doha 3 follows, bowing to the even-minded sants.
rcm.1.3.chaupai.5.core_teaching: Holy company can transform even the worst, as the philosopher's stone turns iron to gold. And when circumstances force good people into bad company, they keep their own nature, like the jewel in a serpent's hood.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Offered as proof that company alone, with no other practice, perfects a person.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Reformed' means their standing rises: honour in this world and a good end hereafter.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'By fate' means the good never seek bad company. They are born into it or bound to it, like the gem born in a snake. Prahlad and Vibhishana are his examples. The gem even counteracts the poison.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation (1883)
commentaries.gist: Same sense: the wicked reformed like vile metal touched by the philosopher's stone. A good man fallen by mischance into evil company still keeps his virtue, like the gem in a serpent's head.

rcm.1.3.chaupai.5.practical_reading: The verse is used both to encourage people who are trying to change through better company and to steady those stuck in difficult surroundings: you do not have to become what is around you.
misreadings: Not a reason to stay in a harmful or abusive environment: the second half describes unchosen circumstance (बिधि बस), and the commentators stress that the good do not choose bad company.
Not a claim that good people are immune to influence. It describes what the truly good do, as an ideal.
cautions: Someone living with an abusive family member could hear 'keep your nature like the jewel' as advice to endure. Pair it with the fact that the text speaks of circumstance, not of choosing to stay.
not_for: someone in danger who needs to leave, not endure
a reader who would hear 'the wicked' as a label for themselves without the hope of the first half
speaks_to: wanting to change and seeking better company
being in a workplace or family whose values you do not share
hope for someone who has gone astray

rcm.1.318.chaupai.3.context: After the four weddings, the brides are leaving Mithila for Ayodhya. The queens weep, and even the parrots and mynas Sita raised cry out her name. Then Janaka and his brother come. Janaka, renowned as the most detached of sages, sees Sita and breaks down. Later Janaka collects himself and sees them off.
rcm.1.318.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Even the most detached and wise heart breaks open at a beloved daughter's leaving. Love sweeps past the boundaries of wisdom, and Tulsidas honours it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: His tears come from love of Janaki, not delusion (compare Ayodhya 286). Others' composure merely slipped. Janaka's fled, because his love was greater.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Was called supremely detached' suggests that today it did not show. First his composure went, and with it knowledge and dispassion.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note
commentaries.gist: That love overflows the banks of knowledge shows the beauty of knowledge: it is love's worth that even the wisest bow to it.

commentaries.who: Manas Mayank, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Renunciation is practised to reach the Lord. How could it hold at the parting from Sita, who is herself that goal?

rcm.1.318.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Used at weddings and send-offs: grief at a child's leaving is not weakness or a failure of wisdom. Even the wise cry.
misreadings: Not a criticism of Janaka or of detachment.
not_for: a parent estranged from a child, for whom the warm embrace may sting
speaks_to: a daughter's or son's wedding and leaving home
people embarrassed by their own tears

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 338, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 338, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 1.318.

rcm.1.54.chaupai.1.context: Sati saw Shiva bow to Ram, who was grieving for Sita in the forest, and could not believe this prince was God. Ignoring Shiva's advice she tested Ram by taking Sita's form. Ram recognised her at once, and she then told Shiva she had done no test. Shiva saw the truth in meditation and resolved not to treat her as his wife in that body. On the way home a heavenly voice praised Shiva's vow. Sati asked what it meant, he would not say, and she guessed that he knew everything. This line opens her remorse. The next line shows her realising he has withdrawn from her.
rcm.1.54.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Facing what she had done, Sati is consumed with worry. She also sees Shiva's depth: he knew her fault and still did not throw it in her face.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Only now does she truly grasp her deed. Not knowing what punishment is coming makes the worry grow. A Padma Purana verse: the pyre burns the dead, worry burns the living.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Not naming her fault, lest it hurt her, is his fathomless depth. Far from punishing, he would not even say it aloud. She weighs his virtues against her failings: he all-knowing and kind, she foolish to deceive him.

commentaries.who: Manas Patrika, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: It is human nature, when trouble comes, to replay one's misdeeds and panic more. She wonders what came over her to hide anything from the one who wished her well.

rcm.1.54.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Readers take it as a picture of remorse after hurting someone who loves us, and of the grace of a partner who does not shame us even when they know.
misreadings: Not a model of never discussing problems in a relationship: Shiva's silence here is mercy, not a rule.
Not an endorsement of the 'deserved' suffering that follows: it describes what happened.
cautions: The arc ends with Sati's death at her father's sacrifice. In the preceding doha (57 क) she blames her deceit on women being 'by nature foolish', a line an editor should not carry into a modern reading.
not_for: someone already drowning in guilt, unless paired with the hope of repair later in the story (Parvati)
a reader whose partner punishes them with silence, who may hear silence praised
speaks_to: remorse after lying to a partner
realising the other person knew all along
being treated more gently than one deserved

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 58, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 58, half-lines 1-2'). NOT 1.54.

rcm.1.54.chaupai.2.context: Sati saw Shiva bow to Ram, who was grieving for Sita in the forest, and could not believe this prince was God. Ignoring Shiva's advice she tested Ram by taking Sita's form. Ram recognised her at once, and she then told Shiva she had done no test. Shiva saw the truth in meditation and resolved not to treat her as his wife in that body. Sati has just realised that Shiva knows and has spared her the shame of hearing it said. Now she reads in his manner that he has withdrawn from her. Unable to speak, she burns inside, and they sit apart on Kailash for a long time until news of her father's sacrifice arrives.
rcm.1.54.chaupai.2.core_teaching: When we know a breach is our own doing, words fail and the heart burns quietly. The verse names that silent, smouldering remorse.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Shiva had resolved that loving Sati as before, after she took Sita's form, would break the path of devotion. Reading his face, she sees this. Her worry came from the fault, her anguish from the abandonment.

commentaries.who: Pt. Sudhakar Prasad Mishra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: She is called 'Bhavani' here because, like Shiva, she is deep: though abandoned, she kept it hidden in her heart.

commentaries.who: Sudhakar Dwivedi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Reads the withdrawal as the traditional penalty: a wife who has offended is set aside rather than harmed, and for a wife no grief is greater. (A period view; editors should not carry it into a reading.)

rcm.1.54.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it to name the silent, consuming guilt that follows a breach of trust, and why it needs to be spoken and repaired rather than left to smoulder.
misreadings: Guilt is a signal to make amends, not a sentence to burn forever.
Not a model of how to respond when a partner errs: Shiva's withdrawal comes from his particular vow.
cautions: Speaks of being abandoned by one's husband. Commentary frames it in patriarchal terms. For a reader whose partner has withdrawn, this can reinforce self-blame.
not_for: a reader in an emotionally abusive marriage
someone whose guilt is out of proportion and needs reassurance
speaks_to: feeling a loved one pull away and knowing why
being unable to speak about one's own wrong

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 58, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 58, half-lines 3-4'). NOT 1.54.

rcm.1.54.sortha.1.context: Sati saw Shiva bow to Ram, who was grieving for Sita in the forest, and could not believe this prince was God. Ignoring Shiva's advice she tested Ram by taking Sita's form. Ram recognised her at once, and she then told Shiva she had done no test. Shiva saw the truth in meditation and resolved not to treat her as his wife in that body. Sati has just guessed that Shiva knows everything, and reproached herself for deceiving him (57 क). The narrator then comments with this image. The next lines show her worry and Shiva's withdrawal.
rcm.1.54.sortha.1.core_teaching: True love lifts the lesser partner to the value of the greater, as water mixed with milk sells as milk. But a drop of deceit splits them, and the sweetness goes.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Mixed with milk, water takes milk's price, colour and taste. That is milk's generosity. Once something sour falls in, the milk splits and the taste is gone: so deceit ends companionship and love.

commentaries.who: Manas Patrika, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Split milk cannot become milk again, and a torn heart does not rejoin. It cites a popular saying that pearls, milk and the heart cannot be mended once broken.

commentaries.who: Sudhakar Dwivedi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Shiva, camphor-white, is the milk, and Sati the water. United, they were worshipped and honoured as one. Deceit separated them and spoiled the union.

commentaries.who: Bhikharidas's verse, cited in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Milk and water show mutual love: water sells at milk's price, and when milk is heated the water burns first, and milk boils over to reach it. Each sacrifices for the other.

rcm.1.54.sortha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it on honesty in close relationships: love raises us, but even small concealments sour trust.
misreadings: Not proof that trust can never be rebuilt: in the Manas itself Sati is reborn as Parvati and, after long austerity, reunited with Shiva.
cautions: Some commentary says a split heart never rejoins. That can feel like a verdict to someone who lied and is trying to repair. Pair it with the Parvati story.
not_for: someone who has confessed and is working to repair trust, who may hear it as hopeless
a person being falsely accused of deceit
speaks_to: keeping a secret from a partner
gratitude for a partner who lifts us

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand soratha 57 (ख), the second of the two closing verses of doha-group 57 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush prints it as 57). NOT 1.54. It comes just BEFORE 58.1-2 in the text, not after.

rcm.1.58.chaupai.3.context: Daksha, Sati's father, holds a great sacrifice and invites all his daughters and their husbands except Shiva and Sati, because Daksha took offence at Shiva in Brahma's assembly long ago. Sati, longing to see her family and the festival, asks to go. Shiva says it is not right to go uninvited where you are resented. She goes anyway, is slighted, finds no share set aside for Shiva, and gives up her body in the sacrificial fire.
rcm.1.58.chaupai.3.core_teaching: One may go uninvited to a friend's, master's, father's or teacher's home. But where someone bears hostility toward you, going brings no good.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: What Shiva warned came true. No one showed Sati affection, courtesy or regard: Daksha did not ask after her, and her sisters smiled mockingly.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Calling her 'Bhavani' shows he has renounced only the Sati body, not his deep love. His vow does not mean her humiliation would not grieve him.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Bhagavata 4.3 and Skanda Purana
commentaries.gist: Shiva warns that she will be dishonoured because she is his. The Skanda Purana says those who enter another's house uninvited meet a humiliation worse than death.

commentaries.who: Manas Patrika, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Shil, sneh, kani' are lost on both sides: they will not honour her, and she, slighted, will lose her composure and affection toward them.

rcm.1.58.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to family gatherings and workplaces: closeness gives you a right to show up, but where you know there is active hostility, protect your dignity rather than walk in hoping for warmth.
misreadings: Not a rule to cut off family; it is a caution about walking into known hostility.
Not victim-blaming: Daksha's insult, not Sati's longing, is the wrong in the story.
cautions: The story ends with Sati's death by self-immolation at the sacrifice. Do not link the verse to that ending for a distressed reader.
not_for: someone grieving a family rupture who wants reconciliation, not justification for distance
a reader at risk of self-harm (because of how the story ends)
speaks_to: deciding whether to attend a family event where you are resented
estrangement from a parent or in-laws

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 62, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 62, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 1.58.

rcm.1.6.doha.1.context: After bowing to saints and, wryly, to the wicked, Tulsidas says the Vedas and Puranas describe creation as virtue and fault kneaded together, and lists pairs of opposites. This doha sums it up. The next line adds that a person turns from fault to virtue only when the Creator grants such discernment.
rcm.1.6.doha.1.core_teaching: The world is a mixture of good and bad. The mark of a saint is the discernment to take the good from everything and leave the rest.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Scripture can name the virtue and fault in each thing, as an expert can tell water in milk. Only the saint actually separates them and takes the good. Compare Bharat as swan (Ayodhya 232).

commentaries.who: Sudhakar Dwivedi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The doha works as a definition of a saint: one who stays clear of faults in this world and takes up only virtues.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation (1883)
commentaries.gist: The Creator made the universe of animate and inanimate, good and evil. A saint, like a swan, extracts the milk of goodness and rejects the worthless water.

rcm.1.6.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it for how we look at people and situations: notice what is good in a person or a place and take that, rather than feeding on faults.
misreadings: Not a call to deny real harm or wrongdoing: the text admits faults exist.
Not license to judge others as 'water'. The discernment is for what one takes in, not for condemning.
not_for: someone processing a serious wrong done to them, who may hear it as 'just focus on the positive'
speaks_to: a mixed experience: a job, family or city with good and bad in it
learning not to dwell on others' faults

rcm.1.66.chaupai.2.context: Reading the newborn Parvati's palm, Narada said her husband would be without qualities or honour, without parents, careless, a matted-haired yogi in inauspicious dress. Her parents were devastated. Narada explains that in Shiva these marks are not faults, for the able are not tainted by them. Here he says a marriage with Shiva would be wholly good, and that if Parvati does austerity, Shiva, who can even erase destiny, will be won.
rcm.1.66.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Shiva is hard to win, yet quickly pleased by sincere effort and hardship. What looks like bad news in Parvati's future becomes good when she seeks him.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Because Shiva is the able Lord, the 'faults' Narada listed are virtues in him. 'Shambhu' means maker of welfare, so 'good in every way' fits. The earlier marriage brought separation; this one brings reunion.

commentaries.who: Sudhakar Dwivedi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Hard to win: Ravana offered his own heads. But he is also Ashutosh, so the hardship need not last long. Vinaya Patrika gives examples of how quickly he pleases.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush and Vishvanath Tripathi
commentaries.gist: As Tripurari he destroyed the impossible Tripura. Likewise he can wipe out what fate has written. Destiny binds those who turn from God and loosens before the devoted.

rcm.1.66.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it to encourage perseverance: what seems out of reach often yields to sincere, sustained effort sooner than we expect.
misreadings: Not a promise that suffering earns rewards on demand.
'Hardship' here is chosen spiritual discipline, not enduring abuse.
cautions: The austerity that follows is extreme (Parvati gives up even dry leaves). Avoid suggesting self-deprivation.
not_for: someone exhausting themselves trying to earn love or approval
speaks_to: a goal that feels out of reach
parents worried about a child's future

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 70, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 70, half-lines 3-4'). NOT 1.66.

rcm.1.67.doha.1.context: After Narada leaves, Maina weeps and begs Himavan to find a suitable husband for Parvati, even against the prophecy. Himavan replies that Narada's word cannot fail, the moon would sooner rain fire. Then he says this doha. Next he gently tells Parvati to do austerity for Shiva.
rcm.1.67.doha.1.core_teaching: Worry cannot change what is beyond our control. Remember the Lord: the one who made our child will see to her good.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: He says 'remember the Lord' because the Lord made Parvati. The one who creates also provides.

commentaries.who: Sudhakar Dwivedi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Himavan holds to the principle that 'he who protects the child in the womb protects it still'. Too much cleverness unsettles faith. Holding to the Lord alone, Himavan sets his own mind and his wife's at rest.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji and S. P. Mishra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Shri-Bhagavan' means the Lord with Lakshmi: pray that Parvati gets a husband as fine as Shri's. Mishra: worship with Shri fulfils every wish.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note
commentaries.gist: 'All worry' means worry over the family and the match, over whether a fit husband will come, and over the inner burning.

rcm.1.67.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers offer it to anxious parents: do your part, but hand the worry you cannot act on to the One who made your child.
misreadings: Trust sits beside action, not instead of it: Himavan immediately advises a concrete step (Parvati's austerity, Gita Press 1.72).
not_for: a parent facing a child's medical emergency who needs action, not reassurance
someone being told to 'just pray' instead of getting help
speaks_to: parents anxious about a child's marriage, health or future
spousal anxiety in a family decision
worry about things outside one's control

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 71 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 71'). NOT 1.67.

rcm.1.70.doha.1.context: Parvati does years of austerity: living on roots and fruit, then leaves, then water and air, then giving up even dry leaves (hence the name Aparna). Her body is reduced to bones. Seeing her so wasted, a voice from the sky speaks. Then the seven sages arrive to test her resolve.
rcm.1.70.doha.1.core_teaching: Sustained devotion bears fruit. When the goal is secured, the hardship should be laid down.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The voice came because her body was so wasted it seemed life would leave it. Unlike to Manu or Ravana, it does not say 'ask a boon', because everyone knew her wish.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Second reason: she would be too shy to ask openly for a husband, as she later tells the sages with hesitation. So the voice simply announced fulfilment.

commentaries.who: Sudhakar Dwivedi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: When she stopped eating even dry leaves the gods cried 'Aparna!', fearing for her life, and Brahma, amazed, spoke.

rcm.1.70.doha.1.practical_reading: Readers take it as permission to stop striving once something is truly won, and as reassurance that long, faithful effort is seen.
misreadings: Not a model of starving or punishing the body to get what you want. The voice's first command is to stop the hardship.
cautions: The surrounding text describes extreme fasting until the body is skin and bone. Do not use it for readers with eating disorders or self-punishing habits, or frame deprivation as admirable.
not_for: someone with an eating disorder or self-harm through deprivation
a reader still waiting with no end in sight, who may feel taunted
speaks_to: the end of a long, hard effort (exams, treatment, a long wait)

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 74 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 74'). NOT 1.70.

rcm.1.72.chaupai.1.context: After Sati gave up her body, Shiva wandered, repeating Ram's name, sometimes teaching sages, sometimes telling Ram's virtues. Meanwhile Parvati was born and performed her austerity. These lines show Shiva in his grief. Soon Ram appears to him and asks him to marry Parvati.
rcm.1.72.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Even the Lord, who is free of desire, feels the grief of separation from one who loved him. He carries it by teaching and telling Ram's story.

commentaries.who: Manas Patrika, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: He fills his days with Ram's story so the grief of losing his single-minded devotee does not overwhelm him. His conduct teaches: speak of Ram to a listener, listen to a speaker, and otherwise remember alone.

commentaries.who: S. P. Mishra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Though desireless, he grieves because he knew Sati as a devotee. Mishra also reports another reading in which the grieving Lord is Ram, pained by Parvati's tapas.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Bhagavata 2.1.5
commentaries.gist: Links the line to Shuka's advice: one who wants freedom from fear should hear, sing and remember Hari, depending on whether a speaker or listener is present.

rcm.1.72.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say grief is not a failure of wisdom: even the wisest feel loss. Shiva's way is to keep teaching, serving and remembering.
misreadings: Not 'the enlightened do not grieve': the verse says the opposite.
Not a recipe to bury grief in busyness: it shows grief held alongside meaningful work.
cautions: Mentions the aftermath of a spouse's death (Sati's self-immolation is the backdrop). Gentle, but name the loss carefully.
not_for: a reader whose partner died by suicide, since Sati's self-immolation is the backdrop
someone who needs permission to stop working and rest in grief
speaks_to: feeling that a spiritual person 'shouldn't' grieve
carrying grief while still working or caring for others

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 76, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 76, half-lines 1-2'). NOT 1.72.

rcm.1.74.chaupai.3.context: The seven sages (Saptarishi), sent by Shiva to test her, find Parvati as if she were austerity in person. They ask whom she worships and what she wants. Shyly, expecting to be laughed at, she says her mind is set on the impossible. The sages then mock Narada and Shiva, and she answers them point by point.
rcm.1.74.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Parvati admits that by worldly judgement her hope is impossible, yet her heart holds to Shiva alone and to her guru's word.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Her hesitation: the sages asked for her secret, she is shy to speak of a husband before elders like fathers, and she expects laughter. 'Daughter of the mountain' explains the 'stone-like' stubbornness she owns to.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note
commentaries.gist: Reads the three images as mind, act and word: the stubborn mind, flying without wings (the deed), and 'I want Shiva always' (the speech).

commentaries.who: V. Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Love makes one 'dull': she means she is too full of love to be reasoned with.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush textual note
commentaries.gist: Some editions add a half-line 'सुनत रिषिन्ह के बचन भवानी...' before this. Manas Piyush and Gita Press treat it as an interpolation.

rcm.1.74.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers use it for quiet, self-aware commitment: you can admit something looks impossible and still choose it with your whole heart.
misreadings: Not praise of stubbornness against all advice: her steadiness rests on trust in her guru and on a worthy goal.
Not a model for pursuing someone who has said no.
not_for: someone fixated on a person who does not reciprocate
a reader whose 'resolve' is harming their health
speaks_to: a choice of partner or vocation that others doubt

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 78, second half of chaupai 3 plus chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 78, half-lines 6-8'). NOT 1.74. Our text starts mid-chaupai: the half-line before it is 'कहत बचन मनु अति सकुचाई। हँसिहहु सुनि हमारि जड़ताई॥'.

rcm.1.76.chaupai.3.context: The sages have mocked Narada's advice and listed Shiva's 'faults', then offered Parvati Vishnu, a 'better' match: handsome, pure and faultless. She laughs and answers each jibe in turn. They had said 'your body is born of a mountain', and this is her reply. Next she says she will not abandon Narada's word, for one who lacks faith in the guru's word finds no happiness.
rcm.1.76.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Parvati turns the sages' taunt into a statement of steadiness: like gold born from stone, which only grows purer in fire, her love does not change under testing.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: She concedes the sages' point and turns it: a mountain-born heart is firm like stone. Her resolve will carry into other births. She cites 'for crores of births I will wed Shambhu or stay unmarried'.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note on the gold image
commentaries.gist: Fire changes everything but gold, which gets brighter as it is heated. So testing only deepens her love. Compare Ayodhya 205 on gold and love.

commentaries.who: Khara and Lamagoda ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Khara: when burned, the stone gives up its hardness, but the gold born of it does not, so her father's resolve may waver but hers will not. Lamagoda: she answers in the sages' own playful tone.

rcm.1.76.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to integrity under pressure: tests and criticism can refine a sound commitment rather than break it.
misreadings: Steadiness is not stubbornness; keep checking that the goal is still worth it.
Not a call to sacrifice health or life ('though the body may break') for a goal.
cautions: 'Let the body go but not the resolve' can be dangerous for a reader with self-harm or eating-disorder risk. Keep the gold image and leave out the body clause.
not_for: someone at risk of harming themselves for a goal
a person in a harmful relationship told to 'hold on'
speaks_to: staying true to a value under ridicule
commitment to a partner or vocation others dismiss

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand 80, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 80, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 1.76.

rcm.1.76.doha.1.context: The sages, testing her, called Shiva a house of faults and Vishnu the home of all virtues, and offered to arrange a match with Vishnu. Parvati, having answered their other jibes, closes with this. She then says that had they come before Narada she would have taken their advice, but she has given her life to Shiva. The sages, satisfied, bless her and report to Shiva.
rcm.1.76.doha.1.core_teaching: Love is not a comparison of qualities. Once the heart has given itself to someone, lists of faults and virtues no longer decide anything.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: She will not argue that Shiva's 'faults' are virtues, nor say a word against Vishnu. Conceding everything, she says her mind is simply absorbed in Shiva. Single-minded devotion to one's chosen deity is the lesson.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Kathasaritsagara and Parvati Mangal
commentaries.gist: 'To each, that is sweet where their mind is fixed.' Tulsidas's Parvati Mangal has her say: does one who loves count faults and virtues?

commentaries.who: Lamagoda ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The line has become a proverb for the single-pointedness of love. Parvati's love rests on an inner bond, not outer qualities.

rcm.1.76.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to devotion to one's chosen deity or path, and to committed love: loyalty does not depend on winning comparisons.
misreadings: Choosing for yourself still means listening honestly to those who care.
Not a reason to ignore real red flags such as abuse or deceit in a partner. Shiva's 'faults' here are only appearances.
not_for: someone whose loved ones are warning of genuine harm in a relationship
speaks_to: choosing one's own path or faith

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand doha 80 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 'doha 80'). NOT 1.76.

rcm.1.8.chaupai.1.context: Before starting, Tulsidas salutes the whole of creation in several rounds: first all gods, demons, humans and creatures as pervaded by Ram, then individual groups, and here every being as full of Sita and Ram. Next he asks them all to treat him as their servant and bless him, since he has no confidence in his own wit.
rcm.1.8.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Seeing every creature as pervaded by Sita and Ram, the poet bows to all of them. Reverence for the divine becomes reverence for every being.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Tulsidas salutes the world three ways, satisfying three schools: as Brahman (Vedanta), as individual souls, and as Prakriti with Purusha (Sankhya), hence the mention of birth-classes here.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Ram-maya' earlier honoured the Lord's majesty. 'Siya-Ram-maya' shows the intimate form living in the poet's heart. Seeing the world so is a ripe stage of love.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note
commentaries.gist: Naming Sita with Ram means bowing to female and male alike, equally. It cites the Adhyatma Ramayana and Padma Purana: all that is feminine is Janaki, all that is masculine is Ram.

commentaries.who: Sudhakar Prasad Mishra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The verse states a Vedantic vision without asking readers to drop ritual or dismiss the gods.

rcm.1.8.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers cite it as a basis for treating every person and creature with reverence: if the divine is in everyone, courtesy is owed to everyone.
misreadings: Not a denial that harm or evil exists: in the same section Tulsidas speaks frankly about the wicked.
cautions: Mentions the 8.4 million births, which implies the rebirth cycle. That is harmless here, but readers outside the tradition may need it explained.
not_for: someone who has been harmed and is being told to revere the person who harmed them
speaks_to: starting a day or a task with gratitude

rcm.1.8.chaupai.6.context: Tulsidas has just confessed that his wit is small and his ambition large. He asks good people to forgive his boldness as parents enjoy a child's lisp, and says the crooked will laugh, those who wear others' faults as ornaments. These lines explain the laughter. The next line compares most people to ponds and rivers that swell only with their own water.
rcm.1.8.chaupai.6.core_teaching: Everyone finds their own work good, whatever its quality. Those who are genuinely glad at someone else's work are rare, and they are the truly good.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar and Baba Janakidas, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Answers the mockers: their own verse may be flat, yet they prize it. They will never rejoice at another's verse, however fine. Manas Piyush prefers this reading.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Applies the first half to Tulsidas himself: whatever others say, everyone likes their own poem. Manas Piyush finds this fits the next half less well.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note
commentaries.gist: Compares it to one's own curd: nobody calls it sour. It cites Dohavali 355: no one dislikes their own conduct, just as a garlic-eater does not notice the smell.

rcm.1.8.chaupai.6.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a check on envy and self-regard: taking real pleasure in a colleague's or friend's good work is a mark of character, and it is rare.
misreadings: Not a call to stop valuing one's own work: Tulsidas goes on to write anyway, trusting the good to receive it kindly.
not_for: someone whose work was just harshly dismissed and needs encouragement, not a lesson in humility
speaks_to: teams and workplaces where credit matters
parents and teachers learning to celebrate others

rcm.1.8.chaupai.7.context: This continues the point of the previous line, that people love their own work and seldom rejoice at another's. Tulsidas gives the image: rivers and ponds rise only with their own water, while the ocean swells when it sees the full moon. The doha that follows admits his luck is small but his hope large, trusting that the good will enjoy the poem and the wicked mock it.
rcm.1.8.chaupai.7.core_teaching: Most people swell only at their own gain. The rare good person rises in joy at someone else's success, as the ocean's tide rises with the full moon.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Rivers and ponds overflow with a little water, while the ocean holds much without spilling. So petty people become intoxicated with a little learning, and the good, full of it, stay within bounds.

commentaries.who: Sudhakar Prasad Mishra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: A swollen river breaks its banks and does damage, just as small people with a little wealth disregard everyone. Their flood lasts a season. The ocean's joy returns every full moon.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editorial note
commentaries.gist: Pairs the images with the previous line: ponds and rivers for those who love only their own poetry, the ocean for those glad at others'. Cites Kishkindha Kand's flooded stream as a petty man made rich.

rcm.1.8.chaupai.7.practical_reading: Teachers use it to invite readers to feel glad at a sibling's, friend's or rival's success: real joy at another's rise is the sign of a large heart.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of being glad at one's own success, only of being glad at nothing else.
not_for: someone who has just suffered a real loss while others prospered, who may need comfort before a lesson
speaks_to: envy at a friend's or sibling's success

rcm.2.11.chaupai.3.context: Dasharath has decided to make Ram crown prince, and Vasishtha has just come to tell Ram to keep vows for the next day's ceremony. As soon as the guru leaves, Ram's first feeling is not pride but disquiet: everything in the brothers' lives has been shared, so crowning only the eldest seems the one blot on a spotless line. Lakshman arrives right after, and Ram welcomes him with loving words.
rcm.2.11.chaupai.3.core_teaching: True affection is uneasy when it is favoured over those it grew up with. Tulsidas holds up Ram's loving regret as a medicine for the selfishness in a devotee's own heart.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The two lines are ordered deliberately: birth, meals, sleep and play are shared bodily life; ear-piercing, sacred thread and marriage are shared rites. Ram is troubled that Bharat and Shatrughna are absent and not even informed.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Primogeniture is family custom, but Ram means the brothers should share in rule too, each with a role; he will not accept the throne in his brothers' absence.

commentaries.who: Vedantabhushan Pt. Ramkumardas, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Raises the objection: Manu's law favours the eldest, other lawgivers favour equal shares. Ram calls the custom unfair yet still honours the received order, so his dignity stays intact.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi and Ramchandra Shukla, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Not grieving for others when you yourself rise is itself 'crookedness' for a devotee; contemplating Ram's simple fairness slowly makes a crooked person straight.

rcm.2.11.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers use it for sibling fairness: when you are singled out (a promotion, an inheritance, a parent's favour), let the first feeling be concern for those who shared the road with you. The Vinayaki tika cited in Manas Piyush applies it directly to brothers who grab the larger share of property.
misreadings: Not a rejection of responsibility or of the eldest's role: Ram does accept his father's plan.
Not a call to refuse every honour; it is about the spirit in which you receive it.
cautions: Can sting for a reader who is the overlooked sibling in a real inheritance or family dispute; frame it as a picture of how a fair heart feels, not as proof that their sibling is wrong.
not_for: a reader in active conflict with a sibling who took everything, on the day of the hurt
only children or people estranged from their siblings, without reframing
speaks_to: someone promoted or rewarded above siblings, friends or co-founders
parents dividing property or attention among children
siblings who grew up close and now face unequal fortunes

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 10, chaupai 3-4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 10, half-lines 5-8'). NOT 2.11.

rcm.2.127.doha.1.context: Ram, entering the forest, asks Valmiki where he should make his dwelling. Valmiki answers with a long list of the kinds of hearts Ram lives in (those whose ears are oceans for his story, whose eyes are thirsty for him, and so on). This doha is the last item in that list; right after it Tulsidas says the sage showed Ram these 'houses' and Ram was pleased, then Valmiki names Chitrakoot as the physical place to stay.
rcm.2.127.doha.1.core_teaching: The heart that loves without asking for anything back is where the divine is most at home. Wanting nothing is what makes the love 'one's own house' rather than a guest room.

commentaries.who: Sudarshan Singh, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Reads the love as like a parent's for an infant: it expects nothing and is happy in the child's happiness. A servant, friend or spouse loves with some expectation; only this kind is fully free of wanting.

commentaries.who: Earlier mahatmas, as reported in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Some read 'nij gehu' as Ram's private inner chamber and so take the doha as describing the sweetest, most intimate devotion (madhurya bhava).

commentaries.who: Sudarshan Singh, in Manas Piyush (on 'nij gehu')
commentaries.gist: Taking the speaker Valmiki as a father figure, 'your own house' means a paternal home: Ram need ask no one's leave to live there, and if it is not fit, making it fit is his own job.

rcm.2.127.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to describe love that is not a transaction: being with someone or something for its own sake, not for what it gives. It also works as a quiet check on prayer that is mostly a list of requests.
misreadings: Not a rule that you must never ask God or anyone for help: it describes the highest kind of love, not a ban on need.
Not a statement that people who want things are unloved.
cautions: Devotional address to Ram; a secular reader may need it framed as 'love with no agenda'.
not_for: someone in acute need who may hear it as 'don't ask for help'
a person being exploited by someone who demands selfless love
speaks_to: wanting a relationship that isn't transactional
someone tired of prayer that feels like bargaining

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 131 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush prints it as 131). NOT 2.127: our id and label are off by four.

rcm.2.146.chaupai.3.context: Sumantra comes back from leaving Ram, Lakshman and Sita at the Ganga. The king keeps asking for his son's message and begs him to bring them back into sight. Sumantra steadies himself and first reminds the king that he is learned, brave and steady, then offers this teaching. Immediately after, he relays Ram's messages; the king cannot bear it and dies a few dohas later.
rcm.2.146.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Pleasure and pain, gain and loss, union and separation arrive by time and karma as surely as day follows night. The steady person holds both alike and uses discernment to hold on to courage.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Day following night cannot be held back by anyone; in the same way what time and karma bring must be lived through. Loss now may be followed by gain later.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The line about fools rejoicing and wailing is true in general but not of grief for Sita and Ram. Dasharath is no fool; Sumantra speaks because he fears the king will die of this love.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji (Pan.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Grief destroys discernment and steadiness, so let it go; reflect with the understanding gained from guru and scripture and steadiness will follow.

rcm.2.146.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers use it to name the rhythm of life: good and bad turns come in cycles, and composure means not being thrown entirely by either. Discernment is the tool, not suppression.
misreadings: Not a claim that grief is foolish: the commentators say this very grief for Ram is not folly.
Not fatalism that excuses inaction; it addresses what has already happened.
cautions: Spoken to a man who dies of grief soon after: the advice did not save him. Using it on Day 1 of grief risks sounding like 'be stoic'.
'Fools rejoice and wail' can sting someone who is crying.
not_for: fresh bereavement
someone who needs permission to cry rather than counsel to be steady
speaks_to: riding out a run of bad news
perspective after a setback at work or in money
someone who tends to swing high and low with events

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 150, chaupais 3-4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush prints the four lines as 150.5-8). NOT 2.146, and our text covers two chaupais, not one.

rcm.2.159.chaupai.3.context: Bharat has come home, learned what his mother did, and gone to Kausalya calling himself a stain on the family. She takes him on her lap, wipes his tears and says this. In the next lines she tells him not to blame anyone, including Kaikeyi, and puts the blame on her own fate instead.
rcm.2.159.chaupai.3.core_teaching: In a terrible time, hold on and let go of self-blame: what time and karma bring cannot be undone. The comfort comes from the one most wronged.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Bharat has been calling himself cursed and is still weeping; these are signs of losing composure, so she asks for steadiness even now, after a king's death and the exile.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji and Ramayan Prakash, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'See the bad time' means troubles come to everyone and also pass; in an evil hour grief is the only harvest, so set it down.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: She answers Bharat's two complaints in order: don't reproach yourself, and don't blame Kaikeyi either; then she takes the fault onto her own fate.

rcm.2.159.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers use it for someone crushed by guilt over harm others caused: the one who lost most refuses to blame them. It models comfort that removes shame without arguing.
misreadings: Not a denial that real wrongs happened; Kausalya names the loss as loss.
Not a reason to dodge one's own real responsibility (our misuse note is right).
cautions: Mentions a death in the family. The 'karma cannot be altered' framing can feel fatalistic to a newly bereaved reader.
not_for: someone who actually caused harm and needs to own it
a reader who hears karma as blame for their loss
speaks_to: guilt over a family member's wrongdoing
being forgiven by the person you expected to blame you

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 165, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 165.5-6). NOT 2.159: our id and label are off by six.

rcm.2.163.doha.1.context: Bharat has returned to Ayodhya to find his father dead and Ram exiled, and has poured out his grief to Kausalya. Vasishtha arrives with the ministers and consoles him with teaching on the inevitability of death. This doha closes that consolation: hold firm and do today's duty. The next lines show that duty: the king's body is bathed, a bier and pyre are prepared on the Sarayu, Bharat stops the queens from following their husband into the fire, and he performs the cremation and the ten-day rites.
rcm.2.163.doha.1.core_teaching: When grief is overwhelming, the guru's counsel is to steady the heart and do the duty that today requires.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (Gita Press), note on doha 169
commentaries.gist: Compares Vasishtha's 'many-sided' teaching with Valmiki and the Adhyatma Ramayana, where the sage explains that death is inevitable for the born and the self is undying, so grief should give way to the rites.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Pandit Ramkumar
commentaries.gist: Bharat rose at once because a guru's word carries great weight; he gave orders to the ministers, and the 'what is due today' is the king's funeral.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Panjabiji
commentaries.gist: Explains why the ministers were summoned: no one had met Bharat on his return and suspicion hung over him, so Vasishtha gathered them to clear it.

rcm.2.163.doha.1.practical_reading: When everything feels unsafe, the next right task is enough: steady yourself and do what today actually requires.
misreadings: Not 'stop grieving and get back to work'; the task Bharat is given is mourning itself, his father's funeral.
Not about ambition or taking the throne.
cautions: The literal 'task today' is cremating a father; avoid a light work framing that erases this, and avoid it for someone newly bereaved unless that is intended.
not_for: someone told to 'just get on with it' who needs room to feel first

rcm.2.165.chaupai.4.context: After Dasharath's funeral rites, Vasishtha gathers the court and Bharat. Before advising Bharat to rule, he speaks of Ram's goodness and of Lakshman's and Sita's love, and is overcome. The next doha has him say, still weeping, that what is destined is powerful.
rcm.2.165.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Even the wisest teacher is overwhelmed by grief and love; wisdom does not remove feeling. The Manas presents this as the greatness of love for Sita and Ram.

commentaries.who: Ramayan Prakash and Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram's 'virtue, gentleness and nature' means how he obeyed his father gladly and said nothing harsh to Kaikeyi even after her cruel words.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: A jnani should be beyond grief and attachment, yet the author of the Yoga Vasishtha sinks in both. This shows how strong the love for Ram, Sita and Lakshman is.

rcm.2.165.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that composure and tears can coexist: the person who has to hold everyone together is allowed to grieve too.
misreadings: Not a sign that wisdom failed: the commentators read it as love's power, not weakness.
cautions: Set right after a funeral; gentle but it is grief context.
not_for: someone looking for practical steps
speaks_to: leaders or elders who feel they must not cry
grieving a person while having to manage others' grief

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 171, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 171.7-8). NOT 2.165.

rcm.2.165.doha.1.context: Vasishtha has just broken down while praising Ram, Lakshman and Sita. Now he speaks to Bharat: destiny is strong, and the six pairs of outcomes lie with Providence. The next line draws the conclusion: so whom should we blame, and at whom be angry in vain? He then urges Bharat to carry out his father's wish and rule.
rcm.2.165.doha.1.core_teaching: Outcomes like loss, death and disgrace are not finally in our control. The point, made explicit in the next line, is that there is no one to blame and no use in anger.

commentaries.who: Pandeyji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Bilakhi' can mean sadly, since even the guru could not prevent this, or 'having considered closely', pre-empting Bharat's question why the guru let it happen.

commentaries.who: Gaud ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Prefers 'grieving': even Vasishtha, son of the Creator, could not hold this back, and he speaks in sorrow. The other reading is strained.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Each of the six pairs plays out in this very story: Ayodhya's loss and the forest-dwellers' gain, Ravana's death, Bharat's fame and Kaikeyi's infamy.

commentaries.who: Nange Paramhans ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The real targets are three: the exile (loss), the king's death and Kaikeyi's disgrace. The opposites are named because these words come as pairs.

rcm.2.165.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to release someone from blaming themselves or others for what was beyond anyone's control, so that grief does not turn into anger or guilt.
misreadings: Not an excuse for inaction or for not taking responsibility (our misuse note is apt).
Not a claim that nothing we do matters.
cautions: Names death directly. 'It was destined' can feel dismissive to a fresh mourner unless framed as freeing them from blame.
not_for: someone who is avoiding responsibility for a real choice
acute fresh grief where 'destiny' sounds cold
speaks_to: blaming yourself for an outcome you couldn't control
anger looking for a target after a loss

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 171 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 171). NOT 2.165.

rcm.2.170.chaupai.7.context: Vasishtha, the ministers and Kausalya have all urged Bharat to take the throne as his father wished. Bharat grants that their advice is simple and good for him, but says his heart is not satisfied. He then asks pardon for answering back, says suffering people's words should not be weighed, and argues that his only good is serving Ram; without Ram the kingdom is a heap of grief.
rcm.2.170.chaupai.7.core_teaching: Bharat admits that sound advice and inner peace can come apart: he understands the counsel but cannot be at peace with it, and says so openly and respectfully.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (word notes and meaning)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'acharat' as 'by following it'. In the next line Bharat asks them to give him advice fit for him ('anuharat'), and asks pardon, since good people don't count a sufferer's words against him.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (meaning of the doha that follows)
commentaries.gist: Bharat then asks whether they think a kingdom is his good or their own convenience: his good lies only in serving Ram, which his mother's crookedness took away.

rcm.2.170.chaupai.7.practical_reading: Teachers use it for the gap between knowing and feeling: you can agree with good advice and still not be at peace, and saying so honestly is better than pretending.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of elders' advice: Bharat praises it before declining it.
not_for: someone looking for permission to ignore all advice
speaks_to: advice you agree with but can't make yourself follow
decisions where duty and heart pull apart

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 177, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 177.5-6). NOT 2.170 and NOT chaupai 7: both numbers in our id are wrong.

rcm.2.176.chaupai.2.context: Bharat has resolved to go to Ram. Just before, he says he can see no other remedy and will set out at dawn. Here he admits that the calamity happened because of him, yet trusts that Ram, seeing him come for refuge, will forgive. Next he describes Ram's gentle nature (he never harmed even an enemy) and asks the assembly for its blessing.
rcm.2.176.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Admitting fault and trusting forgiveness are not opposites: coming face to face, for refuge, is what opens the way to being forgiven.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram has always been kind; going to him for refuge will bring 'special' kindness, which the commentator identifies with Ram later giving Bharat his sandals.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Compares other Manas lines where taking refuge saves even great sinners, and where a tiger is said not to eat one who faces it as a supplicant.

rcm.2.176.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it for going to someone you've hurt (or believe you've hurt), owning your part without excuses, and trusting their goodness rather than rehearsing defences.
misreadings: Not a claim that Bharat was actually guilty: the tradition treats his self-accusation as humility (our note is right).
Not a guarantee that every wronged person will forgive.
cautions: Someone with harsh, unfounded self-blame may take 'I am guilty' as confirmation.
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship who is told to keep going back
speaks_to: guilt that keeps you from approaching someone

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 183, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 183.3-4). NOT 2.176.

rcm.2.185.chaupai.4.context: Guha sees Bharat's army coming to the Ganga and assumes he means to kill Ram; he readies his men to die blocking the crossing. An old man reads a good omen and says Bharat may be coming for another reason. Guha agrees, tells his men to hold the ghats while he goes to learn whether Bharat is friend, foe or neutral, and then sets out with gifts to meet him.
rcm.2.185.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Rash action without understanding the other person brings regret and damages one's own good. Find out someone's intent before treating them as an enemy.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 1)
commentaries.gist: Guha praises the old man because he is himself skilled at reading omens and the elder's years were spent in reflection.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, citing a Sanskrit subhashita
commentaries.gist: Hasty deeds ripen into consequences that hurt the heart like an embedded stake. Compares the sky-voice to Lakshman later (231.3-4), which makes the same point.

commentaries.who: Dinji, in Manas Piyush (word notes)
commentaries.gist: 'Ghat gahahu' means gather and hold the river landing, keeping position while the facts are checked, not disbanding the guard.

rcm.2.185.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to conflict at work or at home: check your assumptions about someone's motives before you act. Guha still keeps his guard posted; caution and openness go together.
misreadings: Not a call to drop all defences: Guha keeps the ghats guarded while he investigates.
not_for: someone facing a known, clear threat who needs to act fast
speaks_to: anger that wants to act right now

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 192, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 192.7-8). NOT 2.185.

rcm.2.196.doha.1.context: Bharat reaches Prayag on his way to Chitrakoot and asks the Triveni for alms, setting aside his kshatriya pride. He asks for none of the four aims of life, only love for Ram's feet in every birth. In the following lines he adds: let Ram think me crooked and people call me a traitor to guru and master, as long as my love keeps growing, like the chataka bird whose love for the cloud only grows when the cloud ignores it, or gold that shines brighter in fire.
rcm.2.196.doha.1.core_teaching: Bharat asks only for love itself, and for it in every life, rather than for any reward, even liberation. In the lines that follow he wants that love whether or not it is returned or praised.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He refuses all four aims up front so they won't be offered instead. Rebirth is welcome if every birth has this love, a one-sided love that doesn't depend on Ram being pleased.

commentaries.who: Ayodhya Dipika (A. Di.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Reads 'birth after birth' as a wish to be born wherever Ram is, so that the love stays and nothing without Ram counts.

commentaries.who: Pt. Yadavshankar Jamdar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: For Bharat love of Ram's feet is both the means and the goal: there is no separate prize beyond the love, so there is no room for dissatisfaction.
