rcm.2.196.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to describe loving something for itself, not for its returns: the devotion is the reward. It can also mark the difference between serving to be noticed and serving because you love.
misreadings: Not a rejection of duty or earning a living: Bharat is a prince who goes on to govern.
Not a sectarian claim that liberation is worthless; it voices the bhakti preference for love over release.
cautions: Rebirth doctrine is assumed.
not_for: someone who needs practical help with money or work right now
speaks_to: someone whose motives in service have become mixed

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 204 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 204). NOT 2.196: our id and label are off by eight.

rcm.2.197.chaupai.4.context: Bharat has just asked Triveni for love of Ram in every birth, even if Ram thinks him crooked and the world calls him a traitor. A soft, auspicious voice rises from the middle of the confluence with this answer. Bharat thrills, the gods shower flowers, and the people of Prayag talk of his pure love; he then goes on to the sage Bharadwaj.
rcm.2.197.chaupai.4.core_teaching: The voice removes Bharat's guilt point by point: he is not crooked but good, his love is boundless, and the love is returned more than he imagines.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Majh Triveni' is apt because Saraswati is in the middle of the confluence; she is the speaker. 'Agadhu': no one, not guru, Guha, Lakshman, Janaka or the gods, could find the bottom of his love.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 1)
commentaries.gist: Bharat's guilt was the charge of crookedness and treachery he laid on himself. 'Good in every way' answers that, and 'none dearer to Ram' answers his fear that Ram would reject him.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 2)
commentaries.gist: By telling him he already has all he asked for, Saraswati shows there is nothing more anyone could give him.

rcm.2.197.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it for people who punish themselves for things they didn't do: sometimes the most useful thing is for someone to say plainly that the guilt is misplaced and that they are loved.
misreadings: Not a statement that guilt is always pointless; it addresses guilt for something one didn't do.
not_for: someone who has really done harm and needs to make amends first
speaks_to: fear that someone you love has turned against you
needing reassurance after a family rupture

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 205, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 205.7-8). NOT 2.197.

rcm.2.198.doha.1.context: Bharat sits before Bharadwaj, head bowed, dreading questions. The sage speaks first: we have heard everything; no one can resist Providence. Then this doha. He goes on to say that even if Bharat had taken the throne he would have done no wrong, that Kaikeyi acted under destiny and repented, and that anyone who calls Bharat guilty is base.
rcm.2.198.doha.1.core_teaching: Bharat should not carry shame for his mother's act, and even she is not to be blamed, because her mind was turned by a higher plan. The sage lifts the shame from both son and mother.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 2)
commentaries.gist: Bharadwaj declares Kaikeyi blameless in front of everyone so that Bharat's shame lifts and no one can blame him. What happens by destiny cannot be stopped.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 2), reconciling the text
commentaries.gist: Earlier the Manas says Saraswati turned Manthara's mind; here Kaikeyi's. Resolution: Saraswati turned Manthara, and through Manthara, Kaikeyi, so both can be credited to her.

commentaries.who: Ramayan Prakash (Ra. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Bharadwaj moves the blame step by step: first to Providence, then to Saraswati, then (as the world sees it) to Kaikeyi, and in the end to destiny itself.

rcm.2.198.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to people ashamed of a parent's or relative's wrongdoing: you are not your family's mistakes. It also models refusing to scapegoat even the one who did the wrong.
misreadings: Not a claim that people are never responsible for what they do: it is a specific mythic framing of Kaikeyi's role in the divine plan.
Should not be used to tell a victim that their abuser 'couldn't help it'.
cautions: The 'a god clouded her mind' framing may sound like excusing harm to someone hurt by a relative.
not_for: someone currently being harmed by the family member in question
speaks_to: shame over a parent's or sibling's actions
being judged for a relative's choices

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 206 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 206). NOT 2.198.

rcm.2.204.chaupai.4.context: Bharat has told Bharadwaj that his only grief is that Ram suffers because of him. The sages are moved and praise him. Bharadwaj consoles him: don't grieve so much, all sorrow will end when you see Ram's feet. He then invites Bharat to be his guest, and goes on to host the whole army with his powers.
rcm.2.204.chaupai.4.core_teaching: The sage gives Bharat a near, concrete hope: the pain will ease once he sees the one he longs for.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: This blesses Bharat's earlier words that the burning in his heart would not go until he saw Ram. It comes true: he finds relief even at the sight of Ram's footprints, and later in the sandals.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji (Pan.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Bharadwaj, who knows all, does not bless him with Ram's return, since he knows Ram will not come back; he offers only comfort and says only what will happen.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 2b)
commentaries.gist: Lists others in the Manas whose sorrow ends at the sight of Ram's feet: Guha, the forest people, Kabandha, Vibhishana, the boatman, Ahalya.

rcm.2.204.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it for the comfort of a reunion ahead: holding on to the next real step (seeing the person, making the call) can ease a grief that argument can't.
misreadings: Not a promise that everything will be fixed: Panjabi ji points out the sage carefully does not promise Ram's return.
not_for: grief for someone who has died, where 'you'll see them' would be hollow
speaks_to: longing to see someone you are estranged from

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 212, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 212.7-8). NOT 2.204.

rcm.2.211.chaupai.2.context: Indra fears that Bharat's love will bring Ram home and wreck the gods' plans, and wants to use illusion on Bharat. Brihaspati tells him to drop the trickery: harming Ram's devotee rebounds on the plotter. He describes Ram's nature: even-handed and untouched by anyone's merit or sin, he has made the world run on action, though he still responds to devotion. The next lines say Ram is angered by offences against his devotees.
rcm.2.211.chaupai.2.core_teaching: God is impartial and does not personally take on anyone's sins or merits; instead the world is ordered so that actions bear their own fruit. Brihaspati uses this to warn Indra that scheming against a good person will come back on him.

commentaries.who: Vaijnath (Vai.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He takes on neither sin (left to Yama) nor merit (left to Brahma); beings reap joy or pain from their own deeds, so he stays untouched. Cites the Brahma Sutra on God's impartiality.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, citing Gita 5.15 with Ramanuja's bhashya
commentaries.gist: The all-pervading Self takes on no one's sin or merit; the sense of 'mine' and 'enemy' comes from ignorance covering knowledge.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, quoting Parashara and Bhishma (Mahabharata, Shanti Parva)
commentaries.gist: Sin is like dye that washing won't remove; deeds follow their doer like a shadow and bear fruit in their own time, knowingly done or not.

rcm.2.211.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers apply it as a reason to act cleanly and not plot against others: you will live with the results of what you do. It is about one's own conduct, not about judging other people's suffering.
misreadings: Not a judgement that people who suffer must have deserved it (our misuse note is right).
Not the whole picture in the Manas: the next line says Ram responds to devotion too, so it is not a cold mechanism.
cautions: 'You reap what you sow' can wound someone who is suffering through no fault of their own.
not_for: someone suffering illness, loss or abuse who may hear it as blame
speaks_to: temptation to scheme or cut corners

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 219, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 219.3-4). NOT 2.211.

rcm.2.212.chaupai.1.context: This closes Brihaspati's counsel to Indra. Ram has promised the gods he will relieve the earth, so he will keep that vow; Bharat only follows Ram's wishes; Indra's agitation comes from his own self-interest. Hearing this Indra is relieved, showers flowers and starts praising Bharat.
rcm.2.212.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Indra's fear of Bharat's goodness comes from his own self-interest; the fault lies in his confusion, not in Bharat. Seeing this clearly turns his anxiety into admiration.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram is true to his word, so he will keep his earlier promise to the gods to lift the earth's burden; he also reassured them at Chitrakoot. Indra has nothing to fear.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar and Panjabi ji (tippani 2), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Indra accepted the good counsel, so he is called 'best of gods'. His joy is relief: had he used illusion on Bharat he would have come to grief.

rcm.2.212.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to look at envy and anxiety about someone else's success: often the threat is in our own interests, not in the other person. Naming that can turn rivalry into respect.
misreadings: Not a rule that all anxiety is selfish; it addresses fear of another person's goodness.
not_for: someone whose fear of another person is well founded (abuse, real threat)
speaks_to: envy of a colleague or sibling

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 220, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 220.1-2). NOT 2.212.

rcm.2.222.chaupai.2.context: At Chitrakoot, Lakshman sees Bharat's army and is sure Bharat has come to attack; he speaks in fury and readies his bow, and the world trembles. A voice from the sky first praises Lakshman's might, then gives this counsel. Lakshman is abashed; Ram and Sita honour him and Ram explains that Bharat could never be corrupted by power.
rcm.2.222.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Any action, right or wrong, should be done after understanding; acting rashly and regretting later is not wisdom. Here it checks a loyal man's anger before he strikes someone he has misjudged.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Placing 'wrong' first hints that Lakshman's plan is wrong; even a right deed earns praise only if done with thought. Cites the proverb that the hasty are foolish and the patient deep.

commentaries.who: Nange Paramhans ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Lakshman's readiness to fight for his master is right; only attacking without checking is a little wrong. The voice is mainly to stop him, like a lion pouncing first, not a general sermon.

commentaries.who: Tripathi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram let Lakshman finish because it is rude to cut someone off and he wanted to know his whole mind; afterwards Ram and Sita honour him so his embarrassment eases.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, citing Bhartrihari's Nitishataka
commentaries.gist: A wise person weighs the outcome before acting; rash deeds ripen into pain that burns the heart like an arrow.

rcm.2.222.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to anger and impulsive decisions: pause, check the facts, then act. Loyalty and passion are good, but they need understanding.
misreadings: Not a call to never act decisively; it asks for thought first, not paralysis.
not_for: a genuine emergency that needs immediate action
speaks_to: anger that wants to act now
jumping to conclusions about someone's motives
impulsive decisions at work or in family conflict

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 231, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 231.3-4). NOT 2.222.

rcm.2.225.chaupai.1.context: Bharat nears Ram's hermitage turning things over: Ram might take him to be party to his mother's plot, or might forgive him for his own goodness' sake. Here he concludes that either way his only refuge is Ram's sandals. The next line praises the chataka bird and the fish, famous for constant love; then Tulsidas describes him walking, slowed by shame and pulled by love.
rcm.2.225.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Whatever the outcome, rejection or honour, Bharat will keep his refuge in Ram. He takes all fault on himself and trusts the master's goodness.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Rejection is mentioned first because that is his fear; when he remembers Ram's nature comfort returns and he names the second possibility. Either way he has no other refuge.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 3)
commentaries.gist: Refuge in the sandals is fitting: a shoe is on the servant's head either way, as a blow if he is scorned or as an honour if he is accepted.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, comparing Vinaya Patrika 177-178, 206
commentaries.gist: Tulsidas's own prayers voice the same stance: even if you abandon me I won't abandon you; like the chataka I keep my vow of love.

rcm.2.225.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it for steady loyalty that doesn't depend on being accepted: doing the right thing and leaving the response to the other. Also used for approaching someone you fear has judged you.
misreadings: Not a call to stay where you are rejected or harmed (our misuse note is right).
'All the fault is the servant's' is Bharat's humility, not a principle that the less powerful party is always to blame.
cautions: 'All fault is mine' can reinforce harmful self-blame in someone already blaming themselves.
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship
someone with harsh self-blame
speaks_to: fear of rejection before a reconciliation
faith that doesn't depend on outcomes

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 234, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 234.1-2). NOT 2.225: our id and label are off by nine.

rcm.2.225.chaupai.3.context: Bharat walks on, body slack with shame and love. His mother's wrong seems to turn him back while devotion and steadiness pull him forward, and thinking of Ram's nature quickens his steps. The next lines compare him to a water-beetle in a current, darting and stalling, and say Guha forgot his own body watching him.
rcm.2.225.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Shame holds him back but remembering the other person's goodness moves him forward. Trust in someone's nature can outpull guilt.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (word notes)
commentaries.gist: 'Dhori' is the extra lead ox yoked in front when a cart is heavily loaded; devotion and steadiness are that extra pull under a heavy load of shame.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (meaning)
commentaries.gist: His body is slack from two things at once: shame about his mother's act and love from remembering Ram's nature.

commentaries.who: Vir Kavi, in Manas Piyush (on the next line)
commentaries.gist: The water-beetle image: in a stream it sometimes halts and then darts ahead, as Bharat's walk alternates between hesitation and haste.

rcm.2.225.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to walking toward a hard conversation: guilt slows you, but focusing on the other person's goodness rather than your own failure helps you keep going.
not_for: someone wanting practical instructions
speaks_to: mixed feelings of shame and love

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 234, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 234.5-6). NOT 2.225.

rcm.2.23.chaupai.2.context: Kaikeyi has just sworn she would throw herself in a well at Manthara's word, even give up son and husband. The poet pictures Manthara as a butcher sharpening the knife of deceit on the stone of her heart, while Kaikeyi, like a sacrificial animal, grazes on green grass without seeing her doom. Then comes this line, and Manthara at once reminds Kaikeyi of the two boons Dasharath owes her.
rcm.2.23.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Words that are sweet to hear can carry a deadly result. Commentators read the image as a warning about flattering counsel that feeds our fears and grudges.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: As sherbet is poured into the mouth of the animal to be sacrificed, Manthara pours honeyed poison into Kaikeyi; the speech is soft first, ruinous after.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note (comparison with Valmiki 2.9)
commentaries.gist: Valmiki calls Manthara 'pāpadarśinī', sharp-eyed for evil; Tulsidas turns that into the images of the knife, the grazing victim and honey laced with poison.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The 'sacrifice' is Kaikeyi's own good name: winning the boons brings her lasting disgrace, which Tulsidas elsewhere calls worse than death.

rcm.2.23.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Used as a test for advice: does it soothe me now and leave me worse later? Teachers apply it to gossip, manipulative friends and counsel that inflames rivalry inside families.
misreadings: Not a claim that all gentle speech is suspect.
Not a verdict that women or servants are schemers; it is about one manipulative speech.
cautions: A reader who was manipulated may hear blame for 'falling for it'; the poet's sympathy here is partly with Kaikeyi as the victim.
not_for: a reader grieving a betrayal by someone close, as a first reading: it can deepen suspicion of everyone
speaks_to: someone realising a 'well-wisher' has been feeding their worst fears
family rivalries stoked by a third party
checking advice before a big decision

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 22, chaupai 2 (lines 3-4) (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 22 (1-3)' and '(4-7)'). NOT 2.23.

rcm.2.235.chaupai.1.context: Bharat has met Ram, and now the whole company from Ayodhya reaches Chitrakoot, every person grieving and longing in their own way. Ram, with Lakshman, meets them all in a moment and eases their burning pain. Tulsidas adds that this is no great thing for Ram, just as one sun is reflected in millions of water pots. He then goes first to Kaikeyi.
rcm.2.235.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Ram meets each distressed person according to the relationship and longing they bring. Compassion, understanding and the power to act are all needed together.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Each epithet matters: compassion alone can't help without knowing what the sufferer needs (sujan), and knowing is useless without power (Bhagavan). Ram has all three, so he relieves them at once.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 2), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Whatever feeling': as disciple, son, brother, friend, king; compares Bal Kand 241, where each person saw the Lord according to their own feeling.

commentaries.who: Shila (Sheela) commentary, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He did not take many bodies, since he is in ascetic dress; each simply saw him as they wished, like one sun reflected in many pots.

rcm.2.235.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to describe good care: meet each hurting person in the way they need, not with one script for all. Seeing what each person longs for is part of compassion.
not_for: someone wanting a strict ethical rule
speaks_to: caring for several grieving people at once

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 244, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 244.1-2). NOT 2.235: our id and label are off by nine.

rcm.2.235.chaupai.4.context: At Chitrakoot Ram sees the mothers, wilted like vines struck by frost. He goes to Kaikeyi first, falls at her feet, and comforts her by laying the blame on time, karma and fate. Then he meets the other queens and tells them all that the world is in God's hands and no one should be blamed. He then greets the gurus' wives, Sumitra and Kausalya.
rcm.2.235.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Ram goes first to the person who caused his exile and takes away her blame, then asks everyone else not to blame anyone. Forgiveness here is active: he puts the guilty one at ease.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi (Vi. Tri.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: All the mothers were grieving but Kaikeyi most, knowing she caused it, so Ram met her first with no trace of resentment; when the others began to blame her he told them the world is in God's hands.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1-2), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Simple nature': Ram had always treated Kaikeyi as mother. 'Time, karma, fate' name three ways of explaining what happened, and the timing of the boon shows each at work.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 3), in Manas Piyush, citing Gita 18.61
commentaries.gist: The final word is that the Lord who dwells in all hearts moves everything; time and karma are only names. Some read Ram as hinting he took the blame himself.

rcm.2.235.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to family ruptures: go first to the one who hurt you and help them carry their remorse, and discourage the rest of the family from piling on blame.
misreadings: Not pretending the harm didn't happen (our misuse note is right).
Not a demand that a victim must comfort the person who hurt them; Ram chooses to.
cautions: 'Blame no one' may feel like erasure to someone still being harmed.
not_for: someone in an ongoing abusive situation
someone not ready to forgive

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 244, chaupai 4 plus doha 244 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 244.7-8 and doha 244). NOT 2.235. Our text runs one chaupai and the doha together.

rcm.2.247.chaupai.1.context: At the Chitrakoot assembly Vasishtha says to Ram: you know every heart; tell us the course that is good for the people, the mothers and Bharat. Then he adds this line to explain why he doesn't decide himself. Ram replies that the remedy is in the guru's hands and he will obey whatever he says.
rcm.2.247.chaupai.1.core_teaching: People in pain cannot weigh things fairly; like a gambler they see only their own stake. So Vasishtha counts himself among them and hands the decision to Ram, and Ram hands it back.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 3)
commentaries.gist: In distress the power to judge goes; the sufferer says whatever seems to bring relief. Compares Vinaya Patrika 34, where the very distressed are not to be blamed for speaking without thought.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The throw that fell is really Ram's (the exile is his dharma), but everyone shouts for their own wish that he come home, as gamblers do.

commentaries.who: Vaijnath (Vai.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Vasishtha means: I will not give an order, because I am one of the distressed.

rcm.2.247.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a reason to delay big decisions in the middle of grief or crisis, and to ask someone steadier to help weigh things.
misreadings: Not a reason to dismiss people who are hurting (our misuse note is right): Vasishtha includes himself.
not_for: someone who needs their distress taken seriously right now

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 258, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 258.1-2). NOT 2.247: our id and label are off by eleven.

rcm.2.249.chaupai.4.context: Asked by Vasishtha and Ram to speak, Bharat says the guru has already said all he could. He recalls his master's nature: he never got angry even at an offender, and from childhood never broke Bharat's heart, even letting him win games he had lost. Then he turns to his own failings and says he has never been able to face Ram out of love and shyness.
rcm.2.249.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Bharat grounds his trust in Ram in small, concrete memories: years of kindness, including letting a little brother win. Those memories are why he dares to hope now.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Constant company often breeds disrespect, yet in all those years Ram never once slighted him.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 4)
commentaries.gist: Raises the objection that Bharat was away for years (Ram went with Vishvamitra; Bharat went to his uncle's), and answers that Bharat did not leave by choice.

commentaries.who: Manas Mayank and Pandey/Vaijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Let me win though I lost' carries a plea: I have lost because of my mother's deed; let me win again now.

rcm.2.249.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it to show how trust is built in small moments, and how remembering someone's past kindness can give courage to approach them after a rift.
not_for: someone whose sibling relationship was hurtful (could sting)
speaks_to: parents thinking about how they treat younger children

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 260, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 260.7-8). NOT 2.249.

rcm.2.252.chaupai.3.context: Bharat has spoken of the suffering mothers and people and blamed himself. Ram answers: your shame is in vain, a being's course depends on God; in my view all the holy of every time and world rank below you. He goes on: even thinking ill of you ruins this world and the next; those who blame your mother have not sat with gurus and saints; remembering your name will wipe out sin.
rcm.2.252.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Ram removes Bharat's guilt by placing outcomes with God and then lifting him up: no one of holy fame anywhere ranks above him.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: This answers Bharat's distress at the suffering mothers and people: grieving that you caused it is pointless, since what people suffer is under Providence and karma.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, citing Valmiki Ramayana 2.22.22 and 2.105.15
commentaries.gist: Joy and sorrow, gain and loss, coming and going with no visible cause are the work of fate; a person does not move by his own will alone.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (meaning)
commentaries.gist: 'The holy of three times are below you' means no one so pure has been, is, or will be.

rcm.2.252.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers use it to answer someone drowning in guilt for others' suffering: what happened is bigger than them, and the people who love them see their worth clearly.
misreadings: Not a statement that people have no agency; it lifts needless guilt.
cautions: 'A soul's course depends on God' can sound fatalistic to someone grieving.
not_for: someone who needs to take responsibility for a real wrong
speaks_to: feeling responsible for a family crisis
needing to hear you are valued

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 263, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 263.5-6). NOT 2.252.

rcm.2.253.chaupai.1.context: Continuing his reply to Bharat's self-blame, Ram swears by Shiva that the earth stands by Bharat's keeping. He tells him not to argue against himself, since love and hostility cannot be hidden. He then proves it: birds and beasts go near sages but flee from hunters, so if even animals know friend from foe, how could humans not know Bharat's love?
rcm.2.253.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Ram tells Bharat to stop building arguments against himself: love shows itself, and everyone, Ram included, can see Bharat's.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 1)
commentaries.gist: Vasishtha, Bharat and Ram each swear by Shiva in this assembly to vouch for their truthfulness.

commentaries.who: Pandeyji (Pan.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Two readings: the earth's protection is in Bharat's hands because Ram has promised to do what he says; or the earth is sustained by Bharat, as his very name means 'one who sustains'.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: This answers Bharat's own words that the sage and Ram know whether his love is true. If even animals tell friend from foe, so can humans; and Ram would have moved away had he doubted Bharat.

commentaries.who: Nange Paramhans ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The two examples, birds and deer, stand for Sita and Ram: both of them know Bharat wishes them well.

rcm.2.253.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it for people who keep arguing themselves into guilt despite clear evidence of their good intent: your love is visible to those who matter; stop prosecuting yourself.
misreadings: Not a claim that hidden malice is impossible to disguise in every case; it reassures Bharat.
not_for: someone being gaslit, who needs to trust their own perception of another's hostility (could cut either way)
speaks_to: fearing that someone doubts your love

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 264, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 264.1-2). NOT 2.253: our id and label are off by eleven.

rcm.2.256.chaupai.2.context: Vasishtha has been pleased and Ram has reassured him, so Bharat says the false pain in his mind is gone. He admits he was afraid of a fear of his own making: the sun is not at fault if someone loses their sense of direction. He lists the real causes (his bad luck, his mother's crookedness, hard fate, hard times) and then says Ram, protector of the surrendered, kept his vow anyway.
rcm.2.256.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Bharat recognises that his dread of rejection was his own confusion, not anything in Ram. The real troubles were circumstance; the relationship itself was never at risk.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 3)
commentaries.gist: The 'root' of fear would be Ram, and there was none on his side. The sun always rises in the east; if someone thinks it rose in the west, the error is theirs. Cites Uttar Kand 73.

commentaries.who: Vaijnath (Vai.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Explains the four causes: misfortune that brought separation, his mother's stubbornness, his own past karma ripening, and the hard times, likened to an evil star rising.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 4b)
commentaries.gist: All four causes repeat things Bharat said in his earlier speech, where he blamed his luck, his mother, fate and the times.

rcm.2.256.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it to name 'apdar', fear we manufacture ourselves. Much of our dread about how someone sees us is our own confusion, like losing one's sense of direction and blaming the sun.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of real hardship: Bharat still names the real causes.
not_for: someone whose fear is well-founded
speaks_to: relief after a feared conversation went well

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 267, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 267.3-4). NOT 2.256: our id and label are off by eleven.

rcm.2.271.chaupai.3.context: At Chitrakoot Janaka's queen visits Kausalya. Kausalya says even Saraswati can't describe Bharat's virtues, any more than one can bail out the sea with a shell. She has always known Bharat to be the lamp of the family, as the king told her again and again; gold and gems are tested, and so are people, by time. Then she checks herself: it is not right to say this today, grief and love reduce one's prudence.
rcm.2.271.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Character is proven by difficult times, as gold by the touchstone. Bharat's behaviour in crisis has confirmed what his father always said about him.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The king kept telling her Bharat was the family's lamp; she did not fully believe it then, and now she has seen it was true.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush, citing a subhashita
commentaries.gist: Gold is tested four ways (rubbing, cutting, heating, beating); a person is tested by generosity, conduct, virtue and action.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 3c)
commentaries.gist: A person is truly good when their nature stays the same in good times and bad; Bharat stayed steady in the worst of times.

commentaries.who: Shila commentary, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: She checks herself because praising Bharat now could seem to push against what he came for, giving up a kingdom to bring Ram back.

rcm.2.271.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that hard times reveal who people are, including ourselves; how someone acts under pressure tells you more than their words in calm times.
misreadings: Not a call to deliberately 'test' people with hardship.
not_for: someone who feels they 'failed the test' in a crisis and is ashamed
speaks_to: seeing someone's true character in a crisis
being judged by how you handled hard times

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 283, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 283.5-6). NOT 2.271: our id and label are off by twelve.

rcm.2.280.chaupai.4.context: Janaka's party has arrived and Janaka asks Bharat what should be done. Bharat says he is a servant, the duty of service is notoriously hard, a master's duty and self-interest conflict, and love clouds judgement. In the doha that follows he asks the elders to decide, keeping Ram's wish, dharma and vow in view, treating him as one who is not free, and recognising everyone's love.
rcm.2.280.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Bharat declines to judge his own case: a servant's duty is hard, his own interest pulls against it, and love blinds as surely as hatred does. So he asks others to decide with everyone's good in view.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note on 293)
commentaries.gist: Keeping Ram's wish, dharma and vow is the servant's duty; wanting everyone's good and love is a kind of self-interest. The two conflict, so deciding is hard.

commentaries.who: Dinji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Bharat means: I think myself guilty while Ram praises my love; either way my judgement is compromised, so you decide. The words are so deep that Tulsidas next calls them 'most wonderful speech'.

commentaries.who: Pandeyji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Paraphrases the request as: keep to Ram's dharma and vow, treat me as dependent, and do what all agree is good for all.

rcm.2.280.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it to explain recusing yourself from a decision you're too close to: love, like anger, distorts judgement, and naming that is wisdom, not weakness.
misreadings: Not a claim that love is bad or that loyalty is foolish.
not_for: someone who needs to trust their own judgement and is being told not to
speaks_to: serving others when your own wishes pull another way

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 293, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 293.7-8). NOT 2.280: our id and label are off by thirteen.

rcm.2.281.chaupai.1.context: Bharat has just answered Janaka in a few words, asking the elders to decide by Ram's wish and everyone's good. Janaka and his court praise both his words and his nature. Tulsidas adds that the speech is like a face in a hand mirror: you hold the mirror but can't grasp the face. The whole party then goes to Ram.
rcm.2.281.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Good speech can be simple to hear yet deep, gentle yet firm, brief yet full of meaning. Bharat's reply is held up as such speech.

commentaries.who: Shila commentary, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Easy to say, soft to hear, hard to understand fully; its sense is clear, yet it is firm toward others.

commentaries.who: Pandeyji / Vaijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Maps each adjective onto Bharat's doha: keeping Ram's wish is easy, keeping dharma hard, 'I am dependent' gentle, 'by all's consent' lovely, 'all's good' firm (hard).

commentaries.who: Dinji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Disagrees on details: 'recognise love' is the firm part, a quiet hint that Janaka, called bodiless (Videha), may not grasp love between brothers.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi (Vi. Tri.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The mirror image explains 'few syllables, boundless meaning': the words are small and easily held, but their meaning can't be grasped whole.

rcm.2.281.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a model for speaking in conflict: few words, kind and firm at once, saying more by saying less.
not_for: someone looking for emotional comfort

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 294, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 294.1-2). NOT 2.281.

rcm.2.285.chaupai.1.context: After Ram tells the assembly he will do what Bharat says, Bharat rises to speak. He opens with twenty epithets of Ram (father, mother, friend, guru, master, worthy, highest good, knower of hearts, simple, good master, ocean of good conduct, protector of those who bow, all-knowing, wise, mighty, friend of the surrendered, prizer of virtues, remover of faults) and then sets himself as the opposite. He goes on to confess that he came against orders.
rcm.2.285.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Bharat names every way Ram is the perfect refuge, and in contrast calls himself the worst servant. The praise prepares the ground for his confession and request.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 1)
commentaries.gist: Twenty epithets in three lines. 'Prabhu' signals power to do even the impossible, here to keep his father's, the guru's and Janaka's words all at once. 'Father, mother': he sustains and pampers like parents.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 1), on 'sarala' and 'susahibu'
commentaries.gist: Simple: though so great he is easy to reach, rising to embrace a boatman. Good master: ordinary masters get angry on hearing of a servant's fault; Ram overlooks faults he has seen.

commentaries.who: Vaijnath (Vai.), citing Bhagavad-guna-darpana, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Defines 'shil' (good conduct) as the great mixing without reserve with the lowly, poor, impure and despised.

rcm.2.285.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a prayer of trust, a list of what one hopes for in a parent, mentor or God, and as a model of humility before asking for something important.
misreadings: Not a reason to see oneself as worthless: 'no one like me' is devotional humility.
cautions: The self-abasing last line can reinforce low self-worth if read alone.
not_for: someone with harsh self-criticism (the last line)
speaks_to: gratitude to a mentor or parent
coming to someone you rely on completely

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 298, chaupais 1-4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 298.1-8, half-lines numbered separately). NOT 2.285, and our text is four chaupais, not one. Manas Piyush prints the start as 'prabhu pitu matu suhrid gur swami' as we do.

rcm.2.285.doha.1.context: Bharat has just confessed that, out of delusion, he overrode the words of Ram and his father and came with the whole company; no one, high or low, ever set aside Ram's command even in thought, and he did. Yet Ram took the boldness as love and service. In this doha he says Ram's own kindness turned his faults into ornaments. He continues with Ram's ways with those who come for refuge.
rcm.2.285.doha.1.core_teaching: Bharat credits Ram's goodness, not his own, with turning his offence into something honoured. Grace can transform even our mistakes.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 3), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Everyone's good comes from Ram's own goodness; compares Vinaya Patrika 152, which lists all whom Ram's goodness helped, from Ahalya to Vibhishana to the simple people of Ayodhya.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (tippani 3)
commentaries.gist: The 'fair fame' is that Bharat is now known as a great lover and saint who gave up a kingdom for Ram.

rcm.2.285.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it for gratitude when someone's generosity turned your mistake into something good, and for the hope that failures can become part of a good story.
misreadings: Not a license to do wrong and expect it to be turned to good.
not_for: someone who has not been forgiven and is still hurting
speaks_to: a mistake that turned out well
a mentor who covered for you kindly

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 298 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 298). NOT 2.285.

rcm.2.286.chaupai.2.context: Bharat describes Ram's way, famous in the world and sung by scripture: even the worst sorts of people, if they come to him for refuge, he takes as his own at a single bow; he sees their faults but never holds them in his heart, and praises their virtues among the good. He goes on: what master so honours a servant? Ram never even thinks of his own kindness, only of the servant's embarrassment.
rcm.2.286.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Ram accepts anyone who turns to him, at once, without holding their past against them, and he publicly praises whatever is good in them.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (word notes)
commentaries.gist: 'Nirisa' means masterless, or one with no God in his understanding (an atheist); 'nisanki' means one who does wrong without fear or shame.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (on 298.1-4, note 1)
commentaries.gist: Ordinary masters turn angry on hearing a servant's fault; Ram does not hold even faults he has seen, as the Manas says elsewhere.

rcm.2.286.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a picture of generous leadership and friendship: don't keep score of people's faults, and speak about their good qualities in public.
misreadings: Not a claim that faults don't matter; it is about acceptance after turning back.
not_for: someone hurt by a person who is being 'accepted' without accountability
speaks_to: someone with a past they're ashamed of
leaders and parents learning to forgive

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 299, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 299.3-4). NOT 2.286.

rcm.2.287.chaupai.1.context: Bharat is near the end of his confession. Whether from grief, love or childish stubbornness, he came setting the command aside; yet Ram, looking at his own nature rather than Bharat's fault, took it all as good. He goes on: I have seen your feet, known your natural kindness, and seen in this great gathering how much you love me despite my great mistake.
rcm.2.287.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Bharat owns that he disobeyed, and marvels that Ram judged it by his own generous nature rather than by the offence.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 1a)
commentaries.gist: Grief is the burning that drove him out; love is his wish to bring Ram back; 'a child's nature' is his stubbornness in ignoring guru, parents, ministers and even Ram's message.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 1c)
commentaries.gist: 'Looking to his own side': Ram does not look at a servant's offence but at his own kindness. Compares Bal Kand 28 and Vinaya Patrika 96-97.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, citing Valmiki Ramayana 2.97
commentaries.gist: In Valmiki too Ram tells Lakshman that Bharat has come only out of love and grief, for no other purpose.

rcm.2.287.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to model honest confession that names mixed motives, and generous reception that judges people by their love rather than by the rule they broke.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of ignoring instructions; Bharat calls it a fault.
not_for: someone being told their disobedience to an abuser was wrong
speaks_to: having acted impulsively out of love
being forgiven more kindly than expected

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 300, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 300.1-2). NOT 2.287.

rcm.2.290.doha.1.context: Bharat has asked Ram to decide and command him. Ram begins his answer: Bharat, you are the upholder of dharma, wise in the world's ways and the Vedas, and skilled in love. Then this doha, after which he speaks of the solar dynasty's way, their father's truthfulness, and what each brother's duty now is: Ram's the forest, Bharat's the kingdom.
rcm.2.290.doha.1.core_teaching: Ram declares Bharat spotless in thought, word and deed, beyond comparison, while saying that propriety and the sad moment keep him from praising his younger brother more.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji (Pan.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Speaking at length among elders is improper; praising a younger brother (who is like a son) to his face is against good manners; and in a time of grief no one can do justice to it anyway.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 2), comparing 259.7 and 283.7
commentaries.gist: The same reticence appears when Vasishtha hesitates to praise Bharat to his face, and when Kausalya checks herself for praising him in a time of grief.

rcm.2.290.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it for affirming someone sincerely and specifically, while also knowing when public praise would be out of place.
not_for: someone looking for advice on what to do
speaks_to: needing to hear you are good

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 304 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 304). NOT 2.290: our id and label are off by fourteen.

rcm.2.292.chaupai.4.context: Ram has told Bharat that obeying father, mother, guru and master is the one practice that brings fame, a good end and prosperity, and that Bharat should bear the hardship and keep the people happy. Trouble has been shared out among all, but Bharat's share for the term will be hardest. Here Ram admits he is saying a hard thing to a tender person, justified by the bad time. The doha that follows compares servant and master to hands, feet, eyes and mouth.
rcm.2.292.chaupai.4.core_teaching: In a crisis it is right to ask the people closest to us to carry hard things, as the hand rises by instinct to shield the body from a blow.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 2)
commentaries.gist: 'Tender': Ram knows Bharat cannot bear separation. 'Hard': asking him to suffer and carry the kingdom. It is justified only because the time leaves no other way: the father is gone and both commands must be kept.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 3-4)
commentaries.gist: An example-and-image figure: the good brother is the hand, the bad time the thunderbolt. The hand rises first to shield the body even if it is hurt; outsiders don't stand by you in such moments.

commentaries.who: Gaud ji, in Manas Piyush (on 306.4)
commentaries.gist: Obeying parents protects reputation, obeying the guru brings a good end, and obeying the master (Ram) brings the power to stay near him.

rcm.2.292.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it for family responsibility in emergencies: the people who love us are asked to carry the heaviest loads, and asking them is honest, not cruel.
misreadings: Not a justification for always loading the 'soft' family member with burdens.
cautions: May sit badly with someone already carrying too much for their family.
not_for: a carer who is burned out and over-relied upon
speaks_to: being asked to step up in a family crisis
asking a loved one for something hard

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 306, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 306.7-8). NOT 2.292.

rcm.2.293.chaupai.4.context: Ram's words have settled the assembly and Bharat is content; his face clears, as if a mute had been given speech. He bows and says the joy of going with Ram and the fruit of his birth are his. Now he will carry out whatever Ram orders, but asks for a support to serve through the term. In the next lines he asks about the coronation gear and to see Chitrakoot's holy places; later Ram gives him his sandals.
rcm.2.293.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Bharat accepts the hard command fully but asks for something concrete to hold on to through the long separation.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 3), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram had only spoken of parents' and guru's orders, not given his own; so here Bharat asks for an order from Ram himself and promises to obey at once.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji (Pan.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He is ready to go but has three requests: a support to cross the sea of separation for fourteen years, instructions about the coronation materials, and leave to see Chitrakoot's holy sites.

rcm.2.293.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to long separations and hard assignments: accept what must be done, and ask for something tangible (a keepsake, a routine, a practice) to carry you through.
not_for: someone who needs to be told they can refuse
speaks_to: needing a ritual or object to get through a long wait

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 307, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 307.7-8). NOT 2.293.

rcm.2.301.doha.1.context: In his parting counsel before Bharat returns to Ayodhya, Ram gives this image of the ruler. The next line says that this alone is the whole of rajadharma, like a wish held secretly in the mind. It echoes an earlier doha (306) where servants are hands, feet and eyes and the master the mouth.
rcm.2.301.doha.1.core_teaching: A leader receives the resources, like the mouth receiving food, but only in order to distribute them wisely so every part of the body is nourished according to its need.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 1)
commentaries.gist: Read with doha 306: there servants are hands, feet and eyes bringing to the mouth; here the mouth's duty is named. 'With discernment' means giving each organ what it needs, neither more nor less, else disease follows.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Discernment' covers place, time, season, friend, foe and neutral; the doha could be expanded into a whole treatise on statecraft, as Gita 6.17 on balanced living could.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi (Vi. Tri.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Society is a body and the leader its mouth; the next line's 'wish hidden in the mind' means this principle should drive all outward action.

commentaries.who: Pandeyji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: This one doha contains all of rajadharma, as large wishes hide in a small mind.

rcm.2.301.doha.1.practical_reading: Widely used in Indian management and civic teaching: leaders take in resources and credit, but their job is to distribute wisely and fairly, not to consume.
misreadings: Not a defence of leaders hoarding: the mouth eats only to feed the body.
not_for: someone looking for personal emotional comfort
speaks_to: anyone with power over shared resources

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 315 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 315). NOT 2.301: our id and label are off by fourteen.

rcm.2.310.chaupai.4.context: After returning, Bharat installs Ram's sandals and lives in a hut at Nandigram, fasting and in ascetic dress. Tulsidas says Ayodhya's wealth was the envy of Indra and Kubera, yet Bharat lived there without attachment. The doha that follows says this is no great feat for Bharat, the vessel of Ram's love, just as a chataka's constancy and a swan's discrimination are simply their nature.
rcm.2.310.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Bharat lives surrounded by royal wealth without enjoying it, because it belongs to Ram; true lovers of Ram turn from luxury without effort.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ayodhya's wealth is Ram's, so calling it vomit would be wrong. Bharat gets the champak image (bees don't settle on champak); the vomit image is for other devotees and other wealth.

commentaries.who: Kharra (an old commentary), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The two images show renunciation inside and outside: 'living without attachment' is inner, 'giving up like vomit' is outward.

commentaries.who: Shila commentary, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: A servant should not enjoy his master's property; Bharat will take it only as prasad once Ram enjoys it, and Ram is now living on roots and fruit.

rcm.2.310.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it for living among comforts or power without being owned by them, and for holding resources in trust rather than as one's own.
misreadings: Not a call to despise money or family wealth; Bharat governs carefully.
The vomit simile is strong; it describes intense dispassion, not a rule for everyone.
cautions: The disgust image can feel harsh or shaming to someone struggling with money.
not_for: someone in financial hardship

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 324, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 324.7-8). NOT 2.310.

rcm.2.42.chaupai.1.context: Ram has entered Dasharath's chamber to find him collapsed, and Kaikeyi has laid out the two boons. In the preceding doha Ram lists the gains: time with sages in the forest, his father's command, and her own consent. Here he adds the fourth, Bharat ruling, and says only a fool would miss such a chance. He then confesses his one real pain: seeing his father so distraught.
rcm.2.42.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Ram reframes a loss of the throne as a cluster of gains: holy company, obedience to his father, his stepmother's wish fulfilled and his brother's good. Commentators insist this is his sincere view, not a polite mask.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (citing Vandan Pathak), in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The four reasons map onto the four aims of life: sages' company brings moksha, the father's word dharma, Kaikeyi's consent kama, and Bharat's rule artha.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Dear as life' means: people strive for the comfort of their life-breath, and here, without effort, the one dear as life receives the kingdom. Cites Valmiki 2.26 on Bharat and Shatrughna being dearer than life.

commentaries.who: Paramahamsa (P. P. Pr.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram repeats the same reasons later to Valmiki, which shows they were not said merely to please Kaikeyi.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: People want a kingdom for the sake of loved ones' happiness; if Bharat gets it, Ram loses nothing. Missing such a moment would be the truest foolishness.

rcm.2.42.chaupai.1.practical_reading: A model for meeting a lost role or promotion by naming honestly what the new path offers and rejoicing in a loved one's gain. Teachers stress it is a choice of perspective made while still feeling the pain (Ram's next lines show his distress at his father).
misreadings: Grace in loss is not pretending it doesn't hurt (our misuse note is right).
Not a demand that a reader be glad about an unjust loss imposed on them.
cautions: Could feel like toxic positivity to someone freshly laid off or displaced; pair with Ram's admission of grief in the next lines.
not_for: victims of real injustice who need validation first
a reader in acute grief
speaks_to: someone who lost a promotion, role or inheritance to a sibling or colleague they love
people trying to see a forced change as an opening

rcm.2.42.doha.1.context: Ram has just told Kaikeyi, with full sincerity, why exile is a gain for him and asked only why his father is so distressed. Kaikeyi, already set on her course, hears every gentle word as a ploy to soften her. The poet answers with the leech image: the water is level, the crookedness is in the leech.
rcm.2.42.doha.1.core_teaching: How we hear words depends on the mind that hears them. When the mind is twisted, even straight speech looks crooked; the fault lies in the hearer, not the speech.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The water has no fault; the leech moves crookedly. Likewise the fault is not in Ram's words but in Kaikeyi's 'kumati'. Raghus do not dress up speech, so Ram's words could not be crafted.

commentaries.who: Punjabiji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Kaikeyi assumed Ram was charming her with soft words so she would withdraw the exile, and resolved not to be fooled.

commentaries.who: Panditji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram's speech is full of reasoning, which is why a suspicious hearer could take it as cleverness.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders the doha as the wicked queen giving his straightforward words 'a perverse twist', like a leech that moves crookedly however smooth the water.

rcm.2.42.doha.1.practical_reading: Applied to conflict and suspicion: when someone keeps reading your plain words as manipulation, the problem may be in the lens, not the message; and when you find yourself doing it, check your own lens.
misreadings: Not licence to dismiss every criticism of your words as the other person's 'twisted mind'.
cautions: Can be weaponised in a relationship ('you just hear everything wrong'); frame it as self-examination first.
not_for: someone being gaslit, who may be told their accurate perception is the 'crooked' one
speaks_to: someone whose good intentions keep being misread
a reader noticing their own suspicion colouring everything
family conflict where trust has broken down

rcm.2.50.doha.1.context: Ayodhya's people are lamenting and cursing Kaikeyi, but Ram walks to his mother Kausalya with a cheerful face and 'fourfold eagerness', his one fear (that the king might hold him back) gone. The doha explains his lightness: kingship had been a tether. Right after, Kausalya, still thinking it is coronation day, blesses him and asks when the auspicious hour is.
rcm.2.50.doha.1.core_teaching: Ram never wanted the throne for himself; losing it felt like freedom. Commentators read it as a sign of his inner detachment and of the forest being where his real work lies.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: An elephant long in captivity stops wanting the forest; a newly caught one suffers in bondage and longs to roam free. Ram's mind is the new one.

commentaries.who: Paramahamsa (P. P. Pr.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The coronation was arranged against Ram's own wish; its cancellation increased the joy of one who is by nature a treasury of bliss.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Kalidasa, Raghuvamsha 12.7
commentaries.gist: Kalidasa too says Ram wept when given the earth and gladly took the command to go to the forest.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as a young elephant with kingship for its chain, the news of exile being the chain's breaking.

rcm.2.50.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it for the relief that can come with losing a role we never wanted: a job, a title, an expectation. It invites the reader to ask which of their 'honours' are really tethers.
misreadings: Losing a role can free you; that does not make every loss a gift (our misuse note is right).
Not a case for dodging duty: Ram embraces a harder duty.
cautions: Ill-suited to someone devastated by a job loss or forced eviction they did not want.
not_for: a reader who has just lost something they deeply wanted
job loss with financial distress
speaks_to: someone relieved after leaving a role that never fit
a person freed from family expectations of a career or position

rcm.2.54.chaupai.2.context: Ram has told Kausalya, who was preparing for his coronation, that he must go to the forest. She cannot hold him back nor tell him to go. If she keeps him, dharma is broken and it looks like a quarrel with Bharat; if she sends him, the loss is huge. Then, remembering a wife's duty and that Ram and Bharat are both her sons, she steadies herself and tells him he has done well, for a father's command crowns all duties.
rcm.2.54.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Duty and love can trap a good heart in a position where every option costs something. The verse names that bind honestly before Kausalya chooses.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Kausalya is the snake, Ram the shrew: keeping him home is swallowing (loss of dharma, disgrace), sending him is releasing (fourteen years of weeping, the 'blindness').

commentaries.who: Nange Paramahamsa, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: In the end the snake swallows and dies; so Kausalya chose death over abandoning dharma, since her husband, her life, would die.

commentaries.who: Manas Mayank, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The snake drops the shrew in water to escape; so Kausalya left the matter to Kaikeyi's decree, keeping both her love and her duty.

commentaries.who: Vedantabhushan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Brothers' conflict' does not mean Ram and Bharat would fight; Kausalya fears Kaikeyi would read any restraint as setting Ram against Bharat.

rcm.2.54.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Used for any parent or caregiver caught between two goods: a child's calling versus wanting them close, a dying parent versus a job. Naming the bind honestly is the first step before choosing.
misreadings: Not saying every dilemma has a clean right answer.
Not a teaching that a mother's love is a weakness to be overcome.
cautions: The snake-and-shrew image is earthy and folk-zoological; explain it gently. The next lines resolve in favour of duty, which can sound like 'love must lose'.
not_for: someone who wants to be told what to do; the verse only describes the bind
speaks_to: parents letting a child move far away for study, work or marriage
caregivers torn between family and career
anyone stuck where both choices hurt

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 55, chaupai 2 (lines 3-4) (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 55, half-lines 3-4'). NOT 2.54.

rcm.2.55.doha.1.context: Kausalya has steadied herself: a father's command crowns all duties, and if it were only Dasharath's she might forbid it, but Kaikeyi's wish counts too, so the forest will be like a hundred Ayodhyas, with forest gods for parents. She admits she cannot ask to come along without unsettling him. This doha is her decision: no insisting, only a plea to keep the bond. Then she blesses him (the next chaupai) and collapses at his feet.
rcm.2.55.doha.1.core_teaching: Real love sometimes means not using love as leverage. Kausalya lets her son go with her blessing and asks only to stay in his heart.

commentaries.who: Munshi Roshanlal, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Kausalya calls her own love false because her life did not leave her on hearing of the exile; even so, she asks Ram to honour the mother-tie from his side and remember her.

commentaries.who: Pt. Yadavshankar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Tulsidas condenses Valmiki's line where Kausalya asks Ram not to give up being her son, and makes it more piercing.

commentaries.who: Paramahamsa (P. P. Pr.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: At the level of ultimate truth her attachment is illusory, yet in everyday reality she is mother and he is son, and that should not be forgotten.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders: she will not press her suit with a show of love beyond what she feels, and prays he will not forget her.

rcm.2.55.doha.1.practical_reading: Read at send-offs: a parent can bless a child's leaving instead of guilt-tripping them into staying, and still say plainly 'don't forget me'. Love that releases is not love that has stopped.
misreadings: Not a claim that a parent's grief at parting is 'fake'.
Not advice to suppress feelings: she voices her grief in the next lines.
cautions: For a parent whose child has cut contact, 'don't forget me' may hurt; for a parent who has lost a child to death, the parting imagery can be raw.
not_for: bereaved parents
parents estranged from a child, without care
speaks_to: parents of children leaving for study, work, marriage or abroad
adult children who feel guilt about leaving ageing parents
anyone tempted to hold someone back with emotional pressure

rcm.2.56.chaupai.1.context: Right after deciding not to hold Ram back, Kausalya blesses him. The image of eyelids is followed by another: the fourteen-year term is water and his loved ones are fish who will survive only while it lasts. She asks him, being compassionate and steadfast in dharma, to find a way to return while all are alive, then breaks down and clings to his feet. Ram lifts her and consoles her; Sita then arrives.
rcm.2.56.chaupai.1.core_teaching: A mother's blessing for safe keeping, joined to a plea: the family's life is tied to his return on time. Love blesses the journey and still asks the traveller to come home.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: The eye is the tenderest organ; the lids shut instantly at the slightest speck and close it in sleep, trusting no one. So should the gods guard Ram.

commentaries.who: Manas Mayank, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The ancestors are the lower lid and the gods the upper; together they protect the pupil.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Gosain' here is not an address to Ram but means Narayan, who along with gods and ancestors is asked to protect him. Manas Piyush finds this the better reading.

commentaries.who: Paramahamsa (P. P. Pr.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Fish die when water runs out: the family will survive only until the term ends. Ram, knowing his father will not live, gives no answer to the plea to return while all live.

rcm.2.56.chaupai.1.practical_reading: A model blessing for anyone setting out on a long absence: wish them protected, and tell them honestly how much their return matters.
misreadings: Not a pressure tactic; it is a blessing that names the family's dependence.
cautions: The 'fish without water' image implies the family may die before the return; Dasharath does. Gentle handling for readers with ailing parents far away.
not_for: someone whose parent died while they were away
readers wrestling with guilt about not returning in time
speaks_to: a parent blessing a child going abroad, to the army, or to a long posting
a traveller who needs to feel held

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 57, chaupai 1 (lines 1-2) (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 57 (1-3)'). NOT 2.56.

rcm.2.67.chaupai.4.context: Sita has just won Ram's consent to come to the forest. Ram comforts her and bows to his mother, who asks him to return soon and end the people's grief and not forget his 'hard-hearted' mother. These lines are her last questions to fate before the doha where she longs to call him 'calf' and 'darling' and hold him again. Ram consoles her in many ways; then Sita bows to her.
rcm.2.67.chaupai.4.core_teaching: A mother's honest fear at parting: she hopes for the day of reunion but doubts she will live to see it. Tulsidas lets grief speak without correcting it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Purushottam Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: While Ram was home her 'dasha' was good; his leaving marks a bad turn. 'Will it turn again' means: will good days return so these eyes see the pair again?

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'When will that hour come' implies fourteen years is very long; despairing of living that long, she asks whether the mother will still be alive to see his face.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Gitavali 2.1-4
commentaries.gist: Compares Tulsidas's Gitavali songs where Kausalya asks how she will bear the house without her child and his voice.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders the lines as Kausalya hoping God may change her lot and asking when the happy day will come that she lives to see his moon-like face.

rcm.2.67.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Gives words to parents and grandparents who fear they won't live to see a far-away child return. It validates the fear rather than dismissing it.
misreadings: Not a prediction of death; it is a mother's fear voiced.
cautions: Directly raises the fear of dying before a reunion; avoid for a reader whose parent died during a separation, unless they seek it.
not_for: readers bereaved of a parent they could not see before death
someone needing hope rather than lament
speaks_to: families facing long separations (deployment, migration, prison terms)
adult children who hear this fear from their parents

rcm.2.73.chaupai.2.context: Lakshman has come to his mother afraid she will stop him going. Sumitra, first shaken, then steadies herself and tells him: your mother is now Sita and your father Ram. Home is wherever Ram lives, as day is wherever the sun shines. She goes on: elders and gods are to be served like one's own life, but Ram is the life of life; go with him and reap the gain of being born.
rcm.2.73.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Home is not a place but the presence of the one you love and serve. Commentators read it devotionally: where Ram is, there is everything that home gives.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note (Gita Press), citing Valmiki 2.37.29 and 2.40.9
commentaries.gist: Vasishtha says the realm will be wherever Ram lives, and Valmiki's Sumitra tells Lakshman to think of the forest as Ayodhya. Tulsidas's line condenses both.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note
commentaries.gist: Ayodhya without Ram is like night; the poet later says Ayodhya looked like a dark night of doom. And Lakshman truly never thought of home again.

commentaries.who: Paramahamsa (P. P. Pr.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Sumitra's words carry spiritual meaning: worldly parents love with some self-interest; Sita (Vaidehi, free of body-attachment) and Ram love without it.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders: where Rama dwells there is Avadh, and wherever the sun's light is, there is day.

rcm.2.73.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Used for migrants, newly-weds and families who move: home is made by people and love, not by an address. Also used devotionally: where God is remembered, there is home.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of one's parents or birthplace; Sumitra herself honours elders in the next line.
Not an instruction to follow anyone anywhere regardless of harm.
cautions: For someone who has no 'people' nearby (isolated migrants, the bereaved), 'home is where your people are' can sharpen loneliness; the devotional reading may land better.
not_for: someone who has lost the person who was their 'home'
people in controlling relationships being pressured to follow
speaks_to: newly married people leaving their parents' home
families relocating for a loved one's work or care

rcm.2.74.chaupai.3.context: Sumitra has told Lakshman that a mother is truly blessed only if her son loves Ram, and that the highest fruit of all good deeds is natural love for Sita and Ram's feet. Here she names the five enemies of that service, then says he will lack nothing in the forest with Ram and Sita as parents, and gives her one instruction: do whatever keeps Ram from hardship. Lakshman leaves at once, like a deer escaping a snare.
rcm.2.74.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Service done well needs a clean heart: Sumitra names five inner disturbances that spoil it and asks for service in thought, word and act.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Each is applied to Lakshman's service: no attachment to home and kin, no anger even at hard words (he stays calm when Sita rebukes him), no envy ('we are both princes'), no pride, no forgetting who Ram is.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: After the five she says 'every kind of distortion', since there are many more; mind, deed and word must all stay pure in service.

commentaries.who: Pandey (Pa.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Service of mind is keeping the moment of service in view; of word, asking fitting orders and speaking sweetly; of deed, the actual work.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders the list as lust, passion, envy, pride and delusion, followed by serving them in heart, word and deed.

rcm.2.74.chaupai.3.practical_reading: A parent's parting advice that works for any young adult leaving home or starting a demanding role: guard against attachment, anger, envy, pride and confusion, and serve wholeheartedly.
misreadings: Not a claim that all feeling is bad; the target is being 'ruled' by these states.
Service here is devotional; it is not a mandate for self-erasure toward any boss or partner.
cautions: 'Not even in a dream' sets an impossible bar if read literally; frame it as an aim.
not_for: someone in an exploitative relationship being told to serve without complaint
speaks_to: caregivers and people in service roles
anyone starting work alongside a sibling or mentor where envy could creep in

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 75, chaupai 3 (lines 5-6) (Gita Press; Manas Piyush vol. 4 'doha 75, half-lines 5-6'). NOT 2.74.

rcm.2.90.chaupai.2.context: On the first night of exile at Shringverpur, Guha sees Ram and Sita asleep on a bed of grass and, grieving, calls Kaikeyi a dull-witted woman who has become an axe to the solar dynasty. Lakshman, keeping watch, answers softly so as not to wake Ram. He goes on: union and separation, friend and foe, wealth and loss are snares of delusion, like a dream where a beggar becomes king; so do not be angry or blame anyone; true waking is detachment and love for Ram.
rcm.2.90.chaupai.2.core_teaching: No other person is the true source of our joy or sorrow; we live out the results of our own actions. The point, in context, is to stop Guha's anger and blame, then lead him toward detachment and devotion.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Guha blamed Kaikeyi for giving sorrow; Lakshman answers from the Mimamsa view that action is primary. He speaks sweetly so as not to hurt Guha or wake Ram, and calls a lowly boatman 'brother'.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Adhyatma Ramayana 2.6.4-8
commentaries.gist: The parallel verse calls it bad thinking to believe another gives us joy or sorrow; one should accept what comes from one's own past acts and keep the mind steady.

commentaries.who: Paramahamsa (P. P. Pr.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Absorbing this principle cures hatred, envy, fault-finding and blaming others, and increases one's capacity to bear pain. Worldly gain and loss follow past karma; spiritual good comes by effort.

commentaries.who: Pt. Purushottam Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The rule is said for all beings, not for Ram, whose deeds are free play, not karmic fruit.

rcm.2.90.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Applied to blame and resentment: instead of locating all your pain in one person, look at the whole chain of causes, including your own part, and stop feeding anger. It returns your peace to your own hands.
misreadings: Not 'you deserve your suffering' (our misuse note is right).
Not an excuse for wrongdoers: commentators say Kaikeyi will bear her own deeds' fruit.
Not a reason to stop seeking justice or protection from harm.
cautions: Karma language can feel like victim-blaming to someone abused, assaulted, bereaved by violence or chronically ill. Do not use for those readers.
Rebirth/past-life karma underlies the traditional reading; keep it light for general readers.
not_for: victims of abuse, violence or injustice
fresh grief, especially after an accident or someone else's negligence
people with depression prone to self-blame
speaks_to: someone stuck in resentment at a relative or ex-partner
family members blaming one person for a shared misfortune
people who want to stop handing their peace to others

rcm.2.91.chaupai.1.context: Lakshman has just told Guha that every pair of opposites (union and separation, friend and foe, heaven and hell) is rooted in delusion, and that the world is like a dream from which the waking gain or lose nothing. From this he draws the practical conclusion: no anger, no needless blame. He continues that only yogis detached from the senses are awake in this night, and that the highest good is love for Ram in thought, word and deed.
rcm.2.91.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Seeing life's ups and downs as a dream seen in the night of delusion, one drops anger and needless blame. Waking up means detachment and love for God.

commentaries.who: Pt. Purushottam Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Guha blamed Kaikeyi, so Lakshman says blame no one in vain. People fault whoever they are angry with; think the matter through and you will see no one is truly at fault. Thus far knowledge; dispassion follows.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: In a dream there is no one else: you yourself become enemy, friend, loss and gain. On waking no one counts the dream-enemy as an enemy, so neither anger nor blame makes sense.

commentaries.who: Paramahamsa (P. P. Pr.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'I and mine, you and yours' is the main dream; still, as one thorn removes another, the guru-disciple relation is a useful dream to end a binding one.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders: reasoning thus, be not angry with anyone nor vainly blame anyone; all are sleepers in a night of delusion seeing many dreams.

rcm.2.91.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Used to cool anger: before blaming, ask whether you are reacting inside a 'dream' of me-and-mine. Many teachers apply it to family quarrels and long-held grudges.
misreadings: Not blaming is not the same as excusing harm (our misuse note is right).
'The world is a dream' is not a licence to ignore suffering or responsibility.
cautions: Calling a loss 'a dream' can feel dismissive to someone grieving or wronged; avoid for fresh loss.
Rests on Vedantic metaphysics; present as perspective, not as a claim that the reader's pain is unreal.
not_for: abuse survivors
fresh grief
someone whose anger is a needed signal of real injustice
speaks_to: someone ready to let go of a grudge
family members caught in mutual blame
people whose anger is hurting themselves most

rcm.2.93.chaupai.3.context: The morning after the night at Shringverpur, the minister Sumantra begs Ram, on the king's behalf, to return so Ayodhya is not left orphaned. Ram raises him and reminds him of Shibi, Dadhichi, Harishchandra, Rantideva and Bali, who bore countless hardships for dharma. Truth is the highest dharma, and he has got it cheaply; abandoning it would bring disgrace, which for an honoured person is worse than a million deaths.
rcm.2.93.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Keeping one's word (here, a father's promise) is the highest dharma. Ram adds that it has come to him cheaply compared to the great kings who suffered for it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Sumantra might say those kings' trials were extreme, so why suffer? Ram answers that truth has no equal, with scripture as proof; making a father's word true crowns all duties.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note citing Valmiki 2.14 and 2.109
commentaries.gist: Valmiki's Kaikeyi and Ram (answering Jabali) say truth is the root of all dharma; gifts, sacrifice, austerity and the Vedas rest on it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Easily obtained': kings gave their lives for ordinary dharma, while Ram gets the highest by a few years in the forest; to drop it would make him look a coward in dharma.

commentaries.who: Growse, The Ramayana of Tulsi Das (1883; 6th ed.)
