commentaries.gist: Renders: there is no virtue equal to truth, as Vedas, Shastras and Puranas declare; he has reached it by an easy road, and abandoning it would spread his disgrace through earth, heaven and hell.

rcm.2.93.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Used for integrity under pressure: when loved ones urge you to break a commitment for comfort, remember that keeping your word is itself the treasure, and often costs less than you fear.
misreadings: Not an argument to keep a promise that harms others or was extracted by abuse.
Not a call to value reputation above people; the following line's stress on disgrace is cultural and should not dominate.
cautions: The next line equates disgrace with a million deaths; avoid quoting that for readers dealing with public shame or suicidal thoughts.
not_for: someone bound by a harmful or coerced promise
a reader overwhelmed by shame
speaks_to: someone tempted to break a commitment because others plead
people holding to integrity at personal cost
those making a hard choice to honour a parent's promise

rcm.2.99.chaupai.3.context: On the far bank of the Ganga, Ram feels awkward that he has nothing to give the boatman who bowed to him. Sita, reading his mind, gladly takes off her jewelled ring; Ram tells Kevat to take his fare, and Kevat clutches his feet. He says he has already received everything, wants nothing more, and will accept whatever Ram gives on the way back. Unable to make him take anything, Ram dismisses him with the boon of pure devotion.
rcm.2.99.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Kevat's real wage is having served and touched the Lord; no fee could match it. Commentators read the refusal as the mark of desireless devotion that receives pure bhakti.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Clutching the feet means: after seeing you, why would I want worldly enjoyment? Don't cheat me with a ring. Faults are the cause, sorrows the effect; both burned away by touching the feet, and poverty, the worst sorrow, too.

commentaries.who: Panjabiji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He had laboured through many births, scorched by sorrow; today, working for Ram, his belly was filled. Plainly: a lifetime ferrying, but today's fare exceeds all.

commentaries.who: Pandeyji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Deferring payment: he had sworn to take no fare; or he keeps Ram in his debt so he returns to this ghat; or each ferried the other across, so they are even.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush (on the doha)
commentaries.gist: Ram, Lakshman and Sita pressed gifts; because he took none, he received pure devotion. Only the desireless receive such grace.

rcm.2.99.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Applied to work and gratitude: some moments of service pay more than money, and the joy of having helped can itself be full payment. It honours working people's dignity.
misreadings: Not an argument that workers should not be paid or should refuse wages.
Not a romanticisation of poverty.
cautions: For readers struggling financially, 'paid in full without money' could ring hollow; emphasise gratitude and dignity, not giving up earnings.
not_for: workers being underpaid or exploited
someone in financial crisis
speaks_to: people in service work who find meaning in it
someone grateful after a meaningful encounter

rcm.3.13.chaupai.6.context: At Panchavati Lakshman asks Ram about knowledge, dispassion, maya and devotion. Ram teaches him, ending with the marks of bhakti: love for the saints' feet, regarding guru, parents and kin as Ram, and then this description of the devotee whose body thrills as he sings. The doha that follows completes it.
rcm.3.13.chaupai.6.core_teaching: Ram says he is held by the devotee whose love shows in body, voice and tears and who is free of desire, pride and pretence. The outward signs count only with the inner purity.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Thrill, choked voice and tears are three of the eight 'sattvic' signs of devotional emotion. Cites Rupa Gosvami's Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu on how they arise.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi (Vi. Tri.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Singing out of desire, pride in one's art, greed for reward or to be called devout may bring some benefit, but it is not loving devotion and cannot win the Lord.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Always in their power': compares other Manas lines where Ram says he guards such devotees and dwells in them as wealth in a miser's heart.

rcm.3.13.chaupai.6.practical_reading: Teachers use it to separate real devotion from performance: feeling that wells up is valued only when it is free of ego, greed and show.
misreadings: Not a test that you must cry or tremble to be devout; the point is freedom from pride and pretence.
not_for: someone who feels spiritually 'dry' and may read it as exclusion
speaks_to: worry that one's practice is hollow

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 16, chaupai 6 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 16.11-12). NOT 3.13: our id and label are off by three.

rcm.3.13.doha.1.context: This doha closes Ram's teaching on bhakti to Lakshman at Panchavati. Lakshman bows at his feet in joy, and some days pass in talk of dispassion, knowledge and right conduct before Shurpanakha arrives.
rcm.3.13.doha.1.core_teaching: Those who rely on Ram alone in speech, action and thought and worship without wanting anything back are where he rests. 'Rest' implies being at home, not just present.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: God dwells in every heart (Gita 18.61) but unmanifest; only in such hearts does he 'rest', since others keep demanding sons, wealth and fame or quarrel among themselves. Calls 'rest' a careful word choice.

commentaries.who: Chakra ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Speech should tell only of God, actions be done for his pleasure, and the mind dwell on him; desire even for heaven or liberation should be absent.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Rest' marks this as Ram's own home, linking to Valmiki's 'jahi na chahia' (Ayodhya 131), where the desireless heart is Ram's own house.

rcm.3.13.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that the divine is most at ease in a person who isn't bargaining: wholehearted, undivided, wanting nothing back.
misreadings: Not a statement that God is absent from people who pray for help; commentators say he dwells in all hearts.
not_for: someone in acute need who must ask for help

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand doha 16 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 16). NOT 3.13.

rcm.3.2.sortha.1.context: Jayant, Indra's son, took the form of a crow to test Ram's power, pecked Sita's foot and fled. Ram's grass-blade arrow chased him through all the worlds; no god would shelter him until Narada sent him back to Ram. When he cried out for protection, Ram let him go with one eye destroyed. This soratha closes the episode.
rcm.3.2.sortha.1.core_teaching: Ram tempers justice with mercy: the offender deserved death, but when he took refuge Ram spared him, leaving a lesser, fitting consequence.

commentaries.who: Dinji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Parvati may have doubted how blinding him in one eye counts as mercy, so Shiva answers at once: by right he should have died.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 3-4), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Mercy is named at the start, middle and end of the episode. Anger usually leaves no room for mercy (compares Parashurama), yet Ram, powerful and provoked, chose kindness.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (Pra. and note 2), citing Valmiki 5.38.35 and Adhyatma Ramayana
commentaries.gist: Taking one eye kept the arrow's word true and taught a lesson; it was the eye that saw and struck. Valmiki also says Ram spared him though he deserved death; Adhyatma says the eye was taken with his consent.

rcm.3.2.sortha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to show mercy and accountability together: the wrongdoer who turns back is spared the worst but still bears a consequence.
misreadings: Grace doesn't erase consequences (our misuse note is right): Jayant loses an eye.
Not a model for victims being expected to forgive their abuser.
cautions: Involves violence and maiming; the 'mercy' includes a punishment.
not_for: a victim of harm who may hear it as pressure to forgive
speaks_to: someone ashamed of a serious wrong who fears there is no way back
parents and managers deciding on discipline

rcm.3.26.doha.1.context: Ram, searching for Sita, finds Jatayu lying wounded after fighting Ravana, remembering Ram's feet. Ram strokes his head and the vulture's pain is gone. Jatayu then tells him Ravana took Sita south, refuses Ram's offer to keep him alive, and dies in Ram's presence.
rcm.3.26.doha.1.core_teaching: Ram's touch and the sight of his face take away all of Jatayu's pain, though he is dying. Both the Lord's touch and the devotee's gaze are named as healing.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The touch comes from Ram's side, the gazing from the devotee's; both end in 'all pain gone'. Either one is enough to remove a devotee's suffering. Lists parallel touches (Sugriva, Hanuman, Bhushundi).

commentaries.who: Mayukh commentary, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: What vanished is the pain of the wounds Ravana gave; the grief for Sita still aches, which is why Jatayu next speaks sorrowfully of her abduction.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram asks him nothing first; the lesson drawn is that one should not question a dying person before easing them.

rcm.3.26.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it for the comfort of presence at the end of life: touch and a loved face can ease what words can't.
misreadings: Not a claim that faith removes physical death or illness; Jatayu still dies.
cautions: Deathbed scene. Gentle, but may be hard for someone recently bereaved or facing a loved one's death.
not_for: someone whose loved one died alone (may sharpen guilt)
speaks_to: sitting with a dying loved one

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand doha 30 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 30). NOT 3.26: our id and label are off by four.

rcm.3.27.chaupai.5.context: Jatayu has declined Ram's offer to keep his body alive. With tears in his eyes Ram tells him he has won a good end by his own deeds, that nothing is out of reach for those devoted to others' good, and sends him to his abode. He also asks Jatayu not to tell Dasharath about Sita's abduction; Ravana will tell him himself. Jatayu takes a divine form, praises Ram, and departs.
rcm.3.27.chaupai.5.core_teaching: Living for others' good makes every aim reachable, including liberation. Ram honours Jatayu's self-sacrifice by sending him to his own abode.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 3), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Serving others brings all four aims: the 'good end' is moksha, and 'nothing is hard' covers wealth, dharma and desire in this world.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: True service of others is impossible while one wants something for oneself, here or hereafter; selfless service is the saint's nature.

commentaries.who: Gaud ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Such liberated servers can even return to the world at will to help others; leaving this worn-out, painful body is good.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 5), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'What can I give you?' shows Ram's generosity: having given everything, he still speaks as if he had nothing to offer.

rcm.3.27.chaupai.5.practical_reading: Teachers use it to honour people who gave themselves for others, and to say that a life of service is itself complete.
misreadings: Not a promise of worldly success for altruists; it is spoken to a dying hero.
cautions: Deathbed and 'leave this body' language. Fine for honouring someone's sacrifice; risky for anyone with suicidal feelings or in fresh grief.
not_for: someone with thoughts of self-harm ('leave this body')
fresh bereavement
speaks_to: honouring a parent or mentor who sacrificed for others

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 31, chaupai 5 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 31.9-10). NOT 3.27: our id and label are off by four.

rcm.3.29.chaupai.1.context: After Jatayu's death and Ram's performing his funeral rites, Shiva sums up for Parvati: Ram is tender-hearted and gracious without cause, giving a lowly flesh-eating bird the end yogis pray for. He adds that those who leave Hari for worldly pleasures are unfortunate.
rcm.3.29.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Ram's grace does not depend on rank or merit: he gave the humblest creature the highest goal.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram's heart melts most at the suffering of the 'deen', meaning people who feel they have no spiritual means of their own, even if they practise.

commentaries.who: Kharra (old commentary), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Objection: Jatayu gave his life for Sita, so how is the grace 'without reason'? Answer: even his strength and courage were Ram's gift (Gita 7.8-11).

rcm.3.29.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that grace isn't earned by status or purity; it reaches the lowest and most unlikely.
misreadings: Not a statement that animals or meat-eaters are worthless; 'lowly' sets up the contrast with the yogi's goal.
cautions: Pt. Ramkumar's note condemns meat-eating; a reader may find that judgemental.
not_for: someone looking for a death-free reading (the setting is a funeral)

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 33, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 33.1-2, where Shiva sums up the Jatayu episode). NOT 3.29: our id and label are off by four.

rcm.3.31.chaupai.2.context: Shabari, an old forest woman of low birth, has waited years for Ram. She washes his feet and feeds him, then stands with folded hands saying she cannot praise him: she is of low birth, dull, and among women, counted lowest of the low, the dullest. Ram answers that he recognises only the bond of devotion, and in the next lines says caste, family, dharma, wealth, strength, kin, virtue and cleverness without devotion are like a cloud without water. He then teaches her the nine forms of devotion.
rcm.3.31.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Shabari voices the social hierarchy that ranks her lowest; Ram sets it aside entirely: the only bond he recognises is devotion.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram calls her 'bhamini', the word he used for Sita, not for bodily beauty: whoever has devotion is beautiful in his eyes. All other ties are born of illusion.

commentaries.who: Ranbahadur Singh, citing the Shandilya Sutra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Experience shows devotion, not learning or birth, is what reaches God: Dhruva as a child, the hunter, Valmiki, Raidas, Namdev and others.

rcm.3.31.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that worth before God is not set by caste, gender, wealth or ability; love is the only credential.
misreadings: The first half is Shabari's harsh self-description, which Ram's reply overturns; never show it alone (our misuse note is right).
Not a teaching that women or lower castes are lesser; it records a hierarchy in order to reject it.
cautions: Contains caste and gender hierarchy language. Manas Piyush's own older notes (Kharra, Pt. Ramkumar) restate caste rankings; do not carry those into readings.
not_for: a reader hurt by caste or gender discrimination if the first half is shown without Ram's answer
speaks_to: feeling unworthy because of background or gender

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 35, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 35.3-4). NOT 3.31: our id and label are off by four.

rcm.3.32.chaupai.2.context: Ram, having eaten Shabari's fruit, teaches her the nine forms of devotion (navadha bhakti): company of saints, love of his stories, service of the guru, singing his virtues, mantra repetition with firm faith, self-restraint and good conduct, then the seventh to ninth. He ends by saying whoever has even one is most dear to him, and Shabari has all. She then directs him to Pampa and Sugriva and gives up her body in yogic fire. These lines give the seventh and eighth forms.
rcm.3.32.chaupai.2.core_teaching: The seventh form is seeing the divine everywhere and honouring good people above God himself; the eighth is contentment with what comes and refusing to dwell on others' faults.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 4), in Manas Piyush, citing Bhagavata 11.2.41
commentaries.gist: Seeing everything as Ram is the mark of his worshippers: earth, water, sky, beings and rivers are all his body, to be bowed to.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand (Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Saints are to be held above Ram because realised saints lead people to him, and because a father loves whoever loves his son more than whoever loves him.

commentaries.who: Kharra (old commentary), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Saints are greater because they stay untouched by the world like a lotus leaf in water.

rcm.3.32.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers use these two as daily practices: look for the good (or the sacred) in everyone, be content with what you have, and stop scanning others for faults.
misreadings: 'Not seeing faults' doesn't mean ignoring harm done to you or others; it is about a habit of fault-finding.
not_for: someone in a harmful situation who needs to see the other person's faults clearly
speaks_to: wanting a simple daily spiritual practice

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 36, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 36.3-4). NOT 3.32: our id and label are off by four.

rcm.3.32.chaupai.3.context: Ram, having eaten Shabari's fruit, teaches her the nine forms of devotion (navadha bhakti): company of saints, love of his stories, service of the guru, singing his virtues, mantra repetition with firm faith, self-restraint and good conduct, then the seventh to ninth. He ends by saying whoever has even one is most dear to him, and Shabari has all. She then directs him to Pampa and Sugriva and gives up her body in yogic fire. This line gives the ninth form and begins the conclusion.
rcm.3.32.chaupai.3.core_teaching: The ninth form is simplicity and honesty with everyone, trusting God, and staying steady through gain and loss. Having even one of the nine is enough, whoever you are.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Guile comes from 'I and mine' and from not fully trusting God. Only when one takes whatever comes as the Lord's gift do elation and despair fall away.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Elation comes from gaining good things and dejection from losing them; once one has found Ram, the gain or loss of passing things stops moving one, as cash means little to one who has the philosopher's stone.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1g), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Woman' is named first because Shabari had called herself lowest for being a woman.

rcm.3.32.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers use it for steadiness and honesty: be straightforward, don't manipulate, trust, and don't ride every high and low.
misreadings: 'Not dejected' is not a rule against sadness; it describes a steady trust underneath.
cautions: Someone in depression may hear 'neither elated nor downcast' as a demand.
not_for: someone in clinical depression
speaks_to: wanting to be more honest and less calculating
feeling excluded from spirituality by gender or background

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 36, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 36.5-6). NOT 3.32.

rcm.3.32.chaupai.4.context: Ram, having eaten Shabari's fruit, teaches her the nine forms of devotion (navadha bhakti): company of saints, love of his stories, service of the guru, singing his virtues, mantra repetition with firm faith, self-restraint and good conduct, then the seventh to ninth. He ends by saying whoever has even one is most dear to him, and Shabari has all. She then directs him to Pampa and Sugriva and gives up her body in yogic fire. This line closes the teaching.
rcm.3.32.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Anyone with even one form of devotion is most dear to Ram, and Shabari, a forest woman of low birth, has them all firmly; the goal yogis strive for is hers today.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The one dear to God is whoever drops every other hope and worships him; cites similar promises to the monkeys, to Guha and to Bhushundi (man, woman or any being).

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Even one of the nine is rare and seldom firm; in her all nine are firm. Her devotion is why he came, and the fruit of seeing him is her own true state.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 1), comparing Adhyatma Ramayana 3.10
commentaries.gist: Adhyatma says the nine are means for anyone, woman, man or animal, practised in sequence; the Manas's 'even one' is far stronger.

rcm.3.32.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that a person written off by society may be furthest ahead spiritually, and that one sincere practice is enough to begin.
misreadings: Not a ranking of devotees over yogis in general; it is said to honour Shabari.
not_for: someone wanting a strict path or method
speaks_to: encouragement to start with one practice

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 36, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 36.7-8). NOT 3.32.

rcm.3.34.doha.1.context: Separated from Sita, Ram walks through the spring forest and describes it to Lakshman as the army of Kama, the god of desire: trees as tents, birds as war-elephants, and so on. Those who stay steady before it have true renown. Then this doha names the three strongest foes. The second doha 38 gives their weapons: greed's are wanting and pretence, desire's is woman alone, anger's is harsh speech.
rcm.3.34.doha.1.core_teaching: Desire, anger and greed can unsettle even the wisest mind in an instant. Knowing their strength is the first defence.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani), in Manas Piyush, citing Gita 2.62 and 3.37
commentaries.gist: The three are really one, desire, taking three forms: dwelling on objects breeds attachment, attachment desire, thwarted desire anger.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 4), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Example: Narada, a home of wisdom, fell to desire on seeing a princess, then to longing, then to anger when thwarted; no one in the world escapes all three.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi (Vi. Tri.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: These are the world's great enemies because they shake even sages who wish everyone well; one must know their strength to protect oneself.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan (Pan. Ra. Va. Sha.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Practical defence: check a craving as it arises, don't answer harsh words, and don't let lustful thoughts settle. Keeping their weapons in view lets one control them.

rcm.3.34.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a humbling reminder that no level of learning or practice makes anyone immune to craving, temper and greed; vigilance, not pride, is the safeguard.
misreadings: Not a statement that feelings of desire or anger are sinful in themselves; it warns of their power to overturn judgement.
cautions: The doha right after it calls woman desire's only weapon. Don't pair them without context; that framing is offensive to many readers today.
not_for: a woman reader if paired with the next doha's 'woman is desire's weapon'

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand doha 38 (ka), the first of two dohas numbered 38 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush prints both under 38). NOT 3.34: our id and label are off by four.

rcm.3.35.chaupai.3.context: Ram has been lamenting Sita and describing desire's army. Shiva explains to Parvati: Ram is beyond the gunas and knows all hearts; he showed the plight of the lovelorn to strengthen dispassion in the steady. Anger, lust, greed, pride and illusion all fall away by Ram's grace; the one the magician favours isn't fooled by the magic show. Then Shiva gives his own testimony. The narrative resumes at Pampa lake.
rcm.3.35.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Shiva states from his own experience that devotion to God is what is real and lasting, while the world is like a dream.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 4), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Lest calling Ram's play a magic show make it seem false, Shiva adds that worship is real and the world dreamlike. In a magic show the place is real, the show false; here the reverse.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 4c), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'My own experience': other sages hold the world real, so Shiva speaks for himself. Kharra adds that in ritual and worship the world is treated as real, in knowledge as unreal.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 4e), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He addresses 'Uma' because it was this very scene of Ram searching for Sita that once deluded her (as Sati).

rcm.3.35.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers use it to put worries in proportion: much of what grips us is passing like a dream, while devotion and what it grows in us endure.
misreadings: Not 'nothing in your life matters' (our misuse note is right); it names what lasts.
Not a denial that suffering is real to the sufferer.
cautions: 'The world is a dream' can feel dismissive to someone in grief or pain.
not_for: fresh grief
someone in acute distress whose pain should be taken seriously
speaks_to: perspective when caught up in worldly worries

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 39, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 39.5-6). NOT 3.35: our id and label are off by four.
data_flags.translation_note: Incomplete. Our text has two lines, but the translation renders only the first. The second line ('puni prabhu gae sarobar tira, pampa nama subhaga gambhira') says: then the Lord went to the shore of the lake called Pampa, lovely and deep. It starts the next...

rcm.3.38.chaupai.2.context: After Ram's lament by Pampa, Narada comes, praises him, and asks for one boon though Ram already knows his heart. Ram answers with this assurance. Narada asks that the name 'Ram' be greater than all the Lord's other names; Ram grants it. Then, seeing Ram pleased, Narada asks why Ram stopped his marriage long ago.
rcm.3.38.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Ram tells Narada there is nothing he withholds from his own; Narada should never lose that trust, even if a past request seemed refused.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 1-2)
commentaries.gist: Ram states his own nature, as he does to Vibhishana in Sundar Kand: he keeps no veil between himself and his devotee; all he has is theirs.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 3-4), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Nothing is dear to Ram except his devotee. 'Never lose this trust' is said for a reason: Narada's earlier request in the Bal Kand was not granted, so his faith could waver.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Narada had also asked 'do what is good for me'; Ram did that instead of the literal request, which is why it seemed refused.

rcm.3.38.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it for trust after an apparent 'no': a loving parent or God may withhold the thing asked for while giving what is really good.
misreadings: Not a promise that every request will be granted literally; the very next scene explains a refusal.
not_for: someone in grief over an unanswered prayer, if read as 'you will get anything'

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 42, chaupais 2-3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 42.3-6). NOT 3.38: our id and label are off by four, and our text runs two chaupais.

rcm.3.39.chaupai.2.context: Narada asks why, when Ram's maya had deluded him, Ram did not let him marry (the Bal Kand story of Vishvamohini, where Narada was given a monkey's face and cursed Vishnu). Ram explains he guards those who rely on him alone as a mother guards a toddler. He goes on to contrast the wise (grown sons) with humble devotees (little children), and the doha calls desire, anger and the like the army of delusion.
rcm.3.39.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Ram stops what his devotee wants when it would harm him, as a mother pulls her toddler away from fire or a snake. The refusal is protection, not rejection.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (meaning and notes)
commentaries.gist: Those who rely on Ram alone are guarded as a mother guards a small child: the moment it runs for fire or a snake, she snatches it away.

commentaries.who: Dinji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Prefers the reading 'bichchhu' (scorpion): first the general claim, then the example of a child grabbing a scorpion, fire or snake.

commentaries.who: Nange Paramhans ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Also defends 'scorpion' from manuscript copies: scorpions are commoner in homes than snakes, as greed besets devotees more than lust or anger, and the Lord guards against it too.

rcm.3.39.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it to reframe a painful 'no' from life or God as possible protection, and to describe how good parents say no.
misreadings: Not a promise that nothing painful will happen (our misuse note is right).
Not a reason to stay passive or refuse medical, legal or emotional help.
cautions: Telling someone their loss was 'for their protection' can wound; use only for a reader reflecting on their own past.
not_for: fresh loss or bereavement
abuse or harm, where 'it was for your good' is dangerous
speaks_to: a relationship that didn't work out, seen in hindsight

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 43, chaupais 2-3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 43.3-6). NOT 3.39: our id and label are off by four, and our text runs two chaupais.

rcm.3.39.chaupai.4.context: Continuing his answer to Narada, Ram compares the wise man (jnani) to a grown son and the humble servant to a small child: a mother still loves the grown son but no longer watches over him as before. The servant leans on Ram's strength, the jnani on his own, and both face desire and anger. So the wise keep devotion even after knowledge. The doha that follows names desire, anger, greed and pride as delusion's army.
rcm.3.39.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Self-reliant wisdom leaves a person to fight desire and anger alone, while humble dependence on God brings his protection; so the wise keep devotion even after attaining knowledge.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Both the child and the servant are free of pride, and pride ruins both: it destroys the jnani's knowledge and the devotee's devotion.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 2), in Manas Piyush, citing Gita 3.37
commentaries.gist: Desire and anger are the enemy. Ram protected Narada from both, then let him fall to them when pride sprouted, to uproot the pride.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush, citing Gita 7.14 and 18.66
commentaries.gist: Maya is hard to cross except by taking refuge in the Lord; it lays many traps for the jnani, while the humble devotee is guarded.

rcm.3.39.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that maturity and knowledge are good, but staying humble and connected protects us better than self-reliance alone.
misreadings: Not anti-intellectual: it asks the learned to keep humility, not to stop learning.
not_for: someone who needs encouragement to become more independent
speaks_to: successful, self-reliant people feeling spiritually alone

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 43, chaupais 4-5 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 43.7-10). NOT 3.39: our id and label are off by four, and our text runs two chaupais.

rcm.3.42.chaupai.1.context: After explaining why he stopped Narada's marriage, Ram is asked by Narada to describe the qualities of saints. Ram lists them over several lines: these come first, followed by japa, austerity and restraint, faith, forgiveness, friendliness, compassion, gladness, dispassion, discernment, humility, no hypocrisy or pride, love of his stories, and selfless service. He ends that not even Saraswati and the Vedas can tell them all. Narada departs, and the Aranya Kand closes.
rcm.3.42.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Good people are embarrassed by praise of themselves and delighted by praise of others; they stay even and calm, keep to what is right, and are simple and kind with everyone.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Their praise is true, yet they shrink from it; the more they hear of others' virtues, the gladder they are. 'Even' toward friend and foe; 'cool' means harsh words from the wicked don't heat them.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Maps the list onto the four attitudes (friendliness, compassion, gladness, equanimity). Gladness at others' virtues is how one treats equals, which prevents envy and rivalry. Saints, unlike seekers, don't even practise indifference toward the wicked.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Never leave right conduct' however things go; compares Lanka Kand, where a saint keeps to what is right despite a million obstacles.

rcm.3.42.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a simple character checklist: deflect praise, celebrate others, keep your temper, stay honest and kind.
misreadings: Not a call for false modesty or refusing all recognition.
not_for: someone with very low self-esteem who already can't accept any praise

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 46, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 46.1-2). NOT 3.42: our id and label are off by four.

rcm.3.7.chaupai.3.context: Sutikshna, a disciple of Agastya devoted to Ram in thought, word and deed, hears that Ram is coming and runs out. On the way he wonders whether the friend of the lowly will really show grace to someone as worthless as himself, listing all he lacks; then he remembers Ram's one habit, that whoever has no other refuge is dear to him, and rejoices that his eyes will see Ram today. Lost in love he forgets the way, dances and turns back; Ram watches hidden behind a tree, then wakes him and embraces him.
rcm.3.7.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Grace does not depend on our qualifications: the one who has nowhere else to go is the one God loves.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Pandit Ramkumar
commentaries.gist: 'One habit' shows that meeting Ram is caused by his compassion, not by spiritual practices; Sutikshna relies not on any practice but on having no other support, as Atri and Sharabhanga also confessed lacking all means.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Pa. Pa. Pra. (Swami Prajnananand)
commentaries.gist: Taking two sayings of Ram together, concludes that 'having no other refuge' is itself a complete form of devotion needing no other means: very simple, yet very hard to attain.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Vijayanand Tripathi
commentaries.gist: The grace Sutikshna hopes for is to be embraced as Ram's own servant, and the 'own servant' is defined as one who has no other hope.

rcm.3.7.chaupai.3.practical_reading: When you feel you have nothing to show, the verse says that very emptiness, honestly owned, is enough to be loved.
misreadings: Not 'effort and practice don't matter'; Sutikshna is described as devoted in thought, word and deed.
Grace does not erase responsibility.
cautions: Strongly devotional; frame for non-devotional readers as being accepted without having to earn it.
not_for: someone who uses self-deprecation to avoid change

rcm.3.7.chaupai.7.context: The sage Sutikshna, hearing that Ram is coming, runs to meet him, lost in love: he forgets direction and who he is, goes forward and back, sings and dances. Ram hides behind a tree to watch. Seeing such love Ram appears inside his heart, and the sage sits motionless in the path, hair on end. Then Ram comes near and tries to wake him.
rcm.3.7.chaupai.7.core_teaching: Ram is moved by love so complete that he first watches unseen and then reveals himself within the devotee's heart, before meeting him outwardly.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He hides so as not to break the spell; if the sage saw him he would stop dancing. Notes Ram hides three times in the Manas: behind a vine, a tree and a bush.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji, with Prajnananand Saraswati, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Like a father secretly watching his child play; but a mother cannot watch such a child for long, so his tenderness overflowed and he appeared in the sage's heart.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, citing Bhagavata 7.7 and 11.14.24
commentaries.gist: Laughing, weeping, singing and dancing without shame are marks of the highest devotee, who purifies the world.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note on the ten states of love)
commentaries.gist: Sutikshna passes through nine of the classic ten states of love, from longing to stupor; Ram hides partly so the shock of meeting does not push him to the tenth.

rcm.3.7.chaupai.7.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that being lost in love or joy, even looking foolish, is not something to be ashamed of, and that sincere longing is itself seen and answered.
misreadings: Not a recommendation to lose touch with reality; it describes ecstatic devotion.
not_for: someone whose emotional overwhelm is distressing rather than joyful
speaks_to: longing to be seen by God or a loved one

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 10, chaupai 7 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 10.13-14). NOT 3.7: our id and label are off by three.

rcm.4.12.chaupai.2.context: Bali has died at Ram's hand after a dialogue in which he accepted Ram. His wife Tara arrives weeping over the body. Ram gives her knowledge; she asks for devotion. After this, Ram has Sugriva perform the funeral rites and has him crowned.
rcm.4.12.chaupai.2.core_teaching: The body that lies here is the five elements; the self is eternal, so the one she loves is not destroyed. Knowledge given by grace removes the delusion, and devotion follows.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: Ram, compassionate, saw the woman's distress and gave knowledge because knowledge removes grief, as Vasishtha consoled Dasharath's queens. First knowledge, then delusion goes, then devotion arises.

commentaries.who: Swami Prajnananand, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Knowledge is given, not achieved by one's own effort. Tara was given knowledge, but not 'firm' knowledge as Dasharath was, which is why she later became Sugriva's wife.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's notes
commentaries.gist: 'Sleeps' echoes Tara's laments in Valmiki, where she begs Bali to rise and speak. Compares Gita 2.11 and 2.20, 2.28: the wise do not grieve for the living or the dead.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation
commentaries.gist: Renders it as the mortal frame sleeping before her while the soul is eternal, so why weep.

rcm.4.12.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Used in grief teaching as a later-stage consolation: the person you loved is more than the body you see. Read with care, it gives a frame for loss, not a rule against crying.
misreadings: Not a rebuke for grieving: Ram responds to Tara's distress with compassion.
Not a claim that the body or the person was worthless.
cautions: Tells a widow over her husband's body not to weep. Do not use early in grief.
'Very lowly body' can sound contemptuous of the dead or of one's own body.
Doctrine of the eternal self may feel dismissive to fresh grief.
not_for: fresh bereavement, especially early days
someone who needs permission to cry
body-image or self-harm contexts
speaks_to: grief after some time has passed
seeking a spiritual frame for death

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 11, chaupai lines 3-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 12: off by one. The text spans two chaupais.

rcm.4.15.chaupai.2.context: After Sugriva's coronation Ram spends the rains on Mount Pravarshan with Lakshman. Missing Sita, he describes the monsoon to Lakshman, pairing each sight with a moral simile. The autumn description follows.
rcm.4.15.chaupai.2.core_teaching: True learning makes a person humble, like clouds that hang low when full of rain. A good person absorbs harsh words without being shaken, as a hill takes the rain.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: Clouds give water as scholars give learning; only the wise bow on gaining learning, the unwise grow arrogant. Harsh words that are like thunderbolts to others are mere raindrops to a saint.

commentaries.who: Panjabiji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Empty clouds stay high; laden with water they come low.

commentaries.who: Swami Prajnananand, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Do not press the stone image too far: rain does soak into hills and feeds springs. The point of likeness is only the bearing.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: 'Bear' implies the saint could retaliate but chooses not to; the lesson is forbearance.

rcm.4.15.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to success and criticism: the more you learn or achieve, the more grounded you should become, and harsh words can be let to run off rather than sink in.
misreadings: Not an instruction to absorb abuse or stay in harmful situations.
Not a claim that good people feel nothing.
cautions: A reader being bullied may hear 'just bear it'; pair with the right to protect oneself.
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship or workplace
someone being harassed
speaks_to: staying humble after a promotion or degree

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 14, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 15: off by one.

rcm.4.15.chaupai.3.context: Part of Ram's monsoon description to Lakshman on Mount Pravarshan. It follows the clouds and hills, and is followed by the filling of lakes and the rivers reaching the sea.
rcm.4.15.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Small minds lose their bounds with small gains, as little streams flood and do damage. And pure water turns muddy on touching the earth, as the soul is clouded when caught in illusion.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: A small stream has no depth, so a little water makes it overflow, wreck homes and fields, and then dry up. So with the petty person: a little money and he cannot contain himself, causes trouble, and soon loses it.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's notes (Bhagavata and Vishnu Purana parallels)
commentaries.gist: Compares Bhagavata 10.20 (streams overflow as an unrestrained person's body and wealth go astray) and Vishnu Purana 5.6 (water leaves its course like the minds of the ill-mannered on getting new wealth).

commentaries.who: Swami Prajnananand, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Sees a pointed reference to Sugriva, who is about to forget Ram once he has his kingdom.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation
commentaries.gist: Renders it as rivulets rushing proudly like mean men puffed up with a little wealth, and water muddied like the soul environed by delusion.

rcm.4.15.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Used as a warning about sudden money or status: notice if a little success makes you careless with others; and as an image for how clear intentions get muddied by the world.
misreadings: Not a judgement on people with little money; the fault is the swagger, not the amount.
not_for: someone ashamed of their modest means
speaks_to: feeling one's ideals get muddied by daily life

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 14, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 15: off by one.

rcm.4.15.chaupai.4.context: Waiting out the rainy season with Lakshman on Mount Pravarshana, Ram reads every sight of the monsoon as a lesson. Just before, he compares muddy rainwater to the soul clouded by maya; here water gathering into ponds is like virtues coming to a good person, and river water reaching the ocean becomes still like a soul that has found Hari. The description continues into autumn.
rcm.4.15.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Good qualities collect in a good person gradually, the way water gathers into a pond; and the soul becomes still on reaching God as a river does in the sea.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Karunasindhuji
commentaries.gist: The rain falls drop by drop and the ponds fill; so a good person becomes an ocean of virtue by gathering one or two qualities at a time from others, like Dattatreya learning from twenty-four teachers.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Panjabiji
commentaries.gist: Wherever rain falls it collects in the pond, its proper vessel; so whoever speaks of a virtue, it goes to the good person who can hold it.

rcm.4.15.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Growth comes in small amounts that add up; you do not need to become good, or capable, all at once.
misreadings: Not 'virtue comes without any effort' as an excuse for inaction (one commentator stresses effortlessness; another stresses gathering).
Not a claim that people without visible virtues are bad.
cautions: Pandit Ramkumar's 'effortless' reading slightly cuts against using it to motivate effort; the 'drop by drop' reading (Karunasindhu) suits a can't-get-started plan better.
not_for: someone needing urgent decisive action

rcm.4.17.chaupai.2.context: The rains are over. Ram tells Lakshman how beautiful autumn is, again pairing each sight with a moral. These lines come right after the kasa grass flowering like old age.
rcm.4.17.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Contentment dries up greed as the autumn star dries the puddles on the roads. A heart without pride and delusion is clear like autumn lakes.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: Only the road water is said to dry completely; so contentment ends greed entirely. Road water is always dirty and keeps people off the road, as greed keeps people away from the greedy man.

commentaries.who: Swami Prajnananand, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Offers a second reading: greed dries up contentment. Until firm devotion comes, a little greed can destroy contentment, as with Sugriva, whose knowledge gave way to sense-greed through bad company.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: Rivers are like saints who wander and help many; lakes like saints who stay in one place. Autumn clearing the water is like a guru clearing the heart.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation
commentaries.gist: Renders it as the rising of Canopus drying the roads as greed is dried up by contentment.

rcm.4.17.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it for wanting less: contentment is not lack of ambition but the end of a restless craving, and with it the mind clears like water after rain.
misreadings: Not a call to give up all goals or accept injustice in the name of contentment.
not_for: someone in real material need, for whom 'be content' sounds dismissive
speaks_to: seeking a clear mind after a turbulent period

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 16, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 17: off by one.

rcm.4.17.chaupai.4.context: In Ram's autumn description, these lines come after the wagtails returning like good deeds in season. They are followed by the clear sky likened to a devotee who has given up all other hopes.
rcm.4.17.chaupai.4.core_teaching: An earth with neither mud nor dust is like the rule of a wise king. Fish panic as the water shrinks, like an unwise family man when his money runs out: the wise plan and work, the unwise only panic.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: 'Abudh' means one without the skill or learning to earn more; a capable person with a large family does not panic but works to support them. The ruler should be neither too hot nor too cold, but act by policy.

commentaries.who: Manas Mayank, quoted in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Builds a detailed parallel: many fish and little water like a big family and little money; clouds gone like income stopped; the fish cannot leave the water as the householder cannot leave home.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's notes
commentaries.gist: All old manuscripts read 'abudh'; some modern editors print 'bibidh'. Compares Bhagavata 10.20.38 on creatures in shallow water and the miserly poor householder.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation
commentaries.gist: Renders it as fish distressed like improvident men of family at the loss of money.

rcm.4.17.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Used as a nudge to prepare for lean seasons, and to respond to money trouble with planning rather than panic.
misreadings: Not a judgement on anyone who is poor or struggling.
Not a claim that worry about money is foolish; the contrast is between panic and wise effort.
cautions: 'Unwise' (abudh) carries a judgement; a reader in financial distress may feel blamed. Keep the focus on planning, not fault.
not_for: someone who has just lost a job or is in debt crisis
someone already ashamed about money

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 16, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 17: off by one.

rcm.4.21.chaupai.4.context: Settled into kingship, Sugriva forgets his promise to search for Sita. Ram, angry, sends Lakshman; Hanuman and Tara intervene. Sugriva comes out, falls at Lakshman's feet and confesses. After this, Hanuman reports the search parties already sent and they go to Ram.
rcm.4.21.chaupai.4.core_teaching: No intoxicant is like sense-pleasure: it can cloud even a sage's mind in a moment. Owning one's lapse humbly brings forgiveness.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: Other intoxicants bewilder the ignorant; sense-pleasure bewilders even the wise. Calling Lakshman 'Nath' means: you made me protected once by killing Bali, and now by your grace I am protected again after the senses nearly undid me.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki parallel)
commentaries.gist: In Valmiki 4.35 Tara makes the same plea, citing Vishvamitra, who spent ten years with the nymph Ghritachi and thought it a day.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Adhyatma Ramayana)
commentaries.gist: There Lakshman says his harsh words came from loving anger and asks Sugriva to forgive them; Vijayanand Tripathi expands Lakshman's reassurance.

rcm.4.21.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Used for owning up when comfort or distraction has made us forget a commitment: name the lapse, apologise without excuses, and get back to the task.
misreadings: Not an excuse ('even sages fall, so it's fine'); Sugriva uses it to confess, not to justify.
cautions: Could feed shame in someone struggling with addiction; pair with the forgiveness that follows.
not_for: someone in active addiction crisis who needs practical help, not a proverb
speaks_to: having let someone down through distraction or comfort

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 20, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 21: off by one. The text reads बिषय (our data has विषय, a spelling variant).

rcm.4.29.chaupai.2.context: The search party, despairing on the southern shore, has spoken of Jatayu's death. His elder brother, the vulture Sampati, hears it, performs his brother's rites, and tells his story: as young birds the two flew toward the sun. He then tells of the sage Chandrama, who foretold that he would help Ram's messengers.
rcm.4.29.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Sampati's own account: his brother turned back, but he in his pride flew on and was burned and fell. Pride is named as the cause of the fall.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: If he had turned back too, the brothers' strength would have been counted equal; he thought himself stronger, so he went on. The fruit of pride is suffering, and he got it.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Sampati tells this story to raise the monkeys' spirits, then tells the sage's prophecy to show he can point them to Sita.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: Compares Adhyatma Ramayana, where the brothers, proud of their strength, flew toward the sun to test it. Adds that by grace his body was not shattered, since it was needed for Ram's work later.

rcm.4.29.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Used as a cautionary tale about overreaching to prove oneself, and about the honesty of naming one's own pride.
misreadings: Not a lesson against ambition as such; the fault named is proud rivalry.
not_for: someone injured or disabled, who may hear it as 'you brought it on yourself'
speaks_to: learning from a fall caused by overconfidence

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 28, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 29: off by one.

rcm.4.30.chaupai.1.context: Sampati has told the monkeys that Lanka lies a hundred yojanas across the sea and that he can see Sita there. As he speaks, his burned wings grow back. He tells them whoever can cross the sea will do Ram's work, and urges courage. Then he leaves, and the monkeys debate who can leap.
rcm.4.30.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Only one with both strength and wisdom can do this task. Sampati's own renewed body is visible proof of what grace can do, so the monkeys should take heart.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: First Sampati told them all to do the Lord's work; now he says one of them must, the one who can leap the sea, and names who is fit. 'Look at me' shows that his wings regrew as he spoke.

commentaries.who: Panjabiji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: It is Ram's work: Ram himself will help and give the wit, so do not panic, just be ready to act.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki parallel)
commentaries.gist: In Valmiki 4.63 Sampati's wings sprout before the monkeys, and he says this is a sign that they will succeed.

rcm.4.30.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to discouragement: look at concrete examples of recovery, including your own, before deciding a task is impossible.
misreadings: Not a promise that a hard task will be easy; it calls for both strength and intelligence.
not_for: someone whose recovery has not come, who may feel the comparison as pressure
speaks_to: a team that has lost heart

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 29, chaupai lines 1-2 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 30: off by one.

rcm.4.30.chaupai.2.context: Right after showing his regrown wings, Sampati gives the monkeys a second argument for courage before he leaves. The monkeys then each state how far they can leap.
rcm.4.30.chaupai.2.core_teaching: If even sinners cross the endless ocean of existence by remembering Ram's name, his own messengers can surely cross a hundred-yojana sea. Drop the fear, keep Ram in mind, and find a way.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: After giving visible proof (his own body), Sampati gives scriptural proof. If sinners can cross the endless ocean of existence, what is a hundred yojanas to you?

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Adhyatma Ramayana)
commentaries.gist: Quotes the Adhyatma Ramayana parallel: those who remember Vishnu cross the ocean of samsara, so Ram's dear devotees can surely cross a mere sea.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Hanuman Bahuk)
commentaries.gist: Cites Tulsi's Hanuman Bahuk, where the monkeys are 'beaten' after looking at the ocean: their joy had gone and their courage failed.

rcm.4.30.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Used to turn fear into planning: hold on to what you trust, then 'make the effort' (karahu upai). Faith here is a reason to act, not to wait.
misreadings: Not a promise that faith removes the need for a plan; the verse ends with 'find a way'.
cautions: Calls fear 'cowardice'; a reader with anxiety may feel judged.
not_for: clinical anxiety or panic, where 'drop your fear' is not helpful on its own

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 29, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id and label say 4.30: off by one.

rcm.4.31.chaupai.3.context: The monkeys have each said how far they can leap; none can cross. Old Jambavant, king of the bears, turns to Hanuman, who has been sitting silent, and reminds him he is the wind's son, a treasury of wisdom. These lines are the climax; Hanuman then grows huge and asks what he should do. Sundar Kand follows.
rcm.4.31.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Being reminded of one's purpose restores forgotten strength. Hanuman grows the moment he hears that his life is for Ram's work.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: Jambavant speaks because he is the eldest and king of the bears, so only he could rouse Hanuman. He asks why the strong one sits silent while all others declare their strength.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Hanuman stayed silent so as not to take the honour of being Ram's envoy from anyone who wanted it; Jambavant understood and asked him to speak.

commentaries.who: Swami Prajnananand, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The silence was Ram's prompting: had Hanuman volunteered first, others could say they could have done it. A true worker does not insist that only he will do the job.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: Valmiki's Uttara Kanda tells of a curse that makes Hanuman forget his strength until reminded; Adhyatma Ramayana has Jambavant say Hanuman was born for Ram's work.

rcm.4.31.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers use it for self-doubt: sometimes we need someone to remind us what we are capable of and what we are here for, and we can be that voice for others.
misreadings: Not a claim that anyone can do anything; it is about a specific gift and purpose being recalled.
not_for: someone told 'you can do anything' while facing real limits, e.g. illness

rcm.4.4.chaupai.1.context: Sugriva, hiding on Rishyamuk hill, sends Hanuman disguised as a brahmin to find out who the two armed strangers are. Ram introduces himself. Hanuman recognises his Lord, falls at his feet, and says he failed to know him because he is deluded like any creature, then asks why Ram too forgot him. This line follows; he then says he knows no method of worship and relies on Ram like a child on its mother, and falls at Ram's feet in his own form.
rcm.4.4.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Hanuman admits many faults but asks not to be forgotten, since every being is bewildered by the Lord's power of illusion and can be freed only by his kindness.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 1)
commentaries.gist: Ordinary masters drop a servant on seeing faults; Ram is said never to count his people's faults, so he should not forget Hanuman either.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (on 'jiva'), citing the arthapanchaka
commentaries.gist: Hanuman's prayer contains the five things a seeker must know: the self (deluded by maya), the Lord, the obstacle (maya), the means (reliance on him), and the goal.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi (Vi. Tri.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He reasons: freedom comes only from your tenderness, and you seem to have forgotten me, and I have no practice of my own; this leaves him overwhelmed at Ram's feet.

rcm.4.4.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that faults don't disqualify us from being loved, and that asking not to be forgotten is a valid prayer.
misreadings: Not a call to dwell on one's faults; the weight falls on the Lord's tenderness.
not_for: someone who needs to hear about their strengths, not their faults
speaks_to: feeling forgotten by God or a mentor

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand 3, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 3.1-2). NOT 4.4: our id and label are off by one (one too high).

rcm.4.4.chaupai.2.context: Sugriva, hiding on Rishyamuk hill, sends Hanuman disguised as a brahmin to find out who the two armed strangers are. Ram introduces himself. Hanuman recognises his Lord, falls at his feet, and says he failed to know him because he is deluded like any creature, then asks why Ram too forgot him. Having asked not to be forgotten, he now confesses he knows no method of worship and states the principle of reliance.
rcm.4.4.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Hanuman claims no spiritual technique, only reliance: as a servant trusts his master and a child its mother and so stays free of worry, the Lord is bound to care for one who depends on him.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: There are two ways a deluded soul crosses maya: by the Lord's tenderness or by practice. Hanuman disclaims practice, so it must be grace. Escape from maya is achieved by grace, not effort.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush, citing Gita 9.22
commentaries.gist: 'Stays free of worry' means the dependent makes no plans for his own welfare; the Lord carries it, as Gita 9.22 promises.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: This is 'karpanya' surrender: the greatest devotee calling himself ignorant. Lessons: drop pride in one's own practices, and even stop worrying how or when one will be saved.

rcm.4.4.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it to relieve the pressure to 'do spirituality right': trust, like a child's trust in a parent, matters more than technique.
misreadings: Not a reason to stop acting or stay in harm's way (our misuse note is right).
Not an argument against practice; Hanuman is humble about his, not idle.
cautions: Someone who had unreliable parents may not find the child-mother image comforting.
not_for: someone who was let down by a parent or carer
speaks_to: anxiety about doing spiritual practice correctly

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand 3, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 3.3-4). NOT 4.4: our id and label are off by one.

rcm.4.4.chaupai.3.context: Sugriva, hiding on Rishyamuk hill, sends Hanuman disguised as a brahmin to find out who the two armed strangers are. Ram introduces himself. Hanuman recognises his Lord, falls at his feet, and says he failed to know him because he is deluded like any creature, then asks why Ram too forgot him. Here, having spoken, he falls at Ram's feet in his true form; Ram lifts and embraces him and then tells him not to feel small.
rcm.4.4.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Once Hanuman drops his disguise and stands in his own form, Ram embraces him and soothes him with his own tears.

commentaries.who: Manas Mayank (Ma. Ma.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He was distressed because Ram said nothing while he spoke. Ram would not accept anyone who came with a disguise; when love filled his heart the pretence fell away and Ram embraced him.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi (Vi. Tri.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Love cannot bear separation or concealment, so the true form appeared by itself once love filled him, as a disguised spy's real form appeared when he praised Ram.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram did not embrace him at the first fall but only after he dropped the brahmin guise: Ram doesn't like pretence. Ram's tears of love cooled the burning in Hanuman's heart.

rcm.4.4.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that being accepted comes after we stop pretending: show up as you are.
not_for: someone who is unsafe being open about who they are
speaks_to: being afraid to be seen as you are

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand 3, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 3.5-6). NOT 4.4: our id and label are off by one.

rcm.4.4.chaupai.4.context: Sugriva, hiding on Rishyamuk hill, sends Hanuman disguised as a brahmin to find out who the two armed strangers are. Ram introduces himself. Hanuman recognises his Lord, falls at his feet, and says he failed to know him because he is deluded like any creature, then asks why Ram too forgot him. Ram has just lifted him and held him; now he reassures him. The doha that follows defines the 'ananya' devotee: one who sees himself as servant and the whole world as the Lord's form.
rcm.4.4.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Ram tells the ashamed Hanuman not to feel small: he is twice as dear as Lakshman. Ram is called impartial, but the servant with no other refuge is especially dear.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram's tears cooled Hanuman's anguish at thinking himself forgotten. Prajnananand reads the anguish as remorse for having approached Ram in disguise.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1c), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram uses the intimate singular 'tu' when most pleased with child-like servants, as he does with others he favours.

rcm.4.4.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it to lift shame: the one who feels most unworthy is told they are deeply valued. It also squares fairness with special love.
misreadings: Not a ranking that disparages Lakshman; it is said to lift Hanuman's shame.
not_for: someone hurt by favouritism
speaks_to: feeling less loved than a sibling or colleague

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand 3, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 3.7-8). NOT 4.4: our id and label are off by one.

rcm.4.6.chaupai.4.context: After Ram and Sugriva swear friendship by fire, Sugriva says he once saw a woman being carried off crying 'Ram!', and shows the cloth she dropped. Ram clasps it to his chest and weeps. Sugriva tells him to set aside grief and promises to serve in every way until Sita is found. Ram then asks Sugriva why he lives in the forest, and hears about Bali.
rcm.4.6.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Sugriva, himself exiled and separated from his wife, steadies the grieving Ram and pledges practical help. Comfort comes with a promise of action.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note 1), citing Valmiki 4.7.5-13
commentaries.gist: Valmiki's Sugriva says much the same at length: give up despair, remember your own steadiness; I too grieve for my wife but have not lost my composure; those ruled by grief find no happiness.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Raghubir' reminds Ram he is a hero; grief undermines courage, so first let go of grief, then steadiness can come.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 2), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He says 'serve', not 'help', because he sees himself as servant. He forgets his own sorrow to comfort Ram, as Ram will forget his own to ask about Sugriva's.

rcm.4.6.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it for being a friend in grief: name the pain, then offer specific help rather than only words.
misreadings: 'Give up grief' here comes with a promise of help; it is not a demand to stop feeling.
cautions: Telling a grieving person to 'stop grieving' can hurt if not followed by real help.
not_for: fresh bereavement, if 'give up grief' is read alone
speaks_to: mutual help between people who are both hurting

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand 5, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 5.7-8). NOT 4.6: our id and label are off by one.

rcm.4.8.chaupai.1.context: Sugriva has told how his brother Bali drove him out and took his wife. Ram vows to kill Bali with one arrow. Then he sets out the duty of a friend: these lines, then steering a friend from wrong to right, revealing their virtues and hiding their faults, giving without hesitation, loving a hundredfold in hard times, and abandoning a friend who flatters to your face and harms behind your back.
rcm.4.8.chaupai.1.core_teaching: A true friend feels a friend's pain as their own, and treats their own huge troubles as small next to a friend's small ones. Ram then acts on this for Sugriva.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1), in Manas Piyush, citing Yajnavalkya Smriti
commentaries.gist: Those not pained by a friend's pain are great sinners, and association with great sinners makes one a sinner too, so one shouldn't even look at them.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 2), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Until you see your own sorrow as dust you won't feel a friend's as heavy or work to remove it. Ram is the example: exiled and bereft of Sita, he set that aside for Sugriva's trouble.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (meaning of 7.3-9)
commentaries.gist: Those without this natural feeling should not force a friendship; a good friend turns you from wrong ways, shows your virtues and hides your faults, and loves a hundredfold in adversity.

rcm.4.8.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Widely quoted on friendship: be moved by a friend's trouble, put your own in proportion, and show up when it matters.
misreadings: Not a demand to ignore your own suffering; it is about not letting it make you blind to a friend's.
Not a license to condemn people who couldn't help.
cautions: A carer already overwhelmed may hear 'your own pain is dust' as dismissal of their needs.
not_for: someone burned out from caring for others
someone whose friends abandoned them (could sting)
speaks_to: reflecting on who showed up for you

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand 7, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 7.1-2). NOT 4.8: our id and label are off by one.
data_flags.translation_note: First line misstated. 'Tinhahi bilokat pataka bhari' is literally 'just looking at them is a great sin'; Pt. Ramkumar explains it as contact with a great sinner. Our 'commit a grave wrong just by being seen' reverses the sense: it is the one who looks...

rcm.4.8.chaupai.10.context: Ram has just shown his strength by tossing Dundubhi's bones and piercing seven palm trees. Sugriva, overwhelmed, speaks words of knowledge and detachment: friends and enemies, joy and sorrow are made of maya, and he asks only to worship Ram day and night. Ram smiles and says Sugriva's words are true, but his own promise will not fail: Bali will be killed.
rcm.4.8.chaupai.10.core_teaching: In a moment of insight, Sugriva sees that even his brother's hostility led him to Ram, so Bali has done him the greatest good, and the feud now seems like a dream fight one is embarrassed about on waking.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: Worldly help is 'hit'; leading someone to God is 'param hit'. Anger that brings you to God is grace. Sugriva means: Ram need not kill Bali now; he would be ashamed to fight him even in a dream.

commentaries.who: Lala Bhagwandin (Deenji), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Reads it as: the fight with Bali was dreamlike, and Sugriva is now embarrassed, seeing that Bali did him no harm but the greatest good.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation
commentaries.gist: Takes the second line as a simile: like a man who dreams he has been fighting and is ashamed of the illusion on waking.

rcm.4.8.chaupai.10.practical_reading: Teachers draw from it that a painful conflict can, in hindsight, be what brought you to something good, and that grudges can look like bad dreams once the mind clears.
misreadings: Not proof that the wrong done to Sugriva was not wrong; Ram still acts on it.
Not a demand that a victim call their wrongdoer a benefactor.
cautions: The story continues to Bali's killing; the insight is not where the episode ends.

Our note says the tradition reads this as kshanik (passing) vairagya. The Manas Piyush pages I read treat the knowledge and detachment as genuine and explain the smile as Ram's maya and his kept promise; I could not source the 'passing' label.
not_for: someone recently hurt by a family member, who may hear it as 'thank your abuser'
speaks_to: a long feud with a sibling or relative
gratitude for an unexpected turn in life

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 7, chaupai lines 19-20 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 8: off by one.

rcm.4.8.chaupai.2.context: Ram and Sugriva have just sworn friendship before fire. Ram first says that a person who is not pained by a friend's pain is a great sinner, and that a true friend sees his own mountain of trouble as dust and a friend's speck as a mountain. This verse continues: people without that instinct should not force friendships; then it begins the list of what a friend does.
rcm.4.8.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Friendship is a disposition before it is a relationship: one who does not naturally feel a friend's pain should not press friendship. A real friend corrects the friend's direction and protects his reputation.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5 (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: A disposition learned from advice comes and goes; a natural one stays steady. Pressing friendship without it, against scripture's warning, is grave wrong. Turning a friend from the wrong road comes before setting him on the right one.

commentaries.who: Panjabiji, quoted in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: If a fault appears in a friend after friendship is made, do not drop him: show him the fear of this world and the next and steer him to the good path.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (parallel texts)
commentaries.gist: Sets these lines beside Bhartrihari's Niti-shataka verse on the marks of a good friend (restrains from wrong, hides secrets, shows virtues, stays in adversity) and Valmiki 4.8, where Sugriva describes friendship.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation (6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders the list as restraining from evil, directing to virtue, publishing the good and concealing the bad.

rcm.4.8.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it to ask what kind of friend one is: someone who quietly steers a friend away from a bad decision and speaks well of them in public, rather than flattering them or broadcasting their failings.
misreadings: Not a call to hide wrongdoing that harms others; the covering is of a friend's faults, not of harm.
Not a rule that one must never criticise a friend; correcting the course is the first duty named.
cautions: The opening line calls those without the instinct 'shatha' (fools, rogues); a writer should not turn that on a reader who struggles with friendship.
not_for: someone whose 'friend' is covering up abuse or crime
someone feeling lonely or friendless, who may hear the first line as blame
speaks_to: wanting to be a better friend
a friend who is drifting toward a bad choice

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 7, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush numbering). Our id says doha 8: off by one.

rcm.4.8.chaupai.3.context: Ram continues his description of a good friend to Sugriva, just after the fire-witnessed pact. After this he describes the false friend, then promises to do Sugriva's work with all his strength.
rcm.4.8.chaupai.3.core_teaching: A true friend shares without keeping accounts, helps to the full extent of his means, and loves most when things go wrong. Adversity is the test of friendship.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: No suspicion in giving and taking means the two friends' wealth becomes one. 'Giving' is named before 'taking' because a friend thinks first of giving. Helping less than one's strength allows is a kind of deceit.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's notes
commentaries.gist: Quotes the Mahabharata's five kinds of strength (arm, allies, wealth, lineage, intellect) to explain 'bal anuman'. Says adversity is where a friend is tested, comparing Anasuya's line that patience, dharma, friend and wife are tested in hard times.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki parallel)
commentaries.gist: Compares Valmiki 4.8, where Sugriva says friends do not divide their gold and ornaments and will give up wealth, comfort and country for each other.

rcm.4.8.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Used as a checklist for friendship: give freely, do what you actually can, and show up more, not less, when a friend is in trouble.
misreadings: Not a demand to give beyond one's means; the measure is one's own strength.
Not a reason to judge every friend who could not help in a crisis; it describes an ideal to practise.
not_for: someone being financially exploited by a 'friend' who invokes this ideal
speaks_to: feeling let down by fair-weather friends

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 7, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 8: off by one.

rcm.4.8.chaupai.4.context: Having listed a good friend's marks, Ram describes the false friend, then adds that a deceitful servant, a miserly king, a bad wife and a false friend are like a stake in the body. He then promises Sugriva his full help.
rcm.4.8.chaupai.4.core_teaching: A friend who is sweet to your face and works against you behind your back, with a crooked mind, should be left. Leaving is the only real protection.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 5
commentaries.gist: The false friend's deceit is in all three: mind (crookedness), speech (made-up sweet words) and action (harm behind). Since such a person will not change, leaving him is the only way to escape his harm.

commentaries.who: Swami Prajnananand, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: A snake's crooked path is visible, but the deceiver's crookedness is hidden, so he is more dangerous than a snake; like a snake's gait, it is his nature and will not be reformed by another's effort.

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation
commentaries.gist: Renders it as one who is fair to your face but an enemy behind your back, whose mind is as tortuous as a snake's.

rcm.4.8.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to two-faced relationships at work or in social circles: notice the gap between what someone says to you and what they do behind you, and distance yourself rather than trying to fix them.
misreadings: Not a licence to drop friends at the first hurt or rumour; it describes settled, deliberate double-dealing.
Not a reason to become suspicious of everyone who is kind.
cautions: May reinforce paranoia in someone already anxious about being betrayed.
not_for: someone with social anxiety who already assumes others are false
a conflict that is really a misunderstanding
speaks_to: discovering a friend has been talking behind your back
setting boundaries with a manipulative person
permission to let go of a toxic friendship

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand doha 7, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 8: off by one.
