rcm.5.1.doha.1.context: Hanuman has just leapt from the shore toward Lanka. The ocean, seeing he is Ram's envoy, tells the mountain Mainaka to rise and give him a rest. Hanuman touches it, bows and flies on. Next the gods send Surasa to test him.
rcm.5.1.doha.1.core_teaching: Hanuman honours the kind offer but will not rest before the task is done. Courtesy toward helpers and single-minded commitment go together.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Mainaka took human form and offered rest (as in Valmiki 5.1). Hanuman honoured it with a touch, and bowed because Mainaka is a god and his father's friend. The bow is also a farewell.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki and Ananda Ramayana)
commentaries.gist: In Valmiki Hanuman says he is pleased with the hospitality but has vowed not to stop on the way, and touches the mountain. In Ananda Ramayana Mainaka asks to be purified by his touch.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: The poet compresses the whole exchange into one doha to show Hanuman's speed: he is half-way across while Mainaka is still being told to rise.

rcm.5.1.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to focus: acknowledge and thank those who offer comfort, but finish what matters before you rest.
misreadings: Not a rule against rest or self-care; it is about not stopping mid-task when something urgent depends on you.
Not a model for refusing all help.
cautions: Could feed burnout or guilt about resting in someone already overworking.
not_for: someone exhausted or burnt out who needs permission to stop
speaks_to: staying focused on an important commitment
distractions on the way to a goal

rcm.5.1.shloka.2.context: Each kand of the Manas opens with Sanskrit invocation verses. This is the second of three at the start of Sundar Kand, between a praise of Ram and the famous verse to Hanuman. It is often recited on its own.
rcm.5.1.shloka.2.core_teaching: A prayer from someone who wants nothing but devotion: since Ram knows every heart, the claim can be checked. It asks for two things: full devotion, and a mind kept clean of desire and the other inner enemies.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: 'No other longing' means not wanting powers, wealth, dharma, pleasure or even liberation. Desire is named first because it is the chief obstacle to devotion.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: 'Nirbhara' has two senses: full and unwavering, and the devotion in which one hands over the whole burden of life to Ram and is free of care. Both apply.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: The second line asks for both gaining (devotion) and keeping (protection from desire and the rest), since even a devotee's clear mind can be muddied, as Narada's was.

rcm.5.1.shloka.2.practical_reading: Recited daily as a centring prayer: say honestly what you want most, and ask for help keeping the mind free of what pulls it away.
misreadings: Not a claim that the speaker has no desires at all; it asks for help with them.
not_for: readers who are not religious, unless framed as an intention
speaks_to: wanting a simpler, more focused inner life

rcm.5.12.chaupai.1.context: Hanuman has dropped Ram's ring before Sita in the Ashok grove, told Ram's story and identified himself as Ram's messenger. Sita, convinced, is moved. After this she asks after Ram and Lakshman and whether Ram remembers her.
rcm.5.12.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Sita, drowning in the sea of separation, finds in Hanuman a ship. Knowing he belongs to Ram, her love for him overflows.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Seeing a devotee makes love rise by itself. Her love had begun when he told Ram's story, held back by doubt; now, sure, it overflowed in tears and thrill.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki parallel)
commentaries.gist: Valmiki 5.34-35: Sita says love for him arose in her mind on seeing him, and she sheds tears of joy on knowing him as Ram's envoy.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush textual note
commentaries.gist: Several manuscripts read बाढ़ी (grew); Bhagavatdas's reads गाढ़ी (deep). Our text uses गाढ़ी.

rcm.5.12.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Used for the moment help arrives in isolation: one messenger, call or friend can be the boat in a sea of loneliness.
misreadings: Not a suggestion that one person can or should carry all of someone's loneliness.
speaks_to: loneliness or separation from a loved one
the relief of a message from someone far away

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 14, chaupai lines 1-2 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 12: off by two.

rcm.5.12.chaupai.5.context: Sita has asked whether Ram ever remembers her and cried that he has forgotten her completely; she is near collapse. Hanuman answers gently. After this he gives Ram's own message about his love.
rcm.5.12.chaupai.5.core_teaching: Sita fears she has been forgotten. Hanuman tells her the opposite: Ram suffers with her, and his love for her is twice hers for him.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: This answers her cry that Ram had forgotten her, just as Ram told Hanuman not to feel slighted when Hanuman thought he had been forgotten: 'you are twice as dear as Lakshman'.

commentaries.who: Swami Prajnananand, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Mother' opens the line because Hanuman, seeing her state, is himself overcome and can only say 'mother' before going on.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Gitavali)
commentaries.gist: In Gitavali Hanuman asks why she speaks so pitifully: Ram's body has grown thin but his heart has grown full of love.

rcm.5.12.chaupai.5.practical_reading: Used for anyone who feels forgotten by someone they love who is far away: the absence may hide a love as great as theirs.
misreadings: Not a promise that every absent person secretly loves you more.
cautions: Could comfort someone falsely about an estranged or abusive partner; frame it as about Ram, not about every relationship.
not_for: someone who has actually been abandoned or rejected

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 14, chaupai lines 9-10 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 12: off by two.

rcm.5.13.chaupai.3.context: Hanuman has dropped Ram's ring to Sita in the Ashoka grove and told her Ram's story. He now gives Ram's message: since their separation everything that once gave joy (moon, breeze, flowers, rain) has turned painful. Speaking would lighten the pain a little, but there is no one who knows it; only Ram's own mind knows the truth of their love, and that mind always stays with her. Sita weeps; Hanuman asks her to hold on, saying Ram's arrows will burn the demons like moths in fire.
rcm.5.13.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Speaking of pain lightens it a little, but some grief is so private that no one else can share it; the heart alone knows the love it misses.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, note on Sundar 15.5
commentaries.gist: Glosses: telling does ease grief, but whom can I tell when no one knows this pain? Only one who understands the pain can be told; so it stays inside, burning.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, further note on 15.5
commentaries.gist: Suggests the hidden sense that Lakshman is with Ram, yet these words are not fit to say to him; and notes the source in the Prasanna Raghava drama.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Pandit Ramkumar
commentaries.gist: Reads the message as a triad: Ram bears the pain in body, says nothing to anyone in speech, and keeps his mind with Sita; 'a little' because only reunion removes the whole pain.

rcm.5.13.chaupai.3.practical_reading: It validates the loneliness of grief: telling helps, but it is hard when no one seems to understand; that is a reason to find the one person who might.
misreadings: Not a claim that talking does not help; the line says it does, a little.
cautions: In the original it is a lover's message; for a breakup or bereavement, keep focus on the loneliness, not on certainty of reunion.
not_for: someone isolated who needs to be encouraged to reach out rather than told no one understands

rcm.5.13.chaupai.4.context: Hanuman delivers Ram's message to Sita: since parting, everything has turned against him; the moon burns like the sun, the cool breeze like a serpent's breath; only his mind knows the truth of their love. This verse ends the message. Then Sita is lost in love and Hanuman urges her to take heart.
rcm.5.13.chaupai.4.core_teaching: The essence of Ram's love is simply this: his mind is always with her. Hearing it, Sita forgets herself in love.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Answers her question whether Ram ever remembers her: his mind lives with her always. Ram suffers in body, says little in words, and his mind stays with her: that is the whole message.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: The constant, undistracted dwelling of the mind on the beloved is the key to 'priti-ras'; lover and beloved appear as two bodies but are one.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: 'Vaidehi' (bodiless) is chosen because she forgets her body on hearing it.

rcm.5.13.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Used to express love across distance: what matters is where the heart stays, not physical presence.
misreadings: Not an argument that physical presence does not matter.
not_for: someone grieving a death, where 'my mind is always with you' may land differently
speaks_to: separation from a spouse or partner

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 15, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 13: off by two.

rcm.5.13.chaupai.5.context: Sita is lost in love after hearing Ram's message. Hanuman steadies her. He goes on to say Ram's arrows will burn the demons like cotton, and that Ram would have come already had he known where she was.
rcm.5.13.chaupai.5.core_teaching: In hardship, steadiness comes first. Recall the one you trust and what he can do, and let fear go.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Patience in calamity is the main thing, so Hanuman tells her four times to hold steady: to hear the message, to remember Ram, for the demons' death, and for Ram's coming.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: Hanuman uses 'mata' when she is overwhelmed and 'janani' when she is composed; the tender word is chosen to bring her back.

rcm.5.13.chaupai.5.practical_reading: Used as a steadying word for someone frightened: breathe, recall what you can rely on, then face the fear.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of fear as weakness.
cautions: 'Give up faint-heartedness' can sound like blame to someone with anxiety.
not_for: clinical anxiety where 'stop being afraid' is unhelpful
speaks_to: fear while waiting for rescue or news

rcm.5.14.doha.1.context: Sita doubts that small monkeys can beat Ravana's mighty demons. Hanuman shows his huge golden form, then becomes small again and says this. Sita is reassured and blesses him.
rcm.5.14.doha.1.core_teaching: Hanuman credits nothing to himself: monkeys have no special strength or wit, but with the Lord's power behind them the smallest can overcome the greatest.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: The huge form and the wise words he just showed are not monkey qualities; they are Ram's power. Ram's power can make the tiny snake eat Garuda, as the monkeys, demons' food, will eat the demons.

commentaries.who: Shyamsundar Das, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Cites a Puranic tale of a snake that took refuge in Vishnu and was empowered to turn on Garuda.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: Compares Hanuman's later answer to Ram (doha 33): by your power, cotton can burn the submarine fire.

rcm.5.14.doha.1.practical_reading: Used against feeling outmatched: what you lack in size or skill, the strength of your cause and those behind you can supply.
misreadings: Not a denial of one's own effort or ability.
speaks_to: feeling small against a powerful opponent
a small team taking on a big task

rcm.5.2.chaupai.5.context: The gods send Surasa, mother of serpents, to test Hanuman's strength and wit. She blocks his path and says she will eat him. He asks to go first and return after his work; she refuses. Next he slips in and out of her mouth, bows and asks leave, and she blesses him.
rcm.5.2.chaupai.5.core_teaching: Hanuman meets force with force, but when force cannot win he becomes tiny and passes through. Knowing when to grow and when to shrink is the wisdom the gods wanted to test.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Surasa grew her mouth without pattern; Hanuman always showed exactly double, only to show her, not to harm her. When she reached her limit he went to the limit of smallness.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: This is a test of divine powers; both show their siddhi of greatness. 'As ... so' covers the three rounds of the contest.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: Her mouth reaching a hundred yojanas, the width of the sea, filled his whole path; the smallest form is the answer to the largest threat.

rcm.5.2.chaupai.5.practical_reading: Used to teach flexibility: some obstacles are overcome by matching strength, others by humility and quick wit.
misreadings: Not a lesson in shrinking oneself to avoid all conflict; it is about choosing the right response.
speaks_to: facing an obstacle that keeps growing
negotiation and knowing when to yield

rcm.5.20.doha.1.context: Hanuman, bound by Meghnad's Brahma-weapon, stands before Ravana. He has told Ravana who he is and why he fought. Now he counsels him: give up enmity, return Sita, and take refuge. After this he urges Ravana to rule Lanka with Ram in his heart and not stain Pulastya's line. Ravana mocks him and orders his tail burned.
rcm.5.20.doha.1.core_teaching: Even to his captor, Hanuman holds the door open: Ram protects whoever bows, and if Ravana seeks refuge, his offence will be forgotten.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Three epithets: he protects the humble (rajas), is compassionate (sattva), and kills the wicked like Khara (tamas). Ravana's offence is not forgivable, yet the Lord forgets it entirely.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: 'Pranat' shows even a bow is enough; 'Kharari' reminds Ravana that only God could have killed Khara, so there is no shame in surrender, and that the alternative is death.

rcm.5.20.doha.1.practical_reading: Used to say that it is never too late to turn around: even after great wrong, an honest turn can be met with mercy.
misreadings: Not a claim that consequences vanish; Ravana's offence is forgiven only if he turns, and he does not.
Not a teaching that victims must forgive.
cautions: Ravana refuses; the story continues to his death.
not_for: someone harmed by another, who may hear it as pressure to forgive the harmer
speaks_to: feeling it is too late to change

rcm.5.21.chaupai.3.context: Continuing his counsel to Ravana in court, Hanuman has just said that speech without Ram's name has no beauty, like a fully ornamented woman without clothes. This verse follows. Next he says a man who turns from Ram finds no protection anywhere.
rcm.5.21.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Wealth and power without a deeper root are like rivers fed only by rain: they swell for a season and then dry up.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Reads the half-line in time: what one had, has and will get is all wasted. Or: what one has will go and be as if never had, like a rain-river that dries up as if water never flowed.

commentaries.who: Panjabiji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: What remains goes; what has been got is as good as not got. For the one turned from Ram, wealth is no means to the highest good.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: Lists several further readings and calls some 'mere wordplay'. Notes that wealth is Lakshmi's grace; it shines only when used for the Lord's work and good deeds.

rcm.5.21.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Used to ask what one's success is rooted in: achievements without values or purpose behind them do not last or satisfy.
misreadings: Not a claim that the wealthy are bad or that money is evil.
not_for: someone in poverty, where a sermon on wealth can sound beside the point

rcm.5.25.chaupai.2.context: After burning Lanka, Hanuman returns to Sita and asks for a token. She gives her hair-jewel (chudamani) and this message for Ram. Next she asks him to remind Ram of the crow incident and to come within a month, or she will not live.
rcm.5.25.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Sita appeals not to Ram's need of her (he needs nothing) but to his pledged nature: he is known as the friend of the helpless, so let him honour that and end her trouble.

commentaries.who: Panjabiji and Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Thus' suggests she showed the gesture of bowing, hands joined, so Hanuman could convey it exactly. 'You lack nothing' means: you value the feeling behind the offering.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: You gain nothing from me, but recall your pledged name. You are able; it is not right that I suffer while you have the power. 'My' goes with both 'lord' and 'trouble'.

rcm.5.25.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Used as a model of prayer or appeal in crisis: humble, direct, and resting on the known kindness of the one asked.
misreadings: Not a substitute for asking concrete help from people around you.
cautions: Part of a message that ends with a threat to her life if Ram is late; keep it separate in fragile contexts.
not_for: someone expecting prayer alone to solve an emergency
speaks_to: praying or asking for help in a crisis
sending a message to someone far away

rcm.5.28.doha.1.context: Hanuman has returned to Ram. Ram asks how Sita is and how she keeps herself alive. Hanuman says her eyes are full, her mind absorbed in Ram's feet, and gives this image. After it he delivers her message and the jewel.
rcm.5.28.doha.1.core_teaching: Sita lives because she guards herself: Ram's name stands watch day and night, remembering him is the closed door, and her lowered eyes are the lock. Life has no way out.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: She sits day and night head bowed, absorbed in meditation, constantly saying the name: with doors shut and chained and guards on watch, how could anyone leave?

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki parallel)
commentaries.gist: In Valmiki 5, Sita says she thinks of Ram constantly and says his name, so she sees and hears only him.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Gitavali)
commentaries.gist: Compares Gitavali 5.18-19, where Hanuman describes her eyes still as a painting and her tongue repeating the name, and Kausalya's similar lament in Gitavali 2.53.

rcm.5.28.doha.1.practical_reading: Used for how remembrance and routine can hold a person together through a long ordeal.
misreadings: Not a claim that devotion replaces help or rescue; Ram goes to rescue her.
cautions: Concerns whether someone will die; a reader with suicidal thoughts needs direct support, not only this image.
not_for: someone in acute crisis or with suicidal thoughts, without added support
speaks_to: holding on during captivity, illness or separation

rcm.5.3.doha.1.context: Entering Lanka at night in a tiny form, Hanuman is stopped by Lankini, guardian of the city. He knocks her down with a blow. She recalls Brahma's sign that when a monkey strikes her the demons' end is near, and counts herself lucky to have seen Ram's messenger. This doha is her praise of good company. She then blesses him to enter.
rcm.5.3.doha.1.core_teaching: Put the joys of heaven and of liberation together on one pan of a scale: they still do not weigh as much as one moment in the company of a saint.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: The scale is the intellect. Heaven stands for ritual action, liberation for knowledge, and satsang for devotion; satsang is both the first step of devotion and its fruit, so it outweighs both.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Bhagavata parallel)
commentaries.gist: The same idea is in Bhagavata 1.18.13, where the sages say they would not weigh heaven or liberation against a moment's company with those devoted to God.

commentaries.who: Panjabiji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The scale image makes it visible: the pan with heaven rises, the pan with satsang stays on the ground because it is heavier.

rcm.5.3.doha.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to value time with good people: a short conversation with someone wise and kind can do more than great achievements.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of other goals; it ranks them by what lasts.
not_for: someone isolated without access to such company, who may feel the lack sharply
speaks_to: finding a mentor or spiritual community
feeling that good company has changed you

rcm.5.30.chaupai.1.context: Hanuman has told Ram how Sita lives and given her message. Ram weeps. He asks how one who relies on him could meet such calamity. Hanuman answers in the next verse.
rcm.5.30.chaupai.1.core_teaching: God, the home of joy, weeps at his devotee's pain, and asks how one who depends on him wholly could be in such trouble.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: The Almighty grieved as if helpless; joy itself grieves at a devotee's pain. One devoted to Ram should not meet calamity: in waking there is none, in sleep nothing is known, and in dream one sees what one dwells on.

commentaries.who: Pandeji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Home of joy' fits: had Sita been happy without him he would have grieved; hearing her love, he is happy, and the tears are of feeling.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: Lists several readings of 'bujhia' (should one ask / could one know calamity even in a dream) from Ramkumar, Deenji and Shrikant Sharan; concludes it means 'should'.

rcm.5.30.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Used to show that the divine is moved by human suffering, and that a devotee's pain is never unseen.
misreadings: Not a promise that devotees never suffer; the next verse redefines what real calamity is.
cautions: Can imply that suffering means lack of faith; pair with the next verse and avoid for those in acute hardship.
not_for: someone whose suffering is ongoing and who may hear 'true devotees don't suffer'

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 32, chaupai lines 1-2 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 30: off by two.

rcm.5.30.chaupai.2.context: Ram has asked whether one wholly devoted to him could meet calamity. Hanuman answers, then assures him the demons are nothing to him. Ram then tells Hanuman he cannot repay him.
rcm.5.30.chaupai.2.core_teaching: The only real calamity is losing the remembrance of God. Outward trouble, like the demons, can be overcome.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Sita remembers with mind and speech; what she lacks is serving Ram in body, and that is her calamity. The demons stand in the way, so killing them ends it.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: Hanuman both affirms and resolves: remembrance is present, so there is no calamity; service is absent, and that will be fixed by victory.

rcm.5.30.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it to reframe hardship: outward trouble can be faced; the deeper loss is losing touch with what gives life meaning. Then act: Hanuman immediately turns to the plan.
misreadings: Not a denial that outward suffering is real; Hanuman still commits to rescuing Sita.
Not 'just pray and it will go away'.
cautions: Can minimise real suffering if quoted alone.
not_for: someone in acute suffering who needs it acknowledged first

rcm.5.31.chaupai.5.context: Ram asks how Hanuman burned Ravana's fortress. Hanuman, pleased and humble, says a monkey's only bravery is jumping from branch to branch; crossing the sea, burning the golden city, killing demons and wrecking the grove were all Ram's doing. The doha follows: nothing is beyond one whom Ram favours.
rcm.5.31.chaupai.5.core_teaching: Hanuman gives all credit for his feats to Ram's power.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: He confines his own effort to branch-jumping and credits the rest to Ram. He even lists the deeds out of order, burning first, which shows lack of pride (or simply answers Ram's question first).

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Hanuman Nataka and Kavitavali)
commentaries.gist: Hanuman Nataka says the sea was crossed by Ram's power and Lanka already burned by Sita's sighs and Ram's anger, the monkey only an occasion; Kavitavali 5.22 says the same.

commentaries.who: Manas Chandrika, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram's ring carried him over, Sita's jewel brought him back, and Lanka burned from her grief and Ram's glory.

rcm.5.31.chaupai.5.practical_reading: Used to model humility about success: give credit to the team, mentors or grace behind an achievement.
misreadings: Not a denial of one's own effort or a reason to refuse praise for real work.
cautions: For someone with low self-worth, may reinforce discounting their own achievements.
not_for: someone who habitually belittles their own achievements

rcm.5.32.chaupai.1.context: Ram has told Hanuman that no god, man or sage has helped him like this and he cannot repay him. Hanuman falls at his feet. Asked to name a gift, he asks only for devotion. Shiva, narrating to Parvati, then says whoever knows Ram's nature cannot care for anything but worship.
rcm.5.32.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Offered any reward, Hanuman asks only for unwavering devotion, and Ram grants it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Other good things give joy; devotion gives the highest joy. He asks now because Ram is pleased, and because a servant should not be 'repaid' as an equal; devotion keeps the Lord favourable always.

commentaries.who: Swami Prajnananand, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Ati sukh' is the joy beyond the senses that the Gita (6.21) calls grasped by the intellect alone.

rcm.5.32.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Used to ask what we really want when offered a reward: steady love for what matters rather than another prize.
misreadings: Not a rejection of all other goods.

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 34, chaupai lines 1-2 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 32: off by two.

rcm.5.35.doha.1.context: Ram's army has reached the shore. In Lanka, Mandodari pleads with Ravana; he laughs. His ministers flatter him that the monkeys are nothing. Tulsidas comments with this doha, then says this was exactly Ravana's case: his court sang his praise.
rcm.5.35.doha.1.core_teaching: When advisers, doctors and teachers say only what pleases, out of fear or hope of reward, the kingdom, the body and righteousness are soon ruined.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Hitopadesha parallel)
commentaries.gist: A Hitopadesha verse says the king whose doctor, guru and minister speak only pleasantly soon loses body, dharma and treasury. A doctor who gives the patient what he craves kills him; a guru who does not stop wrongdoing destroys both.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: The order here is deliberately crossed: Ravana's minister flatters, his doctor Sushen later saves Lakshman, and his 'guru' Shiva never stopped him from opposing Ram.

rcm.5.35.doha.1.practical_reading: Widely quoted for workplaces and families: seek and value people who tell you the truth, and be that person for others.
misreadings: Not licence for harshness; the fault is flattery from fear or self-interest, not kindness.

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 37 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 35: off by two. Dohavali 524 has the same doha with the order 'mantri, guru, vaid'.

rcm.5.36.chaupai.4.context: Vibhishan enters Ravana's court and, invited to speak, gives sober advice: for welfare, fame and good fortune, give up looking at another's wife; then these lines. The doha that follows tells Ravana to drop desire, anger, pride and greed, the roads to hell, and worship Ram.
rcm.5.36.chaupai.4.core_teaching: No power is safe if it is used to harm living beings, and even a little greed spoils the name of an otherwise good person.

commentaries.who: Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Lord of fourteen worlds means all power; 'cannot stand' means it loses the power to protect itself, and merit and self are soon destroyed.

commentaries.who: Swami Prajnananand, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Rule kept by the sword and law alone, without keeping the people content, soon falls; the line also hints at the governments of the poet's own time.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Harming beings is opposing God, who is in all beings. Desire and anger subside, but greed never does, so a little greed outweighs an ocean of virtue.

rcm.5.36.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Used in leadership and ethics: power that harms people does not last, and small greed can undo a good reputation.
misreadings: Not a claim that any self-interest is sinful.
speaks_to: temptation to cut corners for gain

rcm.5.38.chaupai.3.context: Ravana has thrown out his old minister Malyavan for giving the same advice. Vibhishan, joining his palms, says this, then tells Ravana that bad sense has taken over his heart so he takes friend for foe, and loves Sita, the dark night of the demon race.
rcm.5.38.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Both wisdom and folly live in every heart. Which one leads decides whether prosperity or ruin follows.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Ravana had called Vibhishan and Malyavan fools; Vibhishan replies that sense is not decided by calling names but by its fruits. 'Nidana' means calamity and then ruin.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Good sense is sattvic understanding; bad sense is rajasic, which cannot tell right from wrong (Gita 18.31).

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: Cites a Sanskrit subhashita that good and bad sense are the two causes of all fortune and misfortune, and Kaikeyi's 'kumati' as an example of calamity.

rcm.5.38.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Used to remind us that everyone carries both impulses; the work is noticing which one is steering a decision.
misreadings: Not a way to label people as simply good-minded or bad-minded.

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 40, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 38: off by two.

rcm.5.39.chaupai.4.context: Ravana, furious, calls Vibhishan a traitor living on his bread and kicks him. Vibhishan keeps clasping his feet. Shiva, narrating to Uma, comments (line 7); Vibhishan speaks (line 8). Then he leaves with his ministers by the sky road and goes to Ram.
rcm.5.39.chaupai.4.core_teaching: A saint's greatness is to keep wishing well to the one who harms him. Vibhishan, kicked, still treats his brother as a father and tells him plainly where his good lies.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Vibhishan is the limit of goodness and Ravana of wickedness. Returning good for harm is praiseworthy only in a saint; in a warrior or king, kindness to an enemy is counted a fault, as Ram himself says.

commentaries.who: Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Answers Ravana's 'you live by my keeping': you are like a father who raised me, so striking me was fine; a son's duty is to save his father, so I tell you to worship Ram.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki and Adhyatma)
commentaries.gist: Valmiki 6.16 and Adhyatma 6.2 both have Vibhishan call the elder brother 'like a father'.

rcm.5.39.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Used for responding to hurt without hatred: you can keep goodwill and say the truth, and still walk away.
misreadings: Not a rule that one must accept being hit; Vibhishan leaves immediately after.
Commentary itself limits this to saints, not rulers or protectors.
cautions: Mentions physical violence by a family member; do not use to counsel someone to stay with an abuser.
not_for: someone experiencing domestic violence
someone pressured to keep 'being good' to an abuser

rcm.5.39.doha.1.context: Just kicked by Ravana, Vibhishan rises into the sky with his four ministers and says this so all can hear. The moment he leaves, the narrator says, the demons lost their life-force. He goes to Ram's camp full of hopes.
rcm.5.39.doha.1.core_teaching: Vibhishan leaves openly, not in secret: Ram's will is true, this court is doomed, and he is going to Ram for refuge, so let no one call it betrayal.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki parallel)
commentaries.gist: Valmiki 6.17 names the four ministers who went with him (Anala, Panasa, Sampati, Pramati); they later spied on Ravana's camp for Ram, showing he came to serve.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Among the seven limbs of a kingdom the minister is chief; with ministers kept, what is lost can be rebuilt, which is why Vibhishan takes his with him.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: He openly says he is going to Ram so that no one can later blame him for deserting or spying.

rcm.5.39.doha.1.practical_reading: Used for leaving a harmful situation with honesty: say why you go, without hatred, and go towards something better.
misreadings: Not a justification for betraying a group for personal gain; the leaving is open and after honest counsel was rejected.
cautions: Raises family loyalty versus conscience; sensitive for those estranged from family.
not_for: someone who would read it as licence to cut off family impulsively
speaks_to: leaving a toxic workplace or group
after being rejected for honest advice

rcm.5.4.chaupai.1.context: Lankini, humbled, blesses Hanuman and sends him into Lanka. The second line continues into the third: all this happens to the one on whom Ram has looked with grace. Hanuman then enters the city in a tiny form.
rcm.5.4.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Go about your work holding Ram in your heart. For one on whom Ram looks with grace, obstacles turn into help: poison into nectar, enemies into friends, the sea into a puddle, fire into coolness.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Lankini tells him to enter fearlessly; 'all the work' means more than finding Sita. Every item came true for Hanuman: Surasa's threat became a blessing, Lankini an ally, the sea a hoofprint, and later fire did not burn him.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (reading of line 2)
commentaries.gist: Lines 2-3 belong together and are addressed to Garuda (reading गरुड as a vocative): this is Kakbhushundi's comment as narrator, not Lankini's. Kodavram's text reads गरुअ (heavy) instead.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: Contrasts Aranya Kand, where for one turned away from Ram, nectar becomes poison and a friend acts like a hundred enemies.

rcm.5.4.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Used before a hard task: keep in mind whom or what you serve, and difficulties can turn into help along the way.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that faith makes all danger vanish; Hanuman still acts with skill and courage.
cautions: Promises can sound like 'nothing bad will happen'; avoid with readers facing real danger.
not_for: someone in danger who needs practical safety steps
someone whose prayers seem unanswered
speaks_to: starting a daunting job or move

data_flags.attribution_note: Line 1 is Lankini. In Manas Piyush the second line runs into the next (the one on whom Ram looks with grace) and is read as Kakbhushundi's narratorial aside to Garuda, not Lankini's words.

rcm.5.41.chaupai.4.context: Vibhishan arrives at Ram's camp. The guards tell Sugriva, who tells Ram. Ram asks his friend's view; Sugriva says demons are shape-shifters and this one has come to spy, so bind him (line 7). Ram answers (line 8). Hanuman is delighted. Ram then gives his refuge speech.
rcm.5.41.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Ram honours his friend's caution as good policy, but sets above it his vow to protect anyone who comes for refuge.

commentaries.who: Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Sakha' implies Sugriva is eager to weigh the enemy and protect Ram's interests, which is a friend's duty.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Ram refutes Sugriva gently, calling his view good so his friend is not hurt, then explains the duty to the refugee. Sugriva erred by jumping to faults without first praising Ram, as advisers properly do.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki parallel)
commentaries.gist: Valmiki 6.18.33: Ram's vow is to give fearlessness from all beings to anyone who comes once and says 'I am yours'.

rcm.5.41.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Used to show how to overrule caution kindly: acknowledge the concern, then hold to a deeper principle.
misreadings: Not an argument against all caution or security; Ram addresses the risk directly next.

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 43, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 41: off by two.

rcm.5.42.chaupai.1.context: Ram has just said that those who abandon a refugee out of fear for themselves are sinners whose very sight is harmful. He continues to Sugriva with these lines, then explains why a truly wicked person would not come at all.
rcm.5.42.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Ram does not turn away anyone who comes for refuge, whatever their past. The moment a soul truly turns towards him, the weight of countless lives of wrong is wiped away.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Those who abandon a refugee become wholly sinful, while even a great sinner who comes can be freed. Turning to God destroys sin; then worship becomes pleasing; worship purifies the mind; and the pure mind reaches God.

commentaries.who: Ramdas Gaud, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: A sinner as such does not take refuge; the one who repents and then comes is not abandoned. Cites Gita 9.30-31: even the worst who worships single-mindedly is to be counted good.

commentaries.who: Ramshankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: One who sins deliberately, planning to take refuge later and be cleared, hopes in vain.

commentaries.who: Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Reconciles this with Ram's earlier 'I do not like the enemy of brahmins': that was for people living by ordinary duties; this concerns full surrender.

rcm.5.42.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Used to tell people that no past puts them beyond a fresh start, provided the turning is real.
misreadings: Not a licence to keep doing harm or to plan wrongdoing and 'repent later' (Ramshankar Sharan rules this out).
Does not cancel worldly consequences or the duty to repair harm.
cautions: Mentions killing; the hyperbole may need explaining for a general reader.
not_for: someone harmed by another, if it is used to demand they accept the harmer back
speaks_to: deep guilt or shame over the past
returning to faith after a long absence

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 44, chaupai lines 1-2 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 42: off by two.

rcm.5.42.chaupai.2.context: Continuing his answer to Sugriva's suspicion of Vibhishan: after saying he never abandons a refugee, Ram explains why Vibhishan's coming is itself evidence of his good heart. Next he says only the pure-minded reach him.
rcm.5.42.chaupai.2.core_teaching: A wicked heart does not want to turn to God. That Vibhishan came to Ram at all shows his heart is not wicked.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Sin itself blocks worship, so the sinner never likes it. Ram would not reject even Ravana if he came, but a wicked heart will not come; Vibhishan's coming proves his purity. Cites Gita 7.15.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Ramanuja on Gita 7.15)
commentaries.gist: Draws on Ramanuja's bhashya on Gita 7.15, which describes four grades of those who do not take refuge: the deluded, the lowest, those whose knowledge is stolen by maya, and those of demonic disposition.

rcm.5.42.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Used to encourage someone who doubts their own sincerity: the wish to turn toward the good is already a sign of a good heart.
misreadings: Not proof that anyone who shows up has pure motives in every case.
speaks_to: first steps back toward faith or recovery

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 44, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 42: off by two.

rcm.5.42.chaupai.3.context: Ram continues to answer Sugriva's suspicion. Having said the wicked would not come to him, he says what does reach him, then grants that even if Ravana sent Vibhishan as a spy, there is nothing to fear.
rcm.5.42.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Only a clear, honest heart reaches God; he has no taste for deceit and scheming. And even if this were a spy, the camp has nothing to fear.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Gitavali)
commentaries.gist: In Gitavali Ram calls Vibhishan wise, good, pure and a friend; Hanuman adds that a deceiver cannot face the Lord, as darkness cannot face the sun.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Ram humours Sugriva: even granting he was sent, it is no fault of his, for his mind is clear; Ram knows Vibhishan's ways.

commentaries.who: Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Even then' means even if our secrets are known; the repeated 'friend' shows Ram's affection for Sugriva while he overrules him.

rcm.5.42.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Used to value transparency: honesty opens doors that cleverness cannot, and security that comes from strength need not fear the newcomer.
misreadings: Not a claim that suspicion is never justified.

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 44, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 42: off by two.

rcm.5.42.chaupai.4.context: Ram closes his answer to Sugriva. Then, in the doha, he tells Sugriva to bring Vibhishan either way, and the monkeys go to fetch him.
rcm.5.42.chaupai.4.core_teaching: There is no danger from a spy when Lakshman alone can destroy every demon in an instant. And if Vibhishan has come in fear for shelter, Ram will guard him like his own life.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Ram shows divine power here but names Lakshman's, not his own; it is his way never to boast of his own prowess. Lakshman, as Shesha, incarnated to destroy demons.

commentaries.who: Swami Prajnananand, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram never states his own might; even in battle he names Lakshman and others.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki parallel)
commentaries.gist: In Valmiki 6.80 Lakshman offers to use the Brahma weapon to kill all demons, and Ram stops him from destroying many for one.

rcm.5.42.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Used to show that real strength makes generosity possible: one who is secure can afford to protect the frightened.
misreadings: Not a boast of violence; the point is that there is nothing to fear from welcoming the frightened.
cautions: Mentions killing; keep the focus on protection.
speaks_to: fear of being taken advantage of

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 44, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 42: off by two.

rcm.5.43.doha.1.context: Brought before Ram, Vibhishan is overwhelmed by his beauty. He says: Lord, I am Ravana's brother, born a demon, with a tamasic body that loves sin like an owl loves darkness. Then this plea. Ram embraces him at once.
rcm.5.43.doha.1.core_teaching: Vibhishan has come on the strength of Ram's reputation alone: he heard that Ram ends fear and distress, and asks to be saved.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Each epithet answers a lack in him: you are able, I am helpless; you end fear, I am afraid; you remove distress, I am distressed. His only claim is having heard that Ram protects any refugee.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Gitavali parallel)
commentaries.gist: Gitavali 5.43-44 expands the plea: he heard of the stone woman, the boatman, the vulture, Shabari and Sugriva, and comes as the enemy's brother insulted by his own kin.

rcm.5.43.doha.1.practical_reading: Used for the moment of asking for help: you do not need credentials, only to come and ask.
misreadings: Not a formula that guarantees an outcome; it is a plea, and its force is in honesty.
speaks_to: asking for help after a crisis

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 45 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 43: off by two. Ravana's sarcastic echo of the phrase 'श्रवन सुजसु सुनि' in doha 53 is a different doha.

rcm.5.44.chaupai.3.context: Thrown out of Lanka for advising Ravana to return Sita, Vibhishan crosses to Ram's camp; over Sugriva's suspicion Ram receives him, embraces him and seats him close. Ram greets him as 'lord of Lanka', asks after his family's welfare given his bad place of dwelling, then these lines: how did you keep your dharma living day and night among the wicked? I know your ways: wise in right conduct, with no taste for wrong. He adds that it is better to live in hell than to be given the company of the wicked. Vibhishan replies that seeing Ram's feet he is now well.
rcm.5.44.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Ram recognises that keeping one's goodness among cruel people is hard, and affirms that Vibhishan has done it.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Pandit Ramkumar
commentaries.gist: Welfare here means keeping dharma; a place full of the wicked is a bad home however rich, with no respite. 'I know your ways' shows their faults never stuck to him, like a jewel in a snake's hood.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Pa. Pa. Pra. (Swami Prajnananand)
commentaries.gist: Such a place is unfit for practising dharma.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Panjabiji
commentaries.gist: Reads 'friend' as also asking how Vibhishan kept up his friendship with Ram while living there.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, note on the next line
commentaries.gist: On 'better hell than wicked company', cites a Garuda Purana verse: hell exhausts sin, but evil company only increases it.

rcm.5.44.chaupai.3.practical_reading: If you live or work among people who are cruel, it is an achievement just to stay decent; you are seen.
misreadings: Not 'stay among the wicked to prove your goodness'; the next line says better hell than such company, and Vibhishan has left.
cautions: The next line ('better hell than bad company') can feel like blame for someone who cannot leave.
not_for: someone who cannot leave and may hear 'you should have left'
speaks_to: someone being hurt by those around them
staying decent in a toxic workplace or family

rcm.5.44.chaupai.4.context: Ram has embraced Vibhishan and asks after him: Lankesh, are you and your family well, living in a bad place among the wicked day and night? How do you keep your dharma? I know your ways; you are wise and dislike wrong. Then line 7; Vibhishan's reply begins in line 8. The doha says no soul knows peace until it worships Ram.
rcm.5.44.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Better to live in hell than to be given the company of the wicked. And: having seen Ram's feet, Vibhishan is now truly well.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Reads line 7 as Ram's words: Ram himself states the harm of bad company, sparing Vibhishan from having to complain about his brother. Hell is preferred because it at least exhausts sin.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Garuda Purana)
commentaries.gist: Quotes a Garuda Purana verse: better to live in hell than in a wicked house, since hell wears sin away while a bad house increases it.

commentaries.who: Nangeparamhans and Manas Tattva Bhaskar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: In hell one at least remembers God; in bad company never. Hell ends; bad company brings pain now and hell later.

rcm.5.44.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Used to weigh company seriously: who we spend our days with shapes us more than our circumstances.
misreadings: Not contempt for people who live in hard places; it is about corrupting company.
Not a call to cut off everyone with faults.
cautions: Can sound harsh toward family members; Vibhishan's 'wicked company' is his own brother's court.
not_for: someone who cannot leave their environment (a child, a dependant), who may feel condemned
speaks_to: relief after escaping a toxic environment

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 46, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 44: off by two.
data_flags.attribution_note: Manas Piyush (Pt. Ramkumar) reads line 7 ('better to live in hell...') as Ram speaking to Vibhishan, continuing Ram's questions about living among the wicked; Vibhishan's reply starts at line 8. Our data gives the whole verse to Vibhishan.

rcm.5.45.chaupai.4.context: After Ram's teaching on what it means to be well, Vibhishan says all his fear and grief are gone through Ram's grace, then says this. The doha follows: how great is my fortune, that Ram's grace embraced me.
rcm.5.45.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Vibhishan cannot believe his welcome: one who never did good has been embraced by the Lord whom sages cannot reach in meditation. Grace, not merit, did it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: He shows his lowness in body (a demon), mind (low nature) and action (no good deeds), as Shabari did. Even great merit cannot earn sight of the Lord; he comes by his own grace.

commentaries.who: Swami Prajnananand, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Here 'nishachar' is defined as one of low nature and 'adham' as one who does no good, as in Bal Kand 184.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Gitavali)
commentaries.gist: Compares Gitavali 5.36: the form that sages and Shiva cannot see in dreams has taken Tulsi into its lap.

rcm.5.45.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Used for undeserved welcome: the wonder of being accepted by someone far greater than you, without having earned it.
misreadings: The self-description is humility before grace, not a model for self-contempt.
cautions: Harsh self-judgement may echo shame for some readers.
not_for: someone with severe shame or self-hatred, without a reframe

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 47, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 45: off by two.

rcm.5.46.chaupai.1.context: Vibhishan has rejoiced in Ram's grace. Ram now tells him his own nature, as a friend. These lines state his promise to the refugee. The list of loved ones in line 4 leads into the next lines: gathering one's attachments to all these into one cord tied to Ram's feet.
rcm.5.46.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Whoever has harmed all creation, if he comes to Ram afraid and seeking refuge, Ram makes him like a saint at once.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Bhushundi and Shiva are cited as the authorities on Ram's nature; Shambhu in the middle because both others learned it from him. Knowing Ram's nature makes devotion firm.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (gloss of line 3)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'taji mad moh...' as Ram setting aside the refugee's pride, delusion and deceit, not looking at his faults, and at once making him like a saint.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Names the three who know his nature; the fruit of knowing it is that all three worship him constantly.

rcm.5.46.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Used to show that the way back is open even after doing great harm, when a person comes honestly and afraid of who they have been.
misreadings: Not a claim that consequences or the need to repair harm vanish.
cautions: Translation ends with an incomplete list; do not show the fragment on its own.
not_for: victims of harm, if it is used to excuse the harmer
speaks_to: fear of being rejected for one's past

data_flags.translation_note: Two issues. (1) Manas Piyush reads line 3 as Ram setting aside the refugee's pride, delusion and deceit (overlooking them), not as the refugee giving them up first; our translation takes the second reading. Both are possible, but the editor should know. (2) The final...

rcm.5.46.chaupai.3.context: Ram is telling Vibhishan his nature. After the promise to the refugee and a list of relations (mother, father, brother, son, wife, body, wealth, home, friends, family), he describes the devotee he holds dear. The doha then says such devotees, whether seeking with or without desire, are dear to him.
rcm.5.46.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Gather all your scattered attachments into one strong cord and tie your mind with it to God. Such a person, even-minded and free of elation, grief and fear, lives in Ram's heart the way money lives in a miser's.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Withdraw attachment from all these and place it all in Ram; attachment that was a fault becomes devotion when turned to him. Compares Vinaya Patrika 103 and Kavitavali 7.30.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: Attachment is a thin thread that soon breaks; twisted together and tied to the Lord it becomes a cord that cannot break.

commentaries.who: Swami Prajnananand, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Worldly attachment is not dropped all at once; gather it thread by thread, as autumn water dries slowly, and the person gradually becomes free of 'mine'.

rcm.5.46.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Used to reframe love and attachment: not abandoning loved ones, but letting all one's loves be gathered into one devotion that steadies the mind.
misreadings: Not 'give up your family'; the image is of gathering one's loves, not discarding people.
Not a demand to feel no grief or fear at all, instantly.
cautions: 'No grief or fear' can sound like a judgement on someone who grieves.
Even-mindedness as an ideal can be misused to suppress emotions.
not_for: fresh grief
someone in an unsafe relationship who may hear 'detach and endure'
speaks_to: seeking a single centre in life

rcm.5.47.chaupai.3.context: After Ram's speech on his nature and his dear devotees, Vibhishan answers. Next he asks for pure devotion dear to Shiva. Ram says, though you have no desire, I will crown you, and anoints him king of Lanka with sea water.
rcm.5.47.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Vibhishan admits he came with some lingering desire (understood as kingship of Lanka), but love for Ram's feet has washed it away.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Ram had called him 'Lankesh', so Vibhishan knew Ram meant to crown him; he says that wish is gone. Love is a river because the Ganga flows from those feet: it removes the desire and washes the heart clean.

commentaries.who: Baba Jayramdas, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Agrees with Ramkumar that Vibhishan was not a seeker of gain: when Brahma offered a boon he asked only for pure love of the Lord's feet.

rcm.5.47.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Used to show honesty about mixed motives: we often come to good things for partly selfish reasons, and love can transform those reasons.
misreadings: Not a claim that having had a selfish motive invalidates the turning.
speaks_to: desires fading in a larger love

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 49, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 47: off by two.

rcm.5.48.chaupai.4.context: Ram has crowned Vibhishan. Ravana's spies are noticed. At the shore, Ram asks Sugriva and Vibhishan how to cross the deep ocean. Vibhishan answers. Ram agrees and sits on the shore in prayer to the ocean for three days.
rcm.5.48.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Even when you have the power to force a way, right conduct says ask first, humbly.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Sugriva stays quiet, since his last advice was overruled; Vibhishan answers. Ram asked as a man, Vibhishan answered knowing his divinity, like Jambavant and the sages elsewhere. As a king of Raghu's line, Ram should honour proper conduct.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the policy with Dohavali 433: if honey will kill, why give poison; that is, first try conciliation.

rcm.5.48.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Used in conflict and negotiation: try the gentle way first, even from a position of strength.
misreadings: Not a rule of endless appeasement; the sequel shows firmness after patience is ignored.

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 50, chaupai lines 7-8 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 48: off by two.

rcm.5.55.doha.1.context: For three days Ram has sat on the shore asking the ocean for a way. Ravana's spy Shuka has just been released. The ocean does not appear. Ram speaks in anger and calls for his bow. When he aims, the ocean appears, begs pardon and tells him how to build the bridge.
rcm.5.55.doha.1.core_teaching: After three days of patient asking, Ram sees the ocean will not listen to courtesy and shows anger, since an unfeeling party responds only to firmness.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki parallel)
commentaries.gist: Valmiki 6.21.14-16: calm, forgiveness, straightness and kind speech are taken as weakness by the unworthy; fame cannot be won by conciliation alone.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Three days because a pilgrim stays three nights at a tirtha. He shows anger first in words so the ocean may come without the arrow; mercy remains in his heart, and the anger is shown, not felt.

commentaries.who: Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The ocean's dullness is that it ignored Ram first and came only after provoking his anger.

rcm.5.55.doha.1.practical_reading: Used for dealing with someone who ignores repeated, reasonable requests: patience first, then clear firmness, and forgiveness the moment they respond.
misreadings: Not a rule for close relationships or for parenting by fear.
Not permission to intimidate; the firmness follows real patience and ends in forgiveness.
cautions: The proverb 'bhay binu hoi na priti' is often misused to justify fear-based control in families; our data already avoids using it.
not_for: anyone in an abusive or controlling relationship
parenting
partners and close friends
speaks_to: a party that keeps ignoring polite requests
when niceness is taken for weakness

rcm.5.56.chaupai.1.context: Right after the doha on three days of patient asking, Ram calls for his bow. He then fits a fire arrow; the ocean seethes, then comes as a brahmin, apologises, and advises bridging the sea with Nala and Nila's help.
rcm.5.56.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Some efforts are wasted on the wrong ground: pleading with the stubborn, friendship with the crooked, principles to the miserly, wisdom to the possessive, renunciation to the greedy, calm to the angry, sacred stories to the lustful. All are seed sown on barren land.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: The verbs are left out to show one should not do these at all. Seven faults are barren land and seven virtues the seeds, like the seven grains; all seven faults are found in the ocean.

commentaries.who: Manas Tattva Sudha, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Stubbornness, crookedness, miserliness, possessiveness, greed, anger and lust block devotion; humility, love, good policy, knowledge, dispassion, calm and holy stories are the matching means.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Ram asks for the bow aloud to frighten the ocean into coming; the threat is in speech, not in his heart.

rcm.5.56.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Used to recognise when effort is misplaced: know the ground before you sow, and stop pouring energy into someone who will not receive it.
misreadings: Not a licence to write people off quickly or to bully; this follows three days of patience and ends in forgiveness.
cautions: Labels like 'lustful' and 'angry' can feel like judgements if aimed at the reader.
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship who may read 'firmness' as escalation
close family conflicts
speaks_to: wasting energy on someone who will not listen

rcm.5.6.chaupai.1.context: Searching Lanka, Hanuman finds a house marked with Ram's name and tulsi plants; its owner Vibhishan wakes chanting Ram's name. They meet, both moved, and Hanuman tells Ram's story. Unasked, Vibhishan describes his life: he lives among the demons like the poor tongue among the teeth, and wonders whether Ram will ever show grace to one so unsupported. Hanuman reassures him that Ram loves even a lowly, restless monkey like himself.
rcm.5.6.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Living among hostile people is like being the tongue among the teeth: always careful, never safe.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Pandit Ramkumar
commentaries.gist: Having found good company, Vibhishan pours out the pain of bad company without being asked; he says 'our' to include his family; the teeth stand for death-like cruelty, a living hell.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, note on 'bicari'
commentaries.gist: Either the tongue is helpless, shut in with no remedy, or it gets by only through great care, since one slip and it is bitten.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Pandit Ramkumar (third note)
commentaries.gist: The tongue did not choose the teeth, as Vibhishan did not choose his birth; and as the tongue remains when the teeth are pulled, he will remain when the demons are gone.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Lamgodaji
commentaries.gist: Tulsidas's similes come from everyday experience, which is why so many of his lines became proverbs.

rcm.5.6.chaupai.1.practical_reading: It gives words to living or working among people who hurt you: constant care, no rest; and the next lines hold out hope of finding an ally.
misreadings: Not advice to stay in such a situation indefinitely; Vibhishan later leaves Lanka for Ram.
cautions: For someone in an abusive home, pair naming the situation with signposting toward safety and support.
not_for: someone in immediate danger who needs practical help first
speaks_to: living with someone who hurts you

rcm.5.6.chaupai.2.context: Searching Lanka, Hanuman finds a house marked with Ram's name and meets Vibhishan, Ravana's brother. After they exchange who they are, Vibhishan describes his life among the demons and wonders whether Ram will ever be kind to him. Then he answers himself here. Hanuman replies by telling of his own lowliness.
rcm.5.6.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Vibhishan feels he has no birth, practice or love that qualifies him. Yet meeting a true devotee is itself the sign of grace, so he now has hope.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: He declares himself without knowledge (tamas body), action (no practice) and devotion (no love for the feet). He answers his own question because the answer would not sound right from Hanuman's mouth. Hanuman is his doorway to Ram.

commentaries.who: Baba Hariharprasad, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Reads 'tamas body' as lack of action and 'no practice' as lack of knowledge.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Hearing Hanuman's story, Vibhishan knows he is Ram's envoy and that his own good can come through him, so he speaks of his helplessness.

rcm.5.6.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to feeling unworthy: the arrival of a good person or a helping hand can itself be a sign you have not been forgotten.
misreadings: Not a claim that birth decides worth.
cautions: Self-description as low by birth can echo caste or self-contempt; keep the emphasis on hope.
not_for: someone with severe low self-worth who may latch onto the first line

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 7, chaupai lines 3-4 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 6: off by one.

rcm.5.6.doha.1.context: Just after Vibhishan's hope, Hanuman tells him: 'What lineage do I have? A fickle monkey, low in every way; say my name in the morning and you go without food that day.' This doha completes that thought. After it, the narrator says those who forget such a master suffer, and Hanuman finds peace in telling Ram's virtues.
rcm.5.6.doha.1.core_teaching: Hanuman offers his own life as evidence: if Ram was kind to someone as lowly as him, Vibhishan need not doubt. Remembering that kindness moves him to tears.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Hanuman recalls one virtue in particular, Ram's lifting of the lowly, so the singular 'gun' is used. By calling himself lower than Vibhishan, he confirms that grace will surely come to Vibhishan.

commentaries.who: Pandeji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Sakha' marks three likenesses: both share a tamasic nature, both lived under a powerful brother (Bali, Ravana), and the same Ram who helped one will help the other.

commentaries.who: Swami Prajnananand, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: If Ram was kind to me, how much more to those rich in dharma, and to you, a great devotee.

rcm.5.6.doha.1.practical_reading: Used for encouraging someone through one's own story: 'if it happened for me, it can happen for you'.
misreadings: Hanuman's self-description is humility, not a teaching that anyone is truly worthless.
not_for: someone who needs their worth affirmed rather than a shared self-lowering
speaks_to: encouraging a friend who feels unworthy

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Sundar Kand doha 7 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 6: off by one.

rcm.6.110.doha.1.context: After Ravana's death Vibhishan, now king, begs Ram to stay a while, bathe, and see his treasury and palace, and to let him give gifts to the monkeys. Ram answers that all of it is his already. He cannot linger because Bharat is waiting. Next he asks for the quickest way home. The doha after says that if the fourteen years run out he will not find his brother alive.
rcm.6.110.doha.1.core_teaching: Ram turns down a friend's lavish hospitality without hurting him, by making the friend's wealth his own, and shows that a loved one's suffering at home outweighs every comfort on offer.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: 'Your treasury and house are mine' answers Vibhishan's offer of wealth and shows a friend's dharma: treat a friend's goods as your own. Vibhishan called himself a servant; Ram calls him brother and friend.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, citing Padma Purana and Adhyatma Ramayana
commentaries.gist: Bharat's state: matted hair, bark cloth, living in a pit at Nandigram, barely eating, blaming himself for Ram's exile. The Adhyatma Ramayana has Ram picture him the same way, but the Manas's 'constantly repeating my name' is more intense.

rcm.6.110.doha.1.practical_reading: A model for saying no to generous hospitality without offending: honour the offer and give the real reason. Teachers also apply it to how the thought of someone waiting at home makes even small delays feel long.
misreadings: Not a rejection of Vibhishan's friendship; Ram calls him brother and friend in the same breath.
cautions: The next doha links the deadline to Bharat's possible death; mild.
not_for: someone who cannot go home and blames themselves for it
speaks_to: being torn between a host's kindness and the pull of home
someone far from home after a long, hard stretch (deployment, a project, hospital)

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 115 (ka), Gita Press / Manas Piyush numbering. Our ref says 110: off by five.

rcm.6.111.doha.1.context: Vibhishan has flown up in the Pushpak and is showering jewels and clothes on the monkeys, who grab them and even try to eat the gems. Ram laughs with Sita and Lakshman. Tulsidas marvels that the God sages cannot reach is joking with monkeys, and Shiva gives the reason in the next doha.
rcm.6.111.doha.1.core_teaching: The God whom sages cannot reach and scripture can only describe by negation becomes playful and close to simple, unsophisticated companions.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note, citing Bhagavata 10.87.41 and Brihadaranyaka 4.4.22
commentaries.gist: 'Neti neti': the Vedas can only point at him by denying everything finite, since even he cannot reach his own end. The contrast is deliberate: unreachable for sages and scripture, easy for foolish monkeys.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note, with the parallel from Ayodhya Kand 136
commentaries.gist: The same idea appears at Chitrakoot, where the Lord listens to Bhil tribals like a father to his children. Only love is dear to Ram, and Shiva explains this in the next doha.

commentaries.who: Vedantabhushan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Explains why the doha's rhyme seems not to close: the joke is one-sided, since the monkeys do not see that they are being laughed at.

rcm.6.111.doha.1.practical_reading: Used to say that the highest is not distant or stiff. Teachers apply it to ease and laughter in close relationships, and to the idea that simple people are not shut out of the sacred.
misreadings: Not mockery of the monkeys; the commentators read it as intimacy.
not_for: someone in acute grief, where playfulness may feel out of place
speaks_to: feeling too simple or unlearned for spirituality
joy and play after a long struggle

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 116 (first of the two-doha pair numbered 116), Gita Press / Manas Piyush. Our ref says 111: off by five.

rcm.6.111.doha.2.context: This follows the previous doha: Tulsidas has just said the God beyond the sages' meditation is joking with monkeys. Shiva supplies the reason: not practices but pure love draws Ram's grace. The scene then moves on to Ram addressing the monkeys before leaving Lanka.
rcm.6.111.doha.2.core_teaching: Disciplines and rituals have their place, but none draws grace as fully as simple, wholehearted love.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: 'Tasi' means practices do earn some grace: after long effort the Lord sometimes appears in a sage's meditation. Love earns the special kind. The lesson: don't get lost in technique, love the Lord.

commentaries.who: Kharra (anonymous manuscript note), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Love has no pride in it, while yoga, sacrifice and charity keep a sense of 'I am the doer'. That is why love draws more grace.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Nishkeval prem' is innocent, intense love that needs no technique at all, whether or not practices are present.

rcm.6.111.doha.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it to lift the pressure of 'doing it right': sincere affection and attention count for more than perfect ritual. It can reassure people who feel they lack discipline.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of discipline or ethics; the commentary says practices also bring grace, only less.
Not a claim that love is a technique to extract favours.
cautions: Devotional framing; secular readers may need 'love' read broadly.
not_for: someone who wants a structured practice and would hear this as 'don't bother'

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 116 (second half of the pair; Manas Piyush prints both under ॥116॥). Our ref says 111: off by five.

rcm.6.112.chaupai.3.context: Just before this Ram looks at them all with kindness and tells them it was by their strength that he killed Ravana and crowned Vibhishan. Now he sends them home. They are overwhelmed and say that hearing such words gives them 'moha' (they fear thinking they helped God). In the end they go with him to Ayodhya.
rcm.6.112.chaupai.3.core_teaching: After the struggle, Ram releases his companions with a parting gift: keep me in mind and you need fear no one.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: 'Remember' comes before 'fear no one' because remembrance is the cause of fearlessness. Keeping his power in mind, they will never take another master. It cross-refers to 'if my servant hopes in men, what faith is that' (Uttar 46).

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Their work is done. 'All of you' hints that none of them died, so they can see they have nothing to fear. Go home whichever way is easiest, and keep remembering me.

commentaries.who: Karunasindhu, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Esoteric reading: the monkeys who were portions of gods should return to their sources, while Ram's own attendants will go with him.

rcm.6.112.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Applied to endings: when a team, a campaign or a hard season breaks up, take the bond home with you. Remembering who stood with you is a source of courage.
misreadings: Not a promise that nothing bad will happen; it is about not being ruled by fear.
not_for: someone afraid of a real, present danger who needs practical help, not reassurance
speaks_to: the end of a shared ordeal or project
going home after a long time away
courage drawn from faith or from remembered support

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 117, chaupai 3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 5-6), Gita Press numbering. Our ref says 112: off by five.

rcm.6.12.chaupai.3.context: Ravana asks his court for counsel; his ministers flatter him. His son Prahasta says the flatterers will ruin him and urges sending Sita back with a messenger. Ravana insults him harshly ('a bamboo root has sprouted a ghamoi weed'). Prahasta says this line and goes home. The second line is narration: evening comes and Ravana, looking at his twenty arms, goes to his palace, where a dance performance is underway.
rcm.6.12.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Good advice does not take with one who is doomed, just as medicine does not help a patient already in death's grip. Ravana goes off admiring his own arms.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani (via Manas Piyush vol. 6)
commentaries.gist: He who is seized by death gets no benefit from even good medicine; so Ravana hears good counsel but does not accept it, because he is doomed.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki parallels)
commentaries.gist: Valmiki uses the same image for Vibhishan's and Maricha's rejected advice: Ravana, driven by time, would not take good counsel, like a dying man refusing medicine (Valmiki 3.40, 6.16, 6.17).

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: Compares Malyavan's earlier exits: each honest adviser leaves after harsh words, as Prahasta does here.

rcm.6.12.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Used to accept that some people will not take advice however good it is; you can say it once, clearly, and step away.
misreadings: Not a reason to give up on people quickly or to call anyone 'doomed'.
cautions: 'In death's grip' language is sensitive for someone with a seriously ill relative.
not_for: someone whose relative is terminally ill or refusing treatment, where the medicine image may wound

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 10, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 12: off by two.

rcm.6.19.chaupai.4.context: After the bridge is built and the army camped before Lanka, Ram consults his counsellors in the morning; Jambavan advises sending Angad. Ram blesses Angad as a store of intelligence, strength and virtue and asks him to go to Lanka on his errand. These lines are his whole briefing: he trusts Angad's judgement and asks only that he speak so the mission succeeds and Ravana's own good is served. Angad, honoured, bows and sets out.
rcm.6.19.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Speak to an adversary in a way that achieves your purpose and also serves their real good.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Pandit Ramkumar
commentaries.gist: 'Our work' is recovering Sita; 'his good' is Ravana's safety with his family and wealth, if he yields. Calling Angad 'very capable' means he already has every quality an envoy needs.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Gaudji
commentaries.gist: Encouragement from elders lifts the young; by saying 'I know you are capable', Ram makes Angad capable.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing the Manas Mayank and Panjabi commentators
commentaries.gist: Offer a deeper reading: since Ram knows Ravana will not yield while alive, Ravana's true 'good' is liberation through death at Ram's hand.

rcm.6.19.chaupai.4.practical_reading: In a hard conversation with someone who has wronged you, aim for an outcome that gets the work done without humiliating them; trust in a person's ability can itself make them rise to it.
misreadings: Not 'be nice and let them win'; Ram's purpose (Sita's return) is not negotiable.
The esoteric reading (death as Ravana's good) should not be applied to real opponents.
cautions: In the episode that follows, Ravana insults Angad and his dead father; keep the reading on how to speak, not on the confrontation.
not_for: someone facing an abuser, where 'consider their good' could be harmful
speaks_to: preparing for a hard conversation at work
being overlooked and deciding how to speak up

rcm.6.19.doha.1.context: Ram sends Angad as envoy to Ravana. On the way into Lanka Angad meets Ravana's son, who picks a fight, and kills him; word spreads and no one dares stop him. He reaches the door of Ravana's court. Next Ravana laughs and has him brought in.
rcm.6.19.doha.1.core_teaching: Angad walks alone into the enemy's court remembering Ram, fearless as a lion, steady and strong.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: 'Darbar' here means the door of the court; he is called in only later. Since everyone had seen the prince killed, no one stopped him, they only showed the way.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: A lion walks a little, stands, looks around fearlessly and walks on; 'sinha thavani' expresses that fearlessness.

commentaries.who: Bandan Pathak, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He looks this way and that for someone to announce him. 'Dhir' because killing the prince did not shake him; 'bir' because ready for battle.
