rcm.6.19.doha.1.practical_reading: Used before walking into a hard room alone, such as an interview, a hearing or a confrontation: recall what you stand for, and carry yourself with calm courage.
misreadings: Not a model of aggression; the calm is the point.
cautions: The surrounding story includes a killing on the way in.
speaks_to: representing others in a hostile setting

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 18 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 19: off by one.

rcm.6.19.sortha.3.context: Ram has asked his council what to do; Jambavant advises sending Angad as envoy, and Ram tells Angad to do what serves Ram's purpose and Ravana's good. Angad bows, rises and says that whoever Ram favours becomes a sea of virtues (sortha 17 ka). This second sortha is his inner thought. Then he sets out for Lanka.
rcm.6.19.sortha.3.core_teaching: Angad understands the mission is already certain of success; Ram is simply honouring him by sending him. The thought fills him with joy.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Answers Ram's praise of him as 'home of wit, strength and virtue': whoever Ram favours becomes a sea of virtues.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: 'As bichari' marks this as an inner thought; joy and zeal are the companions of heroic sentiment and signs of coming success.

commentaries.who: Panjabiji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram's grace on Hanuman earlier brought him fame; Angad sees that he too is being given the chance to earn honour.

rcm.6.19.sortha.3.practical_reading: Used for doing a task without ego: the outcome does not hang on you alone; being trusted with it is itself the gift.
misreadings: Not an excuse for low effort ('it will happen anyway'); Angad goes and acts boldly.

rcm.6.34.doha.2.context: Angad, enraged by Ravana's taunts, plants his foot in the court and vows that if anyone can move it, Ram will turn back and he forfeits Sita. Meghnad and many warriors try and fail. This doha closes the scene. Then Ravana himself rises to grab the foot, and Angad tells him to grasp Ram's feet instead.
rcm.6.34.doha.2.core_teaching: The monkey's foot stayed planted and the enemy's pride drained away, just as a good person's mind does not let go of right conduct however many obstacles arise.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: Two readings: the foot does not leave the ground, or the ground does not let go of the foot (fearing for its daughter Sita), which Pt. Ramkumar mentions; the grammar favours the first.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: Two images are paired: the deluded man who cannot uproot the tree of delusion, and the saint whose mind holds to dharma despite obstacles, showing strength on both sides.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Kavitavali)
commentaries.gist: Kavitavali Lanka 15-16 describes the foot as if Brahma had made it together with the earth, heavier than Meru.

rcm.6.34.doha.2.practical_reading: Used for steadfastness: when pressure piles up to make you drop your principles, stay planted.
misreadings: Not stubbornness for its own sake; it is firmness in what is right.
speaks_to: standing alone in a hostile room

rcm.6.60.chaupai.2.context: Lakshman has been struck down by Meghnad's shakti. Hanuman has gone for the herb and promised to return before dawn. Half the night has passed and he has not come. Ram lifts Lakshman to his chest and laments as an ordinary man would. Next he asks where that love has gone and says he would rather lose wife than brother. Then Hanuman arrives.
rcm.6.60.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Ram, holding his unconscious brother, remembers his gentleness and all he gave up and endured for Ram's sake.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush vol. 6
commentaries.gist: 'Anuj' carries the thought that the younger should die after the elder. Quotes Hanuman Nataka: you ate after me and slept after me, will you now leave life before me?

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (Valmiki and Gitavali)
commentaries.gist: Valmiki 6.101: rise, you used to console me when I wandered grieving in forests. Gitavali 6.5 gives a parallel lament.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: Lakshman came to the forest because he could not bear to see Ram suffer, as his mother Sumitra had told him.

rcm.6.60.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Used to honour the people who have given things up for us: remembering their gentleness and sacrifice, especially when we fear losing them.
misreadings: Not a reason to demand sacrifice from loved ones.
cautions: Speaks over a gravely injured brother; the scene may be hard for someone keeping vigil by a dying relative, though Lakshman is revived.
not_for: fresh bereavement, if the revival is not mentioned
someone whose loved one did not recover
speaks_to: keeping vigil over a sick loved one
gratitude to a sibling or caregiver

rcm.6.62.chaupai.4.context: Kumbhakarna has been woken to fight. He has already told Ravana that abducting Sita was wrong, yet he goes out to fight for him. Vibhishan, now on Ram's side, comes forward and touches his feet, explaining that Ravana kicked him out for giving good advice. Kumbhakarna embraces him and praises him. In the doha that follows he tells Vibhishan to worship Ram without guile and to go, because he himself is 'in death's grip' and can no longer tell his own side from the other.
rcm.6.62.chaupai.4.core_teaching: A man who has himself chosen loyalty to a doomed brother still sees clearly that the brother who left to follow the right is the true honour of the family, and blesses him rather than calling him a traitor.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: 'Son' shows Kumbhakarna's fatherly tenderness for a younger brother; the Adhyatma Ramayana also has him say 'vatsa'. Being 'in Time's grip' and deaf to advice is said of Ravana by Mandodari, Prahasta, Vibhishan and Valmiki's Maricha too.

commentaries.who: Ramayan Parichaya, Ramayan Pradip and Manas Mayank, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Three 'blessed's mean blessed in all three times and worlds. Or: Vibhishan is the third brother. Or: his mother, his father and he himself are all blessed, or he is blessed in thought, word and deed.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note on Valmiki contrast
commentaries.gist: Valmiki's Ravana called Vibhishan the disgrace of the clan (kulapamsana). Here Kumbhakarna overturns that by calling him its ornament, and it clears the guilt Vibhishan felt about meeting his brother.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Swami, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Read 'nisichar' and 'kul-bhushan' separately: though a rakshasa, you have honoured Pulastya's line, which the rest of us disgraced.

rcm.6.62.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers use the scene for families split by conviction: you can disagree with a sibling's choice, even stay on the other side, and still honour them for following their conscience. It also notes how someone set on ruin cannot hear good advice.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of Kumbhakarna's choice to fight for a cause he knows is wrong; the poem presents that as his being 'in death's grip'.
Not a call to abandon family whenever you disagree; Vibhishan first gave counsel and was thrown out.
cautions: Kumbhakarna goes on to say he is doomed and about to die; for someone estranged from a sibling who is ill or dying the scene can be heavy.
Calls Ravana's state 'in the grip of death'; avoid implying that a stubborn relative is beyond hope.
not_for: someone currently being pressured to cut off family
a reader grieving a sibling they were estranged from, without framing
speaks_to: siblings or relatives who chose different sides
someone who left a family business, faith or path on principle and fears being seen as a traitor
blessing someone even when you can't follow them
giving advice to someone who will not listen

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 63, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id/ref_label say doha 62: off by one against Gita Press / Manas Piyush.
data_flags.translation_note: Our Awadhi text drops a word: the standard reading is 'सुनु सुत भयउ कालबस रावन' (Manas Piyush prints 'सुत'). Our English already says 'Listen, son', so only the sanskrit field needs fixing. Manas Piyush explains 'सुत' as affection: an elder brother speaks to a younger...

rcm.6.76.chaupai.1.context: Meghnad, Ravana's son, has just been killed and the women of the palace are lamenting. Ravana lectures them that everything is perishable and even great demons fell to Time, while he himself behaves as if he were immortal. Tulsidas steps in with the general remark. The night ends and Ravana rides out to his last battles.
rcm.6.76.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Fine words about wisdom cost nothing; living by them is rare. Ravana preaching detachment while clinging to his pride is the example.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: Ravana tells his wives everything dies, citing Madhu-Kaitabha, Hiranyakashipu and others, yet in his pride he thinks himself immortal. That is why the poet calls him 'manda'.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, citing Subhashita Ratna Bhandagara
commentaries.gist: Parallel Sanskrit maxims: many are clever at advising others, but one who rises above his own nature is rare even among thousands. Preaching is easy, keeping to one's own dharma belongs to a great soul.

commentaries.who: Vir Kavi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Wise counsel coming from a base mind is an effect contrary to its cause. He names the figure of speech: the fifth kind of vibhavana.

rcm.6.76.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it against hypocrisy and as a check on oneself: before advising someone in grief, ask whether you live what you are saying. It also warns that consoling words from someone who caused the loss can ring hollow.
misreadings: Not a reason to dismiss all advice because the adviser is imperfect; the content Ravana spoke is called 'pure'.
Not a blanket cynicism about teachers.
cautions: The setting is a mother's and wives' grief over a son killed in war; Ravana's 'all must die' talk is shown as empty. Don't pair it with a reader's fresh bereavement as if their grief were being lectured.
not_for: someone already crushed by self-criticism
a grieving reader who might feel their mourning is being judged
speaks_to: noticing the gap between what one says and does
being lectured by someone who doesn't practise it
someone who gives advice for a living (teachers, parents, managers)

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 77, chaupai 1 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-2), Gita Press numbering. Our ref says 76: off by one.

rcm.6.79.chaupai.3.context: Ravana rides out on a chariot while Ram stands on foot; Vibhishan, out of love, grows anxious and asks how Ram can win without a chariot or armour. Ram answers that the chariot that brings victory is a different one, and describes a chariot made of dharma: courage and fortitude its wheels, truth and character its flag, strength, discernment, self-control and kindness its horses, yoked with forgiveness, compassion and equanimity. Whoever has such a chariot, he ends, can conquer even the great enemy, worldly existence itself.
rcm.6.79.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Real victory rides on inner qualities: courage and steadiness as wheels, truth and character as flag, and self-mastery and kindness as horses.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Pandit Ramkumar
commentaries.gist: Links valour and fortitude to the Gita's list of a warrior's natural qualities (18.43) and to the maxim of courage against enemies and patience in adversity; glosses sila as pure conduct.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, note citing Ramanuja's Gita commentary
commentaries.gist: Defines valour as the capacity to enter battle without fear, and fortitude as the capacity to finish what one has begun even when obstacles arise.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing Vijayanand Tripathi
commentaries.gist: Battle chariots had two wheels; courage and fortitude are the base of the dharma-chariot, and dharma without them is lame and cannot carry anyone through.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush citing the Bandan Pathak commentary
commentaries.gist: Calls this passage the Manas's own battlefield Gita: as Krishna taught Arjuna, Ram teaches Vibhishan the chariot that wins over the unconquerable enemy, worldly existence.

rcm.6.79.chaupai.3.practical_reading: When outer resources look thin compared to the opposition, build the inner chariot: courage to start, patience to continue, truthfulness, and self-control.
misreadings: Not 'resources don't matter'; it is about what ultimately decides the outcome.

rcm.6.8.chaupai.3.context: The bridge is built and Ram's army has crossed. Ravana, hearing the sea has been bridged, is shaken but boasts. Mandodari takes his hand into the palace and pleads: give up enmity with Ram. After these lines she reminds him of Ram's feats (Madhu, Kaitabh, Hiranyakashipu, Bali, Khara-Dushana) and begs him to return Sita.
rcm.6.8.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Pick fights only with those you can beat by wit and strength; the gap between Ravana and Ram is that of a firefly and the sun.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note (parallel texts)
commentaries.gist: Compares Adhyatma Ramayana (Mandodari: no one can conquer Raghava), Valmiki 6.35 (Malyavan: make peace with an equal or stronger foe) and a Shukraniti verse: make peace with the strong, fight only one you can beat by wit.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush editor's note
commentaries.gist: 'Nath' carries her fear of being left without a protector, which comes true later when the demon women are dragged out and Ravana lies 'like an orphan' on the field.

commentaries.who: Baijnath (Bai.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Everyone Ravana defeated was a jiva; Ram is the lord of all jivas, so there is no comparison.

rcm.6.8.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Used as practical advice on conflict: assess honestly before picking a fight, and do not let pride blind you to what you are up against.
misreadings: Not an argument that one should never stand up to the powerful when one is in the right.
not_for: someone facing an abuser or bully, who might hear 'never challenge the stronger'
speaks_to: a partner warning against a reckless fight

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Lanka Kand doha 6, chaupai lines 5-6 (Gita Press / Manas Piyush). Our id says doha 8: off by two.

rcm.7.10.chaupai.4.context: Just before this Ram tells all his companions to bow at Vasishtha's feet and introduces Vasishtha as the family guru by whose grace the demons died. Then he introduces them to the sage as his friends. They are overwhelmed with joy. Next they meet Kaushalya, who blesses them.
rcm.7.10.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Ram introduces those who risked everything for him as friends, not servants, and ranks them above even his own beloved brother.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Though they are servants, Ram by nature calls them friends. The monkeys come from far countries and don't know the sage, so Ram teaches them to bow. Then he introduces them through their bond with him.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's bracketed note, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Etiquette was to bow giving one's father's name. Ram does it for them with one word, 'friends'. That bond would win more of Vasishtha's love than any lineage could.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: What devotees don't know, the Lord teaches them, just as Shrutideva is taught in the Bhaktamal to bow to saints.

rcm.7.10.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Used for honouring the people who carried you through a crisis: introduce them by what they did for you, and don't rank them below family out of habit.
misreadings: Not a slight on Bharat; the commentators read it as praise of the monkeys' sacrifice.
not_for: someone grieving a friend who died helping them, without care
speaks_to: gratitude to friends who stood by you

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 8, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 10: off by two.

rcm.7.104.doha.3.context: In an earlier life Kakbhushundi, a proud Shiva devotee in Ujjain, would not rise when his gentle guru entered Shiva's temple. A voice from the sky (Shiva) cursed him to be born a serpent for a thousand lives. The guru, horrified, sang the Rudrashtakam and then made this plea for his rude student. Shiva softened the curse, and devotion survived through all those births.
rcm.7.104.doha.3.core_teaching: The wronged teacher pleads for the one who wronged him: the student acted from illusion and deserves pity, not wrath. Here mercy flows from the injured party.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Hanuman and the Vedas say the same to Ram: souls wander deluded by your maya. The dull student deserves compassion, not anger. Each epithet (Prabhu, ocean of mercy, Bhagavan, kind to the lowly) names a power to forgive.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: A servant shouldn't overturn his master's order outright, so the guru asks Shiva, who is able, to keep his word yet make the curse end in the student's good soon, rather than after untold ages.

commentaries.who: Vir Kavi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Shiva's anger is calmed by the Brahmin's devotion (a rasa figure called samahita).

rcm.7.104.doha.3.practical_reading: Used to model praying or speaking up for someone who hurt you, seeing their wrong as confusion rather than wickedness, without excusing it.
misreadings: Not a claim that the wrong didn't matter; the guru accepts that a curse is deserved and asks that it be softened.
Not an obligation on victims to plead for those who harmed them.
cautions: The context includes a curse of a thousand serpent births; keep that out of readings for anxious or guilt-prone readers.
not_for: victims of serious harm, who may hear pressure to plead for their abuser
speaks_to: forgiving a student, child or junior who disrespected you
praying for someone who wronged you

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 108: the first of the two dohas Manas Piyush prints together as ॥108 (ख)॥, Gita Press numbering. Our id says '104 doha 3': off by four.

rcm.7.106.chaupai.1.context: After Shiva's curse, softened at the guru's plea, Kakbhushundi passes through many births as animals, gods and humans, keeping up his devotion to Ram. The one pain that never fades is the memory of his teacher's gentleness, which he had insulted. In his final birth he is born a Brahmin and as a boy plays at Ram's deeds. Then comes the episode with the sage Lomash.
rcm.7.106.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Through many lives Kakbhushundi held to his devotion, yet the ache of having wronged a gentle teacher never left him. The memory of someone's kindness can be the deepest remorse.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush prose gloss
commentaries.gist: The 'one thorn' is lasting remorse: he never forgot how gravely he had insulted his gentle guru.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Order of births: first a thousand serpent lives for the curse, then divine bodies to enjoy past merit, then human births of rising station, and finally a Brahmin body.

commentaries.who: Ramayan Pradip, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: His right to worship continued in every body.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, earlier note in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Shows the principle that mental merit counts but mental sin does not: while his disrespect stayed in thought he was not punished, and only the open insult brought the curse.

rcm.7.106.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Used for regret that lasts: the harm we did to someone who was only kind to us stays with us. Teachers treat it as conscience to keep, not self-punishment.
misreadings: Not 'regret forever'; in the story it sits alongside lasting devotion and leads to humility.
cautions: Assumes many rebirths; a reader carrying heavy guilt may hear it as 'this will never leave you'.
not_for: someone already crushed by guilt or with intrusive self-blame
speaks_to: regret over hurting a teacher, parent or mentor
remembering someone's gentleness after they're gone

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 110, chaupai 1 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-2), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 106: off by four.

rcm.7.107.chaupai.8.context: In his last human birth young Kakbhushundi goes to the sage Lomash. Lomash teaches the formless Brahman, but the boy keeps pressing for devotion to the embodied Ram and argues back again and again. The sage's anger shows on his face, and Kakbhushundi admits here that relentless disrespect angers even the wise. Lomash finally curses him to become a crow, which he accepts calmly.
rcm.7.107.chaupai.8.core_teaching: Even the calmest person will flare up under relentless provocation, as sandalwood ignites if rubbed hard enough. The speaker takes responsibility for having been the friction.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Swami, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The text says 'jnani' (the learned), not 'sant': anger arose in a man of knowledge, and true devotee-saints, alike in praise and blame, don't flare up. Lomash is the sandal, and the back-and-forth argument the friction.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: The wise are cool like sandal, but as fire lies hidden in sandal, anger lies subtly in them, held down by discipline. Ordinary rubbing won't light it, only extreme friction.

commentaries.who: Vinayak Rao's tika, citing Mahabharata Vana Parva
commentaries.gist: Neither constant anger nor constant forgiveness is always best, and the wise do not praise forgiving every time. Some anger at extreme provocation is understandable.

rcm.7.107.chaupai.8.practical_reading: Used two ways: to own one's part when one has provoked someone patient, and to forgive oneself or others for snapping after long strain.
misreadings: Not a licence to keep pushing someone until they break.
Not a defence of rage; the speaker is admitting his own fault.
not_for: someone being harmed by another's anger, who may hear it as 'you provoked it'
speaks_to: a patient person who finally lost their temper
owning one's part in a conflict

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 111, chaupai 8 (Manas Piyush half-lines 15-16), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 107: off by four.

rcm.7.108.doha.2.context: Lomash curses Kakbhushundi, who instantly becomes a crow. He bows at the sage's feet, remembers Ram and flies away happy, with no fear or bitterness. Shiva explains why. Lomash then repents, calls him back and blesses him with devotion and the Ram story.
rcm.7.108.doha.2.core_teaching: One who sees their Beloved everywhere has no one left to fight. That is why Kakbhushundi can be cursed and still leave in joy.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: 'Seeing the world full of the Lord': seeing every being as Ram's form, or Ram as the inner mover of all. Either way no room is left for fear or enmity. Compares Bhagavata 11.29 and Isha Upanishad 6.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He bows at the cursing sage's feet because Shiva had taught him to treat a saint as the Infinite. He remembers Ram because remembrance makes the hard easy.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note (on the curse)
commentaries.gist: He leaves joyful and not humbled. He also doesn't change his form of worship out of fear of the curse: he stays devoted to Ram of the Raghu line, not to the formless the sage preached.

rcm.7.108.doha.2.practical_reading: Used to show freedom from resentment: if you can see the sacred in the person who wronged you, there's nothing left to fight over.
misreadings: Not a requirement to accept mistreatment silently.
cautions: In context this follows an unjust curse; don't present it as 'accept injustice cheerfully' to someone being wronged now.
not_for: someone facing ongoing injustice who needs to resist it

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 112 (second of the pair printed as ॥112॥), Gita Press / Manas Piyush. Our ref says 108: off by four.

rcm.7.116.chaupai.1.context: Garuda asked why knowledge and devotion differ. Kakbhushundi has just finished the long 'lamp of knowledge' allegory: knowledge is a lamp, hard to light and easily blown out by maya's winds. Now he turns to devotion as a wish-fulfilling gem that shines by itself and that greed, delusion and maya cannot touch.
rcm.7.116.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Knowledge is a lamp that needs fuel and can be blown out. Devotion is a jewel that shines on its own, day and night, and no wind of greed can put it out.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Garuda asked to have it explained, and 'I have explained' closes the knowledge section. 'Listen' opens the next.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Knowledge and devotion share one conclusion and differ in power. A gem takes the colour of what holds it, as the mind settles once freed of attachment. A chintamani grants every wish, so devotion to Ram grants everything.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The lamp of knowledge can be obstructed, while the gem of devotion can't be: it is unbroken, ageless, priceless and always shining.

commentaries.who: Karunasindhu, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: A pun on 'बुझाई': 'I explained' knowledge, and also 'I showed how the lamp gets blown out'.

rcm.7.116.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use the contrast for steadiness: understanding can flicker under stress, but love and trust can keep shining when the mind is shaken.
misreadings: Not anti-intellectual; the commentary says knowledge and devotion reach the same end.
speaks_to: people who feel their understanding keeps slipping

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 120, chaupais 1-2 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-4), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 116: off by four.

rcm.7.116.chaupai.9.context: Just before this Kakbhushundi says, 'My faith is that Ram's servant is greater than Ram.' These two images explain why: the sea's water reaches the land only through clouds, and the sandal tree's scent spreads only on the breeze. The doha that follows says saints churn devotion's sweetness from the ocean of Brahman.
rcm.7.116.chaupai.9.core_teaching: The divine is like the sea or the sandal tree, but good people are the clouds and breeze that carry its sweetness to everyone. No one gains devotion without them.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Scripture says no one equals Ram, but a saint's tested experience also counts. Kakbhushundi states his own conviction that the servant is greater. He also separates 'dasa' (wholly given over) from 'sevaka' (one who serves but could leave).

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: The sea is deep, fixed, out of reach and salty; clouds draw out sweet water and rain it everywhere. So saints carry Ram's glory to all. Compare Bal Kand 36, where scripture is the ocean and saints the clouds.

rcm.7.116.chaupai.9.practical_reading: Used to honour the people who brought the sacred, or simply goodness, within reach: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend. They are the breeze that carried the scent.
misreadings: Not literally that humans outrank God; it is about how grace reaches people.
speaks_to: gratitude to a mentor, grandparent or teacher
those who serve as carriers of goodness

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 120, chaupai 9 (Manas Piyush half-lines 17-18), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 116: off by four.

rcm.7.117.chaupai.11.context: Just before this: the rise of the wicked brings the world misery, like the ill-omened comet Ketu. Here the rise of the good brings joy, and the answers on the highest virtue and the worst sin follow. Right after come the rebirths of slanderers (as frogs, crows, bats), and then the diseases of the mind.
rcm.7.117.chaupai.11.core_teaching: When good people rise, everyone gains, as the sun and moon serve the whole world. Non-harm is the highest duty, and slandering others the heaviest wrong.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: In power the wicked hurt the world; the rise of the good benefits all. Ahimsa, harming no creature, roots all yamas and niyamas. Slander joins lying to harm: destroying a reputation is like killing many times over.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi on nindā vs parivāda
commentaries.gist: Telling a true fault is parivada, and inventing one is ninda. Either becomes grave when done to wound, while pointing out a fault to help someone improve is not condemned.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Garuda asked which merit the Veda calls highest, and the answer matches his words: 'the Veda knows ahimsa as the highest dharma'.

rcm.7.117.chaupai.11.practical_reading: Used to rank wrongs plainly: gossip and character assassination are not small sins. Celebrate the success of good people, because it lifts everyone.
misreadings: Not a ban on honest criticism meant to help someone improve (the commentary makes this distinction).
cautions: The very next lines describe slanderers reborn as frogs and crows; keep that out of readings.
not_for: someone who has been slandered and needs comfort, not a lecture

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 121, chaupai 11 (Manas Piyush half-lines 21-22), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 117: off by four.

rcm.7.117.chaupai.15.context: This answers Garuda's last and most important question, what the diseases of the mind are. It opens an extended medical allegory: delusion is the root, desire, greed and anger are the three humours, and envy, possessiveness and the rest are skin and throat diseases. The cure comes after: Ram's grace, a true teacher as physician, and devotion as the medicine.
rcm.7.117.chaupai.15.core_teaching: Delusion is the root disease of the mind. From it come desire, greed and anger, which, like the body's three humours out of balance, burn and choke us, and together become a delirious fever.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Bodily diseases don't strike everyone, but mental ones afflict all people in some measure. That is why the verse says 'all people' suffer from them.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Mental diseases are rooted in delusion, bodily ones in 'prajnaparadha' (failed judgement, itself ignorance). Vata, pitta and kapha hold the body and cause disease only when unbalanced; desire, anger and greed do the same in the mind.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi (continued)
commentaries.gist: Desire is vata because vata alone moves and carries the other two wherever it goes, just as desire leads anger and greed.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Just as the three humours together make sannipata, desire, anger and greed together make a great sinner.

rcm.7.117.chaupai.15.practical_reading: A favourite text for a 'psychology of the Manas': treat craving, greed and anger as states that can be diagnosed and treated, not as fixed identity. Teachers like the medical framing because it removes shame.
misreadings: Not a statement about clinical mental illness; 'manas rog' here means moral and emotional afflictions, not depression or anxiety disorders.
Not medical advice.
cautions: Don't use it to suggest that a reader's diagnosed mental illness comes from desire, greed or anger.
not_for: someone with a mental health condition who may hear it as moral blame
speaks_to: people drawn to Ayurveda and psychology

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 121, chaupai 15 (Manas Piyush half-lines 29-30), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 117: off by four.

rcm.7.117.chaupai.17.context: This continues the 'diseases of the mind' allegory. Just before: the endless desires are countless kinds of colic. Just after: pride, deceit, hypocrisy and the like are further diseases, and the doha that follows says one disease can kill and these are many, so how can anyone find peace? The cure comes next.
rcm.7.117.chaupai.17.core_teaching: Possessiveness, envy, mood swings and the burn of others' happiness are diseases that eat at us from within, each matched to a physical illness.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Explains each disease medically. Ringworm is a red, itchy circle (counted among the minor kushthas). Scabies is many small itching, burning pustules. The difference is that ringworm forms a ring and scabies burns.

commentaries.who: Several commentators on 'गरह', in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Most read it as a throat disease such as goitre (Baijnath: from vata-kapha and bad water). Others read graha (possession, seizures), dysentery or gout. Vijayanand Tripathi lists the many grahas of Madhava Nidana.

rcm.7.117.chaupai.17.practical_reading: Used as a self-check list: possessiveness itches, envy burns, mood swings choke, and resentment of others' happiness wastes you. Each is named so it can be treated.
misreadings: Not a statement about people with these physical diseases; the diseases are metaphors.
cautions: Uses leprosy, tuberculosis and skin disease as images of moral fault; avoid with readers who have or care for someone with these illnesses, and avoid stigmatising language.
not_for: readers with chronic illness, especially skin disease, TB or leprosy
someone in a depressive low ('dejection as disease' may shame)

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 121, chaupai 17 (Manas Piyush half-lines 33-34), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 117: off by four.

rcm.7.117.chaupai.6.context: Garuda has asked seven questions. To the first, which body is best, Kakbhushundi answers that the human body is, sought even by moving and unmoving beings, because it can reach liberation and devotion. These lines describe those who waste it. Next come the answers on the greatest sorrow and joy.
rcm.7.117.chaupai.6.core_teaching: Spending a rare human life only on passing pleasures is like throwing away a philosopher's stone for a shard of glass.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Those who don't worship are dull. Those who also chase pleasures are duller still. Worship is the philosopher's stone and pleasures the shard of glass.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Swami, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: They become ever duller and slide toward animal and even inert births.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Seeking happiness, such a person chases the mere appearance of it through great hardship. Their mind clouds further each day until return seems impossible.

rcm.7.117.chaupai.6.practical_reading: Used as a wake-up line about priorities: don't trade what is precious (time, love, the chance to grow) for what glitters briefly.
misreadings: Not contempt for ordinary enjoyment; it is about trading the precious for the trivial.
cautions: Harsh judgement ('dull and duller'); could shame someone in addiction or depression.
not_for: someone in addiction recovery who needs compassion
a reader with low self-worth

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 121, chaupai 6 (Manas Piyush half-lines 11-12), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 117: off by four.

rcm.7.117.chaupai.7.context: These are Kakbhushundi's answers to Garuda's second, third and fourth questions: the greatest sorrow (poverty), the greatest joy (meeting the good), and the nature of saints (doing good in word, thought and deed). He goes on to the wicked, then the highest virtue and worst sin, then the diseases of the mind.
rcm.7.117.chaupai.7.core_teaching: Want is the hardest sorrow in this world and good company the greatest joy, and doing good in word, mind and body is simply what good people are like.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Many sorrows exist, but none like poverty: even a wife may leave the destitute. Kakbhushundi knew it, having gone to Ujjain poor in a famine. Cites sayings that a forest life beats poverty among relatives.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: In the world even the smallest comfort costs money, so the poor suffer most. But some penniless renunciants are deeply happy. The real poverty is delusion ('moha daridra').

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Cold without clothes and hunger without food make one forget every other pain. Meeting saints is the greatest joy: other joys leave craving and end in pain, while this one is whole and good to the end.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Kakbhushundi speaks from experience: meeting one great saint brought him to this highest joy.

rcm.7.117.chaupai.7.practical_reading: Used to take material hardship seriously, without spiritualising it away, and to treasure good company as the best thing life offers.
misreadings: Not a claim that poor people can't be happy (Vijayanand Tripathi rejects that).
Not a reason to look down on the poor.
cautions: For a reader in financial hardship, 'no sorrow like poverty' can validate or deepen despair; pair with the joy-of-good-company half.
not_for: someone in acute financial crisis, unless the reading is careful and practical
speaks_to: loneliness and the value of good friends

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 121, chaupai 7 (Manas Piyush half-lines 13-14), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 117: off by four.

rcm.7.12.chaupai.1.context: Ram has met all the mothers, and Kaikeyi was visibly shrinking with shame when he met her (doha 6). Before going to his own palace, he goes to hers first and puts her at ease. Then he goes home, and Vasishtha orders preparations for the coronation.
rcm.7.12.chaupai.1.core_teaching: Ram goes first to the person who wronged him and is ashamed, and lifts her shame before he goes home himself.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: This shows the greatness of Ram's nature, as in Vinaya Patrika 100. Her shame pained him, so he went to her first to remove her guilt. He had seen it when he met her (doha 6).

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Four reasons: her shame; fine dharma (return to where exile began, showing the boon fulfilled); Bharat had shunned her; and Ram loved Kaikeyi more than his own mother before the exile, so he shows his love undiminished.

commentaries.who: Vinayak Rao's tika, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Quotes a Sanskrit verse for how he may have comforted her: you gave me only my own body to guard in the forest and your small son the whole earth, so your favour plainly fell on me.

rcm.7.12.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it for making the first move toward someone who hurt you and now can't face you. Ease their shame rather than make them earn forgiveness.
misreadings: Not a demand that victims comfort those who harmed them; Ram acts from strength, after the wrong is over and regretted.
cautions: Can feel like pressure on someone still being harmed; keep it to past wrongs and genuine remorse.
not_for: someone in an ongoing abusive relationship
someone not ready to forgive
speaks_to: reconciling with a family member who wronged you and is ashamed

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 10, chaupai 1 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-2), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 12: off by two.

rcm.7.121.doha.2.context: Garuda, his doubts gone, bows at Kakbhushundi's feet with love and returns to Vaikuntha with Ram in his heart. This doha is where Shiva closes the whole Garuda-Kakbhushundi frame. Then he tells Parvati how blessed she is to have heard the story.
rcm.7.121.doha.2.core_teaching: The company of good, wise people is the greatest gain, and it comes as grace, not as something we simply arrange.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: This closes the frame begun when Garuda went to Kakbhushundi. Garuda now bows to him as to a guru, though he came as king of birds and was honoured as one. His doubt is gone, so his mind is steady.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush footnote, citing Bhagavata Mahatmya 2.76
commentaries.gist: Satsang comes when merit gathered over many births ripens. It dispels the darkness of delusion and pride born of ignorance, and discernment dawns.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Keeping Raghubir in his heart' means Garuda now sees Ram as the supreme Self, where before he thought the lord of Vaikuntha the highest.

rcm.7.121.doha.2.practical_reading: Used to treasure the good people in one's life as gifts, not achievements, and to be grateful for meeting the right person at the right time.
misreadings: Not a reason to wait passively for good company; elsewhere the text urges seeking it out.
not_for: someone isolated, who may hear 'you lack grace'
speaks_to: gratitude for a mentor or friend
loneliness and the longing for good company

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 125 (second doha of the pair printed as ॥125॥), Gita Press / Manas Piyush. Our ref says 121: off by four.

rcm.7.126.chaupai.3.context: Each frame has closed: Shiva-Parvati, Yajnavalkya-Bharadwaj, Kakbhushundi-Garuda. Tulsidas now speaks in his own voice to sum up the work. He says that in the Kali age the one means left is remembering, singing and hearing of Ram, and that his own mind found peace this way. The closing prayers and the phalashruti follow.
rcm.7.126.chaupai.3.core_teaching: In a hard age, when elaborate disciplines are out of reach, the simplest means are enough: remember Ram, sing of him and keep hearing his story.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Tulsidas now closes his own dialogue. In Kali, short lives, weak minds, illness and scarce means make yoga, sacrifice, ritual japa, tapas and vows impractical. Cites Bhagavata 1.1.10 and 1.2.14: hear, sing, meditate on and worship the Lord.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: No one can change the season, but in summer one can shelter with khus screens and fans. Remembering Ram is such a shelter in the scorching age of Kali, where living among the wicked makes dharma hard to keep.

commentaries.who: Pande ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Fit the practice to the situation: alone, remember; with good company, sing together; with a good speaker, listen. Say the name aloud, since silent remembrance alone is not enough in this age.

rcm.7.126.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Used to make practice light and possible in a busy life: a name remembered, a song, a story heard is enough to begin.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of ethics or of other paths; it is about what is feasible.
cautions: Devotional and Ram-specific; for a non-devotional reader, frame it as simple practices that keep the mind steady.
not_for: readers who want a philosophical argument
speaks_to: people with no time for elaborate practice

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 130, chaupai 3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 5-6), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 126: off by four.
data_flags.attribution_note: Manas Piyush says plainly that from here on these are Tulsidas's own words, as he closes his own frame of the dialogue. So the speaker is Tulsidas and the listener the reader (his own mind). Our 'Shiva / Tulsidas → Parvati / the reader' should...

rcm.7.126.doha.1.context: Tulsidas has said his own mind found peace in Ram's story. As the poem closes he makes two last prayers in doha form. This is the first: he is the poorest of the poor and Ram the greatest friend of the poor, so let Ram remove his burden. The second asks that Ram be as dear to him as a lover is to the lustful and money to the greedy.
rcm.7.126.doha.1.core_teaching: Tulsidas stakes his whole claim on need, not merit: I am as helpless as anyone could be, and you are as kind to the helpless as anyone could be, so the match is made.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note, citing Vinaya Patrika 242
commentaries.gist: The same pairing runs through Vinaya Patrika: none is as poor as I, no friend of the poor like you; I am crooked and you remove crookedness; I am orphaned and you are the friend of orphans.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Of a work's four anubandhas, this doha states the relationship: a lowly devotee seeking refuge with the friend of the lowly. Only one free of becoming can rescue others from it, and even Brahma admits he is caught.

commentaries.who: Baijnath (continued)
commentaries.gist: Why claim only this relation and not master-servant or father-son? Because 'I can do no service; my only trust is your mercy'.

rcm.7.126.doha.1.practical_reading: A prayer for low moments: you don't have to be worthy to ask. Your need itself is the qualification.
misreadings: Not self-hatred; it is humility used as a claim on grace.
not_for: someone with very low self-worth who might take 'none as poor as I' literally
speaks_to: praying when you have nothing to offer

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 130 (ka), Gita Press / Manas Piyush. Our ref says 126: off by four.

rcm.7.126.doha.2.context: This is the last doha of the Manas, the second of Tulsidas's two closing prayers. Only the closing Sanskrit shlokas and the phalashruti follow. It borrows the two strongest human cravings as the measure of the love he asks for.
rcm.7.126.doha.2.core_teaching: Tulsidas asks to love God with the same effortless, all-consuming pull that lust and greed exert, turning the strongest cravings into the measure of devotion.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Compare Vinaya Patrika 269, with five such loves (water to fish, wealth to the greedy, lover to lover...). The craving lover needs no technique: the beloved fills his mind sleeping and waking, and he gives up everything.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note on Tulsidas's life
commentaries.gist: Cites the tradition (Mul Charit) that Tulsidas himself knew this attachment to his wife before renunciation, as Bilvamangala did. He prays that the same intensity now turn toward Ram.

commentaries.who: Pande ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The direct address suggests Ram appeared to Tulsidas at the end of the work.

rcm.7.126.doha.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say: you already know how to love intensely, so point that capacity at what is highest. It is a frank, unpious picture of devotion.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of lust or greed; they are measures of intensity.
Not a view of women as objects, though the gendered image reflects its era.
cautions: The image is gendered (a woman as the object of a lustful man). Some readers will find it jarring; consider a gender-neutral paraphrase ('as a lover is to one who desires').
not_for: readers sensitive to gendered imagery, without reframing
someone struggling with addiction (craving as a model may be unhelpful)
speaks_to: wanting a deeper, more natural devotion

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 130 (kha), Gita Press / Manas Piyush. The last doha of the poem (only closing Sanskrit shlokas follow). Our ref says 126: off by four.

rcm.7.20.chaupai.2.context: After the coronation Ram sends the monkeys home with gifts. Angad stays behind and pleads. He reminds Ram that his dying father Bali put him in Ram's lap. He has nowhere to go, since Sugriva, his father's killer's ally, now rules, and he is a boy without knowledge, wisdom or strength. Ram embraces him with tears in his eyes and still sends him home with honour, and Angad goes, looking back again and again.
rcm.7.20.chaupai.2.core_teaching: A fatherless young man begs not to be sent away and asks Ram to be the father, mother and teacher he has lost. It shows complete dependence offered in trust.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Angad's epithets fit his plea: all-knowing, ocean of mercy, friend of the afflicted. Dying Bali 'put me in your lap', so Ram is now his father. 'Remember your vow': abandoning me would break your name as refuge.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He calls himself 'deen' (helpless) because his father is dead.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Behind the plea is fear of Sugriva. Angad sees no one who would look after his welfare, so he appeals to Ram as refuge of the refugeless.

commentaries.who: Vir Kavi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Angad never says outright that Sugriva's line will rule and he is unsafe there. He says it indirectly through 'don't abandon me' (paryayokti).

rcm.7.20.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Applied to anyone who has lost a parent and attaches deeply to a mentor or protector, and to the courage of asking plainly, 'please don't send me away.'
misreadings: Not a promise that one will never be sent away; in the story Ram lovingly sends Angad home anyway.
cautions: Mentions a father's death; Angad's father was killed by Ram himself (Kishkindha Kand). Avoid making it a lesson for a newly bereaved child about replacing a parent.
not_for: someone in a dependent relationship that is harmful
a newly bereaved child, without care
speaks_to: clinging to a mentor at a transition

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 18, chaupai 2 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-4), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 20: off by two.

rcm.7.22.chaupai.2.context: After the monkeys have left, Ram bids farewell to Guha, chief of the Nishad boatmen at Shringaverapura, who helped him into exile. He gives him clothes and ornaments and asks him to keep his mind on Ram. Guha weeps at his feet, then goes home and tells his family about Ram's nature.
rcm.7.22.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Ram calls a man of low caste in that society his friend and a brother equal to Bharat, and invites him to keep coming to the royal city: love that ignores rank.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram says 'coming' (meeting) before 'going' (parting). He calls Guha friend and brother, words for an equal, though no one could truly be the Lord's equal. That is how the Lord honours those who love him.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram had already embraced Guha like Bharat (Lanka 120). Guha's joy is at being called friend and brother and invited to the city, said to no monkey. He falls at Ram's feet to say he is only a servant.

rcm.7.22.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Used against caste and class distance: call people by the bond, not the rank, and keep the door open after the crisis is over.
cautions: Manas Piyush's surrounding commentary mentions the Nishad community's 'lower' dharma (they kill animals). Keep caste language out of any reading.
speaks_to: staying in touch after a shared hard time

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 20, chaupai 2 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-4), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 22: off by two.

rcm.7.3.chaupai.1.context: The Uttar Kand opens on the last day of Ram's fourteen-year exile. Ayodhya is anxious, and Bharat in Nandigram has had good omens but no news. He wonders why Ram has not come and whether Ram has forgotten him as crooked. He then envies Lakshman, who was allowed to go along. Just as he is sinking, Hanuman arrives in a Brahmin's form.
rcm.7.3.chaupai.1.core_teaching: At the very edge of a long wait, the faithful heart turns its fear on itself: 'he hasn't come because I am unworthy.' The poem treats this self-doubt with tenderness and answers it at once with Hanuman's arrival.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush (Gita Press)
commentaries.gist: 'Prop' means Bharat cannot live past the deadline, as he says himself a little later. Joy at the omens and grief rise in one mind together. The grief is 'shoreless' because the poet will soon call separation an ocean.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: If Ram fails to come, Bharat's oath before Kaushalya, Dasharath's praise of him and the townspeople's trust would all turn false, and Lakshman's and Guha's old suspicions would seem justified.

rcm.7.3.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers read it as the voice of long waiting, which ends up blaming itself ('they've forgotten me because I'm not good enough'), and as a reminder that this fear is often untrue.
misreadings: Not evidence that Bharat really was crooked; the whole poem presents him as the purest devotee.
Not a promise that every wait ends well on the last day.
cautions: Bharat's life is tied to the deadline: he says he could not live past it, and Manas Piyush cites the Adhyatma Ramayana, where he was ready to enter fire. For a reader in despair, avoid any reading that links waiting and dying.
not_for: a reader with thoughts of ending their life
someone whose person is not coming back (bereavement), unless carefully framed
speaks_to: long waits for someone to come home
the last stretch of a hard period

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 1, chaupai 1 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-2): the first chaupai after the opening doha, Gita Press numbering. Our id/ref say doha 3: off by two.

rcm.7.3.doha.1.context: This closes the opening passage of Bharat's despair on the last day of the exile. Hanuman, sent ahead by Ram (Lanka Kand), arrives in a Brahmin's form just as Bharat is going under. Bharat is overjoyed and asks who he is, and Hanuman gives him the news.
rcm.7.3.doha.1.core_teaching: Rescue comes as a messenger at the moment of sinking. The poem uses the image of the ocean of separation and the ship to show grace arriving in time.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The mind sinks because the sea of separation has no shore. Hanuman comes as the ship. As son of the wind he arrives at wind's speed, and he once saved Sita in the same way from her sea of separation.

commentaries.who: Gaud ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: For fourteen years Bharat's mind was nearly drowned. Hope of the deadline was the plank keeping him afloat, and just as that plank slipped from his hands the ship appeared.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Kaushalya had asked Ram to come back before the deadline so the 'fish' (loved ones) would survive the drying 'water' (the term). Ram did so by sending Hanuman a day early. Bharat, who loved most, was sinking first.

rcm.7.3.doha.1.practical_reading: A picture of help arriving at the lowest point, used to say: hold on a little longer, and notice who comes. A footnote cited in Manas Piyush (Adhyatma Ramayana) has Bharat preparing to die that evening.
misreadings: Narrative of an event, not a guarantee that rescue always arrives in time.
cautions: The cited Adhyatma Ramayana parallel has Bharat preparing to enter fire if Ram does not come. Keep that detail out of readings for someone in despair.
not_for: someone whose rescue did not come (loss, failed waiting), where it can sound like a reproach
speaks_to: being at the end of one's strength
receiving news or help just in time

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 1 (ka), Gita Press / Manas Piyush. Our ref says doha 3: off by two.

rcm.7.39.chaupai.4.context: In the royal garden Bharat, after an apology for being forward, asks Ram to explain how good and bad people differ. Ram begins with this image. The doha that follows completes it: sandal is honoured on the gods' heads, while the axe is heated in fire and hammered. Then come the marks of the good (doha 38) and of the wicked (doha 39 onward).
rcm.7.39.chaupai.4.core_teaching: A good person keeps their own nature even toward someone who harms them, like sandalwood perfuming the axe that cuts it. The next doha makes clear that each nature reaps its own reward.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The wicked insult everyone, saints included. Saints give happiness to everyone, the wicked included. Cross-refers to Sundar Kand 41: a saint's greatness is doing good even to one who does harm.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Answers the objection that the axe doesn't actually become good. The saint's forbearance may later bring the wrongdoer remorse and reform. And either way giving is the saint's work, receiving the other's.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note (second)
commentaries.gist: The saint's 'own quality' is that even when robbed of everything he holds no enmity and prays for the wrongdoer's good sense. He forgives even when harmed.

commentaries.who: Nange Paramhans (and Vir Kavi), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The forgiving saint is honoured even by the honourable. The axe is heated and hammered: harm-doers are punished by the anger of rulers. Vir Kavi notes one is worshipped and one punished.

rcm.7.39.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it for not letting someone else's cruelty change who you are, and for answering harm without becoming harmful. Our misuse note (kindness is not staying within reach of the axe) is well placed.
misreadings: Not advice to stay in harm's way or keep exposing yourself to an abuser.
Not a claim that forgiveness obliges reconciliation.
Not 'if you were truly good you wouldn't mind being hurt'.
cautions: Can be heard as telling victims to endure. Pair with the existing misuse line and with the next doha, where the axe is punished.
not_for: someone currently being abused or bullied who needs to get out
someone who would read it as 'don't complain'
speaks_to: being wronged and wanting to stay decent

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 37, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 39: off by two. Growse's translation places the sandalwood lines just before his 'Doha 38' (sandal on the gods' heads, axe heated and hammered), so even his numbering differs from ours.

rcm.7.4.chaupai.6.context: Hanuman, in a Brahmin's form, has told Bharat that Ram is safe and on his way. Bharat embraces him, and tears flow. These lines are his response. He then asks Hanuman to tell him Ram's story, and next asks whether Ram ever remembers him.
rcm.7.4.chaupai.6.core_teaching: Good news brought at the right moment is a gift beyond any return, and meeting the messenger feels like meeting the beloved.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Meeting Hanuman feels like meeting Ram, so all sorrow ends: meeting a holy person gives the joy of meeting the Lord. 'What can I give you' means nothing in the world matches this news.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush note, citing the Adhyatma Ramayana
commentaries.gist: Parallel: Bharat embraces Maruti, who brings welcome words, and bathes him in tears of joy. Ram once told Hanuman the same, that he could never repay him.

commentaries.who: Ramayan Pradip, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'All sorrows' are the near-delirious laments of the passage just before (why hasn't he come, Lakshman is lucky). Here they are said to be gone in Bharat's own voice.

rcm.7.4.chaupai.6.practical_reading: Teachers use it for gratitude toward people who bring relief: say plainly that you can't repay them, and let them know what their news meant.
misreadings: Not literally 'Hanuman is Ram'; it describes how the messenger's presence felt.
not_for: someone still waiting with no news
speaks_to: gratitude to a messenger or helper

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 2, chaupais 6-7 (Manas Piyush half-lines 11-14), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 4 chaupai 6: off by two, and the text spans two Gita Press chaupais.
data_flags.translation_note: One error. 'बार बार बूझी कुसलाता' means Bharat asked Hanuman again and again about everyone's welfare. Manas Piyush explains this as love, or asking after Ram, Sita, Lakshman and the army one by one. Our 'He asked again and again after everyone's welfare' reads as...

rcm.7.4.chaupai.8.context: Bharat has said he can never repay Hanuman and asked to hear Ram's deeds. Hanuman bows and tells the whole story. Bharat's one question in response is whether Ram ever remembers him as his servant. In the doha that follows Hanuman tells him he is dear to Ram as life, and Bharat embraces him again and again.
rcm.7.4.chaupai.8.core_teaching: After hearing of all Ram's glory, Bharat wants to know only one thing: whether he himself is remembered. It is the humblest and most human question in the scene.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Hanuman bows because Bharat said he could never repay him: 'don't say that, I am your servant.' Ram once said the same to Hanuman, who fell at his feet then too.

commentaries.who: Gaud ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Hanuman surely mentioned Ram's words to Vibhishan about Bharat ('each moment like an age'). That shows a brother's love, but Bharat worships as a servant, so it doesn't satisfy him and he asks whether Ram remembers him as a servant.

commentaries.who: Manas Mayank, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Hanuman puts his head on Bharat's feet to say that his own being is made of this devotion, and that he will tell Ram's story with love, by the power of those feet.

rcm.7.4.chaupai.8.practical_reading: Used to name the ache of 'do they ever think of me?' when someone you love is far away or long silent, and to treat asking as honest, not needy.
misreadings: Not insecurity to be corrected; the commentators treat it as the refinement of devotion.
not_for: someone who has been abandoned in fact, where the answer may be no
speaks_to: wondering whether you matter to someone far away
long-distance relationships, parents of grown children abroad

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 2, chaupai 8 (Manas Piyush half-lines 15-16), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 4: off by two.

rcm.7.40.chaupai.1.context: Right after the sandalwood-and-axe image (doha 37), Ram starts listing the marks of the good. These are the first lines. The list goes on with a soft heart, kindness to the poor, honouring others while seeking no honour, and ends at doha 38 with 'they are dear to me as life'.
rcm.7.40.chaupai.1.core_teaching: The first marks of a good person: not driven by pleasures, rich in character, feeling others' sorrow and joy as their own, even-minded and without enmity, free of greed, resentment, excitement and fear.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Even when pleasures come, their mind isn't snared, because they are a mine of good character. Feeling others' joys and sorrows as their own comes from equanimity, which comes from having no enemy, and that from having no pride.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Others' sorrow is their sorrow' means their own troubles don't distress them, only other people's. He cites the Bhaktamal story of Kevalram, on whose body welts rose when an ox was beaten.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note, citing Gita 12.15 and 12.18
commentaries.gist: 'Enemyless' and 'free of elation, resentment and fear' echo the Gita's devotee who neither disturbs the world nor is disturbed by it, and stays even in honour and dishonour.

rcm.7.40.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Teachers use 'others' sorrow as one's own, others' joy as one's own' as a test of character: can you be glad, not envious, at a friend's success?
misreadings: Not a call to feel nothing about one's own pain; commentators describe an ideal, not a rule for the hurting.
cautions: An ideal portrait; a reader who feels they fall short may hear it as judgement.
not_for: someone already overwhelmed by others' pain (compassion fatigue), without framing
speaks_to: envy at others' success (as its antidote)

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 38, chaupai 1 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-2), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 40: off by two.

rcm.7.40.chaupai.4.context: This closes Ram's list of the marks of the good (doha 38). Immediately after (doha 39) he turns to the nature of the wicked and warns never to keep their company even by mistake.
rcm.7.40.chaupai.4.core_teaching: A truly good person stays steady in self-control and right conduct, never speaks harshly, and is unmoved by praise or blame. Such people are as dear to Ram as life.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Mind the word 'all': if any of these marks is missing, the person is not yet a true saint. Up to 'ye sab lacchan' the path of withdrawal is described, and from here the path of action.

commentaries.who: Manas Mayank, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Like Ganga water, which makes whatever vessel holds it a Ganga-vessel, gold or clay, whoever has these marks is a saint, whatever family they were born in.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram's list covers three kinds of saint. The devotee is described up to 'dear as life like Bharat', the knower up to 'truly a saint', and the karma-yogi from 'shama dama niyama niti' to 'temples of virtue'.

commentaries.who: Karunasindhu, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Shama: gathering mind, intellect, memory and ego onto God. Dama: mastering the ten senses.

rcm.7.40.chaupai.4.practical_reading: 'Never speak a harsh word' and 'take praise and blame alike' are applied to daily speech and to working life: let neither applause nor criticism knock you off course.
misreadings: Not a ban on honest disagreement or firm truth; 'harsh' means wounding speech.
Not an endorsement of caste or birth as the measure of goodness (Manas Mayank explicitly rejects that).
cautions: A demanding ideal; a self-critical reader may feel judged.
not_for: someone who has just been publicly shamed and needs comfort first

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 38, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8) and doha 38, Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 40: off by two.

rcm.7.41.chaupai.2.context: Having described the good, Ram turns to the wicked. He first warns never to keep their company even by mistake, because they ruin the innocent the way an unruly cow leads a gentle one into trouble. Then come these lines on envy and the love of gossip, followed by more marks: lust, anger, causeless enmity, and harming even those who help them.
rcm.7.41.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Envy is an inner fire: it burns at others' good fortune and feeds on hearing others slandered, the exact opposite of the good person who is glad at others' joy.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The heat is 'in the heart': they may look cool outside while burning within. They are the reverse of the saint, burning at others' wealth and happy at others' misfortune.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: 'Wherever they hear' means they go looking for gossip. Slander is the worst sin (Uttar 121), so it is rarely voiced, and these seek it out. Gossip is their livelihood; slander found by chance is 'treasure on the road'.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Answering 'why avoid them if I don't harm them?': their company itself brings harm, like the gentle kapila cow that gets beaten for following the raiding cow into a field.

rcm.7.41.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Used as a mirror more than a weapon: notice the small burn at a colleague's success, and the pleasure of hearing someone criticised. It is also used for choosing company carefully.
misreadings: Not licence to label people 'khal' and write them off; teachers read it mostly as self-examination.
Not a rule against all criticism; it targets relish in running others down.
cautions: Strong judgemental language about 'the wicked'; for a reader who feels envy, frame it as a feeling to notice, not an identity.
not_for: someone already labelled or scapegoated by others
speaks_to: gossip at work or in family groups
understanding why someone resents your success

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 39, chaupai 2 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-4), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 41: off by two.

rcm.7.43.chaupai.1.context: Ram has finished describing the good and the wicked and says such people are found in the Dvapara and Kali ages. Here he sums it up in one line. He goes on to say that those who cause pain while in a human body suffer greatly in the round of births, and that the wise therefore worship him.
rcm.7.43.chaupai.1.core_teaching: All scripture comes down to this: helping others is the highest dharma, and hurting others the lowest wrong.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Sums up the two portraits: doing good marks the saint, causing pain the wicked. 'Verdict of all scriptures' echoes the saying that Vyasa's two words in eighteen Puranas are: helping others brings merit, hurting others sin.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani (continued)
commentaries.gist: Causing pain while in a human body, which holds the treasury of knowledge, brings the 'great' suffering of birth and death. Those without such knowledge get ordinary suffering.

commentaries.who: Ramayan Pradip, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Great crowd of becoming': being born and dying again and again with no release, or being crushed by the burden of supporting a family.

rcm.7.43.chaupai.1.practical_reading: One of the most-quoted lines of the Manas, used as a one-line ethic: before acting, ask whether it helps or hurts someone.
misreadings: Not a call to neglect oneself for others.
cautions: The following lines speak of the suffering of rebirth for those who cause pain; leave that out for readers who fear punishment.
not_for: a caregiver already sacrificing themselves to exhaustion
speaks_to: guilt about having hurt someone (as a way forward)

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 41, chaupai 1 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-2; Manas Piyush itself cross-cites it as '41.1'), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 43: off by two.

rcm.7.45.chaupai.3.context: King Ram calls the citizens, Brahmins and gurus together. He says he speaks without any sense of ownership or royal authority: listen, and act only if it appeals to you. In these lines he adds that whoever follows his counsel is dearest, and that if he says anything wrong they should fearlessly stop him. He then teaches the value of the human body and the ease of devotion.
rcm.7.45.chaupai.3.core_teaching: The ideal ruler invites correction: even the king's words are to be checked against what is right, and citizens should stop him without fear if he goes wrong.

commentaries.who: Gaud ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram speaks as a fellow citizen, not king. 'Anushasan' is guidance, not a command. Those who follow it are dearest, those who don't are not unloved, and those who fearlessly stop him when he errs are dear too.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He addresses the 'townspeople' rather than 'the assembly' because gurus and Brahmins are present, and lecturing them would be unseemly. 'Purajan' takes in everyone gracefully.

commentaries.who: Baba Jayramdas Deen (Manas Sandesh), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Without mamata' goes with his words: he has no insistence that they accept what he says just to please him. That does not mean his words will be against niti.

rcm.7.45.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Widely used for leadership: a good leader asks to be corrected, and the people around them should feel safe saying 'this is wrong'. It applies to parents, managers and teachers.
misreadings: Not a licence for disrespect; the correction is limited to injustice.
speaks_to: building a culture where people can disagree

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 43, chaupai 3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 5-6), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 45: off by two.

rcm.7.46.chaupai.3.context: In his address to the citizens, Ram has said the human body is hard to win, even for gods. Just before this he says the immortal soul wanders through 8.4 million forms. Here he describes the human body as a boat with everything needed to cross. Next he says that one who fails to cross with all this is ungrateful and a self-killer.
rcm.7.46.chaupai.3.core_teaching: A human life is a rare gift of grace, and it comes with everything needed: the body as a boat, grace as a following wind, a true teacher at the helm. Use it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Time, karma, gunas, nature and maya keep the soul cycling through the four kinds of birth. The soul doesn't die, but it feels the pain of each birth and death.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Sometimes, out of compassion' doesn't mean God is usually unkind. Devotees credit every good thing to grace and every lapse to themselves.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note, citing Pancharatra and Gita 9.4-5
commentaries.gist: 'Sometimes' means grace can come at any point in the cycle. No one earns a human birth by karma. God is a friend 'without reason' because nothing we do can benefit him.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Other bodies only use up merit and sin and cannot break maya's ring. Only the human body can strive. So the causeless friend's gift of it is the one way out.

rcm.7.46.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Teachers use the boat image as a call to purpose: you already have the vessel, the help and the guidance, so don't waste the voyage. It can also be gently encouraging: you were given this life for a reason.
misreadings: Not a claim that other creatures are worthless.
Not a threat; the tone is gift, not guilt.
cautions: Assumes rebirth and 8.4 million births; the next lines call those who waste it 'self-killers', a word to avoid with a reader at risk.
not_for: a reader with thoughts of self-harm, if the next lines ('self-slayer') are brought in

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 44, chaupais 3-4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 5-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 46: off by two.

rcm.7.48.chaupai.1.context: Ram has told the citizens that devotion is the easy, joyful path, reached through honouring Brahmins, good company and worship of Shiva. Here he asks what labour it involves and answers: none of the hard practices, only a straight nature and contentment. Next he warns against hoping in men and describes the devotee who wins him.
rcm.7.48.chaupai.1.core_teaching: The path of devotion needs no heroic disciplines, only honesty of heart and contentment with what comes.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Yoga means the eight-limbed discipline, sacrifice means expense and labour, fasts and austerity mean bodily hardship, and devotion needs none of these. 'Simple nature' means no guile: inside and outside alike, words and deeds alike.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note, citing Bhagavata 7.6.19
commentaries.gist: Prahlad tells the demon boys the same: pleasing God takes no great effort, since he is the Self of all and present everywhere.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani (continued), citing Bhagavata 3.27.8
commentaries.gist: Contentment with whatever comes follows from trust: one who remembers him simply is looked after, so be satisfied with what he gives.

rcm.7.48.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Used to lift spiritual perfectionism: you don't need elaborate routines, just honesty, kindness and contentment.
misreadings: Not 'effort is pointless' in life generally; it is about how devotion is reached.
Contentment is not resignation to injustice or to a harmful situation.
not_for: someone whose discontent is a fair response to injustice or deprivation

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 46, chaupai 1 (Manas Piyush half-lines 1-2), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 48: off by two.

rcm.7.48.chaupai.2.context: Directly follows 'what labour does devotion take?' Ram says that one who calls himself Ram's servant yet pins his hopes on people has no real trust, and that he is won by this conduct. Next comes the portrait of the person without grudges, cravings or fears.
rcm.7.48.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Trust that is real rests its final hope on God, not on human patrons. That inward reliance, more than any practice, is what wins Ram.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: This explains contentment: one who leaves Ram to hope in men hasn't treated Ram even as a man, so how is he a devotee? Cites a verse: why fret over food and clothes when the world's sustainer won't neglect you?

commentaries.who: Karunasindhu and Baijnath (footnote), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Read 'nar' as human patrons (kings and the like), or as hoping the way worldly people hope for pleasures. Either way it cancels the trust implied by servanthood.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani on the next line
commentaries.gist: Those enslaved to hope become everyone's slaves. Those whose only hope is the Lord are his servants and dear to him (cites Vinaya Patrika).

rcm.7.48.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to over-dependence on approval, patrons or a single person: put your final weight on something steadier. Our misuse note is apt.
misreadings: Not 'never accept help'; it concerns where the heart's final reliance rests (our existing misuse note is good).
Not a reason to stop acting or to stay in a bad situation.
cautions: Can sound like a reproach to someone who has just leaned on others in a crisis.
not_for: someone who needs to be encouraged to ask for help (e.g. in depression or crisis)

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 46, chaupai 2 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-4), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 48: off by two.

rcm.7.48.chaupai.3.context: Ram has said he is won by simple trust and contentment. Now he describes the devotee in detail: no grudges or quarrels, no hope or fear, every direction joyful. In the next lines this devotee loves good company, counts heaven and liberation as straw, and holds to devotion.
rcm.7.48.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Someone who holds no grudges, picks no fights, and is free of both craving and fear finds every direction full of joy.

commentaries.who: Karunasindhu and Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Vair is a deep grudge held in the mind, always watching for a chance to hurt. Vigraha is an ordinary quarrel that soon passes. The devotee has neither.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Slaves of hope are everyone's slaves. One whose only hope is the Lord is his true servant. With no hope or fear from anyone, every direction becomes joy.
