commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, collecting several commentators on 'anarambha aniketa'
commentaries.gist: Pandit Ramkumar: starts no worldly entanglement, builds no house. Baijnath: claims no doership, lets things happen as Hari wills. Prajnananand Swami: begins no desire-driven action. Ram Vallabhasharan: both words mean freedom from attachment.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, citing B. G. Tilak on Gita 12.16-19
commentaries.gist: 'Sarvarambha-parityagi' and 'aniketa' don't mean leaving home and work. They mean giving up actions done for desired fruits and having no mind trapped in house and family. This fits a householder.

rcm.7.48.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Used as a picture of inner freedom: drop the grudge, stop the fight, loosen craving and fear, and the world opens up.
misreadings: Not a call to quit work or leave home (the commentary explicitly rejects that reading).
Not 'never stand up for yourself'.
not_for: someone currently in danger who needs fear as a signal

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 46, chaupai 3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 5-6), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 48: off by two.

rcm.7.6.chaupai.2.context: The Pushpak is coming down over Ayodhya. Ram tells Angad and Vibhishan how holy and lovely the city is. These lines say it is dearer to him than Vaikuntha, and that bathing in the Sarayu brings people near him. Then the plane lands and the townspeople run out.
rcm.7.6.chaupai.2.core_teaching: The Lord himself says his birthplace is dearer to him than heaven, a strong statement of love for home and of the sacredness of a particular place.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Vaikuntha is famous in both scripture and the world, yet Ayodhya is dearer: Vaikuntha surpasses the three worlds and Ayodhya surpasses Vaikuntha. 'Few know this secret' marks it as a mystery.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Ram doesn't say Vaikuntha is his own realm. 'Vaikuntha' can mean any imperishable divine abode, so sects shouldn't fight over the word. Devotees of Saket may read it in their own way.

rcm.7.6.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Used for the pull of home and roots: even with somewhere 'better' on offer, the place you come from holds you. Also for coming home after long absence.
misreadings: Not a political claim about any modern site; it is about devotion and belonging.
cautions: The Ayodhya birthplace theme is politically charged in India today; keep the reading on home and belonging, not on any dispute.
not_for: someone who cannot go home or has lost a home (displacement), without care
speaks_to: loving an ordinary place more than any famous one

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 4, chaupais 2-3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-6), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 6: off by two.

rcm.7.61.chaupai.2.context: Garuda freed Ram from the serpent-noose in battle and then began to doubt how a God could be bound. Narada and Brahma sent him on. He comes to Shiva, who is on his way to Kubera. Shiva answers him lovingly: a passing talk can't settle such doubt, only long satsang can. He sends him to the crow-sage Kakbhushundi, where Ram's story is told every day.
rcm.7.61.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Deep doubt isn't cured by a quick answer from an authority. It dissolves slowly through long time spent among good people and in hearing what is true.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Shiva speaks with love because Garuda came humbly and with reverence, as to a guru, unlike before. 'All doubts' means getting rid of some of them would not be enough.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Seeing Garuda's humility, his standing as Hari's attendant and his great distress, Shiva teaches lovingly. This is how one should speak to and teach someone who is suffering.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Garuda is learned in the Vedas, and a scholar's doubt is not easy to remove. That is why Shiva prescribes long satsang.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Narada said the same: delusion about God does not go quickly. One must hear the Lord's story from saints for a long time. The compiler adds that the youth of today should take this lesson.

rcm.7.61.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Used for patience with one's own questions. Doubts about faith or life rarely end in one conversation; stay in good company and keep listening.
misreadings: Not a brush-off or a refusal to engage with doubt; Shiva answers with love and sends Garuda where he can be helped.
not_for: someone who needs an urgent practical answer

rcm.7.68.chaupai.6.context: Kakbhushundi has told Garuda the whole Ram story, and Garuda's doubt is gone. He says that seeing Ram's very human deeds (being bound by the serpent-noose) gave him great doubt. Now he counts that confusion as a blessing, because it brought him here. Kakbhushundi, delighted, replies that no one is untouched by delusion.
rcm.7.68.chaupai.6.core_teaching: The confusion that drove us to seek help can, looking back, be the grace that brought us to the right person. Only someone who has burned in the sun knows what shade is worth.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: How is being thrown into delusion grace? Someone in a cooled room doesn't know the joy of a tree's shade, but someone scorched and sweating does. Only one in anguish over the world tastes the joy of satsang.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Only the one who has been in error knows the special joy of the company that removes it.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram's deeds usually show a glimpse of divinity, but where they look wholly human, as in the serpent-noose episode, even the great are confused: Uma at Sita's loss, Garuda here.

commentaries.who: Vir Kavi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Accepting a fault as good because of what it led to is the figure 'anujna'. The shade image is drawn from direct experience ('pratyaksha pramana').

rcm.7.68.chaupai.6.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to hard seasons in hindsight: the crisis that pushed you to a mentor, a friend or therapy can be counted as part of the gift. The verse speaks after relief has come.
misreadings: Not a claim that suffering is good in itself or should be sought.
Not something to tell someone while they are still in the heat.
cautions: 'Your pain is a blessing' lands badly on someone in the middle of pain; this is the voice of someone already relieved.
not_for: someone currently suffering
fresh grief
trauma survivors who could hear it as 'it happened for a reason'
speaks_to: looking back on a crisis that led somewhere good
having been confused or lost and found guidance

rcm.7.69.chaupai.4.context: Garuda has confessed his delusion and is ashamed. Kakbhushundi says that's no wonder: Narada, Shiva, Brahma and the Sanaka sages, leaders among sages and knowers of the Self, were all blinded at some point. These lines widen it to the whole world. The list goes on with pride, youth, possessiveness, envy, grief and worry (next verse) and ends: this is maya's army.
rcm.7.69.chaupai.4.core_teaching: No one is beyond delusion, desire, craving and anger, not even the greatest sages. So being caught by them is human, not a special disgrace.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Kakbhushundi first reassures Garuda and only then teaches. Delight makes teaching take root, while scolding first leaves the listener downcast and deaf to it.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Naming Narada and the others shows all fell to delusion, e.g. Brahma at Ravana's death and in the calf-stealing episode. The list starts with moha because moha is the topic and the root of all the 'diseases'.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush footnote
commentaries.gist: The four sages and four afflictions pair in order: Narada and delusion, Shiva and desire (at Mohini's form), and so on.

rcm.7.69.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Used to take the shame out of failing: the wisest people have been blinded, driven, maddened and burned by these same forces. Self-compassion comes first, then the work.
misreadings: Not an excuse ('everyone does it, so it doesn't matter'); it reassures and then leads to the remedy (grace and devotion).
not_for: someone who has harmed others and needs accountability, not reassurance
speaks_to: shame after losing one's temper or giving in to craving

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 70, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 69: off by one.

rcm.7.7.chaupai.4.context: Ram's Pushpak has landed. He has bowed to Vasishtha and the Brahmins. Bharat then grips Ram's feet and lies flat on the ground and will not be lifted. Ram pulls him up into an embrace. Shiva then says no words can describe their meeting.
rcm.7.7.chaupai.4.core_teaching: The one who blamed himself for fourteen years throws himself down as a servant, and Ram will not leave him there: he forcibly lifts him into an embrace as an equal and a brother.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Bharat won't rise because he is lost in love. Compare Hanuman at Ram's feet in Sundar Kand. When lifting fails, Ram uses force. Bharat falls as a servant and Ram lifts him as master and brother.

commentaries.who: Manas Mayank, cited in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Bharat crossed the ocean of the deadline by leaning on Ram's sandals. Now that the feet themselves have come, how could he let go of his life's support?

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The scene is human and tender (madhurya), but the poet adds an epithet of majesty to the feet ('which gods, sages, Shiva and Brahma bow to') to show how fortunate Bharat is.

rcm.7.7.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers apply it to reconciliation: when someone who blames themselves comes to you in shame, don't leave them on the floor. Lift them up and hold them.
misreadings: Not about Bharat's guilt being real; the poem holds him blameless.
not_for: someone whose reconciliation was refused
speaks_to: shame and self-blame met with acceptance

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 5, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 7: off by two.

rcm.7.7.chhand.2.context: Directly after Ram lifts Bharat and embraces him. Ram asks how he is, and Bharat cannot answer at once. Shiva tells Parvati that this joy lies beyond words and mind. Bharat then says he is well now: Ram saw his distress and pulled him out as he drowned. Ram then embraces Shatrughna and the others.
rcm.7.7.chhand.2.core_teaching: Some joy can't be described, only known by the one who feels it. For Bharat, 'how are you?' can only be answered as 'well now, because you came and pulled me out'.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Love chokes the throat, so words come late. The joy is beyond words (poets can't say it) and beyond mind (it can't reach it; cf. Ayodhya 241). Mind, intellect and ego dissolve in love.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram knows how hard the term was for Bharat. He had said he might not find him alive, and now he sees how wasted he is. So he asks quickly, but Bharat cannot answer quickly.

commentaries.who: Vinayak Rao's tika (Vi. Ti.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Compares Taittiriya Upanishad's 'from which words turn back with the mind'. Earlier Bharat's mind was tossed by doubts. Now, united with Ram after fourteen years, it is absorbed in a bliss like the yogi's.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The mind belongs to nature and keeps swinging between willing and doubting. When the soul leaves those movements behind, it touches a joy the mind can't hold.

rcm.7.7.chhand.2.practical_reading: Used for moments when relief or love leaves you speechless, and for the honest answer to 'how are you?' after a long ordeal: 'better now that you're here.'
cautions: Uses the image of drowning in longing; fine for reunion, but heavy for a reader still apart from someone.
not_for: someone whose loved one will not return

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 5, chhand 2 (Manas Piyush 'दोहा 5, छन्द (2)'), Gita Press numbering. Our ref says 7: off by two.

rcm.7.70.chaupai.2.context: This continues Kakbhushundi's list of what no one escapes. Just before it: the 'delirium' of the gunas, pride, the fever of youth, possessiveness. Just after: the woodworm of desires, the three cravings for children, wealth and fame, and the line 'all this is maya's family'. He then turns to what alone frees one: Ram's grace.
rcm.7.70.chaupai.2.core_teaching: Envy, grief, anxiety and illusion touch everyone. Naming them as universal forces, not personal failures, is the first comfort.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Grief shakes everyone and loosens patience and duty. Even steady men like Janaka and Dasharath were shaken, and the townspeople, Tara and Mandodari lost all composure in their grief.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note on worry
commentaries.gist: Worry burns the chest day and night; the worried are dead while alive. Quotes a saying: the pyre burns the dead, anxiety the living. A snakebite may be survived, but no one escapes the serpent of worry.

commentaries.who: Ramayan Pradip and Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Possessiveness destroys good name, and jealousy actively brings disgrace: people say 'he has so much and is still like this'. Baijnath: fame comes from caring for the highest, and possessiveness is self-interest.

rcm.7.70.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Used to normalise anxiety and grief: they shake everyone, the great included. Teachers pair it with the remedy the text offers next (grace, good company) rather than leave the reader in the list.
misreadings: Not a statement that grief is a failing or a sign of weak faith.
cautions: Groups grief with envy as maya's soldiers; for a mourner, stress that the point is universality, not blame.
not_for: someone in fresh grief who might hear grief called 'illusion'

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 71, chaupai 2 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-4), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 70: off by one.

rcm.7.72.chaupai.2.context: Kakbhushundi has said that Ram's human play deludes the demonic and delights devotees, and that only dull, sense-bound people attribute delusion to the Lord. These five images show how a fault in the seer gets projected onto what is seen. The doha that follows says those sunk in lust, anger and pride, in a dark well, cannot know Ram.
rcm.7.72.chaupai.2.core_teaching: What we see is coloured by our own condition. The jaundiced eye sees a yellow moon. When we judge, especially the divine, we may only be describing our own illness or motion.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The five examples show one thing, superimposition: the world on Brahman, a role on an actor, a mere man on Ram. Jaundice changes form, the 'western sunrise' reverses place, the boat and children project qualities.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Compare Bal Kand 115: those with a dirty mirror and no eyes cannot see Ram's form. There the eyes are missing, here they are diseased, so they see wrongly. Knowledge and dispassion are the heart's eyes.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note (continued)
commentaries.gist: The moon is bright and not yellow, and in the same way Ram is pure and beyond delusion. Whoever has the disease sees the disease in him.

rcm.7.72.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Widely applied to perception and projection: before judging a person or situation, check whether the 'yellow' is in your own eye, and whether you are the one moving.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of all criticism as projection.
In the text it concerns doubts about Ram; widening it to everyday perception is a teaching application.
cautions: Can be used to invalidate someone's honest perception ('you only see that because something's wrong with you').
not_for: someone being gaslit or told their perception is wrong
speaks_to: seeing a situation differently after one's mood shifts

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 73, chaupais 2-3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 3-6), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 72 chaupai 2: off by one, and the text covers two Gita Press chaupais.

rcm.7.73.chaupai.3.context: Kakbhushundi begins to tell how he was himself deluded when the child Ram slipped out of his grasp. Before the story he states Ram's nature: he never lets pride stay in his devotee. Next comes the image of the mother having a child's boil lanced.
rcm.7.73.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Pride is the root of suffering, and Ram's nature is to remove it from those who love him, even if the removal hurts.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: 'Sahaj subhau' is innate, not learned or practised: it is Ram's own way. Others are moved by service, but Ram shows grace to the lowly even without service (Vinaya 162, via Ramayan Pradip).

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He doesn't worry this much about the pride of those who are not his. Ravana's pride was left standing a long time. It is his own devotees he protects from it.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ego is the first seed of creation. 'I am a Brahmin', 'I am a shudra', 'I am wise', 'I am a devotee' are all forms of pride that keep the round of birth going.

rcm.7.73.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Used to reframe a humbling: when life punctures our self-importance, teachers suggest it may be care, not punishment. It also shows ego as the source of much pain.
misreadings: Not a claim that every humiliation is deserved or divinely sent.
cautions: Pairs with the next verse's boil-lancing image; avoid telling someone in pain that their suffering is for their own good.
not_for: someone who has been humiliated or abused by another person
speaks_to: being humbled at work or in life

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 74, chaupai 3 (Manas Piyush half-lines 5-6), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 73: off by one.

rcm.7.73.chaupai.4.context: This follows directly on 'Ram never lets pride stay in his devotee'. The doha that follows says that though the child cries, the mother ignores that pain to cure the disease. Then Kakbhushundi tells how Ram cured his own pride and delusion.
rcm.7.73.chaupai.4.core_teaching: Love sometimes allows a short, sharp pain to prevent a longer harm, as a mother has a child's boil lanced despite the child's tears. The text applies this to the removal of pride.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Great 'mamata' is the reason: 'this one is mine, so how could I let him fall into such suffering?'

rcm.7.73.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it to make sense of painful correction from someone who loves us, and of loss of status or pride that later proves healing. Our existing misuse note matters.
misreadings: Not every pain is for your good (our misuse note is correct).
Never a justification for someone inflicting pain 'for your own good'.
Not 'God is punishing you'.
cautions: A Manas Piyush gloss reads it as God giving the immediate fruit of a fault; do not pass that on to a suffering reader.
The image of a crying child held down may upset parents of sick children.
not_for: someone in grief, illness or trauma who might hear 'this is for your good'
survivors of abuse
speaks_to: painful correction from a parent or mentor
a humbling that later made sense
parents making hard choices for a child's health

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 74, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8) and doha 74 (ka), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 73: off by one.

rcm.7.8.chhand.1.context: After meeting the townspeople, Ram meets his mothers. They run to him like cows hurrying home at dusk to calves left behind. He meets each of them with great love and gentle words, and the pain of separation leaves them. In the doha that follows he meets Sumitra and then Kaikeyi, who is deeply ashamed.
rcm.7.8.chhand.1.core_teaching: A mother's rush toward a returning child is like a cow's evening dash to her calf, and a long separation forced by circumstances ends in a tender, unhurried reunion.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Maps the figure: mothers are cows, Ram and Lakshman calves, fate the herdsman who parted them, fourteen years the day, the evening the return. Only one point is meant: running to the child in great love.

commentaries.who: Shri Nange Paramhans, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Bharat is the herdsman who brought the mothers away from Chitrakoot by force for their protection, to the 'forest' of Ayodhya, leaving the calf Ram behind.

commentaries.who: Vir Kavi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The simile is inverted, since the mothers come from home and Ram from the forest. He names the figure as the second kind of asangati.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar's tippani, second note
commentaries.gist: Ram meets all the stepmothers first and with great love, because the dharma texts say to honour a stepmother ten times one's own mother. He loves them in thought, word and deed.

rcm.7.8.chhand.1.practical_reading: Used for parents and children reunited after separation forced by work, illness, migration or circumstance, and for the instinct of a parent's love.
cautions: A strong image of maternal longing; may be painful for a parent separated from a child or bereaved of one.
not_for: a parent who has lost a child
someone estranged from their mother
speaks_to: working mothers away from young children
coming home to parents after years away

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 6, chhand (Manas Piyush 'दोहा 6 (छन्द)'), Gita Press numbering. Our ref says 8: off by two.

rcm.7.83.chaupai.3.context: The child Ram, pleased with the crow, offers him every boon: siddhis, wealth, liberation, knowledge, dispassion. Kakbhushundi notices that the Lord has not offered devotion. He reflects that all of it without devotion is like food without salt, and asks for unbroken, pure devotion. Ram grants it.
rcm.7.83.chaupai.3.core_teaching: Every gift and pleasure is flat without the one thing that gives it taste. For Kakbhushundi that is devotion.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Ram offered two kinds of thing, pleasures (siddhis, liberation) and virtues (qualities rare even for sages), and Kakbhushundi weighs both against devotion. Joy without devotion doesn't last (Uttar 119: even liberation can't stay without devotion).

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Only someone who doesn't know the joy of worship runs after other joys. Without it the inner burning never stops, so what use is every pleasure when there's no rest?

rcm.7.83.chaupai.3.practical_reading: Used to ask what the 'salt' of one's own life is, the thing without which success and comfort taste flat. In the text that is devotion; teachers widen it to meaning and love.
misreadings: Not a rejection of virtues or pleasures as bad; it is about what gives them savour.
not_for: someone struggling to meet basic needs, who may hear it as dismissing material help

rcm.7.85.chaupai.5.context: This is part of the 'Ram Gita' the child Ram speaks to Kakbhushundi after granting him devotion. He says all creation is his and all are dear, but his devotee is dearest. Just before this he says again and again that nothing is as dear to him as a servant. Next comes the parable of the father and many sons.
rcm.7.85.chaupai.5.core_teaching: Status counts for nothing with Ram: the creator himself without devotion is no dearer than any creature, and the lowliest being with devotion is dear as life.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: Ram has now said three times that the devotee is dearest and adds 'truly' again and again, so no one takes it as mere encouragement to worship. It is doctrine, not flattery.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note on 'ati neech'
commentaries.gist: Even those then counted outcaste (antyaja, chandala, shvapacha) become dear as life through devotion. Caste and stage of life drop away.

rcm.7.85.chaupai.5.practical_reading: Used against status anxiety and hierarchy: worth before the divine doesn't come from rank, learning or power.
misreadings: Not contempt for Brahma or for the learned; it ranks love above rank.
cautions: 'अति नीच' reflects caste language of its time. Render it as 'lowly' and keep caste terms out of the reading.

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 86, chaupai 5 (Manas Piyush half-lines 9-10), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 85: off by one.

rcm.7.86.chaupai.1.context: Ram has said all beings are his and all dear, but the devotee dearest. Now he gives a worldly example: a father's many sons differ in gifts and character, and he loves them all equally, yet the son wholly devoted to him is dear as life, even if he is simple. 'In this way' all beings are Ram's, and the devotee is dearest.
rcm.7.86.chaupai.1.core_teaching: A parent loves every child equally, the scholar, the rich one and the brave one alike. Ram's love for all beings is the same, and wholehearted love draws it closest.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Rejects that question: 'kumara' stands for all offspring. The point is that all beings, male, female, napunsaka, moving and unmoving, are God's children and dear to him.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Maps the sons onto scripture: Brihaspati the scholar, Pracheta the ascetic, Sanaka the knower, Kubera the rich, the daityas the brave, Harishchandra the giver, Dhruva and Prahlad the devoted sons.

rcm.7.86.chaupai.1.practical_reading: Used for parents with very different children, and as reassurance that you don't need to be the clever or successful one to be loved.
misreadings: Not favouritism among children; equal love is stated first.
cautions: Manas Piyush's own note explains the omission of daughters with era-bound gender assumptions; don't repeat it. Use 'children'.
not_for: someone who experienced real parental favouritism, without care

rcm.7.86.chaupai.2.context: This completes the father parable. The devoted son, though simple in every way, is as dear to his father as life, and 'in this way' all moving and unmoving beings, animals, gods, humans and demons, are Ram's children. He goes on to say that whoever worships him with body, word and mind, giving up pride and maya, is dearest.
rcm.7.86.chaupai.2.core_teaching: The simple child whose whole heart belongs to the parent is held dearest. Wholehearted love, not achievement, is what draws Ram closest.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: The devoted son described here is Kakbhushundi himself, devoted in act, word and mind and wanting nothing but devotion. 'Simple in every way' means he has none of the brothers' gifts, while they serve the father only as scripture requires.

commentaries.who: Ramayan Pradip and Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The father doesn't fret at his ignorance and even counts it a virtue. Example: Shravana, who knew no dharma but serving his parents, and whose parents died of grief at losing him.

rcm.7.86.chaupai.2.practical_reading: Reassurance for anyone who feels ordinary or 'not clever': being wholehearted counts for more than being impressive.
misreadings: Not praise of ignorance as such; it values single-minded love.
cautions: The Shravana example in the commentary involves parents dying of grief; leave it out for bereaved readers.
speaks_to: children with learning differences and their parents

rcm.7.86.doha.1.context: This ends Ram's teaching to Kakbhushundi. Having said all beings are his children and the wholehearted devotee is dearest, he declares that any being at all, of any sex or kind, who worships him without guile is supremely dear. The soratha that follows tells Kakbhushundi to worship him, leaving all other hope and reliance.
rcm.7.86.doha.1.core_teaching: Devotion is open to every being without exception of sex, gender, birth or species. What counts is wholeheartedness without guile.
rcm.7.86.doha.1.practical_reading: One of the clearest statements of inclusion in the Manas: no one is shut out by gender, sex or birth. It is used to welcome LGBTQ and gender-diverse readers and anyone told they are 'not eligible'.
misreadings: Don't overstate it as a modern statement on gender identity; it says no category of being is excluded.
cautions: Old commentaries carry hierarchical views of gender and caste; one gloss in Manas Piyush ranks eligibility. Don't import those.
speaks_to: feeling excluded from religion because of gender, sexuality or caste

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 87 (ka), the doha before the soratha that ends section 87, Gita Press / Manas Piyush. Our ref says 86: off by one.

rcm.7.87.chaupai.4.context: Having taught the crow and granted him devotion, the infant Ram goes back to being a baby: with teary eyes and a sulky face he looks at his mother to show he is hungry. She runs, comforts him, nurses him and sings of his deeds. The soratha that follows says Ayodhya's people are always immersed in the joy Shiva himself longs for.
rcm.7.87.chaupai.4.core_teaching: The infinite becomes a hungry baby in his mother's lap. This plain, tender scene of a mother answering her child's need is offered as the highest bliss.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji and Ramayan Pradip, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He can't speak yet, so he shows hunger by look and gesture. 'Soft words' are a mother's endearments, meant to keep him from crying. 'Singing' shows her overflowing joy.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note, citing Gitavali
commentaries.gist: 'Lovely deeds' are his human baby play, with no hint of majesty, which is why they are called lalita. Gitavali poems show Kaushalya rocking and nursing him while gods and sages watch from behind the clouds, envious.

rcm.7.87.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Used to honour the ordinary sacredness of caring for a baby: feeding, soothing and singing are the very joy that saints long for.
cautions: A breastfeeding image; tender for new parents, but painful for those who lost an infant or could not nurse or conceive.
not_for: someone grieving a baby or struggling with infertility

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 88, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 87: off by one.

rcm.7.87.chaupai.8.context: After recounting what Ram taught him, Kakbhushundi gives his own experience: without worshipping Hari troubles don't end, and without Ram's grace his greatness can't be known. Then comes this chain from knowing to trust to love to firm devotion. Next he gives the soratha pair: no knowledge without a guru, no rest without contentment.
rcm.7.87.chaupai.8.core_teaching: Love grows in steps: knowing leads to trust, trust to love, and only love makes devotion firm. Without it devotion has no grip.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush compiler's note
commentaries.gist: A causal chain (karanamala). Worship brings grace, grace reveals his greatness, knowing it brings trust, trust brings love, and love makes devotion firm. Worship is the means and devotion the goal. Sugriva goes through the same chain in Kishkindha Kand.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Till now Kakbhushundi gave Ram's own doctrine. 'Now I tell my experience' marks the turn to what he has tested himself.

commentaries.who: Karunasindhu, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram's grace is recognised when one meets a truly pure saint (cf. Uttar 69).

commentaries.who: F. S. Growse, translation (1883, 6th ed.)
commentaries.gist: Renders the chain as understanding, then confidence, then affection, then consistency of faith, which otherwise 'slips away like oil on water'.

rcm.7.87.chaupai.8.practical_reading: Applied to any relationship or practice: you can't trust what you don't know, or love what you don't trust. Get to know first, and love that lasts follows.
misreadings: Not a demand for intellectual proof before faith; 'knowing' here comes through grace and experience.

rcm.7.87.sortha.5.context: This closes Kakbhushundi's statement of his own experience, as the second soratha in a pair. The first asks whether there is knowledge without a guru, or knowledge without dispassion, or happiness without devotion. This one asks about rest without contentment. Then he urges Garuda to drop argument and doubt and worship Ram.
rcm.7.87.sortha.5.core_teaching: No amount of effort brings rest without contentment, just as no amount of pushing moves a boat on dry land.

commentaries.who: Karunasindhu, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Sahaj santosh' means no elation at what comes and no grief at what goes.

commentaries.who: Ram Balak Das, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Contentment brings happiness ('content with what comes, loving Ram's feet'). In the image, contentment is the water and dispassion the boat.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The two sorathas give pairs of causes: knowledge needs guru and dispassion, happiness needs devotion and contentment. Devotion is the root, and only when it brings natural contentment is there happiness.

rcm.7.87.sortha.5.practical_reading: Used against burnout and endless striving: rest doesn't come from more effort but from a different footing. Teachers apply it to overwork and to chasing the next achievement.
misreadings: Not a call to stop working or to accept injustice; it concerns inner rest.
not_for: someone whose discontent is a just response to deprivation

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 89: the second soratha of the pair numbered 89 (Manas Piyush prints both under ॥89॥), Gita Press numbering. Our id says '87 sortha 5', which matches neither the doha number nor Gita Press's soratha numbering. Growse's translation labels this 'Soratha 5', which may be where our 'sortha 5' label comes from.

rcm.7.95.chaupai.4.context: Kakbhushundi is describing the Kali age into which he was born in an earlier life. Truth is lost, false teachers abound, and just before this guru and disciple are 'blind and deaf to each other'. The list of decay goes on: castes mixed, people sinning and suffering fear, disease, grief and separation.
rcm.7.95.chaupai.4.core_teaching: A teacher's job is to relieve the student's sorrow, not to profit from them. A parent's job is to pass on more than how to earn a living. The verse describes a degraded age in which both have failed.

commentaries.who: Karunasindhu and Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Guru and disciple are 'blind and deaf': the disciple won't listen and clings to pleasures, and the self-interested guru takes anyone on without looking at their qualities, just to 'blow in the ear' and collect fees.

commentaries.who: Baijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: A guru should choose disciples carefully and keep them close until they mature in practice. That is removing their sorrow. Instead these gurus extract money by praise, pressure, then anger. Parents call children away from satsang lest they become mendicants.

commentaries.who: Ram Shankar Sharan and Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The guru doesn't remove the disciple's doubt, which is his real grief, and his taking of money even adds bodily hardship. Parents teach belly-filling skills from childhood rather than learning and good company.

rcm.7.95.chaupai.4.practical_reading: Applied to teachers, coaches, gurus and parents today: are you relieving people's suffering or only collecting their fees? Are you teaching children more than how to make money?
misreadings: Not a ban on teachers being paid; the fault is taking money while ignoring the student's real need.
Not contempt for earning a living; it criticises teaching only that.
cautions: 'Falls into a terrible hell' is punitive language; a reader hurt by an exploitative guru may welcome it, but a teacher who feels inadequate may be crushed by it.
not_for: someone looking for comfort rather than critique
speaks_to: people disillusioned by exploitative gurus or institutions
teachers and mentors checking their motives
parents thinking about values beyond career

data_flags.corrected_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand doha 99, chaupai 4 (Manas Piyush half-lines 7-8), Gita Press numbering. Our id says doha 95: off by four.

shakti_gita.1.39.context: After winning the war with the demons, the gods, led by Vishnu, perform a collective worship (the 'brahma-chakra') hoping the Mother will appear. She appears as a blazing light and a radiant sixteen-year-old form. The gods begin a hymn by admitting that no one can praise her in words (1.41), then ask pardon for trying (1.42-43).
shakti_gita.1.39.core_teaching: Every attempt to praise the divine falls short, and even being forgiven for that is itself grace; the right response is grateful bowing.

commentaries.who: Devi Anugraha Foundation English translation (recent; text and readings unreliable)
commentaries.gist: Prints a different and garbled second verse (e.g. 'moonlight of the world'); useful only as evidence that the text circulates in variant forms. Not used for meaning.

shakti_gita.1.39.practical_reading: Permission to pray clumsily: words will not be enough, and that is fine; the intention is received.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.
speaks_to: people who feel they do not know how to pray

data_flags.corrected_ref: Shakti Gita 1.42-43 in the Mahamandal editions read (1916 and 1957 agree; 1.40 there is the speaker line 'the gods said'). Our '1.39-40' is off by three. The printed Mahamandal editions number speaker lines ('devā ūcuḥ ॥1॥' etc.) as verses, so their numbers run ahead of ours.

shakti_gita.1.47.context: Part of the gods' hymn. Just before (1.48-49) they say she, though formless and beyond the senses, takes a form with qualities for her devotees' good. Just after (1.52-54) they say not even gods understand her, yet she does not withhold her vision from simple devotees who love her feet.
shakti_gita.1.47.core_teaching: Grace does not wait for perfect understanding: to devotees who cannot yet see her true nature, the Mother shows herself in a form and gives both well-being and freedom.
shakti_gita.1.47.practical_reading: You do not have to understand everything to be helped; begin where you are.
misreadings: Not anti-knowledge; the hymn values understanding but says grace is wider.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.

data_flags.corrected_ref: Shakti Gita 1.50-51 in the Mahamandal editions (1916 and 1957 agree). Our '1.47-48' is off by three. The printed Mahamandal editions number speaker lines ('devā ūcuḥ ॥1॥' etc.) as verses, so their numbers run ahead of ours.

shakti_gita.1.51.context: The gods say (1.53) that her devotees, bound by ignorance, do not understand her greatness at all; yet (1.54) those who love her feet with undivided devotion like bees are never turned away from the vision that gives freedom. 1.55 adds that she appears to each in whichever of the five deity forms (Vishnu, Surya, Gauri, Dhisha, Shiva) they like.
shakti_gita.1.51.core_teaching: Simple, single-minded love is enough: the Mother does not withhold herself from devotees who cling to her like bees to a lotus, even if they understand little.
shakti_gita.1.51.practical_reading: Devotion does not require theology; keep returning, like a bee, to what you love in prayer.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.
speaks_to: people who feel they lack learning

data_flags.corrected_ref: Shakti Gita 1.54 in the 1957 Mahamandal edition. Our '1.51' is off by three. The printed Mahamandal editions number speaker lines ('devā ūcuḥ ॥1॥' etc.) as verses, so their numbers run ahead of ours.

shakti_gita.5.133.context: In a chapter on karma, the Mother tells the gods to work joined to her. The next verse explains why: action done without union with her binds, action done joined to her gives the highest freedom (5.136). Then: the world arises from the push and pull of opposites, and her shelter is what lifts one beyond them (5.137-139).
shakti_gita.5.133.core_teaching: Keep doing your work, but do it held in the divine, as shelter and goal; that changes the work from binding to freeing.
shakti_gita.5.133.practical_reading: Before a task, offer it; during it, return to that offering when you notice stress.
misreadings: Not quietism: the Mother explicitly says to keep working.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.

data_flags.corrected_ref: Shakti Gita 5.135 in the 1957 Mahamandal edition (the Devi Anugraha English also numbers it 135). Our '5.133' is off by two.

shakti_gita.5.137.context: The Mother explains (5.137-138) that the world arises and stays through the push and pull of opposites, which bind beings, but one principle frees them. Relying on it, devotees go beyond the pairs and envy (5.139) and, practising desireless action, become fit for liberation (5.140); karmic seeds are then burned (5.141).
shakti_gita.5.137.core_teaching: Relying on the divine lifts a person above the swing of opposites and envy, into steady, fitting work, and prepares them for freedom.
shakti_gita.5.137.practical_reading: When comparison and envy pull at you, return to your own fitting work and your refuge.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.
speaks_to: mood swings between success and failure

data_flags.corrected_ref: Shakti Gita 5.139 in the 1957 Mahamandal edition (Devi Anugraha English also 139). Our '5.137' is off by two.

shakti_gita.6.149.context: Closing chapter 6, the Mother says that when her wise yogi-devotee understands her Prakriti through vidya, she with her Prakriti brings him to union with Brahman (6.148-149); his karmic ropes become like burnt rope (6.150); then her knowledge-form Prakriti takes his actions, holds him in her lap and merges into her (6.151-152). 6.153 calls this merging 'Brahma-sadbhava'.
shakti_gita.6.149.core_teaching: For the wise devotee, the Mother's knowledge-power takes over the burden of action and, like a mother carrying a child, brings him into oneness with her.
shakti_gita.6.149.practical_reading: An image of rest for the over-responsible: some of the weight you carry can be handed over.
misreadings: Not a licence to drop one's duties; it describes the end of the path for the wise devotee.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.
'Merging' language describes liberation and can be read as death; avoid for readers with suicidal thoughts.
not_for: readers in suicidal crisis

data_flags.corrected_ref: Shakti Gita 6.151-152 in the 1957 Mahamandal edition, the penultimate verses of chapter 6 (6.153 closes). Our '6.149-150' is off by two.

shakti_gita.6.27.context: The Mother says beings under ignorance forget her suddenly and get caught in her illusory world (6.28), but when they come to her for refuge she draws them to her in many ways (6.29); devotion is the reason (6.30). She then turns to the three aspects of her being and to how karma binds and frees.
shakti_gita.6.27.core_teaching: Turning toward the divine is met from the other side: the Mother draws those who seek refuge toward herself, by many routes.
shakti_gita.6.27.practical_reading: If you have turned toward faith through unusual or painful routes, this frames them as being drawn, not lost.
misreadings: Not a claim that suffering is sent deliberately as a 'way'.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.

shakti_gita.7.118.context: In chapter 7 the Mother shows her cosmic form and names her powers in the manner of Gita chapters 9-10: she is the Self in all hearts, beginning, middle and end of beings (7.121), then this list (7.122). She goes on: she is woman and man and beyond gender, beyond qualities, and the seed and root of the tree of dharma (7.123-126).
shakti_gita.7.118.core_teaching: The divine Mother is everything a person needs to lean on: goal, support, ruler, mother, home, refuge and friend, the source and end of all.
shakti_gita.7.118.practical_reading: A litany to recite when you feel unsupported: name what you need (refuge, friend, home) and lean on it.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.
not_for: someone grieving their own mother, where 'mother' language may need gentle framing

data_flags.corrected_ref: Shakti Gita 7.122 in the 1957 and 1916 Mahamandal editions (chapter 7, vision of the cosmic form). Our '7.118' is off by four. It echoes Bhagavad Gita 9.18 (verified on vedabase.net).

shambhu_gita.2.43.context: Shiva teaches the ancestors (pitṛs) how creation is held together. Attraction and attachment are rooted in rajas, repulsion and aversion in tamas (2.43); sattva emerges where the two are balanced (2.44). That balance is his sattvic, dharma-formed power, which protects the world (2.45) and holds everything from galaxies to atoms (2.46).
shambhu_gita.2.43.core_teaching: The world is held together by a balance between pull and push; that balance, sattva, is dharma, and it is divine power always working for the good of all.
shambhu_gita.2.43.practical_reading: Balance between wanting and refusing is not weakness; it is the quality that holds a life, and a world, together.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.

data_flags.corrected_ref: Shambhu Gita 2.45 in the Mahamandal edition read. Our '2.43' is off by two.
data_flags.translation_note: 'Gentle power' for sāttvikī is too loose. In context sāttvikī means the sattva-quality power that arises from the balance of attraction (rāga, rajas) and repulsion (dveṣa, tamas), 2.43-44. Better: 'My sattvic power, whose form is dharma...'.

shambhu_gita.4.83.context: Shiva describes to the ancestors the four divisions of the earthly sphere (the ancestors' world, the human world, the world of ghosts and hell) and says Dharmaraja's (Yama's) rule extends over them. If the ancestors make firm daily effort, he says, they can help keep creation in balance without needing Yama's rod. Making people righteous through punishment is good, but effort that keeps them from ever deserving punishment does more for their welfare (vv. 84-86).
shambhu_gita.4.83.core_teaching: Preventing wrongdoing through guidance is better than correcting it through punishment. The context is cosmic governance by the ancestors, not parenting.

commentaries.who: Hindi translation in the Mahamandal edition (1920; no classical commentary exists)
commentaries.gist: Renders vv. 80-86: with firm effort the ancestors can protect creation's harmony without Yama's punishment; making people dharmic by punishment is good, but effort so they never deserve it is considered more beneficial.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Sanskrit text, Shambhu Gita ch. 4)
commentaries.gist: The chapter, framed as Shiva answering the Pitris, maps the worlds and assigns the ancestors a protective role over human welfare; this verse states the preventive ideal within that role.

shambhu_gita.4.83.practical_reading: For a parent, the analogy is: put more energy into setting a child up to do well (routines, example, explanation) than into consequences after the fact. Punishment isn't rejected, just ranked lower.
misreadings: Not a scriptural verdict against all discipline; the previous verse calls punishment-based effort good
Not about parenting in the original; it is an analogy, so don't present it as 'Shiva's parenting advice'
cautions: Late text; label accurately
Surrounding verses discuss hell and ghost-realms; avoid quoting them
not_for: a parent dealing with a child's serious harm to others, where it could read as 'never set consequences'
speaks_to: parents who feel they are always correcting

data_flags.translation_note: Two problems. (1) 'jnani-sannidhau' does not mean the effort is 'made in the company of the wise'; the edition's own Hindi renders the point as how the effort 'is regarded' (by the wise), i.e. 'in the judgement of the wise'. (2) The verse is half...

shambhu_gita.6.75.context: Shiva tells the ancestors how his knowing devotees are freed from karma: those who serve the knower share his merit and those who harm him share his sins, so the knower moves free (6.72-75); knowers of the Self cross the ocean of saṃsāra and taste Brahman's bliss here (6.76). This verse and the next cite scriptural sayings, and conclude that the freed are Brahman itself (6.78).
shambhu_gita.6.75.core_teaching: Knowing the Self carries one across sorrow, because the one God is hidden in every being.
shambhu_gita.6.75.practical_reading: Sorrow is something to cross, not deny: understanding and inner connection are the boat.
misreadings: Not 'the wise do not feel grief'; the image is crossing, not suppressing (our_note is right).
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.

Our_note's sources (Chandogya 7.1.3 'tarati śokam ātmavit', Shvetashvatara 6.11 'eko devaḥ sarvabhūteṣu gūḍhaḥ') are the standard identifications and the Hindi gloss marks them as scriptural quotations; not re-checked against an Upanishad edition here.
not_for: early grief, if offered as 'just know the Self and you'll be fine'

data_flags.corrected_ref: Shambhu Gita 6.77 in the Mahamandal edition read. Our '6.75' is off by two.

shambhu_gita.6.91.context: Shiva describes three grades of devotees. When the distressed, the seekers and those who want things take refuge in him, his Prakriti takes a mother's role, grants their wishes and moves them toward him (6.92-94). For the wanting devotee she acts like a devoted wife (6.95-97), and only the wise devotee merges into her and reaches him.
shambhu_gita.6.91.core_teaching: Whatever brings you to the divine, pain, need or curiosity, is met with motherly care that meets the need and then moves you further.
shambhu_gita.6.91.practical_reading: If you only pray when in trouble or in need, this says that is a legitimate beginning, not a lesser faith.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.
speaks_to: people who pray only in crisis

shambhu_gita.7.53.context: The ancestors end a long hymn praising Shiva as the seed and support of the tree of dharma (7.55), then with this verse hand themselves over. Shiva replies (7.57-59) that he is pleased and wishes them threefold welfare and unhindered progress toward liberation.
shambhu_gita.7.53.core_teaching: A prayer of surrender: we come to you alone; do whatever will truly be good for us, and do it soon.
shambhu_gita.7.53.practical_reading: A prayer for when you do not know what to ask for: hand over the outcome and ask only for what is truly good.
misreadings: Not resignation: the ancestors still ask for action ('do it now').
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.
speaks_to: uncertainty about what to pray for

data_flags.corrected_ref: Shambhu Gita 7.56 in the Mahamandal edition read (chapter on the Shiva-linga). Our '7.53' is off by three.

shambhu_gita.7.65.context: Shiva tells the ancestors to do their duties devotedly but says success needs a mind joined to him (7.66-68). He then offers an easy method (7.69-70): though one without a second, he shows himself to devotees in many vibhutis (7.71) and lists them (7.72-90), ending with the Gita-like teaching that whatever is glorious is from a spark of his power.
shambhu_gita.7.65.core_teaching: Even in demanding work one need not lose devotion; the easy way is to recognise the divine in the best of everything around you.
shambhu_gita.7.65.practical_reading: For busy people: during work, notice something excellent (a skill, a kindness, beauty) and let it remind you of the sacred.
misreadings: This verse only announces the method; the method itself is the vibhuti list that follows.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.

data_flags.corrected_ref: Shambhu Gita 7.69-70 in the Mahamandal edition read. Our '7.65-66' is off by four.

shambhu_gita.7.80.context: Part of Shiva's vibhuti list (7.72-90): among rivers the Ganga, among mantras Om, among images the Shiva-linga. Within a run of 'reverent' things (sights, acts, sounds, touches, smells) he names this embrace. Note the neighbouring verse (7.82) lists, among reverent acts, sexual union free of lust; editors should be aware of the context.
shambhu_gita.7.80.core_teaching: The divine is present in an embrace given with love, affection, devotion and faith; sacred touch is part of the holy.
shambhu_gita.7.80.practical_reading: Hug someone you love today with full attention; the text treats such an embrace as sacred.
misreadings: Not about romantic or sexual touch specifically; the list includes parents, children and devotees.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.
Touch can be a painful theme for readers with abuse histories or who have lost a loved one; use gently.
not_for: readers who have experienced abuse
fresh bereavement where the embrace is no longer possible

data_flags.corrected_ref: Shambhu Gita 7.84 in the Mahamandal edition read. Our '7.80' is off by four.

sur.bgs.10.context: Krishna is in Mathura after killing Kamsa and is sending Uddhav to Braj. Before he goes, Krishna gives him a message for his foster-mother: stay well, we brothers will come soon; since I left no one has called me Kanhaiya, no breakfast, no fresh milk. The rest of the pada asks her to keep his flute and toys safe from Radha and to tell Nand he has been hard-hearted for not sending word. In the story Krishna does not return to live in Braj.
sur.bgs.10.core_teaching: Love in separation runs both ways: Krishna, now a prince, misses the ordinary tenderness of home, a pet name and a mother's food. The commentators use it to show Sur's love is mutual, not only the gopis longing for Krishna.

commentaries.who: Hindi tika in Bhramar Geet-saar (Anita Prakashan, Delhi 1977), pada 10
commentaries.gist: Krishna tells Uddhav to reassure Yashoda. Notes the pada answers critics who say Sur shows only one-sided love: Krishna longs for Nand, Yashoda, Radha, even his toys. The 'Kanhaiya' line shows his ache to hear her pet name again.

commentaries.who: Same edition, notes on the preceding pada
commentaries.gist: Reads this as Krishna's answer to Yashoda's humble message; his promise to come is meant to reassure her that royal splendour has not made him forget Braj.

commentaries.who: Narendradev Shastri, Hindi tika (Agra 1957), pada 10
commentaries.gist: Krishna asks Uddhav to say: let mother be well, we brothers come in four or five days; no one calls me Kanhaiya; keep my flute safe; tell Nand he never sent word after leaving me in Mathura.

sur.bgs.10.practical_reading: For someone living away from parents, it voices what is actually missed: not big things but being called by your home name, being fed. It also models the message home that says 'I am fine, I will come soon' while admitting the ache.
misreadings: Not a promise that a separation will be short; in the story the return does not happen.
Not a complaint against the new place (Mathura): it is about what only home gives.
cautions: The 'four or five days' promise is poignant because Krishna never returns to live in Braj; a reader who has lost a parent may feel this sharply.
For someone estranged from parents, the warm mother image may sting.
not_for: someone whose parent has died recently (the 'I will come soon' line can wound)
someone estranged from or harmed by a parent
speaks_to: living far from parents (study, work, abroad)
missing a parent's small daily care
an adult child who wants to reassure parents

sur.bgs.315.context: Late in the Bhramargeet, the gopis turn from arguing with Uddhava to sending a message. They ask Krishna to come just once, even as a guest of Nanda for half a moment, because breath may fail at any time. They say fate overturned their happiness, recall a joy that even Shiva and the sages lack, and close on Radha weeping for his beauty.
sur.bgs.315.core_teaching: Longing made urgent by the shortness of life: come while there is still time.

commentaries.who: 1977 Kala Mandir tika on Bhramargeet-Saar (vyakhya and vishesh notes)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as the gopis' plea on Radha's behalf: come even as Nanda's guest, since life may end with the wish unmet. Notes the saguna wish to see Krishna and the contrast with the yoga path.

commentaries.who: e-PG Pathshala (INFLIBNET) module on Shukla's Bhramargeet-Saar
commentaries.gist: Notes that by the end Uddhava becomes the gopis' messenger, carrying their appeal back to Krishna. This pada is one of those appeals.

sur.bgs.315.practical_reading: Used as a nudge not to postpone a visit or reconciliation: life is uncertain, so go and see the person now.
misreadings: Not a prediction of death.
Not emotional blackmail; it is a lover's plea, and the devotional object is Krishna.
cautions: Explicitly mentions the breath leaving: sensitive for the terminally ill, the very elderly, or anyone anxious about death.
For someone who already missed a last meeting, it can trigger guilt.
not_for: recent bereavement where the last visit never happened
health anxiety or fear of dying
someone being pressured to return to a harmful person
speaks_to: wanting to see an ageing parent or distant loved one
urge to reconcile before it is too late

data_flags.attribution_note: Speaker needs a note: the tika's prasang says the gopis send this message to Krishna, pointing to Radha's state, and the last line says 'Surdas: Radha laments'. So it is Radha's plea voiced through the gopis, not clearly Radha's own words. Suggest speaker 'the gopis,...

sur.bgs.316.context: In the Bhramargeet, Krishna has left Braj for Mathura and sent Uddhav to teach the gopis formless (nirguna) yoga; most padas are the gopis' replies and laments. In this one they describe their own state: since Shyam left the rains never stop; kohl will not stay in their eyes and streaks their cheeks and breasts black; their bodices never dry; and the flood of tears now threatens to drown Gokul, so they ask Krishna to come and save it.
sur.bgs.316.core_teaching: Not a doctrine but an expression of viraha (love in separation): the loss of the beloved is so total that weeping becomes a season rather than an event. The bhakti tradition treats such longing as a form of love itself, not something to be fixed.

commentaries.who: Hindi tika in Bhramar Geet-saar (Anita Prakashan, Delhi 1977), pada 316
commentaries.gist: Gopis, weeping day and night in Krishna's absence, compare themselves to the rainy season. Last line read as a plea: the tears have flooded Gokul, so save it as you once did by lifting Govardhan. Praised for its emotion and imagery; figures noted: rupaka, atishayokti, upama.

commentaries.who: Narendradev Shastri, Hindi tika, Bhramar Geetsar (Agra 1957), pada 316
commentaries.gist: Gopis describe their viraha: eyes raining since Krishna left, kohl washed onto cheeks, bodice never dry, Gokul flooding with tears; they ask the Lord to rescue it. Notes rupaka and atishayokti.

commentaries.who: Same edition, introduction (on viraha in Sur)
commentaries.gist: Quotes this pada to show the gopis' tears have not stopped since Krishna went to Mathura, then lists the ten classical stages of viraha that Sur depicts.

commentaries.who: e-PG Pathshala (INFLIBNET) module on Bhramargeet-saar
commentaries.gist: Explains the Saar as Shukla's 1920 selection of about 400 Sursagar padas; viraha drives the whole episode, and the gopis answer Uddhav's yoga with love and gentle reproach rather than debate.

sur.bgs.316.practical_reading: Teachers and singers use it to give grief permission: missing someone can feel like weather that does not lift, and saying so plainly is part of loving them. It names the feeling without asking the reader to stop it.
misreadings: Not a call to stay in tears forever or a judgment that one should be 'over it'; it simply describes how separation feels.
Not about romantic loss only in the tradition: the gopis' longing is read as devotion to Krishna.
cautions: Mentions flooding/drowning as hyperbole for tears; fine for most readers, but keep the gloss gentle.
Imagery of tears soaking the bodice and breasts is in the full pada; our excerpt avoids it.
not_for: a reader who needs reassurance that the pain will end soon (the verse offers none)
contexts where the speaker should be shown moving on
speaks_to: someone who has left or moved away
longing after a breakup or separation

sur.bgs.34.context: Uddhava has brought Krishna's advice to practise formless meditation. The gopis reply that love formed in childhood cannot be undone: they recall his playful gait, glance, smile and singing, and his return from the forest in a dancer's dress. They swear by his feet that the yoga message tastes like poison to them, and end with this line.
sur.bgs.34.core_teaching: Love that grew through shared life cannot be talked out of the heart by abstract teaching; the beloved's image stays in every state of mind.

commentaries.who: 1977 Kala Mandir tika on Bhramargeet-Saar (vyakhya and vishesh notes)
commentaries.gist: Says the gopis' hearts have become one with Krishna's image, leaving no room for nirguna practice. Notes that love from childhood companionship cannot be dropped, and that the pada depicts the bhava of remembrance (smriti).

commentaries.who: e-PG Pathshala (INFLIBNET) module on Shukla's Bhramargeet-Saar
commentaries.gist: Frames the whole Bhramargeet as the gopis' saguna love answering Uddhava's nirguna message, often by questioning or mocking rather than arguing philosophically.

sur.bgs.34.practical_reading: It names the experience of someone who keeps surfacing in your mind. Teachers present this as the nature of deep love, not a failure to 'move on'.
misreadings: Not a rule that one should never move on from a person.
In context the beloved is Krishna and the love is devotional; human application is an extension.
Not a general attack on knowledge; it is the gopis' rhetorical stance against a message that ignored their love.
cautions: In grief it can validate remembrance, but may also feed rumination; pair with steadiness.
For a painful breakup it could reinforce fixation on an ex.
not_for: someone trying to leave an unhealthy or controlling relationship
intrusive or obsessive thoughts they want relief from
speaks_to: early grief, when the face keeps returning

sur.bgs.9.context: Before Uddhava sets out for Braj, Krishna dictates messages home. He tells Yashoda not to fret because both brothers will come soon, and says he was hurt that she called herself a mere 'dhai' (wet-nurse) of Devaki's son. He sends respectful word to Nanda about the cows. Then come these lines: Mathura's splendour is joyless without them. The Bhramargeet that follows is the gopis' answer to Uddhava's message of formless yoga.
sur.bgs.9.core_teaching: Rank and luxury in a new place cannot replace the love of the people who raised you; Krishna's heart rests only with them.

commentaries.who: 1977 Kala Mandir tika on Bhramargeet-Saar (vyakhya and vishesh notes)
commentaries.gist: Reads the pada as Krishna's message: he protests Yashoda calling herself a nurse, honours Nanda by touching his feet, worries about the cows, and says Mathura's riches mean nothing without them. Notes the contrast of village warmth with courtly wealth.

commentaries.who: e-PG Pathshala (INFLIBNET) module on Shukla's Bhramargeet-Saar
commentaries.gist: Gives the frame: Krishna sends Uddhava to Braj with a yoga and nirguna message; the gopis win him over, he returns as their messenger, and Krishna's final pada shows his lasting attachment to Braj.

sur.bgs.9.practical_reading: Teachers use it for anyone who has moved away for work or study: success elsewhere does not cancel love for home. Send word, and honour the people who raised you.
misreadings: Not a rejection of ambition or city life; Krishna stays in Mathura for his duties.
Not Krishna disowning his birth parents; the hurt is that Yashoda made herself small.
cautions: Touches foster/birth-mother tension (Yashoda as 'nurse'); handle gently with adoptive or foster families.
For someone estranged from family or unable to go home, the warmth may sting.
not_for: someone who left an abusive or unsafe home
someone whose parent has just died (the promise 'we will come soon' can hurt)
speaks_to: homesickness after moving for work or study
parents whose grown children live far away
adoptive and foster parents whose love deserves honour

data_flags.attribution_note: Speaker (Krishna) is right. Listener needs fixing: the 'pathik' (traveller) is Uddhava, about to leave Mathura for Braj; the 1977 tika glosses it this way. The message is for Yashoda AND Nanda (one line asks Uddhava to clasp Nanda's feet and ask him to look...

sur.vp.1.context: This is the invocation that opens the vinaya section of Sursagar's first skandha. The poet bows to Hari's feet and lists the reversals grace brings, then bows again and again. In the Gita Press arrangement the next padas continue with praise of Hari's compassion.
sur.vp.1.core_teaching: Grace overturns every human limit; the right response is to bow again and again.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 1 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Bows to Hari's lotus feet: by his grace the lame cross mountains, the blind see, the deaf hear, the mute speak, and the poorest walk under a royal umbrella; Surdas bows to that compassionate master again and again.

commentaries.who: NPS Sursagar (Vajpeyi ed. 1950), placement and heading
commentaries.gist: NPS places this pada at the head of skandha 1 under 'mangalacharan', the auspicious opening of the whole Sursagar.

sur.vp.1.practical_reading: Teachers read it as hope that limitation is not the final word, and as a reminder to begin any effort with humility and gratitude.
misreadings: Not a promise of medical cure.
Not a claim that disability is a punishment or a problem to be fixed.
cautions: Uses disability as a metaphor; for disabled readers avoid implying cure is the goal.
The blind-poet story is tradition, not verified biography.
not_for: someone grieving a permanent disability or a failed treatment
someone told their illness persists because of weak faith

sur.vp.107.context: The pada continues: in deserts and forests, in quarrels and wherever fear came, you protected me. The tale of the ocean of mercy cannot be told in one telling. It ends: what use is comfort and wealth where the Lord of the Yadus is not?
sur.vp.107.core_teaching: Hardship kept God near because it kept remembrance constant; ease that brings forgetfulness is the real loss.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 107 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Those troubles that kept me remembering are gone. Then, each time I remembered, you met me, walked beside me, and shielded me as eyelids shield the eye. Wealth and ease without the Lord are worthless.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: The closing line, that comfort without the Lord is useless, shows the pada is less nostalgia for pain than a warning about forgetful comfort.

sur.vp.107.practical_reading: Used to help people see that hard seasons can be times of closeness and meaning, and to stay mindful when life gets easy.
misreadings: Not praise of suffering for its own sake.
Not a reason to seek or prolong hardship.
cautions: Someone in hardship now may not want to hear it 'brings God close'; better for looking back.
not_for: someone in acute crisis now
someone whose hardship included trauma they don't want romanticised
speaks_to: looking back on a hard season
drifting from practice after life got easier
gratitude for protection in hard times

sur.vp.11.context: The pada gives three rescues: Hari left Vaikuntha, Lakshmi and even Garuda to save Gajendra; he lifted Durvasa's curse from Ambarisha while the sage fled as far as Brahma's world; he helped the Pandavas escape the burning lac house. Sur ends by saying his Lord has removed every kind of fear for his people.
sur.vp.11.core_teaching: In crisis, the one who remembers Hari finds him intervening at once, as a true friend does.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 11 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: No friend like Hari: remembered in trouble, he comes between you and the danger at once. Cites Gajendra (he left Vaikuntha, Lakshmi and Garuda), Ambarisha against Durvasa, and the Pandavas in the lac house.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: The pada's examples are all rescues mid-crisis, so the point is prompt help in emergency, not general comfort.

sur.vp.11.practical_reading: Read as encouragement to turn toward God in a crisis and expect not to be alone in it.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that the trouble vanishes.
Not a substitute for calling for human help in an emergency.
cautions: Contains no death language, but 'he always comes' can hurt someone whose prayer in a crisis seemed unanswered.
not_for: someone whose loved one died despite prayers
someone in active danger who needs emergency services first

sur.vp.125.context: The pada tells the mind to love Madhav and drop lust, anger and greed, and gives a string of love-images: the bee sealed inside the lotus; the chatak; the lotus faithful to the sun even as it dries; the moth in the flame; the fish that dies out of water; the pigeon; the deer drawn by music; the wife on the pyre; the thief. It calls love the essence of all rasas.
sur.vp.125.core_teaching: Single-minded love (ananya bhakti) endures hardship and will not accept a substitute.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 125 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Uses the chatak among many examples of faithful love: it bears every hardship in hope of the cloud and never begs water elsewhere. The pada tells the mind to love Madhav this way.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: The surrounding images include the moth burning in the flame and a wife burning with her husband; the pada praises love even unto death, so lift the chatak couplet out carefully.

sur.vp.125.practical_reading: Applied to steadfastness in faith or commitment: wait for what truly nourishes rather than grabbing substitutes.
misreadings: Not a call to endure harm for a person's sake.
Not advice to refuse all help while waiting.
cautions: The full pada includes images of sati (a wife burning with her husband) and self-destroying love; do not quote those or present them as ideals.
not_for: someone staying in an abusive relationship out of 'loyalty'
someone neglecting their needs while 'waiting'
speaks_to: staying faithful during a dry spell in practice
waiting patiently for the right thing

sur.vp.14.context: After the opening, the pada gives examples: Shabari tasted the berries and kept only the sweet ones for Rama, who ate them gladly though they were 'jutha' (already tasted); Krishna, overwhelmed with love, ate the banana peels Vidura offered; he satisfied Durvasa's hunger with one leaf of greens. Sur closes: the compassionate Lord has raised his devotees in every age.
sur.vp.14.core_teaching: God weighs the feeling behind an offering, not its form or correctness.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 14 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Govind accepts everyone's love and responds to the bhava in which each serves. Rama ate Shabari's tasted berries without hesitation; Krishna ate Vidura's banana peels in a rush of love; a leaf of greens satisfied Durvasa.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: All three examples involve offerings that are 'wrong' by ritual rules (tasted fruit, peels, a scrap of greens), which sharpens the point about bhava.

sur.vp.14.practical_reading: Applied to clumsy or imperfect efforts at love or worship: sincerity counts more than polish.
misreadings: Not permission for carelessness when one can do better.
Not a claim that form never matters in a tradition.
not_for: someone hurt because their sincere love was rejected by a person (it speaks of God, not people)
speaks_to: feeling your offering or effort is too small or imperfect

sur.vp.141.context: A short pada. It goes on: in Hari's court everyone sits together, so who is big and who is small? It closes with the touchstone image: at the touch of the paras, the flaw of iron disappears.
sur.vp.141.core_teaching: Refuge in the divine name is never refused; grace surrounds the one who comes, and rank disappears.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 141 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Rama's name is the greatest shelter: the Lord never expels a refugee but keeps him inside a fort of grace. In Hari's court no one is high or low; refuge removes faults as the touchstone removes iron's flaw.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: The pada's two images, an assembly with no ranks and the touchstone, stress that nobody is too low to be admitted.

sur.vp.141.practical_reading: Comfort for someone who fears they will be turned away: in this view the door is always open.
misreadings: Not a claim that chanting alone replaces responsibility.
Not a promise of worldly protection.
not_for: someone who feels rejected by a religious community (it speaks of God, which may not match their experience)

sur.vp.144.context: The pada continues: one whose mind rests at the lotus feet would not take the four goals of life even if offered; with Krishna in the heart, the three worlds weigh like straw. Such a devotee would not leave Vrindavan, the Vamshivat and the Yamuna even for Vaikuntha. Remembering Hari, one does not return to the sea of rebirth.
sur.vp.144.core_teaching: Joyful singing of God gives a happiness that effortful practices and pilgrimages do not.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 144 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: The joy of singing Gopal is not found in chanting, austerity or bathing at countless tirthas. With the mind at his feet, a devotee would refuse even the four goals of life and would not trade Vrindavan for Vaikuntha.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: The pada's later lines (refusing even liberation, preferring Vrindavan to Vaikuntha) show it is about the sweetness of loving devotion, not a dismissal of all practice.

sur.vp.144.practical_reading: Encourages people to sing, chant or play devotional music for joy, not only to perform duties.
