misreadings: Not a rejection of all discipline or practice.
Not a put-down of pilgrimage for those who value it.
not_for: someone who finds singing impossible in fresh grief
speaks_to: people who love music or kirtan

sur.vp.153.context: The short pada adds: water does not drown it and fire does not burn it, such is Hari's name. It closes on the Lord of Vaikuntha as the giver of all happiness.
sur.vp.153.core_teaching: The divine name is the one wealth that cannot be lost, stolen or used up, and it serves in crisis.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 153 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Rama's name is the wealth of us poor: thieves cannot steal it, it never decreases, it helps in calamity, water cannot drown it and fire cannot burn it.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: The extra images (fire and water cannot destroy it) add to the 'secure treasure' theme.

sur.vp.153.practical_reading: Used to give perspective after material loss: some inner resources cannot be taken away.
misreadings: Not a financial plan or a reason to neglect money matters.
Not a romanticising of poverty.
cautions: For someone in real financial hardship, avoid implying poverty doesn't matter.
not_for: someone facing eviction or hunger who needs practical help first
speaks_to: after a loss of money or job

sur.vp.16.context: The pada opens by asking who but the Lord protects a devotee's honour, since he ignores caste and lineage. It recalls that the Yadu clan was destroyed by a curse while Durvasa was chased through three worlds for Ambarisha's sake. Then this couplet, and then Prahlada (Narasimha) and a closing question: who ever took refuge and was not saved?
sur.vp.16.core_teaching: The greatest stoops to the humblest service for those he loves; true greatness shows in service.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 16 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Says the Lord whose foot-water (the Ganga) Shiva carries washed brahmins' feet with his own hands at the Pandavas' Rajasuya. He did not care about caste or clan when protecting devotees.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: The pada sets this act among other examples of the Lord stepping out of his status for devotees (Ambarisha, Prahlada), ending on 'who took refuge and was not saved?'

sur.vp.16.practical_reading: Used to praise humble service by people in power: leaders and elders who do the lowly work themselves.
misreadings: Not a call for anyone to accept humiliation; Krishna's service was freely chosen.
not_for: someone being exploited or made to serve against their will

sur.vp.167.context: The pada goes on: protect the honour of one who has come for refuge and remove the fear of Yama. Sur says he did no yoga, sacrifice or austerity and craved pleasure like a dog after scraps. If Brahma wrote with a wish-tree pen, using the Himalaya ground into the ocean as ink and the whole earth as paper, his faults would still not end. He closes by asking Murari, refuge of the refugeless, to pull him out.
sur.vp.167.core_teaching: The devotee asks to be received not by merit but by the Lord's mercy and the honour of having taken refuge.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika (1955 printing), Hindi bhavartha to pada 167
commentaries.gist: Do not weigh my merits and faults; protect one who took refuge and remove the fear of Yama. I did no spiritual practice, my faults could fill the earth, and none is as merciful as you.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press 1955 printing)
commentaries.gist: The hyperbole of endless faults (Himalaya as ink, earth as paper) makes the plea a total surrender of self-justification, ending 'stretch out your arm'.

sur.vp.167.practical_reading: Speaks to people who feel they don't measure up: they can ask to be accepted as they are.
misreadings: Not an excuse to stop trying to do better.
Not self-hatred as an ideal.
cautions: The full pada is very self-deprecating (dog after scraps, endless faults); for someone with low self-worth or depression, use the opening line only.
not_for: someone with severe self-loathing (the full pada could reinforce it)
speaks_to: shame and feeling not good enough

sur.vp.170.context: The pada continues: you did not let the womb's fire burn me and made my body like gold; born in the world I sinned and spoiled everything from start to end. Sur is fallen, you lift the fallen, and you kept the honour of your pledge.
sur.vp.170.core_teaching: Before we could do anything, God's care was already there; human life is given for remembrance.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 170 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: You did me much good: you gave a human body for remembering you, though I achieved nothing; in the womb, head down and distressed, you did not forget me. You lift the fallen and kept your pledge.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: The pada pairs gratitude with confession: after the womb and the body 'like gold', Sur admits he spoiled everything from birth to end, and rests his hope on the Lord's pledge to lift the fallen.

sur.vp.170.practical_reading: Used for gratitude: we were cared for before we could ask, so look at life as a gift meant for something.
misreadings: Not a claim about fetal consciousness or medicine.
Not a reason to feel guilty about one's life.
cautions: Womb and birth imagery: may be painful after miscarriage, stillbirth or infertility.
not_for: pregnancy loss or infertility
someone struggling with guilt

sur.vp.173.context: The pada is a long confession: what sin have I not done? If you count it, how will your title 'purifier of the fallen' be true? Since birth I have never once said your name; I am a slanderer, glutton, cheat; I wandered door to door like the blind leading the blind. Then this couplet, and a closing line calling the Lord all-knowing and compassionate.
sur.vp.173.core_teaching: God's true greatness is shown not in loving the good but in sheltering the lowly and unworthy.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 173 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Who doesn't like a virtuous, pure servant? A master's lordship is proven when the lowly find refuge with him. The pada argues the Lord's title 'purifier of the fallen' would be empty if he counted sins.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: The couplet is the turning point of the pada: after listing every fault, Sur argues that sheltering such a person is exactly where the Lord's greatness shows.

sur.vp.173.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say grace is not a reward for being good; it also gives a model for how leaders and parents should treat those who struggle.
misreadings: Not a licence to keep doing wrong.
Not a claim that virtue doesn't matter.
cautions: The surrounding confession is harsh self-description; quote this couplet, not the list.
not_for: someone in deep shame who would read the full confession as about them
speaks_to: leaders and parents thinking about how they treat the weakest

sur.vp.176.context: The pada continues: my senses are unconquered, my intellect runs after pleasures, my mind moves the wrong way every day; lust, anger, pride and greed keep me distraught day and night. I have none of yoga, japa, austerity or pilgrimage to my name; how can I please you? Sur's state is such: to whom else can a poor man speak?
sur.vp.176.core_teaching: Even steadiness in devotion is asked for as a gift, because the devotee knows his own mind cannot hold it.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 176 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Asks the compassionate Lord to do whatever is needed so the devotee does not leave his feet even for a moment, admitting that senses, intellect and mind pull away and that he has no spiritual practice to offer.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: The confession of an unruly mind explains why steadiness is asked for rather than promised.

sur.vp.176.practical_reading: Speaks to anyone who keeps slipping on a commitment: ask for help with constancy itself instead of only resolving harder.
misreadings: Not a statement that effort is pointless.
not_for: someone in addiction crisis who needs clinical support, if offered as the only answer

sur.vp.18.context: The pada then lists rescues: Gajendra; Govardhan held for seven days for Braj; Jarasandha killed and kings freed; a dead brahmin's son restored; Narasimha for Prahlada; Draupadi's sari; Ambarisha; the Pandavas from the lac house; Nanda freed from Varuna's noose. Sur, 'refuge of the refugeless', ends by asking who will now remind the Lord of him.
sur.vp.18.core_teaching: Only God truly feels a devotee's pain as his own, and he has always responded.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 18 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Nobody else is pained by a devotee's pain; whenever the lowly suffered, Krishna was kind. Gajendra, helpless and looking in all directions, finally took refuge and was freed.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: The long catalogue of rescues (Gajendra, Govardhan, Prahlada, Draupadi, Ambarisha, the Pandavas) makes 'every time' concrete; the closing plea turns the list into Sur's own request.

sur.vp.18.practical_reading: Comfort for someone who feels nobody really understands their pain.
misreadings: Not a claim that people around you do not care.
Not advice to stop sharing pain with people.
cautions: 'No one else feels your pain' can deepen isolation; pair with encouragement to reach out to people too.
not_for: someone already withdrawing from all human contact
depression with isolation
speaks_to: chronic pain or illness that others don't grasp

sur.vp.2.context: The pada goes on to examples: Draupadi's sari kept growing in the Kuru court; Krishna begged greens at Vidura's house though Vidura had no high caste; he was won by Kubja, who had neither beauty nor virtue; he ran to save Gajendra from the crocodile. It closes on how many lowly people he has carried across.
sur.vp.2.core_teaching: God's natural side is with the unprotected; status, birth and merit do not decide who he helps.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 22 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Says the Lord of the world is the companion of the protectorless and plays many roles for his devotees. Draupadi's cry made him a river of compassion; Vidura's low caste and Kubja's lack of virtue did not matter to him.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: Lists Draupadi, Vidura, Kubja and Gajendra as proof: caste, beauty and strength do not decide whom Hari helps.

sur.vp.2.practical_reading: Speaks to anyone who feels they have no backer: in this view, being without support is exactly what draws God's care.
misreadings: Not a reason to stay without human support.
Not a claim that people with family are less loved.
cautions: Mentions Draupadi's public humiliation; a reader recovering from abuse may find the image heavy.
not_for: someone who needs practical protection now (abuse, danger): point to real help first
speaks_to: feeling alone or without anyone to stand up for you
being looked down on for background or caste

data_flags.attribution_note: Reference error: the ref_label says Sur Vinay Patrika 2, but both Gita Press scans place 'नाथ अनाथनि ही के संगी' at pada 22 (the 1955 index lists it at 22; the other scan shows it between 21 and 23). Traditional attribution to Surdas via the...

sur.vp.211.context: The pada continues with more images: how can one burn a vine one has watered oneself? Shiva left the ocean's jewels and held the poison in his throat. Should a child starve on a goat's dewlap while his mother lives? Though Sur is a great sinner, you are still the purifier of the fallen.
sur.vp.211.core_teaching: God regards his own as a mother regards her child: faults do not cancel belonging.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 211 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Who doesn't honour their own? A mother ignores her child's many faults; no one burns a vine they watered; Shiva took the poison and left the jewels. So the Purifier should accept Sur, sinner though he is.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: The extra images (a self-watered vine, Shiva swallowing poison, a starving child beside its mother) all argue from the protector's own nature.

sur.vp.211.practical_reading: Used to reassure people who fear they have exhausted God's patience; also a model for patient parenting.
misreadings: About God's regard, not a reason to excuse harm done to real people.
Not a demand that a parent tolerate abuse from a child.
cautions: A reader with a cold or absent mother may find the image painful.
not_for: someone hurt by a mother's rejection
victims who might hear 'forgive endlessly'
speaks_to: fear of having failed too often

sur.vp.215.context: The pada continues: by my own reasoning I searched and grasped the fruit of all merit (the name). The Vedas, Puranas, smritis and saints depend on it as a fish depends on water. The eight siddhis, nine treasures and the gods' wealth are husk without you. Grant Sur the grace that carried Ajamila, the courtesan and the hunter across, even if only for one moment at the end.
sur.vp.215.core_teaching: The name of God is the devotee's whole strength; everything else is husk.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 215 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Without your name what strength have I? I chose it after much thought; scripture and saints live on it like fish in water; powers and riches are chaff. Grant Sur that grace, at least at the end.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: The closing request, grace 'even for one moment at the end', ties the name to the hour of death.

sur.vp.215.practical_reading: Comfort when other supports have failed: the name, or prayer, remains when other strengths run out.
misreadings: Not a rejection of skills, effort or other support.
cautions: The pada's close refers to the moment of death; keep that out of readings for the grieving unless intended.
not_for: someone who feels prayer has failed them
speaks_to: when other supports have fallen away
people who chant or pray the name

sur.vp.219.context: The pada continues: through ego I forgot you, and that alone broke our companionship. Ruled by nature I fell into the sea of becoming and wandered bound and orphaned, like a tired deer chasing a mirage. In no birth did I keep the company of saints. Rites, dharma and pilgrimages without worship came to nothing. Place your hand of fearlessness on Sur's head.
sur.vp.219.core_teaching: Grace often comes through the right people arriving at the right time; having been caught, the devotee asks to stay sheltered.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 219 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Keep me in refuge now. By your grace you sent saints and teachers who caught my hand as I was carried off. I lost you through ego and chased mirages; place your fearless hand on my head.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: The rest of the pada explains how he was being 'swept away' (ego, mirages, no satsang), so the rescue is spiritual guidance, not physical rescue.

sur.vp.219.practical_reading: Used to recognise the mentors, friends or counsellors who appeared when life was going under, and to stay close to that help.
misreadings: Not a call to obey any guru uncritically.
cautions: Easily extended to 'any teacher is sent by God'; avoid that for readers hurt by a religious leader.
not_for: someone harmed by a guru or religious authority
speaks_to: gratitude for a mentor or helper

sur.vp.220.context: The pada ends: lotus-eyed, cloud-dark lovely one, let me remain your follower; Sur's Lord is a treasury of kindness to devotees, and I hold your feet. So the acceptance of ups and downs is framed by one request: whatever my state, let me stay yours.
sur.vp.220.core_teaching: Accept life's ups and downs as the Lord's keeping; ask only to remain his in all of them.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 230 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: I will live however you keep me; you know your servants' joys and sorrows, so why recite them? Sometimes food, sometimes hunger, sometimes riding, sometimes carrying loads; only let me remain your servant.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: The closing couplet makes the real request: not a change in fortune but to stay a follower in every state.

sur.vp.220.practical_reading: Used to steady people through financial or status swings: circumstances change, belonging need not.
misreadings: Acceptance is not resignation to mistreatment or injustice.
Not advice to stop trying to improve one's situation.
cautions: 'Sometimes hunger' can sound glib to someone who is actually going hungry.
not_for: someone in food or housing insecurity who needs practical help
someone being told to accept abuse

data_flags.attribution_note: Reference error: the index of the Gita Press edition lists 'जैसे राखहु तैसे रहौं' at pada 230, and the pada sits between 229 and 231 in the body. The id sur.vp.220 and ref_label should be corrected to 230. Traditional attribution to Surdas via the vulgate...

sur.vp.229.context: The pada continues: you are the unknowable yet the lord of the orphaned, kind to the lowly, who plays in the groves; you always helped your servants and fulfilled what they wished. Now whose refuge shall I seek, Lord of the Yadus? Keep me, remove my fear. Sur is devoted to your feet; for what fault have you forgotten your kindness to me?
sur.vp.229.core_teaching: When there is no other capable listener, the plea itself is the turning to God.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 229 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Who will hear me? I see no one but you able to remove my pain. You always helped your servants; take me into refuge and remove my fear. For what offence have you forgotten me?

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: The pada ends in complaint ('why have you forgotten me?'), so it allows honest frustration with God, not only trust.

sur.vp.229.practical_reading: Gives words to people who feel unheard; it also models honest complaint in prayer.
misreadings: Telling God is good; telling a person too is also good.
Not proof that no human can help.
cautions: Speaks from isolation; for someone who is isolated and in despair, pair it with a gentle nudge to reach a trusted person or helpline.
not_for: someone at risk of self-harm if used alone, without a pointer to human help
speaks_to: pain that is hard to explain to others

sur.vp.235.context: The pada continues with a series of absurd swaps: should I leave the wish-cow to milk a goat, get off a horse to ride a donkey, throw away a gold jewel to wear glass, wipe off saffron for soot, trade silk for rags, mango for silk-cotton fruit, the sea for a puddle? It ends with Sur, 'cruel and blind', lying at the door, singing.
sur.vp.235.core_teaching: Exclusive belonging: having been named as the Lord's, the devotee has nowhere else to go.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 235 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: You are my refuge and my master; going anywhere else brings me grief. Called yours, whose should I be called now? Leaving you would be like trading a wish-cow for a goat or silk for rags.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: The string of foolish trades (wish-cow for goat, sea for puddle) turns belonging into common sense rather than duty.

sur.vp.235.practical_reading: Speaks to identity and commitment: once you know where you belong, other options lose their pull.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of other people or relationships.
cautions: Ends with Sur calling himself blind and wretched; fine to leave out.
not_for: someone pressured to stay in a group or relationship by 'where else would you go?'
speaks_to: temptation to drift from a commitment

sur.vp.236.context: The pada continues: leaving everything I came for refuge and held your feet firmly; by your strength your household servants fear no one. It adds that all other gods are paupers and beggars, so he has left them; through your grace Sur has found great happiness.
sur.vp.236.core_teaching: Belonging to God does not depend on being good; the devotee's honour and shame become the Lord's concern.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 236 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Whether good or bad, we are yours; our disgrace and our glory both reflect on you as master. I've come for refuge and held your feet; under your protection your servants fear no one.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: A later line dismisses 'other gods' as beggars; that sectarian edge is in the pada though not in the quoted line.

sur.vp.236.practical_reading: Comfort for people who fear their failures disqualify them from love or faith.
misreadings: Not a licence to stop growing.
Do not quote the 'other gods are beggars' line in inclusive settings.
cautions: Sectarian line about other gods later in the pada.

sur.vp.245.context: The pada continues with examples: Draupadi only said 'refuge' and her garment became endless; Ajamila called his son and the courtesan taught her parrot, and both reached the Lord by the name; Gajendra was freed after a moment's devotion. He took the man-lion form for his devotee. It ends: Sur, blind and guilty, why have you forgotten him?
sur.vp.245.core_teaching: The Lord is the natural protector of those with no one, and he knows the heart without being told.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 245 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: My Lord is such a master of the orphaned: kind to the lowly, full of love, knower of all hearts. Draupadi needed only to say 'refuge'; Ajamila and the courtesan reached him through the name; then why forget blind Sur?

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: The pada closes in complaint (why forget me?), so the praise is also a plea.

sur.vp.245.practical_reading: Comfort for people without family support: someone knows them from within.
misreadings: Not a reason to avoid seeking human support.
cautions: Mentions Draupadi's public humiliation.
not_for: someone who feels God has been absent in a crisis
speaks_to: orphans or those estranged from family

sur.vp.250.context: The pada continues with examples of prompt help: Govardhan lifted for cows and cowherds; Agha, Arishta, Keshi and Kaliya subdued and the forest fire swallowed; Kamsa and his line killed, Jarasandha slain, the guru's dead son brought back; Draupadi's garment made endless. It ends: whose refuge should I seek? There is no other.
sur.vp.250.core_teaching: The Lord is easy to reach, moved by simple remembrance, and quick to give fearlessness.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 250 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: You have never delayed; by nature you are easy to attain and won by remembrance, and have given your devotees fearlessness. You lifted Govardhan for Braj, subdued demons, and made Draupadi's garment inexhaustible.

commentaries.who: NPS Sursagar (Vajpeyi ed. 1950), text of pada 1.121
commentaries.gist: The examples are all instant rescues, supporting 'never delayed'.

sur.vp.250.practical_reading: Encourages people who think God is distant or demanding: in this view a sincere turn of the mind is enough.
misreadings: Not a promise that every request is answered at once.
cautions: 'Never delayed' may hurt someone who waited long for help that never came.
not_for: someone whose prayers for a sick loved one 'were not answered'

data_flags.attribution_note: Text error: our sanskrit has 'भक्तनि अमर दियौ' (gave the undying), but both Gita Press scans and the NPS Sursagar read 'भक्तनि अभै दियौ' (gave fearlessness). Traditional attribution to Surdas via the vulgate Sursagar; the pada is in the Nagari Pracharini Sabha Sursagar (Vajpeyi ed.,...
data_flags.translation_note: Mistranslation following the text error: 'you have always given your devotees what is undying' should be 'you have always given your devotees fearlessness (abhaya)'. Fix both the Braj text and the English. The line ('You never once delayed. You are easy to reach...') is fine.

sur.vp.256.context: The pada goes on: hearing the elephant's cry you ran in haste to free him; you protected Parikshit in the womb; you made Draupadi's cloth grow in the assembly; you comforted the queens of the kings jailed by Jarasandha and freed them; you appeared even when Rahu stole the nectar. Sur ends: my hope rests on you, you are with me in trouble, do as you see fit, everything is in your hands.
sur.vp.256.core_teaching: God is especially the companion of people in narrow straits.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 256 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Hari, you stand by people in trouble: you ran to free the elephant, guarded Parikshit in the womb, saved Draupadi, freed Jarasandha's prisoners. Do as you think best; the poor man's affairs are in your hands.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: The list is longer than our setting says: besides Gajendra, Draupadi and Parikshit it includes Jarasandha's captive kings and the Rahu episode; the close is surrender ('do as you know').

sur.vp.256.practical_reading: For someone cornered (a deadline, debt, a diagnosis): you are not alone in the tight place.
misreadings: Not a guarantee of escape from the situation.
not_for: someone in physical danger who needs emergency help first

sur.vp.258.context: The pada praises the Lord as known to be kind and the giver of fearlessness. It asks which of the hunter, Jatayu, the courtesan or Gajendra was learned, yet he came when they remembered him. He killed Keshi and Kamsa, gave Sudama the wealth of three worlds for a handful of rice, and freed Ahalya at a touch of his foot. Sur asks only for devotion to the Lord.
sur.vp.258.core_teaching: The Lord answers tiny sincere offerings with total generosity.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 258 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: He gave the splendour of three worlds for Sudama's rice and gives everything when pleased by one tulsi leaf; none of the hunter, vulture, courtesan or elephant was a scholar, yet he came when they remembered him.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: Paired in the same couplet with Sudama's rice, the tulsi leaf stands for a humble gift; the pada ends by asking only for bhakti, not for wealth.

commentaries.who: Parallel: Bhagavad Gita 9.26 (our_note's comparison)
commentaries.gist: Krishna says he gladly accepts even a leaf, flower, fruit or water offered with devotion; the same idea of a small sincere gift.

sur.vp.258.practical_reading: Encourages small daily offerings (a leaf, a lamp, a minute of attention) done with love.
misreadings: Not a transaction: offering a leaf to get riches.
Not a claim that bigger offerings are wasted.
not_for: someone told to make offerings for material gain
speaks_to: feeling you have little to give

sur.vp.270.context: A short pada. It goes on: you saved the courtesan, Jatayu, Ajamila, Shabari and Gajendra; make fallen Sur pure and keep the honour of one whose arm you have taken. The next pada in the edition is the famous 'हमारे प्रभु, औगुन चित न धरौ'.
sur.vp.270.core_teaching: A plea from loneliness: the devotee has no one else to mend his life, so asks the Lord to remember him.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 270 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Lord of Braj, take care of me; I have no one else, only you can set my life right. You saved the courtesan, Jatayu, Ajamila, Shabari and the elephant; purify Sur and honour the hand you've held.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: The rescue list shows the plea rests on precedent: those saved were outcasts or helpless, like the speaker.

sur.vp.270.practical_reading: Words for lonely seasons: you can ask to be remembered and helped.
misreadings: A prayer from a lonely place, not advice to cut off from people.
cautions: 'No one else in the world' can mirror depressive isolation; pair with a nudge toward people.
not_for: someone isolated and at risk, if used without pointing to human help

sur.vp.271.context: The pada continues: one stream is called a river, another a drain of dirty water, but when both join the Ganga they become one colour and are called Ganga. So too body is maya and the soul is called Brahman, but mixed together they are spoiled; either separate them, or your vow will be broken.
sur.vp.271.core_teaching: The Lord is samadarshi, impartial like the touchstone: he does not ask where the soul has been, he transforms it.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 271 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Don't hold my faults in mind; your name is 'impartial', so carry me across. The touchstone turns both a worshipped sword and a butcher's knife into gold; a drain and a river both become Ganga.

commentaries.who: NPS Sursagar (Vajpeyi ed. 1950), text of pada 1.220
commentaries.gist: The last couplet adds a Vedantic turn: the soul (Brahman) is spoiled by mixing with maya; the Lord must separate them or his vow fails. The plea ends as a dare, not just a request.

sur.vp.271.practical_reading: Used to say that no past disqualifies a person from grace; also cited for impartial treatment of people.
misreadings: Not a statement that actions have no consequences.
Not about excusing harm to others.
speaks_to: feeling judged by background or history
people rebuilding after prison, addiction or scandal

sur.vp.279.context: The pada continues: a lake fills, overflows, then dries until dust blows; the moon of the second day waxes, then wanes away. Sur's conclusion: let no one trust either prosperity or adversity to last, and therefore serve the Lord, who alone is constant.
sur.vp.279.core_teaching: Fortune and misfortune keep turning like the seasons; trust neither, and anchor in what does not change.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 279 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Serve the Lord of the Yadus, since bodily life swings between fortune and trouble, like trees that flower and shed, a lake that fills and dries, the waxing and waning moon. Trust neither wealth nor calamity.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: The closing warning, trust neither state, makes it a teaching on impermanence as much as consolation.

sur.vp.279.practical_reading: Used to steady people in a downturn (this too will turn) and to humble them in an upswing.
misreadings: Surrender comes after doing your part and reflecting, not instead of it.
Not fatalism: the point is not to cling, not to stop acting.
not_for: someone in acute grief who may hear 'it will pass' as dismissive

sur.vp.281.context: The pada continues: sometimes, getting fickle wealth, a man walks crookedly with pride; sometimes he gathers dust on the road and wails for food. Proud of body, drunk on money and youth, he boasts 'I am great', wastes days in quarrels, play and eating, and regrets it in old age. So, Sur says, take care: without worship there is no happiness.
sur.vp.281.core_teaching: Since circumstances and health will change, use the good days for what matters.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 281 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Not all days pass alike, so remember and worship Hari while the body is healthy. Sometimes wealth makes a man strut, sometimes he begs on the road; pride in body, money and youth gives way to regret in old age.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: The pada's middle is a warning against pride and wasted time, so the line is a call to act now, not only comfort.

sur.vp.281.practical_reading: Teachers apply it as 'use your strength while you have it': start the practice, the visit, the repair now.
misreadings: Not fear-mongering about illness or death.
cautions: Mentions old age and decline; gentle with the ill or elderly.
not_for: someone newly diagnosed or chronically ill (implies the window has closed)

sur.vp.295.context: The pada opens: go somewhere and gain the taste of Hari; take a path where going (death) brings no grief and coming (birth) no elation. After this line it adds: bear the pairs (argument, joy and anxiety) in the heart. If this enters the mind, the happiness is beyond words, and all the siddhis and treasures come of themselves.
sur.vp.295.core_teaching: The conduct of the devotional path: gentle speech, humility toward all, steady cheerfulness, and patience with life's opposites.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 295 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: To find the joy of Hari, take a path free of grief at death and elation at birth: speak gently, be humble with everyone, stay always cheerful, and bear argument, joy and sorrow evenly; then happiness beyond words comes.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: Placed between 'seek Hari-rasa' and 'bear the dualities', the line is practical conduct within a devotional goal.

sur.vp.295.practical_reading: A plain rule of daily conduct: gentle words, no airs, steady good humour.
misreadings: Humility is not self-erasure or accepting disrespect.
'Always joyful' is not a ban on sadness.
cautions: 'Always stay joyful' can feel invalidating to someone depressed or grieving.
not_for: depression or fresh grief
someone being told to stay meek in an abusive setting
speaks_to: people seeking a simple daily rule

sur.vp.297.context: The pada opens by telling the follower of bhakti to give up attachment to wife and children and not to worry about food and clothing, because the sustainer of the world feeds all; whoever keeps an animal at his door feeds it. After our lines it lists further provision: forest fruit for food, springs for thirst, hands for bowls, bark for clothes, the earth for a bed, caves for houses; so drop all worry and love Hari's feet.
sur.vp.297.core_teaching: Providence argued from care already received before we could ask: the one who fed us in the womb will not forget us.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 297 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Whoever takes refuge, how could the Lord forget him? He nourishes the child in the womb and then makes milk from blood; he provides fruit, water and shelter for all creatures; so give up worry and love Hari's feet.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: The opening couplets advise dropping attachment to wife and children and not thinking about food or clothes; the selected lines read better alone.

sur.vp.297.practical_reading: Used to ease worry about provision by recalling care already received, alongside responsible work.
misreadings: Trust alongside work and planning.
The pada's advice to drop concern for family is renunciant counsel, not a model for parents.
cautions: Womb and breastfeeding imagery: sensitive after pregnancy loss or for mothers unable to breastfeed.
The omitted opening lines about leaving family concerns should not be used.
not_for: pregnancy loss or infant loss
someone neglecting dependants in the name of faith

sur.vp.300.context: The pada continues with a sharper edge: whoever leaves the lotus-eyed Lord's greatness to meditate on another god is a fool who leaves the Ganga to dig a well when thirsty. A bee that has tasted lotus nectar won't want karil berries; who would leave the wish-cow to milk a goat?
sur.vp.300.core_teaching: The restless heart roams but has only one real resting place, as a bird at sea can only return to the ship.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 300 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Where else could my mind be happy? Like a ship's bird at sea that finds nowhere to land and returns. Leaving the lotus-eyed Lord for other gods is like digging a well beside the Ganga.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: The couplets after the ship-bird are polemical (other gods as a well beside the Ganga); quote only the opening in inclusive contexts.

sur.vp.300.practical_reading: Used for restless seekers who try many things and keep returning to the same centre: let that return be welcome, not shameful.
misreadings: Not a statement that exploring is wrong.
Do not extend it into the pada's put-down of other deities.
cautions: The rest of the pada disparages worship of other gods.
not_for: interfaith settings if the full pada is used
speaks_to: feeling only one place feels like home

sur.vp.301.context: The pada continues with more images of absorbed love: the deer lost in music, killed by the hunter even without an arrow; the chakori gazing at the moon; the lotus opening at the sight of the sun. Sur asks to hear the Lord's sweet qualities every day.
sur.vp.301.core_teaching: Devotion is the devotee's very life; without it he would wither.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 301 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Your bhakti is my life-breath; without it your servant would wither like a betel leaf without water. Like the deer lost in music, the chakori at the moon, the lotus at sunrise, may I hear your qualities daily.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: The images (deer, chakori, lotus) are all of absorption and delight, so the point is joy, not dependence born of fear.

sur.vp.301.practical_reading: Names a practice that has become as necessary as breath; encourages keeping it daily.
misreadings: Not a statement about dependence on a person.
cautions: The deer image involves a hunter killing an enraptured animal; best left out.
not_for: someone in a codependent relationship who could map it onto a person
speaks_to: people for whom prayer or music is life-giving
returning to practice after a dry spell

sur.vp.32.context: The opening says that, with a master who feeds and sustains the whole world, the one who keeps worrying is immature. Examples follow: Gajendra was freed as soon as he called the name, and Draupadi's sari grew when Duhshasana pulled it. Sur ends by taking refuge at the feet of the Lord who loves devotees.
sur.vp.32.core_teaching: Trust in the Lord's promise of care is the mature stance; anxious fretting shows unripe faith.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 32 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Trusting the Lord's word is what is true; with such a sustainer of the world as master, whoever worries is an incomplete devotee. Cites Gajendra and Draupadi.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: The second half-line (omitted in our data) scolds fretting as 'unripe'; the examples show help arriving at the moment of calling.

sur.vp.32.practical_reading: Used to ease anxiety about provision: do your part, then rest in trust rather than spinning in worry.
misreadings: Not a reason to stop earning, planning or seeking help.
Not a judgment that anxious people lack faith (handle 'unripe' with care).
cautions: The omitted half-line calls worriers 'unripe'; for someone with an anxiety disorder that can feel shaming.
not_for: clinical anxiety where 'just trust' feels dismissive
someone facing real financial danger who needs practical help

sur.vp.37.context: After the opening, the pada gives examples: Hiranyakashipu's blows failed and Prahlada never feared; Dhruva still rules unmoved; Draupadi's honour was saved and Duryodhana's pride broken; Indra's anger against Braj came to nothing when Krishna lifted Govardhan. It ends: those who sing to the Lord and take refuge are saved.
sur.vp.37.core_teaching: The one God has accepted is safe at the root, whatever hostility gathers around them.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 37 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: If Krishna accepts someone, not one hair can be harmed even if the whole world becomes an enemy. Cites Prahlada, Dhruva, Draupadi and the Govardhan episode; ends that those who take refuge are saved.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: Every example (Prahlada, Dhruva, Draupadi, Braj under Indra's storm) is a lone or weak party against a powerful enemy, so the pada is about courage under hostility.

sur.vp.37.practical_reading: Used to give courage under opposition, bullying or public hostility: inner security does not depend on others' approval.
misreadings: Not a guarantee against physical harm.
Not a reason to ignore real threats or refuse protection.
cautions: For someone who has been harmed, 'not a hair falls' can imply they were not held by God; frame as inner safety.
not_for: victims of violence or abuse
someone in danger who needs to seek safety first

sur.vp.423.context: The pada opens: once the mind is fixed on Nandlal, nothing else pleases it; put a fish in milk and it still finds no ease without water. The one given his rasa to drink wanders soft and intoxicated; like a mute who eats jaggery, the joy cannot be told. Then this closing image of the river and the sea.
sur.vp.423.core_teaching: A mind that has truly reached its object does not turn back, as a river that meets the sea does not flow upstream.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 43 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: One whose mind is fixed on Nandlal likes nothing else, as a fish in milk still longs for water; the joy is like a mute tasting jaggery. Like a river that has met the sea, the mind never turns back.

commentaries.who: NPS Sursagar (Vajpeyi ed. 1950), text of pada 2.10
commentaries.gist: The earlier images (fish in milk, mute tasting jaggery) set up the river-sea image as the end of restlessness.

sur.vp.423.practical_reading: Describes the settledness that follows real commitment; encourages trust that the restless phase can end.
misreadings: Not a claim that a committed person never doubts.
not_for: someone forced into a commitment they didn't choose

data_flags.corrected_ref: Sur Vinay Patrika (Gita Press) pada 43, NOT 423 (the Gita Press book has about 309 padas). Closing couplet of 'जाकौ मन लाग्यौ नँदलालहि, ताहि और नहिं भावै'. NPS Sursagar skandha 2, pada 10.
data_flags.attribution_note: Reference error: both Gita Press scans index this pada at 43 and it sits between padas 42 and 44; the edition has no pada 423. Fix the id/ref_label. Traditional attribution to Surdas via the vulgate Sursagar; the pada is in the Nagari Pracharini Sabha Sursagar...

sur.vp.71.context: A short pada addressed to the poet's own mind. Between the two quoted lines it says to stay detached from this boundless world so that the fear of Yama need not be suffered. It closes: by worshipping the Lord, gain something that will help at the end.
sur.vp.71.core_teaching: Belong to God and accept with contentment what life brings, rather than chasing or dreading outcomes.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 71 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Tells the mind to remain Govind's and stay unattached to the world so the fear of death need not be borne; accept with contentment whatever sorrow, joy, fame or fortune comes by one's lot.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text)
commentaries.gist: The pada frames acceptance as part of preparing for the end: bhajan now gives one something to carry at death.

sur.vp.71.practical_reading: Teachers apply it as equanimity: do your work, then receive praise and blame, gain and loss without being thrown.
misreadings: Not acceptance of mistreatment or injustice.
Not passivity about one's circumstances.
cautions: Mentions fear of Yama (death); light touch for grieving readers.
not_for: someone in an abusive situation who might hear 'accept what comes'
fresh trauma
speaks_to: staying centred during praise or criticism

sur.vp.76.context: The pada opens by asking 'what would you lose by living this way?' After this line it says: so what if wealth grew and you built a bigger house? Let there be Hari's stories, worship and lodging for saints in it. Offer wife, children, horses and elephants to Shyam: 'this is my true view', says Sur.
sur.vp.76.core_teaching: Hold your household as God's, and yourself as its steward rather than its owner.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika, Hindi bhavartha to pada 76 (translator credited on archive.org as Sudarshan Singh)
commentaries.gist: Make Nandanandan the owner of the house and live as his servant; what would that cost you? A bigger house and more wealth mean little unless the home holds Hari's stories, worship and saints; surrender family and riches to Shyam.

commentaries.who: Rest of the pada itself (Gita Press text; cross-checked in NPS Sursagar, Vajpeyi ed.)
commentaries.gist: The rest of the pada turns from wealth-building to hospitality and worship at home, so the line is about the purpose of a household, not renouncing it.

sur.vp.76.practical_reading: A householder's bhakti: run the home and money as a trust, with room for prayer, guests and good company.
misreadings: Not a call to give away the house or neglect family.
Not about hierarchy within the family.
cautions: 'Servant/slave' language and 'offer wife and children' may jar for modern readers; the line itself is fine.
not_for: someone losing their home
someone in a controlling household where 'servant' language could be misused
speaks_to: people anxious about wealth and status

surya_gita.3.36.context: The sages ask why even virtuous people are reborn. Surya answers that desire keeps regenerating the seeds of wrongdoing, and desire-driven good deeds earn rewards but don't purify the mind; without a pure mind there's no path to knowledge (vv. 35-38 in the 1967 numbering). This verse marks the turning point: weariness with pleasure and pain. After it he says that from then on, over several lives, one grows in the yoga of knowledge.
surya_gita.3.36.core_teaching: Disenchantment that comes from having lived through enough highs and lows is not a failure; it is where real discernment and freedom from craving begin.

commentaries.who: Hindi translation in the Mahamandal edition (1967; no classical commentary exists)
commentaries.gist: Renders vv. 39-40: even with births driven by desire, scripture on liberation remains meaningful because selfless action can arise; after tasting pleasure and pain a person tires of them, becomes discerning and reaches desirelessness.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Sanskrit text, Surya Gita ch. 3)
commentaries.gist: The verse answers the sages' worry that the virtuous are still reborn: desire-tinged merit doesn't purify; disenchantment opens the path; knowledge then matures over several lives.

surya_gita.3.36.practical_reading: Feeling that the usual rewards no longer move you can be the beginning of a wiser relationship with them, if you let your own judgement, rather than numbness, lead.
misreadings: Not 'nothing matters'; nirveda here leads to discernment, not apathy
Not a claim that suffering is good for you
cautions: Late text; label accurately
Rebirth framing (over several lives) can feel distancing; leave it out of a reading for someone low
Can romanticise numbness; distinguish disenchantment from depression
not_for: someone whose flatness is depression and who needs care, not reframing

surya_gita.6.60.context: In chapter 6 the sages ask to see Surya's cosmic form, are overwhelmed, praise it and ask for his gentle form. Surya tells them to meditate on the cosmic form morning and evening and to be wholly devoted to him. Here they admit their mind is as restless as wind and ask how to restrain it. Next they ask to hear about bhakti and yoga, and Surya begins by defining love and devotion (6.64).
surya_gita.6.60.core_teaching: The sages admit honestly that they cannot simply 'fix the mind' and ask for a method.

commentaries.who: Hindi translation in the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal edition (1967)
commentaries.gist: The sages ask Surya to teach them how to hold back a mind as fickle as wind so they can remember him for lasting peace, and then say they want to hear about devotion and yoga.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text, Surya Gita ch. 6 (same edition)
commentaries.gist: Just before, Surya tells them to meditate on his cosmic form at dawn and dusk and to be wholly devoted to him; just after, he answers with a teaching on love, devotion and four kinds of yoga.

commentaries.who: Parallel: Bhagavad Gita 6.34 (Arjuna)
commentaries.gist: Arjuna tells Krishna the mind is restless, turbulent and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind; the Surya Gita sages use the same wind image.

surya_gita.6.60.practical_reading: Gives permission to admit that one's mind won't sit still and to ask for help or a method instead of forcing it.
misreadings: Not a claim that a restless mind makes one unfit for practice.
not_for: someone with a clinical attention or anxiety disorder looking for treatment advice

surya_gita.6.64.context: Asked about devotion, Surya first defines anuraga as real attachment to an object and says it varies by object: toward children it is affection, toward spouse and friends love, toward parents reverence. This verse adds that the same attachment turned wholly toward him is bhakti. He goes on to distinguish rule-based (vaidhi), passionate (ragatmika) and supreme devotion, and then the kinds of yoga.
surya_gita.6.64.core_teaching: Devotion is not a foreign emotion: it is the familiar human capacity for love, redirected toward the divine.

commentaries.who: Hindi translation in the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal edition (1967)
commentaries.gist: Affection for children is called sneha, for wife and friends prema, for parents shraddha; when a seeker's attachment is in Surya alone, it is called bhakti.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text, Surya Gita ch. 6 (same edition)
commentaries.gist: The definition opens Surya's answer on bhakti and yoga: anuraga is defined first, then sorted by object, and then bhakti is divided into vaidhi, ragatmika and para before he turns to mantra, laya, hatha and raja yoga.

surya_gita.6.64.practical_reading: Teachers use this idea to make devotion approachable: start from how you already love family and friends, and let that feeling widen toward God.
misreadings: Not a claim that loving family is already devotion, or that one must give up human love.
Not a ranking that devalues human relationships.
cautions: For someone estranged from parents or grieving a spouse, the examples may sting.
not_for: someone in fresh grief for a spouse or parent
someone estranged from family
speaks_to: those who love deeply but feel unspiritual

surya_gita.7.54.context: In a chapter on the marks of the freed, Surya lists traits of the videha-mukta: senses still as a painted picture (7.50), mind dissolved like salt in water (7.55). Then this verse: suffering belongs to the one with a mind. 7.57: the jivanmukta still meets pain from prārabdha karma, but how could the one beyond all karma? 7.58-62 warn that anyone who merely thinks 'I am free' is not.
surya_gita.7.54.core_teaching: Suffering is produced by the mind's own projections and resolves; where the mind has dissolved, suffering has nowhere to land.
surya_gita.7.54.practical_reading: Notice how much of a bad day is the mind's commentary (should, if only, what if); loosen one such resolve.
misreadings: Not 'your pain is your fault'.
Not a claim that people who still suffer are spiritually failing; the next verse grants that even the living-free meet pain.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.
Do not offer to someone in physical pain, illness or grief as a teaching that pain is 'just the mind'.
not_for: chronic pain or illness
grief
depression

data_flags.corrected_ref: Surya Gita 7.56 in the 1967 Mahamandal edition (chapter 7, 'Jivanmukta-lakshana-nirupana'). Our '7.54' is off by two.

tulsi_dv.100.context: In Gita Press it closes a short run on reliance on Ram and is followed by dohas on the unity of Shiva and Ram. Kaumudi tika frames it as Tulsi's lament after devotees of other paths all criticised his way.
tulsi_dv.100.core_teaching: In the world people mostly block each other; real good comes from the kind Ram.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: In this world everyone is a hindrance to everyone, nobody is anyone's helper; whatever good happens comes from kind Ram.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Situates it biographically: all the critics opposed my way and none supported it; now my trust is in Ram alone, let him do whatever good he will.

tulsi_dv.100.practical_reading: Read as permission to stop waiting for others' approval and to rest one's hope somewhere steadier.
misreadings: Not a blanket claim that all people are bad or that help from others should be refused.
Can sound cynical if lifted from its devotional frame.
cautions: For someone isolated or depressed, 'no one is a helper' may confirm a distorted belief; pair with encouragement to seek actual support.
not_for: someone who is isolated and needs to be nudged toward people, not away from them
readers with paranoid or persecutory distress
speaks_to: opposition at work or in community

tulsi_dv.101.context: Part of a Gita Press group on Ram's grace and protection (dohas 145-148). The image of the infant reaching for snake and fire is a favourite of Tulsi's; Gita Press notes the same picture in Ramcharitmanas Aranya Kand (the mother who pulls a child back from fire and snake).
tulsi_dv.101.core_teaching: As parents snatch an unknowing child away from a snake or fire, Sita and Ram guard the devotee who does not see the danger he is playing with.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: As parents stop a child playing with a snake or putting his hand in fire, so Sita-Ram, as mother and father, save the child Tulsi when he heads toward the snake or flame of sense-objects.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Mother and father of the world, Sita-Ram, protect the child playing with a serpent and reaching into fire, just as natural parents do.

tulsi_dv.101.practical_reading: Teachers use it to speak of unseen protection and of how much of our safety we never notice; the danger in the commentary is our own pull toward harmful pleasures.
misreadings: Not a promise that nothing bad will ever happen.
Not a reason to take risks because 'someone will catch me'.
cautions: A reader whose child was harmed, or who was not protected as a child, may find the parental image painful.
not_for: someone grieving a child's death or injury
survivors of childhood neglect or abuse, unless carefully framed

data_flags.corrected_ref: Dohavali 147 in Gita Press (both scans) and 146 in Kali Prasad Shastri. NOT 101: Gita Press doha 101 is 'sankara priya mama drohi...' on Shiva-Ram unity.
data_flags.attribution_note: Wrong reference: this is Dohavali 147 (Gita Press), not 101.

tulsi_dv.109.context: One of Tulsidas's autobiographical dohas, in a group on Ram's favour making the weak strong (doha 110 cites Hanuman's role in Sugriva's feud). It matches the begging-childhood verses of Kavitavali (Uttar 57, 73) and Hanuman Bahuk 29.
tulsi_dv.109.core_teaching: When Tulsi lived without Ram's shelter he begged for crusts; since Ram became his helper even kings honour him. The change of fortune is credited to grace, not to his own effort.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: When I was without Ram's support I begged scraps door to door; now that Ram is my helper, kings worship my feet.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Expands in verse: those who once begged crumbs without Ram are now helped by him and kings bow; for the one with Raghuvar in the heart, even gods bow.

tulsi_dv.109.practical_reading: Used as a story of reversal: where you start is not where you end, and the change can come from turning toward a source of strength.
misreadings: Not a prosperity promise (devotion = wealth and status).
The honour from kings is a sign of grace in the tradition, not the goal.
cautions: Poverty imagery: avoid implying that poor people lack God's help.
not_for: someone in present poverty who may hear it as 'you're poor because you lack faith'

tulsi_dv.143.context: Follows doha 174, which lists Ram's grace turning a stone into Ahalya, floating rocks on the sea and reviving fallen monkeys; 176 asks Tulsi to remember the one whose messenger is Hanuman. Ahalya, cursed to stone, was freed by the touch of Ram's feet.
tulsi_dv.143.core_teaching: Remember Ram's liberating feet, drop worry; trouble will pass and the heart's wish will be met.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: Remember the feet of Ram that freed the stone-Ahalya from her curse and give up all anxiety; by such single-minded remembrance your troubles go and your wish is fulfilled.

tulsi_dv.143.practical_reading: Used as a short anti-anxiety practice: when worry loops, turn attention to a remembered act of mercy instead of the feared outcome.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that every wish comes true.
Not a dismissal of real problems that need action.
cautions: The Ahalya story involves deception and a husband's curse; avoid retelling details for readers with sexual-assault trauma.
Promise-of-fulfilment language should be softened.
not_for: someone whose prayers for a specific outcome (health, a child) were not answered
readers for whom the Ahalya story is triggering

data_flags.corrected_ref: Dohavali 175 in Gita Press (scan 2 prints the number) and 175 in Kali Prasad Shastri's index. NOT 143: Gita Press doha 143 is 'jani rama seva sarasa...' (Brahma became Jambavan, Shiva became Hanuman).
data_flags.attribution_note: Wrong reference: this is Dohavali 175 (Gita Press), not 143.

tulsi_dv.152.context: Gita Press heads it 'an easy means of gaining love for Ram'. The next doha (153) warns against a bright outward appearance and sweet speech hiding a bitter mind and dirty deeds.
tulsi_dv.152.core_teaching: For one whose mind, speech and deeds are straightforward, every means of gaining love for Ram becomes straight and easy. Guilelessness is the soil in which love grows.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: If mind, speech and all actions are simple, then every method that produces love for Raghunath is simple; love of God comes very easily through mind, word and deed free of hypocrisy.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: If the mind is guileless, speech clean and deeds praiseworthy, the whole method of producing love for Ram is straight; quotes Manas: the pure-hearted find me, I dislike deceit.

tulsi_dv.152.practical_reading: Teachers apply it as integrity before piety: be the same inside and outside, and devotion stops being complicated.
misreadings: Not 'love makes you straight' (that reverses the causation in both commentaries).
Not a call to naivety; 'sudha' means without guile, not gullible.
not_for: someone in a manipulative environment who may hear it as 'just be simple and trusting'

data_flags.translation_note: Our translation reverses the causation. Both commentaries read: with straight mind, speech and deeds, all the means that give birth to love for Raghubar become straight/easy. Ours says straightness is born OF love. Suggested: 'A straight mind, straight words, straight deeds: then every way to...

tulsi_dv.256.context: Gita Press heads it 'attachment, not householder life, is the obstacle to love of God'. Doha 255 just before warns false renunciants who throw away their begging gear; 257 praises staying at home with contentment.
tulsi_dv.256.core_teaching: Clinging to household life loses the true home; walking out of it loses the worldly home. Live in between, in the household but inwardly free, and build the city of Ram's love there.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: Living as a householder loses one's real home (the next world); renouncing loses the home here; so live in the house like a renunciant and settle the city of Ram's love.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Two homes are meant, the natural and the divine; outwardly keep the household and its duties, renounce mentally, and at times retreat to solitude for bhajan; mere leaving home does not win God.

tulsi_dv.256.practical_reading: A balance teaching for people tempted either to over-identify with family and possessions or to escape them: stay, but hold it lightly.
misreadings: Not a rejection of family life; the heading says household life is not the obstacle.
Not an endorsement of walking out on responsibilities.
not_for: someone who needs to leave an unsafe home: this verse could be misread as 'don't leave'

tulsi_dv.278.context: Second of Tulsi's famous chataka (rain-bird) series, which starts at 277. The chataka is said to drink only rain from one cloud (or the Svati raindrop) and so is the poets' figure of single-minded love. Doha 279 goes further: let the bird not even drink, since love's thirst is better growing.
tulsi_dv.278.core_teaching: Whether the beloved cloud rains on time or stays indifferent for a whole lifetime, the chataka-mind hopes only in it. Love does not depend on being answered.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: O cloud-Ram, whether you rain your grace on time or stay indifferent all my life and never rain, this mind-chataka has hope only in you.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Glosses in verse: the chataka mind never despairs, whether the cloud rains in season or never gives a drop.

tulsi_dv.278.practical_reading: Used for faith in dry seasons: continuing to hope and practise when prayer seems unanswered.
misreadings: Not advice to keep waiting on a person who ignores you (our misuse note already says so).
Not glorification of suffering for its own sake.
cautions: Could validate staying in a neglectful relationship if 'cloud' is read as a human partner.
not_for: someone in an emotionally neglectful relationship
someone told to keep waiting by an exploitative guru or partner
speaks_to: long waiting (for a child, a job, healing)

tulsi_dv.282.context: Gita Press heads it 'Gosvamiji's single-mindedness' and prints it as the opening doha of the chataka series (277 onwards); 278 follows. The rain-bird that waits only for its one cloud stands for undivided devotion.
tulsi_dv.282.core_teaching: All of Tulsi's reliance, strength, hope and faith rest on one object, Ram the dark cloud, as the chataka depends on its one cloud.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: One trust, one strength, one hope and one faith: Tulsidas has become a chataka for the one dark cloud, Ram.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Versifies it: the chataka Tulsidas relies only on the one Ghanashyam; his strength, hope and faith are all in him.

tulsi_dv.282.practical_reading: A verse for focus and loyalty: stop scattering trust across many anxious sources and anchor it in one.
misreadings: Not a rejection of all human relationships.
'One' is devotional single-mindedness (ananyata), not exclusivism toward other people.
cautions: Exclusive devotional language; frame inclusively for a general audience.
not_for: someone being isolated by a controlling partner or group that demands 'only me'

data_flags.corrected_ref: Dohavali 277 in Gita Press (scan 2 prints the number) and 277 in Kali Prasad Shastri. NOT 282.
data_flags.attribution_note: Wrong reference: this is Dohavali 277 (Gita Press and Kaumudi tika), not 282. Setting ('opening of the chataka dohas') is right.

tulsi_dv.405.context: In Gita Press it sits in a run of worldly-wise dohas about the weak and the treacherous. Doha 404 says the weak find no place anywhere; 406 condemns those who swear friendship, learn the household's secrets and then plot, calling those who trust them doomed.
tulsi_dv.405.core_teaching: If the very person in whose lap you sleep in trust turns treacherous, only God can protect you from that.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: If the one in whose lap you trustingly lay your head to sleep plays a treacherous trick, then only God can protect you from it.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Adds a practical gloss: recognise an enemy and guard yourself alertly; if a friend plays foul, Ram protects and brings you through.

tulsi_dv.405.practical_reading: Read as consolation and as realism after betrayal by someone close: you could not have guarded against it, and you are not left alone.
misreadings: Not advice to stop protecting yourself (Kaumudi explicitly says stay alert).
Not blame on the betrayed for trusting.
cautions: Intimate betrayal may include abuse; do not let the verse replace practical safety steps (our misuse note is right).
Doha 406 nearby is harsh toward trusting people; do not pair them.
not_for: someone currently in danger from a partner who needs safety planning, not consolation alone
speaks_to: betrayal by a partner, friend or business associate

tulsi_dv.424.context: Gita Press heads it 'God protects everyone'. Doha 425 follows with 'fighting is to be wholly avoided': the wise avoid battle even with leaves and flowers, citing the Yadavas and Kama.
tulsi_dv.424.core_teaching: If attacked, escaping is fine and defending yourself is fine, but striking back is not; Ram stands guard over everyone's head.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: If someone attacks you it is good to run away, or to stand and block the blow for self-protection; but hitting back is not good, because Ram the protector is over everyone's head.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Running is good, taking cover is good, striking back is not; Ram guards all beings, and no one can kill the one he keeps.

tulsi_dv.424.practical_reading: Used as an ethic of non-retaliation that still allows self-protection: leave, shield yourself, but don't escalate.
misreadings: Not an instruction to endure abuse: the verse explicitly approves fleeing and self-defence.
Not pacifism that forbids protecting others.
cautions: For abuse victims, stress the first half (leaving and shielding are good).
'Over everyone's head' includes the attacker in the commentaries' reading; can feel unjust to a victim.
not_for: someone being told by family or clergy to 'not react' to ongoing abuse
victims of violence seeking justice

tulsi_dv.528.context: Gita Press heads it 'an obedient servant is greater than the master'. Near the end of the Dohavali; the next doha (529) praises the banyan that grows in harmony with its root and gives to all without pride.
tulsi_dv.528.core_teaching: A servant who is expert in his own duty can surpass the master: Ram had to build a bridge to cross the ocean, Hanuman simply leapt it.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: The servant skilled in following his own dharma is greater than the master: Ram crossed the sea by building a bridge, Hanuman crossed the same sea by leaping.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: A servant who is skilled at his own work becomes especially strong: Hanuman leapt the sea while the king himself had to organise a great bridge-building.

tulsi_dv.528.practical_reading: Applied to service and teamwork: excellence in one's own role is a form of greatness, and the devotee's power is the Lord's gift showing through.
misreadings: Not a claim that Hanuman is greater than Ram in the theological sense.
'Out of love' (our line) is not in the doha; the stated reason is mastery of one's own dharma.
not_for: someone being exploited in a 'servant' role at work or home
speaks_to: people in support roles who feel overlooked
pride in doing one's own work well

tulsi_dv.84.context: Gita Press prints this doha under the heading 'the glory of taking refuge' (sharanagati), right after two dohas warning that sense-pleasures make devotion taste flat. It opens a run of short self-portraits in which Tulsidas sets his faults against his reliance on Ram; doha 85 follows directly.
tulsi_dv.84.core_teaching: If Tulsi truly belongs to Ram alone, whatever his quality, then his welfare is secure everywhere and always. Belonging, not merit, is the ground of safety.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as a conditional: if it is true that this Tulsidas, good or bad, is Ram's alone, then he fares well wherever he is and in every time; footnotes Gita 4.11 (the Lord meets people as they approach him).

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Same conditional sense: whatever I am, if I remain only yours, all is well in every world and time; otherwise there is nothing but trouble.

tulsi_dv.84.practical_reading: Teachers use it to separate worth from belonging: you do not have to become good first to be held; the work is to keep turning toward the one you trust.
misreadings: Not a claim that Tulsi is already virtuous; it explicitly sets aside the question of quality.
Not a guarantee of outward success; the 'well-being' is the commentaries' kalyan (ultimate good).
cautions: Mild: 'only yours' language can feel exclusive to readers of other faiths; keep the focus on belonging rather than on rejecting other refuges.
not_for: someone who needs practical help today rather than reassurance
readers hostile to exclusive devotional language

tulsi_dv.85.context: Follows doha 84 in the same 'refuge' cluster. Tulsidas concedes the public verdict on him and names the one quality he can claim; the next doha (86) defines devotion as love for Ram plus walking the path of right conduct.
tulsi_dv.85.core_teaching: Even a person widely seen as full of faults has one thing that can please God: wholehearted trust.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: Paraphrase: people call me a storehouse of faults, but I have one quality, complete trust in you; therefore it is fitting that you be pleased with me.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Adds that the world finds nothing in Tulsi to admire, and he agrees; yet his one great quality is trust in Sita-Ram, who know only how to do good. However bad I am, I know what pleases you.

tulsi_dv.85.practical_reading: Used to encourage people who feel defined by others' judgement: you may not be able to argue with every criticism, but you can still bring trust.
misreadings: Not permission to ignore real faults; the neighbouring dohas (86-88) immediately call for right conduct and honest speech.
Not self-pity; the tone is wry and confident.
cautions: Could reinforce harsh self-talk if the reader is already self-critical; emphasise the 'one virtue' half.
not_for: someone being unfairly scapegoated who needs validation that the accusations are wrong
readers in a shame spiral, if read without the second line
speaks_to: feeling you have nothing to offer

tulsi_dv.95.context: Gita Press heads this doha 'exhortation' (udbodhan). It comes just after Tulsi's self-accusing dohas and before 96, the advice to tell Ram everything. It is a compact rule of devotional life addressed to oneself.
tulsi_dv.95.core_teaching: Direct awe, love, attachment and trust to Ram, and be his without pretence; then even outward loss counts as winning.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: Fear only Ram, place mamata, love and trust in him; for one who is Ram's servant without deceit, even losing is winning.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Prints 'ramahi ura karu' (hold Ram in the heart) instead of 'daru' (fear); explains that worshipping the attribute-free Ram brings victory even when one has not done bhajan well.

tulsi_dv.95.practical_reading: Teachers read it as consolation for setbacks: if your loyalty is undivided and sincere, a lost contest or failed plan is not the final word on you.
misreadings: Not 'losing doesn't matter, so don't try'; the doha is about the inner orientation that survives defeat.
'Fear Ram' is reverent awe, not terror of punishment.
cautions: Text variant: Gita Press 'daru' (fear) vs Kaumudi 'ura' (heart). If a writer builds on 'fear', note it is only one reading.
not_for: someone being pressured to 'accept defeat' in an abusive or unjust situation
readers frightened of a punishing God
speaks_to: wanting to give oneself fully to something

tulsi_dv.96.context: Immediately follows 95 in the 'exhortation' group. Tulsi speaks to himself: having said that sincere belonging turns loss into victory, he now gives the practice, honest disclosure to a kind listener.
tulsi_dv.96.core_teaching: Open your whole heart, merits and faults, to the compassionate Ram; abjectness will shrink and contentment will grow strong.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Dohavali)
commentaries.gist: Tell gracious Ram all your merits and faults with an open heart; your dinata will become weak and your contentment will become very firm.

commentaries.who: Kali Prasad Shastri, Dohavali 'Kaumudi' tika (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'tell all your faults'; says dinata will grow so lean that it cannot come near the stoutness of contentment.

tulsi_dv.96.practical_reading: Used as an image for confession, journaling or prayer: naming everything honestly to a kind presence lightens the weight more than hiding it.
misreadings: Not a promise that problems vanish by being spoken; what changes is the inner state (dinata vs santosha).
Not an instruction to disclose everything to any person; the listener is the 'kripalu' Ram.
not_for: someone whose disclosures have been used against them, if read as 'tell people everything'
speaks_to: starting a journaling or prayer practice

tulsi_gv.2.52.context: After Ram has left for the forest, the Gitavali gives a series of songs on Kausalya's longing in the empty palace. In this pada she handles his childhood bow, arrows and little shoes, sometimes goes to wake him as before, sometimes calls him to eat, and then, remembering he has gone, stands frozen 'like a painted picture'. The next pada (53) has her saying she still cannot believe it is not a dream.
tulsi_gv.2.52.core_teaching: A mother's love keeps reaching for the absent child through his things and her old routines; the poem honours grief as love that has nowhere to go.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Gitavali)
commentaries.gist: Kausalya looks at his play bow, presses his little shoes to heart and eyes, goes to wake him as before or calls him to eat, then stands stunned, remembering the exile; Tulsi says describing it shows his love is shallow.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Gitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Notes that in separation the beloved's belongings become as dear as the beloved, and touching them gives a taste of meeting; cross-references Bharat touching Ram's footprints in the Manas.

tulsi_gv.2.52.practical_reading: Teachers and readers use it to validate the rituals of grief, keeping things, keeping routines, as forms of love rather than failure to 'move on'.
misreadings: Not a lesson to detach or stop grieving; nothing in the poem corrects Kausalya.
Ram is alive in the story; the loss is absence, not death.
cautions: Very strong for empty-nest or separation grief; for a parent whose child has died it may be overwhelming. Ram returns in the story; a bereaved parent's child does not.
not_for: a parent in fresh bereavement for a child, unless chosen with great care
readers who need movement toward hope on the same day
speaks_to: parents whose children have moved away
separation from a child (custody, migration, estrangement)

tulsi_gv.5.42.context: Follows the Gitavali's telling of Vibhishan coming over to Ram and being welcomed (padas 40ff). Tulsi steps back to generalise: refuge in Ram is open to everyone.
