Later stanzas of the pada mention Ajamil saved by calling his son's name and Vibhishan's single bow bearing fruit.
tulsi_gv.5.42.core_teaching: Taking refuge in Ram is good for everyone without exception: rich or poor, high or low, clever or dull, weak or strong, disabled or resourceless.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Gitavali)
commentaries.gist: Everyone who goes to Ram's refuge is well off, rich or poor, great or small, wise or foolish, weak or mighty; even the lame, blind and resourceless who took Ram's highway of devotion were carried through.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Gitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Says this removes any eligibility test from surrender; cites Gita 9.32 that anyone, of any birth, reaches the highest by taking refuge; the royal road is protected as a king's road is policed.

tulsi_gv.5.42.practical_reading: Used as a statement of radical welcome: there is no entry requirement of status, intelligence, strength or ability.
misreadings: Not a claim that the disabled or poor are spiritually deficient; the point is that no condition excludes anyone.
cautions: Disability language (lame, blind) is used as a list of the excluded; handle respectfully for disabled readers.
not_for: readers who may hear disability-as-deficit language as hurtful

tulsi_gv.5.44.context: Vibhishan, now arrived in Ram's camp, introduces himself: Ravana's younger brother, born among rakshasas, he has come having heard of Ram's character. In this verse he declines to list his sorrows. Ram then laughs, calls him close, embraces him like Bharat, touches his head and makes him fearless.
tulsi_gv.5.44.core_teaching: Because the Lord already knows his servant's pain, the servant need not plead; he asks only for a compassionate look, which would tell him he has been accepted.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Gitavali)
commentaries.gist: Vibhishan says: since the Lord knows his servants' joys and sorrows I have not told mine; when you look at me with eyes full of compassion I will know you have accepted me. Ram then embraces him like Bharat.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Gitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Same sense; adds that Ram's embrace and touching his head shows his love for devotees and that Ram, liking him, made him lord of Lanka in his heart.

tulsi_gv.5.44.practical_reading: Applied to prayer or to being with someone who already understands: sometimes the ask is not to explain everything but to be seen kindly.
misreadings: Not a rule that one should never speak one's pain (contrast Dohavali 96, which urges telling everything).
not_for: someone who needs encouragement to speak up about harm rather than stay silent
speaks_to: arriving somewhere new after leaving family

tulsi_gv.5.45.context: Ram's reply in the Vibhishan episode, addressed (per Gita Press) to 'friend Sugriva and Lankapati Vibhishan'. He declares his natural disposition toward those who come for refuge. Vibhishan is overwhelmed with love; Tulsi closes by urging the reader to drop hope and fear and sing of such a Lord.
tulsi_gv.5.45.core_teaching: Ram says that whoever comes to him utterly destitute, dull and with nowhere to go, he serves and never abandons; with arm raised he swears no one is dearer than a servant whose love is without guile.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Gitavali)
commentaries.gist: Ram tells Sugriva and Vibhishan his nature: the fallen, wretched, dull and shelterless who come for refuge he serves and never forsakes; for those with no other means he acts; none is dearer than a guileless servant.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Gitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Connects it to the theology of surrender: the one who has given up other means and depends on Ram alone with great trust is the best candidate; cites Valmiki's Ramayana as 'the great text of surrender'.

tulsi_gv.5.45.practical_reading: Used as a vow of welcome: having nothing and nowhere is not a barrier but the very condition Ram responds to.
misreadings: Not that only the destitute are loved; the qualifier is sincere (non-hypocritical) love.
'Let false love be swept away' is a condition, not a threat.

tulsi_gv.6.7.context: Lakshman has fallen in battle (struck by the shakti weapon). In padas 6-7 Ram laments: he blames himself for his father's death, Sita's abduction and Jatayu's death. Here he tells Sugriva his strength is spent; the monkeys will go home and he will 'accompany his brother'. The monkeys and bears lose heart, and Jambavan rouses Hanuman to fetch the herb (pada 8 is Hanuman's offer).
tulsi_gv.6.7.core_teaching: Even in his own collapse, Ram's heart turns to the person who depends on him: what will become of Vibhishan, whom he promised to make king?

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Gitavali)
commentaries.gist: Ram tells Sugriva his effort is spent; without a brother's arm to share trouble, whom can he trust? The monkeys will go home and he will keep Lakshman company, but his chest burns with worry for Vibhishan.

tulsi_gv.6.7.practical_reading: Used for exhausted caregivers and leaders: even at the end of one's strength, care for those who depend on us can steady us, and help can still arrive (Hanuman).
misreadings: Not a model of giving up; in the story help is about to come.
Our line ('worry for the one who came to me') captures the core; it should not be read as Ram being powerless in the tradition's theology.
cautions: IMPORTANT: 'I will go with my brother' means following Lakshman in death (Shrikant Sharan says so explicitly). Avoid for readers expressing hopelessness or suicidal thoughts; if used, include the rescue that follows.
Self-blame list in the preceding pada (father, wife, Jatayu) may mirror a grieving reader's guilt.
not_for: anyone expressing hopelessness, suicidal thoughts or a wish to 'go with' a dead loved one
fresh bereavement of a sibling
speaks_to: responsibility for dependants while at breaking point

tulsi_hb.10.context: The Hanuman Bahuk is a set of 44 kabitts and savaiyas composed in Tulsidas's old age when he was in acute pain in his arms (Wikipedia dates the illness around 1607 CE); the Sofia study notes the poems first circulated as part of the Kavitavali's longer recension. Verses 1-12 praise Hanuman before the petitions begin; this one portrays his twofold nature.
tulsi_hb.10.core_teaching: Hanuman joins a terrifying strength toward the wicked with a compassionate mind; remembering him removes Tulsi's pain.

commentaries.who: Mahavir Prasad Malaviya 'Vaidya', Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Hanuman Bahuk)
commentaries.gist: Hanuman is the limit of valour, chosen by Ram, vajra-bodied and roaring in battle, yet compassionate and righteous at heart; death to the wicked, guardian of the good, he removes Tulsi's pain when remembered.

commentaries.who: Anjani Nandan Sharan, 'Piyush-varshini' commentary on Hanuman Bahuk (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Word notes: karuna is the feeling, born of another's suffering, that moves one to remove it; dhira means steady and self-controlled. Cites the Mahabharata scene where Hanuman shows Bhima a fraction of his form.

tulsi_hb.10.practical_reading: Used to picture strength and gentleness together: the protector one hopes for is strong against harm and tender toward the hurt.
misreadings: Not a celebration of violence; the fierceness is against 'the wicked' in a protective role.
cautions: Mentions Tulsi's own pain; fine for illness contexts.

tulsi_hb.13.context: The Hanuman Bahuk is a set of 44 kabitts and savaiyas composed in Tulsidas's old age when he was in acute pain in his arms (Wikipedia dates the illness around 1607 CE); the Sofia study notes the poems first circulated as part of the Kavitavali's longer recension. Verses 12-13 are a pair: 12 speaks of those who trust Hanuman's war-cry, 13 of those in whose heart it rings with joy.
tulsi_hb.13.core_teaching: Whoever keeps Hanuman's cry alive with joy in the heart is cared for by Shiva, Parvati, Ram, Sita, Lakshman and the guardians of the world, and the sages and siddhas raise him like a child.

commentaries.who: Mahavir Prasad Malaviya 'Vaidya', Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Hanuman Bahuk)
commentaries.gist: Shiva and Parvati, the world-guardians, Ram, Sita and Lakshman favour the one in whose heart Hanuman's shout rises joyfully; free of sorrow here and hereafter, sages and siddhas rear him like a child.

commentaries.who: Anjani Nandan Sharan, 'Piyush-varshini' commentary on Hanuman Bahuk (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Explains that pada 13 parallels 12: there the fruit of trusting the shout, here the fruit of the shout delighting the heart; glosses hulasati as producing joy.

tulsi_hb.13.practical_reading: Applied as encouragement that courage held joyfully inside (not just fear-driven prayer) draws care toward you.

tulsi_hb.17.context: The Hanuman Bahuk is a set of 44 kabitts and savaiyas composed in Tulsidas's old age when he was in acute pain in his arms (Wikipedia dates the illness around 1607 CE); the Sofia study notes the poems first circulated as part of the Kavitavali's longer recension. From verse 16 the tone turns to complaint: Tulsi asks what he has done wrong to be cut off. This verse praises Hanuman's power and then asks, half-teasing, whether he has grown old or tired just when it is Tulsi's turn.
tulsi_hb.17.core_teaching: Hanuman's name tears through every trouble and worry like a cobweb; so why the delay now?

commentaries.who: Mahavir Prasad Malaviya 'Vaidya', Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Hanuman Bahuk)
commentaries.gist: What you establish even Shankar cannot uproot; Tulsi says all crises and worries burst like spider webs at your name; are you old just for my turn, or tired from protecting the poor, that you delay removing my trouble?

commentaries.who: Anjani Nandan Sharan, 'Piyush-varshini' commentary on Hanuman Bahuk (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Quotes this line while explaining that when a devotee suffers, the wicked mock that God does not listen, and the good feel fear; Tulsi pleads that the same favour be shown him.

tulsi_hb.17.practical_reading: Used both as reassurance about the fragility of worries and as permission to be honest when relief seems late.
misreadings: Not a promise that pain vanishes instantly; Tulsi is complaining that it has not.
Our line makes the name generic ('the one you trust'); in the text it is Hanuman's name.
cautions: The same verse complains about delay; pairing the cobweb image with an ongoing illness may feel glib.
not_for: someone whose illness is worsening, if only the cobweb half is quoted

tulsi_hb.22.context: The Hanuman Bahuk is a set of 44 kabitts and savaiyas composed in Tulsidas's old age when he was in acute pain in his arms (Wikipedia dates the illness around 1607 CE); the Sofia study notes the poems first circulated as part of the Kavitavali's longer recension. In verses 21-23 Tulsi asks Hanuman to remember his own strength and destroy the arm-pain as he once destroyed demonesses.
tulsi_hb.22.core_teaching: Hanuman, who settles the uprooted and uproots the arrogant, is the wish-tree of Ram's servants and the only support of a weak man like Tulsi; let him seize the crocodile-pain in Tulsi's arm and tear its mouth.

commentaries.who: Mahavir Prasad Malaviya 'Vaidya', Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Hanuman Bahuk)
commentaries.gist: You settle the ruined and ruin the proud; remember that strength. You are the wish-tree of Ram's servants and the only support of the weak; with such a master Tulsi is still beaten; seize the crocodile-pain in my arm.

commentaries.who: Anjani Nandan Sharan, 'Piyush-varshini' commentary on Hanuman Bahuk (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Glosses takiya as shelter and reliance; reads 'binu aparadha' as Tulsi being bound and beaten though innocent; explains 'remember your strength' by the sages' curse that made Hanuman forget his power until reminded.

tulsi_hb.22.practical_reading: Applied to dependence without shame: in weakness it is right to lean on a trusted support.
cautions: Context is physical pain and a violent image (tearing the crocodile's mouth); fine for illness, but keep the excerpt gentle.
speaks_to: caregivers' need to lean on someone

tulsi_hb.29.context: The Hanuman Bahuk is a set of 44 kabitts and savaiyas composed in Tulsidas's old age when he was in acute pain in his arms (Wikipedia dates the illness around 1607 CE); the Sofia study notes the poems first circulated as part of the Kavitavali's longer recension. Here Tulsi recalls being taken in as a starving child and then rebukes Hanuman for watching his present suffering.
tulsi_hb.29.core_teaching: Hanuman once called the begging boy and raised him like his own child; Tulsi trusts he will not forget his own now. But the second half complains: you are able in every way, yet you watch your servant suffer like boys amused by a dying sparrow.

commentaries.who: Mahavir Prasad Malaviya 'Vaidya', Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Hanuman Bahuk)
commentaries.gist: I roamed door to door for scraps; you called and reared me like a child, and I trust you won't forget your own. Yet, able as you are, you watch your servant suffer like boys amused by a dying sparrow.

commentaries.who: Anjani Nandan Sharan, 'Piyush-varshini' commentary on Hanuman Bahuk (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Word notes: natapala means protector of the surrendered; sara-sanbhara is the burden of feeding and watching over; parekho as test or delay.

tulsi_hb.29.practical_reading: Shows that gratitude and complaint can live in the same prayer; past care becomes the ground for honest protest.
misreadings: Our excerpt keeps only the tender half; the verse ends in a bitter reproach. Don't present it as purely serene.
cautions: Childhood hunger and abandonment; the 'dying sparrow' image is stark.
not_for: readers who need only comfort today, if the full verse is quoted
speaks_to: people raised in hardship who were helped
feeling forgotten after being cared for

tulsi_hb.30.context: The Hanuman Bahuk is a set of 44 kabitts and savaiyas composed in Tulsidas's old age when he was in acute pain in his arms (Wikipedia dates the illness around 1607 CE); the Sofia study notes the poems first circulated as part of the Kavitavali's longer recension. Tulsi wonders whether the pain comes from his own sins, the three afflictions, or a curse, and reports that nothing has worked.
tulsi_hb.30.core_teaching: Every medicine and charm has failed and the pain grows; Tulsi is Hanuman's servant and Hanuman called him his own, so Hanuman's delay hurts more than the pain itself.

commentaries.who: Mahavir Prasad Malaviya 'Vaidya', Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Hanuman Bahuk)
commentaries.gist: Whether from sin, the three afflictions or a curse, the arm-pain is unbearable; medicines, charms and gods failed; all creation obeys you; you called Tulsi yours, and your delay hurts more than the pain.

commentaries.who: Anjani Nandan Sharan, 'Piyush-varshini' commentary on Hanuman Bahuk (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: In its table of verse uses, lists pada 30 as recited so that one's cause meets no delay.

tulsi_hb.30.practical_reading: An honest model of prayer in chronic illness: saying plainly that nothing is working and that feeling abandoned hurts.
misreadings: Not advice to stop medical treatment (our misuse note is right).
Not proof that illness is caused by sin; Tulsi only wonders.
cautions: The verse floats 'my own sin' or 'a curse' as causes; avoid implying illness is deserved.
Recitation-for-results framing (Piyush) can feel transactional.
not_for: readers who may hear 'illness from sin'
anyone being steered away from medicine toward ritual

tulsi_hb.33.context: The Hanuman Bahuk is a set of 44 kabitts and savaiyas composed in Tulsidas's old age when he was in acute pain in his arms (Wikipedia dates the illness around 1607 CE); the Sofia study notes the poems first circulated as part of the Kavitavali's longer recension. The verse recounts Hanuman's deeds (victory for the monkeys, routing the rakshasas, completing Ram's work) before this closing plea.
tulsi_hb.33.core_teaching: Tulsi asks Hanuman to place his hand on his head; the servant of so reputation-conscious a protector should not be seen suffering.

commentaries.who: Mahavir Prasad Malaviya 'Vaidya', Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Hanuman Bahuk)
commentaries.gist: By your strength the monkeys won and Ram's work was done; gods thrill at your praise; lord of monkeys, place your hand on Tulsi's head, for servants of one who guards his name are never seen unhappy.

commentaries.who: Anjani Nandan Sharan, 'Piyush-varshini' commentary on Hanuman Bahuk (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'hatha pherana' as lovingly placing the hand, and kanigara as one mindful of his own fame; reads the plea as 'it is not fitting that your servant be unhappy'. Notes the variant 'dekhiye/bujhiye'.

tulsi_hb.33.practical_reading: A tender request for touch and reassurance in pain, usable for anyone who wants comfort rather than answers.
misreadings: Not a substitute for medical care (our misuse note).
'Let me not be left alone' (our line) is an interpretive softening; the text appeals to Hanuman's reputation.

tulsi_hb.34.context: The Hanuman Bahuk is a set of 44 kabitts and savaiyas composed in Tulsidas's old age when he was in acute pain in his arms (Wikipedia dates the illness around 1607 CE); the Sofia study notes the poems first circulated as part of the Kavitavali's longer recension. The verse opens 'I have been raised on your crumbs; do not cast me off for a slip', and addresses Hanuman as 'Bholanath' (an epithet of Shiva; Hanuman is traditionally Shiva's form).
tulsi_hb.34.core_teaching: Tulsi is to Hanuman as fish to water and infant to mother; with no other support, he asks Hanuman not to delay and to stroke his aching arm with his long tail.

commentaries.who: Mahavir Prasad Malaviya 'Vaidya', Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Hanuman Bahuk)
commentaries.gist: Raised on your morsels, do not cast me off for lapses; look to your own nature, Bholanath. You are water and I the fish, mother and I the child; protect the distressed child and pass your tail over my arm.

commentaries.who: Anjani Nandan Sharan, 'Piyush-varshini' commentary on Hanuman Bahuk (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Word meanings (ambuchara = aquatic creature, dimbha = infant, luma = tail) and textual variants; links the 'look to your own side' plea to Vinaya Patrika 34's 'forgive, looking to your own nature'.

tulsi_hb.34.practical_reading: Used to express complete dependence in illness, and the wish for gentle touch where it hurts.
misreadings: Not a model of relying on prayer alone (our misuse note).
cautions: Old age and severe pain context; fine for illness plans.

tulsi_hb.40.context: The Hanuman Bahuk is a set of 44 kabitts and savaiyas composed in Tulsidas's old age when he was in acute pain in his arms (Wikipedia dates the illness around 1607 CE); the Sofia study notes the poems first circulated as part of the Kavitavali's longer recension. In verses 39-41 Tulsi reviews his life: a child who turned to Ram and lived on alms, then a young man swept into worldly ways who broke that love, then taken back.
tulsi_hb.40.core_teaching: Even while Tulsi was acting badly, Hanuman adopted him and had him set right by Ram's own hands; Tulsi became a respected Gosain and now reaps the fruit.

commentaries.who: Mahavir Prasad Malaviya 'Vaidya', Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Hanuman Bahuk)
commentaries.gist: As a child I turned to Ram and lived on alms; as a youth I broke that love; while I acted basely Anjani's son took me up and had Ram's hands reform me; now I reap the fruit.

tulsi_hb.40.practical_reading: Used for redemption stories: being claimed before you are good, and changed by that belonging.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of wrongdoing; the verse goes on to say he is now reaping the ripened fruit of his past (Gita Press).
cautions: The closing line 'I am reaping the fruit' can be read as illness being karmic payback; avoid that framing for sick readers.
not_for: someone ill who might hear 'you are reaping your karma'

tulsi_kv.7.11.context: Kavitavali's Uttar Kand is a loose collection of 183 independent quatrains (Sofia study) on Ram's grace, the Name, and Tulsi's own life. This chhand lists quick reliefs Ram gave: Vishvamitra's worries, Ahalya's, King Janak's; even enemies praise his treatment of the brothers of Bali and Ravana.
tulsi_kv.7.11.core_teaching: Ram removed the anxieties of Vishvamitra, Ahalya and Janak in a moment, and even foes praise his conduct toward Sugriva and Vibhishan; he shades the afflicted, the poor and the unprotected with his own hand.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Kavitavali, Indradev Narayan)
commentaries.gist: Ram instantly removed the worries of Vishvamitra, Ahalya and Janak; hearing of Sugriva and Vibhishan, even enemies praise his conduct; he takes the afflicted, poor and helpless under the shade of his own hand.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Kavitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Same; adds that Ravana's own spies and Kumbhakarna praised Ram's treatment of Vibhishan, and that if he is so kind to enemies' brothers, his care for friends is beyond telling.

tulsi_kv.7.11.practical_reading: A protective image for anyone overwhelmed: shelter given personally, not delegated.

tulsi_kv.7.128.context: Kavitavali's Uttar Kand is a loose collection of 183 independent quatrains (Sofia study) on Ram's grace, the Name, and Tulsi's own life. Chhands 127-130 turn on Prahlad: 127 praises Prahlad's love above all other servants, 128 tells the pillar scene, 129 contrasts the Ram within and the Ram outside, 130 the poisonings.
tulsi_kv.7.128.core_teaching: Hiranyakashipu, sword drawn and merciless, faces his son; Prahlad does not run. 'Where is Ram?' 'Everywhere.' 'In the pillar?' 'Yes.' At that cry Narasimha bursts out, kills the tyrant and is calmed only by Prahlad; people's love and faith grew, and from then they began worshipping stone images.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Kavitavali, Indradev Narayan)
commentaries.gist: Sword drawn, merciless, the father faced Prahlad, who did not flee: 'Everywhere'; 'in the pillar?' 'Yes'. Narasimha burst out, slew him, and calmed only at Prahlad's prayer; faith grew and people began worshipping stone images.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Kavitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Adds that even Brahma and Lakshmi could not approach the enraged Narasimha; explains that four kinds of sacred images already existed but after Prahlad people began to see the divine in any stone.

tulsi_kv.7.128.practical_reading: Used for steadfastness under a hostile authority: holding to what you know is true even when the person with power threatens you.
misreadings: Not encouragement to provoke danger.
The violence (tearing the father) is mythic; avoid dwelling on it.
cautions: A father trying to kill his child: very sensitive for survivors of parental violence.
not_for: survivors of parental abuse
children in conflict with parents, if read as 'defy your parents'

tulsi_kv.7.129.context: Kavitavali's Uttar Kand is a loose collection of 183 independent quatrains (Sofia study) on Ram's grace, the Name, and Tulsi's own life. This chhand opens the Prahlad group: Ram, protector of the afflicted, stands wherever he is remembered; the glory of the Name made the false true and the small great; of his many servants Tulsi rates Prahlad's love highest, since he brought God out of a stone.
tulsi_kv.7.129.core_teaching: Wherever anyone in distress remembers kind Ram, he stands there for them; the Name's power has turned the counterfeit genuine and the small great.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Kavitavali, Indradev Narayan)
commentaries.gist: Merciful Ram, protector of the distressed, stands wherever he is remembered; his Name's might made the base precious and the small great; of all his servants Tulsi honours Prahlad's love most, who drew God from stone.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Kavitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Gives Gajendra and Draupadi as afflicted devotees Ram reached wherever they called; Ajamil and Valmiki as the counterfeit and small made great by the Name.

tulsi_kv.7.129.practical_reading: Used for presence: you do not need to be in a temple or in a good state; remembering in the place you are is enough.
misreadings: Not a promise of immediate rescue from every situation.
not_for: someone whose call for help was not answered in a disaster

data_flags.corrected_ref: Kavitavali, Uttar Kand 127 (Gita Press, whose meaning for this line ends at 127; Shrikant Sharan refers to it as chhand 127). NOT 129: chhand 129 is 'antarajamihu ten bade...' (our tulsi_kv.7.182).
data_flags.attribution_note: Wrong reference: this line is Kavitavali Uttar Kand 127 (Gita Press; Shrikant Sharan cites 'chhand 127, arata pala kripala'), not 129.

tulsi_kv.7.182.context: Kavitavali's Uttar Kand is a loose collection of 183 independent quatrains (Sofia study) on Ram's grace, the Name, and Tulsi's own life. Follows 128 (Prahlad and the pillar). Tulsi draws his own conclusion from the story: God came out of the stone, not out of Prahlad's heart.
tulsi_kv.7.182.core_teaching: Ram in visible form, who answers his name, is greater than the Ram who silently dwells within: he runs like a cow that has just calved, milk flowing, at the sound of her calf. Tulsi admits this is his own 'crazy' view: for Prahlad, God emerged from the pillar, not from his heart.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Kavitavali, Indradev Narayan)
commentaries.gist: The embodied Ram outside is greater than the formless indweller, for at his name he runs like a newly calved cow to her calf's cry; Tulsi calls this his own view: for Prahlad God came from stone, not heart.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Kavitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Antaryami is the inner, formless Brahman, present but inaccessible; the embodied Lord answers his name, rushing like a cow that ignores blows to reach her calf, overlooking the caller's sins, as with Gajendra and Draupadi.

tulsi_kv.7.182.practical_reading: Used for personal, relational faith: calling a name and being answered, rather than abstract presence.
misreadings: Not a denial of God within; Tulsi frames it as his personal preference ('my crazy talk').
Not a theological ranking to argue with Advaita readers.
not_for: readers committed to a non-dual or formless view who may find it combative
speaks_to: longing for a responsive, personal God
parents and the image of instinctive love

data_flags.corrected_ref: Kavitavali, Uttar Kand 129 (Gita Press, meaning ends '129'; Shrikant Sharan, after 128). NOT 182: Gita Press 182 is a lament on Kashi's plight in the Kali age.
data_flags.attribution_note: Wrong reference: this is Kavitavali Uttar Kand 129, not 182.

tulsi_kv.7.36.context: Kavitavali's Uttar Kand is a loose collection of 183 independent quatrains (Sofia study) on Ram's grace, the Name, and Tulsi's own life. Chhand 35 lists Ram as all relations; 36 continues and ends: whoever has Ram in life and in death truly lives, the rest walk around as corpses. 37 follows.
tulsi_kv.7.36.core_teaching: Ram is every relationship to Tulsi; he relies on Ram alone and his heart delights in no one else. The verse goes on: one who has Ram in life and death truly lives.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Kavitavali, Indradev Narayan)
commentaries.gist: Ram is mother, father, guru, kin, friend, son, lord and lover; by Ram's oath, my trust is in him, I am dyed in him; who has Ram in life and death truly lives, others are walking corpses.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Kavitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'rama ki saunha' not as an oath but as 'turned toward Ram' (sammukhata); finds here the attitude of exclusive devotion (ananyata).

tulsi_kv.7.36.practical_reading: Used to speak of finding in God what is missing in human relationships, or of a love that gathers up all one's attachments.
misreadings: Not a rejection of human family; it describes where Tulsi's final reliance lies.
The verse's end ('others are walking corpses') is harsh and should not be quoted at non-believers.
cautions: Lists parents and children; for an orphaned or bereaved reader this can be either healing or painful.
The later line calls others 'walking dead'.
not_for: readers who may feel judged by the 'walking corpses' line if quoted

tulsi_kv.7.37.context: Kavitavali's Uttar Kand is a loose collection of 183 independent quatrains (Sofia study) on Ram's grace, the Name, and Tulsi's own life. Gita Press heads this 'love for Ram is the essence'. It follows 36 (Ram as every relation) and precedes 38, a prayer that a body without love for Ram is not worth living in.
tulsi_kv.7.37.core_teaching: Eyes drinking the beauty of Sita-Ram, ears on Ram's story, the Name on the lips, Ram in the heart, understanding, goal, love and strength all in Ram: in Tulsi's own view, that much is the fruit of living.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Kavitavali, Indradev Narayan)
commentaries.gist: Sita-Ram's beauty is water for the fish of the eyes; ears hold his story, lips his name, heart his place; mind, goal, love and strength are in Ram; not speaking for all, Tulsi calls this life's fruit.

tulsi_kv.7.37.practical_reading: Teachers like the humility of 'I don't speak for everyone': a personal statement of what makes life meaningful, not a rule for others.
misreadings: Not a prescription for everyone; Tulsi explicitly limits it to himself.

tulsi_kv.7.48.context: Kavitavali's Uttar Kand is a loose collection of 183 independent quatrains (Sofia study) on Ram's grace, the Name, and Tulsi's own life. Chhands 47-49 are on fearlessness under Ram's protection. 47 says one need not fear even death if Ram is kind; 48 recalls Prahlad's ordeals; 49 says the one with such a master can walk free of worldly worry.
tulsi_kv.7.48.core_teaching: Hiranyakashipu tried snakes, poison, fire and mad elephants on Prahlad; the torments fled and the servants turned away, yet Prahlad felt no despair, relying on Narasimha. So whom should Tulsi fear? If Ram protects, who can kill?

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Kavitavali, Indradev Narayan)
commentaries.gist: Fierce snakes, poison, fire and the tusks of mad elephants were broken; torment itself fled in fear and the frightened servants turned from their orders; Prahlad had no despair, relying on Narasimha; so whom should Tulsi fear?

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Kavitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Retells the ordeals from the Vishnu Purana, where the serpents complain their fangs broke; draws two lessons: the devotee absorbed in love does not register bodily pain, and God's protection makes the attacks futile.

tulsi_kv.7.48.practical_reading: Used for courage under threat: fear loosens when one's sense of safety rests on something larger than the threat.
misreadings: Not a promise of physical invulnerability.
Not a reason to ignore real danger or refuse help.
cautions: Child endangered by a parent: Prahlad story may resonate painfully with readers abused by a parent.
not_for: someone in present danger who needs practical protection
survivors of parental abuse, without careful framing

tulsi_kv.7.50.context: Kavitavali's Uttar Kand is a loose collection of 183 independent quatrains (Sofia study) on Ram's grace, the Name, and Tulsi's own life. Part of a run (47-53) about Ram as the only help when others cannot reach; 51 imagines being dragged off by Yama's messengers with no family to share the ordeal.
tulsi_kv.7.50.core_teaching: In forest, mountain, water, storm, poison, disease, wildfire or among enemies, where no family is near, kind Ram, who has servants like Hanuman, will protect; in all three worlds he is Tulsi's one helper.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Kavitavali, Indradev Narayan)
commentaries.gist: In forest, mountain, water, wind, poison, disease, fire or among foes, with countless dangers and no kin near, gracious Ram, whose servants are like Hanuman, will protect; in all three worlds he is my one helper.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Kavitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Explains each danger (forest storms, poisonous plants, flooded rivers); says Ram protects out of pure grace; mentions Hanuman because Ram's servants carry out his care, so one need not worry how so great a king reaches everywhere.

tulsi_kv.7.50.practical_reading: Used for people facing danger far from family: travellers, migrants, soldiers, patients alone in hospital.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that harm cannot happen.
not_for: someone whose loved one died alone in danger (it may raise 'why wasn't he protected')

tulsi_kv.7.53.context: Kavitavali's Uttar Kand is a loose collection of 183 independent quatrains (Sofia study) on Ram's grace, the Name, and Tulsi's own life. Chhand 51 pictures Yama's messengers dragging one off with no relative to share the ordeal; 52 the boundless sea of existence with no boat; 53 continues the series. Shrikant Sharan says 'where' here means Yama's realm, since worldly ties cannot reach there.
tulsi_kv.7.53.core_teaching: Where no master, friend, spouse, child, sibling or parent is with you, Ram is the one who sincerely forgives all faults of body, speech and mind and quells the terrible pain; amid every crisis he keeps Tulsi safe.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Kavitavali, Indradev Narayan)
commentaries.gist: Where no kind master, friend, wife, son, brother or parent is present, who but gracious Ram forgives without deceit every fault of body, speech and mind and ends the dreadful pain? Amid all crisis he protects me.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Kavitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'where' as the realm of Yama after death, where earthly ties cannot follow; adds that Ram destroys sins through his name, form, deeds and abode; Draupadi and Gajendra illustrate rescue in crisis.

tulsi_kv.7.53.practical_reading: Used for the loneliest hours: illness, dying, or moments no relationship can enter.
misreadings: Not a statement that family is worthless.
cautions: Primary commentary reading is the hour of death and after; our_note 'read of the hour of death' is supported. Use carefully with the dying or bereaved.
not_for: fresh grief where talk of the afterlife may feel dismissive
readers with suicidal thoughts (the setting is death)
speaks_to: fear of what comes after death

tulsi_kv.7.57.context: Kavitavali's Uttar Kand is a loose collection of 183 independent quatrains (Sofia study) on Ram's grace, the Name, and Tulsi's own life. One of the autobiographical chhands (56-57, 72-73); 56 marvels that such a lowly man became Ram's servant. Wikipedia's Tulsidas article cites Kavitavali and Vinaya Patrika for his abandonment after birth.
tulsi_kv.7.57.core_teaching: Abandoned by parents, given no good fate, scorned, timid and hungry like a dog for scraps, Tulsi heard of Ram's nature and laid his need before him just once; Ram, such a master, held back nothing for his welfare here or hereafter.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Kavitavali, Indradev Narayan)
commentaries.gist: Abandoned by parents, with no good fate, scorned, timid and craving a dog's morsels, Tulsi heard of Ram's nature and once poured out his hunger; Raghunath spared nothing in mending his worldly and spiritual life.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Kavitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Cross-references Vinaya Patrika 275 and 272 on his parents leaving him; reads 'showing the empty belly' as expressing desire for welfare in this world and the next, after which Ram took up his whole burden.

tulsi_kv.7.57.practical_reading: Speaks to people with painful origins: one honest cry for help can be enough to be taken in.
misreadings: Not a claim that abandonment was deserved (Tulsi blames fate, not himself, here).
cautions: Parental abandonment and degrading self-description ('like a dog'); powerful for adoptees or neglected children, but handle the self-abasement gently.
not_for: someone who asked for help and was refused, if read as 'once is enough'

tulsi_kv.7.67.context: Kavitavali's Uttar Kand is a loose collection of 183 independent quatrains (Sofia study) on Ram's grace, the Name, and Tulsi's own life. Chhand 66 thanks Ram for making the 'washerman's dog' (belonging to neither house nor ghat) his own; 67 gives a comic self-portrait of uselessness.
tulsi_kv.7.67.core_teaching: High aspirations, terrible luck, unfit for worldly ways, he has no job, trade or skill and could not even manage begging; Ram's name alone saved his stake, otherwise he would not have a hair on his head to offer his ancestors.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Kavitavali, Indradev Narayan)
commentaries.gist: High mind and tastes, very low luck; unfit for social ways, mischievous and a chatterer; neither worldly gain nor the highest goal in reach; no service, mining, farming, trade or begging; Ram's name alone saved his stake.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Kavitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Word notes: langara = naughty, labaru = liar, jabaru = burden, baji = stake; the 'high mind' means high wishes that the unlucky can't fulfil, which only brings pain.

tulsi_kv.7.67.practical_reading: Speaks to people who feel unemployable or out of step with the world: worth and rescue need not come from career success.
misreadings: Not contempt for work; it is self-deprecating humour about his own incapacity.
cautions: Unemployment and poverty; avoid suggesting faith replaces practical help.
not_for: someone in acute financial crisis who needs practical next steps

tulsi_kv.7.7.context: Kavitavali's Uttar Kand is a loose collection of 183 independent quatrains (Sofia study) on Ram's grace, the Name, and Tulsi's own life. Chhand 6 just before says Ram ignored even the misdeeds of his refugees Sugriva and Vibhishan; this one generalises with the sinners saved by a single Name (the courtesan, the elephant, the vulture, Ajamil), and chhand 8 adds Prahlad, Gajendra and Draupadi.
tulsi_kv.7.7.core_teaching: Even when his people commit huge offences, Ram does not hold them in his heart; sinners beyond counting reached the highest abode by saying his name once. So, Tulsi tells himself, worship the friend of the lowly.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Kavitavali, Indradev Narayan)
commentaries.gist: Ram ignores even grave offences of his servants; the courtesan, Gaja, the vulture and Ajamil had countless sins yet one utterance of the Name won them the abode sages cannot reach; Tulsi urges himself to worship him.

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Kavitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Same sense; cites Vinaya Patrika 238 that Ram removes mountain-sized faults and takes in mustard-seed virtues; tells the stories of the courtesan Jivanti and her parrot, and of Gajendra.

tulsi_kv.7.7.practical_reading: Used for people stuck in guilt: grace does not keep a ledger, so the next step is turning back rather than self-punishment.
misreadings: Not a licence to keep doing wrong because it will be ignored.
Not a denial that harm to others needs repair.
cautions: If a reader is the victim of someone else's 'fathomless offences', the verse may feel like it excuses the offender.
not_for: victims of harm who may hear it as letting the wrongdoer off

tulsi_kv.7.73.context: Kavitavali's Uttar Kand is a loose collection of 183 independent quatrains (Sofia study) on Ram's grace, the Name, and Tulsi's own life. Chhand 72 marvels that people now compare the once-crooked Tulsi to Valmiki; 73 recounts his birth and childhood.
tulsi_kv.7.73.core_teaching: Born into a begging family, his birth grieved his parents; as a child he whimpered from door to door thinking four grains of gram were the four aims of life. Now he is the good servant of a mighty master, and even Brahma the fate-writer envies it. Is Ram's name wise or mad, making a straw heavier than a mountain?

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi meaning (Kavitavali, Indradev Narayan)
commentaries.gist: Born into an alms-taking family, his birth grieved his parents; as a child he whimpered from door to door, taking four chickpeas for life's four goals; now Ram's servant, even Brahma envies him. Is the Name clever or crazy?

commentaries.who: Shrikant Sharan, Kavitavali 'Siddhanta-tilak' (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Links the parents' grief to his birth under the inauspicious Mula star; argues from Vinaya Patrika 272 and 275 that he lived with them for a while before being sent away, not abandoned at birth.

tulsi_kv.7.73.practical_reading: Used for dramatic reversal of fortune and for gratitude that refuses to take credit.
misreadings: Not a story that poverty is a curse from birth.
cautions: Parents grieving a child's birth and child hunger; sensitive for readers with similar histories.
not_for: someone currently hungry or destitute who needs material help

tulsi_vp.101.context: The pada asks where else Tulsi could go: which other deity has made a point of seeking out the lowest to save them, and has freed a bird (Jatayu), beasts, a hunter (Valmiki), a stone (Ahalya), trees (the Yamalarjuna) and a foreigner? Gods, demons, sages, nagas and humans are themselves held by maya, so why hand oneself over to them?
tulsi_vp.101.core_teaching: Refuge is sought where there is a record of saving the fallen; the devotee turns to Ram because Ram, unlike the bound beings around, is free to free others.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Asks who else bears the name 'purifier of the fallen' and loves the lowly; lists the bird, beasts, hunter Valmiki, stone Ahalya, trees and Yavana as those saved.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; glosses 'barai' as picking out one by one. Cites Gita 18.61 (the Lord turning all beings on the machine of maya) and the Manas line that Ram makes all dance like puppets, to explain why others cannot save.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: where should I go save your feet, who else is the fallen ones' redeemer and insists on saving sinner after sinner for his name's sake.

tulsi_vp.101.practical_reading: Teachers use the opening line as a song of exclusive trust: when other supports have failed, go back to the one whose nature is to lift the fallen.
misreadings: Not a polemic for a reader to look down on other faiths or deities; it is Tulsi's personal reason for his one refuge.
cautions: The full pada calls other gods 'poor things' under maya; avoid quoting that part in an interfaith or mixed-family context.
not_for: readers from other traditions if the comparative stanza is used
speaks_to: feeling you have nowhere else to go
feeling too fallen to be loved

tulsi_vp.102.context: Tulsi thanks Hari for the human body, the home of every spiritual practice, and says he cannot recount even one favour with a million mouths, yet he asks for more. His mind is a fish that never leaves the water of sense pleasures, so he keeps suffering birth after birth; he asks Ram to make grace the line, the goad-mark on his foot the hook and supreme love the bait, and pull the fish out. Many remedies and gods exist, but only the one who tied the rope of delusion can untie it.
tulsi_vp.102.core_teaching: Human life is a rare gift for practice, but a mind hooked on pleasures cannot free itself by effort alone; release comes from the same higher power that holds the soul in the world.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains the fish image: make your grace the string, the ankusha mark on your foot the hook, supreme love the soft bait, and pierce and draw out my mind-fish; it is play for you.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Calls the pada doctrinal and its image unmatched; reads the last line as: the Lord of maya who tied the soul with ignorance and sent it into the world will himself release it.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the close as there being many Vedic remedies and gods, but the noose of delusion can be loosed only by the one who tied it.

tulsi_vp.102.practical_reading: Gratitude and asking can sit together: be thankful for a human life, then admit honestly what you cannot fix yourself (a compulsion, a craving) and ask for help.
misreadings: Not a claim that God caused a person's specific suffering or addiction to punish them.
Not permission to stop effort; the rest of the Vinaya Patrika asks for both effort and grace.
cautions: 'The one who tied this knot' can be heard by someone in pain as 'God did this to you'; frame it as the power that holds us also frees us.
Rebirth language ('born in many wombs') in the full pada.
not_for: someone in acute addiction crisis needing practical help, if used instead of it
someone angry at God over a loss (the 'binder' line may inflame)
speaks_to: being stuck in a habit or craving you cannot break
feeling grateful for life yet still restless

tulsi_vp.103.context: A complete short prayer. Tulsi asks Ram to remove every other hope and reliance; he wants no good afterlife, clever mind, wealth, powers or fame, only love for Ram's feet that grows daily and asks nothing. Wherever his crooked deeds drag him, birth after birth, let Ram's care not lapse for a moment, as the tortoise never forgets her eggs. Finally he asks that all the love and ties of this body be gathered into one place, in Ram.
tulsi_vp.103.core_teaching: Ask not for outcomes but for undivided, motiveless love, and for God's attention to stay with you even where your own mistakes take you.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads the first line as asking Ram to remove the folly of trusting other means, gods or actions; Tulsi wants no good destiny, wealth or powers, only ever-growing pure love.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; adds that love with a motive is trade, not love.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as a plea that wherever his evil karmas dispose him he may not lose the Lord's love, as the mother-turtle never leaves her eggs.

tulsi_vp.103.practical_reading: Teachers use it to shift prayer from 'fix my circumstances' to 'stay with me in them'; even when habits pull you somewhere you regret, ask not to be left alone there.
misreadings: Not fatalism about karma: the point is being accompanied, not that effort is useless.
'Take away every other hope' is not advice to cut off human relationships; stanza 4 asks that those loves be gathered into the divine, not destroyed.
cautions: Mentions being dragged through many births by bad karma; may feel heavy to someone already blaming themselves.
not_for: someone who needs concrete help and hears 'drop all other reliance' as 'don't seek help'
speaks_to: fear that your own mistakes will take you somewhere you can't come back from
asking to be watched over from a distance

tulsi_vp.105.context: Tulsi's vow of a fresh start. By Ram's grace the night of worldly life has passed, and having woken he will not lay out the bed again. He has found the name as a wish-fulfilling gem and will not let it drop from the hand of his heart; he will test the gold of his mind on the dark touchstone of Ram's form; the senses mocked him while he was their slave, but now, his own master, he will not be laughed at; he will set his mind like a bee on Ram's lotus feet.
tulsi_vp.105.core_teaching: Waking up is a gift of grace, but staying awake is a resolve: don't relitigate the wasted years, just refuse to lie back down.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: my life so far was wasted, but no more; Ram's grace ended the night of worldly maya, and awake I will not spread maya's bedding again.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Reads the first line as 'what I did so far is spoiled, from now I'll take care'; equates it with the proverb 'forget what has passed, look after what lies ahead'.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: I have wasted my time long enough, now no more; the night of existence has passed by Rama's grace and, awake, I'll make my bed no more.

tulsi_vp.105.practical_reading: Used for fresh starts: name the lost time honestly, credit the waking to grace rather than willpower, and make one concrete resolve not to slide back.
misreadings: Not self-condemnation over the past; the commentators read it as 'let bygones go and look ahead'.
Not a promise that relapse can't happen; it is a vow, not a guarantee.
cautions: 'Till now it has been wasted' could sting for someone ashamed of years lost to illness or addiction; stress the second half.
not_for: someone in depression for whom 'just wake up and resolve' may feel like blame
speaks_to: a turning point or new start
waking up from a habit or a numb period

tulsi_vp.125.context: Tulsi complains to Ram, the steady benefactor: his heart is Ram's house, but thieves have moved in - ignorance, delusion, greed, ego, intoxication/pride, anger and lust, 'the enemy of understanding'. They bully him, ignore his pleas, trample him as an orphan; he is one and they are many, no one hears him, and running away won't help. So he tells Ram: it is your house they are looting; my only worry is your bad name.
tulsi_vp.125.core_teaching: Inner vices are intruders in a house that belongs to God; the devotee, unable to evict them alone, hands the problem to the owner with a playful argument that it is the owner's reputation at stake.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Names the seven thieves (ignorance, delusion, greed, ego, pride, anger, lust) who crush him as one without a protector. Reads the close: if they loot your devotee's heart the disgrace is yours, so guard your own house.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same list; quotes a verse attributed to Shankaracharya that lust, anger and greed are thieves living in the body; argues 'bodh-ripu' qualifies Mara (desire), not ignorance.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the heart as Ram's mansion invaded by thieves who trample him as an orphan, ending with his anxiety lest Ram's reputation suffer.

tulsi_vp.125.practical_reading: Teachers use the image to externalise anger, greed or compulsions as intruders rather than one's identity, and to ask for help with them instead of fighting alone.
misreadings: Not an excuse ('it's God's problem, not mine'); our existing misuse note already guards this.
Not saying the person is bad: the heart remains the Lord's house even when occupied.
cautions: Being 'trampled as an orphan' with 'no one hearing my cries' may echo real experiences of abuse; keep the reading on inner states.
not_for: someone facing actual intruders or abuse, where the metaphor could minimise real danger
speaks_to: feeling overrun by anger, greed or craving
shame at what has taken hold of you
feeling outnumbered by your own habits

tulsi_vp.128.context: A litany of Ram's hand: the hand that made fearless those who called once in distress, broke Shiva's bow and ended Janaka's doubt, lifted the boatman Guha and embraced him like a brother, gave the vulture Jatayu funeral rites and his own abode, killed Bali for Sugriva, crowned the frightened Vibhishana, and freed the gods from fear. Its cool shade removes sin, pain and illusion, and Tulsi longs for it night and day.
tulsi_vp.128.core_teaching: The hand that protected the frightened and the outcast in the story is the same hand the devotee asks to feel on his own head; its shade cools sin, distress and illusion.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Walks through each deed of the lotus hand (Janaka's doubt, Guha embraced like a brother, Jatayu given rites like a father, Sugriva, Vibhishana, the gods made fearless) and ends with Tulsi wanting its cool, soothing shade day and night.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading, adding that Jatayu was sent to Saketa; notes the pada blends majesty, sweetness, gentleness and parental tenderness.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as a plea that the Lord sometime lay on his head the lotus hand that gave refuge to those who called the name once in distress.

tulsi_vp.128.practical_reading: Used as a prayer for blessing and reassurance: remembering concrete times protection came, then asking to feel it personally.
misreadings: Not a promise of a physical sign; it is a longing for felt protection.
cautions: Mentions killing Bali and demons in the full pada; the quoted lines are gentle.
not_for: someone grieving a parent whose blessing they can no longer receive, unless handled gently
speaks_to: longing for a blessing or reassurance
fear and needing to feel protected
wanting the comfort a parent's hand on the head gives

data_flags.corrected_ref: DATA ERROR: this is Vinaya Patrika pada 138, not 128. Haritoshini prints it as (138), Thakur as 138, and in the Gita Press 2001 scan it follows pada 137. (Thakur's pada 128 is a different song, 'O my mind, remember Sita's Lord...'). Our text is stanza 1 and stanza 5 (of 5).

tulsi_vp.137.context: The pada argues from examples that one held by Ram's grace cannot be harmed by enemies: Prahlada, the elephant Gajendra, Vibhishana, Dhruva, Ambarisha (whose curser Durvasa still burns with shame), the Pandavas against Duryodhana. It adds that whoever plots a saint's death dies that death, that he who digs a pit for others falls in it, and that for those who hate saints even the wish-tree bears poison; it ends that one whose helper is Ram is always fearless.
tulsi_vp.137.core_teaching: Hostility cannot finally defeat someone held by grace; the devotee need not live in fear of enemies.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as: if Ram's grace is there, others' enmity achieves nothing; not a hair of the devotee is bent though one tries crores of ways; whoever plots a saint's death dies by it.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: how can others' enmity touch such a one; even ten million attempts cannot bend a hair on a devotee's head; then the list from Prahlada to Duryodhana's defeat.

tulsi_vp.137.practical_reading: Teachers use it to steady fear of opponents or gossip: put trust in grace and right conduct rather than in counter-schemes.
misreadings: Not a promise that nothing bad will ever happen (our misuse note is right).
Not a curse on enemies or a wish for their downfall, although the full pada says plotters fall into their own pits.
cautions: The fuller pada contains retribution lines (the plotter dies the death he planned); avoid them for someone in conflict or wishing harm on others.
For someone who has been harmed, 'not a hair is bent' can imply they lacked grace or faith.
not_for: someone who has already been seriously harmed or abused
someone looking for vindication or revenge
speaks_to: fear of people who wish you harm

tulsi_vp.144.context: The pada lists those Ram saved for the honour of his name: Ajamila, a sinful Brahmin who called his son Narayana at death and was spared Yama's hell; the proud elephant Gajendra, rescued from the crocodile on a single remembrance; the hunter (Valmiki), the boatman Guha, the vulture Jatayu and the courtesan Pingala. It ends with Tulsi asking in what conduct he is worse than they, since he still sinks day and night in a terrible well of darkness.
tulsi_vp.144.core_teaching: Ram's protection is unconditional and has a long record; that record is the devotee's argument for being saved too.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Asks who Ram has not kept in his shelter for his name's sake; he is compassionate without cause and removes fear of the round of birth and death.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; stresses that Ajamila was freed even by an accidental 'Narayana', so deliberate remembrance must work too. Notes the pada answers 143's request that Ram camp in Tulsi's heart: how, if the heart is impure? By the name's power.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the opening as: who is there whom you haven't protected for your Name's sake; for no reason you are compassionate and take away the fears of existence.

tulsi_vp.144.practical_reading: Used to reassure people who feel too flawed for help: grace is not a reward, and the stories show it reaching the least likely.
misreadings: Not a guarantee of worldly rescue from every crisis.
'Without reason' does not mean arbitrary; it means not conditioned on merit.
cautions: The full pada ends with Tulsi sinking day and night in a dark well; fine as honest lament, but don't end a reading there for someone depressed.
not_for: someone who prayed and was not rescued from a tragedy (the 'who did he not save' framing can wound)
speaks_to: fear that you are beyond help
feeling you have done nothing to deserve kindness

tulsi_vp.150.context: Tulsi tells Ramabhadra that he both worries and doesn't: all beings suffer, so his lot is common. But is the relationship one-sided? Ram has many like him; he has only Ram. He then admits shame that he is a bad servant who talks like a good one; good or bad, people call him Ram's, and a bad servant, like a bad dog, brings abuse on the master. Seeing no way out of this bind, he asks Ram to do what seems right, look at his list of rescued ones, and not cast off one who has come for refuge.
tulsi_vp.150.core_teaching: Suffering is common to all, so it need not crush; the real fear is whether the love is returned, and the devotee holds on even if it seems one-sided.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads stanza 1 as: I worry and don't, since all beings are vessels of suffering. Reads stanza 2 as a question: is the bond with a great one only from my side? You have many like me; I only you.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Explains the worry is that he is still unfreed; the calm is that all beings share it, so he should not fret over karma's fruits.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: troubled and yet not, since all beings are vessels of affliction; is my bond with such a great one only one-sided? Many are close to you, but I have only you.

tulsi_vp.150.practical_reading: Speaks to the ache of loving someone or something greater who may not notice you, and to finding calm in the fact that suffering is shared, not personal punishment.
misreadings: Not a statement that God really is indifferent; it is the devotee's fear, voiced honestly.
'All beings suffer' is not meant to dismiss one's own pain.
cautions: 'Every soul is a vessel of suffering' may sound fatalistic to someone in fresh pain.
The 'bad servant like a dog' image later in the pada is harsh self-talk.
not_for: someone in an unrequited human relationship who may take it as a call to cling
acute grief, if 'everyone suffers' is foregrounded
speaks_to: feeling your love or devotion is one-sided
feeling like one among many to a teacher, parent or God
anxiety that is also oddly calm

data_flags.translation_note: Stanza 2 is mistranslated. 'नातो बड़े समर्थ सों इक ओर किधौं हूँ' is a question: is my bond with so great a master one-sided? (Poddar, Viyogi Hari and Thakur all read it so). Our 'On one side is my bond with the great and mighty...

tulsi_vp.160.context: A short pada: the Vedas witness that Ram freed the hunter, the courtesan, the elephant and Ajamila, and countless other low ones; whoever took his name, knowingly or not, was barred from hell. So Tulsi has come for refuge: keep him as your own.
tulsi_vp.160.core_teaching: A failing is not a disqualification but the very thing that matches the Lord's nature: the fallen and the raiser of the fallen belong together.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: I am fallen and you raise the fallen, so our pairing is made and my purification is certain. Notes an old-manuscript variant in stanza 3 ('naraka surapura mane') that he prefers to the common reading.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Says the match is mutual: I needed a raiser of the fallen and you needed someone fallen; both wishes are met. Quotes another devotee's kavitt built on the same pairing of sinner and saviour.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: I'm fallen, you the redeemer, so our roles fit perfectly; whoever took the Name knowingly or unwittingly was shut off from hell and heaven.

tulsi_vp.160.practical_reading: Used to turn shame into approach: instead of hiding failure, bring it as the reason to come closer.
misreadings: Not a licence to stay 'fallen' or to keep doing harm because grace will cover it.
cautions: Light and bold in tone; may feel glib to someone carrying serious guilt toward a person they hurt, where repair is also needed.
not_for: someone avoiding responsibility toward people they have harmed
speaks_to: feeling unworthy to pray or return
needing a lighter way to approach God

tulsi_vp.162.context: The pada proves Ram's generosity by examples: the liberation sages fail to reach through yoga and renunciation he gave to the vulture Jatayu and to Shabari without thinking it much; the wealth Ravana got from Shiva by offering his ten heads Ram gave to Vibhishana, and was even shy about giving it. It ends telling the mind: if you want every happiness, worship Ram, who will fulfil all your desires.
tulsi_vp.162.core_teaching: True generosity gives without waiting for service or merit; Ram's kindness to the lowly is of this kind.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Explains that only kindness given without return is real; kindness for return is trade. Only God loves without cause.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the refrain as: who in the world is magnanimous like Rama, who melts for the wretched without their serving him; then Jatayu, Shabari and Vibhishana as proofs.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Says no one in the world melts at the sight of the lowly without prior service as Ram does.

tulsi_vp.162.practical_reading: Teachers use it to describe grace as unearned, and as a model for human giving: help without waiting for the other to have deserved it.
misreadings: Not a promise that worship will deliver every material wish (stanza 4's 'all desires' is devotional hyperbole).
cautions: The closing 'he will fulfil all your desires' can set up disappointment for someone praying for a specific outcome.
not_for: someone bargaining with God for a specific outcome
speaks_to: feeling you have nothing to offer
learning to give without keeping score

tulsi_vp.165.context: Tulsi praises Ram's court for honouring the lowly: the gods, after all their practices, never saw him even in dreams, yet he made brothers of the boatman, bears, monkeys and a demon; he roamed the Dandaka forest with sages but never speaks of it, while he keeps praising Jatayu and Shabari. Stanza 4 cites two Ramayana tales of justice in his kingdom, including keeping in Ayodhya the washerman who slandered Sita. The custom of honouring the poor has always run in this court; only Tulsi seems overlooked.
tulsi_vp.165.core_teaching: In Ram's reckoning, humility counts and pride does not: the proud and accomplished are passed over, the humble are embraced.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'gani' as those blinded by wealth, learning or rank; Ram honoured the humble boatman, bears and monkeys over the proud gods, praised Jatayu and Shabari over sages, and in Ram-rajya the poor have always been honoured.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading: the gods were proud, the bears and monkeys were not; hence the difference in Ram's treatment.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders line 1 differently: Ram disregards honour paid him by the wealthy and gives the poor the fullness of his grace; keeps the ascetic-and-dog and washerman tales and the closing complaint that no one has reminded him of Tulsidasa.

tulsi_vp.165.practical_reading: Reassures people who feel unimpressive or overlooked that worth in the spiritual life is not measured by status; also a mirror for anyone who relies on rank.
misreadings: Not an attack on wealthy people as such; the commentators read 'gani' as pride in wealth or status.
cautions: Stanza 4 refers to the washerman who slandered Sita and to Sita's abandonment; do not bring that story into a reading for someone wronged by a partner.
Ends with Tulsi feeling forgotten; don't leave a lonely reader there.
not_for: someone wronged by slander in a marriage (stanza 4 can sound like endorsement)
speaks_to: feeling overlooked next to impressive people
low status at work or in family

tulsi_vp.166.context: The refrain introduces a catalogue of those Ram embraced: Ahalya, turned to stone by her own fault and freed by the touch of his foot; the violent, forest-dwelling Nishada (Guha), hugged without regard to caste; Jayanta, Indra's son, who wronged Sita yet was spared when he finally came for refuge; the meat-eating vulture Jatayu, given funeral rites like a father; Shabari, a woman of low birth outside both custom and Veda; Sugriva; and Vibhishana, the enemy's brother, welcomed with open arms. The pada ends by telling the mind that a life without devotion wastes even one's mother's youth.
tulsi_vp.166.core_teaching: Ram's kindness looks for no qualification: caste, species, past wrongdoing or being the enemy's kin do not stop it.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Gives the full catalogue: Ahalya freed though without spiritual means, the Nishada embraced without thought of caste, Jayanta sheltered despite his grave offence, Jatayu given a father's rites, Shabari accepted for her love, Sugriva protected, Vibhishana welcomed with outstretched arms.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same catalogue with explanations: Jayanta had pecked Sita's foot as a crow, yet his fear was removed when he came for refuge; Shabari had no standing in society or scripture, yet was given darshan.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the refrain as Rama, the benefactor of the wretched, most tender storehouse of compassion, doing good to others for no reason, then the Ahalya and Nishada stories.

tulsi_vp.166.practical_reading: Used to say no one is outside the circle of care, and to challenge readers to extend kindness across caste, class and grudges.
misreadings: Not a statement that the people listed were worthless; the 'low' labels reflect the social view that Ram ignores.
cautions: The fuller pada uses caste and gender language of its time (Shabari as 'low-born, dull woman'); avoid quoting those descriptors.
Jayanta's offence was an assault on Sita; don't use his pardon to counsel a victim to forgive an abuser.
not_for: someone hurt by caste or gender prejudice if the full pada's labels are quoted
speaks_to: wanting to practise kindness without conditions

tulsi_vp.167.context: After the refrain, Tulsi gives images: whatever skill one has comes easily and gladly to that person, as a small fish swims up the Ganga while a great elephant is swept away; sugar mixed in sand can't be separated by force, yet a tiny ant with a taste for it picks it out. He then describes the state of the yogi who 'sleeps' with the whole world drawn into himself, where grief, delusion, fear, joy, day, night, place and time vanish; until that state, doubt is not uprooted.
tulsi_vp.167.core_teaching: Devotion is easy to describe and hard to live; it is not a matter of strength but of the right 'knack' or taste, which only those who have it truly know.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains the images: the little fish swims against the Ganga while the elephant is swept away; sugar in sand can't be separated by force but an ant with the taste gets it easily.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Argues 'Raghupati-bhagati' is one compound, not a vocative; gives as an example of 'easy to say' the Manas description of the saint (contented, without enmity, etc.), which costs the tongue nothing but is hard to live.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: devotion is hard to perform, simple to tell, and he alone knows who has achieved it; then the fish-and-elephant and ant-and-sugar images.

tulsi_vp.167.practical_reading: Honest about the gap between talking about spiritual life and living it; teachers use it to encourage humility and practice over strength or cleverness.
misreadings: Not a claim that devotion is impossible for ordinary people; the fish and ant show the small can succeed where the mighty fail.
Not discouragement from talking about faith, but a warning against confusing talk with practice.
cautions: Could feed discouragement in someone already feeling they fail at faith; pair with the fish/ant images.
not_for: someone who needs reassurance that they are 'doing it right' and will hear only 'it's hard'
speaks_to: frustration that you can't live what you believe

tulsi_vp.172.context: Tulsi's daydream of a saint's life, asked as a question to himself and Ram: content with whatever comes, wanting nothing from anyone, always at others' service in mind, word and deed; not burning in the fire of harsh words; without pride, calm and cool, speaking of others' virtues, not their faults; dropping the body's worries and bearing joy and sorrow alike. It ends: will Tulsidas, keeping to this path, ever reach unwavering devotion?
tulsi_vp.172.core_teaching: A saint's nature is concrete and ordinary: contentment, service, not reacting to insults, speaking well of others, and steadiness in joy and pain; it is longed for and received by grace, not claimed.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Asks whether by Ram's grace he will ever live with a saint's nature: content with what comes, wanting nothing from men or gods, serving others, keeping the yamas and niyamas; not burning in anger at harsh words.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Calls this pada the poet's true 'inner kingdom', not fantasy; what the yogi reaches in samadhi the devotee inherits by self-surrender. Glosses 'not burning' as not taking insult and flaring in anger, and 'not speaking faults' as covering others' flaws.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as 'Shall I live such a life some day', listing contentment, doing good, not burning at harsh words, counting virtues not vices, bearing pleasure and pain with equanimity.

tulsi_vp.172.practical_reading: Widely used as a checklist for character: when insulted, don't burn; speak of others' good; be content. Framed as a hope, not a standard to beat oneself with.
misreadings: Not a demand to tolerate abuse silently: 'not burning in that fire' is about one's inner anger, not accepting mistreatment.
Not a rejection of ambition or needs; contentment here is freedom from craving.
cautions: Someone in an abusive situation should not be told to 'not burn' at harsh words as if endurance were the goal.
not_for: someone currently being verbally abused who needs to set boundaries
speaks_to: wanting to become a calmer, kinder person

tulsi_vp.177.context: A five-line vow: even if Ram abandons him, Tulsi will not abandon Ram, for whom else could he love? No master so kind and lovely has been heard of, seen or imagined; Tulsi is a dull soul under maya, Ram the Lord of maya; Tulsi is a bad beggar and unworthy son, Ram the generous giver and caring parent. If anyone else had cared to ask after him, Tulsi says, he would have sold himself to them for nothing.
tulsi_vp.177.core_teaching: The devotee's love does not depend on being loved back in a visible way; like a child with parents, the bond holds even when the child is unworthy.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: even if you forsake me I won't leave you, for whose love would I seek leaving your feet? I am the dull jiva under maya, you its Lord.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Adds that there is no other worthy object of love because everything else is impermanent and carries the pain of separation; reads the last line as: had anyone else asked after me, Tulsi would have sold himself for free.

tulsi_vp.177.practical_reading: Used to express loyalty in faith during dry periods when God feels absent: 'even if you seem to leave, I stay'.
misreadings: Not a model for staying in a human relationship where one is being abandoned or mistreated.
cautions: 'Bad son' self-description may hurt someone carrying guilt toward their parents; the 'parents' image can sting after a parent's death or estrangement.
not_for: someone being abandoned by a partner, if read as 'stay no matter what'
speaks_to: feeling abandoned by God or life
staying faithful through a dry season

tulsi_vp.179.context: Tulsi asks where he can go and whom he can tell; for one without any means, Ram alone is the way in the three worlds. Plenty of people play lord, but only Ram's qualities support the supportless. Who else ran to save the elephant, leaving even Garuda behind? Who else made a coward and worthless son like Tulsi precious? Tulsi's spoiled affairs will come right only if Ram makes them; delay will only breed more fault and sorrow.
tulsi_vp.179.core_teaching: When there is no one to tell and no means left, there is still a refuge whose very nature is to support those who have none.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as: where shall I go, who will hear one without spiritual means; for such a one you alone are the refuge in three worlds.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'anghin' as helpless with no shelter; says everyone in the world claims to be the master of all, but the supportless cross only by singing Ram's qualities.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the opening as: where shall I go, whom shall I tell, who will listen to this wretched one; in three worlds you are the only way for those without means.

tulsi_vp.179.practical_reading: For moments of having no one to talk to: the act of speaking the trouble to God is itself the first support.
misreadings: Not a claim that human help is worthless; it mocks self-important 'lords', not friends or helpers.
cautions: A reader who truly has no one may need a pointer to human support too; the verse can deepen isolation if read alone.
The full pada calls Tulsi a coward and worthless son.
not_for: someone in a crisis who needs a helpline or a person, if used as a substitute
speaks_to: being let down by powerful people

tulsi_vp.181.context: Tulsi asks Ram to look his way by any means; he has no other place. His mind is harder than a thousand stones (who else freed a stone, Ahalya?); he wants to perform a sacrifice of love at Ram's feet like Vishvamitra, but fears the demons of the age; he fears his crooked karma as Sugriva feared Bali and wants to live under Ram's arm; delusion strikes him as Ravana struck Vibhishana, and he burns in the three fires of suffering. Each stanza borrows a Ramayana rescue.
tulsi_vp.181.core_teaching: The devotee maps his inner struggles onto Ram's past rescues: as Ram protected Sugriva from Bali, he can protect one hunted by his own past deeds.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Takes each stanza as a parallel: free my stone-like mind as you freed Ahalya; guard my sacrifice of love as you guarded Vishvamitra's from demons.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading: let me live in the shadow of your arm and save me from crooked deeds; explains 'three fires' as bodily, worldly and divine afflictions.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: I am terrified by the terrors of karma like Sugriva by the mighty Vanara-chief Bali; Lord of those without a lord, I long to dwell in the shelter of your arms.
