tulsi_vp.181.practical_reading: Helps someone haunted by the consequences of past actions to ask for protection and a place to stand while they face them.
misreadings: Not a way to escape consequences of one's actions; it asks for shelter while facing them.
cautions: Being 'hunted' by karma could feed guilt in someone already self-blaming.
not_for: someone in real physical danger from a person, where the metaphor might replace practical safety steps
speaks_to: fear of past mistakes catching up

tulsi_vp.182.context: Tulsi says hearing Ram's qualities fills him with longing, but he doesn't know the devotion that pleases Ram: his deeds, nature and times are bad, he has no master, home, wealth, health, steady mind or long life. Whoever he asks for water asks him for nectar instead, so he dares not speak to anyone. So he asks his 'father' to devise the remedy: Ram's glance turns a losing throw into a winning one, makes the unseen seen and the incomprehensible understood. He ends saying he lives in the water of Ram's name like a big fish, and has at least reported his own conduct honestly to his master.
tulsi_vp.182.core_teaching: When one has no qualifications and no ideas left, one can hand the problem over: a single glance of grace can reverse a losing position and bring clarity.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Lists what Tulsi lacks (good deeds, nature, times, master, home, wealth, body, mind, long life); those he asks for water demand nectar; so, father, you devise the remedy, for your glance turns defeat into a good throw.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; in a note sums up Tulsi's plight as bad deeds, low nature, the Kali age, no protector, poverty, lifelong illness and a restless mind, and asks what cure there can be.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: O my father, as I offer myself, do something for me; by your glance even in defeat comes a winning stake.

tulsi_vp.182.practical_reading: For when you've run out of plans: admit it, hand it over, and stay open to seeing what you couldn't see before.
misreadings: Not a promise of a specific outcome (our misuse note is right).
Not a reason to stop seeking practical, medical, legal or emotional help.
cautions: Gambling/dice image ('losing throw') - avoid for readers struggling with gambling.
not_for: someone with a gambling problem
someone awaiting a medical or legal result, if read as a guarantee
speaks_to: not knowing the right way to pray
confusion about what to do next

tulsi_vp.183.context: Tulsi praises Ram as the one who knows the ways of love: the Vedas honour him for removing the pride of the great and the lowliness of the small. He performed the vulture's funeral rites and ate the Bhil woman Shabari's fruits; whoever he honours is honoured by the world and the Veda, and his love is reckoned weightier than yoga or knowledge. Tulsi, though dry of love and in others' control, sits stubbornly at the door of the friend of the poor.
tulsi_vp.183.core_teaching: Love levels: it humbles the proud and raises the lowly, so that both meet as equals.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains the Vedas praise Ram for removing the great one's pride and the small one's lowliness; he did Jatayu's rites and ate Shabari's fruits; whom he honours, world and Veda honour; his love outweighs yoga and knowledge.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Reads 'badai' as the arrogance of the proud and 'chhotai' as the smallness of the small, both removed by Ram's love.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: you know well the ways of love; you do away with the greatness of the great and the smallness of the small.

tulsi_vp.183.practical_reading: Used to describe how real love works in families and communities: it neither flatters status nor lets anyone feel small.
misreadings: Not a call to erase all distinctions or roles; it is about pride and shame melting in love.
speaks_to: feeling superior and wanting to let it go
relationships with a big status gap

tulsi_vp.184.context: The first line is the refrain of a pada on the name in the Kali age: other means have become as useless as a painted sun for dispelling darkness; rituals are mixed with sin like trees that flower without fruit; worship is ruined by hypocrisy and greed, knowledge has become a way to fill the belly; yoga, renunciation and wisdom are mostly talk and costume. Shiva teaches the name to the dying at Kashi. Tulsi ends: keep the mind, love and refuge in Ram's name alone, and Ram will one day pour out his kindness.
tulsi_vp.184.core_teaching: Repeating Ram's name cools the inner burning when elaborate methods have become hollow.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Says the heart's burning goes only by japa of Ram's name; other means in Kali are like a painted sun against darkness; rituals, worship and knowledge have decayed into show and livelihood; Shiva at Kashi teaches the name's power.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Glosses: the mind will be calmed only by japa of the name; other means look easy but fail midway, like trees with lovely flowers and useless fruit.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: by the repetition of Rama's Name the burning of the heart is banished; in Kali other means are as futile as a painting of the sun to dispel darkness.

tulsi_vp.184.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a simple practice for agitation: repeat the name slowly when the mind is on fire.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of all other spiritual practices or of therapy; the critique is of hollow, show-based practice.
Not instant relief; the closing stanza speaks of steady trust over time.
cautions: The fuller pada criticises religious hypocrisy broadly; avoid using it to belittle others' practice.
not_for: someone with a medical cause of agitation, if offered as a replacement for care
speaks_to: needing something simple to hold on to

tulsi_vp.189.context: A walking song in folk idiom. Keep saying Ram as you go, or you'll be seized for the world's forced labour. Crooked karma has handed us, free of charge, a rickety three-cornered litter (the body) with old bamboo and a mismatched frame; its five bearers (the senses) are drunk with desire and stagger, so the rider gets jolted. The road is thorny, there are no provisions, and the traveller has forgotten the name of his village; Tulsi asks Ram to be kind and remove the fear of the world.
tulsi_vp.189.core_teaching: Life is a hard journey in an unreliable vehicle with unruly senses; keeping the name on one's lips is the way to keep walking and not be conscripted into endless drudgery.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: keep saying Ram or you'll be caught in the world's forced labour, from which escape is very hard.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Works out the allegory in detail: karma the carpenter gave the body free; the old bamboo is age-old craving; the three corners are waking, dream and deep sleep.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as a marching refrain, 'Go onward saying Rama', with the rotten three-cornered cot of the body carried by bearers drunk with lust, on a road full of thorns.

tulsi_vp.189.practical_reading: Used as a mantra for hard stretches: when you feel lost, tired and unprovisioned, keep putting one foot in front of the other with the name.
misreadings: Not contempt for the body; the litter image is about not mistaking the vehicle for the destination.
Not a prediction of doom for those who don't chant.
cautions: Rebirth/'forced labour' framing could feel threatening; keep the tone of the refrain, which is companionable ('brother').
not_for: someone with a chronic illness or disability, if the 'rotten body' allegory is emphasised
speaks_to: feeling lost or having forgotten what you're working toward
a long hard stretch of life
being pulled in many directions by cravings

tulsi_vp.191#2.context: Pada 191 is a sequence of dohas on Ram as the one true lover: body-companions are self-interested, gods are business-like, and the classic objects of love in poetry fail their lovers (sound kills the deer, fire burns the moth, water does not die for the fish, the moon ignores the chakor, the cloud pelts the chataka with hail). Ram alone honours love, embraced the boatman like his brother Bharata, and makes the unlucky lucky. Doha 8 (our lines): whoever took refuge in his name, however low, he kept like money tied in his cloth, never checked again. Doha 9: he took in even Tulsi, whose deeds make other sinners.
tulsi_vp.191#2.core_teaching: Once someone takes shelter in the name, Ram keeps them without re-examining their worth: acceptance is not a probation.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Reads the doha: whoever took shelter in his name, however low and sinful, he accepted as one ties money in a knot without testing it, genuine or false.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: however great a sinner, whoever took the Name's refuge was accepted by him, just as a coin is put in the purse and not taken out again to examine it.

tulsi_vp.191#2.practical_reading: Speaks to people who feel they are always being tested and found wanting: in this love, one is not re-weighed every day.
misreadings: Grace does not erase responsibility or consequences (our misuse note).
Not a claim that the person is 'counterfeit'; the image is about not testing.
cautions: Calling someone 'low' or 'sinful' may sting; lead with the coin image.
speaks_to: feeling constantly judged or on probation

tulsi_vp.201.context: Tulsi addresses his own mind: what was gained by a human birth if it never, even in a dream, served others in body, word or mind? The pleasures you chase come unbidden in heaven or hell, at home or in the forest, yet you struggle for them; under delusion you pursued others' wives and enmity and forgot the suffering of the womb; fear, sleep, sex and food are shared by every creature, so a body rare even for gods was wasted in pride. If the sense of 'mine and yours' never left and the mind never settled in Ram, what use is regret once the chance has passed?
tulsi_vp.201.core_teaching: Human life is distinguished from animal life by service and devotion; a life that never helps another has missed its point.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads it: what gain from a human body if it never served others in mind, speech or body; sense-pleasure comes unasked anywhere, yet the mind toils for it; eating, sleeping, fear and mating are common to all beings.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Gives the same bhavartha and glosses 'nij-par-buddhi' as the division between one's own and others'. (The preceding pada 200 in the same commentary uses Kabir sakhis on death to the same end.)

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: what gain being born into this human life when even in a dream you never served in the affairs of others, in speech, thought and deed.

tulsi_vp.201.practical_reading: A plain prompt for today: do one useful thing for someone else, in deed, word or thought.
misreadings: Not a judgment that people who are unwell or unable to help others have wasted their lives.
cautions: The full pada mentions adultery, enmity and the 'suffering in the womb'; keep to the refrain for general readers.
Could induce guilt in someone depressed and unable to function; frame as invitation, not verdict.
not_for: someone bedridden, depressed or burned out by caregiving, who may hear it as accusation

tulsi_vp.217.context: Tulsi explains why he keeps weeping before Ram: if there were anyone else, he would go there. Who else loves the poor, bears the name 'purifier of the fallen', gave Ajamila his abode? Shiva, Brahma, Indra and the guardians were there, but none helped the drowning elephant; in an assembly of capable kings, none clothed Draupadi when she cried out. If Ram is disgusted with him, let him hand Tulsi to someone like himself; otherwise how could Tulsi leave his feet?
tulsi_vp.217.core_teaching: Repeated crying to God is not nagging but the natural result of having no one else who truly helps; the devotee even dares God to find a substitute.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: if there were another refuge I would not keep troubling you with my sorrows; none but you loves the lowly; no god helped the elephant, no capable king clothed Draupadi.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading: he would rather not trouble Ram but finds no one else who removes the pain of the poor.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: if only there were any other, O Lord, why should I time on time tell weeping my long tale of woes to you?

tulsi_vp.217.practical_reading: Gives permission to keep bringing the same sorrow in prayer, again and again, without shame.
misreadings: Not a statement that people around us are useless; it contrasts human limits with divine help.
cautions: Stanza 4 recalls Draupadi's public humiliation; avoid it for readers who have experienced sexual violence.
'If you find me distasteful' may echo a reader's fear of being a burden; reassure.
not_for: survivors of sexual assault (Draupadi stanza)
speaks_to: feeling you keep bringing the same pain
no one else to turn to

tulsi_vp.221.context: Tulsi says he watches day and night for the road by which grace will come, not knowing when. Virtues, knowledge, renunciation and devotion fled in panic at the sight of the Kali age, leaving a store of sins; injustice has made the earth hotter than the sun; he has no other place and his mind is distraught; no one, not even his own body, is his. He ends with a monsoon image: Tulsi is a ripening paddy field drying up, so Ram, dark as a rain cloud, should become the cloud and water it.
tulsi_vp.221.core_teaching: Waiting for grace without knowing when it will come is itself a form of devotion; the devotee keeps watching the road.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: I, a poor one, keep watching for your grace day and night; when it will come cannot be known; virtues and spiritual means fled before the Kali age; the earth burns hotter than the sun with injustice.

tulsi_vp.221.practical_reading: For long waits (for healing, news, a turn in life): keep watching the road, without pretending to know the date.
misreadings: Not passivity: waiting here is attentive and expectant.
cautions: Describes a world of injustice and decay; can feel bleak. Lead with the waiting and the rain-cloud ending.
not_for: someone in an urgent situation who needs action now
speaks_to: not knowing when things will change

tulsi_vp.226.context: Tulsi says: let others rely on what they rely on; for him Ram's name is the wish-tree fruiting with welfare in this age. Karma, worship, knowledge and Vedic doctrine are all true, but like someone who went blind in the monsoon month and sees only green, he sees only the name. He licked leaf-plates like a dog and never filled his belly; now remembering the name he finds nectar served. Where one's love and trust are, there one's work is accomplished; the two syllables are his parents and he sits stubborn as a child before them. He swears, with Shiva as witness, he is not inventing this.
tulsi_vp.226.core_teaching: Tulsi does not dismiss other paths; he simply testifies that for him the name has done everything, and that results follow where one's love and trust are.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: whoever relies on another may do so; for me the name is the wish-tree of welfare in Kali. Karma, worship and knowledge are all true, but like one blinded in Shravan I see only the name.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Stresses Tulsi grants the other paths are genuine; he simply sees only the name. Explains the Shravan-blind image, and reads the last stanza: work succeeds where love and trust are.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: let him put his trust elsewhere who will; for me the wishing-tree of Rama's Name has borne fruit even in Kali; karma, knowledge and worship are still good, but like one gone blind in Shravana I see only green.

tulsi_vp.226.practical_reading: A model for personal faith without judging others: say what has worked for you and trust it wholeheartedly.
misreadings: Not a claim that other paths are false; both commentators note Tulsi calls them true.
Not a guarantee that any wish will be granted.
cautions: Image of licking leaf-plates like a dog may evoke real poverty and shame.
not_for: interfaith settings if read as 'only this works'
speaks_to: finding one simple practice that works for you
after many attempts that never satisfied
being judged for your way of faith

tulsi_vp.227.context: Tulsi proclaims, arms raised, to all companions in worldly and spiritual life that Ram's name alone is his well-wisher. His mother and father abandoned him at birth and fate made him luckless and odd, yet some now call him 'Ram's own' - only because of the name. Without the name he wandered craving food, so pitiable that sorrow itself grieved; now the thorny trees give him mangoes. Saints build both worlds by study and many practices; Tulsi has only the name, the one knot under many windings.
tulsi_vp.227.core_teaching: Out of abandonment and hunger, the name turned a barren life into a fruitful one: the world that gave thorns now gives sweetness.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: I declare to companions in this world and the next that your name alone does me good; parents left me at birth and fate made me unlucky.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading, glossing the trees as people who once slighted him now honouring him; notes the legend that Tulsi's parents abandoned him because of an inauspicious horoscope, adding that no old astrology text prescribes this.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: my parents abandoned me at birth; without the Name I wandered craving for my stomach's sake and even Sorrow grew sad; now by the Name's grace I get mango fruits from the babul and bahera trees.

tulsi_vp.227.practical_reading: Speaks to anyone who began life with very little: what once gave only thorns can, with grace and steadiness, become a source of sweetness.
misreadings: Not a promise of material prosperity through chanting.
cautions: Explicitly about parental abandonment at birth and childhood hunger; may be raw for adoptees or people abandoned by parents. Handle gently.
not_for: someone currently in hunger or homelessness who needs practical help, if read as 'just chant'
speaks_to: being looked down on and now respected

data_flags.translation_note: Stanza 3's last line is slightly off. 'नाम-प्रसाद लहत रसाल-फल अब हौं बबुर बहेरे' = by the name's grace I now get mangoes from babul and bahera trees (Poddar, Viyogi Hari, Thakur): the same thorny trees that gave nothing now yield mangoes (Viyogi Hari: people...

tulsi_vp.229.context: Tulsi swears his tongue would rot if he called himself anyone else's: birth after birth he has lived on Ram's food. In three worlds and three times he sees no friend equal to Ram, and if he deceives Ram may he be a worm in hell for aeons. Even if the age has made his mind a whirligig beetle on the water, it skims the surface and does not sink; Tulsi stays cool and calm because he belongs to a great house.
tulsi_vp.229.core_teaching: Security comes from knowing whose you are: one who belongs to a great house stays calm even when the times toss the mind about.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: may my tongue rot if I call myself another's; birth after birth I have lived on your food; no friend like you anywhere; though Kali has made my mind a whirligig in the river, it will float, not drown.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; adds that the whirligig skims the water without sinking, so the world can't master him.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: may my tongue melt if I say I belong to another master; I have lived off the scraps of your food; Tulsidasa is ever calm by this strength, that he is at a great good place.

tulsi_vp.229.practical_reading: Helps someone steady their identity in unsettled times: the mind may be tossed, but knowing where you belong keeps you afloat.
misreadings: Not a call to swear oaths or curse oneself.
Not servility toward human masters.
cautions: Contains a self-curse (a worm in hell for aeons if deceitful) in stanza 2; omit for anxious or scrupulous readers.
not_for: readers with religious scrupulosity or OCD (oath and hell imagery)
speaks_to: feeling tossed about but wanting to stay calm

tulsi_vp.232.context: Tulsi asks where he would find another friend of the poor: who else understands another's pain, to whom else could he tell his wretchedness? Wherever he turns his mind he finds masters either without compassion or kind but incapable, so he keeps silent rather than expose himself for nothing. He admits his deeds would drown him in a cow's hoofprint while his talk plumbs the ocean; inwardly greedy and a servant of desire, outwardly he calls himself Ram's. Ram knows his heart anyway; he asks to be helped to sing Ram's praise without deceit.
tulsi_vp.232.core_teaching: Real help needs both compassion and capacity; finding that only in God, the devotee brings his sorrow there and admits his own gap between words and deeds.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Explains: no one but Ram does good to others, understands others' pain or consoles; masters are either merciless or merciful but incapable, so I stay silent rather than reveal my secret for nothing; my deeds are tiny, my talk vast.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: where else shall I find another friend of the poor; who besides you would feel another's sorrow; I see lords without compassion, or compassionate but unworthy, so I keep silent.

tulsi_vp.232.practical_reading: For those who have stopped telling people their troubles: it names why (no one both cares and can help) and opens a place to speak.
misreadings: Not advice to stop confiding in people; it is about where ultimate refuge lies.
cautions: Could reinforce someone's isolation ('no one else understands'); pair with encouragement toward trusted people.
not_for: someone withdrawing from all human support in depression
speaks_to: feeling no one understands your pain

tulsi_vp.240.context: Tulsi argues that goodness is whatever pleases Ram, not ritual standing: the courtesan Pingala, the vulture Jatayu and the hunter Valmiki reached Hari's abode without austerities at holy places; King Nriga never left the Vedic path yet suffered for ages as a lizard; the elephant had no initiation yet Ram rushed to him. Ram left high-born gods, sages and Brahmins to be born in a cowherd's house, refused Duryodhana's wealth and ate at humble Vidura's. Ram is won by simple, natural love; everything else is like the wet sheen of water that dries away.
tulsi_vp.240.core_teaching: Virtue is measured by Ram's pleasure, and he is won by simple, sincere love rather than ritual rank, austerity or status.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads: whomever you are pleased with is the truly virtuous; Pingala, Jatayu and Valmiki reached your abode without burning in dung-fire austerities at Prayag; Nriga kept the Vedic path yet suffered; Ram chose a cowherd's home and Vidura's food.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; prints 'karasi' (dung-cake) with 'Kashi' as a variant; glosses 'dichhit' as an initiated sacrificer; says Ram is subject to guileless love and not won by other means.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: whoever you are pleased with is truly pure; the prostitute, vulture and hunter were taken to the Lord's abode, but when did they burn in Kasi and Prayaga?

tulsi_vp.240.practical_reading: Reassures people who feel spiritually 'unqualified' (no rituals, pilgrimages, learning) that sincere love counts most.
misreadings: Not a rejection of all practice or pilgrimage; it says these don't substitute for love.
Not an endorsement of the 'courtesan' label as a moral judgment.
cautions: Nriga's story (a righteous king suffering) could unsettle someone who suffers despite doing right; use carefully.
not_for: someone devoted to pilgrimage or ritual who may hear it as dismissive
speaks_to: feeling you lack the right rituals, learning or background
doubting your worth in a religious community

tulsi_vp.250.context: Tulsi says if he had any other master or place he wouldn't keep pestering Ram; Ram has raised lazy, unlucky ones like him, so Ram is his king and Ayodhya his city. He has not served other deities; the name alone is his welfare, vow and love, his nectar, while other supports are poison. Thieves and watchmen (vices and virtues) are all in Ram's hands, and Ram never delays in helping the suffering, so why delay for him? The ending (our lines): trusting Ram's ways yet frightened by the age's havoc, he asks Ram to say, or have someone say, 'Tulsi, you are mine; don't lose heart.'
tulsi_vp.250.core_teaching: Faith and fear can coexist; what calms the fear is hearing, directly or through someone else, the word of belonging: 'you are mine, don't be afraid'.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains he would not keep calling if he had another master; Ram raised the lazy and unlucky, so Ram is his king; the name is his welfare and the rest is poison; vices and virtues are both in Ram's hand.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; glosses 'kaharu' as injustice and 'jog-chhem' as gaining and keeping; says it is up to Ram whether the thieves (lust, anger) loot him or the watchmen (discernment, dispassion) guard him.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the opening: had there been any other master or place of rest I wouldn't have pestered the Lord again and again; you're my king and Avadha my city.

tulsi_vp.250.practical_reading: In frightening times, it helps to ask for and receive reassurance, even through another person's voice ('have it said'): a friend, teacher or scripture can carry the words 'you are held'.
misreadings: Not a claim that fear means lack of faith; both are present.
cautions: Stanza 2 says he serves no other deity and calls other supports poison; avoid it for mixed-faith readers.
'These times' language can amplify anxiety about the world; keep the focus on the reassurance.
not_for: readers from other traditions if stanza 2 is used
speaks_to: fear about the state of the world
needing to hear 'you are mine, don't be afraid'

tulsi_vp.253.context: Tulsi asks to be kept in Ram's shelter as Ram has kept such people always; no one so kind is known in three worlds and three times. Ram has raised the lazy, unlucky and sinful, and still feels he hasn't repaid the orphans; Ram is capable, and Tulsi, such as he is, is Ram's. Disgusted and frightened by the ways of the age, he asks Ram to say just once, smiling or frowning, 'Tulsi, you are mine'; he swears that this alone would uproot all his sorrow.
tulsi_vp.253.core_teaching: The best argument for future care is past care: as you have kept me until now, keep me still.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads: keep me in your shelter, as you have always taken in people like me; none so kind in three worlds and times; you raised the lazy and sinful and still felt in debt to orphans.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; worries that the age may turn his mind from Ram's feet; quotes Vyasa's lament on the Kali age and a Bhagavata verse that the heart's knot breaks on seeing the Lord.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: O Rama, take me under your refuge as you have ever done; no other is known to be so merciful; I'm yours however I may be.

tulsi_vp.253.practical_reading: Encourages a reader to remember the times they were carried through, and to let that memory ground trust for what's next.
misreadings: Not a claim that suffering will stop because one has been protected before.
not_for: someone who feels they have never been kept or protected (the premise may ring false)
speaks_to: looking back on having been held

tulsi_vp.254.context: Tulsi says Ram's name is his mother and father, kin, beloved, teacher, master, companion and true friend, and his firm love for it is his unshakeable wealth. Shiva churned the vast curd-ocean of a hundred crore Ram-stories and drew out the name as butter; trust in the name is the fruit of all four goals of life; it serves both worldly and spiritual ends, and nothing does as much good.
tulsi_vp.254.core_teaching: Every relationship one needs can be found in the name; love for it is a wealth that does not diminish.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: your name is my parents, kin, lover, guru, master, friend and selfless well-wisher; my single love for it is my unshakeable wealth; Shiva churned the name like ghee from the curd-ocean of countless stories.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; adds that ordinary wealth shrinks when spent while the name-wealth grows daily and is inexhaustible.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the name as mother, father, kin, lover, teacher, lord, friend and companion, and the vow of love for it as his enduring wealth; Shiva churned his countless deeds to extract the name like ghee.

tulsi_vp.254.practical_reading: For someone missing family or mentors, the name (or practice) can become a steady relationship that holds all these roles.
misreadings: Not a call to abandon or replace human family and friends.
cautions: Mention of mother and father may be tender for the bereaved or estranged; the verse can comfort but should be offered gently.
not_for: someone in fresh grief for a parent, if framed as replacement
speaks_to: wanting something that doesn't run out

tulsi_vp.257.context: Tulsi warns that if the friend of the poor pushes the poor away, they have nowhere else. Most people seek their own good, a rare one cares for his dependants, but Ram's feet do good to everyone. He turned glass into gold: the stone (Ahalya), beasts, a bird, Kol and Bhil forest-dwellers and a demon; the Dandaka forest grew holy at his touch and withered trees bloomed. His name helps even those turned against him; no one else destroys sorrow and fault, and one can say anything to so gentle a master.
tulsi_vp.257.core_teaching: Most care is self-interested or limited to one's own circle; divine care extends to everyone, which is why the helpless can rely on it.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: if you remove this poor one he has no other refuge; nearly everyone wants their own good, few do good to their servants; your feet do good to all, good and bad alike.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading ('one in a lakh' cares for dependants); adds that the name helps both the hostile and the devoted; quotes a Rahim doha about being drawn close and then flung away like an arrow, which Tulsi fears.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: if you turn away from this wretch he has no other refuge; all seek their own good, but rarely one who seeks the good of his servants; your feet are good for all.

tulsi_vp.257.practical_reading: Challenges readers to widen their care beyond themselves and their own circle, and comforts those who have no circle.
misreadings: Not cynicism about all people; it contrasts ordinary limited care with universal care.
cautions: Fear of being pushed away may echo rejection by family; reassure.
speaks_to: having no one of your own
wanting to care beyond your circle

data_flags.translation_note: Second line is slightly misread. 'आपको भले हैं सब, आपनेको कोऊ कहूँ' = everyone is good to themselves (seeks their own good), and only someone, somewhere, is good to their own dependants (Poddar, Viyogi Hari, Thakur all read it so). Our 'Everyone is good to...

tulsi_vp.261.context: Tulsi confesses: what he tries to fix would not come right in millions of aeons, but Ram can fix it in a quarter-moment. He traded the priceless jewel of life for wild berries; his mind is dirty, his tongue babbled instead of repeating the name, he took wrong roads and never did good even by mistake; any good deed done by imitation or company he advertised, and he hid his sins, feeding attachment, hatred and anger. Yet the world says Tulsi trusts and loves Ram, and his real support is Ram.
tulsi_vp.261.core_teaching: Self-repair by one's own power is endless; grace can accomplish in a moment what effort alone never finishes.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads: my salvation by my own means won't come in crores of kalpas, but if you wish it, it comes in a quarter moment; I traded life's jewel for the berries of sense pleasure.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; says he wasted life on sense objects and never worshipped; concludes that past, present and future show he has done no good, yet the world says Tulsi belongs to Ram and he trusts Ram.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: by my own efforts it won't be done in a million aeons, but by you it will be achieved in the quarter of a wink; I took mere ber-fruits in exchange for life's priceless jewel.

tulsi_vp.261.practical_reading: Releases perfectionists from the belief that everything depends on their own effort, while still naming honestly what went wrong.
misreadings: Not a reason to stop trying (our misuse note is right).
Not a claim that one's life has been worthless; it is a devotional confession.
cautions: The full pada is harsh self-accusation (never did good even by mistake); avoid quoting it to someone with low self-worth.
not_for: someone with severe self-criticism or depression, if the confession stanzas are used
speaks_to: exhaustion from trying to fix yourself

tulsi_vp.266.context: Tulsi admits the harder he tries to come near, the further he falls; Ram is the same in every age, and Tulsi is still his despite his faults. Finding him separated, the vile age tricked him: turned gold to base metal, a king to a beggar, a good mind to a bad one; he wandered countless hills and forests burning without fire. Only when he went to Chitrakut did he see through the age's tricks, and now he fears his own fears. Hands folded, he reports to Ram that a recognised thief will try to kill, and having said so he is at rest.
tulsi_vp.266.core_teaching: Striving can paradoxically increase the distance; what holds is not the striving but the unchanging nature of the Lord and the fact of belonging to him.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads: the more I want to come near, the farther I go; you are the same in all four ages and I have remained yours though full of sin; the vile age tricked me and turned gold to base metal.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Explains that every effort to come close becomes an obstacle through maya's contact; notes the eternal tie of Brahman and jiva; says he was a part of pure being-consciousness-bliss reduced by the senses to something worth two cowries.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: the more I wish to draw closer to you, the farther away I get; you are steadfast in essence through all four ages, and I'm yours though filled with faults.

tulsi_vp.266.practical_reading: For people who try hard at spiritual or personal growth and feel worse: effort that becomes anxious can push us away; rest in belonging rather than performance.
misreadings: Not an argument that effort is pointless; it is about the paradox of anxious striving.
Grace does not erase responsibility (our misuse note).
cautions: 'Turned gold into base metal, king into beggar' may resonate painfully with someone who lost status or wealth.
speaks_to: trying harder and feeling further away
feeling full of faults yet wanting to belong

tulsi_vp.267.context: Tulsi stages a sit-in (dharna) at Ram's door: he has vowed not to get up his whole life until Ram says 'you are mine'. Yama's messengers pushed him till they tired and couldn't move him; he endured the womb's agony in birth after birth and came out of hell in defiance. Like a child who has dug in for a toy, he will take what he wants, because Ram is kind; he asks Ram to say it quickly, since he is melting with embarrassment, and if Ram is ashamed to say it publicly because of Tulsi's faults, he could say it quietly.
tulsi_vp.267.core_teaching: Devotion can be stubborn: the devotee refuses to leave until he is acknowledged, trusting the Lord's kindness to give in.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: I have vowed to lie at your door and won't rise my whole life until you say 'you are mine', sworn by you; Yama's messengers tired of pushing me.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Calls it Tulsi's satyagraha: he sits in dharna at Ram's door until told 'you are mine', even if life passes.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: having vowed from today to lie at Rama's door, I shall not rise while I live until he tells me 'You are mine'; death's messengers are weary of pushing me away.

tulsi_vp.267.practical_reading: Legitimises persistence in prayer and in seeking acknowledgment: it's all right to keep asking, even stubbornly.
misreadings: Not a model for refusing to leave a person's door who has said no; it is addressed to God.
Surrender follows effort and reflection, not instead of it (our misuse note).
cautions: References to hell and the agony of the womb in stanza 2.
Could be misapplied to human relationships where persistence becomes harassment.
not_for: someone fixated on a person who has rejected them
speaks_to: feeling ignored but unwilling to give up

tulsi_vp.268.context: Tulsi sets his own test for being accepted: when the mind turns around and loves the Lord without guile with the same natural ease it now clings to pleasures. Stanza 2: when it loves Ram as one loves a son, trusts him as a friend, fears him as a king, and holds to him alone like the chataka bird to rain-cloud. Stanza 3: when honour does not elate it nor insult burn it, and it is even in loss and gain, joy and sorrow. Stanza 4: when hearing Ram's qualities brings joy and tears, Tulsi will trust he has become Ram's, and joy will fill his heart.
tulsi_vp.268.core_teaching: The sign of being accepted by God is inner: the heart's natural pull redirected toward the divine, shown in steadiness and spontaneous joy and tears at hearing of him.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: I'll know you have made me yours when my mind turns to you; when it loves you without guile as naturally as it now clings to sense objects.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same bhavartha, adding that while one is a slave of desire one cannot be Ram's servant. Its note on the preceding pada describes the devotee's child-like insistence and urgency to reach the Lord before death.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: then shall I know for sure you've made me yours, when my mind turns towards you with the natural ease it takes to sense objects, loving you spontaneously and abandoning all deceit.

tulsi_vp.268.practical_reading: A gentle self-check: notice where your attention naturally goes, and ask for that same ease to turn toward what you love most.
misreadings: Not a requirement to feel tears or ecstasy as proof of faith.
Not a reason to doubt acceptance when feelings are dry; it is Tulsi's longing, not a test for others.
cautions: Could make someone who feels nothing in prayer worry they are rejected; frame as hope, not criterion.
not_for: someone anxious about whether God accepts them (it sets conditions)
speaks_to: wanting your heart to change, not just your behaviour
noticing where your mind naturally goes
longing for real feeling in faith

tulsi_vp.270.context: Tulsi asks whether Ram will ever look his way, knowing that good or bad he is Ram's own, and put an end to his countless faults. In birth after birth the mind has defeated him; will Ram now let him win? Then Tulsi would have a master, and Ram would earn his name 'lord of the masterless', if he isn't put off by Tulsi's smallness. He asks out of his own fear: Ram is his master, guru, mother, father - everything - so whom else can he tell?
tulsi_vp.270.core_teaching: Belonging comes before goodness: one is Ram's own, good or bad, and that relationship is the basis for asking that faults be removed.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: will you, merciful one, look at me, knowing that whatever I am I am your servant, and end my endless faults; in every birth the mind has beaten me, now let me win.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: will you look towards me in compassion and, knowing that good or ill I'm your own servant, bring my unnumbered faults to an end.

tulsi_vp.270.practical_reading: For someone ashamed of repeated failures: start from 'I still belong', then ask for help to win against the habits that keep winning.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of responsibility for faults; the plea is to have them ended, not ignored.
speaks_to: losing the same inner battle again and again

tulsi_vp.271.context: Tulsi asks Ram, ocean of mercy and protector of refugees, not to cast him off: whatever he is, he is Ram's servant. Others (his vices) have already ruined him, so do not ruin him further; Ram has always mended everyone's affairs, so mend his too. Why fear the world's laughter at taking him in? Treat him with the same nature that made friends of monkeys and a boatman. Guilty as he is, he is Ram's own: a broken arm is still slung from the neck, and a damaged eye is still cared for when it hurts.
tulsi_vp.271.core_teaching: One does not discard a part of oneself because it is broken; in the same way the Lord does not discard a faulty devotee who is still his own.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: whatever I am I'm yours, don't forsake me; I am already spoiled by lust and anger, don't spoil me more; you have always mended everyone; don't fear the world's mockery; though guilty I am yours.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: however I may be I'm your servant, do not forsake me; already ruined by others, be not angry with one lost; though I have done wrong I am still yours; even a broken arm is cared for.

tulsi_vp.271.practical_reading: A powerful image for anyone who feels broken or useless: what is damaged is held closer, not thrown away. Also a model for how families and communities treat their struggling members.
misreadings: Not saying the person is useless; the image is about being kept and tended because one belongs.
cautions: Injury imagery (broken arm, damaged eye) may be literal for someone recently injured or disabled; it can comfort but should be handled carefully.
speaks_to: feeling broken or like a burden
after a failure that made you feel discarded
family members who feel like the 'problem'

tulsi_vp.273.context: Tulsi asks whom else he could tell, who else wishes him well, who else has natural tenderness for servant, friend, sufferer and orphan. Many fallen people crossed the ocean of the world without boat or raft simply because Ram glanced at them - in grace or anger, in sincerity, by accident or sideways. Whichever glance Ram likes, let him cast it quickly on Tulsi and make him his own without delay, for the end of life is very near.
tulsi_vp.273.core_teaching: Divine tenderness is natural, not earned; a single glance of any kind from Ram is enough to carry someone across.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: leaving you, whom do I tell, who is my friend; who else has natural kindness for servant, friend, sufferer and orphan; many sinners crossed without boat because you looked at them in grace, anger, sincerity, by mistake or askance.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Says elsewhere one finds only the self-interested; maps the glances to stories: grace to Ahalya and Jatayu, anger to Ravana and Kansa, sincerity to Guha, Sugriva and Vibhishana, accident to the Yavana.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: leaving you whom shall I tell; who else is a friend to his servant, whose grace falls naturally on the afflicted and orphaned; delay not, for life's end is very near.

tulsi_vp.273.practical_reading: Encourages someone who feels uncared for to bring their need directly, trusting a tenderness that does not depend on merit.
misreadings: Not saying human friends are worthless.
cautions: The full pada ends with 'life's end is near'; avoid for readers who are seriously ill or elderly and anxious about death, unless chosen deliberately.
not_for: someone frightened about approaching death (stanza 3)
speaks_to: feeling that no one wishes you well

tulsi_vp.274.context: Tulsi asks where a sorrowful, poor person can go: who is a master as kind as Ram, who keeps a refugee with no strength left in any part? Other masters take in servants who are rich, talented and serve well; caring for the poor, the talentless and the lazy suits only Ram. Ram knows his heart already; for one as foul-minded as Tulsi, Ram is the only support in three worlds and three times.
tulsi_vp.274.core_teaching: Worldly masters accept the capable; Ram accepts those who have nothing left to offer.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: where shall I go, who is so kind as to shelter a refugee with no strength in any spiritual means; other masters take the rich, virtuous and good servants.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; quotes Vyasa's lament 'at whose door shall I go'; argues 'navin' is an epithet of Ram (ever-young), against commentators who read 'who new would care for the poor'.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: whither shall I go, where is place for a wretched and sorrowful one; who is compassionate like you, who could accept this refuge-seeker devoid of all strength and limbs.

tulsi_vp.274.practical_reading: For people exhausted by illness, grief or burnout: when you have nothing to give, you can still be kept.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of laziness; it describes being accepted without merit.
cautions: Literal reading ('every limb has lost its strength') may touch readers with disability or chronic illness; it can comfort, but avoid implying illness is a moral state.
speaks_to: feeling you have nothing to offer

tulsi_vp.275.context: Tulsi recalls begging from door to door, grinning and falling at feet; the world has kind people able to end sorrow, yet none even spoke to him. His parents left him as a snake leaves its newborn; he blames no one but his own luck, and people shrank from touching his shadow. Seeing his misery, saints told him not to worry: Ram has never cast off even beasts, low ones and sinners who came for shelter. From then on Tulsi became Ram's and was happy, even without much love or faith; seeing what the name's glory and the Lord's gentleness have done for him, he is shy and amazed.
tulsi_vp.275.core_teaching: After universal rejection, a word from good people pointed Tulsi to a refuge that does not reject; he became happy there even before his love and faith were mature.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: I begged at every door, but no one spoke; my parents abandoned me like a snake its young; I blame my fate; people shrank from my shadow.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; discusses the text variant ('tanu-janyo' vs 'tvacha'): Baijnath and Bhatt read it as a snake shedding its skin, but he prefers the Nagari Pracharini reading of a snake abandoning its newborn.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: door to door I told of my wretchedness, baring my teeth and prostrating, yet no one spoke to me; my parents cast me away; a holy man said 'grieve not'.

tulsi_vp.275.practical_reading: For someone who has been turned away repeatedly: one kind voice can point to a place of acceptance; you need not wait until your faith feels strong to be held.
misreadings: Not saying the rejection was deserved; Tulsi blames 'luck', not character.
Grace does not erase responsibility (our misuse note).
cautions: Explicit parental abandonment and social untouchability ('shrank from my shadow') in stanza 2; potentially raw for adoptees or people who faced caste or family rejection.
not_for: someone currently homeless or begging who needs practical help, if used in place of it
speaks_to: being pointed to help by a kind person
gratitude and wonder at unexpected grace

tulsi_vp.30.context: Vinaya Patrika is Tulsi's 'petition' to Ram's court: 279 hymns, the first 43 addressed to other deities and to Ram's courtiers, the rest to Ram (Wikipedia). Padas 25-36 are to Hanuman. This short pada in Raga Sarang begins 'jake gati hai hanuman ki': whoever has Hanuman as refuge has his vow fulfilled, as indelible as a line cut in stone.
tulsi_vp.30.core_teaching: Remembering Hanuman's joyful form releases one from crisis and worry; Shiva, Parvati, Lakshman, Ram and Sita all favour the one on whom Hanuman's kind glance falls, which is a mine of every blessing.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Vinaya Patrika)
commentaries.gist: Whoever relies on Hanuman has his vow fulfilled, firm as a diamond-cut line on stone; he makes the impossible possible; remembering his joyful image ends troubles; the gods favour the one Hanuman looks on kindly.

commentaries.who: Murari Madhusudan Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering
commentaries.gist: English rendering with the same sense: Hanuman's refuge makes one's vow certain; remembering his image frees from sorrow and calamity; his grace is the mine of all good.

tulsi_vp.30.practical_reading: Used as a simple remembrance for anxious moments: call to mind a figure of joyful strength.
misreadings: Not a transaction (recite and win).

tulsi_vp.34.context: Vinaya Patrika is Tulsi's 'petition' to Ram's court: 279 hymns, the first 43 addressed to other deities and to Ram's courtiers, the rest to Ram (Wikipedia). In pada 33 Tulsi protests to Hanuman, demanding to know what fault made Hanuman cast him off. Pada 34 is the apology for that outburst; 35 continues it.
tulsi_vp.34.core_teaching: Don't hold it against the afflicted, the self-seeking, the wretched; they speak without thinking, as people curse heaven in flood or drought. I was at my limit, Lord, and spoke; forgive me by looking to your own goodness. In hard times one remembers the able friend, who forgives and saves.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Vinaya Patrika)
commentaries.gist: Hanuman, do not mind the words of the very distressed, selfish and wretched; they speak in panic, as people curse fate in flood or drought; when Kali's torments reached my limit I spoke ill; forgive me.

commentaries.who: Murari Madhusudan Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering
commentaries.gist: Renders the same: do not take ill the words of the sorely afflicted, the selfish and the wretched who speak without thinking; I spoke being sore afflicted; look to your own ways and forgive me.

commentaries.who: Anjani Nandan Sharan, 'Piyush-varshini' commentary on Hanuman Bahuk (Hindi)
commentaries.gist: Cross-references this pada's 'forgive, looking to your own side' and 'your grace on Tulsi is unconditional and unique' when commenting on Hanuman Bahuk 34 and 16.

tulsi_vp.34.practical_reading: A model for repairing things after lashing out in pain, and for extending the same grace to others who speak harshly when they are suffering.
misreadings: Not permission to abuse others and then demand forgiveness.
Not that anger at God is forbidden; Tulsi expressed it and then reconciled.
speaks_to: after an outburst or angry prayer
caregivers on the receiving end of a patient's anger
guilt about saying harsh things in grief

tulsi_vp.35.context: Vinaya Patrika is Tulsi's 'petition' to Ram's court: 279 hymns, the first 43 addressed to other deities and to Ram's courtiers, the rest to Ram (Wikipedia). Continues the apology to Hanuman begun in 34.
tulsi_vp.35.core_teaching: When hard-pressed one says bitter things; a good master listens, understands, and out of his own goodness does good even to the ill-doer. People flock to a strong, kind helper as rivers to the sea; the fault is all mine, the greatness yours; Tulsi's good comes from your goodness.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Vinaya Patrika)
commentaries.gist: In trouble one speaks ill of one's master, a good master understands and does good even to the bad servant; all run to a strong helper as rivers to the sea; the faults are mine, yours the greatness of forgiving.

commentaries.who: Murari Madhusudan Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering
commentaries.gist: Bitter words come in hard times; the good lord understands and sets things right from his own goodness; nourish the one you took on even if he gives no service; Tulsi's good is your goodness.

tulsi_vp.35.practical_reading: Used for relationships under strain: understanding that pain speaks harshly, and choosing goodness that does not depend on the other person's behaviour.
misreadings: Not a demand that victims keep 'doing good' to someone who harms them.
The 'master-servant' frame is devotional, not a model for human hierarchy.
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship who might hear 'keep being good to the one who hurts you'
speaks_to: being on the receiving end of a loved one's bitterness

tulsi_vp.69.context: Vinaya Patrika is Tulsi's 'petition' to Ram's court: 279 hymns, the first 43 addressed to other deities and to Ram's courtiers, the rest to Ram (Wikipedia). Padas 65-70 are on the Name of Ram; 68 says one keeps burning in the three afflictions until the tongue repeats the Name; 69 lists what the Name is for the needy; 70 follows.
tulsi_vp.69.core_teaching: Remember King Ram's Name with love: it is provision for the unprovided, friend of the helpless, fortune of the unlucky, merit of the meritless, buyer for the poor, family for the low-born, limbs for the lame, eyes for the blind, parents for the hungry, support for the unsupported, a bridge over the ocean of existence; no other Name so lifts the fallen, and it made barren Tulsi fertile.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Vinaya Patrika)
commentaries.gist: The Name is journey-food for the unprovided and helper of the helpless, luck and virtue for those without, honour for the low-born, limbs for the lame, eyes for the blind, parents to the hungry, a bridge over samsara.

commentaries.who: Murari Madhusudan Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering
commentaries.gist: English rendering: provision for the unprovided, companion of the companionless, purchaser for the pauper, high pedigree for the low-born, mother and father to the hungry, support for the supportless, a bridge over existence.

tulsi_vp.69.practical_reading: Used to name, one by one, the forms of lack a reader may feel, and to say there is a source that meets each.
misreadings: Not a claim that disabled or low-caste people are deficient; it reverses exclusion.
The subject is the Name, not a promise of material food.
cautions: Disability and caste language as metaphors of lack; handle carefully.
'Mother and father for the hungry' may be poignant for orphans.
not_for: someone who is literally hungry and needs food today
speaks_to: feeling without resources, family or luck

tulsi_vp.72.context: Vinaya Patrika is Tulsi's 'petition' to Ram's court: 279 hymns, the first 43 addressed to other deities and to Ram's courtiers, the rest to Ram (Wikipedia). Pada 71 marvels that Ram took in Tulsi, who was worth not a counterfeit coin; 72 continues the thought. 73 is 'wake up, dull soul'.
tulsi_vp.72.core_teaching: Ram did Tulsi good from his own goodness, though Tulsi was a traitor to his master. Who is greater than Ram, who smaller than me? People call me Ram's slave and I let them, yet he has not turned from me. Water does not sink the lowly grass floating on its crest, knowing it nourished that grass itself.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Hindi bhavartha (Vinaya Patrika)
commentaries.gist: Ram did me good from his own goodness; I betrayed my master yet he cares for his servant; none is greater than him or smaller than me; water won't drown the straw riding on it, knowing it raised it.

commentaries.who: Murari Madhusudan Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering
commentaries.gist: Rama did good from his own goodness though I rebelled; people call me his slave and I allow it, yet he has not turned away; water does not let the grass it nurtured sink.

tulsi_vp.72.practical_reading: Used for grace that does not depend on deserving: the one who made you will not let you go under.
misreadings: Not that one's actions don't matter; the pada is a confession.
speaks_to: guilt and fear of being abandoned

tulsi_vp.76.context: Pada 76 is one of Tulsidas's autobiographical petitions: he calls himself Ram's slave, named Rambola, who gets food and clothing for saying the name now and then. He recalls being bound by his own deeds and pride, crying out, and being freed; then the moment of acceptance (our lines). The pada ends with him shrugging off people who call him low: he wants no marriage alliance or caste standing, and lives content trusting Ram's love.
tulsi_vp.76.core_teaching: Belonging is given, not earned: a person with no one says plainly 'I want to be yours, I have no one', and is taken by the arm and owned. Once owned, other people's verdicts (low, outcaste) stop mattering.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads the whole pada as Tulsi's story: bound by karma and pride, he cried out; Ram, seeing him burn, freed him; asked who he was, he begged to be his servant.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Calls the pada Tulsi's own 'Ram-story'; notes he treats Ram and guru as one, citing Kabir on the guru.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the scene as the guru touching and caressing his back, taking his arms and making him his own, after Tulsi says he has no one and clings to the feet.

tulsi_vp.76.practical_reading: For someone who feels without family or standing, the pada models saying the need out loud ('I have no one') and letting oneself be claimed; a teacher's hand on the back is the picture of being steadied, not judged.
misreadings: Not a claim that Tulsidas's social rejection was deserved or that caste does not hurt; he refuses to let it define him.
Not a story of earning acceptance through practice: he is taken in at the moment he asks.
cautions: Autobiographical details (orphanhood, being called low) may surface a reader's own family rejection.
The full pada dismisses marriage and caste ties; avoid presenting that as advice for a reader's relationships.
not_for: someone grieving a specific person, where 'I have no one' could deepen isolation without the turn
readers in conflict over marriage or family duties (the full pada brushes those aside)
speaks_to: feeling you have no one anywhere
being newly accepted somewhere after a long time alone
people looking down on you for your background

data_flags.translation_note: First half is right. The last clause 'बोलि सेबक-सुखद, सदा बिरद बहत हौं' is read by both Poddar and Viyogi Hari with Tulsidas as subject: since that day he has always worn the Lord's badge/insignia (the Vaishnava marks: kanthi, tilak, the name) that gladdens devotees....

tulsi_vp.78.context: The pada argues that Ram is the only giver worth asking: everyone else Tulsi tells his poverty to turns out to be poor too; gods, men and sages are masters only until Ram turns his eyes away. Ram has made stones, beasts, trees and birds his own and turned paupers into kings. The ending (our lines) narrows to one request: say once that Tulsidas is yours.
tulsi_vp.78.core_teaching: The deepest request is not for things but to be claimed: one word from the beloved, 'you are mine', outweighs every gift.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Explains: whoever I tell my need to proves needy himself; one who begs from Ram never begs again. Ending: you raise the poor and I am your poor servant, so say just once 'Tulsidas is mine'.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the close as a plea to the compassionate one to say just once that Tulsidasa is his, after listing the stone, tree, bird and beast he made his own.

tulsi_vp.78.practical_reading: Teachers use it to name a need under many needs: to be acknowledged as belonging to someone. It invites a reader to say what they actually want to hear.
misreadings: Not a statement that poverty is a virtue or should be accepted passively.
cautions: A reader who longs to hear 'you are mine' from a parent or partner who will not say it may feel the ache sharply; keep the reading pointed toward being held by the divine, not toward forcing a person.
not_for: someone in a coercive relationship who is told to wait for a word of ownership
speaks_to: wanting to be acknowledged, not just helped
feeling poor or small next to others

tulsi_vp.79.context: A short, complete pada built from paired opposites: kind one and needy one, giver and beggar, sin-remover and famous sinner, Brahman and jiva, master and servant. It ends by leaving the choice of relationship to Ram, asking only that Tulsi find shelter at his feet by any route.
tulsi_vp.79.core_teaching: Every lack in the devotee matches a quality in God, so weakness becomes a reason for closeness rather than distance; the form of the relationship matters less than reaching shelter.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Takes the pairs one by one: you are the giver and I the beggar, the protector of orphans and none is more orphaned than I; you are mother, father, guru, friend and benefactor.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; adds a note that 'chero' means servant or slave, correcting Rameshwar Bhatt's gloss 'disciple'.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the list as Brahman and bound soul, master and slave, and 'father, mother, teacher, friend' as benefactor in every way; take whichever bond you fancy.

tulsi_vp.79.practical_reading: Used to show that one can come to God through whatever relationship feels natural - child, friend, servant - and that admitting one's poverty is itself the opening.
misreadings: Not self-hatred: 'famous sinner' is a devotional convention that sets up the matching quality in Ram.
Not a fixed hierarchy that the reader must adopt; the pada explicitly leaves the choice of bond open.
cautions: The 'father and mother' line may sting for someone estranged from or recently bereaved of a parent; it can also comfort. Handle gently.
not_for: someone working to stop harsh self-talk, if the 'sinner' pairs are read literally
speaks_to: feeling you bring nothing but need
wanting a relationship with God but unsure what form

up_adhyatma.22.context: Just before, the text says the knower must not allow even a moment's carelessness in abiding in Brahman, which the wise call death itself. This verse gives the image; the next says one who reaches the state of the Alone in life stays so after the body falls, and urges constant samadhi.
up_adhyatma.22.core_teaching: Clarity is not won once; like weed closing back over a pond, confusion returns the moment even a wise person stops attending.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar, Thirty Minor Upanishads (1914), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Placed after the warning that carelessness in abiding in Brahman is death itself; the moss image shows that maya re-covers even the wise who are careless for a moment.

commentaries.who: Vivekachudamani (attrib. Shankara), tr. Madhavananda (1921), same verse with translator's note
commentaries.gist: Madhavananda's note: the weed must be held back with a bamboo or the like; in the same way, ongoing meditation is needed to keep ignorance away.

up_adhyatma.22.practical_reading: Insight fades if not practised; keep a daily practice going because old patterns close back in quickly.
misreadings: Not 'you will always fall back, so why try'
Not a reason for anxious self-monitoring
cautions: Can feed guilt in someone who has 'slipped' (relapse, broken habit); frame as care, not failure
not_for: someone harshly self-critical after a relapse
speaks_to: keeping a meditation or prayer practice

up_adhyatma.54.context: One of a run of definitions of the jivanmukta, the one free while living: no 'I' in body and senses, no 'other' in anything else, no difference seen between self, Brahman and world, and evenness whether honoured or reviled. The text then turns to prarabdha karma.
up_adhyatma.54.core_teaching: The mark of inner freedom is staying the same whether the good honour you or the wicked torment you.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar, Thirty Minor Upanishads (1914), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Listed among marks of the jivanmukta: one who keeps equanimity whether revered by the good or reviled by the vicious, next to having no sense of 'I' in the body and no sense of difference.

commentaries.who: Vivekachudamani (attrib. Shankara), tr. Madhavananda (1921), same verse with translator's note
commentaries.gist: The same verse in the Vivekachudamani describes one who feels the same whether his body is worshipped or tormented, as the mark of one liberated in life.

up_adhyatma.54.practical_reading: Praise and criticism both pull at us; practising evenness toward both is a sign of inner freedom, and a goal to grow into.
misreadings: Not a call to tolerate abuse or stay in harmful situations
Not indifference to justice or to others' suffering
cautions: For someone being harassed or abused, 'stay the same' can sound like 'put up with it'; describes an inner state, not a rule about staying
not_for: someone currently experiencing abuse or bullying

up_adhyatma.60.context: The text has just said that knowing 'I am Brahman' burns up karma stored from countless past births, as waking ends the deeds of a dream. Here it qualifies that: prarabdha, the karma that already began this body, still runs its course. It then goes further: for one who truly knows the Self as beyond birth and death, prarabdha does not touch him, and the Veda speaks of it only for those who doubt.
up_adhyatma.60.core_teaching: Knowledge does not stop consequences already set in motion; like a released arrow, they play out, even once you see things differently.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar, Thirty Minor Upanishads (1914), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Follows the claim that 'I am Brahman' destroys stored karma; the arrow aimed at a supposed tiger still strikes the cow. The text adds that for one who knows the Self as unborn, prarabdha has no real hold.

commentaries.who: Vivekachudamani (attrib. Shankara), tr. Madhavananda (1921), same verse with translator's note
commentaries.gist: Work that shaped this body is not destroyed by knowledge before yielding fruit; prarabdha is spent by experience, while stored and future karma burn in knowledge (VC 451-453).

up_adhyatma.60.practical_reading: Changing your understanding doesn't instantly undo the effects of past choices; let them play out with patience instead of self-blame.
misreadings: Not fatalism: it concerns only what has already begun
Not a claim that the person deserved their suffering
cautions: Karma language can feel blaming to someone suffering illness, loss or injustice
Hunting imagery
not_for: someone suffering illness, abuse or loss who may hear 'it's your karma'
speaks_to: living with the consequences of past decisions
after a change of heart, when life hasn't caught up

up_aitareya.31.context: The Aitareya's account of three births. The first is the seed passing from father to mother. Here the unborn child becomes part of the mother, she nourishes it, and she in turn must be cared for. Then she carries the child and the father takes up its care from birth. That care is the second birth; the third comes after the parent's death.
up_aitareya.31.core_teaching: The mother nourishes the child within her, and so she must herself be nourished and protected; care has to flow back to the carer.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), Aitareya bhashya (Sanskrit, GRETIL)
commentaries.gist: The pregnant woman nourishes the husband's self within her by avoiding harmful food and eating well; so she must be nourished and protected by her husband, since no bond in the world lasts without help given in return.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., Aitareya Aranyaka II.5 (SBE 1, 1879)
commentaries.gist: Renders it plainly: she nourishes her husband's self, the son, within her; she who nourishes is to be nourished; she bears the germ, and he raises the child before and after birth.

up_aitareya.31.practical_reading: Whoever is doing most of the caring, whether mother, father or another carer, needs to be cared for too. Ask for help, or offer it, today.
misreadings: Not 'the mother's role is only to carry the father's child'
Not limited to pregnancy; teachers apply the principle to any carer
cautions: Describes conception and pregnancy; sensitive for readers with pregnancy loss or infertility
Frames the child as the husband's self; keep the reading inclusive of single parents and other family shapes
Müller notes some manuscripts open this chapter by asking pregnant women to leave; worth knowing, not quoting
not_for: someone grieving a pregnancy loss

up_aitareya.33.context: Chapter 2 of the Aitareya describes three births of a person: as seed in the father, passed to the mother (first); as the child born and raised (second); and, after the father hands his duties to the son and dies, as rebirth (third). Just before this, the mother nourishes the unborn child and is to be nourished in turn. Just after, the son takes the father's place in good works and the father, his work done, departs. The chapter ends with the sage Vamadeva, who saw through all these births while still in the womb.
up_aitareya.33.core_teaching: In raising a child a parent nurtures a continuation of their own self, and that is how the generations carry on. Shankara adds that this keeps the world going but is not itself the path to liberation.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), Aitareya bhashya (Sanskrit, GRETIL)
commentaries.gist: The father nurtures the newborn through birth rites; the father's self is born as the son, so caring for the son is caring for himself. This is done to keep the worlds continuing, not for liberation.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., Aitareya Aranyaka II.5 (SBE 1, 1879), with Sayana's reading
commentaries.gist: Translates the father as raising the child before and right after birth, which is raising his own self; this is the second birth. Notes that some manuscripts open the chapter by asking pregnant women to leave.

up_aitareya.33.practical_reading: Parenting is not only giving; it shapes the parent too, and continues something of you. Seen that way, the daily care is also self-care and legacy.
misreadings: Not 'your child is an extension of you to be shaped as you like'
Not a claim that only sons carry on the family, even though the original speaks of a son
cautions: The chapter's frame is the cycle of rebirth, and the next sentence is about the parent dying (third birth); don't quote further
The original is father- and son-centred; keep the reading gender-neutral
Can sting for parents of a child who has died, adoptive parents, or people unable to have children
not_for: bereaved parents
people struggling with infertility

up_aitareya.34.context: Chapter 2 of the Aitareya gives a person three births: as seed passing to the mother, as the child born and raised, and, after handing over his duties to the son and dying, as rebirth. This is the third. The chapter closes with the sage Vamadeva, who knew all his births while still in the womb and, rising above, became immortal (2.1.5-6).
up_aitareya.34.core_teaching: The child takes up the parent's work; the parent, duties done and grown old, dies and is born again. Father and son are treated as one self across the generations.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), Aitareya bhashya (Sanskrit, GRETIL)
commentaries.gist: The son takes the father's place for enjoined duties (citing Brihadaranyaka 1.5.17). The father, debts paid and aged, dies and takes a new body by his karma. It is the son's 'third birth' because father and son are one self.

up_aitareya.34.practical_reading: Handing on responsibilities to the next generation is part of a full life; it can be read as permission to let go once your part is done.
misreadings: Not 'children exist to carry on the parent's agenda'
Not a statement that only sons count
cautions: About aging, death and rebirth; the parent's death is the 'third birth'
Avoid for someone whose parent has just died or is dying unless they seek it
Can sting for bereaved parents or the childless
not_for: fresh grief for a parent
bereaved parents
people struggling with infertility
speaks_to: adult children taking on family roles

up_brihadaranyak.188.context: Yajnavalkya is about to leave home for the wandering life and offers to settle his property between his two wives, Maitreyi and Katyayani (2.4.1). Maitreyi asks whether a whole earth full of wealth would make her immortal. He says no, and she then asks for what he knows instead (2.4.3), opening his teaching on the Self.
up_brihadaranyak.188.core_teaching: Wealth can make life comfortable but cannot give what is deathless; not even the hope of it comes through money.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
