commentaries.gist: Maitreyi asks whether rites paid for with the whole earth's wealth could make her immortal. Yajnavalkya: her life would just be like the well-provided; wealth and its works give no hope of immortality.

up_brihadaranyak.188.practical_reading: A clear question to ask of any big goal: will this give me what I really want, or only a more comfortable version of the same life?
misreadings: Not a condemnation of earning or having money
Not a promise that renouncing wealth by itself brings freedom
cautions: For someone in financial distress, 'wealth doesn't matter' can sound glib; the verse is about its limits, not its uselessness
not_for: someone in poverty or debt crisis

up_brihadaranyak.189.context: Maitreyi has just been told that wealth gives no hope of immortality. She sets the property aside and asks for what he knows. In the next verse Yajnavalkya says she was dear to him and now speaks what is dearer still, and he begins the teaching that all things are dear for the sake of the Self.
up_brihadaranyak.189.core_teaching: Once you see something cannot give what matters most, set it down and ask for the real thing.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: Since wealth will not make her immortal, Maitreyi asks what use it is, and requests only what Yajnavalkya knows to be the sole means of immortality.

up_brihadaranyak.189.practical_reading: Before taking a settlement, a promotion or a comfortable option, ask what you actually want from it, and ask the people who know.
misreadings: Not a model of a wife rejecting her rights or inheritance in general
Not contempt for practical provision
cautions: Maitreyi's choice is often held up as an ideal for women to give up property; frame it as her own free intellectual choice
not_for: someone being pressured to give up money or rights they need
speaks_to: a decision point between comfort and meaning
wanting real answers rather than consolation

up_brihadaranyak.191.context: Maitreyi has asked for the teaching that leads to immortality. Yajnavalkya explains that every dear thing is dear for the sake of the Self, so the Self is what must be heard of, reflected on and realised; knowing it, all is known. The following verses give images of the drum, conch and lute, whose sounds are grasped by grasping the instrument.
up_brihadaranyak.191.core_teaching: What we love in any person or thing is, at bottom, the Self; so the Self is the primary object of love and the one thing to come to know.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: Meant to build dispassion for renunciation: spouse, sons and wealth are loved for one's own sake, so love of them is secondary and love of the Self primary. Hence hear of, reflect on and meditate on the Self.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu, SBH vol. 14 (1916)
commentaries.gist: Madhva explicitly rejects reading this as selfish love. 'Atman' here is the Lord Narayana: husband and wife become dear to each other only by his will, which is why mere wishing cannot make someone love us.

up_brihadaranyak.191.practical_reading: Love points beyond the person to something deeper we share with them; teachers use it to loosen possessiveness and to look for what we are really seeking in our relationships.
misreadings: Not 'all love is selfish, so people don't really love you'
Not a reason to withdraw affection from family
cautions: Easy to quote as cynical about love; always include or paraphrase the closing instruction about knowing the Self
Hurts in a failing marriage or after betrayal if read as 'your partner only used you'
not_for: someone just betrayed or abandoned
a parent estranged from a child
speaks_to: asking what we really seek in relationships

up_brihadaranyak.283.context: At King Janaka's debate Kahola asks Yajnavalkya to explain the Brahman that is immediate and direct, the Self within all. Yajnavalkya says it is beyond hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age and death; knowing it, sages drop the desires for sons, wealth and worlds and live by begging. The verse ends: however such a knower behaves, he is just that; all else is perishable. Kahola falls silent.
up_brihadaranyak.283.core_teaching: The drives for children, money and status are one craving in different forms; the knower drops them and passes through learning, inner strength or simplicity, and silence to direct knowledge.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: Having mastered Self-knowledge from teacher and scripture, the knower renounces desires and lives on the strength that knowledge gives, so the senses cannot drag him; then becomes meditative; then a true knower. Shankara uses the passage to defend full renunciation.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu, SBH vol. 14 (1916)
commentaries.gist: After acquiring learning one should establish oneself in the strength of reasoning, then become a muni; passing through meditation and beyond it, one becomes a direct knower. Whatever his condition, such a one stays a beggar for God's grace.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884), footnote
commentaries.gist: Gives the 'become as a child' reading (after Gough and Deussen) but doubts 'knowledge of babes' is an Indian idea, notes Shankara reads it otherwise elsewhere (Vedanta Sutra 3.4.50), and suspects the text may be corrupt.

up_brihadaranyak.283.practical_reading: Wanting children, money and recognition can all be the same restless reaching; teachers use it to invite simplicity, learning that turns into stillness, and less need to prove oneself.
misreadings: Not a command for householders to abandon family
Not anti-intellectual: learning is the first step, not something to skip
'Like a child' does not mean naive or irresponsible
cautions: Lumping the wish for children with greed can hurt people struggling to have children
Renunciation context (begging monks) needs framing for lay readers
not_for: someone grieving infertility
someone whose financial worry is about survival

data_flags.translation_note: Disputed key word. Our 'live like a child' / 'childlike simplicity' follows Müller, Hume and Deussen for bālya. Both Shankara and Madhva read bālya as 'strength' (from bala): Shankara, the strength of Self-knowledge; Madhva, strength of reasoning. Müller's footnote flags the passage as obscure and...

up_brihadaranyak.323.context: This is Gargi's second time on her feet in the debate (in 3.6 Yajnavalkya stopped her from asking too far). She asks the brahmins' permission, then compares her two questions to a warrior's arrows. She asks what space is woven on, and he answers: the Imperishable (akshara), which he then describes by negations (3.8.8).
up_brihadaranyak.323.core_teaching: Gargi frames her questions as a direct challenge, warrior-style; the scene honours searching, fearless questioning in a public assembly.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: With the assembly's leave, Gargi uses the image of a valiant archer of Kashi or Videha holding two deadly arrows to show her questions will be very hard, and dares him to answer if he knows Brahman.

up_brihadaranyak.323.practical_reading: Readers use Gargi as a model of courage in asking hard questions, especially for women speaking up where they are outnumbered.
misreadings: Not hostility for its own sake: her aim is to test whether the teacher truly knows
Not a story of a woman 'put in her place': she ends by declaring him unbeatable on her own judgment
not_for: someone looking for comfort rather than challenge
speaks_to: speaking up in a room that doubts you
preparing for a tough interview or exam

up_brihadaranyak.332.context: Yajnavalkya has just described the Imperishable as the ruler under whose command sun and moon, earth and sky, days and years keep their places (3.8.9). Here he adds that ritual and austerity without knowing it end in finite results, and that knowing it makes one a brahmana. Next he calls it the unseen seer, unheard hearer (3.8.11).
up_brihadaranyak.332.core_teaching: Even thousands of years of worship and austerity come to an end; only knowing the imperishable gives a result that does not run out.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: The Imperishable must exist, since knowing it ends transmigration and rites alone cannot. Rites yield results that are used up; one who dies without this knowledge is pitiable like a bought slave, while one who knows it is a brahmana.

up_brihadaranyak.332.practical_reading: Busy effort, even religious effort, is not the same as understanding; it invites a reader to ask what all their striving rests on.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of ritual or service as worthless; Shankara says they give real but finite results
'Pitiable' is about missing the goal, not a judgment on a person's worth
cautions: Speaks of dying without knowledge as pitiable: avoid for someone whose loved one has just died
not_for: recently bereaved readers
someone with scrupulosity who fears they are 'doing it wrong'

up_brihadaranyak.334.context: Yajnavalkya has just answered Gargi's second question: space is woven on the Imperishable, the unseen seer. Gargi now turns to the brahmins and tells them to be glad if they can leave with a bow, since no one will beat him. She falls silent. Next Vidagdha Shakalya presses him regardless (3.9) and meets a grim end.
up_brihadaranyak.334.core_teaching: Gargi, having tested Yajnavalkya herself, publicly concedes his mastery and counsels her peers to accept it.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: Gargi tells the brahmins to count themselves lucky to escape with a salute; they should not even think of defeating him, since she already said that if he answered her two questions nobody could. Then she stopped.

up_brihadaranyak.334.practical_reading: Knowing when you have met someone who knows more, and saying so openly, is a strength; it also models honest concession after a fair test.
misreadings: Not a story of Gargi being defeated or silenced: her silence follows her own verdict
cautions: The next section (3.9.26) ends with a rival's head falling apart; do not pair it with that
not_for: someone already feeling humiliated or outclassed

up_brihadaranyak.387.context: After Shakalya's fatal failure (3.9.26), Yajnavalkya challenges the silent brahmins in verse. He maps a person's body onto a tree (hair as leaves, skin as bark, blood as sap), then asks: a felled tree sprouts again from its root, but from what root does a person grow again after death? He rules out 'from seed' and says a tree pulled up by its root does not return. No one can answer, and the Upanishad gives its own reply: Brahman, knowledge and bliss.
up_brihadaranyak.387.core_teaching: The riddle points to a root of life that death does not reach; the text's answer is Brahman, consciousness and bliss.
up_brihadaranyak.387.practical_reading: Teachers use the image to ask what in us is deeper than what can be cut away; it is often read at the end of life as a question rather than an answer.
misreadings: Not a promise that the person will literally come back
Out of context it reads as a bleak riddle; the text's own answer follows
cautions: Directly about death and being 'cut down'; Shankara reads it in terms of rebirth, which can feel dismissive in fresh grief
Comes right after a debater's head 'falls apart' in the text
not_for: fresh grief
someone with suicidal thoughts

up_brihadaranyak.418.context: In 4.1 Janaka told Yajnavalkya what six teachers had taught him, and Yajnavalkya showed each was only a partial definition of Brahman. Now the king leaves his seat, bows and asks for teaching. Yajnavalkya points out that for all his learning and wealth he does not know where he goes after death, and begins the teaching on the self in the heart, ending by declaring Janaka has reached fearlessness (4.2.4).
up_brihadaranyak.418.core_teaching: Gathering teachings, honours and wealth is like fitting out a vehicle; it is no use if you do not know your destination.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: Janaka drops his pride and bows. Yajnavalkya says he has fitted his mind with many meditations on Brahman like a traveller's chariot or boat, and is rich and learned, yet lacking Self-knowledge he does not know his destination.

up_brihadaranyak.418.practical_reading: Credentials, reading and success are equipment; the verse asks whether you know what they are for. The king's humility in admitting 'I do not know' is the turning point.
misreadings: Not contempt for learning or wealth: they are the vehicle, just not the destination
cautions: 'When you leave this world' is about death; light to moderate
not_for: someone facing imminent death of a loved one, if the 'where will you go' line is quoted bare
speaks_to: someone who has read a lot but feels stuck

up_brihadaranyak.429.context: Janaka asks what light a person has. Yajnavalkya answers in steps: the sun; when it sets, the moon; then fire; then speech (sound you can follow in the dark); and finally the self. Janaka then asks 'which is the self?' and is told it is the light within the heart, made of consciousness (4.3.7), leading into the long teaching on waking, dream and deep sleep.
up_brihadaranyak.429.core_teaching: When every outer light and sign fails, a person still sits, moves and acts by an inner light, the self, which is distinct from body and senses.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: Sound guides us in the dark, so speech serves as light. When even that stops, as in dream and sleep, a light distinct from body and senses still works: the self, which lights everything and is lit by nothing.

up_brihadaranyak.429.practical_reading: In the darkest periods, when the usual supports and signals are gone, something in us still knows and keeps going; teachers use it to point to that inner witness.
misreadings: Not a claim that outer help is useless: the text values each outer light in turn
not_for: someone needing practical help now, if offered as a substitute for it

up_brihadaranyak.473.context: 4.4 describes dying. In 4.4.1-2 the senses gather into the heart, the self leaves by the eye or head or another opening, and knowledge, deeds and past impressions take hold of it. Here the leech image shows the self reaching the next body before leaving the last; 4.4.4 adds the goldsmith image; 4.4.5-6 say one becomes according to one's desires and deeds.
up_brihadaranyak.473.core_teaching: At death the self, carried by its impressions, already reaches toward a new embodiment before leaving the old, as a leech grips the next blade of grass.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: As a leech grips the next straw before letting go, the transmigrating self casts off this body, makes it senseless, reaches the next body through its impressions and identifies with it, as it makes a dream body.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu, SBH vol. 14 (1916)
commentaries.gist: It is the Lord who removes the soul from the gross body by grasping its subtle body, and who gives the soul knowledge so it understands ignorance; the leech image applies to souls nearing release as well.

up_brihadaranyak.473.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say life is continuous and that our habits and wishes shape what comes next; some apply it to transitions within a life (we tend to grab the next thing before letting go).
misreadings: Not a statement that the dying person has already 'moved on' and so needs no care
The second line does not mean the dead are freed from ignorance (Shankara reads it as the body made senseless)
cautions: Explicitly about death and rebirth; can feel dismissive or frightening in fresh grief
Avoid for readers caring for a dying relative unless they ask about death
not_for: fresh bereavement
someone with suicidal thoughts
parents who have lost a child
speaks_to: questions about what happens at death
making peace with mortality in later life

data_flags.translation_note: Two issues. (1) 'Let go of ignorance' follows Müller and Hume ('dispelled its ignorance') but Shankara reads avidyāṃ gamayitvā as 'making the body senseless', and our own our_note says so; translation and note contradict each other. Madhva reads it as the Lord making the soul...

up_brihadaranyak.474.context: Continues the account of dying. After the leech image (4.4.3), this verse explains how the self makes a new body: as a goldsmith reworks the same gold into a newer, finer shape, the self reworks the same elements. The next verses say one becomes what one desires and does, and that the one free of desire does not go anywhere but becomes Brahman (4.4.6-7).
up_brihadaranyak.474.core_teaching: The self keeps reshaping the same elements into new bodies, finer or not, according to its past deeds and understanding.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: As a goldsmith reworks the same gold, the self repeatedly reworks the five ever-present elements into another, newer form suited to ancestors, celestial singers, gods, Viraj, Hiranyagarbha or other beings, depending on its past work and knowledge.

up_brihadaranyak.474.practical_reading: Often used hopefully: what we are can be refashioned into something better. Teachers add that what shapes the new form is how we live and what we understand now.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that the next life is 'more beautiful' for everyone: the form depends on deeds and knowledge
Not a reason to treat this life or body as disposable
cautions: About death and rebirth; the 'newer and more beautiful' line can sound like a platitude to the newly bereaved
not_for: fresh grief
someone with suicidal thoughts
speaks_to: later stages of grief, when consolation is welcome

data_flags.translation_note: Same issue as 4.4.3: 'letting go of ignorance' (Müller/Hume) vs Shankara's 'making the body senseless'; our_note follows Shankara. Also our translation drops the end of the verse: the new form is that of ancestors, gandharvas, gods, Prajapati, Brahma or other beings, according to one's deeds...

up_brihadaranyak.477.context: Yajnavalkya is explaining to Janaka what happens at death: the self leaves the body like a caterpillar moving to the next blade of grass and makes a new form like a goldsmith reshaping gold. In this verse he says the self takes on whatever it identifies with, and as it acts, so it becomes; then cites the view that a person is made of desire. Next (4.4.6) he says the one attached goes to the fruits of his deeds and returns, while the one free of desire, being Brahman, goes to Brahman.
up_brihadaranyak.477.core_teaching: Desire shapes resolve, resolve shapes action, and action shapes what one attains; the Upanishad uses this to explain rebirth and points beyond it to freedom from desire.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Swami Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: A slight longing, if unchecked, firms into resolve, which leads to action and its results; so desire is the root of transmigration. Without desire, actions bear no binding fruit.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Renders the chain as desire to will, will to deed, deed to what one reaps; the next paragraph contrasts the desiring man, who returns to this world of action, with the desireless one who goes to Brahman.

up_brihadaranyak.477.practical_reading: To keep a resolve, look upstream at what you actually want. Teachers use this verse to say that clarifying desire is the first step of any lasting change.
misreadings: Not a self-help manifestation promise ('want it and you'll get it')
Not a celebration of desire; the passage's goal is freedom from it
cautions: The passage is about death and rebirth; avoid that frame for grieving readers
'You become your deeds' can feel like blame for someone who failed a resolve
not_for: someone in shame over a relapse, without a gentler frame

up_brihadaranyak.486.context: After explaining that the one without desires does not go anywhere but becomes Brahman (4.4.6-7), Yajnavalkya cites a series of verses on the knower. This one says that once a person knows 'I am this', there is nothing left to crave on the body's behalf. The verses that follow praise the wonder of awakening in 'this dense jungle' of the body (4.4.13).
up_brihadaranyak.486.core_teaching: Craving and the suffering that follows the body's ups and downs depend on not knowing who we are; with that knowledge, there is nothing missing to chase.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: 'If' marks how rare this is. Knowing oneself as the one Self of all, there is nothing outside to want and no one else to want it for, so one no longer suffers along with the body.

commentaries.who: Swami Krishnananda (Divine Life Society), discourse on the Brihadaranyaka
commentaries.gist: Birth and suffering come from desire turned outward to the non-self. If the Self is recognised in every object with the same intimacy we feel for our own being, the object stops being an object; that is liberation.

up_brihadaranyak.486.practical_reading: When you notice yourself chasing one more thing for comfort or status, ask: wanting what, for whose sake? The question itself often loosens the grip.
misreadings: Not a recommendation to neglect health or the body's needs
Not 'pain isn't real'
cautions: Can sound dismissive to someone in chronic illness or pain if read as 'stop fretting over your body'
not_for: someone with serious illness or chronic pain
eating-disorder or body-image struggles

up_brihadaranyak.488.context: Part of the closing verses of 4.4 on the knower. The preceding verse speaks of the one who has awakened to the Self in this body; this one says the chance is here and now, and missing it is a great loss. The following verses describe the Self as lord of past and future, beyond fear.
up_brihadaranyak.488.core_teaching: This life is the opportunity to know the Self; not using it is the great loss.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: Read as thanksgiving: in this body, under ignorance's long sleep, we have somehow known Brahman; otherwise endless birth and death would follow. Knowers become immortal; those who take the body as self get sorrow.

commentaries.who: Swami Krishnananda (Divine Life Society), discourse on the Brihadaranyaka
commentaries.gist: The body is given as a vehicle for moving toward God; if it is used only for the senses and this world is taken as all, life has been wasted and that is the great loss.

up_brihadaranyak.488.practical_reading: A nudge not to postpone what matters most; teachers read it as urgency about inner life, not fear.
misreadings: Not a threat of damnation
Not a judgment that people who die without spiritual knowledge are doomed
cautions: 'Great loss' and 'go only to sorrow' can wound someone recently bereaved or anxious about a loved one's death
Can feed scrupulosity or spiritual anxiety
not_for: fresh grief
anxious or perfectionistic readers

up_brihadaranyak.495.context: Near the end of the closing verses of 4.4. Having described the Self as unborn and beyond measure, the text advises the seeker to turn knowledge into direct insight and not get lost in endless words. 4.4.22 follows with the great description of the Self as the lord of all, untouched by good or bad deeds, sought through study, sacrifice, giving and austerity.
up_brihadaranyak.495.core_teaching: Once you have understood the teaching, practise it into insight; more words only tire you.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: Having learned of the Self from teacher and scripture, the seeker should make it direct insight by practising renunciation, calm, self-control, withdrawal, endurance and concentration. A few words on the Self's unity are fine; many words only tire the voice.

commentaries.who: Swami Krishnananda (Divine Life Society), discourse on the Brihadaranyaka
commentaries.gist: Like a mother's advice: don't read or talk too much in the later stages, it drains energy. Some study is needed at first, but practice should follow correct understanding, and much of life may go into understanding the goal properly.

up_brihadaranyak.495.practical_reading: After a point, more books, podcasts and debate become a way to avoid practice; choose one thing you understand and live it.
misreadings: Not anti-learning: understanding comes first
Not a ban on conversation or asking questions
not_for: a beginner who needs to learn more first

up_brihadaranyak.501.context: This seals the long teaching to Janaka. It quotes a verse that the knower's greatness neither grows by good deeds nor shrinks by bad, and from that draws the five qualities (calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, collected) in which one sees the Self everywhere. Janaka responds by offering Yajnavalkya the kingdom of Videha and himself as servant.
up_brihadaranyak.501.core_teaching: The worth of one who knows the Self does not depend on deeds; from that security come calm, restraint, patience and steadiness, and one sees the Self in all.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: Other glories come from work and pass; this one is natural and eternal, unchanged by good or bad work. Knowing it, one becomes calm, controlled, desireless, enduring and concentrated, and sees all as the Self.

up_brihadaranyak.501.practical_reading: Your basic worth is not up for grabs in every success or failure; resting in that makes it easier to be patient, calm and focused.
misreadings: Not a licence to act badly because 'deeds don't touch the knower'
Not a claim that effort and ethics don't matter: the five disciplines are the practice
cautions: 'Not stained by wrong action' can be misused to excuse harm; present with its ethical frame
not_for: someone looking to excuse harm they have done

up_brihadaranyak.533.context: Book 5 opens a supplement after the main teaching of Books 1-4. It begins with the famous verse on fullness and then gives a meditation on Om as space (kha). It is followed by the 'Da Da Da' teaching (5.2) and other meditations.
up_brihadaranyak.533.core_teaching: The source and what comes from it are both whole; nothing is lost when the world arises from the infinite, and the infinite alone remains.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: 'That' is the unconditioned Brahman, 'this' the same Brahman appearing through name and form; both are infinite. The effect comes from the cause without losing infinitude; when its apparent separateness is removed by knowledge, the one infinite alone remains.

commentaries.who: Swami Krishnananda (Divine Life Society), discourse on the Brihadaranyaka
commentaries.gist: From fullness only fullness can come: the whole cosmos is reflected in every particle, and the Absolute loses nothing when the universe emerges, unlike any physical source that is depleted by what it gives.

up_brihadaranyak.533.practical_reading: Recited as a peace chant: you are not a fragment cut off from the whole, and giving does not diminish what is truly full.
misreadings: Not a mathematical claim; 'whole minus whole' is a pointer, not arithmetic

up_brihadaranyak.534.context: In the supplement to the Upanishad, after the verse on fullness and the meditation on Om, comes this short parable. Each group of Prajapati's children, after their studentship, gets the same single syllable 'Da' and hears in it the lesson they most need. The thunder still repeats it. 5.3 then turns to the heart (hṛdaya) as Brahman.
up_brihadaranyak.534.core_teaching: One syllable, three lessons: restraint, giving and compassion. Each hearer took the one they lacked, and every person should learn all three.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: Gods are unruly, humans greedy, asuras cruel, so each heard the lesson for its own fault. All three faults exist in people, so all should learn restraint, giving and compassion; awareness of a fault makes a hint enough.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu, SBH vol. 14 (1916)
commentaries.gist: Madhva reads dama for the gods as humility, not letting power and lordliness make them proud; humans are to give, asuras to be merciful. All beings should practise all three to grow in merit.

up_brihadaranyak.534.practical_reading: Hear the same advice and notice which part stings: that is probably yours. A simple daily check: where do I need restraint, generosity and kindness today?
misreadings: Not 'some people are demons': the three types are tendencies in everyone
Not three separate lessons for three groups only; the text says to learn all three
speaks_to: family or team where each person needs different advice

up_brihadaranyak.56.context: Chapter 1.3 tells how the gods chose the vital breath (prana) as their chanter because it alone could not be pierced by evil. This closing paragraph gives a practice for one who knows that teaching: during the Pavamana chants the sacrificer mutters the three-line prayer, and the Upanishad glosses it at once. The rest of the paragraph turns to winning food and wishes through the remaining chants.
up_brihadaranyak.56.core_teaching: The text itself says all three lines mean one thing: 'make me immortal'. Unreal and darkness both stand for death; real and light for immortality.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: A japa prescribed for one who knows the vital-breath meditation; its fruit is rising to divinity. Shankara takes death as ordinary ignorant thought and action, and the immortal as one's divine nature; the third line sums up the first two.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu, SBH vol. 14 (1916)
commentaries.gist: Madhva restricts the prayer to a special class of souls destined to serve as vehicles of Vayu, who recite it while meditating on Vishnu; it is addressed to Vishnu as the one who leads out of sorrow.

up_brihadaranyak.56.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a short daily prayer for moving from confusion and fear toward clarity; the Upanishad's own gloss lets a reader treat all three lines as one wish to outgrow what dies.
misreadings: Not a general invocation detached from practice: in the text it is a japa within a chant, glossed by the Upanishad itself
Not a prayer for a long physical life; 'immortality' here is the deathless, not avoiding death
cautions: 'Death' is named twice in the gloss; fine for most readers but can jar in fresh bereavement if the gloss is quoted
not_for: someone wanting a prayer for a sick person's recovery (the 'immortality' is not bodily survival)
speaks_to: starting a new day or practice

up_brihadaranyak.62.context: 1.4 opens with the Self alone in the beginning, looking around and seeing nothing but itself, and saying 'I am'. Here that first being feels fear, reasons it away, and fear leaves. Next (1.4.3) he feels no delight alone, longs for a second, and divides into husband and wife, from whom creatures come.
up_brihadaranyak.62.core_teaching: Fear depends on there being something other than oneself; when the first being saw there was nothing besides him, fear dissolved. The Advaita reading takes this as fear born of ignorance and cured by knowing oneness.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: Viraj feared just as we do, from a false notion that he could be destroyed. Right knowledge of the Self removed it, since a second entity that causes fear is only projected by ignorance.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu, SBH vol. 14 (1916)
commentaries.gist: The being is Brahma, who feared from lack of discrimination; he reasoned that no equal exists, his only superior (Vishnu) loves him as a father, and everything lower is under his control, so fear left.

up_brihadaranyak.62.practical_reading: Much anxiety is about what we imagine standing against us; looking straight at the fear and asking 'what exactly am I afraid of?' can loosen it.
misreadings: Not 'you should be alone to be fearless'
Not a dismissal of real external danger; the text is about fear born of a sense of separateness
cautions: For someone frightened because they are actually isolated or unsafe, 'fear comes from a second' could sound like blaming the other person or minimising danger
not_for: someone in real danger from another person
acute loneliness needing company rather than insight
speaks_to: fear of threats that may be imagined

up_brihadaranyak.63.context: Just after the first being overcame fear (1.4.2), he finds no joy in being alone, wishes for a mate, and splits his own body in two to make husband and wife. The verse continues with their union and the birth of humans, then the wife hides in animal forms and the creation of all pairs follows (1.4.4).
up_brihadaranyak.63.core_teaching: The longing for a partner is built into embodied life from the first being onward; the couple is pictured as two halves of one whole. Shankara adds that this shows even the first being was still within desire.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: Viraj's unease shows he is within the relative world. To end it he desired a wife and projected a body the size of man and wife together, then split it, so each partner is half of oneself.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu, SBH vol. 14 (1916)
commentaries.gist: Brahma, alone, felt no delight and wished for a wife; his body held Sarasvati within it, the size of both together, and he then divided it.

up_brihadaranyak.63.practical_reading: Wanting closeness is not a weakness; the text treats it as basic to being human. Teachers also use it to ask whether we expect another person to complete us.
misreadings: Not a claim that unmarried people are incomplete or less
Not a rule that a wife exists to fill a man's space; the original is male-centred and should be read gender-neutrally
cautions: Heteronormative and male-centred framing ('space filled by the wife')
Can sting for the widowed, divorced or involuntarily single if read as 'you are only half'
not_for: recently widowed or divorced readers
people who feel judged for being single

up_brihadaranyak.86.context: Brahman, alone, did not flourish. It projected ruling power (the warrior gods such as Indra and Varuna), then the wealth-producing gods, then the nourisher Pushan, and still did not flourish, so it projected dharma. The next verse (1.4.15) names these as the four varnas and warns that one who dies without knowing the Self is not protected by it.
up_brihadaranyak.86.core_teaching: What is right stands above raw power. Through it the weak can prevail over the strong, and what is right in practice is the same as what is true.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara, Vartika (as cited in Madhavananda's note)
commentaries.gist: The more obvious sense of the simile is that the weak prevail as one does with the backing of the king.

commentaries.who: Swami Krishnananda (Divine Life Society), commentary on the Brihadaranyaka
commentaries.gist: Dharma is the invisible ordering law, the ruler of rulers, which binds even the lawmaker. Strength and weakness depend on one's alignment with it, and truth and righteousness are two sides of one coin.

up_brihadaranyak.86.practical_reading: When you are outmatched, anchor yourself in what is fair and true and in legitimate structures, rather than trying to match force with force.
misreadings: Not a promise that the right side always wins quickly
Not a licence for vigilante 'justice'
Shankara ties dharma here to caste duties; don't present it as a modern human-rights doctrine without saying that is an application
cautions: The surrounding verses (1.4.11-15) describe the creation of the four varnas, and Shankara's commentary links dharma to caste duty; avoid quoting context that reads as endorsing caste hierarchy
For someone being hurt by a person close to them, add practical safety advice; 'dharma will protect you' should not replace seeking help
not_for: someone in immediate danger who needs practical steps first
speaks_to: standing up to someone who hurt you

up_brihadaranyak.92.context: After the creation story, 1.4.15-16 describe the householder's life of ritual duty. Each regular duty makes him a 'world', a support, for some class of beings: gods, sages, ancestors, humans, animals, down to ants. Shankara stresses this describes the ritual householder who has not yet known the Self; 1.4.17 turns to desire as what drives such a life.
up_brihadaranyak.92.core_teaching: By sheltering people, feeding guests and providing for animals, a household becomes a support for all beings, and all beings in turn wish it well.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: The ritual householder, still identified with body and organs, sustains every class of beings through his duties: sacrifice for gods, study for sages, offspring for ancestors, food and shelter for people, fodder for animals.

up_brihadaranyak.92.practical_reading: Ordinary hospitality and care for animals make a home a small world others live by; feeding a guest or a stray is part of a spiritual life, not separate from it.
misreadings: Not 'give so that you are praised'
Not the Upanishad's final word on the good life: Shankara frames it as the ritual householder's path, below Self-knowledge
cautions: Framed around a male householder; keep it gender-neutral
not_for: someone already overburdened by caring for others who needs permission to rest
speaks_to: feeling one's daily care work is small

up_chhandogya.10.context: The Chandogya opens with meditation on Om as the Udgitha, the essence of all essences. After explaining its meaning, the text raises an objection: both the one who understands Om and the one who doesn't perform the rite with it, so why learn? The answer: knowing and not knowing differ, and what is done with knowledge, faith and concentration is stronger. This closes the first section.
up_chhandogya.10.core_teaching: The same outward act carries more power when done with understanding, faith and focused attention.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Against the objection that a medicine works whether understood or not: a merchant who knows gems gets a better price than a forest dweller selling the same stones. Acts done with knowledge, faith and concentration bear more fruit.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: (His 1.1.8.) Both the wise and the ignorant should perform the worship, but knowledge and ignorance differ: worship of the Lord with knowledge, faith and propriety leads to endless reward, that of the ignorant to limited reward.

up_chhandogya.10.practical_reading: Doing the same daily task with understanding and wholehearted attention changes what it yields; it encourages knowing why you do what you do.
misreadings: Not 'only experts should act': both perform the act, the text says
Not a magic formula: 'more powerful' refers to the fruit of a rite done with understanding
not_for: someone already crushed by perfectionism about 'doing it right'
speaks_to: going through the motions at work or in prayer

up_chhandogya.247.context: Chapter 3 has been teaching meditations on the sun and on Gayatri. Here begins Shandilya's meditation: all this is Brahman, and a person becomes after death what their settled conviction is here. The next verses describe what to meditate on: the self in the heart, smaller than a grain of rice yet greater than the worlds, which 'I shall reach on departing' (3.14.2-4).
up_chhandogya.247.core_teaching: Everything rises from, lives in and returns to Brahman; and since a person becomes what they firmly resolve, one should settle the right conviction calmly.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: The world is Brahman because at origin, life and dissolution it is never found apart from it. Meditate calmly, free of love and hate. Volition is firm conviction; as it is here, so one becomes after death.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: The Lord in the heart is the same Lord who pervades the universe: smaller than the atomic soul, greater than the cosmos. 'All this' (sarvam) names him as possessing all qualities; tajjalān names Vishnu who moves on the waters.

up_chhandogya.247.practical_reading: What you repeatedly settle on in your mind shapes who you become; choose your convictions deliberately and hold them calmly.
misreadings: Not 'think positive and you'll get what you want'
'All is Brahman' is not a reason to ignore wrongs in the world
cautions: 'So one becomes on departing' links conviction to after-death state; can worry readers anxious about a loved one's last thoughts
not_for: someone obsessing that their thoughts cause bad events
speaks_to: wanting a sense of the sacred in everything

up_chhandogya.268.context: 3.16-17 treat a person's whole life as a Soma sacrifice: hunger and thirst are the initiation, eating and enjoying are the intermediate rites, laughing and loving are the chants, and these five virtues are the priests' fee. Death is the final purificatory bath (3.17.5). Ghora Angirasa taught this to Krishna, son of Devaki, who then became free of thirst (3.17.6).
up_chhandogya.268.core_teaching: If life is a sacrifice, its real offerings are discipline, generosity, honesty, non-harming and truthful speech.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: These five are the fees of the life-sacrifice because, like a sacrificial fee, they strengthen the merit of the whole undertaking.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: Explains the comparison of a person to a sacrifice step by step (fasting as initiation, eating as the Upasad rites, hymns, then the gifts to priests), reading the whole as a meditation on the Lord.

up_chhandogya.268.practical_reading: Ordinary life becomes worship when it carries these five qualities; a simple checklist for the day.
misreadings: Not a call to harsh self-denial: tapas here is discipline alongside giving and honesty
cautions: The next verse calls death the final rite of the life-sacrifice; don't pair them for the bereaved
speaks_to: people who want spirituality without ritual

up_chhandogya.304.context: Satyakama wants to become a Vedic student and asks his mother his lineage (gotra), which a teacher would require. She says she doesn't know it and tells him to give his name as Satyakama Jabala, after her. He goes to Haridrumata Gautama and repeats her words exactly (4.4.3-4); the teacher accepts him for his truthfulness (4.4.5).
up_chhandogya.304.core_teaching: A mother tells her son the plain truth about his uncertain origins and gives him her own name to carry; that honesty becomes his credential.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Jabala says she was too busy serving many guests in her husband's house to ask his family; she had him in her youth and his father died soon after. So he should call himself Satyakama Jabala.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: Introduces the story of Satyakama (4.4-4.9) as the frame for teaching the four forms of the Lord; the gotra problem is resolved because straightforward truthfulness is taken as the sign of eligibility.

up_chhandogya.304.practical_reading: Telling a child the truth, even an uncomfortable one, and standing behind them gives them something sturdier than a pedigree.
misreadings: Not an occasion to moralise about the mother
Not a claim that lineage doesn't matter in the text's world: it is exactly what the teacher asks for
cautions: Touches on unknown or absent fathers and a mother's past; handle without judgment
Avoid repeating the commentators' caste reasoning (see 4.4.5)
not_for: someone being shamed about their parentage, if the reading dwells on the mother's past
speaks_to: adoptees and people unsure of their origins

up_chhandogya.306.context: Satyakama has gone to Gautama and asked to be his student; the teacher asks his lineage, as was required. The boy repeats his mother's words without softening them. The teacher's response follows in 4.4.5.
up_chhandogya.306.core_teaching: Asked to prove his standing, the boy simply tells the truth, including what he doesn't know.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: A teacher must know a student's family before admitting him. Satyakama says he does not know, he asked his mother, and repeats her words exactly as he remembers them.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: The boy's straightforwardness in admitting he does not know his gotra is itself what qualifies him; the teacher acts on that.

up_chhandogya.306.practical_reading: When asked about a gap in your record or background, a plain honest answer often earns more trust than a polished one.
misreadings: Not a story about lineage being shameful
cautions: Commentators' caste framing (see 4.4.5)
Repeats the mother's words about her youth; keep tone non-judgmental
speaks_to: job or college interviews with gaps to explain

up_chhandogya.308.context: Having heard the boy's honest account, Gautama accepts him and initiates him. He then sends him off with 400 lean, weak cows; the boy vows not to return until they number a thousand (the same verse, our up_chhandogya.309).
up_chhandogya.308.core_teaching: The teacher accepts the student because he did not depart from the truth.
up_chhandogya.308.practical_reading: Integrity opens doors that credentials don't; good teachers and employers notice it.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of caste by birth; most modern readers take it as character outweighing birth
cautions: Shankara and Madhva both explain Gautama's 'only a brahmin would speak so' in caste terms (truthfulness as the mark of a brahmin, Madhva adding that shudras are not straightforward). Do not reproduce that reasoning; modern readers take the story as truth outweighing birth.

up_chhandogya.309.context: The teacher has given the newly initiated boy 400 thin, weak cows to tend. He takes them to the forest vowing not to return until they are a thousand, and stays away for years. When they reach a thousand, a bull, then fire, a swan and a diver bird teach him four quarters of Brahman (4.5-4.8).
up_chhandogya.309.core_teaching: The student accepts an unglamorous task and commits to it for years; his patient faithfulness prepares him for the teaching.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: The boy took the cows to a forest with grass, water and no dangers and stayed years until they became a thousand. Shankara says the story shows faith and austerity are needed for meditation on Brahman.

up_chhandogya.309.practical_reading: Long, patient work on something small and unpromising can be the real training; finish what you take on.
misreadings: Not a lesson that teachers should give pointless tasks
Not 'suffer silently'
not_for: someone exploited by a boss or institution who needs to hear about limits
speaks_to: caring for something fragile over years
long projects with no quick reward

up_chhandogya.326.context: Satyakama returns with the thousand cows, having been taught on the way by a bull, fire, a swan and a diver bird. His teacher sees his face shining like a knower of Brahman and asks who taught him. He says beings other than humans, but asks his teacher to teach him anyway, because knowledge learned from a teacher is best. The teacher teaches him the same, leaving nothing out. Satyakama later becomes a teacher himself (4.10).
up_chhandogya.326.core_teaching: Insight found on one's own is completed and confirmed by learning it from a teacher.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Satyakama had heard from sages that only knowledge learned from a teacher reaches its highest form, so he asks his own teacher, who expounds the same sixteen-part teaching the creatures gave, omitting nothing.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: The bull, fire, swan and diver bird were gods (Vayu, Agni, Brahma, Varuna) teaching casually, not as his acharya; that is why Satyakama still asks his own guru to teach him.

up_chhandogya.326.practical_reading: Even if you have learned a lot alone, go back to a mentor to test and complete it; good teachers confirm without competing.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of self-learning: what he learned was true and the teacher repeats it

up_chhandogya.368.context: 5.1 opens with praise of breath as eldest and best. The senses quarrel over who is greatest and ask their father Prajapati. He gives an indirect test: the one whose leaving makes the body worst off. Speech, eye, ear and mind each leave for a year and the body lives on; when breath begins to leave, it tears the others up like a horse pulling up its tethering pegs, and they concede (5.1.8-12).
up_chhandogya.368.core_teaching: The faculty everything depends on is the quiet one, breath; the showier ones can each be missed.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Prajapati, not wanting to hurt any of them, answers indirectly: the best is the one whose departure leaves the body worst, since a body without life is a corpse no one will touch.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: Breath here is Vayu, the best and oldest of the gods, who works all the senses from within though he chooses to act through them; one who knows him becomes best among equals.

up_chhandogya.368.practical_reading: In families and teams, the person whose absence would hurt most is often the least noisy; it is a gentle check on ego contests.
misreadings: Not a story ranking people's worth
cautions: The test imagery is the body without life (a corpse); light
speaks_to: ego clashes at work or home
feeling unnoticed while holding things together

up_chhandogya.391.context: Shvetaketu went to the assembly of King Pravahana Jaivali, who asked him five questions about where beings go after death; he could not answer one. He returns angry at his father for claiming to have taught him everything. The father admits he doesn't know either, and goes himself to the king to learn (5.3.6-7), who teaches the doctrine of the five fires.
up_chhandogya.391.core_teaching: A father admits openly to his son that he too does not know, and then goes to learn.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: The father tells his son to infer his father's ignorance from his own: had he known, why would he not have told his beloved son when his studies ended? Then he goes to the king.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: Introduces the section the story opens as the teaching of the five fires, which Madhva reads as five aspects of the Lord, taught so that people develop detachment.

up_chhandogya.391.practical_reading: Parents and teachers can say 'I don't know' without losing face, and model going to learn.
misreadings: Not a story about the father failing his son
cautions: The five questions concern where people go after death
speaks_to: parents facing questions they can't answer

up_chhandogya.393.context: The king receives Gautama with honour and offers a boon of human wealth. Gautama declines and asks for the words the king spoke to his son. The king is troubled, tells him to stay a long while, and says this knowledge had never before gone to a brahmin; it had stayed with the kshatriyas (5.3.7). He then teaches the five fires.
up_chhandogya.393.core_teaching: Offered wealth, the learned man asks only for knowledge, even from someone of lower ritual status.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: The king offers wealth such as land; Gautama tells him to keep it and asks for the questions put to his son. The king is perplexed, since a brahmin's request cannot be refused, and asks him to stay.

up_chhandogya.393.practical_reading: When you go to learn, don't be bought off with something easier; ask for what you came for.
misreadings: Not contempt for wealth in general
cautions: Status dynamics between brahmin and king; frame as humility across hierarchies
speaks_to: learning from someone 'below' you in status
staying focused on what you need

up_chhandogya.419.context: Five great householders and scholars, unable to settle what the Self and Brahman are, decide to ask Uddalaka about the Vaishvanara Self. He realises he cannot tell them all of it and sends them, with himself, to King Ashvapati Kaikeya. The king offers them gifts; they ask for the teaching instead (5.11.6).
up_chhandogya.419.core_teaching: A respected teacher knows the limits of his knowledge and points students to someone who knows more.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Uddalaka sees at once why they have come and thinks they will question him about Vaishvanara and he cannot tell them everything, so he decides to direct them to another teacher.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: The Vaishvanara knowledge that follows continues the teaching of the five fires as knowledge of the Supreme; 'great householders' means those who perform a great sacrifice yearly, 'great scholars' those who know the Vedas and their meaning.

up_chhandogya.419.practical_reading: Referring someone to a better expert is a mark of integrity, not weakness.

up_chhandogya.423.context: King Ashvapati offers the visitors as much wealth as he pays each priest at his sacrifice; when they decline, he assumes they see a fault in him and lists his kingdom's virtues. They reply that one should speak of the purpose one came for: the Vaishvanara Self. The king promises an answer in the morning, and they come back with fuel in hand as students.
up_chhandogya.423.core_teaching: State plainly what you came for, and don't be diverted by gifts.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: The scholars say it is the practice of good people to state the purpose of their visit; they seek knowledge of Vaishvanara, which the king knows, so let him teach it. He promises to answer in the morning.

up_chhandogya.423.practical_reading: In meetings and relationships, name what you actually came for instead of accepting a pleasant substitute.

up_chhandogya.455.context: 6.1.1: Uddalaka tells his son that no one in their family is a brahmin only by birth, and sends him to study. He returns at 24, full of himself. The father asks whether he learned the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard; the boy has never heard of it, and the father begins with clay, gold and iron: know one lump of clay and all clay things are known (6.1.4-6). This opens the 'tat tvam asi' chapter.
up_chhandogya.455.core_teaching: Years of study can leave someone proud but still missing the one understanding that makes everything else make sense.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Seeing his son so unlike himself, arrogant and conceited, the father asks about the teaching. The lesson: even having studied all the Vedas, until one knows the Self, life's main purpose is unfulfilled.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: Shvetaketu mastered the Vedas in twelve years and had all the conceit of a precocious youth; the father's question turns him to knowledge of Brahman.

up_chhandogya.455.practical_reading: After a degree or big success, notice any stiffness or superiority; real understanding tends to make people softer and more curious.
misreadings: Not anti-education: the father sent him to study
not_for: someone already crushed by self-doubt
speaks_to: parents of a proud teenager or young adult

up_chhandogya.489.context: Uddalaka teaches that a person has sixteen parts sustained by food. He tells Shvetaketu to fast for fifteen days, drinking only water; the boy then cannot recall the Vedas. After eating he can. The father explains with the ember: one part was left, and food made it blaze again.
up_chhandogya.489.core_teaching: Mind depends on nourishment; even when only a spark remains, it can be fed back to full strength.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: A firefly-sized ember left from a great fire, fed with grass, can burn more than before; one of the boy's sixteen parts remained and, fed by food, blazed up so he recalled the Vedas. Mind is nourished by food.

up_chhandogya.489.practical_reading: When you can't think clearly, look after the body first: food, rest and care can rekindle a mind that feels empty.
misreadings: Not a recommendation to fast for fifteen days
cautions: Involves a long fast; avoid presenting the experiment as advice, especially to readers with eating difficulties
not_for: someone with an eating disorder (fasting story)

up_chhandogya.492.context: 6.8 explains deep sleep: when a person sleeps, he has gone to his own (svam apīta), united with Being. The tethered bird illustrates it: the mind, tired of roaming in waking and dream, settles where it is tied. The section ends with the first 'tat tvam asi' (6.8.7).
up_chhandogya.492.core_teaching: The mind roams everywhere looking for rest and finds it only where it is anchored: in deep sleep it returns to its source.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: As a fowler's tethered bird flies every way and, finding no rest, settles at its tether, the mind, meaning the living self, roams through waking and dream and rests in Being (called prana here) in deep sleep.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: Deep sleep shows dependence: proud of independence while awake, a person is utterly helpless in dreamless sleep, which reveals the soul's dependence on the Lord.

up_chhandogya.492.practical_reading: Restlessness is the mind searching; rest comes from returning to what anchors you rather than from finding a new perch.
misreadings: Not 'thinking is bad'
'Breath' is not only physiology here

up_chhandogya.498.context: Closes the lesson on sleep, hunger, thirst and the root of the body. Having traced everything back to Being, Uddalaka states that this subtle essence is the self of all, and 'you are that'. Shvetaketu asks for more, and eight more illustrations follow (rivers, tree, seed, salt, Gandhara, the dying man, the heated axe), each ending with the same refrain.
up_chhandogya.498.core_teaching: The fine essence underlying everything is the true self of all, and of you.
up_chhandogya.498.practical_reading: Advaita teachers use it to say your deepest identity is not your role, body or story but the same reality as everything; Dvaita teachers use it as a lesson in humility before God.
misreadings: Not 'I am God' as ego-inflation (both schools reject that)
Not a single agreed meaning: the two major schools read it oppositely
cautions: Refrain 'tat tvam asi': Shankara reads identity of the self with Being; Madhva reads 'atat tvam asi', you are NOT that (the Lord). Present both when the refrain is used.
not_for: someone in a dissociative or depersonalised state who needs grounding

up_chhandogya.503.context: After the honey image (6.9: bees' nectar from many trees cannot tell which tree it came from), the rivers flow to the sea and lose their separate names. 6.10.2 applies it: creatures that come from Being do not know they came from it, and whatever they were here (tiger, lion, wolf, insect) they become again.
up_chhandogya.503.core_teaching: Distinct names and identities merge back into one source and do not keep their separateness there.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Rivers like the Ganga and Sindhu flow east and west, are lifted from the sea by clouds and fall as rain to flow back, and once one with the ocean do not know 'I am this river or that'.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: Rivers are conscious deities that cannot distinguish their own waters once in the sea; so souls entering the Lord, home of all, do not retain awareness of their lower personalities, while remaining distinct.

up_chhandogya.503.practical_reading: Used to ease the fear of losing oneself: differences of name and role belong to the journey, not to what we are at source.
misreadings: Not 'individuals don't matter'
cautions: Often used at funerals; for fresh grief, the loss of 'I am this river' can feel like the loss of the person
not_for: fresh grief where the mourner wants the person's individuality honoured

up_chhandogya.508.context: 6.11.1-2: strike a great tree at the root, middle or top and it bleeds sap but lives, pervaded by the living self; when life leaves a branch it dries. 6.11.3 applies it: the body dies when the living self leaves, the living self does not die. Refrain follows.
up_chhandogya.508.core_teaching: Death belongs to the body; the life that animated it does not die.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: The body perishes when separated from the living self, which itself does not perish: we finish work left unfinished before sleep, and newborns show desires from past impressions.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: In the tree there are two: the tree's own soul and the Lord as over-soul; the tree's dependence shows the soul is not the Lord. Madhva again reads the refrain as 'you are not that God'.

up_chhandogya.508.practical_reading: Offered as consolation that what made someone alive is not destroyed with the body.
misreadings: Not a reason to treat death or the body lightly
cautions: Directly about death; comforting to some mourners, dismissive to others in fresh grief
Advaita and Dvaita read the refrain oppositely (see 6.8.7)
not_for: very fresh grief where any 'they didn't really die' message jars
someone with suicidal thoughts

up_chhandogya.509.context: The fifth illustration. The son breaks open a banyan fruit, then a seed, and sees nothing. The father says from that unseen essence the great tree stands, and asks him to have faith. The refrain follows (6.12.3); next is the salt in water (6.13).
up_chhandogya.509.core_teaching: The visible and vast grows from what cannot be seen; grasping that needs trust as well as reasoning.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: From the invisible essence of the seed the huge banyan grows; so from subtle Being grows the world of names and forms. Faith is asked because even something proven by reason and scripture is hard to grasp when subtle.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: Rejects Shankara's reading that the seed is the material cause. The unseen 'animan' is the soul of the tree, invisible in the seed; likewise the Lord within the soul is not seen even by one who knows the soul.

up_chhandogya.509.practical_reading: Big outcomes come from small, invisible beginnings; trust the unseen work of patience, practice or a child's growth.
misreadings: 'Have faith' is not 'stop thinking': the lesson is reasoned and then trusted

up_chhandogya.512.context: The sixth illustration. Salt dissolved overnight cannot be seen or felt, yet every sip tastes of it. The father says Being is likewise present in this body though you don't perceive it. The refrain follows; next, the man from Gandhara (6.14) on how one comes to know it.
up_chhandogya.512.core_teaching: What is present everywhere may not be visible; it is known by another kind of contact.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Melted salt cannot be seen or touched yet is in the water and known by taste; so Being, root of the world, is right here in the body, unperceived by the senses but knowable by other means.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: Shankara's question 'why is Being not perceived?' makes no sense for Advaita, where Being is everything; the real question is why the Lord within the soul is not seen, as dissolved salt is not seen.

up_chhandogya.512.practical_reading: Something you can't point to can still flavour everything; used for presence of the sacred, and of love that isn't visible.
speaks_to: feeling God or meaning is absent

up_chhandogya.515.context: The seventh illustration answers how one comes to know Being. A man brought blindfolded from Gandhara and abandoned cries out; someone removes the blindfold and gives directions, and asking from village to village he gets home. So one with a teacher knows.
up_chhandogya.515.core_teaching: We are like travellers led away blindfolded; a compassionate teacher removes the blindfold and points the way, but we still walk it ourselves.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: A merciful person removes the blindfold and points north; asking village to village, the man reaches Gandhara, unlike one who is foolish or distracted by sights. The blindfold is delusion; the teacher points to one's own Being.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: Through the teacher the soul reaches the Lord, who is distinct from it yet within it.

up_chhandogya.515.practical_reading: When you feel lost, ask for directions and then keep asking along the way; a guide helps but you still do the walking.
misreadings: Not passive dependence on a guru
cautions: The verse speaks of delay 'until release' (death)
not_for: someone harmed by a controlling teacher

up_chhandogya.518.context: The eighth illustration. At a deathbed relatives ask 'do you know me?'; the person knows them until speech merges into mind, mind into breath, breath into heat, heat into Being. Then he does not know them (6.15.2). Shankara says the order is the same for knower and non-knower, but the knower does not return.
up_chhandogya.518.core_teaching: At death the faculties withdraw one into another until all returns to Being; the dying person stops recognising others not because they are lost, but because they are returning to the source.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Relatives ask the dying man 'do you know me?'; he knows them until his faculties merge in order into Being. The process is the same for all, but the knower stays in Being while the ignorant returns to birth.

up_chhandogya.518.practical_reading: Gives words to the experience at a deathbed when a loved one stops recognising us: something is withdrawing inward, not simply being lost.
misreadings: Not a medical description to apply to a specific patient
cautions: A vivid deathbed scene: very sensitive for anyone sitting with a dying relative or recently bereaved
Not suitable for readers facing a parent's dementia without care in framing
not_for: fresh grief
a reader whose relative is currently dying unless they ask
someone with suicidal thoughts
speaks_to: sitting with the dying (only if the reader seeks it)
later reflection on a death witnessed

up_chhandogya.521.context: The ninth and last illustration. A man accused of theft must grasp a heated axe; if guilty, covered in falsehood he is burned; if innocent, covered in truth he is not burned and is released. 6.16.3: just so, the one whose self rests in the true is not burned, and the refrain closes the chapter: Shvetaketu understood.
up_chhandogya.521.core_teaching: Truth protects and untruth burns; the one whose self rests in what is true is freed.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: The axe touches both men alike, yet the one given to untruth is burned and the one given to truth is released. So the knower, resting in Being, is not reborn; one resting in the unreal returns to birth.

up_chhandogya.521.practical_reading: Living truthfully gives a kind of protection under pressure; dishonesty makes every trial harder.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of trial by ordeal
Not a claim that innocent people never suffer
cautions: Trial by ordeal and punishment imagery; could wound someone falsely accused or punished
not_for: someone wrongly convicted or harmed despite innocence
speaks_to: being tempted to lie under pressure

up_chhandogya.526.context: Narada asks Sanatkumara to teach him; asked what he knows, he lists the four Vedas, the epics, grammar, mathematics, logic, ethics, astronomy, the arts and more (7.1.2). Then comes this confession. Sanatkumara tells him all of it is name, to be honoured as Brahman, and leads him step by step upward to the infinite (bhuma), where happiness lies.
up_chhandogya.526.core_teaching: Knowing a great deal doesn't remove sorrow; Narada admits his learning hasn't touched the self, asks for help, and that honest admission begins the teaching.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Narada knows only the words and rituals, not the self. His sorrow is the ache of not having fulfilled life's purpose. Even a sage needed a teacher; the story shows nothing but self-knowledge gives the highest good.

commentaries.who: Swami Lokeswarananda (Ramakrishna Mission), Chandogya Upanishad
commentaries.gist: Narada felt his scholarship was pointless without knowing the Self, like a donkey carrying sandalwood without enjoying its scent; with humility he asks to be taken across sorrow and helped to feel life's purpose fulfilled.

up_chhandogya.526.practical_reading: You can be accomplished and still feel empty, and saying so to someone wiser is the first step out. Narada, the most learned of all, did exactly that.
misreadings: Not anti-education; Sanatkumara honours each level as a step
Not 'your sadness means you're spiritually lacking'
cautions: Gentle and safe; the main risk is implying study was a waste for a reader who invested heavily in it
not_for: no strong contraindication

up_chhandogya.581.context: Sanatkumara leads Narada up a ladder: truth rests on understanding, understanding on thinking, thinking on faith, faith on steadfastness, steadfastness on action (kriti), action on happiness (7.22), happiness on the infinite (7.23).
up_chhandogya.581.core_teaching: Steady commitment comes only from doing; practice is what makes devotion firm.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Action here means restraining the senses and concentrating the mind; only when this is present do devotion and the other steps, up to true understanding, come about.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: Each step names a quality of the Lord: one who knows him as Creator (kriti) knows him as firm (nishtha), and so on up the ladder.

up_chhandogya.581.practical_reading: Waiting to feel committed before acting gets it backwards; acting steadily builds the commitment.
misreadings: Not busyness for its own sake: Shankara reads 'action' as inner discipline
not_for: someone exhausted who needs rest more than action

up_chhandogya.582.context: Sanatkumara is leading Narada up a ladder from name and speech through mind, will, thought, strength, food and so on. Just before: one serves only when one acts, and 'action' here, says Shankara, means restraining the senses and concentrating the mind (7.21). This verse: one acts only when one gets (expects) happiness. Next: the infinite alone is happiness; there is none in what is small (7.23).
up_chhandogya.582.core_teaching: People act only for some expected good, so the real question is what happiness actually is; the Upanishad's answer is that only the infinite, not anything limited, is happiness.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: One acts only once one has resolved that some good is to be gained; 'having obtained' really refers to the expected result. Lest anyone think the truth reveals itself automatically, the text adds that happiness must itself be investigated.

commentaries.who: Swami Lokeswarananda (Ramakrishna Mission), Chandogya Upanishad
commentaries.gist: Glosses it as: a person works when there is happiness in it and doesn't bother otherwise, so one must understand the true nature of that happiness. Links the preceding 'action' to disciplined practice.

up_chhandogya.582.practical_reading: If you can't get started, ask honestly what good you expect from the task. Often the block is that you don't see any. Finding the real reason it matters, not just forcing yourself, is what moves you.
misreadings: Not 'only do what feels fun'
Not a productivity hack; the passage is heading toward the infinite as the only real happiness
cautions: If paired with the next section (no happiness in the finite), it can sound dismissive of ordinary joys; frame gently
not_for: anhedonia from depression, where 'find the joy' can sound like blame

up_chhandogya.583.context: The summit of the ladder. Narada began (7.1) as a man who knew many texts but not the Self and was in sorrow. Sanatkumara now says happiness is only in the infinite. 7.24 defines it: where one sees, hears and knows nothing else.
up_chhandogya.583.core_teaching: Lasting happiness is not in any limited thing but only in the infinite.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: The finite always breeds longing for more, longing causes pain, and what causes pain is not happiness, like a fever. So there is no happiness in the small; the infinite alone, where nothing more is wanted, is happiness.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: Bhuma is a name of the Lord Vishnu, the highest in the ascending series of his attributes; the bliss described is his.

up_chhandogya.583.practical_reading: Notice how every small satisfaction points to wanting more; the verse invites looking for contentment in something that doesn't run out.
misreadings: Not a rejection of small joys as worthless
not_for: someone in depression who can't access small joys, if it reads as 'your happiness isn't real'

up_chhandogya.585.context: Narada asks what the infinite rests on. Sanatkumara says on its own greatness, or not even that. He explains: in the world, 'greatness' means owning cattle, gold, servants, wives, land and houses, one thing resting on another; he does not mean that. 7.25 then says the infinite is above, below, everywhere, and is oneself.
up_chhandogya.585.core_teaching: Worldly greatness always depends on possessions and other people; true greatness rests on nothing outside itself.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: A person like Caitra becomes 'great' by depending on cows, horses and the like; Sanatkumara denies that the infinite rests on anything other than itself in that way.

up_chhandogya.585.practical_reading: Worth that depends on what you own or whom you command is borrowed; ask what your worth rests on.
misreadings: Not contempt for family or property
cautions: Lists wives and slaves among possessions; flag the historical framing
speaks_to: identity tied to wealth or a job title
after a loss of status or property

up_chhandogya.612.context: 8.1-3 teach about the small space in the lotus of the heart, which contains all. 8.3.1-2 say our true desires are covered by untruth; that is why a dead relative cannot be seen. The buried treasure image follows. 8.3.3: this self is in the heart, and one who knows it goes daily to the heavenly world.
up_chhandogya.612.core_teaching: Every night in deep sleep we pass over the treasure of our own true self without finding it, because untruth, desire and ignorance carry us off.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Living and dead loved ones and all one longs for are found in the space of the heart. As people walk over buried gold unknowing, creatures enter Brahman daily in deep sleep and miss it, carried off by untruth.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: The soul's true desires already exist in it and become manifest in release; they are covered over by untruth, which is why they are not realised now.

up_chhandogya.612.practical_reading: What you seek may be closer than you think, buried under distraction; slowing down is a way of 'knowing the spot'.
misreadings: Not 'you will literally meet your dead relatives' (though the first half is often read consolingly)
cautions: The omitted first half speaks of dead relatives being 'found' there: potentially consoling in grief but also easily over-promised
not_for: fresh grief if it sounds like a promise of reunion
speaks_to: later stages of grief (with the first half)

data_flags.attribution_note: The narrator/Upanishad (Prajapati's teaching begins only at 8.7). Listed as 'Prajapati's teaching (narrator)'; better just 'narrator'.

up_chhandogya.639.context: Indra and Virochana lived 32 years with Prajapati, who told them the self is what is seen in the eye; they looked at their reflections in water, dressed up, and took the body to be the self. Virochana went home satisfied and taught the asuras body-worship; 8.8.5 says that is why people who don't give or believe are called asura and adorn their dead. Indra turns back with a doubt (8.9.1).
up_chhandogya.639.core_teaching: Settling for the body as the self is a half-truth that seems to work and satisfies quickly, and the Upanishad calls it the demons' doctrine.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Prajapati, seeing them leave without realising the Self, warns aloud that whoever follows this will come to grief, hoping they hear. Virochana, satisfied, preaches that the body alone is to be worshipped and served for both worlds.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: The reflection gets all the body's good and bad qualities, which should have shown it is not Brahman; Virochana's failure to see this shows his ineligibility, due to impurity of heart.

up_chhandogya.639.practical_reading: A warning against grooming, appearance and comfort as the whole of life; it asks whether we stopped at the first satisfying answer.
misreadings: Not a rejection of caring for the body
cautions: Can be used to shame people who care about appearance or fitness
not_for: someone with body-image or eating issues if it reads as shaming

up_chhandogya.641.context: Indra, on his way back to the gods, realises the reflection-self shares every condition of the body, including blindness, lameness and death, and sees no good in it. He returns to Prajapati with fuel in hand (8.9.2) and is told to stay another 32 years (8.9.3).
up_chhandogya.641.core_teaching: If you are only your body, you share all its losses and its death; seeing that clearly is the start of seeking further.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Indra, endowed with qualities like compassion, kept pondering the teaching on the way, and part of the water-pot lesson came back to him: if the reflection is the self, it must share the body's blindness and death too.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: Indra actually knew the truth and only acted out the doubt, going and returning repeatedly to mislead the asuras and the ignorant.
