up_chhandogya.641.practical_reading: A model of honest doubt: Indra doesn't settle for a comfortable answer but goes back and asks again.
misreadings: Not a claim that disabled bodies are lesser
cautions: Uses blindness and lameness as examples of loss; can hurt disabled readers
not_for: readers with disabilities if the framing is careless
someone newly injured or diagnosed

up_chhandogya.644.context: Indra returns with his doubt. Prajapati agrees, promises to explain the same self further, and asks him to live another 32 years as a student. Then he teaches the dream self (8.10), which Indra also questions; then the deep-sleep self (8.11); and finally the bodiless self (8.12).
up_chhandogya.644.core_teaching: The teacher affirms the student's doubt and asks for more time and preparation before going deeper.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Prajapati confirms Indra is right that the reflection is not the Self. Since Indra did not grasp what was clear to the faultless, some defect obstructs him, so he must live another 32 years as a student to remove it.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: The repeated returns were Indra's choice, made knowingly so that the asuras and the ignorant would think he had not yet understood.

up_chhandogya.644.practical_reading: Deep understanding takes time; a good teacher honours your questions and asks you to keep going rather than handing over a quick answer.
misreadings: Not that teachers should withhold for the sake of it
not_for: someone already exhausted by endless waiting

up_chhandogya.655.context: After 101 years Indra receives the final teaching. The body is mortal and the dwelling of the deathless, bodiless self. While identified with the body one is held by pleasure and pain; the bodiless is untouched. 8.12.2-3: as wind and clouds rise from space and take their own form, so the serene one rises from the body and appears in its own form.
up_chhandogya.655.core_teaching: The body is mortal and caught in pleasure and pain; the self that dwells in it is deathless and untouched by them.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: 'Held by death' means constantly seized by it, said to create detachment from the body. The body is the seat of the immortal self; embodiment is false identification, and when knowledge ends it, pleasure and pain do not touch.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu
commentaries.gist: The individual soul is always subject to pleasure and pain dependent on others, even in release it receives joy from God; only the bodiless Supreme Brahman is untouched, his bliss self-originated.

up_chhandogya.655.practical_reading: Pain and pleasure come with having a body; knowing that you are more than them can loosen their hold.
misreadings: Not a call to ignore pain or neglect health
Madhva reads 'bodiless' as God, not the individual
cautions: 'Held by death' is strong; for the terminally ill or bereaved, introduce gently
Can feel dismissive to someone in chronic pain
not_for: someone in acute physical pain or newly diagnosed
fresh grief
speaks_to: being tossed between highs and lows

up_chhandogya.663.context: This is the final verse of the Chhandogya, closing the eighth chapter's teaching on the self (Prajapati's instruction of Indra comes just before). Having taught that knowledge of the self is the goal, the text ends by sketching the whole life of a householder who reaches it: study at the teacher's house, return home, family, continued recitation, inward-gathered senses and non-harm, to the end of life.
up_chhandogya.663.core_teaching: An ordinary householder's life, lived with study, a clean and settled home, virtuous children, an inward-gathered mind and non-harm, is itself a path to the highest world. The commentators add that such a life done with knowledge bears exceptional fruit.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganath Jha
commentaries.gist: Ends the Upanishad by showing that ordinary duties done by a knower bring exceptional results. Serving the teacher outranks other duties; the harm exception means only scripturally ordained occasions; 'not returning' means staying in Brahma's world until it dissolves.

commentaries.who: Swami Lokeswarananda (Ramakrishna Order), drawing on Shankara
commentaries.gist: Reads it as a life plan: serve and learn from the teacher, marry, keep studying in a pure place, raise good children, check the senses, practise non-violence; the earlier chapters' worship purifies the mind for this.

commentaries.who: Max Müller's note (SBE 1)
commentaries.gist: Reports a commentator who says even a wandering mendicant causes some trouble to others, so begging is allowed only at sacred places; notes that others read the exception differently.

up_chhandogya.663.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a portrait of a steady, good life: keep learning after formal study ends, keep a clean and settled home, bring up children well, rein in the senses, and do as little harm as you can.
misreadings: Not a claim that only renunciants reach the goal; the verse is about a householder
The exception for 'sanctioned' harm is about Vedic ritual, not permission to hurt people when convenient
'Virtuous children' is not a reproach to people without children
cautions: The original is framed for a male twice-born student (teacher's house, Vedic study); widen it gently for a general reader
'Raise virtuous children' can sting for the childless or for parents estranged from their children
Ends on not returning (no rebirth), which may need framing for someone grieving
not_for: someone struggling with infertility or childlessness
someone whose home life is in crisis, who may hear it as a standard they are failing
speaks_to: building a settled, ordinary good life
new parents or newly-weds setting the tone of a home
people finishing formal education and wondering how to keep learning
wanting a simple daily ethic: study, restraint, non-harm

up_dakhsinamurti.26.context: The sages at a long sacrifice ask the ever-living Markandeya the secret of his long life and joy; he answers that it is knowledge of Shiva as Dakshinamurti, and gives the mantras and meditation forms. Asked again how that knowledge dawns, he gives this lamp image, then a second image of fire churned from two fire-sticks. The passage goes on to say Brahma himself gained his power to create by worshipping Dakshinamurti.
up_dakhsinamurti.26.core_teaching: Knowledge of the divine is not manufactured; when letting go, devotion and wakefulness are in place, it shines of itself in the dark, as a properly prepared lamp gives light.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1953)
commentaries.gist: The seeker should regard the innermost self as the lamp of knowledge. Its light appears of its own accord in delusion's darkness; Shiva's secret is like fire latent in the fire-sticks until churning brings it out.

commentaries.who: P. R. Ramachander's translation (surrounding text)
commentaries.gist: Places the lamp image right after the three Dakshinamurti mantras and meditation forms, and before the note that Brahma gained the power to create by worshipping Dakshinamurti.

up_dakhsinamurti.26.practical_reading: You cannot force insight, but you can prepare for it: loosen your grip on what you crave, give your heart to something higher, stay awake. Light then comes in its own time.
misreadings: Not 'just wait and enlightenment will happen'; the lamp has to be filled and the sticks rubbed
'Detachment' is not coldness toward people
cautions: Embedded in a mantra and ritual text for Shiva as Dakshinamurti; the surrounding verses are esoteric
not_for: someone in acute crisis who needs practical help now, not a long view of inner growth
speaks_to: feeling stuck in confusion or a dark season
people who practise and feel nothing is happening
devotional seekers wanting to know how devotion and understanding fit together

up_devi.15.context: Just before, the gods praise her as Speech, Lakshmi and Aditi, and give a coded form of her root mantra (verse 14). This verse names her as the Self's own power, holding noose, goad, bow and arrow, and promises that one who knows her crosses grief. Next the gods address her as Mother and ask her protection.
up_devi.15.core_teaching: The Goddess is the Self's own power and the great wisdom; knowing her in this way carries a person across sorrow.

commentaries.who: Wikipedia summary of the Upanishad (drawing on Warrier and on scholars such as Brooks and Coburn)
commentaries.gist: Treats verse 15 as an iconographic description: the Great Goddess carries noose, goad, bow and arrow and enchants all.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Renders her as the Self's power that enchants all, with the four emblems, and as the great and holy Science; the promise of crossing grief stands as its own short verse.

up_devi.15.practical_reading: Sorrow is crossed not by suppressing it but by knowing the power that lives in you as your own self; the verse points to that inner resource.
misreadings: 'Crosses beyond grief' is a direction of travel, not an order to stop grieving
'Enchants the world' does not mean she is a trickster to be feared
cautions: On a grief day, avoid implying that a person still grieving has not 'known' enough
not_for: very fresh bereavement, where 'crossing grief' may sound like being hurried
speaks_to: grief that needs a sense of inner strength
women and devotees who find strength in the Goddess as the Self's own power

up_devi.16.context: Right after the promise that whoever knows her crosses grief, the gods turn to her as Mother and ask protection on every side. The text then lists the whole Vedic pantheon and much more as her forms, ending in a salutation to her as time itself; the next verse praises her as remover of distress.
up_devi.16.core_teaching: The Mother who is asked for protection is the same power that appears as all the gods and forces of the world.

commentaries.who: Wikipedia summary of the Upanishad (drawing on Warrier and others)
commentaries.gist: Verse 18 venerates her as the Vasus, Rudras and Adityas, all gods, even demons and ghosts, the three gunas, the planets and time: everything that was, is and will be.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Gives the plea to the Mother for protection in every way as a short verse of its own, followed by the long list of her forms ending in a salutation.

up_devi.16.practical_reading: A simple prayer of trust: ask to be held on every side, while remembering that the forces around you are not foreign to that same Mother.
misreadings: A child's prayer for protection, not a promise that nothing will go wrong
cautions: The full verse also names demons and ghosts as her forms; if quoting more than our excerpt, explain the all-inclusive theology
not_for: someone who has just lost a loved one despite praying for protection
speaks_to: wanting the comfort of a mother-figure in prayer

up_devi.19.context: After the long list of her forms (the gods, the gunas, the planets, time), the devotee bows to her as the one who removes distress and gives both worldly enjoyment and freedom. The next verses give her seed mantra in coded form.
up_devi.19.core_teaching: The Goddess is praised as both comfort in this life and freedom beyond it, a refuge who removes distress.

commentaries.who: Wikipedia summary of the Upanishad
commentaries.gist: Verse 19 states that she is infinite, pure, Shiva, the refuge and the giver of what is good.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Renders her as banishing distress and granting pleasure and deliverance alike; the verse follows the salutation that closes the catalogue of her forms.

up_devi.19.practical_reading: In a painful stretch, a devotee can name what they need: relief now and freedom in the long run, and bow to the one they trust to give both.
misreadings: 'Takes away pain' is a devotee's praise, not a promise of a particular outcome; it does not replace care or treatment
Not a claim that worldly enjoyment is worthless; she gives both
cautions: Avoid implying that continued pain means weak devotion
not_for: someone in serious medical or mental-health crisis if presented as a substitute for help
speaks_to: people who want a short daily line of praise
holding worldly hopes and spiritual hopes together

up_devi.25.context: After the coded seed-mantra verses (20-23) and a meditation picture of the Goddess seated in the lotus of the heart, glowing like the dawn sun, with noose and goad and gestures of boon and fearlessness (24), the devotee bows to her as destroyer of great fear. The next verses explain why she is called unknowable, endless and one-yet-many.
up_devi.25.core_teaching: The Goddess is approached as compassion itself, the one who ends great fear and settles great difficulty.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Renders her as dispeller of the gravest fears, vanquisher of obstacles and wearer of great mercy's form, directly after the heart-lotus meditation image.

commentaries.who: Wikipedia summary of the Upanishad
commentaries.gist: Describes the preceding meditation (verses 20 and 24): seated in the lotus heart, glowing like the morning sun, with noose and goad, gestures dissolving fear, three-eyed and red-robed.

up_devi.25.practical_reading: When fear is large, picture compassion as a presence in your own heart and bow to it; let that steady you enough to take the next step.
misreadings: Praise of her compassion, not a promise that hardship will disappear; seek practical help too
not_for: someone angry at God after a loss, who may find praise language jarring
speaks_to: a crisis that feels too big
wanting a short prayer for courage

up_devi.29.context: Verses 26-27 explain her names: unknowable because even Brahma does not know her essence, endless, unborn, one and many, the source of all mantras and the witness of emptiness. This verse adds that nothing is beyond her, and explains the name Durga. The frightened devotee's bow follows at once.
up_devi.29.core_teaching: She is called Durga because she brings beings safely through what is hard to pass, and nothing stands above her.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Renders the line as: beyond her is nothing; she is renowned as the unapproachable; then joins it to the frightened devotee's bow to the one who steers across the sea of worldly life.

commentaries.who: NIOS lesson on the Durga Suktam
commentaries.gist: Presents Durga as the inner strength that lets a person overcome difficulties and face hard situations.

up_devi.29.practical_reading: Name the hard place you are in, and remember the tradition's promise: the one called Durga is the one who gets people through such places.
misreadings: Not a promise of escape from hardship; the image is of being carried through it
not_for: someone for whom the hard place ended in loss; 'rescue' may sound hollow
speaks_to: going through a hard passage (illness, job loss, exams, a move)
wanting to understand the name Durga

up_devi.30.context: Having explained that she is called Durga because she rescues from hardship, the Upanishad has the devotee, afraid of the round of worldly existence, bow to her as the pilot across its sea. Then come the benefits of reciting the text: release from sins and obstacles, recitation morning and evening, and its use in consecrating images.
up_devi.30.core_teaching: Fear of the endless round of existence becomes the very reason to turn to the Goddess, who carries the devotee across it.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Has the devotee, afraid of life, bow to the inaccessible one who guards against sin and pilots him across the sea of worldly existence; the recitation benefits follow.

commentaries.who: Wikipedia summary of the Upanishad
commentaries.gist: Summarises verses 26-28: she is unknowable, endless, the source of all mantras, with nothing beyond her, and is the pilot of worldly life.

up_devi.30.practical_reading: When the whole cycle of striving, loss and starting again feels frightening, a devotee can admit that fear honestly and hand it over in a bow.
misreadings: 'Afraid of worldly life' is spiritual weariness with samsara, not a wish to stop living
cautions: Present 'bhava-bhita' carefully: do not use it with a reader who has expressed hopelessness about living; avoid phrasing like 'frightened by life'
not_for: anyone expressing suicidal feelings or hopelessness, where 'afraid of life' could be heard as agreement
speaks_to: wanting to surrender a burden in prayer

up_devi.9.context: The gods ask the Goddess who she is; she answers that she is Brahman, the source of nature and spirit, the five elements and all the gods. The gods then bow to her as Shiva, Prakriti and the great Goddess, and this verse is their act of taking refuge, borrowed from the Vedic Durga Suktam. Hymns to her as Speech, Lakshmi and Aditi follow.
up_devi.9.core_teaching: The worshipper takes refuge in Durga, the radiant power behind all action, trusting her to dispel darkness.

commentaries.who: Swami Vimalananda's gloss on the Durga Suktam (quoted on the Advaita-l list)
commentaries.gist: Vairochani is the Supreme's own power shining in many forms; she lives in actions and their results and makes them effective, or is the power people call on so their work bears fruit.

commentaries.who: NIOS (National Institute of Open Schooling) lesson on the Durga Suktam
commentaries.gist: Presents Durga as the power residing in actions and their results, the inner strength that helps a person face and get through hard situations.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Places the verse just after the gods salute her as Shiva and as blessed Prakriti, and renders its close as a plea to the hard-to-reach one to dispel the gloom.

up_devi.9.practical_reading: When a task or a season feels too dark to face, turn to the source of strength behind your effort and ask for the courage to go through it.
misreadings: Taking refuge is not a guarantee that hardship will vanish
Not a call to give up effort; the verse links her to action and its fruit
cautions: Explicitly devotional; for a reader outside the Shakta tradition, frame it as a prayer they may borrow, not a claim they must accept
not_for: someone who feels abandoned by God in grief, who may hear 'she dispels darkness' as a broken promise
speaks_to: feeling surrounded by darkness or confusion
wanting to pray when words are hard to find
devotees of the Goddess around Navaratri

up_isha.1.context: The opening verse of the Isha, an 18-verse Upanishad that closes the White Yajurveda Samhita. It sets the theme that the Lord pervades everything; the next verse speaks to those who want to live out a full life of work, and verses 6-7 return to seeing the self in all.
up_isha.1.core_teaching: Because everything belongs to the Lord, one should hold things without grasping and not covet wealth; the schools differ on whether this means renunciation or contented use of what is given.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: Cover the world with the thought that the Self is all. Such a knower renounces desires for son and wealth; 'bhunjitha' means protect yourself by that renunciation. Covet no one's wealth, since nothing really belongs to anyone.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: All movement in nature is caused by the indwelling Lord, so everything is His. Enjoy what He has allotted you and do not go begging from the rich, even a king; ask the Lord alone.

up_isha.1.practical_reading: Treat what you have as entrusted, not owned: enjoy it, share it, and stop measuring yourself against other people's wealth.
misreadings: Not a call to neglect your finances; it is about how you hold what you have
Not a license for indulgence; 'enjoy' is tied to letting go
cautions: For someone in poverty, 'do not covet' can sound like being told to accept injustice; stress the inner freedom, not resignation
not_for: someone in real financial distress who needs practical help, if framed as 'just let go'
speaks_to: starting a new financial chapter (job, inheritance)

up_isha.15.context: After verses on knowledge and ignorance and on the manifest and unmanifest, the Upanishad turns to prayer. This verse asks Pushan, the nourishing Sun, to uncover the face of Truth hidden by a golden lid. Verse 16 continues the address to the Sun ('the person there, I am he'), and 17-18 are the final prayers at death.
up_isha.15.core_teaching: The dazzle of what shines hides the truth behind it; the seeker asks for that covering to be lifted so the real can be seen.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: The prayer of one who did his duties and worshipped Brahman in the sun, asking at death for the way to it. The 'True' is Brahman in the solar orb; the golden lid covers its entrance.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: The golden disc is the solar orb that hides the body of Vishnu, the True. Pushan, the full Lord, reveals that form himself to devotees who love the True.

up_isha.15.practical_reading: Teachers often apply it to the 'golden lids' in our lives (success, money, approval) that are attractive enough to stop us looking further, and to the honest wish to see things as they are.
misreadings: The modern 'gold hides truth' reading is an application; the commentators read the golden lid as the sun's disc
cautions: Traditionally a deathbed prayer; if used with someone facing death, it can be moving, but say so gently
not_for: someone in fresh grief if the deathbed framing is foregrounded without care
speaks_to: wanting clarity in a confusing situation
being dazzled by success or status

up_isha.18.context: The Isha ends with the prayers of one about to die: verse 17 asks breath to return to the immortal wind and the body to end in ashes, and asks the mind to remember its deeds. Verse 18 asks Agni, who knows every path and every deed, to lead by the good road and keep sin away, and offers many salutations.
up_isha.18.core_teaching: A prayer to be guided by the straight path, kept from crookedness, and led toward the highest good, by a divine guide who knows all one's ways.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: The dying worshipper asks for the good road, the northern path, not the southern one of coming and going, to the fruits of his deeds; asks that deceitful sin be removed; and, unable to serve further, offers many salutations.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: Agni is Hari, leader of the universe. The prayer asks to be led by the path of no return to the treasure of liberation, and that Hari, who knows our efforts, remove the sin binding us to rebirth.

up_isha.18.practical_reading: A morning or bedtime prayer: ask to be led by the straight way today, to have crookedness kept from you, and offer thanks.
misreadings: 'Wealth' is not material riches in either commentary
cautions: The setting is a deathbed prayer; for a general daily reading the guidance theme works, but don't hide the context
not_for: someone newly bereaved if the deathbed context is foregrounded without care
speaks_to: facing a decision and wanting guidance
starting a journey or new venture

up_isha.2.context: Verse 1 says everything is pervaded by the Lord: enjoy by letting go and covet no one's wealth. Verse 2 speaks to those who want to live out a full life. Verse 3 warns that those who destroy their own self go to sunless worlds.
up_isha.2.core_teaching: A full life of work is compatible with inner freedom if action is done in the right spirit. The commentators differ on what that spirit is.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), S. Sitarama Sastri tr.
commentaries.gist: Verse 1 is for those able to renounce. This verse is for those who want a full life and cannot renounce: for them, doing the enjoined rites is the only way bad karma won't stick. Renunciation remains the higher path.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), Srisa Chandra Vasu tr. 1909
commentaries.gist: 'Doing' means acting without desire for results while worshipping the Lord. Neglecting this is a fault even for the wise, so everyone should keep working. Verse 1 teaches detachment; verse 2 adds that action must go with it.

up_isha.2.practical_reading: Keep doing your work wholeheartedly, for a long life, but loosen your grip on outcomes so the work does not stick to you.
misreadings: Not a call to overwork
Not a promise of a long life
Shankara does not treat this as the highest path; don't present it as the Upanishad's last word on action versus renunciation
cautions: On a 'running on empty' action day, frame it as working without clinging, not 'keep pushing'
'A hundred years' may sting for someone seriously ill
not_for: a reader facing terminal illness

up_isha.6.context: Verses 4-5 describe the self as unmoving yet swifter than mind, far and near, within and outside everything. Verse 6 draws the consequence for how one sees others, and verse 7 adds that for such a seer there is no delusion or grief.
up_isha.6.core_teaching: Seeing the one self in all beings removes the sense of 'other' that breeds aversion and fear.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: Addressed to the renunciant seeking freedom. Revulsion arises only when one sees something bad as separate from oneself; one who sees the pure self everywhere has nothing left to recoil from.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: The Self here is the Supreme Lord, support and inner ruler of all beings, not the individual soul. Knowing that all power is His, the devotee becomes fearless and stops anxiously protecting himself.

up_isha.6.practical_reading: When someone repels or frightens you, pause and look for what you share with them; the recoil often eases when they stop being wholly 'other'.
misreadings: Not a demand to tolerate abuse or to stay close to people who harm you
Not a claim that all behaviour is equally acceptable
cautions: For someone hurt by another person, do not use it to imply they should stop feeling aversion to the one who hurt them
not_for: survivors of abuse or violence, where 'see yourself in the abuser' would land badly
speaks_to: caregivers struggling with a patient's illness or ageing body

up_isha.7.context: Continues verse 6. Having said that the one who sees the self in all feels no aversion, the Upanishad asks rhetorically what delusion or grief can remain for one who sees oneness. Verse 8 then describes the self as radiant, bodiless and pure.
up_isha.7.core_teaching: Grief and confusion rest on ignorance of oneness; for the one who truly sees it, they have no ground.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: Delusion and grief are the seeds of desire and action and belong to the ignorant; for one who sees the self as one and pure like space, the whole cycle is uprooted with its seed.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: The Lord in whom all beings rest has always dwelt within them. One who knows this, and sees Vishnu everywhere as one, has no delusion or sorrow because he knows the truth.

up_isha.7.practical_reading: In a moment of confusion or sorrow, widen the frame: you are not alone and not separate. Teachers use the verse to loosen isolation, not to forbid feeling.
misreadings: Not an instruction that a wise person should not grieve, or that grief shows a lack of wisdom
Describes the end state of realisation, not a test to pass today
cautions: Asks 'what sorrow can there be?' and so can sound dismissive of fresh grief; do not use on Day 1 of a grief plan or for a recent loss
not_for: fresh bereavement
someone ashamed that they are still grieving
speaks_to: readers drawn to Vedanta's big picture

up_kath.1.1.11.context: Nachiketa has waited three nights at Death's house without food; Yama, returning, offers three boons in amends. Nachiketa's first wish (1.1.10) is that his father be calm, free of anger toward him, and welcome him back. Yama grants it in this verse; the second boon will be the fire ritual, the third the question about death.
up_kath.1.1.11.core_teaching: The first thing Nachiketa asks of Death is not for himself but for peace with his father, and Death grants it: the father's anger will pass and his love return.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: By Death's permission your father will feel toward you as affectionately as before, trust you, sleep peacefully the rest of his nights, and lose his anger on seeing you released from Death's jaws.

commentaries.who: Madhva tradition, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: Your father will love you as before; sent back by me, you will be recognised like someone returning from another city, and Uddalaka's son, freed of anger, will see you released from death. The boon includes forgiveness of Nachiketa's faults.

up_kath.1.1.11.practical_reading: Repair with family can come first, even before your own ambitions. Ask for peace in the relationship, and trust that anger can soften.
misreadings: Not a promise that every estranged parent will relent
cautions: Can be painful for someone whose parent died unreconciled
not_for: someone whose parent died before they could reconcile
victims of abusive parents, if read as 'go back and make peace'
speaks_to: a parent and child after a fight
wanting a relative's anger to cool

up_kath.1.1.4.context: Vajashravasa, wanting heaven, performs a sacrifice in which he gives away all he owns, but the cows are old and spent. His young son Nachiketa, filled with faith (shraddha), sees that such gifts bring no merit. He asks to whom he himself will be given; on the third asking, the father snaps that he gives him to Death.
up_kath.1.1.4.core_teaching: A son's persistent, dutiful question exposes the emptiness of a hollow gift, and provokes an angry word that sets the whole teaching in motion.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: As a good son should, Nachiketa wanted to avert the harm a defective sacrifice would bring his father, even by offering himself to complete it. Ignored, he asked again; the father, irritated that a boy should speak so, cursed him.

commentaries.who: Madhva tradition (Gati-Sara, quoted in Madhva's bhashya), tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: The boy told his father that decrepit cows should never be given and that he should rather give his son to a priest. Hearing this, the father cursed him; another Katha recension spells the curse out in detail.

up_kath.1.1.4.practical_reading: Children often see through adult gestures; the story invites parents to hear an awkward question as care, not cheek, and to watch what they say in anger.
misreadings: Not a story of a child's rebellion; both commentators read Nachiketa's question as dutiful concern for his father
Not an endorsement of the father's anger
cautions: A parent 'giving a child to Death' is stark; take care with readers estranged from a parent or who heard cruel words from one
Mentions death directly
not_for: someone who has lost a child
a reader who suffered parental abuse
speaks_to: a young person who sees hypocrisy in elders
parents who said something harsh in anger

up_kath.1.1.5.context: Just after his father, in anger, says 'To Death I give you', Nachiketa reflects. He is not the worst of sons or pupils, yet his father has said this. Concluding that the words, though spoken in anger, must not be made false, he goes on (next verse) to comfort his regretful father and urge him to keep his word.
up_kath.1.1.5.core_teaching: Even when wronged by an angry word, Nachiketa examines himself calmly and chooses to honour his father's truthfulness.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: Among sons or pupils I am first or middling, never the worst, yet father gives me to Death. What could Death do with me? Clearly he spoke in anger, but his word must not be falsified.

commentaries.who: Madhva tradition, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: Renders the second line as: what object of Yama's will he accomplish through me today? Madhva adds no separate comment on this verse.

up_kath.1.1.5.practical_reading: When someone you love says something hurtful, you can take stock of yourself honestly, neither crushed nor defiant, and decide how to respond with integrity.
misreadings: Not boasting or defiance of death; the commentators read it as sober reflection
cautions: Speaks of being sent to Death
not_for: a reader with suicidal thoughts if 'going to Death' is presented as brave
speaks_to: being unfairly treated by a parent or boss

up_kath.1.1.6.context: Nachiketa's father, regretting his angry words, is grieving. Nachiketa urges him to keep his word, as their ancestors and good people always have, because life is short and falsehood gains nothing. He then goes to Yama's house, where Death is away for three nights.
up_kath.1.1.6.core_teaching: Because life is brief and passes like a crop, there is nothing to be gained by breaking one's word; keep faith with the truth.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: Recall how your father and grandfather acted, and how good people act now: none of them broke his word. Since mortals decay and are reborn like corn, falsehood gains nothing; keep your truth and send me to Death.

commentaries.who: Madhva tradition, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: Reads it as a reflection on mortality: look at those who died before me and those now dying who will follow, and learn that a person ripens and dies like corn and is born again like corn.

up_kath.1.1.6.practical_reading: Life is short; don't trade your integrity for a moment's relief. A promise kept, even a hard one, is worth more than an easy way out.
misreadings: Not a counsel of fatalism; in Shankara's reading it is an argument for keeping one's word
cautions: Rebirth imagery ('born again like grain') can feel dismissive to someone freshly bereaved
Mentions death
not_for: fresh grief, if used as 'everyone dies like grain'
speaks_to: perspective on how short life is

data_flags.translation_note: The words are rendered literally, but our translation and line lose the point Shankara draws: look at how our forefathers acted and how good people act now (none broke his word); since a mortal ripens and falls like grain, what is gained by falsehood? So...

up_kath.1.2.2.context: Nachiketa has refused Yama's offers of wealth, long life and pleasures and insisted on knowing what happens after death. Yama now begins to teach: the good and the pleasant are two different things that pull a person different ways; whoever takes the good fares well, whoever chooses the pleasant misses the goal (1.2.1). After this verse he praises Nachiketa for rejecting 'the chain of wealth' in which many sink.
up_kath.1.2.2.core_teaching: The good and the pleasant come to everyone mixed together; the wise person examines and separates them and chooses the good, while the careless grab the pleasant for gain and security.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: They arrive mixed and hard to tell apart; the wise sift them like a swan separating milk from water and choose the good; the dull take the pleasant (cattle, children) to sustain the body.

commentaries.who: Madhva tradition, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: Renders it: the good and the pleasant reach a soul through past causes; the wise examine and choose the good, while the ordinary person chooses pleasant objects and their acquisition and preservation.

up_kath.1.2.2.practical_reading: When you want more, pause and ask whether this is good for you or just pleasant right now. Both feel similar in the moment; the work is telling them apart.
misreadings: Not 'pleasure is bad'; it ranks the two, it doesn't condemn enjoyment
'Getting and keeping' isn't a ban on financial security
cautions: Calls the other chooser 'manda' (dull, foolish); avoid labelling the reader
not_for: someone in poverty for whom 'getting and keeping' is survival

up_kath.1.2.22.context: Yama is describing the self to Nachiketa: smaller than the small and greater than the great, seated far yet going everywhere (1.2.20-21). This verse draws the consequence for grief. The next verse says this self is not won by study or cleverness.
up_kath.1.2.22.core_teaching: The self is unchanging and all-pervading within changing bodies; knowing oneself as that removes the ground of grief.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: The self is bodiless like space yet present in the passing bodies of gods, ancestors and humans; it is unchanging and all-pervading. Knowing it as 'I am he', the wise have no occasion to grieve.

commentaries.who: Madhva tradition, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: Renders it: the wise, knowing that Self as resting unembodied in changing bodies, great and all-pervading, becomes fully liberated. Madhva reads the Self here as the Supreme Lord.

up_kath.1.2.22.practical_reading: When everything around you is shifting, look for what in you is steady and watching; teachers use this to steady anxiety, not to forbid sadness.
misreadings: Not a rule that a wise person must not grieve, or that grief shows ignorance
Not a dismissal of the body's importance
cautions: 'The wise do not grieve' can feel dismissive to a grieving reader; avoid on early grief days
not_for: fresh bereavement
someone told to 'stop grieving'
speaks_to: illness or ageing of one's own body
seekers wanting the core Vedanta teaching

up_kath.1.2.23.context: Having described the self and said the wise do not grieve, Yama explains how it is (and is not) attained: not by lectures, intelligence or much learning. The next verse adds the moral and mental conditions.
up_kath.1.2.23.core_teaching: The self is not a prize of scholarship; it opens to the one who wholly turns to it (Shankara) or whom the Lord chooses by grace (Madhva).

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: Hard to know, the self is still knowable by right means: not study, memory or learning. One who seeks the self alone, free of desire, attains it by the self, and it reveals its nature to him.

commentaries.who: Madhva tradition, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: The Lord is obtained by the one He elects; His grace comes not through scholarship or memory but through devotion, wholly by His will. Calm and self-control (next verse) are the means by which grace falls.

up_kath.1.2.23.practical_reading: You cannot think or read your way to the deepest things; what is needed is sincere longing and openness. Keep studying, but don't mistake information for transformation.
misreadings: Not anti-learning; the commentators reject learning as sufficient, not as useful
Grace reading is not favouritism: Madhva ties it to devotion and discipline
cautions: 'The one it chooses' can sound exclusionary to someone who feels spiritually unworthy
not_for: someone who already feels rejected by God, if 'chosen' is stressed
speaks_to: people who feel they 'know a lot' but feel nothing

up_kath.1.2.24.context: Follows the verse that says the self is not won by learning. Here Yama names what is required: turning from wrongdoing, calm senses, a collected mind and a mind at rest. The next verse asks who can know where this self dwells, for whom priests and warriors are food and death a sauce.
up_kath.1.2.24.core_teaching: Understanding of the self requires a changed life: turning from wrongdoing and calming and gathering the mind.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: One who has not turned from forbidden acts, whose senses are active, mind scattered, or mind restless even for the fruit of concentration cannot attain it. Only one with all four, taught by a teacher, attains the self by knowledge.

commentaries.who: Madhva tradition, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: If the Lord is seen only by grace, why practise? Because knowledge is needed to win that grace: one who has ceased from evil and is controlled and concentrated obtains Him; grace naturally falls on such a person.

up_kath.1.2.24.practical_reading: Insight follows character. Before chasing more knowledge, stop the habits you know are wrong and give your mind some quiet.
misreadings: Not a claim that a person who has done wrong can never change; it describes the turning needed
cautions: Could feed shame in someone already self-critical
not_for: someone struggling with addiction who is already full of self-blame, without a supportive frame
speaks_to: people who read a lot but stay restless
wanting a practical first step in spiritual life

up_kath.1.3.14.context: Closes the chariot section. After the ladder from senses to the highest self and the instruction to merge speech into mind and mind into the self (1.3.13), the Upanishad calls everyone to rise and seek teachers, warning that the path is as hard as a razor's edge. The next verses describe the self beyond sound and touch.
up_kath.1.3.14.core_teaching: Wake up from the sleep of ignorance and seek out those who know; the way is real but demanding.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: Arise: turn toward self-knowledge; awake: end ignorance's sleep, the seed of all misery. Learn from excellent teachers. The Shruti speaks like a mother from compassion; the path is razor-sharp because what is to be known is so subtle.

commentaries.who: Madhva tradition, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: Renders it: awake, arise, approach the great teachers and learn; the sages say the road is hard to travel and crossing samsara is as difficult as a razor's edge.

up_kath.1.3.14.practical_reading: Stop drifting; find good teachers or mentors and commit, knowing the road will ask for care and effort.
misreadings: Not a call to frantic activity; the waking is inner
'Razor's edge' is about care, not danger to the reader
not_for: someone exhausted or burnt out who needs rest, not a summons
speaks_to: starting a demanding course of study
young people needing a call to purpose
after a setback, getting back up

up_kath.1.3.3.context: The third valli opens with two selves in the cave of the heart and the Nachiketa fire as a bridge. Yama then gives the chariot image (1.3.3-4), develops it with good and bad horses (1.3.5-9), lists the ascending order of senses, objects, mind, intellect and the great self (1.3.10-11), and ends with the call to arise and awake (1.3.14).
up_kath.1.3.3.core_teaching: A person is like a chariot: the self rides, the intellect drives, the mind holds the reins and the senses pull toward their objects. The journey depends on the driver's discernment.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: The image is for the self caught in worldly life, able to travel toward freedom. The intellect guides like a driver; the mind, willing and doubting, holds the senses like reins. Only the conditioned self is the 'enjoyer'.

commentaries.who: Madhva tradition, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: Renders the rider as the individual soul (jiva) seated in the chariot, and reads 'the enjoyer' or sufferer as the soul joined with senses and mind but without buddhi.

up_kath.1.3.3.practical_reading: Notice who is driving today: your considered judgment, or whichever sense or craving pulls hardest. Strengthen the driver, keep the reins in hand.
misreadings: Not a teaching that the body or senses are bad; they are the chariot and horses, needed for the journey
not_for: someone with a disability or chronic illness if 'the body is just a vehicle' is pressed too hard
speaks_to: students and young adults building discipline

up_kath.1.3.5.context: Continues the chariot image. After naming the parts, Yama contrasts the driver who lacks discernment, whose horses bolt, with the one who has it, whose horses obey. Verses 7-9 add where each ends up: the first keeps returning to worldly life, the second reaches the goal, Vishnu's highest place.
up_kath.1.3.5.core_teaching: Without discernment and a disciplined mind the senses run wild; with them, the same senses become willing servants.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: When the intellect-driver cannot tell what to do or avoid and the mind-reins are slack, the sense-horses become unruly; when the driver discerns and holds the reins firmly, they can be let go or stopped at will.

commentaries.who: Madhva tradition, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: These two verses show that controlling the senses lets the mind be controlled; control of thought is an indirect means to liberation.

up_kath.1.3.5.practical_reading: Training beats force: build small daily habits of attention so that the senses learn to follow your judgment.
misreadings: Not a call to suppress all pleasure; good horses still run
cautions: Avoid shaming language ('vicious') about a reader's own impulses
not_for: someone with ADHD or compulsive disorders if framed as pure willpower

up_kath.2.1.1.context: Opens the second chapter. Having said the self is seen only by a subtle intellect, Yama now explains why it is usually missed: the senses are built to face outward. The next verse adds the second obstacle, desire for outward things.
up_kath.2.1.1.core_teaching: Our senses naturally turn outward, so we miss what is within; a rare person who longs for the deathless turns the gaze back and sees the self.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: This valli names the obstacle to seeing the self: the senses go out to their objects by nature. A rare discerning person, wanting immortality, turns them back like reversing a river's current and sees the inner self.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: Vyatrinat means 'subdued': the Lord himself checks the outflowing senses and turns them inward when he wills a person to see him; so the devoted sage sees the God within.

up_kath.2.1.1.practical_reading: It is not a personal failing that your attention flies outward; that is how we are made. Build moments that turn it back: a pause, a breath, a question about what is watching.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of the senses or of the outer world
not_for: someone in a dissociative or depressive state, if 'withdraw the senses' is pressed

up_kath.2.1.2.context: Follows the verse on outward-facing senses. Shankara: the second obstacle is desire for outward pleasures. Those who chase them walk into death's net; the wise, knowing the sure immortality within, do not seek the permanent among impermanent things. The next verses say that by which one knows form, taste and the rest is this self.
up_kath.2.1.2.core_teaching: Running after outward pleasures traps us in the cycle of loss and death; the wise stop looking for lasting security in things that cannot last.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: Desire for outward enjoyments, here or hereafter, is the second obstacle. Pursuing them, people fall into death's net (ignorance, desire, action) and its misery. Knowers of Brahman covet nothing here, rising above desire for sons, wealth and worlds.

commentaries.who: Madhva tradition, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: Renders it: men of small understanding go after outward desires and fall into Yama's wide noose; the self-controlled, knowing liberation, do not seek the permanent in the unstable.

up_kath.2.1.2.practical_reading: Notice where you are trying to buy permanence with impermanent things: status, possessions, someone's approval. Enjoy them, but rest your security elsewhere.
misreadings: Not a ban on enjoying life
'Childish' is the text's word, not a label for the reader
cautions: Mentions death
not_for: someone in grief over a lost person, where 'do not seek the lasting in what passes' may sound cold
speaks_to: disillusionment after getting what you wanted

up_kath.2.2.11.context: Yama has given images of the one self entering all forms, like fire and air taking the shape of what they enter (2.2.9-10). This verse answers the worry that if the self is in everything it must suffer everything. The following verses say the eternal joy belongs to the wise who see it within.
up_kath.2.2.11.core_teaching: The one self in all beings is not touched by the world's suffering, as the sun that lights every sight is not soiled by what it shows.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: The sun reveals even filth yet is not soiled. Likewise the self is untouched by the world's misery, which comes from ignorance superimposing action and agency on it, as a snake is imagined on a rope.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu, citing the Kurma Purana
commentaries.gist: As the sun-deity is the inner eye, untouched by defects of the physical eye, so the Lord, independent and separate from all souls, is not touched by their sorrows; the soul is his dependent reflection.

up_kath.2.2.11.practical_reading: There is a place in you that witnesses pain without being destroyed by it. Teachers use this to give a sufferer somewhere to stand, not to deny the pain.
misreadings: Not 'suffering is unreal, so ignore it' or 'others' pain is not your concern'
Not an argument against compassion
cautions: 'Untouched by the world's sorrow' can sound uncaring to someone in pain; frame as inner refuge
not_for: someone in acute grief, if read as 'your true self does not feel this'
speaks_to: caregivers and helping professionals at risk of burnout
people overwhelmed by news of suffering
wanting an inner refuge in pain

up_kath.2.2.15.context: Closes the fifth valli. Nachiketa has asked how that supreme bliss, indescribable, can be known: does it shine by itself or not (2.2.14)? Yama answers that it is the light by which all lights shine. The sixth valli then opens with the image of the eternal fig tree with roots above.
up_kath.2.2.15.core_teaching: The self or Brahman is the light behind all lights; nothing illumines it, and everything shines by it.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: Sun, moon, stars, lightning and fire cannot illumine Brahman, their own self. They shine after it, as hot water or a firebrand burns by fire's heat. That they shine at all shows Brahman is self-luminous.

commentaries.who: Madhva tradition, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: Renders it as 'that Form' which sun, moon, stars, lightning and fire do not reveal; when He shines, all is lit after Him, and by His light all this becomes bright.

up_kath.2.2.15.practical_reading: On a dark day, remember that awareness itself is what lets you see anything at all, including the darkness. It is used in prayer and meditation as a reminder of a light that does not go out.
misreadings: Not a statement about astronomy
Not a rejection of the natural world's beauty
speaks_to: feeling that one's inner light has gone out

up_kath.2.3.15.context: Near the end of Yama's teaching: the previous verse says when all desires lodged in the heart fall away, the mortal becomes immortal and attains Brahman here. This verse restates it as the cutting of the heart's knots. The next verse speaks of the 101 channels of the heart and the one that leads upward at death.
up_kath.2.3.15.core_teaching: Freedom is the undoing, here and now, of the knots of false identification and desire that bind the heart; that is the whole teaching.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: The knots are ignorance-born convictions like 'I am this body', 'this wealth is mine', 'I am happy or miserable'. When knowledge of oneness with Brahman destroys them, their desires die and the mortal becomes immortal while alive.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: When a person is wholly freed from the bonds of false knowledge he attains immortality; all the scriptures' instructions aim at this.

up_kath.2.3.15.practical_reading: Name one knot you carry, a fixed idea of who you are or what you must own, and loosen it a little today. Freedom is found in this life, not only after it.
misreadings: 'Becomes immortal' is not about the body not dying
cautions: The next verse is about the soul's exit at death; quote this verse on its own
speaks_to: feeling knotted up or stuck in old patterns
letting go of a rigid self-image
seekers wanting the heart of the Upanishads in one line

up_katharudra.17.context: The text lays down the rite of renunciation: the man settles his sons, performs farewell rites, discards sacred thread and possessions, and wanders, living on alms. Verses 5-7 list the few things he gives up and where he may sleep; this verse gives inner rules on comfort, praise and blame; the next verses turn to celibacy and then to the self as light and bliss.
up_katharudra.17.core_teaching: Keep to the middle with the body, neither pampering nor punishing it, and stay even under praise and blame.

commentaries.who: A. A. Ramanathan's translation (Adyar), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Places the verse among the renunciant's rules, just after where he may bathe and sleep (river sands, temples) and just before celibacy; renders it as avoiding extremes of comfort and hardship and staying unmoved by praise or blame.

up_katharudra.17.practical_reading: Look after your body without indulging or punishing it, and when praised or criticised, don't let either knock you off balance or make you lash out.
misreadings: Not a call to ignore real criticism; it is about not retaliating
Not an endorsement of harsh asceticism; it warns against it
cautions: The surrounding text (verse 3) lists ritual starvation, drowning or entering fire among options for the renunciant; never quote that context to a general or vulnerable reader
Rules addressed to a male renunciant; adapt for householders
not_for: someone with an eating disorder if 'don't comfort the body' is stressed
speaks_to: reacting to online praise or criticism
over-exercise or crash dieting, or the opposite

up_kaushitaki.126.context: Indra has offered Pratardana a boon and taught 'I am prana, the conscious self (prajnatman)'. He then shows how each organ (speech, smell, sight and so on) is one portion of prajna (3.5-6). This verse argues the point from experience: without prajna no sense makes anything known, as when we say our mind was elsewhere. The next verse turns from objects to the knower.
up_kaushitaki.126.core_teaching: No sense works on its own: seeing, hearing and the rest make anything known only through consciousness, as everyday absent-mindedness shows.

commentaries.who: Shankarananda's commentary, as translated by Cowell and quoted by Müller (SBE 1)
commentaries.gist: The organ cannot exist without prajna, nor its objects without the organ. Since what cannot exist without another is identical with it, objects are one with the organs and the organs one with prajna, like cloth and its threads.

commentaries.who: E. B. Cowell's translation and notes (1861)
commentaries.gist: Notes that the other recension has the person, not the organs, say 'my mind was elsewhere', and that 'body' here stands for the skin as organ of touch.

up_kaushitaki.126.practical_reading: You only truly hear, taste or see what you attend to. Bring your mind back to the person in front of you or the meal on your plate.
misreadings: Not a productivity tip in the original; it is an argument that consciousness is the ground of experience
not_for: someone with a cognitive impairment if framed as personal failure

up_kaushitaki.131.context: After showing that no sense works without consciousness (3.7), Indra redirects the inquiry from each object and function to its knower. He then explains that objects and senses depend on each other and both rest on prana-prajna like a wheel's rim on spokes and spokes on the hub; that self is not increased by good deeds nor diminished by bad, and is Indra's own self.
up_kaushitaki.131.core_teaching: Instead of chasing each experience, turn to the one who experiences: the conscious self behind speech, sight, action, pleasure and pain.

commentaries.who: Shankarananda's commentary, as summarised in E. B. Cowell's notes (1861)
commentaries.gist: The 'speaker' is the soul, witness of all the organs' activity and itself one with joy. Speech and mind stand for all the organs; the clauses in between stand for all their objects.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, translation and notes (SBE 1)
commentaries.gist: Renders the conclusion: the ten objects depend on prajna and the ten subjects on objects; neither exists alone; both rest on prana, which is the conscious self, blessed and immortal, like rim, spokes and hub of a wheel.

up_kaushitaki.131.practical_reading: When pleasure or pain is loud, step back to the one noticing it. That shift can give room to respond rather than react.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of feelings or experiences; it relocates attention to the knower
cautions: Later in the same section the self 'makes' some do good and others bad deeds; avoid quoting that line out of context, it can sound fatalistic
not_for: someone in acute physical pain if presented as 'just observe it'
speaks_to: anxiety, where stepping back to the observer helps

up_kaushitaki.3.context: King Chitra, about to sacrifice, chose Aruni as his priest; Aruni sent his son Shvetaketu, and Chitra asked him a riddling question about the worlds after death. Shvetaketu could not answer and asked his father, who admitted he did not know either; both went to Chitra as pupils, fuel in hand. Chitra praises Aruni for not being too proud and teaches the two paths after death.
up_kaushitaki.3.core_teaching: A learned father and son admit their ignorance and go together, humbly, to learn from someone who knows.

commentaries.who: Shankarananda's commentary, as summarised in E. B. Cowell's translation (1861)
commentaries.gist: The story opens the Upanishad to show that even great sages like Gautama and Shvetaketu received knowledge of Brahman only from a teacher, through humility; so modern students too must be humble to receive it.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, translation and notes (SBE 1)
commentaries.gist: Explains Chitra's obscure question as about the two roads after death (the path of the gods and the path of the fathers) and notes that the text was already corrupt when the commentary was written.

up_kaushitaki.3.practical_reading: Saying 'I don't know, let's find out together' is a strength. A parent and child can learn side by side, and the expert should be willing to become a student.
misreadings: Not a story of a father's failure; the king praises his lack of pride
cautions: The teaching that follows is about what happens after death
speaks_to: professionals facing a question beyond their expertise

data_flags.translation_note: The father's middle sentence is misread. Our 'We have studied the Veda and take what others give us' loses 'sadasi' (in his hall/assembly). Müller: only after learning the proper portion of the Veda in Chitra's own dwelling shall we obtain what others give us. Cowell:...

up_kaushitaki.93.context: The second chapter of the Kaushitaki is about breath (prana) as Brahman and related rites. It ends with the father's transmission: when near death, the father, dressed in new white cloth beside a prepared fire, hands each faculty to his son, who accepts each. The son then walks around him and leaves; the father blesses him with fame and honour. If the father recovers, he lives under his son's authority or becomes a wandering ascetic.
up_kaushitaki.93.core_teaching: A dying parent passes on the whole of a life, its faculties, deeds, joys and sorrows, and the child consciously receives them; continuity is made explicit.

commentaries.who: Shankarananda's notes, in E. B. Cowell's translation (1861)
commentaries.gist: Adds ritual detail: the water-pot is placed north or east of the fire; notes the other recension's variants (the father meets the son from above; thoughts and desires instead of mind and knowledge).

commentaries.who: Max Müller, translation and notes (SBE 1)
commentaries.gist: Describes the full rite and the son's departure; notes that the final instruction is unclear: Müller takes it as performing the funeral duties, while Cowell reads it as having the son duly receive the tradition.

up_kaushitaki.93.practical_reading: Many people find comfort in naming what they inherit from a parent, not just possessions but ways of seeing, working and feeling, and in consciously taking it up.
misreadings: Not a claim that a child must carry a parent's sorrows as a burden forever
cautions: This is a deathbed rite: handle with great care for anyone recently bereaved or caring for a dying parent
Father-to-son framing; widen to any parent and child
not_for: someone estranged from or harmed by a parent, for whom 'I take your joys and sorrows into me' may be distressing
very fresh grief unless the reader has asked for it
speaks_to: after a parent's death, reflecting on what was passed on

up_maha.104.context: Chapter 3 is the young sage Nidagha's lament. Back from bathing at countless holy places, he tells Ribhu that the pilgrimage has only stirred a question: everything is born to die, wealth and family breed anxiety, life is like a drop on a leaf-tip. He says a life is worth the name only if in it one reaches the place of highest peace and grieves no more; then comes this verse; and he adds that the rest are 'old donkeys'. Next he says scripture, knowledge, mind and body become burdens without discernment.
up_maha.104.core_teaching: Mere biological life is shared with trees and animals; a human life is truly lived when the mind is nourished by reflection on what matters.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: A lifetime counts if in it the bliss of Brahman is attained and the misery of worldly existence ends. Trees, beasts and birds live too; he alone truly lives whose mind is sustained by meditation.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: only he really lives whose mind is sustained by contemplation; those without spiritual rebirth are only old donkeys.

commentaries.who: Yoga Vasishtha parallel (Rama's lament on life), tr. Vihari-Lala Mitra
commentaries.gist: Mitra's rendering of the parallel: plants have vegetable life, beasts animal life, humans a thinking life, but true life lies beyond the succession of thoughts; those not born again live well.

up_maha.104.practical_reading: Being busy is not the same as being alive. Give your mind some time each day to reflect on what you are living for.
misreadings: Not contempt for animals, plants or people with cognitive disabilities
cautions: The next line calls the unreflective 'old donkeys'; don't quote it
not_for: someone struggling just to get through the day, who may hear 'mere living' as a judgment
speaks_to: feeling like life is on autopilot

up_maha.106.context: Chapter 3 is the young sage Nidagha's lament. Back from bathing at countless holy places, he tells Ribhu that the pilgrimage has only stirred a question: everything is born to die, wealth and family breed anxiety, life is like a drop on a leaf-tip. Having said that only a reflective life is truly lived, he lists four things that become loads without the right inner condition. The next verse turns to ego as the root of misfortune.
up_maha.106.core_teaching: Things meant to help (scripture, knowledge, mind, body) become burdens when the inner condition for using them (discernment, dispassion, calm, self-knowledge) is missing.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: To one whose reasoning is fully developed, scripture is a burden; to one blinded by passion, even knowledge of Brahman is a burden; to one without composure, the mind; to one who does not know the self, the body.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: Renders it: scripture burdens one who lacks discrimination, knowledge one who is attached, mind one without security, body one ignorant of the self.

commentaries.who: Yoga Vasishtha parallel, tr. Vihari-Lala Mitra
commentaries.gist: Knowledge encumbers the unthinking, wisdom the passionate, intellect the restless, and the body is a heavy load to one ignorant of his soul.

up_maha.106.practical_reading: If your learning, your thoughts or your own body feel heavy, the fix may be inner: calm, clarity and self-understanding, not more information.
misreadings: Not anti-intellectual; it names what learning needs in order to help
cautions: 'The body is a burden' can resonate painfully with someone with chronic illness, body-image struggles or self-harm thoughts; frame carefully or avoid for such readers
not_for: someone expressing that their body or life is a burden in a self-harm sense
speaks_to: feeling weighed down by one's own mind

up_maha.107.context: Chapter 3 is the young sage Nidagha's lament. Back from bathing at countless holy places, he tells Ribhu that the pilgrimage has only stirred a question: everything is born to die, wealth and family breed anxiety, life is like a drop on a leaf-tip. After the four burdens, he turns to ahamkara, the I-maker: misfortune, anguish and craving all come from it, and whatever he enjoyed under its sway was unreal. The next verses describe his restless mind and his craving.
up_maha.107.core_teaching: The sense of a separate, grasping 'I' is the root of calamity, anguish and craving; no enemy is worse.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Ruin, misery, anguish and all exertion spring from being ruled by individuality; no enemy is stronger. Whatever was enjoyed under its sway is without substance; freedom from individuality alone is real.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: Danger, mental ailments and desire all arise from ego; there is no more dangerous enemy; only freedom from ego is real.

up_maha.107.practical_reading: When you notice trouble, worry or wanting building up, ask how much of it is about protecting or inflating your sense of 'me'.
misreadings: Not a call to self-hatred or erasing healthy self-respect
cautions: For a reader with low self-worth, distinguish ego (grasping self-importance) from the self that deserves care
not_for: someone with very low self-esteem or depression, if read as 'your self is the enemy'
speaks_to: people noticing how their 'I' fuels stress

up_maha.109.context: Chapter 3 is the young sage Nidagha's lament. Back from bathing at countless holy places, he tells Ribhu that the pilgrimage has only stirred a question: everything is born to die, wealth and family breed anxiety, life is like a drop on a leaf-tip. After naming ego as the enemy, he describes his own mind: it runs everywhere to no purpose like a village dog, and (next verse) has left him dull, eaten up by it as by a street dog, with craving as its partner. Then he says mastering the mind is harder than drinking the ocean.
up_maha.109.core_teaching: Left to itself, the mind runs restlessly and aimlessly, like a stray dog roaming the village.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: The highly distracted mind leaps hither and thither to no purpose and strays far, like a dog wandering the whole village; Nidagha adds that he feels eaten up by that street-dog mind, with covetousness as its partner.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: The mind runs hither and thither in vain and with zeal, like a dog in the village; the speaker says he has been made inert by thirst and eaten by his mind.

up_maha.109.practical_reading: Notice the stray-dog mind without scolding it. Naming the wandering ('there it goes again') is the first step to calling it home.
misreadings: Not a judgment that a wandering mind is shameful; Nidagha is describing himself honestly
not_for: someone with a diagnosed attention or anxiety disorder, if framed as a moral failing

up_maha.111.context: Chapter 3 is the young sage Nidagha's lament. Back from bathing at countless holy places, he tells Ribhu that the pilgrimage has only stirred a question: everything is born to die, wealth and family breed anxiety, life is like a drop on a leaf-tip. Having described his wandering mind, he says mastering it is harder than drinking the ocean, uprooting Meru or eating fire; the mind is the root of all objects, and when it goes the three worlds go, so it must be treated with effort. Next he describes craving as a mouse and a monkey.
up_maha.111.core_teaching: Mastering the mind is the hardest of tasks, harder than any heroic feat.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Mind-control is harder than drinking the ocean, uprooting Meru or eating fire. The mind is the root of all objects: while it exists the three worlds exist; when it goes, they go. So treat it with great effort.

commentaries.who: Yoga Vasishtha parallel, tr. Vihari-Lala Mitra
commentaries.gist: Rama says subduing the mind is harder than drinking the ocean or upsetting Sumeru; the mind causes all exertions and must be cured with care.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: Containing the mind is impossible even by drinking the ocean, uprooting Meru or eating fire; mind is the cause of objects, so it should be cured with effort.

up_maha.111.practical_reading: If you struggle to steady your mind, you are not weak; the tradition itself calls this the hardest task. Expect slow progress and keep at it.
misreadings: Not 'it's impossible, so give up'; Ribhu's answer (chapter 4) gives the means
cautions: Pair with Ribhu's answer (e.g. 4.2-3 or 4.106-107) so the reader is not left with only the difficulty
not_for: someone already hopeless about changing, if offered without the answer that follows

up_maha.113.context: In the Yoga Vasishtha parallel (1.17), Rama describes craving: it dries him like the sun dries mud, dances like a demoness in the dark forest of his mind, drags him like a bull led by a nose-rope, and throws a net over people through attachment to children, friends and spouse. This verse comes early in that catalogue. In the Maha Upanishad version, the young Nidagha voices the same lament to his teacher Ribhu.
up_maha.113.core_teaching: Craving quietly undermines every good resolve or virtue we try to build, the way a mouse gnaws through a string.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (on the Yoga Vasishtha parallel, 1.17.8)
commentaries.gist: Craving cuts through whatever eagerness one has for the wealth of virtues such as discernment and dispassion; the 'string' is a lute's gut string.

commentaries.who: Bhaskarakantha, Mokshopaya-tika (on the Mokshopaya parallel, 1.16.8; Sanskrit Wikisource)
commentaries.gist: Reads the verse with 'adhitastham' and glosses it as a resolve one has trained and made firm: even a firm commitment gets gnawed through.

up_maha.113.practical_reading: If you keep making good resolutions and watching them fray, the problem may be the background wanting that nibbles at them, not your character. Notice the craving itself.
misreadings: Not 'you are weak-willed'
Not a condemnation of all desire; it targets restless craving
cautions: The surrounding lament is very bleak; quote this verse alone
Attribution and numbering need an editor's check before publishing the reference
not_for: someone already self-blaming about addiction, without a supportive frame

up_maha.114.context: Chapter 3 is the young sage Nidagha's lament. Back from bathing at countless holy places, he tells Ribhu that the pilgrimage has only stirred a question: everything is born to die, wealth and family breed anxiety, life is like a drop on a leaf-tip. After saying craving gnaws his good qualities like a mouse gnawing a string (3.22), he calls it a restless monkey, then a bee in the heart-lotus that flits from hell to sky; of all sorrows, craving lasts longest, and the only charm against it is to stop brooding.
up_maha.114.core_teaching: Craving is like a restless monkey: it leaps where it shouldn't, keeps reaching even when full, and never stays put.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Covetousness, the fickle monkey, lands where no one can leap, relishes fruit even when sated and never rests long anywhere; giving up the mind's brooding is the mantra that exorcises it.

commentaries.who: Yoga Vasishtha parallel, tr. Vihari-Lala Mitra
commentaries.gist: The greedy are as unsteady as a flouncing monkey that never rests, goes where others cannot, and craves fruit even when sated.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: Thirst is a fickle monkey: it sets foot in impassable places, hankers after fruits even when filled, and never rests long; abandoning brooding is the charm against it.

up_maha.114.practical_reading: Next time you reach for more while already full (food, scrolling, shopping), picture the monkey and pause before the next leap.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of all wanting
not_for: someone in addiction recovery if used as shaming rather than insight

up_maha.144.context: Chapter 3 is the young sage Nidagha's lament. Back from bathing at countless holy places, he tells Ribhu that the pilgrimage has only stirred a question: everything is born to die, wealth and family breed anxiety, life is like a drop on a leaf-tip. Near the end of his lament, Nidagha says even oceans dry up and the gods Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva perish; dangers and fortunes come in a moment, birth and death too. He concludes that sense-objects are worse than poison and begs Ribhu to wake him with knowledge, or he will sit silent like a painted figure.
up_maha.144.core_teaching: Misfortune and fortune, birth and death all arrive in a moment; nothing in the world lasts.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Even the creator, Hari and Shiva waste away; all beings rush to destruction like waters to the undersea fire. Dangers and prosperity come in a moment; birth and death happen in an instant; all is transient.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: Dangers come for a moment, so does wealth; birth and death are only for a moment: everything dies. The brave are killed by those not brave.

up_maha.144.practical_reading: Hold good days lightly and bad days patiently; both arrive suddenly and both pass. Let that make you value what is here now.
misreadings: Not a promise that bad times will soon end
Not nihilism; it is the disillusion that precedes Ribhu's teaching
cautions: Spoken in despairing dispassion; on its own it can deepen hopelessness
Mentions death; avoid for fresh bereavement
not_for: fresh grief
someone feeling hopeless or depressed
speaks_to: after a sudden reversal of fortune

up_maha.150.context: Chapter 4 is Ribhu's answer to Nidagha's lament. He says Nidagha already knows what is to be known and only needs the mind's confusion wiped away, then names four gatekeepers of freedom (calm, inquiry, contentment, good company) and goes on to describe the free person, inquiry, calm and contentment in turn, before teaching that the world is the mind's projection and that the mind must be stilled by the mind. These are the opening lines of that answer, right after Ribhu says he will sweep away the delusion born of the mind's impurity. Next he says knowledge should be cultivated first, through scripture, good company, austerity and self-control.
up_maha.150.core_teaching: Calm, inquiry, contentment and good company guard the door of freedom; make friends with even one of them wholeheartedly and the other three follow.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Four doorkeepers: control of senses, inquiry into one's real nature by reasoning about cause and effect, contentment with what has come, and company of knowers of Brahman. Win one with full effort and all four are mastered.

commentaries.who: Yoga Vasishtha parallel (Vasishtha to Rama), tr. Vihari-Lala Mitra
commentaries.gist: Four guards watch the gate of liberation: peace, judgment, contentment and good company. Cultivate all, or three or two; at the least secure one, even at great cost, and it wins over all four.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: Lists the four as control of inner and outer senses, enquiry, contentment and contact with good people; resort to at least one with all effort, giving up everything, and the others are achieved too.

up_maha.150.practical_reading: You don't have to fix everything at once. Pick one door this week: a little more calm, honest self-inquiry, contentment, or time with good people, and let it open the others.
misreadings: 'Setting all else aside' is about focus, not abandoning responsibilities
speaks_to: a practical plan for inner change

up_maha.165.context: Chapter 4 is Ribhu's answer to Nidagha's lament. He says Nidagha already knows what is to be known and only needs the mind's confusion wiped away, then names four gatekeepers of freedom (calm, inquiry, contentment, good company) and goes on to describe the free person, inquiry, calm and contentment in turn, before teaching that the world is the mind's projection and that the mind must be stilled by the mind. Having said that the sense 'I am never the doer' leaves only the equanimity called immortality, Ribhu tells Nidagha that noble souls are born in the world, always cheerful like autumn moons (4.17). This verse continues their portrait; next they shine through friendliness and other virtues, even and gentle, keeping their bounds like the ocean.
up_maha.165.core_teaching: People of settled goodness do not wilt in adversity, do not grasp beyond what is fitting, and enjoy walking the way of the good.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Under 'the state of a jivanmukta': they do not droop in adversity, as a gold lotus does not fade at night though the sun has set; they do not aspire beyond the prescribed limit and delight in upright conduct.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
