commentaries.gist: Men of noble qualities, ever cheerful like autumn moons, are not depressed in danger, like a gold lotus at night; they do not aspire beyond what is destined and delight in the path of good people.

commentaries.who: Yoga Vasishtha related image (Vasishtha on contentment), tr. Vihari-Lala Mitra
commentaries.gist: A mind bright with contentment does not shrivel like a lotus in the dark night of adversity.

up_maha.165.practical_reading: Resilience can look like a lotus that stays open after dark: you can keep your shape in hard times by not grasping for more and staying with what is good.
misreadings: Not a demand to look cheerful when suffering
'Not wanting beyond what is at hand' is not a ban on ambition
cautions: Could be heard as 'good people don't get depressed'; avoid with readers in depression
not_for: someone in clinical depression, who may hear it as a judgment

up_maha.178.context: Chapter 4 is Ribhu's answer to Nidagha's lament. He says Nidagha already knows what is to be known and only needs the mind's confusion wiped away, then names four gatekeepers of freedom (calm, inquiry, contentment, good company) and goes on to describe the free person, inquiry, calm and contentment in turn, before teaching that the world is the mind's projection and that the mind must be stilled by the mind. Ribhu has just said that neither wealth, friends, kin, bodily austerity nor pilgrimage reaches the goal, only mastery of the mind (4.28). He now praises shama, calm: in a calm mind all sorrows dissolve; all beings trust the calm one like a mother; no elixir or fortune gives such joy. Definitions of the calm and the content person follow.
up_maha.178.core_teaching: Sorrow, craving and anxiety cannot survive in a truly calm mind, any more than darkness in sunlight.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Under 'the real form of quiescence and its fruit': whatever sorrows, unquenchable desires and anguish exist stand dissolved in those whose minds are tranquil, all functions abated, as darkness in the sun's rays.

commentaries.who: Yoga Vasishtha parallel (Vasishtha on calm), tr. Vihari-Lala Mitra
commentaries.gist: Whatever misery, anxiety and intolerable difficulty may overtake a man are lost in the tranquil mind like darkness in the sun.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: All miseries, hankerings and unbearable mental pain are lost in people with a calm mind, like darkness in the sun.

up_maha.178.practical_reading: Calm is not a reward for solving your problems; it is what lets many of them dissolve. Practise small calming habits before and during trouble.
misreadings: Not 'if you still suffer, you are not calm enough'
Not a substitute for treatment of anxiety disorders
cautions: Can sound like blame to someone with clinical anxiety; offer as encouragement, not diagnosis
not_for: someone in a panic or mental-health crisis if given as the whole answer
speaks_to: the value of a daily calming practice

up_maha.179.context: Chapter 4 is Ribhu's answer to Nidagha's lament. He says Nidagha already knows what is to be known and only needs the mind's confusion wiped away, then names four gatekeepers of freedom (calm, inquiry, contentment, good company) and goes on to describe the free person, inquiry, calm and contentment in turn, before teaching that the world is the mind's projection and that the mind must be stilled by the mind. Continuing his praise of calm, after saying sorrows vanish in a calm mind, Ribhu says all creatures trust the calm person as children trust their mother. Next: no elixir or fortune gives the joy of inner calm.
up_maha.179.core_teaching: A calm person becomes a refuge: everyone, difficult or gentle, comes to trust them as children trust a mother.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: As children, naughty or soft-natured, are deeply attached to their mother, so all beings, furious or meek, come to have faith in a yogin who has developed tranquillity.

commentaries.who: Yoga Vasishtha parallel, tr. Vihari-Lala Mitra
commentaries.gist: As all children, good or bad, trust their mother, so all beings rely on the person of even disposition.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: All creatures grow calm in a serene person, like children, mischievous or soft, in their mother.

up_maha.179.practical_reading: Your calm is a gift to others. Parents, teachers, managers and carers find that a steady presence settles even difficult people.
misreadings: Not a promise that every hostile person will become friendly
cautions: Mother imagery may be painful for someone who lost or lacked a mother
not_for: someone dealing with an abusive person, if read as 'stay calm and they will come round'

up_maha.180.context: Chapter 4 is Ribhu's answer to Nidagha's lament. He says Nidagha already knows what is to be known and only needs the mind's confusion wiped away, then names four gatekeepers of freedom (calm, inquiry, contentment, good company) and goes on to describe the free person, inquiry, calm and contentment in turn, before teaching that the world is the mind's projection and that the mind must be stilled by the mind. Third line of the praise of calm: after saying calm dissolves sorrow and wins everyone's trust, Ribhu says no elixir and no fortune gives the joy of calm within. He then defines the calm person: unmoved by pleasant or unpleasant sights, sounds, touch and taste, clear as the moon in death, festival or battle.
up_maha.180.core_teaching: Neither longevity potions nor wealth bring the happiness that inner calm gives.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Neither the elixir of life nor the caresses of the Goddess of Wealth give a person the happiness he finds inwardly by subduing his passions.

commentaries.who: Yoga Vasishtha parallel, tr. Vihari-Lala Mitra
commentaries.gist: Neither a cooling nectar nor the embrace of prosperity satisfies the soul as much as inner contentment of the mind.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: Not by drinking elixirs nor by the embrace of wealth does one get as much joy as by inner peace.

up_maha.180.practical_reading: Before chasing the next health fix or financial goal, notice that the happiness you want may be closer: in a quieter mind.
misreadings: Not anti-health or anti-wealth; it ranks inner calm above them
cautions: For someone in poverty or illness, avoid implying their material needs don't matter
not_for: someone in financial or medical crisis if used to dismiss real needs

up_maha.185.context: Chapter 4 is Ribhu's answer to Nidagha's lament. He says Nidagha already knows what is to be known and only needs the mind's confusion wiped away, then names four gatekeepers of freedom (calm, inquiry, contentment, good company) and goes on to describe the free person, inquiry, calm and contentment in turn, before teaching that the world is the mind's projection and that the mind must be stilled by the mind. After praising calm, Ribhu turns to the third gatekeeper, contentment: those who drink its nectar delight in the self. These two verses define the content person; next he says liberation in life arises when thought delights in what has come, as a chaste wife welcomes her husband.
up_maha.185.core_teaching: Contentment means letting go of what hasn't come, staying even with what has, and enjoying what is here without longing for more.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: The content person gives up delusion about things apart from the Atman, rests even when the Atman is attained, feeling neither fatigue nor elation; sweet-tempered and upright, he enjoys the Atman to his heart's content.

commentaries.who: Yoga Vasishtha parallel (Vasishtha on contentment), tr. Vihari-Lala Mitra
commentaries.gist: Contentment is giving up fruitless desires, calm in what is obtained, feeling neither pain nor elation.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: The contented one gives up longing for what is not got, is even toward what is got, ignores grief and joy, does not admire what is not got, enjoys what has actually come, and is benign in conduct.

up_maha.185.practical_reading: Write down what you already have that you have stopped enjoying. Enjoy it today, and loosen your hold on the things you keep waiting for.
misreadings: Not complacency or giving up goals
Not suppressing feelings about loss
not_for: someone in fresh grief over a person, if 'let go of what has not come' is applied to the lost person

up_maha.221.context: Chapter 4 is Ribhu's answer to Nidagha's lament. He says Nidagha already knows what is to be known and only needs the mind's confusion wiped away, then names four gatekeepers of freedom (calm, inquiry, contentment, good company) and goes on to describe the free person, inquiry, calm and contentment in turn, before teaching that the world is the mind's projection and that the mind must be stilled by the mind. Ribhu has said that one who knows the self as bliss fears nothing, and described the supreme as beyond the beyond and worshipped by all gods (4.70-71). This verse gives the two key phrases: 'I am Brahman' for the great, and the two words 'mine' and 'not mine' for bondage and freedom. Next he warns against getting caught in debates about soul and God.
up_maha.221.core_teaching: Bondage and freedom turn on the sense of 'mine'; dropping possessiveness frees, and the conviction 'I am Brahman' is the root of liberation.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: The surest means of liberation is always to hold the attitude 'I am Brahman'. 'Mine' and 'not-mine' stand for bondage and release: with the rise of 'mine' the creature is bound, with 'not-mine' it is freed.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: As a rule, 'I am Brahman' leads the great to liberation, whereas 'not mine' and 'mine' give liberation and bondage respectively.

up_maha.221.practical_reading: Notice where 'my' is tightening your chest: my plan, my status, my way. Try holding one of those as 'not mine' today and see what loosens.
misreadings: Not a call to stop caring for family or property; it is about clinging
cautions: 'Not mine' applied to a child or partner can sound cold to a parent or a grieving spouse
not_for: someone grieving a child or partner, if 'not mine' is applied to the lost person

up_maha.248.context: Chapter 4 is Ribhu's answer to Nidagha's lament. He says Nidagha already knows what is to be known and only needs the mind's confusion wiped away, then names four gatekeepers of freedom (calm, inquiry, contentment, good company) and goes on to describe the free person, inquiry, calm and contentment in turn, before teaching that the world is the mind's projection and that the mind must be stilled by the mind. Ribhu is giving 'the cure for the disease called mind': cut the mind with the knife of non-imagining and rest in the state beyond ideas. He then says restlessness is the mind's nature, as heat is fire's; the mind without it is immortal and is liberation. The following lines urge destroying that restlessness through inquiry and effort.
up_maha.248.core_teaching: Restlessness is the mind's nature, as heat is fire's; seeing this is the starting point, and a mind freed of it is called freedom.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Fickleness belongs to the mind as heat to fire; it comes from ignorance of the self. A mind free of it is immortal existence and liberation, like motionless air becoming space or purified quicksilver becoming still.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: Nowhere is the mind without fickleness; it is its nature, as heat is fire's. The mind without wavering is called amrita, and that is liberation in the scriptures.

up_maha.248.practical_reading: Don't be discouraged that your mind wanders; that is what minds do. The practice is to work with it patiently, not to be shocked by it.
misreadings: Not 'restlessness is fine, do nothing'; the teaching goes on to its stilling

up_maha.255.context: Chapter 4 is Ribhu's answer to Nidagha's lament. He says Nidagha already knows what is to be known and only needs the mind's confusion wiped away, then names four gatekeepers of freedom (calm, inquiry, contentment, good company) and goes on to describe the free person, inquiry, calm and contentment in turn, before teaching that the world is the mind's projection and that the mind must be stilled by the mind. Ribhu has just said that only the mind is skilled enough to control the mind, as only a king can control a king. He then gives this image: people seized by craving's crocodile and swept by whirlpools have their own mind as the only boat; cut the mind's noose with the mind and lift yourself across. Next he tells Nidagha to drop each vasana as it arises.
up_maha.255.core_teaching: The mind that binds is also the only means of release: use your own mind to cut its bonds, because no one else can do the crossing for you.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: For those clutched by avarice's crocodile and sinking in the ocean of existence, the only saving boat, their own mind, stands aloof. Cut the binding rope of mind with mind and rescue yourself; it cannot be crossed any other way.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: For those caught by desire's crocodile and tossed by whirlpools, only the mind is the life-boat. Break the mind's rope with the mind and lift yourself out of worldly life, which cannot be crossed through another.

up_maha.255.practical_reading: Help from others matters, but the last step is yours: use your own understanding to undo the thought patterns that hold you.
misreadings: Not 'don't accept help'; it says the inner work cannot be outsourced
Not a claim that anyone who is struggling simply hasn't tried hard enough
cautions: For someone in a mental-health crisis, 'no one else can carry you over' could sound isolating; pair with encouragement to seek support
not_for: someone in acute crisis who needs to hear that help is available
speaks_to: taking responsibility for one's inner life

up_maha.260.context: Chapter 4 is Ribhu's answer to Nidagha's lament. He says Nidagha already knows what is to be known and only needs the mind's confusion wiped away, then names four gatekeepers of freedom (calm, inquiry, contentment, good company) and goes on to describe the free person, inquiry, calm and contentment in turn, before teaching that the world is the mind's projection and that the mind must be stilled by the mind. Ribhu has told Nidagha to drop each vasana as it rises, then the vasana of difference, then even the ideas of being and non-being; this destruction of mind is the destruction of ignorance, and it consists in not placing reliance on whatever is perceived (4.110). This half-verse sums it up; next he says ignorance exists only for the dull, not for one of clear insight.
up_maha.260.core_teaching: Not clinging is itself freedom; clinging is itself suffering.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Destroying the mind's fancies destroys ignorance. Give no interest to whatever is perceived: absence of interest is nirvana, the extinction of the mind.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: Avoiding desire toward whatever is seen is the destruction of mind and of ignorance; freedom from desire is extinction (liberation), and taking up desire is misery.

up_maha.260.practical_reading: When something hurts, ask what you are gripping. Loosening the grip, even a little, often eases the pain.
misreadings: Not clinging is not the same as not caring
cautions: Very compressed; on a grief day it can sound like 'you suffer because you were attached'. Avoid with fresh loss
not_for: fresh bereavement
someone blamed for 'being too attached' to a person they lost
speaks_to: people drawn to short, memorable lines

up_maha.369.context: Chapter 5 continues Ribhu's teaching: the seven stages of ignorance and of knowledge, the danger of vasanas (latent tendencies), three kinds of 'I'-sense, and how a wise person lives among worldly affairs. Ribhu has said that the world turns, bound by the thread of vasanas, which bring misery when they grow and well-being when cut off (5.86). This verse adds that craving binds even the wise and well-born like a chained lion. The next verse says that with real effort, done as guided, anyone succeeds.
up_maha.369.core_teaching: No amount of courage, learning or status protects anyone from being chained by craving.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Taking undue interest in things is the storehouse of misery; vasanas bring misery when they prevail. However valiant, learned, noble or excellent, one is enslaved by greed like a lion in fetters.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: Though intellectual, extremely learned, high-born and eminent, one is bound by cravings as a lion is with a chain.

up_maha.369.practical_reading: Successful, capable people are not immune to craving; it can bind them all the more. Don't assume achievement means freedom.
misreadings: Not a claim that the strong are weak; it shows craving's power over anyone
not_for: someone already ashamed of an addiction, without a hopeful frame (pair with 5.88)

up_maha.370.context: Chapter 5 continues Ribhu's teaching: the seven stages of ignorance and of knowledge, the danger of vasanas (latent tendencies), three kinds of 'I'-sense, and how a wise person lives among worldly affairs. Directly after saying craving binds even the great like a chained lion, Ribhu answers with hope: with supreme effort and perseverance, acting calmly as the scriptures guide, who would not succeed? He then describes three kinds of 'I'-sense, two that free and one that binds.
up_maha.370.core_teaching: Steady, calm, well-guided effort brings success; even strong craving can be overcome.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: By manly effort and perseverance, calmly following the course the scriptures lay down, who will not achieve success? The next lines distinguish freeing and binding kinds of I-sense.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: Resorting to supreme personal endeavour and perseverance, and conforming unwaveringly to scriptural conduct, who may not win perfection?

up_maha.370.practical_reading: Effort works best when it is steady, guided and unhurried. Make a plan, follow good advice, and keep going without panic.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that effort controls every outcome
'Without anxiety' is not 'without care'
cautions: Could add pressure to someone already overworking; stress 'without anxiety'
not_for: someone burnt out, if read as 'try harder'

up_maha.40.context: Shuka, Vyasa's son, already knows the truth by his own insight but is not at rest in it; when his father's explanation does not satisfy him, Vyasa sends him to King Janaka. Janaka keeps him waiting seven days at the gate, seven in the courtyard, and seven in the women's quarters, where he is plied with pleasures. Shuka stays unmoved; Janaka then bows to him and teaches him that release is the dropping of mental tendencies (vasanas).
up_maha.40.core_teaching: A mind settled in truth is not shaken by luxury or delay; it stays even, clear, silent and content.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Janaka tests Shuka with three weeks of waiting and, in the harem, with beautiful women and intoxicating food. None touch his mind in samadhi, as a breeze cannot move a firm mountain; he stands like the full moon.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Shuka, unattracted, remains pure, equable, silent and composed like the full moon; Janaka, recognising his nature, bows and asks what more he could desire.

up_maha.40.practical_reading: Test your steadiness not only in hardship but in comfort and flattery. A settled mind can enjoy a good meal without being owned by it.
misreadings: Not a claim that enjoyment is wrong; the point is not being moved by it
cautions: The story uses women as temptations; avoid that framing

up_maha.452.context: Chapter 5 continues Ribhu's teaching: the seven stages of ignorance and of knowledge, the danger of vasanas (latent tendencies), three kinds of 'I'-sense, and how a wise person lives among worldly affairs. Ribhu has said that when wealth and family grow, grief grows too, and that the very enjoyments that breed passion in a fool breed dispassion in the wise (5.168-169). Hence this practical rule for everyday dealings; next, the mark of the wise: no longing for future pleasures, natural enjoyment of present ones. He goes on: the wise neither abandon worldly affairs nor get engrossed in them.
up_maha.452.core_teaching: In daily life, let go of what is lost and take up what comes, without clinging either way.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: So, Nidagha, knower of truth, in your daily conduct feel unconcerned with whatever is lost and take hold of whatever is attained; the wise neither abandon worldly affairs nor get engrossed in them.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: With your awareness of truth, cultivate indifference to whatever has perished among life's activities and accept whatever offers itself.

up_maha.452.practical_reading: After a loss at work or in money matters, don't keep re-litigating it; turn to what has just arrived and use it well.
misreadings: Not advice to stop grieving a person; the setting is worldly transactions (vyavahara)
cautions: Do not use for the death of a loved one: 'let go of what is lost' would land as dismissive
not_for: bereavement
pregnancy loss
end of a marriage in its early days
speaks_to: moving on after a failed project

up_maha.453.context: Chapter 5 continues Ribhu's teaching: the seven stages of ignorance and of knowledge, the danger of vasanas (latent tendencies), three kinds of 'I'-sense, and how a wise person lives among worldly affairs. Follows the rule 'let go of what is lost, take up what comes' (5.170). Ribhu now names the mark of the wise; next he says a person of gnosis, free of desire and aversion, is no more stained than a lotus leaf by water.
up_maha.453.core_teaching: The wise naturally stop pining for future pleasures and fully enjoy what has already come.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Absence of longing for pleasures not yet attained, with natural enjoyment of what comes unsought, is the innate quality of the pandita, the jivanmukta who has perceived the supreme Self.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: The mark of a discriminating person is spontaneous indifference to experiences that do not come of themselves and hearty acceptance of those that do.

up_maha.453.practical_reading: Enjoy today's meal, today's company, today's small win, without the background hum of 'and next...'.
misreadings: Not a ban on planning or hope
'Unforced' means this should not be a grim effort of suppression
not_for: someone whose present is painful (illness, grief), if told to 'enjoy what has come'

up_maha.467.context: Chapter 5 continues Ribhu's teaching: the seven stages of ignorance and of knowledge, the danger of vasanas (latent tendencies), three kinds of 'I'-sense, and how a wise person lives among worldly affairs. Ribhu has explained how ideation (sankalpa) sprouts from pure awareness and grows into misery, and urged Nidagha to uproot each idea with care, cutting ideas by ideas and the mind by the mind (5.178-184). He closes the chapter with this image of husk and tarnish, and the call to be industrious.
up_maha.467.core_teaching: Our flaws may be natural, like husk on rice or tarnish on copper, but effort removes them; so keep working on yourself.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: As paddy husk and copper's tarnish come off only by labour, so does the impurity of the individual self. Though innate, it need not stay; it is surely removable, so put forth effort.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: As paddy husk or the black coating on copper is destroyed by effort, so may a person's mental impurities be. Like the grain's, the self's innate impurity can be destroyed; there is no doubt, so strive.

up_maha.467.practical_reading: Don't despair of a habit or trait just because it feels like 'who I am'. Patient polishing works on copper and on people.
misreadings: 'Impurity' is not a statement that the person is bad or dirty
cautions: Words like 'impurity' or 'stain' can trigger shame; use 'rough edges' or 'tarnish' language in readings
not_for: someone struggling with shame or self-loathing, if 'impurity' is stressed

up_maha.532.context: Chapter 6 describes the person liberated while living (jivanmukta). Just before, Ribhu says one who rests in the state beyond all, filled with pure awareness, is neither agitated nor elated and does not sink in worldly life (6.63). These verses give the outward marks; next he urges Nidagha to roam the world as such a person, free of fever, seeming to engage but inwardly untouched.
up_maha.532.core_teaching: A free person does the work at hand, treats friend and foe alike, speaks kindly and perceptively, and so moves through the world without sinking.

commentaries.who: Upanishad Brahmayogin, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Fulfilling daily tasks as they occur, seeing friend and foe alike, free of attachment and aversion, the sage neither grieves nor longs; speaking agreeably when asked and reading others' thoughts at a glance, he does not drown in worldly existence.

commentaries.who: A. G. Krishna Warrier's translation (Adyar)
commentaries.gist: One who does what falls to his lot, sees foe and friend alike, and is free of likes and dislikes is neither sad nor hopeful; who says what pleases all and speaks pleasantly when asked never suffers in this life.

up_maha.532.practical_reading: A good day's template: do the task in front of you, be fair to people you like and dislike, speak gently, and try to understand what others really mean.
misreadings: 'Saying what is agreeable to all' is not people-pleasing or dishonesty
'Seeing friend and foe alike' does not mean ignoring real danger
not_for: someone facing an abuser, if 'see foe as friend' is applied

up_maha.536.context: In the last chapter of the Maha Upanishad, Ribhu describes the jivanmukta, someone free while still living. Just before, he says such a person does each day's tasks as they come, treats friend and foe alike and speaks pleasantly. This verse belongs to a run of refrains telling Nidagha to 'move through the world' in that way; it is followed by the 'this one is mine, that one is not' verse.
up_maha.536.core_teaching: A free person can be fully engaged in worldly work while the inner self stays untouched by its excitement and anxiety. Action is not abandoned; only the inner identification with being the anxious doer is dropped.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered in T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar's Adyar translation (1941)
commentaries.gist: The liberated sage keeps a show of interest in worldly affairs, like a temple-tower figurine that only seems to hold the tower up, while the heart stays still; like a skilled actor, partly to set an example.

up_maha.536.practical_reading: Teachers use it for people in demanding jobs or caregiving: give the task your full energy and visible effort, but don't let the urgency take over your inner life. The busyness is real; the panic is optional.
misreadings: Not a licence to be fake or manipulative with people
Not advice to suppress feelings; it describes inner freedom, not emotional numbness
Not a call to withdraw from work
cautions: The commentary's 'actor' image can sound like pretending; present it as role-playing without being swallowed by the role
Someone burned out may hear 'stay calm inside' as another demand; pair it with rest, not more effort
not_for: someone in acute burnout who needs permission to stop
grief, where 'calm inside' can feel like being told not to feel
speaks_to: people in high-pressure roles (doctors, managers, parents of young children)
wanting to stay engaged without losing oneself

up_maha.539.context: Still describing how the liberated person lives, Ribhu contrasts narrow and generous minds. Just before, Nidagha is told to act in the world like a skilled actor, inwardly detached. In the Upanishad's own frame (per the Adyar commentary) the verse leads into identifying with the cosmic self (Virat), so that all beings are one's own family; then comes the teaching that bondage is the mind's pull toward objects.
up_maha.539.core_teaching: Dividing people into 'mine' and 'not mine' is a mark of a small mind; a large-hearted person treats everyone as family. In the Upanishad this flows from seeing one self in all, not merely from social niceness.

commentaries.who: Yoga Vasishtha 5.18.61 with the Tatparya-prakasha commentary (Pansikar ed., Sanskrit)
commentaries.gist: Same first line; the second half says the noble have an unveiled mind, which the commentary explains as a mind free of the narrowing 'only this one is my kin', seeing sameness everywhere.

up_maha.539.practical_reading: Used today as an ethic of inclusion: notice when you sort people into 'ours' and 'theirs' (family, caste, nation, team) and widen the circle of care. Teachers also apply it to everyday generosity toward strangers and colleagues.
misreadings: Not a political slogan about borders or a claim that all differences are unreal in practical life
Not a demand to treat strangers exactly as one's own children or to neglect one's own family
The verse itself is about inner largeness, not about a world government
cautions: Extremely well known and often quoted out of context; keep its Upanishadic frame (seeing one self in all)
Someone hurt by family may find 'everyone is family' painful; family here is a circle of goodwill, not obligation to an abuser
not_for: someone estranged from an abusive family
use as a rebuke to a person setting healthy boundaries
speaks_to: workplace or community conflict between groups
migrants and people far from home

up_maitrayani.13.context: This closes King Brihadratha's lament. After listing everything that passes away, he asks what use pleasures are if those who enjoy them keep returning to this world, and begs the sage to pull him out. In the next section Shakayanya, pleased, begins teaching him about the self.
up_maitrayani.13.core_teaching: Pleasures cannot lift someone out of the round of repetition; the king sees himself trapped like a frog in a well and asks a teacher for a way out. Asking for help is the turning point.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Renders the image as a frog in a dry well and the plea as 'thou art my way' repeated twice; notes the commentator's reading of a disputed word in the clause about who feeds on pleasures.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Reads the king as already disgusted with worldly life and asking to be reclaimed; the teacher is the only resort for people of his kind who have fallen into this miserable existence.

up_maitrayani.13.practical_reading: Feeling stuck, as if the walls of your life are all you can see, is a reasonable moment to ask for guidance. Teachers use the frog image for the limited view we get trapped in, and the plea as a model of humbly asking for help.
misreadings: Not a statement that the person is helpless or worthless
Not a rejection of all enjoyment; it questions pleasure as the answer to the deeper problem
cautions: The 'return here again and again' refers to rebirth; may need gentle framing
Language of being trapped can resonate with depression; pair with the sage's positive response that follows
not_for: acute crisis or suicidal feelings, where 'lift me out of this world' could be misread
someone who needs practical rather than spiritual help
speaks_to: ready to ask for help or find a mentor

up_maitrayani.78.context: Near the end of the Maitri, after long passages on sacrifice and meditation, a run of eleven verses on the mind is given. Just before this one, the text says thoughts become still like a fire without fuel, and that even a truth-loving mind can be pulled by sense objects. Next it says a serene mind wipes out good and bad deeds.
up_maitrayani.78.core_teaching: Our experience of the world is shaped by the mind, and we gradually become what we dwell on. So the work is to clean up the mind with steady effort.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Translates it as thoughts alone causing the round of births and notes how close this is to the opening of the Dhammapada; records a manuscript reading 'samsara' in place of the commentator's text.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: The mind alone is worldly existence because it hides Brahman; it should be uprooted by study and by seeing there is no mind apart from Brahman. Whatever one sets the mind on, one finally becomes.

up_maitrayani.78.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say: watch what you feed your attention (worries, grudges, screens, gratitude), because you become what you dwell on. Mental hygiene is daily work.
misreadings: Not 'think positive and everything will be fine'
Not a claim that outer problems are imaginary or that suffering is your own fault
cautions: Can sound like blaming someone's own mind for their anxiety or depression; frame as an invitation, not an accusation
Not a substitute for treatment of clinical anxiety or OCD (where 'purify your thoughts' can feed obsession)
not_for: someone with OCD or intrusive thoughts
trauma survivors who might hear 'it's all in your mind'
speaks_to: anger or resentment that keeps replaying

up_maitrayani.8.context: Brihadratha has handed his kingdom to his son and gone to the forest for long austerity. When the sage Shakayanya appears and offers a boon, the king asks to be taught the self. Shakayanya first tries to put him off, and the king answers with this lament on the decay of the body and of everything in the world. It builds to the 'frog in a well' plea for help.
up_maitrayani.8.core_teaching: Everything we see, from insects to kings to the stars, comes into being and falls apart. The king's lament is the turning point that makes him ready to ask what does not perish.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., SBE 15 (1884), with notes drawing on Ramatirtha's commentary
commentaries.gist: Places the line in the king's verse lament (gatha) on the body's impurity and the world's decay; notes manuscript variants in the grass/trees compound and in the list of departed kings, which even the commentator calls corrupt.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Frames the speech as a verse disparaging worldly existence: whatever is mortal is perishable like flies and gnats that perish as quickly as grass, so pursuing desires in such a body is pointless.

up_maitrayani.8.practical_reading: Teachers use the king's survey of impermanence as an honest starting point: noticing that things pass is not pessimism but the beginning of asking what really matters. It can help someone loosen their grip on status or possessions.
misreadings: Not a claim that life is worthless or that one should despair
Not contempt for small creatures; the image is about how briefly they last
cautions: A stark verse about everything dying; risky for a reader who is depressed, grieving or has suicidal thoughts
The wider passage describes the body in disgusting terms (bones, mucus, faeces); don't quote around it
not_for: fresh grief
depression or hopelessness
anyone in crisis
speaks_to: after a loss of status, job or wealth
people chasing achievement who feel empty

up_maitrayani.80.context: Fourth and fifth of the verses on the mind at Maitri 6.34. Just before, a serene mind is said to burn up good and bad deeds and gain lasting happiness. Just after, the text says the mind is of two kinds, pure and impure, according to whether it is touched by desire.
up_maitrayani.80.core_teaching: We already have a great capacity for focus; it is just spent on objects. Turned toward the highest, the same intensity would free us.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Renders the verse plainly as a conditional: thoughts fixed on Brahman as firmly as on worldly things would bring freedom; it sits among verses Ramatirtha's commentary treats as summary slokas.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Adds that bondage comes from the mind straying outward instead of facing the inner self; the same saturation the mind has with pleasures, if absorbed in Brahman, would liberate anyone.

up_maitrayani.80.practical_reading: Your capacity for devotion is visible in what you already obsess about; teachers suggest redirecting some of that energy toward what you most value. A gentle, encouraging verse about attention.
misreadings: Not a scolding for enjoying anything
Not a promise that liberation is quick or easy
cautions: Mild verse; few risks. Avoid implying the reader is failing spiritually.
not_for: someone already harsh on themselves about lack of discipline
speaks_to: distraction and phone or media habits
wanting to deepen a spiritual practice

up_maitrayani.86.context: This is the last of the eleven verses on the mind at Maitri 6.34. It comes right after the image of water poured into water, fire into fire: a mind merged in the self can no longer be told apart and is free. The prose that follows says those who neglect the fire rites and meditation miss the place of Brahman. The same verse opens the Amritabindu Upanishad, which pairs it with the pure and impure mind.
up_maitrayani.86.core_teaching: What binds or frees us is not the world itself but the mind's attachment to it. The same mind that hooks onto things can let go of them, and in letting go there is freedom.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Gives the verse as the last of eleven slokas on mind; notes the manuscript reading 'vishayasaktam muktyai' and the commentator's view that the preceding line is easy, which Müller disputes.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: The mind engrossed in worldly pleasures leads to bondage; freed from their influence it leads to liberation. Explanations of liberation other than this inward turn are called mere book learning.

commentaries.who: Amritabindu Upanishad 1-2, tr. K. Narayanasvami Aiyar (1914)
commentaries.gist: The same verse follows the teaching that mind is pure or impure according to desire; the aspirant should therefore keep the mind free of longing for sense objects.

up_maitrayani.86.practical_reading: Freedom starts with noticing what your mind is hooked on; you cannot always change circumstances, but you can work on the grip. Teachers use it to introduce non-attachment as a skill.
misreadings: Not 'your suffering is your own fault'
Not a claim that external injustice or illness doesn't matter
'Free of objects' does not mean blank or uncaring
cautions: Can feel dismissive to someone facing real external hardship (abuse, poverty, illness)
For clinical anxiety or depression, add that skills and support matter; this is not a cure
not_for: victims of abuse or injustice, where it could sound like 'just change your attitude'
fresh grief

up_maitreya.24.context: Chapter 1 of the Maitreya Upanishad retells the Maitri story of Brihadratha. In chapter 2 the sage Maitreya goes to Kailasa and asks Shiva for the highest truth. Shiva answers by turning outer temple worship into an inner one: the body is the shrine, the living self is Shiva, and ignorance is the stale offering to clear away. The verses that follow redefine knowledge, meditation, bathing and purity, then describe the renunciant's life.
up_maitreya.24.core_teaching: The truest temple is your own body and the divine is your own deepest self; real worship is dropping ignorance and recognising 'I am That'.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar tr., Maitreya Upanishad II (Thirty Minor Upanishads, 1914)
commentaries.gist: Gives the verse as Mahadeva's reply to Maitreya's request for the highest truth, followed by the renunciant's rules: begging food, contemplating non-duality, the body as impure and to be washed.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), on the parallel verses in the Skanda Upanishad, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Explains this as mental worship, the essential means to self-knowledge: the jiva is the Shiva installed in the body-temple, ignorance is thrown away like faded flowers from the altar, and worship is the conviction 'I am the deity'.

up_maitreya.24.practical_reading: Teachers use it to make worship inward and daily: treat your body with respect as a shrine, and clear away what clouds your sense of the sacred in you. It also supports self-respect.
misreadings: Not 'I am God, so I can do as I please'
Not a rejection of temple worship for householders; it is addressed to renunciants
'Body is a temple' here is not a fitness slogan, though care for the body fits
cautions: The same chapter soon calls the body impure and foul, so don't pair the two passages carelessly
Strongly non-dual ('I am Shiva'); some devotional readers may find it presumptuous
not_for: someone with an eating disorder, if it slips into rules about purity
readers strongly committed to dualist devotion, without explanation

up_maitreya.25.context: Continuing his answer to Maitreya, Shiva redefines four daily religious acts in inner terms: knowledge, meditation, ritual bathing and ritual purity. The next lines tell the renunciant to drink the nectar of Brahman, beg only enough food to keep the body going, and live alone thinking of the One.
up_maitreya.25.core_teaching: Outer rituals point to inner disciplines: real knowledge is seeing oneness, real meditation is a mind let go of objects, real bathing is washing out mental stains, real purity is mastery of the senses.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar tr., Maitreya Upanishad II (1914)
commentaries.gist: Renders the four definitions as cognition of everything as non-different from oneself, drawing the mind from sense objects, purifying the mind's impurities, and subduing the senses.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), on the Skanda Upanishad parallel, as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (1941)
commentaries.gist: Knowledge is seeing the identity of the individual and the Supreme; ablution is giving up impure mental tendencies (vasanas); purification is control of both inner and outer senses.

commentaries.who: Skanda Upanishad, tr. K. Narayanasvami Aiyar (1914)
commentaries.gist: The same four definitions appear, followed by begging for alms, living alone and dwelling on the non-dual One as the path to liberation.

up_maitreya.25.practical_reading: Teachers use it to reinterpret daily routines: as you bathe, also let go of a grudge; as you clean, also rein in a habit. It helps people for whom ritual has gone mechanical.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of physical hygiene or of ritual for those who value it
'Seeing no difference' is not denial of real differences in need or justice
cautions: Addressed to renunciants; for householders frame it as an inner layer added to ordinary life, not a call to abandon it
not_for: someone with OCD around cleanliness or purity
readers who may take 'restraint of the senses' as a demand for harsh self-denial

up_mundaka.1.1.3.context: The Mundaka opens with the lineage of the teaching from Brahma down to Angiras. Then Shaunaka, a wealthy householder, comes to Angiras in the prescribed way with one question: what is it that, once known, makes everything known? Angiras answers by distinguishing two kinds of knowledge.
up_mundaka.1.1.3.core_teaching: The seeker asks for the one reality behind all the variety of things, the way knowing gold lets you understand every gold ornament. Asking that question properly, with humility, is where the path starts.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: 'Duly' shows the rule for approaching a teacher applies to everyone, not only Shaunaka. The question assumes one cause of all variety, as knowing gold lets one know all the different gold pieces.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909), translator's note on Madhva's reading
commentaries.gist: Treats the question as threefold: what authoritative teaching reveals rites and deities, what more must be known to grasp their fruit, and what more is needed actually to gain it.

up_mundaka.1.1.3.practical_reading: Behind many scattered worries lies one real question; teachers use Shaunaka as a model of bringing that question humbly to someone who knows. Success in worldly life (he was a rich householder) did not answer it.
misreadings: Not a promise of encyclopaedic knowledge of every fact
Not a claim that worldly learning is useless
cautions: Low risk. Mentions a formal teacher relationship; for readers without a guru, frame as seeking good guidance.
not_for: someone needing immediate practical comfort in crisis
speaks_to: successful people who feel something is missing
curiosity about what life is ultimately about

up_mundaka.1.1.4.context: Asked for the one thing that makes all known, Angiras first says there are two kinds of knowledge to be known, the higher and the lower. He lists the four Vedas and six auxiliary sciences as lower, and calls the higher that by which the imperishable is reached. The following verses describe that imperishable as the source of all beings.
up_mundaka.1.1.4.core_teaching: All learning, even of scripture, is lower knowledge; the higher knowledge is the direct knowing of what never perishes. Shankara stresses this is not mastering the Upanishad's words but realising what they point to.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: Lower knowledge concerns the means and fruits of good and bad acts; higher is knowing the supreme self. Even the Upanishads as mere words are lower; the higher is the realisation they convey, needing a teacher and renunciation.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: The same Vedas are lower when used only for ritual and higher when understood as speaking of Vishnu; there is really one body of scripture, read in two ways.

up_mundaka.1.1.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it to separate information and skill from wisdom: degrees and expertise are valuable but do not by themselves settle the question of meaning. Keep learning, and also seek what learning points beyond.
misreadings: Not contempt for science, skills or education
Not a claim that the Vedas are false; Shankara keeps them as valid in their sphere
cautions: Calling all learning 'lower' can sting a student under exam pressure; frame as two complementary kinds.
not_for: someone who left education and feels inadequate, if it is read as dismissing their worth
speaks_to: students and professionals who feel knowledge isn't enough

up_mundaka.1.2.12.context: Having shown that rituals win only temporary worlds, Angiras says the thoughtful person, after examining those worlds, grows dispassionate because the uncreated cannot be produced by action. Such a person should go humbly to a qualified teacher. The next verse tells the teacher to give the full teaching to a calm, ready student.
up_mundaka.1.2.12.core_teaching: Whatever is achieved by effort is itself temporary; what is eternal cannot be manufactured. Seeing this, a seeker turns humbly to a teacher who both knows the texts and lives the truth.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: Everything action can do is produce, reach, refine or modify; none of these yields the eternal. Disgusted with such ends, the seeker should go to a teacher, since even a scholar should not seek Brahman-knowledge on his own.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as mastering and then letting go of desire for worlds gained by works, because the uncreated world of Brahman is not won through created ones; then approaching an inspired teacher with humility.

up_mundaka.1.2.12.practical_reading: Teachers use it when achievement stops satisfying: you cannot build your way to peace, so look for someone wiser and learn. A good mentor needs both knowledge and lived integrity.
misreadings: Not a rejection of work or achievement as such
Not a demand to obey any self-proclaimed guru; the verse specifies learning and real grounding
The word 'brahmana' should not be used to exclude anyone
cautions: The original names a brahmana as the seeker; keep the reading caste-neutral.
Guru language can be exploited; stress the teacher's qualifications.
not_for: someone recovering from abuse by a spiritual teacher
people under financial pressure who need achievement to survive
speaks_to: looking for a mentor or teacher

up_mundaka.1.2.8.context: Angiras has just described the Vedic sacrifices and their heavenly rewards, then called them 'unsafe boats' that cannot carry one across. This verse describes those who trust in rituals and rewards while thinking themselves wise. The next verses say such people return to lower worlds once their merit runs out, and that a true seeker turns away from works to find a teacher.
up_mundaka.1.2.8.core_teaching: People who equate religious busyness or status with wisdom wander in circles of suffering, and lead others the same way. Self-satisfaction blocks learning.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: They flatter themselves that they know all that is worth knowing, and wander afflicted by old age and sickness, like blind men following a blind guide into ditches and thorns.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: Rendered as fools, wise in their own eyes and oppressed by misery, going round and round like the blind led by the blind; no separate bhashya note on this verse.

up_mundaka.1.2.8.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a check on spiritual or intellectual arrogance and on following confident leaders blindly. Ask whether you, or the people you follow, are actually seeing.
misreadings: Not a licence to call others blind or to mock religious people
Not a rejection of all ritual; it targets treating ritual reward as the final goal
cautions: Harsh tone; use for self-examination, not as a judgement on the reader's loved ones.
not_for: someone already ashamed after being deceived (it can sound like blame)
readers in fresh grief
speaks_to: being misled by gurus, influencers or confident experts

up_mundaka.2.2.4.context: In the previous verse Angiras tells the seeker to take up the great weapon of the Upanishad as a bow, fit to it an arrow sharpened by meditation, draw it with a mind absorbed in That, and hit the imperishable. Here he explains the image: Om is the bow, the self the arrow, Brahman the target. The verses after describe Brahman as that in which the worlds are woven.
up_mundaka.2.2.4.core_teaching: Meditation on Om carries the attention, as a bow sends an arrow, to rest in Brahman; with undistracted focus the self becomes one with its aim. Shankara: the 'hit' is the end of identifying with the body.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: Repeating Om purifies the self so it settles in Brahman unobstructed, as a bow drives an arrow home. The arrow is the supreme self appearing as the individual; the hit is dropping the notion that the body is the self.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: Translates the arrow as the mind and says the one with concentrated thought enters the target; the translator's note reads the verses as teaching hearing, reflection and meditation on Brahman as a method of worship.

up_mundaka.2.2.4.practical_reading: Teachers use the archer to teach steady attention: a single point of focus, a support like a mantra or breath, and no distraction. It also applies to work that needs deep focus.
misreadings: Not just a productivity tip; the target in the text is Brahman
Not about aggression or competitiveness
cautions: Low risk. Avoid turning it into pressure to perform.
not_for: someone exhausted and needing rest rather than more focus

up_mundaka.2.2.8.context: Angiras has been describing Brahman as the inner controller dwelling in the heart, to be meditated on as Om. This verse states the fruit of seeing it. The next verses describe Brahman as the stainless light in the golden sheath, the light by which sun, moon and fire shine.
up_mundaka.2.2.8.core_teaching: Directly seeing the highest unties the knot of desire and ignorance, ends doubt, and exhausts accumulated karma. Shankara adds that the karma that has already produced this present life still runs its course.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: The knot is the mass of desires lodged in the intellect, not in the self. On seeing the self as 'I am He', doubts end and stored karma is destroyed, except the karma already bearing fruit as this birth.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: Madhva glosses 'parāvara' as Vishnu, compared with whom even the highest beings are low; the translator's notes read the knot as the bonds of ignorance, desire and karma on the soul, cut when the Lord is seen.

up_mundaka.2.2.8.practical_reading: Teachers use it for the relief of real clarity: when you truly understand, inner knots and endless second-guessing fall away. It also offers hope that the past need not define you.
misreadings: Not a promise that consequences of past actions vanish instantly in practical life
Not intellectual certainty or winning an argument
cautions: Talk of karma wearing away may raise questions of guilt; keep it hopeful rather than transactional.
not_for: someone using it to dismiss responsibility for recent harm

up_mundaka.3.1.1.context: The third Mundaka opens with this image right after the teaching that the knot of the heart is cut by seeing the highest. The next verse says the bird that eats, sunk in the same tree, grieves at its helplessness, but when it sees the other, the Lord, and his glory, its grief goes. Shankara treats the verse as a summary restatement of the truth from a new angle.
up_mundaka.3.1.1.core_teaching: In each of us there is the self that tastes the joys and pains of action, and the witness that only watches. Recognising the witness brings freedom from the eater's sorrow.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: The tree is the body; the eating bird is the individual self tasting pleasure and pain through ignorance; the other is the ever-free Lord who directs by mere presence as witness, as a king rules simply by being there.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: The soul eats bitter and sweet fruit alike, as if sweet; the Lord does not eat the soul's karmic fruit and never suffers. The verse shows the soul and God as distinct even while dwelling together.

up_mundaka.3.1.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to teach the observer stance: alongside the part of you caught up in events, there is a part that can watch without being swept away. Mindfulness practice often starts here.
misreadings: Not detachment as coldness toward others
Not a claim that experience doesn't matter
cautions: Low risk. Advaita and Dvaita disagree whether the birds are finally one or two; avoid presenting either as the only reading.
not_for: someone dissociating after trauma, where 'just watch' may deepen disconnection
speaks_to: feeling lonely (the companion bird is always there)

up_mundaka.3.1.2.context: 3.1.1: two birds, close companions, sit on one tree; one eats the fruit, the other just watches. This verse: the person sunk on that tree grieves, confused by helplessness, until he sees the other, the Lord, and his greatness, and then sorrow leaves. 3.1.3 goes on: seeing the shining creator, the knower shakes off merit and demerit and reaches the highest sameness.
up_mundaka.3.1.2.core_teaching: We suffer while we identify with the struggling self; seeing the calm witnessing presence (the Lord) and its greatness frees us from sorrow.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: The soul is deluded by the Lord's own free power and grieves; it is freed when it sees the ever-worshipped Lord as distinct from itself. The translator's note: discontent binds, contentment frees.

up_mundaka.3.1.2.practical_reading: When you feel helpless and swamped, step back and notice the part of you that can watch the struggle without being lost in it. That steadier view eases the grief, even if circumstances don't change.
misreadings: Not 'your grief is just ignorance'
Advaita says you ARE the other bird, Dvaita says you see God as other; don't flatten these
cautions: Shankara's own examples of grief are a dead son and a dead wife; don't quote the bhashya to someone bereaved
Promises sorrow 'leaves'; for fresh grief, say 'eases' rather than 'ends'
not_for: acute fresh grief, if presented as 'grief is delusion'
speaks_to: being lost in one's own story

up_mundaka.3.1.4.context: This follows the two-birds image (3.1.1-3): the one who sees the radiant Lord is freed from grief and becomes stainless. This verse describes how such a knower lives. The next verse (3.1.5) says the Self is reached through truth, austerity, right knowledge and self-control.
up_mundaka.3.1.4.core_teaching: One who sees the one Self shining in all beings finds delight within, has nothing to prove in argument, and remains engaged. The commentators disagree about what that engagement is.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Seeing only the Self everywhere, the knower has nothing else to talk about. 'Active' means knowledge, meditation and freedom from desire. Mixing ritual work with knowledge is rejected, because outer activity and inner delight conflict.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), Srisa Chandra Vasu tr.
commentaries.gist: Seeing that the Lord is the real doer, the knower stops boasting 'I act'. He contemplates the Lord's play, and when not absorbed he stays active in worship and duties and teaches seekers.

up_mundaka.3.1.4.practical_reading: A joy that does not depend on winning arguments or outside props, together with steady engagement in one's own work, without the need to dominate.
misreadings: Not 'avoid all disagreement'; conflict avoidance is not the point
For Shankara 'active' does not mean hustle; for Madhva it means service and worship
'Delight in the Self' is not self-absorption
cautions: On a 'running on empty' day, 'active' should not be heard as 'do more'
not_for: someone who needs to speak up, for example about abuse; do not read it as 'stay quiet'
speaks_to: needing an inner source of joy
people worn out by constant argument

data_flags.translation_note: Two loose spots. (1) 'Does not talk over others' and the line 'the wise stop arguing' are modern glosses of na ativadi. Shankara: he does not talk of anything other than the Self. Madhva (Vasu tr.): he no longer claims 'I am the doer' and...

up_mundaka.3.1.6.context: Angiras is listing the aids to self-knowledge: truth, austerity, right knowledge and continence (3.1.5). This verse praises truth as the strongest of them. The next verse describes Brahman as vast, self-luminous and near, seen within by the wise.
up_mundaka.3.1.6.core_teaching: Truthfulness is the decisive aid on the spiritual path; the truthful prevail, and the path of the sages is kept open by truth. Shankara stresses truthful speech; Madhva reads Truth as the Lord himself.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: It is the person who speaks truth who wins, as the world sees liars defeated by the truthful. Truth keeps the path of the gods open for sages free of deceit, pride and desire.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: Satya is Vishnu, called true because he has all good qualities; those opposed to him are 'untrue' and do not reach him. The highest abode of truth is Vishnu's Vaikuntha.

up_mundaka.3.1.6.practical_reading: Teachers use it to encourage honesty when lying looks easier: truth builds a road you can keep walking. Integrity is part of spiritual practice, not separate from it.
misreadings: Truth wins in the long run; it is not a promise of quick or worldly victory (our misuse note is right)
Not a licence for blunt cruelty in the name of truth
Not a nationalist slogan in its original setting
cautions: Someone who told the truth and suffered for it may find 'truth always wins' hollow; frame it as the path, not a guaranteed outcome.
not_for: someone punished for honesty and still hurting, without acknowledgement of that cost
speaks_to: temptation to lie or cut corners

up_mundaka.3.2.2.context: The second section of the third Mundaka opens by praising those who worship the knower of Brahman without desire. This verse contrasts the person driven by desires with the one whose desires are fulfilled in the self. The next verse says the self is not won by study or intellect but reveals itself to the one it chooses.
up_mundaka.3.2.2.core_teaching: Brooding on desires keeps us bound to chase them, life after life; for one fulfilled in the self, desires dissolve even here and now.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: Renouncing desire is the primary aid to liberation. Whoever covets objects, brooding on their virtues, is reborn wherever desire leads; for one whose desire is the self, desires stop arising because their causes are destroyed.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: One who thinks objects of desire are the highest is born where they can be enjoyed; but desires vanish even on earth for one who aspires to the highest and whose mind is content. Direct knowledge alone ends desire entirely.

up_mundaka.3.2.2.practical_reading: Teachers use it to show that wanting tends to breed more wanting, while inner contentment loosens desire's grip. Notice which desires you keep feeding by dwelling on them.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of all wanting or of healthy ambition
'Whole in himself' does not mean self-sufficient isolation
cautions: Rebirth is assumed ('born here and there'); keep it gentle for readers who don't hold that belief.
not_for: someone grieving a lost desire (a child, a partner) who may hear 'stop wanting'

up_mundaka.3.2.4.context: The previous verse says the self is not reached by study, intellect or much learning, but by the one it chooses. This verse adds the human side: strength, care and the right kind of discipline are needed. The next verses describe sages who, having attained it, enter the All.
up_mundaka.3.2.4.core_teaching: Self-knowledge needs inner strength, attentiveness and the right kind of discipline; whoever strives with these means reaches Brahman's home.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: Strength is that born of steadiness in the self; heedlessness is distraction by attachment to family and possessions; tapas here means knowledge, and its mark is renunciation. With these aids, the knower's self enters Brahman.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909), with translator's notes
commentaries.gist: The austerity must be sattvic and scripturally sanctioned. Hearing and reflection support devotion but are secondary; the chief means is grace, received by the devotee who strives and prays.

up_mundaka.3.2.4.practical_reading: Teachers use it against both laziness and showy austerity: real progress needs inner strength and attentiveness, with practice aimed at the right goal. Effort and grace work together.
misreadings: 'Weak' does not mean physically weak or ill
Not a call to harsh self-mortification
cautions: 'Not won by the weak' can wound someone who is depressed, disabled or exhausted; clarify that strength here is inner resolve.
not_for: someone with depression or chronic illness who already feels weak
a reader in grief
speaks_to: procrastination in spiritual or personal practice
practice that has become showy or rigid

up_mundaka.3.2.8.context: The preceding verses describe the sages who know Brahman entering the All at death, their parts returning to their sources. This verse gives the image of rivers entering the sea. The next verse says the knower of Brahman becomes Brahman, crossing grief and sin.
up_mundaka.3.2.8.core_teaching: As rivers lose their separate names in the sea, the knower lets go of the identity built from name and form and reaches the highest. Advaita reads this as merging; Dvaita as reaching God without losing the self.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: As the Ganga and other rivers give up their distinct identity in the sea, the knower, freed from name and form created by ignorance, reaches the self-luminous Person beyond the unmanifest.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: Rivers only seem to lose name and form to ordinary eyes; the wind knows each drop and returns it as rain. Likewise the freed soul keeps its individuality; name and form are never actually lost.

up_mundaka.3.2.8.practical_reading: Teachers use it for letting go of a small, defensive sense of self and finding belonging in something larger. It can also speak to the ego's fear of losing itself.
misreadings: Not a description of death as annihilation
Not a call to erase one's personality or culture
cautions: Often read at funerals; for fresh grief, 'giving up name and form' may feel like loss of the person; use the Dvaita reading or hold back.
not_for: fresh bereavement unless handled gently
someone fearing loss of self in depression or dissociation

up_narayana.16.context: The verse is a visualisation to hold in mind before worship or recitation: Vishnu lying on the cosmic serpent, calm, vast as the sky, dark as a rain-cloud, with Lakshmi. It stands outside any narrative and is used at the start of the Vishnu Sahasranama and in daily prayer. The Narayana Upanishad itself is a short prose text on everything coming from and returning to Narayana, and on the eight-syllable mantra 'Om namo Narayanaya'.
up_narayana.16.core_teaching: A meditation image of God as utterly peaceful even while resting on a serpent, holding up the universe; bowing to him takes away the fear that comes with worldly life.
up_narayana.16.practical_reading: Commonly recited at the start of prayer or before sleep to settle fear; the image of calm repose on a serpent is often explained by teachers as peace amid danger. (Not sourced to a classical commentary.)
misreadings: Not an Upanishadic statement of doctrine; it is a devotional visualisation
Not a promise that worldly dangers will disappear
cautions: Do not cite it as Upanishad scripture in user-facing text.
Sectarian (Vaishnava) image; fine for devotional plans but label clearly.
not_for: plans presenting Upanishadic philosophy
readers expecting a sourced scriptural teaching
speaks_to: anxiety and fear before sleep or exams
wanting a calming image to hold

data_flags.attribution_note: Reference and speaker are both wrong: it is a devotional dhyana verse of uncertain origin, not Upanishadic text. Our own our_note already says it is 'appended to printed editions and is not part of the Upanishad's own text'; the ref should not present it as...

up_niralamb.13.context: The Niralamba Upanishad opens by promising to explain, in question-and-answer form, what must be known to end suffering. It defines Brahman, Ishvara and the jiva, then says Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, the gods, humans, women, animals and the castes are all Brahman. This answer on jati comes next; the following questions define karma, knowledge, happiness, heaven and hell.
up_niralamb.13.core_teaching: Caste is not in the body or in the self; it is a social convention for practical life. At the level of the self, there is no birth-group at all.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Glosses jati as division based on birth and says it belongs neither to skin colour, blood, flesh, bone nor the self; it is a convention that comes from everyday transactions.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar tr., Niralamba Upanishad (1914)
commentaries.gist: Places the answer right after the teaching that gods, humans, women, animals and the castes are all Brahman, with no manyness at all; caste cannot refer to the body and is merely conventional.

up_niralamb.13.practical_reading: Used today to argue that birth-group identity says nothing about a person's worth or inner nature. Teachers apply it against caste prejudice and, by extension, racial or colour prejudice.
misreadings: The text calls caste a convention, not unreal for all purposes; avoid overstating it as a social reform manifesto in its own time
Not a claim that caste discrimination doesn't happen
cautions: Caste is a live and painful issue; do not use the verse to dismiss someone's experience of discrimination ('caste doesn't really exist')
Avoid naming specific castes
not_for: contexts where it would be used to deny lived discrimination

up_niralamb.21.context: In the same catechism, after defining happiness as knowing Brahman and sorrow as dwelling on worldly objects, the Upanishad defines heaven and hell. It then goes on to bondage (thoughts of 'I' and 'mine') and liberation. The answers keep turning external religious ideas into states of mind and company.
up_niralamb.21.core_teaching: Heaven and hell are not only places after death; good company lifts us now, and company sunk in hollow pursuits drags us down.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Companionship with the good is the heavenly state; companionship with people enamoured of the illusory pleasures of worldly life is hell, because it leads toward hell's torments.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar tr., Niralamba Upanishad (1914)
commentaries.gist: Translates svarga as association with Sat, noting it can mean good people or Brahman, and naraka as association with what produces worldly existence, the false.

up_niralamb.21.practical_reading: Teachers use it to stress how much the people around us shape our inner life: choose friends and influences that bring out the best in you. It fits advice on friendships, online spaces and habits.
misreadings: Not a licence to look down on or shun people as 'worldly'
Not a denial of afterlife teaching elsewhere; it gives an inner meaning
cautions: Can be used to justify cutting people off harshly; stress choosing influences, not condemning individuals.
not_for: someone isolated with no supportive company, who may feel condemned to 'hell'

up_prashn.19.context: Kabandhi asked where creatures come from. Pippalada answers with paired principles (life and matter, sun and moon, the two paths after death) and says householders who keep their vows reach the world of the moon. This verse closes the answer: the pure world of Brahman belongs to those free of crookedness, falsehood and deceit.
up_prashn.19.core_teaching: The pure state belongs to those without crookedness, lies or pretence. Shankara: householders' many dealings make these faults hard to avoid, so the path suits those whose lives remove their causes.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as the pure Brahma-loka for those with no crookedness, falsehood or dissimulation; the translator's note sums up the first question as a hierarchy of creative pairs under Vishnu.

up_prashn.19.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a simple integrity check: no twisting, no lying, no pretending. Being the same inside and outside is its own kind of purity.
misreadings: Not a claim that householders cannot be honest
Not a promise of heaven as a reward for good behaviour
cautions: Shankara's view that householder life breeds deceit may feel judgemental to families; present it as a warning about pressures, not a verdict.
not_for: someone consumed by guilt over past dishonesty, without a word on repair

up_prashn.23.context: Bhargava asked which powers sustain a creature and which is greatest. Pippalada tells a story: space, wind, fire, water, earth, speech, mind, eye and ear each boast that they hold up the body. Breath, the chief, tells them not to be deluded; they don't believe it, so breath begins to leave and all the others are pulled along. Convinced, they praise breath in the hymn that follows.
up_prashn.23.core_teaching: The vital breath is the support of all the faculties; when it goes, everything goes with it. The story teaches humility to the parts that think they run the whole.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: Seeing their lack of faith, Prana seemed to rise from the body in indignation; all the others rose and settled with it, as bees follow their king. Giving up disbelief and seeing Prana's greatness, the senses praise it gladly.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), as reported in S. C. Vasu's translation (1909)
commentaries.gist: Madhva takes 'abhimāna' to mean the body, not pride; Prana began to go out of the body to convince the doubting powers. The translator sets this against Shankara's 'wounded pride' reading.

up_prashn.23.practical_reading: Teachers use it for teamwork and humility: the flashy parts depend on a quiet centre that holds everything together. It is also used to introduce breath awareness.
misreadings: Not a medical claim
Not praise of pride; in Shankara's reading breath acts to correct the others' disbelief
cautions: Describes life leaving the body; could touch someone who recently watched a person die.
not_for: someone who recently sat with a dying person
respiratory illness or ICU contexts
speaks_to: taking the basics for granted (health, breath, support staff)

up_prashn.3.context: Six seekers devoted to Brahman come to the sage Pippalada with fuel in hand, hoping he will explain everything. Here he asks them to stay another year with discipline, continence and faith before asking. After the year each asks one question, which gives the Upanishad its six chapters.
up_prashn.3.core_teaching: Deep questions need preparation; the teacher asks for a year of disciplined living first. His 'if we know' shows humility, not doubt.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: Though they had already practised austerity, they are to live another year with special care for continence and faith and in service of the teacher. 'If we know' shows the teacher's freedom from conceit, not uncertainty.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909), translator's note
commentaries.gist: The 'if' shows the teacher's modesty; the pupil should come without doubting the teacher and serve him, and the teacher must love the pupil.

up_prashn.3.practical_reading: Teachers use it to value patience and readiness: some answers only make sense after you have lived differently for a while. It also models a teacher who admits limits.
misreadings: Not a demand that anyone wait a year before seeking help
Not an excuse for gatekeeping knowledge
cautions: Celibacy (brahmacarya) may need gentle framing for householders as general self-restraint.
not_for: someone in crisis who needs help now
speaks_to: building discipline before a big change

up_prashn.72.context: This opens the last of the six questions. Sukesha tells Pippalada that a Kosala prince once asked him about the person of sixteen parts; he admitted he didn't know rather than bluff, and the prince drove off in silence. Now Sukesha asks Pippalada where that person is. Pippalada answers that the person is right here within (Vasu's Madhva translation: 'in this heart').
up_prashn.72.core_teaching: Honest 'I don't know' is better than an impressive bluff; lying withers a person from the root. The story also shows how hard this knowledge is to get.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: The story spurs seekers by showing how hard this knowledge is. Sukesha explains his ignorance so the prince would believe him; a liar is destroyed in both worlds. Knowledge should go to the worthy, and falsehood never be spoken.

commentaries.who: Madhva school (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu (1909), translator's note
commentaries.gist: Gives the same story; the note says this last chapter shows the Lord rules souls even when released, and presents Prana as the great saviour and mediator.

up_prashn.72.practical_reading: Teachers use it to give permission to say 'I don't know', at work, as a parent, or as a teacher. Integrity costs a moment of embarrassment; lying costs much more.
misreadings: Not shame at not knowing; the point is honesty about it
Not a literal curse that liars will physically wither
cautions: Low risk. Avoid making it a threat ('liars dry up').
not_for: someone already ashamed of past lies, if presented as a curse
speaks_to: parents and teachers asked hard questions

up_shiv_sankalp.1.context: Book 34 of the White Yajurveda opens with six verses, each ending with the refrain 'may that mind of mine be of auspicious resolve'. This first verse describes the mind as divine, travelling far in waking and in sleep. The following verses praise the mind as the means of sacrifice, the seat of wisdom and memory, and the charioteer of the person.
up_shiv_sankalp.1.core_teaching: The mind is a powerful, far-roaming light that illumines all the senses; the prayer is that this power be turned to good intentions.
