commentaries.who: R. T. H. Griffith, notes to his translation (Texts of the White Yajurveda, 1899)
commentaries.gist: Says the first six verses form a hymn regarded as an Upanishad, named Shivasankalpa from its refrain; glosses the refrain as having an auspicious resolve and the 'one light' as illuminator of the senses.

up_shiv_sankalp.1.practical_reading: Used as a morning or bedtime prayer for good intentions; teachers apply it to setting the mind's direction before the day, since the mind will wander anyway.
misreadings: Not a demand to stop the mind from wandering
Not a magic formula to control thoughts
cautions: Low risk. Gentle prayer.
not_for: someone with intrusive thoughts who may feel guilty for 'bad intentions'

up_shiv_sankalp.6.context: This closes the six-verse prayer on the mind. After praising the mind as wisdom, memory and the hub in which all knowledge is set like spokes, the hymn ends with the charioteer image. The next verse in the Samhita begins unrelated ritual verses in praise of food.
up_shiv_sankalp.6.core_teaching: The mind steers a person the way a charioteer steers horses; since it decides where we go, we pray that it be set on good.

commentaries.who: R. T. H. Griffith, translation and notes (Texts of the White Yajurveda, 1899)
commentaries.gist: Renders the mind as guiding men like a skilful charioteer with reins, dwelling in the heart and swiftest; notes that the six verses are a separate hymn called Shivasankalpa and that the rest of book 34 is a miscellany.

up_shiv_sankalp.6.practical_reading: Teachers use the charioteer image for self-direction: the mind holds the reins of your actions, so steady it with good intentions. A short daily prayer for clear direction.
misreadings: Not mind over body in a harsh sense
Not a claim that one can control all outcomes
cautions: Low risk.
not_for: someone blaming themselves for things outside their control
speaks_to: students and young adults choosing a direction

up_shwetashwetar.1.1.context: The Upanishad opens with a group of Brahman-seekers raising the basic questions together. The next verse lists the candidate causes then debated (time, nature, necessity, chance, the elements, the person) and rejects them. Through meditation the sages then see the power of God hidden in its own qualities as the true cause.
up_shwetashwetar.1.1.core_teaching: The Upanishad starts from honest, shared questions about origin, sustenance, destiny and why we live through joy and sorrow. Inquiry, not belief, opens the text.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), as reported in Röer's 1853 translation notes
commentaries.gist: 'Kim' may ask what Brahman's nature is, or whether Brahman is a cause at all, and if so whether material, efficient or both. 'Where we rest' means at the world's dissolution.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884), note
commentaries.gist: Translates 'Is Brahman the cause?', saying Shankara himself prefers this when he later recaps the question as 'is Brahman the cause or time and the rest'; notes textual errors in Röer's edition.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma, The Svetasvatara Upanisad (1916), notes citing commentators
commentaries.gist: Lists three commentarial readings of the first question; observes that we evidently don't control our own joy and sorrow, so some overseer must govern them.

up_shwetashwetar.1.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it to honour big questions: where did I come from, what sustains me, where am I going, who or what governs my ups and downs. Asking them together, with others, is itself a spiritual act.
misreadings: Not doubt for its own sake; the questions lead to meditation and an answer
Not a fatalistic claim that we have no say in our lives
cautions: Low risk. 'Who governs our sorrows' can raise the problem of suffering; don't force an answer on the reader.
not_for: someone in acute grief who needs comfort rather than open questions
speaks_to: after a major life event that shakes assumptions

up_shwetashwetar.1.15.context: The preceding verses compare the self to fire hidden in fire-sticks: present but unseen until drilled out, as meditation on Om draws out the self from the body. This verse gives four more images of something hidden in a substance and drawn out by effort. The next verse says the self pervades all like butter in milk, rooted in self-knowledge and austerity.
up_shwetashwetar.1.15.core_teaching: The self is already present within, as oil is in seed or fire in wood, but it has to be drawn out by truthfulness and disciplined effort.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853), following Shankara's commentary
commentaries.gist: Each image implies a process: pressing the seed, churning the curd, digging the riverbed, rubbing the sticks; likewise the self is perceived within by one who looks with truth and with austerity that subdues senses and mind.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884), notes
commentaries.gist: Explains 'streams' as dry riverbeds that give water when dug; notes the line reads better with the Brahmopanishad's variant, and that the seeker and the self sought are the same.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: The Supreme Self is to be found not somewhere outside but in one's own mind, obtained by meditation as oil by pressing and fire by friction; tapas here is concentration of mind and senses.

up_shwetashwetar.1.15.practical_reading: Teachers use it for patience in inner work: what you seek is not missing, only hidden, and steady practice (honesty, discipline, meditation) brings it out the way churning brings out butter.
misreadings: Not 'you already have it, so no effort is needed'
Not harsh asceticism; tapas is focused effort
cautions: Low risk.
not_for: someone exhausted, if 'effort' is stressed over 'already within'

up_shwetashwetar.3.17.context: The preceding verse, borrowed from the Purusha hymn, says the Supreme has hands, feet, eyes and ears everywhere. This verse corrects any literal reading: he lights up the work of every sense but has no senses himself. The next verse describes the embodied self in the city of nine gates.
up_shwetashwetar.3.17.core_teaching: The Lord gives every sense its power without having senses; he rules all yet is also the shelter, and in one reading the friend, of all.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853), notes following Shankara
commentaries.gist: He shines through the qualities of the outer senses and of the mind (sound, colour, doubt, decision) yet has none of these organs; renders the close as lord, ruler and infinite support of all.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Separate from all senses yet reflecting their qualities, the lord and ruler and great refuge of all; in the neighbouring note, Shankara explains 'ten fingers beyond' as endless or as the heart's position.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: The verse removes the hint from 3.16 that God literally has hands and feet; he is the life-giver and sole master of the senses, only seeming to have them. Records 'friend' as another reading.

up_shwetashwetar.3.17.practical_reading: Teachers draw comfort from it: the power behind all things is not distant but a refuge, and in the popular reading a friend. It suits prayers of trust.
misreadings: Not that God is a human-like friend with needs; he is beyond the senses
The 'friend' wording depends on a variant; avoid overstating it as the only reading
cautions: If quoting 'friend', mention it is one reading.
not_for: readers who need strict textual precision without the variant explained
speaks_to: longing for a sense of being held

up_shwetashwetar.3.20.context: After describing the all-pervading Person who has no senses yet works through them all, the seer turns inward: this vast reality is also smaller than the smallest and lives in the heart. The next verse is the seer's own testimony: 'I know this unageing, ancient one, the self of all'.
up_shwetashwetar.3.20.core_teaching: The infinite lives in the heart of every being; seeing it, by grace and with grasping dropped, ends sorrow.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884), translation and note
commentaries.gist: One who has left grief behind sees the majesty of the passionless Lord by the Creator's grace; Müller had to alter his Katha translation because the Shvetashvatara recension reads 'akratum' and 'īśam'.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853), following Shankara
commentaries.gist: Renders it as seeing the glorious ruler as devoid of action, by the grace of the creator, and so becoming free from grief; notes the verse is taken from the Katha with different readings.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: The verse teaches that spiritual vision depends on grace; records both readings of 'dhātu-prasāda', the Creator's grace or the purity of the senses and mind.

up_shwetashwetar.3.20.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say the sacred is not far away but in your own heart, and that grace and letting go of grasping open the way. It is a verse of hope after sorrow.
misreadings: Grace is not a reward for being good enough (our misuse note is right)
Not passivity: the Katha context pairs it with inner discipline
cautions: Promises freedom from sorrow; for fresh grief present it as a horizon, not a demand to stop grieving.
not_for: someone in acute grief who may hear 'you should be free of sorrow by now'

up_shwetashwetar.3.5.context: Chapter 3 praises the one Rudra who rules the worlds and asks him for good understanding (3.4). Verses 5-6 are prayers taken from the Yajurveda: show us your kind form, and turn your arrow away from people and creatures. The chapter then shifts to the vast Person who pervades all.
up_shwetashwetar.3.5.core_teaching: The same power that can be fearsome has a kind, peaceful face; the devotee asks to be looked on with that face.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853), notes following Shankara
commentaries.gist: Rudra here stands for the supreme spirit; notes the verses come from the Vajasaneyi Samhita and that Mahidhara, the Yajurveda commentator, explains 'giriśanta' as Shankara does.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as a prayer to the mountain-dweller to look on us with his most blessed, auspicious, not-terrible form that reveals no evil; cites the Yajurveda parallels.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: Calls this a prayer for the manifestation of God's benevolent being and for grace bringing all that is good; explains 'giriśanta' as one who spreads happiness, with Kailasa a later association.

up_shwetashwetar.3.5.practical_reading: Used as a prayer when life feels harsh: asking to see the kind face of what frightens us. Teachers relate it to trusting that even hard forces have a benevolent side.
misreadings: Not a bargain to avoid all misfortune
Not a claim that God is only gentle; the verse acknowledges the fearsome side
cautions: Low risk. Rudra's 'fearsome' side may need a word for readers unfamiliar with it.
not_for: someone who may hear it as a promise that nothing bad will happen

up_shwetashwetar.4.11.context: Just before, the text calls nature (prakriti) maya and the great Lord its wielder, with the world made of his parts. This verse says knowing that one ruler of all sources brings lasting peace. The next verse repeats the earlier prayer to Rudra for good understanding.
up_shwetashwetar.4.11.core_teaching: One Lord stands behind every origin, and the whole world gathers into him and comes forth from him; knowing him brings a peace that does not end.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853), notes
commentaries.gist: Reads the sources as nature (first producer) and intellect, ego and subtle elements (derived producers), noting the Samkhya colour of the verse; the boon he grants is liberation, the peace absolute.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Translates: whoever has discerned the one who rules every germ, in whom all comes together and comes asunder, the blessing-giving adorable god, passes for ever into that peace.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: He is the independent governor and support of every cause, primary and secondary; notes another commentator reads 'comes together' as 'gains stability'; the peace is final, without return.

up_shwetashwetar.4.11.practical_reading: Teachers use it to ground peace in a sense of a single source behind life's comings and goings; things gather and scatter, but the ground remains.
misreadings: Not a promise that life's events will become peaceful
Not merely intellectual knowledge of a doctrine
cautions: Low risk.
not_for: someone needing practical help, if offered as a substitute

up_shwetashwetar.4.14.context: This verse comes in a run of 'knowing him, one attains...' sayings in chapter 4 (4.11 peace, 4.15 cutting death's bonds, 4.16 freedom from all fetters). Just before, the seer offers worship to the god who rules all two- and four-footed beings. Here he is described as the subtle, many-formed creator in the middle of the world's confusion.
up_shwetashwetar.4.14.core_teaching: Right in the middle of the world's tangle is the subtle, kind One who made and holds it all; knowing him brings unending peace.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Renders 'kalila' as chaos: the subtle, many-formed creator stands amid it and alone wraps the whole world; Müller glosses Shiva as 'the happy one'. Knowing him, one passes into peace for ever.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: The chaos is the world of appearances, the work of maya, like a fortress hard to overcome, with the Supreme as its untouched witness; another commentator reads it as darkness hiding him through ignorance.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853)
commentaries.gist: Renders 'within that which is impervious', glossed as the creation, with the subtle creator enveloping the universe; knowing the blessed one brings absolute peace.

up_shwetashwetar.4.14.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say peace is found in the middle of chaos, not after it ends: the kind presence is already inside the confusion.
misreadings: Peace here is inner steadiness, not a promise that outside chaos will stop (our misuse note is right)
cautions: Low risk; good for overwhelm.
not_for: someone who may feel told their real problems don't matter
speaks_to: overwhelm and chaos at work or home

up_shwetashwetar.4.15.context: Continuing the chapter's sayings on what knowing the Lord brings, this verse speaks of him as the world's guardian through time, hidden in all beings. The next verse compares him to the fine film on ghee, hidden in all beings, and says knowing him frees one from all fetters.
up_shwetashwetar.4.15.core_teaching: The Lord guards the world through time and is hidden in every being; sages and gods find their essence in him, and knowing him cuts through the bonds of death.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884), with Shankara's gloss in note
commentaries.gist: Shankara takes 'in time' as in former ages; sages and deities are 'united' in him because they find their true essence in Brahman. Knowing him cuts death's fetters.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: The verse points to the great sages who realised the Supreme and adds that we too, by the same methods, can be freed; the noose of death is glossed as darkness, ignorance, maya.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as the preserver at the due time, concealed in all beings, with whom the Brahma-seers and deities are united by concentration; knowing him cuts the bonds of death.

up_shwetashwetar.4.15.practical_reading: Teachers use it for steadiness about time and mortality: a guardian presence runs through the ages and through every being, and knowing it loosens the fear of death.
misreadings: Not a promise of physical immortality
Not a promise that loved ones will be protected from harm
cautions: Mentions death directly; for the recently bereaved, 'cutting death's noose' can feel hollow.
not_for: fresh grief after a death, unless handled carefully

up_shwetashwetar.4.21.context: The preceding verses say no one can grasp him above, across or in the middle, no likeness of him exists, and he is known only in the heart. Here the seer turns to personal prayer: someone afraid comes to the Unborn and asks to be protected by his kind face. The next verse is a Vedic prayer for family and livestock.
up_shwetashwetar.4.21.core_teaching: Fear can be the doorway to refuge: recognising the Unborn, one who is afraid turns to him and asks for protection by his gracious face.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), as reported in Röer's notes (1853)
commentaries.gist: 'Dakṣiṇa' means either auspicious or southern, the face turned to the south; Röer adds that the person is perturbed by the misery of the world.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Translates it as someone coming near trembling with the words 'Thou art unborn' and praying that Rudra's gracious face protect him for ever; notes the alternative senses of 'dakṣiṇa'.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: This verse and the next are prayers, since freedom from evil and reaching God depend on grace; the fearful one fears birth and the rest and turns to Rudra, destroyer of pain.

up_shwetashwetar.4.21.practical_reading: A prayer for anyone afraid. Teachers use it to say fear does not disqualify you; it can be what brings you to ask for help.
misreadings: A prayer for protection, not a guarantee that nothing bad will happen (our misuse note is right)
Not a replacement for medical, legal or emotional help
cautions: Very suitable for anxious readers; avoid implying that prayer alone will solve a crisis.
not_for: someone in immediate danger who needs practical help first

up_shwetashwetar.4.22.context: This closes chapter 4 right after the prayer of the frightened devotee. It is an old Rig Vedic prayer to Rudra not to harm children, lives, cattle or warriors, offered by people bringing oblations. Chapter 5 then turns to knowledge and ignorance in the imperishable Brahman.
up_shwetashwetar.4.22.core_teaching: A parent's and community's prayer: spare our children, our lives and livelihood; we keep calling on you.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884), note
commentaries.gist: Lists the Rig Veda and Samhita parallels and variant readings; notes 'sadasi' in the Shvetashvatara seems to rest on Shankara alone, while Shankarananda and Vijnanatman read 'sadam it', always.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as a plea not to injure children, grandchildren, lives, cows or horses, nor slay valiant men in anger, since the worshippers always invoke Rudra with oblations.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: Treats it with 4.21 as a prayer depending on God's grace, and glosses the grammar: prohibitive forms meaning 'do not destroy', 'bhāmita' as exasperated, worshippers 'full of oblations'.

up_shwetashwetar.4.22.practical_reading: Used by parents praying for their children's safety, and in times of illness or danger to family.
misreadings: Not a promise of a particular outcome (our misuse note is right)
Not a picture of an arbitrary angry god to be bribed
cautions: Mentions harm to children; may be very painful for parents who have lost a child or whose child is seriously ill
Does not replace medical help
not_for: bereaved parents
parents of a child in critical care, unless chosen by them

up_shwetashwetar.6.11.context: In the last chapter the seer describes the one God who, like a spider spinning thread, covers himself with what comes from nature. This verse is the fullest statement of that God as the hidden self in all beings. The next verse says the wise who see him in themselves have eternal happiness, not others.
up_shwetashwetar.6.11.core_teaching: One God is hidden in every being as its inner self: the witness of all actions, pure awareness, untouched by qualities.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884), with Shankara's gloss on the next verse
commentaries.gist: Translates the list of epithets; on the following verse notes Shankara's view that actions belong to the organs of living beings and do not affect the Highest Self, which stays passive.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: Each epithet answers an objection: 'one' against many souls, 'self-luminous' against materialism, 'hidden' because maya veils him, 'all-pervading' and 'inner self' so that pervading does not mean a second thing.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'mere thinking' as thought without any particular thought, and 'without qualities' as free of the three gunas; Röer reads the context through Samkhya, where only nature acts and the soul witnesses.

up_shwetashwetar.6.11.practical_reading: Teachers use it to ground respect for every being (the same divine is hidden in all) and to describe the inner witness that watches without being stained by what happens.
misreadings: Not pantheism in the sense that every act is divine or excused
'Overseer of actions' is not a surveillance image
cautions: Low risk.
not_for: someone who may hear 'witness' as being told to detach from pain they need to feel

up_shwetashwetar.6.18.context: Near the end of the Upanishad, after describing the Lord as the eternal among eternals and the light by which all shines, the seer makes a personal act of refuge as one seeking liberation. The next verse describes that God as partless, actionless, peaceful and the last bridge to immortality.
up_shwetashwetar.6.18.core_teaching: The source of all creation and revelation is also the light that makes self-knowledge dawn in us; the seeker, longing for freedom, takes refuge there.

commentaries.who: Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884), notes reporting commentators
commentaries.gist: Records the manuscript variants 'light of his own thoughts' and 'grace of his own thoughts'; Shankarananda explains the former as the witness of one's own understanding.

commentaries.who: Siddheshwar Varma (1916), notes
commentaries.gist: The prayer shows God's grace as a means to true knowledge, as in chapter 3; he is the illuminator of spiritual understanding, and 'creates' can mean in every cycle of creation.

commentaries.who: E. Röer tr. (1853)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as the seeker approaching the protection of the God who manifests knowledge of himself, who at the start of creation made Brahma and gave him the Vedas.

up_shwetashwetar.6.18.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a closing prayer of surrender after effort: having inquired and practised, the seeker asks for the light of understanding. It can be recited before study or meditation.
misreadings: Refuge is not a substitute for effort (our misuse note is right)
'Brahma' is the creator deity, not Brahman, the absolute
cautions: Low risk.
not_for: someone who wants purely secular framing

up_skand.1.context: The Skanda Upanishad opens with this thanksgiving and goes on to say that when the inner instruments fall away, only consciousness remains, which is Hari, Mahadeva and Brahman alike. It declares that Shiva and Vishnu are one, that the jiva is Shiva, and repeats the 'body is a temple' verses found in the Maitreya Upanishad.
up_skand.1.core_teaching: Even a trace of the Lord's grace is enough to make one steady and to reveal one's true nature as pure consciousness, one with Shiva; nothing is higher than that.

commentaries.who: Upanishad-brahma-yogin (Advaita), as rendered by T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar (Adyar, 1941)
commentaries.gist: Frames the verse as the knower's realisation of identity between Brahman and the self: by a bit of grace he has not swerved from the path, is wisdom itself, and is Shiva, Brahman not different from the inmost self.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar tr., Skanda Upanishad (1914)
commentaries.gist: Renders the opening as 'I am indestructible through a small portion of thy grace'; notes the text's identification of Shiva and Vishnu would shock sectarian partisans who quarrel over supremacy.

up_skand.1.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a gratitude prayer: a little grace is enough to steady us. It also models a non-sectarian devotion that sees Shiva and Vishnu as one.
misreadings: Not ego inflation ('I am God, so I am above others')
Not a sectarian claim of Shiva over Vishnu; the text identifies them
cautions: Strongly non-dual; some devotional readers may need the grace framing emphasised.
not_for: readers with a strictly dualist devotional view, without explanation

up_taittiriya.103.context: Anuvaka 7 opens by saying that in the beginning was non-being, from which being arose; that made itself, so it is called self-made. This verse says that self-made reality is rasa, the essence or 'flavour' that makes life sweet, and that getting it brings joy. The next lines ask who could even breathe if this bliss were not in the space of the heart.
up_taittiriya.103.core_teaching: The self-existent reality is the very essence and sweetness of life; whoever finds it becomes joyful. Joy comes from this source, not from objects.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Brahman exists because it is rasa, what gives satisfaction. Desireless sages, owning no outer sources of pleasure, are seen full of joy as if they had them; Brahman alone is their source of joy.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Brahman is the supreme essence in a creation that is flavourless in itself; by this rasa the world appears flavourful. For those who have realised the Self, this bliss is direct experience, not inference.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Brahman is called rasa because it is to be relished with love; people love dharma only as a means to heaven, but Brahman is loved for itself, so it must be bliss itself.

up_taittiriya.103.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say the deepest joy is not borrowed from things: the sweetness we taste in life comes from a source within, which is why contented people can be happy with little.
misreadings: Not hedonism ('life is about pleasure')
Not a claim that ordinary joys are worthless; they are drops of the same bliss
cautions: For someone in depression, 'joy is within' can feel like an accusation; offer gently.
not_for: clinical depression, without care
fresh grief

data_flags.translation_note: 'Sukṛtam' is mistranslated as 'well made'. In context (2.7 begins: Brahman made itself by itself, hence it is called su-kṛtam, 'self-made') it means 'that which is self-made', the self-caused (Mahadeva Sastri: 'the self-cause'). Suggested: 'That which is self-made is indeed the essence (rasa). Having found...

up_taittiriya.108.context: Anuvaka 8 opens with the gods and natural forces moving out of fear of Brahman. Then it announces an inquiry into bliss: take the happiest imaginable human (young, good, learned, quick, steady, strong, owning the whole earth's wealth) as one unit, and multiply a hundredfold step by step up to the bliss of Brahma. At every step, a learned person free of desire is said to have that same bliss.
up_taittiriya.108.core_teaching: Even the greatest worldly happiness is a small measure compared with the bliss available as desire thins; a wise person free of craving already has the higher joys.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: The question is whether Brahman's bliss is produced by contact, like worldly pleasure, or is inherent. Worldly pleasure is a fragment of Brahman's bliss, growing a hundredfold at each level as ignorance, desire and karma lessen.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Whatever admits of more and less must culminate in something limitless; so ordinary bliss, raised step by step, points to the immeasurable bliss, taught for those whose gaze is turned outward.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Explains each qualification: youth because children and the old can't enjoy; good because a hostile youth suffers; learned, prompt, steady and strong, since lacking any of these would spoil enjoyment.

up_taittiriya.108.practical_reading: Teachers use it to put success in perspective: imagine having everything (youth, health, learning, wealth) and the text says a person free of craving already has more. Contentment outweighs accumulation.
misreadings: Not a put-down of health, learning or wealth; they define the unit of joy
Not literal arithmetic of happiness
cautions: The ideal is a 'young man'; keep the reading gender- and age-neutral.
not_for: someone in poverty or illness who may feel their lack is being idealised

up_taittiriya.124.context: After the hundredfold ladder of bliss, anuvaka 9 opens with this verse, which the commentary treats as summing up the teaching that Brahman is beyond speech and thought. It is followed by the sentences on the knower no longer being tormented by regret over good left undone or wrong done.
up_taittiriya.124.core_teaching: The bliss of Brahman is beyond words and thought; whoever knows it as their own self has nothing left to fear.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Words denote conditioned things and fail to reach the unconditioned non-dual bliss; the mind, which moves with words, turns back too. The knower of this bliss as the self fears nothing.

commentaries.who: Later Advaita gloss following Shankara's in Mahadeva Sastri (1903), probably Sayana
commentaries.gist: If Brahman is beyond words, how does scripture teach it? Words like 'That thou art' remove ignorance without naming Brahman directly, as calling a sleeper's name wakes him without describing him.

up_taittiriya.124.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say the deepest reality is felt rather than explained, and that touching it dissolves fear. Silence and contemplation can go where explanations can't.
misreadings: Not anti-intellectual; words are still used to point
Fearlessness is not recklessness
cautions: Low risk; good for anxiety. Avoid implying that a fearful reader 'doesn't know' enough.
not_for: someone needing concrete practical help

up_taittiriya.125.context: Right after 'the knower of Brahman's bliss fears nothing', an objection is raised: surely there is fear about one's good and bad deeds? The text answers that such regrets do not burn the knower. The next sentences say the knower treats both good and evil as the self and is strengthened, not weakened, by them.
up_taittiriya.125.core_teaching: For one who knows the self, the burning regret over good undone and wrong done falls away, because the self is not the doer whose account is being kept.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: As death approaches a person is tormented by 'why didn't I do right? why did I do the forbidden?', fearing hell. These two do not afflict the knower of Brahman as they afflict one who does not know.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: One who knows the self as non-agent is untouched, since the fruit of action belongs to the agent. Such regrets overtake the ignorant in their last moments; the knower burns good and evil in the fire of knowledge.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Everyone near death regrets merit not earned in youth and sins committed; such thoughts trouble all others but do not assail one who has known Brahman.

up_taittiriya.125.practical_reading: Teachers use it to release crippling guilt and regret so a person can live and act well now. Freedom from self-torment is the ground for genuine amends.
misreadings: Not a licence to stop caring about harm done (our misuse note is right)
Not moral indifference; the commentators assume ethical life precedes this knowledge
cautions: The commentaries set it at the moment of death; avoid with readers facing terminal illness unless chosen
Could be misused to excuse an abuser's lack of remorse
not_for: someone who has recently harmed another and hasn't made amends
victims, if read as their abuser's absolution

up_taittiriya.127.context: The third section opens with a story: Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him Brahman. Varuna names food, breath, eye, ear, mind and speech as doors, and gives a definition: that from which beings are born, by which they live, into which they return. Bhrigu goes off to practise tapas and comes back with successive answers: food, breath, mind, understanding, and finally bliss.
up_taittiriya.127.core_teaching: Brahman is that from which all beings come, by which they live, and into which they return; a good teacher points the way, and the student must discover it through his own disciplined reflection.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Varuna names food and the senses as gateways to perceiving Brahman, then gives its definition: that with which beings stay one at birth, life and dissolution. Seek to reach Brahman so defined through those gateways.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: The story shows Brahma-vidya comes only through a teacher, approached with faith and a pure mind; Bhrigu asks after turning away from every pleasure short of liberation.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Upanishad stories like this extol the teaching rather than serve ritual recitation; Varuna, a most friendly teacher, gives the definition without being asked, likening beings to waves and foam in one ocean.

up_taittiriya.127.practical_reading: Teachers use it for learning by discovery: the best teachers give pointers and a question, then let you work it out. Also a model of a parent who teaches by guiding rather than telling.
misreadings: Not that food is God; food is the first gateway
Not a refusal by the father to teach
cautions: Mentions death ('into which they enter at death'); mild.
speaks_to: big-picture questions about origin and purpose

up_taittiriya.132.context: Bhrigu has concluded that food is Brahman, but sees food-born beings come and go and returns to his father. Varuna does not correct him directly; he repeats: seek Brahman through tapas, tapas is Brahman. This repeats after each answer (breath, mind, understanding) until Bhrigu realises that bliss is Brahman.
up_taittiriya.132.core_teaching: Real understanding comes through sustained, concentrated inquiry; the teacher keeps sending the student back until the student sees for himself.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Repeating 'tapas' shows it is the best means: as long as the definition is not fully met and the thirst for more light remains, practise concentration. Varuna calls tapas Brahman by courtesy, because it is the closest means.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: By repeatedly saying 'seek Brahman by tapas', the text shows that perception of the self is possible only through such concentrated devotion.

up_taittiriya.132.practical_reading: Teachers use it for perseverance in learning and self-inquiry: partial answers are steps, so keep going deeper. Good teachers don't hand over answers too quickly.
misreadings: Tapas here is concentrated reflection, not self-torture
Not a refusal to help
cautions: Low risk.
not_for: someone exhausted who needs rest, not more effort

up_taittiriya.146.context: Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him Brahman. Varuna gives only a test (that from which beings are born, by which they live, into which they return) and tells him to seek it through tapas. Bhrigu proposes food, breath, mind and understanding, returning each time; on the fifth inquiry he sees that bliss fits. The text then calls this the wisdom of Bhrigu and Varuna, and the next anuvaka turns to reverence for food.
up_taittiriya.146.core_teaching: The source, support and end of all beings is bliss, meaning a non-dual fullness at the core of the self, not a passing pleasure. It is found by going inward layer by layer through patient, concentrated reflection.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), in A. Mahadeva Sastri's 1903 translation
commentaries.gist: With a mind purified by tapas, Bhrigu saw that breath, mind and understanding fell short, went inward step by step, and found bliss, the innermost, to be Brahman. So composure of the outer and inner senses is the means.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara, Vartika on Shankara's bhashya (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: The knower sets aside all five sheaths and rests in the support that lies beyond cause and effect. The 'highest space' is the self, where the distinction between 'I' and 'you' falls away.

commentaries.who: Unmarked commentary passage in Mahadeva Sastri's edition (which translates Shankara and Sayana)
commentaries.gist: Small pleasures are mixed with pain: the effort to get them, comparison with greater ones, and their loss. The bliss meant here is glimpsed in deep sleep and absorption, and is more than the mere absence of pain.

up_taittiriya.146.practical_reading: Teachers use it to look beneath achievements and comforts for a quieter gladness that is already there. It is also a model of learning by repeated honest reflection rather than borrowed answers, and of a parent who gives clues instead of conclusions.
misreadings: Not 'life is about having fun': the commentators set this bliss against ordinary pleasures
Not an instruction to feel happy; it describes the ground of being, not a mood
'Entering joy at death' is a statement about the source of beings, not a promise about how dying feels
cautions: Mentions death ('into joy they enter'), which may sting for the recently bereaved
For a low reader, 'everything is born of joy' can feel invalidating; present it as something uncovered slowly, as Bhrigu did
not_for: fresh grief
a reader being told to 'just be positive'
speaks_to: parents or teachers who guide by questions

up_taittiriya.149.context: After Bhrigu realises that bliss is Brahman (3.6), the text draws out vows and contemplations. Anuvakas 7-10 pair a vow with a contemplation of food: do not belittle food, do not reject food, make plenty of food, turn no one away. Here, breath and body are food and eater to each other.
up_taittiriya.149.core_teaching: Because food was the first doorway to knowing Brahman, it should be honoured, never despised; life and body sustain each other as food and eater.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Since Brahman was known through food, regard food as a teacher and never condemn it; the vow praises food as a means of knowing Brahman. Breath and body rest in each other, so each is both food and eater.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara and Sayana, per Mahadeva Sastri's note (1903)
commentaries.gist: They differ from Shankara: the vow belongs to the contemplation of food as Brahman, so the devotee should never belittle food, treating it as a guru; breaking the vow makes the contemplation defective.

up_taittiriya.149.practical_reading: Teachers use it for gratitude and respect toward food: don't complain about or waste it. A footnote in the edition adds that a renunciant should not condemn even poor food that comes by chance.
misreadings: Not a rule against dietary choices or fasting
Not about forcing oneself to eat
cautions: Be careful with readers who have eating disorders; avoid framing around eating amounts.
not_for: someone with an eating disorder
someone experiencing food insecurity, if framed as 'don't complain'

up_taittiriya.158.context: The last of the food vows in the Bhriguvalli, following the contemplation of earth and space as food and eater. Whoever practises it must never refuse lodging to anyone who comes, and so must earn plenty of food to feed guests; the wise say 'food is ready for him'. The section then says food given generously and respectfully comes back the same way.
up_taittiriya.158.core_teaching: Hospitality is a sacred vow: never turn away someone seeking shelter, and so work to have enough to share.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: The one who contemplates earth and space must not turn away anyone seeking lodging; since lodging implies food, he should earn plenty of food by every means. The wise say 'food is ready' rather than send a guest away.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: A host who lets a guest go hungry loses all good here and hereafter; earn food by officiating, teaching, accepting gifts. Food given in one's prime and with respect returns the same way, at the same stage of life.

up_taittiriya.158.practical_reading: Teachers use it for generosity and open-door hospitality: earn well partly so that you can share. In a modern key, welcome guests, newcomers and people in need.
misreadings: 'By whatever means' is not a licence for dishonest earning; the commentators assume proper means
Not a demand to put oneself or family at risk by admitting anyone
cautions: Someone financially struggling may feel guilty; frame as sharing what one can.
Personal safety comes first.
not_for: someone in financial hardship
someone who cannot safely open their home
speaks_to: work as a means to share

up_taittiriya.43.context: Lesson 8 taught meditation on Om. Lesson 9 guards against thinking meditation makes ordinary duties unnecessary: it lists right conduct, truth, austerity, restraint, calm, the sacred fires, guests, social duties and raising children, each paired with 'and study and teaching'. The lesson ends with three teachers' views on which single duty matters most.
up_taittiriya.43.core_teaching: Every duty in life should be kept company by continued learning and sharing what one learns; study is not a phase that ends.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Study and teaching are repeated with every duty to show they must be pursued with special care while all the others are done, since knowledge of the Veda, on which the highest good depends, comes only through study.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: A seeker of liberation cannot rely on contemplation alone; he must also practise right speech, study and teaching. Even a renunciant should not give up study; neglect obstructs meditation.

up_taittiriya.43.practical_reading: Teachers use it for lifelong learning alongside every role: keep studying and keep sharing what you know, whether you are working, parenting or caring for others.
misreadings: Not a claim that study alone is enough
Not limited to Vedic study in a modern reading, but don't erase its original meaning
cautions: The full list includes begetting children; avoid quoting that part to readers facing infertility.
not_for: someone overwhelmed by obligations who may hear another 'should'

up_taittiriya.49.context: This opens the teacher's famous graduation address in the Shiksha Valli, given when the student has learned the Veda and is about to return home to married life. Shankara notes the teacher now explains the meaning of what was memorised. The address goes on through duties to family, gods, ancestors, parents, teachers and guests, and how to give.
up_taittiriya.49.core_teaching: As a student goes out into life, the teacher's first counsel is: speak the truth, do what is right, and never stop learning.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Speak what you know by proper evidence and what is fit to say. A student should not leave the teacher's house without inquiring into dharma; the teacher now explains the meaning of what was learned by heart.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Truth-speaking means saying a thing as it was perceived, without hypocrisy or intent to harm; dharma means the prescribed rites such as the fire offering.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Truth-speaking stands for the related virtues too, such as non-harming and not stealing; the two short commands together mean all scriptural duties should be observed.

up_taittiriya.49.practical_reading: Teachers use it as advice for any graduation or new beginning: be honest, act rightly, keep learning. Often quoted at convocations.
misreadings: Not a set of rigid rules; it's a summary of values
Truth here includes not harming, not just blunt factual speech
cautions: Low risk.

up_taittiriya.50.context: Continuing the graduation address: after paying the teacher a fitting fee, the student should marry and continue the family line. Then comes a run of 'do not be careless about' sayings: truth, dharma, welfare, prosperity, study and teaching. Next come duties to the gods and ancestors and the honouring of parents, teachers and guests.
up_taittiriya.50.core_teaching: A good life keeps several threads unbroken: gratitude to teachers, family, truth, rightness, health and safety, prosperity, and continued learning and teaching.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Self-preservation has physical means like medicine and ritual means; wealth likewise. Health and wealth must not be neglected, since without them one cannot do the works that lead toward liberation.

up_taittiriya.50.practical_reading: Teachers use it to show the tradition values health, safety and prosperity, not only renunciation: take care of yourself and your livelihood while keeping truth and learning.
misreadings: Not a command that everyone must have children
Not a licence for greed; prosperity sits alongside truth and dharma
cautions: 'Do not cut off the line of your family' can hurt readers facing infertility, child-free by choice, or LGBTQ+; Shankara even mentions rites to obtain a son. Consider omitting that clause in readings
Gender assumptions (son, line of descent) need neutral framing
not_for: readers struggling with infertility or pregnancy loss
people pressured by family to marry or have children
speaks_to: neglecting health or finances for work

up_taittiriya.52.context: In the graduation address, after warning against neglecting rites for gods and ancestors, the teacher names four people to be honoured as divine: mother, father, teacher and guest. Immediately after, he adds that only blameless actions, and only the teachers' good conduct, are to be followed.
up_taittiriya.52.core_teaching: Treat your mother, father, teacher and guests with the reverence due to the divine; do not neglect what you owe to those who came before.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Mother, father, teacher and guest are to be worshipped as deities, not regarded as mere human beings.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Worship your mother as you would a deity such as Rudra, Vishnu or Vinayaka. Rites for the gods include vratas taught in the Puranas; for ancestors, the annual ceremonies.

up_taittiriya.52.practical_reading: Teachers use it for gratitude and respect toward parents, teachers and anyone who comes to your door; 'Atithi Devo Bhava' is also India's hospitality motto.
misreadings: Honouring parents does not mean accepting mistreatment or giving up your conscience (our misuse note is right; the very next verse limits following elders to their good conduct)
Not idol-worship of people
cautions: Painful for those with abusive, absent or deceased parents; pair it with the next verse's limit
For those whose parents have died, frame as remembrance
not_for: survivors of parental abuse
someone estranged for their safety
fresh grief for a parent, without care

up_taittiriya.53.context: Right after telling the student to honour parents and teachers as gods, the teacher limits it: follow only blameless actions, and only the good conduct of your teachers, not the rest. The address continues with how to treat people better than oneself and how to give.
up_taittiriya.53.core_teaching: Even revered elders and teachers should be imitated only in what is good; the student keeps his own moral judgement.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Do only acts free from blame and sanctioned by the practice of the wise; follow the teachers' own good conduct where it agrees with scripture, not their contrary acts, even though teachers do them.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Avoid evil acts, and even acts open to the least suspicion of evil, though practised by the wise; follow the teachers only where they accord with scripture and the practice of the good.

up_taittiriya.53.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say respect is not blind obedience: learn from elders' virtues, not their faults. It is a healthy counterweight to 'treat your parents as god'.
misreadings: Not permission to dismiss elders whenever convenient
Not a rejection of tradition
cautions: The Parashurama example in Sayana mentions matricide; don't quote it in a reading for distressed readers.
speaks_to: disillusion with a mentor or parent

up_taittiriya.54.context: Continuing the address: after limiting imitation to good conduct, the teacher says how to treat learned people better than oneself, then gives the six-fold teaching on giving. Next he says what to do when unsure about right action.
up_taittiriya.54.core_teaching: Honour those wiser than you, and give in the right spirit: with faith, generosity, modesty, a sense of awe, and understanding.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Honour superior brahmanas with seats and relieve their fatigue, or keep silent in their assembly and just grasp what they say. Give only with reverence, never with irreverence; give liberally, with modesty, with fear, with friendliness.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Read with Gita 17: giving to show off wealth is tamasic, from shame before equals rajasic, from fear of sin sattvic. Or the whole passage is about sattvic giving: give in proportion to your means.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara's Vartika (Advaita), notes marked (S.) in A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: In their discourses do not hurry to speak; grasp the essence of what they say and never contradict them even if you could.

up_taittiriya.54.practical_reading: Teachers use it for the ethics of giving today: give respectfully and humbly, in proportion to your means, aware of the person you give to. And listen more than you talk around people wiser than you.
misreadings: Not 'give out of fear of punishment' in a modern anxious sense
'Better than us' was about learned brahmanas; apply it to the wise of any background, not as caste deference
cautions: Caste wording in the original ('brahmanas'); keep the reading inclusive.
not_for: someone in financial hardship who may feel pressure to give

up_taittiriya.56.context: Near the end of the graduation address the teacher admits that rules will not cover every case. When unsure about an action or about conduct, follow the thoughtful, independent, gentle people around you who care about what is right; do the same in dealing with people under accusation. The address closes: this is the instruction, the teaching, the secret of the Veda.
up_taittiriya.56.core_teaching: When rules run out, look to people who are thoughtful, independent, kind and committed to the right, and act as they would, including in judging the accused.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: In doubt about a rite or custom, act as the brahmanas of that country and age would: able to judge, well-versed, not driven by others, not cruel, seeking dharma, unswayed by desire. Likewise toward people suspected of wrongdoing.

commentaries.who: Sayana's commentary (Advaita), tr. A. Mahadeva Sastri (1903)
commentaries.gist: Gives examples of real doubts: contradictory rules on timing of rites, regional customs such as cross-cousin marriage or eating meat. In such cases follow the wise of your own place and time who are free of attachment and aversion.

up_taittiriya.56.practical_reading: Teachers use it for moral uncertainty: find wise, kind and independent-minded people and ask how they would act. It also counsels fairness and restraint toward someone accused.
misreadings: Not 'follow the crowd' or local majority opinion; the qualities named are demanding
Not deference to a caste group; in a modern reading, the qualities are what matter
cautions: Original names brahmanas as the reference group; keep inclusive.
not_for: someone surrounded only by harsh or manipulative 'advisers'
speaks_to: how to treat someone accused or in scandal

vishnu_gita.1.58.context: The frightened gods praise Vishnu as the one whose power moves them (1.60). Here they confess that they exist only by his being, yet forget him through maya (1.61). They add that he cures their forgetting by sending hardship as discipline, which is his mercy (1.62), then take refuge and ask for teaching so that fear and want end (1.63-66).
vishnu_gita.1.58.core_teaching: We exist only because the divine exists, yet we forget it; that forgetting, not the divine's absence, is the root of our fear.
vishnu_gita.1.58.practical_reading: A remembering practice: before a fearful task, recall what holds your existence before you recall what threatens it.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.
The next verse frames calamity as God's corrective discipline for forgetting; do not pair the two in readings for someone suffering, as it can sound like 'your suffering is punishment'.
not_for: someone in fresh suffering if the next verse's 'calamity as discipline' is brought in

data_flags.corrected_ref: Vishnu Gita 1.61 in the 1919 Mahamandal edition. Our '1.58' is off by three.

vishnu_gita.1.60.context: Suta asks Vyasa how the Lord once freed the gods from fear. Vyasa explains that creation is a play of opposites in which gods and anti-gods alternate in power. The frightened gods praise Vishnu: they move only by his power, forget him through maya, and he cures their delusion through adversity, which they call his compassion. Then comes this verse, and they ask to be taught so they never fall into delusion again. Vishnu replies that they slipped from right conduct and forgot their duty, which is why fear seized them, and he teaches dispassion.
vishnu_gita.1.60.core_teaching: Fear rooted in confusion can be dissolved by turning for shelter and asking to understand. The gods ask not only for rescue but to be taught, so the confusion does not return.

commentaries.who: Hindi translation in the Mahamandal edition (1919; no classical commentary exists)
commentaries.gist: Renders the gods' plea: we seek refuge in you, lover of those who seek shelter; act so that our delusion-born fear is destroyed. The next verse asks for teaching so they never fall into delusion again.

commentaries.who: Context of the hymn (Sanskrit text, Vishnu Gita ch. 1, vv. 60-70 in the 1919 numbering)
commentaries.gist: The gods say they move only by Vishnu's power yet forget him through maya, and he cures this through adversity, which they call his mercy. Vishnu replies that they lapsed from right conduct and forgot their duty, hence the fear.

vishnu_gita.1.60.practical_reading: Saying plainly 'I'm afraid and I need help making sense of this' is a legitimate first step. Ask for clarity, not just relief.
misreadings: Not 'your fear is your own fault'. Vishnu's reply in the text does tie the gods' fear to their own lapse, but do not import that onto a reader facing real danger at work
Not passivity: the gods go on to ask for teaching
cautions: A late text: label it accurately
The hymn's idea that adversity is the Lord's corrective (v.62 in the 1919 edition) can feel like blame to someone being harmed
not_for: someone who needs practical safety steps, such as harassment at work, unless paired with action

vishnu_gita.1.98.context: The gods asked how to be free of fear. Vishnu explains that attachment to perishable things born of ignorance breeds fear: the body fears age and death, wealth fears kings and thieves, youth fears old age, beauty fears decay, pleasure fears disease, family fears downfall (vv. 101-103 in the 1919 numbering). This verse adds honour, virtue, power and learning. The next verse says even heaven carries envy and the fear of falling, and only dispassion is fearless; then Vishnu recites Bhagavad Gita 2.13-15 to the gods.
vishnu_gita.1.98.core_teaching: Every good thing we hold, even honour, virtue, power and learning, brings its own fear of losing it; only dispassion (vairagya) is free of fear.

commentaries.who: Hindi translation in the Mahamandal edition (1919; no classical commentary exists)
commentaries.gist: Lists the fears attached to each possession (honour fears abasement, virtue fears the wicked, power fears critics, learning fears debaters) and concludes that only the state of dispassion is truly without fear.

vishnu_gita.1.98.practical_reading: If you feel you're never good enough, notice that every achievement brings a new thing to defend. Security comes less from more achievement than from holding achievements more lightly.
misreadings: Not 'don't seek honour, skill or learning'
Not a claim that your fears are irrational; they are the natural shadow of what you value
cautions: Late text; label accurately, and consider crediting the idea to Bhartrihari
Surrounding verses list fears of death and family loss; don't quote them to a grieving reader
not_for: someone facing real threats (harassment, legal danger), where 'hold it lightly' would dismiss them

viv.1.apple_standard.context: In the second Karma-Yoga class he says calm and renunciation cannot be forced on people who have not yet lived through their desires, and admits he has met hardly twenty truly calm people. Here he argues that each person must pursue their own ideal; the elided lines picture a child ordered to walk twenty miles. Right after, he says one standard for everyone only makes people hate themselves, and that our duty is to encourage each person toward their own highest ideal.
viv.1.apple_standard.core_teaching: People differ by nature, so each should be measured against an ideal that fits them, not against someone else's. Forcing one ideal on all breeds struggle and self-hatred.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 2)
commentaries.gist: He follows the image by saying a single standard for all creates an unnatural struggle that leads people to hate themselves; our duty is to encourage each to live up to their own highest ideal.

commentaries.who: Same chapter, closing story (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 2)
commentaries.gist: He ends the chapter with the king who learns that the monk and the householder are each great in their own place.

commentaries.who: Parallel in Karma-Yoga ch. 4 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He makes the same point about nations: he is not the measure of the universe, and others' duties should be seen through their own eyes.

viv.1.apple_standard.practical_reading: Used against constant comparison: with siblings, colleagues, other parents or social media. Ask what growth looks like on your own path rather than borrowing someone else's yardstick.
misreadings: Not moral relativism that excuses harm; it is about ideals and temperaments, not about ethics toward others
Not 'never aim higher'; he says each should strive toward their own highest ideal
cautions: The elided sentences picture a child made to walk until it dies or arrives half dead; do not pull them in for a parent or a grieving reader
not_for: someone using 'my own standard' to dismiss feedback about harm they caused
speaks_to: career pressure to follow someone else's path
feeling like a failure by another's measure

viv.1.assimilate_grow.context: On the Parliament's last day he says anyone hoping for unity through one religion's victory holds an impossible hope. He uses a seed that takes in earth, air and water yet grows into its own plant. Right after, he says the Parliament proved holiness belongs to no one church, and ends with 'Help and not Fight'.
viv.1.assimilate_grow.core_teaching: Faiths should learn from each other's spirit while each stays itself and grows by its own nature; neither conversion nor merging is the goal.

commentaries.who: Context of the address (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: The seed absorbs earth, air and water but becomes its own plant; so each religion should take in the others' spirit without becoming them.

commentaries.who: His opening address, 11 September 1893 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: Two weeks earlier he told the Parliament his tradition holds not only toleration but acceptance of all religions as true.

viv.1.assimilate_grow.practical_reading: Applied to mixed families, migration and new workplaces: learn deeply from others without having to give up who you are.
misreadings: Not a call to blend all religions into one
Not a claim that differences don't matter; he keeps each tradition's individuality
not_for: someone being pressured to convert, if read as 'you must absorb their way'
speaks_to: keeping one's identity while learning from others

viv.1.blows_inner_fire.context: Opening Karma-Yoga, he says the goal of life is knowledge, not pleasure, and that pleasure and pain both leave impressions that make up character, misery sometimes teaching more. This sentence sums up that point. He then argues that all knowledge is already within us and experience only uncovers it.
viv.1.blows_inner_fire.core_teaching: Suffering, as much as joy, shapes character, and history's great people were often formed more by hardship than by praise.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 1)
commentaries.gist: Just before, he says good and evil share equally in moulding character and in some cases misery teaches more; just after, that knowledge is uncovered from within, not added from outside.

commentaries.who: Same idea later: "Sadhanas or Preparations for Higher Life" (CW, wisdomlib)
commentaries.gist: He tells hearers we pass through hell to reach heaven, so they should bless their mistakes and not look back.

viv.1.blows_inner_fire.practical_reading: Teachers use it to help people find meaning in a hard season after the fact: what did that difficulty draw out of you?
misreadings: Not a reason to seek hardship or to keep someone in it
Not something to say to a person in fresh pain ('it's good for you')
cautions: Can romanticise suffering: for someone in grief, abuse, illness or poverty it may sound like their pain is a lesson they needed
Best offered as reflection on a past hardship, not a present one
not_for: fresh grief
someone in an abusive situation
acute crisis or depression
speaks_to: looking back on a hard season with some perspective
students or young workers facing early rejection

viv.1.come_up_lions.context: Describing the despair of a world bound by cause and effect, he says a Vedic sage answered with 'children of immortal bliss', and that the Hindu refuses to call anyone a sinner. This passage follows. Next he says we are not bodies or matter, and that above all laws stands One by whose command the wind blows and death walks the earth.
viv.1.come_up_lions.core_teaching: Human beings are divine and free at heart; calling them sinners slanders human nature. Wake from the false belief that you are weak.

commentaries.who: Context of the paper (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He builds this on the Upanishadic address 'children of immortal bliss' and says Hindus refuse to call people sinners; he goes on to say we are souls, not matter.

commentaries.who: Svetasvatara Upanishad 2.5 (Max Müller, via IntraText)
commentaries.gist: The verse he draws on calls on all the 'sons of the Immortal' to hear the prayer.

commentaries.who: Parallel: "Practical Vedanta I" (CW vol. 2, London 1896)
commentaries.gist: Instead of telling people they are sinners, he says, Vedanta tells them their nature is pure and teaches them the strength already within.

viv.1.come_up_lions.practical_reading: Used for shame and low self-worth: you are more than your worst label.
misreadings: Not a denial of wrongdoing or accountability
Not a pep talk that one can simply decide not to be depressed
cautions: 'It is a sin to call a man so; a standing libel' may offend readers whose faith holds a doctrine of sin
The following lines ('ye are not bodies') can land oddly for someone who is ill or disabled
not_for: readers in a Christian context who may hear an attack on their faith
clinical depression if offered as 'just think differently'

viv.1.dependent_on_me.context: He has just quoted his master: look on your children as a nurse does, caring fully yet ready to leave without a pang. Then this line. He goes on: no one in the universe depends on us; nature helps all, and helping is only a privilege by which we educate ourselves.
viv.1.dependent_on_me.core_teaching: Thinking others depend on us breeds attachment, and attachment brings pain; we help as a privilege, not as their indispensable saviour.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 6)
commentaries.gist: Right after, he says not one beggar depends on our charity and the course of nature will not stop for us; helping others is a privilege by which we educate ourselves.

commentaries.who: Parallel in Karma-Yoga ch. 5 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: No beggar we help owes us anything; we owe him for letting us exercise charity.

viv.1.dependent_on_me.practical_reading: Teachers use it for over-functioning and control: care fully, but drop the belief that everything collapses without you.
misreadings: Not a reason to neglect children, patients or anyone who really relies on you
Not 'your care doesn't matter'
cautions: The surrounding nurse image (ready to leave the children without a pang) can hurt new parents, carers, or bereaved parents
For a carer whose dependant has died, 'no one depends on me' may sound like their care was pointless
not_for: new parents
bereaved parents or carers
someone already feeling useless or unneeded

viv.1.dont_think_result.context: He has just quoted the Gita's 'to work we have the right, but not to the fruits' and asked why we care for results. Before that he says even low motives like fame have a place, but we should move toward higher ones. After this he turns to the tension between intense work and rest.
viv.1.dont_think_result.core_teaching: Help and good work should not be governed by what we expect back, gratitude or success.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 1)
commentaries.gist: He quotes the Gita on the right to work but not its fruits, then says to leave fruits alone; he grants even selfish motives as a start but urges higher ones.

commentaries.who: Gita 2.47 (vedabase.io, Prabhupada)
commentaries.gist: The verse separates duty from its fruits, warns against seeing oneself as cause of the results, and also rules out escape into inaction.

viv.1.dont_think_result.practical_reading: Used for people-pleasing and outcome anxiety: do the helpful thing without scripting how the other person should respond.
misreadings: Not 'never plan or measure'; it is about not letting expected returns drive the work
Not permission to ignore consequences for others
not_for: someone being exploited who is told not to expect fairness
speaks_to: helping someone who may never thank you

viv.1.duty_disease.context: He says ordinary duty is on a lower plane, though we must still do it, and that a certain sense of duty causes great misery. The elided lines picture 'slaves to duty' with no time to pray, dying in harness like a horse, and say the only true duty is to work unattached, giving all to God. After, he calls much so-called duty attachment or greed dressed up.
viv.1.duty_disease.core_teaching: Duty can turn into a compulsion that eats life; the remedy is not to stop working but to work free and at rest inside.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 7)
commentaries.gist: Around this line he says the ordinary idea of duty causes misery, that slaves to duty die in harness, and that true duty is to work unattached as free beings.

commentaries.who: Parallel in Karma-Yoga ch. 4 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: Duty is seldom sweet; it runs smoothly only when love oils it, otherwise it is constant friction.

viv.1.duty_disease.practical_reading: Used for burnout and work that follows you home: keep the work, drop the inner whip.
misreadings: Not permission to drop real responsibilities
Not a critique of caring for family as such
cautions: Elided lines include 'dying in harness like a horse'; do not pull them in for an exhausted or depressed reader
The next lines call family attachment 'morbid attachment of flesh for flesh', which can hurt carers
not_for: carers of a sick relative who cannot simply rest
someone looking for an excuse to abandon commitments

viv.1.duty_next_to_us.context: He has been speaking of family duties: a mother puts her children first, children see parents as the divine on earth. This line introduces his retelling of the Mahabharata story of the young ascetic humbled first by a housewife and then by a butcher (the Vyadha), both enlightened through ordinary duty.
viv.1.duty_next_to_us.core_teaching: Rise by doing well the work in front of you; strength gathered there carries you to the highest.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 4)
commentaries.gist: He uses the housewife and the butcher, who reached insight by doing their ordinary duties unattached, to show any station done well leads to the highest.

commentaries.who: Mahabharata, Vana Parva sec. 214 (Ganguli, wisdomlib)
commentaries.gist: In the source story the fowler presents his parents as his highest teachers and sends the Brahmana home to console his own parents.

commentaries.who: "On Indian Women" interview, 1898 (CW, wisdomlib)
commentaries.gist: He retells the same story: the wife nursing her husband and the butcher Dharma-Vyadha found enlightenment through common faithfulness and duty.

viv.1.duty_next_to_us.practical_reading: Used when people feel stuck or unworthy: begin with the next ordinary task, done fully.
misreadings: Not 'stay in your station forever' or a defence of caste-bound work
cautions: The preceding lines on a mother's duty to put children first may add guilt for struggling parents
not_for: someone told to accept an unjust situation as their 'duty'
speaks_to: overwhelm: what is the one next thing

viv.1.duty_sweet_love.context: He says duty's purpose is to thin the lower self so the higher can shine, then admits duty is seldom sweet. The elided line asks how parents, husbands and wives could do their duties otherwise, given daily friction. Next he says the highest freedom in small irritations is to forbear.
viv.1.duty_sweet_love.core_teaching: Duty without love is friction; love makes it sweet, and love can only live where there is freedom.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 4)
commentaries.gist: Duty is seldom sweet; love oils its wheels; and real freedom in daily friction is forbearance, not being a slave to temper.

commentaries.who: Parallel in Karma-Yoga ch. 7 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He warns that duty can become a disease, and asks for work done as free beings rather than slaves.

viv.1.duty_sweet_love.practical_reading: Applied to family life and caregiving: when duty grinds, look for where love has gone and where freedom has been lost.
misreadings: Not 'if your duty feels heavy you don't love enough'
cautions: The lines that follow blame jealous wives and claim a chaste, loving wife can reform a brutal husband; never pull them in, especially for anyone facing domestic abuse
not_for: domestic abuse
someone told to stay and love harder
speaks_to: marriage going through a dry patch

viv.1.end_and_means.context: After the butcher story he describes an Indian yogi who never teaches directly but sheds light on a question days later. This is the secret of work that yogi gave him. He follows: do the work as worship, wholly, and the Vyadha and the housewife show that unattached duty leads to the highest.
viv.1.end_and_means.core_teaching: Make the present task the whole of your attention, so that means and goal become one.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 4)
commentaries.gist: He passes on the yogi's secret, then says to do the work as the highest worship, as the butcher and the housewife did, and so be illumined.

commentaries.who: "Sketch of the Life of Pavhari Baba" (CW vol. 4)
commentaries.gist: He recalls Pavhari Baba scouring a copper pot as carefully as he worshipped, and quotes his secret of work: love the means as if it were the end.

commentaries.who: "Work and its Secret", Los Angeles 1900 (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He opens that lecture saying a great man taught him to give the means as much attention as the end.

viv.1.end_and_means.practical_reading: Used for focus and for craft: wash the dish as if washing the dish were the point.
misreadings: Not 'goals don't matter'

viv.1.five_minutes.context: Near the end of the chapter he says that, apart from the fully realised, everyone must work, but we should never think we can help the universe; we only help ourselves in the world's gymnasium. Then this line against self-importance. He goes on: only God's life is infinite, so give up fruits and do good for its own sake.
viv.1.five_minutes.core_teaching: Our sense of being indispensable is an illusion; seeing that frees us from attachment to our work.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 7)
commentaries.gist: Just before, he says remembering work as a privilege keeps us unattached; just after, that God alone is infinite and we should do good for its own sake.

commentaries.who: Parallel in Karma-Yoga ch. 5 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He says not to worry or lose sleep over the world, since it will go on without you.

viv.1.five_minutes.practical_reading: Used against ego and over-identification with a role: a corrective for pride, not a verdict on anyone's worth.
misreadings: Not 'your life doesn't matter'
Not a reason for despair or nihilism
cautions: High risk for a depressed, suicidal or grieving reader: 'we all die, and in five minutes the world forgets us' can confirm feelings of worthlessness or that the dead are forgotten
not_for: depression
suicidal thoughts
fresh grief
someone already feeling invisible
speaks_to: perfectionists who think everything rests on them

viv.1.forbear.context: Right after saying duty is sweet only through love and love shines only in freedom, he asks whether being a slave to anger and jealousy is freedom. The next sentences turn to married couples, blaming jealous wives and fault-finding husbands, and claim a chaste, loving wife can reform almost any man.
viv.1.forbear.core_teaching: Being ruled by irritation is bondage; the freest response to small daily frictions is restraint.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 4)
commentaries.gist: He calls slavery to anger and jealousy the opposite of freedom; the next lines on wives and husbands are dated and gendered.

commentaries.who: Inspired Talks, 25 July 1895 (CW vol. 7)
commentaries.gist: He says to be grateful even to one who curses you, as it gives a mirror and a chance to practise self-restraint.

viv.1.forbear.practical_reading: Used for small irritations at home or work: not every slight needs an answer.
misreadings: Not tolerance of mistreatment or abuse
Applies to 'little roughnesses', not to serious harm
cautions: The very next lines say a chaste, loving wife can conquer a brutal husband and that women are as brutal as men; never pull them in for anyone facing domestic violence
Gendered, dated framing
not_for: domestic abuse
harassment
anyone being told to put up with harm
speaks_to: daily irritations with family or colleagues

viv.1.frog_in_well.context: A previous speaker had asked delegates to stop abusing each other; he answers with a story of a frog born in a well who calls the sea-frog a liar because nothing can be bigger than his well. This is the moral, and he names his own religion first. He closes by thanking America for trying to break down these walls.
viv.1.frog_in_well.core_teaching: Religious quarrels come from each side taking its own small world for the whole.

commentaries.who: Context of the talk (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: The whole short talk is the frog story told to explain why religions disagree; he includes himself as a Hindu in the well.

commentaries.who: Letter to Diwanji Saheb, Chicago (CW vol. 8)
commentaries.gist: He uses the same image for his own countrymen, who he says have become frogs in the well, unaware of the wider world.

viv.1.frog_in_well.practical_reading: Used for intellectual humility: notice where you have mistaken your corner for the whole world.
misreadings: Not a claim that all views are equally right
speaks_to: moving out of a small community

viv.1.good_impressions.context: He explains that each act leaves an impression in the mind; someone who keeps thinking and doing bad becomes a machine driven by bad impressions. This line gives the reverse. After it he says good tendencies can grow so strong that one cannot do evil even if one wishes, and then character is established.
viv.1.good_impressions.core_teaching: Character is built from accumulated impressions; good thoughts and deeds pile up until they carry us toward good automatically.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 3)
commentaries.gist: Just before, he says bad impressions force a man to do evil like a machine; just after, that enough good impressions make evil almost impossible and character becomes firm.

commentaries.who: Parallel in Karma-Yoga ch. 1 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He defines character as the sum of tendencies left by pleasure and pain on the mind.

viv.1.good_impressions.practical_reading: Used for habit change: small good acts repeated really do reshape us.
misreadings: Not a verdict that people with bad habits are bad people
cautions: The preceding lines say a man full of bad impressions 'cannot help it' and will be a bad man; avoid for someone with addiction or deep shame
not_for: someone convinced they are irredeemable
