speaks_to: parents thinking about what children absorb

viv.1.grateful_to_helped.context: He has said the world does not wait for our help and that a beggar we help owes us nothing; thinking we have done the world good is a foolish thought that brings misery. The elided line asks why we should expect anything in return. Afterwards: is it not a privilege to worship God by helping others?
viv.1.grateful_to_helped.core_teaching: The helper should be grateful to the helped, for the chance to serve; expecting thanks breeds unhappiness.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 5)
commentaries.gist: No beggar owes us a cent; we owe him for letting us practise charity; helping is a privilege by which we worship.

commentaries.who: Inspired Talks, 25 July 1895 (CW vol. 7)
commentaries.gist: Thank God for the world as a moral gymnasium, but never imagine you can help the world.

viv.1.grateful_to_helped.practical_reading: Used for resentment in helping roles: shift from 'they owe me' to 'I was given a chance'.
misreadings: Not a reason to tolerate exploitation or unpaid labour
Not 'you have no right to feel hurt'
cautions: Carers or partners whose effort is taken for granted may hear 'your hurt is your fault'
not_for: someone being exploited
unpaid carers already burnt out

viv.1.help_not_fight.context: The closing lines of his last Parliament address, after the seed image. The elided words say that anyone who still dreams of one religion surviving and the others perishing has his pity. He ends with the words written on every religion's banner.
viv.1.help_not_fight.core_teaching: Every tradition has produced saints, so none can claim holiness alone; the future lies in helping, assimilating and harmony.

commentaries.who: Context of the address (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He argues from the Parliament itself that every system has produced people of the highest character.

commentaries.who: His opening address (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He had begun the Parliament hoping its bell would toll the death-knell of sectarianism and fanaticism.

viv.1.help_not_fight.practical_reading: Applied to family, community and online conflict over belief: choose help over fight.
misreadings: Not a denial that real differences exist

viv.1.inside_the_machine.context: He says we are dragged along by the world-machine and there are only two ways out: drop all desire and step aside, which almost no one can do, or plunge in and learn the secret of work, the way of Karma-Yoga. After this he says the way out lies through the machine itself, and that God does not need our help.
viv.1.inside_the_machine.core_teaching: Freedom need not mean escape: one can stay inside ordinary life and learn to work in a way that frees.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 8)
commentaries.gist: Of the two exits, renunciation is nearly impossible; the other is to work inside the machine, and through it come out.

commentaries.who: Parallel in Karma-Yoga ch. 1 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: His ideal worker is calm as in a cave while moving through a crowded city.

viv.1.inside_the_machine.practical_reading: Used when someone wants to flee their life: change how you work before changing where you are.
misreadings: Not 'never leave a job or relationship'
not_for: someone who needs to leave a harmful situation

viv.1.judge_character.context: He has said every big work is made of countless small ones, like a wave made of tiny waves. This passage follows. Next he calls karma's effect on character the greatest power we deal with, and the human being a centre that draws in and sends out all the forces of the universe.
viv.1.judge_character.core_teaching: Real greatness shows in everyday conduct and consistency, not in rare heroic moments that any occasion can bring out.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 1)
commentaries.gist: He builds from the image of a wave made of minute waves to argue that small daily actions reveal and make character.

commentaries.who: Parallel in Karma-Yoga ch. 2 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He says even a coward turns brave under praise; the true test is doing good when no one approves.

viv.1.judge_character.practical_reading: Used for integrity and parenting: how you treat a waiter or a junior colleague says more than one big gesture.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of genuine courage in a crisis
not_for: someone ashamed of one bad day, if read as a verdict on their whole character

viv.1.love_no_pain.context: He contrasts love with possessive jealousy: a man who wants a woman always at his bidding is a slave, not a lover, because his 'love' brings pain when she does not obey. This line follows. After it he says that when we can love family and world without pain or jealousy we are fit to be unattached, and quotes Krishna on working without gain.
viv.1.love_no_pain.core_teaching: True love has no painful reaction of jealousy or possession; what brings that pain is attachment wearing love's name.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 3)
commentaries.gist: His example is a jealous, controlling lover; he calls that a slave's morbid affection, not love.

commentaries.who: "Work and its Secret", Los Angeles 1900 (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He says misery comes not from loving but from wanting love in return.

viv.1.love_no_pain.practical_reading: Used for jealousy and control in relationships: if your 'love' demands obedience, look again.
misreadings: Not 'if a relationship hurts, you never loved'
Not 'grief means your love was false'
cautions: Strong caution for grief: 'if it does not [bring bliss], it is not love' can tell a bereaved reader their pain shows their love was false
People hurt by a partner may read it as blaming their own love
not_for: grief or bereavement
someone in an abusive relationship
heartbreak, read as 'you didn't really love'

viv.1.make_ourselves.context: He says only what we earn is really ours: a cheat may grow rich and find it a burden; a fool may own every book but read only what he deserves. Our karma decides what we deserve and can take in. This line follows, then: if the present came from past action, the future can be built by present action.
viv.1.make_ourselves.core_teaching: Our present self came from our own past acts, so our future self can be shaped by what we do now.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 1)
commentaries.gist: He uses 'deserving' produced by karma to argue that what we are is our making, so what we will be is in our hands.

commentaries.who: "The Cosmos: The Microcosm", New York 1896 (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He urges taking full responsibility and knowing oneself the creator of one's destiny.

viv.1.make_ourselves.practical_reading: Used for agency: whatever brought you here, the next choices are yours.
misreadings: Not a claim that every circumstance or injustice is your own fault
Not 'the poor or the sick deserve it'
cautions: The surrounding 'deserve' language can read as blame for illness, poverty, disability or abuse; frame it forward, not backward
not_for: victims of abuse or injustice
chronic illness or disability
grief
speaks_to: young adults taking charge of their life

viv.1.master_not_slave.context: He says we wrongly take nature as ourselves and get attached, so we work like slaves, not freely. This line sums up the teaching. Next: ninety-nine per cent of people work like slaves and reap misery; work through freedom and love, since love cannot exist in a slave.
viv.1.master_not_slave.core_teaching: Work hard, but from inner freedom and love, not from selfish compulsion.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 3)
commentaries.gist: Attachment to nature makes us work like slaves; work through freedom and love.

commentaries.who: Parallel in Karma-Yoga ch. 7 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He describes duty turned into compulsion as living a slave's life.

viv.1.master_not_slave.practical_reading: Used for burnout and resentment: same task, different inner stance.
misreadings: Not a comment on people in actual servitude or exploitative jobs
cautions: The slavery metaphor may jar for readers in coercive or exploitative work
not_for: people in forced or exploitative labour

viv.1.misery_attachment.context: In 'Freedom' Vivekananda says the whole universe is struggling toward freedom and that Karma-Yoga is the science of working well. He then gives this line as Karma-Yoga's message, illustrated by two burned paintings: a stranger's loss barely touches us, but losing our own painting hurts because we have made it 'mine'. He follows with the lotus leaf that sits in water without getting wet, and two routes to non-attachment: self-reliance for those without belief in God, offering the fruits of work to God for believers.
viv.1.misery_attachment.core_teaching: Work itself does not make us miserable; our identification with it and its results does. Work wholeheartedly, but hold the outcome as not 'mine'.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Complete Works vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. VII)
commentaries.gist: The burned-painting example: the same loss hurts only when it is ours; 'mine' extends to house, children and body. Advises enjoying things without claiming them.

commentaries.who: Same chapter, later paragraphs
commentaries.gist: Non-attachment is the basis of all the yogas: a person in a cave can be attached and a king free. Duty becomes a burden when it hardens into compulsion; act freely and expect no praise, like the many unknown people who work silently.

commentaries.who: Lecture chronology (vivekananda.net)
commentaries.gist: Lists 'Freedom' among the New York Karma-Yoga talks, dated 10 January 1896.

viv.1.misery_attachment.practical_reading: When work is draining you, look for where you have fused your worth with the outcome; keep doing the task well but loosen the 'this must go my way' grip.
misreadings: Not 'stop caring about your work'.
Not a denial that workload, poor conditions or exploitation cause real exhaustion.
cautions: For genuine burnout from overwork, 'it is your attachment' can sound like blame; acknowledge the load first.
not_for: someone exhausted by unsafe or exploitative conditions who needs to change the conditions
speaks_to: work that has become your identity

viv.1.monkey_mind.context: He has just defined pratyahara as gathering the mind in from the senses, the start of real character. Then the traditional story of a restless monkey made drunk, stung by a scorpion, and finally possessed by a demon. He applies it to the mind: desire, then jealousy of others' success, then pride. Next comes the first practice: let the mind run and watch it.
viv.1.monkey_mind.core_teaching: The mind is restless by nature and made worse by desire, envy and pride; that is why control is hard and must be learned patiently.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (CW vol. 1, Raja-Yoga ch. 6)
commentaries.gist: The story sets up his first practical lesson: sit and let the mind run while simply watching it.

commentaries.who: Preface to Raja-Yoga (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He warns that, with few exceptions, Yoga can be safely learned only in direct contact with a teacher.

viv.1.monkey_mind.practical_reading: Used to normalise a restless mind: the chatter is the mind's nature, not your failure.
misreadings: Not a moral condemnation of having a busy mind

viv.1.moral_gymnasium.context: This is his own recap at the close of the fifth class, which he calls 'today's lecture'. The elided points say helping is a privilege and that God, not we, sustains the world. He adds: avoid fanaticism, which is opposed to love, and the calmer we are the better we work.
viv.1.moral_gymnasium.core_teaching: The world is not ours to fix; it is a training ground where serving others strengthens us.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 5)
commentaries.gist: His four-point summary: we are debtors to the world, God sustains it, we should not hate anyone, and we should avoid fanaticism.

commentaries.who: Inspired Talks, 25 July 1895 (CW vol. 7)
commentaries.gist: Same image a few months earlier: thank God for the world as a moral gymnasium, but never imagine you can help the world.

viv.1.moral_gymnasium.practical_reading: Used to reframe hardship at work or home as practice in patience and service.
misreadings: Not 'you have no rightful claims on anyone'
cautions: 'The world does not owe us anything' can hurt people who are owed justice, such as abuse survivors or unpaid carers
not_for: someone denied justice or wages
speaks_to: frustration that the world won't change

viv.1.no_duty_ugly.context: The proud ascetic, sent by the housewife, finds the butcher selling meat, hears from him the teaching that forms the Vyadha-Gita of the Mahabharata, and asks why such a sage does such filthy work. The butcher calls him son and gives this answer, then says his birth placed him there, he learnt the trade as a boy and does it unattached, serving his parents.
viv.1.no_duty_ugly.core_teaching: No honest work is degrading in itself; what matters is doing one's duty well and without attachment.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 4)
commentaries.gist: The butcher says he learned the trade as a boy, does it unattached, serves his parents, and gained his insight without yoga or renunciation.

commentaries.who: Mahabharata, Vana Parva sec. 214 (Ganguli, wisdomlib)
commentaries.gist: In the epic the fowler explains his birth by a curse from a past life, and calls his parents his highest teachers.

commentaries.who: "On Indian Women" interview, 1898 (CW, wisdomlib)
commentaries.gist: He cites the butcher Dharma-Vyadha as one who reached enlightenment through common faithfulness and duty.

viv.1.no_duty_ugly.practical_reading: Used for dignity in unglamorous or stigmatised work.
misreadings: Not a defence of caste-bound occupations or of keeping people in work they were born into
Not a claim that all work is ethically equal
cautions: The butcher's next words, 'my birth placed me in these circumstances', can be read as caste fatalism; frame around dignity, not birth
not_for: someone trapped in work by caste or class pressure
speaks_to: students looked down on for their background

viv.1.not_hate_ourselves.context: He says teaching only the highest ideal, 'resist not evil', would condemn most people, make them feel always wrong, and that constant self-disapproval breeds more vice than any weakness. This line follows. Next: one who has no faith in himself can never have faith in God, so duty and morality must vary with circumstance.
viv.1.not_hate_ourselves.core_teaching: Ideals pitched too high breed self-hatred, which degrades; growth starts from faith in oneself.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 2)
commentaries.gist: He warns that the highest ideal taught to everyone breeds self-condemnation, and that the gate to degeneration opens for one who hates himself.

commentaries.who: "Practical Vedanta I", London 1896 (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He calls one who does not believe in himself the real atheist, and says faith in oneself does everything.

viv.1.not_hate_ourselves.practical_reading: Used for perfectionism and shame: self-respect is the ground of growth, not its reward.
misreadings: Not 'never feel remorse'
cautions: The preceding sentence says the gate to degeneration has opened for one who hates himself; a self-critical or depressed reader could hear a verdict, so offer only this line
'No faith in himself, no faith in God' can wound believers in depression
not_for: severe depression if read as 'your self-hatred has doomed you'

viv.1.position_of_giver.context: He asks whether we expect anything back from our children for what we give them, and says to treat a city or a state the same way. This passage follows. He then contrasts working like slaves with working as master of one's mind, and says the world is guided by might and mercy.
viv.1.position_of_giver.core_teaching: Give as a free offering, as a parent to a child; attachment and pain come only from expecting a return.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 3)
commentaries.gist: He uses parents' giving to children as the model, then extends it to any person, city or state.

commentaries.who: Parallel in Karma-Yoga ch. 5 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He says a beggar owes us nothing and we should be grateful for the chance to help.

viv.1.position_of_giver.practical_reading: Used for giving in families and friendships without keeping accounts.
misreadings: Giving freely is not letting yourself be used
Not an argument against fair pay or reciprocity in relationships
cautions: The next lines call right and justice 'baby's talk'; do not pull them in for someone seeking justice
not_for: someone being financially or emotionally exploited
speaks_to: resentment toward adult children or siblings

viv.1.potentially_divine.context: The lines first appear as a motto closing the Preface to Raja-Yoga, right after he explains how Patanjali differs from Sankhya. They recur in his commentary on Yoga Sutra II.25, where he says ignorance joins the soul to nature and the aim of all religion is to be free of nature's control; the yogi seeks it through control of the mind.
viv.1.potentially_divine.core_teaching: Every soul is divine already; religion is the work of manifesting that by mastering inner and outer nature, by any of the four yogas, and all else is secondary.

commentaries.who: Preface to Raja-Yoga (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He presents the statement as the book's motto after explaining the Sankhya basis of Patanjali's system.

commentaries.who: Commentary on Yoga Sutra II.25 (CW vol. 1, Raja-Yoga)
commentaries.gist: He repeats it after explaining that freedom from ignorance ends the soul's bond to nature, the goal of all religions.

commentaries.who: Publication (Wikipedia)
commentaries.gist: Raja Yoga was published in July 1896.

viv.1.potentially_divine.practical_reading: Used as a summary creed: whatever your path, the goal is to bring out the best that is already in you.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of rituals, scriptures or temples as worthless; he calls them secondary, not useless
not_for: readers devoted to a ritual tradition who may hear contempt
speaks_to: seekers unsure which path is right

viv.1.silence_in_activity.context: Near the end of the first class he weighs two pictures, the whirl of work and quiet retreat, and says neither alone is perfect: the recluse is crushed by the world, the busy man suffers in quiet. This ideal joins both. He then says to begin humbly, taking work as it comes and noticing selfish motives.
viv.1.silence_in_activity.core_teaching: The ideal worker carries inner stillness into the busiest life and full energy into the quietest.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 1)
commentaries.gist: He presents this as the ideal of Karma-Yoga, then says we must start from the beginning, growing less selfish each day.

commentaries.who: Parallel in Karma-Yoga ch. 8 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He says not to flee the world-machine but to learn the secret of work inside it.

viv.1.silence_in_activity.practical_reading: Used for staying calm in a busy city job, or energised in a quiet one.
misreadings: Not a standard to beat yourself with; he says start where you are
cautions: Anxious readers may hear one more ideal they are failing; pair with his 'begin from the beginning'
speaks_to: balancing meditation with a busy job

viv.1.sneers_ridicule.context: He has said duty differs by circumstance and that one idea runs through all his teaching: condemn weakness; the Vedas repeat 'fearlessness'. This line follows. He then turns to his closing story, the king who learns that monk and householder are each great in their own place.
viv.1.sneers_ridicule.core_teaching: Do your duty without being governed by the mockery of others; fearlessness is the Vedic ideal.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 2)
commentaries.gist: He ties this to the Vedic word 'fearlessness', then tells the story of the king, the monk and the householder.

commentaries.who: Same chapter (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 2)
commentaries.gist: He also says neither monk nor householder should look down on the other; each is great in his own place.

viv.1.sneers_ridicule.practical_reading: Used for social courage: choosing an unpopular path, career or belief.
misreadings: Not 'fear is shameful'
Not 'ignore all criticism'
cautions: 'Fear is a sign of weakness' can shame people with anxiety, panic or trauma; keep the focus on mockery, not on fear itself
not_for: anxiety disorders
trauma survivors
speaks_to: being mocked for faith or values

viv.1.state_of_mind.context: He says the world is neither good nor evil; each person makes a world for himself. The young are optimistic and the old pessimistic, and both are foolish. After this line he says fire is neither good nor bad in itself, depending on use, and that the world is perfect in being fitted to its purpose.
viv.1.state_of_mind.core_teaching: Whether life seems good or evil depends largely on the mind that meets it.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 5)
commentaries.gist: Each man manufactures his own world; fire warms or burns depending on use; so the world.

commentaries.who: "The Gita III", San Francisco 1900 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He says the world is not as bad as we think; we make our own ghosts and demons.

viv.1.state_of_mind.practical_reading: Used for perspective and cognitive reframing in ordinary troubles.
misreadings: Not a denial of real hardship, injustice or trauma
cautions: For trauma, grief or poverty, 'neither good nor evil by itself' can sound like the pain is only in the head
He calls the old 'foolish' for complaining; avoid for elderly readers
not_for: trauma
grief
clinical depression

viv.1.streams_to_sea.context: In his first Parliament speech he says he is proud of a religion that sheltered persecuted Jews and Zoroastrians, then quotes a hymn he says he has repeated since boyhood. After it he cites the Gita's 'whosoever comes to Me, through whatsoever form, I reach him' and condemns sectarianism and fanaticism.
viv.1.streams_to_sea.core_teaching: Different people take different paths by temperament, straight or winding, and all lead to the same Lord as all rivers reach the sea.

commentaries.who: Context of the address (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He follows the hymn with the Gita's promise that whatever way people come, God meets them.

commentaries.who: Shiva Mahimna Stotra v. 7 (sanskritdocuments.org)
commentaries.gist: The verse names Veda, Sankhya, Yoga, Pashupata and Vaishnava paths, chosen by temperament, all reaching Shiva as rivers reach the ocean; the hymn is ascribed to Pushpadanta.

commentaries.who: First Public Lecture in the East, Colombo 1897 (CW vol. 3)
commentaries.gist: He quotes the same verse, naming the Mahimnah-stotra, as India's lesson of sympathy beyond mere toleration.

commentaries.who: Gita 4.11 (vedabase.io)
commentaries.gist: The Gita verse he cites next: Krishna responds to people as they approach him, and all follow his path.

viv.1.streams_to_sea.practical_reading: Used for respecting other people's paths, including within one family.
misreadings: Not a claim that all paths are identical in content

viv.1.suppress_anger.context: Commenting on the sutra that recommends friendliness, mercy, gladness and indifference toward the happy, the miserable, the good and the evil, he says most daily trouble comes from not holding the mind steady: when someone harms us we react, the mind goes out in waves, and we lose power. This passage follows. Next comes sutra I.34 on breath.
viv.1.suppress_anger.core_teaching: Each impulse of hatred or anger that is mastered, not acted out, becomes stored strength that can turn into higher powers.

commentaries.who: Context of the commentary (CW vol. 1, Raja-Yoga, YS I.33)
commentaries.gist: He ties it to the four attitudes of I.33 and to the mind losing power each time it reacts to harm.

commentaries.who: Inspired Talks, 25 July 1895 (CW vol. 7)
commentaries.gist: He says to bless one who curses you, since it is a chance to practise self-restraint.

viv.1.suppress_anger.practical_reading: Used for reactivity: pause before answering in anger and the pause itself becomes strength.
misreadings: Not 'bottle up feelings'
Not 'ignore harm done to you'; anger at real harm still needs safe expression and action
cautions: 'Suppress' can be heard as denying feelings; for abuse or trauma survivors it may sound like they must swallow anger
not_for: abuse victims
people with trauma whose anger needs room

viv.1.take_up_one_idea.context: He criticises people who take up each new practice for its novelty and drop it; one must stick with a thing to the end, and only one who 'can become mad with an idea' sees light. This passage follows. Next he says the first step is not to disturb the mind: avoid disturbing people, places and foods, and for the highest, avoid all company.
viv.1.take_up_one_idea.core_teaching: Real attainment comes from devoting oneself wholly to one aim, not dabbling in many.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (CW vol. 1, Raja-Yoga ch. 6)
commentaries.gist: He attacks 'nibbling at things', then advises avoiding disturbing company, and for the highest seekers all company.

commentaries.who: Preface to Raja-Yoga (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He cautions that Yoga is safely learnt only with a teacher, with few exceptions.

viv.1.take_up_one_idea.practical_reading: Used for focus: commit to one project or practice long enough to see results.
misreadings: Not 'drop your family and friends for your goal'
cautions: The surrounding text praises becoming 'mad with an idea' and avoiding all company; risky for anyone isolated, depressed, manic or obsessive
not_for: isolation or loneliness
mania or obsessive thinking
someone told to cut off support

viv.1.through_their_eyes.context: He has described how strangers are exploited abroad and carry home false impressions, and how sailors and traders behave badly in foreign lands, which may be why the Chinese call Westerners 'foreign devils'. This line follows. Next: 'I am not the standard of the universe'; we should do the duty of our birth and position.
viv.1.through_their_eyes.core_teaching: Judge other people and cultures by their own frame, not by ours.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 4)
commentaries.gist: He says duty changes with environment, and that he must fit himself to the world, not the world to him.

commentaries.who: "Hints on Practical Spirituality", Los Angeles (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He gives the example of English travellers condemning a French bullfight while the French condemned English prize-fighting.

viv.1.through_their_eyes.practical_reading: Used for cross-cultural empathy at work, in marriage, and with in-laws.
misreadings: Not 'never judge harmful practices'

viv.1.tolerance_acceptance.context: After thanking the audience in the name of the oldest order of monks and of millions of Hindus, and acknowledging speakers who credited the East with toleration, he says this. He then says he is proud of a nation that sheltered persecuted Jews and Zoroastrians, and quotes the hymn of many streams reaching one sea.
viv.1.tolerance_acceptance.core_teaching: His tradition goes beyond tolerating other religions to accepting them all as true.

commentaries.who: Context of the address (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He moves from this claim to India's shelter of refugees and the hymn of many rivers reaching one sea.

commentaries.who: First Public Lecture in the East, Colombo 1897 (CW vol. 3)
commentaries.gist: Back home he says the world must learn from India not only toleration but sympathy.

viv.1.tolerance_acceptance.practical_reading: Used for respect in mixed families, workplaces and neighbourhoods: go beyond putting up with others.
misreadings: Not a claim that every belief or practice is beyond question

viv.1.true_to_nature.context: In a lecture on the prophets he says they were messengers of God whom he worships, but they are dead and we are alive and must go ahead. Religion is not imitating Jesus or Mohammed; be Jesus rather than an imitation. After this line he says that if you do not exist, God does not exist for you, and the prophets are signposts, not resting places.
viv.1.true_to_nature.core_teaching: The highest religion is authenticity: grow from your own nature with self-trust rather than imitating even great prophets.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Ida Ansell notes)
commentaries.gist: The prophets are signposts urging us onward; religion is not imitation; the notes mark gaps with dots.

commentaries.who: "The Common Bases of Hinduism", Lahore 1897 (CW vol. 3)
commentaries.gist: He tells Indian youth to have faith in themselves and not imitate, since working at others' dictation erodes independence.

viv.1.true_to_nature.practical_reading: Used for authenticity: stop copying someone else's life, even a good one.
misreadings: Not a rejection of teachers or prophets; he says he worships them
cautions: A shorthand transcript with gaps; wording is not his polished text
Nearby lines ('be not an imitation of Jesus, but be Jesus') may offend Christian or Muslim readers
not_for: readers who may take it as disrespect to their prophet
speaks_to: finding one's own way in faith

viv.1.truth_to_truth.context: Defending image worship, he says the Hindu does not abuse anyone's idol: if a man can realise his divinity through an image, that is not sin, and passing beyond that stage does not make it an error, as childhood is not a sin for an old man. This line follows. Next: all religions, from fetishism up, are attempts of the soul to grasp the Infinite, each a stage.
viv.1.truth_to_truth.core_teaching: Spiritual growth moves from lesser to greater truth; earlier stages are not errors to be despised.

commentaries.who: Context of the paper (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He applies the idea to image worship and to every religion as a stage in the soul's ascent.

commentaries.who: "Christ, the Messenger", Los Angeles 1900 (CW vol. 4)
commentaries.gist: He repeats it with the image of travelling toward the sun, which looks bigger at every stage yet is the same sun.

commentaries.who: Notes taken down in Madras, 1892-93 (CW, wisdomlib)
commentaries.gist: Already in India he named passing from lower to higher truth, never from error to truth, as a mark of Hinduism.

viv.1.truth_to_truth.practical_reading: Used for kindness toward one's own past beliefs and toward people at other stages.
misreadings: Not 'every claim is equally true'

viv.1.unknown_heroes.context: Just before, he says the way out of misery is to give up the idea of happiness, since the two are linked, and that the only way beyond death is to give up the love of life. The elided line calls the known Buddhas and Christs second-rate heroes beside the unknown ones. After: those unknown leave their ideas to the world and found no schools in their name.
viv.1.unknown_heroes.core_teaching: Seeking credit spoils good work and brings misery; the greatest people worked silently and passed unknown.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 7)
commentaries.gist: He describes unknown sages whose thoughts later find voice in famous teachers, and who put forward no claims for themselves.

commentaries.who: Parallel in Karma-Yoga ch. 2 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He calls doing good without the approval of others the highest sacrifice.

viv.1.unknown_heroes.practical_reading: Used for quiet service: carers, teachers and parents whose work is never in the papers.
misreadings: Not a reason to let others take credit unchallenged at work
Not 'your work is worthless if unseen'
cautions: The sentences just before say the only way beyond death is to give up the love of life; never pull them in for a depressed or self-harm-risk reader
The elided line calls Buddha and Christ 'second-rate heroes', which can offend
not_for: suicidal or depressed readers if surrounding lines are used

viv.1.wait_and_watch.context: Right after the monkey simile he gives the first lesson: sit and let the mind run. The elided lines say knowledge is power, you cannot control the mind until you know what it does, and you may be shocked by hideous thoughts that arise. After it he says thoughts lessen over months with patient daily practice.
viv.1.wait_and_watch.core_teaching: Begin not by fighting the mind but by watching it; with daily patience it grows calmer.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (CW vol. 1, Raja-Yoga ch. 6)
commentaries.gist: Watching the mind comes first; over months the thoughts thin out, but practice must be daily and patient.

commentaries.who: Preface to Raja-Yoga (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He reminds students that Yoga is safely learnt in direct contact with a teacher.

viv.1.wait_and_watch.practical_reading: Used as a beginner's meditation: notice thoughts without wrestling them.
misreadings: Not 'suppress your thoughts'
cautions: The elided lines warn that hideous thoughts may surface; for people with intrusive thoughts, OCD or trauma, unguided open watching can be distressing; suggest a teacher or therapist
not_for: severe intrusive thoughts or trauma without support

viv.1.weakness_as_forgiveness.context: Introducing the Gita, he describes Arjuna seeing kin on both sides and refusing to fight, and says life is a continuous fight for all of us. This passage follows. Next: only someone who could strike and forbears earns merit; we often give up through laziness and cowardice and call it bravery; and he renders the Gita's call to give up faint-heartedness.
viv.1.weakness_as_forgiveness.core_teaching: Forgiveness and renunciation count only when chosen from strength; we often dress up fear and weakness as virtue.

commentaries.who: Context of the class (CW vol. 1, Ida Ansell notes)
commentaries.gist: Merit lies in the one who could strike yet forbears; he then turns to Krishna's call to give up faint-heartedness.

commentaries.who: Gita 2.3 (vedabase.io, Prabhupada)
commentaries.gist: Glosses klaibyam as impotence and hṛdaya-daurbalyam as weakness of heart; the purport calls Arjuna's pity weakness, not virtue.

viv.1.weakness_as_forgiveness.practical_reading: Used for honest self-examination: am I forgiving, or avoiding a hard conversation?
misreadings: Not a push to retaliate
Not 'forgiveness is weakness'; chosen forgiveness is the real thing
cautions: Abuse survivors who chose not to fight back must not hear 'cowardice'
Gendered 'unmanliness' framing
'Laziness and cowardice' language can read as blame
not_for: abuse survivors
trauma responses like freezing

viv.1.without_approbation.context: He says he will read passages from the Mahanirvana Tantra on the householder: devoted to God, working constantly, offering the fruits to God. This passage sits inside that reading. Next: the householder's great duty is to earn a living honestly and to please his parents as visible representatives of God.
viv.1.without_approbation.core_teaching: The hardest and highest thing is to keep doing good without needing gratitude, fame or approval.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 2)
commentaries.gist: Presented within his rendering of the Mahanirvana Tantra on the householder's duties: honest living, care of parents, service of God and the poor.

commentaries.who: Parallel in Karma-Yoga ch. 1 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: Great occasions make even small people heroic; true greatness is the same in everyday conduct.

viv.1.without_approbation.practical_reading: Used for unseen goodness: carers, parents, people doing right in organisations that don't notice.
misreadings: Not 'never ask for credit you are due'
not_for: someone being exploited and told to want no recognition

viv.1.witness.context: He has said the idea that the world exists for our enjoyment holds us down: millions leave it each year and the world does not feel it; we are as much for the world as it is for us. This passage gives two rules. Next comes his master's image of the nurse who cares fully for a child yet can leave without a pang.
viv.1.witness.core_teaching: Work fully, but drop attachment and keep an inner witness that does not get pulled into the fray.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. 6)
commentaries.gist: The two rules are to give up attachment and to stay a witness while working; the nurse image illustrates both.

commentaries.who: Parallel in Karma-Yoga ch. 7 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He says we only help ourselves in this gymnasium of the world, and should never think we help the universe.

viv.1.witness.practical_reading: Used to stay steady in conflict or crisis at work: act, but don't get swept up.
misreadings: Not emotional detachment from loved ones
Not passivity; 'go on working' is half the instruction
cautions: The preceding lines ('millions pass out of it every year; the world does not feel it') can wound a grieving reader
not_for: fresh grief
someone already numb or dissociated

viv.2.angels_unawares.context: He says the great preparations for yoga are mental: a quiet life, freedom from anxiety, and not trying to keep comfort while seeking the Self (the fool grabbing a crocodile for a log, from the Vivekachudamani). He quotes 'seek ye first the kingdom of God'. Then this passage; next, meditation as the greatest help.
viv.2.angels_unawares.core_teaching: Give yourself wholly to an ideal; the struggle brings growth, and even mistakes may turn out to be gifts.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He sets this between renunciation ('seek ye first the kingdom') and meditation as the greatest help.

commentaries.who: "Sadhanas or Preparations for Higher Life" (CW, wisdomlib)
commentaries.gist: He tells listeners to bless their mistakes, since they have been angels unawares, and to hold on to the ideal.

viv.2.angels_unawares.practical_reading: Used for self-compassion about mistakes made while striving.
misreadings: Not 'mistakes have no consequences'
cautions: 'Leave no place in the mind for anything else' can feed obsession or isolation
not_for: obsessive or manic states

viv.2.atheist_himself.context: He says all the difference between people lies in faith in themselves, which he has found in his own life and which grows as he ages. Then this contrast. Next: it is not selfish faith, because Vedanta teaches oneness, so faith in oneself means faith in all and love for all.
viv.2.atheist_himself.core_teaching: Faith in one's own divine nature is the heart of religion; lacking it is the real atheism.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He insists this is not selfish faith: since all are one, faith in yourself is faith in all.

commentaries.who: Karma-Yoga ch. 2 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He says one who has no faith in himself can never have faith in God.

viv.2.atheist_himself.practical_reading: Used for self-belief: trust your capacity as you trust a friend's.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of belief in God
Not arrogance; he grounds it in oneness
cautions: Believers in a crisis of confidence may hear 'you are an atheist'
Atheist readers may find the word used as a slur
not_for: severe depression, where self-belief is not a choice

viv.2.calm_mind_works.context: He says Vedanta's real activity is joined to unshakable calm; asked how one can work without passion, he says he once thought so but learned that less passion means better work. The elided lines say letting feelings loose wastes energy and shatters nerves, and that great workers were calm. After: the ideal is always ahead of the real.
viv.2.calm_mind_works.core_teaching: Calm, forgiving balance, not passion or anger, produces the most work.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He presents calm as the condition for real activity and says he learned this with age.

commentaries.who: Karma-Yoga ch. 1 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: His ideal worker moves through a city with a mind calm as in a cave.

viv.2.calm_mind_works.practical_reading: Used for anger at work and in family: steady beats stormy.
misreadings: Not 'feelings are wasteful' in general
cautions: Grieving or traumatised readers may hear that their emotions are wasted energy
Not a reason to suppress anger at real injustice
not_for: fresh grief
someone whose anger needs to be heard

viv.2.cannot_give_up.context: He says the Gita teaches to work with the whole mind yet without attachment, so we can quit whenever we like. This sentence follows. Next: we know clinging hurts us yet cannot tear away, like a bee that came to sip honey and got its feet stuck in the pot.
viv.2.cannot_give_up.core_teaching: Our deepest sorrow is clinging to something that is failing and harming us, unable to let go; we must be able to attach and detach at will.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: The bee stuck in the honey-pot shows how we get caught by what we came only to enjoy.

commentaries.who: Karma-Yoga ch. 6 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He gives two rules for work: drop attachment and remain a witness.

viv.2.cannot_give_up.practical_reading: Used for sunk-cost traps: a failing venture, a habit, a relationship that only hurts.
misreadings: Not advice to abandon every hard commitment
Not 'quit whenever it gets difficult'
not_for: someone being urged to give up care of a dependant

viv.2.child_teaches_himself.context: Vivekananda argues that earlier attempts at religious harmony failed because they tried to boil all religions down to a few shared doctrines, producing more quarrelling sects. His own 'little plan' is not to destroy anyone's faith but to help each person grow along their own line. The child and plant analogy supports this: no one makes another spiritual; a helper can only remove obstacles. He then describes four types of mind (active, emotional, mystical, philosophical) that a universal religion must serve.
viv.2.child_teaches_himself.core_teaching: Growth, whether a child's or a seeker's, comes from inside; those who help can create opportunities and protect from harm, but cannot force the growing.

commentaries.who: Surrounding lecture (Complete Works vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: The analogy belongs to his argument 'help, do not destroy': stop assuming you can make others spiritual; serve the different types of mind instead of forcing one mould.

commentaries.who: Vedanta Society of Northern California, monthly reading of this lecture
commentaries.gist: Reads the passage as following from his view that God is the centre of all religions and each person moves toward it along a different path, so one should meet people where they are and help them forward.

commentaries.who: Lecture chronology (vivekananda.net)
commentaries.gist: Dates 'The Ideal of a Universal Religion' to New York, 12 January 1896.

viv.2.child_teaches_himself.practical_reading: For a parent: today, instead of pushing a skill or lesson, remove one obstacle (a distraction, a fear, a missing tool) and give one opportunity, then step back and let the child do the growing.
misreadings: Not 'leave children to it'; providing and protecting is the hedge he describes.
Not a rejection of teaching; it redefines the teacher's job.
cautions: In context it is about spiritual growth; applying it to parenting is a natural but modern extension.
Parents of children with special needs may hear 'the child teaches himself' as dismissive of the support they give; stress the hedge.
not_for: a parent dealing with a child in danger or crisis, where active intervention is the hedge
speaks_to: trust in a child's own growth

viv.2.condemn_none.context: He says all differences, between virtue and vice, heaven and hell, life and death, are of degree, not kind, so we have no right to look down on anyone less developed. This passage follows. Next: criticism wastes energy, since all are seeing the same thing, and he turns to the idea of sin.
viv.2.condemn_none.core_teaching: Since all differ only in degree, condemn no one: help if you can, otherwise bless them and let them go their way.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: His ground is oneness: differences are of degree, so contempt is unjustified.

commentaries.who: "The Ideal of a Universal Religion" (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He gives nearly the same rule: help if you can; if not, stand by and do no harm.

viv.2.condemn_none.practical_reading: Used against harsh judgment of others, online and off.
misreadings: Not approval of harm
Not a reason to stay where you are mistreated
not_for: someone being told not to name abuse

viv.2.creator_of_destiny.context: He says blaming others only weakens us: blame none, stand on your own feet, and say 'this misery I suffer is of my own doing', since what I made I can unmake. This passage follows. Next he says to let the dead past bury its dead, since good thoughts and deeds stand ready like angels to defend us.
viv.2.creator_of_destiny.core_teaching: Stop blaming others; take responsibility and know that the strength to shape your future is within you.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: Just before, he asks hearers to call their misery their own doing so that they can undo it.

commentaries.who: Karma-Yoga ch. 1 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: We are responsible for what we are and can make ourselves what we wish.

commentaries.who: "Unity in Diversity", London 1896 (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He says we make our own fortunes and our own suffering, then put our hands over our eyes and call it dark.

viv.2.creator_of_destiny.practical_reading: Used for agency after a setback: whatever happened, you can author what comes next.
misreadings: Not 'everything that happens to you is your fault'
Not a reason to blame the sick, the poor or victims
cautions: The sentence just before says to own your misery as your own doing; for abuse victims, the ill, the bereaved or the depressed this reads as blame. Use only the forward-looking part
not_for: abuse or assault survivors
grief
chronic illness
depression

viv.2.difference_sign_of_thought.context: He says beyond swords there are crueller weapons, contempt, social hatred and ostracism, used on those who think differently, and asks why everyone should think alike; he does not want to live in a grave-like land. This line follows. Next he asks how contradictory religions can all be true.
viv.2.difference_sign_of_thought.core_teaching: Disagreement is a sign of thinking minds; a thoughtful person should welcome a world of differing views.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He condemns contempt and ostracism toward those who think differently.

commentaries.who: "Address at the Final Session", Chicago 1893 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: Each faith should keep its individuality while learning from others.

viv.2.difference_sign_of_thought.practical_reading: Used for families and teams where disagreement feels threatening.

viv.2.do_not_destroy.context: He says attempts to unify religion by binding all to a few doctrines only made more sects; he offers his own plan for discussion. First maxim: do not destroy; iconoclastic reformers do no good; build. This passage follows. Second maxim: take people where they stand and lift them from there.
viv.2.do_not_destroy.core_teaching: Build, don't tear down: help if you can, do no harm if you can't, and never attack anyone's sincere convictions.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: This is the first point of his plan; the second is to take each person where they stand.

commentaries.who: "Practical Vedanta I", London 1896 (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: Condemn none; help if you can, or bless and let them go.

viv.2.do_not_destroy.practical_reading: Used in arguments about belief and in parenting: don't demolish, build up.
misreadings: Not 'never challenge harmful beliefs'; he says 'so far as they are sincere'

viv.2.eyes_of_love.context: Near the close of the lecture he says those who worship through ceremonies and forms are not in error; it is a journey from lower to higher truth, as darkness is less light. This line follows. Then: what is within is without; we see impurity only if it is in us; and Vedanta lets us work with contentment.
viv.2.eyes_of_love.core_teaching: See others with love, knowing they are walking a path we have walked too.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He grounds the line in the idea that all forms of worship are steps from lower to higher truth.

commentaries.who: "Paper on Hinduism", Chicago 1893 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: Same idea: humanity travels from truth to truth, not from error to truth.

viv.2.eyes_of_love.practical_reading: Used for patience with younger people, beginners or one's former self.

viv.2.fear_of_death.context: He argues that if existence depended on memory, forgotten years of childhood were never lived, which is too narrow an idea of the self; we are only struggling toward true individuality, which is infinite. He alone lives whose life is in the whole universe. This passage follows. Next: fearlessness comes only when one can say 'I am in all lives, I am the universe'.
viv.2.fear_of_death.core_teaching: We truly live only when identified with all life; the narrow separate life is a kind of death, and that is why we fear death.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He leads into this from memory and individuality, and on to the fearlessness of one who sees himself in all.

commentaries.who: "Unity in Diversity", London 1896 (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He quotes the Upanishad that one who sees many here goes from death to death; see the One and be free.

viv.2.fear_of_death.practical_reading: Used to ease self-centred anxiety: widening care beyond oneself can loosen fear.
misreadings: Not a statement that ordinary life is worthless
Not a reason to welcome death
cautions: High risk: 'living this little life is death, simply death' could be read by a depressed or suicidal reader as devaluing their life
For fresh grief, the abstract 'one life' can feel dismissive of a particular person's loss
not_for: suicidal thoughts
depression
fresh grief
terminal illness without careful framing
speaks_to: fear of death in a philosophical mood

viv.2.grow_from_inside.context: He says no one can teach even a child; the child teaches himself. Our duty is to give opportunities and remove obstacles, as a hedge protects a plant that grows by itself. This line follows. Next: an outside teacher only removes obstructions; there is no teacher but your own soul.
viv.2.grow_from_inside.core_teaching: Spiritual growth cannot be imposed; it unfolds from within, and teachers only clear the way.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: Plant and hedge image; the teacher only removes obstacles; 'help if you can, but do not destroy'.

commentaries.who: "Practical Vedanta II", London 1896 (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: Looking back, he says, the help that came was always from within ourselves.

viv.2.grow_from_inside.practical_reading: Used for parenting and teaching: protect and provide; don't force.
misreadings: Not a rejection of teachers, mentors or therapy; he gives them the role of removing obstacles
not_for: someone in crisis who needs outside help now

viv.2.hands_before_eyes.context: He says that disbelief in the glory of one's own soul is what Vedanta calls atheism, and that nothing, sex, race or age, bars anyone from the ideal because it is already realised. This passage follows. Next he says darkness and weakness never existed, and calls those who cry that they are weak fools.
viv.2.hands_before_eyes.core_teaching: All power is already ours; the darkness we complain of is our own covering, and removing it reveals the light that was always there.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He insists the ideal is already realised in everyone; nothing bars anyone from it.

commentaries.who: "Unity in Diversity", London 1896 (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: Same image: you make yourselves suffer, put your hands before your eyes, and say it is dark.

commentaries.who: "The Gita III", San Francisco 1900 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: Same image again: we cover our eyes and cry for light; take the hands away.

viv.2.hands_before_eyes.practical_reading: Used for hope: what feels like permanent darkness may be a covering that can lift.
misreadings: Not 'your suffering is self-inflicted'
cautions: The very next lines call people 'fools' who cry that they are weak; depressed readers may hear contempt or blame
Not suitable as 'just choose to see the light' for clinical depression
not_for: clinical depression
grief
trauma

viv.2.help_from_within.context: He says that so long as we don't know our real nature we are beggars, crying to imaginary beings for help that never comes, and a whole life passes in weeping and hoping; 'be free; hope for nothing from anyone'. This passage follows. Next: the rich man's parlour is always full of hopefuls who never get anything.
viv.2.help_from_within.core_teaching: Looking back, real help came from within us, not from others; self-reliance rests on knowing our real nature.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He precedes this with crying to imaginary beings and the advice to hope for nothing from anyone.

commentaries.who: "Practical Vedanta IV", London 1896 (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He says he cried for years and was helped in the end, but the help came from within.

viv.2.help_from_within.practical_reading: Used for self-reliance: your own effort was never wasted.
misreadings: Not a reason to refuse help, therapy, medicine or a crisis line
Not a claim that no one will help you
cautions: Strong caution: the surrounding lines ('hope for nothing from anyone', prayers to 'imaginary beings') can discourage a person in crisis from reaching out, and can offend believers
not_for: anyone in crisis or at risk of self-harm
isolated or lonely readers
believers who rely on prayer

viv.2.hundred_thousand_ways.context: He says no single philosophy, myth or ritual will ever be held by all; we can only lessen friction by recognising the need for variety. The long elision (about 300 words) includes the image of photographing the sun at each stage of a journey toward it. After the water-in-vessels image: yet God is One, and India has long tried to work out this harmony.
viv.2.hundred_thousand_ways.core_teaching: Truth can be put in countless ways, each true as far as it goes; God appears to each in the shape of the vessel that holds Him.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He moves from accepting variation to the sun photographed at each stage, then the water in vessels.

commentaries.who: "Christ, the Messenger", Los Angeles 1900 (CW vol. 4)
commentaries.gist: He uses the journey toward the sun again: it looks different at each stage yet is the same sun.

viv.2.hundred_thousand_ways.practical_reading: Used for openness to other people's ways of seeing God or meaning.
misreadings: Not 'nothing is false'

viv.2.language_of_soul.context: He says one branded an atheist may meet the teacher who speaks his language and become deeply spiritual; we each eat in our own way, as Hindus eat with their fingers. This passage follows. Next: when the right teacher comes, we grasp it at once; so religions face a huge task, since human minds are of many types.
viv.2.language_of_soul.core_teaching: Spiritual truth satisfies only when it reaches us in a form fitted to our own nature.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: The 'atheist' who meets the right teacher, and eating in one's own way, illustrate the point.

commentaries.who: "The Ideal of a Universal Religion" (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: God, like water, takes the shape of each vessel.

viv.2.language_of_soul.practical_reading: Used for seekers who feel religion has never 'spoken' to them.
speaks_to: searching for a practice that fits

viv.2.little_mental_universe.context: He says 'practical' is relative: Indians who keep an arm raised for years are not fools but often brilliant people. This line follows. Next: English passengers raged at a bullfight in Marseilles, while the French threw out English prize-fighters as cruel.
viv.2.little_mental_universe.core_teaching: We wrongly treat our own small framework of values as the measure of everything.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: The bullfight and prize-fight story shows each nation condemning the other's cruelty.

commentaries.who: Karma-Yoga ch. 4 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: See others' duty through their own eyes; never judge other peoples' customs by your standard.

viv.2.little_mental_universe.practical_reading: Used for cross-cultural humility and for judging family members less.
misreadings: Not 'no practice can be criticised'

viv.2.love_in_return.context: He says if love is give-and-take, it follows the laws of buying and selling and a blow will come, like a mirror that returns our grimace; we get caught not by what we give but by what we expect. This line follows. Next: desire is the father of misery, and the one who asks nothing back is the most successful.
viv.2.love_in_return.core_teaching: Love hurts us not because we love but because we expect love back.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: Love as trade brings rises and falls; the man who asks no return is the truly successful one.

commentaries.who: Karma-Yoga ch. 3 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: True love brings no painful reaction; possessive clinging is something else.

viv.2.love_in_return.practical_reading: Used for relationships that have become bookkeeping: give without the ledger.
misreadings: Wanting care from a partner or parent is human; this is not 'you should expect nothing'
cautions: A grieving reader, or a child who lacked a parent's love, may hear that their longing is a fault
not_for: grief
neglect or abuse survivors

viv.2.means_and_end.context: The lecture's first lines. The elided words say he learned this from a great man whose life demonstrated it, and that our defect is being so drawn to the alluring goal that we neglect the means. After: causes produce effects, so once the means are right we can almost let the ideal go.
viv.2.means_and_end.core_teaching: Give the means as much care as the goal; if the means are right, the end will follow.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He argues from cause and effect: perfect the means and the goal will come.

commentaries.who: "Sketch of the Life of Pavhari Baba" (CW vol. 4)
commentaries.gist: Pavhari Baba's secret of work: love the means as if it were the end. Likely the 'great man' meant here.

commentaries.who: Karma-Yoga ch. 4 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He passes on a yogi's advice to join end and means into one.

viv.2.means_and_end.practical_reading: Used for goals and anxiety: focus on today's process, not the distant result.
misreadings: Not 'the goal doesn't matter'

viv.2.mistakes_made_me.context: He says help comes from within: he cried for years, was helped in the end from within, and had to undo his own mistakes; no aspiration in his life was in vain. This passage follows. The elided sentence says he does not mean you should go home and commit mistakes on purpose. Next: goodness is our nature; mistakes come from weakness, weakness from ignorance; he prefers 'mistakes' to 'sin'.
viv.2.mistakes_made_me.core_teaching: Every mistake helped make us who we are; don't brood over them, since our essential goodness cannot be destroyed.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He frames mistakes as products of ignorance, not sin, and insists our pure nature remains.

commentaries.who: "Sadhanas or Preparations for Higher Life" (CW, wisdomlib)
commentaries.gist: Bless your mistakes; they have been angels unawares; hold on to the ideal.

viv.2.mistakes_made_me.practical_reading: Used for regret and shame: your past, mistakes included, is part of how you got here.
misreadings: Not 'mistakes don't matter'
Not a licence for harm to others
cautions: Readers who caused serious harm need accountability alongside this
not_for: someone avoiding responsibility for serious harm

viv.2.never_mind_failures.context: He says we must hear the ideal until it fills the blood, meditate on it, and fill the mind with the highest thoughts day after day. This passage follows, with his joke that only a cow never lies. Next: the ideal is to see God in everything; if you can't, see Him in the one thing you love most; there is infinite life before the soul.
viv.2.never_mind_failures.core_teaching: Failures and lapses are natural and even give life its meaning; keep returning to the ideal however often you fall.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He follows with a gentle method: see God first in what you love most, then widen; take your time.

commentaries.who: "Sadhanas or Preparations for Higher Life" (CW, wisdomlib)
commentaries.gist: Do not look back on little mistakes; hold on to the ideal and march on.

viv.2.never_mind_failures.practical_reading: Used for persistence after relapse: in habits, sobriety, meditation or study.
misreadings: Not 'failure doesn't matter'
cautions: 'The beauty of life' can sound glib after a major loss
The following 'infinite life before the soul' assumes rebirth
not_for: fresh grief or catastrophic loss

viv.2.nothing_is_lost.context: He says realisation takes long preparation: striking a light takes a second, making the candle takes long. This passage follows, with his free rendering of Arjuna's question and Krishna's reply in Gita 6. Next he says breathing and posture are only physical helps; the real preparation is mental, starting with a quiet life free of anxiety.
viv.2.nothing_is_lost.core_teaching: No sincere effort is wasted; what we build carries forward, into the next birth if not this one.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He sets this between the long preparation needed and the mental groundwork of a quiet life.

commentaries.who: Gita 6.38 (vedabase.io)
commentaries.gist: Arjuna asks whether one who fails in yoga perishes like a cloud torn away, with no footing in either world.

commentaries.who: Gita 6.40 (vedabase.io)
commentaries.gist: Krishna says such a person meets no ruin here or hereafter; no one who does good comes to a bad end.

viv.2.nothing_is_lost.practical_reading: Used for discouragement about slow progress: small efforts count.
misreadings: Not a promise of results in this life
cautions: The passage relies on rebirth and offers the childhoods of Jesus, Buddha and Shankara as evidence; some readers will not share that frame
not_for: readers who reject rebirth, if offered as proof

viv.2.razor_edge.context: He is reading through the Katha Upanishad: the chariot of the senses, the Atman hidden from the senses but seen by the pure, and one who realises Him escapes death. 'But it is very difficult.' This passage follows. Next he says realisation is the central idea of all the Upanishads.
viv.2.razor_edge.core_teaching: The path is hard and dangerous like a razor's edge, but one must keep going and not lose heart until the goal is reached.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He gives this after saying realisation of the Atman is very difficult, then calls realisation the core of the Upanishads.

commentaries.who: Shankara on Katha Up. 1.3.14 (wisdomlib)
commentaries.gist: Shankara addresses those asleep in ignorance, urges going to knowing teachers, and says the path is hard because its object is so subtle.

viv.2.razor_edge.practical_reading: Used for long hard efforts: keep walking even when the path is narrow.
misreadings: Not 'never rest'
Not 'push through every warning sign'
not_for: burnout, if read as 'never stop'

viv.2.reason_not_authority.context: A Roman Catholic had told him reason is too weak to trust; he replies that priests are weaker still and he will follow reason, which gives some chance of truth, and sympathise with those who reach no belief by it. This line follows. Next: what matters is realisation, which comes from thinking; the glory of man is that he thinks.
viv.2.reason_not_authority.core_teaching: Honest reasoning, even if it leads to unbelief, is better than blind belief on authority.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He sets reason against priestly authority and asks for sympathy toward those who find no belief.

commentaries.who: "The Way to the Realisation of a Universal Religion", Pasadena 1900 (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: Thinking beings must differ; he wants to live among people of differing opinions.

viv.2.reason_not_authority.practical_reading: Used for doubters: questioning is not betrayal.
cautions: 'Two hundred millions of gods' and the Catholic exchange may offend some readers
not_for: readers in a fragile faith crisis who need support more than argument

viv.2.remedy_weakness.context: He says there are two ways: show people their weakness or their strength. Everyone knows their disease; thinking all the time that we are diseased won't cure us, medicine is needed. This passage follows. Next: teach people the strength within; instead of calling them sinners, Vedanta says they are pure and perfect.
viv.2.remedy_weakness.core_teaching: Dwelling on weakness doesn't cure it; thinking of and building strength does.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He uses a medical analogy: knowing the disease is not enough, medicine is needed; teach strength, not sin.

commentaries.who: "Paper on Hinduism", Chicago 1893 (CW vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: He refuses to call human beings sinners and calls them children of immortal bliss.

viv.2.remedy_weakness.practical_reading: Used against rumination: shift attention from what is wrong to what can be built.
misreadings: Not 'depression can be cured by positive thinking'
Not a rejection of treatment; he himself says medicine is needed
cautions: For depressed or anxious readers, 'stop brooding, think of strength' can feel like blame; pair with his own point that medicine is needed
not_for: clinical depression if offered as the cure

viv.2.still_small_voice.context: Part of his London Jnana-Yoga series. Just before this paragraph he argues that the modern habit of covering life's sores with optimism cannot last, since the covering is eventually stripped off. He then grants that we are all bound in Maya and asks whether there is any way out; right after, he contrasts the religious answer with 'practical' advice to just make the best of a bad world, which he calls a life of pretence.
viv.2.still_small_voice.core_teaching: Every honest person eventually feels that life is a kind of prison; yet in that very place a quiet voice keeps saying there is a way across. Religion, for him, begins when that voice is heard, often only after self-reliance has collapsed.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2, 'Maya and Freedom')
commentaries.gist: He sets out two answers together: the bold claim that this world is Maya, and the hopeful claim that there is a way beyond it. He rejects 'make the best of it' as hypocrisy.

commentaries.who: Bhagavad Gita 7.14 (the verse he paraphrases; vedabase.io)
commentaries.gist: Krishna says his Maya made of the three gunas is hard to get past, but those who take refuge in him cross beyond it. Vivekananda sets this beside Jesus' 'Come unto me' as the same voice.

viv.2.still_small_voice.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that the moment of feeling utterly at the end of one's strength is not only a loss but the moment a deeper call can be heard.
misreadings: Not a claim that life is worthless or that suffering should be accepted passively
Not a proof text for one religion: he deliberately pairs the Gita and the Gospel
cautions: Opens with a bleak picture (the world as prison, life and death as synonyms) that may deepen low mood if the reading stops before the hopeful turn
Says the old feel it most; avoid implying older readers are disillusioned
not_for: someone in acute crisis who needs practical help rather than metaphysics
readers who would hear 'prison' as confirmation of hopelessness
speaks_to: feeling trapped or that nothing will change
the point where one's own strength has run out
seekers asking what religion is for

viv.2.stony_heart.context: The lecture argues that we need both the power to attach ourselves fully and the power to detach at will. Just before this line he describes people who never love: like a wall, they are never hurt, but they are only a wall. He concludes it is better to be attached and caught than to be a wall, then says the goal is to keep the full power of love and still be higher than the gods by being able to let go.
viv.2.stony_heart.core_teaching: Avoiding love to avoid pain also shuts out joy; hardness is not freedom. The aim is to love completely and keep the strength to let go.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2, 'Work and its Secret')
commentaries.gist: Right after the line he says such hardness is weakness and death, a soul not yet awakened; what he wants is the mighty power of love together with the power to detach.

commentaries.who: Related passage, same lecture
commentaries.gist: Earlier he says attachment is the source of our pleasures and also of our misery, and that only one who can both attach fully and detach when needed gets the best out of life.

viv.2.stony_heart.practical_reading: Applied to people who have shut down after being hurt: closing the heart buys safety at the price of joy; the work is to stay open while learning to let go.
misreadings: Not a call to cling or to stay in harmful attachments
Not a rebuke of people who are grieving or numb; he is describing a chosen hardness
cautions: Someone numb from trauma or depression may hear 'stony' as blame; frame numbness as protection, not failure
not_for: acute depression or trauma-related numbness
someone in an abusive bond being told to stay open
speaks_to: after a heartbreak, deciding never to love again

viv.2.strength_is_life.context: This comes in the same Los Angeles lecture, right after he quotes the Gita's call to work without being caught. He compares misery to microbes that only take hold of a weakened body; then he moves on to attachment as the source of both pleasure and pain.
viv.2.strength_is_life.core_teaching: Misery is always around us, but it gets a grip only when the mind is weak; building inner strength is therefore the real protection.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2, 'Work and its Secret')
commentaries.gist: He links weakness to slavery and every kind of misery, and immediately after the line describes strength as lasting happiness and weakness as constant strain.

commentaries.who: Same saying in a Calcutta conversation, 22 January 1898 (CW vol. 5, diary of S. N. Sen)
commentaries.gist: He repeats the phrase while urging shraddha, faith in oneself as the deathless Atman, saying this faith is what the country lost.

viv.2.strength_is_life.practical_reading: Teachers use it as a call to tend the mind like the body: build habits of courage and self-trust so that hard events do not take hold so deeply.
misreadings: Not a judgement on illness, depression or anyone who is struggling
Not 'only the strong deserve to live'
Not denial of real external causes of suffering
cautions: 'Weakness is death' can sound like blame to someone ill, disabled or depressed; pair it with the idea that strength can be built and helped
not_for: someone with clinical depression or chronic illness who may hear it as fault-finding
grief in its early days
speaks_to: feeling battered by many small worries

viv.2.strike_a_match.context: In the last of four London lectures on practical Vedanta he argues that the will is almighty and what we need is character. Just before this he says that telling people their nature is evil, so they sit weeping over past false steps, only weakens them. After it he asks his hearers to see the pure Self even in the worst person and call it out instead of condemning.
viv.2.strike_a_match.core_teaching: Brooding over past wrongs does not remove them; bringing in the light of one's true nature does, at once. Put energy into building character, not into lament.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2, 'Practical Vedanta IV')
commentaries.gist: He says teaching people that they are evil sends them toward more evil, and asks that we hail even the vilest person as the pure, deathless Self rather than condemn him.

commentaries.who: Same image elsewhere: 'The Common Bases of Hinduism', Lahore 1897 (CW vol. 3)
commentaries.gist: He uses the dark room again for reform: crying 'it is dark' does nothing; bring in light and suggest higher things, starting from faith in people.

commentaries.who: Same image: 'Reply to the Madras Address' (CW vol. 4)
commentaries.gist: Positive, constructive teaching lasts; bring in light and darkness leaves by itself.

viv.2.strike_a_match.practical_reading: Used against rumination and shame: instead of replaying a mistake, take one constructive step that expresses who you want to be.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of making amends to people one has harmed
Not a claim that remorse is always wrong; his target is paralysing self-condemnation
cautions: Readers carrying heavy guilt may need to hear that accountability and repair still matter
not_for: someone who has seriously harmed another and is avoiding responsibility
fresh grief over a death, where 'light in a moment' sounds glib
speaks_to: after a failure, wanting to start again

viv.2.temple_of_man.context: After telling the Upanishadic story of Satyakama, he argues that worshipping the living person in front of us is the most practical religion. Just before, he says the human body is the highest temple; just after, he notes that this idea frightens people who prefer inherited theories, and adds that each must have his own path though the path is not the goal.
viv.2.temple_of_man.core_teaching: Freedom comes the moment we truly see God in every human being and stand in reverence before each person; that is the most practical worship.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 2, 'Practical Vedanta II')
commentaries.gist: He contrasts the Vedantic claim that nothing is not God with building churches while ignoring the living God within people, calling the human soul the only God to worship.

commentaries.who: Parallel: Rameswaram temple address, 1897 (CW vol. 3)
commentaries.gist: He tells pilgrims that seeing Shiva in the poor, weak and diseased is real worship, and image worship only preliminary.

viv.2.temple_of_man.practical_reading: Teachers turn it into a daily practice: treat each person you meet today, including difficult ones, as sacred.
misreadings: Not a rejection of all temples or rituals; he calls the path not the goal, not wrong
Not a reason to tolerate abuse in the name of seeing God in the abuser
not_for: someone currently being harmed by another person

viv.3.arise_awake.context: On his return from the West the Hindu community of Kumbakonam presented him an address; this is his reply. Just before, he says the poor and downtrodden must hear that behind everyone, strong or weak, high or low, is the Infinite Soul. He quotes the Katha Upanishad and then calls on 'modern Hindus' to de-hypnotise themselves through their own scriptures.
viv.3.arise_awake.core_teaching: No one is truly weak, because the soul is infinite; wake up from the belief in weakness, stand up and keep going until the goal is reached.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 3, 'The Mission of the Vedanta')
commentaries.gist: He addresses this to every man, woman and child regardless of caste or birth, as the cure for centuries of inactivity and self-forgetting.

commentaries.who: Shankara on Katha Upanishad 1.3.14 (wisdomlib)
commentaries.gist: Shankara reads the verse as the scripture speaking like a compassionate mother to beings asleep in ignorance: turn toward Self-knowledge, approach teachers who know, and realise the Self, for the path is razor-sharp.

viv.3.arise_awake.practical_reading: Used as a call to stop accepting a small, defeated picture of oneself and to commit to a goal with persistence.
misreadings: Not a hustle slogan about worldly success; in the Upanishad the goal is Self-knowledge
Not a dismissal of real limits like illness or exhaustion
cautions: Strongly national in context (addressed to 'modern Hindus'); present the universal point
Can feel demanding to someone depleted
not_for: burnout, where the need is rest
acute depression, where 'just get up' can wound

viv.3.be_not_afraid.context: The CW introduction says the official Calcutta reception was held at Raja Radha Kanta Deb's house in Sobhabazar a week after his arrival. These are the closing words of his reply: just before, he says great power has always been with the people and calls for young heroes to carry India's spiritual ideas abroad; he then thanks the audience and states his wish to serve.
viv.3.be_not_afraid.core_teaching: Fear makes a person nothing and is the chief cause of misery; fearlessness is itself a kind of heaven, so wake up and keep going.

commentaries.who: Context of the reply (CW vol. 3, Calcutta reply)
commentaries.gist: He frames fearlessness as the condition for the 'great work' he lays before the young: carrying the teaching of their forefathers across the world.

commentaries.who: Shankara on Katha Upanishad 1.3.14 (the refrain he ends with)
commentaries.gist: Shankara takes 'arise, awake' as a call to wake from the sleep of ignorance, the seed of all misery, by approaching teachers and realising the Self.

viv.3.be_not_afraid.practical_reading: Applied to everyday anxiety: notice how much suffering is fear of what might happen, and act anyway.
misreadings: Not contempt for anxious people
Not advice to ignore real danger
cautions: Someone with an anxiety disorder may hear 'the moment you fear, you are nobody' as shaming
not_for: clinical anxiety or panic
situations of real physical danger

viv.3.dare_to_be_free.context: A Jnana-Yoga lecture that moves from Sankhya dualism to Advaita: there is only the Atman. Just before the line he says that once we know the Atman alone is real, the world's miseries and even its goodness stop disturbing us. Just after, he warns that Jnana is for the bravest, who smash even their sensory idols, and mocks people who claim 'I am not the body' only to cure a headache.
viv.3.dare_to_be_free.core_teaching: Real freedom asks the courage to think to the end and then live what one has seen, not stop halfway out of fear.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 3, 'The Free Soul')
commentaries.gist: He presents this as what the Jnana-Yogis teach, and immediately says Jnana is very hard, meant for the boldest who give up even cherished ideas about the body.
