viv.3.dare_to_be_free.practical_reading: Used to encourage integrity between conviction and action: if you have truly seen something, let it change how you live.
misreadings: Not licence to do whatever one likes; 'free' here means free of the false self
Not an invitation to reckless choices because 'nothing is real'
cautions: Surrounding text calls the world a dream; avoid using it to minimise someone's real troubles
not_for: someone considering a rash, harmful decision
someone whose suffering would be dismissed as unreal
speaks_to: afraid to act on one's convictions

viv.3.dares_to_differ.context: Speaking in Madras after his return from the West, Vivekananda first addresses the Theosophical Society: Hindus are grateful for its work and he respects Mrs Besant, but respect does not mean accepting everything, and he denies the rumour that Theosophists helped his success in America. This passage then observes that 'sympathy' lasts only while one agrees. He goes on to describe how Theosophists and some Christian missionaries opposed him in America, and later in the lecture lays out his plan for reform from within and for strength over weakness.
viv.3.dares_to_differ.core_teaching: Much professed tolerance is conditional: support lasts only as long as you agree, and disagreement reveals it.

commentaries.who: Surrounding lecture (Complete Works vol. 3)
commentaries.gist: The remark comes right after he rejects the rumour that Theosophists made his American success, and just before he recounts how Theosophists and some missionaries worked against him there.

commentaries.who: Swami Nikhilananda's biography (vivekananda.net)
commentaries.gist: Records that in this lecture he criticised Theosophists who had tried to undermine his work in America and later claimed credit, while noting many Theosophists in India were genuine well-wishers.

commentaries.who: Lecture chronology (vivekananda.net)
commentaries.gist: Dates 'My Plan of Campaign' to 9 February 1897 at the Victoria Public Hall, Madras.

viv.3.dares_to_differ.practical_reading: If someone's warmth vanished when you disagreed with them, the change says something about the conditions they placed on it; you need not conclude you were wrong to differ.
misreadings: Not proof that everyone who withdraws after a disagreement was false.
Not encouragement to provoke disagreement to test people.
cautions: Original target is organisations and public critics, not family or partners; applying it to 'someone close' is an extension. Avoid using it to write off a relationship after one quarrel.
not_for: someone whose disagreement involved hurting the other person
a quarrel that may still be repaired
speaks_to: hurt from a friend turned critic

viv.3.do_not_become_others.context: His first Lahore lecture, given after a joint welcome by the Arya Samaj and the Sanatana Dharma Sabha. He has just quoted Manu that one may take knowledge even from the lowest-born; then he tells his hearers not to be pulled out of Indian life or think India would be better off if everyone dressed and behaved like another race.
viv.3.do_not_become_others.core_teaching: Learn freely from everyone, but digest what you learn in your own way; do not turn into an imitation of someone else.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 3, 'The Common Bases of Hinduism')
commentaries.gist: He grounds the point in Manu's verse about learning from anyone, then argues that a national life thousands of years old cannot simply be reversed by copying another people.

viv.3.do_not_become_others.practical_reading: Applied to personal growth: take good ideas, habits and skills from mentors and other cultures, but adapt them so they fit who you are.
misreadings: Not a rejection of learning from the West or from others
Not cultural chauvinism
cautions: The context is nationalist and uses caste language from Manu; present the general principle
not_for: readers who might take it as a reason to reject outside help or new ideas
speaks_to: learning from a mentor without losing oneself

viv.3.hospitality_west.context: Late in his long Lahore lecture on Vedanta he praises the English for their sympathy with their own people and charity to strangers, giving an example of a public appeal that raised money at once. Right after this sentence he turns on his audience: in India even a small joint-stock company collapses because people cheat each other, and imitating England is useless without a foundation of love; he urges the young men of Lahore to raise the banner of Advaita.
viv.3.hospitality_west.core_teaching: Gratitude for kindness received abroad, used to show his audience that love and sympathy are the real foundation of a strong society.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 3, 'The Vedanta')
commentaries.gist: The thanks is a hinge: from Western sympathy for one's own people he moves to Indian disunity and argues that only Advaita gives a basis for real love.

viv.3.hospitality_west.practical_reading: Can be read as a model of honest gratitude toward people outside one's own group, and of learning from their virtues.
misreadings: Not uncritical praise of the West; elsewhere in the same lecture he is critical
On its own the sentence is thin; it needs the surrounding argument
cautions: Out of context it is an autobiographical aside with little teaching; it is a weak standalone reading
not_for: as a standalone comfort verse; it carries little on its own

viv.3.make_children_strong.context: In his Jaffna lecture he argues that the idea of the impersonal teaches us not to think of ourselves as weak, because all knowledge, power and purity are already within. He then turns this into advice on bringing up children, and adds that only Vedanta gives this life-giving idea of the soul.
viv.3.make_children_strong.core_teaching: Bring children up on confidence in their own inner nature, not on fear and empty forms, so that they can stand on their own feet and bear life.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 3, 'Vedantism')
commentaries.gist: It follows directly from his point that whatever we think we become; teaching a child weakness produces weakness.

commentaries.who: Parallel: 'My Plan of Campaign', Madras 1897 (CW vol. 3)
commentaries.gist: He calls for man-making education and rejects whatever weakens body, mind or spirit.

viv.3.make_children_strong.practical_reading: Parents and teachers read it as: build a child's self-respect and courage before rules, and explain the why behind practices.
misreadings: Strong does not mean hard, harsh or emotionless
Not a licence for harsh discipline
cautions: A parent of a child with illness or disability may hear 'strong' as a standard their child fails; stress inner confidence
not_for: a parent grieving a child or caring for a very ill child

viv.3.real_worship.context: During his visit to the Rameswaram temple he was asked to speak to the people gathered there. He has just said that religion lies in love, not ceremony, and that a pilgrimage place is made holy by holy people. After this passage he tells the parable of two gardeners, one who flatters the master and one who quietly tends the garden.
viv.3.real_worship.core_teaching: The heart of worship is to be pure and to do good to others; serving God in suffering people pleases Him more than worship that sees Him only in images.

commentaries.who: Context of the address (CW vol. 3, Rameswaram)
commentaries.gist: He says one who serves even one poor person as Shiva, without regard to caste, creed or race, pleases Shiva more than the temple-only worshipper; the gardener parable makes the same point.

commentaries.who: Parallel: 'Practical Vedanta II', London 1896 (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: He calls the living human being the highest temple and says worship of that God is the most practical religion.

viv.3.real_worship.practical_reading: Applied as: let your spirituality show up in how you treat the sick, poor and weak around you today.
misreadings: Not a rejection of temple worship, which he calls preliminary, not useless
Not 'good works are enough without inner purity'; purity comes first in the sentence
not_for: readers hurt by religious communities who may hear it as a demand to serve more

viv.3.realised_not_heard.context: In his Lahore lecture on the common ground of Hindu sects he says India's great word is anubhuti, realisation, and that its scriptures alone keep saying the Lord is to be seen. After the line he adds that mere intellectual assent is nothing, and that the best proof of God is that people have seen Him.
viv.3.realised_not_heard.core_teaching: Religion is meant to be experienced and lived, not just heard, memorised or agreed with.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 3, 'The Common Bases of Hinduism')
commentaries.gist: He presents realisation as one of the shared bases of all Hindu sects and grounds belief in God and the soul on the experience of seers past and present.

viv.3.realised_not_heard.practical_reading: Teachers use it to move people from reading about spirituality to practice: prayer, meditation, service, and honest reflection.
misreadings: Not anti-study: elsewhere he values learning; he objects to learning without realisation
Not a claim that only mystics can be religious
not_for: someone who feels guilty for not having 'experiences'
speaks_to: feeling religion is just ritual or words

viv.3.refuses_to_learn.context: Comes right after the seed-and-tree image and just before he quotes Manu on learning even from the humble. He is warning against imitation but insisting that India still has much to learn from others.
viv.3.refuses_to_learn.core_teaching: Willingness to learn is a sign of life; refusing to learn is a kind of death.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 3, 'The Common Bases of Hinduism')
commentaries.gist: Balanced against 'do not imitate': take what is good from others, but absorb it in your own way.

viv.3.refuses_to_learn.practical_reading: Applied to pride and defensiveness at any age: staying teachable keeps one alive.
misreadings: Not a call to accept every idea uncritically
cautions: 'Already dead' is harsh; avoid aiming it at older readers or the grieving
not_for: bereavement contexts, where 'dead' language jars

viv.3.reject_as_poison.context: In this Madras lecture he says what India needs is strength and faith in itself; occultism and mysticism have weakened it. He calls for 'man-making' religion and education, then offers this as the test of truth. After it he says truth must be strengthening and enlightening and that, from long experience, mysticisms are generally weakening.
viv.3.reject_as_poison.core_teaching: Judge teachings by their effect: what leaves you weaker in body, mind or spirit should be rejected; truth makes people stronger and clearer.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 3, 'My Plan of Campaign')
commentaries.gist: He applies the test chiefly to occult and mystical fads, saying they contain some truth but on the whole weaken people.

commentaries.who: Parallel: 'Vedantism', Jaffna (CW vol. 3)
commentaries.gist: He makes the same move with children: teach them strength and the soul's glory, not weakness.

viv.3.reject_as_poison.practical_reading: Used as a filter for media, habits and relationships: notice what consistently leaves you weaker, and step away from it.
misreadings: Not a rule that anything painful or difficult is false; growth can be hard
Not a reason to reject medicine or therapy because it feels uncomfortable
cautions: Could be misread as 'if something makes you feel weak (e.g., admitting depression) it is wrong'
not_for: someone avoiding necessary but uncomfortable treatment or truths
speaks_to: choosing what to read or follow

viv.3.seed_becomes_tree.context: Just before, he urges his audience to have faith in themselves, be proud of their ancestors and not imitate, since working at others' dictation slowly kills even the power of thought. The seed image follows as the model for learning without imitation; right after come 'that man who refuses to learn is already dead' and Manu's verse on learning from anyone.
viv.3.seed_becomes_tree.core_teaching: Like a seed that takes in earth, air and water and still becomes its own kind of tree, take everything others can give you and grow into yourself.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 3, 'The Common Bases of Hinduism')
commentaries.gist: The image resolves his double message: do not imitate, yet take what is good from others; let that be your position.

viv.3.seed_becomes_tree.practical_reading: Applied to students, immigrants and anyone shaped by many influences: absorb, then become more fully yourself.
misreadings: Not isolationism
Not a claim that one's nature is fixed and cannot grow

viv.3.servant_first.context: The closing paragraph of the Jaffna lecture. He laments jealousy and the wish for precedence even in worship, calls it slavery that everyone wants to command and no one to obey, and blames the loss of the old brahmacharya training. He then urges them to avoid jealousy and do deeds that will outshine their ancestors.
viv.3.servant_first.core_teaching: Learn to obey and serve first; the ability to lead grows out of that, and jealousy over precedence destroys joint work.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 3, 'Vedantism')
commentaries.gist: He presents obedience as the cure for a culture where everyone wants to command; command will come by itself to the one who has learned to obey.

commentaries.who: Parallel: letter 'To my Brave Boys', 19 November 1894 (CW vol. 4)
commentaries.gist: He tells Alasinga to be the servant while leading and not to 'boss' others, which he says kills organisations.

viv.3.servant_first.practical_reading: Used in leadership and team settings: earn the right to lead by serving and by not competing for status.
misreadings: Not a call for blind obedience to anyone
Not a justification for exploiting junior people
cautions: 'Obey' can land badly for someone in a controlling relationship or workplace
not_for: someone in an abusive or coercive situation

viv.3.whatever_you_think.context: Just before, he describes the glory of the soul in Gita-like terms (no weapon cuts it, no fire burns it) and says power comes from believing in it. After the line he adds that all knowledge, power and purity are already within, unexpressed only because we do not believe it; this, he says, is what the idea of the impersonal teaches.
viv.3.whatever_you_think.core_teaching: We grow into what we habitually believe about ourselves, so believe in the strong, pure Self within rather than in your weakness.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 3, 'Vedantism')
commentaries.gist: He ties the saying to Vedanta: the soul is already all-powerful and pure, and belief is what lets this come out.

commentaries.who: Parallel: Inspired Talks, 26 June 1895 (CW vol. 7)
commentaries.gist: He says we are what our thoughts have made us, so take care of what we think.

viv.3.whatever_you_think.practical_reading: Teachers use it for self-talk: notice the labels you put on yourself and replace defeating ones.
misreadings: Not 'positive thinking cures everything'
Not blame for illness or misfortune
cautions: Could imply depressed people chose their state; present it as practice, not accusation
not_for: clinical depression where thoughts are a symptom

viv.3.where_we_agree.context: Near the end of his Lahore lecture, given to a hall welcomed jointly by the Arya Samaj and the Sanatana Dharma Sabha. He has just said religion must be as free to all as air and must not be spread by forming little sects that fight over differences. After this sentence he uses the dark-room image: do not cry about darkness, bring in light, and begin by believing in people.
viv.3.where_we_agree.core_teaching: Build on what people share and do not organise around quarrels; differences tend to resolve themselves when the common ground is strong.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 3, 'The Common Bases of Hinduism')
commentaries.gist: He sets this against forming sects to fight over differences and calls positive suggestion the secret of reforming people.

viv.3.where_we_agree.practical_reading: Applied to families, teams and communities in conflict: start with shared ground and let smaller disputes wait.
misreadings: Not a call to hide or deny real injustice
Not relativism: he still holds firm views
not_for: situations of abuse where 'leave differences alone' would excuse harm

viv.4.agony_at_the_heart.context: The CW heading says only that Balaji Rao had just had 'a severe domestic affliction'; a letter of 27 April 1893 from Khetri to Dr Nanjunda Rao says Balaji had lost his son. The letter opens with Job's 'the Lord gave and the Lord hath taken away', says sorrow is when the inner eye opens, and urges him to keep saying 'Thy will be done'. This prayer is its closing paragraph, ending in Krishnarpanam and a wish for his peace.
viv.4.agony_at_the_heart.core_teaching: A prayer that admits honestly that the heart fights against acceptance, and asks Krishna for the strength to reach surrender anyway.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 4, 'A Message of Sympathy to a Friend')
commentaries.gist: Written just before he sailed for America; it mixes Job, the Gospels, Tennyson and the Gita, and treats the moment of loss as when the inner eye can open.

commentaries.who: Letter from Khetri to Dr Nanjunda Rao, 27 April 1893 (CW vol. 6)
commentaries.gist: Confirms the bereavement: he is very sorry that Balaji has lost his son, and says for us there is only calm submission.

viv.4.agony_at_the_heart.practical_reading: For a grieving reader it gives permission to say that acceptance is not yet possible, while still praying toward it.
misreadings: Not a demand to stop grieving or to 'just accept'
Not saying God caused the death as punishment
cautions: Written to a father who lost his son; 'the Mother's hand that is striking' implies God sent the loss, which can hurt
Soldier-obey imagery ('ours but to do and die') can feel cold in fresh grief
not_for: readers angry at God who will hear 'striking hand' as cruelty
non-theistic readers in fresh grief

viv.4.calm_of_heart.context: A short poem in which peace is described through paradoxes: power that is not power, light in darkness, the space between joy and sorrow. This is the third stanza; the poem ends by calling peace the goal of life, where the tear-drop goes.
viv.4.calm_of_heart.core_teaching: Peace is not somewhere else; it is the pause already present between sounds, words and surges of feeling.

commentaries.who: The poem itself (CW vol. 4, 'Peace')
commentaries.gist: Its stanzas build a run of in-between images (death between two lives, lull between two storms) to show peace as what joins opposites, not their absence.

viv.4.calm_of_heart.practical_reading: Used as a mindfulness prompt: notice the small pauses in the day and rest in them.
misreadings: Not a claim that passion or grief is bad
cautions: Later lines mention 'death between two lives' and 'eternal death unmourned'; check which stanza is shown

viv.4.circle_of_light.context: The closing passage of his lecture on Christ. He has just said that all the great messengers are manifestations of the same God and bore the world's burden; then he says every person is in a small way a prophet carrying a cross. He ends with salutations to past prophets, to those working for humanity now, and to those still to come.
viv.4.circle_of_light.core_teaching: Everyone quietly carries a burden, and no one, however low, has lost the inner light that keeps them in touch with the divine.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 4, 'Christ, the Messenger')
commentaries.gist: The lecture opens with waves rising and falling and treats prophets as the high waves; this ending brings the same dignity to every ordinary life.

viv.4.circle_of_light.practical_reading: Used to restore self-respect to someone who feels worthless: you carry a real burden, and something in you is still untouched.
misreadings: Not a statement that suffering is deserved
Christian imagery (cross) used by a Hindu monk; not conversion language
cautions: 'However low and degraded' may sting someone already ashamed; lead with the light, not the degradation

viv.4.deep_down_calm.context: The third sentence of the condolence letter: it follows Job's 'the Lord gave, the Lord hath taken away', which he calls the secret of existence. It is followed by 'Blessed are they that mourn' and the idea that the inner eyes open when the world seems cut away under us.
viv.4.deep_down_calm.core_teaching: However hard the surface storm, there is a layer of calm and peace underneath that the storm does not reach.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 4)
commentaries.gist: He grants that the heart is wrung and the horizon looks like solid misery, and says that this is when the inner light breaks through.

commentaries.who: Letter from Khetri, 27 April 1893 (CW vol. 6)
commentaries.gist: Shows the occasion: Balaji Rao had lost his son.

commentaries.who: Parallel: letter to Mrs Ole Bull, 20 January 1895 (CW vol. 5)
commentaries.gist: Uses the same sea image: the surface rises and sinks, but for the observant soul each sinking reveals more.

viv.4.deep_down_calm.practical_reading: Used to say that grief and a deeper steadiness can exist together; one need not end the storm to find the floor beneath it.
misreadings: Not a claim that the loss does not matter
Not 'you should already feel the calm'
cautions: Written for the death of a child; deliver it with acknowledgement of the storm, not as a correction
not_for: someone who would hear 'bliss' as dismissing their loss in the first hours

viv.4.education_religion.context: A letter to a Madras friend arguing about faith, knowledge and love and then about religion and society. Just before these lines he insists that religion should not reform society and society should not legislate religion ('Hands off!'). After them he says the only duty of the teacher in both cases is to remove obstructions; the Lord does the rest.
viv.4.education_religion.core_teaching: Education and religion both draw out what is already present in a person; the teacher's job is to clear obstacles, not to pour things in.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 4, 'What we Believe in')
commentaries.gist: The paired definitions support his 'hands off' principle: since perfection and divinity are already within, the teacher removes obstructions and lets growth happen.

commentaries.who: Parallel: class talk 'Concentration and Breathing' (CW vol. 6)
commentaries.gist: He says the essence of education is concentration of mind, not collecting facts.

viv.4.education_religion.practical_reading: Teachers and parents apply it as: trust what is already in the learner and remove what blocks it.
misreadings: Not anti-schooling
Not a claim that people need no help; removing obstacles is real work

viv.4.hearts_purified.context: In this address on what prepares a person for devotion, he lists aids such as music and then kriya, work: doing good to others. He says the memory of God does not come to the selfish. After the line he lists the five daily sacrifices of the householder (study, worship, ancestors, humans, animals) and says a householder's door should be open to the poor.
viv.4.hearts_purified.core_teaching: Serving others purifies the heart, and a purified heart is where God can be felt.

commentaries.who: Context of the address (CW vol. 4, 'The Preparation')
commentaries.gist: He places service among the practical preparations for devotion and ties it to the householder's duty to share his home with those in need.

viv.4.hearts_purified.practical_reading: Used to suggest that when prayer feels dry, practical kindness can open the heart again.
misreadings: Not salvation by works alone
Not a demand to give beyond one's means
not_for: someone already exhausted by caregiving

viv.4.hold_on_brave_heart.context: A six-stanza poem of encouragement to Ajit Singh, Raja of Khetri, Vivekananda's friend and patron. It moves from the clouded sun, through winter always followed by summer, heavy duties and fleeting pleasures, to the claim that no honest work is lost; a fifth stanza tells the wise few to guide the many gently, and the last promises help from those who see far and from the Lord.
viv.4.hold_on_brave_heart.core_teaching: Dark stretches alternate with light ones, and sincere effort is never wasted even when hopes fail, so keep going a little longer.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text: the whole poem (Complete Works vol. 4)
commentaries.gist: Stanza 2 adds that winter is always followed by summer and life alternates like waves; stanza 4 that no work or struggle is lost though hopes and strength fail; stanza 5 is advice to a leader of the masses.

commentaries.who: Addressee: Ajit Singh of Khetri (Wikipedia)
commentaries.gist: Ruler of Khetri who financed Vivekananda's 1893 voyage and supported his mother; the poem is addressed to a powerful friend and patron, not to a stranger in crisis.

commentaries.who: vivekananda.net text of the poem
commentaries.gist: Gives the same six stanzas with no date or circumstances of composition; the date remains unestablished in the sources checked.

viv.4.hold_on_brave_heart.practical_reading: On a day when work feels shaky, take the poem as permission to stay steady for one more stretch while remembering that effort is not wasted even if this particular outcome fails.
misreadings: Not a guarantee of a specific outcome ('victory is sure' is poetic encouragement).
Not advice to stay in a harmful or dangerous workplace.
cautions: In a plan called 'When work feels unsafe', 'hold on' must not read as 'put up with harassment, danger or abuse'. If unsafe means unsafe, the right step is to get help or leave.
Stanza 5 has an elitist ring (the wise few guiding the masses); avoid quoting it out of context.
not_for: workplace harassment or physical danger
someone who has already held on too long and needs permission to stop

viv.4.live_for_others.context: He thanks the Maharaja, whose help made his journey possible, describes America, and lays out his plan to educate India's poor through travelling teachers. Just before the line he notes that Americans do not care whether India's poor live or die, and asks why they should when India's own rich think only of themselves. He then urges the prince to raise India and leave a name worth honouring.
viv.4.live_for_others.core_teaching: Life is short and vanities pass; only a life given to others is fully alive.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 4, 'Our Duty to the Masses')
commentaries.gist: Addressed to a ruler with means, it is a direct appeal to use power for the education of the poorest.

commentaries.who: Parallel: letter to Rakhal (CW vol. 6)
commentaries.gist: He quotes Sanskrit sayings that the good live for others and the wise give themselves for others, and says he can secure his own good only by doing others good.

viv.4.live_for_others.practical_reading: Used as a challenge to people with resources or privilege, and as a reminder that meaning grows from contribution.
misreadings: Not a call to burn out or neglect oneself and one's family
'More dead than alive' was aimed at the privileged and selfish, not at the sick or struggling
cautions: Avoid using the 'dead' phrasing with someone depressed or in grief
not_for: burnout
depression, where 'more dead than alive' could wound

viv.4.love_pays.context: The letter opens by telling Alasinga to push on with the organisation, needing only love, sincerity and patience, and calls love the only law of life. After 'Struggle' and 'Be not afraid', he says money, name, fame and learning do not count; love and character do. He then moves on to the need for social liberty.
viv.4.love_pays.core_teaching: What really carries a work forward is not money, fame or learning, but love and character.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 4, 'To my Brave Boys')
commentaries.gist: Written to young workers with no money or standing: he tells them that none lives but one who loves and that feeling for the poor brings power.

viv.4.love_pays.practical_reading: Applied when someone feels they lack the credentials or resources to do good: love and integrity matter more.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of money or education as useless; he says they do not 'pay' compared with love

viv.4.no_winter.context: A poem of encouragement to the Maharaja of Khetri, his patron. The first stanza says that if the sun is hidden, hold on, victory will come. The second (this one) points to the seasons and the waves. Later stanzas say no work is lost and no struggle is vain, and that the good and wise lead though the masses learn their worth late.
viv.4.no_winter.core_teaching: Hard times always give way to better ones, just as winter gives way to summer and every hollow becomes a crest; so stay steady and brave.

commentaries.who: The poem itself (CW vol. 4)
commentaries.gist: Its stanzas move from enduring gloom to the assurance that no good effort is wasted and that the heirs to one's work will come.

viv.4.no_winter.practical_reading: Used to help someone ride out a bad season by remembering that conditions change.
misreadings: Not a promise that a specific loss will be undone
cautions: In grief, 'summer came behind' may sound like 'you'll get over it'; better for setbacks than for bereavement
not_for: fresh bereavement

viv.4.praise_blame_one.context: A long poem in stanzas, each ending with the refrain 'Om Tat Sat, Om'. Just before this stanza the monk renounces all heavens, hopes and fears and declares 'I am the Self in all'. This stanza tells him not to care how the body fares; the next says truth cannot come where lust, fame and greed live.
viv.4.praise_blame_one.core_teaching: Whether people garland you or kick you, say nothing; where everything is one Self, praise and blame have nobody to land on.

commentaries.who: The poem itself (CW vol. 4, 'The Song of the Sannyasin')
commentaries.gist: It is addressed to the renunciant and asks complete indifference to the body and to others' treatment, grounded in 'I am the Self in all'.

viv.4.praise_blame_one.practical_reading: Used to loosen dependence on approval and fear of criticism.
misreadings: Not a reason to stay silent under abuse
Not indifference to others' suffering
cautions: 'Kick this frame; say naught' could read as accepting violence; present it as freedom from approval, not tolerance of harm
Later stanzas contain monastic lines about women and wives that will not suit many readers
not_for: someone experiencing abuse or bullying

viv.4.requiescat.context: Goodwin, the English stenographer who took down and transcribed his lectures from early 1896, died at Ootacamund on 2 June 1898, aged 27. The poem, written two months later, blesses his soul on its way, honours his service and sacrifice, and in its last stanza says he is one with That which comes as death and life and asks him to keep helping the world.
viv.4.requiescat.core_teaching: A blessing for someone who has died: their service is complete, they are free, and loving memory keeps their place among us.

commentaries.who: The poem itself (CW vol. 4)
commentaries.gist: It moves from blessing the soul's journey to remembrance, then to union with That which is both death and life.

commentaries.who: Wikipedia, 'J. J. Goodwin'
commentaries.gist: Gives Goodwin's death on 2 June 1898 at Ootacamund aged 27, his work as stenographer from 1896, and dates the poem to August 1898.

viv.4.requiescat.practical_reading: Can be read aloud or prayed for someone who has died, especially one remembered for faithful service.
misreadings: Not a statement that grief should end
cautions: Directly about a death; suitable for bereavement but the 'blissful' tone may feel premature in the first days
not_for: a death that was violent or traumatic, where 'blissful' may jar
speaks_to: loss of a friend or colleague

viv.4.servant_while_leading.context: In the practical part of the letter he tells Alasinga to start a central association on religious grounds, avoid violent social reform and work hard. After these lines he warns Alasinga not to 'boss' the other friends just because the letters come to him, saying this kills organisations, and asks for no hypocrisy or roguery.
viv.4.servant_while_leading.core_teaching: Lead as a servant, stay unselfish, refuse to listen to gossip about one friend from another, and be patient.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 4, 'To my Brave Boys')
commentaries.gist: He follows with a warning against bossing others, which he calls what kills all organisations.

commentaries.who: Parallel: 'Vedantism', Jaffna (CW vol. 3)
commentaries.gist: He says first learn to be a servant, then you will be fit to be a master.

viv.4.servant_while_leading.practical_reading: Used as rules for team leaders and volunteers: serve, avoid gossip, be patient.
misreadings: Not a call to tolerate wrongdoing in a team for the sake of harmony

viv.4.struggle_motto.context: Comes right after he urges the young men to feel for the poor until the heart nearly breaks and then pour themselves out at the Lord's feet. After this he says 'Be not afraid' and that money and fame do not pay; love does.
viv.4.struggle_motto.core_teaching: Keep struggling both when everything is dark and when things begin to improve; effort does not stop with success.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 4, 'To my Brave Boys')
commentaries.gist: It is offered as his own testimony to young workers before he tells them not to fear and that love is what pays.

viv.4.struggle_motto.practical_reading: Used to encourage persistence, and to remind those who have just succeeded not to relax their effort.
misreadings: Not glorification of overwork
cautions: Can sound exhausting to someone already depleted
not_for: burnout or chronic illness

viv.5.bob_up_soon.context: Vivekananda had returned to India in December 1900 and spent spring 1901 touring East Bengal and Assam; after about two months of hard travel he collapsed and came back to Calcutta to recover. The letter opens with a joke about Mary's letter wandering the world, then reports the Raja of Khetri's death and his own poor health, says he would like to go to Europe for a long talk with her, and claims three-quarters of his restlessness has gone. He closes with love to friends and lifelong gratitude to Mary's mother.
viv.5.bob_up_soon.core_teaching: Not a doctrine but an honest note from a teacher at a low point: he names grief and illness without disguise and still expects the tide to turn.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (Complete Works vol. 5, letter CIII)
commentaries.gist: Written after a strenuous East Bengal and Assam tour left him collapsed; the bad news and the expectation of recovery sit in one short paragraph between banter and affectionate greetings.

commentaries.who: Vivekananda's last years (Wikipedia)
commentaries.gist: From 1901 his asthma, diabetes and insomnia limited him; he died at Belur Math on 4 July 1902, about fourteen months after this letter.

viv.5.bob_up_soon.practical_reading: You can say plainly that things are bad right now and, in the same breath, decide to wait for the turn rather than conclude it will never come.
misreadings: Not a promise that health or fortune will return on schedule.
Not a brush-off of grief; he names the loss first.
cautions: Mentions an accidental death (the Raja's fall).
His health did not recover; he died the following year. Do not frame 'bob up' as a guarantee, especially for a reader who is seriously ill.
not_for: someone with a terminal diagnosis, if read as a promise of recovery
very fresh bereavement where 'bob up soon' may feel rushed
speaks_to: a low patch after loss plus illness
losing hope but not giving up
being honest about a bad season

viv.5.great_convictions.context: Written from the Hale home in Chicago to his Madras disciples. He comments on press criticism, then asks whether they can raise the masses while keeping their spiritual nature, and become Western in energy yet Hindu to the backbone. He says they were born to do it; this line follows, then 'Onward for ever!' and a motto of sympathy for the poor.
viv.5.great_convictions.core_teaching: Believe in yourselves; deep convictions give birth to great deeds.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 5, Epistles I, VII)
commentaries.gist: The line closes a challenge to raise India's poor; a postscript asks them not to publish the letter but to spread the idea of educating the masses.

viv.5.great_convictions.practical_reading: Used to encourage people facing a big task to build conviction before action.
misreadings: Not a claim that conviction alone guarantees success

viv.5.hero_in_silence.context: He apologises for harshness in earlier letters, says he works in America as he did in India, relying on the Lord. Just before the line he praises America as a field where a hundred hands help for every opponent. After it he writes 'How many Buddhas die before one finds expression!' and says he believes in God, in man, and in going to hell to save others, and that no nation can hate others and live.
viv.5.hero_in_silence.core_teaching: Anyone can act brave when success is certain or when being praised; the real hero keeps working quietly without either.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 5, Epistles I, XXI)
commentaries.gist: Set amid his account of American generosity and his insistence that India must stop hating others, the line praises unseen, unrewarded work.

viv.5.hero_in_silence.practical_reading: Used to honour quiet, unseen effort, such as caregiving, maintenance work or long projects.
misreadings: Not contempt for people who need encouragement
cautions: 'Idiots' and 'cowards' are harsh; lead with the second half

viv.5.not_in_a_day.context: A quick note written the day before he sailed for England. He welcomes Dr Nanjunda Rao's proposed magazine for boys, suggests popular stories from Sanskrit literature, says he has no money to send, and then gives this advice. He adds that the person and the life are the secret of power, tells him to keep the letter and read the last lines whenever worried or jealous, and calls jealousy the bane of the nation.
viv.5.not_in_a_day.core_teaching: Keep going bravely, do not expect quick results, keep the highest ideal, stay steady, and avoid jealousy and selfishness.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 5, Epistles I, LXI)
commentaries.gist: He explicitly asks the recipient to re-read these lines whenever he feels worried or jealous, making it a practice for hard moments.

viv.5.not_in_a_day.practical_reading: Used as a re-read-when-anxious note for anyone building something slowly.
misreadings: Not a call for endless patience with harmful situations

viv.5.ridicule_opposition.context: Writing from America, Vivekananda reminds the Maharaja that he is persistent: he has started a movement with a few hundred followers, plans to train some sannyasins to carry it on, and says the more the Christian priests oppose him the more determined he is to leave a mark. He plans to go to London by late August and winter between London and New York before returning to India. He then frames opposition as a stage and welcomes it, so long as he stays steady, pure and faithful to God.
viv.5.ridicule_opposition.core_teaching: Resistance is a normal stage of any new work, not a final verdict on it; the task is to stay steady and true while it lasts.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (Complete Works vol. 5, letter XLVII)
commentaries.gist: The line comes amid practical plans for his American work and a remark that clergy opposition only hardens his resolve; he welcomes persecution on condition that he himself remains pure and faithful.

commentaries.who: Addressee: Ajit Singh of Khetri (Wikipedia)
commentaries.gist: The Maharaja was his patron and close friend who had paid for his journey to the 1893 Parliament, which explains the letter's frank report on progress and setbacks.

viv.5.ridicule_opposition.practical_reading: If your resolve is being laughed at or resisted, treat that as a stage to pass through; check your own conduct, then keep going.
misreadings: Not proof that opposition means you are right; he pairs it with staying pure and steady.
Not a license to dismiss all criticism as ridicule.
cautions: Can feed grandiosity ('I am ahead of my time'); pair it with honest self-checking.
not_for: someone whose plan is meeting opposition because it harms others
speaks_to: early resistance to a new habit or project

viv.5.same_unity.context: An interviewer visited him in South Belgravia during the 1896 London season to ask what message India had for England. Asked to sum up his mission, he says it is the philosophy of religion, the kernel shared by all forms once the non-essential parts are stripped away; unity is behind them all. He goes on to say people fight over the non-essential while the essential is love of God and of man.
viv.5.same_unity.core_teaching: Under all the names people give the divine there is one unity that animates all life; the essential is love of God and of human beings.

commentaries.who: Context of the interview (CW vol. 5, 'India and England')
commentaries.gist: He presents this as the common basis of all religions and criticises fighting over outward forms.

viv.5.same_unity.practical_reading: Used in interfaith settings and for readers from mixed backgrounds as a reason for respect.
misreadings: Not a claim that all religions are identical in every teaching
Not a dismissal of particular traditions
not_for: readers who feel their tradition's distinctiveness is being erased

viv.5.soul_is_a_star.context: The CW heading says he wrote to Mrs Ole Bull, whom he called 'Dhira Mata', on the loss of her father. He says he had a premonition of the death, calls such deaths turning points, and argues the soul only seems to move, like the moon behind clouds, so the felt presence of the departed is true. This passage closes the letter.
viv.5.soul_is_a_star.core_teaching: The departed is not lost: each soul is like a star set in God, and the dead have only laid down a garment and stand where they always were.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 5, Epistles I, XXXI)
commentaries.gist: He builds from the moving-moon image to the claim that the sense of the departed being near is intellectually sound, then prays that the father be free.

viv.5.soul_is_a_star.practical_reading: Offered to the bereaved as a picture of the dead held safely in God, and of a bond that is not broken.
misreadings: Not a denial that loss hurts
Not a guarantee of reunion in a particular form
cautions: Raises rebirth and karma ('dragged by the unseen power of his own past actions'), which can unsettle a grieving reader; consider showing only the first sentences
He says he does not write when such grief strikes, which can sound distant
not_for: readers who would find rebirth teaching distressing
very fresh grief where metaphysics feels distant

viv.6.behind_my_work.context: He opens with news of friends and his reluctance to interfere in a dispute, then shifts into a reflective, almost dreamlike passage: bonds are breaking, work has lost its taste, he hears his Master calling and feels nirvana near. He says his best moments have been when drifting, and he is drifting again. This line names the hidden motives of his past; after it he cries 'Mother, I come', a spectator now, not an actor.
viv.6.behind_my_work.core_teaching: Looking honestly at his own past, he sees ego behind even his best work, and finds that as those motives fade he is left in peace, carried rather than striving.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 6, Epistles II, CLVIII)
commentaries.gist: The admission sits inside a passage of release: he has given up his place as leader and feels calm, peaceful and distant from his former role.

viv.6.behind_my_work.practical_reading: Used to encourage honest self-examination of motives without self-hatred, as a step toward freedom.
misreadings: Not a confession that his work was worthless
Not a recommendation to stop caring about one's work
cautions: Same letter speaks of the body falling away and nirvana; a distressed reader could hear a longing for death. Keep the focus on releasing ego
not_for: someone with suicidal thoughts, given the surrounding 'release' language
someone already drowning in self-criticism
speaks_to: after leaving a role or retiring

viv.6.essence_of_education.context: A talk on the power of concentration, which he calls the main difference between humans and animals. He warns that concentration without the power of detachment causes great suffering. After this passage he says his own development was one-sided: he had concentration without detachment, and the most intense suffering of his life came from that; he learned detachment only later.
viv.6.essence_of_education.core_teaching: Education should train the mind itself, its power to focus and to let go, rather than stuff it with facts.

commentaries.who: Context of the talk (CW vol. 6, 'Concentration and Breathing')
commentaries.gist: He pairs concentration with detachment and offers his own life as a warning of what happens when only the first is developed.

commentaries.who: Parallel: letter 'What we Believe in' (CW vol. 4)
commentaries.gist: He defines education as the manifestation of the perfection already in a person.

viv.6.essence_of_education.practical_reading: Used by teachers and learners to prioritise attention training (focus, rest, switching) over memorising.
misreadings: Not anti-knowledge
Not a dismissal of exams for students who must take them

viv.6.fearful_to_hurt.context: A short letter. He opens by saying he does not want to work, he wants to rest, but karma drives him on like cattle hurried to slaughter. He calls all this our fear, the beginning of misery and disease. After the lines he calls it a mass of nonsense we build around ourselves and longs to be fearless and daring.
viv.6.fearful_to_hurt.core_teaching: Anxious over-caution backfires: fear of hurting people hurts them more, and trying too hard to avoid evil leads us into it.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 6, Epistles II, CLV)
commentaries.gist: The letter is written in fatigue and frustration, and 'we' includes himself; he ends wishing to become fearless.

viv.6.fearful_to_hurt.practical_reading: Used for people-pleasers and anxious carers: excessive fear of causing pain can itself cause it; act clearly and kindly.
misreadings: Not permission to be careless of others' feelings
cautions: The cattle-to-slaughter image is dark; the letter's mood is weary
not_for: someone who has genuinely hurt others and needs to take care

viv.6.glad_blunders.context: From the same reflective passage as 'Behind my work was ambition'. Just before, he says bonds are breaking, love dying and work tasteless; he hears the Master call and feels nirvana before him. After the line he says he leaves none bound, the old man is gone, the guide and leader has passed away and the boy-student is left; he has long given up his place as leader.
viv.6.glad_blunders.core_teaching: He accepts his whole life, birth, suffering and mistakes included, with gratitude, as he lets go into peace.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 6, Epistles II, CLVIII)
commentaries.gist: Said while stepping back from leadership; he describes himself as spectator rather than actor and speaks of freedom whether or not the body falls.

viv.6.glad_blunders.practical_reading: Used to help people make peace with their past, including mistakes, rather than wishing it away.
misreadings: Not a death wish; our_note is right to say so
Not a claim that suffering is good in itself
cautions: Surrounding lines ('whether this body will fall and release me') could be heard as welcoming death; do not use with suicidal readers
not_for: suicidal ideation
fresh trauma, where 'glad I suffered' could feel invalidating

viv.6.nothing_lasts.context: A very short letter (as printed, with an omission at the start). After this line he adds that life is not eternal and he is thankful for it; that suffering is the lot of the world's best and bravest until things are set right; that it is a discipline that breaks the dream; and that he is glad to be one of nature's sacrifices.
viv.6.nothing_lasts.core_teaching: Low moods pass, because nothing lasts forever.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 6, Epistles II, CXLVIII)
commentaries.gist: The comfort leads straight into his own view of suffering as the lot of the brave and a discipline that breaks the dream; he says he rejoices in his sufferings in sane moments.

viv.6.nothing_lasts.practical_reading: Used as a light, kind reminder that a bad mood or season will pass.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of serious depression ('never mind')
cautions: The very next sentence says life is not eternal and he is thankful for that; do not show it to a reader in despair
'Never mind' can feel dismissive if the gloom is deep
not_for: clinical depression or suicidal thoughts (because of the next sentences)
speaks_to: anxiety about a phase lasting forever

viv.6.one_thing_at_a_time.context: The short notes sketch the eight limbs of Raja-Yoga: yama (non-injury, truthfulness, non-covetousness, chastity, purity in thought, word and deed), a firm upright seat, about half an hour of breath control with Om repeated mentally, then withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation and samadhi. The instruction to do one thing at a time closes the list.
viv.6.one_thing_at_a_time.core_teaching: Concentration grows by giving one task, while you do it, your full attention, rather than scattering yourself.

commentaries.who: Surrounding notes (Complete Works vol. 6, 'On Raja-Yoga')
commentaries.gist: The line caps a compressed outline of the eight limbs, so it reads as the practical form of concentration (dharana) in daily work.

commentaries.who: Raja-Yoga, 'Pratyahara and Dharana' (Complete Works vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: Makes the same point at length: would-be yogis must stop nibbling at many things, take up one idea and let it fill thought and life; dharana is confining the mind to one point.

viv.6.one_thing_at_a_time.practical_reading: Pick the single next task, close everything else for a short block, and give that one task all your attention until the block ends.
misreadings: Not a demand for perfection or hours of unbroken focus.
Not a rule that one may only ever have one project.
cautions: For someone with ADHD or high anxiety, 'to the exclusion of all else' can sound impossible; frame it as a short, kind experiment.
not_for: someone whose difficulty starting comes from depression, where focus advice can add guilt

viv.6.power_of_detachment.context: He says yogis claim full control of the mind is possible, then names the ethical danger: fixing the mind on something and being unable to pull it away. This line follows. He then says concentration and detachment must be developed together, and later admits his own greatest suffering came from lacking detachment.
viv.6.power_of_detachment.core_teaching: Most suffering comes from being unable to let the mind go from what grips it; that ability can be trained alongside focus.

commentaries.who: Context of the talk (CW vol. 6, 'Concentration and Breathing')
commentaries.gist: He says the two powers must grow together to be safe, and that his own most intense suffering came from having concentration without detachment.

commentaries.who: Parallel: 'Work and its Secret', Los Angeles 1900 (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: Only one who can attach fully and also detach when needed gets the best of life; being unable to love at all is no answer.

viv.6.power_of_detachment.practical_reading: Used for rumination and obsessive worry: practise shifting attention deliberately, not only focusing harder.
misreadings: Not 'stop caring about people'
Not emotional coldness; elsewhere he rejects the 'stony' heart
cautions: 'Almost all suffering' can sound like blame for suffering from external causes like illness or loss
not_for: fresh bereavement, where 'detach' sounds like 'stop loving'

viv.6.strive_to_be_great.context: After news about his Raja-Yoga book, he says he does not want anyone he loves to become a lawyer, although his own father was one; India needs pluck and scientific genius, so he wants Mohin to be an electrician. The quoted lines follow, with an omitted sentence that only America brings out the best in everyone. He ends that an electrical engineer can make a living in India.
viv.6.strive_to_be_great.core_teaching: What matters is to try for something great and useful; even failure after such striving is a satisfaction, and it takes daring to cut a new path.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 6, Epistles II, XCIX)
commentaries.gist: His hopes for Mohin are tied to India's need for science and courage rather than more lawyers.

commentaries.who: Letter to John Fox, Paris, 14 August 1900 (CW vol. 8)
commentaries.gist: The CW editors identify Mohin as Mahendranath Datta, Swamiji's younger brother; Vivekananda sends him blessings and says he likes boldness and adventure.

viv.6.strive_to_be_great.practical_reading: Used to encourage young people to attempt ambitious, useful work and to see honest failure as no disgrace.
misreadings: Not contempt for law as a profession (he is giving a personal preference)
cautions: The lawyer remark may put off some readers
speaks_to: young people choosing an unusual path

viv.6.the_cup.context: A three-stanza poem in which God speaks to 'My child'. The first stanza says this cup was assigned from the beginning and that much of its dark drink is the child's own brew from long ago. The second says this is a painful road, while a friend walks an easier one and will also come to God. The quoted third stanza calls it a joyless task meant for no other hand and asks for acceptance without understanding.
viv.6.the_cup.core_teaching: Your particular burden is measured for you and has its place in God's universe; you are not asked to understand it, only to take it and look to God.

commentaries.who: The poem itself (CW vol. 6, 'The Cup')
commentaries.gist: Spoken by God; it frames suffering as both assigned and partly self-made, and compares the hearer's hard road with a friend's easier one without ranking them.

viv.6.the_cup.practical_reading: Used to help someone stop comparing their road with others' and carry their own task with faith.
misreadings: Not acceptance of abuse or injustice; act where you can (as our misuse field says)
Not 'you deserve your suffering'
cautions: The first stanza says the dark drink is partly 'your own brew of fault and passion', which can feel like blame; consider showing only the third stanza
Asks for acceptance without understanding, which can frustrate someone wanting answers
not_for: victims of abuse or injustice
someone blaming themselves for a loss
speaks_to: a hard duty that feels unchosen

viv.6.three_essentials.context: He is glad the young doctor has come to know Sri Ramakrishna and praises his vairagya. He then sets out the difficulties of renouncing hastily and says India needs a few thousand who will sacrifice themselves. The quoted lines are his caution: no haste; purity, patience, perseverance and love. He closes saying everything comes right if one is pure and sincere.
viv.6.three_essentials.core_teaching: Do nothing in haste: purity, patience, perseverance and above all love are what bring success, and there is all the time needed.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 6, Epistles II, LI)
commentaries.gist: Written to a young man eager to give up everything; he encourages the aim but slows the pace.

commentaries.who: Parallel: letter from Reading, England, 4 October 1895 (CW vol. 6)
commentaries.gist: Repeats that purity, patience and perseverance overcome all obstacles and that great things are necessarily slow.

viv.6.three_essentials.practical_reading: Used to slow down people rushing into big life decisions or measuring themselves by fast results.
misreadings: Not a reason to postpone everything indefinitely

viv.6.tropics_or_poles.context: The letter begins with practical news (a trip to the Leggetts, staying put to save money). It then turns into a prayer: he asks whether God will leave him now after carrying him all his life, says nothing exists without God's mercy, and dismisses worries about the 'right sort of presentation'. He signs as her 'ever obedient son', calling her 'mother'.
viv.6.tropics_or_poles.core_teaching: Wherever he goes, God is with him as guide, friend and his real Self; in loneliness he asks never to lean on anyone but God.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 6, Epistles II, LXII)
commentaries.gist: A practical letter that becomes a prayer of trust, written while he was alone and struggling in New York.

viv.6.tropics_or_poles.practical_reading: Used to comfort people who are alone far from home, moving, or emigrating.
misreadings: Not a rule never to accept help from people
cautions: 'Never seek help from any being but Thee' could discourage someone from reaching out for support; frame it as trust, not isolation
not_for: someone isolated who needs to be encouraged to seek human help

viv.6.weary_take_my_hand.context: Class notes on devotion, describing stages of love and then prayer, praise and meditation. He gives several model prayers in a row: to be taken by the hand like a child, this one, and then one asking God to help us bear the small burden of our life and never leave us.
viv.6.weary_take_my_hand.core_teaching: A simple prayer for the tired: wanting nothing else but God, admitting weariness, and asking to be led and sheltered.

commentaries.who: Context of the notes (CW vol. 6, 'On Bhakti-Yoga')
commentaries.gist: One of a series of short prayers he gives students; the next asks God, who bears the universe, to help us bear our little burden.

viv.6.weary_take_my_hand.practical_reading: Can be used as a prayer at the end of an exhausting day.
misreadings: Not a rejection of ordinary goods for everyone
not_for: non-theistic readers

viv.7.i_am_near.context: He thanks Prof. Wright for letters of introduction to the Parliament of Religions, mentions plans to see Boston's Sanskrit library, and copies out a poem. The poem sees God in the moon, stars and sea; then, when calamity seems to crush him, he hears God whispering 'I am near'. It goes on to see God in a mother's lullaby, children's play, friendship, and all scriptures, ending 'I am thine'.
viv.7.i_am_near.core_teaching: In moments of calamity the poet hears God say 'I am near', and that makes the heart strong enough to fear nothing.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 7, Epistles III, IX)
commentaries.gist: Written a week before the Parliament opened, while he was a stranger in America depending on others' help.

viv.7.i_am_near.practical_reading: Used to comfort anxious or frightened readers with a sense of God's nearness.
misreadings: Not a promise that nothing bad will happen
cautions: 'A thousand deaths no fear' mentions death; fine for most uses
not_for: non-theistic readers

viv.7.neither_seek_nor_avoid.context: A day's notes on happiness and misery as gold and iron chains, both hiding the blissful Atman. Just before, he quotes Ramakrishna that all is God but the tiger-God is to be avoided, and speaks of the sky as God's censer. After the line he tells the story of the mosquito apologising to the bull, who says the mosquito can do him no harm.
viv.7.neither_seek_nor_avoid.core_teaching: Take what comes without chasing or running; true freedom is not gritting one's teeth but being unaffected.

commentaries.who: Context of the talk (CW vol. 7, Inspired Talks, 25 June 1895)
commentaries.gist: He sets this beside Ramakrishna's tiger-God saying, which keeps it from meaning passivity before danger, and the bull-and-mosquito story about not being disturbed.

viv.7.neither_seek_nor_avoid.practical_reading: Used to loosen anxious control: stop forcing outcomes and stop dodging what must be faced.
misreadings: Not passivity about problems you can fix (as our misuse field says)
Not tolerance of danger: the tiger-God saying in the same notes says to avoid it
not_for: someone in danger or abuse

viv.7.round_us_this_minute.context: The CW heading says it was written on the death of Prof. Wright's daughter, aged 16. He opens with the sad news reaching him, then these lines; he goes on to say the Wrights are strong and pure and have surely thrown off the illusion that anyone can die, quotes the Katha Upanishad's lines on the one eternal amid the changing, and prays for their peace.
viv.7.round_us_this_minute.core_teaching: Forms pass but the spirit, being in God, does not; those we have lost are around us now, only changed in how they are present.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 7, Epistles III, XXXV)
commentaries.gist: A short condolence: after the core comfort he quotes the Upanishadic promise of peace to one who sees the eternal in the changing.

viv.7.round_us_this_minute.practical_reading: Offered to bereaved readers as a sense that the dead are near.
misreadings: Not a denial of grief
cautions: Calls the world an 'illusion' and death a 'lie and delusion' right after; to a parent who has lost a child that can feel dismissive. Use the 'round us this minute' sentence on its own
not_for: very fresh grief where 'illusion' language would wound
speaks_to: feeling the presence of the departed

viv.7.thoughts_live.context: A day's notes on working without the little self. Just before, he says to get rid of the little 'I' and let God work. After the line he says each thought carries our character, so even a pure person's jests do good; then: desire nothing, look for no return.
viv.7.thoughts_live.core_teaching: We become what our thoughts make us, and thoughts have far-reaching effects, so guard them.

commentaries.who: Context of the talk (CW vol. 7, Inspired Talks, 26 June 1895)
commentaries.gist: Set inside teaching on selfless work: the influence of the pure comes through their thoughts, even unconsciously.

commentaries.who: Parallel: 'Vedantism', Jaffna (CW vol. 3)
commentaries.gist: Whatever you think, that you will be: think yourself weak and you will be weak.

viv.7.thoughts_live.practical_reading: Used for mindfulness of thought habits and their effect on others.
misreadings: Not blame for intrusive or anxious thoughts
cautions: People with OCD or intrusive thoughts may fear their thoughts 'live'; reassure them
not_for: OCD or intrusive-thought anxiety

viv.7.want_a_bit_of_peace.context: Vivekananda tells Mrs Blodgett that after six months of intense work he has relapsed into nervous exhaustion and fever, though his heart and kidneys are sound, and that he will rest a few days in the country before going to Chicago. He mentions introducing Miss Noble, whom he calls his daughter, to a Chicago friend. The closing lines bless her and then admit he badly wants some peace and ask for her prayers.
viv.7.want_a_bit_of_peace.core_teaching: Even a great teacher reaches the end of his strength and says so plainly, asking others for help.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (Complete Works vol. 7, letter LII)
commentaries.gist: Health relapse after six months of lecturing; plans a short country rest before Chicago; arranges for Sister Nivedita's work; ends with the plea for peace and prayers, love to Kate and greetings to friends.

commentaries.who: Vivekananda chronology, May 1900 (vivekananda.net)
commentaries.gist: Places him at Camp Taylor, California, as guest of Alice Hansbrough on 2 May 1900, when he wrote to Mrs Blodgett and to Sister Nivedita.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda in California (Wikipedia)
commentaries.gist: He reached California on 3 December 1899; Roxie Blodgett was among his Los Angeles hosts; he left California for Chicago on 30 May 1900.

viv.7.want_a_bit_of_peace.practical_reading: If you are running on empty, it is allowed to say it out loud and ask someone to hold you in their thoughts or give you an hour off.
misreadings: Not a sign of spiritual failure; the point is honest need.
cautions: Written by a monk to a friend, not about parenting; its use for parents rests on the shared exhaustion.
not_for: someone who needs practical steps rather than permission to feel tired

viv.8.all_right_long_run.context: Near the end of a lecture on whether Vedanta could become the religion of the future. He has listed what Vedanta does not offer: no single book, no chosen person set above others, no clay idols. Here he says it knows no sin, only mistakes; after the passage he adds that God is our own Self, so fear of God is the real superstition.
viv.8.all_right_long_run.core_teaching: There are mistakes but no sin in Vedanta; calling anyone a sinner is the one real error. Our present is built from mistakes and successes alike, so honour both and go forward.

commentaries.who: Context of the lecture (CW vol. 8, 'Is Vedanta the Future Religion?')
commentaries.gist: It follows his claim that we are all spirit and precedes his argument that God is one's own Self, whom it is absurd to fear.

commentaries.who: Parallel: 'Practical Vedanta IV', London 1896 (CW vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: Teaching people their nature is evil only weakens them; bring in the light instead of weeping over past steps.

viv.8.all_right_long_run.practical_reading: Used to free people from shame and to look at past mistakes as part of what made them.
misreadings: Not 'nothing anyone does is wrong' or a dismissal of harm done to others
Not contempt for other religions' ideas of sin, though his phrasing is sharp
cautions: 'None of this nonsense' about Satan and sin may offend Christian or Muslim readers
Someone who caused serious harm may misuse 'no sin'
not_for: readers whose faith centres on sin and redemption
someone avoiding accountability
speaks_to: looking back on a messy past

viv.8.come_good_come_evil.context: The letter opens saying he is 'very happy', not from optimism but because his power of suffering is growing and the world's joys and sorrows are losing meaning. The line is in an exuberant postscript: he says he enjoys good and evil alike, was both Jesus and Judas, and that as 'the diamond mine' he plays with pebbles of good and evil; he ends 'I am peace'.
viv.8.come_good_come_evil.core_teaching: Face everything bravely: good and bad both come and go, and from the standpoint of the Self they are only play.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 8, Epistles IV, CLXV)
commentaries.gist: Written in a mood of non-dual exaltation; he quotes the Upanishadic idea that fear remains while there are two.

viv.8.come_good_come_evil.practical_reading: Used to encourage courage in uncertainty: whatever comes, meet it rather than hide.
misreadings: Not a statement that evil is acceptable or that one should not resist harm
Not 'I enjoy evil' in an ethical sense; it is about the witness Self
cautions: The postscript's 'I enjoy the evil' and 'I was Judas' can shock out of context
not_for: someone harmed by another, for whom 'welcome evil' would wound

viv.8.comfort_no_test.context: The series heading says these notes were recorded by Miss S. E. Waldo and copied from her notebook by Saradananda in 1896. Just before, he tells of two men who laughed at the moon causing tides but believed a Puranic tale. After the line he says whoever seeks truth must not cling to comfort, the Jnani must give up desires and body-identification, and this self-sacrifice underlies all religious sacrifice.
viv.8.comfort_no_test.core_teaching: Whether something feels comfortable says nothing about whether it is true; real truth often is not comfortable, and finding it asks us to let go of comfort.

commentaries.who: Context of the discourse (CW vol. 8, Jnana-Yoga IV)
commentaries.gist: He follows the line with the call to give up desire and identification with the body, calling this inner sacrifice the root of all sacrifice.

viv.8.comfort_no_test.practical_reading: Used to encourage honesty with oneself, even when the truth about a situation is unwelcome.
misreadings: Not a claim that comfort is bad or that true things must hurt
cautions: Not a comfort verse; avoid for grief or acute distress
not_for: grieving or distressed readers seeking comfort

viv.8.early_violet.context: A two-stanza poem (eight lines each). The first lists hardships: frozen ground, cold wind, no companion, a gloomy sky, love failing, vice reigning. The second asks the violet not to change its nature but to keep giving its scent freely.
viv.8.early_violet.core_teaching: Even if love fails and wrong seems to win, keep your own good nature and keep giving freely.

commentaries.who: The poem itself (CW vol. 8, 'To an Early Violet')
commentaries.gist: All the hardships come first, from loneliness to failed love, before the single request to remain sweet and pure.

viv.8.early_violet.practical_reading: Used to encourage people not to let others' unkindness make them bitter.
misreadings: Not advice to stay in a cold or abusive situation; keeping your nature does not mean staying put (as our misuse field says)
cautions: Could be read as telling someone mistreated to keep giving to the person mistreating them
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship

viv.8.exchange_grief.context: The closing paragraph of his condolence letter on the death of Mary's father, George W. Hale, in whose Chicago home he had stayed. After saying experience is the only real teacher, he contrasts her sheltered life with his own life of continual blows (poverty, betrayal, his own foolishness), names his pessimism, and then makes this offer. He signs as her 'ever faithful brother'.
viv.8.exchange_grief.core_teaching: A friend who has suffered much offers, if it were possible, to take her grief in place of his own, and leaves the rest to the Mother.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 8, Epistles IV, CLVI)
commentaries.gist: He is unusually open about his own suffering and pessimism, which makes the offer sound like solidarity rather than instruction.

commentaries.who: Editorial note on the Hale family (CW vol. 8, 'An Interesting Correspondence')
commentaries.gist: Explains that Mary Hale was a daughter of Mr and Mrs Hale, whom he called Father Pope and Mother Church, and that the Hale sisters were like sisters to him.

viv.8.exchange_grief.practical_reading: Used to show that real comfort can be honest companionship in pain rather than advice.
misreadings: Not a suggestion that grief can be traded away
cautions: He calls her life 'sheltered' and his own far worse; out of context this can sound like comparing griefs

viv.8.faith_totters.context: Written on hearing that a public meeting in Calcutta had honoured his work in America; he sends them the printed report. He weeps at God's mercy, admits that his faith still sometimes wavers and his mind gets despondent, then declares that God as Father and Mother never leaves His children. He closes 'Blessed, blessed art Thou'.
viv.8.faith_totters.core_teaching: Even while overwhelmed by God's mercy he confesses that his faith sometimes wavers; doubt and despondency come even to the devoted.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 8, Epistles IV, XXIII)
commentaries.gist: The confession sits between tears of gratitude and a firm affirmation that God never abandons His children.

viv.8.faith_totters.practical_reading: Used to reassure believers that wavering faith is normal and not a failure.
misreadings: Not evidence that his faith was weak; he presents it as human frailty
cautions: 'Weeping like a woman' is a dated gendered phrase
Same passage as viv.8.never_never_never (identical translation field)
not_for: non-theistic readers

viv.8.heart_lives_on.context: The opening of the condolence letter. He has received news of Mr Hale's death the day before and says he is sorry, because the heart lives on despite monastic training, and Mr Hale was one of the best people he met. He then acknowledges that Mary and the family must be miserable, especially as it is her first such grief.
viv.8.heart_lives_on.core_teaching: Even a monk trained in detachment grieves; the heart goes on feeling, and that is no failure.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 8, Epistles IV, CLVI)
commentaries.gist: He names his own sorrow first, then turns to hers, and goes on to speak of his own guilt after his father's death.

commentaries.who: Editorial note on the Hale family (CW vol. 8)
commentaries.gist: Identifies Mary Hale as daughter of Mr and Mrs Hale, close friends whom he addressed as Father Pope and Mother Church.

viv.8.heart_lives_on.practical_reading: Gives permission to grieve even to people who think their faith or discipline should prevent it.
misreadings: Not a criticism of detachment practice
speaks_to: spiritual people who feel they should not grieve

viv.8.lotus_bees.context: Fragmentary notes. Just before, he says society must be outgrown and renunciation means one cannot serve God and Mammon. After the line come other short sayings: a handful of strong men can move the world; we need heart, brain and arm; it is God who works, not you; when heart and brain conflict, follow the heart.
viv.8.lotus_bees.core_teaching: Develop your own depth of thought and love first; those who need it will be drawn to you without your chasing them.

commentaries.who: Context of the notes (CW vol. 8, 'The Religion of Love')
commentaries.gist: One of a string of compressed sayings; the surrounding notes balance self-belief with 'it is God who works, not you'.

viv.8.lotus_bees.practical_reading: Used to shift focus from seeking recognition or followers to inner growth.
misreadings: Not a promise of popularity
Not a reason to withdraw from people

viv.8.mental_hell_lifted.context: He thanks Mary for inviting him to Chicago, says he is busy trying to earn his passage home, and that his health is better but strength has not returned. He wishes for a few days' rest with the Hale sisters, then says the last two years were especially bad: he has lived in mental hell, now partly lifted. He thanks Mary for being the sweetest notes in his jarring life and says he has never known a peaceful moment.
viv.8.mental_hell_lifted.core_teaching: A great teacher admits two years of mental torment, only partly lifted, and hopes for better days.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 8, Epistles IV, CLVII)
commentaries.gist: Written ten days after his condolence letter to her; it mixes practical worries about money and health with this rare admission of inner suffering.

viv.8.mental_hell_lifted.practical_reading: Used to reassure readers that severe inner struggle happens even to spiritual giants, and that partial relief is real relief.
misreadings: Not a diagnosis; do not read modern clinical terms into it
cautions: Strong language ('mental hell'); appropriate for someone struggling if paired with hope, but avoid amplifying despair
speaks_to: long periods of depression or strain

viv.8.never_never_never.context: The same short letter as viv.8.faith_totters: he weeps with gratitude at news that a Calcutta public meeting honoured him, confesses his faith sometimes wavers, then affirms that God as Father and Mother never leaves His children and urges them to take refuge like children.
viv.8.never_never_never.core_teaching: There is a God, Father and Mother, who never abandons His children; put theories aside and take refuge in Him like a child.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 8, Epistles IV, XXIII)
commentaries.gist: The affirmation comes straight after his admission of despondency, so it reads as faith reasserted, not faith never shaken.

viv.8.never_never_never.practical_reading: Used to reassure those who feel abandoned that they are not.
misreadings: Not a claim that suffering proves God's absence or presence
cautions: 'Weeping like a woman' is dated
Identical passage to viv.8.faith_totters
not_for: non-theistic readers

viv.8.not_good_enough.context: Right after admitting his own sorrow at Mr Hale's death, he says he has lost many people and that the strangest pain when someone dies is the sense of not having been good enough to them. He recalls months of pain after his father's death, because he had been so disobedient, and tells Mary, who was dutiful, that any such feeling is only a form of sorrow.
viv.8.not_good_enough.core_teaching: Guilt after a death, the feeling of not having been good enough to the person, is common, and is really a form of grief rather than a judgement.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 8, Epistles IV, CLVI)
commentaries.gist: He shares his own regret about his father to normalise hers before reassuring her.

commentaries.who: Editorial note on the Hale family (CW vol. 8)
commentaries.gist: Gives the relationship: the Hales were close friends and Mary like a sister to him.

viv.8.not_good_enough.practical_reading: Used to help the bereaved see guilt as part of grief and to be gentle with themselves.
misreadings: Not a claim that the reader was in fact a bad child or friend
cautions: Mentions his own disobedience to his father; readers with real conflict with the dead may need more than this

viv.8.smiles_and_tears.context: Middle of the condolence letter: after calling her guilt a form of sorrow, he says life is now beginning for her in earnest, that books and lectures teach less than experience, and that we learn through smiles and tears. He adds that her mother has the solace of her religion and wishes we could all dream good dreams, before contrasting her sheltered life with his own.
viv.8.smiles_and_tears.core_teaching: We learn through both joy and sorrow; we may not know why it works this way, but seeing that it does is enough.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 8, Epistles IV, CLVI)
commentaries.gist: Written to someone meeting her first great grief; he offers experience, not doctrine, as the teacher.

viv.8.smiles_and_tears.practical_reading: Used to help someone accept that painful experience also teaches, without needing to explain why.
misreadings: Not 'your loss happened to teach you something'
cautions: 'It is best as it is' just before can sound like approval of the loss; consider omitting it
not_for: very fresh grief, where 'lessons' language can hurt

viv.8.soul_of_light.context: On his return to Belur Math on 9 December 1900 he learned that Captain Sevier had died at Mayavati (on 28 October 1900). In this letter of 26 December he tells MacLeod that Sevier died before he could arrive, was cremated in Hindu fashion, and that Mrs Sevier is calm. He also says he is calm and strong, feels foolish about his earlier anxiety over the Math, and asks MacLeod to tell Mrs Bull she was always right. The four lines come just before his closing greetings.
viv.8.soul_of_light.core_teaching: Looking back and ahead, he finds that all is well; even in his deepest sorrow there is a core of light.

commentaries.who: Full letter (CW vol. 6, Epistles II, CLXVII)
commentaries.gist: The lines close a letter mixing grief for Sevier, calm, relief that his brother monks managed well, and an apology to Mrs Bull.

commentaries.who: Wikipedia, 'Charlotte Sevier'
commentaries.gist: Gives Captain Sevier's death date as 28 October 1900.

commentaries.who: Swami Nikhilananda's biography (vivekananda.net)
