commentaries.gist: Says he reached Belur Math on 9 December 1900 and was told there of Sevier's death.

viv.8.soul_of_light.practical_reading: Used to say that light can be found inside sorrow, not only after it.
misreadings: Not 'you should not be sad'
cautions: Written about two weeks after he learned of a friend's death; suitable for grief but 'all is right' can sound premature to the newly bereaved
not_for: the first days after a loss
speaks_to: looking back on a hard year

viv.8.take_things_easy.context: A newsy letter to Shashi, who was running the work in Madras. He asks Shashi to look after Alasinga, who is overworking, and passes on news: two lectures in Calcutta by Miss Noble and Sharat, some monks recovering from influenza, and Holy Mother eating with the Western women. The quoted line comes after that news, followed by 'a few strong strokes and rest on your oars' and plans for next year's festival.
viv.8.take_things_easy.core_teaching: Good work needs rest as well as effort; trust that you are looked after, keep your health and don't strain.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (CW vol. 8, Epistles IV, CXXIV)
commentaries.gist: The advice to Alasinga and to Shashi frames rest as part of good work, not a lapse from it.

viv.8.take_things_easy.practical_reading: Used directly for overworkers: alternate effort with real rest.
misreadings: Not a call to laziness

vr.1.2.16.context: Valmiki has just watched a hunter kill the male of a pair of mating krauñca birds and, moved by the female's cry, has burst out with a curse on the hunter. Still looking at the bird, he turns inward and asks what it was that came out of him. In the next verses he thinks it through and tells his disciple the words have the form of a new metre, the śloka.
vr.1.2.16.core_teaching: Even a self-controlled sage can speak out of grief, and the mature response is to stop and examine what was said rather than defend it. That pause is what turns a raw outburst into something he can understand and use.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka), on 1.2.40 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Tilaka maps the episode onto rasa theory: the slain bird and its mate are the cause of the emotion, and the sage's anxious reflection in v.16 is counted as a passing (vyabhicāri) feeling within the larger grief that becomes karuṇa rasa.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa), on 1.2.14 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Govindarāja insists the outburst was not whim or anger: it came from seeing a clear wrong (killing a creature in the act of mating) joined with tender compassion for the bereaved bird.

vr.1.2.16.practical_reading: After words said in pain or anger, take a breath and ask honestly what came out and why, before either regretting it wholesale or justifying it. Strong feeling, examined, can become insight or creative work.
misreadings: Not a teaching that grief or compassion is wrong; the commentators treat his feeling as righteous.
Not a call to self-punishment after an outburst; the verse moves to reflection, not shame.
cautions: Context involves a violent killing of a bird and a curse; mild, but note for very sensitive readers.
not_for: someone who is being blamed for normal grief; it could read as 'you should not have reacted'
a reader looking for comfort for a fresh loss (the verse is about self-examination, not consolation)
speaks_to: having snapped or said something harsh in grief or shock
noticing your own reaction and wanting to understand it
creative people turning pain into work

vr.1.2.36.context: After Brahma has visited, approved the new metre and told Valmiki to tell Rama's whole story, the disciples chant the krauñca verse over and over and marvel at it. This verse is their exclamation. Right after it, Valmiki resolves to compose the entire Ramayana in such verses.
vr.1.2.36.core_teaching: A private grief, given form and shared through repetition, becomes something lasting that others can receive. The poem's own origin story says its compassion (karuṇa) is born from sorrow.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Tilaka gives a full rasa analysis: the grief (śoka) is the underlying emotion; through poetic universalisation and the disciples' repeated chanting, personal sorrow becomes the aesthetic experience of karuṇa rasa.

vr.1.2.36.practical_reading: Teachers use this as the founding image of turning pain into something made: a song, a poem, a journal entry said aloud to others. Shaping and repeating grief can change how it sits in you.
misreadings: Not a claim that grief should be quickly converted into productivity.
Not 'grief is good'; the verse honours the sorrow that the poem grows from.
cautions: Gentle for grief, but 'sorrow can become something you make' may feel premature in the first days of a loss.
not_for: very fresh, acute grief where making anything feels impossible
someone pressured to 'be productive' about loss
speaks_to: people writing, singing or creating after a loss
grief that has begun to settle and wants a form

data_flags.attribution_note: Speaker is not the narrator: in itihasa.io (and Griffith, Book I canto 2) the line is spoken by Valmiki's disciples, who keep chanting the verse and say to one another, astonished, that the grief has become a śloka. Suggest speaker 'Valmiki's disciples', listener 'one another'.

vr.1.21.21.context: Vishvamitra has asked for young Ram to protect his sacrifice from demons, and Dasharatha, terrified, has refused and angered the sage. Vasishtha steps in, lists Vishvamitra's powers and says there is no reason for doubt. This verse is his clinching point; in the next verse Dasharatha, calmed, agrees to send Ram.
vr.1.21.21.core_teaching: The sage does not need Ram; Ram needs what the sage can give. A parent's fear can misread an opportunity for the child as a threat.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads the particle 'ca' as 'even though': though fully able to deal with the demons himself, Vishvamitra asks for Ram purely for the prince's good, implying he means to hand over his whole store of divine weapon-knowledge.

vr.1.21.21.practical_reading: When a mentor, school or opportunity asks to take your child (or you) out of a safe place, ask whether the request is really for their growth. Letting go can be the protective act.
misreadings: Not a rule that parents should hand children to any authority who asks; the case rests on Vasishtha's trusted judgement of this particular sage.
Not dismissing a parent's fear as foolish.
cautions: For a parent whose child faces real danger (illness, war, an unsafe situation), this could feel like being told to stop worrying.
not_for: a parent grieving a child who left and came to harm
situations of coercion or where the 'mentor' is untrustworthy
speaks_to: parents sending a child away to study, train or work
anxiety about letting someone you love take a risk
resisting a mentor's offer out of fear

vr.1.33.8.context: Kushanabha's hundred daughters refused the wind-god Vayu's demand that they become his, saying their father decides whom they marry; Vayu in anger entered their bodies and left them deformed. When they tell their father, he praises their forbearance in this panegyric, comforts them, and then looks for a suitable husband for them.
vr.1.33.8.core_teaching: Forbearance is praised as containing the fruit of every other virtue: generosity, truth, sacrifice, honour and dharma. The world itself is held up by people who can bear and not retaliate.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Forbearance is equated with charity, truth and the rest because it yields the fruit of all of those duties together.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Agrees with Tilaka and adds a pun: kṣamā also means the earth, so 'the world rests on kṣamā' plays on the earth that bears everything.

vr.1.33.8.practical_reading: Commonly cited as a hymn to patience and forgiveness: not hitting back when wronged, and holding steady so that others can rely on you.
misreadings: Not an instruction that victims of assault or abuse should stay silent or forgive the abuser.
Forbearance here is not passivity; the daughters had already firmly refused Vayu.
cautions: The daughters were harmed by Vayu after refusing him; praising their forbearance can read as praising silent endurance of sexual violence. Use with great care or avoid in any plan touching abuse, harassment or trauma.
Should not be used to tell a woman to tolerate mistreatment.
not_for: survivors of assault, abuse or harassment
anyone in an unsafe relationship
readers being pressured to 'forgive and forget' a serious wrong
speaks_to: everyday irritation and the urge to retaliate
holding back a harsh reply at work or home
someone who chose not to take revenge and wonders if that was weak

vr.1.44.10.context: Bhagiratha has brought the Ganga down and led her over the ashes of his 60,000 ancestors (Sagara's sons), freeing them. Brahma appears, tells him to perform the water rites for them, and praises him for completing what Sagara, Amshuman and Dilipa had tried and failed to do. Next he says this descent has earned Bhagiratha a great store of dharma.
vr.1.44.10.core_teaching: A task that defeated several generations can be completed by the one who persists; the earlier efforts were not wasted but carried forward into his success.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Glosses samatikrāntā as 'crossed over', the vow brought through to completion.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Same gloss, and reads the fame as one esteemed by the greatest sages.

vr.1.44.10.practical_reading: Used to honour long, multi-generation or long-delayed effort: finishing a family's unfinished task, a degree or project years in the making, or a cause many people worked on before you.
misreadings: Not a claim that earlier generations failed through weakness; the text treats their efforts with respect.
cautions: Ancestral rites for the dead are in the background; mild.
not_for: someone who has just failed and feels it is final (it celebrates success, may sting)
a reader burdened by family expectations they never chose
speaks_to: carrying on a parent's or family's unfinished work

vr.1.53.9.context: King Vishvamitra, a guest at Vasishtha's hermitage, has seen the wish-granting cow Śabalā feed his whole army and asks for her, offering a hundred thousand cows. Vasishtha refuses, saying she is bound to him like fame to a self-mastered person and that his offerings, rites and learning depend on her. The king keeps raising the offer, then tries to take her by force.
vr.1.53.9.core_teaching: Some things cannot be priced because a whole way of life depends on them; no offer, however large, makes them tradeable.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explains the next line's comparison: Śabalā is inseparable from Vasishtha just as fame born of learning and austerity never leaves a self-mastered person.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: With Tilaka, lists the rites resting on Śabalā (offerings to gods and ancestors, daily fire rites, offerings to all beings) to show why she cannot be sold.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explains how even Vedic learning depends on her: her milk gives the purity of mind and bodily vigour that study needs.

vr.1.53.9.practical_reading: Applied to values, relationships, integrity or a vocation that someone offers money or status to buy: knowing what is not for sale.
misreadings: Not a general refusal to negotiate or share.
Not about stubbornly hoarding possessions; the cow sustains his duties to others.
cautions: Vishvamitra later uses force and Vasishtha's sons die in the fighting; keep that in view if building a plan around the episode.
not_for: someone who genuinely must sell a cherished thing to survive (could feel like judgement)
a reader in a real coercive situation where refusing is unsafe
speaks_to: pressure to compromise integrity for money or promotion
protecting something precious from a powerful person
boundaries with people who think everything has a price

vr.1.63.9.context: Vishvamitra had been practising severe austerity at Pushkara when the nymph Menaka came to bathe nearby; he invited her to stay and ten years passed. Waking from it, he sees the gods' plot to rob his austerity and is filled with remorse. He then sends the frightened Menaka away gently and goes north to practise harder.
vr.1.63.9.core_teaching: Absorption in desire can quietly swallow years; the turning point is recognising it honestly, taking ownership, and recommitting.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka), on 1.63.12-13 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Vishvamitra spares Menaka because he sees the fault as his own (she stayed at his request), and by not cursing he shows he has kept his vow to conquer anger.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa), on 1.63.12-13 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Has him say the offence is his alone, as one who had become a slave to desire; so he dismisses her with gentle words instead of punishing her.

vr.1.63.9.practical_reading: Used for 'where did the time go' moments: years lost to a distraction, a habit or a relationship that pulled you off course, and the choice to own it and start again without blaming others.
misreadings: Not a warning against women or love as such; the commentators stress he blamed himself, not Menaka.
Not a call to self-hatred; he regrets and resumes his practice.
cautions: Sexual desire is the context; frame carefully. Avoid shaming language about lost years.
not_for: someone grieving a relationship (could read as 'it was a waste')
readers prone to harsh self-criticism or depression about lost time
speaks_to: realising a habit or distraction has eaten months or years
regret over drifting from a goal
taking responsibility instead of blaming the tempter

data_flags.translation_note: Two issues. (1) 'As if they were a single day and night' slightly misstates: the Sanskrit (ahorātrāpadeśena) says ten years passed under the guise of days and nights, i.e. unnoticed, as if just a day and night. Acceptable as a paraphrase. (2) 'This obstacle came...

vr.1.64.15.context: Indra sent the nymph Rambha to tempt Vishvamitra; seeing through it, the sage angrily cursed her to become stone, and then realised that his anger had cost him his austerity. Restless and unpeaceful, he resolves never again to give in to anger or speak, and then vows not even to breathe for a thousand years while he dries his body in tapas.
vr.1.64.15.core_teaching: Anger quietly undoes years of hard-won discipline, and as long as the senses are unmastered there is no peace. The response is a firm, concrete vow of restraint.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'I will not speak' as a vow against harsh or cursing speech, the kind that just cost him his tapas.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Agrees with Tilaka: the vow is to give up curse-like speech.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as total silence and even holding the breath, since passions like anger arise only when the breath moves.

vr.1.64.15.practical_reading: After an angry outburst that cost you something, make a specific, keepable resolution about speech, such as not replying while angry.
misreadings: Not a call to suppress all emotion or never speak up.
His breath-holding vow is ascetic hyperbole, not advice.
cautions: The following verses describe extreme austerity (not breathing, drying up the body); do not present as a practice.
not_for: someone who suppresses anger to the point of harm, or is being silenced
a reader in an abusive relationship told to 'not speak'
speaks_to: seeing how anger undid long effort
wanting a concrete rule for speech

data_flags.corrected_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 1.64.16 + 1.64.17. Line 1 is 1.64.16 = Baroda critical edition 1.63.15 (last verse of CE sarga 63); line 2 is 1.64.17, Southern-only (not in the CE). Our id 1.64.15 is one verse early.

vr.1.65.3.context: Vishvamitra has taken a thousand-year vow of silence and fasting. When it ends and he is about to eat, Indra comes disguised as a brahmin and begs his food, and the sage gives it away without a word. Through all such tests anger does not get in, and soon after the gods acknowledge him a brahmarshi.
vr.1.65.3.core_teaching: Real mastery is not the absence of provocation but the absence of an opening for anger: shaken outwardly, inwardly undisturbed.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'like wood' as standing still as a log, and 'antaram' as an opening: anger found no gap to enter.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Stresses that he bore every obstacle and provocation patiently.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'antaram' as the inner mind: anger never reached it.

vr.1.65.3.practical_reading: A picture of growth after repeated failure: the same provocations still come, but they no longer get inside. Useful for anyone working on temper over a long time.
misreadings: Not praise of emotional numbness; 'like wood' describes stillness in austerity, not not caring.
Not a claim this is quick or easy; it follows two failures.
cautions: Ascetic extremes (thousand-year fast) are mythic; avoid suggesting deprivation.
not_for: someone already numb or dissociated who might take 'like wood' as an ideal

vr.1.77.20.context: The last sarga of the Bala Kanda: after the weddings and Parashurama's challenge, the family returns to Ayodhya and Bharata leaves for his uncle's home. Valmiki closes the book with Ram and Sita's happy early years, saying their love grew by each other's qualities and that their hearts spoke to each other without words.
vr.1.77.20.core_teaching: A marriage begun by the elders' choice deepens as each comes to love the other's character; love is something that grows, not only something found.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Ram's love had two roots, respect for his father's choice and Sita's beauty and goodness; Sita's love was twice as intense, flowing simply from his being her husband; their hearts read each other's unspoken thoughts.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: On the next line, says each heart understood the other directly, by its own heart.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Takes that mutual understanding as knowing by insight (buddhi).

vr.1.77.20.practical_reading: Speaks to arranged and long marriages: love that keeps growing because you keep seeing who the other person is.
misreadings: Not an argument that arranged marriage is superior or that wives should love more than husbands.
Govindarāja's 'Sita loved twice as much' should not be turned into a gender prescription.
cautions: Readers know the later separation and Sita's ordeal; for someone in a painful marriage, an idealised picture may sting.
not_for: someone in an unhappy or coercive marriage
recent divorce or widowhood
a reader pressured into an arranged match
speaks_to: newly married couples, especially arranged marriages
renewing appreciation in a long marriage

vr.2.1.10.context: The Ayodhya Kanda opens with Bharata away at his uncle's and Dasharatha thinking of making Ram crown prince. Valmiki paints a long portrait of Ram's qualities to show why the king and people want him. This verse follows the line calling him free of envy and peerless, and precedes the one on remembering kindness and forgetting wrongs.
vr.2.1.10.core_teaching: Inner calm shows in speech: open gently, and do not let another's harshness set the tone of your reply.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Ram mirrors Dasharatha's noble bearing like a lamp lit from a lamp, and never retorts even when spoken to harshly.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka), on the preceding verse (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: With Govindarāja, defines Ram's freedom from envy (anasūyaka) as never finding fault in others' good qualities, the trait this verse continues.

vr.2.1.10.practical_reading: In arguments at home or work, speak first and softly, and when someone is harsh, decline to escalate. Calm speech is presented as a sign of inner steadiness, not weakness.
misreadings: Not a rule never to stand up for yourself or others; Ram acts firmly elsewhere.
Not about suppressing all disagreement.
cautions: For someone being verbally abused, 'do not answer back' could sound like advice to endure it.
not_for: people in abusive relationships
someone who already over-accommodates and needs to assert themselves
speaks_to: wanting to be someone who lowers the temperature

vr.2.1.11.context: Part of the same opening portrait of Ram's virtues in Ayodhya Kanda sarga 1, just after the verse on gentle speech. It is followed by the picture of Ram spending even breaks from weapons practice in the company of elders rich in conduct and wisdom.
vr.2.1.11.core_teaching: Gratitude should be quick and generous, grievance short-lived; this is possible because the person is master of his own mind.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Ram is pleased by a single benefit even if done by chance, and forgets a hundred, meaning countless, wrongs.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'ātmavattā' as having an inner faculty that is under one's own control; that is what lets him let go of injuries.

vr.2.1.11.practical_reading: Keep a long memory for kindness and a short one for slights: notice and thank small help, and stop rehearsing old grievances.
misreadings: Not 'forget abuse and stay in harm's way'; it is about not nursing grudges, not about ignoring danger.
Not a demand that a wronged person instantly forgive.
cautions: Could pressure someone hurt by serious betrayal or abuse to 'just let it go'.
not_for: survivors of serious harm still processing it
someone told by an abuser to forget what happened

vr.2.100.16.context: Bharata has reached Ram at Chitrakoot. Before hearing the news of their father's death, Ram embraces him and asks a long series of 'I hope...' (kaccit) questions on statecraft: honouring elders, waking early to plan, consulting well, starting good work promptly, choosing wise ministers, fair justice and more. This one is about how to take counsel.
vr.2.100.16.core_teaching: Good decisions need a small circle: alone you miss the other side, with too many you never agree and plans leak.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Deliberating alone fails to weigh pros and cons fairly; with too many, unanimity is impossible and counsel leaks.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi), on the preceding verse (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explains that the last watch of the night is when a king should think through how to achieve the state's aims, the habit this question builds on.

vr.2.100.16.practical_reading: For big decisions, consult a few trusted people, not no one and not everyone, and keep plans private until they are ready.
misreadings: Not secrecy for its own sake or a licence to exclude stakeholders.
Not literally about government only.
cautions: Few; administrative in tone.
not_for: someone in grief or crisis needing comfort (it is practical, not consoling)
speaks_to: people who either decide alone or crowd-source everything

vr.2.100.17.context: Next in Ram's kaccit questions at Chitrakoot, after the one on taking counsel. It is followed by asking whether other kings learn of Bharata's undertakings only after they are done, and whether a single wise counsellor is preferred to a thousand fools.
vr.2.100.17.core_teaching: Once you have decided on a worthwhile, low-cost task, begin it promptly; delay lets the opportunity's value drain away.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the phrase as small means, great fruit, and quotes a maxim that time drinks up the fruit of what is not done quickly.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi), on the next verse (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Takes the kings who should learn of one's work only once it is done as subordinate regional rulers.

vr.2.100.17.practical_reading: Against procrastination: if a small action will pay off well, do it now.
misreadings: Not 'act without thinking'; the verse requires deciding first (viniścitya).
cautions: Few.
not_for: someone burnt out or depressed who cannot start things (may feel like pressure)
speaks_to: starting a small habit or task
leaders with too many pending decisions

vr.2.100.20.context: Among Ram's kaccit questions at Chitrakoot, after asking whether Bharata keeps his plans from being guessed. Here he asks if Bharata prefers one wise man to a thousand fools. Next he says even thousands of fools give a king no real help, while one capable minister can bring great prosperity.
vr.2.100.20.core_teaching: Quality of counsel beats quantity: one wise adviser is worth more than a crowd of foolish ones, especially in hard times.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explains the grammar: 'a thousand fools' is in the ablative with an implied 'setting aside', i.e. preferring one wise man over them.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi), on the next verse (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'ayutāni' as tens of thousands: even that many fools are no help.

vr.2.100.20.practical_reading: Seek one trusted, wise mentor or adviser over many loud opinions, particularly when things are going wrong.
misreadings: Not contempt for ordinary people; it is about whom a leader relies on for counsel.
cautions: 'Fools' language may feel harsh; paraphrase gently.
not_for: a reader feeling stupid or inadequate

vr.2.100.51.context: Late in Ram's kaccit questions, a cluster on justice: is an innocent man ever punished without examination by jurists, is a thief caught red-handed ever freed for a bribe, do ministers judge disputes between rich and poor without greed. This verse warns of the consequence. Next he asks whether Bharata honours the old, children and learned men with gifts, affection and gentle words.
vr.2.100.51.core_teaching: Injustice to the innocent, through careless or self-serving judgement, rebounds on the one in power and destroys what he holds dear.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: The tears of the falsely accused destroy the sons and cattle of a king who rules for pleasure without investigating right and wrong; he also warns against punishing without examination by jurists or freeing a thief for a bribe.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka (attributed on this page to Nāgojī Bhaṭṭa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)

vr.2.23.9.context: Ram has just said the exile is Destiny's doing and no one is to blame. Lakshman, enraged, rejects this: only the faint-hearted follow fate, and heroes overpower it by effort. He goes on to threaten to show the world today what human might can do; Ram calms him and keeps to his decision.
vr.2.23.9.core_teaching: Lakshman's case: one who can counter fate with effort does not collapse when fate goes against him. The epic voices this through an angry speaker and Ram does not adopt it here.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Even granting that the parents' decision is fate-driven, Lakshman says such fate should be disregarded; only a coward submits to it.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Agrees with Tilaka: self-respecting heroes overpower fate by human strength and never lose heart.

vr.2.23.9.practical_reading: Taken on its own, it encourages answering bad luck with renewed effort instead of fatalism.
misreadings: Not the epic's final verdict: Ram rejects using force here and keeps his father's word.
Not a licence for anger or rebellion against elders.
Not a claim that anyone who suffers simply didn't try hard enough.
cautions: Spoken in rage just before Lakshman threatens violence; a reading must separate the teaching on effort from the urge to fight.
Can imply blame on people whose setbacks are beyond their control (illness, disability, systemic issues).
not_for: chronic illness, disability or grief where effort cannot change the outcome
someone already blaming themselves for not trying hard enough
speaks_to: fatalism or giving up after a setback
students or job seekers after rejection

vr.2.24.20.context: Kausalya, desperate, wants to follow Ram to the forest. Ram tells her that a wife must not abandon her husband, that Bharata will look after her, and asks her to keep the old king from being destroyed by grief. The verses that follow (Southern-only) state at length that a wife's highest duty is serving her husband, and Ram ends by asking her to wait for his return with rites and worship.
vr.2.24.20.core_teaching: Instead of adding his mother's departure to his father's loss, Ram gives her a task of care: keep watch over the grieving old man.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis (commentators unnamed for this note), on 2.24.22-24 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Ram answers her fear about the co-wives by assuring her that righteous Bharata will attend on her, while she must guard the king from dying of grief once Ram has gone.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa), on 2.24.28-29 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Ram also prescribes rites and worship for her so that idleness does not deepen her grief while she waits.

vr.2.24.20.practical_reading: When a family is hit by a loss, giving the grieving a concrete way to care for each other can steady them. Look after the elder who is taking it hardest.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of the surrounding verses' claim that a wife's only duty is to serve her husband.
Not a denial of the mother's own grief.
cautions: Adjacent Southern-only verses (2.24.25-28) teach strict wifely service and Tilaka elaborates them; do not import that framing into a modern reading.
Dasharatha does die of grief soon after; avoid implying the caregiver could have prevented it.
not_for: someone who blames themselves for failing to save a grieving relative
readers sensitive to gender-role prescriptions
speaks_to: adult children moving away while a parent is unwell
caring for a grieving parent or grandparent
someone who wants to help in a family crisis

vr.2.25.2.context: Kausalya has accepted that she cannot hold Ram back. Controlling her tears, she performs protective rites and pours out a long blessing: go, come back soon, and may the dharma you keep protect you; then she invokes the gods of shrines, the sages, the seasons and more to guard him in the forest.
vr.2.25.2.core_teaching: The goodness a person keeps, gladly and steadily, becomes his own protection. A mother's blessing turns his life's discipline into a shield.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads the variant 'dhṛtyā' (with steadfastness) beside 'with love', and notes the active verb stresses that dharma itself directly guards Ram.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka), on the next verse (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Takes the 'shrines' in the following blessing as temples of the gods where Ram has bowed; Govindarāja reads them as crossroad shrines.

vr.2.25.2.practical_reading: A blessing to say over someone leaving home: may the good you live by keep you safe. It also reminds the traveller that integrity is a kind of protection.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that good people never suffer; Ram suffers greatly in the forest.
Not a transactional 'do good and nothing bad will happen'.
cautions: For someone whose good, careful child was harmed, the idea that dharma protects could hurt.
not_for: bereaved parents
someone who feels their goodness 'failed' to protect them
speaks_to: parents blessing a child leaving for study or work
anyone wanting to bless a loved one in a hard season

vr.2.29.2.context: Ram has just described at length the dangers of the forest (wild beasts, thorns, hunger, cold) to persuade Sita to stay in Ayodhya. In tears, she answers that these faults are virtues to her, and then goes through them one by one, arguing that with him she will fear nothing.
vr.2.29.2.core_teaching: Love changes how hardship is weighed: what is a danger alone becomes bearable, even good, when shared with the beloved.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka; the page attributes this gloss to Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Because she is led on by love for Ram, every forest hardship turns into a virtue for her.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads the word as qualifying the hardships: in her beloved's company they feel as pleasant as cuckoo-song, sandal-paste and mountain breezes; he also reads her face as only slightly tearful.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Takes the word describing her as 'deeply attached to her husband' rather than 'tear-streaked'.

vr.2.29.2.practical_reading: In relationships, facing difficulty together can be chosen and even welcomed: a move, a lean year, an illness, when the bond comes first.
misreadings: Not a claim that a partner must follow wherever the other goes; this is Sita's own argued decision.
Not romanticising danger or deprivation.
cautions: Readers know Sita's later abduction; avoid implying her choice 'caused' it.
not_for: someone staying in a harmful relationship out of love
a reader pressured to follow a partner against their own wishes
speaks_to: couples facing a hard move, job loss or long illness together
choosing to stand by someone in difficulty
partners being 'protected' from a decision they want to share

vr.2.30.9.context: Ram still refuses to take Sita. She grows sharper: in the previous verse she tells him he can be the obedient one to Bharata, for whose sake he has been passed over, and here insists he cannot leave without her; whether it is austerity, wilderness or heaven, it must be with him. She goes on to say walking behind him will be no more tiring than a pleasure-couch. Ram eventually agrees.
vr.2.30.9.core_teaching: Shared life is not conditional on comfort: whatever the setting, the point is to be together.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads the previous verse as Sita's retort: Ram may be the one submissive to Bharata, for whose sake his coronation was stopped; she will share austerity, forest or heaven with Ram alone.

vr.2.30.9.practical_reading: A vow-like line for partners: I don't want only the good parts with you; whatever comes, let it be together.
misreadings: Not 'a wife must follow her husband'; Sita overrules Ram here.
Not glorifying hardship for its own sake.
cautions: Context includes Sita's sharp words to Ram, which a reading should not omit if it describes her as merely devoted.
not_for: someone in a controlling relationship
recently widowed readers (the 'with you' may wound)
speaks_to: standing by a partner in crisis
claiming your place in a shared decision

vr.2.34.28.context: Rama has come to take leave. Dasharatha, bound by his promise to Kaikeyi, blesses his path and admits that Rama's truthful resolve cannot be turned back, but begs him to stay just this one night so that he and Kausalya can see him and give him every comfort, and to leave at dawn. He adds that Rama is doing a very hard thing for his father's sake, that it gives him no joy, and that he was deceived by a woman like fire hidden under ash.
vr.2.34.28.core_teaching: A heartbroken parent, unable to stop a child's departure, asks only for one more night together.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rama Varma (Tilaka) and Govindaraja (Bhushana) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Tilaka reconstructs the day: Rama had spent three watches taking leave and giving away his wealth, so 'now' points to the night about to fall; both gloss the last word as 'you will depart at dawn'.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Bhushana on the following verses (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explain that Rama goes 'for my sake' in the sense of protecting his father's truth and welfare hereafter, while the exile itself is hateful to Dasharatha; Kaikeyi is compared to live coals under ash.

vr.2.34.28.practical_reading: Gives words to a parent's longing at a child's leaving, and to the child's mix of love and resolve.
misreadings: Not a reproach of the child who must leave; Dasharatha himself says Rama's resolve cannot be turned.
cautions: The surrounding lines blame Kaikeyi harshly; and Dasharatha dies of grief soon after. Avoid both for a reader far from ageing parents.
not_for: someone whose parent died while they were away (could intensify guilt)
speaks_to: leaving home for work or study
missing family meals and time together

vr.2.40.8.context: Ram, Sita and Lakshman are about to mount Sumantra's chariot for the forest. Sumitra has just told Lakshman that the family's code is generosity, sacrifice and giving one's life in battle, so he must guard Ram even at the cost of his body. Then, saying 'go, go', she gives this blessing; next Sumantra urges Ram to start the fourteen years that very day.
vr.2.40.8.core_teaching: A mother releases her son by relocating home for him: the people he serves will be his parents, the place he goes will be his home.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of all three commentators (Tilaka, Bhūṣaṇa, Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Plain sense: so that homesickness does not shake him, Lakshman should treat Ram as his father, Sita as his mother Sumitra, and the forest as Ayodhya.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Adds further readings, including a Vaishnava one: Dasharatha as Vishnu borne by Garuda, Janaka's daughter as Lakshmi, Ayodhya as unconquerable Vaikuntha. Śiromaṇi argues against this at length.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja and Śivasahāya, on 2.40.7 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Sumitra cites the family code of giving one's life in battle to tell Lakshman he must protect Ram even at the cost of his own body.

vr.2.40.8.practical_reading: For parents letting a child go: tell them where to find family and home in the new place. For the one leaving: home can be made wherever you are with people you serve and love.
misreadings: Not a call to cut ties with one's own parents.
The Vaishnava reading is one commentator's devotional layer, not the plain sense.
cautions: The previous verse speaks of laying down one's life to protect Ram; leave it out of comforting readings or frame carefully.
not_for: someone estranged from family who may hear 'replace your parents'
a grieving parent whose child left and did not return
speaks_to: a child leaving for college, work or marriage
joining a new 'family' at work or in service

vr.2.44.17.context: Sumitra continues consoling Kausalya: with Lakshman marching ahead of Ram as his guard, nothing is beyond Ram's reach. She declares with certainty that Kausalya will see him back, and next pictures him bowing at her feet like the rising moon.
vr.2.44.17.core_teaching: A companion's firm reassurance: the separation will end; let go of grief and confusion.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Notes the verb form is a definite future, stressing the certainty of Ram's return; on the previous verse, Lakshman would never walk ahead as guard unless Ram were the Supreme Person.

vr.2.44.17.practical_reading: How to sit with someone who is weeping: stay, name what is solid (he is protected, he will return), and say it with conviction.
misreadings: Not a rule that grief must be cast off quickly.
Not usable as a promise about someone who has died.
cautions: 'Let go of this grief' is risky for any bereaved reader; this is about a living person's temporary absence.
not_for: bereavement
uncertain outcomes (missing person, serious illness)
speaks_to: comforting a friend whose family member has gone away
separation from a child or spouse for a set time

vr.2.44.9.context: Ram has left and Kausalya is lamenting. Sumitra comforts her: Ram is not to be pitied; the sun will not scorch him, the forest breeze will serve him in every season, and here the moon will embrace him at night like a father. She goes on to recall his divine weapons and says Kausalya will see him return.
vr.2.44.9.core_teaching: Consolation through trust: the person you cannot reach is still held, here by the natural world itself.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Cites the Upanishadic idea that wind and sun act out of awe of the Lord: so the sun will not scorch Ram, and the moon embraces him like a father.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Notes the forest breeze will serve him tempered to the season, cool or warm as needed, part of nature's service to Ram.

vr.2.44.9.practical_reading: For a parent worrying about a child far away: imagine the child held and cared for where they are, and let that ease the night.
misreadings: Not literal protection by the moon; it is poetic consolation.
Not a dismissal of the mother's worry.
cautions: Reassurance can feel hollow to a parent whose child is in real danger.
not_for: bereaved parents
someone whose loved one is missing or in danger
speaks_to: worry for a loved one travelling or posted abroad

vr.2.46.22.context: Crowds of townspeople have followed Ram to the Tamasa river and are sleeping under trees, refusing to go home. Ram tells Lakshman he does not want them to suffer for his sake. Before dawn they slip away, confusing the tracks, so the citizens will return to Ayodhya.
vr.2.46.22.core_teaching: A leader's duty runs one way: lift people out of trouble, even trouble they made themselves, and never pull them into one's own.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: With the other two, contrasts 'ātmakṛtāt' (sorrow from the citizens' own deeds) with 'ātmanā' (sorrow caused by the prince): a true prince rescues subjects from their own woes and inflicts none.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Same reading as Tilaka; the page states all three commentators agree.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Same reading as Tilaka and Govindarāja.

vr.2.46.22.practical_reading: For managers, parents and anyone with responsibility: help people out of their messes, and don't make them carry your troubles out of loyalty to you.
misreadings: Not a reason to hide your struggles from people who love you.
Not paternalism that denies people agency.
cautions: Our note says 'atmakrita is best taken as suffering caused by the prince himself'; the commentators read it the other way (the citizens' own doing). Update the note.
not_for: someone isolating themselves and refusing help (could reinforce it)
speaks_to: parents not wanting children to bear their burdens
people whose loyal friends are sacrificing for them

vr.2.58.14.context: Sumantra has returned from leaving Ram at the Ganga and reports Ram's messages to the king and queens. Ram asks his mother to keep up the fire rites, serve the king, drop her pride toward the other queens and honour Kaikeyi, and to treat Bharata as king.
vr.2.58.14.core_teaching: Ram, the one wronged, asks his mother to keep the household whole by setting aside both status-pride and resentment, even toward the co-wife who caused the exile.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Abhimāna is ego from being chief queen; māna is jealous pique toward co-wives. Reads the last phrase as 'honour Kaikeyi, whom the king follows', and notes Kataka's reading 'salute Kaikeyi'.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Same distinction of the two prides; construes the line as 'treat the king and noble Kaikeyi alike'.

vr.2.58.14.practical_reading: In a family rift, someone has to drop status and grievance so the household can function; sometimes it is asked of the injured party.
misreadings: Not a rule that the wronged must defer to those who wronged them in every case.
Not a denial that Kaikeyi did wrong.
cautions: Asks a wronged woman to defer to the one who wronged her; avoid using with readers in abusive or toxic family situations.
Surrounding lines ask her to serve the king 'like a god'; do not import that.
not_for: readers suffering ongoing mistreatment from a family member
someone being pressured to reconcile with an abuser
speaks_to: sibling or step-family rifts after a conflict
dropping ego to keep peace at home

vr.2.58.18.context: The charioteer Sumantra returns to Ayodhya and tells the grieving Dasharatha what Ram said at parting: Kausalya should drop pride and honour Kaikeyi and treat Bharata as king; Bharata, as prince regent, should serve their father on the throne and not displace the old king; and, weeping, Ram asked that Bharata look on Kausalya as his own mother. Dasharatha dies of grief soon after, so Bharata never gets to act on this.
vr.2.58.18.core_teaching: Ram asks his brother to rule only as the old father's agent, honouring him rather than pushing him aside.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rama Varma (Tilaka) and Govindaraja (Bhushana) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Gloss the key verb as 'do not depose him from the throne' (Tilaka) or 'do not obstruct him' (Bhushana); Bharata should serve as prince regent while their aged father reigns.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Bhushana on the preceding verses (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explain Ram's advice to Kausalya to drop pride of rank and jealousy toward co-wives, and that a king is senior by office, not years, so even his mother should honour Bharata as king.

vr.2.58.18.practical_reading: As parents age, help them without taking over; let them keep their dignity and say in their own life.
misreadings: Not 'never make decisions for an ageing parent' where safety requires it.
cautions: Dramatic irony: the father dies of grief soon after; avoid pairing with a reader whose parent is dying unless intended.
not_for: someone whose parent is controlling or abusive
speaks_to: caring for ageing parents from a distance

vr.2.62.13.context: Kausalya, in grief, had bitterly reproached Dasharatha for exiling Ram. Seeing the king in anguish with folded hands, she is shaken, places his hands on her head and begs forgiveness. She says she knows he is truthful and that grief made her speak; the next verse is the famous line that grief destroys fortitude, learning, everything; there is no enemy like grief.
vr.2.62.13.core_teaching: Grief can make even a wise person speak against what she knows; the remedy is to name it and repair the relationship.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi), on 2.62.14-16 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Kausalya says she spoke rashly and improperly only because grief destroys both steadiness and the settled understanding of dharma that comes from learning.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) and Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa), on the preceding verse (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Differ on construing the previous line about a wife whom her husband has to placate; both frame her apology as restoring proper relation with the king.

vr.2.62.13.practical_reading: After saying hurtful things in grief, apologise plainly: acknowledge the other's goodness and own that pain spoke. It also invites forgiveness for others who lash out while grieving.
misreadings: Not 'grieving people must not express anger'.
Not a claim that Kausalya's complaint was baseless.
cautions: The preceding verse frames wifely duty in strong terms; keep it out of a modern reading.
not_for: someone whose grief-anger is justified and who is being pushed to apologise
speaks_to: apologising after an argument during a family crisis
understanding a grieving relative's harsh words

vr.2.62.14.context: Kausalya has just apologised to Dasharatha for her bitter words, saying grief for her son made her speak. She explains with this verse what grief does, and adds that a blow from an enemy can be borne but even a slight grief cannot. She notes Ram has been gone five nights that feel like five years; the king, consoled, falls asleep.
vr.2.62.14.core_teaching: Grief can undo steadiness and even what one knows to be right; it is named here to explain, and excuse, words spoken in pain.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi), on 2.62.14-16 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Kausalya pleads she spoke rashly and improperly only because grief wipes out both fortitude and the firm grasp of dharma gained from scripture.

vr.2.62.14.practical_reading: Explains why grieving people say or do things unlike themselves, and why grace is owed to them, and to yourself. Also a reason to delay big decisions in fresh grief.
misreadings: Not a command to suppress grief; it describes grief's effects to excuse lapses.
Not a reason to treat grieving people as irrational in everything.
cautions: Calling grief 'an enemy' may feel harsh to someone who experiences grief as love; frame as describing its effects on judgement.
Spoken in a household where the king is about to die of grief.
not_for: someone told their grief is a weakness
a reader who needs permission to grieve rather than a warning about it
speaks_to: why decisions feel impossible after a loss

vr.2.63.11.context: Dasharatha has just recalled how, as a young prince famed as an archer who could hit by sound alone, he committed a sin. Here he says this sorrow is self-made, like poison a child swallows unknowingly. Next he compares himself to the man deluded by palāśa flowers, and then tells the full story of shooting the hermit boy at the river.
vr.2.63.11.core_teaching: Owning the past: present suffering is traced honestly to one's own earlier act, done in ignorance rather than malice.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa), on 2.63.11 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the 'renown' of the young archer as fame for shooting by sound; also reads a second sense, 'having heard the sound (of the boy's pitcher)'.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi), on 2.63.11 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Agrees with Govindarāja on both senses of the phrase.

vr.2.63.11.practical_reading: Taking responsibility for consequences of a past mistake, even an unintended one, without excuses; seeing that ignorance can still cause great harm.
misreadings: Not a teaching that every sorrow is self-caused; Dasharatha says this about his own case.
Not a reason to blame people for their misfortunes.
cautions: Concerns the accidental killing of a young man; heavy.
Can deepen guilt for someone who has caused harm by accident.
not_for: someone who caused an accidental death or injury and is in acute guilt
readers being blamed for their illness or loss

vr.2.63.7.context: Late at night, five or six days after Ram's departure, Dasharatha wakes and remembers a wrong from his youth. He begins by saying each person reaps the fruit of his own deeds, then this verse on rash action, then the parable of the man who cuts a mango grove to water flashy palāśa trees. He goes on to confess how, as a young prince proud of shooting by sound, he killed a hermit boy.
vr.2.63.7.core_teaching: Before acting, weigh how much is at stake, what it will lead to and what could go wrong; acting without this is childish, however grown one is.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Distinguishes the 'aims' (worldly goals) from the 'actions' (rites aimed at the next world): both need weighing before one begins.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Applies it to Dasharatha himself: indulging in the trivial sport of hunting led to the catastrophic loss of his son; the mango and palāśa parable follows.

vr.2.63.7.practical_reading: Pause at the start: how big is this, where does it lead, what could go wrong? Useful for impulsive decisions, from money to words to risky fun.
misreadings: Not a claim that every misfortune is punishment for a careless act.
Not a counsel of paralysis; it is about weighing, not avoiding action.
cautions: Spoken by a dying man about killing a boy by mistake; the frame is heavy.
not_for: someone grieving a death caused by an accident they feel responsible for (could intensify self-blame)
a reader already paralysed by overthinking
speaks_to: young people tempted by thrill or showing off

vr.2.64.19.context: Dasharatha has confessed to the blind sage that he killed his son by mistake. Weeping, the sage says that if Dasharatha had not confessed, his head would have burst; a knowing killing of a forest ascetic by a warrior would topple even Indra. He then asks to be taken to his son's body and, after lamenting, curses Dasharatha to die grieving for a son.
vr.2.64.19.core_teaching: Voluntary confession changes the consequences of a wrong: it does not erase them, but it saves the confessor from the worst.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of all three commentators (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: All gloss the verb as 'would split asunder'.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi), on the next verse (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Notes the a-fortiori argument: if a knowing attack on a forest hermit would bring down even Indra, how much more a mortal king; so Dasharatha's unknowing act plus confession spared him instant ruin.

vr.2.64.19.practical_reading: Owning up honestly, without being caught, changes what follows. Teachers use it for confession, apology and accountability.
misreadings: Not a claim that confession erases consequences; Dasharatha is still cursed and dies of grief.
Not literal: heads do not burst.
cautions: Embedded in the story of a killed boy and a curse of grief; heavy context.
Our 'line' ('you were spared') is fair but should not imply he escaped consequences.
not_for: someone grieving a child
a person coerced into confessing
speaks_to: deciding whether to confess a mistake

vr.2.64.9.context: Dasharatha, having shot the hermit boy and heard his dying words, carries the water pot to the boy's blind, aged parents. Hearing footsteps, the father thinks his son has returned late, begs him not to be angry if they have hurt him, and says this. Dasharatha then speaks in a faltering, terrified voice and confesses.
vr.2.64.9.core_teaching: The depth of dependence and love between aged parents and a child; the pathos is that the son is already dead.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka), on 2.64.11 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explains Dasharatha's reply as spoken in a voice choked with emotion, without clear consonants.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa), on 2.64.11 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads the same phrase as 'with indistinct syllables' and a variant meaning 'utterly terrified'.

vr.2.64.9.practical_reading: Used by teachers to show the weight of care for aged parents and the gravity of harm done to a family's only support.
misreadings: Not a comforting verse; it is a moment of dramatic irony and grief.
cautions: Very painful: a parent speaking to a child who is already dead. Avoid for bereaved parents unless the plan is explicitly about lament.
The only commentary found concerns the next verse, not this one.
not_for: bereaved parents
anyone who has lost a child
readers who caused an accident
speaks_to: adult children who are their parents' main support

vr.2.7.27.context: Manthara, Kaikeyi's maid, sees Ayodhya decorated, learns Ram is to be crowned, and rushes to warn Kaikeyi that this spells ruin. Kaikeyi instead rejoices, gives Manthara a jewel and says she makes no distinction between Ram and Bharata. Only in the next sarga does Manthara work on her fears and envy.
vr.2.7.27.core_teaching: Kaikeyi's first, natural response is generous joy; the later envy is not native to her but talked into her.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Her words mean she feels no difference in the affection that comes from motherhood between Ram and Bharata; Tilaka also says her repeated 'dear news' shows overflowing joy.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Agrees that the repetition in the previous verse expresses rapture, not a flaw in style.

vr.2.7.27.practical_reading: Our first reactions are often more generous than the stories others later feed us; notice who is stoking comparison and return to your own first, kinder response.
misreadings: Not evidence that Kaikeyi is simply a villain; the text shows her good-hearted at first.
Not a claim that jealousy never arises on its own.
cautions: The reader knows what follows (Kaikeyi's demand and the exile); use as a 'before' picture, not an ending.
not_for: someone grieving a relationship destroyed by a third party's manipulation (may feel too neat)
speaks_to: being glad for someone else's success
noticing influence from a friend or relative who stirs envy

vr.2.72.25.context: Bharata, summoned from his uncle's home, arrives in a strangely silent Ayodhya and finds his father absent from his mother's rooms. Kaikeyi tells him Dasharatha has died. He weeps, asks of what illness, and envies those who were with him; in his confusion he then imagines his father simply hasn't heard he has come. He does not yet know Ram is exiled.
vr.2.72.25.core_teaching: The grief of the one who was absent: not just the loss, but having missed the last days and the chance to care.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'saṃskṛtaḥ' as honoured with funeral rites by Ram.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Takes it as 'served during his final illness'; in the next verse Bharata, in denial, imagines his father just doesn't know he has arrived.

vr.2.72.25.practical_reading: Names the particular pain of not being there when a parent died: living abroad, stuck at work, arriving too late.
misreadings: Not blame on the absent child.
cautions: Speaks directly to a parent's death; appropriate for grief plans but gentle handling needed.
Could intensify guilt for readers who missed a parent's death.
not_for: readers in acute guilt without a consoling frame around it
speaks_to: missing a parent's death or funeral
adult children living far from parents
grief mixed with guilt for absence

vr.2.72.27.context: Still not grasping the death, Bharata imagines his father would have bent down to smell his head had he known Bharata was there. Then he asks where that comforting hand is. Next he asks Kaikeyi to tell Ram, now his father and brother, that he has come, and only then learns of the exile.
vr.2.72.27.core_teaching: Grief lives in small bodily memories: the hand that used to brush the dust off.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the verb as 'wipes clean'.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Same gloss as Tilaka.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explains the unusual verb form grammatically; with the others reads the next line as 'tell Ram I have come'.

vr.2.72.27.practical_reading: Gives permission to miss the small things: a parent's touch, a gesture, a voice. Used in grief writing to honour specific memories.
misreadings: Not a call to 'move on'; it is lament.
cautions: Directly about losing a father; tender but intense for fresh grief.
not_for: someone with a painful or abusive relationship with a parent (idealised memory may jar)
speaks_to: sons and daughters after a father's death

vr.2.75.15.context: Kausalya, grief-stricken, has bitterly told Bharata he now has the kingdom he wanted and should send her to Ram too. Bharata, with folded hands, protests that he knew nothing, and then swears a long series of oaths calling ruin on whoever consented to Ram's exile. Convinced, Kausalya embraces him.
vr.2.75.15.core_teaching: When falsely blamed, appeal to what the other already knows of your love, and stand by your innocence.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Because another's inner innocence cannot be seen directly, Bharata turns to solemn oaths to make it credible; losing a scripture-guided mind is the gravest curse he calls down.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Agrees the oaths, though phrased generally, are aimed at Bharata himself.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Adds that from loss of wisdom all ruin follows, which is why that curse comes first.

vr.2.75.15.practical_reading: For being wrongly blamed in a family crisis: answer the hurt person gently, remind them of the relationship, and be patient while they see the truth.
misreadings: Not a teaching to swear oaths; the oaths are Bharata's dramatic response.
cautions: Kausalya's accusation comes from grief; avoid making her the villain.
not_for: someone who actually did contribute to harm and wants absolution
speaks_to: being blamed for a relative's wrongdoing

vr.2.77.21.context: On the thirteenth day after the cremation, Bharata and Shatrughna collapse with grief at the pyre site while collecting the bones. Vasishtha tells Bharata the rites are unfinished and he must not delay, and then gives this teaching. Sumantra likewise raises Shatrughna and speaks of the birth and passing of all beings.
vr.2.77.21.core_teaching: Some conditions come to every creature without exception; since they cannot be avoided, the bereaved must rise and carry on with what remains to be done.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Names the three pairs: hunger and thirst, grief and delusion, old age and death.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Gives the same three pairs as Govindarāja.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Cites other readings: birth and death, pleasure and pain, gain and loss; and Kataka's citation of the six stages of being (arising, growing, decaying, perishing and so on).

vr.2.77.21.practical_reading: In grief, remembering that loss and death come to everyone can ease the sense of being singled out, and help one return to necessary tasks.
misreadings: Not 'stop grieving'; Vasishtha is getting Bharata through the remaining rites.
Universality of death is not meant to minimise a particular loss.
cautions: 'You should not be like this' can feel dismissive in early grief; use after the first days or with framing.
Directly about a father's funeral rites.
not_for: the first hours or days of bereavement
someone who needs their grief validated before being told to rise
speaks_to: needing to function for practical tasks while grieving

data_flags.translation_note: Our translation inserts the list of the three pairs (hunger and thirst, grief and confusion, old age and death) as if in the verse. The verse says only 'three pairs'; the list is Govindarāja's and Śiromaṇi's gloss. Our note already says so; the translation should...

vr.2.8.8.context: Kaikeyi has rejoiced at the news and even rewarded Manthara. Manthara refuses the gift and begins her campaign: first she frightens Kaikeyi for Bharata, then here she paints Kausalya as the lucky one, and next she pictures Kaikeyi waiting on Kausalya with folded hands like a servant.
vr.2.8.8.core_teaching: The voice of envy works by counting another's blessings for you and casting you as the loser in comparison.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: After stoking fear for Bharata, Manthara now deliberately kindles co-wife jealousy, picturing Kaikeyi standing before Kausalya like a servant.

vr.2.8.8.practical_reading: Watch for the 'lucky them' voice, from others or inside your head, that turns someone else's good news into your loss.
misreadings: Not a teaching to admire; it is Manthara's manipulation, quoted as a warning.
Not proof that women or servants are schemers.
cautions: The verse is the speech of a manipulator; a reading must frame it as a warning, not counsel.
not_for: a day meant to comfort; it is diagnostic, not consoling
someone who is the target of a manipulator and blames themselves
speaks_to: a friend or relative who stirs jealousy
envy at a sibling's or colleague's milestone

vr.2.82.11.context: After the funeral rites, Vasishtha convenes the court and tells Bharata that his father gave him the kingdom and Ram has kept his word by leaving, so Bharata should rule. Bharata, weeping, refuses: Ram, the eldest and most virtuous, deserves it. He then resolves to go to the forest and bring Ram back.
vr.2.82.11.core_teaching: Some gains are not one's to take, however lawfully offered; Bharata counts himself and the kingdom alike as Ram's.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: A Śrīvaiṣṇava reading: both the kingdom and Bharata belong to Ram as his dependents; one possession cannot rule another unless the owner commissions it, so Vasishtha should state their true relation.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads the last phrase as Bharata asking Vasishtha to state the righteous means by which Ram himself may take up the kingdom.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka (attributed on this page to Nāgojī Bhaṭṭa), on 2.82.9 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Calls Bharata dharma-knowing because he knows the rule that the eldest is crowned, and says he desires the duty of serving his elder brother.

vr.2.82.11.practical_reading: Turning down a benefit that comes from someone else's wrong, even when it is offered legitimately: an inheritance, a promotion, a credit that belongs to another.
misreadings: Not a rule that younger siblings must always defer.
Not a rejection of responsibility; Bharata later rules as Ram's trustee.
cautions: Few; it is a strong moral moment. Avoid implying anyone who accepts an inheritance is a usurper.
not_for: someone who needs to claim what is rightfully theirs and is being guilted out of it
speaks_to: being offered something that rightfully belongs to someone else

data_flags.attribution_note: Speaker Bharata is right, but the listener is Vasishtha, the family priest, who has just urged him (before the assembled ministers and people) to accept the throne. The 'you' in 'you ought to declare what is right' is singular, addressed to Vasishtha. Suggest listener 'Vasishtha,...

vr.2.84.9.context: Bharata's huge army reaches the Ganga at Shringaverapura on its way to find Ram. Guha, king of the Nishadas and Ram's friend, fears Bharata means Ram harm, posts five hundred boats each with a hundred armed young boatmen, and says the army may cross only if Bharata proves well-meaning. He then goes to meet Bharata with gifts to learn his intent.
vr.2.84.9.core_teaching: Prudent loyalty: be ready to defend, but make the final judgement on what the other person actually intends, and go find out.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka (attributed on this page to Nāgojī Bhaṭṭa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Guha warns his men against hasty battle: if Bharata is well-disposed to Ram (or, in the other reading, free of malice), the army crosses safely; otherwise the boatmen will attack from the boats.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Stationing the boats on the southern bank blocks any crossing without Guha's consent, while keeping them ready to ferry the army at once if Bharata proves loyal.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Notes the scale of preparation (a hundred boatmen on each of five hundred boats) and that Guha's gifts include silks, showing he approaches with courtesy.

vr.2.84.9.practical_reading: When someone's arrival looks threatening, prepare sensibly but don't decide their intent for them; meet them, ask, and then act.
misreadings: Not a call to treat strangers as enemies.
Not naive trust either: Guha keeps his guard up.
cautions: Guha offers meat and fish to Bharata in the text; a vegetarian-household reading might want to skip that detail.
not_for: someone in real danger from a person with a record of harm (could read as 'give them the benefit of the doubt')
speaks_to: suspicion of a relative or colleague's motives

vr.2.97.12.context: Ram has told Lakshman that Bharata has come at the right time to see them and would never wrong them even in thought. Here he asks when Bharata ever did Lakshman harm, or what new fear makes him suspect him. Next he forbids harsh words to Bharata: any unkindness to Bharata would be unkindness to Ram himself. Bharata indeed arrives in grief, seeking Ram's return.
vr.2.97.12.core_teaching: Judge a person by their record, not by appearances or fear; suspicion without past cause wrongs the innocent.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Glosses Bharata's visit as timely and Ram's question as asking when Bharata ever did any past wrong; on the next verse, an offence against the Lord's devotee is felt by the Lord as against himself.

vr.2.97.12.practical_reading: Before assuming the worst about someone, ask: what has this person actually done before? Check fear against history.
misreadings: Not 'never be cautious'; it concerns someone with a good record.
Not a claim that past behaviour guarantees future behaviour in every case.
cautions: For readers who have been harmed by someone previously trusted, the logic 'he never wronged you before' may feel naive.
not_for: someone in a relationship with a person who has a history of harm

vr.2.97.4.context: At Chitrakoot, Lakshman sees Bharata's army approaching, assumes Bharata has come to kill them, and wants to fight. Ram replies that killing Bharata to win a kingdom would bring infamy after he promised to keep his father's word, and that any wealth gained by ruining kin or friends is poisoned food. He adds that he wants dharma, wealth, pleasure and even the earth only for his brothers' sake.
vr.2.97.4.core_teaching: Gain bought by destroying family or friends is poison: it should be refused outright.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka), on 2.97.3 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explains the infamy Ram fears: people would say he broke his pledge to his father, killed Bharata and seized the kingdom the father had given Bharata.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Agrees on the infamy and likens wealth won by killing kin to cakes mixed with poison.

vr.2.97.4.practical_reading: Refuse any inheritance, promotion or deal that requires breaking a family member or friend; the 'win' will poison you.
misreadings: Not a rule against ever pursuing a fair claim within a family.
Not a judgement on anyone who received an inheritance during a family dispute.
cautions: Few; mild violence implied in context (Lakshman wants to fight).
not_for: someone already being exploited by family and needing to assert their rights
speaks_to: business partners or siblings in conflict
workplace politics where you could rise by undermining a colleague

vr.2.97.7.context: Continuing his answer to Lakshman at Chitrakoot, Ram has just sworn by his weapon that he wants kingship only for his brothers' welfare. Here he says the earth is not hard for him to win, but he would not want even Indra's rank through wrong. Next he says any happiness without his brothers may burn to ash.
vr.2.97.7.core_teaching: Restraint is meaningful because it is chosen from strength: Ram could take the kingdom and refuses because it would be wrong.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Ram disclaims the kingdom not from inability, since his valour could easily win the earth, but because he spurns even Indra's throne if tainted by wrong.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Same reading; on the next verse, Ram invokes fire to burn any joy not shared with his brothers.

vr.2.97.7.practical_reading: When you have the power or opportunity to take something by cutting corners, the question is not 'can I' but 'is it right'.
misreadings: Not boasting; capability is mentioned to show the refusal is free.
Not a rejection of ambition as such.
cautions: Few.
not_for: someone powerless in their situation (the 'I could if I wished' framing may not fit)

vr.3.10.17.context: Rama answers Sita's plea for non-violence. He explains that the sages begged his protection and that he would give up life, Sita and Lakshmana before breaking a promise to them, but he first thanks her: she spoke from love, and her words honour her lineage. He then goes on, bow in hand.
vr.3.10.17.core_teaching: Honest counsel, even when it disagrees, is a sign of love, and the right response is gratitude. Rama receives the advice warmly and still keeps the promise he has made.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Distinguishes sneha (fondness) from sauhārda (good-heartedness that seeks the other's welfare): fondness alone would not offer correction, so Sita's counsel shows both.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Links Sita's praise of dharma to her Janaka heritage and her mercy to her own nature; as his partner in dharma she must also share his vowed course.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri has Rama say she spoke in fitting words prompted by affection, then explain that the ascetics' plight bound him by promise.

vr.3.10.17.practical_reading: Teachers use it for receiving criticism from people close to you: thank them, credit the love behind it, then decide on the merits.
misreadings: Not 'anyone who criticises me loves me' (our misuse note is right).
Not Rama yielding: he thanks Sita and keeps his vow; counsel is honoured, not obeyed by default.
not_for: someone being controlled or belittled under the label of 'advice'
