speaks_to: receiving hard feedback from a partner, parent or friend
someone hurt that a loved one questioned them

vr.3.41.20.context: Ravana has threatened Maricha with death unless he helps abduct Sita. Maricha, who has met Rama's arrows before, makes a last appeal, prophesies the ruin of Ravana and Lanka, and says he would rather die at Rama's hands. This verse, in a different metre, closes his speech; he then goes as the golden deer.
vr.3.41.20.core_teaching: People bent on their own ruin cannot hear good advice from those who wish them well; refusing counsel is itself a sign of approaching downfall.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Notes that Maricha ends with a general maxim: those whose life is spent and who stand near death cannot tolerate wholesome advice.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: Maricha says Ravana ignores his well-meant words just as those whose last hour has come ignore friends' counsel.

vr.3.41.20.practical_reading: Used to warn against the stubbornness that rejects every warning; also a mirror to ask whose advice we have stopped listening to.
misreadings: Not a licence to predict doom for people who reject our advice.
Maricha himself then complies; the verse is about Ravana, not a model of how to respond.
cautions: Language of being 'as good as dead' is harsh; avoid for anyone facing illness or mortality.
not_for: grief, terminal illness
someone who already blames themselves for not listening
speaks_to: someone being warned by friends and refusing to listen
reflecting on a past mistake made despite warnings

vr.3.43.6.context: The jewelled deer appears near the hermitage. Lakshmana warns that it is Maricha's illusion, like a cloud-city in the sky, since no such deer exists. Sita interrupts, captivated, and asks Rama to catch it; Rama goes, and the abduction follows.
vr.3.43.6.core_teaching: Lakshmana reasons from experience: what is too wondrous to exist in nature is a trap. The warning is sound but unheeded, and the whole loss follows from that moment.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) and Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Both explain that Maricha's power of illusion has itself taken the shape of a deer.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Defines the gandharva-city as a fleeting sky mirage of wondrous, shifting forms; since such a deer cannot exist, it must be a trick.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: Lakshmana says the radiant fawn is a magician's device that does not exist on earth; Sita, smiling, interrupts him, wanting it as a pet.

vr.3.43.6.practical_reading: Applied to scams, offers and attractions that look too perfect: pause and test before you chase.
misreadings: Not blame of Sita: the epic presents the moment as fated and as Ravana's crime.
Not cynicism about all beauty or good fortune.
cautions: Retelling can tip into blaming the person who was deceived; keep the focus on the deceiver and on the value of a second voice.
not_for: victims of fraud or abuse who may feel blamed
grief over a loss that followed a choice
speaks_to: someone tempted by a deal, offer or person that seems too good
anyone who wishes they had listened to a warning

data_flags.corrected_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 3.43.7-8 (Southern, itihasa.io) = Baroda CE 3.41.6-7. Our text is two ślokas; id 3.43.6 is off by one.

vr.3.50.15.context: Ravana is flying off with Sita when the aged vulture Jatayu, friend of Dasaratha, confronts him. Jatayu argues that Rama killed Khara justly and that carrying off Sita is like tying a venomous snake in one's cloth. This maxim rounds off his warning before he challenges Ravana to fight.
vr.3.50.15.core_teaching: Take on only what you can carry and digest without harm. Spoken to Ravana, it means: Sita is a burden that will destroy you.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of all three commentators (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Gloss the burden as a heavy load and 'anāmaya' as not causing disease; Govindarāja sees ironic praise (vyājastuti) in the address, as earlier in the speech.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri renders it as general wisdom: carry only the weight that will not crush you and eat only what will not make you sick; then asks who would undertake a dishonourable act that will cost him his life.

vr.3.50.15.practical_reading: Often quoted as a rule of proportion: do not grab more than you can handle; ambition and appetite need limits.
misreadings: Our note is right: in context this is a rebuke to a wrongdoer, not gentle advice about workload.
Not a reason to avoid all challenge or growth.
not_for: someone whose load was imposed on them (caregivers, the poor) — it can sound like blame
speaks_to: greed, wanting what is not yours

vr.3.50.18.context: Jatayu, who says he is sixty thousand years old, sets his age against Ravana's youth, chariot, armour and arrows, and still refuses to let him take Sita. He fights, tears apart Ravana's chariot, and is cut down; Rama later finds him dying and performs his funeral rites.
vr.3.50.18.core_teaching: Courage does not wait for equal strength: an old, unarmed creature stands up to an armed abductor because it is right.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Notes Jatayu admits being worn by age and by duties, and unarmed, yet still challenges Ravana.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'my Vaidehi' as 'my daughter-in-law', since Jatayu was Dasaratha's friend; the protection is family duty.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: Jatayu says he is very old, Ravana young and armed on a chariot, yet he will not escape unhurt if he carries Vaidehi off.

vr.3.50.18.practical_reading: Used to honour elders and anyone who stands up for someone weaker despite poor odds; doing right does not depend on winning.
misreadings: Not a recipe for reckless confrontation; the epic honours the stand but Jatayu dies.
Not a claim that age is no handicap.
cautions: Jatayu is killed; in a reading for a frightened or elderly person, avoid implying they should put themselves in danger.
not_for: someone in physical danger who needs to stay safe
victims who could not fight back (it can sound like a reproach)
speaks_to: older people who feel they no longer count
bystanders deciding whether to speak up
standing for a principle against stronger opponents

vr.3.65.4.context: Having found the hermitage empty, Rama blazes with world-ending fury and threatens to destroy the three worlds. Lakshmana, palms joined, reminds him of his gentle nature and argues that only one chariot and one track are visible, so one culprit must be found and dealt with.
vr.3.65.4.core_teaching: Punish the one who did wrong, not everyone; anger should be aimed by evidence, not spread over the whole world.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Lakshmana infers a single offender because there is only one wrecked chariot and one track.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Adds Lakshmana's concern not to harm righteous rakshasas such as Vibhishana in a general slaughter.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: why destroy the worlds for one man's sin; it is not yet known whose shattered chariot this is or who fought here.

vr.3.65.4.practical_reading: Applied to collective blame: when hurt by one person, do not punish a group, family or whole community.
misreadings: Our note is right: Lakshmana is not asking for forgiveness, but for targeted, just response.
Not a reason to suppress anger at real wrong.
not_for: someone who has not yet been allowed to feel their anger
speaks_to: anger after betrayal that spills onto everyone
prejudice after a bad experience with one person
parents or managers punishing a group for one person's act

data_flags.translation_note: Second half overreaches. 'nanu jānāmi kasyāyam' is read by itihasa.io as 'I do not (yet) know whose this chariot is', and Shastri likewise says it is not yet known; Govindaraja's text reads 'na tu'. Suggest: 'Whose broken war-chariot this is, we do not yet know.'...

vr.3.66.17.context: Lakshmana, the younger brother, has been consoling Rama and urging effort. He says that not even Brihaspati could teach Rama, that he is only repeating what Rama himself taught him, and that he will rouse the wisdom grief has put to sleep. He then urges Rama to turn his strength on the guilty enemy alone.
vr.3.66.17.core_teaching: Grief does not destroy a person's wisdom; it only puts it to sleep for a while, and a friend can help wake it.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Lakshmana disclaims presumption by saying his insight was given by Rama himself; he only rouses knowledge veiled by grief. The gods' inability to fathom Rama's mind hints at his divinity.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: Lakshmana says Rama often taught him this, that no one, not even Brihaspati, could teach Rama, and that he would arouse the power sorrow has quenched.

vr.3.66.17.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say: you have not lost your judgement, it is resting under grief; a friend's job is to remind, not lecture.
misreadings: Not a demand to stop grieving; it trusts the grieving person's own wisdom.
cautions: Gentle verse, but it sits in a speech that soon urges action; do not rush a bereaved reader toward 'getting back to work'.
not_for: readers who need permission to grieve rather than to recover
speaks_to: someone grieving who feels they have 'lost themselves'
people whose usual competence has deserted them

vr.3.66.5.context: Rama is wailing like an orphan. Lakshmana clasps his feet and consoles him: Dasaratha won him by great austerity, and trouble comes to every living being. He follows with examples of great figures who suffered (Yayati, Vasishtha, the trembling earth, the eclipsed sun and moon).
vr.3.66.5.core_teaching: No living being is spared adversity; misfortune touches like fire and also passes. Lakshmana says this to steady Rama, not to dismiss his loss.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: On 'take heart' cites the Chandogya teaching that while one has a body, pleasant and unpleasant cannot be escaped; on the previous verse he cites the Gita: the great set the example others follow.

vr.3.66.5.practical_reading: Teachers use it to remind a suffering person that pain is universal and not permanent, as a hand on the shoulder rather than an argument.
misreadings: Not 'your pain is small' or 'get over it'.
'Passes in a moment' is consolation, not a timetable for grief.
cautions: Shastri's rendering of the next part says it is not worthy of Rama to grieve even if Sita is dead; avoid importing that line into a grief reading.
not_for: fresh bereavement (the 'passes quickly' frame can feel dismissive)
long-term illness or chronic pain
speaks_to: acute distress after a loss or shock

data_flags.corrected_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 3.66.6 (Southern, itihasa.io). Southern-only verse, absent in Baroda CE; itihasa notes it is also missing from the Govindaraja and Shivasahaya texts and commented only by Tilaka. Our id 3.66.5 is off by one.

vr.3.66.9.context: Part of Lakshmana's list of examples showing that adversity reaches even the greatest: Yayati fell from heaven, Vasishtha lost a hundred sons, the earth itself quakes, and the sun and moon undergo eclipse.
vr.3.66.9.core_teaching: Even the sun and moon, on which the world depends, are eclipsed; misfortune is no proof of weakness or of having lost one's light.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Calls sun and moon 'dharma' because they witness all dharma; cites Manu that rain comes from the sun; glosses eclipse as being seized by Rahu and Ketu.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: the sun and moon, the eyes of the world and symbols of virtue by which all is ordered, suffer eclipse; even the gods are subject to fate.

vr.3.66.9.practical_reading: Used to tell a capable person in a dark patch that an eclipse is temporary and does not change what they are.
misreadings: Not fatalism ('nothing can be done'); Lakshmana's point is to rouse Rama to act.
cautions: In the same speech Lakshmana says Rama should not lament even if Sita is dead; keep that out of a grief reading.
not_for: fresh bereavement if used to minimise the loss
speaks_to: high achievers going through failure or depression

vr.3.72.7.context: Freed from his monstrous form, Kabandha rises in a radiant body and tells Rama how to recover Sita. He explains that a person struck by misfortune should ally with another in the same plight; Rama and Lakshmana, stripped of kingdom and with Sita abducted, are such people. So Rama must make a friend of such a fellow sufferer, and Kabandha names Sugriva, driven out by his brother Vali and living on Mount Rishyamuka.
vr.3.72.7.core_teaching: Some troubles cannot be met alone; find an ally who shares your kind of trouble, because without that friendship success is not in sight.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindaraja (Bhushana) and Rama Varma (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Read the preceding verse through royal policy: of the six expedients, the one Rama needs is alliance (samashraya), and one touched by deep misfortune is best allied with another who shares that lot.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindaraja and Rama Varma on 3.72.9-10 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Because the brothers have lost their kingdom and suffered Sita's abduction, they are in a phase of misfortune and must befriend a fellow sufferer; without it Kabandha sees no recovery of Sita.

vr.3.72.7.practical_reading: Reach out to someone who has been through what you are going through; shared experience makes for help that actually works.
misreadings: Not 'use people'; the alliance with Sugriva becomes a real, mutual friendship.
Not a claim that only fellow sufferers can help.
cautions: The commentators frame this as statecraft (strategic alliance), so avoid overstating it as purely emotional support.
not_for: someone who has been hurt by a friend and is not ready to trust
speaks_to: needing a support group or peer

vr.3.74.12.context: Rama and Lakshmana reach Shabari's hermitage near Pampa. She tells them her teachers, Matanga's disciples, ascended to heaven when Rama reached Chitrakuta, telling her to wait for him; she offers him the forest foods she has gathered. She then shows him the hermitage and leaves her body.
vr.3.74.12.core_teaching: Shabari's long, patient waiting is expressed in simple service: everything she gathered was for Rama. Devotion is shown in faithful preparation.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) and Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Both record the traditional account (sampradāya) that from the time Rama reached Chitrakuta, Shabari gathered fruit daily and tasted each kind to check its sweetness; Tilaka cites the Padma Purana for this.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: thus the blessed ascetics spoke to her, and for Rama she has gathered wild fruits of many kinds from the borders of Lake Pampa.

vr.3.74.12.practical_reading: Used for faithful waiting and humble preparation: love shows itself in small, constant acts long before the moment arrives.
misreadings: Not a claim that waiting alone earns reward; her life of service to her teachers is the ground of it.
cautions: Shabari dies (ascends) right after this meeting; mention gently if used for an elderly or dying reader.
not_for: someone in an abusive situation being told to 'wait patiently'
speaks_to: people waiting a long time for something they hope for
elders who feel their devotion goes unseen

vr.3.74.22.context: Shabari shows Rama the wonders of Matanga's grove: the seven seas that came at the old sages' wish when they were too weak to travel, their bark garments that never dry, and the lily garlands from their worship that never fade. She then asks leave to give up her body and join them.
vr.3.74.22.core_teaching: What the sages offered in devotion has not faded, long after they have gone; the power of their practice lingers in the place.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja, Rāma Varmā and Śivasahāya (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: All three explain the hermitage marvels: the seas gathered at the sages' mere wish; garments stay wet through contact with their holy bodies; the garlands stay fresh because they were offered with intense devotion.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: the bark robes left hanging after their ablutions are still wet, and the azure lotuses offered in worship have not faded.

vr.3.74.22.practical_reading: Used for the lasting trace of good people: their practice and love still mark the places and people they served.
misreadings: A miracle narrative, not a literal claim about flowers that a modern reader must accept.
cautions: Mentions teachers who have died and Shabari's own death next; good for remembrance, but handle with care for fresh grief.
not_for: someone who needs practical help more than consolation
speaks_to: remembering a teacher, parent or elder who has died
visiting a place that holds someone's memory

vr.3.9.19.context: Sita, walking behind Rama into the Dandaka forest, worries that his vow to kill rakshasas will draw him into violence without provocation. She tells of an ascetic whom Indra, disguised as a warrior, left a sword to guard; carrying it everywhere, he slowly grew cruel and fell. This verse sums up the parable before she asks Rama to keep his weapons for real need.
vr.3.9.19.core_teaching: Habitual contact with an instrument of harm changes the one who handles it, the way fire changes whatever it touches. Sita uses the precedent to ask that force be used only with cause.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads the fire simile as a law of change: just as fire alters any object it touches, a weapon kept close alters the mind of the person who bears it.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) and Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Treat 'caused by contact with a weapon' as describing the story itself: this precedent shows what weapon-contact produces.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Renders the summary plainly: carrying arms works a change in the carrier's mind as fire changes wood; Sita then asks Rama not to slay rakshasas without provocation and to honour the code of peace in the forest.

vr.3.9.19.practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that what we handle daily (tools of power, anger, harsh speech, even devices) quietly shapes our temperament, so keep such things for their proper use.
misreadings: Not pacifism in the absolute: Sita grants that a kshatriya protects the afflicted; her objection is to violence without cause.
Not a criticism of Rama's character; she frames it as care and leaves the decision to him.
cautions: The parable ends with the ascetic falling into hell; keep that detail out of readings for someone already frightened of their own anger.
not_for: victims of violence (it is about the one who wields force)
someone needing to defend themselves now
speaks_to: noticing how a role, tool or habit is changing you
people in jobs that involve power over others (security, policing, management)
someone who keeps anger 'at hand' and feels it hardening them

vr.3.9.26.context: Closing her counsel on non-violence, Sita praises dharma as the source of wealth and happiness. Right after this she says she spoke only out of a woman's affection and that Rama, who knows the three worlds, should decide.
vr.3.9.26.core_teaching: Dharma, and the lasting happiness it brings, is reached by effortful self-discipline; ease and pleasure do not produce real happiness.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explains that true felicity is never gained through comfort or absence of hardship but by chastening body and mind with vows.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Names the kind of vows meant, such as the cāndrāyaṇa fast; Govindarāja's text reads a passive 'is not obtained', matching the critical edition.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri's version: saints won bliss by self-denial, and happiness is not born of pleasure; through duty the world is conquered, duty being its marrow.

vr.3.9.26.practical_reading: Used to say that the good life is built by small daily disciplines, not by chasing comfort; satisfaction follows effort.
misreadings: Not a call for harsh self-punishment; the context is restraint in the forest, not mortification for its own sake.
Not a rejection of all pleasure; it says pleasure is not the route to lasting happiness.
cautions: For someone depressed or exhausted, 'wear yourself down' can sound like a demand to push harder; frame it as steady practice, not strain.
not_for: burnout, illness, someone who needs rest
people with eating disorders (vows of fasting are the commentators' example)
speaks_to: someone noticing that comfort has not made them happy

vr.4.1.101.context: Arriving at Lake Pampa in spring, Rama is overwhelmed by longing for Sita: every bird and mated deer reminds him of her. Lakshmana answers the long lament by praising resolute energy, adding that energetic people do not sink in their undertakings and that by energy alone they will recover Sita; he then urges Rama to put grief behind him and remember his own great nature. Rama regains his steadiness and walks on past the lake.
vr.4.1.101.core_teaching: Energy of will is the strongest resource a person has; with it, little in the world is out of reach.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rama Varma (Tilaka) and Shivasahaya (Shiromani) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Both explain that every kind of effort is rooted in utsaha, so nothing is unattainable for one who has it, and by it alone the brothers will recover Sita.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rama Varma (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: On the next verses, Tilaka says Rama's nature is pure sattva, so Lakshmana's brief reminder is enough for him to drop the grief he had taken on.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindaraja (Bhushana) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads Rama's 'grief and delusion' theologically as compassion and tenderness, which Rama restrains so as to act within scriptural bounds.

vr.4.1.101.practical_reading: Used to say that when you feel flattened, the first step back is energy itself, a small act of will, before plans or results.
misreadings: Not 'positive thinking fixes everything'; Lakshmana links energy to the concrete task of searching for Sita.
Not a rebuke of grief as weakness; Rama's grief is treated by the commentators as love, which he then channels.
cautions: The surrounding verses tell a grieving man to cast grief aside; on a Day 1 'see' slot this can feel like being told to cheer up. Pair it with the lament that precedes it.
not_for: clinical depression where 'find your energy' may feel impossible or blaming
fresh grief in its first days
speaks_to: starting again after a loss or setback
needing a nudge to take the first step

vr.4.10.6.context: Sugriva tells Rama how the rift began: Vali chased a demon into a cave; when blood flowed out Sugriva thought him dead, sealed the cave and returned. The ministers made him king. When Vali came back furious, Sugriva bowed, explained he was crowned against his will, and offered the kingdom back; Vali refused, took his wife and drove him out.
vr.4.10.6.core_teaching: Sugriva owns the situation, explains without excuses, and asks pardon; he offers to return what he holds. A rift can begin from honest misunderstanding.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Sugriva was consecrated by force, not from ambition; he asks pardon for an offence that came by fate and says he remains Vali's servant as before.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'despondency' as the citizens' fear that the realm would perish without a ruler; reads 'as before' as remaining crown prince.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: seeing him in distress, the people and ministers placed him on the throne without his wishing it; he begs pardon and offers the kingdom back as a trust.

vr.4.10.6.practical_reading: Used for apologies after misunderstandings: explain honestly, ask forgiveness, offer to make it right, even if the other may not accept.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that a sincere apology will be accepted; Vali refuses.
Sugriva's account is one-sided; Vali's dying words (4.22) admit fault on his side too.
not_for: someone being pressured to apologise for harm done to them
speaks_to: family rifts over inheritance, roles or property
apologising when you did not intend harm

vr.4.15.22.context: Still at the door, Tara urges Vali to give up enmity with Sugriva, seek Rama's friendship, and win his brother back with gifts and honour, making him his closest confidant.
vr.4.15.22.core_teaching: A younger brother, near or far, remains one's own family and deserves care; reconciliation is wiser than war.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads 24-25 together: Tara judges friendship with Rama and affection with Sugriva to be Vali's proper course, since a younger brother must be cherished.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) and Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explain 'there or here': whether Sugriva stays far off on Rishyamuka or lives in Kishkindha, he is in every way Vali's kinsman, unequalled on earth.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: do not quarrel with your younger brother; reconcile with Sugriva and put hatred far away.

vr.4.15.22.practical_reading: Used for estranged siblings: distance and old injury do not undo the bond; the stronger party can make the first move.
misreadings: Not an argument that the wronged party must reconcile on any terms; here Tara addresses the one who did the wronging.
cautions: Vali refuses and dies within the hour; sensitive for someone who lost a sibling while estranged.
not_for: someone estranged from an abusive relative
speaks_to: the older or stronger sibling in a rift

vr.4.15.7.context: Sugriva, defeated the day before, is back at the gate roaring for a fight. Vali storms out; Tara embraces him and pleads. She asks him to drop this anger and fight in the morning, reasoning that Sugriva's quick return means he has a powerful ally (Rama). Vali dismisses her and dies.
vr.4.15.7.core_teaching: Anger that rushes in like a flood should be set aside, as one throws off last night's faded garland on rising, and the decision taken calmly in the morning.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka, Bhūṣaṇa and Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: All explain the double simile and that Tara's practical point is postponement: put anger down now and fight tomorrow morning; waiting will neither add enemies nor make him look weak.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: On the following verses: Tara infers a special cause from Sugriva's unusual confidence, so her counsel is reasoned, not timid.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: abandon this torrent-like anger as one throws aside a faded garland on rising; fight Sugriva tomorrow at dawn.

vr.4.15.7.practical_reading: Used as advice to sleep on it: do not act in the surge of anger; let it drop and decide in the morning.
misreadings: Not 'never feel anger'; it is about not acting inside the flood.
Not a counsel of cowardice: Tara argues postponement costs nothing.
cautions: Vali ignores her and is killed shortly after; avoid making the reading about what happens to those who don't listen if the reader has just lost someone after a quarrel.
not_for: someone whose anger is a justified response to ongoing abuse
speaks_to: about to send the angry message or make the angry call

vr.4.2.16.context: Sugriva, hiding on Rishyamuka, sees two armed strangers (Rama and Lakshmana) and panics, sure Vali has sent them. Hanuman calms him: Vali cannot come here, there is nothing to fear yet, and a ruler should read people from their signs and conduct before deciding.
vr.4.2.16.core_teaching: Panic lets the mind jump ahead of the facts; steady yourself and judge by evidence before reacting.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads verses 16-17 as one sentence and takes the exclamation 'aho' to imply Sugriva is above ordinary monkey nature, so the fickleness is unworthy of him.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Says Hanuman is dispelling Sugriva's fear that Vali himself has come in disguise.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: Hanuman tells Sugriva his simian nature is showing, since by giving way to distraction he cannot see clearly, though he is intelligent and able to read others.

vr.4.2.16.practical_reading: Used for anxiety spirals and catastrophising: name the jumpiness, then look at what is actually in front of you.
misreadings: Not mockery of an anxious person; Hanuman pairs the rebuke with reassurance and practical advice.
cautions: For someone with an anxiety disorder, 'your mind is flighty' can sound like blame; pair it with Hanuman's calm reassurance.
not_for: someone facing a real, present danger
speaks_to: over-reading threats at work or in relationships

vr.4.22.23.context: With his last breath Vali advises his young son Angada how to live at his uncle Sugriva's court: obey the king, be attentive to place and time, bear pleasure and pain, and keep a measured distance. Vali dies right after this verse.
vr.4.22.23.core_teaching: Neither be too familiar nor too distant with those in power over you; both extremes are serious mistakes, so keep to the middle.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of all three commentators (as reported) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Gloss 'antaradṛk' as taking the middle way between over-familiarity and aloofness.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Cites the maxim that with kings, fire and teachers, too close brings ruin and too far brings no benefit.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: be neither too attached to anyone nor hold anyone in contempt; both extremes are a great error, so follow the middle course.

vr.4.22.23.practical_reading: Used for workplace and family relationships with authority: friendly but professional, warm but not overfamiliar.
misreadings: Not advice for intimate relationships; the context is serving a ruler.
cautions: These are a dying father's last words to a child; touching for a reader who lost a parent, but can be heavy.
not_for: close friendships or partnerships where full openness is the point

vr.4.22.3.context: Mortally wounded by Rama's arrow, Vali revives briefly and sees his victorious brother. He asks Sugriva not to hold his wrongs against him, then hands him the kingdom, entrusts Angada and Tara to him, and gives him his golden garland.
vr.4.22.3.core_teaching: At the end, Vali asks forgiveness, admitting he acted under a delusion he could not resist.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explains the offence as due to demerit from a previous life.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Takes the offence concretely: banishing Sugriva and taking his wife, driven by fated delusion.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: Vali, in a clear and affectionate tone, asks Sugriva not to approach him with ill will, as he was carried away by a fatal loss of understanding.

vr.4.22.3.practical_reading: Used for deathbed or late-life reconciliation: asking pardon openly, even when one partly blames circumstances.
misreadings: Our note is right: the plea leans on fate; the acts that follow (giving the kingdom and his family into Sugriva's care) are what make the amends real.
Not a template for excusing harm as 'not my fault'.
cautions: Deathbed scene; take care with readers facing the death of an estranged relative.
not_for: someone pressured to forgive a person who has not changed
speaks_to: someone receiving an apology they are unsure how to take

vr.4.22.4.context: Same dying speech: Vali reflects that the two brothers were not destined to have happiness together; brotherly affection turned out otherwise. He then gives Sugriva the kingdom.
vr.4.22.4.core_teaching: Vali sees, too late, that brotherly love and the kingdom could not both be held; what should have been affection became rivalry.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Commentators on 4.22.1-6 (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Note that Vali revives with faint breath to speak, and that the 'blameless fame' he mentions is his reputation for invincibility; Govindarāja reads 'tāta nānyathā' here.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: it seemed it was not their destiny to live at peace; though friendship is natural between brothers, with them it was different.

vr.4.22.4.practical_reading: Used to reflect on what rivalry over money, status or inheritance costs a family; the bond is worth more than the prize.
misreadings: Our line 'It went the wrong way' fits; avoid reading it as pure fatalism that excuses both brothers.
cautions: Deathbed regret; sensitive for those who lost someone before reconciling.
not_for: fresh grief over an unreconciled death
speaks_to: sibling rivalry over property or position
regret over a relationship lost to competition

vr.4.24.9.context: After Vali's death Sugriva, now king, sees Tara and Angada grieving and is overcome by remorse. He tells Rama that Vali, though stronger, had spared his life, while he has killed his brother; he speaks of entering the fire.
vr.4.24.9.core_teaching: Weighed honestly, no gain is worth a brother's death; even an ambitious person who reflects would find no joy in it.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) and Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: On 9-10: Vali refrained from killing Sugriva for fear of lowering his own greatness; Govindarāja reads it as 'by not transgressing his greatness'.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: how could anyone approve a brother's murder or set the joy of a kingdom against the grief of his death; first anger made him glad, then great sadness seized him.

vr.4.24.9.practical_reading: Used for remorse after a hard-won victory: count the human cost of what you fought for.
misreadings: Not a general condemnation of competition; it is about victory bought with a loved one's loss.
cautions: Sugriva goes on to speak of self-immolation in this sarga; avoid for readers with suicidal thoughts or acute guilt.
not_for: someone in acute guilt or self-harm risk
someone who did not cause the loss they grieve
speaks_to: remorse after a family dispute or lawsuit
winning at the cost of a relationship

vr.4.27.24.context: Sugriva is crowned and the rains set in; Rama and Lakshmana camp on Mount Prasravana. Seeing the moon rise, Rama cannot sleep for thinking of Sita. Lakshmana, himself sad, speaks gently: enough of this anguish; grief ruins every purpose; summon your effort and wait for the season.
vr.4.27.24.core_teaching: Unchecked grief drains away every purpose; a friend reminds the grieving person of what they already know so they can recover their resolve.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Notes Lakshmana speaks with conciliatory gentleness.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Commentators (Tilaka, Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Gloss 'enough of anguish' as 'let there be no agitation of mind', and say excessive grief ruins all undertakings.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: Lakshmana, equally afflicted, asks Rama to cease mourning, since one who grieves never succeeds.

vr.4.27.24.practical_reading: Used as a loving nudge after a long period of sorrow: grief is real, but it should not consume everything you still mean to do.
misreadings: Our misuse note is right: not a rule that grief must be cut short.
The speaker shares the sorrow; it is not a lecture from outside.
cautions: 'Enough' can feel brutal to the freshly bereaved; best for prolonged distress with a goal still in reach (Sita is alive).
not_for: early bereavement or death of a loved one (in the story the loved one is alive and recoverable)
speaks_to: someone whose sorrow is crowding out a goal still possible

vr.4.27.29.context: Continuing the night conversation on Prasravana, Lakshmana urges Rama to uproot grief, wait out the rainy season, and rekindle his valour like a fire under ashes. Rama praises his brother's affectionate counsel and agrees to wait.
vr.4.27.29.core_teaching: Some seasons are for waiting, not acting: when conditions make action impossible, wait for the right time and keep resolve alive.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) and Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: On the surrounding verses, gloss 'vyavasāya' as strenuous effort; Lakshmana is rekindling Rama's resolve, not asking him to give up.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: wait till autumn, as it is now the rainy season, then destroy Ravana, his kingdom and kin; Lakshmana wants to revive Rama's dormant valour like a fire under ashes.

vr.4.27.29.practical_reading: Used for strategic patience: when the roads are closed, rest, prepare, and act when the season turns.
misreadings: Our note is right: waiting is not giving up.
Not an excuse for indefinite delay; Rama does act when autumn comes (and Sugriva's over-delay is criticised in 4.29-4.33).
not_for: situations needing urgent action now (safety, health)
speaks_to: a project or plan blocked by circumstances
job seekers in a slow market
recovery periods after illness or injury

vr.4.28.62.context: Rama describes the rainy season to Lakshmana. He chooses not to press Sugriva, who has just been reunited with his wife after long suffering, trusting that once rested he will see the season has turned and remember the help he received. Rama adds that an ungrateful person wounds the hearts of the good.
vr.4.28.62.core_teaching: Give a friend time and trust their gratitude; a person who has been helped will, after rest, remember what they owe.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of itihasa.io commentarial note (commentator not specified) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Rama waits for the clearing of both the rivers and Sugriva's goodwill, trusting that a helped hero reciprocates, while an ungrateful one pains the noble.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: Rama does not wish to press Sugriva, who is reunited with his wife after long suffering; when rested he will remember his promise; ingratitude wounds honest hearts.

vr.4.28.62.practical_reading: Used for patience with people who owe you: give them room before you remind them.
misreadings: Our misuse note is right: patience has limits; when autumn comes and Sugriva delays, Rama sends Lakshmana with a stern message.
not_for: someone being repeatedly let down by a person who never follows through
speaks_to: waiting on a friend, colleague or family member to follow through
managers giving a team recovery time

vr.4.29.7.context: Autumn has come. Sugriva, crowned and lost in pleasure with Ruma and Tara, has left the state to his ministers. Hanuman approaches him tactfully: he has his throne, now he must attend to his friend; help given late is no help, so order the search before Rama has to ask.
vr.4.29.7.core_teaching: Help that comes after the moment has passed fails a friend, however large it is; timeliness is part of loyalty.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: What is not done at the proper time is as good as not done, even if done later with great effort.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: On the next verses: Rama, though anxious, does not himself point out the lapsed time, which shows his gracious character.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: Hanuman tells Sugriva that the delay is not yet serious so long as Rama has not had to call on him, but waiting until compelled will be too late.

vr.4.29.7.practical_reading: Used to say: show up when it matters; a late gesture, however grand, does not replace being there in time.
misreadings: Not shaming for honest delays beyond one's control.
not_for: someone already crushed by guilt for missing a moment that cannot be undone (e.g. a death)
speaks_to: someone procrastinating on a promise to a friend
people who show up only after the crisis
comfortable success causing neglect of old commitments

vr.4.3.19.context: Hanuman, disguised as a mendicant, has just addressed Rama and Lakshmana on Sugriva's behalf. Rama, impressed, tells Lakshmana that someone who speaks like this must know the Vedas and grammar, and praises the envoy's composure and diction.
vr.4.3.19.core_teaching: Good speech is brief, clear, unhurried, pleasant to hear and spoken in a steady voice; such speech shows inner composure and learning.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) and Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explain 'resting in the chest' and 'passing the throat' as stages of speech (madhyamā, then vaikharī), and 'avyatham' as free of harsh-sounding syllables.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Cites the Śikṣā list of six virtues of recitation, such as sweetness and distinct syllables, glossing polish as grammatical purity.

vr.4.3.19.practical_reading: Taught as a guide to speaking well in interviews, meetings and hard conversations: concise, clear, unrushed, calm in tone.
misreadings: Not a rule that only polished speakers are trustworthy.
not_for: people with speech disabilities or stammers (could read as judgement)
speaks_to: preparing for an interview, pitch or difficult talk
people who ramble or rush when nervous

vr.4.32.15.context: Hanuman tells Sugriva that autumn, the agreed season, has come and he has forgotten. Rama, grieving his stolen wife, will speak harshly through Lakshmana, which is no wonder; Sugriva should bear it, bow to Lakshmana and ask pardon.
vr.4.32.15.core_teaching: When someone in deep pain, whom you have let down, speaks harshly, even through someone else, bear it patiently and make amends.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) and Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Gloss 'through another' as words heard through Lakshmana.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Stacks the reasons to bear the words: Rama is robbed of his wife, stricken with grief, and the supreme lord.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: grieving his wife, Rama will speak harshly through Lakshmana, which is no wonder; having acted improperly, Sugriva should bow to Lakshmana and ask pardon.

vr.4.32.15.practical_reading: Used for receiving the anger of a hurting person you have failed: hear it out without defensiveness, then repair.
misreadings: Our misuse note is right: patience with a hurting person's outburst, not tolerance of ongoing abuse.
Key condition: Sugriva is at fault; it is not a general rule to absorb anyone's harshness.
cautions: Do not offer to someone who is the target of repeated verbal abuse.
not_for: victims of abuse or domestic violence
someone blamed for what was not their fault
speaks_to: you let someone down and they are angry
caregivers facing a grieving relative's outbursts
teams handling an upset client after a real failure

data_flags.corrected_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 4.32.16 (Southern, itihasa.io) = Baroda CE 4.31.16. Our id 4.32.15 is off by one.

vr.4.32.7.context: Hearing that Lakshmana has arrived in fury, Sugriva tells his ministers he has done nothing wrong and that a friend angry without cause makes him anxious; friendship is easy to make and hard to keep. Hanuman then tells him plainly that the lapse is his own.
vr.4.32.7.core_teaching: Making friends is easy; keeping friendship is hard, because minds change and affection can break over small things.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Calls it a worldly maxim; fickle minds break affection over a slight inequality.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Hardness lies in guarding friendship against whisperers; in the next verse Sugriva shows gratitude, fearing he cannot repay Rama.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: easy to contract a friendship, very hard to sustain it, since the fickle mind can break it for the most trivial reason.

vr.4.32.7.practical_reading: Used to remind that friendships need tending: small neglects, left unrepaired, can end them.
misreadings: Irony in context: Sugriva speaks as if the problem were Rama's touchiness, while the lapse is his own (Hanuman corrects him).
not_for: someone blaming a friend's 'fickleness' for a hurt they caused

vr.4.33.39.context: Lakshmana storms into Kishkindha; Sugriva sends Tara to meet him. Tara, calm and courteous, answers his fury: this is no time for anger, anger should not be turned on one's own, and a well-wisher's lapse should be borne. She then explains Sugriva's lapse and that preparations are under way.
vr.4.33.39.core_teaching: Do not turn anger on your own allies; bear the lapse of someone who sincerely wants your good.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: 'Not the time' because the moment for the search has not yet been lost.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Because anger would only delay the work.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Because Sugriva is overcome by desire, so his lapse deserves allowance; Govindaraja reads 'na cātikopaḥ', 'not excessive anger'.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: this is not the time for recrimination; restrain anger against her lord, who has Lakshmana's interests at heart, and forgive his folly.

vr.4.33.39.practical_reading: Used for keeping alliances intact: when a friend slips, address it without turning on them.
misreadings: Our misuse note is right: about lapses by people who mean well, not repeated mistreatment.
Govindaraja's reading suggests moderation, not suppression, of anger.
not_for: someone repeatedly let down or exploited by the same person
speaks_to: anger at a teammate, partner or friend who dropped the ball

vr.4.35.9.context: Lakshmana has rebuked Sugriva harshly. Tara answers: Sugriva is not ungrateful or false; after long hardship he lost track of time, as the sage Vishvamitra once spent ten years with Ghritachi thinking it a day. People of real character do not give way to anger without first examining the facts. She then shows the army is already being gathered.
vr.4.35.9.core_teaching: People of strong character examine before they let anger take them; reflection comes first.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Notes Tara's turn: having first conceded a lapse to calm Lakshmana, she now shows that on examination Sugriva has committed no fault.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: Tara says Sugriva has not merited such harsh words; after long adversity and sudden good fortune he lost track of time, like Vishvamitra with Ghritachi.

vr.4.35.9.practical_reading: Used to appeal to someone's better self before they act in anger: check the facts first.
misreadings: Not that strong people never feel anger; it is about not being ruled by it before reflection.
not_for: someone whose anger at a real, verified wrong is being dismissed
speaks_to: about to react to a perceived betrayal
leaders handling a subordinate's apparent failure
appealing to an angry person's best self

vr.4.36.20.context: Sugriva has humbly owned his lapse and promised help. Lakshmana, calmed, says only Rama and Sugriva could admit fault while holding power, urges Sugriva to come and console Rama, and asks forgiveness for his own harsh words.
vr.4.36.20.core_teaching: Lakshmana takes responsibility for his own harsh words and asks pardon; reconciliation runs both ways.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) and Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Both stress his tact: he makes clear the threats were his own, so Sugriva will not think Rama dictated them; Rama's words were only a grief-stricken lament.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Glosses Rama's 'speech' as lament (vilāpa) born of separation from Sita.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: Lakshmana asks Sugriva to forgive the reproaches he spoke because of Rama's deep distress.

vr.4.36.20.practical_reading: Used as a model apology after an outburst on someone else's behalf: own your words, do not pin them on the person you were defending.
misreadings: Not a retraction of the legitimate complaint; Sugriva did lapse.
speaks_to: speaking up for a hurting friend and overdoing it

vr.4.49.6.context: The southern search party has failed to find Sita and much of Sugriva's deadline has gone. Angada rallies the exhausted monkeys: drop fatigue and gloom, search again, since persistence brings results and sitting idle will bring Sugriva's and Rama's anger. Gandhamadana seconds him.
vr.4.49.6.core_teaching: Those who persist see results; despondency is no reason to sit idle with closed eyes.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'it is not fitting for us to close our eyes', i.e. sit idle without doing our duty, even having fallen into despondency.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Takes the word as loss of enterprise or enthusiasm; Tilaka notes the repeated 'search' in the previous verse shows urgency.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: banishing languor, despondency, torpor and fatigue, let us search every region again; perseverance and ardour lead to success.

vr.4.49.6.practical_reading: Used to rally a tired team or oneself: results come to those who keep working, so do not let discouragement turn into inaction.
misreadings: Not 'despair is permanent'; the verse says despair must not stop you, not that you cannot recover from it.
cautions: Our translation's 'you cannot rise again' could frighten a depressed reader; fix before use.
not_for: clinical depression framed as laziness
speaks_to: job seekers or students after repeated rejection
long projects with no results yet

data_flags.translation_note: Second half misstated. The Sanskrit says that, having fallen into deep despondency, it is not proper (for us) to 'close our eyes' (sit idle) — Govindaraja — or to lose our drive — Shivasahaya. Our 'once you sink into deep despair, you cannot rise again'...

vr.4.62.13.context: Sampati, Jatayu's elder brother, tells the monkeys his story. Long ago his wings were burnt shielding Jatayu from the sun; grounded on the Vindhya, he wanted to die. The sage Nishakara told him to wait: Rama's envoys would come, he would point them to Sita, and his wings would return. Sampati has just done so, and his wings grow back.
vr.4.62.13.core_teaching: The sage could heal Sampati at once but holds back, because by staying where he is, as he is, Sampati will do something the world needs.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) and Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Nishakara could restore the wings that day but refrains, since with wings Sampati would fly off restlessly; staying here, he will serve the worlds, the princes, sages and Indra.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Textual note (Govindarāja) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Govindaraja reads 'notsaheyam', shifting the sense to the sage's reluctance rather than ability.

vr.4.62.13.practical_reading: Used for people sidelined by injury, age or disability: your present place may be exactly where you are needed; usefulness is not over.
misreadings: Not a promise that every limitation will be healed; Sampati's wings return in the story.
cautions: Sampati wished to die (Shastri's chapter makes this explicit); careful with readers in despair: emphasise purpose, not the death-wish.
not_for: someone in crisis who needs medical help rather than meaning-making
speaks_to: people grounded by illness, disability or age
those who feel useless after retirement or job loss
waiting for a role to become clear

vr.4.66.28.context: Closing his speech, Jambavan recalls his own past feats (circling the earth at Vishnu's three strides, gathering herbs at the churning of the ocean) and says he is now old and his strength has gone; Hanuman alone has every quality the task needs.
vr.4.66.28.core_teaching: An elder honestly names his own decline and hands the task to the one now able: this is your time.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) and Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Both read 'among us at this time, you alone have every excellence needed for the feat', a grammatical point that sharpens the handover.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri's chapter frames Jambavan's whole speech as an appeal to Hanuman to undertake the leap for the good of all.

vr.4.66.28.practical_reading: Used for mentorship and succession: elders can honour their own past and still pass the work on with grace.
misreadings: Not 'old people are useless'; Jambavan's wisdom is what makes the leap possible.
cautions: Speaks of declining strength with age; can sting a reader grieving their own decline unless the mentoring role is foregrounded.
not_for: older readers already feeling discarded (unless framed as the elder's gift)
speaks_to: handing over a role or business
young people being trusted with responsibility

vr.4.66.7.context: On the southern shore, each monkey says how far he can leap; none can cross a hundred leagues. Jambavan, the old bear-king, turns to Hanuman sitting apart in silence and reminds him of his birth from the Wind god and his powers, which a curse had made him forget. Hanuman then grows for the leap.
vr.4.66.7.core_teaching: You have exceptional strength, mind and courage; why hold yourself back? A friend's recognition can wake abilities one has forgotten.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the question as 'why do you not make yourself ready to leap the ocean?'

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'why do you not know yourself?' (as in the critical edition) and glosses viśiṣṭam as surpassing all beings.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: Jambavan asks why Hanuman, learned and equal in strength to Rama, Lakshmana and Sugriva, sits apart in silence.

vr.4.66.7.practical_reading: Used to encourage someone underselling themselves: name their gifts and ask what is stopping them.
misreadings: Not pressure to perform; Jambavan reminds Hanuman of who he is, the leap follows from that.
The CE reading ('know yourself') is worth using: the point is self-recognition.
not_for: someone exhausted or ill being pushed to 'step up'
speaks_to: someone holding back from an opportunity

vr.4.7.10.context: Sugriva has shown Rama Sita's dropped jewels and Rama breaks down. Sugriva, who has himself lost wife and kingdom, says he does not give in to grief though only a monkey, and that the steady person who reflects never sinks in loss, money trouble or mortal danger; this verse is the counterpart about the one who gives in.
vr.4.7.10.core_teaching: Constantly giving way to despair makes a person sink helplessly, like an overloaded boat; reflection keeps one afloat.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) and Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Distinguish the three crises of the previous verse (separation from a loved one, loss of wealth, mortal danger); the reflective person deliberates and does not sink, the unreflecting one sinks like a laden boat.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri's version keeps the core: one overwhelmed by despair is in danger; Sugriva urges Rama to banish sorrow and revive courage.

vr.4.7.10.practical_reading: Used to warn against letting despair become a habit; it adds weight until one cannot stay afloat.
misreadings: Not 'grieving people are fools'; the word targets habitual surrender, and Sugriva softens it immediately (4.7.14).
cautions: Calling the grieving 'foolish' can wound; for bereavement, pair with 4.7.14 or avoid.
not_for: fresh grief or clinical depression (risks shaming)
speaks_to: after a setback, deciding whether to keep going
people who have lost a job or money

vr.4.7.14.context: Right after his advice on despair, Sugriva softens: he speaks as a friend, not a teacher, and asks Rama, out of regard for their friendship, not to grieve. Rama wipes his tears, embraces Sugriva and says he is himself again.
vr.4.7.14.core_teaching: Comfort works best when given as a friend beside you, not as a teacher above you.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka, Bhūṣaṇa and Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: All read 'brūmi' (I say) and explain that Sugriva speaks out of the duty of friendship, not as an instructor, asking Rama to honour their bond.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: On the previous verse: when a person is engulfed by sorrow even their life is at risk, which is why a friend must speak.

commentaries.who: H. P. Shastri's English translation (1952), on wisdomlib
commentaries.gist: Shastri: Sugriva says he speaks for Rama's good as a friend, not to instruct; Rama wipes his tears and returns to himself.

vr.4.7.14.practical_reading: A model for consoling: speak as a peer, own that you are not an authority, and appeal to the relationship.
misreadings: 'Do not grieve' here is a friend's plea, not a rule that grief is wrong.
cautions: Still ends with 'do not grieve'; for fresh bereavement, foreground the friendship, not the instruction.
not_for: early bereavement if 'do not grieve' is the takeaway

vr.4.7.9.context: After the fire-witnessed pact of friendship, Sugriva shows Rama the ornaments Sita dropped; Rama weeps. Sugriva, who has himself lost his wife and kingdom, says that even he, a mere monkey, does not grieve like this, asks Rama to hold back his tears, and gives this maxim. He goes on to compare the despondent person to an overloaded boat that sinks, and joins his palms begging Rama to take up his strength again.
vr.4.7.9.core_teaching: In loss, money trouble or danger, the person who holds steady and reasons things out with his own mind does not go under.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindaraja (Bhushana) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)

vr.5.12.10.context: Hanuman has searched Ravana's palace, inner apartments and much of Lanka without finding Sita. He dreads facing Jambavan, Angad and the waiting monkeys empty-handed and even thinks he might fast to death. Then he rallies: freedom from despondency is the root of success and the highest happiness; he will search again where he has not looked. He goes on to search the remaining places and later finds Sita in the Ashoka grove.
vr.5.12.10.core_teaching: Refusing to lose heart is the root of success and itself the highest happiness; so search again where you have not yet looked.

vr.5.21.14.context: Ravana has come to the Ashoka grove offering Sita wealth, queenship and power, and threatening her. Trembling, she puts a blade of grass between them and answers: she warns that Lanka will fall through his single crime and that those he has wronged will rejoice at his end. In this verse she says no wealth or power can tempt her, and in the next ones adds that having rested on Rama's arm she could not rest on another's, and urges Ravana to return her and seek Rama's friendship.
vr.5.21.14.core_teaching: Sita declares that power and riches cannot buy her, because she is as inseparable from Rama as sunlight is from the sun. Her integrity is not a negotiating position but who she is.

vr.5.30.18.context: Hanuman, hidden in the tree above Sita, plans how to speak to her without terrifying her. He reasons that if he speaks refined Sanskrit like a brahmin she will remember Ravana's disguise as a mendicant and take him for Ravana (5.30.18); yet he must speak human words, or he cannot comfort her at all (this verse). He then worries she may still cry out and alert the guards, and settles on softly praising Rama from the branches.
vr.5.30.18.core_teaching: To comfort a frightened person you must speak in words they can understand and trust; Hanuman chooses ordinary human speech over impressive formal language.
