commentaries.gist: Takes 'human speech' to mean the vernacular of the Kosala people, because that regional speech is what Sita knows intimately and would find reassuring.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Says Hanuman fears that formal grammatical Sanskrit would frighten her, so he resolves to use ordinary human language, and to speak while still hidden in the foliage.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Monkey chatter would be unintelligible, so human speech is unavoidable; a brahmin's diction would recall Ravana's disguise when he abducted her.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 30
commentaries.gist: Has Hanuman conclude that he must use the human tongue, since otherwise he cannot give the blameless lady courage.

vr.5.30.18.practical_reading: When someone is frightened or grieving, speak plainly and in their own idiom; comfort depends on being understood, not on sounding learned.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of Sanskrit or learning; the point is fitting speech to the listener's fear.
Not an instruction to hide one's identity; Hanuman reveals himself as soon as she can trust him.
not_for: a reader wanting comfort for themselves today (this is guidance for the comforter)
speaks_to: someone about to break hard news or comfort a frightened person
parents, carers, doctors, teachers explaining to someone anxious
a person who over-prepares and over-formalises when someone needs warmth

vr.5.30.34.context: Hanuman has found Sita and is considering what to do if she cries out and the guards attack. He knows he could kill thousands of rakshasas, but if he were killed or captured no one else could leap the ocean and Rama's mission would fail. So he refuses to turn a mission already as good as achieved into a gamble, and plans to approach Sita quietly.
vr.5.30.34.core_teaching: A prudent agent does not risk a nearly-secured result for a fight whose outcome is uncertain; secure the essential task first.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'asatyāni' as battles whose victory is never certain; no prudent envoy would endanger a mission already settled in its outcome.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Whoever exposes a sure undertaking to needless battle-risk becomes the destroyer of his master's cause, foolish and deserving blame.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Battles now are 'unreliable' because they would put Sita's very life at risk.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 30
commentaries.gist: Has Hanuman say battles are hazardous and he dislikes so uncertain an enterprise; a wise person takes no needless risk.

vr.5.30.34.practical_reading: Before a dramatic move, ask whether it risks what you have already nearly secured; finish the certain part first, then take on the uncertain one.
misreadings: Not a rule against all risk or courage; Hanuman fights later, once the essential task is done.
Not cowardice: he is sure he could win, but will not stake the mission on it.
not_for: someone paralysed by fear of any risk, who needs encouragement to act
speaks_to: someone tempted by a confrontation that could derail a near-finished goal
founders, managers, students near the finish line

vr.5.30.40.context: Having weighed the dangers of speaking openly, Hanuman decides to stay hidden in the branches and begin by extolling Rama, the one Sita's whole mind is fixed on, so she is not startled. In these two verses he resolves to deliver Rama's good words in a sweet voice and arrange everything so she can believe him. The next sarga is his gentle recital of Rama's story.
vr.5.30.40.core_teaching: Hanuman plans to win a terrified listener's trust by starting gently with what she loves most (Rama) and speaking sweetly, rather than by asserting himself.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (on 5.30.41) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Without showing his monkey form, Hanuman will keep Sita calm purely by singing Rama's praises.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'samādadhe' as answering every doubt Sita might raise, and notes Hanuman speaks from inside the tree's boughs.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'samādadhe' in a future sense, 'I shall speak it all properly', and reads the preceding verse's compound as Sita whose mind is fixed on Rama.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 30
commentaries.gist: Has Hanuman resolve to speak gently of Rama, praising his piety and renown in sweet tones, and do everything to win her confidence.

vr.5.30.40.practical_reading: To earn the trust of someone frightened or suspicious, begin gently with what matters to them and speak softly; trust is built before your own agenda.
misreadings: Not manipulation or flattery: Hanuman speaks truthfully ('avitatham' in 5.30.44) and only to relieve her fear.
cautions: Two verses merged under one id.
not_for: a reader wanting personal consolation (this is about how to approach another)
speaks_to: someone approaching an estranged or frightened person
a new caregiver, teacher or counsellor building trust

data_flags.translation_note: Minor: the Sanskrit says he will deliver Rama's own auspicious, dharma-filled words ('vacanāni' of Rama, 'samarpayan' = handing over), not 'good and true words about Ram'. In the narrative he in fact recites Rama's story (5.31), and the prior verse speaks of praising Rama, so...

vr.5.34.5.context: Hanuman has just told Sita that Rama is well and asks after her, and that Lakshmana bows to her. Thrilled in every limb, Sita, who the night before had resolved to end her life, quotes a folk proverb: joy comes to one who stays alive, even after a hundred years. A moment later her suspicion that he is Ravana in disguise returns, and Hanuman has to win her trust again.
vr.5.34.5.core_teaching: Sita recognises the truth of a folk saying: as long as one stays alive, joy can still come, however long the wait. The commentators draw the moral that one should bear great sorrow and keep living.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Because Sita kept her life through unbearable grief and has now heard unhoped-for news of Rama, she praises the popular saying as true; their gloss draws the lesson that one should endure even great sorrow and go on living.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka (on 5.34.7) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: The joy at this meeting is mutual: Hanuman rejoices at having found the queen, Sita at seeing Rama's messenger.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 34
commentaries.gist: Has Sita, trembling with delight at news of the two brothers, say the wise hold that happiness comes to a man even after a hundred years.

vr.5.34.5.practical_reading: A verse of hope for long waits: staying alive through a dark stretch keeps open the chance that good news, reunion or joy will still come.
misreadings: Not a promise of a specific outcome or timeline.
Not a reason to dismiss present pain ('it will be fine eventually'); Sita had suffered for months and nearly died.
cautions: Sita had decided to hang herself the night before (5.28); suitable as a protective line for someone in despair, but any reading should also point a reader in crisis to immediate help.
The joy here is reunion with a living person; for fresh bereavement it can sound like a hollow promise.
not_for: fresh grief over a death, where 'joy will come' can feel dismissive
speaks_to: someone in a long, dark wait (illness, separation, unemployment, legal limbo)
a reader who has thought of giving up on life

vr.5.36.44.context: Hanuman has given Sita Rama's ring and describes Rama's state: he barely sleeps, wakes calling her name, sighs at every flower, and strives only to win her back. Sita's sorrow lifts at hearing Rama praised, yet she grieves at hearing of his grief. Valmiki pictures her as an early-autumn night whose moon is still partly veiled by the last clouds.
vr.5.36.44.core_teaching: Valmiki's image for mixed feeling: relief and sorrow can be present at once, like a moon half clear, half veiled.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Sita is freed from the sorrow born of doubt by hearing of Rama's sleepless love, yet struck with an equal sorrow on hearing of his torment.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Admires the simile: like an autumn night with its moon partly clear and partly clouded, Sita is both brightened and shadowed.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (on 5.36.44) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Rama's sleeplessness and murmuring of Sita's name show the steadfast love of the best of men in separation.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 36
commentaries.gist: Sita is delighted by Rama's praises but grieved to hear of his pain, like the autumn moon passing into a dark cloud and reappearing.

vr.5.36.44.practical_reading: Gives permission to feel two things at once: good news about someone you love can bring relief and fresh pain together.
misreadings: Not a demand to resolve the feeling into one; the verse simply describes both.
not_for: someone needing a clear action step
speaks_to: mixed feelings at news from a distant or suffering loved one
long-distance relationships, families separated by migration, hospital or prison

vr.5.38.32.context: Sita gives Hanuman a secret token for Ram: the story of the crow that attacked her, at which Ram once loosed a Brahma-weapon. Then she reproaches him: he used such a weapon for a mere crow, so why does he pardon the one who carried her off? She asks for energetic compassion, saying that though she has him as protector she seems protectorless, and reminds him that he himself taught that compassion is the highest dharma.
vr.5.38.32.core_teaching: Sita feels abandoned despite being loved, and asks that love show itself in decisive action.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rama Varma (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Having given a token known only to Ram, Sita adds a reproachful plea: he used the Brahma-weapon for a crow on her account, so why pardon her abductor? With him as lord, she seems lordless.

commentaries.who: valmikiramayan.net word notes (via sanskritdocuments.org mirror)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the line as Sita asking Rama, best of men and of great strength, to show her mercy: with him as protector she still looks protectorless. The previous note concerns the Brahma-missile hurled even at a crow.

vr.5.38.32.practical_reading: Names the ache of feeling alone even when someone loves you, and the honest wish that their love would show up in action.
misreadings: Not a statement that she has been abandoned; she is certain of Ram's love and is urging him to act.
cautions: Its edge is reproach; for someone who has been left, it can deepen blame toward the person who left.
not_for: someone left permanently, where the hope of rescue is not real
speaks_to: waiting for someone to come through

vr.5.39.20.context: Hanuman is about to leave Lanka with Sita's token. Gazing at him again and again, she asks him to stay one more day hidden somewhere and leave tomorrow: his nearness would give her a moment's release from her great sorrow, and once he goes she fears for her very life until he returns and doubts how the army will cross the sea. Hanuman reassures her and then departs.
vr.5.39.20.core_teaching: A frightened, lonely person asks for presence: simply having a friend near brings a moment's relief from sorrow.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Śiromaṇi (on 5.39.22) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: On the next verse, once Hanuman leaves, uncertainty about his return leaves her life itself in doubt; Śiromaṇi reads it as a rhetorical question.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 39
commentaries.gist: Has Sita ask him to tarry one day in a hidden spot, saying his presence will let her forget her misfortune for a while.

vr.5.39.20.practical_reading: Presence itself heals: sometimes what helps most is staying a little longer with someone who is struggling, even without solving anything.
misreadings: Not a sign that Sita is weak; she has endured months of captivity.
cautions: The next verse speaks of doubt about her survival; keep context gentle.
not_for: someone who needs to be told to let go of a relationship
speaks_to: loneliness, especially during illness or isolation
someone saying goodbye to a visitor, child, or friend
the comforter wondering whether just being there matters

vr.5.39.40.context: At parting, Hanuman promises Sita that Rama and Lakshmana will soon come on his back with a vast army, destroy Lanka, kill Ravana and take her home. This verse is his summary: take heart, wait for the time, and you will soon see Rama blazing like fire. He then adds that she will be reunited with Rama like Rohini with the moon, and see the far shore of her grief.
vr.5.39.40.core_teaching: Hanuman asks Sita to take heart and wait for the appointed time, because help is truly on its way; waiting is asked of her only because others are acting.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Both gloss 'kālakāṅkṣiṇī' as being intent on counting the days remaining until Rama arrives.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Because she will soon see Rama, she should be expectant and take comfort; the next verse's reunion like Rohini with the moon means she will attain union with Rama.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 39
commentaries.gist: Hanuman's parting reassurance to Sita that Rama will soon come and free her (chapter read for context).

vr.5.39.40.practical_reading: When help is genuinely on its way, the task is to steady yourself and count the days rather than despair; Hanuman's own action stands behind the promise.
misreadings: Not a call to passive waiting where no help is coming.
Not a timeline promise.
cautions: Its promise of rescue and violence against the captor ('Ravana slain') is part of the context; keep focus on 'take heart'.
not_for: someone whose situation has no rescue coming (can feel like false hope)
speaks_to: waiting for test results, a visa, a release, a reunion
someone in a hard place who knows help is coming
families awaiting a loved one's return

vr.5.41.6.context: Having comforted Sita and taken her token, Hanuman decides his mission is not complete until he has also gauged the enemy's strength. He dismisses conciliation, gifts and division as useless with the rakshasas and settles on force. The verse before says a good envoy accomplishes extra tasks without harming the main one; this verse adds that one must know many ways to a goal. He then smashes the Ashoka grove to provoke a fight, which leads to his capture and the burning of Lanka.
vr.5.41.6.core_teaching: Effective agents are resourceful: they understand a goal from several angles and do not depend on one method.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (on 5.41.5-6) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Bhūṣaṇa (on 5.41.7) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Hanuman wants to learn the relative strength of the enemy before returning so his master's command is fully done; otherwise he could not answer if asked about Ravana's army.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 41
commentaries.gist: Has Hanuman set aside negotiation, gifts and dissension as useless here and choose valour, noting that a skilful messenger achieves his main aim and others besides.

vr.5.41.6.practical_reading: Don't rely on a single plan; understand a goal well enough to have several routes to it, and add value beyond the brief without endangering the core task.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of using force; in context Hanuman's 'many ways' leads to provoking a fight, and later he regrets the anger that followed.
Not 'do everything at once'; the preceding verse insists extra tasks must not harm the main one.
cautions: Belongs to the run-up to the burning of Lanka; pair with 5.55.3-10 if using the arc.
not_for: someone already overwhelmed who needs to simplify
speaks_to: professionals and students stuck on one approach

vr.5.55.10.context: Looking at the burning city, Hanuman fears Sita has died in the fire. He calls himself an arsonist who forgot Sita and betrayed his master, and here concludes that in anger he has cut the root of the mission; since no part of Lanka seems unburnt, she must have perished. He considers throwing himself into fire or the sea, but then reasons that Sita's virtue protects her, notes that his own tail did not burn, hears celestial beings say she is safe, and goes to see her before leaving.
vr.5.55.10.core_teaching: Hanuman sees that a moment's anger can undo the very purpose one has worked for. His fear proves mistaken, but the lesson about anger stands.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Take 'this task' as the burning of Lanka, done as an effortless trifle, which destroyed the root of Rama's main purpose.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'this task' as the great mission of finding Sita, nearly finished with only the report to Rama left, now ruined at its root.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 5.55.11-12) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Because no spot is seen unburnt, Hanuman infers Sita's death; Śiromaṇi calls it perversity of judgement, and Govindarāja explains the next verse as resolving to give up his life at once.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 55
commentaries.gist: Has Hanuman reproach himself as a shameless wrongdoer who, forgetting Sita, has slain his lord by fire.

vr.5.55.10.practical_reading: Before acting in anger, ask what you came to do; the cost of a small outburst can be the thing you care about most.
misreadings: Not proof that Sita died: Hanuman's fear is mistaken, and the sarga resolves it.
Not a counsel to self-punishment; Hanuman's despair passes once he thinks clearly.
cautions: Immediately followed by Hanuman resolving to end his life (5.55.12-13); never quote that part to a reader in distress, and always give the resolution.
Two verses merged.
not_for: someone consumed by guilt or shame already
a reader with suicidal thoughts (context)
speaks_to: regret after an outburst that harmed a relationship or project
someone who sabotaged a near-finished effort through impulse

vr.5.55.3.context: Hanuman, captured and with his tail set on fire, has burned much of Lanka. Looking at the blazing, terrified city, he is seized by dread that Sita may have died in the fire, and turns on himself. This verse opens a series of reflections on anger: blessed are those who quench rising anger with wisdom. He curses himself, considers ending his life, then reasons that Sita's own power must have protected her, hears from celestial beings that she is safe, and goes to see her again.
vr.5.55.3.core_teaching: Hanuman, realising what his anger may have cost, praises those who use understanding to stop anger as it rises, the way water puts out fire.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Hanuman concludes that anger was the root of his reprehensible act; the repetition of 'mahātmānaḥ' is no flaw, as it comes from his overwhelming distress.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the 'great souls' as people of supreme self-discipline, and notes Govindarāja's reading 'best of men'.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Śiromaṇi (on 5.55.1-2) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Having put out his tail in the sea, Hanuman sees the city's ruin and fears Janaki herself has burned; dread and self-condemnation rise in him.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 55
commentaries.gist: Has Hanuman reflect that he has done something reprehensible and that blessed are the great souls who extinguish anger born in them as water quenches fire.

vr.5.55.3.practical_reading: Notice anger at the moment it rises and use judgement to put it out before it acts; even heroes learn this after the damage.
misreadings: Not a teaching that anger is never felt by good people; Hanuman, the ideal devotee, felt it.
Not a call to suppress justified grievance; it is about stopping anger from acting blindly.
cautions: Followed by intense self-condemnation and thoughts of ending his life (5.55.7-13); a reader prone to shame should get the arc's resolution (Sita is safe) too.
not_for: someone whose anger is a response to abuse they are suffering (it can sound like 'you should calm down')
speaks_to: someone who has just lost their temper and regrets it
parents, partners, managers working on reactivity
after an outburst at work or home

vr.5.55.5.context: Part of Hanuman's reflection on anger after burning Lanka, just after praising those who quench rising anger. The verse before says an angry man will commit any sin, even kill his teachers and insult the good; the one after says he is truly a man who sheds anger by forbearance as a snake sheds its old skin. He then curses himself for having forgotten Sita.
vr.5.55.5.core_teaching: Anger destroys discrimination: in rage a person loses the sense of what must not be said or done.

commentaries.gist: Has Hanuman say the one who gives way to wrath cannot tell when to speak and when to be silent, and no wrong is beyond him.

vr.5.55.5.practical_reading: In a heated moment, assume your judgement about what to say is compromised; pause before speaking or sending.

vr.6.1.12.context: Hanuman has returned with Sita's jewel and message. Rama praises his feat as unmatched and says that by finding Sita, Hanuman has saved Rama, Lakshmana and the whole Raghu line. Then a pang: in exile he has nothing fitting to give in return. In the next verse he gives his embrace as his 'all', and holds Hanuman close.
vr.6.1.12.core_teaching: Rama's gratitude is so great that being unable to repay it pains him; the next verse shows that the gift of oneself is the fitting return.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: The distress of being unable to repay at once overshadows even his joy at news of Sita.

vr.6.10.17.context: Disturbed by the omens in Lanka since Sita's arrival, Vibhishana goes to Ravana's palace in the morning and, before his ministers, urges that Sita be returned as the only remedy, asking not to be blamed if he speaks out of misjudgement or attachment to life. In this verse he explains why he alone speaks: the ministers have shrunk from saying it, but what he has seen and heard must be told; Ravana should weigh it and act. Ravana, feverish with infatuation, rejects him.
vr.6.10.17.core_teaching: When those around a leader stay silent out of fear, a loyal advisor must still report what he has seen and heard, and leave the decision to the leader.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explains why Vibhishana speaks when senior counsellors like Prahasta are present: they withdrew out of fear of Ravana, which exposes the cowardice of men who think themselves warriors; his brotherly bond compels him.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (on 6.10.26-27) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: The narrator calls the advice fit for all three times: it redeems the past by expiating the abduction, helps the present, and protects the future by keeping dharma.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Bhūṣaṇa (on 6.10.23-24) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)

vr.6.111.11.context: Over Ravana's body, his chief queen Mandodari laments. She has just declared that Rama was Vishnu in human form who slew Ravana for the world's good. Here she names the deeper cause: long ago Ravana conquered his senses (through austerities) and so conquered the three worlds; now those same senses, as if avenging that old defeat, have conquered him. She goes on to recall the signs she saw (Khara's death, Hanuman's entry into Lanka) and her own unheeded pleas to make peace with Rama.
vr.6.111.11.core_teaching: Ravana's power came from early self-mastery; his fall came when he let his senses rule him again. Self-control won is not self-control kept.

not_for: someone in early recovery who could hear it as fatalistic
recent widows or widowers

vr.6.113.29.context: After Ravana's death, Hanuman brings Sita news of victory and offers to kill the rakshasis who tormented her for months. She quotes an old saying sung by a bear who, though betrayed by a hunter he had sheltered, refused to give him up to a tiger: the noble do not return evil for evil. Hanuman praises her as Rama's worthy wife and takes her message to Rama.
vr.6.113.29.core_teaching: Sita, now free and able to punish, chooses compassion: the noble keep their own standard of conduct and do not answer cruelty with cruelty, since everyone errs.

vr.6.116.10.context: After the victory Rama, before the assembled army, tells Sita he fought to clear his family's name, not for her, and that he cannot take her back after she lived in another man's house. If after their love grown together and their long life together he still does not know her, she is lost forever. She asks why he did not reject her when Hanuman came, which would have spared everyone a war, then asks Lakshmana for a pyre and enters the fire; Agni returns her unharmed.
vr.6.116.10.core_teaching: Sita protests with dignity that a long shared life should have taught Rama who she is; being unknown by the one closest to you is a permanent wound.

vr.6.16.20.context: After Ravana insults Vibhishana as a traitor in open court, Vibhishana rises into the air with four companions and answers. Elder brothers deserve respect, he says, but he cannot bear such words; people under Time's sway reject good advice. This verse is his famous maxim. He adds that he cannot watch his brother perish like a burning house, asks forgiveness, wishes him well and leaves for Rama's camp.
vr.6.16.20.core_teaching: Flatterers are always available; honest, beneficial counsel is rare, and so is the person willing to hear it.

vr.6.18.23.context: Sugriva still fears Vibhishana is a spy. Rama first says no rakshasa could harm him even if he wanted to, then recalls a tale of a dove that welcomed and even offered its own flesh to the hunter who had caught its mate and came to it for shelter. If a bird could do that, how much more should he. He then quotes the sage Kandu on protecting refugees and makes his vow.
vr.6.18.23.core_teaching: An argument from the lesser to the greater: if even a bird sheltered the one who wronged it when he came for refuge, a person of dharma must do no less.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Contrasts the dove, a mere bird that offered its flesh to its mate's captor, with Rama, dharma in bodily form; also recalls a monkey who rescued a hunter, reminding Sugriva of his own lineage's dharma.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Because a bird's conduct alone lacks scriptural force, Rama goes on to cite the authoritative verses of the sage Kandu.

commentaries.gist: Vibhishana cannot harm Rama at all; Rama, able to slay all fiends by a wish, invokes the dove as the traditional example.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 18
commentaries.gist: Rama's speech to Sugriva on sheltering refugees, leading to Kandu's verses (chapter read for context).

vr.6.18.23.practical_reading: Hospitality and protection toward someone in need should not depend on whether they have been on the 'other side'.
misreadings: As our note says: it describes the protector's duty, not a duty on the injured to host those who hurt them.
Not an endorsement of self-sacrifice to abusers.

Do not use for readers recovering from betrayal or abuse.
not_for: a survivor of abuse or betrayal (it can sound like 'host the one who hurt you')
speaks_to: questions of welcoming refugees, migrants or outsiders
someone deciding whether to help a former rival who is now in need

vr.6.18.26.context: Part of Rama's argument for accepting Vibhishana. After the dove example, he quotes the sage Kandu: one must not kill an enemy who comes begging for refuge with joined palms; and here, whether he comes in distress or in pride, an enemy who seeks refuge must be protected even at the cost of one's life. Kandu adds that failing to do so from fear, delusion or desire is a sin the world condemns, and the refugee who dies unprotected takes away the protector's merit.
vr.6.18.26.core_teaching: The duty to protect anyone who seeks refuge does not depend on their attitude or past: even a proud former enemy must be shielded, even at great personal cost.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: The previous verse forbids killing a supplicant foe so as to avoid cruelty; this verse goes further and commands defending him even with one's life; failing through fear, distraction or greed is a sin all condemn.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'distressed or proud' as making the supplicant's merits or faults irrelevant; a disciplined person must protect him or incur sin and public blame.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Kandu's verses enjoin giving up one's transient life to save any supplicant.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 18
commentaries.gist: Has Rama introduce the sacred verses of Kandu, son of Kanva, and conclude that refusing shelter to those who ask is a grave wrong.

vr.6.18.26.practical_reading: Protection of the vulnerable should not be conditional on whether we like them or whether they come humbly.
misreadings: Not a duty imposed on the weak or wounded toward those who harmed them; it is addressed to one who has power to protect.
Not a literal call to die for anyone who asks.
cautions: 'Even at the cost of his own life' can be heavy for a reader already self-sacrificing or in a caregiving crisis.
not_for: exhausted caregivers or people in abusive situations who may hear 'sacrifice yourself'
speaks_to: those in positions of power or care (leaders, teachers, guardians)
someone asked for help by a person they dislike

vr.6.18.3.context: After hearing his allies' doubts and Hanuman's argument that Vibhishana is sincere, Rama gives his own view: he will never abandon one who comes in friendship, even if he has faults. Sugriva objects again that a man who deserts his own brother in calamity may desert anyone. Rama then argues that Vibhishana cannot harm him, tells the story of the dove, cites the sage Kandu, and makes his vow of refuge.
vr.6.18.3.core_teaching: Rama will not turn away someone who comes to him in friendship, even if that person is flawed; the righteous see no fault in accepting him.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'mitrabhāva' as the attitude of one taking refuge, even if only outwardly feigned, and cites a Vedic rule that one who has surrendered is never handed back even if deserving death.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'friendship' as standing for the attitude of a friend or servant; on Sugriva's reply, he notes Sugriva thinks debating Vibhishana's guilt is pointless since he abandoned his brother.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 18
commentaries.gist: Has Rama say he will never refuse one who presents himself as a friend, and that even if mistaken, no honest man could reproach him.

vr.6.18.3.practical_reading: Make room for people who come to you in good faith even if they carry faults or a bad history; acceptance need not wait for perfection.
misreadings: Not a demand that victims welcome back those who harmed them; Rama is the powerful party, and the refugee has done him no wrong.
Not naivety: Rama has heard and weighed every objection.
cautions: For readers who have been hurt, 'never turn away anyone' can feel like pressure to tolerate harmful people; keep the protector framing.
not_for: someone being pressured to reconcile with an abuser
speaks_to: someone deciding whether to give a newcomer, a reformed person or an outsider a chance
teams and communities welcoming people with a past
a reader who fears they are too flawed to be accepted

vr.6.18.31.context: Having cited the dove and the sage Kandu, Rama concludes with his own vow: to anyone who comes to him even once and asks for protection saying 'I am yours', he grants safety from all beings. He orders Sugriva to bring the newcomer, 'whether he is Vibhishana or Ravana himself'. Vibhishana is brought, falls at Rama's feet, and is accepted.
vr.6.18.31.core_teaching: Rama's vow: a single sincere act of surrender, 'I am yours', is enough for him to grant complete protection. The Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition treats it as the Lord's promise of refuge (śaraṇāgati).

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Rama crowns scripture, Kandu's tradition and the dove's example with his own vow: a single surrender wins fearlessness, even for Ravana in disguise.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: The present tense 'I give' marks Rama's eternal, natural dharma; he distinguishes release from fear of rebirth for one who knows, and safety from all beings for one who says 'I am your servant'.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: 'This is my vow' proclaims an unconditioned resolve; Rama commands Sugriva to bring the supplicant even if it were Ravana.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 18
commentaries.gist: Has Rama swear that any being who seeks refuge with him saying 'I am thine' is assured of his protection, whether it be Vibhishana or Ravana himself.

vr.6.18.31.practical_reading: For devotees, a promise that one honest turning toward the divine is enough; in human terms, a model of offering unconditional safety to those who ask for help.
misreadings: Not a magic formula that removes all consequences; Vibhishana still serves and fights.
Not a demand on victims to protect their aggressors.
cautions: Highly devotional; secular readers may prefer the human 'protect those who ask' reading.
not_for: a reader who rejects devotional framing

a seeker beginning a spiritual practice
people afraid to ask for help

vr.6.19.4.context: Granted refuge, Vibhishana comes down from the sky with his four companions, falls at Rama's feet and says Lanka, friends and wealth are left behind and his kingdom, life and happiness now rest in Rama. Hearing this, Rama comforts him and looks at him as if drinking him in, then asks him to describe the rakshasas' strengths and weaknesses. Vibhishana tells him about Ravana, Kumbhakarna, Prahasta and Indrajit.
vr.6.19.4.core_teaching: Rama receives the one who has surrendered not coolly but with comfort and visible delight.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Rama comforts Vibhishana, apologising for the delay caused by the council's debate, and gazes on him with the utmost affection.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Since service in battle will come later, Rama first invites service by speech, asking for intelligence.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 19
commentaries.gist: Has Rama speak in soothing tones while seeming to consume him with his gaze.

vr.6.19.4.practical_reading: When someone arrives in need, welcome them warmly and attentively before asking anything of them.
cautions: Southern-only half-verse; CE readers will not find it.
not_for: a reader wanting an action step
speaks_to: someone afraid of how they will be received after leaving a group, job or family

vr.6.21.11.context: Rama has lain on kusha grass by the shore for three nights, asking the Ocean for a passage, and the Ocean has not appeared. Angered, he tells Lakshmana that his forbearance is being taken for weakness, damns patience toward such a one, calls for his bow and threatens to dry up the sea. He then shoots, the sea churns, Lakshmana tries to restrain him, and the Ocean appears, offers Nala's bridge, and Rama redirects the arrow at its request.
vr.6.21.11.core_teaching: Forbearance is a virtue, but when it is mistaken for weakness by one who will not respond to gentleness, firm action becomes appropriate.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explains why an Ikshvaku prince sets aside patience: forbearance has its proper season and application; he also notes Rama calls for bow and arrows in stages, giving the Ocean time to relent.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka, Śiromaṇi and Bhūṣaṇa (on 6.21.19-24) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: All three gloss the threatened destruction of sea-creatures and the Ocean being forced to overflow the bounds it normally keeps.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 21
commentaries.gist: Has Rama say forbearance and gentle speech are seen as weakness by those who lack them, call for his bow, and Lakshmana try to restrain him.

vr.6.21.11.practical_reading: Patience and gentleness come first, but they are not unlimited; if they are exploited, firm and clear action is legitimate, used to open the way rather than to punish.
misreadings: Not a licence for anger whenever one feels slighted; as our note says, it must be read with the three days of patient asking before and the restraint after.
Not an endorsement of destroying what stands in one's way; Rama redirects the arrow when the Ocean yields.
cautions: Contains images of killing sea-creatures; keep to the core line.
Readers who are themselves volatile may take it as permission for rage.
not_for: someone already prone to explosive anger
as a stand-alone verse without the context of prior patience
speaks_to: someone whose kindness keeps being exploited (at work, by a landlord, by a manipulative person)
people-pleasers learning to set firm boundaries

vr.6.21.6.context: Rama has lain on darbha grass by the shore for three nights asking the Ocean for passage; the Ocean has not even appeared. Angry, his eyes reddened at the corners, Rama tells Lakshmana that gentleness is wasted on the arrogant, that the world honours the boastful man who punishes freely, and that fame and victory are not won by conciliation alone; he takes up his bow and starts to shoot. The Ocean then rises, asks for mercy and tells him Nala can build a bridge.
vr.6.21.6.core_teaching: The virtues of the good (calm, forbearance, honesty, kind speech) are read as weakness by those who lack them.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindaraja (Bhushana) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Notes that Rama's eyes are reddened only at the corners, a sign of measured, controlled anger rather than rage.

commentaries.who: valmikiramayan.net word notes (via sanskritdocuments.org mirror)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the key compound as virtues that give weak results when directed toward those who have no virtues.

vr.6.21.6.practical_reading: When your patience and kindness are repeatedly ignored, it may be time to add firmness; the problem is the other person's misreading, not your virtue.
misreadings: Not permission to drop kindness; Rama spent three days in patient request first.
Not an endorsement of the boastful 'punish freely' type he describes next; he is bitterly describing how the world behaves.
cautions: The verse sits in an angry speech that praises force; a reader who is hurt may hear it as license for retaliation. The episode itself ends with Rama redirecting his arrow when the Ocean responds.
not_for: someone already inclined to anger or revenge
situations where the 'unworthy' party is a child or someone vulnerable
speaks_to: being ignored after repeated polite requests

vr.6.22.42.context: When Rama's anger finally brings the Ocean before him, the Ocean asks him to spare it and says the monkey Nala, son of the divine architect Vishvakarma, can build a bridge. Nala steps forward: his mother was granted a boon that she would bear a son equal to Vishvakarma; the Ocean has reminded him of it, and he would not have praised his own abilities unasked. Then this verse: I can build it, let the monkeys start today. Hundreds of thousands of monkeys rush to the forest to haul trees and rocks.
vr.6.22.42.core_teaching: Once reminded of an ability he had kept quiet about, Nala owns it plainly and calls for work to start that very day.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindaraja (Bhushana) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Explains Nala's earlier silence: he had forgotten his gift until the Ocean reminded him, and boasting unasked at the start of a task inspires little trust.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rama Varma (Tilaka) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Attributes Nala's prior silence to modesty, embarrassment at self-praise.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Shivasahaya (Shiromani) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'let them build' as Nala telling the monkeys to gather materials under his direction.

vr.6.22.42.practical_reading: You may have abilities you have stopped noticing; when someone names them, say yes plainly and begin today.
misreadings: Not boasting; the commentators stress Nala's modesty.
Not 'do it all alone'; the whole army builds.
not_for: someone pressured to overcommit

vr.6.34.11.context: Ravana has tried to break Sita with a conjured head of Rama. Sarama, a kind rakshasi, has comforted her, explained the illusion and offered to help. Sita says Ravana bewilders her with sorcery, has her threatened and abused, and even in the grove she has no peace for fear of him. So she asks Sarama to find out whatever is being said or decided and tell her. Sarama wipes her tears and goes to learn Ravana's intentions.
vr.6.34.11.core_teaching: In fear and uncertainty, Sita asks a friend not for rescue but for the truth about what is being decided; honest information is itself a kindness.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis (on 6.34.11-12) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Sita asks Sarama to report any discussion or final decision about her release or continued captivity; gentle-spoken Sarama strokes her tear-wet face and wipes away her tears.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja, Rāma Varmā and Śivasahāya (on 6.34.9-10) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 34
commentaries.gist: Has Sita ask Sarama to tell her exactly what Ravana has resolved to do.

vr.6.34.11.practical_reading: When someone is anxious about decisions being made about them (a diagnosis, a court case, a job), clear, honest information is often the greatest help a friend can give.
misreadings: Not a request to spy for malice; it is a captive's plea for clarity about her own fate.
cautions: Context includes psychological abuse (threats, a fake severed head); keep context light.
not_for: someone who has said they do not want to know details yet
speaks_to: someone waiting on decisions they cannot control (medical, legal, immigration, layoffs)
a friend wondering how to help someone anxious

vr.6.59.131.context: In their first direct battle, Ravana has struck down Lakshmana and many monkey heroes. Hanuman's blow stuns Ravana; Rama then shatters his chariot, bow and crown. Seeing him helpless and spent, Rama refuses to kill an exhausted enemy and tells him to go back to Lanka, catch his breath, and return armed to see Rama's strength. Ravana returns to Lanka humiliated, his pride broken, and wakes Kumbhakarna.
vr.6.59.131.core_teaching: Rama will not strike an exhausted, disarmed enemy: a code of fair fighting and magnanimity in strength, combined with a clear warning.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Rama explicitly gives Ravana leave to go under his eyes, and mocks him as 'king of night-prowlers', a deceitful fighter; he spares him to avoid the reproach of killing a battle-weary foe.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Rama bids him rest in Lanka and come back with chariot and bow to witness his might.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (on 6.59.141) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Seeing Ravana with no other refuge, compassionate Rama only cuts off his crown, breaking his pride and leaving him like a fangless serpent.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 59
commentaries.gist: Has Rama tell the weary Ravana he will not deliver him to death, grant him a reprieve to return to Lanka, and invite him back to test his prowess.

vr.6.59.131.practical_reading: Strength is shown in restraint: do not press an advantage against someone who is spent; give them room to recover, even in a contest.
misreadings: As our note says, it is a warrior's fairness and a warning, not gentle advice to rest.
Not forgiveness or reconciliation; the war continues.

speaks_to: someone in a position of advantage over a rival or opponent

vr.6.63.4.context: With the war going badly, Ravana has had his giant brother Kumbhakarna woken from months-long sleep and laments his losses. Kumbhakarna laughs: this is the disaster the council foresaw when Ravana ignored his well-wishers (meaning Vibhishana). The fruit of the sinful deed has come quickly. Here he says the act was never thought through at the outset; out of pride in strength alone its consequences were never weighed. He goes on to lecture on right order in policy, then, loyal, agrees to fight.
vr.6.63.4.core_teaching: Ravana's disaster came from acting on pride in his strength without weighing the consequences beforehand.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 6.63.2-4) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: All identify the 'earlier counsel' with the council where Vibhishana spoke, read 'ignoring well-wishers' as disregarding them; Tilaka and Bhūṣaṇa cite a dictionary sense of 'anubandha' as the arising of harm, i.e. Ravana never weighed what abducting Sita would bring.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Bhūṣaṇa (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (on 6.63.1) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Kumbhakarna laughs because Ravana is reaping the fruit of rejecting Vibhishana's advice.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 63

vr.6.63.4.practical_reading: Before a big decision, especially one driven by confidence or pride, sit down and trace where it leads.
misreadings: Not 'I told you so' for its own sake; Kumbhakarna still fights for his brother.

not_for: someone already full of regret about a past choice (can deepen self-blame)

vr.6.63.5.context: Continuing his rebuke after being woken, Kumbhakarna says a ruler who, relying on his power, does later what should come first and first what should come later, cannot tell good policy from bad. He adds that acts done out of place and time are spoiled like offerings poured into unconsecrated fires, and describes the right way: deliberate with ministers first. Then he agrees to fight for his brother.
vr.6.63.5.core_teaching: Order matters: deliberation should precede action. A leader who acts first and consults afterward has lost the ability to judge.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (on 6.63.6) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 63
commentaries.gist: Has Kumbhakarna say one who, trusting his own power, leaves until last what should be first, or does first what should follow, cannot tell wise from foolish.

vr.6.63.5.practical_reading: Consult and plan before acting, not after; when a decision has gone wrong, check whether the steps were taken in the wrong order.
misreadings: Not a rule against ever acting quickly; it targets acting on power without prior deliberation.
not_for: a reader needing comfort rather than critique
speaks_to: managers, founders, parents making big decisions
someone about to act before consulting the people affected

vr.6.65.4.context: Mahodara, a courtier, has argued against Kumbhakarna fighting alone and proposed a scheme instead. Kumbhakarna rebukes him and tells Ravana he will rid him of his fear by killing Rama today: heroes don't thunder in vain like rainless clouds; they don't praise themselves but do hard deeds without display. He adds that Mahodara's counsel would please only timid, foolish kings who think themselves wise, then goes to battle, where he dies.
vr.6.65.4.core_teaching: Real courage shows itself in hard deeds, not in boasting.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Valiant men cannot bear to praise themselves with their own tongues; they achieve hard feats without displaying their ability in words.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads the verbs as collective singulars: a hero neither tolerates insult from others nor esteems himself highly.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 6.65.3) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 65
commentaries.gist: Has Kumbhakarna say heroes do not thunder in vain like rainless clouds, need not boast, and achieve the hardest feats without bluster.

vr.6.65.4.practical_reading: Let your work speak; when tempted to announce or overclaim, do the hard thing quietly instead.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of Kumbhakarna's cause; he fights for Ravana's unjust war.

not_for: someone with low self-worth who needs to learn to name their strengths
speaks_to: people tempted to self-promote or over-promise

vr.7.40.10.context: As the allies take leave, Hanuman asks a boon: may his love and devotion stay fixed on Rama, and may he live as long as Rama's story is told on earth; may celestial women recite it to him, and hearing the nectar of Rama's deeds, he will dispel his longing as the wind scatters clouds. Rama rises from the throne, embraces him and grants it, and gives him his own necklace.
vr.7.40.10.core_teaching: For Hanuman, hearing Rama's story is how he bears separation from Rama; the story keeps the beloved present.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Glosses Hanuman's longing as the yearning to be with Rama.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the longing as the hard-to-bear sorrow born of parting, which the recited story will scatter like a breeze dispersing a thin cloud.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 40
commentaries.gist: Has Hanuman ask that the Apsaras recount Rama's history to him, so the nectar of his deeds will dispel his anxieties as wind chases clouds.

vr.7.40.10.practical_reading: When separated from someone or something you love, return to their story; telling and hearing it can ease the ache.
misreadings: Not an escape from life; Hanuman's listening is devotion that sustains him.
cautions: Southern-only verse.
not_for: readers who want no devotional framing
speaks_to: missing a loved one far away
devotees who find comfort in kathā, bhajan or reading
grief that seeks comfort in memories and stories

vr.7.40.12.context: Hanuman has asked to live as long as Rama's story is told. Rama rises, embraces him and grants it: as long as the worlds last, the story will last, and with it Hanuman's fame and life. Then he says that for each of Hanuman's services he would give his life, and hopes he never has to repay, since one repays only when the benefactor is in trouble. He places his own pearl necklace on Hanuman's chest.
vr.7.40.12.core_teaching: Rama grants Hanuman life as long as his story lasts, and declares a debt of gratitude he hopes never to repay, because repaying would mean Hanuman had fallen into misfortune.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (on 7.40.21) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: A person becomes eligible for a return favour only in calamity; so wishing to repay a benefactor amounts to wishing him distress, and Rama silently prays misfortune never touches Hanuman.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 7.40.19-20) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Rama ratifies the boon: as long as the worlds endure the story endures, and with it Hanuman's fame and life; Tilaka says this grants Hanuman permanence for the whole cosmic age.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 7.40.22-23) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Rama then fastens his moon-bright pearl necklace with a cat's-eye centre on Hanuman, who glows like golden Meru crowned by the moon.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 40
commentaries.gist: Has Rama say he would give his life for every service and still remain Hanuman's debtor, that the memory will ever abide in his heart, and that one turns to those one has helped in misfortune.

vr.7.40.12.practical_reading: Some kindnesses cannot be repaid; carry them as a grateful debt and wish your benefactor never to need anything from you.
misreadings: Not a refusal to repay kindness; it is a wish that the friend never be in need.
cautions: Text varies between editions; if quoting the Sanskrit, note that two lines are not in the itihasa.io southern text.
not_for: someone carrying unhealthy obligation or guilt toward a benefactor
speaks_to: deep gratitude toward a mentor, parent, friend
someone who has been helped greatly and cannot repay

vr.7.40.6.context: After the coronation, Rama sends his allies home. He has told Sugriva to rule Kishkindha and cherish his companions, and embraced him repeatedly. Now he tells Vibhishana to rule Lanka by dharma, never let his mind turn to unrighteousness, and always remember Rama and Sugriva with love; then go, free of worry. The assembly applauds. Hanuman then asks his boon.
vr.7.40.6.core_teaching: Rama's parting wish to a friend: rule rightly, and keep the bond alive in memory with love.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 7.40.9-10) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Śiromaṇi glosses wise kings as those with dharma-guided judgement; Tilaka and Govindarāja read 'dhruvam' as for a long time.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Finds a veiled warning in asking to be remembered with Sugriva: Vibhishana must never take on Ravana's arrogance, or Rama and Sugriva would deal with him as they did with Ravana.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 40
commentaries.gist: Rama, having embraced Sugriva again and again, speaks affectionately to Vibhishana as he sends his allies home.

vr.7.40.6.practical_reading: At partings, ask only to be remembered with love, and send friends off free of worry.
misreadings: Tilaka's 'veiled warning' reading shows the line is not only sentimental; it also reminds a new ruler of accountability.
not_for: fresh bereavement (being 'remembered' can sound like a death)
speaks_to: farewells: friends moving away, colleagues leaving, graduations

vr.7.48.14.context: Composing herself, Sita gives Lakshmana a message for Rama: he knows she is pure and devoted; she has been abandoned out of his fear of ill fame, and it is her part to ward off reproach from him. He should treat the citizens as his brothers, which is his highest dharma. She does not grieve for herself as much as for the people's slander. She adds that a husband is a woman's god, kinsman and teacher, asks Lakshmana to look at her (visibly pregnant) and leave. Lakshmana bows, unable to speak.
vr.7.48.14.core_teaching: Sita, though wronged, speaks with composure: what grieves her most is not her own hardship but the false talk that caused it.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads the message as turning to statecraft: Rama should treat citizens like brothers, and act so as to remain free of public reproach.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Notes that Sita disregards both bodily hardship and the ignorant townsfolk's gossip, grounding her sacrifice in devotion.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 7.48.17) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: All gloss her request that Lakshmana look at her as showing she is visibly pregnant, so there is a witness.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 48
commentaries.gist: Sita's lament and message to Rama at the river (chapter read for context).

vr.7.48.14.practical_reading: When falsely accused, it is natural to feel the injustice of the lie more than the hardship; naming that can help.
misreadings: Not a model of a wife accepting abandonment as right; our note is correct that she is the one wronged.
The 'husband is a woman's deity' line that follows must not be used to counsel submission to an unjust partner.
cautions: Context is a pregnant wife abandoned because of gossip; handle with care for readers facing separation, slut-shaming or community judgement.
Verse boundaries are tangled across editions.
not_for: a reader being pressured to accept mistreatment from a spouse
speaks_to: someone hurt by rumours or false accusations
people judged by their community (caste, gossip, social media)

vr.7.48.6.context: Lakshmana, in anguish, has just told Sita on the bank of the Ganga that Rama has abandoned her because of public gossip about her time in Lanka, and that he must leave her near Valmiki's hermitage. Sita, pregnant, faints, then speaks: her body seems made for sorrow; what sin did she commit? Before, she lived in the forest happily following Rama; now how can she live alone, and to whom will she tell her grief? She adds she cannot drown herself, because Rama's line would end with her child.
vr.7.48.6.core_teaching: Sita voices the loneliness of an innocent person cast out: the worst of the exile is having no one to share her sorrow with.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (on 7.48.5-6) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Contrast this solitary banishment with the earlier forest exile, which she bore gladly as long as she followed Rama.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (on 7.48.5-6) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads a devotional nuance: with Rama present, even apparent suffering was joy; without him, she is alone with her grief.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Śiromaṇi (on 7.48.7) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: She cannot answer the sages who will ask why she was cast off, because she committed no wrong to justify it.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 48
commentaries.gist: Has Sita ask how, abandoned by all, she can live in solitude, and to whom she will confide her affliction.

vr.7.48.6.practical_reading: Names the particular pain of isolation in sorrow; the first help for someone cast out is someone to listen.
misreadings: Not a sign that she deserved it; the commentators stress she committed no wrong.
cautions: The next verses mention her thought of drowning herself in the Ganga (rejected for her unborn child); do not quote them to a vulnerable reader.
Pregnancy and abandonment by a spouse; sensitive for readers facing separation, divorce or single parenthood.
not_for: a reader in active crisis without a pointer to real support
speaks_to: someone newly isolated by divorce, migration, illness or family rejection
the loneliness of grief with no one to talk to

vr.7.49.10.context: Lakshmana has left Sita weeping alone at the Ganga. Valmiki, told by the hermit boys, comes with the guest-offering. He tells her he knows by his inner sight that she is sinless, that she is now under his care, that the women ascetics near his hermitage will look after her like their own child, and here: accept this welcome, trust me, let your fever of sorrow go, think of this as coming home. Sita bows at his feet, says 'so be it', and follows him; the sages' wives welcome her. Her twin sons Kusha and Lava are born there.
vr.7.49.10.core_teaching: Valmiki offers a wronged, abandoned woman belief, safety and a home: the first answer to rejection is welcome.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Complete the simile: dwell here just as in your own home; Tilaka glosses 'like a calf' in the previous verse as 'like one's own child'.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Calling Sita 'child' (vatse) reveals Valmiki's friendship with Janaka as well as Dasharatha.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 7.49.17-18) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Sita's quiet 'so be it', with bowed head and joined palms, shows dignity amid devastation; the sages' wives are the women ascetics he mentioned.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 49
commentaries.gist: Has Valmiki come with the arghya, tell Sita he knows her purity by his spiritual vision, and assure her she is under his protection.

vr.7.49.10.practical_reading: When someone arrives at your door rejected or shamed, believe them, make them safe, and let them feel at home.
misreadings: Not a suggestion that the abandonment was fine because she found shelter.
cautions: Two verses with different speakers merged.
not_for: a reader who has nowhere to go (could feel like a fairy-tale rescue)
speaks_to: someone starting over after being cast out (divorce, family rejection, displacement)
volunteers, hosts, shelter workers, teachers welcoming newcomers

vr.7.53.4.context: After Sita's banishment, Rama has grieved and not held court for four days. Lakshmana has just consoled him, and Rama, pleased, calls him a rare kinsman. Here he says four days without attending to the citizens' business cuts him to the core; he orders the subjects, priest, ministers and all men and women with petitions summoned, adding that a king who does not attend to his people's affairs daily falls into a dreadful hell. He then tells the story of King Nriga, cursed for keeping petitioners waiting.
vr.7.53.4.core_teaching: Even in private grief, Rama feels his neglect of people who depend on him as a wound, and returns to duty.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Supply 'have passed' to the elliptical opening; Śiromaṇi joins verses 4 and 5 as one sentence: the lapse torments Rama, so he summons everyone to fulfil their petitions at once.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 53
commentaries.gist: Has Rama say four days have passed since he attended to his people's interests and his soul is tormented, then summon the petitioners.

vr.7.53.4.practical_reading: Grief can take us away from responsibilities; when ready, return to them without self-punishment, starting with whoever has been waiting.
misreadings: Not a demand to suppress grief and get back to work immediately; Rama took four days.
The 'king falls into hell' line that follows is about rulers' duty, not a threat to grieving readers.
cautions: The grief here follows Rama's own unjust abandonment of Sita; a reading must not present him simply as the sufferer.
Southern-only passage.
not_for: someone in fresh grief being pushed back to work too soon
speaks_to: someone returning to work or caregiving after a personal crisis
leaders and public servants who have let things slide

vr.7.72.10.context: Shatrughna, sent by Rama to kill the demon Lavana, has founded and ruled the city of Madhura (Mathura) for twelve years. On a visit home he reports that all is done, says twelve years apart from Rama have been too long, and asks not to be sent away again: like a calf without its mother, he cannot live far away any longer. Rama embraces him, tells him not to lose heart since a king must protect his people, invites him to visit from time to time, and asks him to stay seven nights before returning.
vr.7.72.10.core_teaching: Shatrughna voices raw homesickness and longing for his brother after long service far away.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the plea as 'grant my request to stay with you', likening long absence from Rama to a calf separated from its mother.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śiromaṇi and Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (on 7.72.11) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Twelve full years have elapsed; with duty done, Shatrughna's pent-up longing breaks out, and the commentators let its simplicity speak.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 72
commentaries.gist: Has Shatrughna report Lavana's death, say twelve years far from Rama are enough, and ask not to remain away like a calf separated from its mother.

vr.7.72.10.practical_reading: Gives voice to homesickness after long service far from family; it is not weakness to say you miss home.
misreadings: Not childishness; the same verse reports a hard task completed.
not_for: someone grieving a parent's death (the 'motherless calf' image may be too raw)
speaks_to: migrants, soldiers, students, workers posted far from family
adult children missing parents or siblings

vr.7.72.14.context: Shatrughna has begged to stay near Rama after twelve years ruling Madhura. Rama embraces him, tells him not to despond, since kings do not lose heart abroad and must protect their subjects; he may visit from time to time. Here Rama says Shatrughna is dearer to him than life, but the kingdom must be looked after; so stay seven nights, then return with your people. Shatrughna, in a subdued voice, agrees, stays seven nights and goes back.
vr.7.72.14.core_teaching: Rama holds love and duty together: he affirms his brother is dearer than life, gives him time together, and still sends him back to his responsibility.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (on 7.72.15-16) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Rama softens stern duty with warmth, inviting regular visits; Śiromaṇi notes his balanced candour: Shatrughna is beloved beyond life, yet the realm's protection cannot be neglected.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (on 7.72.17-18) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Because protecting Mathura cannot be set aside, Rama grants a seven-night reunion; Shatrughna's subdued 'so be it' shows him putting longing under dharma.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 72
commentaries.gist: Has Rama say he too cherishes Shatrughna more than life, yet the kingdom's security comes first; stay seven days, then return to Madhura.

vr.7.72.14.practical_reading: Love does not cancel duty: make time to be together fully, then return to your responsibilities, and plan the next visit.
misreadings: Not coldness: Rama embraces him and affirms his love first.
cautions: The response to homesickness is 'go back'; for a lonely reader that can feel hard. Pair with the invitation to visit (7.72.15).
not_for: someone wanting permission to come home for good
speaks_to: parents and adult children who live apart
families saying goodbye at the end of a visit
people whose work keeps them far from loved ones

vr.7.83.15.context: Having finished other duties, Rama proposes to perform the Rajasuya, the imperial sacrifice. Bharata gently objects that it would bring the destruction of many royal lines and suffering on earth, and Rama, the protector of all, should not do it. Rama is pleased, praises Bharata's words as firm and righteous, and gives up the plan: the wise should not do what afflicts the world, and good advice should be accepted even from the young. Lakshmana then proposes the Ashvamedha instead.
vr.7.83.15.core_teaching: A wise leader drops a plan that would harm people, and accepts good counsel even from a younger person.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka and Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Both read 'bālānāṃ tu' as 'even from the young'; by accepting Bharata's correction, Rama shows the humility of a dharmic ruler, opening the way for the non-violent Ashvamedha proposal.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of the three commentators (on 7.83.19) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: All unpack the compound for the Rajasuya that was 'about to enter my resolve'; Tilaka and Śiromaṇi supply that Rama turns back his intention.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 83
commentaries.gist: Has Rama renounce the Rajasuya on Bharata's counsel, say the wise should never do what harms the world, and that good advice should be taken even from a child.

vr.7.83.15.practical_reading: Be willing to drop your own grand plan when someone, even someone junior, shows it would hurt people.
misreadings: Not that elders are always wrong; the point is openness to good counsel from any quarter.
not_for: a reader needing comfort rather than guidance
speaks_to: managers, parents and teachers receiving feedback from juniors or children
leaders weighing projects with human costs

vr.7.97.4.context: Years after the banishment, Valmiki brings Sita to Rama's assembly during the Ashvamedha and swears to her purity. Rama answers with joined palms: he accepts Valmiki's word; Sita proved herself before the gods long ago, yet public slander was powerful, and knowing she was innocent he abandoned her out of fear of the people; he asks Valmiki's forgiveness, acknowledges Kusha and Lava as his sons, and wants Sita proven pure before the world. Sita instead calls on the Earth, which rises and takes her; she does not return.
vr.7.97.4.core_teaching: Rama admits he abandoned Sita knowing she was innocent, because he feared public opinion, and asks pardon; the confession does not undo the wrong, and Sita refuses another trial.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā's Tilaka (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Clears Rama of private suspicion: knowing Sita sinless, he banished her purely from fear of public talk; he consents to a fresh proof only to silence that slander.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya's Śiromaṇi (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'fear of the people' as dread of scriptural censure, and says Rama begs Valmiki's pardon for the offence of the abandonment.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja's Bhūṣaṇa (on 7.97.2) (AI synthesis on itihasa.io, not peer-reviewed)
commentaries.gist: Rama's 'so it is' means the proof must be done not for his own trust, which Valmiki's oath already gave, but for the public.

commentaries.who: Hari Prasad Shastri's translation (wisdomlib), chapter 97
commentaries.gist: Has Rama say that though convinced of her innocence, he cast off Sita from fear of the people, ask the brahmin's pardon, and acknowledge the twins.

vr.7.97.4.practical_reading: Admitting a wrong done under social pressure is necessary but does not by itself repair it; giving in to what people say can cost the people we love most.
misreadings: As our note says: the admission does not undo the wrong.
Not a defence of putting reputation over justice; the commentators' attempts to excuse Rama should not be presented as the verse's meaning.
cautions: Leads directly to Sita leaving for the earth; for readers who were disbelieved or abandoned it may be painful.
Commentators largely defend Rama; a reading should not force that frame on a hurting reader.
not_for: a reader being pressured to accept an apology and reconcile
speaks_to: someone who gave in to family or community pressure and hurt an innocent person
people facing honour or reputation pressures
the person wronged who hears an apology that comes too late

yv.1.1.7.context: The Yoga Vasishtha opens with a frame story: the Brahmin Sutikshna, unsure whether action or knowledge leads to liberation, asks the sage Agastya. Agastya answers with this image of two wings and then tells the story of Karunya, who stopped all ritual action because two scriptures seemed to point in opposite directions, until his father set him straight.
yv.1.1.7.core_teaching: Freedom is not reached by knowledge alone or by action alone but by both working together, as a bird needs both wings to fly.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: As a bird reaches its goal only with both wings, the highest state needs knowledge and action together, though not at the same instant: action purifies the mind, knowledge removes ignorance, as a mirror needs both cleaning and light.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. I)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders the two wings as knowledge and acts, and the following verse as: neither acts nor knowledge alone produce emancipation. Agastya then introduces Karunya's story to illustrate it.

yv.1.1.7.practical_reading: Teachers use this verse against two opposite traps: thinking without ever acting, and busyness without reflection. When stuck waiting for certainty, take the next small step and keep reflecting as you go.
misreadings: Not a claim that action and contemplation must happen at the same moment; the commentary explicitly denies that
Not a dismissal of either study or work as unnecessary
cautions: In Advaita reading, 'action' here means duty and ritual that purify the mind; a modern 'just do things' gloss is a simplification
not_for: someone exhausted or burnt out who needs rest rather than a push to act
a reader in acute grief
speaks_to: feeling stuck between overthinking and doing
students and professionals who read a lot but don't act
people who keep busy but feel directionless

yv.1.10.19.context: Dasharatha has noticed his son is changed since his pilgrimage and sends for news. The servant says Rama barely eats, avoids company, sees beautiful things with sorrowful eyes and calls everything unreal before falling silent (v.18). After this verse he says Rama seeks lonely places, lives like a wandering ascetic, and neither laughs, sings nor cries. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha then ask to hear Rama himself.
yv.1.10.19.core_teaching: An outside observer's description of withdrawal: no joy in humour, pleasure or work, only silence. The text treats it seriously and responds with care and conversation, not scolding.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
