commentaries.gist: Brief gloss only: 'does not rise' means he does not feel delight; the surrounding verses are explained as signs of a turning away from enjoyments.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. X)
commentaries.gist: The attendant's whole report (vv. 9-28) lists the symptoms: little eating, avoiding company, calling all things unreal, solitude, no laughing, singing or crying; the king is distressed.

yv.1.10.19.practical_reading: Losing the spark for jokes, pleasures and work is worth noticing and naming. In the story, the people around Rama noticed, worried, and brought help; it's okay to let someone do that for you.
misreadings: Not a portrait of spiritual achievement to imitate
Not 'withdrawal is wisdom'; the sages treat it as a state needing guidance
cautions: This describes classic signs of depression (anhedonia, withdrawal). Our 'misuse' field rightly says to talk to someone or a doctor if it lasts weeks; keep that
The sages' reading that Rama's state is dispassion, not illness, should not be applied to a real reader
not_for: anyone with suicidal thoughts, without a clear pointer to help

yv.1.10.9.context: Rama has returned from a pilgrimage across the land and has withdrawn: he neglects his daily duties, eats little, and sits apart. His worried attendants report this to the king. In the following verses they list his symptoms (he performs his rites only sometimes, refuses food, takes no pleasure in play), and in the next chapter Rama is brought before the court, where the king and the sages question him gently.
yv.1.10.9.core_teaching: The verse simply reports that Rama has changed since his journey. The book treats this withdrawal as the start of a real search for meaning that needs a wise listener.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. X)
commentaries.gist: The servants tell the king they themselves have wasted away with worry; Rama has been dejected since the pilgrimage, carries out his daily rites only half-heartedly, and has stopped eating and enjoying pastimes.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: The commentator gives no separate gloss on this narrative verse; the chapter's colophon titles it 'Raghava's dejection' (rāghava-viṣāda), placing it as the opening of Rama's dispassion.

yv.1.10.9.practical_reading: Loss of interest after a big experience (travel, a loss, a milestone) can signal that old goals no longer fit. It deserves attention and a good conversation, not dismissal.
misreadings: Not a romanticisation of depression as a spiritual stage
Not a claim that withdrawal is always a sign of wisdom
cautions: Rama's symptoms (not eating, withdrawing, neglecting duties) overlap with clinical depression; a reading must not suggest that such symptoms need only spiritual reframing. Encourage talking to someone, including professionals.
not_for: someone in a severe depressive episode if the reading implies it is 'just a phase of awakening'
speaks_to: feeling flat or changed after travel or a major life event
parents or friends worried about someone who has withdrawn

yv.1.11.37.context: Rama has been brought before the court, pale and silent. The king and Vasishtha speak to him; then Vishvamitra asks why his eyes are so restless and what is troubling him, noting that the usual causes of distress don't apply to a prince like him. This verse is his closing invitation; Rama, encouraged, sheds his gloom and begins his long account of what troubles him.
yv.1.11.37.core_teaching: A respected teacher invites the troubled young man to say openly what is on his mind, promising that speaking it out is the way to be freed of the anxieties.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Construes it as: speak, and you will obtain all that you wish; once what you want is gained, the mental afflictions will not split you open again. The next verse's 'speech of the sage' is read as Vishvamitra's.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra has Vishvamitra ask Rama to state his heart's craving so it can be settled for good; Rama then shakes off his sorrow like a peacock at the sound of thunder.

yv.1.11.37.practical_reading: The first step out of a heavy silence is often being asked kindly and given room to speak. It also models how to ask someone who has withdrawn: gently, without judgement.
misreadings: Not a promise that every wish will be granted
Not a claim that talking alone cures everything
cautions: Our record has no prasang attached to this verse (prasang is null); link it to the 'Rama comes home and loses interest' story
not_for: a reader who has tried to speak up and been dismissed, if framed as 'just talk and it goes away'
speaks_to: people who find it hard to ask for help
anyone wanting to support a withdrawn friend or child

yv.1.12.15.context: Asked by Vishvamitra why he is so low, Rama explains that after his pilgrimage he began to reflect: people are born to die and die to be born, pleasures are unstable, the world is built by the mind, and he has been chasing mirages like a deer. This verse caps that reflection. He then says such thinking made him lose all taste for the world, and asks the sages what this world really is.
yv.1.12.15.core_teaching: Rama questions the worth of everything he has and asks who he really is. The text treats this questioning as the healthy start of inquiry, not as despair to be fixed.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Unpacks the questions: who am I, what is this world in essence and why has it come, is it all false or partly true? If false, let it be false: no one loses anything.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XII)
commentaries.gist: Places the verse in Rama's account of how pilgrimage reflections on birth, death and the mind's projections drained his interest in pleasures and led to questions about reality.

yv.1.12.15.practical_reading: When nothing you own or do feels meaningful, the Yoga Vasishtha treats that emptiness as the doorway to a real question (who am I, what matters?) to be explored with a teacher, not a dead end.
misreadings: Not a recommendation to quit your job or responsibilities
Not nihilism: it is the question that opens the teaching, not its conclusion (our 'misuse' field already says this)
'Mithya' here is philosophical (not ultimately real), not 'pointless'
cautions: For a reader whose 'nothing matters' is depression, validating detachment could deepen it; pair with a grounding verse and gentle encouragement to talk to someone
Rama's lament runs for many chapters and is very bleak; don't quote other lines from it to a low reader
not_for: someone with signs of clinical depression or suicidal thoughts, unless paired with care and the answer verses

yv.1.12.22.context: Late in Rama's first lament he says the thought of how to end sorrow burns him like fire inside a hollow tree (v.21). In this verse he admits he holds back tears because of what his people would think. The next verse says his face shows nothing, his crying is tearless, and only the discernment in his heart sees it when he is alone. He ends by saying his mind finds no rest, like a chained wild elephant.
yv.1.12.22.core_teaching: Rama admits the hidden weight of sorrow he carries and that he hides it out of fear of how his own people would see him. Saying this aloud to the sages is where his help begins.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: worldly misery sits on his heart like a rock and stops his breath; he wants to weep but holds back for fear of his people; his tearless grief is known only to his own consciousness in solitude.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Sanskrit, Vairagya 12.21-27)
commentaries.gist: Before: anxiety burns him like fire in a hollow tree. After: tearless, blank-faced crying seen only in solitude; prosperity deludes; his mind finds no rest, like a chained elephant.

yv.1.12.22.practical_reading: Many people carry grief or strain silently because they fear looking weak to family or colleagues. Noticing that you're holding back, and finding one safe person to tell, is the first relief.
misreadings: Not praise for keeping a stiff upper lip (our 'misuse' field says this well)
Not a statement that crying is shameful
cautions: Rama's lament is unrelievedly bleak; follow with something that opens a way forward
not_for: no strong contraindication
speaks_to: men or eldest children expected not to cry

yv.1.13.11.context: Still on wealth and fortune, Rama has said riches bring woe and conceal poison like a cultivated aconite plant. Here he names three rare types of person. The verses that follow describe wealth as a deep, rough cave and a great mountain river.
yv.1.13.11.core_teaching: Wealth, courage and power tend to bring their own vice (blame, boasting, partiality); the person who holds them without that vice is rare.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Raises the objection that some rich people are righteous and famous, and answers with this verse: yes, but such people are rare. He calls the verse self-explanatory.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders the three rarities as a rich man without blemish, a brave man without vanity, and a master without partiality.

yv.1.13.11.practical_reading: Used as a checklist for leaders and achievers: have the money without the arrogance, the courage without the bragging, the authority without favouritism.
misreadings: Not proof that the rich, brave or powerful are bad
Not a male-only standard; the point applies to anyone
not_for: someone feeling powerless or poor, if used to sneer at others
speaks_to: parents talking about character with teens

yv.1.13.8.context: Rama's lament begins with wealth (Lakshmi, fortune). In this chapter he says riches breed vices the way milk feeds a snake's poison, that they soil the learned and brave like dust on gems, and that they bring woe rather than happiness. The next verses list the three rare kinds of men (v. 11).
yv.1.13.8.core_teaching: People are often kind to everyone until money and status harden them, the way cold wind turns soft snow into hard ice.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Explains 'cool and soft to touch' as a figure for compassion and courtesy, 'vātyā' as a gathering of winds, and 'made harsh' as made hard to bear.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as people being gentle to friends and strangers until riches harden their hearts, as wind stiffens frost; the surrounding verses say wealth corrupts the learned, the brave and the gentle.

yv.1.13.8.practical_reading: A check on how success or money is changing how we treat people, and a reminder to keep the warmth we had before.
misreadings: Not a claim that all wealthy people are cruel
Not a call to stay poor
cautions: Can feed resentment toward richer relatives or colleagues; frame it as self-examination
not_for: someone in financial hardship who may hear it as consolation-by-contempt for the rich
speaks_to: someone newly promoted or newly well-off
feeling hurt by a friend who changed after success

yv.1.14.10.context: After wealth, Rama turns to life itself: the body is like foam on the sea and he takes no pleasure in mere living. In this verse he defines real living. Next he says trees, animals and birds also 'live', but only one who lives by reflection truly lives, and that scripture is a burden to the undiscerning and knowledge a burden to the passionate.
yv.1.14.10.core_teaching: A life counts as truly lived when it reaches what is really worth reaching, the lasting peace after which grief doesn't return; mere survival is not enough.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'what is to be attained' as the supreme human goal that must necessarily be reached, and 'supreme repose' as the bliss of liberation while living; the next verse's 'mere living' is life without reflection.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XIV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders true living as gaining what is worth gaining so that there is no more sorrow; the following verses contrast vegetable and animal life with a life lived by understanding.

yv.1.14.10.practical_reading: A prompt to ask what you are actually living for, beyond getting through the days, and to measure a life by inner peace reached rather than years or possessions.
misreadings: Not a statement that ordinary lives are worthless
Not a reason to despise one's own life when one feels it lacks meaning
cautions: The surrounding verses disparage 'mere living' and the body (foam on the sea); for a reader who feels their life has no value, this framing could deepen hopelessness. Pair with an affirming verse.
not_for: anyone expressing that their life is not worth living
acute grief
speaks_to: feeling that life is only routine
graduates or retirees asking what comes next

yv.1.16.22.context: Rama, asked why he has grown so withdrawn, gives a long lament. This chapter is about the mind: he says it is hotter than fire, harder to master than a mountain is to cross and tougher than a thunderbolt (v.21). After this verse he compares it to a sea full of whirlpools, says subduing it is harder than drinking the ocean or uprooting Meru, and that it is the root of all trouble and must be treated like an illness.
yv.1.16.22.core_teaching: The untrained mind grabs at whatever attracts it and then abandons it, including worthwhile work, almost at once. Rama is naming the problem honestly; Vasishtha's later teaching is that the mind can be trained.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary)
commentaries.gist: The mind attaches instantly to sense objects and just as quickly abandons even long-practised good activities, like a boy who drops his long-pursued studies the moment he is handed some toy.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: Surrounding verses call the mind restless and dull at once, harder to subdue than drinking the ocean, the cause of every exertion, and something to be treated like a disease; Rama asks how to master it.

yv.1.16.22.practical_reading: Starting and dropping tasks is an old, ordinary feature of the mind, not a personal defect. Naming the pattern is the first step; the YV's own answer is patient, repeated training rather than self-blame.
misreadings: Not a diagnosis that you are lazy or broken
Not a claim that the mind can't be trained: it is Rama's complaint, which the rest of the book answers
Not a comment on attention disorders; don't present it as medical insight
cautions: Nearby verses are very bleak about the mind (a demon seizing a child, v.20); quote this one alone
A reader with diagnosed ADHD may find a 'scripture says your mind is a bird on meat' framing shaming; keep it general
not_for: someone already harshly self-critical about focus, unless paired with the 'train it gently' verse (2.9.33)
speaks_to: starting many things and finishing none

yv.1.16.25.context: At the end of his account of the mind, Rama says subduing it is harder than drinking the ocean or uprooting Mount Meru (v. 24). Here he states its central role, and in the next verse he says hundreds of joys and sorrows spring from the mind like forests from a mountain, but fall away when cut by discernment.
yv.1.16.25.core_teaching: The world we experience depends on the mind, so the mind is the patient: it must be deliberately treated, the way one treats an illness.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'to be treated' as: to be removed, like a disease. The following verse is read as discernment thinning out the mind's hundreds of pleasures and pains.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders the mind as the cause of all exertions and the seat of the three worlds; its weakening weakens worldliness, and it needs careful cure.

yv.1.16.25.practical_reading: When life feels overwhelming, change begins with working on the mind that experiences it, deliberately and consistently, the way one follows a treatment.
misreadings: Not a claim that external problems are imaginary
Not 'it's all in your head' blame
cautions: For a reader with mental illness, 'your world is your mind' can sound like blame; stress that treatment, including professional help, fits the verse's own medical image
not_for: someone facing real external injustice or crisis, if used to dismiss it
speaks_to: feeling that one's outlook colours everything
someone starting a meditation, therapy or self-care routine

yv.1.16.3.context: Rama now describes the mind. Just before this he says it wanders like a hungry village dog; just after, that it is always empty, caught in the net of bad hopes, and roams like a deer that has lost its herd. Later in the chapter he says the mind is harder to master than drinking the ocean (v. 24) and is the cause of everything (v. 25).
yv.1.16.3.core_teaching: The restless mind can't be filled by acquisitions; like a woven basket in water, whatever is poured in runs out, so the emptiness remains.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Defines the 'karaṇḍaka' as a woven bamboo or cane container, and reads the surrounding verses as the mind roaming without discernment, never coming to rest.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as the mind seldom finding anything, and even with a good store, being as little content as a wicker vessel filled with water.

yv.1.16.3.practical_reading: If each new purchase, achievement or relationship fades quickly, the problem may be the container, not the contents. Teachers use it to turn attention from getting more to steadying the mind.
misreadings: Not a claim that wanting things is shameful
Not a counsel of despair: Rama names the problem that Vasishtha's teaching later addresses
cautions: Nearby verses are harsh about the mind; quote this one alone
not_for: someone in material need, for whom 'riches don't satisfy' can sound glib
speaks_to: chasing the next goal and feeling empty after each
shopping or scrolling to fill a gap
high achievers who never feel satisfied

yv.1.17.14.context: After the mind, Rama turns to craving (tṛṣṇā), which he says withers his good qualities the way a mouse gnaws a lute string. Just before this verse, craving pulls people up and down like a bucket in a well; just after, attachment to family spreads its net like a hunter catching birds.
yv.1.17.14.core_teaching: Craving is tied deep inside us and leads us around, the way a nose-rope leads a bullock wherever the driver wants.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'in the body' as threaded through the inner mind, paralleling the nose-rope threaded through a bullock's nose; what the person is made to haul is the load of countless means for gains in this world and the next.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XVII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as a man led about like a beast of burden by avarice, which bends his heart as a string bends the beast and is hard to break.

yv.1.17.14.practical_reading: Notice what keeps pulling you: the urge to check, buy, prove or acquire. Seeing the rope is the first step to not being led by it.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of all desire or ambition
Not a claim that addiction is simply a moral failing
cautions: For someone struggling with addiction, pair it with practical support; the verse names the pull, it doesn't solve it
not_for: someone in early recovery who could hear it as shaming
speaks_to: feeling driven by wants one doesn't endorse

yv.1.17.43.context: Near the end of Rama's chapter on craving, after many images of how craving deceives and wears people down, he says what would release it: dropping 'cintā'. The following verses return to craving's power, grabbing anything like a fish at bait and making even serious people shallow.
yv.1.17.43.core_teaching: Craving is fed by repeatedly dwelling on what we want; stop the dwelling and the sorrow it brings falls away. This is called the cure for the disease of craving.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Introduces the verse as the means to give up craving. 'Cintā' here means repeatedly calling sense objects to mind; he cites the Gita's line that dwelling on objects breeds attachment.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XVII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as people getting rid of misery by being freed from anxieties, with abandoning cares called the best remedy for avarice.

yv.1.17.43.practical_reading: When a want keeps looping in your head, stop feeding it with attention: change what you look at, rehearse it less, and the grip loosens.
misreadings: Not 'stop caring about real problems'
Not 'anxiety is a choice'; it is about rumination on desires
cautions: For someone with an anxiety disorder, 'just give up worry' can feel invalidating; use the sense of letting go of fixation, not suppressing fear
not_for: clinical anxiety, if read as 'just stop worrying'
someone worried about a real danger

yv.1.17.50.context: Rama's chapter on craving piles up images: craving is like a lamp flame that is bright but burns and blackens (v. 49), like a dark Vindhya slope (v. 51). This verse says how quickly it can diminish even the greatest.
yv.1.17.50.core_teaching: Craving alone can reduce a wise, brave, steady person to something as light and worthless as grass, in an instant.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: 'Like Meru' means weighty; 'steady' means firm in not grasping. Craving shrinks such a person to grass by reducing him to begging; he quotes a verse that a supplicant is lighter than cotton.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XVII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as penury having the power to debase the best of men to straw in a moment, regardless of wisdom, heroism and gravity.

yv.1.17.50.practical_reading: No achievement or status protects us from being made small by wanting; staying grounded in what we value matters more than reputation.
misreadings: Not contempt for people who ask for help or are in need
cautions: The commentary's link to begging could shame people who must ask for help; avoid that angle in a reading
not_for: someone who has had to ask for financial help
speaks_to: a capable person ashamed of how a want or habit has diminished them

yv.1.26.11.context: Late in his lament Rama surveys a world turned upside down: enjoyments are great diseases and cravings mirages (v. 10). Here he locates the enemy inside: the senses and the mind. Following verses call ego a stain and the intellect weak.
yv.1.26.11.core_teaching: Our worst harm comes from within: senses and mind turned against us. The commentary explains this as the self, identified with the mind, causing its own suffering.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: The mind is the enemy because it causes bondage; the self, taking itself to be the mind, in a sense strikes itself by means of the mind, i.e. makes itself suffer.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XXVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as our very senses being our enemies before which truth gives way; the surrounding verses list friends as ties, enjoyments as disease, and ambition as a mirage.

yv.1.26.11.practical_reading: Many struggles are inner: self-sabotage, harsh self-talk, habits that undo our own plans. Seeing that clearly is the start of change; Vasishtha later teaches that the same mind can lift itself.
misreadings: Not a reason for self-blame or self-punishment
Not a claim that outside harms don't exist
cautions: 'The self strikes the self' must never be used near self-harm or suicidal thoughts; avoid for readers in crisis
Rama's lament here is bleak; it is the question, not the book's answer
not_for: anyone with self-harm history or suicidal ideation
someone being harmed by another person
speaks_to: feeling one is one's own obstacle

yv.1.26.21.context: In the same bleak survey Rama says compassion no longer rises and meanness comes easily (v. 20). Here: courage gives way, people rise and fall, bad company is easy and good company hard. Next: all things come and go, and wishes bind us to the world.
yv.1.26.21.core_teaching: Firmness erodes easily, and bad influences are always at hand while good company is rare, so good company is worth seeking out on purpose.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XXVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as patience turning into impatience, man subject to birth and death, good company rare and bad company within everyone's reach.

commentaries.who: Context in the text (Vairagya 29.22, Mumukshu 11.59)
commentaries.gist: Rama ends his lament (1.29.22) saying no trouble survives the company of the noble; Vasishtha later makes good company one of the four gatekeepers of liberation (2.11.59).

yv.1.26.21.practical_reading: Good company doesn't happen by default; choose and protect it. Be wary of how easily we drift toward people or feeds that pull us down.
misreadings: Not a licence to label people as 'bad' and shun them
not_for: someone isolated with no supportive people, if it adds blame
speaks_to: someone noticing their circle is pulling them down

yv.1.26.39.context: Rama has just said that not even great discernment can steady the mind (v. 38). Here he names the one person he thinks happy. Then he returns to life as an ocean of waves struck by the fire of death.
yv.1.26.39.core_teaching: The truly happy person is the awakened one whose mind is cool and settled within, yet who actively helps others and feels their pain.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Comments that such awakening is extremely rare, the point of the verse being that happiness belongs only to the rare enlightened person.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XXVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as: one whose endeavour is to do good to others and who feels for their woes is truly intelligent and happy under the influence of his cool judgment.

yv.1.26.39.practical_reading: Happiness here combines inner calm with active care for others; calm without care, or care without calm, falls short.
misreadings: Not a reference to the historical Buddha or a Buddhist claim unless a source says so
Not 'be happy by absorbing others' pain'; the mind stays cool
cautions: Caregivers already overloaded by others' pain may hear 'feel their pain' as more burden; emphasise the cool mind
not_for: a carer near burnout, unless framed around inner coolness
speaks_to: someone asking what real happiness looks like

yv.1.27.19.context: Rama describes people coming and going like leaves on trees, born again and again without reflection (v. 18). Here he asks who can sleep after an empty day of roaming. Next he says the rich man, just as he settles down to enjoy his gains, is cut off by death.
yv.1.27.19.core_teaching: A day spent in restless activity without any good work leaves no real rest; rest follows days that contain something worthwhile.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XXVII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as people returning home after travelling far and near, yet none finding rest by day or night except the virtuous few who live by honest dealings.

commentaries.who: Context in the Sanskrit text (Nirnaya Sagar ed.)
commentaries.gist: The verse sits among Upajati-metre verses on restless, fruitless activity: people come and go like leaves (v. 18); the rich man, just as he settles down to enjoy his gains, is cut off by death (v. 20).

yv.1.27.19.practical_reading: At day's end, ask whether at least one thing done was genuinely good. Busy days can still feel empty; one meaningful act can change how a day rests.
misreadings: Not a diagnosis of insomnia as moral failure
cautions: Don't use for readers with insomnia, anxiety or depression in a way that implies poor sleep means a wasted life
not_for: someone with clinical sleep problems
new parents sleeping badly
speaks_to: feeling restless at night after a hollow day

yv.1.27.9.context: This chapter is in a longer metre. Just before, Rama says people who are not crushed by trouble, not puffed up by good times and not captivated by beauty are rare (v. 8). Here he redefines bravery. Next he says no action of the restless lasts to the end.
yv.1.27.9.core_teaching: Real courage is not winning battles but crossing the ocean of one's own body, senses and churning mind.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Says those who cross the ocean of body and senses, with its passions as waves, by discernment and dispassion are the true heroes, and that this is rare.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XXVII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as battle fighters who withstand war elephants being less brave than those who withstand the surges of the mind amid the currents of the senses.

yv.1.27.9.practical_reading: Self-mastery, such as staying steady under provocation or temptation, takes more courage than outward victories, and deserves to be recognised as courage.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of soldiers or physical courage as worthless
not_for: veterans or bereaved military families, if it seems to belittle battlefield courage
speaks_to: someone who feels weak for struggling inwardly

yv.1.28.17.context: This chapter describes ceaseless change: the world is like a dancer whose glances flash like lightning (v. 16). Here Rama says those days, people and deeds are now memory, and we too will soon go. Next: things decay and arise daily with no end to this 'accursed' course.
yv.1.28.17.core_teaching: Everything that once seemed grand, including people, wealth and achievements, passes into memory, and so will we; this is a call to see clearly what lasts.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Briefly glosses the 'great ones' as those who once shone with festivals and splendour, the point being that even they survive only as memory.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XXVIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as the days, the great men and their deeds being retained only in memory, and such being our case too in a short time; the chapter describes the world's unending flux.

yv.1.28.17.practical_reading: Remembering that this time will also pass can loosen our grip on status and grudges and turn us toward what matters now.
misreadings: Not a call to despair or nihilism
cautions: Mentions our own death; can land heavily on someone grieving or elderly and frightened; not for Day 1 of a grief plan
not_for: fresh grief
someone with health anxiety or a terminal diagnosis, unless gently framed
speaks_to: someone over-invested in status or a grudge

yv.1.29.22.context: Rama closes his lament by asking the sage to scatter the mist over his heart with the light of knowledge (v. 21). This verse, the last of the chapter, voices his hope. In the next chapter he summarises and turns to direct questions about how to live.
yv.1.29.22.core_teaching: There is no mental affliction that doesn't fade through the company, and so the teaching, of noble-minded people, as the moon dispels night.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Construes: afflictions that do not perish through association with the noble-minded, and its fruit (their instruction), simply do not exist in the world.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XXIX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as no anxieties that cannot be ended by the society of good-minded men, as moonbeams remove night's darkness.

yv.1.29.22.practical_reading: Seek out wise, kind people when troubled; their presence and counsel can ease what we can't ease alone.
misreadings: Not a promise that company replaces professional help for serious illness
cautions: 'No trouble survives' is absolute; for severe depression it could make a reader feel broken if company hasn't helped
not_for: someone who has no access to supportive people right now, unless paired with practical steps
speaks_to: someone deciding whether to reach out to a mentor or friend

yv.1.30.17.context: Having finished his lament, Rama turns to questions: how can the mind become clear like a lake (v. 16)? Here: how can one active in the world stay unbound? Next: how can one treat others as oneself and others' goods as straw, and who has crossed the ocean of the world whose example to follow?
yv.1.30.17.core_teaching: Rama's key question: is it possible to be fully active in the world and still not be stained or bound by it, like water on a lotus leaf? The whole teaching answers yes.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XXX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as asking how one engaged in worldly affairs can remain untainted, pure and intact like a water drop on a lotus leaf; the next questions ask for an exemplar who crossed the ocean of the world.

commentaries.who: Context in the Sanskrit text (Nirnaya Sagar ed.)
commentaries.gist: The verse is one of a string of questions in the chapter titled 'Statement of purpose' (how can the mind become clear, v. 16; how to treat others as oneself, v. 18). No separate gloss on v. 17.

yv.1.30.17.practical_reading: The aim is not to escape work or family but to engage fully without being swallowed by worry and attachment.
misreadings: Not detachment as coldness toward people
not_for: someone in grief who may hear 'untouched' as 'you shouldn't be affected'

yv.1.31.17.context: Rama asks how to escape sorrow and says there is no ending of it without a method (yukti) (v. 16). Here he asks for that method. Then he asks how great people of old reached peace. The chapter ends with Rama vowing to stop eating, acting and finally breathing if he does not find an answer, and falling silent.
yv.1.31.17.core_teaching: Rama asks for a practical method that lets him go on with his work without sorrow, or failing that, the best way of handling life's affairs.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XXXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as a request for the best instruction to ward off the world's miseries, either by dealing with affairs or by renouncing them; the chapter closes with Rama's vow to withdraw from all activity if unanswered.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Treats vv. 16-17 together without a separate gloss; the following verses are read as Rama asking how the noble-minded of old achieved peace.

yv.1.31.17.practical_reading: The question many people really have: not 'should I quit?' but 'how do I keep doing this without it crushing me?' The book's answer is inner freedom while acting.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of quitting work or family
Not a promise of a quick technique
cautions: The same chapter ends with Rama threatening to stop eating and give up his body; never cite the surrounding verses to someone in distress
not_for: someone with suicidal thoughts, if the chapter context is drawn in
speaks_to: feeling trapped in a job or caregiving role

yv.1.31.7.context: Rama asks what course or refuge can save him from the unknown tracks of future births (v. 6), then flatters his teachers' power with this verse. He goes on to ask how this troublesome world can be enjoyed by anyone not deluded, and asks for the skill to live without sorrow (v. 17).
yv.1.31.7.core_teaching: Nothing in heaven or earth is so trivial that wise people cannot make it beautiful; Rama is expressing trust that his teachers can transform his bleak view.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'the wise' as minds empowered by austerity and knowledge like the sages present; nothing exists that they could not make delightful. He cites stories where a guru's curse turned into heaven or a death sentence was averted.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XXXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as nothing being so trifling on earth or in heaven that the gifted cannot raise it to consequence; the next verse asks how this vapid world can be relished except through ignorance.

yv.1.31.7.practical_reading: A wise eye can find worth and beauty in ordinary, even dull things; seek out those who see that way and learn to see that way yourself.
misreadings: Not 'everything is beautiful if you are positive', dismissing real hardship
cautions: The chapter ends (vv. 21-26) with Rama vowing to give up food, water and finally the body if he gets no answer; never quote that context to a distressed reader
not_for: someone in crisis, given the chapter's ending

yv.2.11.58.context: Vasishtha has urged Rama to keep away from the ignorant and those who keep bad company, and to honour the virtuous (v. 57). Here he gives the fruit of good company. Next comes the famous list of the four gatekeepers at liberation's door (calm, inquiry, contentment, good company) and the advice to cultivate at least one with full effort, since it brings the others.
yv.2.11.58.core_teaching: Regular contact with good people grows discernment, and discernment bears both a good life in the world and liberation.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Introduces the verse simply as stating the fruit of the preceding advice (keeping good company), and moves straight on to the four gatekeepers.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as wisdom gained through association with good people, like a tree yielding fruits of both enjoyment and liberation; the next verse names the four guards at the gate of liberation.

yv.2.11.58.practical_reading: Spend regular time with people whose judgement you admire; their good sense rubs off and improves both everyday life and inner life.
misreadings: Not a rejection of people who are struggling
not_for: isolated readers without access to such company, unless paired with books or online communities

yv.2.13.53.context: In the chapter on calm (śama), the first gatekeeper (Mumukshu sarga 13), Vasishtha has just called calm auspicious, peace itself and the remover of error (v. 52). Here he says calm wins over even enemies. He goes on to say calm minds shine like moonlit seas, and that the calm are honoured above kings.
yv.2.13.53.core_teaching: A person who is deeply calm, cool and clear within disarms hostility; even enemies tend to become friends.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as one content with quiet and clearness of soul, with a stoical mind, making friends of enemies; the chapter praises calm as the best state and the cure of error.

commentaries.who: Context in the Sanskrit text (Nirnaya Sagar ed.)
commentaries.gist: The verse sits in a run of praises of śama (vv. 52-81) that end with the refrain 'such a one is called calm'; the commentator's short glosses here explain the images (moonlight, milky ocean) rather than this verse.

yv.2.13.53.practical_reading: Staying calm and clear in conflict often lowers the temperature; many opponents soften when they meet steadiness rather than aggression.
misreadings: Not a duty to placate or stay with someone abusive
Not a promise that every enemy will change
cautions: Never use for someone in an abusive relationship as advice to 'stay calm and they'll change'
not_for: domestic abuse or harassment victims

yv.2.13.64.context: Vasishtha tells Rama to bear up under disease, disaster or greed with an even mind and to soothe the mind with the nectar of calm (v. 63). Here calm makes every act and meal sweet. Next he says a mind soaked in calm heals even wounds, and that no demon, enemy, tiger or snake troubles the calm.
yv.2.13.64.core_teaching: Everything done or eaten with a calm, cool mind tastes truly sweet; without calm, nothing really satisfies.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as whatever you do or eat with calm coolness of mind being sweeter to the soul than any sweet taste; the previous verse urges equanimity in disease and disaster.

commentaries.who: Context in the Sanskrit text (Nirnaya Sagar ed.)
commentaries.gist: The preceding line asks Rama to 'comfort the mind with sprinklings of the nectar of calm'; the next says a mind steeped in calm heals even cut limbs. No separate gloss on v. 64.

yv.2.13.64.practical_reading: Eat a meal or do a chore slowly and calmly today; the same ordinary things feel richer when the mind is settled.
misreadings: Not a claim that calm makes bad situations good
cautions: Food framing: avoid for readers with eating disorders
not_for: eating disorders

yv.2.13.67.context: After saying that no imp, demon, enemy, tiger or snake troubles a calm person (v. 66), Vasishtha calls calm an armour. Next: a king in his palace isn't as graceful as a calm person, and people are more delighted seeing a calm person than a dear one.
yv.2.13.67.core_teaching: Calm is like armour: the causes of suffering strike it but don't pierce it, as arrows glance off adamant rock.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: One whose limbs are all well protected by armour made of nectar-like calm; 'pierce' means afflict, and 'sorrows' means the things that cause sorrow.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as one whose mind and body are guarded by the armour of meekness never being pierced by the shafts of adversity, like the thunder-stone impenetrable to arrows.

yv.2.13.67.practical_reading: Cultivating calm doesn't stop hard things happening, but it keeps them from getting all the way in.
misreadings: Not 'calm people don't feel pain'
Not a call to numb emotions
cautions: For someone in raw pain, 'sorrows can't pierce you' may sound like a reproach; better for steady days
not_for: fresh grief
trauma

yv.2.13.72.context: This verse begins a series of definitions, each ending 'he is called śānta (calm)': one even toward all beings who neither craves nor rejects (v. 73), whose mind is the same inside and out, unshaken in death, festival or battle (v. 75), cool within and not drowning in things (v. 78).
yv.2.13.72.core_teaching: A calm person is one who meets the pleasant and the unpleasant through all the senses without being carried up into elation or down into dejection.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as the one called meek who feels neither pleasure nor pain at the sight, touch, hearing or taste of anything good or bad.

commentaries.who: Context in the Sanskrit text (Nirnaya Sagar ed.)
commentaries.gist: The verse opens a run of definitions (vv. 72-80) each ending 'he is called calm', covering evenness to all beings, sameness inside and out, steadiness in death, celebration and war.

yv.2.13.72.practical_reading: Notice the swings in a day, the lift at good news and the slump at bad, and practise meeting both with the same steadiness.
misreadings: Not emotional flatness or indifference
Not suppressing joy
cautions: Our note calls it a parallel to the Gita's sthitaprajña; that is our observation, not a commentary claim
not_for: depression with anhedonia, if 'not elated' is heard as an ideal of numbness
speaks_to: mood swings around feedback, social media likes, markets

yv.2.13.78.context: Among the definitions of the calm person: Vasishtha has described the one whose glance spreads grace (v. 77). Here, cool within and active but not confused. Next: one whose mind does not shrink even in terrible calamities, and whose mind, like space, is not stained though he deals with the world. The chapter ends urging Rama to follow calm as the great ones did.
yv.2.13.78.core_teaching: Calm is not withdrawal: the calm person is fully active in the world, cool inside, not swallowed by things, and clear-headed.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Explains that though engaged with objects as a man of affairs, he does not sink into them, i.e. does not become attached.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra's v. 78 describes one who feels a cool calmness within (the rest of his line is lost at a page break), followed by one untroubled by life's long tribulations who does not take the body to be himself.

yv.2.13.78.practical_reading: You don't need to step away from work or family to be calm; aim to be engaged and unhurried inside at the same time.
misreadings: Not detachment as disengagement

yv.2.14.11.context: Vasishtha has said that prosperity and liberation are all fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree of inquiry (v. 10). Here minds opened by inquiry float. Next: those who act with inquiring minds receive the finest fruits, while sorrows are the blossoms of non-inquiry growing in a fool's heart.
yv.2.14.11.core_teaching: Minds opened by inquiry and discernment don't go under in misfortune; like dried gourds in water, they stay afloat.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Viveka here means inquiry; minds that blossom by it do not sink, meaning they do not fall into despair; the gourds are dried bottle-gourds.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XIV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as minds of great men expanded by reasoning never being immersed under currents of calamity but floating like gourds on water.

yv.2.14.11.practical_reading: Understanding a hard situation clearly, rather than drowning in it, keeps us afloat while it passes.
misreadings: Not 'thinking people never suffer'
cautions: If someone is sinking, the verse could imply they lack discernment; frame as encouragement, not judgement
not_for: someone in severe depression, if implied that clear thinking alone should keep them afloat

yv.2.14.2.context: Opening the chapter on the second gatekeeper, Vasishtha says one should inquire constantly, with a mind purified by understanding the teachings (v. 1). Here inquiry is medicine. Next: the world is a forest of troubles whose shoots of desire, once cut by the saw of inquiry, don't grow back.
yv.2.14.2.core_teaching: Sustained inquiry sharpens understanding until it sees the highest truth; it is the great remedy for the chronic illness of worldly suffering.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'sharpness' as skill at plunging into subtle truth; inquiry is what develops that skill.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XIV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as understanding sharpened by reasoning coming to see the transcendent state, reasoning being the best medicine for the chronic disease of worldliness.

yv.2.14.2.practical_reading: When stuck in a recurring problem, ask honest questions about it (what is really happening, what do I assume?) instead of only reacting.
misreadings: Not endless overthinking or rumination
Not intellectual cleverness for its own sake
cautions: For ruminating or anxious readers, distinguish inquiry from looping worry
not_for: acute crisis where reflection is not yet possible

yv.2.14.50.context: This is the chapter on vichara, the second of the four gatekeepers to freedom. Vasishtha praises inquiry at length: an un-reflecting person suffers more than a sick man, and one should steady the mind by oneself through inquiry and carry it across the sea of delusion (v.49). Here he defines inquiry. He then says truth is known only through inquiry, truth brings rest in the self, and that rest ends sorrow.
yv.2.14.50.core_teaching: Inquiry means honestly asking who you really are and how you came to be caught in this round of trouble, and reasoning it through. Vasishtha says this leads to knowledge, knowledge to inner rest, and rest to the end of sorrow.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Two questions: am I the body and its parts or something different (the 'you' side), and how did worldly life arise on its ground (the 'that' side), reasoned in line with scripture, sages and the teaching tradition.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XIV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as reasoning within oneself about where the evil of worldliness began; surrounding verses say reason brings truth, truth brings peace, and peace dispels sorrow.

yv.2.14.50.practical_reading: When life feels pointless, sit down with the questions directly: what in me is actually suffering, and how did I get into this pattern? Write them out rather than just feeling them.
misreadings: Not rumination or self-blame ('what is wrong with me?'); it is calm investigation
Not purely intellectual debate; the aim is inner rest
cautions: Nearby verses are harsh about those who don't inquire (better to be a frog in mud or a worm in filth, v.46; a stone heart, v.51); never quote those to a low reader
'Who am I?' can be destabilising for someone dissociating; keep the exercise concrete
not_for: acute crisis, where reflection can turn into rumination

yv.2.14.53.context: Vasishtha has said that without inquiry nothing true is properly known (v. 52). Here he sets out the chain from inquiry to the end of sorrow. The chapter then closes with a verse urging Rama, endowed with calm, to let clear inquiry shine and make his actions bear fruit.
yv.2.14.53.core_teaching: Inquiry leads to knowing what is real; that brings rest in oneself; that rest becomes calm of mind; and calm ends all sorrow.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Tattva is the permanence of the real; knowing it brings steadiness of mind, and from that rest comes calm, which is the end of all sorrow.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XIV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as knowledge of truth coming by reasoning, peace of mind by truth, and the tranquillity of mind dispelling human misery; the closing verse urges weighing everything with reason.

yv.2.14.53.practical_reading: Calm can't be forced directly; it follows from seeing a situation truly. Start by asking clear questions.
misreadings: Not a quick fix for sorrow
cautions: 'End of all sorrow' is a spiritual goal; don't promise it to someone suffering now
not_for: fresh grief, where 'end of all sorrow' can sound dismissive
speaks_to: people interested in reflection or meditation
someone seeking inner peace through understanding

yv.2.15.1.context: This opens the chapter on the third gatekeeper. Vasishtha goes on: the contented regard a kingdom as straw (v. 2), are never shaken by adversity (v. 3), and find wealth poisonous compared with contentment's nectar.
yv.2.15.1.core_teaching: Contentment is the highest good and is itself happiness; the contented person reaches the deepest rest.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Contentment, as about to be defined, is the highest good, i.e. liberation, and also happiness; it is praised by naming the means after its fruit. 'Rest' is the end of the mind's restless distraction.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as contentment being the chief good and true enjoyment, the contented man getting the best repose; the contented think sovereignty no better than rotten straw.

yv.2.15.1.practical_reading: Notice what is already enough today; contentment is a practice of appreciating what is here, which brings real rest.
misreadings: Not complacency or giving up on goals
Not a reason to accept injustice
cautions: Avoid using it to tell people in hardship to be content with their lot
not_for: someone facing poverty or injustice, if read as 'be satisfied with less'

yv.2.15.11.context: Vasishtha has named four 'gatekeepers' of freedom and gives this chapter to the third, contentment. Just before, he says a mind without contentment cannot reflect knowledge, like a tarnished mirror (v.9). Right after, he defines the contented person as one who does not crave what has not come and enjoys what does come, in its order (v.12).
yv.2.15.11.core_teaching: Happiness depends on the state of the mind more than on possessions: a content, untroubled mind is already rich. The chapter defines contentment as not craving the unobtained and receiving what comes evenly.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary)
commentaries.gist: Passes over v.11 without separate comment, but glosses the chapter: contentment is called the highest good because in it lasting freedom from sorrow is tasted; v.3 notes that even in poverty or separation a contented mind is not lost.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XV)
commentaries.gist: Surrounding verses say the content regard sovereignty as rotten straw, that great fortunes wait on a contented mind like servants on a king, and that contentment settles anxieties as rain settles dust.

yv.2.15.11.practical_reading: Before measuring your life by what you lack, check whether the mind is at peace with what is here; a settled mind turns a modest life into a rich one.
misreadings: Not a claim that poverty is fine or that material need is imaginary
Not an instruction to stop working or striving; v.14 of the same chapter asks for 'manly effort' to drop craving
cautions: For a reader in real financial hardship or illness this can sound like 'just be content'; the verse itself says freedom from adhi and vyadhi is part of the condition
not_for: someone struggling to pay for food, rent or treatment
acute illness (the verse assumes freedom from vyadhi)
speaks_to: someone downsizing or living simply by choice

yv.2.15.19.context: Closing verses of the chapter on contentment. Before it, the contented person is said to shine like the full moon by pure conduct (v.18). After it, the chapter ends saying even celestials and great sages bow to the one adorned with equanimity (v.20); the next chapter turns to good company.
yv.2.15.19.core_teaching: An even, contented person is a joy to others; the sight of such calm gives people more delight than accumulated money gives its owner.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Samata here means an even-minded view toward everything, born of contentment.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as more delight from seeing the placid face of a contented person than from piling up wealth; v.20 says the even-minded are honoured by gods and sages.

yv.2.15.19.practical_reading: Your calm is a gift to the people around you; a steady, unhurried presence at home or work often matters more to them than what you earn or buy.
misreadings: Not about physical good looks
Not a rule that one must look cheerful all the time
cautions: Could press someone who feels depressed to 'put on a calm face'; it praises inner evenness, not masking
not_for: someone in depression being told to appear serene
someone grieving
speaks_to: parents or leaders who feel they must provide more and more
someone realising their mood shapes the household

yv.2.16.19.context: Vasishtha has praised good company at length. In v.18 he lists the four means of crossing worldly life (contentment, good company, inquiry, calm); this verse ranks each as the highest of its kind. He goes on to say these four are the pure means to break bondage (v.20) and that practising one brings the rest (vv.21-22).
yv.2.16.19.core_teaching: Four inner resources, contentment, good company, inquiry and calm, are the real wealth, path, knowledge and joy; each is described as supreme by naming it after what it yields.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: In each phrase the result is figuratively identified with its means: contentment is 'gain' because it yields what gain is sought for, and so on for all four.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: contentment the best gain, good company the right course, reasoning the true knowledge, quietism the highest bliss; whoever practises these crosses the world's sea (v.20).

yv.2.16.19.practical_reading: A simple four-part check for a day: have I been content, did I spend time with good people, did I think clearly about what matters, did I find some calm?
misreadings: Not a dismissal of material gain or formal learning; it ranks inner goods above them
not_for: acute crisis where a list of ideals may feel abstract

yv.2.16.3.context: Opening of the chapter on the fourth gatekeeper, good company. Vasishtha has just said such company helps people everywhere in crossing worldly life and grows the flower of discernment (vv.1-2). After this he calls it frost on the lotus-pond of calamity and the cutter of the tree of ignorance (vv.4-5), and says it should not be given up even in the worst plight (v.8).
yv.2.16.3.core_teaching: The company of the wise changes how life's hardest facts appear: loneliness, loss and even death lose their sting when seen in their light.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: 'Empty' means empty of relatives and wealth, a place of sorrow; in the company of the wise it becomes as if filled.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: the society of the learned makes solitude feel like company, death like a festivity, difficulty like ease; v.17 adds that this 'medicine' allays the afflictions of poverty and death.

yv.2.16.3.practical_reading: When life feels empty or frightening, seek out people whose understanding steadies you, a teacher, a wise friend, a satsang; how you see your situation changes in their presence.
misreadings: Not a claim that death is literally happy or that loss should be celebrated
Not 'only spiritual people are worth knowing'
cautions: 'Death feels like a festival' can wound someone in fresh grief; use only with care and framing about perspective, not about the loss itself
not_for: the first days after a death
someone who has no access to good company and may feel blamed
speaks_to: loneliness after a move or breakup
someone isolating in a hard time
value of a support group or satsang

yv.2.16.32.context: Having said that practising any one of the four gatekeepers brings the others, Vasishtha urges Rama to win the mind by effort and grow at least one, 'grinding teeth on teeth' if need be (vv.27-30). Just before this verse he says that once one fruitful virtue gains strength, the faults of the mind wane (v.31). After it he pictures desire as a river with good and bad banks that you can steer by effort (vv.33-34).
yv.2.16.32.core_teaching: Qualities compound: strengthening one virtue strengthens the others and weakens faults, while letting one fault grow feeds the rest and erodes virtues. So start with one.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Of two mutually opposed things, when one grows its whole kind grows with it; the commentator calls this a well-known principle.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: cultivating virtues makes them grow and suppresses vice, while fostering vice increases vices and suppresses good qualities; the next verse likens desire to a river steered between good and bad banks.

yv.2.16.32.practical_reading: Pick one small good practice and keep it; it tends to pull others along. Equally, notice which single bad pattern is quietly dragging the rest down.
misreadings: Not a threat that one lapse ruins everything
Not a claim that people are simply good or bad
cautions: A reader with harsh self-judgment may read the second half as doom; stress the first half and the chapter's call to start with one
not_for: someone in shame spirals who may hear only 'faults multiply'
speaks_to: starting a turnaround after a slump
someone overwhelmed by trying to fix everything at once

yv.2.16.8.context: After chapters on calm, inquiry and contentment, Vasishtha describes the fourth gatekeeper of freedom: the company of the wise. Just before this verse he says such company makes solitude feel like companionship, turns hardship into ease and grows discernment. Just after, he calls it a lamp on the right path. He ends by saying that practising any one of the four gatekeepers brings the others.
yv.2.16.8.core_teaching: However bad things get, and however powerless you feel, keep some contact with wise and good people. It is one of four entry points (with calm, inquiry and contentment) to freedom, and any one of them strengthens the others.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary on the Yoga Vasishtha)
commentaries.gist: Introduces the chapter as the fourth gatekeeper and adds that serving even one of the four bears fruit. Glosses 'not even a little' as not even for a moment.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: The surrounding verses say wise company clears inner darkness, heals mental ills, eases the pain of poverty and death, and is worth more than pilgrimage, gifts or austerities.

yv.2.16.8.practical_reading: In low times people tend to withdraw. Teachers read this as: keep at least one thread to someone who steadies you (a mentor, a satsang, a wise friend), even for a few minutes.
misreadings: Not 'only keep positive people around you' or drop friends who are struggling
Not a demand to socialise when depleted; brief contact counts
'Good company' means wise and decent people, not just any crowd
cautions: Nearby verses say wise company makes death feel like a festival (16.3) and that those who neglect it are fuel for hell (16.16); do not quote these to someone grieving
Where the 'company' is the source of harm, steer towards safe, chosen people
not_for: someone whose circle is harming them
a socially anxious reader pressured to perform

yv.2.4.12.context: Vasishtha opens the long 'effort vs fate' teaching (Mumukshu sargas 4-9). Just before, he defines real effort as action of mind and body along the path taught by the good; anything else is a madman's flailing. After this verse he gives examples of beings who reached the status of Indra or Shiva by effort, and says effort is of two kinds, past and present (v. 17).
yv.2.4.12.core_teaching: Whoever genuinely wants something and works for it steadily and in the right order will reach it, unless they give up halfway.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: 'Step by step' is there to show that setbacks come only from skipping what the right procedure requires; an action carried out completely is bound to bear fruit. The following verses confirm this with examples.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. IV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as one who wishes for riches and perseveres surely gaining them, or else stopping short midway; just before, effort following the counsel of the good succeeds, otherwise it is a madman's antics.

yv.2.4.12.practical_reading: Persistence in the right method matters more than a perfect start. When progress stalls, check the method and keep going rather than quitting midway.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that every goal is reachable by effort alone (Vasishtha himself limits this at 2.6.21)
Not blame for those whose efforts failed through no fault of their own
cautions: Can feel blaming to someone who worked hard and still lost (illness, job loss, infertility); pair with 2.6.21
not_for: someone grieving a loss that effort could not prevent
chronic illness
speaks_to: someone tempted to quit a long project

yv.2.4.17.context: After examples of beings who rose by effort, Vasishtha divides effort into two kinds. The commentator raises the objection that past karma accumulated over countless ages seems too vast to conquer, and v. 18 replies that energetic, sustained practice joined with wisdom can crush even Mount Meru.
yv.2.4.17.core_teaching: There are two kinds of effort: what we did before and what we do now. Present effort can soon overcome the effects of the past.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'is overcome' as 'is overpowered'. He raises the objection that endless past karmas from countless ages can't be beaten by present effort, and points to the next verse: they share a root, so destroying that root conquers them all.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. IV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as actions being of two kinds, of former and present lives, with present acts generally superseding past ones; the next verse says energy with constant practice can break even Meru.

yv.2.4.17.practical_reading: You are not locked into the results of old habits or mistakes; consistent effort now can redirect them.
misreadings: Not 'everything bad that happens is your past karma'
Not 'past trauma can be willed away'
cautions: Rebirth framing ('former lives', per Mitra) can feel like blame to someone suffering; use the this-life reading
not_for: trauma survivors, if implied they can simply overpower the past
speaks_to: people who feel defined by past failures

yv.2.5.12.context: Vasishtha has said to keep up effort until the bad effects of past action subside (v. 11). The commentator raises the objection 'why isn't the past stronger?', and this verse answers. Next: overcoming bad fortune with a resolute mind, one should work to cross the world; don't be like idle human donkeys.
yv.2.5.12.core_teaching: Past faults are reliably calmed by present good action, just as yesterday's ailment is cleared by today's remedy.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Answers the doubt 'why shouldn't the past be stronger?': yesterday's disorder, such as indigestion, is cleared by today's measures, such as fasting. The next verse is read as overpowering past ill-fortune with a resolute mind.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. V)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as the evils of bad fortune being removed by meritorious acts of this life, as the bad result of yesterday's act is averted by today's remedy.

yv.2.5.12.practical_reading: A bad day or a mistake can be repaired; what you do well today begins to correct it, as a remedy corrects an ailment.
misreadings: Not 'good deeds erase harm done to others without making amends'
not_for: someone who caused serious harm, if read as skipping accountability

yv.2.5.20.context: Vasishtha says relying on supposed fate is like running from your own arms thinking they are snakes (v. 19). Here he mocks the phrase 'fate drives me'. Next: so by effort first cultivate discernment, then study the scriptures of self-knowledge.
yv.2.5.20.core_teaching: 'Fate is pushing me' is the excuse of a defeated mind; good fortune turns away from people who don't look to the example of those who succeeded by effort.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Reads the compound as people whose sight has not fallen on the best, those like Vishvamitra who reached their goals by effort alone; on seeing such people, prosperity withdraws.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. V)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as perverse minds being pleased to think themselves guided by fortune, with prosperity fleeing far from those who depend on fortune.

yv.2.5.20.practical_reading: Notice when 'it's fate' or 'it's just how things are' is really a reason not to try; look at people who changed their situation and learn from them.
misreadings: Not aimed at people grieving losses they could not prevent
Not a judgement on people with depression who struggle to act
cautions: Harsh tone ('burnt minds'); avoid for readers who are depleted, depressed or grieving
not_for: grief
depression
disability or chronic illness
speaks_to: motivation for a capable but resigned person

yv.2.5.30.context: Vasishtha says it is seen and known that action brings success, and only the dull expect it from luck (v. 29). Here he blames idleness. Next: after childhood a young person should seek the company of the wise and study, examining his own faults and strengths.
yv.2.5.30.core_teaching: Laziness is the great obstacle: without it, almost anyone could become prosperous or learned.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Raises 'if effort works, why doesn't everyone strive?' and answers: idleness, a calamity because it destroys prosperity. The main point is to give up idleness and, from childhood on, devote oneself to good company and the like.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. V)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as no one failing to be rich or learned but for idleness, through which the earth is filled to the sea with indigent and beastly men; the next verse urges youth to seek the wise.

yv.2.5.30.practical_reading: Use it only on yourself: where is inertia, not lack of ability, keeping me from learning or building something?
misreadings: Not an explanation of poverty; poverty has structural causes
Not contempt for the poor
cautions: Literal reading blames the poor and calls them beasts; do not serve in general plans; never to someone in financial hardship
not_for: anyone poor, unemployed, ill or disabled
general audiences without editing
speaks_to: self-motivation for students and young adults

yv.2.5.5.context: Vasishtha argues that what people call fate is just past effort. He says lawful effort leads to success (v. 4); here past and present effort are like two butting rams. He goes on: where harm comes despite proper effort, one's own (past) effort is the stronger force at work; and push on with teeth gritted.
yv.2.5.5.core_teaching: Past and present effort contend like two rams; the stronger wins. So put every means and skill into making today's effort the stronger one.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: 'Huḍa' means a ram; the two efforts are sometimes evenly matched and sometimes not, and here the weaker one subsides.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. V)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as fortune and exertion contending like two rams of unequal strength, the stronger winning; therefore apply yourself diligently so today overcomes tomorrow.

yv.2.5.5.practical_reading: Old patterns push one way and new intentions another; strengthen the new one daily, with skill and support, so it wins the contest.
misreadings: Not 'struggle against yourself harshly'
Not a claim that willpower alone settles everything
not_for: exhausted or depleted readers who need rest first
speaks_to: feeling pulled between old and new self

yv.2.6.1.context: Opening a new chapter, Vasishtha draws the conclusion of the previous one: fate is just past effort. Next he says results follow effort, and that crying 'oh fate!' is like crying 'oh, it hurts!' (vv. 2-3).
yv.2.6.1.core_teaching: Since fate is only the result of past effort, set aside the fatalistic attitude and lift yourself up through good company and sound teaching.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Because nothing called fate exists apart from past effort, throw far away the fatalist attitude, 'I depend on it and am not free', and lift oneself out of the cycle of rebirth.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. VI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra continues: whatever one attempts, one meets its reward by exertion, and fate is nothing other than that same exertion.

yv.2.6.1.practical_reading: Stop waiting for luck to change; choose good influences and good ideas, and use them to pull yourself forward.
misreadings: Not 'you caused your own suffering'
Not a rejection of grace or help from others; the means named are other people and teachings
cautions: Rebirth/samsara framing in the commentary; keep the reading this-worldly for general users
not_for: fresh grief or tragedy, where 'fate is your own past effort' would wound

yv.2.6.18.context: Vasishtha has said that when a beggar is made king by the royal elephant, people call it fate but it is really someone's effort (v. 17). Here: past and present effort strike each other, and the calm one wins. Next: present effort is stronger because it is directly at hand; hail can ruin a year's crop, but one should not grieve over what is beyond one's power (vv. 20-22).
yv.2.6.18.core_teaching: Past and present efforts keep contending, and either can prevail; the person who stays unagitated is the one who wins.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Present effort is the kind that can actually be made now; past effort is already over and done, so it cannot be renewed. (OCR of this gloss is partly damaged.)

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. VI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as present acts destroying those of the past and the reverse also happening, but human exertion being always successful; the next verse says the present is stronger because it is evident.

yv.2.6.18.practical_reading: Setbacks from old habits will happen; staying calm, not panicking, is what lets steady effort win over time.
misreadings: Not 'calm people always succeed'

yv.2.6.2.context: Right after setting fate aside (v. 1), Vasishtha says results follow effort in proportion, so 'fate' is just another name for effort. Then he says 'oh fate!' is like 'oh, it hurts!' (v. 3), and that fate is the earlier action, as easily beaten as a boy by a strong man (v. 4).
yv.2.6.2.core_teaching: Results come in proportion to effort; if you want to use the word fate, it can only mean that same effort.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. VI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as one readily meeting the reward of what one attempts, this being the effect of exertion; fate is no other than the same thing.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Introduces the verse briefly with its first word, without further gloss; in the next verse he explains 'fate' as simply the name for earlier action.

yv.2.6.2.practical_reading: Put attention on what you can do; treat 'luck' as the delayed result of past work, not an outside force.
misreadings: Not a denial that chance events happen
Not proportional 'deservingness' for suffering
not_for: grief, accident or illness

yv.2.6.21.context: In the middle of his case for effort Vasishtha concedes a limit: a hailstorm can wipe out a year's crop (v. 20). Here he says not to agonise over such losses beyond one's power, since otherwise one would have to weep daily over death. Next: all things arise through place, time, action and means, and the one with more effort wins; so cross the ocean of the world with effort, good teachings and good company.
yv.2.6.21.core_teaching: Some losses are beyond our power; tormenting ourselves over them is as pointless as weeping every day because we cannot stop death.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. VI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as it not becoming us to grieve the loss of long-earned treasure, since sorrow avails nothing over what is beyond our control; it follows the image of hail ruining a year's harvest.

commentaries.who: Context in the Sanskrit text (Nirnaya Sagar ed.)
commentaries.gist: In the surrounding verses Vasishtha admits that past effort sometimes overpowers present effort, like hail on a crop (v. 20), before giving this limit. The commentator's gloss on vv. 20-22 is illegible in the scan.

yv.2.6.21.practical_reading: Grieve real losses, but don't add the second wound of blaming yourself for what you never controlled.
misreadings: Not 'don't feel loss' or 'don't grieve'
Not 'death doesn't matter'
cautions: Mentions death; the 'weep every day' line can sound dismissive to fresh grief. Better on a 'steady' or 'why' day than Day 1
not_for: fresh bereavement on Day 1
someone whose loss involved real negligence by others
speaks_to: self-blame over outcomes outside one's control

yv.2.6.3.context: Vasishtha has said fate is only a name for effort (v. 2). Here he likens 'oh fate!' to the cry 'oh, it hurts!' Next he says fate, being past action, can be overcome like a child by a strong man, and that yesterday's bad conduct is improved by good conduct today.
