yv.2.6.3.core_teaching: Exclaiming 'fate!' in hard times is like crying out in pain: it expresses distress rather than naming a real power controlling us.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: Explains that what is then meant by 'fate' is simply past action; that is what the word refers to.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. VI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as people labouring hard exclaiming 'how painful!' and those suffering under fate crying 'hard is fate!'; the next verse calls fate a name for past actions, overcome like a boy by a youth.

yv.2.6.3.practical_reading: When you catch yourself saying 'it's my fate', hear it as 'this hurts'; acknowledge the pain, then look at what can be done.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of pain
cautions: Better than its neighbours for gentle use, but the chapter around it argues hard against fate; avoid for fresh loss
not_for: recent bereavement or trauma
speaks_to: someone who habitually says 'it's my fate'

yv.2.7.12.context: In a chapter arguing that effort, not fate, governs life, Vasishtha says help comes from three sources (scripture, a teacher and one's own effort) and that all of them work through effort. Then he gives this verse as the essence of the scriptures. He goes on: teachers tell their students to pursue with effort what is excellent and lasting, and results come in proportion to effort.
yv.2.7.12.core_teaching: When the mind is caught up in harmful things, deliberately redirect it toward good ones; this redirecting by effort is the heart of all teaching.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Introduces the verse as the essential point, useful for the matter in hand, distilled from the scriptures just mentioned; the preceding verse is glossed as: worldly success comes by one's own effort, knowledge by effort plus scripture plus teacher.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. VII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as the 'long and short of all the Sastras': diligence guards the mind from evil by applying it to what is good and right.

yv.2.7.12.practical_reading: When you notice yourself sliding into a craving, comparison or unhelpful habit, don't just resist it; give the mind a better thing to do instead, and repeat.
misreadings: Not 'think only positive thoughts' or suppress hard feelings
Not a moral judgement that wanting things is bad; it is about where attention is placed
cautions: The same chapter says fate is a consolation only for weak minds (v.15) and that people go to hell for lack of effort (v.9); don't quote those to someone struggling
Effort framing can feel like blame for someone depressed or exhausted
not_for: someone in burnout or depression who needs rest more than effort

yv.2.7.17.context: Vasishtha is building his case that effort, not fate, brings results. Just before, he says effort's results are seen every day, as in people who travel far to earn (v.16), and fate is a comfort only for weak minds (v.15). After this he says the wise escape hard straits by effort while the fatalist sits idle, and each gets fruit according to how he strives.
yv.2.7.17.core_teaching: Results come from doing. Eating fills you, walking gets you there; waiting for fate does neither.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Very brief: the verse completes the previous point, that the fruit of effort is plainly 'seen to be fruitful' in everyday life.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. VII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: the eater is sated, the walker proceeds, the speaker is a speaker; action makes the man. Next verses: the wise escape difficulties by exertion, while the idle fatalist gets nothing.

yv.2.7.17.practical_reading: When a resolve stalls, take one concrete step today; the verse's examples are tiny physical acts, not grand plans.
misreadings: Not 'success is purely your own doing' or contempt for those facing bad luck
Not a call to overwork
cautions: The chapter is scornful of fatalists and the weak-minded (v.15, v.18); keep quotes to this verse
For someone whose effort is blocked by illness, poverty or others, 'effort always bears fruit' can sting
not_for: someone exhausted, ill or facing obstacles beyond their control

yv.2.7.21.context: Vasishtha continues the argument and gives examples, such as Vishvamitra rising to brahminhood by effort (v. 20). Here he defines fate as the timing of effort's fruit. Next: fate is never seen and doesn't live in another world; people use the word for the result of action, and growth and ageing show no separate fate.
yv.2.7.21.core_teaching: Results come from effort, sooner or later according to circumstances; that arrival of the result is what people call fate.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: If one has great devotion to fate, then let one regard effort itself as fate rather than imagining some other false thing; 'phala-prāpti' means the attainment of the result.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. VII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as the reward of industry that comes sooner or later at any time or place being what the wise call fortune; the next verses say no one has ever seen fate.

yv.2.7.21.practical_reading: When results are slow, it doesn't mean effort failed; timing depends on circumstances. Keep going.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that results will always come
not_for: grief

yv.2.9.30.context: Vasishtha has just argued that no one else can make you understand; you must use your own discernment (v. 29). Here is the river of tendencies. Next: turn the mind from bad to good (v. 31), lead it like a child, gently and gradually (vv. 32-33), and even if old habits are thick, thicken the good ones today (v. 34).
yv.2.9.30.core_teaching: Our tendencies flow like a river in two channels; by deliberate effort we must steer the flow into the good one.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: The mind-river flows two ways; following Yoga teaching, blocking one channel makes it run doubly in the other. Then lead the mind like a child, gently and by degrees, not by force, citing the Gita's 'little by little'.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. IX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as the current of desires flowing between good and evil channels, to be turned to the right course by our own activity; the next verse urges Rama to exert himself to redirect the mind.

yv.2.9.30.practical_reading: Don't just fight a bad habit; give its energy a better channel, and redirect gently and repeatedly rather than by force.
misreadings: Not harsh suppression of desires

yv.2.9.33.context: Vasishtha argues that one's tendencies (vasanas) flow along a good and a bad channel and must be steered into the good one by effort. He says the mind is like a child. This verse gives the method. He goes on: whatever you have practised has become strong in you, so from today strengthen good tendencies; we become what we practise.
yv.2.9.33.core_teaching: Train your mind as you would raise a child: settle it, soothe it and guide it gradually with steady effort, rather than jolting it.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Quickly bring the child-mind to its natural evenness by dropping the swings of attachment, soothe it, then restrain it gradually in the self; never abruptly by force, lest agitation break concentration. Cites Gita 6.25.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. IX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as training the mind like a child, slowly, by gentleness and indulgence rather than force and hurry; next verses urge directing habits toward good from now on.

yv.2.9.33.practical_reading: Treat your own mind the way a good parent treats a child: no shaming, small steps, consistent gentle redirection. Self-improvement works better as patient training than as self-punishment.
misreadings: Not 'no effort needed': the verse insists on steady effort
Not permission to indulge every impulse; gentleness is a method, not a lack of direction
cautions: The very next verses say 'we become what we practise'; fine, but avoid implying a reader's struggles are their own bad habits
not_for: no strong contraindication

yv.2.9.39.context: Vasishtha has said that when unsure which tendency is at work, lean toward the good, since there is no harm in it (v. 38). This verse gives the reason: we become what we practise. Next: so cultivate good tendencies, master the five senses, and until you know the truth, follow what teachers and scripture establish.
yv.2.9.39.core_teaching: We become whatever we repeatedly practise; this is plainly seen in people, even from childhood, so practise the good.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary, Nirnaya Sagar ed. 1937)
commentaries.gist: There is really no room for doubt here: practice is seen in other fields too to make the practised thing firm. The next verse is read as: practise good tendencies until knowledge of truth dawns.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (V. L. Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. IX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as whatever one practises, one becomes perfect in it in time, as study from childhood makes the learned free from error; the previous verse says to lean toward the good when in doubt.

yv.2.9.39.practical_reading: Small daily practices shape who we become; choose them deliberately.
misreadings: Not 'you are only your habits, unchangeable'

yv.3.16.24.context: Queen Lila, devoted to King Padma, fears losing him and calls learned brahmins to ask how a person can escape death (vv.19-23). They answer with this verse. She then resolves that if he dies first, his soul should not leave the palace, and begins long worship of the goddess Sarasvati, who grants her boons (vv.25-41).
yv.3.16.24.core_teaching: Effort and devotion can achieve a great deal, but no practice wins freedom from bodily death; the story then moves Lila from this fear toward understanding.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Glosses the request as immortality for both her husband and herself, and the following verses as her private reflection on the brahmins' answer.

commentaries.who: Context of the story (Mitra tr. 1891, Utpatti ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: holy men may succeed in everything by austerity, prayer and rites, but none attains immortality here; Lila, fearing her lord's death, then turns to worship of Sarasvati.

yv.3.16.24.practical_reading: Love that tries to guarantee a loved one will never die meets a hard limit; the story invites shifting from controlling death to understanding life, while still caring fully.
misreadings: Not fatalism about medical care
Not a dismissal of prayer or discipline; it names one thing they cannot do
cautions: Mentions death directly; for someone with a seriously ill partner or parent it can land as hopelessness unless framed as the start of Lila's journey
not_for: someone currently at a deathbed
fresh bereavement (use the later teaching of the story instead)
speaks_to: anticipatory fear of losing a spouse or parent
new parents' fear for a child's safety

yv.3.16.50.context: After Sarasvati's boons, time passes and King Padma dies. Lila wastes with grief: pale, mute, about to die like a female chakravaka parted from its mate (vv.44-49). This verse closes the chapter. In the next, Sarasvati tells her to cover the body with flowers, promises he will return, and begins teaching her about the nature of worlds and death.
yv.3.16.50.core_teaching: Grace meets grief first with compassion, like first rain reaching a stranded fish; the teaching that follows comes only after that.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Sarasvati is compassionate because Lila had worshipped her over many births, and her compassion culminates in giving knowledge of truth; 'compassion' here implies consolation as its fruit.

commentaries.who: Context of the story (Mitra tr. 1891, Utpatti ch. XVI-XVII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: the goddess took pity on her excess of grief, like the first shower on dying fishes in a drying pond; ch. XVII opens with Sarasvati's practical comfort before any doctrine.

yv.3.16.50.practical_reading: When someone is crushed by loss, the first response is compassion and presence; explanations can wait. If you are the one grieving, help may come before understanding does.
misreadings: Not a promise that the dead return (Lila's story uses this to teach about illusion and consciousness)
cautions: Describes a widow near death from grief; tender for the newly bereaved but should not hint at the story's later 'restoration' as a promise
not_for: someone who will read the story's sequel as 'your loved one will come back'
speaks_to: carers wanting to know how to sit with someone grieving

yv.5.10.9.context: As Janaka sits absorbed, his chamberlain enters and lists the waiting baths, worship, brahmins and meals (vv.2-8), ending with this call. Important: Janaka does not rise at once. He keeps reflecting, calls the kingdom fleeting and resolves to stay apart (vv.10-12; Mitra's longer chapter continues his reasoning). Only at the start of ch.11 does he rise and do his duties without the sense of being the doer.
yv.5.10.9.core_teaching: The ordinary call of duty and punctuality; in the story it tests Janaka's insight, which he then carries back into his daily work.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. X)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: rise and do the prescribed duties, since it does not become the best of men to be late; yet the king stayed in meditation, calling royalty transitory, before concluding his inner self is unaffected by action.

commentaries.who: Context of the next chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: having thought it through, Janaka rose for his daily rites without the sense of agency, doing duties as they came without concern for reward.

yv.5.10.9.practical_reading: Insight does not cancel the day's work; get up and do what is due, but let the doing come from a settled mind.
misreadings: Not 'busyness is virtue'
Not that reflection is a waste of time; Janaka's pause is what changes how he works
cautions: Our note implies Janaka returns to work straight after this call; in the text he first keeps reflecting and only rises in ch.11
not_for: someone exhausted or ill who needs rest
burnout where 'get up and do it' is the wrong message
speaks_to: getting back to work after a period of withdrawal

yv.5.11.6.context: Janaka has overheard the sages' songs and reflected. He rises to do the day's work without clinging and, after the day's duties, speaks to his mind at night. V.5: restless mind, the world does not make you happy; calm does. V.6 is this verse. V.7: like a watered tree putting out a hundred branches, desire makes you endlessly needy. V.8: births and worldly troubles grow from this net of thoughts, so drop it and turn to calm.
yv.5.11.6.core_teaching: The troubled world we live in is largely built and enlarged by our own unchecked imagining; quieting that habit shrinks it.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Glosses calm (v.5) as an undistracted state whose essence is the self's own happiness. Desire (v.7) leaves one with endless needs, and births and worldly troubles grow from the net of thoughts about objects (v.8).

commentaries.who: Context of the episode (Mitra tr., Upasama chs. IX-XI)
commentaries.gist: Janaka does not renounce his kingdom: he does the day's duties without a sense of doership, then at night gently counsels his restless mind.

yv.5.11.6.practical_reading: Notice when you are spinning 'what if' scenarios. Each one adds weight; come back to the task in front of you.
misreadings: Not a claim that worries are imaginary or that real risks are not real
Not a call to stop planning
cautions: For 'work feels unsafe', don't imply the danger is all in the reader's head; real threats need real action
For 'far from parents', worry about ageing parents is a form of love; acknowledge that
not_for: someone facing real danger or abuse who needs to act

yv.5.12.14.context: After his reflection Janaka becomes a jivanmukta who rules the Videhas, untouched by joy or sorrow (vv.9-12), his mental impressions dissolved as in deep sleep (v.13). This verse describes his relation to time. Vasishtha then draws the lesson: Janaka gained this by his own inquiry, not by a guru, scripture or merit alone, and praises prajna (vv.15-27).
yv.5.12.14.core_teaching: When the mind's stored impressions wane, worry about past and future falls away and one meets each moment lightly and gladly.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: This is the fruit of the waning of vasanas: linking past and future comes from them, breeding aversion to past harms and craving for future gains; seeing only the present, natural bliss continues, hence 'smiling'.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: unmindful of the past and heedless of the future, he enjoys the present with a glad heart; he did his duties while his mind stayed in contemplation.

yv.5.12.14.practical_reading: Planning is fine; the trouble is the mental replay and rehearsal. Bring attention back to what is in front of you and meet it with some lightness.
misreadings: Not 'never plan'; Janaka goes on ruling a kingdom
Not forced cheerfulness
cautions: 'Smiling' should not be imposed on someone in sorrow
not_for: acute grief
someone who needs to plan urgently (debt, medical decisions)

yv.5.12.23.context: Vasishtha praises prajna after Janaka's story: the lamp of insight dispels dullness (v.19), crosses disasters like a boat (v.20), while the dull are blown about like straw (v.21). The previous verse says the wise cross the ocean of samsara even without help or scripture. Next he says prajna should be grown first through scripture and good company, like watering a plant (v.24).
yv.5.12.23.core_teaching: Clear understanding is the decisive resource; it carries a task through without outside help, while poor judgment wastes even great advantages.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: In the world the person of good counsel prevails even without allies, while the foolish fall even with large armies; or, spiritually, insight reaches the goal of all aims while delusion loses even what is primary.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra frames the passage as praise of percipience: it lets one see past and future, cross dangers like a boat, and pass the world's ocean without friends or scriptures.

yv.5.12.23.practical_reading: Before adding resources or people to a problem, invest in thinking it through clearly; good judgment often matters more than help.
misreadings: Not 'never ask for help'
Not contempt for people who struggle
cautions: A reader who feels they have 'ruined' something may take it as a verdict on their intelligence
not_for: someone who just failed and is blaming themselves

yv.5.12.26.context: Continuing the praise of prajna: grow it through scripture and good company like watering a sapling (v.24); a deed rooted in it bears sweet fruit in time (v.25). After this verse Vasishtha calls dullness the boundary of all sorrows and the seed of the tree of samsara, to be cut first (v.27).
yv.5.12.26.core_teaching: Give at least as much effort to growing understanding as you give to earning, and give it first.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The same kind and degree of effort is needed, no more; one need not labour beyond what one already spends on worldly gain.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: the exertions made for outward property should first go to improving the understanding; intellectual growth should precede outward circumstances.

yv.5.12.26.practical_reading: Audit your week: if hours go to career and money, set aside real, scheduled effort for reading, reflection or practice too.
misreadings: Not against earning a living
not_for: someone in financial crisis for whom earning is urgent
speaks_to: students choosing between grades and learning

yv.5.21.10.context: Following v.9 on discernment as a friend, Vasishtha says only one's own steadiness (dhairya) lifts one from crisis. Next he says one should raise one's own mind by dispassion, scripture and greatness of spirit (v.11), and that no wealth gives what greatness of mind gives (v.12).
yv.5.21.10.core_teaching: In the end it is one's own inner steadiness that carries one through a crisis; outer supports are not the final resource.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The compounds describe one who has given up all wealth and, by severing inner attachment, pushed kin aside as with a hand; such a person's own fortitude raises himself out of crisis.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: when bereft of property and friends, one has no help in adversity but one's own patience and reliance on God; the next verses urge elevating the mind by learning and dispassion.

yv.5.21.10.practical_reading: When outside help runs out, draw on your own steadiness: one small decision, one next step. Accepting help when it comes is not a failure of this.
misreadings: Not 'go it alone' or 'don't ask for help'
Not a praise of cutting off family
cautions: Can deepen isolation for someone already abandoned; pair with the reminder that help is welcome
The commentator's reading (pushing relatives away) should not be presented to a family-estranged reader as an ideal
not_for: suicidal crisis (needs outside help, not self-reliance)
abuse situations where reaching out is vital
speaks_to: someone whose support has fallen away
job loss with no safety net
immigrants or people far from family

yv.5.21.14.context: Vasishtha has said greatness of mind gives what no wealth can (v.12) and that those tossed up and down by desire have minds always feverish (v.13). This verse gives the shoe image. Next: the mind becomes full through dispassion and empty through desire (v.15), and craving dries the heart like Agastya drinking the ocean (v.16).
yv.5.21.14.core_teaching: Change the mind rather than trying to change the whole world; a mind that is whole finds the world sweet, as a shod foot finds every road smooth.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: All three kinds of suffering are rooted in faults of mind; when the mind is filled with the nectar of Brahman, the whole world appears full of bliss, just as the ground seems leather-covered to one wearing soft shoes.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: a mind full of knowledge finds the world filled with ambrosia and moves over it easily, like one walking in shoes; desirelessness fills the mind more than fulfilled desires.

yv.5.21.14.practical_reading: Instead of waiting for every person and circumstance to change, work on the inner 'shoes': contentment, perspective, less craving.
misreadings: Not 'outer problems don't matter' or a reason to ignore injustice
cautions: Can sound like blaming someone's mind for real external harm (abuse, discrimination)
not_for: someone suffering abuse or injustice that needs to be addressed outwardly
speaks_to: chronic irritation with people and circumstances

yv.5.21.6.context: Punya and Pavana, at peace, live on in the forest and finally attain nirvana (vv.1-3). Vasishtha reflects that relatives and possessions go with no one (v.4) and that the remedy for desires is not feeding them (v.5). This verse gives the fire image. He then urges Rama to rise, look on the world with compassion, and act (v.7).
yv.5.21.6.core_teaching: Rumination and craving feed on attention; withdraw the fuel of repeated thought and they die down by themselves.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Not thinking about sense objects is itself the way to renounce them; 'edhate' means grows.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: hankering after objects swells appetite as thinking swells thought, as fire grows with fuel and dies without it; suppressing appetites frees us better than fostering them.

yv.5.21.6.practical_reading: When a worry or craving loops, stop arguing with it and stop feeding it; turn attention to a task or the breath and let it burn out.
misreadings: Not 'ignore real problems'
Not thought-suppression by force; the image is of not adding fuel
cautions: People with OCD or intrusive thoughts may read this as 'just don't think it'; that can backfire, so frame gently
not_for: clinical anxiety or OCD presented as a cure

yv.5.21.9.context: Vasishtha has called the desireless state the pure 'Brahmic' state in which even a dull person is not deluded (v.8). This verse names viveka and dhi as companions. Next (v.10) he says nothing but one's own fortitude lifts one out of a crisis, and (v.11) that the mind should be raised by dispassion, scripture and greatness of spirit.
yv.5.21.9.core_teaching: Discernment and clear understanding are companions you can take anywhere; with them, crises do not overwhelm you.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Discernment is the friend; 'dhi' is understanding whose mark is awakening to the highest truth.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: one walking with reason as companion and understanding as consort does not fall into the hidden pitfalls along life's way.

yv.5.21.9.practical_reading: In a crisis, slow down and consult your own clear judgment as you would a trusted friend before reacting.
misreadings: Not 'you don't need people'
not_for: someone in acute emergency needing outside help now

yv.5.22.34.context: Vasishtha tells Rama the story of Bali, who has ruled for ages. Sated, Bali asks what use his sovereignty and fading pleasures are: the same bathing, eating and sleeping, actions rising and falling like waves. He asks what deed would leave nothing further to do. He then remembers asking his father Virochana about the final state and Virochana's parable of the king and his minister, the mind, and he calls his teacher Shukra for instruction.
yv.5.22.34.core_teaching: Repeating the same pleasures and duties without any aim that ends the need for more looks absurd to a thoughtful mind. That disenchantment opens the inquiry; it is not the conclusion.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The daily round brings nothing new, so craving for it is cause for shame. Bali is looking for an aim that, once gained, leaves nothing more to do, and he sees none in pleasure.

commentaries.who: Context of the story (Mitra tr., Upasama chs. XXII-XXVI)
commentaries.gist: Bali's weariness leads him to recall Virochana's teaching that mastering the mind, the minister, wins everything, and he seeks Shukra's guidance. The answer is inner mastery, not escape.

yv.5.22.34.practical_reading: Treat the 'same day again' feeling as a prompt to ask what your days are for, not as a verdict that they are worthless. Bali's next step is to look for teaching, not to walk away.
misreadings: Not advice to quit your work or duties
Not proof that life is meaningless; the story goes on to an answer
Not contempt for people whose work is routine
cautions: Used alone it can deepen hopelessness in burnout or depression; pair it with the story's resolution, as our misuse note says
The chapter mentions repeated births
not_for: a reader who already feels worthless
depression, unless the follow-up verse comes with it

yv.5.24.19.context: Virochana tells Bali that the world is a transformation of the mind and that conquering it conquers all (vv.14-15). Bali asks for the method (v.16). Virochana: total disinterest in sense objects is the supreme method that tames the mind (vv.17-18). This verse adds that it is hard unpractised and easy when practised; it grows step by step like a watered creeper (v.20) and cannot be had by wishing, as rice cannot grow unsown (v.21).
yv.5.24.19.core_teaching: Dispassion is not a gift you either have or lack: practice turns what seems impossible into something natural.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Glosses the surrounding verses: anāstha means non-craving and yukti means the method; the creeper image shows it widens and becomes evident with practice, and 'shathatman' is the mind greedy for pleasure, which cannot get it without practice.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXIV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: it is hard to get rid of serpentine desires without continued practice of indifference to worldly affairs; Bali then asks how such indifference takes root.

yv.5.24.19.practical_reading: Whatever inner change you are attempting, expect it to feel impossible at first; repeat it daily and it becomes easy.
misreadings: Not 'it's easy, so you're failing if it's hard'
not_for: someone who has been practising hard and feels blamed for not progressing

yv.5.31.35.context: Hiranyakashipu has been killed by Vishnu as the man-lion and the demons are routed. Prahlada reflects that Hari cannot be beaten by weapons and has outlasted all their past wars (vv.30-33), so the only way to 'overcome' him is to take refuge in him (v.34). This verse states that resolve; next he calls Hari the cause of creation and dissolution (v.36) and vows refuge (v.37).
yv.5.31.35.core_teaching: When every other way is closed, complete, wholehearted refuge in God is the way through.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: With one's whole nature, every kind of understanding and every effort and undertaking, he alone is the refuge for those seeking shelter; there is no other way.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: Prahlada, having found one expedient against Hari's might, resolves to have recourse to him with full contrition, as the true refuge and only resort of all.

yv.5.31.35.practical_reading: When you have tried everything and are cornered, wholehearted surrender, putting your whole mind and effort into trust rather than resistance, can open a new way.
misreadings: Not passivity; the verse asks for all of one's effort turned in one direction
cautions: Speaks from defeat and the death of a parent (Prahlada's father has just been killed); can be strong for someone at rock bottom
not_for: readers uncomfortable with theistic devotion (the verse names God)

yv.5.31.37.context: Following his resolve (v.35) and praise of Hari as cause of all (v.36), Prahlada makes this vow. Then he names the mantra that never leaves his heart (v.38), declares 'Hari is the sky, earth, world; I am Hari, full of Vishnu' (v.39), and says one should worship Vishnu by becoming Vishnu (v.40).
yv.5.31.37.core_teaching: Refuge is a decision made in a moment and then lived always and everywhere, until one feels filled by the divine.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Having decided, he resolves on surrender with his whole being; asked whether he takes refuge only in some place or time, he answers: everywhere, being full of Narayana in all places, times and things.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: from this moment he will think only of the unborn Narayana and rely on him, who is present everywhere and full in himself.

yv.5.31.37.practical_reading: Turning points can be chosen: 'from today' you can begin a practice of trust and remembrance and let it grow into every hour.
misreadings: Not a one-time ritual; it is a lifelong orientation
not_for: non-theistic readers
speaks_to: someone who has been running from faith

yv.5.31.38.context: Directly after vowing refuge (v.37). He then identifies himself with Hari (v.39) and states that a non-Vishnu worshipping Vishnu gains no fruit; one must worship Vishnu as Vishnu (v.40), which ends the chapter. In the following chapters he worships in his shrine and mind until Vishnu appears.
yv.5.31.38.core_teaching: A short prayer held continuously in the heart becomes as natural as air in the sky.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: He resolves on continuous japa of this Vedic mantra; it is taken without 'Om' because the form with pranava needs a pure place and is not for unbroken repetition; 'from the heart' marks mental japa as primary.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: obeisance to Narayana is his faith for success in all undertakings, and he prays it may abide in his heart as wind in empty air.

yv.5.31.38.practical_reading: Keep one short prayer or name in the mind through the day, silently, while walking or working; it steadies the heart.
misreadings: 'Every aim' is praise of the name, not a promise of particular outcomes
cautions: Commentator's point that the mantra without Om suits continuous silent repetition is useful practical guidance
not_for: non-Vaishnava or non-theistic readers without adaptation
speaks_to: people who find long prayers hard

yv.5.33.19.context: Prahlada worships Vishnu inwardly and in his shrine until the demons of his city also turn devotee and the gods are astonished (ch.32-33). Vishnu reassures the gods and comes through the underworld to Prahlada's shrine (vv.16-17). Prahlada, overjoyed, sings this hymn, which continues with Hari's beauty and attributes.
yv.5.33.19.core_teaching: God is the shelter of exactly those who have no other shelter; the devotee approaches with that trust.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Treasure-house because the three worlds are kept safe within him; remover of inner and outer darkness; self-luminous light beyond sun and moon; protector of those with no other refuge; called unborn, unfailing and Lord in relation to the three gunas.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXXIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: Prahlada adores Hari, unborn and undecaying, receptacle of the three worlds, dispeller of darkness, refuge of the helpless and friendless.

yv.5.33.19.practical_reading: When you feel you have nowhere to turn, this is a prayer for exactly that state.
not_for: non-theistic readers
speaks_to: guilt and shame ('remover of every stain')

yv.5.36.1.context: Through chs.34-35 Prahlada inquires into the Self, realises it and passes beyond his old ego, saying his great dangers are gone. Ch.36 opens with this greeting. He goes on: who else is a friend in the three worlds (v.2); you were near all along, yet far by many births (v.5); salutations to you who are Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma and all.
yv.5.36.1.core_teaching: Realisation is described as remembering, not acquiring: the Self was always there and is now recognised, greeted like an old friend and as the Lord.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXXVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra titles it a hymn to the Soul: Prahlada thanks the Lord beyond all things found within himself, calls him his only friend, present everywhere, long distant and now near.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (on the end of ch.35)
commentaries.gist: Glosses Prahlada's state just before: he marvels at his former ego as at a dream after waking; his mind, now of the form of boundless Brahman, has shed the cloud of 'I'; all great calamities are gone.

yv.5.36.1.practical_reading: Moments of deep peace can feel like coming home to something you had forgotten; treat them as remembering who you are.
misreadings: Not self-worship in an ego sense; the 'I' that is greeted is beyond the ego
not_for: readers in acute distress (abstract)
speaks_to: returning to faith after a long gap

yv.5.41.3.context: Prahlada sat in samadhi so long that his kingdom fell into disorder (ch.37). Vishnu comes, wakes him and asks him to live liberated and rule (chs.38-40). Prahlada speaks for the first time: this verse, then 'by your grace I am settled; in samadhi or out of it I am the same' (v.4). He is then installed as king.
yv.5.41.3.core_teaching: Endless calculation and duty exhaust the mind; rest in the Self heals it, and that rest feels brief even when long.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: He was wearied by weighing what helps the asuras and hurts the gods; 'a moment' is said because in samadhi one does not register the length of time.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XLI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: Lord, I was much tired with many state affairs and thoughts of my people's weal and woe, and have now found a little rest from my labour.

yv.5.41.3.practical_reading: If decision fatigue and responsibility have worn you out, real inner rest, not just distraction, is what restores you, and it can be found even briefly.
misreadings: Not a call to abandon responsibilities; Vishnu sends him back to rule
speaks_to: managers and carers with decision fatigue

yv.5.41.4.context: Straight after v.3. Prahlada continues: I have seen you within for long with a pure mind, and now see you outside too (v.5); I was in that boundless vision not from grief, delusion, or fear of the world (v.7); where the One exists there is no sorrow or loss (v.8). Vishnu then installs him as king.
yv.5.41.4.core_teaching: True steadiness does not depend on being in meditation; it continues through ordinary life.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: 'Sthiti' is abiding in one's own nature through knowledge of truth; 'rupena' is the absolute nature; he is the same in samadhi and outside it, and in embodied and bodiless liberation.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XLI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: by thy grace I am settled in myself, and in trance or waking I enjoy tranquillity of mind at all times.

yv.5.41.4.practical_reading: Aim for the calm of practice to carry into the rest of the day: the test of meditation is how you are afterwards.
misreadings: Not 'I no longer need practice'
not_for: someone who feels guilty that their calm doesn't last
speaks_to: meditators whose calm vanishes at work

yv.5.43.25.context: Vasishtha is in a sharp passage: Vaishnava devotion was devised for those who flee scripture, effort and inquiry (v.20); worship is the secondary method when practice is lacking (v.21); win your own mind or you are a 'forest donkey' (v.24). After this verse: Vishnu dwells within every person and those who leave him to seek an outer Vishnu are low (v.26); the conch-bearing form is secondary (v.27).
yv.5.43.25.core_teaching: Give your own mind the same loving, patient appeal you give the gods; winning it over is the real work.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Supplies only the implied comparison: just as entreaty is made to Madhava, so it should be made to one's own mind.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XLIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: people seek favour from gods and great men but not from their own hearts, which can give every blessing; the next verse places Vishnu within every person.

yv.5.43.25.practical_reading: Talk to your own mind kindly and persistently, as you would pray: ask it to settle, to let go, to choose well.
misreadings: Not 'prayer is useless'
Not 'worship yourself'
cautions: The surrounding verses disparage image worship and call devotion a device for those who avoid effort; avoid quoting them in a devotional plan
not_for: strongly devotional readers if presented with its polemical context
speaks_to: people who pray but neglect inner work

yv.5.43.32.context: Vasishtha softens: one who lacks self-discernment should worship the four-armed Lord, and by that worship and austerity the mind becomes pure in time (vv.30-31). This verse: daily practice and discernment clear the mind, as a mango ripens. Next: so by the occasion of Hari's worship the Self gains the fruit by itself (v.33).
yv.5.43.32.core_teaching: Clarity is a ripening: steady daily practice plus discernment surely brings it, gradually and naturally.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: 'Soon' signals that clarity is certain to come; 'sahakara' names the state of the mango when its flower and fruit are most fragrant.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XLIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: daily practice of self-control and meditation purifies the mind, which like the mango gains its virtues one by one; worship of Hari can likewise lead there.

yv.5.43.32.practical_reading: Do the small practice every day and stop checking whether you are 'there yet'; ripening happens on its own schedule.
misreadings: Not 'it will be quick'

yv.5.43.9.context: Rama asks: if everything is won by effort, how did Prahlada wake only by Vishnu's boon (v.3)? Vasishtha: Prahlada earned it himself; the Self and Narayana are one, like sesame and its oil (vv.4-8). This verse gives two routes. Next: even long-pleased, Madhava cannot give knowledge to one who does not inquire (v.10); inquiry from effort is the main cause, boons secondary (v.11).
yv.5.43.9.core_teaching: Awakening can come by one's own inquiry or through God reached in devotion; in this chapter both are finally one's own effort, since Vishnu and the Self are not two.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: 'By its own power' means by the strength of inquiry made through one's own effort; 'through Vishnu's body' means via the effort that takes the form of devotion.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XLIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: sometimes the soul wakes by its own intuition, sometimes by the grace of the personal Vishnu through faith; but the god, however pleased, cannot give knowledge to one without reasoning.

yv.5.43.9.practical_reading: Whether you lean on prayer or on reflection, the work of seeing clearly is still yours; grace and effort meet in the same place.
misreadings: Not that grace is irrelevant
Not that devotion is lesser for everyone; but the chapter does rank inquiry first
cautions: Devotional readers may be uncomfortable with the chapter's ranking; use the verse with the effort-and-grace framing
speaks_to: devotees who also want to think

yv.5.61.2.context: King Suraghu of the Kiratas, troubled by the duty to punish and reward, is taught by the sage Mandavya and settles in the vision of the one Self (chs.55-60). Vasishtha urges Rama to do likewise (v.1). This verse: holding that view, the mind no longer burns. Next: discernment brings relief like grabbing a firm tuft of grass while falling into a pit (v.3); then the story of Suraghu and his friend Parigha begins.
yv.5.61.2.core_teaching: Seeing life from the vision of the one Self removes the mind's burning, as light removes a child's terror of the dark.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Sin is reversed when knowledge of truth uproots it; the child, having obtained light, no longer suffers; the chapter tells of Suraghu's meeting with Parigha.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. LXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: act like Suraghu, relying on the sole existence of the Supreme; with this sight the mind no longer pants or sorrows, as a child is not afraid of the dark once it has a lamp.

yv.5.61.2.practical_reading: Much of our distress is fear in the dark; a clearer way of seeing, from a teacher, a text, a reflection, can work like turning on a light.
misreadings: Not that one insight ends all difficulty forever
speaks_to: moral distress at work (Suraghu's problem was judging others)

yv.5.64.33.context: Vasishtha says liberation's method is gained from contact with great souls, like a boat from a ferryman (v.31), and a wise person should not live in a 'desert' with no good person-tree giving fruit and cool shade (v.32). This verse paints the good person as a champak. Next: where there is no such person, one with some discernment should not sleep in the heat of delusion (v.34); and 'the self is the friend of the self' (v.35).
yv.5.64.33.core_teaching: Good people are like shade trees: their kind words and smiles give the tired immediate rest, so seek them out and stay near them.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The good person is the champak tree; each adjective is to be applied to both, tree and person.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. LXIV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: good men are flowering champak trees; their cooling words are the shady leaves and their smiles the blossoms; let men resort to such bowers, for without them the world is a burning desert.

yv.5.64.33.practical_reading: Notice who in your life gives you rest with a few kind words, spend time with them, and try to be that shade for someone else.
misreadings: Not a judgement on people who have no such friends
cautions: The next verse says not to live where no such people are; a lonely reader may feel stuck
not_for: someone isolated with no access to supportive people, unless paired with v.35 (self as friend)
speaks_to: gratitude for a kind friend or elder

yv.5.66.34.context: Vasishtha tells of two boys raised in sage Atri's hermitage on Mount Sahya. When their fathers die they mourn, then spend long years apart in austerities without gaining knowledge. Meeting again as old men, Vilasa asks if Bhasa is at peace. Bhasa answers that no one rests while desire and fear remain, and describes life's stream of duties and the spinning mind. In the next chapter both turn to self-knowledge and become free while living.
yv.5.66.34.core_teaching: A mind swept along by endless tasks and the 'done, doing, still to do' reckoning never rests. Rest comes from understanding, not from more effort or harder austerity.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The 'bird of the mind', bound in the net of reckonings, is stupefied. Around it he explains the river of activity running through every birth, and the body as the precious instrument for life's highest aim.

commentaries.who: Context of the story (Mitra tr., Upasama chs. LXV-LXVII)
commentaries.gist: Years of grief and hard austerity without understanding left both friends restless. Their honest exchange turns them to self-knowledge, and they are freed while still living.

yv.5.66.34.practical_reading: Notice the to-do loop running in the background. The answer the story gives is not a better list but stepping back to understand what the mind is doing.
misreadings: Not 'stop doing your tasks'
Not that hard work is pointless; the story's point is effort without understanding
cautions: The story opens with the death of both fathers and long mourning; useful but tender for the bereaved
For a parent of small children, don't imply the busyness is a personal failing
not_for: someone in crisis who needs practical help more than reflection

yv.5.9.46.context: Janaka, shaken by the Siddhas' songs, sits alone and reviews his life: heavenly rewards are short-lived, good is mixed with evil, beings far greater than he have perished (vv.38-45). He then says prized fortunes are calamities and accepted adversities are fortunes (46-47), that the world is a play of the mind (48) and that calling things 'mine' is a strange new script (48).
yv.5.9.46.core_teaching: Whether something is a fortune or a calamity depends on how the mind holds it: clung-to wealth breeds trouble, while hardship that turns one toward wisdom becomes real wealth.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Varied riches (jewels, elephants, wealth, family) are won with great effort, painful to protect and bound to perish, so they are calamities; poverty, loss of kin or kingdom become fortunes if they lead to good company, austerity and awakening.

commentaries.who: Context of the soliloquy (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. IX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: prosperity is mere vexation that proves a calamity, while feared adversities may become true prosperity by freeing one from worldly entanglement.

yv.5.9.46.practical_reading: Look at what you are proudest of and what you most resent: the first may be costing you peace, and the second may be pushing you toward something better.
misreadings: Not a reason to romanticise poverty or loss
Not a rule against enjoying success; the problem is the mind's clinging
cautions: Telling someone in acute hardship that it is 'really a fortune' can feel dismissive; offer as a later reflection, not first comfort
not_for: the immediate aftermath of a loss or disaster
someone in poverty being told to be grateful
speaks_to: a setback that redirected a career or life
job loss or failure seen in hindsight

yv.5.9.59.context: Janaka has realised the world tree grows from the mind and resolves to stop being fooled by appearances (vv.55-58). Here he ends his repeated self-pity. Next he declares 'I am awake, I am glad, I have seen the thief, the mind' (v.60) and resolves to rest in the Self. Then his doorkeeper arrives (ch.10).
yv.5.9.59.core_teaching: Once one sees that the mind itself was the source of feeling lost, repeated self-lament can be set down; the verse marks a turning from despair to awakening.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Whatever I lamented over and over before is finished; from now on I do not grieve.

commentaries.who: Context of the soliloquy (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. IX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: he had wailed long over the depravity and loss of his soul and now ceases, knowing he is not utterly lost; next he finds the robber of his soul to be his own mind.

yv.5.9.59.practical_reading: When you notice an old loop of 'I'm finished, I'm ruined', you can name it and set it down; often the voice saying it is the problem, not the facts.
misreadings: Not 'stop grieving the dead'
Not a command to suppress tears
cautions: Do not use on Day 1 of a grief plan; in context it is about self-pity and spiritual despair, not mourning a person
Our setting line should be revised from 'replaying his losses' to 'his old cries of being lost'
not_for: recent bereavement
someone who has not yet been allowed to grieve
speaks_to: a moment of resolve to change the inner narrative

yv.6a.115.1.context: Late in the Nirvana teaching. Rama asks what the three terms mean (v.2); Vasishtha tells how Bhringisha, though he knew the truth, found no rest amid the restless world and asked Shiva for a settled inner conviction (vv.3-8); Shiva answers with this same triad (v.9) and defines each in turn (vv.11-40).
yv.6a.115.1.core_teaching: The liberated life is not withdrawal: act fully, experience fully, let go fully, all with doubts dropped and steadiness held.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The chapter describes the marks of the liberated-while-living for Bhringi; they are called three 'vows' with respect to the time of practice, but at maturity they become natural marks of the liberated.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. CXV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: strive to be the greatest in deeds, enjoyment and 'bounty', relying on unshaken endurance and defying cares; these three were explained long before by Shiva.

yv.6a.115.1.practical_reading: Throw yourself into your work, take life's experiences as they come, and hold everything lightly enough to let go.
misreadings: 'Great enjoyer' is not hedonism; v.21 defines it as hating nothing and craving nothing
speaks_to: people who think spirituality means withdrawing

yv.6a.115.17.context: One of ten definitions of the 'great doer' (vv.11-20): one who does right or wrong as it comes without doubt, acts without expectation, without ego, without agitation (vv.11-16). After this: one who is even in action and inaction, keeps equanimity by nature, and whose mind is the same in birth, life and death (vv.18-20). The 'great enjoyer' follows.
yv.6a.115.17.core_teaching: Great action is timely, fitting and unattached: do what the moment requires without clinging to it.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Glosses the great doer's conduct as in keeping with the world's ways; the following verse means one who, firm in the Self, stays even toward prescribed and forbidden action.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. CXV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: he does his duties best who has his wits ready at the fittest time and sits unconcerned at other times like a silent sage.

yv.6a.115.17.practical_reading: Do the right thing at the right time in the way the task needs, then put it down; don't carry it around afterwards.
misreadings: Not detachment as not caring about quality

yv.6a.115.26.context: Among the definitions of the 'great enjoyer' (vv.21-33): one who hates nothing and craves nothing but enjoys what comes (v.21), watches the world as a witness (v.23). Just before this, v.25 says he regards old age, death, calamity, kingship and poverty alike as 'delightful' (the commentator: delightful as Brahman). After: non-violence, equanimity and contentment flow from him like moonbeams (v.27); he eats bitter and sweet alike (v.28).
yv.6a.115.26.core_teaching: The 'great enjoyer' is large enough to receive big joys and big sorrows without being overturned, as the ocean takes in every river.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: He receives joys and sorrows with an even attitude, for experience; in v.25 old age, death and poverty are 'delightful' because seen as Brahman.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. CXV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: he is the man of greatest gratification who bears all ups and downs of fortune with equal fortitude, as the deep sea holds its waves.

yv.6a.115.26.practical_reading: Let life's highs and lows flow in without being swept away; you can feel them fully and still remain yourself.
misreadings: Not emotional numbness
cautions: The neighbouring verse calls death and poverty 'delightful'; avoid quoting it to someone suffering them
not_for: fresh bereavement if read as 'take it evenly'

yv.6a.115.43.context: After Shiva's three definitions, Vasishtha tells Rama to stand in this view, free of fever (v.40), contemplate Brahman as ever-risen and pure with nothing else besides (vv.41-42), and closes the chapter with this verse on acting outwardly while turned inward.
yv.6a.115.43.core_teaching: Inner anchoring makes outer work sustainable: act fully in the world while resting inward, and weariness and ego both fall away.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. CXV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: look always to the inner soul and do outward actions with the body, forsaking egoism; freed from care you will reach supreme felicity.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Frames the chapter as the marks of the jivanmukta; the 'vows' become natural traits at maturity, which is the state this closing verse describes.

yv.6a.115.43.practical_reading: Keep a thread of inner quiet through the workday, a breath, a remembrance between tasks, and you will tire less.
misreadings: Not 'withdraw from people'
speaks_to: people who meditate but lose it at work

yv.6a.26.12.context: Vasishtha has flown to Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who has seen many world-ages. In ch.25 Bhushunda explains his samadhi through watching the meeting-point of inbreath and outbreath. In ch.26 he lists the habits of mind behind his long, untroubled life, each verse ending 'so I live long, free of illness'; ch.27 closes the episode.
yv.6a.26.12.core_teaching: Constant accounting of what one has gained and will gain is a source of strain; being free of it is part of a healthy, long life.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Introduces ch.26 as Bhushunda giving the causes of his long life after describing breath-based self-knowledge. No gloss on v.12; on v.10 he says Bhushunda judges having and lacking as fit to drop, and so lives long.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. XXVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: 'this boon I gained today, that better one I shall have tomorrow' are ruinous thoughts of mortals, unknown to him, which is why he lives long and unailing.

yv.6a.26.12.practical_reading: Pause the inner ledger of gains and next targets; enjoy what has come without immediately reaching for the next thing.
misreadings: Not against goals or ambition as such
not_for: someone in genuine need of basics

yv.6a.26.18.context: Vasishtha has flown to Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who has seen many world-ages. In ch.25 Bhushunda explains his samadhi through watching the meeting-point of inbreath and outbreath. In ch.26 he lists the habits of mind behind his long, untroubled life, each verse ending 'so I live long, free of illness'; ch.27 closes the episode.
yv.6a.26.18.core_teaching: Worry is a kind of fever; freedom from the daily 'what happened, what will happen' fever keeps body and mind well.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Introduces ch.26 as Bhushunda giving the causes of his long life after describing breath-based self-knowledge. On v.18 he glosses 'sampannam' as 'obtained'.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. XXVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: he does not think about what he did today or must do tomorrow, nor ails under the fever of vain thoughts about past and future, and so stays sound.

yv.6a.26.18.practical_reading: When you catch yourself scanning yesterday and tomorrow, call it the 'fever' and let it pass; tend to today.
misreadings: Not a claim that worry alone causes disease
cautions: The 'free of illness' refrain should not imply that ill people worried themselves sick
not_for: someone with serious illness who may hear blame

yv.6a.26.28.context: Vasishtha has flown to Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who has seen many world-ages. In ch.25 Bhushunda explains his samadhi through watching the meeting-point of inbreath and outbreath. In ch.26 he lists the habits of mind behind his long, untroubled life, each verse ending 'so I live long, free of illness'; ch.27 closes the episode.
yv.6a.26.28.core_teaching: Knowledge should not puff up the mind; humility in learning is another of Bhushunda's keys to a long, sound life.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Introduces ch.26 as Bhushunda giving the causes of his long life after describing breath-based self-knowledge. On v.28: 'auddhatya' is immodesty; the mind does not become unruly or proud.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. XXVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: whenever he comes to know the truth he never feels proud, but wants to learn more, and this has lengthened his life (Mitra's 'desire to learn more' is his own addition).

yv.6a.26.28.practical_reading: Each time you learn or achieve something, notice any swagger, and let it turn into curiosity instead.
misreadings: Not anti-intellectual

yv.6a.26.34.context: Vasishtha has flown to Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who has seen many world-ages. In ch.25 Bhushunda explains his samadhi through watching the meeting-point of inbreath and outbreath. In ch.26 he lists the habits of mind behind his long, untroubled life, each verse ending 'so I live long, free of illness'; ch.27 closes the episode.
yv.6a.26.34.core_teaching: Sharing others' joys and sorrows and being a friend to all is part of a healthy life; Bhushunda pairs it next with steadiness in adversity (v.35).

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Introduces ch.26 as Bhushunda giving the causes of his long life after describing breath-based self-knowledge. No gloss on v.34 survives in the OCR; on vv.35-36 he notes Bhushunda does not cling to gains or losses.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. XXVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: he is happy at others' happiness and sorry at their misery, and this universal fellow-feeling keeps him alive and fresh.

yv.6a.26.34.practical_reading: Let yourself be glad for others' good news and moved by their trouble; friendship and fellow-feeling are good for you too.
misreadings: Not a call to absorb everyone's pain without limits
cautions: Readers who are carers or highly empathic may need the next verse's balance (steady in adversity)
not_for: carers at risk of compassion fatigue, unless balanced

yv.6a.26.8.context: Vasishtha has flown to Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who has seen many world-ages. In ch.25 Bhushunda explains his samadhi through watching the meeting-point of inbreath and outbreath. In ch.26 he lists the habits of mind behind his long, untroubled life, each verse ending 'so I live long, free of illness'; ch.27 closes the episode.
yv.6a.26.8.core_teaching: Freedom from brooding over past and future, and resting attention in the present, is the first of Bhushunda's keys to a long, untroubled life.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Introduces ch.26 as Bhushunda giving the causes of his long life after describing breath-based self-knowledge. On v.8 he glosses only: the 'drishti' is present-moment seeing, and 'atmana' means by the mind.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. XXVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: he never thinks of past and future; his sight is fixed on the present, while (Mitra adds) his meditative mind sees past and future as present.

yv.6a.26.8.practical_reading: Notice how often the mind runs back to regrets or forward to fears; return it to what is in front of you, again and again.
misreadings: Not 'never plan or learn from the past'
cautions: Bhushunda's ease rests on long practice; don't present it as a quick fix
not_for: acute grief where the past cannot simply be dropped
speaks_to: older readers reflecting on long life

yv.6a.29.108.context: Vasishtha recalls to Rama how, living as an ascetic on Kailasa, Shiva and Parvati came to him; he worshipped them, and Shiva asked whether his austerities were unhindered and his fears quieted (vv.95-106). Vasishtha replies in vv.107-113 praising remembrance of Shiva. He then asks Shiva how God should truly be worshipped, which leads to Shiva's teaching on inner worship.
yv.6a.29.108.core_teaching: For one whose mind is absorbed in the joy of remembering God, nothing seems out of reach and fear loses its hold.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Glosses the frame: Vasishtha answers with humble, conciliating speech; v.108 itself is left without comment, and v.109 is read as praise that there is no being who does not bow to Shiva.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. XXIX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: nothing is unattainable and nothing to be feared for one who remembers the three-eyed god always and whose heart is filled with rapture by that remembrance.

yv.6a.29.108.practical_reading: When fear rises, deliberately turn the mind to what you love and trust most; remembrance itself steadies you.
misreadings: Not a promise that hardship will not come
cautions: 'Nothing is hard to reach' can sound like a guarantee; frame as the felt confidence of devotion
not_for: non-theistic readers

yv.6a.29.111.context: Part of Vasishtha's reply to Shiva's enquiry after his welfare (vv.107-113), praising smarana. Immediately after, he asks Shiva his doubt about true worship, and Shiva teaches that the real God is consciousness itself and real worship is inner.
yv.6a.29.111.core_teaching: Remembrance of God links past, present and future merit, holds wisdom and steadiness, opens the door to freedom, and puts the devotee above calamity.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Remembrance is the fruit of merit cultivated earlier, waters present merit and sows the seed for what is still to be done; 'all calamities' means present and future ones.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. XXIX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: remembrance brings the reward of past lives' merit and waters the present; it is the jar of knowledge's nectar, the gateway to salvation, a priceless gem, and it tramples all calamities.

yv.6a.29.111.practical_reading: A habit of remembering the divine is cumulative: it grows from past practice, nourishes today and prepares tomorrow.
misreadings: Not a guarantee against misfortune; it is about standing above it
cautions: Translation currently trails off; fix before use
not_for: non-theistic readers
speaks_to: those building a daily remembrance habit

data_flags.translation_note: Incomplete sentence. 'Tanoti caishyato bijam' completes v.110b: remembering you is the fruit of past merit, the watering of present merit, and sows the seed of future merit (the commentator: of what is yet to be done). Our translation ends 'Holding the great wish-jewel of remembering...

yv.6a.39.2.context: Shiva has taught that the true deity is consciousness, present in everything (ch.38). Here he begins the inner worship: the purest of purifiers, destroying all darkness (v.1); it goes on in every state (v.2); one should constantly meditate on Shiva dwelling in the body as one's own Self, the cause of all perception (v.3), whether lying, rising, walking or standing (v.4).
yv.6a.39.2.core_teaching: The highest worship needs no special place or time: it is continuous inner attention to the divine as one's own awareness, carried into every activity.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The chapter describes the inner worship of Shiva as the inner Self; it destroys all ignorance, and in v.2 'gata' means it accompanies every kind of activity.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. XXXIX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: this inward worship rests on mental meditation and goes on in every state, sitting or walking, waking or sleeping, worshipping Shiva in the body in spirit.

yv.6a.39.2.practical_reading: You don't need a shrine to worship; bring quiet attention to the presence within while you commute, work, cook or lie down.
misreadings: Not a rejection of temple worship; Shiva also describes outer worship elsewhere
speaks_to: busy people who can't keep long rituals

yv.6a.93.29.context: SENSITIVE CONTEXT. Urged by Kumbha that he has not truly renounced, Shikhidhvaja burns his hut and belongings (vv.1-11). Told he still has not given up everything, he decides his body is what remains and rises to hurl it off a cliff (vv.15-17). Kumbha stops him: the body is innocent, a dumb tool moved by something else; destroying it is not renunciation (vv.18-27). He asks what then moves the body (v.28); this verse answers: not giving up body, kingdom or hut. The answer that follows is the mind (vv.30-43).
yv.6a.93.29.core_teaching: Real letting go is not done by destroying the body or abandoning outer life; it is the mind that must be released.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The body is not the offender; the ego that agitates it is. Renouncing by throwing away the body cannot succeed, since a body fit for knowledge is rare, and the root of birth and action regrows.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. LXXXXIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: Kumbha interrupts the prince as he goes to dash his body from the crag, calls the body innocent and harmless, and says neither forsaking realm, body nor burning hut and chattels makes renunciation of all.

yv.6a.93.29.practical_reading: Dramatic outer changes, quitting, leaving, punishing yourself, do not by themselves bring peace; the work is with the mind that drives them.
misreadings: Not 'never change your life'
Not a dismissal of genuine renunciation; it relocates it to the mind
cautions: The verse answers a man about to throw himself from a cliff. Never use it lightly or with imagery of falling; if used for someone with thoughts of self-harm, the message must be explicitly protective (the body is innocent; do not harm it) and paired with crisis resources
Our setting line omits the suicide attempt; an editor must know it
not_for: a reader in active suicidal crisis without professional support framing
speaks_to: someone who wants to escape their life (quit, move, cut off everyone) to find peace

yv.6a.93.43.context: Continuing after v.29: Kumbha says the 'all' to be renounced is the mind, which takes the forms of body, world and kingdom (vv.30-41); giving it up ends all ills (v.42). This verse concludes the point. Next: when the mind is given up, duality dissolves and what remains is peaceful, clear and one (v.44). Shikhidhvaja's awakening follows in later chapters, and he finally returns with Chudala to rule.
yv.6a.93.43.core_teaching: To renounce the mind's grasping is to renounce everything; when that is done, reality is directly known.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Giving up the mind makes total renunciation possible, failing which it is impossible; once achieved, the supreme reality of boundless bliss is experienced.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. LXXXXIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: resignation of the mind is what makes renunciation of all; succeed in that and you know the truth and the true felicity of the soul.

yv.6a.93.43.practical_reading: Instead of asking what to give up outwardly, ask what your mind is clinging to; letting that go is the real renunciation.
misreadings: Not 'stop thinking' or numbness
cautions: Same scene as 6a.93.29 (attempted self-destruction just before)
speaks_to: people considering monastic or radical life changes

yv.6b.44.32.context: Rama asks Vasishtha to describe the tree of samadhi with its creepers and flowers (v.1). Vasishtha describes it: its creepers are clarity, truth, steadiness, equanimity, peace, friendliness, compassion (v.23); it cools the directions like a rain cloud (v.27); as the tree of discernment grows in the heart's forest it spreads shade and coolness (vv.30-31). This verse: the tired mind-deer rests there. The rest of the chapter describes that deer's long, hunted wanderings.
yv.6b.44.32.core_teaching: The restless, hunted mind finds its rest in the cool shade of discernment and meditation, as a lifelong traveller finally rests.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The mind-deer, wearied in the wilderness tracts of samsara, rests in that shade; the following verses detail its many causes of exhaustion; even on a good path it is thrown off by the clamour of disputants.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. XLIV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: the deer-like mind, tired of wandering the world's deserts, rests under this cool shade like a traveller worn out from birth; it is hunted by the passions and chases the mirage of ego.

yv.6b.44.32.practical_reading: If your mind feels like it has been running all its life, give it a daily place of shade: a few minutes of stillness and reflection.
cautions: Later verses describe the deer hunted and falling into a pit; use only this verse's restful image
